en: The First Fascicle of the Commentary on the Meaning of the *Nidāna* (Origination) within the "Introductory Chapter" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
1. Prologue Chapter 1: Exposition on the Meaning of the Origin The Buddha has come from the Great Path of Prajñāpāramitā; The Buddha has reached the ultimate depths of the Ocean of Prajñāpāramitā;
The Buddha is unimpeded regarding the characteristics and meanings of Prajñāpāramitā; I prostrate to the peerless Buddha of Prajñāpāramitā.
The two views of existence and non-existence are extinguished without remainder;
the true nature of all phenomena is what the Buddha has taught—eternally abiding, indestructible, and pure of afflictions. I prostrate to the Dharma revered by the Buddha.
The great ocean of the noble assembly acts as a field of merit, adorned by those in training and those beyond training;
the seeds of craving for future existence are forever exhausted, and since the notion of "mine" has ceased, its roots are likewise removed.
Having abandoned all worldly activities, they dwell in the abode of manifold virtues.
Foremost among all the multitudes, I bow my head to the truly pure and virtuous Saṃgha.
Having single-mindedly paid homage with reverence to the Triple Gem, And to Maitreya and others who save the world;
To Śāriputra, foremost in wisdom, And Subhūti, who dwells in non-contention and emptiness.
Now, according to my ability, I wish to expound the meaning of the true reality of great wisdom and the other shore;
I pray that all you virtuous ones of noble wisdom will listen to my words with single-minded compliance!
Question:
For what causes and conditions did the Buddha preach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*?

The teachings of all Buddhas are not spoken of their own accord without purpose or for minor reasons; they are like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which does not move without purpose or for minor reasons.
"For what great causes and conditions does the Buddha now preach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*?
The answer is:
Within the Tripiṭaka, the Buddha extensively employs various analogies to preach the Dharma for the śrāvakas, yet he does not speak of the bodhisattva path.

Only in the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* of the *Madhyama Āgama* does the Buddha grant Maitreya Bodhisattva the prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, and your name shall be Maitreya," yet it likewise does not describe the various practices of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha now wishes to expound extensively upon the practices of all bodhisattvas for the sake of Maitreya and others; therefore, he preaches the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who cultivate the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*; the Buddha preaches the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for their sake, desiring that they attain further increase in this samādhi.
As it is said in the "First Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:

"The Buddha manifested his supernormal powers and emitted golden light that illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; he manifested a vast body, with pure radiance and various wondrous colors filling the void of space."
The Buddha was in the midst of the assembly, upright and most exquisite, with none able to equal him.
He was like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, standing amidst the great ocean.
When the bodhisattvas beheld the Buddha’s supernormal transformations, their mindfulness of the Buddha samādhi increased all the more. For this reason, he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva was first born, he emitted a great radiance that pervaded the ten directions. He walked seven steps, looked around in all four directions, and uttered a lion’s roar, speaking these verses:
"My births from a womb are ended; this is my very last body.
I have already attained liberation, and I shall now deliver sentient beings."

Having made this vow, his body gradually grew in stature; desiring to leave his kinsmen behind to renounce the world and cultivate the unsurpassed path, he rose in the middle of the night for contemplation and saw that the musicians, the queen, and the court ladies appeared like putrid corpses.

He immediately commanded Chandaka to saddle the white horse; at midnight, he leaped over the city walls and traveled twelve yojanas until he reached the forest where the seer Bhārgava resided. There, he shaved his hair with a sword and exchanged his exquisite precious robes for a coarse cotton *saṃghāṭī*.
By the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he practiced austerities for six years, consuming only a single sesame seed or a single grain of rice each day, and thought to himself:
"This place is not the path!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva left the place of asceticism and went beneath the Bodhi tree, sitting upon the diamond seat.

King Māra led eighteen billion followers to come and destroy the Bodhisattva; however, by the power of his wisdom and merit, the Bodhisattva subdued the hosts of Māra and immediately attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, Mahābrahmā Śikhin, the lord of the trichiliocosm, together with the various devas of the form realm, Śakra Devendra and the various devas of the desire realm, as well as the four heavenly kings, all went to the Buddha’s dwelling and entreated the World-Honored One to first turn the wheel of Dharma;
it was also because the Bodhisattva recalled his original vow and his great kindness and great compassion that he accepted their invitation to preach the Dharma.
That which is the profound nature of all phenomena is the Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, the Buddha preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are those who doubt that the Buddha has attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Why is this? All dharmas are immeasurable and innumerable; how could a single person know all dharmas?
The Buddha abides in the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, pure as space; amidst these immeasurable and innumerable dharmas, he himself utters these sincere words:
"I am the Omniscient One.
Desiring to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, for this reason he preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are ready to be delivered; yet because the Buddha’s great merit and wisdom are immeasurable, difficult to know and difficult to understand, they are deluded by evil teachers, their minds sink into false teachings, and they do not enter the Right Path.
For the sake of such people, he gives rise to a mind of great kindness and extends his hand of great compassion to them, causing them to enter the Buddha-way;
for this reason, he manifests his most wondrous merits and exerts his great supernormal powers.
As it is said in the "First Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:

"The Buddha entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi. Arising from that samādhi, he surveyed the worlds of the ten directions with his divine eye; all the pores of his body smiled, and from the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet, he emitted six hundred koṭis of nayutas of light rays of various colors. From his toes up to the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, he likewise emitted six hundred koṭis of nayutas of light rays of various colors from each place, universally illuminating the immeasurable and innumerable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, making them all brilliantly clear."
The Buddha arose from samādhi and, desiring to proclaim the true mark of all dharmas and to sever the knots of doubt of all sentient beings, he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are wicked and heterodox persons who, harboring feelings of jealousy, slanderously say:
"The Buddha’s wisdom does not transcend that of ordinary men; he merely deludes the world with illusory arts."

In order to sever that sense of arrogance and false pride, he manifests immeasurable power of spiritual transformation and immeasurable power of wisdom, and within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he speaks of himself:
"My spiritual virtues are immeasurable; I am preeminent throughout the three realms and serve as the refuge and protection for all."
"If one gives rise to a single evil thought, one incurs immeasurable transgression;
if one gives rise to a single pure faith, one enjoys the happiness of humans and devas and will certainly attain the fruit of Nirvana.
Furthermore, it is said in order to cause people to believe and accept the Dharma:

"I am the Great Teacher, endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; I have established the dwelling place of the Noble Lord, attained mastery over the mind, can roar the lion's roar, and turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma, being the most honored and supreme in all worlds."
Furthermore, wishing to cause sentient beings to rejoice, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying:
"You all should give rise to great joy!"
Why is this? All sentient beings have entered the net of false views and are deluded by heterodox teachers and evil masters; I, however, have emerged from all such evil masters and nets of falsehood.

The Great Teacher endowed with the ten powers is difficult to encounter; you have now met him. I shall, according to the occasion, open up for you the profound treasury of the Dharma, such as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, so that you may take from it as you please.

Furthermore, all sentient beings are afflicted by the diseases of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Since beginningless birth and death, no one has been able to cure this illness, and they have constantly been led astray by the evil teachers of external paths.
I have now appeared in the world as the Great King of Physicians; I have gathered the medicinal herbs of all dharmas, which you should take.
For this reason, the Buddha has preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, some may think: "The Buddha is the same as other humans;
he too undergoes birth and death, and truly experiences the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, old age, and illness."
The Buddha, wishing to sever that thought, preached this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He declared:

"My body is inconceivable; even the Brahma Kings and other celestial progenitors, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have sought to measure my body and investigate my voice, yet they could not fathom them—how much less my wisdom and samādhis?"
As it is said in a verse:
"Within the true reality of all phenomena, The Brahma kings and others,
All the lords of heaven and earth, Are deluded and cannot comprehend it!"
"This Dharma is profound and wondrous; none are able to fathom it.
When the Buddha appears, he fully elucidates and explains it, its brilliance like the sun shining.

Furthermore, when the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, Bodhisattvas from other directions arrived at that time, desiring to measure the Buddha’s body. They ascended through space beyond immeasurable Buddha-fields until they reached the world-system of Flower-Top Buddha, yet they saw the Buddha’s body as it was before. The Bodhisattvas then said:
"Space has no boundaries, and the Buddha's virtues are likewise;
Were one to attempt to measure his body, It would be a futile labor that could never reach its end!
Ascending beyond the realm of space, Across immeasurable Buddha-fields,"
Beholding the body of the Lion of the Śākyas, it is as before and not different!
The Buddha’s body is like a mountain of gold, radiating great brilliance;
adorned with the primary and secondary marks, it is like the blooming of spring flowers.

Just as the Buddha’s body is immeasurable, his radiance and voice are likewise immeasurable; the merits of all Buddhas, such as morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom, are entirely immeasurable.
The three secrets as described in the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* should be explained in detail here.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was first born, he took seven steps upon touching the ground and spoke words of his own accord; having finished speaking, he became silent, just like other infants who neither walk nor speak, being nursed for three years and gradually raised by their mothers until they grow up.
However, the Buddha’s body is infinite and transcends all worlds; yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests as an ordinary person.

When an ordinary person is born, because their physical faculties, sense organs, and mental consciousness have not yet matured, they do not yet fully comprehend the four modes of deportment—sitting, lying down, walking, and standing—nor their speech and silence, nor any of the various human behaviors.
As the days, months, and years pass, one gradually practices and learns until being able to fully embody human laws.
Why is it that the Buddha, at birth, was immediately able to speak and walk, yet later could no longer do so?
This is why they appear strange!

It is solely for this reason that, through the power of skillful means, they manifest human conduct and adopt human deportment, so as to cause all sentient beings to have faith in the profound Dharma.
If, when a bodhisattva is born, he is immediately able to walk and speak, people of the world will think:
"Now we see this person, who has never existed before in the world; he must be a deva, a nāga, a ghost, or a spirit. The Dharma he studies must certainly be beyond our reach."
Why is this? Our physical bodies, subject to birth and death, are dragged along by the fetters and karma, and thus lack self-mastery.
Who, then, could possibly reach such a profound Dharma?
By doing so, they would sever themselves from the possibility of becoming a worthy vessel for the noble ones.
For the sake of such people, he was born in the Lumbinī Grove.

Although he was already capable of proceeding to the foot of the Bodhi tree to attain Buddhahood, through the power of skillful means, he manifested as an infant, a small child, a youth, and an adult.
Throughout various periods, he sequentially experienced amusements, arts, riding, and the five desires, fully possessing the ways of humanity.

Later, gradually beholding the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, he conceived a mind of weary aversion. At the midpoint of the night, he leaped over the city walls to leave the household life and went to the hermit Udraka Rāmaputra; though he appeared as his disciple, he did not practice that dharma.

Although he constantly employs supernormal powers and recollects his past lives—having observed the precepts and practiced the Path during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha—he now manifests the cultivation of ascetic practices for six years in order to seek the Way.
Although a bodhisattva presides over a trichiliocosm, he manifests the defeat of Māra’s armies and the attainment of the unsurpassed path.
Because he accords with worldly conventions, he manifests these various transformations.
Now, because the power of great supernormal knowledge and wisdom is manifested within this *Prajñāpāramitā*, all people should know that the Buddha’s body is infinite, transcending all worlds.
Furthermore, there are those who are ready to be delivered, yet they may fall into the two extremes:
some, due to a lack of wisdom, seek only physical pleasure;
others, for the sake of the path, practice and become attached to asceticism.
Such individuals as these have lost the correct path to nirvāṇa within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Desiring to extricate them from these two extremes and lead them into the Middle Way, the Buddha has therefore preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Furthermore, in order to distinguish between the fruits and retributions of making offerings to the birth-body and the dharma-body, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was taught, as explained in the "Chapter on the Stūpa of Śāriputra."
Furthermore, it is taught in order to explain the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and the characteristics of one who is non-retrogressive.
It is also taught for the sake of [counteracting] the illusions of Māra and the deeds of Māra.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of those in future generations, as a cause and condition for making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, because he wished to bestow the predictions of the three vehicles, he preached this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, this *Prajñāpāramitā* shall go to the south; from the south it shall go to the west; and during the final five hundred years, it shall go to the north."

Among them, there are many sons and daughters of good family who have faith in the Dharma, who offer material gifts such as various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, pennants, music, lamps, and precious jewels.
Whether one writes it oneself, teaches others to write it, recites or hears it being read, correctly contemplates it, or practices it, thereby making an offering of the Dharma—
by reason of these causes and conditions, such a person will experience various kinds of worldly happiness and,
in the end, attain the three vehicles and enter nirvana without remainder.
Thus, for the sake of observing the causal conditions within these various chapters, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is taught.
Furthermore, because the Buddha wishes to explain the characteristics of the ultimate *siddhānta*, he teaches this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
There are four kinds of *siddhānta*:
first, the world-view *siddhānta*; second, the individual-person *siddhānta*; third, the therapeutic *siddhānta*; and fourth, the ultimate-meaning *siddhānta*.
Within the four *siddhāntas*, all twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma are entirely true and without contradiction.

Within the Buddha-dharma, there are things that are true by virtue of the *loka-siddhānta*; there are things that are true by virtue of the *pratyātmagati-siddhānta*; there are things that are true by virtue of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and there are things that are true by virtue of the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
As for "the existence of worlds," there are phenomena that exist because they arise from the combination of causes and conditions; they have no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For example, a chariot exists because the pole, axle, spokes, rim, and so forth are combined; there is no separate chariot apart from these parts.
It is the same with human beings: they exist through the combination of the five aggregates, and there is no separate person.

If the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the worldly consensus) did not exist, how could the Buddha, who speaks the truth, say: "With my pure divine eye, I see sentient beings according to their good and evil karma dying here and being born there to receive retribution;
those with good karma are born among devas and humans, while those with evil karma fall into the three evil realms"?
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"When one person appears in the world, many people receive blessings; he brings forth merit, happiness, and benefit—this is the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
As it is said in the *Dharmapada*:
"A god can save himself; how could another possibly save him?
When a god practices wholesome wisdom, he is most capable of saving himself.
As the Buddha said in the *Bimbisāra-rāja-āgamana-sūtra*:
“Ordinary people do not hear the Dharma; ordinary people are attached to a self.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Buddhadvirātra-sūtra*:
“From the night the Buddha first attained the Way until the night of his parinirvāṇa, all the sūtras and teachings spoken during these two nights are entirely true and non-erroneous.”
"If there were truly no person, why would the Buddha say, 'With my divine eye, I see sentient beings'?
Therefore, one should know that the existence of a person is according to the worldly standpoint (loka-siddhānta), and not according to the ultimate standpoint (paramārtha-siddhānta)."
Question: The first *siddhānta* is the ultimate reality; it is called "first" because it is real, whereas the others should not be real. Answer:

Not so! These four *siddhāntas* each possess their own reality—suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). From the perspective of the world-view *siddhānta*, they do not exist; from the perspective of the ultimate truth *siddhānta*, they do exist.
It is the same with persons and so forth: they exist according to the world-view (loka-prasiddha-siddhānta), but they do not exist according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-siddhānta). Why is this?
Because persons exist due to the causal conditions of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha); thus, there are such things as "persons."
For example, milk exists because its causes and conditions—color, fragrance, taste, and touch—exist;
if milk were truly non-existent, the causes and conditions of milk would likewise not exist.
Since the causal conditions for milk truly exist now, milk itself must also exist;
it is not like the "second head" or "third hand" of a single person, which exist as mere conventional designations without any causal conditions.
Characteristics such as these are called the *loka-prasiddha-tantra* (the universal standpoint).
What is the *pudgala-prasiddha-tantra* (the individual standpoint)?
It refers to preaching the Dharma by observing the mental activities and conduct of individuals; regarding a single matter, some may accept it while others do not.
As it is said in the sūtras:
"Because of karma with mixed retribution, one is born into a mixed world and experiences mixed contact and mixed sensation.
Furthermore, the *Bhārgavīya-sūtra* states:
"No person attains contact; no person attains feeling.
Question: How are these two sūtras to be reconciled?
The answer is:
Because there are those who doubt the future life, do not believe in the retribution of sin and merit, commit unwholesome deeds, and fall into the view of annihilationism;

in order to sever their doubts, cause them to abandon those evil practices, and uproot that view of annihilationism, it is said that there is the world of mixed birth, mixed contact, and mixed feeling.
This Pūraṇa maintains the view that there is a self and a soul, thereby falling into the extreme of eternalism.
Pūraṇa asked the Buddha,
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Who experiences it?

If the Buddha were to say, "So-and-so experiences it," one would fall into the view of eternalism; the person's view of self (*ātman*) would become twice as firm and could not be shifted. For this reason, he does not speak of there being an experiencer or a toucher.
Characteristics such as these are called the *prātipauruṣika-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for the benefit of individuals).
Regarding the *pratipakṣika-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy), there are phenomena that exist when applied as remedies, yet lack inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
For example, medicinal herbs, foods, and drinks that are heavy, hot, oily, sour, or salty are called medicine for wind disorders (*vāta*), but are not medicine for other disorders;
medicinal herbs, foods, and drinks that are light, cold, sweet, bitter, or astringent are called medicine for heat disorders (*pitta*), but are not medicine for other disorders;
and medicinal herbs, foods, and drinks that are light, pungent, bitter, astringent, or hot are called medicine for cold disorders (*ślesman*), but are not medicine for other disorders.
The treatment of mental illnesses within the Buddha-dharma is also like this:
the contemplation of impurity is called an effective remedial method for the illness of sensual desire,
but it is not called effective nor a remedial method for the illness of anger.
Why is this? Contemplating the faults of the body is called the contemplation of impurity;
however, if one who is prone to anger contemplates such faults, it will only increase the fire of their hatred.
Contemplating a mind of loving-kindness is called an effective remedial method for the disease of hatred;
however, it is not called an effective method nor a remedial method for the disease of desire.
Why is this so? It is because loving-kindness seeks out what is beneficial and contemplates the virtues among sentient beings;
whereas if a person of lustful desire were to seek out what is beneficial and contemplate virtues, it would only serve to increase their lustful desire.
The contemplation of causes and conditions is called an effective remedial method for the disease of ignorance;
however, it is not called effective, nor is it a remedial method, for the diseases of greed and hatred.
Why is this so? Because false contemplation arises first, giving rise to false views; false views are themselves delusion.
Question:
As it is said in the Buddha-dharma that the twelve links of dependent origination are profound, as in this passage:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:

'This dharma of dependent origination is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, difficult to awaken to, and difficult to contemplate; only those with subtle minds and skillful wisdom can comprehend it.'"
"If foolish people find even shallow and superficial teachings difficult to understand, how much more so the profound principle of dependent origination?
Why, then, do you now say that 'foolish people should contemplate the dharma of dependent origination'?"
The answer is:
A foolish person does not mean one who is as ignorant as cattle or sheep;
rather, such a person seeks the true path but, because they contemplate it with a distorted mind, gives rise to various false views.
Thus, for such foolish persons, one should contemplate causes and conditions; this is called the skillful remedial method (*pratipakṣa-dharma*).
For those who act with hatred or lust, and who seek their own pleasure while wishing to afflict others—among such people, [hatred and lust] are neither skillful nor remedial methods.
For these two types of persons, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) are the skillful and remedial methods.
Why is this? Because these two contemplations can extract the poisonous thorns of hatred and desire.
Furthermore, sentient beings who are attached to the inversion of permanence do not understand that all phenomena exist through a process of similarity and continuity.
When such a person contemplates impermanence, this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint), not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why?
Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.
As it is said in a verse:
"To perceive the impermanent as permanent Is called a perversion;
Since there is no impermanence within emptiness, Where could one see permanence?"
Question: It is the ultimate truth that all conditioned phenomena are associated with impermanence; why then do you say that impermanence is not real? Why is this so?
All conditioned phenomena possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; since they arise first, abide next, and cease last, how can you say that impermanence is not real?
Answer: Conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) should not possess three characteristics. Why is this?
Because the three characteristics are not real.

If arising, abiding, and ceasing were the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), then within "arising" itself there should also be three characteristics, because arising is a characteristic of the conditioned;
likewise, each of these [other characteristics] would also have to possess three characteristics, leading to an infinite regress. This applies equally to abiding and ceasing.
If birth, abiding, and cessation each lacked further birth, abiding, and cessation, they should not be called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Why? Because the characteristics of conditioned phenomena would be absent.
For this reason, the impermanence of all phenomena is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, if the true nature of all things were impermanent, there would be no retribution for karmic actions.
Why is this? Because "impermanence" means the loss through arising and ceasing; it is like a rotten seed that does not produce fruit.
In this way, there would be no karmic action, and if there is no karmic action, how could there be a retribution?
Now, all dharmas of the worthy and the noble possess karmic retribution; they are to be trusted and accepted by those of wise intelligence, and one should not say they do not exist.
For this reason, all dharmas do not have the nature of impermanence.
Through such immeasurable causes and conditions as these, it cannot be said that all phenomena lack the nature of impermanence.
That all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent, and likewise suffering (*duḥkha*) and non-self (*anātman*), is also thus.
Characteristics such as these are called the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies).

As for the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth), the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), all treatises and verbal expressions, and everything that is either dharma or non-dharma—all of these can be analyzed, refuted, and dismantled one by one;
however, the true Dharma practiced by the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats cannot be refuted and cannot be dismantled.
That which was not universally applicable within the three *siddhāntas* is here fully applicable.
Question: In what way is it applicable?
The answer is:
That which is called "supernormal power" (abhijñā) is free from all faults, immutable, and invincible. Why is this so?
Because all other treatises and all other *siddhāntas* (established tenets) except for the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established tenet) are subject to refutation.
As stated in a verse in the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*:
"Each relying on their own views, They give rise to conceptual proliferation and contention."
If one can recognize that as wrong, this is what is meant by knowing right view.
One who refuses to accept the Dharma of others is called a foolish person;
one who engages in such contentious debate is truly a foolish person.
"If one relies on one's own views, / And gives rise to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*),
/ If this were pure wisdom, / There would be nothing that is not pure wisdom.
In these three verses, the Buddha explains the characteristics of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established conclusion).
It is said that the sentient beings of the world rely on their own views, rely on their own doctrines, and rely on their own discourses, thereby giving rise to contention and strife;
conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is the root of contention and strife, and conceptual proliferation arises based on various views.
As it is said in a verse:
"Because there is the grasping of dharmas, there are various discourses; if there were no grasping, what would there be to discourse upon?
Regarding views such as 'grasping exists' or 'grasping does not exist,' this person has completely eliminated them all."

The practitioner who can know this as it truly is does not accept or cling to any phenomena or any conceptual proliferations; they do not view these as real, do not engage in dispute or contention, and are able to know the nectar-like flavor of the Buddha-dharma.
If it were not so, one would be slandering the Dharma.
If one does not accept another's teaching, neither understanding nor adopting it, such a person lacks wisdom.
If that were the case, then all those who engage in debate would be devoid of wisdom.
Why is this? Because each [person] does not accept the dharma of the other.
That is to say, some people claim that their own dharma is the supreme truth and pure, while asserting that the dharma of others is false and impure.

For example, there are worldly methods of governance; thus, these methods of governance involve punishments, executions, and various forms of impurity. Worldly people accept and practice them, considering them to be truly pure;
yet among other renunciants, noble, and holy persons, they are the most impure.

The practices of renunciants among the non-Buddhists—such as standing on one leg amidst the five fires or plucking out their hair—are considered by the followers of the Nirgranthas to be marks of sublime wisdom, yet others describe these as the ways of the foolish.
In these various ways, the renunciants of other paths, as well as laypeople and brahmins, each consider their own dharma to be excellent and all others to be false speech.
Within this Buddha-dharma, there are also Vātsīputrīya bhikṣus who say:
"Just as the dharma of the eye exists through the combination of the four great elements, so too does the dharma of a person exist through the combination of the five aggregates."
The *Vātsīputrīya Abhidharma* states:

"The five aggregates are not separate from the person, and the person is not separate from the five aggregates; one cannot say that the five aggregates are the person, nor can one say that the person exists apart from the five aggregates. The person is subsumed within the fifth category of the 'inexpressible' (*avaktavya*) dharma-treasury."
The followers of the Sarvāstivāda school say:

"The self (pudgala) cannot be found when sought through all modes, at all times, and within all dharma-gates; it is like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise, which are eternally non-existent."
Furthermore, although the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*) truly exist, there is no person (*pudgala*) within them.
Moreover, there are those among the Mahāyāna followers of the Buddha’s teachings who say:
"All phenomena (*dharma*) are neither arising nor ceasing; they are empty and non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise, which are eternally non-existent."
All such masters of debate likewise maintain their own doctrines while refusing to accept those of others, asserting: "This alone is the truth; all else is false speech."

If one personally receives their own Dharma, makes offerings to their own Dharma, and practices their own Dharma, yet does not receive or make offerings to the Dharma of others, it constitutes a fault.
If one were to consider this purity as attaining the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then there would be nothing that is not pure.
Why is this? Because all those [beings] cherish their own nature (*dharmatā*).
Question:
If all views are flawed, what is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established truth)? Answer:
Transcending all paths of language, where the movements of the mind cease, being entirely without support and not indicating any phenomena;
the true reality of all phenomena (dharmas), which has no beginning, middle, or end, and is neither exhausted nor destroyed—this is called the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate established truth).
As stated in the verses on the meaning of the Mahāyāna:
"Where language comes to an end, and the activities of the mind cease;
neither arising nor ceasing, phenomena are like nirvāṇa."
To speak of the sphere of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called the worldly dharma;
to speak of the sphere of non-action is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"All is real, all is not real, and all is both real and not real."
"All things are neither real nor unreal; this is called the true mark of all dharmas.
Thus, in various sūtras such as these, the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate tenet) is taught.
This meaning is extremely profound, difficult to see and difficult to understand; because the Buddha wishes to explain this meaning, he preaches the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, he preaches this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in order to inspire faith in the Buddha-dharma within great masters of debate, such as the Brahmin Dīrghanakha.
There was a brahmin named Dīrghanakha, and others such as Śreṇika Vatsagotra and Saccaka Kātyāyana; these great masters of debate in Jambudvīpa declared:
"All arguments can be refuted, all speech can be undermined, and all tenets can be overturned; therefore, there is no real dharma that is trustworthy or worthy of reverence."
As it is said in the *Śāriputra-mūla-parivarta-sūtra*:
Śāriputra’s maternal uncle, Mahākauṣṭhila, was defeated in debate by his sister Śāri when they discussed the Dharma.
Kūṭadanta reflected and thought to himself:
"This is not due to my sister's own power; she must be carrying a man of wisdom who has entrusted his words to her mouth.
If such is the case even before birth, what will it be like once he is born and grows up?"
Having reflected thus, he gave rise to a mind of pride; for the sake of engaging in extensive debate, he left the household life to become a brahmin.
He entered the kingdom of South India and began to study the scriptures.
The people asked,
"What do you seek in your aspirations?
What sutras are you studying?"
Dīrghanakha replied,
"I wish to read all eighteen kinds of great sūtras.
The people said to him:
"Even if you were to exhaust the span of your entire life, you would still not be able to know even one [of these], let alone know them all.
Long-nailed (Dīrghanakha) thought to himself:
"In the past, out of arrogance, I was defeated by my sister; now these people have again treated me with contempt and insult."
For these two reasons, he made a vow to himself:
"I shall not clip my nails until I have completely read the eighteen kinds of scriptural texts.
When people saw that his nails were long, they called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).

By means of the power of wisdom derived from various scriptures, such a person uses various forms of censure—arguing that this is the Dharma and that is not the Dharma, this is appropriate and that is inappropriate, this is real and that is unreal, this exists and that does not exist—to refute the arguments of others.
For example, just as a powerful, mad elephant that tramples and crushes cannot be restrained by anyone,

so too the brahmin Dīrghanakha, having defeated all the masters of debate with the power of his own arguments, returned to the village of Nāla in Rājagṛha, the capital of Magadha, to his place of birth.
Arriving there, he asked people, "Where is my sister's son now?"
Someone said to him:
"Your nephew, having just reached the age of eight, has mastered all the scriptures;
by the time he is sixteen, his debating skills will surpass all others."
"There is a member of the Śākya clan, a practitioner of the Way surnamed Gautama, who has taken him as his disciple.
Upon hearing this, Dīrghanakha immediately gave rise to arrogance and, conceiving a lack of faith, spoke these words:
"If my sister's son is so exceptionally intelligent, by what artifice has that man enticed and deceived him into shaving his head and becoming his disciple?"
Having spoken these words, he went straight to where the Buddha was.
At that time, Śāriputra, having received the precepts for only half a month, stood attending the Buddha by his side, fanning him with a fan.
The brahmacārin Dīrghanakha, having seen the Buddha and finished his greetings, sat to one side and thought to himself:
"All arguments can be refuted, all speech can be undermined, and all attachments can be overturned; among these, what is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?"
What is the ultimate truth?
What is its nature?
What are its characteristics?
"Is it not inverted?

Reflecting thus, it was as if one were seeking the very bottom and shore of the great ocean; though searching for a long time, one could not find a single dharma that was truly real enough to enter the mind.
"By what line of reasoning did he obtain my nephew?
Having thought this, he said to the Buddha,
"Gautama!..."
"I do not accept any dharma.
The Buddha asked Long-claw:
"Do you accept this view that 'I do not accept any dharma'?"
Regarding the meaning of what the Buddha has questioned you about: you have already drunk the poison of false views; now you must expel this poisonous vapor by saying:
"I do not accept any dharma. Do you accept this view?
At that time, just as a fine horse perceives the shadow of a whip and immediately awakens to enter the right path, so it was with the brahmin Dīrghanakha;
upon receiving the shadow of the Buddha’s words entering his mind, he immediately abandoned his arrogance, felt shame, and bowed his head, reflecting thus:
“The Buddha has placed me within the gateway of defeat in two positions.”
If I were to say, "I accept this view," that would be a gross point of defeat easily recognized by many: "How can you say for yourself that you do not accept any dharma, yet now accept this view?"
This is a case of manifest lying; it is a coarse point of defeat, known by many people.
The second point of defeat is subtle; I wish to accept it because it is not known by many.
Having formed this thought, he replied to the Buddha, "Gautama!
I do not accept any phenomena; I do not even accept this view."
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

"If you do not accept any phenomena, and you do not even accept this view, then there is nothing accepted; in this you are no different from the common people. Why then do you exalt yourself and give rise to arrogance?"

Thus, the brahmin Dīrghanakha was unable to provide an answer; realizing he had fallen into defeat, he immediately conceived reverence for the Buddha’s omniscience and gave rise to faith. He thought to himself:
"I have fallen into defeat, yet the World-Honored One does not proclaim my failure, nor does he speak of right or wrong, nor does he take it to heart."
The Buddha’s mind is supple and exceedingly pure;
all grounds for verbal discourse have ceased, and he has attained the Great and Profound Dharma. This is a state worthy of veneration, wherein the purity of mind is supreme.

Because the Buddha taught the Dharma to sever their wrong views, they immediately attained freedom from dust and defilement while still in their seats, and achieved the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
At that time, upon hearing these words, Śāriputra attained arhatship.
This brahmin Dīrghanakha left the household life to become a śramaṇa and attained the state of a mahābala-arhat.

Had this brahmin Dīrghanakha not encountered even a trace of the Prajñāpāramitā—the dharma corresponding to the ultimate truth that transcends the four propositions—he would not have attained even a small degree of faith, let alone the fruits of the path of renunciation.
The Buddha, wishing to guide such great masters of debate and those of sharp faculties, preached this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which all Buddhas teach the Dharma:
first, by observing the minds of others to deliver them according to their capacity; second, by observing the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Now, because the Buddha wishes to expound the true mark of all dharmas, he preaches this *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As it is said in the "Chapter on Marks and Non-Marks," the devaputras asked the Buddha:
"This *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely profound; how does it manifest its marks?"
The Buddha told the devaputras:

"Emptiness is precisely the mark; it is the mark of signlessness, the mark of wishlessness, the mark of neither arising nor ceasing, and the mark of non-action; it is the mark of eternal non-arising, the mark of suchness, and the mark of quiescent extinction."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of preaching the Dharma:
first, that which concerns points of contention; second, that which concerns points free from contention.
That which concerns points of contention is as explained in other sūtras.
Now, because one wishes to clarify the state of non-contention, this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is taught.

It is the same for having marks or being markless, having substance or being without substance, having a basis or being without a basis, having opposition or being without opposition, having superiority or being unsurpassed, and for worlds or non-worlds.
Question:
Since the Buddha possesses a heart of great compassion, he should teach only the Dharma of non-contention; why then does he teach the Dharma of contention? Answer:
All dharmas free from contention are signless, eternally quiescent, and ineffable;

yet, the current teaching on giving and so forth, as well as on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and other such dharmas, is spoken solely for the sake of quiescence and the absence of conceptual proliferation.
Those of sharp faculties understand the Buddha’s intention and do not give rise to contention;
those of dull faculties do not understand the Buddha’s intention, and because they grasp at signs and cling with their minds, they give rise to contention.
This Prajñāpāramitā is a state free from contention, for all dharmas are ultimately empty.
If ultimate emptiness were obtainable or subject to dispute, it would not be called "ultimate emptiness.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is named the "Place Beyond Dispute," because both existence and non-existence are extinguished therein.

Furthermore, in other sūtras, all phenomena are generally explained by way of three categories: namely, the category of the wholesome, the category of the unwholesome, and the category of the indeterminate.
Now, because he wishes to explain the characteristics of those phenomena that are neither wholesome, nor unwholesome, nor indeterminate, he preaches the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the dharmas of neither training nor beyond training; the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and the dharmas not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*); visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*), invisible and resistant (*anidarśana-sapratigha*), and invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*); superior, middling, and inferior dharmas; small, great, and immeasurable dharmas—these and other such triads of dharma-gates are likewise [to be understood].
Furthermore, in other sūtras, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught according to the dharma-gate of the śrāvakas.
In this regard, a bhikṣu contemplates the thirty-six impurities within his own body to eliminate the disease of desire and greed;
he likewise contemplates the external body and both the internal and external bodies.
Now, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, I wish to explain the perfection of wisdom through an alternative formulation.
As it is said:

"The bodhisattva contemplates the internal body; he does not give rise to applied or sustained thought regarding the body, and he does not apprehend the body, because there is nothing to be apprehended."

Thus one contemplates the external body and contemplates both the internal and external body; yet regarding the body, one does not give rise to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), for one does not apprehend the body, because there is nothing to be apprehended.
To contemplate the body within the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) without giving rise to the applied and sustained thought of "body" is extremely difficult;
the same applies to the other three foundations of mindfulness.
The same applies to various sets of four dharmas, such as the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the four dhyānas, and the four truths (*catuḥsatya*).
Furthermore, in other sūtras, the Buddha taught that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
now, because he wishes to teach a different method regarding these same five aggregates, he speaks the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
As the Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva views form as permanent, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom;
if they view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom."
To practice the impermanence of form is not to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not to practice the perfection of wisdom.
The five aggregates of clinging, the five destinies, and various other such sets of fivefold dharmas are likewise.
The remaining sixfold, sevenfold, eightfold, and so forth, up to immeasurable dharmas, are also like this.
Just as the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless, the explanation of the causes and conditions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
Because this matter is so vast, I have now briefly concluded the exposition on the arising of the causes and conditions of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

2. Thus have I heard: at one time. Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter One. Thus have I heard: at one time. Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Two. [Sūtra] Thus have I heard: at one time.
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason do the sūtras of the Buddhas begin with the expression "Thus" (evam)? Answer:
"The ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom.
The meaning of "thus" (*evam*) is precisely faith.
If there is pure faith within a person's mind, that person can enter the Buddha-dharma.
If one lacks faith, such a person cannot enter the Buddha-dharma.
One who does not believe says, "This matter is not so," which is the characteristic of lack of faith.
One who has faith says, "This matter is thus."
For example, just as an ox-hide that has not been softened cannot be bent or folded, so it is with a person who lacks faith.
For example, just as an ox-hide that has already been softened can be fashioned into whatever use is required; so it is with one who possesses faith.
A person of faith is also like this.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"Faith is like a hand."
"Just as a person with hands enters a mountain of jewels and takes whatever treasures they wish at will;

so too is it with faith: one who possesses it enters the mountain of the Dharma’s treasures—the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), path (*mārga*), and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*)—and takes whatever they desire at will."
Lacking faith is like being without hands; if a person without hands enters a mountain of jewels, they will be unable to take anything.
It is the same with a lack of faith: entering the jewel-mountain of the Buddha-dharma, one gains nothing at all.
The Buddha said:
"If a person has faith, that person can enter the great ocean of my Dharma and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa; their shaving of the head and donning of the saffron robe will not be in vain."

If one lacks faith, such a person cannot enter the ocean of my Dharma; like a withered tree that produces neither flowers nor fruit, they will not attain the fruits of the śramaṇa. Although they may shave their heads, don the dyed robes, read various sūtras, and be capable of posing difficult questions and providing answers, within the Buddha-dharma they gain nothing at all.
For this reason, such meanings are present at the very beginning of the Buddha-dharma, because they constitute the characteristics of wholesome faith.
Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is profound and far-reaching; only another Buddha can fully know it.
If a person possesses faith, although they have not yet attained Buddhahood, by the power of that faith they are able to enter the Buddha-dharma.
For example, when Brahmā Sahāmpati requested the Buddha to first turn the wheel of Dharma, he addressed the Buddha with this verse:
"In Jambudvīpa, which has first appeared, There are many impure dharmas; [Please turn the wheel of Dharma to purify them. "
"I pray you open the gate of ambrosia; you shall proclaim the path of purity!
The Buddha replied in verse:
"My Dharma is exceedingly difficult to attain; it can sever all fetters and afflictions."
"One whose mind is attached to the three realms of existence cannot understand this!
The Brahmā King addressed the Buddha:
"O Virtuous One!..."
In this world, there are superior, middling, and inferior types of wisdom.

Those whose minds are gentle, supple, and upright are easily delivered; yet if such persons do not hear the Dharma, they will fall back into various evils and hardships. This is like lotus flowers in water—some are already grown, some are ripening, and some have not yet emerged from the water; if they do not receive the sunlight, they cannot bloom.
The Buddha is also like this; out of great compassion and pity for sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them.
The Buddha thought:
“The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—all preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; I, too, should do likewise.”
Having reflected thus, he accepted the invitation from the Brahma King and the other devas to preach the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"I now open the gate to the flavor of the Deathless; Whoever has faith shall find joy."
"Among all people, he preaches the sublime Dharma; he does not preach for the sake of causing distress to others.

In this verse, the Buddha does not say that the person who practices giving attains joy, nor does he say that the person who is learned, observant of precepts, patient, energetic, meditative, or wise attains joy; he speaks only of the person of faith.
The Buddha’s intention was this:

"My foremost Dharma is profoundly deep, subtle, immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable; it is unmoving, non-reliant, and non-attached—a Dharma of non-apprehension that no one other than an omniscient person can understand."

Therefore, among the dharmas of the Buddha, the power of faith is primary; it is by the power of faith that one can enter, for neither giving, nor ethical discipline, nor meditative concentration, nor wisdom can bring about initial entry into the Buddha-dharma.
As it is said in verse:
"The minds of people in the world are stirred; They love the fruits and rewards of merit, yet do not love the causes of merit;
They seek existence, but do not seek cessation."
"Having previously heard the teachings of false views, my mind became attached and deeply immersed in them.
How can I understand this most profound Dharma without faith?
Just as Devadatta’s great disciples, such as Kokālika and others, fell into the evil realms because they lacked faith in the Dharma.
This person lacks faith; though they seek within the Buddha-dharma by means of their own wisdom, they are unable to find it.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound.
As Brahmādeva taught to Kokālika, he spoke this verse:
"To attempt to measure the immeasurable Dharma is what the wise do not attempt.
One who seeks to measure the immeasurable Dharma will surely sink into ruin."

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "thus" (*evam*): if a person’s mind is virtuous and upright in faith, such a person may listen to the Dharma; if they lack these characteristics, they will not understand it.
As it is said in a verse:
"The listener gazes intently as if drinking from thirst; With single-minded focus, they enter into the discourse.
Leaping with joy, their heart is moved by both sorrow and delight upon hearing the Dharma— To such a person as this, one should preach."

Furthermore, the meaning of "thus" (evam) stands at the beginning of the Buddha-dharma; it is the root of all benefits—benefits in this life, benefits in future lives, and the benefit of nirvana—and faith constitutes its great power.
Furthermore, all those who have left the home life as non-Buddhist outsiders think to themselves, "My dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is the foremost in purity.

Thus, such people praise the dharma they practice themselves while disparaging the dharma of others. Consequently, they engage in physical combat and strife in the present life, and in future lives they fall into hell, undergoing various immeasurable sufferings.
As it is said in verse:
"Because of attachment to one's own dharma, One reviles the dharma of others;
Even if one is a practitioner who maintains the precepts, One shall not escape the suffering of hell!"
In this Buddha-dharma, one abandons all craving and all views; all pride of self is completely severed and no longer clung to.
As it is said in the *Raft Simile Sūtra*:
"If you understand my teaching of the raft simile, then even wholesome dharmas should be abandoned, let alone unwholesome dharmas."
The Buddha himself does not dwell upon nor rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, much less upon other dharmas that involve attachment.
For this reason, the beginning of the Buddha’s teaching proclaims: "Thus."
The Buddha’s intention was as follows:

"My disciples have no attachment to dharmas, no defilement regarding dharmas, and no partisan factions; they seek only liberation from suffering and do not engage in frivolous discourse concerning the characteristics of dharmas."
As stated in the *Aṭṭhaka-vagga*, in the verse of the challenge posed by Māgandiya:
"Within the fixed nature of all phenomena, One arbitrarily gives rise to various conceptions;
Since one has completely abandoned both the internal and external, How can one ever attain the Path?"
The Buddha replied:
"It is not attained through seeing, hearing, knowing, or perceiving, nor is it attained by upholding the precepts;
it is not attained by not seeing, hearing, and so forth, nor by not upholding the precepts."
"Thus one completely relinquishes all discursive arguments, and likewise relinquishes 'I' and 'mine.
By not grasping at the characteristics of any phenomena, one may thus attain the Way. Māṅkatika asked:
"If it is not through seeing, hearing, and so forth, nor is it attained by maintaining the precepts;
if it is not through not seeing, hearing, and so forth, nor is it attained by not maintaining the precepts—
according to my contemplation, one attains the Way by maintaining the 'dumb' method!"
The Buddha replied:
"You rely on the gate of false views; I know your deluded path.
If you did not perceive these delusive thoughts, at that time you would naturally remain mute!"
Furthermore, "My teaching is the truth, while other teachings are falsehood;
my teaching is supreme, while other teachings are unreal"—this is the root of contention.
Now, the meaning of "Thus" (evam) demonstrates to people the dharma of non-contention; having heard what others have said, one speaks of them without fault.
For this reason, at the beginning of all the Buddha's sutras, it is titled "Thus."
The meaning of "thus" has been briefly explained.
Now, the term "I" shall be discussed.
Question:
If it is said within the Buddha-dharma that all phenomena are empty and that there is no self whatsoever, why does the beginning of the Buddhist sūtras state, "Thus have I heard"?
The answer is:
Although the disciples of the Buddha know that there is no self, they speak of a "self" in accordance with worldly conventions; it is not a real self.
It is like using gold coins to buy copper coins—no one would laugh at this.
Why is this? Because the nature of buying and selling is such.
It is the same with the term "self": although it is spoken of within the context of the dharma of non-self, it should not be challenged, as it conforms to worldly convention.
As stated in a verse from the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Is there an arhat bhikṣu, whose outflows are forever exhausted,
who, in this final body, can speak of 'I'?"
The Buddha replied:
"There is an arhat bhikṣu whose outflows are forever exhausted;
in his final body, he is able to say, 'I exist.'"
The self is spoken of within the context of worldly conventions (*saṃvṛti*), not within the context of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
For this reason, although all phenomena are empty and without self, there is no fault in speaking of a "self" by way of worldly convention.
Furthermore, there are three roots of worldly language:
first, false views; second, pride; and third, names.
Among these, two kinds are impure and one kind is pure.
All ordinary persons have three kinds of speech:
that of the false, that of arrogance, and that of mere names;
those who have seen the Path and are in training have two kinds of speech:
Pride is names;
all noble ones speak in one way:
by means of names.

Although internally one does not contradict the true Dharma, one follows the conventions of worldly people and thus transmits these words; because this removes the false views of the world, one conforms to worldly custom without dispute.
For this reason, setting aside two kinds of impure speech, one employs a single type of expression in accordance with the fundamental worldly conventions.
Therefore, when a disciple of the Buddha speaks of a "self" in conformity with worldly custom, there is no fault.
Furthermore, if a person clings to the mark of selflessness (*anātman*) as being real and considers all else to be false speech, that person should raise this objection:
"If the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is selflessness, why do you say, 'Thus have I heard'?"

"Now, for all the disciples of the Buddhas, all phenomena are empty and non-existent; within this, the mind does not cling, nor do they speak of clinging to the true mark of phenomena, much less clinging to a mind within the dharma of non-self."
For this reason, one should not raise the objection: "Why do you speak of a self?
As a verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"If there were something that was not empty, Then there would have to be something that is empty."
If even the non-empty cannot be attained, how much less can the empty be attained?
Ordinary people perceive the non-empty, and they likewise perceive the empty;
yet to not see seeing and to have no seeing—this is truly called Nirvana.
The non-dual gate of peace can shatter all false views;
that which is the sphere of action of all Buddhas is called the Dharma of Non-Self.
This concludes the brief explanation of the meaning of "self."
Regarding "hearing," it shall now be explained. Question:
As for hearing, how does one hear?
Is it heard by means of the auditory faculty?
Is it heard by means of auditory consciousness?
Or is it heard by means of mental consciousness?
If it is the ear-faculty that hears, it should not hear because the ear-faculty lacks cognition.
If it is the ear-consciousness that hears, it should not hear because the ear-consciousness is momentary and thus incapable of discrimination.
If it were the mental consciousness that hears, the mental consciousness likewise could not hear.
Why? Because the five consciousnesses first cognize the five sense-objects, and only thereafter does the mental consciousness cognize them.
The mental consciousness cannot cognize the five sense objects of the present; it cognizes only the five sense objects of the past and future.
If the mental consciousness could cognize the five sense objects of the present, then even those who are blind or deaf would be able to perceive forms and sounds.
Why is this? Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) has not been destroyed.
He replied:
It is not the ear faculty that hears sound, nor is it the ear-consciousness, nor is it the mental consciousness.
The act of hearing sound arises from the convergence of many causes and conditions; one cannot say that a single dharma alone can hear sound.
Why is this? Because the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) lacks sentience, it should not hear sounds;
because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is formless, non-obstructive, and locationless, it likewise should not hear sounds.
Because sound is devoid of sentience and lacks sense organs, it cannot cognize itself.
At that time, when the ear-organ is unimpaired, the sound reaches a range where it can be heard, and the mind desires to hear;
through the conjunction of the faculty, the object, and the mind, auditory consciousness arises.
Following auditory consciousness, mental consciousness immediately arises and is able to discern—that various causes and conditions enable the hearing of sounds.
For this reason, one should not raise the objection:
"Who hears the sound?"
"In the Buddha-dharma, there is not even a single dharma that can act, see, or know.
As it is said in a verse:
'There is karma and there is its fruit, But there is no agent who performs the karma or experiences the fruit.'"
This is the foremost profundity, which the Dharma-Buddha is able to perceive.
Though empty, it is not annihilated; though continuous, it is not eternal;
and yet neither merit nor demerit is lost—such is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
The brief explanation of "hearing" is concluded.
Now, the meaning of "one" shall be explained. Question:

Within the Buddha-dharma, dharmas such as number and time do not truly exist, because they are not subsumed within the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), or elements (dhātus). Why, then, do you speak of "one time"?
Answer: There is no fault in there being "one time" (a single moment) according to worldly convention.
If one fashions images of deities out of clay, wood, or other materials and pays them homage with the thought that they are the deity, there is no fault.

The same applies to the statement regarding "one time" (*ekakṣaṇa*). Although in reality there is no such thing as one time, there is no fault in speaking of "one time" in accordance with worldly convention.
Question:
It should not be that there is no "one time."
The Buddha himself said:
"When one person appears in the world, many people obtain happiness; who is this person?
It is the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
As it is said in a verse:
"I practiced without a teacher or protector; My resolve was peerless and without equal.
By accumulating a single practice, I attained Buddhahood; Spontaneously, I realized the Noble Path."
In these and other such ways, the Buddha has taught "one" in various places; therefore, there ought to be a "one.

Furthermore, it is because of the combination of one dharma that a thing is called "one. If, in reality, there were no single dharma, why would a single thought arise with respect to a single object, rather than two or three?
From two objects, two minds arise, neither one nor three;
from three objects, three minds arise, neither two nor one?
If numbers truly do not exist, then from a single object, two minds should arise, and from two objects, a single mind should arise.
The same applies to three, four, five, and six [dharmas].
For this reason, it is certain that within a single object there exists one dharma; because these dharmas combine, a single mind arises within that single object.
Answer:
Whether "oneness" is identical to the "thing" or whether "oneness" is different from the "thing," both positions entail logical faults.
Question:
If they were one, what fault would there be?
The answer is:
if "one" and "jar" were identical in meaning, it would be like the case of Indriya and Śākya, which are also identical in meaning.
If that were so, then wherever there is "one," it should be a jar;
for example, just as wherever there is a tinduka tree, there is also a śāla tree in every such place.
Now, all things such as clothing and so forth ought to be the same as a jar, because "one" and "jar" are one and the same.
Thus, wherever there is oneness, it should all be a jar;
for just like a jar and clothing, all would be a single entity without any distinction.
Furthermore, "one" is a numerical category; therefore, "vase" should also be a numerical category.
Since the substance of a vase possesses five attributes, "one" should likewise possess five attributes.
A jar has color and is resistant;
a "one" should likewise have color and be resistant.
If wherever it is located it is not called a jar, then now one should not say "jar" and "one" are identical!
If one speaks of "one," it does not include the jar; if one speaks of the "jar," it likewise does not include "one," because "jar" and "one" are not different.
Furthermore, if one wishes to speak of "one," one should speak of the "jar";
if one wishes to speak of the "jar," one should speak of "one"—in this way, there would be confusion.
Question:
If such a fault exists in the case of identity, what is the error in the case of difference? Answer:
If "one" were different from the jar, then the jar would not be one;
if the jar were different from "one," then "one" would not be the jar.
If the jar is joined with "one" and thus the jar is called "one," then now that "one" is joined with the jar, why is "one" not called the jar?
Therefore, one cannot say that the jar is different from oneness. Question:
Although the jar is one because it is conjoined with the number one, oneness itself does not constitute the jar.
Answer: Among all numbers, "one" comes first. Since the one is different from the jar, the jar does not constitute "one.
Because "one" does not exist, "many" also does not exist.
Why is this? Because there is first one and subsequently many.
Thus, within such diversity, even "one" cannot be found.

For this reason, when seeking a single dharma within these two categories, it cannot be found. Because it cannot be found, how could it be subsumed under the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), or elements (dhātus)?

It is only because the disciples of the Buddha follow conventional language that they speak of "one"; in reality, the mind does not cling to it, knowing that the names of numerical dharmas exist merely as designations.
For this reason, within the Buddha-dharma, speaking of "one person," "one teacher," or "one time" does not incur the fault of falling into false views.
This concludes the brief explanation of "one."
Regarding "time," it shall now be explained. Question:
In India, there are two ways of designating "time."
The first is called *kāla* (time), and the second is called *samaya* (occasion).
Why does the Buddha not speak of *kāla* but instead speak of *samaya*?
The answer is:
If one says "kāla," there is likewise doubt in both cases.
The questioner asks:
Because it is easy to pronounce, one should say "kāla."
The two syllables "kāla" and the three syllables "samaya" are difficult to pronounce due to their reduplication.
The answer is:
"In order to eliminate wrong views, 'samaya' is spoken, and 'kāla' is not."
Question: Some say:
"All things in heaven and on earth, whether beautiful or ugly, have time as their cause," as stated in a verse from the *Kālasūtra*:
"When the time comes, sentient beings ripen; when the time arrives, it urges them on.
Time can awaken people; therefore, time is the cause."
"The world is like a chariot wheel; the changes of time are like its revolving rim.
Human beings are also like a chariot wheel, sometimes ascending and sometimes descending.
Furthermore, another person said:
"Although all things, whether beautiful or ugly, in heaven or on earth, are not produced by time, yet time is an unchanging cause and is substantially existent.
Because the dharma of time is subtle, it cannot be seen or known; however, one can know that time exists through its effects, such as flowers and fruits."
Regarding "last year" and "this year," "long" and "short," or "slow" and "fast"—by observing these characteristics, although time itself is not seen, one can know that time exists.
Why is this? Because by seeing the effect, one knows that there is a cause.
"For this reason, there is the phenomenon of time; because the phenomenon of time is indestructible, it is eternal.
He replied:
"For example, a lump of clay is the present time, the dust of the earth is the past time, and the jar is the future time."
Because time is eternal, past time does not become future time;

according to your scriptural doctrine, time is a single entity. For this reason, the past world does not become the future world, nor does it become the present world, because they would otherwise be confused with one another.
In the past world, there was also no future world; for this reason, there is no future world.
It is the same for the present world. Question:

"When you accept that there is earth-dust at the time of the past, if there were such a thing as a 'time of the past,' there would necessarily also have to be a 'time of the future. For this reason, temporal dharmas must truly exist.
He replied:
"Have you not heard what I previously stated: the jar of the future world and the earth-dust of the past world?"

The future world does not become the past world; when one falls into the characteristic of the future world—that is, at the time of the characteristic of the future world—how can it be called the time of the past?
For this reason, the time of the past also does not exist.
Question: Why is it that there is no time?
There must necessarily be time.
The present has the characteristic of the present; the past has the characteristic of the past; the future has the characteristic of the future.
The answer is:
if all three periods of time possessed their own specific characteristics, then everything would be exclusively the present period, and there would be no past or future times.
If the future were to exist right now, it would not be called "future," but should instead be called "present.
For this reason, that statement is incorrect.
[The opponent] asks:
The past time does not function within the characteristics of the future or the present; the past time functions within the past, and the future time functions within the future.
For this reason, each respective dharma-characteristic exists at its own time.
The answer is:
if that which has already passed were to pass again, it would destroy the characteristic of the past.
If the past were not the past, it would lack the characteristic of the past.
Why? Because it would have abandoned its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The future world is also like this.
For this reason, the dharma of time has no substantial reality; how then could it produce the beauty and ugliness of heaven and earth, as well as various things such as flowers and fruits?
For various reasons such as these to eliminate false views, the term *kāla* (time) is not used; instead, *samaya* (occasion) is spoken of.

One observes the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), and conventionally designates this as "time"; there is no separate time apart from these.

That which is called direction, time, separation, conjunction, unity, difference, length, shortness, and so forth—these names arise from the mental attachments of ordinary people, who claim they are substantially existent dharmas;
for this reason, one must discard worldly names, language, and conventional dharmas.
Question:
If time does not exist, how can there be the precept that permits "eating at the proper time" and prohibits "eating at the improper time"? Answer:
I have already stated previously that while the names of worlds exist as conventional phenomena (*dharmas*), time is not a real phenomenon; you should not raise objections to this!

Furthermore, these are the rules for establishing precepts within the Vinaya; they are real within the context of the world, yet they do not constitute the characteristics of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya-dharma-lakṣaṇa*), because the characteristics of a self (*ātman*) and of phenomena (*dharma*) cannot ultimately be found.

Moreover, it is for the sake of restraining the scolding and reproach of the masses, for the desire to protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure for a long time, and to establish the ritual protocols for disciples, that the World-Honored Ones of the three realms have established these various precepts.
Within this, one should not seek:
"What reality is there?
What names and so forth are there?"
What is associated? What is dissociated?
What is the nature of phenomena as such?
What is this dharma that does not have such characteristics?
For this reason, this matter should not be questioned!
[The opponent] asks:
If "eating at the improper time," "medicines taken at the proper time," and "robes worn at the proper time" are all *kalpa*, why is *samaya* not mentioned?
Answer: This is taught within the Vinaya and is not permitted for laypeople to hear; how then could non-Buddhists have heard it and thereby give rise to wrong views?
Other sūtras are accessible to all who may hear them; therefore, the term *samaya* is used here to ensure that they do not give rise to wrong views.
"Samaya" is a deceptive name; "time" (*kāla*) is likewise a conventional designation.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, "samaya" is frequently mentioned, whereas "kāla" is rarely mentioned; because it is rare, one should not raise an objection based upon it.
Thus have I heard at one time: the brief explanation of the individual meanings of these five phrases is hereby concluded.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Volume One;
General Explanation of the First Chapter: An Exposition on "Thus Have I Heard."
Volume Three, Part Two. Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by imperial decree. 3. General Exposition on “Thus Have I Heard”: Commentary on the Preface. “Thus have I heard: [The commentary states: “‘Thus’ (evam) refers to the fact that the Dharma was taught exactly as it was; ‘I’ (mayā) indicates that it was heard by me personally; ‘heard’ (śrutam) means that it was received through the auditory faculty. ... [The text continues with the commentary on the introductory formula] ... [End of Volume Three, Part Two]
Regarding the phrase "At one time," it shall now be explained in general.
A question is asked:

If all Buddhas are omniscient persons who are self-enlightened without a teacher, do not follow the instructions of others, do not receive teachings from others, do not employ paths taught by others, and do not preach the Dharma based on what they have heard from others, why is it said, "Thus have I heard"?
Answer: As you have said, the Buddha is an omniscient person who is self-arisen and without a teacher; he should not be thought to speak by hearing the Dharma from another.

The Buddha-dharma is not limited to that which is spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth; all true and virtuous speech, all subtle and excellent words in the entire world, originate from within the Buddha-dharma.
As it is said in the Buddha’s Vinaya:
"What is the Buddha-dharma?
The Buddha-dharma is spoken of by five kinds of persons:"

First, that which was spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth; second, that which was spoken by the Buddha’s disciples; third, that which was spoken by rishis; fourth, that which was spoken by devas; and fifth, that which was spoken by emanated persons.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Śakradevendra-pratilabdha-mārga-sūtra*, the Buddha told Kauśika:
"The true and virtuous speech, the subtle and excellent discourse found in the world, all originate from within my Dharma."
As it is said in the *Buddhastotra*:
"All the virtuous speech in the world arises from the Buddha-dharma;
there is no eloquent teaching that is without fault, nor any that surpasses the words of the Buddha."
Although there may be [good speech] elsewhere, nothing that is wholesome and free from fault is anything other than a remnant of the Buddha-dharma.
Even if there are well-spoken words among the various non-Buddhist paths, they are like insects gnawing through wood and accidentally forming characters.
Superior, middling, and inferior dharmas mutually destroy one another; like extracting gold from iron, who would believe it?
It is like finding ox-head sandalwood within an eranda tree.
