Just as from bitter seeds there may come sweet, excellent, and beautiful fruit;
if one is able to have faith, such a person will believe that within the external scriptures there are naturally produced words of excellence.
All true words of excellence emerge from the Buddha;
like sandalwood fragrance, they come from Mount Malaya.
Apart from Mount Malaya, there is no source for sandalwood.
"Thus, with the exception of the Buddha, there is no one who can speak words of ultimate truth.
Furthermore, "Thus have I heard" is spoken by Ānanda and other great disciples of the Buddha; because it enters into the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma, it is called the Buddha-dharma.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he lay down with his head to the north between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara, intending to pass away.
At that time, Ānanda, because he had not yet eliminated his attachment to kinsmen and had not yet transcended desire, sank into an ocean of grief and could not emerge from it on his own.
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha said to Ānanda, "You,
who are the guardian of the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha, ought not to sink into an ocean of grief like an ordinary person!"
"All conditioned phenomena are characterized by impermanence; do not be sorrowful or distressed!
Furthermore, the Buddha has entrusted the Dharma to you; if you are now filled with grief and despondency, you will lose what you have received."
"You should ask the Buddha:
'After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, how should we practice the Path?
Who shall serve as our teacher?'"
"How can we live together with this wicked-mouthed Chandaka?
What words did the Buddha speak at the beginning of the sutras?"—
in this way, one should ask the Buddha about such various matters concerning the future.

Upon hearing these words, Ānanda’s distressed mind was slightly revived; aided by the power of mindfulness and the Way, he went to the side of the Buddha’s final bed and questioned the Buddha regarding this matter.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Whether now before me, or after my passing, you should rely upon yourselves and rely upon the Dharma, and not rely upon anything else.”
How does a bhikṣu rely upon himself, rely upon the Dharma, and not rely upon anything else?
In this regard, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, constantly maintaining one-pointedness of mind and wisdom, practicing with diligence and vigor, and removing worldly greed and sorrow;
he likewise contemplates the body externally and both internally and externally in the same manner.
The foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena are also like this.
This is called a bhikṣu who relies upon himself, relies upon the Dharma, and does not rely upon anything else.
From this day forward, the Prātimokṣa Sūtra shall be our Great Teacher;
regarding the physical and verbal actions as taught in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, we should act accordingly.
"Ānanda, after my parinirvāṇa, you should govern the bhikṣus according to the Brahma-dharma.
If there are those whose minds are soft and submissive, you should teach them the Saṃthakātyāyana-sūtra; they will then be able to attain the Path."
Furthermore, regarding the treasury of the Dharma-gems accumulated by me over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this treasury should first be introduced as follows:
"Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in a certain region, in a certain land, in a certain grove of trees."

Why is this? All Buddhas of the past began their sutras with these words; all Buddhas of the future will likewise begin their sutras with these words; and even at the time of their final parinirvāṇa, the Buddhas of the present instruct [their disciples] to utter these words.
"Now, after my parinirvāṇa, the beginning of the sūtras should also state: 'Thus have I heard:
at one time.
Therefore, you should know that this is the Buddha's instruction; it is not the Buddha himself saying, "Thus have I heard."
The Buddha is one who possesses all-knowledge and is self-enlightened without a teacher; therefore, it would be inappropriate for him to say, "Thus have I heard.
If the Buddha were to speak of himself as saying, "Thus have I heard," then there might be grounds for the objection that he has something he does not know.
Ānanda questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha taught him this: there is no fault in what these disciples say, namely, "Thus have I heard.
Furthermore, so that the Buddha-dharma might long abide in the world, the elder Mahākāśyapa and other arhats asked Ānanda:
"In what place did the Buddha first preach the Dharma?"
"What Dharma did he teach?
Ānanda replied:
"Thus have I heard:"
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, where he taught the Noble Truth of Suffering to five bhikṣus.
"I have attained vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening through right mindfulness within the Dharma, without having heard it from another."
This sutra should be explained in detail therein. As it is explained at length in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the earth shook in six ways; all rivers flowed backward; violent winds broke out; black clouds rose up on all sides; evil thunder and lightning flashed; hail and rain fell in torrents; meteors fell everywhere; lions and other fierce beasts roared and howled; and the devas and people of the world all wailed aloud.
The gods, humans, and others all uttered these words:
"How swift is the Buddha’s entry into nirvana!
The Eye of the World has been extinguished!"
At that moment, all grasses, trees, medicinal plants, flowers, and leaves split open simultaneously;
all the kings of mountains, including Mount Sumeru, shook and trembled; the waters of the ocean surged with waves, the earth quaked violently, and mountain cliffs collapsed;
the various trees were broken and snapped, and smoke rose from all four directions, most terrifying to behold.
The ponds, pools, rivers, and streams were all turbid and fouled; comets appeared during the day.
All people wept and wailed, the devas were filled with sorrow, and the celestial maidens choked with grief, their tears flowing freely.
The various learners remained silent and unhappy, while those beyond learning reflected that all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent.
Thus, the devas, humans, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and nāgas were all filled with great sorrow.
The various Arhats, having crossed the ocean of old age, sickness, and death, thought to themselves:
"I have already crossed the river of ordinary beings' craving; the bond of old age, sickness, and death has been torn asunder.
Having seen the four great serpents within the casket of the body, I shall now enter the Nirvana of extinction without remainder!"
The various great Arhats each followed their own inclinations, casting off their bodies and entering parinirvāṇa in various places among mountain forests, flowing springs, and mountain valleys;
furthermore, other Arhats flew upward into the air like the king of geese, manifesting various supernatural powers to inspire pure faith in the hearts of the multitude, and then entered parinirvāṇa.
The gods from the Six Heavens of Desire up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, seeing that all the Arhats had entered parinirvāṇa, each thought to themselves:
"Now that the Buddha-sun has set, the light of the disciples' various meditative concentrations, liberations, and wisdoms has also faded away."
These sentient beings suffer from various diseases of lust, anger, and ignorance; now that these physicians of the Dharma are swiftly entering parinirvāṇa, who will be there to treat them?
The lotuses of disciples born within the great ocean of immeasurable wisdom have now withered;
the tree of the Dharma has been broken down, and the clouds of the Dharma have dispersed and vanished.
When the Great Wisdom Elephant King has passed away, the elephant calf follows him as well;
now that the merchant of the Dharma has departed, from whom shall we seek the treasure of the Dharma?
As the verse says:
“The Buddha has entered eternal peace in parinirvāṇa; the assembly that had extinguished all fetters has also passed away.
Thus the world is empty and devoid of wisdom; the darkness of delusion increases as the lamp of knowledge is extinguished!”
At that time, the devas prostrated at the feet of Mahākāśyapa and spoke in verse:
"The elder has already eliminated desire, anger, and pride;
His form is like a pillar of purple-gold, Majestic from top to bottom, wondrous beyond compare; His eyes are clear and pure, like lotus flowers!"
Having praised him in this way, he addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
Do you know, O Noble One?"
The Dharma-ship is about to break apart, the Dharma-city is about to collapse, the Dharma-ocean is about to dry up, the Dharma-banner is about to fall, and the Dharma-lamp is about to go out;

those who preach the Dharma are departing, those who practice the Way are gradually diminishing, and the power of evil men is increasingly flourishing; you must establish the Buddha-Dharma with great compassion!
At that time, Mahākāśyapa’s mind was like the great ocean—tranquil, still, and unmoving—and after a long while he replied:
“You have spoken well!
It is truly as you say; before long, this world will be blind and shrouded in darkness through lack of wisdom.”
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa accepted the invitation in silence.
At that moment, the devas prostrated at Mahākāśyapa’s feet and suddenly vanished, each returning to their own place.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa reflected:
"How can I now cause this Buddha-dharma, so difficult to encounter throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, to endure for a long time?"
Having reflected thus, he thought: "I know this Dharma such that it may be made to endure for a long time; I ought to compile the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya, forming the Three Piṭakas."
In this way, the Buddha-dharma can endure for a long time, and people of future generations will be able to receive and practice it.

Why is this? Because throughout his successive lives, the Buddha diligently endured hardships out of compassion for sentient beings; having mastered these teachings through study, he expounded them for the sake of others.
"We, too, should receive and employ the Buddha’s teachings, proclaiming and transforming [sentient beings].
At that time, after Mahākāśyapa had finished speaking these words, he stood upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, struck the bronze *gandi*, and spoke this verse:
"O disciples of the Buddha!"
"If you have mindfulness of the Buddha, you should repay the Buddha's kindness; do not enter nirvana!
This sound of the *gandi* and Mahākāśyapa’s voice reached throughout the trichiliocosm, so that all heard and knew it.
All the disciples who possessed supernatural powers gathered together at Mahākāśyapa’s location.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed those gathered in the assembly:

"The Buddha-dharma is about to perish. For three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha underwent various forms of diligent suffering out of compassion for sentient beings, and through study, he attained this Dharma."
After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, those disciples who know the Dharma, uphold the Dharma, and recite the Dharma will all likewise pass away following the Buddha.
Now that the Dharma is about to perish, future sentient beings are truly to be pitied; they will lose the eye of wisdom and remain in the darkness of ignorance and folly.

Out of great compassion, the Buddha takes pity on these beings; we should therefore receive and apply the Buddha’s teachings, and only enter nirvāṇa at our own discretion once the compilation of the scriptural collections (piṭaka) is complete.
The entire assembly that had gathered received the instruction and remained there.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa selected one thousand people; with the exception of Ānanda, they were all arhats who had attained the six supernormal powers, both shared liberation and unimpeded liberation;

they had all attained the three types of clear knowledge, possessed mastery over meditative concentration, and were able to enter various samādhis in both forward and reverse order, all without obstruction.

He recited and studied the Tripitaka and was knowledgeable in both internal and external scriptures; he had read and mastered all eighteen kinds of great sutras of the various non-Buddhist schools and was able to debate them all, thereby subduing those of heterodox views.
Question:
At that time, there were countless Arhats such as these; for what reason were exactly one thousand selected, rather than more?
The answer is:
When King Bimbisāra attained the Way, eighty-four thousand members of his retinue also each attained the Way.
At that time, the king issued an edict within the palace to constantly provide meals as an offering for one thousand people.
King Ajātaśatru did not cease this practice.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa reflected and said:
"If we continue to beg for alms as we have always done, non-Buddhists will come and forcibly challenge us with difficult questions, thereby causing the Dharma activities to be neglected."
"Currently, in the city of Rājagṛha, meals are constantly provided to support a thousand people; it is here that they may reside to compile the collection of the Sūtras.
For this reason, one thousand people were selected, and no more could be taken.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, together with a thousand followers, arrived at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha and addressed King Ajātaśatru:
"Provide us with food to be sent to us daily; for now, we are compiling the scriptural collections and may not travel elsewhere."
During the three months of the summer retreat in this central land, on the fifteenth day of the first month when the *poṣadha* was being recited, the Saṃgha assembled.

Mahākāśyapa entered into meditative concentration and, observing with his divine eye, considered: "Who among those now in this assembly has not yet exhausted their afflictions and should be expelled?"
Only Ānanda alone had not yet exhausted [his outflows]; the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine people had their outflows already exhausted, being pure and stainless.
Mahākāśyapa arose from his meditative concentration and, amidst the assembly, took Ānanda by the hand and led him out, saying:
"Now, within this pure assembly, we shall collect the scriptural treasury."
"Your fetters are not yet exhausted; you should not remain here!
At that moment, Ānanda was filled with shame and wept bitterly, thinking to himself:
"For twenty-five years I have attended upon the World-Honored One, serving him at his side, yet I have never experienced such anguish as this."
"The Buddha is truly of great virtue, possessing compassion and forbearance.
Having thought this, he said to Mahākāśyapa:
"I possess the power; it would have been possible for me to attain the Way long ago."
However, according to the Dharma of all Buddhas, an Arhat is not permitted to be provided with attendants for service;
for this reason, I have left behind residual fetters and have not severed them completely.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"You have yet another transgression!
The Buddha’s intention was not to permit women to leave the household life, yet you earnestly entreated him until he allowed them to enter the Path."
"For this reason, the Buddha’s True Dharma shall decline after five hundred years; this is your *duṣkṛta* offense!
Ānanda said, "I felt compassion for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Furthermore, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time possesses fourfold assemblies; why should our Śākyamuni Buddha alone be without them?"
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, near the city of Kuśinagara, his back was in pain; he spread out his uttarāsaṅga robe folded fourfold as a bed and said to you:
'I need water.'"
“Since you did not provide [the water], this is your *duṣkṛta* offense!
Ānanda replied, “At that time, five hundred carts crossed the stream, making the water turbid; for this reason, I did not take it.”
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"Even if the water were turbid, the Buddha possesses great supernormal power and could make the turbid waters of the great ocean clear and pure.
Why did you not give it to him?"
"This is your fault; go and perform a *duṣkṛta* confession!
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"The Buddha asked you:..."
"If there is a person who has well cultivated the four bases of psychic power, they can remain for a kalpa, or for slightly less than a kalpa;
the Buddha, having well cultivated the four bases of psychic power, wishes to remain for a kalpa, or for slightly less than a kalpa."
"You remained silent and did not answer.
When I questioned you up to three times, you still remained silent.
Had you answered the Buddha:"
"The Buddha’s four bases of psychic power were well-cultivated; he could have remained for a full kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa.
Because of you, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa prematurely. This is your *duṣkṛta* offense!"
Ānanda said:
“Māra has clouded my mind; for this reason I remained silent.
It was not out of malice that I did not answer the Buddha.”
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
“You folded the Saṃghāṭī robe for the Buddha and stepped upon it with your feet; this is a duṣkṛta offense of yours.
Ānanda said:

"At that time, a great wind arose; no one was there to help me hold my robe. The wind blew it toward me so that it fell at my feet. It was not out of a lack of reverence that I stepped on the Buddha's robe."
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"The Buddha possessed the mark of the concealed organ; for you to display it to women after his parinirvāṇa—how shameful!
This is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) on your part!"
Ānanda said: "At that time, I thought to myself:

'If all women were to see the Buddha’s mark of the concealed organ, they would feel ashamed of their female forms and desire to obtain male bodies, so as to cultivate the marks of a Buddha and plant the roots of merit.'"
"For this reason, I have shown [this] to women so that they would not, out of shamelessness, intentionally break the precepts.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"You have committed six kinds of *duṣkṛta* offenses; you must repent for them all before the Saṃgha!"
Ānanda said,
“Yes! I shall follow the instructions of the Elder Mahākāśyapa and the Saṃgha!”
At that time, Ānanda knelt with palms joined, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, and repented for six kinds of *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Mahākāśyapa led Ānanda out from among the Saṃgha by the hand and said to him:
"Exhaust all your outflows (*āsrava*) first, and only then may you enter."
"Since your residual fetters are not yet exhausted, do not come!
Having spoken thus, he closed the door himself.
At that time, the Arhats deliberated, saying:
"Who is capable of compiling the Vinaya Piṭaka?
The Elder Aniruddha replied, "Śāriputra was the second Buddha;

he had an excellent disciple named Gavāmpati (translated into Chinese as 'The Cow-Chewer'), who was gentle, harmonious, and refined, constantly dwelling in seclusion, abiding in tranquil stillness, and capable of knowing the Vinaya Piṭaka."
"He is currently staying in the Śirīṣa Tree Garden in the heavens and has sent a messenger to invite you.
Mahākāśyapa said to a junior bhikṣu:
"It is now your turn to serve as the monk's messenger."
The junior bhikṣu asked,
"What commission does the Saṃgha have for me?
Mahākāśyapa replied:
“The Saṃgha has sent you to the Śirīṣa Grove in the heavens, to the dwelling place of the Arhat Gavāṃpati.
Delighted and leaping with joy, that bhikṣu accepted the Saṃgha’s command and said to Mahākāśyapa:
“When I arrive at the abode of the Arhat Gavāṃpati, what matters should I report?”
Mahākāśyapa said: "Having arrived, tell Gavāmpati:
'The Arhats such as Mahākāśyapa, whose outflows are exhausted, have all assembled in Jambudvīpa.'"
“The Saṃgha has a great Dharma-affair; you should come quickly!

This junior bhikṣu prostrated with his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, circumambulated them three times to the right, and then, like a garuḍa soaring through the sky, he went to where Gavāmpati was. Prostrating with his head at his feet, he spoke to Gavāmpati, saying:
"O virtuous one of gentle goodness!
You have few desires and are content, always dwelling in meditative concentration!
The Great Kāśyapa sends his greetings and says this:"
"Now the Sangha has a great Dharma matter; you should come down quickly to behold the assembly of various jewels.
At that time, Gavāmpati felt doubt arise in his mind and said to the bhikṣu, "Does the Sangha not have some matter of dispute that it calls me here?"
"Is there no one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Has the Buddha-Sun entered parinirvāṇa?
The bhikṣu replied:
"It is indeed as you say; the Great Teacher, the Buddha, has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Gavāmpati said, "The Buddha’s parinirvāṇa was too swift! The Eye of the World has been extinguished!"
"He who can follow the Buddha as a general turning the wheel of Dharma— where is my preceptor Śāriputra now?
He replied,
"He has already entered nirvāṇa."
Gavāmpati said: "The Great Teacher and his generals have each departed separately; what can be done about it!
Where is Mahāmaudgalyāyana now?"
The bhikṣu said,
“He too has attained parinirvāṇa. Gavāmpati said:
"The Buddha-dharma is about to disperse; the Great Man has passed away, and sentient beings are to be pitied.
He asked:
"What is the Elder Ānanda doing now?"
That bhikṣu said:
"Venerable Ānanda, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you were filled with grief, weeping, and despondency, unable to compose yourself."
Gavāmpati said: "Ānanda is distressed because he still possesses the fetter of craving; thus, separation gives rise to suffering.
As for Rāhula, what of him?"
He replied, "Because Rāhula has attained arhatship, he is without sorrow or grief; he merely contemplates the mark of impermanence in all phenomena. Gavāmpati said:
"Having severed craving that is so difficult to sever, one is free from sorrow. Kauṇḍinya said:
"I have lost my Great Teacher who has transcended desire; dwelling here in this Śirīṣa grove, what would there be for me to do?"
"My Upādhyāya and my Great Master have both already entered parinirvāṇa; I can no longer descend to Jambudvīpa, but shall remain here in parinirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, he entered into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), leaped up into the air, and his body emitted radiance.

Furthermore, he manifested water and fire, touched the sun and moon with his hands, and displayed various supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). From his own heart he produced fire that consumed his body, while from within his body water flowed forth in four streams, descending to where Mahākāśyapa was.
A voice arose from within the water, reciting this verse:
“Kauṇḍinya bows his head in homage To the Great Virtuous Saṅgha, the foremost among the wondrous assembly.
Hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall follow him, Just as when a great elephant departs, the elephant calf follows!”
At that time, the junior bhikṣu took the robes and bowl and returned them to the Saṅgha.
During this interval, Ānanda contemplated all dharmas, seeking the exhaustion of the remaining outflows;
that night he sat in meditation and practiced walking meditation, earnestly seeking the Way.
This Ānanda possessed great wisdom but little power of concentration; for this reason, he did not immediately attain the Way.
Only when concentration and wisdom are equal can one quickly attain it.

As the final watch of the night was passing, being utterly exhausted, he lay down to rest; as he turned over onto his pillow, before his head had even reached the cushion, he attained awakening in a state of vast clarity.
Just as when a flash of lightning appears, those in the dark see the path;
so too did Ānanda enter the diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*), shattering the mountain of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
he attained the three knowledges (*traividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and common liberation (*sāmānyavimukti*), becoming a great-power Arhat.
That very night, he arrived at the door of the Sangha hall, knocked,
and called out. Mahākāśyapa asked,
"Who is knocking at the door?"
He replied, "I am Ānanda. Mahākāśyapa said:
"Why have you come? Ānanda replied,
"Tonight I have attained the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*)."
Mahākāśyapa said, "I did not open the door for you; you must come through the keyhole!
Ānanda replied:
"Very well! he replied, and by means of his supernormal power, he entered through the keyhole of the door, prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, and confessed:
"Mahākāśyapa!..."
"Do not reproach me further!
Mahākāśyapa placed his hand upon Ānanda’s head and said,
"I acted thus for your sake, so that you might attain the Way."
"You have no resentment, and I am likewise; this you should realize for yourself.
For example, just as a hand painting the void leaves no stain or attachment, so too is the mind of an Arhat: it attains non-attachment amidst all phenomena."
"Return to your original seats.
At that time, the Saṃgha deliberated again, saying:
"Kauṇḍinya has already entered parinirvāṇa; who else is capable of compiling the Dharma-piṭaka?"
The Elder Aniruddha said:
"This Elder Ānanda is among the Buddha’s disciples one who constantly attends upon the Buddha, is able to retain the sūtras he hears, and is always praised by the Buddha;
this Ānanda is capable of compiling the Sūtra Piṭaka."
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa placed his head upon Ānanda’s head and said:
“The Buddha has entrusted you with the preservation of the Dharma-treasury; you ought to repay the Buddha’s kindness!”
"In what place did the Buddha first preach the Dharma?
All the great disciples of the Buddha who were able to protect the treasury of the Dharma have entered parinirvāṇa; you alone remain."
"You should now follow the Buddha's intention; out of compassion for sentient beings, you must collect the treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Ānanda, having paid homage to the Saṃgha, sat upon the lion throne.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, the holy Lion-King— Ānanda is his son.
Seated upon the lion throne, He gazes upon the assembly, yet none see the Buddha.”
Such a great assembly of virtuous ones, in the absence of the Buddha, loses its majestic power;
it is like the sky when the moon is absent—the constellations remain, yet they lack splendor.
You, O man of great wisdom, speak! You, son of the Buddha, should now expound [the Dharma].
"In what place did the Buddha first teach? Now you should reveal it!
At that time, the Elder Ānanda, with single-minded devotion, joined his palms toward the direction where the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and spoke thus:
"When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, at that time I was not there."
Thus it was heard by successive transmission:
For the sake of the five bhikṣus, the Buddha first opened the gate of the deathless and preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
The truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path— Ājñātakauṇḍinya first attained the vision of the Path;
eighty thousand hosts of devas likewise entered the tracks of the Path!
When these one thousand arhats heard these words, they ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
They all said: "Alas!"
"The power of impermanence is great! While we saw with our own eyes the Buddha preaching the Dharma, now he says, 'I heard it!
Then he spoke in verse:
'I beheld the marks of the Buddha’s body, Like a mountain of purple gold. "
When the marks of excellence and all virtues have ceased, only the name remains alone.
Therefore, one should employ skillful means to seek escape from the three realms;
diligently accumulate all roots of goodness, for Nirvana is the supreme bliss!
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha spoke in verse:
"Alas! The world is impermanent!
Like the moon reflected in water or a plantain tree, he whose merit filled the three realms has been destroyed by the wind of impermanence!"
At that time, Mahākāśyapa spoke again in verse:
"The power of impermanence is exceedingly great; Whether foolish or wise, poor or wealthy, noble or base, Whether one has attained the Way or not— None can escape it!"
"It is not through clever words or exquisite jewels, nor by the power of deception or strife;
like fire consuming all things, the nature of phenomena is such that they are impermanent.
Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"From the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra* to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, they were compiled into the four Āgamas:
the *Ekottarika-āgama*, the *Madhyama-āgama*, the *Dīrgha-āgama*, and the *Saṃyukta-āgama*."
"This is called the Sūtra Piṭaka.
The Arhats asked again:
"Who is able to clearly compile the Vinaya Piṭaka?"
They all said, "The Elder Upāli is foremost among the five hundred arhats in the mastery of the Vinaya; we now request him.
They then made their request, saying:
"Arise and sit upon the lion throne!
Declare where the Buddha first preached the Vinaya and established the precepts.
Having received the instruction of the Saṃgha, Upāli sat upon the lion throne and declared:
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, Sudinna, the son of the householder Kalandaka, committed his first act of sexual misconduct; for this reason and cause, the first *pārājika* offense was established.

The meaning of the two hundred and fifty precepts is arranged into three sections: the Seven Dharmas, the Eight Dharmas, the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya, the Ekottara, the Upāli-questions, the Miscellaneous Section, and the Good Section;
such as these eighty sections constitute the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Arhats further reflected:
"Who is capable of clearly and thoroughly compiling the Abhidharma Piṭaka?
They thought:
“Venerable Ānanda, among the five hundred arhats, you are foremost in understanding the meaning of the sūtras; we now request your presence.
They then made this request:
“Rise and take your seat upon the lion throne!”
"In what place did the Buddha first preach the Abhidharma?
Having received the instruction of the Saṃgha, Ānanda sat upon the lion throne and said:
"Thus have I heard:"
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Those who possess the five fears, the five offenses, and the five enmities, and do not eliminate or extinguish them—for this reason, they experience immeasurable suffering of body and mind in this present life, and furthermore, they will fall into the evil realms in future lives."

All those who are free from these five fears, five sins, and five enemies, by reason of these causes and conditions, experience various kinds of physical and mental happiness in this present life, and in future lives will be born in the blissful realms of the heavens.
What are the five fears that should be avoided?
First, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, drinking intoxicants.
Passages such as these are called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

Once the collection of the Three Piṭakas was completed, the devas, spirits, nāgas, and celestial maidens made various offerings; they rained down celestial flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and divine garments, making offerings because of the Dharma.
Thereupon he spoke these verses:
"Out of compassion for the world, He compiled the Dharma of the Three Pitakas;
The One of Ten Powers and All-Knowledge Proclaimed the lamp of wisdom that dispels ignorance!"
Question: From where did the *Aṣṭagrantha Abhidharma*, the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, and so forth originate? Answer:
While the Buddha was in the world, the Dharma was free from contradiction or error;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the first council, it was likewise as when the Buddha was present.
A hundred years later, King Aśoka convened a great *saṃghāṭī* assembly; because the great Dharma masters engaged in divergent discussions, various schools with distinct names came into being.

From that time onward, the lineage passed down successively to the Brahmin practitioner Kātyāyana, who possessed sharp faculties and great wisdom. Having mastered all the scriptures of the Tripitaka, both internal and external, he composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (The Foundation of Knowledge) in eight chapters (*aṣṭagrantha*) in order to explain the Buddha’s words; the first chapter therein is the "Dharma Supreme in the World" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Later, because subsequent disciples were unable to fully comprehend the *Aṣṭagrantha* (Eight Divisions), they composed the *Vibhāṣā*.
Some say that among the six divisions of the *Abhidharma*,

the third division consisting of eight chapters titled "The Analysis of Worldly Realms" (*Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga*) was actually the third division of the *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātuprakaraṇa-sūtra) composed by Maudgalyāyana.
Within the six sections, the first section consists of eight chapters: four chapters were composed by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra, and four chapters were composed by Arhats of Kaśmīra;
the remaining five sections were composed by various masters of the treatises.
Some say: While the Buddha was still in the world, Śāriputra composed the Abhidharma by interpreting the Buddha’s words;
later, the Vātsīputrīya practitioners and others recited it, and thus it is known even today as the *Śāriputra-abhidharma*.

Mahākātyāyana, during the time of the Buddha, interpreted the Buddha’s words and composed the Piṭakas—*piṭaka* being the Qin term for "basket" or "repository"—which are still practiced today in South India.
This is because they all provide extensive explanations of the Buddha’s words.
For example, regarding the teaching on the five precepts:
how many are with form, and how many are without form?
How many are visible, and how many are invisible?
How many are with resistance, and how many are without resistance?
How many are with outflows, and how many are without outflows?
How many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)? How many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
How many have retribution (*savipāka*)? How many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
How many are wholesome (*kuśala*)? How many are unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
How many are determinate (*niyata*) and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Such categories as these are called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, there are the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):

The latent tendency of sensual desire, the latent tendency of ill will, the latent tendency of craving for existence, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of views, and the latent tendency of doubt.
Of these seven latent tendencies, how many are bound to the realm of desire, how many are bound to the realm of form, and how many are bound to the formless realm?
How many are abandoned by the vision of the truths?

How many are abandoned by cultivation? How many are abandoned by the vision of suffering? How many are abandoned by the vision of origin? How many are abandoned by the vision of cessation? How many are abandoned by the vision of the path?
How many universal proclivities (paryavasthāna) are there, and how many non-universal ones?
There are ten knowledges (jñāna):

knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Of these ten knowledges, how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
How many are conditioned (saṃskṛta) and how many are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?
How many have outflowing objects (sāsravālambana) and how many have non-outflowing objects (anāsravālambana)?
How many have conditioned objects as their condition? How many have unconditioned objects as their condition?
How many have objects in the desire realm as their condition? How many have objects in the form realm as their condition? How many have objects in the formless realm as their condition?
How many have objects that are unbound as their condition?
How many are cultivated within the paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and how many are cultivated within the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
At the time of attaining the four fruits, how many are acquired and how many are lost?
Such analysis of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) is also called Abhidharma.
The Abhidharma consists of three types:
first, the *Abhidharmakāya* and its meaning, briefly stated as three hundred and twenty thousand words;
second, the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, briefly stated as three hundred and sixty thousand words.
Third is the *Kṣudraka* (Miscellaneous Collection), which briefly comprises three hundred and twenty thousand words.
The *Kṣudraka* extensively compares various matters according to their categories; it is not the *Abhidharma*.
The general meaning of the brief explanation of "Thus have I heard:
at one time" is hereby concluded. 4.
Commentary on the Term *Bhagavat* from the First Chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. [Sūtra]: *Bhagavat*.
[Treatise] Now it shall be explained. [Commentary]:
What is meant by the term Bhagavat?
Regarding "Bhagavān": "Bhaga" means "virtue" (*guṇa*) and "vān" means "possessing"; thus, he is called the "Possessor of Virtue.

Furthermore, "bhaga" means "discrimination" (*vibhāga*) and "vān" means "skillful"; because he skillfully discriminates the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, he is called "Bhagavān."
Furthermore, "Bhaga" means "fame," and "Va" means "existence"; thus, it is called "one who possesses fame. There is no one who has attained such fame as the Buddha.
The wheel-turning sage-kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors cannot equal the Buddha, let alone all other ordinary beings! Why is this so?
The wheel-turning sage king is bound by the fetters, whereas the Buddha has already transcended them;
the wheel-turning sage king is submerged in the mire of birth, old age, sickness, and death, whereas the Buddha has already crossed over;
the wheel-turning sage king is a slave to affection and craving, whereas the Buddha has forever abandoned them.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells amidst the calamities of the world’s wilderness, whereas the Buddha has already transcended them;
the Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells within the darkness of ignorance, whereas the Buddha dwells within the supreme light;
the Wheel-Turning Sage King may at most govern the four continents, whereas the Buddha governs immeasurable worlds.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses mastery over wealth, whereas the Buddha possesses mastery over the mind;
the Wheel-Turning Sage King craves celestial pleasures, whereas the Buddha does not even cling to the bliss of the Peak of Existence;
the Wheel-Turning Sage King seeks happiness from others, whereas the Buddha finds happiness within his own mind.
For these reasons, the Buddha excels the wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin).
It is likewise with all other Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors; they are merely slightly superior to the wheel-turning sage-kings.
Furthermore, "Bhaga" means "to destroy," and "Va" means "able. Because this person is able to destroy lust, anger, and ignorance, he is called "Bhagavān."
Question:
If Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas also destroy lust, anger, and ignorance, how do they differ from the Buddha? Answer:
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have destroyed the three poisons, their residual traces are not yet exhausted;
it is like incense in a vessel: although the fragrance has been released, the lingering scent still remains.
Furthermore, when fire burns wood or grass as fuel, smoke arises and charcoal and ash remain because the power of the fire is weak;
the Buddha’s three poisons are forever exhausted without remainder, like the fire at the end of an eon that burns Mount Sumeru until all the earth is consumed, leaving neither smoke nor charcoal.
Just as Śāriputra had the residual habit-energy of anger, Nanda the residual habit-energy of lust, and Pilindavatsa the residual habit-energy of pride;
it is like a person bound in chains who, though initially released, still finds their gait unsteady.
At that time, the Buddha arose from meditation and began walking in meditation (caṅkrama). Rāhula followed the Buddha as he walked, and the Buddha asked Rāhula, "Why are you so emaciated?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha with a verse:
"If a person eats oil, they gain strength; if one eats ghee, they obtain a fine complexion;
but eating sesame dregs and vegetables yields neither beauty nor strength—this the Great Virtuous World-Honored One should know for himself!"
The Buddha asked Rāhula,
"Who is the senior elder (sthavira) among this assembly?
Rāhula replied:
“Upādhyāya Śāriputra,” the Buddha said,
“Śāriputra eats impure food.”
At that time, Śāriputra heard these words and immediately spat out his food, making this vow:
"From this day forth, I shall no longer accept invitations from others."
At that time, King Prasenajit, the householder Sudatta, and others went to where Śāriputra was and said to him:
“The Buddha does not accept invitations from people without cause; yet, Venerable Śāriputra, you likewise do not accept invitations. How then shall we laypeople attain great faith and purity?”
Śāriputra said: "Our Great Teacher, the Buddha, has said:
'Śāriputra eats impure food.'"
"Thus, we may not now accept invitations from others.

Thereupon, King Prasenajit and the others went to where the Buddha was and said to him, "The Buddha does not constantly accept invitations, and Śāriputra likewise does not accept them; how then can our minds attain great faith?"
"I pray that the Buddha will command Śāriputra to return and accept the invitation.
The Buddha said, "This man’s mind is firm; it cannot be turned back."
At that time, the Buddha cited a past-life cause and condition:
"In the past, there was a king who was bitten by a venomous snake. As the king was on the verge of death, he summoned various skilled physicians and ordered them to treat the snake venom."
Then the physicians said,
"If you cause the snake to suck [the poison] back out, the toxic vapors will be exhausted.
At that time, the physicians each performed incantations and magical arts, and the snake that had bitten the king immediately came to the king's location.
The physicians piled up wood and lit a fire, commanding the snake, "Go back and suck out your own venom; if you do not, you shall enter this fire!
The venomous snake reflected:
"Since I have already spat out my venom, how can I go back and suck it up?"
"This matter is more grievous than death!
Having thus resolved with a settled mind, he immediately entered the fire.
At that time, the venomous snake was Śāriputra.
"From lifetime to lifetime his mind remains firm and cannot be moved.

Furthermore, the Elder Pilindavatsa was constantly afflicted with eye pain. When this man went begging for alms, he would always cross the Ganges River; upon reaching the riverbank, he would snap his fingers and say:
"Little maid, stop!"
"Do not flow!
The water immediately split in two, allowing him to pass through to beg for alms.
Then the deity of the Ganges went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha:
“The disciple of the Buddha, Pilindavatsa, constantly reviled me, saying:
‘Little slave, stop! Do not flow!
The Buddha told Pilindavatsa, “Apologize to the River Goddess!”
Pilindavatsa immediately joined his palms and said to the goddess Gaṅgā:
"Little maid, do not be angry!
I now repent and apologize to you!"
At that time, the great assembly laughed at him,
saying, "How can one offer an apology and yet proceed to insult?
The Buddha spoke to the River Goddess Gaṅgā:
“Did you see Bakkula join his palms in repentance?
Although he spoke these words while repenting without pride, you should know that they were not evil.

For five hundred lifetimes, this man has always been born into brahmin families; he has always been self-conceited and noble, looking down upon others. What he has practiced since the beginning was merely verbal, yet in his heart there was no arrogance.”
"In this way, although these Arhats have severed the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they still possess residual traces.

As for the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whether someone cuts off one arm with a sword or another anoints one arm with sandalwood paste, their mind regards them as equally as their left and right eyes; thus, they are forever free from residual traces."
The brahmin woman Ciñcā Māṇavikā, using a wooden bowl as a pretext, slandered the Buddha in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
"You have caused me to become pregnant; why do you not feel concern?
Give me food and clothing!"
"You have no shame, deceiving and deluding others!
At that time, the five hundred Brahmin teachers and their followers all raised their hands and cried out: "It is so!"
"It is so! We understand this matter.
At that time, the Buddha showed no change in his complexion, nor did he show any sign of shame.

This matter was immediately revealed; the earth shook violently, and the various devas made offerings, scattering many kinds of famous flowers and praising the Buddha’s virtues, yet the Buddha showed no sign of joy.
Furthermore, when the Buddha ate horse fodder, he felt no sorrow or distress;
when the celestial kings presented him with food complete with a hundred flavors, he did not feel joy. His mind was single-pointed and without duality.
In such various matters as food and drink, clothing and bedding, and in diverse situations such as praise or censure, honor or contempt, his mind remains without variation.
For example, when genuine gold is burned, forged, and polished, it suffers neither increase nor decrease.
For this reason, although an Arhat has severed the fetters and attained the Way, they still possess residual tendencies and thus cannot be called a Bhagavat.
Question:
Does the Bhagavat have only this one name,
or does he have other names as well?
Answer: The Buddha’s merits are immeasurable, and his names are likewise immeasurable;
these names take up the most prominent ones, as they are the ones most widely recognized by people.
Furthermore, there are other names, such as Tathāgata and so forth.
Why is he called Tathāgata?
Because he understands according to the nature of phenomena and speaks according to the nature of phenomena.
Just as all Buddhas have come by way of the path of peace and security, the Buddha has likewise come; he will no longer go into further existence. For this reason, he is called Tathāgata.
He is also named Arhat. Why is he named Arhat?
"A-ra" means "thief," and "ha" means "to kill"; thus, he is called the "Slayer of Thieves."
As the verse says:
"The Buddha takes patience as his armor, diligence as his sturdy mail,
the precepts as his great horse, and meditative concentration as his excellent bow."
"Wisdom is the excellent arrow;
externally it destroys the army of Māra, and internally it extinguishes the thieves of the afflictions.
This is called an Arhat. Furthermore, "A" means "not," and "Raha" means "birth"; thus, it is called "non-birth."
The seeds of the Buddha-mind do not grow in the fields of future lives, for they have shed the husks of ignorance.
Furthermore, "Arhat" means "one who should receive offerings."

Because the Buddha has eradicated all fetters and afflictions and attained all-encompassing wisdom, he deserves the offerings of all the heavens, the earth, and all sentient beings; for this reason, the Buddha is named Arhat.
He is also named Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is he named Samyaksaṃbuddha?
"Samyak" means "right," "saṃ" means "universal," and "buddha" means "to know. Thus, it signifies one who has attained right and universal knowledge of all phenomena.
Question: What is "right and universal knowledge" (samyak-saṃbodhi)? Answer:
Knowing suffering as it truly is, knowing its origin as it truly is,
knowing its cessation as it truly is, and knowing the path as it truly is—
this is called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, one knows that all dharmas truly possess an indestructible nature, neither increasing nor decreasing.
What is meant by "indestructible nature"?
It is where the sphere of mental activity ceases, the path of language is cut off, and it remains unmoving, like the state of nirvāṇa, transcending all dharmas.
For this reason, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore,
[he knows] the names of all worlds throughout the ten directions, the names of sentient beings encompassed within the six realms of existence,
the causes and conditions of those beings' past lives, and their places of birth in future lives.

To fully know all such phenomena—the mental characteristics of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as well as their various fetters and afflictions, their various roots of goodness, and their various means of deliverance—is what is called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He is also named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; in the language of Qin, this means "Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct.
Why is he called "Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct"?
The three knowledges—knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows—are called the three vidyās.
Question:
What is the difference between the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the clear knowledges (vidyā)? Answer:
To directly know the events of past lives is called *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledge);
to know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past is called *vidyā* (clear vision).
To directly know dying here and being born there is called *abhijñā*.
To know the causes and conditions of practice so that their convergence is never lost is called *vidyā* (clear knowledge).
To directly exhaust the fetters (*saṃyojana*) without knowing whether there will be further rebirth or not is called *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledge);
if one knows the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) such that there is no further rebirth, this is called *vidyā*.
These are the three knowledges (vidyā) obtained by great Arhats and great Pratyekabuddhas.
Question:
If that is so, what difference is there between them and the Buddha?
Answer: Although they have attained the three knowledges (*traividya*), their knowledge is not fully perfected; the Buddha’s is entirely perfected—this is the distinction.
Question:
What is incomplete? What is complete?
The answer is:
The knowledge of past lives possessed by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—whether regarding themselves or others—is likewise not all-encompassing.
Some Arhats know one lifetime, or two, three, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even eighty thousand kalpas; beyond that, they can no longer know. Therefore, it is incomplete.
The clarity of the divine eye regarding future ages is also like this.

Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), at the times of arising, abiding, and ceasing, [the Buddha perceives] the various fetters (*saṃyojana*): they arise in such a way, abide in such a way, and cease in such a way.

Within the patience toward the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), one fully realizes all the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned.

One knows that such fetters and latent tendencies are liberated, thereby attaining a corresponding liberation from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and attaining a corresponding liberation from unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), continuing thus up to the patience following the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) within the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*).
This is not perceived by the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas because their wisdom is limited and their speed [of realization] is slight.

Thus he knows the causes and conditions of past sentient beings and the exhaustion of their outflows; it is the same for the future and the present. For this reason, the Buddha is said to be "endowed with clear knowledge and conduct."
"Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the actions of body and speech. Only the Buddha’s bodily and verbal actions are fully perfected; all others possess defects.
This is called being "endowed with wisdom and conduct" (*vidyā-caryā-sampanna*).
He is also called *Sugata*: "*Su*" in the Qin language means "good," and "*Gata*" means either "gone" or "spoken. Thus, it signifies "well-gone" or "well-spoken."
"Those who go well" depart through various profound samādhis and immeasurable great wisdoms, as the verse says:
"The Buddha’s omniscience is the great chariot; By practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one enters nirvāṇa."
This is called "departing well.
To speak well means to teach according to the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, speaking without attachment to the craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

One must observe the power of the disciple's wisdom; even if one were to employ every skillful means, supernatural powers, and the power of knowledge to transform such a person, there would be nothing that could be done.
This person can be delivered quickly, while that person can be delivered slowly; this person should be delivered at this particular stage;
for this person one should preach on generosity, or on morality, or on nirvana;
for this person one should preach on the five aggregates, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four noble truths, and other such dharmas that enable entry into the Path.
To preach the Dharma in this manner, knowing the various capacities and wisdom of his disciples, is called "speaking well.
It is also called *lokavid* (world-knower):
"*loka*" means "world" in the language of Qin, and "*vid*" means "to know"; thus, it means "knowing the world."
Question: How is the world known? Answer:
He knows two kinds of worlds:
first, the world of sentient beings; second, the world of non-sentient beings.
Furthermore, he knows the world as it truly is, the cause of the world, the cessation of the world, and the supramundane path.
Furthermore, knowing the world is not according to worldly convention, nor is it according to the knowledge of non-Buddhists;
one knows that because the world is impermanent, it is suffering, and because it is suffering, it is without self.

Furthermore, to know the characteristics of the world—neither permanent nor impermanent, neither finite nor infinite, neither departing nor not departing—and likewise to remain unattached to such characteristics; to perceive them as pure, eternally indestructible, and like space: this is called knowing the world.
It is also called *anuttara*, which in the language of Qin means "unsurpassed.
Why is it unsurpassed?
Because the dharma of nirvāṇa is unsurpassed.
The Buddha knows this nirvana for himself without hearing it from another, and he also guides sentient beings to bring them to nirvana.
Just as among all phenomena nirvana is supreme, so too is the Buddha supreme among sentient beings.
Furthermore, in maintaining the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and in teaching and transforming sentient beings, there is no one who can equal him, let alone surpass him!
Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. Furthermore, "A" means "non-" and "nuttara" means "answerable.
The teachings of all non-Buddhist paths are answerable and subject to refutation, for they are neither real nor pure.
The Buddha-dharma cannot be answered and cannot be refuted; it transcends all paths of language, and because it is truly pure, it is therefore called "without answer."
He is also named Puruṣadamyasārathi:

"Puruṣa" means "great man" in the language of Qin; "damya" means "one who can be transformed"; and "sārathi" means "charioteer. Thus, he is called the "Charioteer of Great Men Who Can Be Transformed."

Because the Buddha possesses great kindness, great compassion, and great wisdom, he at times uses gentle and beautiful speech, at times harsh and cutting speech, and at times mixed speech; by means of these, he disciplines and guides beings so that they do not lose the Way.
As the verse says:
“The Buddha-dharma is the chariot, the disciples are the horses; The Real Dharma is the treasure, and the Buddha is the trainer.
If the horse leaves the path and loses the correct track, It must be treated in this way to bring it under control.”
If there is slight disharmony, it is treated with light discipline; by delighting in the good and establishing it, one attains the supreme path.
If it cannot be disciplined, it is then relinquished; through such mastery, one becomes unsurpassed.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of trainers:

first, parents, elder brothers, elder sisters, and relatives; second, the laws of officials; third, the laws of teachers—these three kinds of laws govern one in this life; fourth, King Yama governs one in future lives; and the Buddha benefits one with the happiness of this life, the happiness of future lives, and the happiness of Nirvana; therefore, he is called a Teacher.
The four kinds of worldly governance mentioned above do not endure for long and cannot achieve lasting fulfillment.
The Buddha brings people to maturity through the threefold path, constantly following that path without losing it, just as fire does not abandon its own characteristics until its extinction;
the Buddha causes people to attain wholesome dharmas in this same way, never abandoning them until death.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Teacher who tames and transforms men. Question:
Since the Buddha also transforms women and enables them to attain the Way, why do you speak only of "men"?
The answer is:
because men are honored and women are humble; because women follow men; and because men are the masters of worldly affairs.
Furthermore, women have five obstacles:
One cannot become a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra Devendra, a Māra Devendra, a Brahmā Devendra, or a Buddha; for this reason, it is not spoken of.
Furthermore, if it were said that a Buddha is the teacher and tamer of women, it would be disrespectful.
If one speaks of a "man" (puruṣa), everything is included.
For example, when a king arrives, he cannot come alone; he must necessarily have attendants.
Likewise, when speaking of a man, those with both sexual organs, those without organs, and women are all included. For this reason, it is called "man."
For these reasons, the Buddha is called the "Tamer and Teacher of Men Capable of Being Converted.
He is also called *Śāstṛdevamanuṣyāṇām*:
"*Śāstṛ*" means "Teacher" in the language of Qin; "*deva*" means "heavenly beings"; and "*manuṣyāṇām*" means "human beings. Thus, he is named the "Teacher of Heavenly Beings and Humans."
What is meant by "Teacher of Gods and Humans"?

The Buddha demonstrates and guides what should be done and what should not be done, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. When people follow his teachings and do not abandon the Dharma, they attain liberation from afflictions as their reward; thus he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Question:
Since the Buddha is able to deliver dragons, ghosts, spirits, and others who have fallen into rebirth in other realms, why do you speak only of him as the "Teacher of Gods and Humans"? Answer:
Those delivered from rebirth in the other realms are few, while those delivered from rebirth among gods and humans are many.
It is like a person of white complexion who, though having black moles, is not called a "black person," because the black is so slight.
Furthermore, among humans, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are thin and the mind of renunciation is easily attained;
among devas, wisdom is sharp.
For these reasons, the Path is easily attained in these two realms, whereas it is not so in other realms.
Furthermore, when one speaks of "devas," it encompasses all celestial beings; when one speaks of "humans," it encompasses all those born upon the earth.

Why is this? Because among the heavens, the devas are supreme, and upon the earth, humans are supreme. Therefore, to speak of devas is to encompass everything within the heavens, and to speak of humans is to encompass everything upon the earth.

Furthermore, among human beings, one may receive the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara), attain the path of seeing the truths (darśana-mārga), the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), and the various fruits of the paths.
Some people say that these cannot be attained in other realms of existence.
Some may say: "One obtains [the fruit] to some extent.
It is easily obtained and frequently attained among gods and humans; for this reason, the Buddha is the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Furthermore, among humans, the causes for happiness are numerous, whereas in the heavens, the retributions of happiness are numerous;
wholesome dharmas are the causes of happiness, and happiness is the retribution for wholesome dharmas.
In other realms, the retributions for wholesome causes are few. For this reason, the Buddha is the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
He is also named Buddha, which in the language of Qin means "the Knower.
What dharmas does he know?
He knows all dharmas—past, future, and present; those categorized as sentient beings and those not categorized as sentient beings; and those that are permanent and those that are impermanent.
Because he attained clear and complete awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, he is named Buddha.
Question:
Other people also know all dharmas; for example, Maheśvara (translated into Chinese as "Mahādeva" or "Great Sovereign"), who has eight arms, three eyes, and rides a white ox.
For example, there is the deity Viṣṇu (in the language of Qin, "Pervasive Pervasion"), who has four arms, holds a conch and a discus, and rides upon a garuḍa.
There is also the deity Kumāra (in the language of Qin, "Child"), who carries a rooster and a bell, holds a red banner, and rides upon a peacock; both are great generals among the devas.
These various devas each claim to be great and all profess themselves to be omniscient.
There are those who become their disciples, study their scriptures, and receive their teachings, asserting that they are omniscient.
Answer: This should not be [the basis for] omniscience. Why? Because:
Because of attachment to the mind of anger and arrogance.
As a verse says:
“If one [worships] painted images or clay statues, Or hears of the devas in the sutras and praises the devas,”
These four kinds of devas each hold various weapons and staves in their hands.
Whether it be because their strength is inferior and they fear others, or because their minds are unwholesome and they terrify others—
these devas will certainly and inevitably fear others, whether due to a lack of power or out of dread.
This deity is always feared by all, yet it cannot eliminate the suffering of decline.
Those who serve and revere it do not escape drowning in the ocean of sorrow in this present life;
those who neither revere nor make offerings to it are not hindered from enjoying wealth and happiness in this present life.
One should know that all things are false and devoid of reality; therefore, the wise do not rely on the heavens.

If the various sentient beings in the world revolve like a cycle due to the causes and conditions of their karma—being born in the heavens through the condition of merit, or among humans through the condition of mixed karma—[they remain subject to suffering].
"Worldly actions depend upon causes and conditions; therefore, the wise do not rely on celestial deities.
Furthermore, regarding these three heavens: if one loves them, they desire that all one's wishes be fulfilled; if one hates them, they desire that one's lineage be extinguished for seven generations.
The Buddha is not like this.

When he was still a bodhisattva, even if an enemy or a robber came wishing to kill him, he would still offer his own body’s flesh, head, eyes, marrow, and brain as an offering; how much more so when he had attained Buddhahood and no longer cherished his own body!
For this reason, only the Buddha alone should receive the title of "Buddha.
One should take refuge in the Buddha and regard the Buddha as one's teacher; one should not serve celestial deities.
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses two qualities:
First is the power of great merit and supernormal faculties; second is the foremost pure mind, wherein all fetters and afflictions are extinguished.
Although the devas possess merit and supernormal powers, because their fetters and afflictions are not extinguished, their minds are not pure;
because their minds are not pure, their supernormal powers are also slight.
Although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have extinguished their fetters and possess pure minds, because their merit and virtue are meager, their power and influence are slight.
The Buddha is called "superior to all people" because he is fully perfected in these two dharmas;
other people do not surpass all others.
The name Bhagavān means "Possessor of Virtue," as has already been explained. He is also called Asama, which in the language of Qin means "Unequaled";

he is also called Asamasama, which in the language of Qin means "Unequaled by the Unequaled"; he is also called Lokanātha, which in the language of Qin means "World-Honored One"; he is also called Pāraga, which in the language of Qin means "One Who Has Crossed to the Other Shore"; he is also called Bhadanta, which in the language of Qin means "Great Virtue"; he is also called Śīlaguṇa, which in the language of Qin means "Virtue of Morality. Such are his immeasurable names and titles.
The names of his parents were Siddhārtha, which in the language of Qin means "Accomplished Benefit.
Because at the time he attained the Way he realized all dharmas, he is named Buddha, one who should receive the offerings of devas and the people of the world.
Such as these are called "Virtuous" (Mahāpuṇya) or "of Great Virtue" (Mahāguṇa).
In this way, various names are established according to one's virtues.
Question:
"You love the son of the Kṣatriya clan, Prince Śuddhodana, named Siddhārtha; for this reason, you greatly praise him, saying he is 'All-Knowing,' yet there is no such person as an All-Knowing One!"
The answer is: No!
Because of your evil and heterodox views, you harbor jealousy and hatred toward the Buddha and utter falsehoods; there truly is one who possesses all-knowledge.

Why is this? Among all sentient beings, the Buddha’s physical form, complexion, and countenance are incomparably upright and handsome; endowed with the marks, virtues, and radiance, he surpasses all other people.
Even a person of small capacity, upon seeing the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, knows him to be one possessed of all-knowledge, let alone a person of great capacity!
As it is said in the *Gopaka-upama Sūtra*:
King Bimbisāra of Magadha invited the Buddha and his five hundred disciples for three months.
The King, wishing to offer fresh milk, curd, and butter to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, told the cowherds to settle nearby and deliver fresh milk, curd, and butter every day.
When the three months had ended, the king took pity on these cowherds and said to them, "Go to see the Buddha, and upon your return, resume your work as cowherds.
The cowherds then set out for the place where the Buddha was; along the way, they discussed the matter among themselves, saying:
“We have heard people say that the Buddha is the All-Knowing One; we are lowly and inferior persons—how could we possibly discern whether there truly exists one who is All-Knowing!”

Because the brahmins were fond of ghee and curds, they frequently visited the cowherds and formed close bonds with them; consequently, the cowherds heard the names of various sūtras and scriptures from the brahmins.
Therefore it is said:

"The methods for treating illness, the methods of warfare, the methods of astrology, the methods of sacrificing to the heavens, the arts of song and dance, and the methods of debate and inquiry—Prince Śuddhodana has extensively studied and mastered these sixty-four worldly arts; thus, if he were to know such things, it would not be considered difficult."
"Since his birth, he has never tended cattle; we shall question him regarding the secret methods of cattle-tending. If he can explain them, he is truly an omniscient one."
Having made this deliberation, he proceeded into the Bamboo Grove and saw the Buddha’s radiance illuminating the forest.

Advancing further to seek the Buddha, he saw him sitting beneath a tree, appearing like a mountain of gold; it was as if clarified butter had been cast into a fire, its flames brilliantly bright, resembling molten gold scattered throughout the bamboo grove. The color of the purple-gold light was such that one could never tire of gazing upon it, and his heart was filled with great joy. He said to himself:
"Now, regarding this Lion of the Śākyas—whether omniscience exists or not—"
There is none who does not rejoice upon seeing him; this matter alone is sufficient.
His radiance is the foremost illumination, his countenance is most noble, and his physical marks and majestic virtue are complete, matching his name as a Buddha.
Each and every mark is clearly distinct, and his majestic spiritual power is fully perfected;
virtue and merit naturally envelop him, such that none who behold him fail to love him.
With a halo surrounding his body, those who gaze upon him can never look away with satiety!
If one possesses all-encompassing wisdom, one must necessarily possess these meritorious qualities.
All manner of painted images and statues adorned with precious jewels,
when compared to this wondrous body, cannot serve as a metaphor for it.
"One who can fulfill all contemplations, / Causing one to attain the supreme bliss;
/ Seeing him, pure faith arises— / He must surely be the All-Knowing One!
Having reflected thus, he prostrated to the Buddha, sat down, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How many qualities must a cowherd possess to cause his herd of cattle to multiply?
And how many qualities must he lack to prevent the herd from increasing and to deprive it of peace and security?”
The Buddha replied:
"There are eleven qualities by which a cowherd can cause his herd to multiply.
What are these eleven?"

He knows the form; he knows the marks; he knows how to groom; he knows how to dress wounds; he knows how to produce smoke; he knows the good paths; he knows the places suitable for cattle; he knows the best fords; he knows the safe places; he knows when to leave milk behind; and he knows how to care for the owner of the cattle.
If a cowherd knows these eleven dharmas, he can cause his herd of cattle to multiply;
so too it is with a bhikṣu: by knowing these eleven dharmas, he can increase wholesome qualities.
"How does one know form?
One knows black, white, and variegated colors;
so too, monks, does one know that all forms are the four great elements and are produced by the four great elements."
"What is knowing the signs?
One knows the auspicious and inauspicious signs of a cow; when it joins with another herd, one recognizes it by those signs.
A bhikṣu is also like this: seeing the signs of wholesome karma, he knows that person is wise."
Seeing the signs of evil karma, one knows this person is a fool.
"How can they be scraped and brushed?
For while the various worms grow the sores by drinking the blood, scraping and brushing removes the harm."
It is the same for a bhikṣu: the worms of evil and wrong thoughts drink the blood of his roots of goodness and cause the wound of the mind to grow; when these are removed, he is at peace.
"What is meant by 'covering the wound'?"
Just as one uses clothing or blades of grass to protect oneself from mosquitoes, gadflies, and thorns, so too is the bhikṣu:

through mindfulness and right contemplation of the Dharma, he covers the wounds of the six sense-faculties, ensuring that he is not harmed by the stinging thorns of afflictions such as greed, desire, and hatred.
"How does one know that smoke is being produced?
When mosquitoes and gadflies are removed, and a cow sees smoke from afar, it comes toward the house.

It is the same for a bhikṣu: he speaks according to what he has heard, thereby removing the mosquitoes and gadflies of the fetters (saṃyojana), and using the smoke of the Dharma teaching to lead sentient beings into the house of the true mark of non-self and emptiness."
"How does one know the path?
One knows the paths—good and bad—by which cattle come and go;
so too is it for the bhikṣu: he knows the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to nirvāṇa, and is thus able to leave behind the evil paths of nihilism and eternalism."
"How does one know the place suitable for cattle?
It is that which enables the cattle to breed and thrive with few ailments.
A bhikṣu is also like this: when the Buddha-dharma is preached, he attains the pure joy of the Dharma, and all his roots of goodness flourish."
"What is meant by 'knowing the crossing'?
It means knowing an easy entry and an easy passage where there are no waves or evil creatures;
so too is it for a bhikṣu: he is able to go to a bhikṣu of great learning and inquire about the Dharma."

The teacher of the Dharma knows the sharpness or dullness of another's faculties and the lightness or heaviness of their afflictions, enabling them to enter a favorable crossing and attain deliverance in peace and security.
"How does one know the place of peace and security?"
One knows that the dwelling place is free from tigers, wolves, lions, evil insects, and venomous beasts;

likewise, a bhikṣu knows that the four foundations of mindfulness are secure, being free from afflictions, evil Māras, and venomous beasts. When a bhikṣu enters therein, he is secure and free from harm.

"What is meant by 'leaving over milk'? Because a mother cow loves her calf, she gives it milk; by leaving some milk behind, the mother cow is pleased, so that the calf's supply does not run dry. Thus, both the owner of the oxen and the cowherd benefit day by day.

It is the same for a bhikṣu: when laypeople and householders provide robes and food, one should know how to exercise moderation and measure, so as not to exhaust their resources. Then the donors will rejoice, their faith will remain unbroken, and the recipients will never lack for anything."
"How is one who tends to oxen to be known?

Because great bulls are able to protect the herd, they should be nurtured and guarded so as not to let them become emaciated; they should be given sesame oil to drink, adorned with necklaces, marked with iron horns, groomed, and praised with words of commendation.

A bhikṣu is also like this: among the Saṃgha there are great persons of majestic virtue who protect and benefit the Buddha-dharma, subdue non-Buddhists, and enable the eight assemblies to plant various roots of goodness; they should be respectfully served and honored according to what is appropriate."
Having heard these words, the cowherds reflected thus:

"What we know does not exceed three or four matters, and what our masters, the herdsmen, know does not extend beyond five or six; yet now, having heard this teaching, we marvel at such an unprecedented thing!"
"If one knows this matter, it is the same for all others; he is truly an omniscient person, and there is no further doubt.
This sūtra should be explained in detail here.
For this reason, we know that there exists one who possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajña*).
Question:
There should not be anyone in the world who possesses all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because there is no one who perceives an Omniscient One.
He replied:
It is not so! There are two kinds of non-perception; one cannot conclude that something does not exist simply because it is not perceived.
First, there are things that actually exist but are not seen because they are obscured by causes and conditions.
For example, it is like the origins of a person's clan, the weight of Mount Sumeru, or the number of grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges; these exist but cannot be known.
Second, they do not truly exist, and because they do not exist, they are not seen.
It is like a second head or a third hand, which are not seen because they are concealed by causes and conditions;
likewise, you do not see the Omniscient One because he is concealed by causes and conditions, but it is not that there is no Omniscient One.
What are the causes and conditions for concealment?
It is that one has not yet attained the fourfold faith and the mind clings to evil and heterodoxy;
because you are thus concealed by these causes and conditions, you do not see the Omniscient One.
Question: Because the objects of knowledge are immeasurable, there can be no person who possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajña*).
All phenomena (*dharma*) are immeasurable and boundless; even if many people were to combine their efforts, they could not know them all, let alone a single person!
For this reason, there is no person who possesses all-knowledge.
The answer is:
just as all phenomena are immeasurable, so too is wisdom immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless.
It is like a box: if the box is large, the lid is also large; if the box is small, the lid is also small. Question:
The Buddha himself taught the Buddha-dharma; he did not teach other sutras.
If such things as medical prescriptions, astrology, mathematics, and worldly classics— these kinds of teachings—
are not expounded by one who is an omniscient person,
for what reason? For this reason, it is known that he is not an omniscient person.
The answer is:
Although one knows all dharmas, one speaks because of their utility and does not speak because they are not useful;
one speaks because someone asks and does not speak because no one asks.
Furthermore, all phenomena (*dharma*) can be briefly summarized into three kinds:
first, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); second, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); and third, ineffable phenomena (*anabhilāpyadharma*). These already encompass all phenomena.
Question: Because the fourteen difficult questions were not answered, we know that [the Buddha] was not an omniscient person.
What are these fourteen difficult questions?
The world and the self are eternal; the world and the self are impermanent; the world and the self are both eternal and impermanent;
the world and the self are neither eternal nor impermanent. The world and the self are finite; they are infinite; they are both finite and infinite; they are neither finite nor infinite.

After death, there is a soul that departs to a future life; after death, there is no soul that departs to a future life; after death, there is both a soul that departs and no soul that departs; after death, there is neither a soul that departs nor no soul that departs to a future life.
Is this body the self? Is the body one thing and the self another?
If the Buddha were an omniscient person, why did he not answer these fourteen difficult questions?
The answer is:
Because this matter lacks reality, it is not answered.
That all phenomena are eternal is illogical;
that all phenomena are annihilated is likewise illogical.
For this reason, the Buddha did not answer.
It is like a person asking how many liters of milk can be obtained by milking a cow's horn; this is an improper question and should not be answered.
Furthermore, the world is infinite, like a wheel which has neither beginning nor end.
Furthermore, to answer this question is profitless and carries the fault of falling into evil and heterodox views.
