as a close relative of the World-Honored One who constantly attends upon the Buddha, he must certainly have this thought:
"I am an attendant of the Buddha and know the treasury of the Dharma-jewel; as for the path to the exhaustion of outflows, I do not fear losing it.
For this reason, he was not very earnest.
Question:
For what causes and conditions did the Venerable Ānanda receive his name?
Was it due to causes and conditions from a previous life?
"Was this name given by his parents?
Or was it established based on causes and conditions?
He replied:
This is due to causes and conditions from previous lives, as well as names given by one's parents; it is also established based on causes and conditions.
Question:
What are the causes and conditions from previous lives?
The answer is:
In a previous life, Śākyamuni Buddha was a potter named Mahāprabha.

At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, whose disciples were named Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda. The Buddha and his disciples went together to the potter’s house to stay for one night.
At that time, the potter made offerings of three things—a grass seat, a lamp, and honey syrup—to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. He then made this vow:
"In a future age of the five evils of old age, sickness, death, and affliction, may I become a Buddha, just as this present Buddha is named Śākyamuni;
and may the names of my Buddha’s disciples also be like the names of this present Buddha’s disciples."
By virtue of the Buddha’s vow, he received the name Ānanda.
Furthermore, in life after life, Ānanda made this vow:
"Among the assembly of the Śākyamuni Buddha’s disciples who are foremost in learning, may I be the most preeminent, and may my name be Ānanda."
Furthermore, Ānanda, because he practiced patience and eliminated anger throughout his successive lives, by virtue of these causes and conditions, he was born with a handsome appearance.
Because his parents saw that he was so handsome and all who beheld him were filled with joy, they named him Ānanda; "Ānanda" means "Joy" (in the language of Qin).
These are names based on causes and conditions from previous lives.
How were they named by their parents?
Formerly, there was a king of the Solar Lineage named Siṃhahanu (Lion Cheek). That king had four sons:
The first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana.
He had one daughter, named Amṛtaprabhā.
King Śuddhodana had two sons:
the Buddha and Nanda.
King Śuklodana had two sons:
Bhadrika and Tiṣya.
King Droṇodana had two sons:
Devadatta and Ānanda.
King Amṛtodana had two sons:
Mahānāman and Aniruddha.
Queen Amṛtārasā had one son, named Śubhāla.

Within this [realm], the Bodhisattva Siddhārtha gradually grew up; he renounced the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and went forth into homelessness at midnight. He traveled to the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Uruvilvā and practiced austerities for six years.
At that time, because King Śuddhodana cherished his son, he constantly sent messengers to inquire after him, wishing to know news:
"Has my son attained the Way?
Is he ill?"
"Or has he died?
The messenger came and informed the king:
"The Bodhisattva possesses nothing but skin, bone, and sinews holding him together; his life-force is extremely feeble!"
"Whether today or tomorrow, it will not be long.
When the king heard these words, he was filled with great sorrow and sank into an ocean of distress, thinking:
"My son has neither become a Wheel-Turning King nor attained Buddhahood; how bitter is this decline! He is dying without having achieved anything!"
Thus afflicted by grief, bewildered and overwhelmed,
the Bodhisattva then abandoned the place of asceticism and partook of milk-rice of a hundred flavors, whereby his body was fully restored.
Having bathed in the waters of the Nairañjanā River, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree and sat upon the Vajrāsana, making this solemn vow:
"I shall not break this cross-legged meditation until I have attained all-knowledge;
until I have attained all-knowledge, I shall never rise.
At that time, Māra led a host of eighteen billion to the Bodhisattva’s location, daring to challenge the Bodhisattva to determine who would prevail.
By the power of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, he utterly shattered the demonic army.
The Māra, unable to prevail, withdrew and thought to himself:
"The Bodhisattva cannot be defeated; I shall instead afflict his father."
He went to King Śuddhodana’s presence and spoke deceptively:
"Your son has already passed away this very night.
Upon hearing these words, the king was struck with terror and fell from his bed, like a fish on hot sand.
At that time, the king wept bitterly and spoke in verse:
"Āyudha’s words were empty; The auspicious omens bore no fruit.
The favorable name for gaining profit— Of all these, nothing was obtained!"
At that time, the deity of the Bodhi tree was filled with great joy; taking celestial *mandārava* flowers, she went to King Śuddhodana’s presence and spoke these verses:
“Your son has already attained the Way, And the hosts of Māra have been shattered and dispersed.
His radiance is like the rising sun, Universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions!”
The king said:
"Previously a deity came and told me, 'Your son has already passed away. Now you come and say, 'He has defeated Māra and attained the Way.
Since these two statements are contradictory, which one can be trusted?"
The tree spirit spoke again:
"It is truly not a falsehood.
The celestial being who arrived earlier spoke deceitfully, claiming his task was finished; it is Mara, harboring jealousy, who has come to trouble you."
"Today the devas and nāgas have made offerings of flowers and incense, and silken banners hang suspended in the air;
from your son’s body radiates a light that illuminates heaven and earth.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind was liberated from all suffering and affliction.
The king said:

"Although my son has renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he has now attained the status of a Dharma-Wheel-Turning King; he will certainly obtain great benefit and shall have nothing lost."
The king’s heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, a messenger from the house of King Droṇodana arrived and addressed King Śuddhodana, saying,
"Your noble younger brother has fathered a son."
The king’s heart was filled with joy, and he said, "Today is most auspicious; it is a day of rejoicing!
He then spoke to the messenger, saying:
"This child shall be named Ānanda.
This was how his parents bestowed a name.
How, then, is a name established based on causes and conditions?
Ānanda was upright and pure, like a fine, bright mirror; whether old or young, beautiful or ugly, all facial features and physical forms were reflected within his body.
His person was so radiant and pure that when women saw him, their lustful minds would immediately be stirred; for this reason, the Buddha permitted Ānanda to wear a shawl to cover his shoulders.
Because Ānanda causes those who see him to feel joy in their hearts and eyes, he is named Ānanda.
Thereupon, the author of the treatise praised him, saying:
"His face is like the pure full moon; His eyes are like blue lotuses."
The vast waters of the Buddha-Dharma flow into Ānanda’s heart!
They enable the minds and eyes of people to behold them, bringing great joy to all who see;
for all who come seeking to see the Buddha, he manifests them all with perfect propriety.
"In this way, although Ānanda was able to attain the path of arhatship, for the sake of providing service and offerings to the Buddha, he did not personally exhaust his outflows.
Because of these great merits, although he was not yet an *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training), he was counted among the *aśaikṣas*;
although he had not yet abandoned desire, he was counted among those who had abandoned desire."
For this reason, among the five thousand counted together, because they were in reality not yet arhats, it says: "except for Ānanda.

**Commentary on the Meaning of the Fourfold Assembly, Chapter Seven, from the First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra.** [Sūtra] Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all of whom had seen the Noble Truths.
[Treatise] Question:
Why are there five thousand bhikṣus, while each of the other three assemblies consists of five hundred? Answer:
Women generally possess little wisdom and are heavily burdened by the defilements of affliction; they seek only pleasure and delight.
Because their conduct is dominated by craving, few are able to sever the fetters and attain the realization of liberation.
As the Buddha said:
"This Dharma of dependent origination is foremost in its profundity and difficult to attain;
that all afflictions are exhausted and one attains nirvana through the departure from desire is even more difficult to perceive."
For this reason, women cannot attain much; they are not like bhikṣus.

Because upāsakas and upāsikās have households, their minds are not pure and they cannot exhaust the outflows (āsravas); at best, they can realize the Four Noble Truths and become those in training (śaikṣa).
As a verse says:
"Though the peacock has colors that adorn its body, It cannot fly as far as the wild goose;
Though the white-robed layperson possesses the power of wealth and status, The merit of leaving the home-life is superior!"
For this reason, although these bhikṣuṇīs have left the household life and abandoned worldly occupations, their wisdom is limited; therefore, there are five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who are arhats.
The two assemblies of white-robed laypeople, because their domestic affairs were so pressing, also attained the Way, numbering five hundred each.
A question was asked:
"If you have praised all five thousand arhats, why do you not praise the three other assemblies?"
Answer: Since the great assembly has already offered praise, it is known that others have done so as well.
Furthermore, if he were praised individually, the followers of external paths would criticize him, saying:
"Why do you praise the bhikṣuṇīs?
This is because they give rise to slander.
If one were to praise a layperson (*avadātavasana*), one should say:
"It is for the sake of making offerings.
For this reason, he does not praise [them].
Question:
In other Mahāyāna sūtras, the Buddha is accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering either eight thousand, sixty thousand, or one hundred thousand.
This *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the foremost among all such sūtras.
As it is said in the "Chapter on Entrustment":
"If one forgets all other sūtras, the transgression is slight;
but to lose even a single phrase of the Prajñāpāramitā is a very great transgression."

For this reason, one knows that the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the foremost and greatest; among all the foremost sūtras, it shall have the foremost great assembly. Why is this? Because the number of śrāvakas is small, consisting of only five thousand bhikṣus, and five hundred each of bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Answer: Because this great sūtra is extremely profound and difficult to understand, the assembly of śrāvakas is small.
It is like a king who possesses genuine treasures which he does not show to ordinary people, but shows only to those great persons who have faith and affection for them.
It is like when a king deliberates on state affairs; he consults with his great ministers—men of trust, affection, and wisdom—while other minor officials are not permitted to enter.

Furthermore, these six thousand five hundred people have all attained the Way. Although they do not fully comprehend the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are all able to believe in it because they have attained the four untainted faiths (*anāsrava-śraddhā*).
In other sutras, although the assembly of śrāvakas is large and diverse, not all have attained the Way.
Furthermore, herein, from among the many millions of arhats previously praised, the most excellent five thousand are selected;
the same applies to the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Victors are difficult to encounter; therefore, they are not many.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 3.
Commentary on the Bodhisattva within the First Chapter, Scroll 4.8.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
8. Commentary on the Bodhisattva [Sūtra]. [Sūtra]: Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
[Treatise] Question:
If counting from the top, the Bodhisattvas should come first, followed by the Bhikṣus, Bhikṣuṇīs, Upāsakas, and Upāsikās, because the Bodhisattvas rank next after the Buddha;
if counting from the bottom, the Upāsikās should come first, followed by the Upāsakas, Bhikṣuṇīs, Bhikṣus, and Bodhisattvas.
Question: Why is it that the bhikṣus are mentioned first, followed by the other three assemblies, and the bodhisattvas are mentioned last? Answer:
Although the bodhisattva should properly follow the Buddha, because their afflictions have not yet been exhausted, the arhat is mentioned first.

Although the wisdom of the arhats is slight, it is already matured; although the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is vast, their afflictions are not yet exhausted. For this reason, the arhats are mentioned first.
The Buddha-dharma is of two kinds:
first, the secret; second, the manifest.
Within the manifest, Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats are all fields of merit, because their afflictions have been exhausted without remainder.

Within the Secret [Teachings], it is said that various bodhisattvas have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), their afflictions are already severed, they possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and they benefit sentient beings.
Because of the manner in which the Dharma is manifested, the Arhats are mentioned first and the bodhisattvas are mentioned later.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, through the power of skillful means, manifests entry into the five realms of existence and experiences the five desires in order to guide sentient beings;
however, if he were to appear above the Arhats, gods, and worldlings would give rise to doubt and wonderment. For this reason, it is explained later.
Question:
It may be so for [the stage] after the arhat; why, then, is it placed after the upāsaka and upāsikā? Answer:
Although the fourfold assembly has not yet exhausted their outflows, because they will do so before long, they are collectively termed the "assembly of śrāvakas.
It would be inconvenient to speak of bodhisattvas within the midst of these four assemblies.
Just as a bhikṣuṇī, because she has attained immeasurable discipline, ought to rank after the bhikṣus and before the śrāmaṇeras;
yet the Buddha, for the sake of convenience in ritual protocol, places her after the śrāmaṇeras.
These bodhisattvas are likewise; although they ought to rank above the three assemblies of those still in training (śaikṣa), they are mentioned later for the sake of convenience.
Furthermore, some say:
"Because the merit and wisdom of a bodhisattva surpass those of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha, they are treated separately."
Question: In the sūtras of the Śrāvakas, only the fourfold assembly is mentioned; why, then, is the bodhisattva assembly mentioned separately here? Answer:
There are two kinds of paths:
first, the path of the śrāvaka; second, the path of the bodhisattva.
The fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās constitutes the path of the śrāvaka; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constitute the path of the bodhisattva.

For this reason, in the Śrāvaka teachings, at the beginning of the sūtras there is no mention of "the Buddha dwelling in such-and-such a place together with so many bodhisattvas," but rather it simply says, "the Buddha dwelt in such-and-such a place together with so many bhikṣus."
As it is said:
"The Buddha was at Vārāṇasī together with five bhikṣus;
the Buddha was in the kingdom of Gayā together with a thousand bhikṣus."
"The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī together with five hundred bhikṣus.
In various sūtras such as these, it is not stated that he was accompanied by a certain number of bodhisattvas.
Question:
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
those who have left the household life and those who remain at home.
Lay bodhisattvas are generally included among the upāsakas and upāsikās;
monastic bodhisattvas are generally included among the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Question: For what reason are they now explained separately? Answer:
Although they are collectively included within the fourfold assembly, they ought to be explained separately.
Why is this? This bodhisattva will necessarily fall among the fourfold assembly, yet there are those within the fourfold assembly who do not fall among the bodhisattvas. Who are they?

There are those who follow the path of the śrāvaka, those who follow the path of the pratyekabuddha, those who seek rebirth as devas, and those who seek a pleasant existence for themselves; these four types of persons do not fall within the ranks of the bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because such a person has not yet resolved their mind by saying, "I shall become a Buddha.

Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), all names and the characteristics of birth-and-death are severed; they have transcended the triple world and do not fall within the category of sentient beings.

Why is this? Because once a śrāvaka has attained the path of arhatship and entered parinirvāṇa, they no longer even fall within the category of sentient beings; how much more so, then, for a bodhisattva?
As stated in a verse from the *Upasīvanāgara* section of the *Pārāyaṇa*:
"Once extinguished, does one emerge again from nowhere?
Or, once eternally extinguished, does one not emerge?"
"Once you have entered nirvana, do you abide eternally?
I pray that you of great wisdom will explain the truth of this!
The Buddha replied:
“Cessation is that which is immeasurable; it destroys causes, conditions, names, and signs.
It transcends all paths of speech, vanishing all at once like the extinguishing of a fire.”

"If even an Arhat has severed all names and designations, how much more so for a Bodhisattva who can shatter all dharmas, know the true mark, and attain the Dharma-body—how could they not sever them?"
For this reason, among the four assemblies of the Mahāyāna, the bodhisattvas are mentioned separately.
Question:

Why is it that at the beginning of Mahāyāna sūtras, both the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas are mentioned, whereas at the beginning of Śrāvaka sūtras, only the assembly of bhikṣus is mentioned and the assembly of bodhisattvas is not?
Answer: It is because one wishes to distinguish the meanings of the two vehicles:
the Buddha Vehicle and the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The Śrāvaka-yāna is narrow and limited, whereas the Buddha-yāna is vast and expansive;
the Śrāvaka-yāna seeks self-benefit for oneself, while the Buddha-yāna benefits all beings.

Furthermore, the Śrāvaka-yāna primarily teaches the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), whereas the Buddha-yāna teaches both the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because these various distinctions are taught as two paths, the Mahāyāna sūtras speak of both the assembly of śrāvakas and the assembly of bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the verses praising the Mahāyāna:
"One who has attained this Great Vehicle Is able to bestow all happiness."
Benefiting others with the true Dharma, may they attain the Unsurpassed Way!
Those who have attained this Mahāyāna, out of compassion for all beings,
give away their heads and eyes as alms, relinquishing them as if they were mere grass or wood!
Those who have attained this Mahāyāna uphold the pure precepts,
Like the yak that cherishes its tail, they do not spare even their own bodies or lives!
Those who have attained this Mahāyāna are able to achieve unsurpassed patience;
If one’s body were to be cut and mangled, one would regard it as if grass were being severed!
Those who attain this Mahāyāna are diligent without weariness;
they practice with ceaseless effort, like one bailing out the great ocean!
Those who have attained this Mahāyāna extensively cultivate immeasurable concentrations;
through the power of supernormal knowledges and the noble path, they attain purity and mastery!
Those who have attained this Mahāyāna discern the characteristics of all phenomena.
The indestructible wisdom of reality has already been fully attained therein!
With inconceivable wisdom and the power of immeasurable compassion,
one does not enter into dualistic dharmas, but contemplates all phenomena with equanimity.
Donkeys, horses, camels, and elephants—though they may be similar, they cannot be compared;
so it is with Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, regarding their greatness and smallness.
Great compassion is the axle, and wisdom is the two wheels.
Vigor is the swift horse; precepts and concentration are the bit;
the mind of patience is the armor; and dhāraṇī is the bridle.
This Mahāyāna vehicle can carry all across!

Question: In the Śrāvaka sūtras, only the assembly of bhikṣus is mentioned at the beginning; why, then, in the Mahāyāna sūtras, is only the assembly of bodhisattvas not mentioned at the beginning? Answer:
The Mahāyāna is vast and expansive; all vehicles and all paths enter into the Mahāyāna.
The Śrāvaka vehicle is narrow and limited, and thus cannot accommodate the Mahāyāna.
It is like the Ganges River, which cannot receive the great ocean because it is narrow and small.
The great ocean can receive all streams because of its vastness;
the Mahāyāna Dharma is likewise.
As a verse says:
“The Mahāyāna is like the ocean, while the Hīnayāna is but water in a cow’s footprint;
because it is small, it cannot contain the great—the analogy is just so. Question:
What is called bodhi?
What is called sattva?
The answer is:
"Bodhi" refers to the path of all Buddhas; "sattva" means either a sentient being or a great mind.
This person desires to fully attain the merits of the path of all Buddhas, and their mind cannot be severed or broken, like a mountain of vajra—this is called the "great mind."
As the verse says:
"The teachings of all Buddhas— Wisdom, as well as ethical discipline and meditative concentration— Are able to benefit all beings; This is what is called bodhi."
"His mind cannot be moved; he is able to endure and accomplish the work of the Way;
it is neither severed nor broken—this mind is called *sattva*.
Furthermore, the praise of the sublime Dharma is named "sa," and the essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the sublime Dharma is named "tva."

Because the bodhisattva’s mind benefits both self and others, because he delivers all sentient beings, because he knows the true nature of all phenomena, because he practices the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and because he is praised by all worthies and sages, he is called a *bodhisattva*.
Why is this so? Because among all dharmas, the Buddha-dharma is supreme;
since this person desires to take up this dharma, they are praised by the worthy and holy ones.
Furthermore, such a person seeks the path of the Buddha for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from birth, old age, and death; therefore, they are called a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, three kinds of paths are all *bodhi*:
first, the path of the Buddha; second, the path of the Śrāvaka; and third, the path of the Pratyekabuddha.
Although the path of the pratyekabuddha and the path of the śrāvaka attain awakening, it is not termed "bodhi";
it is only within the merit of a Buddha that awakening is termed "bodhi."
This is called a bodhisattva. Question:
From what point onward is one given the name "bodhisattva"?
The answer is:
Because they possess great vows, their minds are unshakable, and they are diligent and non-regressive;
by virtue of these three matters, they are called Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, some say:
"At the initial arousal of the mind, one makes the vow:
'I shall become a Buddha and deliver all sentient beings.'"
From that time forward, one is called a Bodhisattva.
As it is said in a verse:
"When first generating the mind, one vows, 'I shall become a Buddha.'"
"Having transcended all worlds, he is worthy of receiving the offerings of the world.

From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the ninth stage of unimpeded penetration, when one enters the diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*), the period between these points is called a bodhisattva.
"There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
those who are subject to regression (vivartika) and those who are non-regressive (avivartika);
they are like arhats who are subject to falling away and those who are not."
An *avaivartika* bodhisattva is called a "true bodhisattva";
because of this true bodhisattva, all other regressive bodhisattvas are also designated as "bodhisattvas."
For example, those who have attained the four stages of the path are called the true Sangha;
because of this true Sangha, all those who have not yet attained the path are also designated as the Sangha.
Question:
How does one know whether a bodhisattva is *vivaṛtīya* (receding) or *avaivartika* (non-receding)?
The answer is:

in the "Avaivartika Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha himself explains the characteristics of the *avaivartika*; such-and-such characteristics constitute receding, while such-and-such characteristics constitute non-receding.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva excels in the cultivation and mindfulness of a single dharma, they are called an avaivartika bodhisattva.
What is this one dharma?
It is to always collect all wholesome dharmas with a single-minded focus.
As it is said:
"Because all Buddhas have gathered all wholesome dharmas with a single mind, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there is a single dharma that a bodhisattva attains which is the mark of being irreversible (*avaivartika*).
What is this one dharma?
It is upright diligence.
As the Buddha asked Ānanda:
“Ānanda! Do you speak of diligence?
“So it is, World-Honored One!”
“Ānanda! Do you praise diligence? “So it is, Sugata!”
“Ānanda! Constantly practice, constantly cultivate, and constantly maintain mindfulness of diligence, until it enables people to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
As explained at length in the sutra.
Furthermore, when one attains two dharmas, at that time these are the marks of an avaivartika.
What are these two dharmas?
One who truly knows that all phenomena are empty,
yet remains mindful of not abandoning any sentient being—
such a person is called an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Furthermore, one attains three dharmas:
first, if one single-mindedly makes a vow desiring to achieve the Buddha-way, it shall be like a vajra—immovable and indestructible;
second, regarding all sentient beings, a heart of compassion penetrates to the very bone and marrow.
Third, having attained the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, one is able to see all Buddhas of the present.
At that time, one is called an *avaivartika*.
Furthermore, among the followers of Kātyāyanīputra within the Abhidharma, they say:
"What is meant by 'Bodhisattva'?
One who has awakened themselves and is further able to awaken others is called a Bodhisattva.
One who will certainly become a Buddha is called a Bodhisattva."

"Bodhi" refers to the wisdom of one who has exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya). Because such a person is born from wisdom, is protected by those with wisdom, and is nurtured by those with wisdom, they are called a Bodhisattva.
He further said:
"Once one has generated the mind of *avaivartika*, from that point onward one is called a bodhisattva.
He also said:
"If one leaves behind five things and attains five things, this is called a bodhisattva.
What are these five things?
Leaving behind the three evil realms and being constantly reborn among gods and humans;..."
They shall be free from poverty and low birth, always attaining noble status;
they shall be free from the conditions of non-masculinity, always obtaining a male body;
and they shall be free from all physical deformities, deficiencies, or ugliness, with all their faculties complete.

Free from negligence, joy, and forgetfulness, he constantly remembers his past lives; having attained this wisdom of recollecting past existences, he always remains aloof from all unwholesome dharmas, stays far away from evil people, constantly seeks the Dharma, and gathers disciples.
"Such a person is called a bodhisattva.
He further said:
"From the time one has planted the karma for the thirty-two marks onwards, one is called a bodhisattva."
Question: At what time did he plant the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks? Answer:
After three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, one then plants the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks.
Question: For how long a duration is a period called an "asaṃkhyeya"?
Answer:
Among gods and humans, those who are able to calculate reach a point where they can no longer know the maximum number; this is called one asaṃkhyeya.
For example:

One one is called two; two twos are called four; three threes are called nine; ten tens are called a hundred; ten hundreds are called a thousand; ten thousands are called ten thousand (*myriad*); ten million is called a *koṭi*; ten million *koṭis* are called a *nayuta*; ten million *nayutas* are called a *vibhūta*; ten million *vibhūtas* are called a *gata*; beyond the *gata* is the *asaṃkhyeya*.
In this manner, one cycles through three asaṃkhyeyas:
when the first asaṃkhya is fulfilled, one enters the second asaṃkhya;
when the second asaṃkhya is fulfilled, one enters the third asaṃkhya.
It is like the method of calculation: one calculates from one up to one hundred; when the hundred is completed, one returns to one.
In this same way, when a bodhisattva has passed through one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, they begin again from one.
During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, the mind did not know of itself whether it would become a Buddha or not;
during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, although the mind was able to know that it would certainly become a Buddha, one did not yet proclaim with the mouth, "I shall become a Buddha";

during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, the mind clearly and fully knew for itself that it would attain Buddhahood, and one spoke these words aloud without any fear or hesitation: [I shall become a Buddha].
"I shall become a Buddha in a future age.
From the past Śākyamuni Buddha up to Ratnaśikhin Buddha, this constitutes the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa;
during this period, the Bodhisattva was forever free from a female body.
From the time of the Buddha Ratnaśikhin until the Buddha Dīpaṃkara constitutes two asaṃkhyeyas.

During this period, the Bodhisattva made offerings to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara with seven blue lotuses; he spread out a deerskin garment and laid his hair over the mud. At that moment, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon him the prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
From the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha until Vipaśyin Buddha constitutes the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
When these three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, it is at that time that the Bodhisattva plants the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks.
Question:
In what place can the karma for the thirty-two marks be planted? Answer:
It is within the desire realm, not the form or formless realms;
among the five destinies of the desire realm, it is planted within the human destiny;
and among the four continents, it is planted within Jambudvīpa.
It is planted in the body of a man, not in that of a woman;
it is planted when a Buddha appears in the world, but cannot be planted when no Buddha appears;
it is planted by taking the Buddha’s body as its object, but cannot be planted by taking anything else as its object.
Question:
Regarding these karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks, among the three types of karma—bodily, verbal, and mental—to which category of karma do they belong?
Answer:
The seeds of mental karma, not those of bodily or verbal karma. Why is this?
Because this mental karma is sharp.
Question:
Regarding the mental karma that constitutes the thirty-two marks, which consists of the six consciousnesses— is it of the nature of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
or is it of the nature of the five [sensory] consciousnesses?
Answer: This is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), not the five sensory consciousnesses. Why is this so?
The five consciousnesses are incapable of discrimination; for this reason, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is planted.
Question: What are the characteristics of its initial planting?
Answer: Some say:
"The mark of the feet being firmly planted was planted first."
Why is this? Because one must first establish [the basis], and only then can the other characteristics be planted. Some say:
"The mark of the deep blue eyes is first planted; having attained this mark of the eyes, one views sentient beings with great compassion.
Although these two phrases exist as such, it is not necessarily so.
If it is at the time when the causal conditions harmonize that this constitutes the "first seed," why must one necessarily establish the foot as the beginning?
Question: Is a single volition the seed?
Are they produced by many types of volition?
The answer is:
thirty-two types of volition produce the thirty-two marks; each type of volition produces one mark, and each mark is adorned with a hundred merits.
Question:
How much constitutes one unit of merit? Answer:

Some say: "There is the karmic retribution of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), who enjoys blessings and happiness throughout the four continents and attains sovereign power; this is called one merit."
"In this manner, one hundred merits constitute a single mark.
Furthermore, some say:
"To act as Śakra-devānām-indra and attain sovereignty over the two heavens is called one merit."
Again, some say: "To become the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and attain sovereignty within the desire realm—this is called one merit.
Again, others say:
"Excluding the Bodhisattvas who are destined for succession, the merit and reward obtained by all other sentient beings is called one unit of merit.
Furthermore, some say:

"When the kalpa of heaven and earth comes to an end, it is through the collective merit and virtue of all sentient beings that the retribution of the trichiliocosm is established; this is called one unit of merit."
Furthermore, some say:
"This merit is immeasurable and cannot be known through analogy:
suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were blind and sightless, and there were one person who could cure them all; this would constitute a single unit of merit."
All people are afflicted by poison, yet one person can treat them so that they are healed;
all people are destined for death, yet one person can rescue them so that they are delivered;
all people have violated their precepts and their right view, yet one person can instruct them so that they attain pure precepts and right view.
"Such as these constitute a single unit of merit.
Furthermore, another person said:
"This merit is immeasurable and beyond analogy."
When this bodhisattva enters the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he contemplates great practices in his mind and plants the causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks.
For this reason, this merit is immeasurable; only a Buddha can know it.
Question: At what time can a bodhisattva plant the seeds for the thirty-two marks? Answer:
At the slowest, it takes one hundred kalpas; at the fastest, ninety-one kalpas.
The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni accomplished the thirty-two marks by practicing for ninety-one great kalpas.
As it is said in the sutra:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Puṣya.
At that time, there were two bodhisattvas:"
One was named Śākyamuni and the other was named Maitreya.
Puṣya Buddha wished to examine whether the mind of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was pure and mature;
he observed him and saw that his mind was not yet pure and mature, whereas the minds of all his disciples were pure and mature.
Furthermore, while the mind of Maitreya Bodhisattva was already pure and refined, his disciples were not yet so.
At that time, Puṣya Buddha thought to himself:
"The mind of a single person can be easily and swiftly transformed, whereas the minds of a multitude are difficult to treat with such speed."
Having reflected thus, Puṣya Buddha, wishing to cause the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni to quickly attain Buddhahood, ascended Mount Himavat and entered the fire-samādhi within a jeweled cave.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was a non-Buddhist rishi; while ascending a mountain to gather medicinal herbs, he saw the Buddha Puṣya seated within a jeweled cave, having entered the fire-samādhi and emitting radiance.
Having seen him, his heart was filled with joy, faith, and reverence;

he stood upon one foot, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and gazed at him with single-minded focus, his eyes never blinking for seven days and seven nights, praising the Buddha with this single verse:
“Neither in heaven nor on earth is there anyone like the Buddha; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is none who can compare.”
"I have seen all that exists in the world, and there is none like the Buddha!

For seven days and seven nights he gazed intently at the World-Honored One without blinking his eyes; thus he transcended nine *kalpas* and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within ninety-one *kalpas*.

Question: If the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was intelligent and widely learned, capable of composing various excellent verses, for what reason did he praise the Buddha with a single verse for seven days and seven nights?
The answer is:
Śākyamuni Bodhisattva valued the mind’s contemplation and did not value profuse speech.
Had he used further verses to praise the Buddha, his mind might have become distracted; therefore, for seven days and seven nights, he praised the Buddha with a single verse.
Question:
Why is it that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni’s mind was not yet fully matured while his disciples were fully matured,
whereas the Bodhisattva Maitreya’s own mind is fully matured while his disciples are not yet fully matured?
Answer: It is because the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni has a greater mind for benefiting sentient beings and less for himself,
whereas the Bodhisattva Maitreya acts more for his own sake and less for the sake of sentient beings.

From the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until Kāśyapa Buddha, during the ninety-one great kalpas in between, he completed the accumulation of the causal conditions for the thirty-two marks and fulfilled the six pāramitās.
What are the six?

They are the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Question:
How is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:
He is able to give everything without any obstruction; even when giving away his own body, his mind feels no attachment or regret.
This is like King Śibi, who gave his own body for the sake of a pigeon.
The Buddha Śākyamuni himself was once a king named Śibi.
This king had attained the *Namo-rakṣa-dhāraṇī*, possessed great diligence, and was endowed with a heart of compassion; he regarded all sentient beings as a mother loves her own child.
At that time, there was no Buddha in the world, and Śakra Devānām Indra’s life was ending and he was about to fall.
He thought to himself:
"Where is there a Buddha, a person of all-knowledge?"
Having questioned him everywhere without being able to resolve his doubts, and knowing that he was not the Buddha, he returned to the heavens and sat there in sorrowful anxiety.
Viśvakarman, the celestial master of skillful transformations, asked him:
"Lord of Devas, why are you so sorrowful?"
He replied, "I sought an omniscient person but could not find one; for this reason, I am sorrowful.
Viśvakarman said:
“There is a great bodhisattva who is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; before long, he shall become a Buddha.
Śakra replied in verse:
“The bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Mind, Like fish eggs or the blossoms of the mango tree,”
"The causes for these three matters are many during the time [of practice], but when the fruit is realized, it is very rare!
Viśvakarman replied:

"This King Śibi of the Uśīnara clan maintains the precepts and exerts diligence; he possesses great kindness and great compassion, as well as meditative concentration and wisdom. Before long, he will become a Buddha."
Śakra Devānām-indra said to Viśvakarman:
"We shall go to test him to see whether he possesses the marks of a Bodhisattva or not.
You become a pigeon and I will become a hawk; you then feign fear and enter under the king's arm, and I shall pursue you."
Viśvakarman said:
"How can this Great Bodhisattva be troubled by such matters?
Śakra Devānām Indra spoke in verse:
"I have no evil intent; I am like pure gold that must be tested.
By testing the Bodhisattva in this way, I shall know whether his mind is firm or not.
Having spoken this verse, Viśvakarman immediately transformed himself into a pigeon with red eyes and red feet.
Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a hawk and flew swiftly in pursuit of a dove.
The dove came straight into the king’s armpit; its whole body trembled with fear, its eyes darted about, and its voice was choked with terror.
At that time, a great multitude of people spoke among themselves, saying:
"This king is most magnanimous and benevolent; all should place their trust in him.
Even this small bird, a pigeon, has come to take refuge with him as if entering its own home."
"The marks of a Bodhisattva are such that he will surely become a Buddha before long.
At that time, the hawk was perched on a nearby tree and said to King Śibi:
"Return the dove to me; this is what I have received!"
The King then said to the hawk:
"I accepted this previously; it was not you who accepted it.
When I first resolved my mind upon enlightenment, I accepted this for the sake of delivering all sentient beings."
The hawk said:
"The King wishes to deliver all sentient beings; am I not among them?
Why do you alone show me no compassion and snatch away my food for today?"
The king replied:
"What food do you require?
I shall make a vow."
"Whosoever among sentient beings comes to take refuge in me, I shall surely protect and deliver them.
Whatever food you require, I shall also provide it to you.
The hawk said:
"I must have freshly slaughtered, hot meat," the king thought to himself:
"Such a thing is difficult to obtain; it cannot be acquired except by killing living beings!"
"How could I kill one to give to another?
With his mind thus resolved through reflection, he spoke this verse himself:
"This flesh of my own body Is always subject to old age, sickness, and death."
"Before long it will rot and stink; I must give it to him.
Having reflected thus, he called for someone to bring a knife and cut the flesh from his own thigh to give to the hawk.
The hawk said to the king:
"Although you have given me this warm meat, you must act according to reason so that the weight of the meat equals that of the dove; do not deceive me!"
The king said, "Bring the scales!
He placed the meat on one side against the dove; the dove's body grew heavier, while the king's meat grew lighter.
The king ordered his men to cut off both thighs, yet they remained light and insufficient;

next, he had them cut off both calves, both hips, both breasts, and the flesh of his neck and spine until the meat from his entire body was exhausted, yet the dove’s body still weighed more while the king’s flesh remained light.
At that time, the close attendants and inner relatives set up curtains and screens to keep the onlookers at a distance, saying, "The King is now in such a state;
there is nothing left to behold! King Śibi spoke:
"Do not block the people; let them enter and look!
He then spoke this verse:
"Gods, humans, and asuras— let everyone come and behold me!"
With a great mind and unsurpassed resolve, one seeks to attain the Way of the Buddha.
If one seeks the Way of the Buddha, one must endure these great sufferings;
if one cannot maintain a steadfast mind, then one should cease such intentions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva smeared his hands with blood, grasped the scale and attempted to ascend it, fixing his mind so as to offer his entire body for the sake of the pigeon.
The hawk said,
"Great King!
"This matter is difficult to accomplish; why do you act thus?
Return the pigeon to me!
The king said:
"The pigeon has come to take refuge with me; I shall never give it to you.
Throughout countless lifetimes, I have lost my body without benefiting any being; now, I wish to exchange this body for the path to Buddhahood."

As he grasped the scale with his hands, at that moment, the Bodhisattva’s flesh was exhausted and his tendons severed; unable to control himself, he fell as he tried to ascend. He reproached his own mind, saying:
"You must remain firm; do not succumb to confusion!"
"All sentient beings have fallen into the great ocean of sorrow and suffering; you alone have made a vow to deliver them all, so why are you weary and despondent?
This suffering is very slight, whereas the suffering of the hells is vast; compared to that, this does not even equal one-sixteenth part!"
I now possess wisdom, diligence, moral discipline, and meditative concentration, yet I still suffer from this pain; how much more so for those in the hells who lack wisdom!
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with a single-minded desire to ascend, again grasped the scale and said to the men,
"Support me! At that moment,
the Bodhisattva’s mind was firm and free from regret.
The devas, nāga kings, asuras, ghosts, spirits, and humans all praised him greatly, saying:
"For the sake of a mere small bird, he acts in such a way! This matter is truly rare!"

Immediately, the great earth shook in six ways, the great oceans surged with waves, withered trees blossomed with flowers, and the heavens rained down fragrant showers and scattered famous flowers; celestial maidens sang praises:
"You shall surely attain Buddhahood!"
At that time, the seers from the four directions who were mindful of me all came and praised me, saying:
"This is a true Bodhisattva; he will surely attain Buddhahood soon.
The hawk spoke to the pigeon:
"Having undergone such trials and not begrudging his own body or life, he is truly a Bodhisattva!
He then spoke these verses:
Born from the ground of compassion, The sprout of the tree of omniscience.
"We should provide offerings; we ought not to give rise to grief!
Viśvakarman said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Lord of Devas!..."
"You possess supernatural power; you can restore this king's body to its former state.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "There is no need for me."
"This king has made this vow himself; with a great and joyful mind, he disregards his own body and life to inspire all beings and cause them to seek the path of the Buddha.
Śakra spoke to the king:
"As you cut your flesh, did your heart not feel weary or distressed?"
The King said, "My heart is joyful; it is neither distressed nor submerged. Śakra said:
"Who will believe that your mind did not sink?
At that time, the Bodhisattva made this true vow:

"If, while my flesh was being cut and my blood flowing, I remained without anger or vexation, and sought the path of Buddhahood with a single-minded resolve without despondency, then may my body be restored to its former state immediately."
As soon as he finished speaking, his body returned to its original state.
When humans and devas saw this, they were all filled with great sorrow and joy, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence:
"This Great Bodhisattva will surely become a Buddha; we ought to serve and support him with our whole hearts."
"May you quickly attain the path of Buddhahood and remember us!
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and Viśvakarman each returned to their respective heavens.
Such various manifestations as these constitute the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*.
Question:
How is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:

One should not begrudge even body or life in order to protect and uphold the pure precepts; as King Sutasoma did for the sake of the great king Kalmāṣapāda, he would rather sacrifice his own life than violate the prohibitions.
In the past, there was a king named Sutasoma. This king was diligent in upholding the precepts and always relied upon truthful speech.
One morning, he mounted his chariot and, accompanied by his court ladies, entered a garden for recreation.
As he was leaving the city gate, a brahmin came to beg and said to the king:
"Your Majesty is a person of great merit and virtue, while my own body is poor and destitute; please have compassion for me and grant me a small amount of alms!"
The king said, "Yes!
I respectfully accept the Tathāgata’s instruction; I shall bestow these gifts upon you once I have returned from my excursion."
Having spoken these words, he entered the garden to bathe and sport.
At that time, a king of birds named Mṛgapāda flew through the air and seized the king from among the court ladies, carrying him away just as a golden-winged garuḍa seizes a nāga from the ocean.
The women wept and wailed, their lamentations filling the entire garden;
the city, both inside and out, was thrown into a state of alarm, agitation, and terror.
Mṛgāra placed the king upon his back, leaped into the air, and reached his dwelling, where he set him among the ninety-nine other kings.
King Susumu shed tears like falling rain, and King Mṛgāra said to him:
"Great Kṣatriya king!
Why do you weep like a small child?"
"In human life there is death; where there is meeting, there must be parting.
King Sudassana replied, "I do not fear death;
I greatly fear the loss of my integrity."
"Since my birth, I have never spoken a falsehood.
This morning, as I was leaving my door, a brāhmaṇa came to beg from me, and I promised him at that time, saying:
'I shall give you alms later.'"
"Without considering impermanence, you have betrayed his heart and brought upon yourself the sin of deception; that is why you weep!
King Mṛgapada said, "If this is what you intend, yet you fear the sin of lying, I grant you seven days to return. Once you have finished giving alms to the brahmins, you may come back."
"If you do not return within seven days, I possess the strength of two wings and it will not be difficult for me to seize you.
King Sudassana returned to his own country, where he bestowed gifts as he pleased, installed the crown prince as king, and held a great assembly for the people, apologizing and saying:
"My wisdom was not all-encompassing and my governance did not accord with the Dharma; may you look upon me with loyalty and forbearance!"
"As for me today, my body is no longer my own; I shall now return.
The people of the entire kingdom and all his kinsmen prostrated themselves, entreating him:
"We pray that Your Majesty will take heed and provide compassionate protection for this land; do not harbor further anxieties regarding the ghost-king Mṛgā-pāda!"
"We shall establish iron fortifications and deploy elite troops; though Mṛgāra is divine, he will not fear us!
The King said, "That cannot be done!"
And he spoke in verse:
"Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder for ascending to heaven.
Truthful speech makes one small become great; false speech leads one into hell."
"Now, guarding my word of truth, I would rather cast off my body and life than harbor any regret in my heart.
Having reflected thus, the king set out immediately and arrived at the abode of King Mṛgāra.
Mṛgapada saw him from afar and said with joy:
"You are a man of truth; you have not violated your pledge.
All people cherish their own lives, yet you have escaped death only to return and fulfill your promise; you are a great man!"
At that time, King Śuddhodana praised truthful speech, saying:
"One who speaks truth is a human being; one who does not speak truth is not a human being.
In this way, he praised truthful speech in various ways and censured false speech.
Upon hearing this, Mṛgāra’s faith became pure and serene, and he said to King Sutasoma:
"Since you have spoken so well, I now release you;
having been liberated, the ninety-nine kings shall also grant you leave to return each to his own kingdom as you wish."
When he had spoken thus, the hundred kings each returned to their own places.
Such various characteristics within these Jātaka tales constitute the fulfillment of the Śīlapāramitā (Perfection of Ethical Discipline).
Question:
How is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:
If someone comes to revile one, or beats, strikes, cuts, flays, dismembers, or takes one's life, the mind does not give rise to anger.
It is like the Bhikṣu Kṣānti, who, when King Kali severed his hands, feet, ears, and nose, remained firm and unmoved in heart.
Question:
How is the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:

If there were one with a great mind and diligent effort like the Bodhisattva Mahātyāga, who for the sake of all beings vowed to drain the great ocean with this single body until it was completely dried up, maintaining a concentrated mind without slackening.
It is also like when he praised the Buddha Puṣya, keeping one foot raised for seven days and seven nights without blinking his eyes.
He asked:
"How is the dhyāna-pāramitā fulfilled?"
The answer is:
It is like how all non-Buddhist practitioners attain mastery within their meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, it is like the seer Śāṇakavāsin, who, while sitting in meditation, had no inhalation or exhalation; birds nested within his spiral-topknot (*śaṅkhakeśa*) and gave birth there, remaining unmoving and unshaken until the fledglings flew away.
Question:
How is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:
The Bodhisattva, with a great mind, reflects and discerns, just as the Brahmin minister Govinda divided the great earth of Jambudvīpa into seven parts;
he likewise divided all the various large cities, small towns, villages, and settlements into seven parts.
The Prajñāpāramitā is thus.
Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, this bodhisattva was a disciple under Kāśyapa Buddha; maintaining pure precepts and practicing meritorious deeds, he was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven.
Question:
Why is it that the Bodhisattva is born in the Tuṣita Heaven, rather than being born above it or below it;
for he possesses such great merit and virtue that he ought to be able to take birth at will?
Answer: Some say that when the karma of causes and conditions has matured, one ought to be born therein.
Furthermore, the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*) in the lower stages are thick and turbid, while those in the higher stages are sharp;
however, in the Tuṣita Heaven, the fetters and afflictions are neither thick nor sharp, because wisdom there is peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, it is because one does not wish to miss the time of a Buddha’s appearance in the world.
If one were born in a lower realm where life is short, the Buddha might not have appeared by the time of one's death;
if one were born in a higher realm where life is long, one's lifespan would not yet be exhausted when the Buddha appears. Thus, one would miss the opportunity.
The lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven coincides with the time when a Buddha appears in the world.
Furthermore, because the Buddha always dwells in the Middle Way:
among the six heavens of the desire realm and the Brahma realms, Tuṣita is situated three above and three below.

In that world, he will surely be born in the Middle Kingdom; at midnight he will descend as an embryo, and at midnight he will depart from the kingdom of Kapilavastu; by practicing the Middle Way, he will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
in the middle of his life he will preach the Dharma for the sake of others, and at midnight he will enter Nirvana without remainder.
Because they delight in the Middle Dharma, they are reborn in the Middle Heaven.
Thus the Bodhisattva’s birth in the Tuṣita Heaven is complete.
Thereupon, he contemplates the human realm through four ways of observation:
First is the observation of time; second, the observation of the land; third, the observation of the lineage; and fourth, the observation of the place of birth.
What is the observation of time?
There are eight kinds of time, and it is within these that a Buddha appears:

First, when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years; second, when the human lifespan is seventy thousand years; third, when the human lifespan is sixty thousand years; fourth, when the human lifespan is fifty thousand years; fifth, when the human lifespan is forty thousand years; sixth, when the human lifespan is thirty thousand years; seventh, when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years; and eighth, when the human lifespan is over one hundred years.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"When the human lifespan is one hundred years, the time for a Buddha’s appearance has arrived.
This is called the contemplation of the time.
How does one contemplate the land?
All Buddhas are always born in the Central Land, where gold, silver, and precious objects abound, food and drink are abundant and exquisite, and the land is pure.
How does one contemplate the lineage?
The Buddha was born into two types of lineages:
either the Kṣatriya or the Brāhmaṇa.
Because the Kṣatriya caste possesses great power and the Brāhmaṇa caste possesses great wisdom,
the Buddha is born among those who are honored at any given time.
How does one contemplate the place of birth?
"What kind of woman can conceive a Bodhisattva who possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa and is also able to protect her own pure precepts?
Having reflected thus, [he concluded that] only the queen of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu in the Middle Country could conceive the Bodhisattva.
Having reflected thus, he descended from Tuṣita Heaven and entered his mother’s womb without losing right wisdom.
It is asked:
For what reason do all Bodhisattvas in their final body come from heaven and not from among human beings?
Answer: Because they ride upon the supreme path, among the six realms of existence, the heavenly realm is the highest.
Furthermore, when descending from the heavens, various auspicious omens appear that have never occurred before.
If it were from the human realm, the human realm could not possess this.
Furthermore, humans revere and honor the devas.
Question:

All ordinary beings enter the mother's womb with a defiled mind in continuous succession and are associated with all forms of false wisdom; how, then, can it be said that a Bodhisattva enters the mother's womb with right wisdom?

Answer: Some say that while all sentient beings enter the mother’s womb with a mind of false wisdom during the process of rebirth, the Bodhisattva enters the mother’s womb with right wisdom because he does not lose his mindfulness.

While dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one knows that one is dwelling in the intermediate state; at the time of entering the womb, one knows that one is entering the womb; at the stage of the *kalala*—the period of seven days when the union of the red and white essences occurs—one knows that one is dwelling in the *kalala*; at the stage of the *arbuda*, the second seven-day period which has the appearance of a sealed blister, one knows that one is dwelling in the *arbuda*; at the stage of the *peśī*, the third seven-day period which has the appearance of coagulated curd, one knows that one is dwelling in the *peśī*; at the stage of the five protuberances (*paṃca-peśī*), one knows that one is dwelling in the five protuberances;
and at the time of birth, one knows that one is being born. To maintain such mindfulness without loss is called "entering the mother’s womb with right wisdom."
Furthermore, when other beings dwell in the intermediate state (antarābhava), if they are male, they conceive a lustful desire for their mother, thinking:
"This woman shall engage in sexual union with me."
If he is a man, he conceives hatred toward his father;
if she is a woman, she conceives a lustful mind toward her father, thinking:
"This man shall consort with me."
He gives rise to anger toward his mother.
Such a mind of anger or a mind of lustful attachment does not exist in a bodhisattva.
The bodhisattva has already previously understood who is the father and who is the mother.
"This father and this mother were able to nourish my body; depending upon my parents, this physical body was born, and by means of it, I attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This pure mind that recollects the parents and enters the womb in succession is called 'entering the mother's womb with right wisdom.'"
When this Bodhisattva has completed ten months, possessing correct wisdom and never losing mindfulness,
he emerges from the womb, takes seven steps, and utters these words:
"This is my final body."
...and so on, until he brought the physiognomist before him, saying:
"Examine my son; does he truly possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?
If he is endowed with these thirty-two marks, there are two possible destinies for him:..."
"If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves the home life, he shall become a Buddha.

The physiognomists said, "The Prince of the Earth truly possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King, and if he leaves the home life, he shall become a Buddha."
The king asked,
"What are the thirty-two marks?
The physiognomist replied:
First, the mark of level soles:
the entire sole of the foot touches the ground, with no space between it and the earth such that not even a needle could be inserted.
Second, the mark of two wheels on the soles: [the soles bear the signs of two wheels].

With its thousand spokes, rim, and hub, these three features are fully complete; it is spontaneously accomplished without depending on human labor. Even the celestial artisans, such as Viśvakarman, could not create such a wondrous form.
Question:
For what reason is it impossible? Answer:
This Viśvakarman, the celestial master artisan, does not conceal his wisdom;
this is the retribution for his wholesome karma of the wheel-mark.
This celestial artisan has obtained wisdom as a result of his birth-retribution.
These wheel-marks are obtained through the roots of goodness and wisdom cultivated over successive lifetimes.
Viśvakarman obtained this wisdom in a single lifetime;
these wheel-marks, however, arise from wisdom developed over immeasurable kalpas.
For this reason, even Viśvakarman cannot create such things, let alone other artisans.
Third is the mark of long fingers:
the fingers are slender, elongated, and straight; they are well-proportioned in sequence and beautifully formed, with the joints set at varying intervals.
Fourth, the mark of broad and level heels.
Fifth, the mark of webbed fingers and toes:
like a king of geese, when the fingers are spread they appear, and when not spread they do not appear.
Sixth, the mark of softness of hands and feet:
they are as delicate as fine karpāsa wool, surpassing all other parts of the body.
Seventh, the mark of high and full insteps:
When he steps upon the earth with his feet, it is neither too broad nor too narrow.

The color of the soles of his feet is like that of a red lotus; the webbing between his toes and the color of the edges of his feet are like genuine coral; his toenails are like pure red copper; the upper part of his insteps is the color of true gold; and the hair on the upper part of his insteps is the color of blue *vaiḍūrya*.
His feet are magnificent and beautiful, like sandals adorned with various jewels and diverse ornaments.
Eighth is the mark of the calves of an eneya deer:
his calves are like those of the eneya deer, tapering and slender from top to bottom.
Ninth, the mark of standing upright with hands reaching the knees:
without bending forward or leaning back, he can touch his knees with his palms.
Tenth, the mark of the concealed private organ:
It is like the precious elephant-treasure and the precious horse-treasure. Question:
When a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for what cause and condition do his disciples see the mark of the sheathed organ?
The answer is:
It is for the sake of delivering the multitude and resolving their doubts that he displays the mark of the concealed organ.
Furthermore, some say:
"The Buddha manifested as a horse-treasure and an elephant-treasure, showing them to his disciples and saying:
'My private organ is likewise concealed in a sheath.
(11) Eleventh, the mark of the body being proportionate in height and breadth:"
Like the nyagrodha tree, the body of the Bodhisattva is symmetrical at its midpoint, with equal proportions on all four sides.
Twelfth is the mark of body hair growing upward:
the hairs on his body all grow upward and are fine.
Thirteenth, the mark of a single hair growing from each pore:
the hairs do not tangle; they are the color of blue lapis lazuli, curling to the right and pointing upward.
Fourteenth, the golden-hued mark:
Question: What kind of golden color? Answer:
If iron is placed beside gold, it does not appear; gold as it exists today, when compared with the gold from the time of the Buddha’s presence, does not appear;
the gold from the time of the Buddha’s presence, when compared with the Jāmbūnada gold, does not appear;

the Jāmbūnada gold, when compared with the golden sand on the path of the wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin) in the great ocean, does not appear; and that golden sand, when compared with the golden mountain...
Then it does not appear; compared to Mount Sumeru, the Golden Mountain does not appear;

compared to the golden necklaces of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Mount Sumeru does not appear; compared to the gold of the Yāma Heaven, the golden necklaces of the Trāyastriṃśa gods do not appear;
compared to the gold of the Tuṣita Heaven, the gold of the Yāma Heaven does not appear.
The gold of the Tuṣita Heaven does not appear when compared to the gold of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;

the gold of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven does not appear when compared to the gold of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and the gold of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven does not appear when compared to the color of the Bodhisattva’s body.
Such a color is called the mark of golden hue.
Fifteenth is the mark of the fathom-wide radiance:
on all four sides there is a radiance of one fathom, and within this light the Buddha is most supremely dignified and majestic, like the pure and bright precious light of the various devas and kings.
Sixteenth is the mark of fine and thin skin:
dust and dirt do not adhere to his body, just as a lotus leaf does not receive dust or water.
If a bodhisattva walks upon a mountain of dry earth, the soil does not stick to his feet.
When the Sālavana wind blows, it shatters earthen mountains into dust, yet not even a single grain of dust touches the Buddha’s body.
Seventeenth is the mark of the seven protuberances being full and rounded:
his two hands, two feet, two shoulders, and the back of his neck—these seven places are all full, well-proportioned, and their color is so pure and superior that it excels the rest of his body.
Eighteenth, the mark of the fullness of both armpits:
they are neither high nor deep.
Nineteenth, the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion.
Twentieth, the mark of a great straight body:
among all people, his body is the largest and most upright.
Twenty-first, the mark of well-rounded and beautiful shoulders:
There is nothing that can compare to this for treating the shoulders.
Twenty-second is the mark of forty teeth:
neither more nor less. Other people have thirty-two teeth; their bodies have over three hundred bones, and their skull bones number nine.
The Bodhisattva has forty teeth and a single bone in his head.
The Bodhisattva’s teeth and bones are many, while the bones of his head are few;
in other people, the teeth and bones are few, while the bones of the head are many.
For this reason, he differs from the bodies of other persons.
Twenty-third is the mark of even teeth:
all his teeth are equal, neither coarse nor fine, with no gaps between them.
Regarding the mark of closely set teeth: those who do not know it would say they are but a single tooth, for there is not enough space between the teeth to admit even a single hair.
Twenty-fourth is the mark of white teeth:
they surpass even the radiance of the King of Snowy Mountains.
Twenty-fifth, the mark of lion-like jaws:
his jaws are broad and even like those of the lion, the king among beasts.
Twenty-sixth, the mark of obtaining the supreme taste among all tastes:
Some say: When the Buddha places food in his mouth, all such food becomes the most sublime flavor. Why is this?
Because within all these foods there exists the cause for the most excellent flavor;
yet, as there is no person possessing such characteristics who can activate that cause, they do not obtain the most excellent flavor.
Furthermore, some say:

when a bodhisattva raises food to his mouth, at that moment nectar flows from two places on either side of the throat, blending with all flavors; because these flavors are pure, it is called "the supreme flavor among flavors."
Twenty-seventh is the mark of the broad tongue:
this Bodhisattva’s broad tongue extends from his mouth and covers all parts of his face up to the hairline;
yet when it is withdrawn back into his mouth, it does not even fill the cavity of his mouth.
Twenty-eighth is the mark of the Brahma-voice:
like the fivefold voice that issues from the mouth of the Brahma King;
the first of these is as deep as thunder.
2. It is clear and resonant, reaching far so that those who hear it find joy;
3. It enters the heart, inspiring reverence and love;
4. It is precise and easy to understand.
Fifth, the listeners never grow weary.
The Bodhisattva’s voice is likewise; five kinds of sounds issue from his mouth with the characteristics of the kalaviṅka bird’s call, which is as lovely as the song of the kalaviṅka bird;
and it has the characteristics of the sound of a drum, like the deep and far-reaching resonance of a great drum.
Twenty-ninth, the mark of truly blue eyes:
like a beautiful blue lotus.
Thirtieth, the mark of eyelashes like those of a cow:
Like the eyelashes of a bull king, they are long, beautiful, and not disordered.
Thirty-first is the uṣṇīṣa mark:
the Bodhisattva has a bone protuberance on his crown, like a fist in size, situated upon the top of his head.
The thirty-second is the mark of the white hair:
a single white hair grows between the eyebrows, neither too high nor too low; it is pure white and curls to the right, extending five feet in length.
The physiognomist said:
"The thirty-two marks of a great man are thus present in Prince Dīpaṃkara; the Bodhisattva possesses these marks.
He asked:
The Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the thirty-two marks, and the Bodhisattva likewise possesses the thirty-two marks; what is the difference between them?
The answer is:
the marks of a Bodhisattva excel those of a Wheel-Turning Sage King in seven respects.
The characteristics of a bodhisattva are:
first, purity and excellence;
second, clarity and distinctness.
Third, the state of non-loss;
fourth, fulfillment;
fifth, profound penetration.
Sixth, he follows the course of wisdom and does not follow the ways of the world;
seventh, he follows the practice of detachment.
The marks of a Wheel-Turning Sage King are not like this.
Question: What is meant by "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa)? Answer:
They are called "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) because they are easily known; for example, water is distinguished from fire by means of their marks. Question:
For what reason does a bodhisattva possess exactly thirty-two marks, neither more nor less?
Answer: Some say:
"The Buddha adorns his body with the thirty-two marks because they are upright and orderly."
If they were few, the body would not be upright; if they were many, the features of the Buddha’s body would be disordered.
These thirty-two marks are upright and unconfused; they cannot be increased, nor can they be diminished.
"Just as the Buddha-dharma can neither be increased nor diminished, so too are the marks of his body.
He asked: "For what reason does the Bodhisattva adorn his body with these marks?"
The answer is:
There are those who, upon seeing the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha’s body, attain purity of faith; for this reason, he adorns his body with these marks.

Furthermore, because the Buddhas are supreme in all matters, their bodily color, majestic power, lineage, family, wisdom, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and liberation—all such things—are preeminent. If the Buddha did not adorn his physical marks, these qualities would be diminished.
Furthermore, some say:
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi dwells within this body; if the marks of the body are not majestic, Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi does not dwell within this body."
For example, suppose a man wishes to marry the daughter of a noble and wealthy family. The girl sends a messenger to speak to that man, saying:

"If you wish to marry me, you must first adorn the chamber, remove all filth, smear it with fragrant incense, and arrange beds and couches with quilts, mattresses, and cushions; provide curtains, canopies, banners, parasols, flowers, and incense, ensuring everything is magnificently decorated; only then shall I come to your house."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is also like this: it sends forth the messenger of wisdom to the place where the bodhisattva dwells in future ages, saying:
"If you wish to obtain me, first cultivate the primary and secondary marks to adorn yourself; only then shall I dwell within your body.
If you do not adorn your body, I will not dwell there."
For this reason, the bodhisattva cultivates the thirty-two marks to adorn his own body, for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually grew up; having witnessed the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, a sense of weary renunciation arose within him. He left home at midnight, practiced asceticism for six years, and then partook of the sixteen-virtue-strengthening honeyed milk-gruel offered by the brahmin girl Nandā.
Having finished his meal, he destroyed eighteen thousand billion ghost armies and hosts of Māras beneath the Bodhi tree and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is asked:
By attaining what merit is one called a Buddha?
Answer: One is called a Buddha because one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Furthermore, some say:

“He has attained the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the three types of penetration, the unimpeded knowledges, and the three bases of mindfulness—namely: first, when receiving teachings with reverence, the Buddha feels no joy;
second, when not receiving teachings or not being revered, the Buddha feels no sorrow;

third, whether revered or not revered, his mind remains unchanged. Because he fully knows the general and specific characteristics of all dharmas, including great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he is called a Buddha.”
Question: For what reason is one who has not yet attained the Buddha-way called a bodhisattva, whereas one who has attained the Buddha-way is not called a bodhisattva? Answer:
Before attaining the Buddha-way, one’s mind is characterized by attachment and seeking, desiring to grasp *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; for this reason, one is called a bodhisattva.
Once the Buddha-way has been accomplished, because one further acquires the various distinct great merits of a Buddha, there is another name: one is called a Buddha.
For example, when a prince has not yet become king, he is called a "prince";
once he has become king, he is no longer called a "prince.
Having become king, although he is indeed the son of a king, he is no longer termed a "prince."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: one who has not yet attained the Buddha-way is called a Bodhisattva, while one who has already attained the Buddha-way is called a Buddha.
Within the Śrāvaka-dharma, the disciples of Mahākātyāyanīputra explain the meaning of the characteristics of a Bodhisattva in this way.
The followers of the Mahāyāna say:
"These disciples of Kātyāyanīputra are people of saṃsāra; they do not recite or read the Mahāyāna sūtras, and thus they are not great bodhisattvas!"

Not knowing the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), one might nonetheless, by virtue of one's own sharp faculties and wisdom, compose treatises within the Buddha-dharma, establishing meanings regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*), knowledge (*jñāna*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the faculties (*indriya*), and so forth; yet even in these, there are errors here and there—how much more so when attempting to compose a treatise on the Bodhisattva path?
For example, a person of little strength cannot even cross a small ditch by leaping over it, let alone a great river;
in such a great river, one knows they will sink and perish.
It is asked:
What is loss?
The answer is as stated above:
"One who has passed through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas is called a bodhisattva.
Throughout those three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he gives away his head, eyes, marrow, and brain without any regret in his heart; this is something that neither arhats nor pratyekabuddhas can equal.
Long ago, when the Bodhisattva was a great *satpuruṣa* (worthy man), he was crossing the great ocean when a violent wind wrecked the ship.
He said to the merchants:
"Seize my head, hair, hands, and feet; I shall carry you across."
Once the crowd had seized him, he took his own life with a knife.
By the nature of the great ocean, it does not retain corpses; immediately, a swift wind blew him to the shore.
If one who possesses such great compassion is said to be "not [a Bodhisattva]," then who indeed is a Bodhisattva?

When the practice during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa was completed and he had not yet entered the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he received the prediction of his future buddhahood from Dīpaṃkara Buddha. At that moment, he ascended into the void and beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in the sky, praising Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Dīpaṃkara Buddha said:
"After one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
Having received such a prediction, to say that at that time he was not yet a bodhisattva would surely be a great error!
The disciples of Kātyāyanīputra say:

"During the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there have been no marks of a Buddha, nor has there been any causal condition for planting the marks of a Buddha; how, then, can one know that this is a bodhisattva?"
"All dharmas first possess signs, and only then can their reality be known; if there were no signs, they could not be known.
The Mahāyāna practitioner says:
"Receiving the prediction of Buddhahood, ascending into the void, and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions—these are not great signs?"
