Having been prophesied by the Buddha that they shall become Buddhas, those who are to become Buddhas possess these great marks; yet you abandon these great marks to pursue the thirty-two marks!
“The thirty-two marks are possessed even by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin), and the various devas and Māras can also manifest these marks through transformation.
Nanda, Devadatta, and others all possess thirty marks;
the Brahmin Vāṣpa has three marks, and the wife of Mahākāśyapa possesses the mark of golden hue.”
Even among people of the present day, each possesses one or two marks, such as blue eyes, long arms, or an upper body like that of a lion;
since there are various such marks, some more and some fewer, why do you value these marks so highly?
"In which sūtra is it stated that during the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, a bodhisattva does not plant the causes and conditions for the marks?
For example, Nanda bathed the Buddha Vipaśyin and vowed to attain purity and handsome features;
furthermore, at the stūpa of a pratyekabuddha, he applied blue pigment to the wall, fashioned an image of the pratyekabuddha, and thereupon made a vow: [may I become pure and handsome]."
"May I always attain a golden-colored body.
He also constructed a tiered platform for the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
By virtue of these three causes and conditions of merit, he experienced happiness in life after life; wherever he was born, he was always handsome and dignified.

By the remainder of this merit, he was born among the Śākya clan in Kapilavastu as a disciple of the Buddha; he attained thirty of the marks of a Great Man, was pure and handsome, and upon leaving the household life, attained the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha declared that among his five hundred disciples, the bhikṣu Nanda was foremost in physical beauty.
Since these marks were easily obtained, why do you say, "They were planted during ninety-one great kalpas and realized in the remainder of one lifetime"?
"This is a great loss!
You say: 'During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one does not know whether one will become a Buddha or not.'"
During the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he knew that he would become a Buddha, yet he did not proclaim it himself;
during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, knowing that he had attained Buddhahood, he was able to proclaim it for others.
"Where did the Buddha speak these words?
In which sutra do these words appear?
Are they spoken within the Tripiṭaka of the Śrāvaka-dharma?"
"If it is taught within the Mahāyāna?
The disciples of Kātyāyanīputra replied:
"Although it is not spoken by the Buddha's own mouth within the Tripiṭaka, the underlying principle ought to be so!"
"It is stated thus in the 'Bodhisattva Chapter' of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*.
He replied: "In the Mahāyāna it is said:"
"At the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one knows: 'I shall become a Buddha.

For example, from the time the Bodhisattva Acāra first generated the mind in the presence of the Buddha Dīrghabāhu, until he attained the Way of the Buddha at the Vajrāsana, no inverted or impure thoughts arose during that interval.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, there are four kinds of bodhisattvas and four kinds of predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*):
there are those who receive a prediction before they have yet resolved their minds for awakening;
and there are those who receive a prediction at the very moment they resolve their minds for awakening.
There are those who have received a prior prediction of enlightenment that others all know, while they themselves do not know;
and there are those who have received a prior prediction of enlightenment that both others and themselves fully know.
Why do you say, "During two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he knew he had received the prediction of enlightenment but did not proclaim it himself"?
Furthermore, the Buddha said, "He cultivated merit for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, desiring to deliver sentient beings"; why then do you speak of "three asaṃkhyeya kalpas"?
The three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have a measure and a limit.
A question is asked:
"Although these words exist within the Mahāyāna, I am still unable to believe them entirely."
The answer is:
This is a great loss!
These are the true teachings of the Buddha, spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth; you show no gratitude or reciprocity!
You have been born from within the Mahāyāna; why do you say that you cannot believe it at all?
Furthermore, the discourse on the Mahāyāna should be explained here in detail.
Furthermore, regarding these karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks, they are planted within the Desire Realm, not within the Form or Formless Realms.

It may be granted that they cannot be planted in the Formless Realm, as it is devoid of body and form, and these thirty-two marks are the adornment of the body; however, why can they not be planted in the Form Realm?

Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are many Brahma kings who constantly invite the Buddha to first turn the wheel of Dharma; their wisdom is pure and they are able to seek the path of the Buddha. Why, then, do you say that they cannot plant the causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks?
Furthermore, it is said:
"One can plant [the seeds] in the human realm, not in other realms.

For instance, Sagara the Naga King is a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, Anavatapta the Naga King is a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage, and Rāhu the Asura King is likewise a great Bodhisattva. Why, then, do you say that "in other realms one cannot plant the causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks"?
Regarding your statement:
"The *Jambudvīpa* variety can be planted among humans,

but it cannot be planted in Uttarakuru," there is an interpretation that this is because the people there lack the sense of self (*ātman*), are attached to pleasure, and do not possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
In the two regions of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha, merit, wisdom, and lifespan are superior to those in Jambudvīpa; why, then, can [the marks] not be planted there?
Furthermore, you say:
"One thought plants one mark."

This mind undergoes sixty births and cessations in the space of a finger-snap; since it does not abide within a single moment of thought and lacks the capacity for discernment, how could it plant the marks of a Great Man?
This mark of a Great Man cannot be produced by the planting of a single thought; for this reason, it is through the convergence of many thoughts that one mark can be planted.
It is like a heavy object that one person cannot carry alone, which must necessarily rely on the strength of many people.
Regarding such marks of excellence, it is necessary to attain a great mind and bring together many thoughts before one can plant them.
For this reason, they are called the "marks of a hundred merits.
One plants these merits through a hundred great thoughts; thus they are named the marks of a hundred merits. It should not be understood that a single thought plants a single mark.
If one cannot even contemplate a single matter or cultivate a single deed for other matters, how much less so for the marks of the hundred merits!
Why, then, is it said that "the mind of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was not yet fully matured, while the minds of his disciples were;
the mind of the Bodhisattva Maitreya is fully matured, while the minds of his disciples are not"?
Where is this statement found?
It is not in the Tripiṭaka nor in the Mahāyāna; these words originate solely from your own mind.
You merely see that when the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was in a jeweled cave, he beheld Buddha Puṣya and praised him with a single verse for seven days and seven nights.
Maitreya Bodhisattva also praised Puṣya Buddha in various ways; however, this is not mentioned in the *Avadāna-sūtra*, which you do not know.

Because you lack the underlying causes and conditions for understanding this, you claim that "the disciples of Maitreya have minds that are not yet pure and mature. Such assertions are entirely erroneous!
You said:

"A bodhisattva is able to give away all things without any sense of attachment or regret; just as King Śibi, for the sake of a pigeon, cut off his own flesh to give to a hawk, yet his heart felt no remorse."
"Bestowing wealth and treasures as a gift is called the inferior gift;
bestowing one's own body as a gift is called the middling gift;
bestowing various things with a mind free from attachment is the superior gift."
Why do you praise the middle grade of giving as the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*?
Although this giving is great in mind and abounds in compassion, it may involve both wisdom and a lack of wisdom.
Just as a person does not spare their own body for the sake of parents or relatives, or does not spare their own body for the sake of a lord;
by this analogy, one knows that not sparing one's body for the sake of the pigeon constitutes giving within this context.
Question:

Because the bodhisattva acts for the sake of all sentient beings, as their parent, as their lord, and for the sake of all people—for these reasons, it is not merely that he does not begrudge his own body that constitutes the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*.
Answer:

Although one acts for the sake of all sentient beings, this mind is not pure; one does not know that one's own body is devoid of a self, nor does one know that the one who grasps is without a person and without a master.
Not knowing that the true nature of the object given cannot be described as being either identical or different, one becomes mentally attached to these three things;
this is called impurity. While one may obtain the retribution of merit within the world, one cannot proceed directly to the path of the Buddha.
As it is said regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*, that the three things are unobtainable and one does not cling to them—this constitutes the fulfillment and perfection of the *dānapāramitā*.
In this manner, up to the *prajñāpāramitā*: "To be able to distinguish the great earth, cities, and villages into seven parts—this is the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*."

"This Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless, like the waters of the great ocean; even the devas, noble ones, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice cannot know its limits—it is only a bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth bhūmi who can know them. How then can you say, 'To divide the great earth, cities, and villages into seven parts is called the fulfillment of Prajñāpāramitā'?"
This matter is a method of calculation; being able to analyze the stages is but a small fraction of the conventional *prajñāpāramitā*, like one or two drops of water in the great ocean.
True Prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it can reveal the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This Prajñāpāramitā has no place from which it comes and no place to which it goes; it cannot be found when sought in any location.
It is like a magical illusion, like an echo, like the moon reflected in water—once seen, it vanishes.

Out of compassion, the various sages, though [the truth] is of a single characteristic, have expounded this Prajñāpāramitā—the precious treasury of the wisdom of all Buddhas—by means of various names; your statement is a great error!
You have spoken of four kinds of observations:
"observing the time, observing the land, observing the lineage, and observing the place of birth.

A Buddha appears in the world when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years; Buddhas appear in the world during lifespans of seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, or twenty thousand years; and it is when the human lifespan is one hundred years that a Buddha appears in the world."
"If the Buddhas always have compassion for sentient beings, why do they appear in the world only during these eight specific times and not at other times?
The Buddha-dharma does not depend on time; just as a good medicine cures an illness as soon as it is taken, so too the Buddha-dharma does not depend on time."
Question:

Although Bodhisattvas have compassion for sentient beings and the Buddhas do not wait for a specific time, when the human lifespan exceeds eighty thousand years, people possess long lives and much pleasure; their fetters such as defilement and craving are thick, and their faculties are dull, making it a time when they cannot be transformed.
If it were after a hundred years, when human lifespans are short and suffering is abundant, and the various fetters such as anger and the like have become even thicker—
this being a time of pleasure or a time of suffering rather than a time for attaining the Way— for these reasons, the Buddha does not appear in the world.
The answer is:

The lifespans of the various devas extend for many millions of years; because they possess the causal conditions from previous lives, even though their pleasures are manifold and their defiled attachment is thick, they are able to attain the Way—how much more so, then, for those among humans who do not experience such great pleasure!
The thirty-six kinds of impurity are easy to transform through teaching; for this reason, when the human lifespan exceeds eighty thousand years, a Buddha should appear in the world.
In that time, because people are free from illness and their minds are joyful, all people possess sharp faculties and merit.
Because they possess merit and sharp faculties, they should easily attain the Way.
Furthermore, during the time of the Buddha Siṃhadundubhisvararāja, the human lifespan was one hundred thousand years;
during the time of the Buddha Vidyārāja, the human lifespan was seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
and during the time of Amitābha Buddha, the human lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"Why do you say, 'When more than eighty thousand years have passed, no Buddha shall appear in the world'?
He asked:

"In the Mahāyāna sūtras there is such a thing, but in my teaching there are no Buddhas of the ten directions; there are only one hundred Buddhas of the past, such as Śākyamuni and Krakucchanda, and five hundred Buddhas of the future, such as Maitreya."
Answer: Within the Mahāyāna treatises, various causes and conditions are set forth to speak of the Buddhas of the three periods and the ten directions. Why is this so?

In the worlds of the ten directions, there are various sufferings and afflictions such as old age, sickness, death, lust, anger, and ignorance; for this reason, the Buddha should appear in those lands.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If there were no old age, sickness, death, or afflictions, the Buddhas would not appear in the world.
Furthermore, where there are many sick people, there should be many physicians.
In the *Dīrgha Āgama* among the teachings for you disciples, King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Buddha in verse:
"I prostrate to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; I likewise take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha."
Your sutra states: "To all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, I prostrate; to Śākyamuni Buddha, I take refuge. By this, it is known that there are other Buddhas in the present.
If there were no other Buddhas in other lands, why would he first prostrate to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and subsequently offer a separate refuge to Śākyamuni Buddha?

This king has not yet abandoned desire; because he attained the Way under Śākyamuni Buddha, his heart of reverence and affection is profound, and thus he offers refuge to him, whereas toward other Buddhas he merely prostrates.
Question:

The Buddha himself stated, "In one world-system, two Buddhas do not appear at the same time, nor can two wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) appear at the same time. For this reason, there should not be other Buddhas existing in the present.
The answer is:
Although these words have been spoken, you do not understand their meaning.
When the Buddha said that two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously within a single trichiliocosm, he did not mean that there are no present Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions.
Just as within the world-system of the four continents, two wheel-turning sage-kings never appear at the same time, for such a person of great merit has no enemies with whom to coexist in the world.
For this reason, there is but one Wheel-Turning Sage King in the four continents;
likewise, within a trichiliocosm, no two Buddhas appear simultaneously.

The sūtras state that the Buddha and the wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) are of one kind; why then do you believe that there are other wheel-turning sage kings in the other four continents, yet do not believe that there are other Buddhas in the other trichiliocosms?

Furthermore, a single Buddha cannot deliver all sentient beings; for if a single Buddha were able to deliver all sentient beings, there would be no need for other Buddhas, and only one Buddha would ever appear.

As with the Buddhas of all times, they pass into extinction after having delivered those beings who were ready for deliverance, just as a fire is extinguished when a candle is consumed; this is because conditioned phenomena are impermanent and empty by nature.
For this reason, there must currently be other Buddhas remaining.

Furthermore, sentient beings are immeasurable, and their suffering is likewise immeasurable; therefore, there must arise Bodhisattvas of great resolve, and there must also appear immeasurable Buddhas in the world to deliver all sentient beings.
Question: As it is said in the sūtras:
"In immeasurable ages, a Buddha appears from time to time, just as the flower of the udumbara tree appears only once in a great while."
If the Buddhas of the ten directions were as numerous as they are pervasive, then Buddhas would be easy to encounter and easy to find, and it could not be said that they are difficult to meet!
The answer is: It is not so!

This is said with reference to a single great trichiliocosm, wherein a Buddha appears from time to time over immeasurable eons; it does not mean that such a thing is difficult throughout all the worlds of the ten directions.
Furthermore, because sentient beings do not know how to show reverence and do not diligently apply themselves to seeking the Way, for this reason it is said:
"A Buddha appears from time to time only once in immeasurable eons."

Furthermore, because these sentient beings have reaped the karmic retribution of their many sins, they fall into the evil realms; for immeasurable kalpas they do not even hear the name of a Buddha, let alone see one.
It is because of such people that it is said that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult.
Question:
If there are currently many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, why do they not come to deliver all sentient beings from their sins, evils, and sufferings?
The answer is:

Sentient beings have accumulated the stains of sin over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; although they possess various other merits, they lack the merit required to see the Buddha, and therefore do not see him.
As a verse says:
"While the reward for good merit is not yet near, and the sins of decline have not been eliminated,
one cannot perceive in the present those of great virtue and power."
The great virtuous sages, whose minds are free from discrimination,
Compassionately regard all people, wishing to deliver them all at once.
When the merit and virtue of sentient beings have ripened, And their faculties of wisdom are likewise sharp,
If one encounters the conditions for deliverance, one attains liberation immediately.
Just as a great dragon king sends down various rains according to his vow,
so too do sin and merit follow one’s original actions, each received exactly as it was sown.
Question: If one possesses merit and wisdom oneself, such a person the Buddha can deliver;
if one lacks merit and wisdom, the Buddha does not deliver them.
If that were so, one would possess merit and wisdom inherently and would not depend on the Buddha for deliverance!
The answer is:
this merit and wisdom arise from the causes and conditions of the Buddha.

If a Buddha does not appear in the world, the various bodhisattvas teach the path through the causes and conditions of the ten wholesome actions, the four immeasurable minds, and the various causes and conditions regarding the retributions of sin and merit in future lives.
If there were no Bodhisattvas, there would be various sūtras stating that when people obtain this Dharma, they practice the causes and conditions for merit.
Furthermore, although people may possess merit and wisdom, if a Buddha does not appear in the world, they will receive retribution within this world and be unable to attain the Way;
only if a Buddha appears in the world can they attain the Way—this constitutes a great benefit.

For example, although a person possesses eyes, they cannot see anything when the sun has not yet risen; it must wait for the light of the sun before they can see. One cannot say, "I have eyes, so what use is the sun?"
As the Buddha said:
"Two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view:
first, hearing the Dharma from others; second, internally reflecting upon it in accordance with the Dharma."
Because of their meritorious deeds, they are able to give rise to wholesome thoughts;
because of their sharp faculties and wisdom, they are able to contemplate in accordance with the Dharma.
For this reason, it is known that they attain deliverance through the Buddha.
There are many such various errors and contradictions!
Because I wish to compose a treatise on the Prajñāpāramitā, I cannot further discuss other matters at length.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Volume Four.
Commentary on the Ninth Chapter, "Mahāsattva," within the First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra. Volume Five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. 9. Commentary on the Mahāsattva [Sūtra]. [Sūtra]: The Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Question:
What is meant by "mahāsattva"? Answer:
"Mahā" means great;
"sattva" refers to a sentient being, or it is called "valiant mind.
Because this person's mind is capable of performing great deeds, never retreating or turning back, and possesses a great valiant mind, they are called a Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, a Mahāsattva is so called because he is the foremost among many sentient beings; thus, he is named a Mahāsattva.

Furthermore, because he gives rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion among many sentient beings, establishes the Great Vehicle, is able to practice the Great Path, and attains the state of supreme greatness, he is named a Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, because he has perfected the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), he is called a Mahāsattva.
As for the characteristics of a Mahāsattva, they are described in the *Buddhastotra-gāthā*:
"Only the Buddha alone is supreme; The father and mother of the three realms, the All-Knowing One."
Peerless among all equals, I bow my head to the World-Honored One, whose likeness is rare!
Ordinary people practice benevolence for their own benefit, seeking recompense by bestowing wealth and gifts;
but the Buddha’s great compassion and kindness are free from such concerns, benefiting enemies and kin, the hateful and the loved, with equal impartiality!

Furthermore, because he is certainly able to preach the Dharma to destroy all the great false views, great craving and pride, and the great egoism of all sentient beings as well as his own self—namely, these various afflictions—he is called a Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, sentient beings are like the great ocean, having no beginning, no middle, and no end;
even if a wise mathematician were to calculate for immeasurable eons, they could never reach the limit.
As the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:

"Suppose all the worlds in the ten directions, even unto the limits of space, were merged into a single body of water. If countless and immeasurable sentient beings were to join together, each holding a single hair, to take one drop and depart; and if further, incalculable numbers of sentient beings were to do as before, joining together to hold a single hair and take one drop and depart—until that great body of water was entirely exhausted without remainder, yet the sentient beings would still not be exhausted."

Because these sentient beings are thus infinite, immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable, he is able to rescue and deliver them all, causing them to leave behind suffering and affliction and to abide in the bliss of unconditioned tranquility.
Because they possess this great mind and desire to deliver many sentient beings, they are called *mahāsattvas*.
As stated in the *Acintya-sūtra*, the laywoman Uṣāṇā said to the bodhisattva Sudhana:

"The various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of delivering a single person; nor for the sake of two, three, or even ten people; nor for a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million; nor for ten million, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred billion, or even a trillion."
It is not for the sake of *ayuta* billions of sentient beings that they resolve their minds;
nor for *nayuta* billions, nor for *ayuta* sentient beings;
nor for *bimbara*, nor *gagaṇa*, nor *agala*, nor *pavara*, nor *mavara*, nor *pada*, nor *tapasa*. It is not...
Not Vibhāha, not Abhaya, not Smara, not Apaga, not Maghava, not Viraja, not Saṃghama, not Viśāla,
not Yamapa, not Vija, not Viluha, not Vibhāti, not Vigra.
It is not *tā*, nor *tūlā*, nor *aparaṇa*,
nor *thavara*, nor *vibhaya-bha*, nor *makkhā*, nor *duṇayakkhā*,
nor *ḍhava-ra*, nor *vibhara*, nor *pucchata*, nor *abhagada*, nor *vissatha*.
Neither Nepāla, nor Arbuda, nor Pāṇḍava, nor Bhadrāśva,
nor Aṭaṭa, nor Hahava, nor Huhuva, nor Utpala, nor Aṭata,
nor Ahirbudhnya, nor Mālutā, nor Kṣaya, nor Ulkā.
Many, not Maśu-yama, not Samatha, not Vimatha,
not Pramatha, not Āpamdhara, not Vāmandhara, not Mathara,
not Khandumathara, not Vemathara, not Paramathara, nor...
Śivadara, na Piṇḍila, na Vetala, na Tīra, na Cīra, na Kīra, na Nīla, na Sīra, na Pāra,
na Mīra, na Varavara, na Meru, na Khīru, na Matūra.
Not *sumula*, not *apaya*, not *kṣamara*, not *mamara*,
not *āttada*, not *kṣila*, not *vīlava*, not *karava*,
not *ahababa*, not *vīvaba*, not *babba*, not *āravba*, not *sala*.
Not Brahman, not Meru, not Māra, not Tamra, not Pāṇḍara,
not Nikama, not Avarta, not Nidhiśa, not Accha, not Trisrotas, not Vāmana, not Āpata, nor...
It is not an *udumbara*, nor a *padma*, nor a *saṃkha*, nor a *gati*, nor an *udagamana*, nor an *asaṃkhyeya*,
nor an *asaṃkhyeyāsaṃkhyeya*, nor immeasurable (*aprameya*), nor immeasurably immeasurable (*aprameyāprameya*),
nor boundless (*ananta*), nor boundlessly boundless (*anantānanta*), nor incomparable (*asama*).
It is not non-equal and not equal; it is not incalculable, nor is it incalculable-incalculable; it is not uncountable, nor is it uncountable-uncountable;
it is not inconceivable, nor is it inconceivable-inconceivable; it is not unspeakable, nor is it unspeakable-unspeakable.

They do not resolve their minds for the sake of sentient beings equal in number to the atoms of a single land; nor do they resolve their minds for the sake of sentient beings equal in number to the atoms of two, three, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten million, a billion, or even an *ayuta*, a *nayuta*, or even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of lands.

They do not resolve their minds for the sake of sentient beings equal in number to the atoms of a single Jambudvīpa; nor do they resolve their minds for the sake of sentient beings equal in number to the atoms of Godānīya, Uttarakuru, or Pūrvavideha.
They do not resolve their minds for the sake of sentient beings equal in number to the atoms of a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, or a great trichiliocosm.

It is not for the sake of two, three, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, a hundred million, a billion, ten billion, a hundred billion, or even an unspeakably unspeakable number of sentient beings, equal to the dust motes of a trichiliocosm, that they resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].

"He does not resolve his mind for the sake of making offerings and providing for a single Buddha, nor even for the sake of making offerings and providing for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas;

he does not resolve his mind for the sake of making offerings and providing for as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a single land, nor even for the sake of making offerings and providing for as many Buddhas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms."

"They do not resolve their minds for the sake of purifying a single buddha-field, nor even for the sake of purifying as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably, unspeakably many trichiliocosms."

"One does not resolve to attain enlightenment for the sake of upholding even a single Buddha-dharma, nor even for the sake of upholding as many Buddha-dharmas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms."

"It is not for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of Buddhas is not interrupted in a single trichiliocosm that they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], nor even for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of Buddhas is not interrupted in as many trichiliocosms as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms."

"They do not resolve their minds for the sake of analytically knowing the vows of a single Buddha, nor do they resolve their minds for the sake of analytically knowing the vows of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems."

"They do not resolve their minds for the sake of adorning a single Buddha-field, nor even for the sake of adorning as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms."

"They do not resolve their minds for the sake of discerning knowledge of the assembly of disciples of a single Buddha, nor even for the sake of discerning knowledge of the assemblies of disciples of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosm worlds."

"They do not resolve their minds for the sake of upholding the Dharma-wheel of a single Buddha, nor even for the sake of upholding the Dharma-wheels of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosm worlds."

"It is not for the sake of knowing the various minds of a single person that they resolve their mind; it is not for the sake of knowing the various faculties of a single person; it is not for the sake of knowing the sequential succession of kalpas within a single trichiliocosm; nor is it for the sake of discerning and severing the afflictions of a single person that they resolve their mind, up to and including not for the sake of discerning and severing the afflictions of as many people as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosms."
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas made this vow: "We shall bring all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to full maturity;

we shall fully provide offerings and support to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions; we vow to purify all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions; we shall firmly uphold all the teachings of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions because we distinguish and know all Buddha-lands; because we fully know the assemblies of all the Buddhas' disciples; because we distinguish and know the various minds of all sentient beings; because we know how to sever all the afflictions of all sentient beings; and because we fully know the various faculties of all sentient beings—it is for these reasons that the bodhisattvas resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
With these ten gates as the foremost, up to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya gates—these are the Dharma-gates of the Path that Bodhisattvas should know and enter!
In brief, such is the true path of these bodhisattvas:
they enter into and know all dharmas because they know them through wisdom, and because they adorn all buddha-fields within the bodhisattva path.
Uśanas said: "Good son!
My vow is as follows:
"Since the beginning of this world, all sentient beings have been entirely pure, and all afflictions have been completely severed.
Sudhana asked, "What kind of liberation is this?"
Uśanas replied, "This is called the Banner of Sorrowless Tranquility.

I know this single gate of liberation, but I do not know the great minds of the bodhisattvas, which are like the waters of the great ocean, capable of upholding and receiving all the teachings of the Buddhas."
The minds of all Bodhisattvas are unshakable, like Mount Sumeru;
all Bodhisattvas are like the King of Medicines, able to eliminate all afflictions;
all Bodhisattvas are like the sun, able to illuminate and dispel all darkness.
All Bodhisattvas are like the earth, for they can sustain all sentient beings;
all Bodhisattvas are like the wind, for they can benefit all sentient beings;
all Bodhisattvas are like fire, for they can burn away all the afflictions of the various non-Buddhists.
All bodhisattvas are like clouds, able to rain down the water of the Dharma;
all bodhisattvas are like the moon, their light of merit and virtue able to illuminate all;
all bodhisattvas are like Śakra-devānām-indra, protecting all sentient beings.
"This path of the Bodhisattvas is profoundly deep; how could I possibly know it all!
Because these Bodhisattvas give rise to great vows, desiring to accomplish great deeds and desiring to reach the Great State, they are called "Mahāsattvas."
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of a mahāsattva within this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha himself has declared:
"Such and such characteristics are the characteristics of a mahāsattva."
Śāriputra, Subhūti, Pūrṇa, and the other great disciples each spoke on their respective chapters; these should be explained in detail herein. Chapter Ten:

Explanation of the Bodhisattva’s Merits within the First Chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. [Sūtra] They have all attained dhāraṇīs and various samādhis; they practice emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); they have already attained equal patience (*samartha-kṣānti*).
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason are the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas praised by means of these three matters in this specific sequence? Answer:
In order to bring forth the true merits of all bodhisattvas, one should praise what is praiseworthy and believe what is worthy of belief;
thus, one praises the bodhisattvas by means of the profound and pure Dharma that cannot be believed by any ordinary sentient beings.

Furthermore, although the name "Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" has been mentioned previously, the reason why one is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has not yet been explained. It is because of the attainment of various meritorious qualities—such as the *dhāraṇīs*, *samādhis*, and the *kṣāntis*—that one is named a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Question: The meaning of the sequence has already been understood; for what reason is it called "dhāraṇī"? What is a dhāraṇī?
The answer is:
"Dhāraṇī" means "able to hold" in the language of Qin, or it means "able to obstruct.
As for "able to hold," it refers to gathering various kinds of wholesome dharmas and being able to maintain them so that they are neither dispersed nor lost.
It is like a complete vessel filled with water; the water does not leak or scatter.
As for "being able to obstruct": when unwholesome roots of evil arise in the mind, one can obstruct them so that they do not arise;
if one wishes to commit an evil transgression, one maintains restraint so as not to do it.
This is called a dhāraṇī.
This dhāraṇī may be associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind;
it may be with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
The formless (ārūpya) is invisible and non-obstructive;
it is subsumed under one base (dhātu), one entrance (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha):
the dharma-base (dharmadhātu), the dharma-entrance (dharmāyatana), and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
"Known by nine knowledges" (the *Dan* commentary notes:
excluding the knowledge of exhaustion);
"cognized by one consciousness" (the *Dan* commentary notes:).
First is the single consciousness.
Such is the meaning of the *dhāraṇī* of the Abhidharma-dharma.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* is able to maintain all the teachings they have heard without loss, by virtue of the power of mindfulness.
Furthermore, this dhāraṇī-dharma constantly follows the bodhisattva, like a tertian malaria;
this dhāraṇī does not leave the bodhisattva, like a spirit possessing a person;
this dhāraṇī always accompanies the bodhisattva, like the observance of wholesome and unwholesome precepts.
Furthermore, this dhāraṇī sustains the bodhisattva and prevents them from falling into the pit of the two stages;
it is like a compassionate father who loves his son: when the son is about to fall into a pit, he holds him and prevents the fall.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva has attained the power of dhāraṇī, no māra kings, māra subjects, or māra followers can shake him, destroy him, or overcome him;
it is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be moved by the mere blowing of the breath from ordinary people.
Question:
How many kinds of this dhāraṇī are there? Answer:
This dhāraṇī is of many kinds.
One is called the *śrutadhara-dhāraṇī*.
One who attains this dhāraṇī does not forget or lose any speech or phenomena heard by the ear; this is called the *śrutadhara-dhāraṇī*.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of discerning knowledge; one who attains this dhāraṇī can discern and fully know all sentient beings and all phenomena, whether great or small, beautiful or ugly.
As a verse says:
"Elephants, horses, and gold; wood, stone, and various garments; men, women, and water—these are all diverse and not the same."
"The names of all things are one, yet the principles of their worth—whether noble or base—are distinct; having attained this dhāraṇī, one is able to discern them all.
Furthermore, there is the Sound-Entry Dhāraṇī; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī hears all spoken sounds and voices without feeling joy or anger.
Even if all sentient beings were to revile and abuse him with harsh words for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, his mind would feel no hatred.
A question is asked:
Since a bodhisattva has not yet exhausted all outflows (āsrava), how can he endure such evils for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges?
The answer is:
I previously stated that it is by virtue of attaining the power of this dhāraṇī that one is able to do so.
Furthermore, although this bodhisattva has not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), he possesses great wisdom and sharp faculties, enabling him to contemplate and eliminate thoughts of anger.
He reflects thus:
"If the faculty of hearing does not reach the edge of the sound, to whom would the harsh sound attach?"
Furthermore, it is like the sound of abuse: upon hearing it, it simply passes by. If one does not engage in discrimination, who would become angry?
Ordinary people are attached to a self; they discriminate between right and wrong and thereby give rise to resentment and hatred.
Furthermore, if a person can understand that all words arise and perish as they occur, such that the preceding and succeeding do not coexist, then they will have no anger.
They will also know that among all phenomena there is no internal master; who then would revile, and who would be angry?

If someone hears words from distant lands and strange tongues, what is considered good here may be considered evil there; since such likes and dislikes have no fixed standard, one should not feel anger even when reviled.
If one understands that the sounds of speech have no fixed nature, then there will be neither anger nor joy.
If a loved one reviles one, one feels no resentment despite the abuse;
yet upon hearing harsh words from a stranger, anger arises.
It is like encountering wind and rain: one enters a house or takes up an umbrella.
Just as one puts on boots when there are thorns in the ground,
or kindles a fire in great cold and seeks water in the heat; so too,
regarding these various afflictions, one merely seeks the means to avert them without feeling anger toward them.
Abusive speech and all other evils are likewise treated in this way; one merely uses compassion to quell these evils, without giving rise to a mind of anger.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, for their nature is entirely empty.
If someone should become angry and revile them, or strike or kill them, these are like a dream or a magical illusion; who is there to be angry, and who is there to revile?

Furthermore, if someone were to praise and make offerings to a Bodhisattva who has attained patience—providing clothing, food, bedding, medicine, flowers, incense, and necklaces—for as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River over the course of eons, the mind of that Bodhisattva would remain unmoved, neither rejoicing nor becoming attached.
Question:
We already understand the various causes and conditions for why a bodhisattva does not become angry; however, we do not yet know why they do not feel joy even when their actual merits are praised.
Answer:
One knows that various forms of offerings and reverence are all impermanent;
for now, due to certain causes and conditions, they come to offer praise and worship, but later,
when other causes and conditions arise, they may become angry, perhaps striking or even killing one— therefore, one does not take pleasure in them.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"It is because I possess merit and wisdom that they come to praise and make offerings to me;
this is praise for my merit, not praise for me as a person. Why, then, should I feel joy?"
Furthermore, because this person seeks their own karmic reward, they perform causes and conditions for my sake and make offerings to me as a meritorious act;
it is like a person who sows grain, irrigates, and tends to it, yet the earth feels no joy.
Furthermore, if someone makes offerings to me and I were to receive them with joy, my own merit would become diminished, and others would also obtain little merit; for this reason, I do not rejoice.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being like dreams and echoes; who is there to praise, and who is there to rejoice?
Since I have not yet attained liberation within the three realms, my outflows are not yet exhausted, and I have not yet realized the Buddha-way, how could I rejoice upon receiving praise?
If one is to be praised with joy, it is the Buddha alone.
Why? Because all his merits are already fully perfected.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva receives various forms of praise, offerings, and provisions, no joy arises in their mind.
Such characteristics as these are called "entry into the dharani of sounds."

Furthermore, there are the dhāraṇīs named: the Dhāraṇī of Tranquil Extinction, the Dhāraṇī of Boundless Revolutions, the Dhāraṇī of Contemplating According to the Grounds, the Dhāraṇī of Majestic Virtue, the Dhāraṇī of Flower Adornment, the Dhāraṇī of Pure Sound, the Dhāraṇī of the Treasury of Space, the Dhāraṇī of the Treasury of the Ocean, the Dhāraṇī of Discerning the Grounds of All Dharmas, and the Dhāraṇī of Illuminating the Meaning of All Dharmas.
These and others constitute a brief explanation of five hundred dharanī gates; if explained extensively, they are immeasurable.
For this reason, it is said that all bodhisattvas have attained dharanis.
Regarding "all samādhis," there are three samādhis:
emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*). Some say:
"To contemplate the five aggregates as being without self and without what belongs to a self is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To abide in this samādhi of emptiness and not give rise to the three poisons for the sake of future lives is called non-action (*apranihita*).
This is because one relies upon the departure from the ten marks (*daśanimitta*):"
"Because of the five sense objects, male, female, arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is called signlessness (animitta).

Some say: "Abiding within this samādhi, one knows the true mark (lakṣaṇa) of all dharmas, which is so-called ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā); this is called the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi)."
"Having known this emptiness, there is non-action.
What is meant by non-action?
It is not to contemplate whether phenomena are empty or not empty, existent or non-existent, and so forth."
As the Buddha said in a verse from the *Dharmapada*:
"To see existence is to be terrified; To see non-existence is likewise to be terrified.
Therefore, do not cling to existence, Nor should you cling to non-existence."
This is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
What is the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)?
All phenomena are without signs; all phenomena are neither accepted nor clung to. This is called the wishless samādhi.
As a verse says:
"Speech has ceased, mental formations have also been extinguished; neither arising nor ceasing, it is like the mark of nirvāṇa."
"Furthermore, the eighteen kinds of emptiness are called the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*);
various commentaries state:

not seeking [existence] within the five modes of existence—namely, birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava*), death-existence (*maraṇa-bhava*), intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), and karmic existence (*karma-bhava*)—is called the samādhi of non-action (*apranihita-samādhi*)."
To destroy all marks and not give rise to recollection is called the samādhi of signlessness (animitta-samādhi). Question:
There are various methods of dhyāna-concentration; for what reason are only these three samādhis specifically designated?
Answer:
Within these three samādhis, because one contemplates that which is proximate to nirvāṇa, it causes the mind to be neither high nor low, but equal and unmoving; this is not the case in other states.
For this reason, these three samādhis alone are so designated.
Among other meditative concentrations, some are characterized by excessive craving, some by excessive pride, and some by excessive views;
yet within these three samādhis lies the foremost true meaning and true benefit, which can provide access to the gate of nirvāṇa.

For this reason, among all the dharmas of dhyāna-concentration, these three methods of emptiness constitute the three gates of liberation and are also called the three samādhis; because these three samādhis are the true samādhis, other concentrations may also be designated as "concentrations."

Furthermore, excluding the four fundamental dhyānas, from the stage of *anāgamya* up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), these are called concentration (*samādhi*) and also called samādhi, but they are not dhyāna;
the four dhyānas are called concentration, are called dhyāna, and are also called samādhi;
all other concentrations are likewise called concentration and are also called samādhi.

Such as the various meditative dharmas, namely: the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four analytical knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
Furthermore, some say:
"There are twenty-three kinds of all samādhi dharmas. Others say:
"Sixty-five kinds. Some say:
"Five hundred kinds."

Because the Mahāyāna is the greatest, there are immeasurable samādhis, namely: the samādhi of the universal adornment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); the samādhi that can illuminate all phenomena of the three periods of time; the samādhi of non-discriminative knowledge that observes the depths of the nature of phenomena; the samādhi of entering the bottomless Buddha-dharma; the samādhi of illumination like space, bottomless and boundless; the samādhi of observing the power of the Tathāgata’s practice; the samādhi of the lion’s roar of the power of the fearless adornment of the Buddha; the samādhi of the revolving treasury of the gate of the nature of phenomena; the samādhi of the moon pervading all worlds with unimpeded adornment; and the samādhi of the light of the Dharma-cloud of universal adornment. It is through such immeasurable samādhis as these that Bodhisattvas attain realization.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna" within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there are briefly one hundred and eight samādhis:
the first is named Śūraṅgama-samādhi, up to the Ākāśāsaṅgānupalipta-samādhi;
if explained extensively, there are immeasurable samādhis.
For this reason, it is said that all bodhisattvas attain the various samādhis.
Regarding the phrase "practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness," a question is asked:
Question: Since it has already been stated that Bodhisattvas attain various samādhis, for what reason is it further said that they "practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness"? Answer:

Previously, the names of the samādhis were mentioned, but their characteristics were not explained. Now, wishing to explain those characteristics, it is therefore said that they "practice emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness."
If there is someone who practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, this is called attaining the samādhi of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
As a verse says:
"If one maintains pure precepts, This is called a true bhikṣu."
If one is able to contemplate emptiness, this is called attaining samādhi.
If one is able to practice with diligence, this is called a person on the path.
If one attains nirvāṇa, this is called true bliss.
Regarding the phrase "having already attained equal patience" (samaropa-kṣānti):
it is asked,
what is meant by "equal" (sama)?
What is "patience" (kṣānti)?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of equality.
Sentient beings are equal, and dharmas are equal.
Patience is also of two kinds:
patience toward sentient beings and patience toward dharmas.
What is equality toward sentient beings?
Among all sentient beings, to have an equal mind, equal mindfulness, equal affection, and equal benefit—this is called equality toward sentient beings.
Question:
By the power of loving-kindness and compassion, one should maintain equal mindfulness toward all sentient beings, but one should not maintain equal contemplation. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva practices the true path, which is non-perverted and in accordance with the characteristics of dharmas;
how then can he regard virtuous people and unvirtuous people, great men and small men, humans and animals as equal?

Among those who are unwholesome, there truly exists the characteristic of being unwholesome; among those who are wholesome, there truly exists the characteristic of being wholesome. This is likewise true for great persons and small persons, as well as for humans and animals.
Just as the characteristic of a cow resides within a cow, and the characteristic of a horse resides within a horse;
the characteristic of a cow does not reside within a horse, nor does the characteristic of a horse reside within a cow, because a horse does not become a cow.
Question: Since sentient beings each have their own distinct characteristics, how can one contemplate them as being equal without falling into error?
Answer: If good characteristics and unwholesome characteristics were real, then the Bodhisattva would fall into error.
Why is this? Because it destroys the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*).

For all phenomena lack the characteristic of being truly wholesome, lack the characteristic of being truly unwholesome, lack many characteristics, and lack few characteristics; they are neither human nor animal, and neither one nor different.
For this reason, your objection is incorrect.
As it is said in the verse on the characteristics of all phenomena:
“Neither arising nor ceasing, Neither discontinuous nor permanent, Neither identical nor different,”
Neither going nor coming, the dharma arisen through causes and conditions, which extinguishes all conceptual proliferation—the Buddha is able to teach this; to him I now pay homage.
Furthermore, among all sentient beings, one does not cling to various marks; the mark of a sentient being and the mark of emptiness are equal and without distinction.
To contemplate in this way is called the equality of sentient beings.
If a person is equanimous and free from obstruction in their mind, entering directly into the stage of non-retrogression, this is called attaining "equal patience" (samaropa-kṣānti).
A Bodhisattva who has attained equal patience feels neither anger nor malice toward any sentient being, just as a compassionate mother loves her child.
As a verse says:
"View sounds as like echoes, and bodily actions as like reflections;
when one perceives people in this way, how could one not practice forbearance?"
This is called the patience regarding the equality of sentient beings.
What is called the patience regarding the equality of dharmas?

Whether they be wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—such dharmas as these enter the gateway of non-duality and enter the gateway of the true nature of dharmas; having thus entered, they are fully realized.

In this context, when one deeply penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the mind enters directly with forbearance, free from contention and without obstruction; this is called "forbearance regarding the equality of phenomena" (*dharma-samatā-kṣānti*).
As a verse says:
"All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, Neither non-born nor non-extinguished."
"Neither arising and ceasing, nor not arising and ceasing; neither not arising and ceasing, nor not not arising and ceasing.
[The commentary by Dan states: "Having already attained liberation..."

Because one has attained detachment from false views, it is called "liberation. Regarding "emptiness" and "non-emptiness," the marginal note says: because one does not grasp at emptiness, it is called "non-[emptiness].

When all such [extremes] are entirely relinquished, all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is extinguished; the path of speech is cut off, and one enters deeply into the Buddha-dharma. With a mind that is unimpeded, immovable, and non-retrogressive, this is named "the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); it is the initial gateway for assisting the path to Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is said: "He has already attained equal patience.
[Sūtra]: He attains the unimpeded dhāraṇī.
[Śāstra]: Question:
Question: Previously it was already stated that bodhisattvas attain dhāraṇīs; why is it now stated again that they "attain the unimpeded dhāraṇī"?
Answer: Because the unimpeded dhāraṇī is the greatest.
Just as among all samādhis, the King of Samādhis is the greatest, like a king among men;
and just as among all liberations, the Unobstructed Liberation is the greatest—[the commentary notes:
this is that which is attained at the time of attaining Buddhahood and the Way].
Among all these dhāraṇīs, the Unobstructed Dhāraṇī is the greatest; for this reason, it is explained again.
Furthermore, although it was previously stated that the bodhisattvas have attained dhāraṇīs, it was not known what kind of dhāraṇīs they were.
There are minor dhāraṇīs, such as those obtained by universal monarchs, sages, and others;
the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, the dhāraṇī of discerning sentient beings, and the dhāraṇī of taking refuge in protection without abandonment.
Other people also possess such minor dhāraṇīs as these.
This unimpeded dhāraṇī is not attained by non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas who have newly begun their training;
it belongs exclusively to those bodhisattvas of immeasurable merit, wisdom, and great power. For this reason, it is explained separately.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas, having fully perfected their own benefit, desire only to benefit others; they preach the Dharma and transform beings inexhaustibly, taking the unimpeded dhāraṇī as their foundation.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas constantly practice the unimpeded dhāraṇī.
[Sūtra] These are entirely the five supernormal powers.

[Śāstra] They are: the power of mastery over will (*ṛddhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the recollection of one's own past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
What is the supernormal power of mastery (ṛddhi)? There are three kinds of mastery:
that of arrival, that of transformation, and noble mastery.
There are four kinds of reaching [a destination]:
first, the body can fly through the air without obstruction, like a bird;
second, one brings the distant near, arriving there without having traveled.
Third, vanishing from here and appearing there;
fourth, being able to reach [any destination] in a single thought-moment.
As for transformation: the large can be made small, the small can be made large, the one can be made many, and the many can be made one; all various things can be transformed.
The transformations of the non-Buddhists last at most seven days;
the transformations of the Buddhas and their disciples are sovereign and have no limit of duration.
As for the "noble power of mastery" (ṛddhi-vaśitā), one is able to contemplate undesirable and impure things among the six external sense objects and cause them to become pure.
That which is capable of contemplating even lovely and pure things as impure is the noble *ṛddhi-dharma*, possessed by the Buddha alone.
This supernormal power of mastery (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) arises from the cultivation of the four bases of power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
These, such as the supernormal power of the bases of psychic mastery (*ṛddhipāda-abhijñā*), arise sequentially because they take form as their object; they cannot be attained simultaneously.

As for the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), it consists of obtaining a purified form (*rūpa*) derived from the four great elements of the form realm within the eye; this is called the divine eye.

That which is seen by the divine eye includes all sentient beings and objects within the six realms of existence of its own level and lower levels; whether near or far, concealed or subtle, there is no form that it cannot illuminate.
There are two kinds of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*):
first, that obtained through karmic retribution (*vipākaja*); second, that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanāja*).
Among these five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), the divine eye is obtained through cultivation, not through retribution.
Why is this? Because one attains it by constantly recollecting various kinds of light.
Furthermore, some people say:

"Because these bodhisattvas have attained the power of the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they are not subsumed within the six realms of existence; yet, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they manifest through their dharma-body throughout the ten directions and the triple world.
As for bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the dharma-body, they may attain it either through cultivation or as a result of karmic retribution."

Question: Since the merits of these bodhisattvas surpass those of arhats and pratyekabuddhas, why is it that they praise the minor divine eye (divyacakṣus) shared by ordinary persons, rather than praising the bodhisattvas’ wisdom-eye (prajñācakṣus), dharma-eye (dharmacakṣus), and buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus)?
The answer is:
There are three kinds of devas:
first, the nominal devas; second, the devas by birth; and third, the pure devas.
Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin-rāja*) and other great kings are called "nominal devas" (*prajñapti-deva*);
those from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the highest realm of existence (*bhavāgra*) are called "birth devas" (*upapatti-deva*);
and all Buddhas, Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats are called "pure devas" (*viśuddha-deva*).
This pure deva cultivates and attains the divine eye; this is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).

The pure divine eye of the Buddha and the *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas cannot be attained by any ordinary person with the five supernormal powers who is free from desire, nor can it be attained by *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.
Why is this? A lesser arhat, applying his mind with limited focus, perceives a thousand-world system;
applying his mind with greater focus, he perceives a two-thousand-world system.
A great arhat, with a slight application of mind, sees two thousand worlds;
with a great application of mind, he sees a trichiliocosm.
It is the same for a pratyekabuddha.
This is called the supernormal power of the divine eye.
What is called the supernormal power of the divine ear?
It is the attainment of pure matter derived from the four great elements of the form realm within the ear, by which one is able to hear all sounds.
The sounds of devas, the sounds of humans, and the sounds of the three evil realms.
How does one cultivate and attain the supernormal power of the divine ear?
By constantly recollecting and attending to various kinds of sounds.
This is called the supernormal power of the divine ear.
What is the supernormal power of knowing past lives?
It is the constant recollection of former existences.

From days, months, years, and ages until the time within the womb, and even throughout past lives—one life, ten lives, a hundred lives, or thousands of millions of billions of lives—even up to the great Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas who know eighty thousand great kalpas;
the great Bodhisattvas and Buddhas know immeasurable kalpas.
This is called the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
What is called the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?

It consists in knowing whether the minds of others are defiled or undefiled; it is attained by constantly maintaining mindfulness while observing for oneself the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind.

Furthermore, one contemplates the signs of joy, anger, fear, and dread in others; having seen these signs, one subsequently knows their minds—this is the first gateway to the knowledge of others' minds.
This concludes the brief explanation of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
[Sūtra] It says: "One's words shall certainly be believed and accepted.
[Śāstra] Gods, humans, nāgas, asuras, and all great beings will believe and accept one's speech; this is because it is the retribution for not engaging in frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
As for the retribution for frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): even if one speaks the truth, no one will believe or accept it.
As a verse says:
"Those who fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) Have flames of fire issuing from their mouths."
A great sound issues from the four directions; this is the retribution for verbal transgressions.
Though one may possess extensive learning and eloquence, preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly, because of the karma of lack of sincerity and faith, no one will believe or accept it.
"If you wish to possess extensive learning and be trusted and accepted by others,
you should therefore be sincere and must not engage in frivolous speech!
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, there shall be no indolence."
[Treatise] The dharma of indolence destroys the wealth, profit, and merit of laypeople, and it destroys the joy of rebirth in heaven and the joy of nirvana for those who have left the household life.
It causes both the reputation of the laity and that of the renunciants to perish; as a great loss and a great thief, nothing surpasses indolence.
As a verse says:
"Laziness submerges the virtuous mind; the darkness of delusion destroys the light of wisdom.
All sublime vows are extinguished, and even great undertakings are lost!"
For this reason, it is said: "There is no further indolence.
[Sūtra] He has already abandoned gain and fame.
[Śāstra] This dharma of gain and fame is like a thief; it destroys the root of merit.
Just as heavenly hail damages the five grains,
so too do gain, offerings, and fame destroy the sprouts of merit, preventing them from growing.
As the Buddha taught through this parable:
"Just as a rope made of hair binds a person until it cuts the skin and severs the bone,
so too does one who craves gain and offerings sever the root of their merit."
As it is said in a verse:
"Having entered a sandalwood grove, one gathers only its leaves;
Having entered a mountain of the seven treasures, one seeks instead for crystal."
There are those who enter the Buddha-dharma, yet do not seek the bliss of Nirvana;
instead, they seek profit and offerings—such people are deceiving themselves!
Therefore, disciples of the Buddha who wish to obtain the taste of the Deathless (Amṛta), [should strive accordingly].
One should abandon the poison of worldly entanglements and diligently seek the bliss of Nirvāṇa!
Just as a shower of evil hail destroys the five grains,
so too does attachment to gain and offerings shatter shame, modesty, and the dhūta ascetic practices.
"In this life they burn their roots of goodness, and in future lives they fall into hell;
like Devadatta, they are submerged by their own pursuit of gain and honor.
For this reason, it is said: "Having already abandoned gain and fame."
[Sūtra] He preaches the Dharma without any expectation.
[Śāstra] Out of great loving-kindness and compassion, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude; he does not preach for the sake of food, clothing, fame, or power.
This is because of his great compassion, because his mind is pure, and because he has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As a verse says:
"Though one possesses great learning, eloquence, wisdom, and skill in speech, And may beautifully expound all dharmas to transform the minds of others,
If one's own conduct does not accord with the Dharma and is improper, It is like clouds and thunder that do not bring rain."
Though possessing vast learning, great erudition, and wisdom, One who is slow of speech and unskilled in eloquence cannot reveal the treasury of the Dharma;
It is like a light drizzle falling without thunder.
Lacking extensive learning and devoid of wisdom, unable to preach the Dharma and lacking noble conduct—
such a corrupt Dharma teacher is shameless, like a small cloud that brings neither thunder nor rain.
Possessing vast learning, profound wisdom, and eloquent speech, he skillfully explains all dharmas to transform the minds of others;
practicing the Dharma with a correct mind, he is fearless, like a great cloud and thunder pouring down a torrential rain.
The Great General of the Dharma holds the mirror of the Dharma, Illuminating the treasury of wisdom of the Buddha-dharma;
Holding and reciting it, he widely proclaims and rings the bell of the Dharma, Like a ship upon the sea, ferrying all across.
Just as a king of bees gathers all manner of flavors, he speaks according to the Buddha’s words and follows the Buddha’s intent;
assisting the Buddha to clarify the Dharma and deliver sentient beings—such a Dharma teacher is extremely difficult to encounter!
[Sūtra] He has transcended the patience regarding the profound Dharma.
[Śāstra] What is the "profound Dharma"?
The twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda) are called the profound Dharma.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is extremely profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to know!
Furthermore, because one is forever free from the net of sixty-two false views arising based on the past and future worlds, it is called the "profound Dharma."
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"An uninstructed worldling, if he wishes to praise the Buddha, his praise is very limited; that is to say, he may praise the purity of the precepts or praise his freedom from all desires."
"If one can praise this profound Dharma that is difficult to understand and difficult to know, this constitutes truly praising the Buddha.
Regarding this, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, the three gates of liberation are called the profound Dharma.
As the Buddha taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the devas praised him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"This Dharma is profoundly deep!
The Buddha said, "As for this profound Dharma, emptiness is its meaning; non-action and signlessness are its meaning."
Furthermore, to understand that the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) are truly indestructible and immovable is called the "profound Dharma.
Furthermore, setting aside the power of mental conceptualization and wisdom, one dwells solely within the pure true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena with a concentrated mind.
For example, when the heat is intense, one perceives what is not yellow as yellow;
because of the power of conceptual thought and mental cognition, one views all phenomena through a distorted lens—this is called the "shallow dharma.
For example, when a person’s eyes are pure and free from the influence of heat, they see yellow as truly yellow.
Thus, by removing the internal mental perception and the power of intellectual knowledge, the eye of wisdom becomes pure and perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It is like a genuine crystal: if a yellow object is placed within it, it appears yellow; if blue, red, or white objects are placed within it, it changes color accordingly.
The mind is likewise: because ordinary persons possess the power of internal mental perception and intellectual knowledge, they perceive the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
To contemplate the true reality of all phenomena as being neither empty nor non-empty, neither existent nor non-existent,
and to enter deeply into this Dharma without wavering and without any obstruction— this is called the "patience for the profound Dharma" (gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti).
"Crossing over" (*tāraṇa*) means attaining the profound Dharma, being fully perfected and without obstruction, and reaching the other shore; this is what is called "crossing over.
[Sūtra] Attaining the power of fearlessness.
[Treatise] The various bodhisattvas achieve the power of the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*).
Question:
Since the bodhisattva’s task is as yet unfinished and he has not yet attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), for what reason is it said that he has attained the four fearlessnesses?
Answer: There are two kinds of fearlessness:
the fearlessness of a bodhisattva and the fearlessness of a Buddha.

Although these bodhisattvas have not yet attained the fearlessnesses of a Buddha, they have attained the fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva; therefore, they are said to "have attained the power of fearlessness."
Question:
What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva? Answer:

First, because they are able to retain everything they hear, because they have attained all dhāraṇīs, because they constantly recollect them without forgetting, and because they preach the Dharma in the midst of the assembly without fear.

Second, because he knows the causes and conditions for the desire of all sentient beings to attain liberation, as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, and thus preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate, the Bodhisattva has no fear when preaching the Dharma amidst the great assembly.

Third, he does not see anyone—whether from the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below—who might come to pose a challenge or question such that he would be unable to answer in accordance with the Dharma.
Because he does not perceive even the slightest such sign, he teaches the Dharma in the midst of the assembly without fear.

Fourth, because all sentient beings listen to and receive his answers to their inquiries, and he is able to skillfully sever the doubts of all sentient beings by answering them according to their wishes and in accordance with the Dharma, the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma in the midst of the great assembly without fear.
[Sūtra] He transcends all demonic activities.
[Śāstra] There are four kinds of Māras: first, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*);

second, the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*); third, the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and fourth, the Māra of the Lord of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*).
Because these bodhisattvas have attained the bodhisattva path, they destroy the demon of afflictions;
because they have attained the dharma-body, they destroy the demon of the aggregates;
because they have attained the path and the dharma-nature body, they destroy the demon of death.

Because he is always single-minded, because his mind does not cling to any place, and because he has entered the immovable samādhi, he destroys the Māra of the Lord of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
For this reason, it is said that he "transcends all demonic activities."
Furthermore, in this "Chapter on Awakening to Māra" within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha himself speaks of the deeds and activities of Māra.
Because these deeds and activities of Māra have been completely transcended, it is called "having transcended the activities of Māra."
Furthermore, with the exception of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything remaining is entirely termed "Māra.

This includes all afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), desires (*kāma*), bonds (*bandhana*), graspings (*upādāna*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), as well as the Māra King, the Māra subjects, and the Māra people.
All such things as these are collectively termed "Māra.
Question: Where is it stated that the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), such as the bond of desire (*kāma-bandhana*) and so forth, are called Māra?
The answer is:
In the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the Buddha spoke these verses to the Māra King:
"Desire is your first army; Grief and sorrow are your second army."
The army of hunger and thirst is the third; the army of craving is the fourth and fifth;
the army of sleep is the sixth; the army of fear is the seventh;
and the army of latent venom is the eighth.
The ninth army is gain and offerings, attached to false fame;
the tenth army is self-exaltation and contempt for others.
Such are your armies, O people of all the world.
And all the various devas— none are able to break it.
With the arrow of wisdom, through the power of cultivated concentration and insight,
I shall crush your demonic host, like an unbaked clay jar sinking into water.
Cultivate wisdom with a single mind to deliver all beings;
my disciples who are diligent, constantly mindful of cultivating wisdom,
and practice in accordance with the Dharma, will surely attain Nirvana.
"Though you do not wish to release him, he shall reach where you cannot reach!
At that time, upon hearing this, the Māra was overcome with grief and immediately vanished;
the wicked hosts of Māras likewise disappeared and were no longer seen.
This is called the Māra of the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Question:
Within the five aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*), where is this said to be Māra?
The answer is:
On Mount Makula, the Buddha instructed his disciple Rādha:
“Form is Māra; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise Māra.”
Furthermore, if one wishes to create a material body in a future life, this is a point of movement;
if one wishes to create an immaterial body, this too is a point of movement;
if one wishes to create a body with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception, these are all points of movement.
Movement is the bondage of Māra; non-movement is non-bondage, through which one attains liberation from evil.
Herein, it is said that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are Māra.
As for the Māra of the Lord of Gods (Indra), the subjects of Māra, and the followers of Māra—they are themselves Māra, so there is no need to speak of them further.
Question: Why is he called Māra? Answer:
He robs one of the life-force of wisdom and destroys the roots of goodness—the merit of the Path and the Dharma; for this reason, he is called Māra.
Various non-Buddhist practitioners say:
"He is named the Lord of Desire, also named Flower-Arrow, and also named Five-Arrows" (the *Dan* manuscript adds a note stating:).
The five desires are arrows, for they destroy various wholesome dharmas.
Within the Buddha-dharma, these are called Māra; such karma and such activities are termed "the works of Māra."
What constitutes such demonic activities?
They are as explained in the "Chapter on Awakening to Demons" (Jue mo pin).

Furthermore, when people transmigrate through the world experiencing suffering and pleasure, it is due to the causes and conditions of the fetters (saṃyojana), and also due to the power and causes and conditions of the Demon King (Māra-rāja).

This Māra is named the enemy of all Buddhas and the thief of all noble ones; he destroys the work of all those who flow against the current and takes no delight in Nirvāṇa—this is what is called Māra.
This Māra has three types of activities:
jesting, idle chatter, singing, dancing, and lewd glances—these arise from craving;
binding, beating, whipping, torturing, piercing, cutting, hacking, and lopping off—these arise from hatred.
Scorching the body, freezing oneself, plucking out one's hair, self-starvation, entering fire, leaping into abysses, and throwing oneself from cliffs—such acts as these arise from ignorance.
They involve great faults and impurity, and are attachments to the mundane world; all of them are the deeds of Māra.
To loathe benefit, to reject nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa, is also the work of Māra.
To be submerged in the great ocean of suffering and remain unaware of it—
such immeasurable things as these are all the works of Māra.
Having already abandoned and relinquished them, this is called "transcending all demonic activities.
[Sūtra] All karmic obstructions are completely liberated.
[Śāstra] To be liberated from all evil karma is termed "the liberation of karmic obstructions."
Question: If there are three kinds of obstructions—
the obstruction of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa), the obstruction of karma (karmāvaraṇa), and the obstruction of retribution (vipākāvaraṇa);
Question: Why, when abandoning the two obstacles, do you speak only of the obstacle of karma? Answer:
Because among the three obstacles, the power of karma is the greatest.
The various karmas accumulated over even hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are not lost, not burned, and not destroyed; they do not vanish when the time for their retribution arrives.
These karmas are able to endure for a long time and bestow their retribution when conditions harmonize;
