they are like seeds of grain or grass in the earth, which sprout when the proper season is reached, neither being lost nor destroyed.
Even the all-knowing wisdom of these Buddhas, which is most supreme and honored like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, cannot overturn these various karmas; how much less so can ordinary people!
As a verse says:
"The wheel of birth and death carries people along;
The various afflictions and fetters turn it with great power and autonomy, Such that no one can stop it."
The karma created by oneself in previous lives transforms into various forms;
the power of karma is the greatest, peerless within the world!
Previous karma is sovereign, leading people to undergo their retributions.
Driven by the power of karma, one revolves, circling within the sea of birth and death.
Though the waters of the great ocean may dry up and Mount Sumeru and the earth be utterly exhausted,
the karmic causes and conditions of previous lives are neither burned away nor destroyed.
All karmas, having long been accumulated and gathered, follow the doer wherever he goes;
just as a creditor pursues a debtor without ceasing,
so too these fruits of karma cannot be turned aside by anyone.
There is no place of escape, nor can one avoid it by seeking mercy.
Among the sentient beings within the three realms, it pursues them without a moment’s separation, like the Kālarākṣasa;
this is the karma described by the Buddha.
As wind does not enter what is solid, as water does not flow upward,
and as space is not subject to harm, so too is it with karma that has not been performed.
Though the power of various karmas is immeasurable, they do not pursue one who did not create them.
When the time for retribution arrives, it neither perishes nor is lost.
From the earth it flies up to heaven; from heaven it enters the Snowy Mountains;
from the Snowy Mountains it enters the ocean—it is never separated from one’s presence in any place.
"Constantly following me, never forsaking me for even a single moment;
until the time when there is no longer loss, it is like a star rushing toward the moon.
For this reason, it is said: "All karmic obstructions are entirely liberated."
[Sūtra] Skillfully expounding the dharma of dependent origination.

[Śāstra] Regarding the dharma of the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination: through various gateways of the Dharma, one can skillfully explain how afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and phenomena (*vastu*) arise in successive succession and continuity; this is called the twelve links of dependent origination.
Among these, the three factors of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are called afflictions (*kleśa*);
the two factors of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are called karma;
and the remaining seven factors are called the substantial entities (*vastu*).

Regarding these twelve links of dependent origination: the first two are subsumed under the past life, the last two are subsumed under the future life, and the middle eight are subsumed under the present life.
This is a brief explanation of three factors:
afflictions, karma, and suffering.
These three matters serve as causes and conditions for one another in a reciprocal cycle:

afflictions are the cause and condition for karma; karma is the cause and condition for suffering; suffering is the cause and condition for further suffering; suffering is the cause and condition for afflictions; afflictions are the cause and condition for karma; karma is the cause and condition for suffering; and suffering is the cause and condition for further suffering. This is called being causes and conditions for one another in a reciprocal cycle.
All afflictions of past lives are called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
From ignorance arises karma, which is capable of producing the fruits of the world; therefore, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).

From volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), a defiled mind arises; it is the primary cause of the body. Just as a calf recognizes its mother through the recognition of her specific characteristics, this is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
This consciousness arises simultaneously with the four formless aggregates (*skandha*) and the form in which it dwells; these are collectively termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Within this name-and-form, the six sense organs such as the eye arise; this is called the "six entrances" (ṣaḍāyatana).
The conjunction of the sense organ, the object, and consciousness is called "contact" (sparśa).
From contact arises "feeling.
When one becomes attached within feeling, this is called "craving.
Seeking due to the causal condition of craving is called "clinging."
From grasping the karma that serves as the cause and condition for future existence, this is called "existence" (*bhava*).
From existence, one again receives the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in a future life; this is called "birth" (*jāti*).
From birth, the maturation and decay of the five aggregates is called "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Old age, death, birth, sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and wailing—these various afflictions and distresses constitute a collection of manifold sufferings.

If one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena with single-mindedness and purity, then ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are extinguished, and so on, until this entire collection of manifold sufferings is extinguished.
These are the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination; to be thus able to skillfully avoid attachment to false views and to expound them for others is called "skillful.

Furthermore, within this contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, to sever craving for dharmas, to have no mental attachment, and to know the true mark (lakṣaṇa) is called "skillful."
As it is said in the "Inexhaustible Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"Ignorance is inexhaustible like space; volitional formations are inexhaustible like space; and so on, up to the accumulation of all suffering is inexhaustible like space."
A bodhisattva should understand it in this way!
One who understands in this way abandons the limit of delusion and should have no point of entry.
One who contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in this manner is sitting at the site of enlightenment and attains sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
[Sūtra] “Since incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, he has made great vows.
[Śāstra] The meaning of “incalculable” (*asaṃkhyeya*) has already been explained in the “Chapter on the Meaning of Bodhisattvas.”
Regarding the meaning of "kalpa," the Buddha explained through a simile:

"Suppose there were a stone mountain four thousand li high, and a long-lived person who comes once every hundred years with a fine, soft cloth to wipe it; even when this great stone mountain is completely worn away, the kalpa would not yet have ended."
Suppose there were a great city four thousand *li* in size, filled with mustard seeds without being leveled;
if a person of long life were to come once every hundred years and take away a single mustard seed, the kalpa would still not be exhausted even when the mustard seeds were all gone.
In this manner, for incalculable kalpas, the Bodhisattva makes great and correct vows to deliver and liberate sentient beings.

"Vow" (praṇidhāna) refers to the essential oath of the Great Mind: the resolve to certainly deliver all sentient beings, sever all fetters and afflictions, and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is what is called a "vow."
[Sūtra]: His countenance is serene and pleasant; he always inquires after others' welfare first, and his speech is not coarse.

[Śāstra]: Because the root of anger has been uprooted, because envy has been eliminated, because he constantly cultivates great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), and great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and because the four kinds of wrong speech have been severed, he attains a serene and pleasant countenance.
As it is said in verse:
"If one sees a mendicant on the road, One should attend to them with four kinds of hospitality:
First, look upon them with kind eyes; Second, go out to meet them and respectfully inquire after their welfare."
One should provide excellent offerings of seats and fulfill all desires through giving;
with such a mind of generosity, the path of the Buddha is as if held in the palm of one's hand.
If one can eliminate these four kinds of faults—the poison of false speech and verbal transgressions—[the path is attained].
Divisive speech, harsh words, and frivolous talk— by abandoning these, one obtains a great and beautiful retribution.
When a person of gentle virtue seeks the Way and desires to deliver all sentient beings,
they eliminate the four types of evil verbal karma, just as a horse is guided by a bridle!
[Sūtra] He attains fearlessness within the great assembly.
[Śāstra] Because of his greatness, because of his solid virtues and wisdom, and because he has attained the supreme *dhāraṇī* of eloquence, he attains fearlessness within the great assembly.
As a verse says:
"The wisdom and virtue within are meager, While outwardly one is skilled in beautiful words;
Just as a bamboo has no core within, It merely displays its exterior."
"With inner wisdom and virtue profound, And outwardly skilled in the words of the Dharma;
Like a wondrous diamond, Possessing strength both within and without.

Furthermore, because he has accomplished the dharma of fearlessness, he is handsome, of noble birth, and possesses great power; his observance of precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, eloquence, and so forth are all perfected. For this reason, he is without fear.
For this reason, one is fearless in the midst of the great assembly.
As a verse says:
"One with meager virtue and no wisdom should not occupy a high seat."
As a jackal sees a lion, it crouches and hides, not daring to emerge.
One of great wisdom has nothing to fear; they should occupy the lion’s throne.
Just as when the lion roars, all the beasts are struck with dread!
Because he has gathered immeasurable and boundless power of wisdom and merit, he possesses fearlessness.
As a verse says:
"If a person extinguishes all evils, even down to the smallest transgression..."
Such a person of great virtue has no wish that remains unfulfilled.
This person possesses great wisdom and is free from affliction within the world;
therefore, for such a person, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are one.

Furthermore, it is because the Bodhisattva alone attains the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). As stated in the *Vinapanarāja-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva alone attains the four fearlessnesses, as previously explained.
[Sūtra] They skillfully expound the Dharma for countless billions of kalpas.
[Śāstra] Such Bodhisattvas diligently cultivate various roots of goodness, such as heedfulness (*apramāda*), within their own bodies.
These Bodhisattvas have accumulated merit and wisdom not for one, two, three, or four lifetimes, but for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
As a verse says:
“For the sake of sentient beings, one has resolved upon the Great Mind;
if there are those who show no respect and give rise to arrogance, their transgression is so great it cannot be described, let alone if they further add an evil mind!”

Furthermore, throughout incalculable and immeasurable kalpas, this bodhisattva has cultivated the body, cultivated morality, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom; amidst arising and ceasing, bondage and liberation, and the adverse and the favorable, he has personally and clearly realized the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
There are three kinds of understanding:
understanding through hearing, understanding through meaning, and understanding through realization.
Within the various gates of the Dharma teachings, one is without any obstruction, attaining the skillful means of preaching the Dharma and the perfection of wisdom.
What these bodhisattvas have spoken is like the speech of noble ones; it should all be accepted with faith.
As a verse says:
"Though one possesses wisdom, if lacking extensive learning, One will not know the true nature of reality."
Just as in the midst of great darkness, one with eyes sees nothing;
so too, one with much learning but no wisdom does not know the true meaning.
Just as in the midst of great light, there may be a lamp but no eyes.
"One who is learned and possesses sharp wisdom—this is what should be accepted as spoken [by the Buddha].
One who lacks wisdom and lacks clarity is called a 'human-bodied ox. He asked:
One should say that he has skillfully preached the Dharma for countless billions of kalpas; why, then, do you speak of "emerging"?
The answer is:

it is easy to preach the Dharma among those who lack wisdom and among one's own disciples, but it is difficult to preach the Dharma among those who are widely learned, possess sharp intelligence, and are skilled in debate.
If a Dharma teacher of limited wisdom is timid and withdrawn in this matter,
whereas one who is highly learned and of great erudition is bold and joyful amidst difficult inquiries, he shall possess great majestic virtue within the entire assembly.
As stated in a verse from the *Devasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"The radiance of his face, eyes, and teeth Shines universally throughout the great assembly;
It outshines the light of all the devas, So that their various splendors no longer appear."
For this reason, it is called "being able to attain liberation through skillful preaching of the Dharma over incalculable billions of kalpas.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 5, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* First Chapter: Exposition of the Ten Similes.
Treatise on the Explanation of the Ten Similes, Volume Six, Part One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by imperial decree. [Sūtra] One thoroughly understands that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like space, like echoes, like the city of the Gandharvas, like dreams, like shadows, like images in a mirror, and like transformations.
[Treatise] These ten similes are for the purpose of explaining the dharma of emptiness. Question:
If all dharmas are empty like an illusion, for what reason are there dharmas that can be seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and cognized?
If, in reality, nothing exists, there should be nothing that can be seen, nor even anything that can be cognized.
Furthermore, if one falsely perceives what does not exist, why is it that one does not see sounds or hear forms?
If all things are equally empty and non-existent, why is there that which is visible and that which is invisible?

Since all dharmas are empty—just as, for example, the first fingernail does not exist and the second fingernail likewise does not exist—why is it that one does not see the second fingernail but sees only the first?
For this reason,
it is known that the first nail is visible because it truly exists, while the second nail is invisible because it does not truly exist.
The answer is:
Although the characteristics of all phenomena are empty, there are still distinctions between what is visible and what is invisible.

For example, like illusory elephants, horses, and various other objects, although one knows they lack substantial reality, their forms can be seen and their sounds heard; they correspond to the six sense faculties without being confused with one another.
All phenomena are likewise: though empty, they can be seen and heard without being confused with one another.
As it is said in the *Sūtra of the Virtuous Woman*:
“The Virtuous Woman addressed the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
Is ignorance present within?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is there anything external? The Buddha said:
"No. "Is there anything internal or external?
The Buddha said:
"No. "World-Honored One,
does this ignorance come from a previous life?"
The Buddha said: "No. [He asked:
"Does it go from this world to the next world?"
The Buddha said, "No.
[He asked again,] "Does this ignorance have one who brings it into being or one who causes it to cease?"
The Buddha said: "No. [The interlocutor asked:
"Is there a single dharma that possesses a fixed, real nature, which is called ignorance?"
The Buddha said, “No.
At that time, the girl Guṇavati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If ignorance has no internal existence, no external existence, nor both internal and external existence; if it does not proceed from a previous life to this life, nor from this life to a future life; and if it lacks any true intrinsic nature, how can there be the arising of suffering through the conditions of ignorance leading to volitional formations, and so forth?"
“World-Honored One!
It is like a tree: if it had no roots, how could it produce stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit?
The Buddha said:

"Although the characteristics of all phenomena are empty, because ordinary beings lack learning and wisdom, they give rise to various afflictions therein. With afflictions as the causal condition, they perform actions of body, speech, and mind; with those actions as the causal condition, they produce a future body; and with that body as the causal condition, they experience suffering and pleasure."
Within this, there is no real agent that creates afflictions, nor are there any actions of body, speech, or mind, nor is there anyone who experiences suffering or pleasure.
It is like a magician who conjures various things through illusion.
"What do you think?
Is there anything internal produced by that illusion? He replied:
"No. "Is there anything outside? He replied:
"No. "Is there anything internal or external? He replied:
"No. "From the past life to the present life, and from the present life to the future life? He replied:
"No. "Is there anyone who is born or dies among those created by illusion? He replied:
"No. "Is there truly one dharma that is created by illusion? He replied:
"No. The Buddha said,
"Have you ever seen or heard of musical performances created by illusion?"
She replied, “I have both heard it and seen it.
The Buddha asked the virtuous woman:
"If illusion is empty, deceptive, and without reality, how can it produce music from within itself?
The Virtuous Woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One! [How is this so?]"
"This is merely an illusory appearance; though it has no fundamental basis, it can nevertheless be heard and seen.
The Buddha said, "Ignorance is also like this: though it exists neither internally, nor externally, nor both internally and externally;"

There is no transition from the past life to the present life, nor from the present life to the future life; furthermore, there is no substantial nature. There is neither one who is born nor one who perishes; yet, conditioned by ignorance, the formative forces arise, and so on until the accumulation of the aggregates of suffering occurs.
Just as when an illusion ceases, that which is produced by the illusion also ceases;
so it is with ignorance: when ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations are exhausted, and so on until the entire accumulation of suffering is exhausted.
"Furthermore, this analogy of illusion demonstrates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty and lack solidity;
as it is said:
'All conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions, deceiving the childish, dependent on causes and conditions, lacking self-mastery, and not enduring for long.'"
For this reason, it is said that "all bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are like illusions.

Regarding "like a mirage": because dust is stirred by the wind and sunlight, one sees it in the wilderness as if it were a wild horse; those without wisdom, upon first seeing it, mistake it for water.

The marks of male and female are likewise so: the sun of the fetters and afflictions heats the dust of all conditioned phenomena, and the wind of false recollection whirls within the wilderness of birth and death; those lacking wisdom perceive them as having a single characteristic, namely, as male or female.
This is called "like a mirage.
Furthermore, if one sees a mirage from afar, one perceives it as water, but when near, there is no perception of water.

It is the same for those without wisdom: if they are far from the Noble Dharma, they do not know non-self and do not know that all dharmas are empty; thus, amidst the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas—which are by nature empty dharmas—they give rise to the notion of a person, the notion of male, and the notion of female.
By approaching the sublime Dharma, one realizes the true nature of all phenomena; at that time, various delusive conceptualizations are entirely eliminated.
For this reason, it is said that "Bodhisattvas know all phenomena to be like a mirage."
Regarding the phrase "like the moon in water": while the moon actually exists in the void of space, its reflection appears in the water;

likewise, while the moon of the true mark of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) exists in the void of suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the reflections of the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self" appear within the water-like minds of ordinary beings, devas, and humans.
For this reason, it is called "like the moon in water.
Furthermore, when a small child sees the moon in the water, he rejoices and wishes to seize it; when an adult sees it, he laughs.
Ignorant people are also like this: because of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they perceive a "self";
because they lack true wisdom, they perceive various phenomena;
having perceived them, they rejoice and desire to grasp their marks.
The male form, the female form, and so forth—
these are laughed at by the noble ones who have attained the Path.
As it is said in a verse:
"Like the moon in water or water in a mirage, like obtaining wealth in a dream or seeking life after death—
if someone truly desires to obtain these things, that person is deluded and will be laughed at by the sages!"
Furthermore, it is like seeing the reflection of the moon in still water; if the water is stirred, it is no longer seen.
In the still water of the mind of ignorance, one sees the reflections of the self, pride, and various fetters (*saṃyojana*);
but when the water of the mind is stirred by the staff of true wisdom, the reflections of the self and the various fetters are no longer seen.
For this reason, it is said: "All bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are like the moon in water.
As for "being like space," it has only a name but no real dharma.
Space is not an object that can be seen; however, because one looks from a distance, the visual faculty undergoes a transformation and perceives a pale blue color.

All phenomena are likewise: they are empty and non-existent. Because people are far removed from untainted, true wisdom, they abandon the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and their minds become attached to various miscellaneous things such as self and other, male and female, houses, and cities.
It is like a child looking up at the blue sky and thinking there is a real color; someone flying up to a great distance sees nothing at all, yet because of the distance, they perceive it as blue.
All phenomena are likewise.
For this reason, it is said to be "like space.
Furthermore, just as the nature of space is eternally pure, yet people call it impure when it is obscured by clouds and mist, so too are all phenomena:
their nature is eternally pure, yet because they are obscured by lust, anger, and the like, people call them impure.
As a verse says:
"Just as in the summer months, when thunder, lightning, and rain / And dark clouds cover the sky, making it impure;
/ So too it is with the ignorant ordinary person, / Whose mind is constantly shrouded by various afflictions."
Just as when the sun first appears in winter, it is constantly obscured by the gloom of dark clouds;
though one may attain the first fruit or the second path, one still remains veiled by the defilements of desire.
Just as when the sun is about to rise in springtime, it is obscured by dark clouds;
though one has abandoned the defilements of desire and attained the third fruit, the remnants of ignorance and pride still shroud the mind.
Like an autumn day free from clouds and mist, And like the waters of the great ocean, pure and clear;
Having accomplished what was to be done with a mind free of outflows— Thus does the Arhat attain purity.
Furthermore, space has no beginning, no middle, and no end; all phenomena are likewise so.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said to Subhūti in the Mahāyāna:
"Space has no prior existence, no middle existence, and no subsequent existence; all phenomena are likewise so."
That sutra should be explained in detail here.
Therefore, it is said: "All dharmas are like space. Question:
Space is a substantially existent phenomenon. Why?

If space were not a substantially existent phenomenon, then actions such as lifting or lowering, coming or going, contracting or extending, or exiting or entering would be impossible, because there would be no locus for movement.
Answer: If the phenomenon of space were truly existent, space would have to have a place of abiding. Why is this?
Where there is no place of abiding, there is no dharma.
If space were to abide within a cavity, it would mean that space abides within space; for this reason, it should not abide within a cavity.
If it were to abide within a solid substance, that substance would not be empty, and thus it could not abide therein, as there is nothing for it to occupy.
Furthermore, you state that "the dwelling place is empty space. However, within a solid stone wall, there is no dwelling place;
if there is no dwelling place, then there is no empty space. Since empty space has no dwelling place, there is no such thing as empty space.
Furthermore, because there is no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no space.
All phenomena each possess their own characteristics; because characteristics exist, one knows that phenomena exist.

For example: earth has the characteristic of solidity, water the characteristic of moisture, fire the characteristic of heat, wind the characteristic of motion, consciousness the characteristic of cognizing, wisdom the characteristic of discernment, the world the characteristic of arising and ceasing, and nirvāṇa the characteristic of eternal cessation.
"Because this space is without characteristics (animitta), it does not exist.
Question: Space does have characteristics; you say it does not exist because you do not recognize them. The absence of form (rūpa) is the characteristic of space.
Answer: It is not so!
Formlessness (ārūpya) is simply the destruction of form; there is no other distinct dharma, just as when a lamp is extinguished, there is no further dharma remaining.
For this reason, there is no characteristic of space.
Furthermore, this phenomenon of space does not exist. Why is that?
Because of form, you claim that the state of formlessness is the characteristic of space.
If that were so, then before form has arisen, there would be no characteristic of space.
Furthermore, you say:
"Form is an impermanent phenomenon, whereas space is an eternal phenomenon.
If that were so, space would have to exist prior to the existence of form, because it is eternal.
If form does not yet exist, then there is no formless realm;
if there is no formless realm, then there is no characteristic of space;
if there is no characteristic, then there is no phenomenon.
For this reason, space exists as a mere name but lacks substantial reality.
As it is with space, so it is with all phenomena: they exist only as provisional designations and lack substantial reality.
For this reason, it is said that "all bodhisattvas know that all dharmas are like space.
Regarding "like an echo": whether in deep mountains or narrow valleys, or in deep, secluded ravines, or within vast empty halls;
when there is a sound from speech or a sound from striking, and a sound arises from that sound, it is called an "echo."
The ignorant person says there is a person who utters the sound;
the wise person reflects in their mind:
"This sound is not produced by a person; it is simply because of the contact with sound that another sound arises, which is called an echo."
The phenomenon of resonance is empty and can deceive the faculty of hearing.

For example, when a person wishes to speak, the wind within the mouth called *udāna* returns to the navel; upon touching the navel, resonance issues forth. When the resonance issues forth, it touches seven locations and then recedes; this is what is called speech.
As it is said in verse:
"The wind named udāna Rises from the navel and moves upward;
This wind touches seven places: The neck, the gums, the teeth, and the lips."
The tongue, the throat, and the chest—within these, speech arises.
The fool does not understand this; deluded and attached, they give rise to anger and ignorance.
The person of middle capacity possesses wisdom; they neither become angry nor remain attached.
Nor is there any delusion; one merely follows the characteristics of all phenomena.
Whether bending or straightening, contracting or extending, or in the speech of the past, future, and present—there is nowhere a creator to be found.
Is this matter an illusion?
Is it a wooden automaton?
Or is it a matter within a dream?
I am oppressed by the heat of my breath; is this real, or is it unreal?
Who can know the truth of this matter?
This skeletal figure, bound by sinews, can produce such vocal sounds, like molten gold cast into water.
For this reason, it is said that "all bodhisattvas know all dharmas to be like echoes.
Regarding "like a *gandharva* city": when the sun first rises, one sees city gates, watchtowers, palaces, and people entering and exiting; as the sun rises higher, these vanish.
This city can only be seen with the eyes but has no reality; it is called a *gandharva* city.
Suppose there is a person who has never before seen a city of the Gandharvas. At dawn, looking toward the east, he sees it and thinks it is a real place of delight.
He hastens toward it, but as he draws closer, it vanishes; as the sun rises higher, it disappears entirely.
Driven to the utmost exhaustion by hunger and thirst, he sees a shimmering vapor like a mirage and mistakes it for water. He runs toward it in haste, but as he approaches, it vanishes again.

Exhausted and distressed by hardship, he reached a remote mountain and a narrow valley where he cried out loudly; hearing an echo, he thought there were inhabitants living there, but though he searched with all his might, he saw nothing.
Through reflection, he attained self-awakening, and his longing heart was stilled.

It is the same with ignorant people: within the empty aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), they perceive a self and various phenomena, becoming attached through lust and anger; they run wild in all directions, seeking pleasure to satisfy themselves, yet through their perversions and deceptions, they reach the utmost exhaustion and distress.
If, by means of wisdom, they know there is no self and no real phenomena, then at that time their perverted aspirations will cease.
Furthermore, the city of the gandharvas is not a city, yet the human mind conceives of it as a city;
ordinary people are likewise: what is not a body they conceive of as a body, and what is not a mind they conceive of as a mind.
Question:
A single matter can be understood; why provide so many analogies? Answer:
I have already answered this previously: this Mahāyāna is like the water of the great ocean, encompassing all dharmas;
because the Mahāyāna possesses many causes and conditions, there is no fault in employing numerous analogies.
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva possesses profound and sharp wisdom, he employs various dharma-gates, various causes and conditions, and various parables to dismantle all phenomena;
for the sake of explaining them to others, he should cite many parables.

Furthermore, within all the teachings of the Śrāvakas, there is no simile of the city of the Gandharvas; rather, there are various other similes for impermanence—“form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion”—as well as the simile of emptiness in the *Māyājāla-sūtra*.
Because this metaphor of the city of the Gandharvas is distinct [from others], it is explained here. Question:
In the teachings for the Śrāvakas, the body is compared to a city; why is the city of the Gandharvas used as a metaphor here?
Answer:

In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, the city is used as a metaphor for the fact that the various conditions (*pratyaya*) truly exist, though the city itself is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
In contrast, the city of the Gandharvas lacks even those various conditions; it is like a whirling firebrand that merely deceives the eyes of people.
In the Śrāvaka teachings, a city is used as a metaphor in order to refute the notion of a self;
here, because Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties and penetrate deeply into the emptiness of all phenomena, a *gandharva-nagara* (city of the Gandharvas) is used as a metaphor.
For this reason, it is said that "it is like a city of Gandharvas.
As for "like a dream," it is as if in a dream there is no real substance, yet one calls it real; upon waking and realizing it was non-existent, one laughs at oneself.

People are also like this: while asleep amidst the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), they cling to what is actually non-existent; when they attain the awakening of the Path and realize it is not real, they likewise laugh at themselves.
For this reason, it is said that "it is like a dream.
Furthermore, in a dream, one sees things that do not exist due to the power of sleep;

likewise, people also see various things as existing when they do not, due to the power of the sleep of ignorance—namely, the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," male and female, and so forth.
Furthermore, just as in a dream one feels joy when there is no cause for joy, anger when there is no cause for anger, and fear when there is no cause for fear;

so it is with the sentient beings of the three realms: because they sleep in ignorance, they feel anger when they should not feel anger, joy when they should not feel joy, and fear when they should not feel fear.
Furthermore, there are five types of dreams:
if the body is out of balance and the heat element is predominant, one frequently sees fire, yellow, and red;
if the cold element is predominant, one frequently sees water and white.
If wind-energy (*vāyu*) is predominant, one frequently sees things flying or sees black objects;
furthermore, because one habitually reflects upon and dwells upon what has been heard and seen, one sees them in dreams;
or else it may be that a deity grants a dream in order to make one know future events.
These five kinds of dreams are all devoid of substantial reality and are merely false perceptions.
Human beings are likewise: due to the power and conditions of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), sentient beings within the five realms perceive four kinds of self:
the aggregate of form is the self, form belongs to the self, form is within the self, and the self is within form.
As it is with form, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—four times five makes twenty.
Having attained the path and awakened through true wisdom, one knows that they are without reality.
Question: One should not say that "a dream has no reality. Why is this?
Consciousness arises when it encounters causes and conditions;
within a dream, consciousness has various conditions—if these conditions did not exist, how could consciousness arise?
He replied:
It does not exist!

It is seeing what should not be seen, such as seeing a human head with horns in a dream, or dreaming that one’s body flies through the void; yet humans truly have no horns, nor does the body fly. Therefore, it is without reality.
Question:
Human heads truly exist, and horns also truly exist elsewhere;
it is because the mind is deluded that one sees human heads as having horns.
Space truly exists, and those who fly also truly exist;
it is because the mind is deluded that one perceives one's own body flying, yet this is not without reality.
He replied:
Although human heads truly exist and horns truly exist, the notion that a human head grows horns is a false perception.
Question: The world is vast, and the causes and conditions from previous lives are manifold and diverse; [how can one say this?]

There may be other countries where people have horns growing from their heads, or have only one hand or one foot; there are people one chi tall, and people with nine heads. What is so strange about people having horns?
The answer is:
It might be possible for people from other countries to have horns; however, if one dreams that people known in this very country have horns, that cannot be so.
Furthermore, if a person dreams of the limits of space, the limits of direction, or the limits of time, how could such things possess reality?
Where is there no space, no direction, and no time?
For this reason, one sees what does not exist within a dream.
You previously stated:
"How can consciousness arise without an object?
Although there are no objects such as the five sensory realms, it arises with *dharma* as its object because it is transformed by the power of one's own mental reflection and recollection.
It is like when a person says, "There are two heads"; from those words, a conceptualization arises.
It is just as in a dream, where what does not exist is seen as existing.
All phenomena are likewise; although all phenomena do not exist, they can be seen, heard, and known.
As it is said in verse:
"Like a dream, like a phantom, like a gandharva city;
so too are all phenomena."
For this reason, it is said that "all bodhisattvas know all phenomena to be like dreams.
Regarding "like a shadow": a shadow can only be seen and cannot be grasped;
so too are all phenomena—though they are seen, heard, sensed, and known by the faculties such as the eye, they are in reality unobtainable.
As a verse says:
"This true knowledge and wisdom cannot be grasped from any side;
like a great mass of fire, it also cannot be touched."
"The Dharma cannot be received, nor should it be received. Furthermore,
just as a shadow appears when light is obstructed and does not appear when it is not, so too,
when the light of right view is obscured by the fetters and afflictions, the shadows of the marks of a self and the marks of phenomena arise.
Furthermore, it is like a shadow: when a person leaves, the shadow goes; when a person moves, the shadow moves; when a person stands still, the shadow stands still.

The shadows of good and evil karma are likewise: when one departs for the next life, they go; while one dwells in this life, they remain. Because the retribution is never severed, they emerge when the time for the ripening of transgressions or merits arrives.
As a verse says:
"He pursues [the enemy] even through the air; he pursues him even among mountain rocks;
he follows him even beneath the earth; and he enters even into the waters of the sea!"
"Constantly following everywhere, the shadow of karma never departs.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like shadows.
Furthermore, just as a shadow is empty and non-existent, such that its reality cannot be found when sought;
All phenomena are likewise empty and devoid of reality.
Question:
It is not the case that a shadow is empty and devoid of reality!
Why is this? The *Abhidharma* states:
"What is called the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*)?"

Blue, yellow, red, white, black, indigo, purple, light, brightness, shadow, and so forth, as well as the three types of manifest form produced by bodily action—these are called the visible base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
"How can you say it does not exist?

Furthermore, a shadow truly exists because there are causes and conditions—the tree serves as the cause and the light serves as the condition; when these two things come together, a shadow arises. How can you say it does not exist?"
If there were no shadow, then other phenomena that exist through causes and conditions would likewise all be non-existent!

Furthermore, this shadow-substance can be seen to have length or shortness, largeness or smallness, coarseness or fineness, curvature or straightness; when the form moves, the shadow also moves—all these matters are visible. For this reason, it must exist.
The answer is:
A shadow is truly empty and non-existent. As for your claim that this is taught in the Abhidharma, it was composed by those who interpret the meaning of the Abhidharma;
they expound a particular dharma-gate, yet people do not grasp its underlying intent and instead cling to it as being real.
As it is said in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"The atom is the most subtle; it cannot be broken and cannot be burned.
Thus, it is eternal!
"Furthermore, there are dharmas within the three periods of time that emerge from the future into the present and enter the past from the present, without anything being lost.
This, then, would be permanence!
Furthermore, it is said:
"All conditioned phenomena arise and perish anew at every moment, never remaining.
If this were so, it would constitute the characteristic of annihilation!
Why is this? Because that which previously existed is now non-existent.
Various such divergent explanations contradict the Buddha’s words and cannot be used as proof.

A shadow is now different from material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); whereas the arising of a material phenomenon must necessarily involve odor, taste, tangibility, and so forth, a shadow is not thus, and for this reason it is non-existent.
For example, a jar is known by two faculties:
the eye faculty and the body faculty.
If a shadow were an existing entity, it should be perceivable by two sense organs; however, such a thing does not occur.
For this reason, a shadow is not a real substance, but is merely a phenomenon that deceives the eye;
it is like a firebrand held in the hand and whirled rapidly to form a circle—it is not real.
A shadow is not a substantial entity!
If a shadow were a substantial entity, it should be possible to break or destroy it;
yet as long as the form is not destroyed, the shadow ultimately does not perish. For this reason, it is empty.
Furthermore, a shadow is dependent upon a form and lacks independence; therefore, it is empty. Although it is empty, the mind arises and the eye perceives it.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like shadows."

Regarding the phrase "like a reflection in a mirror": a reflection in a mirror is not produced by the mirror, nor by the face, nor by the one holding the mirror; it is neither produced spontaneously, nor does it arise without causes and conditions.
Why is it not produced by the mirror?
If the face has not yet reached the mirror, there is no image; for this reason, it is not produced by the mirror.
Why is it not produced by the face?
Without a mirror, there is no reflection.
Why would it not be produced by the one holding the mirror?
Without a mirror and without a face, there is no reflection.
Why is it not produced spontaneously?
If there were neither a mirror nor a face, there would be no reflection; the reflection exists only by depending upon the mirror and the face.
For this reason, it is not produced spontaneously.
Why is it not without causes and conditions?
If it were without causes and conditions, it would exist eternally;
if it existed eternally, it should appear even when the mirror is removed or the face is removed. For this reason, it is not without causes and conditions.
All phenomena are likewise: they are not self-made, not made by another, not made by both together, and not without causes and conditions.

Why are they not self-made? Because a "self" cannot be apprehended; because all phenomena produced by causes lack autonomy; and because all phenomena are dependent upon causes and conditions. Therefore, they are not self-made.
Nor is it created by another; since the self does not exist, the other likewise does not exist. If it were created by another, then the power of demerit and merit would be lost.
There are two kinds of creation by another:
that which is wholesome and that which is unwholesome.
If it were wholesome, it should bestow all happiness; if it were unwholesome, it should bestow all suffering.
If happiness and suffering were mixed, by what cause and condition would it bestow happiness?
For what reason is suffering given?
If it were shared, there would be two faults:
the fault of oneself and the fault of another.
If suffering and pleasure arose without causes and conditions, people would always experience pleasure and be free from all suffering;
if there were no causes and conditions, people would not create the causes for pleasure or eliminate the causes of suffering.
All phenomena necessarily have causes and conditions, yet due to ignorance, they do not know this.
For example, as a person seeks fire from wood, water from the earth, and wind from a fan;
such various things each have their own causes and conditions.
These are the causes and conditions for the conjunction of suffering and pleasure, and it is from these causes and conditions for the conjunction of suffering and pleasure that they arise.
Due to the causal conditions of karma from previous lives, and through the conditions of either wholesome or unwholesome conduct in this present life, one obtains suffering or pleasure.

When these various causes and conditions of suffering and pleasure are sought in reality, there is no person who creates them and no person who receives them; it is the empty five aggregates that create them, and the empty five aggregates that receive them.
When ignorant people obtain pleasure, their lustful minds become attached to it; when they encounter suffering, they give rise to anger.
When that pleasure ceases, they seek to obtain it again.
It is like a small child who sees a reflection in a mirror and feels joy and attachment; once the attachment is lost, he breaks the mirror in search of it, which the wise laugh at.
Losing happiness and seeking it again is likewise so; it is also ridiculed by the noble ones who have attained the Way.
For this reason, it is said that all phenomena are like images in a mirror.
Furthermore, just as a reflection in a mirror is truly empty, neither arising nor ceasing, yet deceives the eyes of ordinary people;
so too are all phenomena empty and without reality, neither arising nor ceasing, yet deceiving the eyes of ordinary beings.
Question: A reflection in a mirror arises from causes and conditions; there is a face, a mirror, a person holding the mirror, and light. Because these factors combine, the reflection arises.
Based on this reflection, one experiences sorrow or joy; thus it acts as both cause and effect. Why, then, do you say that "it is truly empty, neither arising nor ceasing"?
The answer is:
Because they arise from causes and conditions and lack independence, they are empty;
if a phenomenon were truly existent, it likewise could not arise from causes and conditions.
Why is this? If [the effect] already exists within the causes and conditions, then the causes and conditions would have no function;
if [the effect] does not yet exist within the causes and conditions, then the causes and conditions likewise would have no function.
For example, if curd already existed within milk, then this milk would not be the cause of the curd, because the curd already exists beforehand.
If the curd did not exist beforehand, then just as there is no curd in water, this milk likewise would not be the cause.
If curd could arise without a cause, why would it not also be produced from water?
If milk is the causal condition for curd, then milk itself is not independent; milk, too, arises from causes and conditions.
Milk exists because of the cow, and the cow arises from grass and water; thus, there is no end to this, as all things possess causes and conditions.

For this reason, regarding the effect within its causes and conditions, one cannot say it exists, nor can one say it does not exist, nor can one say it both exists and does not exist, nor can one say it neither exists nor does not exist. All phenomena arise from causes and conditions and lack intrinsic nature, like a reflection in a mirror.
As the verse says:
"If a phenomenon arises from causes and conditions, The nature of that phenomenon is truly empty;
If this phenomenon were not empty, It would not exist through causes and conditions."
For example, like a reflection in a mirror: it is neither the mirror nor the face, nor is it the person holding the mirror; it is not self-existent, yet not without cause.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, and furthermore, it is neither both existent and non-existent.
"This statement is also not accepted; such is called the Middle Way.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like reflections in a mirror.
Regarding "like a transformation," there are fourteen transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*):
The first dhyāna has two [spheres]:
the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
the second dhyāna has three:
The desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna;
the third and fourth [dhyānas]:
the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna.
The four dhyānas consist of five stages:
the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
These are the fourteen transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta), which perform eight kinds of transformations:
First, they can make things small, even down to the size of a minute atom;
second, they can make things large, even to the extent of filling empty space;
third, they can make things light, even as light as a goose feather.
Fourth, he possesses mastery:
he can make the large small and the long short, and so forth in various ways.
Fifth, he possesses sovereign power: because no person of great strength can humble him, it is said that "he possesses sovereign power."
Sixth, the ability to travel to distant places;
seventh, the ability to shake the earth;
eighth, the ability to obtain everything according to one's wishes.
One body can become many bodies, and many bodies can become one;
they pass through stone walls as if they were open space, walk upon water and tread upon emptiness, and reach out their hands to touch the sun and moon;
they are able to transform the four great elements.
Earth becomes water and water becomes earth; fire becomes wind and wind becomes fire; stone becomes gold and gold becomes stone.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of such transformations:
the medicinal herbs, precious objects, and magical arts of the desire realm can transform various things.
Those with supernormal powers can transform various objects through the power of their spiritual faculties;
the classes of devas, nāgas, and spirits can transform various objects through the power of their karmic retribution at birth;
and those born in the form realm can transform various objects through the power of their karmic retribution at birth and their cultivated meditative concentration.

Just as a magically conjured person has no birth, old age, sickness, or death, and neither suffering nor pleasure—being distinct from a human being—and for this reason is empty and lacks reality, so too are all phenomena:
they are all devoid of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like transformations.
Furthermore, that which is born through transformation has no fixed substance; it arises merely from the mind and performs various functions, yet none of these possess any reality.
The human body is also like this: it originally has no cause, but the body of the present life arises from the mind of a previous life; all of these lack any reality.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like illusions."
Just as when a mind of transformation ceases, the transformation itself ceases;
so it is with all phenomena: when causes and conditions cease, the fruit also ceases, lacking any independent autonomy.
Just as a magical creation, though truly empty, can cause sentient beings to give rise to sorrow and suffering, anger, joy and pleasure, or delusion and confusion; [so too are all phenomena].
All phenomena are likewise: although they are empty and lack substantial reality, they can cause sentient beings to give rise to joy, anger, sorrow, fear, and so forth.
For this reason, it is said that "all phenomena are like magical transformations."
Furthermore, just as the phenomena produced by transformation have no beginning, no middle, and no end, so too are all phenomena.
Just like a transformation, when they arise they come from nowhere, and when they cease they go nowhere.
All phenomena are likewise.
Furthermore, like the characteristics of a magical transformation, they are as pure as space, free from any defilement or attachment, and cannot be sullied by either sin or merit;
all phenomena are likewise, for they are, by their very nature, eternally pure, just as the dharma-nature, suchness, and the limit of reality are.

For example, there are four great rivers in Jambudvīpa, each of which has five hundred tributary streams; though these waters are variously impure, they all become pure once they enter the waters of the great ocean.
Question: One should not say that the matter of transformation is empty. Why is this?
The mind of transformation is also obtained through the cultivation of meditative concentration; from this mind, one produces various transformations—whether of persons or of phenomena.
Since these transformations possess causes and possess effects, how can they be empty?
Answer: As has already been answered regarding the reflection, it shall now be answered again.
Although these causes and conditions exist, the fruit of transformation is empty.

For example, when one says with the mouth, "there is nothing," although this arises from the mind and is spoken by the mouth, one cannot claim that because the mind and mouth exist, that which is said—"there is nothing"—is itself something existent.
If one says, "there is a second head or a third hand," although these arise from the mind and mouth, one cannot say that there actually are such heads or hands.
As the Buddha said:
"By contemplating non-arising, one attains liberation from arising;
by relying on the unconditioned, one attains liberation from the conditioned."
"Although one contemplates that unarisen phenomena are non-existent, they can still function as causes and conditions; the same applies to the unconditioned.
Although transformations are empty, they too can produce the causes and conditions for the mind."
For example, although the nine similes such as illusions and mirages do not exist, they can give rise to various kinds of mental states.
Furthermore, these manifested phenomena cannot be found when sought among the six causes and four conditions; because the six causes and four conditions therein are incompatible, they are empty.
Furthermore, emptiness does not consist in mere non-perception; rather, it is called "empty" because things lack practical utility.
For this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are like illusions."
Question:
If all dharmas are empty and without distinction according to these ten similes, why are only these ten matters used as analogies, rather than mountains, rivers, rocks, walls, and so forth?
Answer: Although all phenomena are empty, there are distinctions among them; there is emptiness that is difficult to understand and emptiness that is easy to understand.
Now, the emptiness that is easy to understand is used as a metaphor for the emptiness that is difficult to understand.
Furthermore, all phenomena are of two kinds:
those where the mind becomes attached and those where the mind does not become attached.
One uses the state where the mind is unattached to understand the state where the mind is attached.
Question:
Why are these ten similes points where the mind does not become attached? Answer:
These ten things do not abide for long, because they are easily produced and easily extinguished; for this reason, the mind does not become attached to them.

Furthermore, there are those who understand the ten similes as phenomena that deceive the ears and eyes, yet do not know that all phenomena are empty; therefore, these similes are used to illustrate all phenomena.

If there are those who become attached to these ten similes and fail to understand the various difficult arguments, taking them to be [the ultimate] existence, these ten similes will not serve their purpose; for them, other dharma-gates should be further explained.
Question:

If all dharmas are entirely empty, neither arising nor ceasing, then I already know that these various analogies such as the ten similes, as well as the various reasoned arguments based on causes and conditions, are all empty.
If all phenomena were entirely empty, one should not speak of this analogy;
if one speaks of this analogy, then they are not empty.
The answer is:
I have taught emptiness to refute the existence of all phenomena.
As for what is being discussed now: if you speak of existence, it has already been refuted;
if you speak of non-existence, there should be no objection!
For example, it is like an administrative bhikṣu who raises his hand and cries out in a loud voice, "The assembly, be silent!
This is using sound to block sound; it is not a seeking of sound.
For this reason, although all phenomena are said to be empty, neither arising nor ceasing, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, it is also said that they are not non-existent.
For this reason, it is said that "all phenomena are like transformations."
[Sūtra] Attaining unimpededness and fearlessness.
[Śāstra] Within the various aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and causal conditions, the mind is unimpeded, inexhaustible, and undying; this is called unimpededness and fearlessness.
Question:
As it was previously stated that all bodhisattvas are fearless amidst immeasurable assemblies, why is "unimpeded fearlessness" now mentioned again?
Answer: Previously, the causes of fearlessness were explained; now, the fruits of fearlessness are explained.

Among all assemblies, even within the assembly of bodhisattvas, he preaches the Dharma inexhaustibly and engages in debate without diminution, his mind free from doubt or difficulty, because he has already attained unimpeded fearlessness.
Furthermore, as previously stated, [the Buddha] is fearless amidst immeasurable multitudes; however, it was not explained by what power he is fearless.
For this reason, the fearlessnesses are further explained here, because he has attained the power of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-bala*).
Question:
If bodhisattvas also possess the unhindered knowledges and the fearlessnesses, what is the difference between a Buddha and a bodhisattva? Answer:
As I have previously stated, because the bodhisattvas themselves possess the power of fearlessness, they are fearless regarding all dharmas; this is not the fearlessness of a Buddha.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of unimpeded dharmas:
first, those that apply to all places; second, those that do not apply to all places.

Regarding those that do not apply to all places: for example, one may enter into a single scripture or even into hundreds of thousands of scriptures with unimpeded mastery, or enter into a single assembly or even into hundreds of thousands of assemblies without fear.
It is the same with all bodhisattvas: they are unimpeded within their own wisdom, yet not within the wisdom of a Buddha.
It is like when the Buddha set down his alms bowl; neither the five hundred arhats nor the various bodhisattvas such as Maitreya were able to take it up.
It is the same for all bodhisattvas: they are unimpeded within the power of their own strength, yet they encounter impediments within the power of the Buddha’s wisdom.
For this reason, it is said that "all bodhisattvas attain the unimpeded and the fearlessnesses."
[Sūtra] He fully knows the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings, and delivers them by means of subtle wisdom.
[Śāstra] Question:
In what way does he "fully know the mental activities of sentient beings"?
Answer:

It is because they know that the minds of sentient beings move through various phenomena in every place, like sunlight shining everywhere; thus, the Bodhisattva fully knows the inclinations and tendencies of the mental activities of sentient beings and instructs them accordingly.
It is said that there are two types of inclinations among all sentient beings:
first, those whose minds constantly seek pleasure;
and second, those who possess discerning wisdom and are able to distinguish between good and evil.
Do not follow after the mind; you should follow wisdom and reproach your own heart.
For countless eons, you have accumulated various karmas without ever feeling satiated, yet you have merely pursued worldly pleasures, failing to realize they are suffering.
Do you not see that attachment to worldly pleasures leads to affliction? That taking birth in the five realms of existence is entirely the work of the mind—who is it that causes this?
You are like a mad elephant, trampling and destroying everything without restraint—who is there to tame you?
If one attains skillful self-mastery, one will be free from worldly afflictions.
One should know that dwelling in the womb is impure and its suffering and distress are like those of hell;
once born into this world, there are the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, along with myriad forms of grief and lamentation.
If you are born in the heavens, you shall inevitably fall back down;
there is no peace within the three realms, so why do you delight in and cling to them?
Thus, in various ways, he rebuked his mind, vowing not to follow it.
This is how a bodhisattva knows the mental activities of sentient beings.
Question:
What is meant by "liberating them through subtle and wondrous wisdom"?
In this context, what is called subtle wisdom?
And what is called coarse wisdom?
The answer is:
Skillful worldly wisdom is called coarse wisdom; practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, the wisdom of generosity is coarse wisdom, while the wisdom of ethical discipline and meditative concentration is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, the wisdom of morality, concentration, and insight is called coarse wisdom; the wisdom of meditative absorption (dhyāna) is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, the wisdom of meditative absorption is called coarse wisdom; non-reliant meditative absorption is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, grasping at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is coarse wisdom; not grasping and not rejecting the characteristics of phenomena is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, destroying ignorance and other afflictions to attain the characteristics of phenomena is called coarse wisdom;

entering into the true nature of phenomena—like pure gold that is neither diminished nor lost, like a diamond that is neither broken nor destroyed, and like space that is untainted and unattached—is called subtle wisdom.
Having personally attained such immeasurable and subtle wisdom, the bodhisattvas further teach it to sentient beings.
For this reason, it is said: "All bodhisattvas fully know the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings, and deliver them by means of subtle wisdom."
12. Commentary on the Unimpeded Mind: The Twelfth Section of the Commentary on the Unimpeded Mind within the First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra. [Sūtra] The mind is unobstructed.
[Treatise] What is meant by "the mind being without obstruction"?
It means that regarding all those who are enemies, kin, or neither enemy nor kin, the bodhisattva maintains a mind of equanimity, free from any hindrance.
Furthermore, among all sentient beings in every world, if they come to harm or oppress him, his mind feels no resentment;
yet if they offer various forms of respect, he likewise feels no joy.
As a verse says:
"The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have no attachment in their hearts;
toward non-Buddhists and evil people, they harbor no hatred or anger."
"Purity such as this is called the absence of hindrance in the mind.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction in the mind regarding all phenomena.
Question:
If this bodhisattva has not yet attained the Buddha-way and has not yet attained all-knowledge (sarvajñā), how is it that his mind is unimpeded regarding all phenomena?
The answer is:
because this bodhisattva has attained immeasurable and pure wisdom, his mind is unimpeded regarding all phenomena.
Question:
Since the various bodhisattvas have not yet attained the path of Buddhahood, they should not possess immeasurable wisdom;
since they still possess residual fetters, they should not possess pure wisdom.
The answer is:
These bodhisattvas do not possess the physical bodies born of karmic fetters within the three realms; they have all attained mastery over the dharma-body and transcended old age, sickness, and death.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, they move through the worlds.
To adorn the Buddha-fields and to transform sentient beings;
having already attained mastery, one who wishes to become a Buddha is able to do so.
Question:
If a Dharma-body Bodhisattva is no different from a Buddha, why is he called a "Bodhisattva"?
Why does he pay homage to the Buddha and listen to the Dharma?
If he were different from the Buddha, how could he possess immeasurable pure wisdom?
The answer is:
Although this bodhisattva possesses the Dharma-body and is free from old age, sickness, and death, he differs slightly from a Buddha.
It is like the fourteenth day of the month, when people harbor doubts as to whether the moon is full or not.
In this way, although a bodhisattva can act as a Buddha and can preach the Dharma, they have not yet truly attained Buddhahood.
A Buddha is like the moon on the fifteenth day, fully perfected and beyond doubt.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of "immeasurable purity" (*apramāṇa-viśuddhi*):
first, that which actually has a measure, yet is called immeasurable by those who are unable to measure it.
For example, the waters of the ocean or the sands of the Ganges are called immeasurable because people cannot measure them.
In relation to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is not "immeasurable.
It is likewise with the immeasurable pure wisdom of a Bodhisattva; because it cannot be measured by any devas, humans, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, it is called "immeasurable wisdom.
When a Bodhisattva attains the path of non-arising, all fetters and afflictions are severed, and thus they attain pure wisdom.
Question:
If at that time all fetters have already been severed, what further remains to be severed at the time of attaining Buddhahood? Answer:
This purity is of two kinds:
first, when one attains Buddhahood, all fetters are completely eliminated, and one attains true purity;
second, when a bodhisattva relinquishes the physical body and attains the dharma-body, they sever all fetters and achieve purity.
For example, just as a single lamp can dispel darkness and perform its function, yet there may be a larger lamp that is twice as bright;
so it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Although what has been severed by a Bodhisattva is said to be severed, compared to what has been severed by a Buddha, it is still not yet exhaustive.
This is called “having attained immeasurable pure wisdom, one’s mind is without obstruction regarding all phenomena.
[Sūtra] One achieves great patience.
[Śāstra] Question:

Question: Previously, "equal patience" (samarṣa-kṣānti) and "dharma-patience" (dharma-kṣānti) were already explained; for what reason is "the accomplishment of great patience" (mahākṣānti-sampanna) now mentioned again? Answer:
When these two types of patience increase, they are termed "great patience."
Furthermore, the patience of equanimity (*samaropa-kṣānti*) consists of being able to endure all things among sentient beings;
the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomika-dharma-kṣānti*) consists of enduring within the profound Dharma.
Through the increase of these two patiences, one realizes them and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Finally, the physical body perceives all the Buddhas of the ten directions manifesting before it, seated in mid-air; this is called "the accomplishment of Great Patience" (*mahākṣānti*).

It is, for example, like in the Śrāvaka Dharma, where the increase of the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) is called the stage of Summit (*mūrdhan*), and the increase of the stage of Summit is called the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); there is no other distinct dharma that increases to become something else.
The same applies to equal patience (*samarṣaṇā*) and great patience (*mahākṣānti*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of patience:

patience toward beings (*satvakṣānti*) and patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Patience toward beings refers to enduring among sentient beings; for example, even if beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to inflict various evils upon one for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one’s mind remains free from anger.
Though they perform various acts of reverence and offering, their minds find no joy.
Furthermore, one observes that sentient beings have no beginning; if there were a beginning, there would be no causes and conditions.
If there are causes and conditions, there is no beginning; and if there is no beginning, there should likewise be no end.
Why is this? Because the beginning and the end are mutually dependent.
If there were no beginning or end, the middle would likewise not exist.

When observing in this manner, one does not fall into the two extremes of eternalism or nihilism; by viewing sentient beings through the path of peace and security, one does not give rise to false views—this is called the patience of birth.
To have no obstruction in one's mind regarding the extremely profound Dharma is called "Dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti).
Question:
What is the extremely profound Dharma?
Answer: As previously explained in the section on the profound patience regarding dharmas (*gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti*).

Furthermore, as for "profound dharmas": within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), fruits arise successively; yet the fruit does not exist within the cause, nor is it non-existent. That which emerges from this is called the profound dharma.

Furthermore, by entering the three gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—one attains the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, this is called the profound Dharma.
Furthermore, one contemplates all phenomena as neither empty nor non-empty, neither possessing marks nor markless, and neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
when the mind likewise does not cling during such contemplation, this is called the profound Dharma.
As it is said in verse:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are called the characteristic of emptiness; they are also called provisional designations, and they are also called the Middle Way."
If a phenomenon were truly existent, it should not return to non-existence;
that which was previously existent and is now non-existent is called "annihilation.
It is neither eternal nor annihilated, and neither existent nor non-existent.
"When consciousness ceases, speech also comes to an end.
To have unimpeded faith in this profound Dharma, neither regretting nor sinking back, is called "the accomplishment of great patience."
[Sūtra] Skillfully delivering [beings] according to reality.
[Śāstra] There are the teachings of non-Buddhists which, though they deliver sentient beings, do not deliver them according to reality. Why is this?
Because various false views, fetters, and latent tendencies remain,
although the followers of the Two Vehicles have those whom they deliver, it is not as they ought to deliver them. Why is this?
They lack omniscience because their skillful means and resolve are meager;
only the Bodhisattvas can deliver others skillfully and in accordance with reality.

It is like two ferrymen crossing people: one uses a floating bag or a raft of grass to ferry them across, while the other uses a large vessel; the difference between these two modes of transport is vast and profound.
The Bodhisattva’s skillful ferrying of sentient beings is likewise.
Furthermore, it is like treating an illness: through bitter medicine, acupuncture, or moxibustion, one may be cured despite the pain;
yet if there were a wondrous medicine named Sudarśana, the mere sight of it by a patient would heal all their ailments.
Although they are alike in curing illness, their methods differ in quality.
It is the same with the teaching and deliverance of people by Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.

As for ascetic practices (dhūta), meditating with a diligent mind during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and attaining the Way by contemplating suffering—this is the teaching of the Śrāvakas.
To contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena as neither bound nor liberated, so that the mind attains purity— this is the teaching of the Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the *Pūrva-yoga* of Mañjuśrī,
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“Virtuous One!

In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Siṃhaghoṣarāja. The lifespan of that Buddha and of sentient beings was ten trillion *nayuta* years, and the Buddha delivered sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.”
The name of the land is Thousand Radiances. All the trees within that land are composed of the seven treasures, and from these trees issue immeasurable, pure sounds of the Dharma:
the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-ceasing, and non-existence. When sentient beings hear them, their minds are liberated and they attain the Way.

"When King Siṃhaghoṣa Buddha first preached the Dharma at his inaugural assembly, nine hundred and ninety million people attained the path of Arhatship, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas was likewise."

All these bodhisattvas have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); they enter various dharma-gates, behold immeasurable buddhas whom they honor and make offerings to, are able to deliver immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, attain immeasurable dharani-gates, and are able to attain immeasurable varieties of samādhis.
The bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds and newly entered the gateway to the Path were beyond counting.
The immeasurable adornments of this buddha-field could not be fully described.
When the Buddha had finished his work of transforming beings, he entered nirvana without remainder.
The Dharma remained for sixty thousand years, and the sounds of the Dharma no longer issued from the trees.
At that time, there were two bodhisattva bhikṣus:
one named Priyamūla and the other named Jayamati.
"This Dharma Master Nandendriya is upright in his demeanor and does not abandon worldly ways, nor does he discriminate between good and evil.
Nandendriya’s disciples are intelligent and delight in the Dharma, taking pleasure in hearing profound meanings;
yet their teacher does not praise few desires and contentment, nor does he praise the practice of the precepts or the dhūtas, but speaks only of the purity of the true mark of all phenomena."
He said to his disciples:

"The characteristics of all dharmas—whether the characteristic of lust, the characteristic of anger, or the characteristic of delusion—are themselves the true characteristic of all dharmas, which is without any obstruction."
By these skillful means, he teaches his disciples to enter the wisdom of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇajñāna*).

At that time, among all people, the disciples are without anger and without regret; because their minds are without regret, they attain patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*); because they have attained patience toward beings, they then attain patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*), remaining as immovable as a mountain amidst the true Dharma.
“The Dharma Master Śreṣṭhamati maintained the precepts with purity and practiced the twelve dhūtas; he attained the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions.
However, the disciples of Śreṣṭhamati were of dull faculties and full of craving; they discriminated between what was pure and what was impure, and their minds consequently wavered.”
On another occasion, Jeta entered a village and went to the house of Udāyin’s disciple, where he sat upon a prepared seat;
there he praised the observance of precepts, fewness of desires, contentment, the practice of dhūta austerities,
and meditative seclusion in quiet places, while disparaging Udāyin, saying:

"This person preaches the Dharma and teaches others to enter into wrong views; they describe lust, anger, and delusion as being without obstruction. Such a person is one who practices in a mixed manner, not one who is purely pure."
This disciple, possessing sharp faculties and having attained the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), asked Jayamati:
"Virtuous One!
What is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of this dharma of sexual desire?"
He replied, “Lust is the characteristic of affliction. He asked:
"Is this affliction of sensual desire within,
or is it without? He replied:
"This affliction of sensual desire does not exist within, nor does it exist without;
if it were within, it should not arise dependent upon external conditions;
if it were without, it would have no concern with me and should not afflict me."
The householder said:

"If sensual desire does not come from within, nor from without, nor from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below; and if, when sought everywhere for its true nature, it cannot be found, then this phenomenon is neither born nor extinguished.
If it lacks the characteristics of birth and extinction and is empty and non-existent, how could it cause affliction?"
When Jayamati heard these words, his heart was displeased; unable to offer a reply, he rose from his seat and spoke these words:
"Nandendriya deceives many people, leading them into false paths."

“At that time, this Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati had not yet learned the Dhāraṇī of Sounds; upon hearing what the Buddha spoke, he would immediately feel joy, but upon hearing the words of non-Buddhists, he would become angry.
Hearing of the three unwholesome [paths], he was not pleased; hearing of the three wholesome [paths], he was greatly delighted.
Hearing discourse on birth and death, he felt sorrow; hearing of nirvāṇa, he felt joy.”
"From the householder's home to the grove of trees, he entered the vihāra and said to the bhikṣus:
'You should know that this person, the bodhisattva Priyamūla, is deceitful and causes many people to fall into evil and heterodox views.'"
