"Why is this? Because the characteristics of lust, anger, and delusion, as well as all dharmas, are all characterized by non-obstruction.
At that time, Nandendriya had this thought:
"This person harbors great anger and is shrouded by evil karma; he is destined to fall into a grave transgression!
I shall now preach the profound Dharma for him; though he may have nothing to attain in this present life, it will serve as a causal condition for the Buddha-way in future lives."
At that time, Nandimukha assembled the Sangha and, with single-minded concentration, recited these verses:
“Lust itself is the Way; Hatred and delusion are likewise so.
Within these three things, Lie the immeasurable paths of all Buddhas.”
If there is someone who discriminates between lust, anger, and delusion on one hand, and the Path on the other,
that person is far from the Buddha, as distant as heaven is from earth.
The Path and lust, anger, and delusion are one and the same in their fundamental equality.
If a person hears [of desire] and feels fear, they are far removed from the Buddha-way.
The nature of lust neither arises nor ceases; it cannot cause the mind distress.
If a person calculates in terms of "self," lust will lead them into the evil realms.
"To perceive existence and non-existence as distinct is not to be free from existence and non-existence;
if one knows that existence and non-existence are equal, one transcends and excels to attain the Buddha-way.

When he had spoken these and other verses, numbering more than seventy, thirty thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and eighteen thousand śrāvakas, because they were unattached to all dharmas, all attained liberation.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Jitāṃśu immediately fell into hell and underwent suffering for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of years!
Upon being reborn among humans, he was constantly slandered for seven hundred and forty thousand lifetimes, and for immeasurable kalpas he did not hear the name of a Buddha."

As these offenses gradually thin out, one is able to hear the Buddha-dharma and leave the household life to pursue the Way; yet, one again abandons the precepts, repeating this for sixty-three thousand lifetimes while constantly forsaking them.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, one acts as a śramaṇa; although one does not abandon the precepts, the faculties remain dull and obscured.

"This Bodhisattva Joyful Faculty (Nandendriya) has now become a Buddha in the eastern direction, past hundreds of thousands of billions of buddha-fields; his land is named Jewel Adornment, and his Buddha is named King of Radiance Surpassing the Sun."
Mañjuśrī said: "At that time, the bhikṣu Jayamati was my very self; I recall that at that time I underwent such immeasurable suffering."
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha:
"If there are those who seek the path of the three vehicles and do not wish to undergo various sufferings, they should not destroy the characteristics of all phenomena nor harbor anger."
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
"Having heard these verses, what benefit have you obtained?
He replied:

"Upon hearing this verse, I attained the end of all suffering; in every lifetime, I have obtained keen faculties and wisdom, being able to understand profound dharmas and skillfully expound their deep meanings, becoming the foremost among all bodhisattvas."
Passages such as these are called "skillfully explaining the characteristics of all dharmas.
This is termed "skillful deliverance according to reality.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.
The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise, Volume Thirteen, Chapter Seven: Explanation of the Vows for Buddha-fields within the First Chapter,
composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. 13. Treatise on the Vows for Buddha-lands [Sūtra]: "I vow to receive immeasurable worlds of all Buddhas."
[Treatise] Bodhisattvas, seeing that the worlds of the Buddhas are immeasurably adorned and pure, give rise to various vows.
There are Buddha-worlds where there is no suffering whatsoever, even to the point that the names of the three evil realms do not exist;
having seen these, the bodhisattvas themselves make this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, there shall be no manifold sufferings in my world, nor even the names of the three evil realms; it shall be thus.
My Buddha-world shall be adorned with the seven treasures, always possessing pure radiance day and night, without sun or moon.
Then he made this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, my world shall likewise always be adorned with pure radiance.
All sentient beings in that Buddha-world shall practice the ten wholesome paths and possess great wisdom; clothing, bedding, food, and drink shall arrive according to their thoughts.
Then he made this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, the clothing, food, and drink of the sentient beings in my world shall also be like this.

There shall be a Buddha-world consisting purely of Bodhisattvas, whose physical bodies possess the thirty-two marks of a Buddha and whose radiance shines through all things; even the names 'Śrāvaka' and 'Pratyekabuddha' do not exist there, nor are there any women. All shall practice the profound and wondrous path of the Buddha, traveling to the ten directions to teach and transform all beings.
Then he made this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, the sentient beings in my world shall also be like this.
I vow that all such various adornments and purities of immeasurable Buddha-worlds as these shall be attained."
For this reason, it is called "vowing to receive immeasurable Buddha-worlds. Question:
Since the practices and deeds of bodhisattvas are pure, they naturally obtain pure retribution; why must they necessarily establish vows before they can attain them?
For example, when a farmer harvests grain, why would he need to make further wishes?
The answer is:
if one performs meritorious deeds without making vows, there is nothing to establish or direct them; it is the vow that acts as a guide and leader, enabling what is accomplished.
It is like melting gold: according to what the smith fashions, the gold has no fixed form.
As the Buddha has said:
there are those who cultivate the merit of minor giving and the merit of minor precepts, yet do not understand the methods of dhyāna.

Hearing that among humans there are those who possess wealth and pleasure, their minds constantly dwell upon this with attachment; they long for it without relinquishing it, and after the end of their lives, they are reborn among those who possess wealth and pleasure.
Furthermore, there are those who cultivate the merit of minor giving and the merit of minor precepts, yet do not know the methods of dhyāna.

Hearing that there are the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven—where beings are single-mindedly intent on sensual desire and transformations come from themselves to provide for them—and hearing of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, where others transform sensual desires and provide them for one’s enjoyment, continuing thus in succession, and therefore it is named "Mastery over Others' Transformations"—they constantly wish for and delight in these states, and after the end of their lives, each is reborn therein.
All of these are obtained through the power of vows.
It is the same for a bodhisattva: they cultivate the vow for a pure world and subsequently attain it.
For this reason, one knows that by means of a vow, one receives superior fruits.
Furthermore, the task of adorning a Buddha-field is a great undertaking; it cannot be accomplished by the practice of merit alone, but requires the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
For example, although the strength of an ox can pull a cart, it must rely on a driver to reach its destination.
It is the same with the aspiration to purify a world: merit is like the ox, and aspiration is like the driver.
Question:
If one does not make a vow, will one not obtain merit? Answer:
Although one may attain [merit], it is not as good as having a vow;
for a vow can assist merit, and by constantly recollecting what one has practiced, one's merit increases.
Question:
If making a vow results in a karmic retribution, then why would a person who commits the ten unwholesome deeds not receive the retribution of hell if they do not vow for it?
The answer is:

although sins and merits have fixed retributions, one who makes a vow cultivates a small amount of merit; because of the power of that vow, they obtain a great fruit of retribution, as previously explained.
Among transgressions, the retribution is suffering; all sentient beings wish to obtain happiness and none wish for suffering. Therefore, they do not desire hell.
For this reason, the retribution for merit is immeasurable, whereas the retribution for sin is limited.
Some say: The greatest sin lies in the Avīci Hell, where one receives retribution for one kalpa;
the greatest merit lies in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, where one receives retribution for eighty thousand great kalpas.
The vows of the bodhisattvas to purify their worlds also involve entering the path and attaining nirvana over immeasurable kalpas; this constitutes eternal bliss.
Question:

As stated in the "Niraya Chapter," regarding the sin of slandering the *prajñāpāramitā*, when the kalpa of this world comes to an end, one goes to the hells of other directions. Why, then, is it said that "the greatest sin receives retribution in hell for one kalpa"?
Answer: For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha-dharma employs two paths of teaching:
first, the path of the Buddhas; second, the path of the śrāvakas.
The Buddha taught that one who commits the five heinous crimes within the path of the śrāvakas will undergo retribution in hell for one kalpa;

however, regarding one who destroys the Dharma of the Buddha within the path of the bodhisattvas, it is said that when this kalpa ends, they shall go to other regions to undergo immeasurable suffering.
The merit of the Śrāvaka-dharma is the foremost, whereby one receives [its fruits] for eighty thousand kalpas;
the great merit within the Bodhisattva path leads to receiving [its fruits] for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
For this reason, merit must be accompanied by a vow; this is called "vowing to receive immeasurable Buddha-worlds."
[Sūtra] One recollects the immeasurable Buddha-lands and the samādhis of the Buddhas, which are constantly present before one.
[Śāstra] "Immeasurable Buddha-lands" refers to the Buddha-lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

“Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi” (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) means that one constantly perceives all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time with the mind’s eye, as if they were present before one.
Question: What is meant by Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi?
Answer: There are two kinds of Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*):
first, within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, one perceives with the mind's eye a single Buddha-body filling the ten directions; [the second is as follows].
Second, regarding the Bodhisattva path within immeasurable Buddha-fields, one recollects the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions.
For this reason, it is said: "Recalling immeasurable Buddha-fields, the samādhi of all Buddhas is constantly present before one."
Question:
Since the samādhis of a bodhisattva are of various kinds and immeasurable, for what reason is only this Bodhisattva’s Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi praised as being constantly present?
Answer: Because this bodhisattva recollects the Buddha, they are able to enter the path of the Buddha.
For this reason, the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha is constantly present before them.
Furthermore, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) can eliminate various afflictions as well as transgressions from previous lives;

other samādhis, however, may be able to eliminate lust but not anger, or able to eliminate anger but not lust, or able to eliminate delusion but not lust or hatred, or able to eliminate the three poisons but not transgressions from previous lives.
This Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) can eliminate various afflictions (*kleśa*) and various transgressions.
Furthermore, this Buddha-remembrance samādhi possesses great merit and virtue and is able to deliver sentient beings;
for those bodhisattvas who wish to deliver sentient beings, no other samādhi possesses such merit and virtue as this Buddha-remembrance samādhi, which can swiftly extinguish all transgressions.
As it is said:
In the past, there were five hundred merchants who entered the sea to gather treasures;
they encountered the makara fish-king opening his mouth, and as the seawater rushed into it, their ship was driven along with great speed.
The boatman asked the person on the upper deck,
"What do you see? He replied:
"They see three suns appearing, white mountains arrayed, and the waters rushing forward as if entering a great pit.

The boatman said, "This is the opening of the mouth of the King of Makara fish; one is the actual sun, the two others are the fish's eyes, the white mountains are its teeth, and the rushing waters are entering its mouth."
"We are finished!
Let each of us seek the various heavenly deities to save ourselves!
At that time, each person sought out the deity they served, but it was of no benefit whatsoever.
Among them, a lay follower who observed the five precepts said to the crowd:
"We should together recite 'Namo Buddha. The Buddha is supreme; he is able to rescue us from suffering and calamity!"
The multitude, with one mind and in unison, cried out, "Namo Buddha.

These fish had been disciples of the Buddha who had violated the precepts in a previous life; having attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajātismara*), they heard the sound of the name of the Buddha being invoked and their hearts were moved by repentance and awakening. They immediately closed their mouths, and the boatmen were thus delivered.
Because of mindfulness of the Buddha, one can eliminate grave offenses and be rescued from all sufferings and calamities; how much more so for the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha!

Furthermore, the Buddha is the King of Dharma and the Bodhisattvas are the Generals of Dharma; that which is honored and revered is solely the World-Honored Buddha. Therefore, one should constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, by constantly recollecting the Buddha, one obtains various merits and benefits.
For example, just as a high minister who has received exceptional favor and grace constantly thinks of his sovereign;

so too is the Bodhisattva: knowing that all manner of merits and immeasurable wisdom are obtained from the Buddha, and because he recognizes the gravity of this debt of gratitude, he constantly recollects the Buddha.

Regarding your question, "How can one constantly recollect the Buddha without practicing other samādhis?", the present statement says "constantly recollects" but does not say "does not practice other samādhis. Because the practice of the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi is predominant, it is said that one "constantly recollects."

Furthermore, although the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have been explained previously, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) has not yet been discussed; therefore, it is explained now.
[Sūtra] It is able to invite immeasurable Buddhas.
[Treatise] There are two kinds of "invocation":
first, when the Buddha has first attained the Way, the bodhisattva performs the invocation three times at night and three times by day—six times in total.
Baring the right shoulder and joining the palms, he says:

"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, when the immeasurable Buddhas have first attained the Way but have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma, I, [Name], entreat all those Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, so as to deliver and liberate them all."

Second, when the Buddhas wish to relinquish their immeasurable lifespans and enter parinirvāṇa, the bodhisattva likewise, three times during the night and three times during the day, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and said:

"The immeasurable Buddhas in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, I, [name], entreat you to remain long in the world for incalculable kalpas, to deliver all beings, and to benefit sentient beings."
This is called "being able to invite immeasurable Buddhas.
A question is asked:

According to the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma, they should naturally preach the Dharma to extensively deliver sentient beings; whether invited or not invited, such is the inherent nature of the Dharma. Why, then, is it necessary to invite them?

If it were possible to invite the Buddhas by facing them directly before one, that might be so; however, since one does not even see the Buddhas in the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions, how can they be invited?
Answer: Although the Buddhas must inevitably preach the Dharma and do not wait for an invitation, the one who invites them should also obtain merit.
It is like a great king who, despite having abundant fine food, will surely grant favor and merit to anyone who requests it, because he records the sincerity of that person's heart.

Furthermore, it is like the mind of loving-kindness that contemplates all sentient beings and wishes for them to obtain happiness; although the sentient beings themselves obtain nothing, the one who contemplates gains great merit.
Inviting the Buddha to preach the Dharma is likewise so.
Furthermore, there are Buddhas who, being uninvited by anyone, enter parinirvāṇa without preaching the Dharma.
For example, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna entered parinirvāṇa because no one had invited him.
Subsequently, the bodies of transformation Buddhas and the stupas made of the seven treasures appeared all at once, in order to testify to and expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

This was also like the case of the Buddha Susaṃtata, whose disciples’ fundamental practices were not yet mature; he thus entered parinirvāṇa prematurely, leaving behind a transformation Buddha for one kalpa to deliver sentient beings.
Now this Śākyamuni Buddha, after attaining the Way, remained in silence for fifty-seven days without preaching the Dharma;
he said of himself:
"My Dharma is exceedingly profound, difficult to understand and difficult to know!"
"All sentient beings are bound and attached to worldly dharmas; there is no one capable of liberating them. It would be better to remain silent and enter the bliss of nirvana.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-rāja, and the various devas joined their palms in respectful salutation and entreated the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings for the first time.
The Buddha then silently accepted the invitation; later, he went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī and turned the Wheel of Dharma.
If this is so, how can you say that the invitation was of no benefit?
Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma regards all sentient beings with impartiality, without distinction of noble or base, nor light or heavy;
if there is someone who invites him, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of that invitation.
Although sentient beings may not personally invite the Buddha face-to-face, the Buddha constantly perceives their minds and hears their invitation;

even if the Buddhas were to neither hear nor see them, the act of inviting the Buddha would still possess merit—how much more so when the Buddha both hears and sees it, yet derives no benefit from it?
Question:
Since you know that requesting the Buddha is beneficial, why do you request specifically by means of these two matters? Answer:
The other matters need not be requested, but these two matters must certainly be requested;
for if they were explained without being requested, there would be those among the non-Buddhists who would say:
"The essence of the Way is eternally fixed; why then do you cling to dharmas and engage in so much talk and activity?"
For this reason, it must be requested before being spoken.
If someone were to say:
"If one knows the characteristics of all phenomena, one should not be attached to life and remain long in the world, but should instead enter nirvana early."
For this reason, it was necessary to request [the teaching].
Had he taught without being requested, people would have said that the Buddha was attached to the Dharma and desired to make it known;
for this reason, he waited for a request before turning the wheel of Dharma.
The various followers of external paths are personally attached to their own doctrines; whether invited or uninvited, they preach them to others on their own initiative.

The Buddha, however, is neither attached to nor does he crave any phenomena. Out of compassion for sentient beings, if there is one who invites the Buddha to speak, the Buddha then speaks for them; yet the Buddhas do not initially turn the wheel of Dharma without being invited.
As a verse says:
"What do the Buddhas declare to be real? What is that which is unreal?
Both reality and unreality— These two things are unattainable."
"Such is the true nature of reality, which does not engage in conceptual play regarding all phenomena;
yet out of compassion for sentient beings, he employs skillful means to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, if the Buddha were to preach the Dharma on his own initiative without being requested, it would imply that he was manifesting himself and adhering to a doctrine of his own, and he would consequently have to answer the fourteen difficult questions.

Now, when the various devas invite the Buddha to preach the Dharma, it is solely for the purpose of severing old age, sickness, and death, which is a state free from frivolous proliferation; therefore, there is no fault in not answering the fourteen difficult questions.
For these reasons, it was necessary to request him before he could turn the wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, as the Buddha was born among humans and acts according to the ways of a Great Man, although he possesses great compassion, he does not preach unless requested;
if he were to preach without being asked, he would be ridiculed by the non-Buddhists.
For this reason, one must first request [the teaching].
Furthermore, as the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) revere Brahmā, if Brahmā himself makes the request, the minds of the non-Buddhists will be subdued.
Moreover, according to the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, one should constantly perform three activities during the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night.
First, at dawn, baring the right shoulder, join the palms and pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:

"I, [Name], whether in this life or throughout immeasurable kalpas of past lives, have committed evil karma and offenses of body, speech, and mind; before the present Buddhas of the ten directions, I repent them, praying that they may be extinguished and eliminated, so that I shall never commit them again."
At midday, evening, and night, one should likewise do so three times.

Second, one should recollect the merits performed by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as all the merits possessed by their assemblies of disciples, and rejoice in them while encouraging and assisting them.

Third, to exhort and entreat all Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions to turn the wheel of Dharma for the first time, and to request that these Buddhas remain in the world for immeasurable eons to deliver and liberate all beings.
When a bodhisattva practices these three matters, their merit is immeasurable, and they draw closer to attaining Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is necessary to make this request.
[Sūtra] They are able to sever various views, fetters, and all afflictions.
[Treatise] There are two kinds of "views":
first, eternalism; second, annihilationism.
Those with the view of eternalism perceive the five aggregates as permanent and their minds find acceptance and delight therein.
Those with the view of annihilation see the cessation of the five aggregates and find mental acceptance and delight therein.
Most sentient beings fall into these two views.
The Bodhisattva personally severs these two and is also able to eliminate the two views of all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Middle Way.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of views:
the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of views:
All phenomena are endurable; all phenomena are not endurable; all phenomena are both endurable and not endurable.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of views:
that the world is eternal, that the world is impermanent, that the world is both eternal and impermanent, and that the world is neither eternal nor impermanent.
The same applies to whether the self and the world are finite, infinite, both, or neither;
and whether one exists after death, does not exist after death, both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of views:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Such various views as these, up to and including the sixty-two views, are all abandoned.
These various views arise from various causes and conditions, are observed through various gates of wisdom, and are heard from various teachers.
Such various characteristics can act as the cause for various fetters and latencies, and can bring about various sufferings for sentient beings; these are called "various views."
The meaning of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) will be explained in detail later.
As for "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*), there are ten:

the envelopment of anger, the envelopment of concealing transgressions, the envelopment of drowsiness, the envelopment of sleep, the envelopment of frivolity, the envelopment of restlessness, the envelopment of shamelessness, the envelopment of lack of dread, the envelopment of avarice, and the envelopment of envy.
Furthermore, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) bind and entangle the mind, they are all termed "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*).
As for "affliction," it is so called because it causes the mind to be vexed and brings about distress.
There are two kinds of afflictions:
internal attachment and external attachment. Internal attachment refers to the five views, doubt, pride, and so forth;
external attachment refers to lust, anger, and so forth.
Ignorance is both internal, external, and common to both.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of fetters:
first, those belonging to craving; second, those belonging to views.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
those belonging to lust, those belonging to hatred, and those belonging to delusion.
These are called afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*): some say there are "ten envelopments," while others say there are "five hundred envelopments.
Defilements (*kleśa*) are called all the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*):
there are nine fetters and seven proclivities, which together constitute the ninety-eight fetters.
As stated in the meaning of the *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma*:
the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and the ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) constitute the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the *Vātsīputrīya-abhidharma*, the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are likewise [counted] as five hundred envelopments.

In this way, these various afflictions (*kleśa*), the bodhisattva is able to sever for himself through various skillful means (*upāya*), and is also able to skillfully sever the afflictions of others.

For example, when the Buddha was in the world, there were three brothers—the eldest, the middle, and the youngest—who heard that in the city of Vaiśālī there was a courtesan named Āmrapālī, in Śrāvastī there was a courtesan named Sumana, and in Rājagṛha there was a courtesan named Utpalavarṇā.

There were three men who each heard people praising three women for their incomparable beauty; day and night they focused their thoughts on them, their minds attached and unable to let go, so that in their dreams they dreamed of engaging in sexual union with them.
Having awakened, he thought to himself:
"She did not come, nor did I go, yet the act of lust was accomplished.
Because of this, he attained realization:
"Are all dharmas likewise?
Thereupon, he went to where the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla was and asked about this matter.
Bhadrapāla replied:
"All phenomena are truly thus: they all arise from mindfulness.

In this way, he skillfully taught the emptiness of all phenomena through various means to these three people; at that time, the three immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
These bodhisattvas are likewise; they skillfully preach the Dharma in various ways for the sake of all sentient beings, severing all views, fetters, and afflictions.
This is called "being able to sever various views, fetters, and all afflictions."
[Sūtra] They sportively give birth to hundreds of thousands of samādhis.

[Śāstra] Because the bodhisattvas’ minds are disciplined through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and by the power of pure wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), they are able to produce various kinds of samādhis.
What is samādhi? When the virtuous mind dwells in one place without movement, this is called samādhi.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of samādhi:
There are the samādhis with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, and without vitarka or vicāra.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of samādhi:
samādhi bound to the desire realm, samādhi bound to the form realm, samādhi bound to the formless realm, and unbound samādhi.

The bodhisattva samādhis employed herein are as previously described; because they have not yet been perfected within the Buddha-samādhis, yet are practiced and cultivated with diligence, it is said that they "can produce" them.
Question:
For what reason do the bodhisattvas produce and sport within these hundreds of thousands of kinds of samādhis? Answer:

Sentient beings are infinite, and their mental activities differ: some possess sharp faculties while others are dull; regarding the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), some are thick while others are thin.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva practices hundreds of thousands of kinds of samādhi to sever these afflictions (*kleśa*).
For example, if one wishes to make poor people very wealthy, one must prepare all kinds of wealth and provisions; only when everything is fully prepared can one then rescue those who are poor.
Furthermore, just as a person who wishes to extensively treat various illnesses must prepare a variety of medicinal herbs before being able to cure them,
so too does a bodhisattva, wishing to extensively deliver sentient beings, practice hundreds of thousands of diverse samādhis.
Question:
One should merely bring forth this samādhi; for what reason, then, does one further sport within it? Answer:
When a Bodhisattva’s mind gives rise to various samādhis and delights in entering and emerging from them with mastery, this is called "play" (līlā);
it is not the play of fettered attachment. "Play" signifies mastery;
just as a lion is sovereign and fearless among deer, it is therefore called "play."
These bodhisattvas possess mastery over all samādhis; they are able to emerge from them, enter them, and likewise [remain within them].
Other people, regarding samādhi, may be able to enter it with mastery, but cannot master remaining in it or emerging from it;
or they may master remaining in it, but cannot master entering it or emerging from it.
There are those who can emerge at will, but cannot abide or enter at will;
there are those who can enter and abide at will, but cannot emerge at will;
and there are those who can abide and emerge at will, but cannot enter at will.
Because these bodhisattvas possess mastery in three ways, it is said that they “sportively give birth to hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
[Sūtra] These and other such immeasurable merits are accomplished by all the bodhisattvas.
[Treatise] These bodhisattvas dwell together with the Buddha; were one to wish to praise their merits, they could not be exhausted even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.
For this reason, it is said that they have "accomplished immeasurable merit."
[Sūtra] Their names were: Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla (in the language of Qin,
"Good Protector"), Bodhisattva Ratnākara (in the language of Qin, "Jewel Accumulation"), Bodhisattva Nāyaka ("Guide"),
Bodhisattva Naradatta ("Narada"), Bodhisattva Jyotipāla ("Star-Attainer"), and Bodhisattva Varuṇa ("Water Deity").
The Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva Lord of Devas, the Bodhisattva Great Intention, the Bodhisattva Beneficial Intention,
the Bodhisattva Increasing Intention, the Bodhisattva Non-Vain Vision, the Bodhisattva Good Progress, the Bodhisattva Superior Power,
the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence, the Bodhisattva Never-Relinquishing-Diligence, the Bodhisattva Sun-Treasury, and the Bodhisattva Unimpaired Intention.
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas such as Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī (translated into Chinese as Miaode),
Ratnamudrādhara, Nityotkṣiptahasta, and Maitreya— countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas,
all of whom were *ekajātipratibaddha* heirs to the position of the Honored One.
Regarding the "stages":
[The Treatise] states that these various bodhisattvas, together with the Buddha, were dwelling on Vulture Peak in the city of Rājagṛha.
Question:
Question: Since there are so many bodhisattvas in this way, why are only the names of twenty-two bodhisattvas mentioned? Answer:
Bodhisattvas are immeasurable—ten million, a hundred million, a billion; they could not be fully described. If one were to describe them all, they could not be contained within written words.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas herein:
those who live at home and those who have left the home life.
The sixteen bodhisattvas beginning with Śubhavyūha are bodhisattvas who live at home;
The lay bodhisattva Bhadrapāla is a long-time resident of Rājagṛha;
the prince bodhisattva Ratnākara is a native of Vaiśālī;
and the elder’s son bodhisattva Jyotipāla is a native of Campā.
The lay bodhisattva Śreṣṭhin was a native of Śrāvastī;
the brahmin bodhisattva Nalada was a native of Mithilā;
and the upāsaka Varuṇa was a bodhisattva.
Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and other such bodhisattvas are bodhisattvas who have left the household life.
Avalokiteśvara and others have come from buddha-fields in other directions.
If one speaks of those living at home, this includes all bodhisattvas dwelling in households.
The same applies to those who have left the household life and those from other regions. Question:
What special excellence does the Bodhisattva Susthitamati possess that he is mentioned first?
If the greatest were placed first, one should have mentioned Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
if the smallest were placed first, one should have mentioned Bodhisattvas who are still in their physical bodies and have only recently resolved to attain enlightenment.
The answer is:
It is neither because of greatness nor because of smallness; it is because the Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha is a long-time resident of Rājagṛha and is the greatest among the lay bodhisattvas.
The Buddha was in Rājagṛha and wished to preach the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, it is taught at the very beginning.
Furthermore, this Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha possesses immeasurable and manifold merits, as the Buddha himself manifested before him in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* Sūtra to praise those merits.
Question: If Maitreya Bodhisattva should be titled "the Successor," why do the other bodhisattvas also say, "those who shall succeed to the Honored Position"? Answer:
These bodhisattvas shall all succeed to the position of Buddha in the buddha-fields of the ten directions.

**Commentary on the Emission of Light, Chapter 14 of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra** [Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One personally prepared a lion throne, sat upon it cross-legged, straightened his body, and fixed his mindfulness before him. He entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi (King of Samādhis), into which all other samādhis are fully contained.
[Treatise] Question:
Since the Buddha has attendants and various bodhisattvas, for what reason does he personally prepare the lion throne? Answer:
This was created through the Buddha’s transformative power (nirmāṇa) in order to bring satisfaction to the great assembly; for this reason, Ānanda was unable to spread it.
Furthermore, because it was produced by the Buddha’s mind, it is said that he "spread it himself."
Question: Why is it called the "Lion Throne"?
Is it because the Buddha transformed himself into a lion, or did a real lion come, or was it made of gold, silver, wood, or stone?
Furthermore, since the lion is not a virtuous beast, it is unnecessary for the Buddha; moreover, as there is no cause or condition [for its presence], it should not come!
The answer is:
this is merely called "lion"; it is not an actual lion.
The Buddha is the lion among men; therefore, wherever the Buddha sits—whether on a couch or upon the ground—it is called a "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*).
It is just as the place where a king of the present day sits is also called a lion throne.
Furthermore, the King summons men of prowess, who are also called "human lions";
people refer to the king as a "human lion" as well.
Moreover, just as a lion strides alone among four-footed beasts without fear and is able to subdue them all;
The Buddha is also like this; because he has completely subdued all among the ninety-six kinds of paths and is without fear, he is called the "Lion among Men.
Question:
There are many ways of sitting; for what reason does the Buddha exclusively use the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*)?
The answer is:
Among all methods of sitting, the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka) is the most secure and comfortable, causing no exhaustion;
this is the method of sitting for one who practices dhyāna, as it holds the hands and feet steady and prevents the mind from wandering.
Furthermore, among all four modes of physical deportment, this is the most secure.
This is the sitting posture for attaining the Way through meditative concentration; when the Māra King sees it, his heart is filled with anxiety and fear.

Sitting in this manner is the dharma of those who have left the household life; when one sits cross-legged beneath the forest trees, all who see it are filled with great joy, knowing that this practitioner will surely attain the Way.
As a verse says:
"If one sits with legs crossed, The body at ease, entering samādhi;
One’s majestic virtue is revered by all, Like the sun illuminating the world."
Having removed sleep and sloth that shroud the mind, the body is light and free from fatigue;
awakening is likewise agile and easy, sitting at ease like a coiled dragon.
Seeing him depicted in the lotus posture, even the King of Māras is filled with sorrow and fear.
"How much more so for one who has entered the Way, sitting peacefully without wavering.
For this reason, one sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that his disciples should sit in this manner.

There are followers of external paths who either constantly stand on tiptoe seeking the Way, or remain perpetually standing, or carry their feet upon their shoulders—such are their eccentricities; their minds are submerged in the sea of heterodoxy and their bodies lack peace and stability.
For this reason, the Buddha taught his disciples to sit with legs crossed and the body held straight.
Why straighten the body?
Because when the mind is easily rectified, the body remains upright in its seated posture and the mind does not become indolent;
one should align the mind and rectify the intention, binding mindfulness to what lies before.
If the mind wanders and scatters, one should collect it and bring it back.
Because one desires to enter samādhi, all various wandering thoughts must likewise be collected;
by binding the mindfulness in this manner, one enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
What is meant by the "King of Samādhis Samādhi"?
This samādhi is the most supreme and sovereign among all samādhis, and it is able to take immeasurable dharmas as its objects.
Just as among all people the king is foremost, and among kings the universal monarch (cakravartin) is foremost, and throughout the heavens above and the earth below the Buddha is foremost;
so too is this samādhi, for it is the most supreme among all samādhis.
Question:
If all samādhis should be foremost by virtue of the Buddha's power, for what reason is only the Samādhirāja specifically called the foremost?
Answer:
Although all the samādhis practiced by the Buddha are supreme by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, there must nonetheless be degrees of distinction among all dharmas.

Just as the various treasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, though they surpass all the treasures of other kings, still possess internal distinctions among these rare jewels, with their value and quality differing vastly.
Regarding this King of Samādhis Samādhi, by which concentration is it subsumed,
and what are its characteristics? Some say:
The Samādhirāja-samādhi is named the "Mark of Sovereignty" (vaśitā-lakṣaṇa); it is well-comprised within the five aggregates and resides in the fourth dhyāna. Why is this?

All Buddhas, while practicing the Path of Seeing the Truths (darśana-mārga) within the fourth dhyāna, attain the stage of Anāgāmin and immediately realize the Buddha-way within eighteen moments of mind.
Having relinquished his life-span within the fourth dhyāna, he arises within the fourth dhyāna and enters nirvana without remainder.
Within the fourth dhyāna, there are eight places of birth and abiding.
The liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) mostly reside within the fourth dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna is called "unshakable" (*āneñjya*), for it is free from obstructive factors that hinder meditative concentration.

In the desire realm, various sensual desires obstruct the mind of concentration; in the first dhyāna, the mind is moved by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); in the second dhyāna, it is moved by great joy (*prīti*); in the third dhyāna, it is moved by great bliss (*sukha*); but in the fourth dhyāna, there is no such movement.
Furthermore, the first dhyāna is consumed by fire, the second dhyāna is reached by water, and the third dhyāna is reached by wind; the fourth dhyāna is free from these three afflictions.
Therein, inhalation and exhalation cease, and equanimity and mindfulness are pure.
For this reason, the Samādhirāja-samādhi should be situated within the fourth dhyāna, like a precious object placed in a secure treasury.
Furthermore, some say:
"Who is able to know the characteristics of the Buddha’s samādhis?"
The teachings of all Buddhas are of one mark, which is marklessness; they are immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable.
If even other samādhis are immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable, how much more so the King of Samādhis!
This samādhi can be known only by a Buddha.
If even a Buddha’s supernormal powers and observance of the precepts are beyond comprehension, how much more so this King of Samādhis!
Furthermore, as for the Samādhirāja-samādhi (King of Samādhis), because all samādhis enter into it, it is called the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
It is like the myriad rivers and streams of Jambudvīpa all entering the great ocean, or like all the people being subject to the king.
Question:
Since the Buddha possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and there is nothing he does not know, for what reason must he enter this Samādhirāja-samādhi before he can know [it]?
Answer:
In order to clarify that wisdom arises from causes and conditions, he refutes the claims of the six non-Buddhist teachers who say, "Our wisdom is always present at all times and knows eternally."
For this reason it is said: "Because the Buddha enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi he knows; if he does not enter it, he does not know. Question:
If this is so, then the power of the Buddha is diminished!
The answer is:
When entering this Samādhirāja-samādhi, it is not considered difficult; one attains it immediately upon thought.
It is not like the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or various lesser bodhisattvas who seek entry through expedient means.
Furthermore, upon entering this Samādhirāja-samādhi, he causes the six supernormal powers to penetrate throughout the ten directions, becoming limitless and immeasurable.
Furthermore, when the Buddha enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi, he manifests various transformations and displays great supernormal powers.
If one were to manifest supernatural powers without having entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi, some might think:
"The Buddha uses the power of illusion or the power of incantations; or perhaps it is through the supernatural power of a mighty dragon, or he is a deva and not a human."
Why is this? Because a single body manifests immeasurable bodies through various transformations of light, they are called "non-humans.
To sever this doubt, the Buddha entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
Furthermore, if the Buddha were to enter any other samādhi, the devas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas might be able to fathom and know it;
although one would say that the Buddha’s spiritual power is great, it would still be conceivable, and thus their reverent heart would not be profound.

For this reason, when he enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi, all the various holy ones, including even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, are unable to fathom or know it; they do not know upon what the Buddha’s mind relies nor what its object of perception is.
For this reason, the Buddha enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
Furthermore, there are times when the Buddha emits great radiance and manifests great supernormal powers:

as at the time of his birth, the time he attained the Way, the time he first turned the Wheel of Dharma, the time of the great assembly of devas and sages, or when he defeated the non-Buddhists; on all such occasions, he emits great radiance.

Now, wishing to manifest its extraordinary excellence, he emits a great radiance so that all devas, humans, and sentient beings of the ten directions, as well as all arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, may see and know it.
For this reason, he enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
Furthermore, there are inferior, middling, and superior levels of radiant supernormal power (*ṛddhi*):
incantations and illusions that can produce transformations of light are the inferior;
The gods, nāgas, and spirits who obtain radiance and supernormal powers as a result of their retribution possess the intermediate level;
those who enter various samādhis and, by the power of the mind and merit of the present life, emit great radiance and manifest great supernormal powers possess the superior level.
For this reason, the Buddha enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
Question:
Since each of the various samādhis has its own distinct characteristics, how can all samādhis be entirely contained within it?
Answer: When one attains this King of Samādhis Samādhi, all samādhis are attained; therefore, it is said that "one enters into them all.
By the power of this samādhi, all samādhis—immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable—are attained.
For this reason, it is called "entry.
Furthermore, when one enters this Samādhirāja-samādhi, one can enter any other samādhi whenever one wishes to do so.
Furthermore, upon entering this Samādhirāja-samādhi, one is able to observe the characteristics of all samādhis, as if looking down from a mountain peak.
Moreover, when the Buddha enters this Samādhirāja-samādhi, he is able to observe all worlds throughout the ten directions, and he is also able to observe all sentient beings.
For this reason, he entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi, surveyed the world with his divine eye, and smiled with his entire body.
[Treatise] Question:
How is it that the World-Honored One, having entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi without performing any deliberate action, arises from that concentration and gazes upon the world?
The answer is:
The Buddha enters the Samādhirāja-samādhi, wherein all the jewel-treasuries of the Buddhadharma are entirely opened and inspected.
Having observed within this Samādhirāja-samādhi, he reflects to himself:
"This Dharma-treasury of mine is immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable!
Thereafter, he arose calmly from samādhi and, observing sentient beings with his divine eye, he perceived their poverty and suffering.

This treasury of Dharma is obtained through causes and conditions; all sentient beings are likewise capable of obtaining it, yet they remain seated in the darkness of ignorance, neither seeking nor striving for it.
For this reason, I smile with my whole body.
Question:
The Buddha possesses the Buddha-eye, the wisdom-eye, and the Dharma-eye, which are superior to the divine eye; why then does he use the divine eye to observe the world?
Answer:
Because that which is seen by the fleshly eye is not all-pervasive;
the wisdom-eye knows the true mark of all dharmas;
and the dharma-eye sees by what skillful means and by practicing what dharma a person attains the Way.
The Buddha-eye is defined as the clear and thorough knowledge of all phenomena as they manifest before one.
Today, the divine eye perceives worlds and sentient beings without obstruction or hindrance, whereas the other eyes are not so.
Although the wisdom-eye, the dharma-eye, and the buddha-eye are superior, they do not perceive the dharmas of sentient beings;
if one wishes to see sentient beings, one must rely solely on two eyes:
the fleshly eye and the divine eye.
Because the fleshly eye is not all-pervasive and is subject to obstructions, one employs the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) for observation.
Question: Since this eye now resides in the Buddha, why is it called the "divine eye"?
Answer:
This eye mostly exists among the devas; it is the divine eye (divyacakṣus) whose vision is unimpeded by mountains, walls, or trees.
It is obtained through the power of human diligence, observance of precepts, and the practice of meditative concentration (dhyāna), rather than being a result of one's birth.
For this reason, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
Furthermore, because people generally honor the heavens and take the gods as their masters, the Buddha accords with the inclinations of human beings; for this reason, it is called the divine eye.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of devas:
devas by designation, devas by birth, and pure devas.
As for devas by designation:
The Heavenly Kings and the sons of heaven are these.
Those born in the heavens are the Śakras, Brahmās, and the various devas.
The Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*) consist of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats.
Among those in the Pure Heavens, the Buddha is the most honored; thus, there is no fault in referring to him here as possessing the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
Regarding the phrase "observing the world with the divine eye": the sentient beings of the world constantly seek peace and happiness, yet they instead encounter suffering;
their minds are attached to a self (*ātman*), though in reality there is no such self within them.
Sentient beings constantly fear suffering yet constantly practice suffering, like a blind person seeking a good path who instead falls into a deep pit.
Having contemplated these various matters, he smiled with his whole body.
Question:
Laughter arises from the mouth, and sometimes the eyes laugh; why then do you say "the entire body laughs"? Answer:
The Buddha is the Honored One in the world who has attained mastery; he can cause his entire body to be like his mouth or his eyes, and for this reason, he is able to smile with his whole being.
Furthermore, because all his pores open, it is called "smiling";
and because he smiles with joy from his mouth, all his pores open.
Question:
The Buddha is most venerable; for what reason does he smile? Answer:
Just as the great earth does not shake without cause or for minor reasons, so too is the Buddha:
he does not smile without cause or for minor reasons; it is now because of a great cause that his entire body smiles.
What makes it "great"?
Because the Buddha wishes to preach the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, innumerable sentient beings shall continue the lineage of the Buddhas; this constitutes the great causal condition.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"In life after life, I was once a small insect and an evil person; gradually accumulating the roots of all virtues, I attained great wisdom.
Now I have personally realized Buddhahood, possessing immeasurable, supreme, and greatest spiritual powers."
"All sentient beings may likewise attain this; why then do they undergo toil and suffering in vain, only to fall into inferior realms?
It was for this reason that he smiled.
Furthermore, there are small causes with great fruits and small conditions with great retributions.
If, in seeking the Buddha-way, one praises a single verse, recites "Namo Buddha" once, or burns a pinch of incense, one will certainly attain Buddhahood;

how much more so for one who hears and understands that all dharmas are truly neither arising nor ceasing, neither non-arising nor non-ceasing, yet whose practice of the karma of causes and conditions is never lost!
It is for this reason that I smile.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā is pure like space; it cannot be given, nor can it be taken.

Through various skillful means, radiant splendors, and divine virtues, the Buddha seeks to transform and discipline the minds of all sentient beings, so that they may subsequently believe in and accept the Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, he emits light because of his smile.
There are various causes and conditions for smiling:

some smile out of joy; some smile out of anger; some smile out of contempt for others; some smile upon seeing something extraordinary; some smile upon seeing something shameful; some smile upon seeing the customs of distant regions; and some smile upon seeing rare and difficult-to-encounter things.
This is now the foremost rare and difficult matter:
the characteristics of all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing; they are empty stillness, without characters or names, beyond speech and beyond description.
Yet, one wishes to establish names and set up characters to preach for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain liberation—this is the foremost difficult matter.
For example, suppose there were a great mass of fire extending for a hundred yojanas, and a person carrying dry grass entered it and passed through without burning even a single leaf;

this would be extremely difficult. The Buddha is likewise: carrying the "grass" of the names of the eighty thousand dharma-aggregates, he enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and passes straight through without obstruction, unburnt by the fire of defiled attachment. This is extremely difficult; it is because of this difficult feat that he smiles.
Because of such various rare and difficult-to-encounter events, he smiled with his entire body.
[Sūtra] From the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet, he emitted six hundred trillion rays of light.
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason does the Buddha first emit light from his body? Answer:
This was already answered within the "Causes and Conditions for the Buddha’s Smile," but it shall now be explained further.
When someone sees the Buddha’s immeasurable body emitting great radiance, because their mind is pure with faith and reverence, they know that he is no ordinary person.

Furthermore, because the Buddha wishes to manifest the divine signs of the radiance of wisdom, he first emits light from his body; when sentient beings perceive that the Buddha’s bodily light has appeared, they know that the radiance of wisdom must likewise emerge.
Furthermore, all sentient beings are constantly attached to sensual pleasures, and among the five desires, form is the foremost.
Upon seeing this wondrous light, their minds will inevitably become enamored with it and abandon their original attachments;
this causes their minds to gradually distance themselves from desire, after which one may preach wisdom for them.
Question:
Other devas and humans are also able to emit light; what is the distinction between the radiance emitted by the Buddha and theirs? Answer:
Although the various devas and humans are able to emit light, it is limited and finite;
that which is illumined by the sun and moon reaches only the four continents;
but the light emitted by the Buddha fills the trichiliocosm, emerging from within this trichiliocosm and pervading as far as the lower directions.
The radiance of other beings can only bring people joy;
the radiance emitted by the Buddha can cause all who hear the Dharma to attain liberation—this is what distinguishes it.
Question:
Just as the head is the highest part of a single body, for what reason does he first emit light from below the feet?
Answer:
That the body finds its place of support is entirely due to the feet.

Furthermore, although within a single body the head is noble while the feet are base, the Buddha does not value his own radiance nor seek gain and offerings; for this reason, he emits light from the base parts of the body.
Furthermore, when various nāgas, great serpents, and spirits emit light from their mouths, it serves to harm and poison objects before them;
yet if the Buddha emits light from his mouth, sentient beings are struck with fear, wondering, "What is this great radiance!"
Furthermore, fearing that he might be harmed, he therefore emitted light from beneath his feet.
A question is asked:
"The six hundred million billion rays of light beneath his feet, up to the *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown, can all be counted;"
Even the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system cannot be filled, let alone the ten directions!
The answer is:
this bodily light is the source of all lights; from this source, its branches and streams are immeasurable and innumerable.
For example, it is like the *kālakūṭa* insect, whose body is minute; yet when it encounters the wind, it grows larger until it is able to swallow and devour all things.
Light is also like this: when it encounters sentient beings who can be saved, it increases boundlessly.

[Sūtra] From each of the ten toes, the two ankles, the two calves, the two knees, the two thighs, the waist, the spine, the abdomen, the back, the navel, the heart, the *śrīvatsa* mark on the chest, the shoulders, the arms, the ten fingers of the hands, the neck, the mouth, the forty teeth, the two nostrils, the two eyes, the two ears, the *ūrṇā-kośa*, and the *uṣṇīṣa*, he emitted six hundred trillion rays of light.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the radiance from the soles of your feet is able to illuminate the trichiliocosm as well as the worlds of the ten directions, why do you emit six hundred trillion rays of light from each part of your body?
Answer: I previously stated that the light from his feet illuminates the lower direction but does not fill the other directions; therefore, he further emits light from his body parts. Some say:
Among all parts of the body, the feet are the most significant because they serve as the foundation for standing; the others are not so.
Therefore, the Buddha first emitted six hundred trillion rays of light from beneath his feet to manifest this to sentient beings.
Just as among the thirty-two marks, the first—the mark of the feet standing firmly on the ground—possesses spiritual power throughout all parts of the body.
Question:
By relying on which samādhi, by relying on which supernatural power (*abhijñā*), and within which meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) does he emit this radiance?
Answer:

This light is emitted from within the Samādhirāja-samādhi; among the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), it is the power of psychic transformation (ṛddhividhi); and among the four dhyānas, it is emitted from the fourth dhyāna.
Within the fourth dhyāna, there are the fire-kṛtsnāyatana (fire-totality) and the fire-abhibhv-āyatana (fire-mastery), from which light is emitted.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was first born, when he first attained enlightenment, and when he first turned the wheel of Dharma, he emitted immeasurable light that filled the ten directions; how much more so would he not emit light when teaching the Mahāprajñāpāramitā?
For example, the jewel of a wheel-turning sage king constantly emits light that illuminates the king’s army for one yojana on each of its four sides;
the Buddha is likewise, and because of his connection with sentient beings, he constantly radiates his natural light even when not entering samādhi.
Why is this? Because the Buddha, the Sangha, and the Dharma Jewel have been perfected.
[Sūtra] From these various rays of light, a great radiance issued forth, pervasively illuminating the trichiliocosm.

From this trichiliocosm, he shines universally upon all worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Question:
Just as the characteristic of fire is to flame upward, the characteristic of water is to moisten downward, and the characteristic of wind is to move horizontally;
This radiant fiery energy ought to ascend; how then can it pervade the trichiliocosm as well as the worlds of the ten directions?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of radiance.
The first is the element of fire, and the second is the element of water.
The sun-gem is the element of fire, and the moon-gem is the element of water.
Although the characteristic of fire is to blaze upward, the fire within the human body reaches everywhere, both above and below.
The fire of the sun is also like this; therefore, during the summer months, the earth and water become entirely hot.
For this reason, we know that fire does not always move upward.
Furthermore, these rays of light, by the power of the Buddha, reach everywhere throughout the ten directions.
It is like a strong bow shooting an arrow: it reaches wherever it is directed.
Question:
Why does it first illuminate the eastern direction, and only later the south, west, and north?
Answer:
Because the sun rising in the east is considered the superior direction, the Buddha, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, first illuminates the east.
Furthermore, there is another difficulty [in the opposing view].
If it first illuminates the south, one should ask:
"Why does it not first illuminate the east, west, and north?
The same applies if it first illuminates the west or the north.
Question:
When will this radiance be extinguished? Answer:
By means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), the Buddha can remain as long as he wishes; once he relinquishes that power, it ceases.
The Buddha’s light is like a lamp, and his supernormal power is like the oil; if the Buddha does not relinquish his supernormal power, the light will not be extinguished.
[Sūtra] The light radiates beyond worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; it is likewise so throughout the ten directions.
[Śāstra] Question:
What constitutes a trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu)?
The answer is:
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the Buddha explains in detail:

one thousand suns, one thousand moons, one thousand Jambudvīpas, one thousand Aparagoyānīs, one thousand Uttarakurus, one thousand Pūrvavidehas, one thousand Sumeru mountains, one thousand abodes of the Cāturmahārājika devas, one thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, one thousand Yāma heavens, one thousand Tuṣita heavens, one thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, one thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, one thousand Brahmakāyika heavens, and one thousand Mahābrahmā heavens—this is called a small chiliocosm, and it is termed a *cūlikā*.
Taking one *cāturdvīpaka* world as a single unit, counting up to one thousand of these constitutes a "second-order intermediate world system" (*dvisāhasra madhyama lokadhātu*).
Taking one such second-order intermediate world system as a single unit, counting up to one thousand of these constitutes a "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra lokadhātu*).
The first thousand is the small chiliocosm, the second thousand is the medium chiliocosm, and the third is called the great chiliocosm.
Because it is a triple-thousandfold enumeration, it is named "great chiliocosm" (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*);
because it is a thousand times two [thousand], it is called "three thousand."
This is a collective designation.
From ten billion suns and moons up to ten billion Great Brahmā heavens, this is called a trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu).
All of these arise at one time and perish at one time.
Some say: the period of abiding lasts for one kalpa, the period of destruction lasts for one kalpa, and the period of returning to formation lasts for one kalpa.
This trichiliocosm is likewise destroyed in three ways during a great kalpa (mahākalpa):
Water, fire, and wind;
likewise, the minor kalpas are destroyed in three ways:
by sword, by disease, and by famine.
This trichiliocosm is situated in space;
upon the wind is water, upon the water is earth, and upon the earth are human beings.
Mount Sumeru has two celestial abodes:
The abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, the abodes of the Thirty-three Gods,
and the remaining abodes such as those of the Yāma gods— all these lands of the seven treasures, produced by the causes and conditions of merit,
are lifted into the air by the wind; even up to the Great Brahmā Heaven, all are lands of the seven treasures, all situated upon the wind.

This light shone universally throughout this trichiliocosm; having finished illuminating it, the remaining radiance extended beyond, shining upon worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
and so it was likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Question:
This light shines afar; why does it not perish? Answer:
The radiance takes the Buddha’s spiritual power as its basis; because this basis exists, it does not perish.
It is like a dragon spring: by the power of the dragon, the water is never exhausted.
These radiances, through the power of the Buddha’s mind, shine universally throughout the ten directions, remaining undiminished along the way.
Question:
Just as there are various great rivers within Jambudvīpa that even exceed the Ganges in size, why is it always said, "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges"?
Answer: The sands of the Ganges are numerous, whereas those of other rivers are not so.
Furthermore, this Ganges is the birthplace and the place where the Buddha traveled; it was seen with his own eyes by his disciples, and therefore it is used as a metaphor.
Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in Jambudvīpa, he emerges from the northern side of the four great rivers of Jambudvīpa and enters the great oceans of the four directions.
Within the Snowy Mountains to the north lies Lake Anavatapta;
within this lake are golden lotuses made of the seven precious gems, as large as chariot canopies.
The Nāga King Anavatapta is a Mahāsattva Bodhisattva of the seventh stage.
On the four sides of this lake there are four flowing streams:
from the east the Elephant-Headed stream, from the south the Ox-Headed stream, from the west the Horse-Headed stream, and from the north the Lion-Headed stream.
From the eastern Elephant Head [Mountain] issues the Ganges River, whose bed contains golden sand;
from the southern Ox Head [Mountain] issues the Sindhu River, whose bed likewise contains golden sand;
from the western Horse Head [Mountain] issues the Vakṣu River, whose bed likewise contains golden sand.
In the north, the river Śītā issues from the head of the Lion; its bed likewise consists of golden sand. These four rivers all originate from the northern mountains:

the Gaṅgā issues from the northern mountains and flows into the eastern sea; the Sindhu issues from the northern mountains and flows into the southern sea; the Vakṣu issues from the northern mountains and flows into the western sea; and the Śītā issues from the northern mountains and flows into the northern sea.
Among these four rivers, the Gaṅgā is the greatest;

the people from all four distant regions regard its scriptures as teaching that the Gaṅgā is a river of merit and auspiciousness, such that if one enters it to bathe, all sinful defilements and evils are entirely eliminated.
Because people revere and serve this river and all recognize it, the sands of the Ganges are used as a metaphor.

Furthermore, the names of other rivers change from age to age, whereas this Ganges does not change from lifetime to lifetime; for this reason, the sands of the Ganges are taken as the metaphor, and no other river is chosen.
Question:
How much sand is there in the Ganges River? Answer:
It cannot be known by any calculation; only a Buddha and a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body can know its number.
A Buddha and a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body can count and know the exact number of atoms produced and destroyed within all of Jambudvīpa, let alone those of the sands of the Ganges.
Once, while the Buddha was sitting under a tree in the grove outside the Jeta Grove, a brahmin came to where the Buddha was and asked him,
"How many leaves are there on this forest grove?"
The Buddha immediately replied,
"There are a certain number.
The brahmin felt doubt in his mind:
"Who can testify to this?
The brahmin went to the side of a tree, plucked a few leaves from it and hid them, then returned to ask the Buddha,
"Exactly how many leaves are there in this grove?"
He immediately replied:
"Now there are only a few leaves remaining.
He spoke thus according to what he had taken.
When the brahmin realized this, his heart was filled with great reverence and faith; he sought ordination under the Buddha and later attained the path of an arhat.
For this reason, it is known that the Buddha can know as many things as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Question:
How many people, upon encountering the Buddha’s radiance, will necessarily attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If encountering the radiance leads one to attain the Way, why does the Buddha, who possesses great compassion, not constantly emit radiance so that all beings may attain the Way?
"Why is it necessary to maintain precepts, practice meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom before one attains the Way?
He replied:
"Sentient beings attain liberation through various causes and conditions; these are not the same for all."

There are those who attain liberation through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), those who attain liberation through observing the precepts and expounding the Dharma, and those who attain liberation through the touch of light upon their bodies.
It is like a city with many gates of entry; though they differ, the destination reached by each is no different.
There are those who attain liberation when the light touches their bodies, yet there are also those who do not attain liberation even upon seeing the light or having it touch their bodies.

[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One smiled from every pore of his body and emitted a radiance that illuminated the trichiliocosm and extended further to worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Question:
Previously, he already manifested a smile from his entire body; for what reason does he now manifest smiles from all his pores?
The answer is:
Smiling with the entire body is a coarse manifestation; now, smiling from every pore is a subtle manifestation.
Furthermore, when the entire body previously smiled, the radiance was limited in number; now, as every pore smiles, the radiance is infinite.
Furthermore, those who had not yet been delivered by the radiance of his entire body now attain deliverance upon encountering the radiance from a single pore.
It is like shaking a tree to gather fruit: that which is ripe falls first;
as for that which is not yet ripe, it requires further shaking.
Furthermore, it is like catching fish: if the first net does not suffice, one must use a subsequent net to catch them.
The causes and conditions for the laughter are as explained above.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll Seven.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Chapter One:
The Explanation of the Emission of Light, Part Fourteen, Continued; Scroll Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. [Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One, with his constant radiance, illumined the trichiliocosm; it likewise reached the Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and so it was throughout the ten directions.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Question:

Previously, the Buddha already manifested a smile from his entire body and emitted light from his pores; why does he now again emit his constant radiance (*nityaprabhā*) to illuminate the ten directions?
The answer is:
There are those who see a different radiance and think it is not the Buddha’s light.
When they see the Buddha’s constant radiance grow ever greater, their hearts rejoice; realizing, "This is truly the Buddha’s light," they will ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Question: What is meant by "constant radiance" (*nityaprabhā*)? Answer:

The Buddha’s body has a radiance extending one zhang in each of the four directions; the Bodhisattva possesses this from birth, which is one of the thirty-two marks known as the "Mark of the One-Zhang Radiance."
Question:
For what reason does the Buddha’s radiance always extend only one fathom and not more? Answer:
The constant radiance of all Buddhas is immeasurable, perpetually illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.

The supernatural body-radiance of Śākyamuni Buddha is likewise immeasurable, extending for one zhang, a hundred zhang, or even thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of zhang, until it fills the trichiliocosm;
this extends throughout the ten directions, in accordance with the constant law of all Buddhas.
However, because sentient beings in this world of five turbidities possess little merit and little wisdom, [the Buddha] receives a radiance of one zhang;
for if he were to receive more light, the eyes of these present beings—whose blessings are meager and whose faculties dull—would be unable to endure its brilliance.
Just as a person whose eyes lose their sight upon seeing the body of a celestial being because the light is so intense and the eyes are so weak,
if sentient beings possess sharp faculties and heavy merit, the Buddha manifests immeasurable radiance for them.
Furthermore, there are those who, upon seeing the Buddha’s constant radiance (*nityaprabhā*), attain liberation through joy.
For example, when a king bestows the remains of his regular meal upon his subordinates, those who receive it rejoice greatly;

the Buddha is likewise. There are those who do not feel joy in their hearts when seeing the Buddha’s various secondary rays of light, yet upon seeing the Buddha’s constant radiance, they will certainly reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and smiled with a serene countenance.
From the root of his tongue, he emitted immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of rays of light; each of these rays transformed into a golden jewel-flower with a thousand petals.
Upon each of these flowers, there is a transformation Buddha seated in the full lotus posture, preaching the six pāramitās;
any sentient being who hears this will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, this was likewise the case in all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
[Treatise] Question:
Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses such great virtue and is so deeply revered, for what reason does he extend his broad and long tongue, which appears to be a minor physical trait?
Answer: The three kinds of light previously emitted illuminated the sentient beings of the ten directions, enabling them to attain liberation.
Now, he wishes to orally expound the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep; it is difficult to understand, difficult to know, and difficult to believe and accept. For this reason, he extends his broad and long tongue as a witness.
With such a mark upon his tongue, his speech is necessarily truthful.

Once in the past, after the Buddha had completed the *varṣā* retreat in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, Ānanda followed the Buddha on a journey through various countries, intending to reach the city of the brahmins.
The Brahmin king, knowing the Buddha’s divine power and his ability to transform the masses and move the hearts of all, thought as he arrived there: "Who now would find pleasure in me?
I shall therefore establish a restriction:
'If anyone gives food to the Buddha or listens to his words, they shall pay a fine of five hundred gold coins.'"
After the restriction had been established, the Buddha arrived in that country and, taking Ānanda with him, entered the city with his alms bowl to beg for food.
All the people in the city closed their doors and did not respond; the Buddha emerged with his bowl empty.

At that time, there was an old servant in a certain household who, carrying a broken earthen vessel filled with foul-smelling dregs, went out the door to discard it; he saw the World-Honored Buddha approaching with an empty bowl.
The old man saw the Buddha’s excellent marks and signs:
his golden complexion, the white hair-tuft, the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, and the fathom-wide halo; he also saw that the alms bowl was empty and contained no food.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"Such a divine person ought to partake of celestial food; that he now lowers his body to wander for alms with a bowl must surely be because of his great compassion for all beings.
With pure faith, he desired to provide excellent offerings, but finding no way to fulfill this wish, he felt ashamed and spoke to the Buddha:
"I intended to provide an offering, but was unable to obtain anything; now, if the Buddha requires this meager food, please accept it!
Knowing that his mind was pure with faith and reverence, the Buddha reached out his hand and received the alms-food in his bowl.
