At that moment, the Buddha smiled, emitting light of five colors that illuminated heaven and earth, before returning to enter through the mark between his eyebrows.
Ānanda joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha: “Indeed,
World-Honored One!”
"I now wish to hear the meaning of the reason for this smile!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see that old woman who, with a heart of faith, gave food to the Buddha?"
Ānanda said, “I see it.
The Buddha said:
"Because this old woman gave food to the Buddha, she shall enjoy happiness and blessings among devas and humans for fifteen kalpas and not fall into the evil realms;
later, she will obtain a male body, leave the household life to study the Way, become a pratyekabuddha, and enter nirvana without remainder."
At that time, a brahmin standing beside the Buddha spoke this verse:
“You are of the solar lineage, of the Kṣatriya caste, The crown prince of King Śuddhodana.
Yet for the sake of food, you utter a great falsehood; How heavy must be the retribution for such foul food?”
At that time, the Buddha extended his broad and long tongue, covering his face up to the hairline, and said to the brahmin:
"In the scriptures you have studied, have you ever seen anyone with such a tongue who would speak falsely?"
The brahmin said, “If a person’s tongue can cover their nose, their words are free from falsehood; how much more so for one whose tongue reaches as far as the hairline?
My heart believes that the Buddha certainly does not speak falsely; I simply did not understand how such a small gift could yield such a great reward.”
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"Have you ever seen anything rare in this world, something difficult to behold?
The brahmin replied:

"Look! Once, while traveling on a road with some brahmins, I saw a nyagrodha tree whose shade covered five hundred merchant wagons and yet did not even exhaust its extent; this is what is called a rare and marvelous thing!"
The Buddha asked,
"As for the seed of this tree, what is its size?
He replied:
"It is as large as one-third of a mustard seed.
The Buddha said,
"Who would believe your words?"
"The tree is so large, yet the seed is exceedingly small!
The Brahmin said,
"It is indeed so!"
“World-Honored One!
I have seen it with my own eyes; it is not false.
The Buddha said:

"I am likewise; seeing that this old woman, with pure faith, has made an offering to the Buddha and shall obtain a great fruit of retribution, just as this tree—wherein the cause was small yet the reward is vast—it is due to the excellence of the Tathāgata’s field of merit."
The Brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding attained; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he repented before the Buddha, saying, "My heart was devoid of propriety;
in my folly, I did not believe in the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him in various ways, and he attained the first fruit of the Path.
Immediately raising his hand, he cried out in a loud voice:
"All you people! The gate of ambrosia is open; why do you not come forth!"
All the brahmins within the city each presented five hundred gold coins to the king to welcome and make offerings to the Buddha, all saying:
"Having attained the flavor of the Deathless, who would begrudge these five hundred gold coins!"
When all the people had departed, the restrictive laws were abolished.
This Brahmin king, together with his ministers and subjects, took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma; all the city dwellers attained pure faith.
Thus the Buddha manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue for the sake of those who lack faith.
Question:
Just as he manifested the tongue-mark to cover his face for the sake of the brahmins, why does the radiance of this tongue-mark now extend even to the trichiliocosm?
The answer is:
[His tongue] covered his face up to the hairline because of his minor faith;
now, because the great matter of the Prajñāpāramitā has arisen, the mark of the broad and long tongue covers the trichiliocosm.
Question:
It was already difficult for all the people within this single city to see this mark of the tongue that covers the face;
how much more so now, when the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is being preached, for this entire great assembly—including immeasurable multitudes from this world and other directions—to be able to see it all?
Furthermore, since what the human eye can perceive does not exceed a few li, the claim that [the tongue] now pervades the trichiliocosm is perhaps too vast to be easily believed!
The answer is:
By means of skillful means, the Buddha borrows his supernatural power so that all may see the mark of the tongue covering this trichiliocosm.
If his supernatural power were not exerted, even those in the tenth stage would not know the Buddha’s mind;
if his supernatural power were exerted, even animals could know the Buddha’s mind.
As it is said in a later chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"All people see the assembly of Akṣobhya Buddha as if facing him directly with their own eyes."
"Furthermore, it was as the Buddha had described the various adornments and purities of Amitābha Buddha’s world.
Ānanda said:
'I only wish to see it.'"
The Buddha then immediately caused the entire assembly to behold the majestic purity of the world of Amitāyus Buddha.
Their vision of the Buddha’s tongue was likewise so.
After the Buddha had covered the entire trichiliocosm with his broad and long tongue, he then smiled.
The causes and conditions for this smile are as explained above. Question:
Question: Previously, the light of the tongue-mark was already emitted; for what reason is the tongue-faculty now again emitting light?
Answer: It is because he wishes to cause all beings to gain renewed faith.
Furthermore, because the color of his tongue’s appearance was like coral, and it was mutually inspired by its golden radiance and purity, he again emitted light.
Moreover, these various lights transformed into thousand-petaled precious golden lotuses.
From the mark of his tongue emerged this thousand-petaled precious lotus flower of golden hue, its radiance shining through all, like the sun first rising.
It was asked:
"For what reason does he manifest these precious flowers within the light?"
Answer: Because the Buddha wished to sit.
Question:
"Various couches may be used for sitting; why necessarily a lotus flower?
He replied:
"The couch is the practice for sitting used by laypeople in the world."
Furthermore, because the lotus is soft and pure, he wishes to manifest his supernormal powers by being able to sit upon it without causing the flower to be damaged;
furthermore, in order to adorn the sublime Dharma-seat;
and furthermore, because all other flowers are small, none possess such fragrance, purity, and magnitude as this flower.
The lotus among humans does not exceed a foot in size;
the lotuses in the Mandākinī Pond and the Anavatapta Lake are as large as a carriage canopy;
the precious lotuses in the heavens are even larger than these, such that they can accommodate one sitting in the full lotus posture.
The lotus upon which the Buddha sits is hundreds of thousands of millions of times more excellent than this.
Furthermore, the calyx of this flower is adorned, pure, fragrant, and sublime, fit for sitting.
Moreover, when the kalpa comes to an end and all is consumed by fire, everything becomes empty; yet this remains so.
By the power of the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings, winds from the ten directions arrive and, meeting and colliding with one another, are able to support the great waters.
Upon these waters is a man with a thousand heads and two thousand hands and feet, named Viṣṇu.
From the navel of this man emerges a wondrous jewel lotus flower of golden hue with a thousand petals; its light is brilliantly radiant, as if ten thousand suns were shining together.
Within the lotus, there was a person sitting in the full lotus posture; this person further possessed immeasurable radiance and was named the Brahmā King.
This Brahmā King gave birth to eight sons from his mind, and these eight sons gave birth to heaven, earth, and the people.
This Brahmā King has exhausted all lust and anger without remainder; for this reason it is said:
"If there is a person who cultivates pure conduct through meditation and severs sensual desire, they are said to be practicing the Brahma-way."
The Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma, which is sometimes called the Dharma-wheel and sometimes the Brahma-wheel.
Because this Brahma King sits upon a lotus flower, the Buddhas, in accordance with worldly convention, sit cross-legged upon precious flowers and preach the six pāramitās.
Those who hear this Dharma will ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
A question is asked:
"The Buddha Śākyamuni manifests as immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; how can he preach the Dharma simultaneously?"
As stated in the *Abhidharma*:
"At one time, there are not two minds.
If the emanated Buddha speaks, the emanator should remain silent; [otherwise, it would contradict this principle].
When the master of the transformation speaks, the transformed beings should also remain silent.
Why, then, do they all simultaneously preach the six pāramitās?
The answer is:
To speak in this manner is merely the transformative teaching of non-Buddhists and śrāvakas.

Just as the Buddha’s transformations are produced by the inconceivable power of immeasurable samādhis, so too, when the Buddha speaks himself, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of transformed Buddhas also speak simultaneously.
Furthermore, the various non-Buddhists and śrāvakas cannot create emanations within their own emanations;
whereas the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can create emanations within his emanations.
Moreover, after the parinirvāṇa of the various non-Buddhists and śrāvakas, they cannot leave behind emanations; [the Buddha can].
Just as after the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has passed into parinirvāṇa himself, he can still leave behind a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) that is no different from the Buddha himself.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma*, there are no two minds at one time;
likewise, the Buddha is the same: when he speaks through a transformation, he has no mind at that moment.
The Buddha, through his mental intention, desired that the emanations speak; they then all spoke.
A question is asked:
"If the Buddha now wishes to expound the *prajñāpāramitā*, why does he have the emanation-Buddhas expound the six *pāramitās*?"
Answer: These six pāramitās and the prajñāpāramitā are a single dharma without distinction.
If these five pāramitās do not attain the prajñāpāramitā, they are not called "pāramitās."

Just as with the dānapāramitā, if one does not obtain the prajñāpāramitā, one sinks into the world of phenomena subject to exhaustion, perhaps attaining the parinirvāṇa of the path of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha;
however, if it is conjoined with the prajñāpāramitā, it is called a pāramitā and is able to reach the path of Buddhahood.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā and the six pāramitās are one dharma without distinction.
There are two kinds of Prajñāpāramitā:
first, that which is adorned; second, that which is not yet adorned.
It is like a person who adorns their body with fine necklaces and ornaments; if there is another who does not wear them, they are said to be "unadorned.
It is also like a king who comes accompanied by various officials and attendants, which is called "the king's arrival";
if he has no officials or attendants, he is called "solitary."
In this way, it is so for worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise throughout the ten directions.
A question is asked:

"If the Buddha possesses such great supernormal power, with countless thousands of millions of billions of emanation Buddhas preaching the six *pāramitās* throughout the ten directions to deliver all beings, then everyone should have attained deliverance; there should be no remainder!"
The answer is:
There are three obstructions:
sentient beings within the three evil realms are unable to understand or know [it].
Whether among humans or in the heavens, whether small or large, whether aged or afflicted by great illness;
and even up to the formless realms and the heaven of non-perception—none can hear it, none can know it.
Question:
Why is it that not all those who are able to hear and understand attain the Way? Answer:
Furthermore, they should not all attain the Way.
Why is this? Because of their fetters and karmic obstructions.
There are those for whom the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are heavy; their minds are constantly shrouded by these fetters, and for this reason they do not fully attain the Way.
Question:
If the Buddhas of the ten directions should likewise dispatch emanations to preach the six *pāramitās*, and we ourselves possess no three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), why is it that we do not hear them?
Answer: Beings of the present age are born into an evil world and thus enter among the three obstructions.

Being born after the Buddha’s passing, they face the retribution of unwholesome karma; there are those with the obstruction of evil and sinful karma in their world, and there are those with the obstruction of heavy and thick fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Those who fall behind the Buddha are mostly hindered by heavy and dense fetters (*saṃyojana*):

some have thin lust but thick anger; some have thin anger but thick lust; some have thin lust but thick ignorance; some have thin ignorance but thick anger; and so forth, with these qualities alternating between being thick or thin.

Because they are obstructed by these fetters and afflictions, they do not hear or know the Dharma preached by the Transformation Buddhas, nor do they see the radiance of the Buddhas; how much less can they attain the Way!
It is like the rising of the sun: a blind person does not see it and thus claims that there are no sun or moon in the world, yet what fault is there in the sun?
Furthermore, just as when thunder and lightning shake the earth, a deaf person does not hear it—what fault is there in the sound?

Now, the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly preach the Dharma, and they constantly dispatch transformation-buddhas to the worlds of the ten directions to preach the six pāramitās; yet because of their sinful karma and their blindness or deafness, they do not hear the sound of the Dharma.
For this reason, they do not fully hear or see.
Although the sages possess great compassion, they cannot cause everyone to hear [the Dharma] or see [the Buddha].
Only when one's transgressions are about to be extinguished and merit is about to arise can one then see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
[Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One remained upon the lion throne and entered the Lion’s Play Samādhi; by his supernormal power, he caused the trichiliocosm to tremble in six ways.
[Treatise] Question:
Why is this samādhi named "Lion’s Play" (Siṃhavikrīḍita)? Answer:
Just as a lion pounces upon a deer, playing with it at its own will,
so too does the Buddha enter this samādhi and is able to cause this earth to revolve in various ways, making it shake in six different manners.
Furthermore, regarding the Lion’s Play: just as when a lion sports in the sun, all other beasts dwell in peace;

so too is it with the Buddha. When he enters this samādhi, he causes the trichiliocosm to tremble, enabling sentient beings in the three evil realms to find rest simultaneously and attain peace and security.
Furthermore, the Buddha is called the "Lion among Men. The *Siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Lion’s Play) is the Buddha’s play-samādhi.

When he enters this samādhi, he causes this great earth to quake in six ways; all sentient beings in the evil realms and hells are thereby granted liberation and reborn in the heavens—this is what is meant by "play."
Question:
For what reason does the Buddha enter this samādhi? Answer:
He wishes to shake the trichiliocosm in order to deliver sentient beings from the three evil realms and establish them within the two [noble] paths.
Furthermore, regarding the three types of transformations mentioned above that issue from the Buddha’s body, people’s faith may not yet be deep;

now, by shaking the great earth, he desires to cause sentient beings to know that the Buddha’s spiritual power is immeasurable, capable of moving all external things, so that their faith becomes pure, their hearts rejoice, and they all attain liberation from suffering.
Question:
Since there are Arhats and various devas who are also able to shake the earth, why do you speak of this specifically as the Buddha’s supernatural power? Answer:
The various arhats and devas are unable to move it completely; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can cause the great earth to quake in six ways.
Question:
For what reason does the Buddha shake the trichiliocosm?
Answer: It is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to know that all things are empty and impermanent.
There are some people who say:
"The great earth, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, and the great ocean—all these possess permanence.
For this reason, the World-Honored One caused the earth to shake in six ways to demonstrate this causal condition, so that people might realize impermanence.

Furthermore, just as a person wishing to dye a garment first removes dust and dirt, so too does the Buddha first cause the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm to behold his supernatural power, thereby softening their minds through reverence, and only then preach the Dharma; for this reason, the earth quakes in six ways.
What are the six kinds of movement?
[Sūtra] The east rises and the west sinks; the west rises and the east sinks;
the south rises and the north sinks; the north rises and the south sinks.
The edges surge while the center subsides; the center surges while the edges subside.
[Śāstra] Question:
For what reason are there exactly six kinds of movement?
Answer: Earthquakes are of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior.
As for the inferior grade, there are two types of movement:
Sometimes it surges in the east and subsides in the west; sometimes it surges in the south and subsides in the north; or [it surges] at the periphery and in the center.
Regarding the center, there are four types:
either east, west, south, and north; or east, west, periphery, and center; or south, north, periphery, and center.
The superior [type] consists of six kinds of movements.
There are various causes and conditions that cause the earth to shake violently, as the Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are eight causes and eight conditions that cause the earth to quake."
As explained elsewhere.
Furthermore, some say: "There are four kinds of earthquakes: [text continues as in the source]."
"The fire moves, the dragon moves, the garuḍa moves, and the celestial kings move.
Among the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the moon revolves through them once every month:

if the moon reaches the mansion of Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇā, Jyeṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Uttarabhādrapadā, or Viśākhā—within these six mansions—if at that time the earth shakes as if it were collapsing, this shaking belongs to the Fire Deity.

At that time, there will be no rain; the rivers and streams will dry up; the year will be unfavorable for wheat; the Son of Heaven will meet with misfortune, and the high ministers will suffer calamity.
If, among these six lunar mansions—Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvaphalgunī, Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, and Āśleṣā—the earth should quake as if collapsing, such a movement belongs to the Dragon Deities (Nāgas).

At that time, there will be no rain; the rivers and streams will dry up; the year will be unfavorable for wheat; the Son of Heaven will meet with misfortune, and the high ministers will suffer calamity.
If, among these six lunar mansions—Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, and Ārdrā—the earth shakes or collapses, such a movement belongs to the Garuḍa.
At that time, there will be no rain; rivers and streams will dry up; the year will be unfavorable for wheat; the Son of Heaven will meet with misfortune, and high ministers will suffer calamity.

If the earth quakes as if collapsing during the nine lunar mansions of Heart (Jyeṣṭhā), Horns (Viśākhā), Room (Anurādhā), Maiden (Śravaṇā), Void (Śatabhiṣaj), Well (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Net (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Pincer (Abhijit), and Dipper (Śravaṇā), this movement belongs to the Heavenly Emperor (Indra).

At such a time, there will be peace and security, abundant rains, and the five grains will flourish; the Son of Heaven will be auspicious, high ministers will receive blessings, and the myriad people will live in tranquility.

Furthermore, there are small and great causes and conditions for the shaking of the earth: there is that which shakes a single Jambudvīpa, and there is that which shakes the four continents, a thousandfold world system, a two-thousandfold world system, or a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
Minor tremors occur due to minor causes and conditions:
when a person of merit is born or dies, the earth of a single country shakes; this is called a minor tremor.
Major tremors occur due to major causes and conditions:
Just as when the Buddha was first born, when he first attained Buddhahood, and when he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, the trichiliocosm shook throughout; this is called a great trembling.
Now, because the Buddha wishes to assemble a great multitude of sentient beings, he causes this earth to quake in six ways.
Furthermore, within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha bestows predictions upon various bodhisattvas that they shall become Buddhas;
as the Buddha is the great sovereign of heaven and earth, at that time the Earth Deity rejoices greatly:
"I have now obtained my lord!
For this reason, the earth shakes.
It is like when a sovereign is first established: the ministers and subjects rejoice, all cry out "Ten-thousand-year reign!", leaping, dancing, and singing.

Furthermore, it is due to the causes and conditions of the merit of the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm that there exist this great earth, mountains, rivers, trees, and all such things; yet these sentient beings do not realize their impermanence!

Therefore, by means of the great power of his merit and wisdom, the Buddha shakes this world and the merit of its sentient beings, causing them to realize that it is meager, that all things are subject to destruction, and that everything returns to impermanence.
[Sūtra]: The earth becomes entirely soft and supple, causing sentient beings to feel harmony and joy.
[Śāstra]: Question:
When the earth quakes, how can it cause the minds of sentient beings to attain harmony and joy?
Answer: Because the mind follows the body, when the body attains pleasant things, the mind becomes joyful.
As for "joy," it refers to those with whom one dwells and the articles that serve the body, which are able to cause the mind to rejoice.
Now, because the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm are of mixed and evil nature, their minds being coarse and wild, and lacking in wholesome deeds;
for this reason, the World-Honored One has moved this great earth, causing it all to become soft and supple, so that these beings may obtain benefit for their minds.
For example, when the gods enter the Nandana Grove of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, their minds all become supple, joyful, harmonious, and serene, and no coarse thoughts arise;
even when the asuras mobilize their armies and come to attack, they harbor no intention to fight at all.

At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra led the host of devas into the Karkaśa Garden; because the trees, flowers, and fruits in this garden were harsh and unpleasant, with coarse and foul qualities, a mind of contention immediately arose among the devas and humans.
The Buddha is likewise; because this great earth is coarse, harsh, and foul, he transforms it to make it soft and supple, causing the minds of all sentient beings to attain joy.
Furthermore, just as when incantations or medicinal herbs are wafted into someone's nose, a mind of anger arises and they immediately engage in strife;
yet there are other incantations and medicinal herbs that can cause people's hearts to become harmonious, joyful, and full of gladness, so that they face one another with a spirit of respect.
If even incantations and medicinal herbs can produce such effects, how much more so when the ground of the entire trichiliocosm becomes soft?

[Sūtra] Within this trichiliocosm, those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the eight states of no-leisure were immediately liberated and attained rebirth in the heavens, from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the realm of Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
[Treatise] Question:

If the Buddha, upon entering the Lion’s Play Samādhi, can cause those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and the other eight difficult conditions to all attain liberation and be reborn in the Four Heavenly Kings’ realm up to the Heaven of Control over Others’ Emanations, then what further need is there to cultivate merit and perform wholesome deeds in order to obtain such karmic fruits?
Answer: As explained above, those with abundant merit and virtue attain deliverance upon seeing the light;
those whose karmic defilements are deep awaken only when the earth trembles.
For example, when the sun rises and shines upon a lotus pond, those that are ripe open first, while those that are unripe have not yet blossomed.
It is the same with the Buddha: he first emits his radiance, and those whose merit is mature and whose wisdom is sharp attain liberation first;
those whose merit is not yet mature and whose minds of wisdom are not sharp do not yet attain it for this reason.
The Buddha’s great compassion equally delivers all beings, without hatred or attachment.
It is like the fruit of a tree: when a person shakes the tree, the ripe fruit falls first;
the Buddha is likewise. This trichiliocosm is like the tree, and the one who shakes it is the Buddha.
Those who have already been delivered have their fruit ripened; those who have not yet been delivered have their fruit still arising.
Question:

For what reason does a wholesome mental state, by way of its causal conditions, lead to rebirth in the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but not in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is:
The Buddha wishes to deliver these sentient beings so that they may attain the realization of the Path.
However, because there is no physical body within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), it is impossible to preach the Dharma for them.

Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no sense of weariness; thus it is difficult to attain the Path. Because the pleasures of dhyāna are so abundant, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes dull.

Furthermore, by means of his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the Buddha causes the earth of this trichiliocosm to become soft and supple. Because sentient beings’ minds are filled with faith and joy, they are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
however, because they do not practice the four dhyānas or the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they cannot be reborn in the realms of form or the formless realm.
Question:
Since the five aggregates are impermanent, empty, and without self, how can one be born among gods or humans?
Who dies and who is born?
Answer: This matter has already been explained in detail within the "Chapter Praising the Bodhisattva"; now I shall answer briefly.

Regarding your statement that "the five aggregates are impermanent, empty, and without self," in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the five aggregates possess neither permanence nor impermanence, neither existence nor non-existence, and neither self nor non-self.
If one seeks a real self as the non-Buddhists do, it cannot be found;
there is only a provisional designation, existing through the combination of various causes and conditions, and possessing this name.
For example, when illusory beings kill one another, people see them die;
when the illusory arts cause them to rise again, people see them live.
The names "birth" and "death" exist, yet they lack reality.
Within the phenomena of the world, birth and death truly exist; within the reality of ultimate marks, there is no birth and death.
Furthermore, those who undergo birth and death possess birth and death; those who do not undergo birth and death have no birth and death.
Why is this? Because one who is not subject to birth and death can, through great wisdom, destroy the characteristic of birth.
As it is said in a verse:
"Although the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma are empty, they are nevertheless not annihilated;
although there is arising, it is not eternal, and the various karmic actions are never lost.
All dharmas are like plantain trees; everything arises from the mind."
If one knows that phenomena lack substantial reality, this mind is likewise empty.
If someone conceptualizes emptiness, this is not the practice of the Path.
All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; because one conceives of existence, their true mark is lost.
"With mindfulness, one falls into the net of Māra; without mindfulness, one attains liberation.
Because the mind moves, it is not the Way; non-movement is the Dharma-seal.

[Sūtra] These devas and humans, recognizing their own past lives, were all filled with great joy. They came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
[Treatise] Question:
When the various devas are born, they know three things for themselves:
they know the place from which they have come; they know the field of merit where they have practiced; and they know the merits they originally performed.
Question: When one is born into this human life, if these three things are absent, how can one know past lives?
Answer: The human realm is indeterminate; some possess such knowledge, while others do not.
Furthermore, by relying on the Buddha’s supernatural power, one can know past lives.
A question is asked:
The gods possess the five supernormal powers as a result of their retribution; they naturally know their own past lives and are thus able to reach the Buddha’s presence.
Although people may know their past lives through the Buddha’s supernatural power, since the place where they dwell is distant, how can they reach the Buddha’s presence?
The answer is:
there are some who possess supernormal powers acquired as a result of their birth, such as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and noble beings (*ārya*).
Or there may be someone who, by means of the Buddha's supernatural power, asks:
"A person is born after ten months and is nursed with milk for three years; after reaching the age of ten, they are able to emerge on their own."

Now, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, we have all been liberated from the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions; having been reborn among devas and humans, we have immediately arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling place.
While it is understandable for devas to do so, how could humans—whose dharmic nature is not yet perfected—be able to come here?
Answer: The modes of birth for the five destinies each differ:
those in the heavens and those in the hells are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
There are two types of birth for hungry ghosts:
birth from a womb or miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
For humans and animals, there are four types of birth.
There are birth from eggs, birth from moisture, birth by transformation, and birth from a womb.

Regarding birth from eggs: for example, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ had thirty-two sons; Mother Viśākhā gave birth to thirty-two eggs, which hatched to produce thirty-two boys, all of whom were powerful warriors.
Migāra is the name of the eldest son; his mother attained the fruit of the third path—such as these are called those born from eggs.
As for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), such as the courtesan Ambapālī and the Wheel-turning Sage King born from the crown of the head—such as these are called those born from moisture.

Regarding those born by transformation (*upapāduka*): for example, when the Buddha was traveling with the fourfold assembly, among the community of bhikṣuṇīs there was a bhikṣuṇī named Āravā who was born by transformation from the earth;
likewise, at the beginning of the kalpa, all humans were born by transformation—such as these are called those born by transformation.
Those born from a womb are born like ordinary humans.
Those born by transformation grow instantly to full size and are able to reach the Buddha’s presence.
Some are able to reach the Buddha’s presence because they have obtained supernatural powers as a result of their past retribution.
Furthermore, by virtue of the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), they were able to reach the place where the Buddha was.
[Sūtra] Thus, in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, the earth shook in six ways;
all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and the other eight difficult conditions immediately attained liberation and were reborn in the heavens, reaching as far as the sixth heaven.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the three thousandfold world system is immeasurable and incalculable, and sentient beings therein are exceedingly numerous, why does [the Buddha's compassion] further extend to the sentient beings of worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
Answer:

The power of the Buddha is immeasurable; even though he delivers sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, he still considers that number small, and for this reason, his reach extends to the ten directions.
Question:
If Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his great supernormal powers, extensively delivers beings throughout the ten directions, why is there a need for other Buddhas?
Answer:
Sentient beings are infinite, and thus they do not ripen at one and the same time.
Furthermore, the causes and conditions of sentient beings differ from one another; as it is said in the Śrāvaka-dharma:
"Regarding the disciples of Śāriputra, even the Buddhas themselves could not deliver them, let alone others."

Furthermore, here we speak only of worlds in the eastern direction equal in number to the sands of a single Ganges River; we do not speak of two, three, four, or even ten million billion Ganges-sands of worlds.
Furthermore, because worlds are infinite and immeasurable—if they were finite and measurable, sentient beings would have reached their end.
For this reason, there are immeasurable worlds in the ten directions where the Buddhas should deliver beings.

[Sūtra] At that time, among the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, those who were blind regained their sight; those who were deaf regained their hearing; those who were mute were able to speak; those who were insane regained their sanity; those who were distracted attained concentration; those who were naked obtained clothing; those who were hungry and thirsty became fully satiated; the sick were healed; and those with physical deformities became complete.
[Treatise] Question:
Sentient beings suffer from hundreds of thousands of kinds of afflictions; if the Buddha possesses supernatural powers, why does he not universally cause them all to attain liberation?
Answer:
All are to be saved; for now, I shall briefly explain only the coarse [afflictions].
Just as various fetters and latent tendencies are briefly explained as the three poisons. Question:
It would suffice simply to say, "the blind gain sight"; why then is it said, "those born blind"?
The answer is:
those who are born blind do so because of grave offenses committed in previous lives.
If even those with grave offenses can still be made to see, how much more so those with minor ones?
Question:
How is it that grave offenses from previous lives cause one to be born blind?
The answer is:

If one destroys the eyes of sentient beings, or plucks out the eyes of sentient beings, or destroys the eye of right view by claiming that there is neither sin nor merit, such a person will fall into hell after death; when their retribution is exhausted and they become human again, they will be blind from birth.

Furthermore, if one steals the fire-jewels or various lamps and lights from a stūpa of the Buddha, or the jewels and lamps and lights from the stūpas of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, or seizes the light from other fields of merit.
Thus, blindness resulting from various kinds of karmic causes and conditions in previous lives is due to past-life karma;
whereas blindness resulting from illness or injury in the present life is due to present-life conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the ninety-six kinds of eye diseases that even the medicinal king Jñānaka cannot cure, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can enable one to see again.
Furthermore, first they cause them to obtain sight, and afterwards they cause them to obtain the eye of wisdom.
It is the same for the deaf who obtain hearing.
Question:
If there are those who are blind from birth, why not mention those who are deaf from birth?
The answer is:
those who are blind from birth are many, while those who are deaf from birth are few; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Question:
By what causes and conditions does one become deaf? Answer:
Deafness is the result of causes and conditions from previous lives:
having received the instructions of one's teacher, yet refusing to accept or practice them while instead responding with anger, one suffers deafness because of this transgression.

Furthermore, it results from cutting off the ears of sentient beings, or piercing their ears, or stealing the *gaṇḍī*, bells, conchs, or drums belonging to a Buddha-stūpa, a saṃgha-stūpa, or the fields of merit of various virtuous persons; for these reasons, one incurs this retribution.
Such are the various causes and conditions of past lives and the causes and conditions of the present life—
whether it be illness or being struck— that through these present-life conditions one becomes deaf.
Question:
A mute person is unable to speak; for what kind of offense did they become mute? Answer:
In previous lives, they cut off others' tongues, or stuffed their mouths, or administered harmful drugs so that they could not speak;
or when hearing the instructions of teachers or the admonitions of parents, they interrupted their speech and rejected their teachings;
or they became people of evil and heterodox views, disbelieving in sin and merit, and destroying right speech.
Having emerged from the retribution of hell and been born into the world as a human, one is mute and unable to speak.
It is for various causes and conditions such as these that one is mute. Question:
"Those who are mad regain their sanity. What constitutes madness?
The answer is:

having committed offenses in previous lives, one disrupts others' meditative concentration, destroys meditation huts, and employs various incantations to cause people to become angry, engage in strife, or indulge in lustful desire.
In this world, the various fetters and afflictions are thick and heavy.
It is like a Brahmin who has lost his field of merit and whose wife has also died; he immediately goes mad and runs about naked.
Furthermore, for example, when the bhikṣuṇī Ciñcā-Kauṇḍinya was still a laywoman, her seven sons all died; because of her great grief and sorrow, she lost her mind and went mad.
There are those who, being consumed by great anger that they cannot control, become utterly insane.
There are foolish people who, due to their evil and heterodox views, smear their bodies with ashes, pluck out their hair, go naked, and in their mad delusion eat excrement.
There are those who, due to wind-disorders (*vāta*) or heat-disorders (*pitta*), become insane when their illnesses are severe;
there are those possessed by malevolent spirits (*pāpīyān yakṣa*); and there are those who become insane from foolishly drinking rainwater.
Thus losing one's mind, these various conditions are called madness.
Because of seeing the Buddha, the madness is immediately rectified.
Question:
"Those who are distracted attain concentration. If "madness" constitutes distraction, by what means is it distinguished?
The answer is:
there are those who are not mad but whose minds are frequently scattered; their will is like that of a monkey, unable to abide in one-pointedness—this is called a distracted mind.
Furthermore, when there are pressing affairs and one is in a state of haste, the mind becomes attached to various matters; thus, one loses mental power and is unable to receive the Way.
Question:
What are the causes and conditions for a distracted mind?
The answer is:
When wholesome states of mind become thin and one follows after unwholesome states, this is called mental distraction.
Furthermore, such a person does not contemplate impermanence, does not contemplate the signs of death, and does not contemplate the emptiness of the world.
Attachment to life and preoccupation with worldly affairs cause one to scatter in various directions; therefore, the mind is distracted.
Furthermore, failing to find internal joy within the Buddha-dharma and instead seeking pleasurable things externally while pursuing the causes of pleasure results in a distracted mind.
Because such distracted people are able to see the Buddha, their minds attain concentration.
A question is asked:
Previously it was said that "the mad regain their sanity," but now it is said that "the naked obtain clothing. Aside from those who are insane, how can there be others who are naked?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of madness:
first, that which everyone knows to be madness; [the second is that which others do not recognize as such].
Second, because of evil and perverse views, one strips oneself naked, yet others do not realize one is insane.
As it is said:
In a country of South India, there was a Dharma Master who sat upon a high seat to expound the meaning of the five precepts; among the assembly, many non-Buddhists came to listen.
At that time, the king raised an objection, saying:

"If it is as you have said—that one who gives alcohol or drinks alcohol oneself receives the retribution of madness and folly—then among the people of the present age, those who are mad should be many and those who are sane should be few;
yet now, those who are mad are fewer and those who are not mad are more numerous. For what reason is this so?"
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners said:
"Excellent! This challenge is most profound!"
"This bald man on his high seat will certainly be unable to answer, for the King possesses sharp intelligence.
At that time, the Dharma Master pointed his finger at the various non-Buddhist practitioners and spoke of other matters; the King understood them immediately.
The various non-Buddhists said to the king:
"Your Majesty’s question was exceedingly profound; you did not know how to answer it. Out of shame for your ignorance, you merely raised your finger and spoke of other matters."
The King said to the non-Buddhists:
"The Dharma Master on the high seat has already finished his response by pointing; out of consideration for you, he did not speak it aloud.
When he pointed at you earlier, saying that you were mad, he meant that your madness was no small matter."
You smear your bodies with ashes, go naked without shame, and eat excrement from human skulls;
you pluck out your hair, lie upon thorns, and hang upside down to smoke your noses;
in winter you enter the water, and in summer you roast yourselves by fire.
Such various practices as these are not the Path; they are all signs of madness.
Furthermore, according to your own Dharma, if one sells meat or salt, one immediately loses the status of a Brahmin;
yet when you receive a cow as a gift at a temple, you sell it immediately and claim that you have attained the Dharma.
If an ox is simply meat, then this is a deception of people; is this not a failure?
Furthermore, to say that "entering the waters of the Ganges River removes all defilements of sin" implies that sin and merit have neither cause nor condition.
Selling meat or selling salt—what fault is there in this?
Entering the waters of the River Ganges and claiming that one’s sins can be removed—if it could remove sin, it could likewise remove merit; who, then, would possess any auspiciousness?
Regarding such matters as these, which have neither cause nor condition, to insistently treat them as causes and conditions is madness.
All such various signs of madness belong to you;
because the Dharma Master wishes to protect you, he points them out but does not speak of them.
This is called "the naked madman.
Furthermore, there are those who are impoverished and without clothing, or whose garments are tattered and worn; by the power of the Buddha, they are caused to obtain clothing.
Question:
"The hungry shall obtain satiety, and the thirsty shall obtain drink. What, then, constitutes hunger and thirst? Answer:
Because their merit is meager, they lacked the causes in past lives and lack the conditions in the present life; for this reason, they suffer from hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, such persons in past lives robbed the Buddhas, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their parents and close relatives of food;
thus, even though they encounter the era of a Buddha, they still remain hungry and thirsty because their transgressions are so grave.
Question:
Now, there are those born in an evil age who obtain fine food and drink, while those born in the age of a Buddha suffer further hunger and thirst.
If it were the case that a person with transgressions should not be born in the age of a Buddha, and a person with merit should not be born in an evil age, for what reason is this so?
Answer: The causes and conditions of karmic retribution differ for each individual.
There may be someone who possesses the causes and conditions to see the Buddha, yet lacks the causes and conditions for food and drink; [and so forth].
There may be those who possess the conditions for food and drink, yet lack the conditions for seeing the Buddha;
it is like a black snake that lies down embracing a maṇi jewel, while an arhat goes begging for alms but receives none.
Furthermore, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who left the household life to seek the Way;
one observed the precepts, recited the sūtras, and practiced seated meditation, while the other extensively sought out donors to cultivate various meritorious deeds.
When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, one of them was born into the family of an elder, while the other became a great white elephant whose strength was capable of defeating enemies.
The elder’s son left the household life to study the Way and attained the six supernormal powers as an arhat; however, due to his meager merit, it was difficult for him to obtain almsfood.
On another day, he entered the city with his alms bowl to beg for food, but was unable to obtain any anywhere.
Upon arriving at the stable of the white elephant, he saw that the King had provided the elephant with all manner of abundant provisions.
He spoke to the elephant, saying:
"Both you and I are guilty of a transgression.
The elephant was immediately overcome with grief and did not eat for three days.
The elephant keeper became terrified and sought out a practitioner of the Way; upon seeing him, he asked:
"What incantation have you cast that has caused the king’s white elephant to fall ill and be unable to eat?
He replied, "This elephant was my younger brother in a previous life; we both left the household life to study the Path together during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha."
I merely observe the precepts, recite the sutras, and practice seated meditation, but do not practice giving;
my younger brother merely seeks out donors extensively to perform various acts of giving, but does not observe the precepts nor engage in study.
Because he did not maintain the precepts, recite the sutras, or practice seated meditation, he has now become this elephant;
because he extensively practiced the giving of alms, his food and drink are fully provided for and all things are abundant.
"Because I practiced only the Way and did not cultivate the practice of giving, although I have now attained the Way, I am unable to obtain alms-food.
For this reason, because the causes and conditions were different, even though he encountered the era of a Buddha, he still remained hungry and thirsty.
Question: How are these sentient beings satiated? Answer:
Some say: "The Buddha, by means of his supernormal power, transformed [the offerings] into food, causing them to be fully satiated. Others say:
"The Buddha's light touches their bodies, causing them to be free from hunger and thirst.
It is like a wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel: if someone thinks of it, they will no longer suffer from hunger or thirst; how much more so when encountering a Buddha!"
"The sick shall be healed. There are two kinds of illness:
first, various illnesses arise due to the retribution of karmic actions performed in previous lives;
second, various illnesses also arise due to the provocation of cold, heat, and wind in the present life.
In this world, there are two kinds of illness:
first, internal illness, wherein the five viscera are disordered, resulting in chronic knots and long-standing ailments;

second, external illness, such as being struck by runaway chariots or galloping horses, crushed by earthslides or falling from heights, or injuries from weapons, blades, and staves—these various forms of disease.
Question:
By what causes and conditions does one become ill? Answer:
Because in previous lives they delighted in using whips and staves, torturing and flogging, and imprisoning others—inflicting various forms of harm—they now suffer from disease in this life.
Regarding their present illness, they do not know how to care for themselves; they are irregular in their diet and inconsistent in their sleeping and rising.
Because of these matters, various illnesses arise.
Thus there are four hundred and four types of illness; by the supernatural power of the Buddha, he causes those who are ill to be healed.
As it is said:

When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, a certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to a meal at his home. There were five causes and conditions for the Buddha to remain in the vihāra and not go to receive the food:

first, he wished to enter meditative concentration; second, he wished to preach the Dharma to the devas; third, he wished to wander about and inspect the rooms of the bhikṣus; fourth, he wished to visit the sick bhikṣus; and fifth, if the precepts had not yet been established, he wished to establish them for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Buddha took a door-bolt in his hand and entered the quarters of the bhikṣus. There he saw a bhikṣu suffering from illness, with no one to attend to him, lying in his own excrement and urine, unable to rise or move about.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“What is troubling you?
You are alone and have no one to look after you!”
The bhikṣu replied, "Venerable sir!
By nature I am indolent; when others were ill, I did not look after them at all."
"Therefore, I am ill, and others do not even look after me!
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
"I shall look upon you.
Then Śakra Devānām-indra washed his hands with water, and the Buddha rubbed his body with his hand.
As he rubbed his body, all his pains were immediately healed, and his body and mind became peaceful and secure.

At that time, the World-Honored One gently supported the sick bhikṣu as he rose, led him out of the room to wash and dress, and then slowly escorted him back inside, where he provided him with a fresh mat and bade him sit.
The Buddha said to the sick bhikṣu:

"For a long time you have not diligently sought to attain what has not yet been attained, to reach what has not yet been reached, or to realize what has not yet been realized; thus you have endured various sufferings and afflictions, and in this way, there shall yet be even greater suffering for you!"
Having heard this, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s grace is immeasurable and his supernormal powers are infinite; by touching me with his hand, my pain has been instantly removed, and my body and mind are filled with bliss!"
For this reason, the Buddha used his supernormal powers to cause the sick to recover.
Regarding the phrase "those with impaired physical forms attain completeness," who are called "those with impaired physical forms"?
If there are those who, in previous lives, destroyed the bodies of others—severing their heads, cutting off their hands and feet, or breaking various parts of their limbs;
or who destroyed images of the Buddha, mutilated the noses of Buddha images, or damaged the forms of various worthy sages;
or who destroyed the likenesses of their own parents.
Because of these offenses, one receives a physical form that is frequently incomplete.
Furthermore, as a retribution for unwholesome dharmas, one receives an ugly body;
or in this present life, one may be plundered by bandits or subjected to execution, resulting in mutilation and destruction through various causes and conditions.
Some suffer from diseases of wind, cold, or heat, with malignant sores breaking out on their bodies and their limbs rotting away; this is called physical deformity.
Through the great grace of the Buddha, they all attain full restoration.
For example, there was a slave in the Jeta Grove named Gendī; Gendī means "continuity" in the language of Qin. He was the nephew of King Prasenajit;
he was handsome and brave, and his disposition was gentle and virtuous.
When the King’s principal consort saw him, her heart was captivated by him; she immediately called him aside in secret, wishing to bring him under her influence.
But Khandika would not comply. The consort became furious and slandered him to the King, yet she herself ended up being punished for his crime.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately dismembered him limb by limb and cast the remains among the graves;
yet before his life had even ceased, that very night tigers, wolves, and rākṣasas came, intending to devour him.
At that time, the Buddha went to his side; when his radiance shone upon him, the man’s body was immediately restored to health, and his heart was filled with great joy.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he immediately attained the three paths.
The Buddha took him by the hand and led him to the Jetavana.
The man said:
"My body has already been broken and discarded; the Buddha has restored my body. Now, for the remainder of this life, I shall offer my body as a gift to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
The next day, King Prasenajit, having heard of these matters, came to the Jetavana and said to Kāṇḍīn:
"I repent my transgression toward you!
You were truly without fault; I unjustly punished and harmed you. I shall now divide the kingdom with you and rule half of it."
Ganḍi said: "I am already weary of it; the King is likewise without fault.
This is the retribution for the calamities and transgressions of my past lives!"
"I now offer my body to the Buddha and the Sangha; it shall not be returned.
Thus, if there were sentient beings whose bodies were maimed or incomplete, they were immediately restored to wholeness upon receiving the Buddha’s radiance.
Therefore it is said:
even those with physical deformities all attain completeness; having received the Buddha’s radiance, they are immediately restored to health.
[Sūtra] All sentient beings come to regard one another with minds of equality.
They were like fathers and mothers, like elder and younger brothers, like elder and younger sisters, and also like close relatives and spiritual friends.

At that time, sentient beings practiced the ten paths of wholesome action, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, and were free from all blemishes; they were serenely happy, just as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna.
They all attained excellent wisdom, maintained the precepts to guard themselves, and did not afflict other sentient beings.
[Treatise] Question:

These sentient beings have not yet abandoned desire, lack meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and have not attained the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*); how then can they "attain an impartial mind" (*samacitta*)?
The answer is:
These [beings] are not equal in terms of meditative concentration; rather, they are free from enmity and ill will toward all sentient beings.
Because of this, they regard one another with virtuous minds.
Furthermore, regarding "equanimity of mind" (*samacitta*), it is stated in a sutra:
"What is meant by equanimity of mind?
To regard one another as one would one's own parents—this is called equanimity of mind."
Question: Is it that one regards all sentient beings as one’s own parents, brothers, and sisters?
Answer: Yes.
"No, indeed! One regards the elderly as one's parents, those of middle age as elder brothers, and the young as younger brothers; it is the same for sisters.
Because of an equalizing mind, all are regarded as one's own kin."
Question: How is it that one who is not a parent calls them "parent," and so on, up to one who is not a relative calls them "relative"?
Does this not constitute falling into false speech?
Answer: Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, there are no sentient beings who have not been one's father, mother, brother, sister, or close relative.
Furthermore, within the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there are no fathers, mothers, or brothers.
Because people are attached to the notion of a self and calculate things through inversion, they designate others as "father," "mother," "brother," and so forth.
Now, by the power of the mind of goodness, they regard one another as father and mother; this is no empty talk.

Furthermore, it is like a person who, out of a sense of righteousness, serves one who is not his father as a father, and serves one who is not his mother as a mother; the same applies to brothers and sons.
It is like a person who, when their own son behaves wickedly, casts him out and abandons him;
yet, if a child of another clan acts virtuously, they raise him as their own son.
To regard others in this manner is what constitutes an impartial mind.
As it is said in verse:
"To regard the wives of others as one's mother, To see the wealth of others as fire,
And to view all beings as one's own kin— This is what is called right view."
At that time, sentient beings practiced the ten paths of wholesome action.
Regarding the three types of physical actions:
abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, and abstaining from sexual misconduct;
The four paths of action of speech are:

abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech; the three paths of action of mind are: [abstaining from covetousness, abstaining from malice, and abstaining from wrong view].
Not coveting, not harming, and not holding wrong views.
One does not kill living beings oneself, does not instruct others to kill, praises those who do not kill, and seeing others who do not kill, rejoices on their behalf;
this applies likewise to the four types of wrong views.
Question:
The last three paths of action are not karma, whereas the first seven paths of action are karma; why, then, are they called the "ten paths of wholesome karma"? Answer:
Because they proceed from the minor to the major, they are collectively termed "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Although the latter three are not themselves karma, they can initiate karma;
furthermore, they arise for the sake of karma. For these reasons, they are all collectively designated as paths of action.
Regarding the phrase, "Purifying the holy life (brahmacarya) so that it is free from all blemishes and impurities":
A question is raised:

Since the previous exposition on practicing the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) is already sufficient in principle, why is it stated here once again that one "purifies the holy life"?
Answer: There are those who practice the ten paths of wholesome action but do not cease sexual activity;
now, this practice is further praised as the "Brahma-conduct" because it involves the total eradication of lustful desire, and is thus called "purely cultivating the Brahma-conduct."

Regarding the phrase "free from all blemishes and impurities": those who engage in sexual misconduct have foul bodies and a stinking reputation; for this reason, the person who has severed sexual desire is praised as being "free from all blemishes and impurities."
Regarding the phrase "serenely joyful":
a question is asked,
"What kind of joy is this?"
The answer is:
This happiness is of two kinds:
internal happiness and the happiness of nirvāṇa.
This bliss does not arise from the five sensory objects; it is like a spring in a rock, where water emerges from within and does not come from without.

Mental bliss is also like this: by practicing equanimity of mind, cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and attaining the ten paths of wholesome action, one becomes pure and free from defilement—this is called internal bliss.
Question:
To which realm is this pleasure bound?
Is it bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
Answer: This joy is bound to the desire realm and also unbound;
it is not bound to the form or formless realms.
Now, regarding the statement, "For example, as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna": if this were bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one should not say "for example.
For this reason, it is known that it is not bound to the realm of form.
This mind of the desire realm gives rise to joy and bliss that pervades the entire body;
it is like a warm medicinal oil soaking the body, making it supple, harmonious, and pleasant.

As for "non-attachment," one attains the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, contemplates all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, and attains true wisdom. When the mind has no point of attachment, there is the bliss of signlessness (*animitta*); this is what is meant by non-attachment.
Question: The Buddha said that Nirvana is the supreme bliss; why then do you speak of "the bliss of the third dhyāna"? Answer:
There are two kinds of happiness:
the happiness of sensation and the happiness of the exhaustion of sensation.
The happiness of the exhaustion of sensation is the happiness of nirvana without remainder, wherein all five aggregates have been exhausted and will never arise again.
That which can eliminate sorrow and affliction, bringing joy to the mind, is called pleasant feeling;
such fulfillment of pleasant feeling exists within the third dhyāna.
For this reason, it says, "It is like the bliss of the third dhyāna. Question:
Since there is also the experience of bliss in the first and second dhyānas, why does it mention only the "third dhyāna"?
The answer is:
Joy is of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior.
The inferior is the first dhyāna; the middling is the second dhyāna; and the superior is the third dhyāna.
The first dhyāna has two types:
the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya);
the faculty of pleasure associated with the five consciousnesses, and the faculty of joy associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
In the second dhyāna, there is the faculty of joy associated with the mental consciousness;
in the third dhyāna, there is the faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness.
Throughout all three realms, apart from the third dhyāna, there is no other faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness.

These five consciousnesses are incapable of discrimination and do not know the characteristics of names; in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, when the visual consciousness arises, the mental consciousness has already arisen.

For this reason, the faculty of pleasure associated with the five consciousnesses cannot fulfill pleasure, whereas the faculty of pleasure associated with the mental consciousness can fulfill pleasure.

For this reason, among the various merits within the third dhyāna, because pleasure (sukha) is predominant, there are no liberations (vimokṣa), spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), or totalities (kṛtsnāyatana).
Beyond this third dhyāna, there is no further pleasure; for this reason, it says, "For example, as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna."
Regarding the statement that "all sentient beings shall all obtain excellent wisdom, uphold the precepts, maintain self-restraint, and not afflict other beings":
one asks, for what reason is it said that "all obtain excellent wisdom" immediately after [the mention of] happiness?
Answer: When a person has not yet attained happiness, they are able to perform meritorious deeds;
however, once they have attained happiness, their minds become excessively attached to that pleasure, and thus they do not perform meritorious deeds!
Therefore, following the attainment of happiness, one sequentially gains excellent wisdom.
"Excellent wisdom" means observing the precepts, maintaining self-restraint, and not harassing sentient beings.
Question:
Observing the precepts is called "self-restraint" and is also called "not harassing sentient beings. For what reason, then, are both "self-restraint" and "not harassing sentient beings" mentioned?
Answer: Goodness of body and speech is called "observing the precepts" (śīla);
restraining the mind and directing it toward goodness is called "self-restraint," and is also termed "not afflicting sentient beings."
All merits are subsumed within the aggregate of morality (śīla-kāya), the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-kāya), and the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-kāya).
To say "one who well upholds the precepts" refers to what is subsumed within the aggregate of morality;
to say "one who well guards oneself" refers to what is subsumed within the aggregate of concentration.
"Not afflicting sentient beings" refers to virtues such as loving-kindness within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); these are subsumed under the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*).
Question: Since there is no one who would say they "do not like to maintain the precepts," why does it now say "liking to maintain the precepts"?
Answer: It is like those Brahmins attached to worldly dharmas who say:
"One who abandons the home life and zealously upholds the precepts is a person who severs the lineage."
"Furthermore, one who acquires wealth through their own efforts can extensively cultivate merit; such a person possesses this kind of fortune.
But for one who has left the household life and lives on alms, if they cannot even provide for themselves, how could they possibly perform various meritorious deeds?"
Thus, those who praise the observance of precepts also include worldlings who follow the methods of governance; they criticize those who prioritize self-restraint, saying:

"A person should govern the world through the law, rewarding the good and punishing the wicked. The law must not be transgressed, nor should one show favoritism toward the honored or the kin. By establishing laws to save the world, the benefit is great; why then use only oneself to be good, remaining self-contained and doing nothing?"
"The world is in chaos and lacks order; people are in distress and not being rescued!
This is called criticizing the preference for self-preservation.
Furthermore, there are those who criticize the preference for not harassing sentient beings, saying:

"If one cannot retaliate against an enemy, bind a thief, punish the wicked, or impose discipline upon the guilty; if one cannot ward off calamities or rescue those in distress, then silence is of no benefit—what use is this?"
Thus, one should censure what is unwholesome so as not to afflict sentient beings.
As it is said:
"If a person lacks courage and vigor, what is the use of being born into this world?"
"To see one's parents in distress and not rescue them, like a wooden figure standing on the ground"—
various unwholesome words such as these are called "reproaching those who do not harm sentient beings."
These devas and humans all attain excellent wisdom; they uphold the precepts, maintain self-restraint, and do not afflict sentient beings.

By practicing these wholesome dharmas, their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure; they have nothing to fear or dread, and being free from feverish distress, they possess a fine reputation and good renown, being loved and respected by others—this is what constitutes approaching the gate of Nirvana.
When their life is about to end, they see their merit and their hearts rejoice; they are without sorrow and without regret.
If they have not yet attained nirvana, they will be reborn in the worlds of the Buddhas or in the heavens.
For this reason it is said:
"One attains excellent wisdom, maintains the precepts, and self-restrains oneself, not harassing sentient beings.
— *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 8.
The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise, Part One: The Remainder of the Commentary on the Emission of Light, Scroll Nine.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.

Translated by Imperial Decree. [Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; within the trichiliocosm, his virtue was uniquely supreme, and his radiance, physical form, and majestic power were so magnificent as to pervade the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
For example, the light and color of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, are exceptionally sublime, such that no other mountains can equal them.
[Treatise] Question:
By what power does the Buddha’s virtue stand preeminent among all sentient beings, and why are his radiance and majestic majesty so towering and magnificent?

Since the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, the various devas, and the sages also possess great power, radiance, and majestic virtue, why do you say that only the Buddha’s virtues are exceptionally venerable?
The answer is:
Although these noble ones possess radiance and majestic virtue, they are finite and limited.
They are like the various stars; once the sunlight has emerged, they vanish and do not appear.

The Buddha has accumulated great merit over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas until all perfections are complete; because the causes and conditions are vast, the retribution is likewise vast, whereas other beings do not possess this.

Furthermore, throughout his successive lifetimes, the Buddha practiced various ascetic disciplines, constantly bestowing upon sentient beings his head, eyes, marrow, and brain in immeasurable and innumerable instances; how could it have been merely his kingdom, wealth, wife, and children?

All various kinds of ethical discipline, various kinds of patience, various kinds of diligence, and various kinds of meditative concentration, as well as incomparable, pure, indestructible, and inexhaustible wisdom—having practiced these throughout successive lifetimes, they have been fully perfected.
By the power of this fruit, one attains an immeasurable and extraordinary majesty; for this reason, it is said that "because the causes and conditions are great, the retribution is also great."
Question:
If the Buddha’s supernatural power is immeasurable and his majestic virtue is so sublime as to be beyond description, for what reason did he undergo the retribution for nine offenses?
First, the Brahmin woman Sundarī slandered him, and five hundred Arhats were also slandered along with him.
Second, the Brahmin woman Ciñcā tied wooden bowls to her belly and slandered the Buddha;
third, Devadatta pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha, injuring his big toe;
fourth, a splinter of wood pierced his foot.
Fifth, when King Virūḍhaka raised an army and slaughtered the Śākyas, the Buddha suffered from a headache;
sixth, at the invitation of the Brahmin Aṅgada, he ate horse fodder;
seventh, due to the movement of a cold wind, his back ached.
Eighth, the six years of ascetic practice;
ninth, entering a Brahmin village to beg for food and returning with an empty bowl.
Furthermore, during the eight nights before and after the winter solstice, when cold winds shattered the bamboo, he sought out the three robes to ward off the chill.
Furthermore, he suffered from fever, and Ānanda stood behind him fanning the Buddha.
In such ways as these, the Buddha underwent even the minor affairs of the world.

If the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) is immeasurable—such that throughout the trichiliocosm and even in the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, his radiance, physical form, and majestic virtue are so sublime—why then does he undergo various retributions for sins?
Answer:

The Buddha was born among humans as a human parent, receiving a human body and strength; yet the strength of a single finger-joint surpasses that of ten million billion nayutas of white elephants, and his power of supernormal feats is immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable.

This son of King Śuddhodana, having grown weary of the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, left the household life and attained the Way of the Buddha—how could such a person undergo the retribution of sin, being tormented by cold, heat, and the like?
Just as the Buddha’s supernatural power is inconceivable, how could there be any afflictions such as cold or heat within that which is inconceivable?
Furthermore, the Buddha has two kinds of bodies:
first, the Dharma-nature body; second, the body born of parents.

This Dharma-nature body fills the voids of the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless; its physical form is upright and majestic, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, possessing immeasurable radiance and immeasurable voices. The assembly listening to the Dharma also fills the voids, for this assembly is likewise the Dharma-nature body, which cannot be seen by those subject to birth and death.
It constantly manifests various bodies, various names, various places of birth, and various skillful means to deliver sentient beings, eternally saving all without a moment’s rest.
Such is the Buddha of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya-buddha*), who is able to deliver sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Those who undergo various retributions for their transgressions are the birth-body Buddhas (*janma-kāya-buddha*); these birth-body Buddhas preach the Dharma in succession according to human laws.
Because there are two kinds of Buddhas, there is no fault in receiving various karmic retributions for offenses.

Furthermore, at the very moment a Buddha attains the Way, all unwholesome dharmas are completely severed and all wholesome dharmas are fully accomplished; how could there then be any actual unwholesome dharma-retribution remaining to be received?
It is solely out of compassion for sentient beings of future ages that he manifests these skillful means to undergo such sufferings.

Furthermore, just as Aniruddha received immeasurable happiness for countless lifetimes because he gave food to a pratyekabuddha—whereby his thoughts of food and drink were fulfilled at will—how much more so for the Buddha, who in life after life cut his own flesh and extracted his marrow to give to sentient beings; how could he then fail to obtain alms and return with an empty bowl?
For this reason, it is known that the Buddha employs skillful means (*upāya*) to save sentient beings, and thus accepts these various karmic offenses.
How does he employ skillful means out of compassion for future generations?
Because the merit of the fivefold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples is meager, they are unable to obtain the various requisites for their livelihood when they beg for them.
The laypeople said:
"If you cannot even obtain food and clothing, and cannot eliminate your own illnesses, how can you attain the Way to benefit others?
To this, the five groups [of monastics] should reply:
"Although we have no small means for sustaining our lives, we possess the merit of practicing the Path.
The many sufferings we endure today are the retribution for the sins of our past lives;
the merit we cultivate now will bring benefit in the future."
Even when our Great Teacher, the Buddha, entered a village of brahmins to beg for alms, he could not obtain any and returned with an empty bowl;

the Buddha also suffered from various ailments, and even when the Śākyas were being punished for their crimes, the Buddha suffered a headache—how much more so for us, people of meager merit and low station!

Upon hearing this, the laypeople’s anger subsided; they then provided the bhikṣus with the four kinds of offerings, whereby the bhikṣus attained physical well-being, sat in meditation, and realized the Way.
This is for the sake of skillful means; it is not that they truly undergo punishment.
As it is said in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*:
When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, he spoke to Ānanda:
"I have a feverish wind-disorder arising within my body; I shall need cow's milk.
Take my bowl and beg for some cow's milk.
Ānanda took the Buddha’s bowl and entered Vaiśālī at dawn, arriving at the gate of a lay devotee’s house and standing there.
At that time, Vimalakīrti was walking there and saw Ānanda standing with his almsbowl;
he asked Ānanda, "Why are you standing here at this early hour with your almsbowl?"
Ānanda replied, “The Buddha’s body has a slight ailment that requires cow’s milk;
this is why I have come here. Vimalakīrti said:
"Stop! Stop, Ānanda!"
Do not slander the Tathāgata!
The Buddha is the World-Honored One; having transcended all unwholesome dharmas, how could he have any illness?
Do not let the non-Buddhists hear these coarse words, for they will disparage the Buddha and say:
"If even the Buddha cannot save himself when he is ill, how can he save others?
Ānanda replied, "This was not my own idea;
I received the Buddha’s direct command that I must obtain cow's milk."
Vimalakīrti said:
"Although this is the Buddha’s command, it is a skillful means; because we live in this present age of the five corruptions, he delivers all beings by means of such a manifestation."
If in future ages there are sick bhikṣus who seek medicinal decoctions from laypeople,
and the laypeople say:
"If you cannot even cure your own illness, how can you cure others?"
The bhikṣus said:
"If even our Great Teacher still suffers from illness, how could we—whose bodies are like blades of grass or mustard seeds—not fall ill?
For this reason, lay followers provide the bhikṣus with various medicinal decoctions so that they may remain at ease, practicing meditation and the Path.

If there are non-Buddhists and seers who can eliminate the illnesses of others through medicinal herbs and incantations, how much more so should the Tathāgata, with his omniscience and merit, be able to eliminate illness from his own body?
"You should remain silent, take your bowl, and fetch some milk, so that no other person or follower of a different school may hear of it.
From this, we know that the Buddha employed skillful means; he was not actually ill.
The causes and conditions for all transgressions are likewise thus.
