This bodhisattva is also like this: born into a world of mixed [qualities], their sharp wisdom is difficult to approach.
It is like a person who, having undergone diligent hardship from a young age, possesses many capabilities and is capable of much;
or like a horse that has been raised but not ridden—it can no longer be put to use.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattvas in this Sahā world possess many skillful means, they are difficult to approach; this is not the case in other places.
As the Buddha said:
"I recall my own past lives, when in a single day I bestowed a thousand lives upon others."

For the sake of delivering sentient beings, although they are fully endowed with all merits, the six pāramitās, and all Buddha-activities, they do not become Buddhas, but constantly deliver and liberate sentient beings through skillful means.
For this reason, the bodhisattvas in this Sahā world are difficult to approach.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi received from the Buddha Ratnākara a thousand-petaled golden lotus flower and set out together with countless monastic and lay bodhisattvas, as well as various young men and maidens.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi possesses great power and supernormal faculties, he ought to be able to come; but how do these bodhisattvas—whether monastics or laypeople, as well as boys and girls—arrive here of their own accord?
The World of Many Treasures lies at the very eastern edge; the distance is vast and far-reaching— is this by one's own power of practice,
or by the power of the Buddha Ratnākara,
or by the power of the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi?
"Is this by the power of Śākyamuni Buddha?
He replied,
"It is entirely due to the power of these four kinds of people."

These bodhisattvas, whether they are householders or those who have left the home life, are either non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who have accomplished the five supernormal powers and have well cultivated the four bases of psychic power; this is due to their past karmic conditions with Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as through their own personal efforts and the power of the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi. Why is this so?
Among them, those whose power and influence were weak were able to come because of the power of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha.
It is like when a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) flies up into the sky: his fourfold army, as well as his palaces, pavilions, livestock, and beasts—all fly along;
for the merit of the Wheel-Turning Sage King is so great that he can cause everything to follow him in flight.

It is the same here: those whose power and influence are weak have all been able to come because of the power of the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, as well as the power of Buddha Ratnākara and the illumination of Śākyamuni’s light.
If they lacked power themselves, yet could have come even by the light of Śākyamuni Buddha alone, how much more so when there were three!
Question:
Why did this Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi not come alone, but instead brought many people with him?
Answer: Because it is appropriate for there to be attendants.
For example, when a king goes out, he must necessarily have a retinue.
Furthermore, this is because of the karmic conditions between the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi and Śākyamuni Buddha. Why is this so?
Within that great assembly, two groups have come together; therefore, we know that those with the necessary karmic conditions have arrived, while those without such conditions remain behind.
Question:
For what reason does this bodhisattva come together with these householders, renunciants, boys, and girls?
Answer:
The seven assemblies of the Buddha’s disciples are:
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Upāsakas and upāsikās are householders; the other five groups are renunciants.
Within both the renunciant and householder states, there are further two types:
the great and the small.
The "small" refers to boys and girls;
the remainder are considered "large. Question:
The great should go; how can the small come?
He replied:
"It depends on one's merit, not on whether one is great or small."
If one loses the benefits of merit and practices unwholesome dharmas, one is young despite being old;
if one possesses the benefits of merit and practices wholesome dharmas, one is great despite being young.
Furthermore, when this small person comes from afar, people see him and exclaim:
"Though small, he is able to do such a thing; he has come from afar for the sake of the Dharma!
This also demonstrates that the Buddha-dharma can be practiced by both the small and the great.
In the teachings of the non-Buddhists, only Brahmins are permitted to practice their dharma, while those who are not Brahmins are not;
in the Buddha-dharma, there is neither great nor small, neither insider nor outsider, and all are able to practice it.
For example, when taking medicine, the primary aim is to eliminate the illness, regardless of whether it is expensive or inexpensive, or whether the patient is high-born or low-born, great or small.
[Sūtra] They all made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddhas of the eastern direction.
[Treatise] Question:
If one were to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the eastern direction, since those Buddhas are so numerous, when would it ever end? When could they possibly come to this world?
The answer is:
These bodhisattvas do not perform the dharma-offerings of humans or devas, but practice the dharma of bodhisattva offerings themselves.

Regarding the dharma of bodhisattva offerings: their bodies enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and as their bodies move straight forward, immeasurable bodies emerge from their sides, manifesting various kinds of offering objects that fill all buddha-worlds.
It is like when a dragon king travels, water flows from his body and rains down universally upon the world.
A question is asked:
These bodhisattvas wish to go to Śākyamuni Buddha; why do they make offerings to various buddhas along the way?
Answer:
The Buddhas are the foremost field of merit; if one makes offerings to them, one obtains a great reward.
It is like a person who extensively cultivates their fields and enterprises in order to obtain a great harvest of grain.
The bodhisattvas see that by making offerings to the Buddhas, they obtain the fruit of Buddhahood; for this reason, they make offerings.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva always respects and honors the Buddha, just as a person respects and honors their parents.

The various bodhisattvas, having received the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, attained various samādhis, various dhāraṇīs, and various supernormal powers; out of gratitude for this kindness, they made extensive offerings.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja attained from the Buddha the samādhi of the "Body of All Manifestations" (*sarvavikurvaṇa-rūpakāya-samādhi*) and reflected:
"How shall I make offerings to the Buddha and to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*?"
Immediately, he flew up into the heavens and, by the power of samādhi, rained down the seven treasures, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies as offerings to the Buddha.
Having emerged from samādhi, his mind was still not yet satisfied.
For twelve hundred years, he consumed various fragrances and drank various fragrant oils; thereafter, wrapping his body in celestial white cotton cloth, he set it ablaze, making this vow:
"May the radiance of my body illuminate as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in eighty Ganges Rivers!"
Then the Buddhas in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in eighty Ganges Rivers praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! To make offerings with one's own body is the foremost;
it surpasses making offerings of kingdoms, cities, wives, and children by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond the reach of any analogy."
For twelve hundred years, his body remained burning without extinguishing.

Furthermore, by making this offering to the Buddha, one obtains immeasurable renown, merit, and benefit; all unwholesome matters are entirely eliminated, and all roots of goodness increase. One shall constantly receive the rewards of such offerings in both this life and future lives, and after a long time, one will attain Buddhahood.
By making such offerings to the Buddha, one attains various and immeasurable benefits.
For this reason, all Bodhisattvas make offerings to the Buddha.
[Sūtra] Carrying various flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, ointments, robes, banners, and canopies, they proceeded toward the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
[Śāstra] Question:
One should simply say "prostrates"; why is it called "prostrating with the head at the feet"?
The answer is:
Among the parts of a human body, the head is the most noble, for it is where the five sensory faculties reside and it occupies the highest position;
the feet are the most base, for they tread upon impure places and occupy the lowest position.
Therefore, one uses the rites esteemed by the noble to honor those who are humble, because of the value placed upon making offerings.
Furthermore, there are inferior, middling, and superior forms of salutation:
the inferior is the bowing of the hands (*yī*), the middling is kneeling (*guì*), and the superior is prostrating with the head to the ground (*jīshǒu*).
To prostrate with one's head at the feet is the supreme form of offering.
For this reason, within the Buddha’s Vinaya, a bhikṣu of lower standing grasps both feet of a bhikṣu of higher standing with both hands and prostrates with his head.
Question: There are four modes of physical conduct:
sitting, standing, walking, and lying down. For what reason does he stand facing one direction?
The answer is:
One should not walk for the sake of coming, nor should one lie down for the sake of receiving respect and offerings; this matter is easy to understand, so why is it worth asking?
One should ask: "Are you sitting or standing?
For one who sits shows a lack of reverence for the offering;
one who stands shows reverent worship of the Dharma.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, all those who have left home as non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) and all laypeople (*avadātavasana*) come to where the Buddha is and sit.
The non-Buddhists sit because they hold their own doctrines in high regard and thus slight the Buddha;
the laypeople sit because they are like guests.
The bodies and minds of all members of the five assemblies belong to the Buddha; therefore, they are established [in this position].
As for those Arhats who have attained the Way, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and others, because they have already accomplished what was to be done, they are permitted to sit;
others, though they may have attained the three lower paths, are not permitted to sit, because their great task is not yet completed and the thieves of the fetters have not been destroyed.
It is like the king’s ministers, who sit because they have performed great meritorious services;
among these bodhisattvas, although there are those in white robes, they stand because they have come from afar to make offerings to the Buddha.
[Sūtra] He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata Ratnakūṭa sends his greetings to the World-Honored One:
Are you free from affliction and illness? Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Is your physical strength and well-being secure?"
Furthermore, he offered these thousand-petaled golden lotuses to the World-Honored One.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the Buddha Ratnākara possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), why does he inquire after Śākyamuni Buddha’s welfare, asking whether he has little affliction or illness, whether his daily life is light and easy, and whether his physical strength is peaceful and at ease?
The answer is:
It is the nature of all Buddhas to know and yet ask questions.
For example, in the Vinaya, when the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka constructed a cave made of red bricks, the Buddha saw it and, though already knowing, asked:
“Ānanda! What is this being made?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"This is the son of a potter who has gone forth; his name is Daṇḍaka. He built a small grass hut, but it was constantly destroyed by cowherds; after it was built three times and destroyed three times, he therefore built this earthenware hut."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Break down this earthen cave!
For what reason?
The followers of external paths may say:
"While the Great Teacher, the Buddha, was still present, the teachings concerning the outflows (āsrava) were being promulgated!
It is in such instances that he knows the answer but asks intentionally.

Furthermore, although the Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom, he accords with worldly conventions; when people of the world exchange greetings, the Buddha likewise exchanges greetings. Since the Buddha was born among humans and partakes of human conditions—such as cold and heat, birth and death—which are equal to those of others, the manner of his greetings should also be equal.
Furthermore, within a world, those of great nobility and those of great meanness should not exchange greetings with one another;
however, by virtue of the Buddha’s power, they ought to exchange greetings.

Moreover, this Many-Jewels World is pure and magnificently adorned, and the color, form, and radiance of the Buddha’s body are likewise vast; if one were not to exchange greetings, people would say that one was being disrespectful.

Furthermore, he wished to demonstrate that although the physical forms, colors, and radiances of the Buddha-worlds may vary in their excellence, their wisdom and spiritual powers are equal and without difference; for this reason, he inquired after his well-being.
Question: Why does he ask, "Are you free from illness and free from affliction? Answer:
There are two kinds of illness:
first, illness caused by external conditions; second, illness caused by internal conditions.
As for the external, such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, weapons, staves, falling, being crushed by earth, and various other such external afflictions—these are called "disturbances."
The internal refers to immoderation in food and drink, irregularity in sleeping and rising, the four hundred and four diseases, and various other such conditions; these are called internal illnesses.
Since both types of illness cause suffering for all who possess a body, he asked:
"Are you free from little affliction and little ailment?"
Question: Why does he not ask, “Are you free from affliction? Are you free from illness? but instead ask, “Do you have little affliction? Do you have little suffering? Answer:
The Sage truly knows that "the body is the root of suffering; there is no time when it is not ill.
Why is this? This body is a composite of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and their natures are incompatible, each harming the other.
It is like a malignant ulcer that never ceases to cause pain; if one applies medicine to it, it may achieve slight improvement but cannot be cured.
The human body is also like this: it is constantly ill and constantly treated; because it is treated, one lives, but if it were not treated, one would die.
For this reason, one cannot ask whether there is "no affliction" or "no illness," because external afflictions—
namely wind, rain, cold, and heat— are constantly present as sources of distress.
Furthermore, there are four bodily postures:
sitting, lying down, walking, and standing. Sitting for too long causes extreme distress; likewise, lying down, standing, or walking for too long all cause distress.
For this reason, he asks, "Are you free from much affliction and free from much illness?
A questioner asks:
Since asking about being "free from much affliction and free from much illness" would have been sufficient, why does he further say, "Are you light and agile in your movements and rest?"
The answer is:
Although a person’s illness has subsided, they have not yet fully recovered; for this reason, one asks, “Are you light and well in your movements and rest?
The questioner asks: [Why is this so?]
Why is it asked, "Are you strong and at ease?
The answer is:

there are those whose illnesses have been cured; although they are able to walk, sit, and rise, their physical strength is not yet sufficient to undertake tasks or perform actions, such as carrying light objects or lifting heavy ones. Therefore, one asks about their "strength."
There are those who, though their illness has been cured and they are able to lift heavy objects and carry light ones, have not yet attained peace and happiness;
for this reason, he asks: "Are you at peace and happy? He asks:
If one is free from illness and possesses strength, why has one not yet attained peace and happiness?
The answer is:
there are those who are impoverished, terrified, and sorrowful, and thus do not attain peace and happiness; for this reason, the question is asked.
"Are you at ease?
Furthermore, there are two methods of inquiry:
inquiring after the body and inquiring after the mind.
If one says, "Are you free from minor afflictions and illness? Are you light and at ease in your movements and rest, as well as in your physical strength? this is an inquiry concerning the body.
If one says, "Are you at peace and happy? this is an inquiry concerning the mind.
The various internal and external ailments are called physical illnesses;

the various afflictions such as lust, anger, jealousy, stinginess, greed, sorrow, and fear, as well as the ninety-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*), the five hundred entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and various desires and aspirations, are called mental illnesses.

Because one inquires after each individual's illness, it is said: "Are you free from affliction and disease? Are you light and agile in your movements and rest? Is your physical strength at ease and in comfort? A questioner asks:
"It may be appropriate to inquire in this manner regarding humans, but even for the devas such an inquiry would not be fitting; how much less so for the Buddha?"
Answer: The Buddha’s body is of two kinds:
first, the body of supernatural transformations; second, the body born of parents.
The physical body born of one's parents is inferior to that of the devas because it is subject to human laws; therefore, one should inquire after their well-being according to human custom. Question:

All noble sages have minds free from attachment; they do not crave the body, do not cherish life, do not loathe death, and do not rejoice in birth. If this is so, what is the purpose of inquiring after their well-being?
Answer: Because he conforms to worldly conventions, he accepts greetings according to human custom;
likewise, when sending greetings, he does so according to human custom as well.
"The thousand-petaled golden lotus" is as described above.

[Sūtra] At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having accepted these thousand-petaled golden lotuses, scattered them toward the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction.
[Treatise] Question:
Since there is no one superior to the Buddha, for what reason does he now scatter flowers as an offering toward the Buddhas of the eastern direction?
It was as when the Buddha first attained the Way, he thought to himself:
"If a person has no one to revere, their undertakings will not succeed; who in the worlds of the ten directions is worthy of reverence and service?
I wish to take them as my teacher and serve them!"
At that time, Brahmā, the King of Devas, and the other gods said to the Buddha:
"The Buddha is unsurpassed; there is none who surpasses the Buddha.

The Buddha himself also observed with his divine eye that throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, within all the worlds, there was no one superior to the Buddha, and he thought to himself:
"I practice the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; that which has now enabled me to attain Buddhahood is what I revere, it is my teacher, and I shall reverently make offerings to and serve this Dharma."

"It is like a tree named 'Excellent and Firm' (Sudṛḍha). This tree has been in the earth for a hundred years with its branches and leaves fully developed; yet in a single day it grows to a height of a hundred *zhang*. Once this tree has emerged, it seeks a great tree to provide shade for its body."
At that time, there was a deity in the forest who spoke to the tree Suḍāṭhika, saying:
"In this world, there is none greater than you; all trees shall dwell within your shade."

The Buddha is also like this: having been born within the stages of a bodhisattva for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he sat for a single day beneath the Bodhi tree at the Vajrāsana and, truly knowing the characteristics of all dharmas, attained the path of Buddhahood.
At that time, he thought to himself:
"Who may I honor and serve as my teacher? To whom shall I offer my service, respect, and offerings?
Then, Brahmā Śikhin and the other devas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha is supreme; there is none who surpasses the Buddha.
For what reason, then, does one now again make offerings to the Buddhas of the eastern direction?
The answer is:
Although the Buddha is unsurpassed, and there is none who exceeds the Buddha within the worlds of the three periods of time and the ten directions, one nevertheless performs offerings to him.
Offerings are categorized as superior, middling, or inferior:
to offer to one who is inferior to oneself is an inferior offering;
Making offerings to those superior to oneself is the supreme offering;
making offerings to those equal to oneself is the middling offering.
Making offerings to the Buddhas is the middling offering.
Just as the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Arhat bhikṣuṇīs, entered nirvāṇa on the same day at the same time, so too at that moment,
the upāsakas who had attained the three paths lifted five hundred couches,
while the Four Heavenly Kings lifted the couch of the Buddha’s foster mother, Mahāprajāpatī.
The Buddha stood before her, holding an incense burner and burning incense as an offering.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You all should assist me in making offerings to the body of my wet nurse."

At that time, the various Arhat bhikṣus each, by means of their supernormal powers, went to Mount Malaya, gathered sandalwood fuel from the ox-head variety, and assisted the Buddha in preparing the funeral pyre; this was the lower form of offering.
For this reason, although one does not seek a specific fruit, one practices equal offerings.
Furthermore, only a Buddha should make offerings to a Buddha; other people do not know the virtues of a Buddha.
As it is said in verse:
"The wise can revere wisdom; In discourse on wisdom, the wise find joy.
The wise can understand wisdom, Just as a snake knows its own feet!"
For this reason, the Buddhas, who possess all-knowledge, are able to make offerings to the All-Knowing One.
Furthermore, these Buddhas of the ten directions have, in life after life, exhorted and assisted Śākyamuni Buddha.
Just as a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage contemplates all phenomena as empty and non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing—
having contemplated thus, their mind does not cling to any world-system, and they desire to relinquish the six perfections and enter nirvana.
It is, for example, like a person who, while dreaming, constructs a raft to cross a great river; with hands and feet weary, they give rise to thoughts of distress and weariness.
While in the midst of the current, they awaken from the dream and think to themselves:
"Where is there any river that needs to be crossed?"
At that time, his diligent mind completely relaxed.

The Bodhisattva was likewise; established in the seventh stage, he attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and all mental activities ceased as he desired to enter nirvana.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all emitted radiance, illuminating the Bodhisattva’s body, and stroking his head with their right hands, they said: “Good son!
Do not give rise to such a thought!
You should remember your original vow to deliver sentient beings.
Although you understand emptiness, sentient beings do not; you must accumulate all merits, teach and transform sentient beings, and enter nirvana together with them!
"You have not yet attained the golden-colored body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, immeasurable radiance, or the thirty-two karmic actions.
You have now merely attained one dharma-gate of non-arising; do not be so greatly elated!"
At that time, having heard the instructions of all the Buddhas, the Bodhisattva returned to his original resolve to practice the six *pāramitās* in order to deliver sentient beings.
It was through such assistance that he attained the Way of the Buddha at its inception.
Furthermore, when the Buddha first attained the Way, he reflected within his mind:
"This Dharma is exceedingly profound; sentient beings are ignorant and of meager merit. I too have been born in this age of five corruptions; what should I do now?"
Having reflected thus, I thought: "I shall divide a single Dharma into three parts and establish it as the Three Vehicles to deliver sentient beings.
While I was engaged in this contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all manifested radiant light and praised me, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
We, too, dwell within this world of five corruptions; we shall divide a single Dharma into three parts to deliver sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha heard the voices of the Buddhas of the ten directions and was filled with great joy, exclaiming:
“Homage to the Buddha!

Thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions everywhere provide encouragement and assistance to bring about great benefit; out of awareness of this profound debt of gratitude, he offers flowers as an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
There is no supreme merit that surpasses this merit. Why is this?
These flowers are produced by the power of the merit of the Buddha Ratnākara; they are not flowers born from water.
Puming is a Dharma-body Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who has sent these flowers here to offer to Śākyamuni Buddha.
Śākyamuni Buddha knows that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the foremost field of merit; therefore, by making offerings to them, one’s merit is manifold.
Why is this? Because a Buddha makes offerings to a Buddha himself.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are four kinds of giving:
First, the giver is pure while the recipient is impure;
second, the giver is impure while the recipient is pure;
third, both the giver and the recipient are pure.
Fourth, the giver is impure and the recipient is impure.
Now, by giving to the Buddhas of the eastern direction, both parties are pure; this merit is the greatest.
For this reason, the Buddha himself makes offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Question: Since all noble ones (ārya) do not receive retributive fruits and will not be born again, why is it said that the merit of this giving is the greatest?
The answer is:
Although there is no one to receive this merit, its characteristic is inherently vast;
if there were someone to receive it, the retribution would be immeasurable.
Because the noble ones know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and empty, they relinquish them and enter nirvana; they relinquish even this merit as well.
It is like a ball of heated gold: although one may see its beauty with the eyes, it cannot be touched by the hand, for it would burn the person's hand.
Furthermore, it is like a person who has an ulcer and must apply medicine to it;
if there were no ulcer, the medicine would have no application.
A person’s body is likewise: it is constantly oppressed by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, which are just like the breaking out of an ulcer.
To provide clothing, bedding, food, and drink for warmth and comfort is like applying medicine to a wound.
It is like a foolish person who, out of greed for the medicine, does not seek to remove the wound;
yet if there were no wound, the medicine would likewise be useless.
The Buddhas regard the body as a wound; because they have abandoned this bodily wound, they likewise do not receive the medicine of karmic retribution.
For this reason, although they possess great merit, they do not undergo its retribution.
[Sūtra] The lotus flowers that were scattered filled the Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
[Śāstra] Question:
The flowers are few while the worlds are many; how can they fill them?
Answer: By virtue of the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), he possesses the eight kinds of spontaneous transformations as described above:

he can make the large small and the small large; he can make the light heavy and the heavy light; he moves with sovereign freedom and without obstruction, reaching wherever he desires; he can shake the great earth, and whatever he wishes is accomplished.

All the great sages have attained these eight kinds of mastery; therefore, the Buddha is able to fill worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with a single small flower.
Furthermore, he showed the sentient beings their future rewards of merit, saying: "These few flowers fill the worlds of the eastern direction.
He also exhorted the bodhisattvas of the east, saying: 'The fruit and reward obtained by planting merit in the field of the Buddha shall likewise fill immeasurable lands.
Although you have come from afar, you should rejoice; having encountered this great field of merit, your reward shall be immeasurable! "
[Sūtra] Upon each flower there is a bodhisattva, sitting cross-legged and preaching the six pāramitās;
those who hear this Dharma shall all eventually attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] Question:
Previously, the Buddha used the radiance of his tongue-mark to manifest a thousand-petaled jeweled flower, upon each of which there was a seated Buddha;
for what reason are there now, upon each flower, seated Bodhisattvas?
The answer is:
The flowers above were emanated by the Buddha, and therefore there are Buddhas seated upon them;
these flowers are those offered by the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, and for this reason there are Bodhisattvas seated upon them.
Furthermore, while those sentient beings above should attain liberation by seeing the Buddha seated, these sentient beings here should attain liberation by seeing the Bodhisattva seated.
He sits cross-legged and preaches the six *pāramitās*;
those who hear this Dharma will ultimately reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as previously explained.

[Sūtra] All the bodhisattvas, whether ordained or lay, as well as the boys and girls, bowed their heads at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, each offering articles of worship to honor, revere, respect, and praise Śākyamuni Buddha.

These bodhisattvas, both monastic and lay, as well as the boys and girls, each by the power of their own roots of goodness and merit, were able to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
[Treatise] As it is said in verse:
“The path by which all the Noble Ones have come, The Buddha has likewise come;
The true nature and that which is departed— The Buddha is also thus, without distinction.”
The noble ones speak according to reality, and the Buddha likewise speaks according to reality;
for this reason he is called the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
With the armor of patience his mind is firm, and with the bow of diligence his strength is mighty.
With the sharp arrows of wisdom, he destroys the thieves of pride.
He is worthy of receiving all offerings from gods and men;
for this reason, he is called a Buddha and an Arhat.
Truly knowing the true nature of suffering, And truly knowing the origin of suffering,
Knowing the true nature of the cessation of suffering, And knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering—
Truly understanding the Four Noble Truths, Which are certain, real, and unchangeable.
Therefore, throughout the ten directions, he is titled Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having attained the subtle and wondrous three knowledges (vidyā) and being fully endowed with pure conduct,
he is thus titled Bhagavat and Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna.
Having understood all phenomena, he has attained the wondrous Way for himself;
yet at times he teaches through skillful means out of compassion for all beings.
He eliminates old age, sickness, and death, leading them to the place of peace and security.
For this reason he is called a Buddha, and for this reason he is a Sugata.
Knowing whence the world comes, and also knowing the path to the cessation of the world—
for this reason he is called a Buddha, a Lokavid.
With the eyes of dhyāna, precepts, wisdom, and so forth, none can equal him, much less surpass him;
for this reason he is called the Buddha, the Anuttara.
With great compassion he delivers sentient beings, teaching and training them with gentleness and goodness.
For this reason he is called Buddha, Puruṣadamyasārathi;
with wisdom free from afflictions, he proclaims the supreme liberation—
for this reason he is called Buddha, Devamanuṣya.

"The movements and non-movements of the three periods of time, All phenomena, whether exhaustible or inexhaustible— Beneath the tree of enlightenment, he knows them all; Therefore, he is named Buddha.

[Sūtra] To the south, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world situated at the very edge called Free from All Sorrow. The Buddha there is named Virtue of No-Sorrow, and the Bodhisattva is named Free from Sorrow.

To the west, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world situated at the very edge called "Extinction of Evil. The Buddha there is named Jewel Mountain, and the bodhisattva is named Ritual Mind.

To the north, beyond as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world situated at the very edge named Vijaya; the Buddha there is named Vijitarāja, and the bodhisattva is named Vijayin.

Below, across as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world situated at the very edge named "Excellent" (Sādhu). The Buddha there is named "Virtuous Excellence" (Sādhuguna), and the Bodhisattva is named "Flower Supreme" (Puṣpadatta).

Above, passing through as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River, there is a world situated at the very edge called *Nandi*. The Buddha there is named *Nandideva*, and the bodhisattva is named *Nandiprāpta*.
In this way, all [directions] are just like the eastern direction.
[Treatise] Question:
According to the Buddha’s Dharma, there are in reality no names for the various directions; why is this so?

That which is not subsumed within the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), or the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and is likewise absent from the four scriptural collections (*piṭaka*), is said to be a real dharma (*bhūta-dharma*) that cannot be found even when sought through causes and conditions. Why, then, is it stated here that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions come?
Answer: It is spoken of as "direction" (dis) because it follows what is transmitted by conventional worldly dharmas; however, when one seeks the reality of "direction," it cannot be found.
Question:
Why do you say it is "without direction"?
You do not mention it in your fourfold collection of dharmas (catuṣkoṭi-dharmapiṭaka), whereas I do mention it in my sixfold collection of dharmas (ṣaḍdharmapiṭaka).
It is not subsumed within your categories of aggregates (skandha), sense-bases (āyatana), or elements (dhātu), whereas it is subsumed within my category of substantial entities (dravya).
This "direction" (方) is both existent and permanent, because it is a constant characteristic and possesses a defining mark.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The place where the sun rises is the east; the place where the sun sets is the west; the place where the sun travels is the south; and the place where the sun does not travel is the north."
The day is divided into three parts:
the first part, the middle part, and the last part.
According to the direction of the sun's division, the first part is the eastern direction; the same applies to the southern and western directions.
That which is not traversed by the sun is without spatial division.
"There" and "here," or "this" and "that," constitute the characteristic of direction (*dig-lakṣaṇa*);
if there were no "direction," there would be no "there" or "here. Thus, "there" and "here" are the characteristic of direction, rather than direction itself.
Answer: Not so!
Mount Sumeru stands in the midst of the four continents; the sun revolves around Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four worlds beneath heaven.
When it is midday in Uttarakuru, the sun rises in Pūrvavideha; for the people of Pūrvavideha, that is the east.
When it is midday in Pūrvavideha, the sun rises in Jambudvīpa; for the people of Jambudvīpa, that is the east.
In reality, there is no beginning. Why is this?
Because every direction is the east, every direction is the south, every direction is the west, and every direction is the north.

Your claim that "the place where the sun rises is the east, the place where the sun travels is the south, the place where the sun sets is the west, and the place where the sun does not travel is the north" is incorrect.
Furthermore, there are places where the sun does not appear; this constitutes a lack of "direction," because the characteristic of direction (*dig-lakṣaṇa*) is absent.
Question:
I am speaking of the "characteristic of direction" within a single country, while you raise an objection based on four countries. For this reason, the eastern direction is not without a beginning.
The answer is:

If, within a single country, the sun were to coincide with the eastern direction, this would constitute having a limit; because it has a limit, it is impermanent; and because it is impermanent, it is not all-pervading.
For this reason, "directions" have only a name but no reality.

[Sūtra] At that time, this trichiliocosm was transformed into jewels; flowers covered the ground everywhere, and silk streamers, banners, and canopies were suspended. Fragrant trees and flowering trees were all magnificently adorned.
[Treatise] Question:
By whose supernatural power was the earth transformed into jewels? Answer:
This is the result of the Buddha’s immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations.
While some may possess incantations, illusions, or various spirits, nāga kings, and devas who can transform minor objects,
none— neither other men nor even Brahmādeva— are capable of transforming the entire trichiliocosm into precious jewels.

When the Buddha enters the four dhyānas and the fourteen transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*), he is able to cause the flowers, incense, trees, and all the lands of the trichiliocosm to be completely adorned;
all sentient beings become harmonious and unified, and their minds turn toward goodness.
Why is this? It is to adorn this world for the purpose of expounding the Prajñāpāramitā;
it is also to adorn it for the sake of the visiting bodhisattvas from the ten directions, as well as for the devas, humans, and those of the world.

It is like a person inviting a noble guest: if invited by a single family, one adorns that family; if by a lord of a nation, one adorns that nation; if by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), one adorns the four continents; and if by a Brahmā Heaven King, one adorns the trichiliocosm.

The Buddha is the sovereign of immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, as many as the sands of the Ganges; this is because bodhisattvas from other regions, as well as devas and people of the world, have come as guests.

Furthermore, when these and other people behold this manifested transformation and its adornments, they give rise to the Great Mind and a heart of pure joy; from the Great Mind they initiate great deeds, and from great deeds they obtain great retribution. When receiving this great retribution, they again give rise to the Great Mind. Thus, through successive stages of growth, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, this world is transformed so that it becomes entirely composed of jewels.
What are called "jewels"?
There are four kinds of jewels:
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
There are further seven kinds of jewels:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musāragalva, agate, and red pearls—this pearl being extremely precious, not coral.
Furthermore, there are other treasures:

the *māragata* pearl, which emerges from the beak of the golden-winged garuḍa and is green in color, capable of warding off all poisons; the *indranīla* or celestial blue pearl; the *mahānīla* or great blue pearl; the *padmarāga* or red-light pearl; *vajra*; dragon pearls; wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*); jade, shells, coral, amber, and various other such things called treasures.
These jewels are of three kinds:
human jewels, celestial jewels, and bodhisattva jewels. Human jewels possess little power;
they have only pure radiance and color, which removes poison, dispels demons, and eliminates darkness, as well as various sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
The celestial jewel is both vast and superior; it constantly follows the celestial body, can be commanded, and can be spoken with. It is light and not heavy.
The Bodhisattva-jewel surpasses the celestial jewel, for it can encompass the affairs of both human jewels and celestial jewels;
furthermore, it can cause all sentient beings to know the causes, conditions, origins, and endings of dying here and being born there, just as one sees the reflection of one's face in a clear mirror.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-jewel is supreme, for it can produce various sounds of the Dharma;

if fashioned into a precious crown as a head ornament, it rains down banners, streamers, flower-canopies, and all manner of ritual implements upon the Buddhas of immeasurable worlds in the ten directions to make offerings to them.
Furthermore, they rain down robes, bedding, and various articles for daily life; according to the needs of sentient beings, they bestow all such diverse things as gifts.
Through these and other various kinds of treasures, they eliminate the suffering and distress of poverty among sentient beings.
Question:
From where do these various precious jewels originate? Answer:

Gold is extracted from mountain rocks, sand, and red copper; pearls are found within the bellies of fish, inside bamboo, and within the brains of snakes; dragon-pearls are found within the brains of dragons; coral grows from stone-trees in the ocean; mother-of-pearl is produced from the shells of insects; silver is extracted from scorched stones; and the remaining varieties, such as lapis lazuli and crystal, all emerge from mountain caves.
The wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) arises from the Buddha’s relics;
when the Dharma is about to perish, all relics transform into wish-fulfilling gems,
just as ice that has passed a thousand years transforms into crystal beads.
Such various jewels as these are the ordinary treasures among humans.
That which is adorned by the Buddha throughout all worlds is the most supreme; it is something that the devas cannot obtain. Why is this so?
These arise from great merit.
The various flowers and banners are as previously described.
As for the incense trees, they include the agallochum sweet-scented tree (*agaru*), the *tagara* wood-fragrance tree, sandalwood (*candana*), and other such varieties of incense trees.
There were various kinds of flowering trees, such as the Campaka tree with yellow blossoms, the Aśoka tree with *an-ūpa* (sorrowless) flowers, and the Bakula tree with red blossoms.
[Sūtra] It is, for example, as in the worlds Padmavyūha and Samantakusuma, where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, and other Bodhisattvas of great majestic power all dwell.
[Treatise] Question:
Why is it said, "For example, like the world-system Puṣpasaṃcaya"? Answer:
That world constantly possesses pure flowers, whereas this world undergoes transformation all at once; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.
According to the method of parable, the small is used to illustrate the great.
Just as a person’s face is beautiful, it is like the full moon.
Question:
There are further pure worlds in the ten directions, such as the World of Bliss of Amitābha Buddha; for what reason is only the world of Samantakusuma used as a metaphor?
Answer: The world of Amitābha Buddha is not like the world of Flower Accumulation (Puṣpasaṃcaya). Why is this?

Although the Buddha led the bhikṣu Dharmākara to observe the pure worlds of the ten directions, because his power of merit was slight, he was unable to see those supremely wonderful and pure worlds; for this reason, his world was not as excellent.
Furthermore, when the Buddha transformed this world, it was exactly like the world Padmavati.
For this reason, it is said: "It was as if it were the world Padmavati."
Question:

There are other great bodhisattvas, such as Vimalakīrti, Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and so forth; why does [the text] not state that these bodhisattvas dwell there, but mentions only Mañjuśrī and Susthitamati?
The answer is:

From every single pore of this Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, there constantly emerge worlds of Buddhas and various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, filling the ten directions to transform sentient beings, without any fixed place of abiding.

Mañjuśrī manifests emanations and enters the five realms of existence; he may appear as a śrāvaka, as a pratyekabuddha, or as the body of a Buddha. As it is said in the *Śūraṅgamasamādhi Sūtra*: "In past lives, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was the Buddha Nāga-jāti-guru," and "For seventy-two billion lifetimes, he was a pratyekabuddha"—these things can indeed be spoken of and described.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is immeasurable and ineffable; his dwelling place cannot be known.
If he were to dwell anywhere, he would have to dwell within all worlds; therefore, it is not spoken of.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and the bodhisattvas of great majestic power," this should also be understood as a general reference to Samantabhadra and all other such great bodhisattvas.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha knew that everyone had assembled: those from all worlds—whether the world of devas, the world of Māras, or the world of Brahmā;
whether śramaṇas, brahmins, or gods; whether gandharvas, humans, asuras, and so forth; as well as all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had succeeded to the position of the Honored One.
[Treatise] Question:
The Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) is immeasurable; yet, if all sentient beings of the ten directions were to come together in this assembly, all worlds would have to become empty.
If they do not come, then there must be something that the Buddha’s immeasurable supernatural power cannot accomplish!
The answer is:
They should not all come. Why is this?
The worlds of the Buddhas are boundless and immeasurable; if they were all to come, they would thereby become finite.

Furthermore, in each of the ten directions there is a Buddha who likewise teaches the Prajñāpāramitā, as it is stated in the forty-third chapter of that *Prajñāpāramitā*: "In each of the ten directions, a thousand Buddhas appear, all of whom teach the Prajñāpāramitā."
For this reason, they should not all come.
Question:
If there are Buddhas of the ten directions, all of whom preach the Prajñāpāramitā, for what reason do the bodhisattvas of the ten directions come?
Answer: As already explained in the chapter on "The Arrival of Samantaprabha Bodhisattva," he has come because of his causal connection with Śākyamuni Buddha.

Furthermore, it is due to the original vows of these bodhisattvas that wherever the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, they shall listen to, receive, and make offerings to it; for this reason, they have come from afar.
Desiring to accumulate merit through the power of his own body, and also to demonstrate to all sentient beings:
"I have come from afar to make offerings to the Dharma; why do you, who reside in this world, not make offerings?"
Question: Since the Buddha is unattached to phenomena (*dharma*), for what reason does he manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) seven times to cause sentient beings to assemble in great numbers?
Answer:

This Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to know and difficult to understand, and inconceivable; for this reason, he has extensively assembled the great bodhisattvas so that those who have newly resolved their minds may attain faith and joy.
For example, the words of an ordinary person are not trusted by others, whereas those of a noble and eminent person are certainly accepted with faith.
Question: For what reason does it say, "whether in the world of devas, or the world of Māras, or the world of Brahmā"?
It would suffice simply to say "the world of devas and the world of humans. Why is this?
Because among the ten epithets [of the Buddha], he is called the "Teacher of Devas and Humans"; for this reason, one should speak only of "devas and humans."

Answer: The various devas possess the divine eye and the divine ear; they have sharp faculties and great wisdom, and they know for themselves that they have come. For this reason, it is called the "deva world."
Question:
If the world of devas already includes Māra and Brahmā, for what reason are they mentioned separately as "whether Māra or Brahmā"?
Answer:
In the heavens, there are three great lords:
Śakra Devānām-indra, the lord of two realms;
and Māra-rāja, the lord of the six heavens of the desire realm.
In the Brahma-world, Mahābrahmā is the sovereign.
A question is asked:
"Since the Yama Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven all have their own sovereigns, why are there only three sovereigns [in the formless realms]?"
The answer is:
Śakra Devānām Indra dwells upon the earth, and the Buddha likewise dwells upon the earth; he constantly comes to the Buddha’s presence, possesses great renown, and is widely known by many people.
The Māra King constantly comes to harass the Buddha; furthermore, he is the sovereign of the entire realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
The Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, and Nirmāṇarati Heaven all belong to the Māra King.
Furthermore, regarding the world of devas, all devas within the three realms are subsumed under this category;
however, because Māra is the sovereign of the entire desire realm, he is mentioned separately.
Furthermore, Māra constantly harasses the Buddha; yet he has now come to listen to the Prajñāpāramitā so that others may increase their faith.
Question: There are many great devas within the realm of form (rūpadhātu); why then does it say only that "the Brahma-world has assembled"?
Answer: The gods in the higher realms lack vitarka and vicāra and do not delight in distracted minds; furthermore, it is difficult for them to hear [the teaching].
In the Brahma-world, there are four consciousnesses, and thus it is easy to hear.
Furthermore, because the Brahma-world is proximate;
moreover, "Brahma" signifies freedom from desire and purity, and by mentioning the Brahma-world here, all the devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are collectively indicated.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa when other heavens were yet devoid of inhabitants, the Brahmā King was alone in the Brahma palace, silent and without anyone else; his mind was not pleased, and he thought to himself:
"Why is it that no beings are born here?"
At that time, among the Ābhāsvara devas, those whose life-span was exhausted were destined to be reborn according to their thoughts.
Brahmā then had this thought:
"These gods did not exist before; they have come into being because of my thought. I am the one who can create these gods."
At that time, the various devas also each thought to themselves:
"I was born from the Brahmā King; the Brahmā King is my father.
For this reason, it is simply called the "Brahma-world."

Furthermore, when those in the heavens of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas see the Buddha and hear the Dharma in the desire realm, or when they encourage and assist bodhisattvas, their visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, and tactile consciousness all take up their objects within the Brahma-world.
For this reason, the "Brahma-world" is mentioned separately.
Question:
Why are only "śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas" mentioned, and not kings, householders, or other groups of people?
Answer: There are two classes of wise people:
śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Those who have left the household life are called śramaṇas; those who remain in the household life are called brāhmaṇas.
Others have their minds set upon worldly pleasures, and for this reason they are not mentioned.
Brāhmaṇas study extensively in wisdom and seek merit, while those who have left the household life seek the Path in its entirety; therefore, only śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are spoken of.
Those whose lineage has been pure for seven generations within their families, and who have all received the precepts upon reaching six years of age, are called Brahmins.
Among these śramaṇas and brahmins, there are those who possess moral virtue and wisdom; it is for this reason that it is so said.
Question: The celestial world has already been explained previously; why is "heaven" (deva) mentioned again now? Answer:
The "worlds of devas" refers to the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; "Māra" refers to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and "Brahmā" refers to the Form Realm.
Now, when "devas" is mentioned here, it refers to those within the Desire Realm such as the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens.
As for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, because its physical forms are exquisitely sublime, it is called "Love-body" (Kāmadhātu-priya-kāya).
Question:
Why is it that only the "gandharva" is mentioned, while the other spirits and nāga kings are not? Answer:
These gandharvas are celestial musicians who follow the devas; their minds are gentle, yet their power of merit is slightly less than that of the devas.
The various spirits (yakṣas) are subsumed within the realm of spirits, and the dragon kings (nāgarājas) are subsumed within the realm of animals.

The Kinnaras are also celestial musicians who all belong to the devas; they dwell and sit together with the devas, and their food, drink, and musical performances are all identical to those of the devas.
This king of the Gandharvas is named Tuṅgila, which in the language of Qin means "tree."
These gandharvas and kiṃnaras always dwell in two places; their habitual abode is among the mountains of ten jewels.
At times, they perform music for the devas in the heavens; these two groups constantly alternate between the upper and lower realms.
Human beings are born within the four continents; there are four types of births, ranging from an extremely long lifespan of immeasurable years to an extremely short lifespan of ten years.

Asuras possess malicious minds and engage in strife, yet they do not break the precepts; having extensively cultivated the merit of giving, they are born to dwell on the shores of the great ocean, where they also possess walled cities and palaces.
These are the names of the asura kings: Vemacitra, Bali, Rāhu, and others such as these are called asura kings.
As it is said:
once, when the asura king Rāhu desired to devour the moon, the Moon Devaputra, terrified, went quickly to the Buddha’s presence and spoke this verse:
“O World-Honored Buddha, accomplished in great wisdom, I now take refuge in you and pay homage;
Rāhula is tormenting me—may the Buddha, out of compassion, grant me protection!”
The Buddha spoke these verses to Rāhula:
“The moon can illuminate the darkness and bring coolness; It is the great lamp of light within the void of space.
Its color is pure white and it possesses a thousand rays; Do not swallow the moon! Release it quickly!”
At that time, Rāhula was terrified and his sweat poured forth; he immediately released the moon with haste.
Seeing Rāhula release the moon in such a state of panic and fear, the Asura King Bali spoke this verse in question:
“O Rāhula, for what reason Do you release the moon so hastily, trembling with fear and dread?”
“Your body is dripping with sweat like that of a sick man; your mind is so terrified and uneasy!
At that time, Rāhula replied with a verse:
“The World-Honored One has exhorted me with a verse, yet I will not release even one-seventh of the moon’s head.”
"Even if I were to obtain a livelihood, it would not be secure; for this reason, I now release this moon!
The Asura King Bali spoke in verse:
"The Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter; they appear in the world only after a vast interval of time."
When these verses of purity were spoken, Rāhu immediately released the moon.
He asked: “Why did you not speak of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts?”
The answer is:
Those in the hells have minds distracted by great suffering and cannot receive the Dharma;
those in the animal realm have minds shrouded by ignorance and cannot be transformed.
Because the bodies of hungry ghosts are scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, they are unable to receive the Dharma.

Furthermore, although some among the animals and hungry ghosts occasionally come to listen to the Dharma, they merely give rise to a mind of merit and are incapable of receiving the Path; therefore, it is not taught to them.
Question:
If that is so, then the gandharvas and asuras should also not be mentioned. Why?
Because they are already included within the realm of ghosts and spirits (preta).
Answer: The Buddha did not speak of "inclusion" (saṃgraha); why, then, do you now say there is inclusion?
This is the teaching of Kātyāyanīputra and others.
Just as the power of the asuras is equal to that of the devas, and they sometimes defeat the devas in battle;

and just as the gandharvas are the musicians of the devas who share in their blessings and joys, possessing wisdom capable of distinguishing the beautiful from the ugly—why should they not be able to receive the teachings of the Way?
As it is said in the *Devatā-varga* of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
"The mother of the yakṣa Pūrṇavasu was staying at a place where the Buddha had traveled to lodge.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma, the ambrosia; two children, a boy and a girl, began to weep. Their mother spoke a verse to stop them:"
“‘O Uttara, do not make a sound; O Pūrṇa-vasu, do not weep!
I have now heard the Dharma and attained the realization of the Path; you, too, shall surely attain it just as I have.’”
For this reason, one knows that among the spirits and deities there are those who have attained the Way.
Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada is superior even among the bodhisattvas, let alone other beings!

Just as the Tumburu Kinnara King and the Gandharva King went to the Buddha’s dwelling, playing the lute in praise of the Buddha, the trichiliocosm shook throughout, and even Mahākāśyapa could not remain settled in his seat.

If such people as these cannot attain the Way, why is it that the various Asura kings and Dragon kings all go to the Buddha’s dwelling, inquire about the profound Dharma from the Buddha, and receive answers regarding its deep meaning according to their questions? Why, then, do you say they cannot attain the Way?
Question:

Among the sentient beings of the five destinies, the Buddha is the teacher of gods and humans; he does not speak of the three evil paths because they lack merit and lack the capacity to receive the path.
"These dragons and ghosts have all fallen into the evil realms.
He replied:
"The Buddha also did not explicitly teach the five destinies; those who speak of the five destinies are the monks of the Sarvāstivāda school."
The Vātsīputrīya school asserts that there are six destinies (*gati*).
Furthermore, there ought to be six destinies. Why is this?
The three evil realms are exclusively places of retribution for sin;
if one has much merit and little sin, these are termed asuras, gandharvas, and so forth, and their birthplaces should be distinct [from those realms].
For this reason, one should speak of six realms of existence.
Furthermore, although those in the three evil paths also receive the merit of the Path, it is so slight that they are said to have none.
As for the various Bodhisattvas who succeed to the position of the Honored One, it is as previously explained.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Volume Ten.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Commentary on the First Chapter, Section Sixteen:
The Causes and Conditions Concerning Śāriputra, Volume Eleven.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty, by imperial decree. 16. The因缘 (Nidāna) of Śāriputra. [Sūtra] The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
[Treatise] Question:
The Prajñāpāramitā is the dharma of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; for what reason does the Buddha address Śāriputra rather than the Bodhisattvas?
Answer: Among all the disciples, Śāriputra’s wisdom is the foremost, as the Buddha said in a verse:
“The wisdom of all sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One;”
"If one were to compare Śāriputra’s wisdom and erudition,
he would still not equal even a single sixteenth part [of this person].
Furthermore, Śāriputra possesses great merit through his wisdom and vast learning.
At the age of eight, he recited eighteen sections of the sutras and thoroughly understood the principles and meanings of all scriptures.
At that time, there were two dragon kings in the kingdom of Magadha:
one named Kṛtī and the other named Agara.

Rain falls in its proper season, and the land knows no years of famine; moved by this, the people regularly assemble in great numbers at the dragon’s dwelling during the second month of spring to hold a grand festival, making music and discussing the Dharma for the duration of that day.
From antiquity to the present, this assembly has never ceased; thus, it is named after the Dragon to designate this gathering.
On this day, according to established custom, four high seats are prepared:
the first for the king, the second for the crown prince, the third for the great ministers, and the fourth for the debaters.
At that time, Śāriputra, though only eight years old, asked the assembly,
"For whom have these four high seats been prepared?
The assembly replied:
"To serve as king, crown prince, minister, or scholar.
At that time, Śāriputra observed the Brahmins and others present; seeing that none surpassed him in spirit or bearing, he ascended the debating throne and sat cross-legged.
The multitude was filled with wonder and suspicion; some thought him a foolish child lacking in knowledge, while others believed his wisdom and capacity surpassed that of men.

Although they marveled at his spiritual marvels, each still harbored self-importance and felt ashamed of his youth, so they would not speak with him themselves but sent their young disciples to convey their inquiries.
The depth of his responses and the excellence of his reasoning were truly transcendent!
At that time, the various masters of treatises marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; both the ignorant and the wise, the great and the small, all submitted to him.
The King was greatly delighted and immediately commanded the relevant officials to grant him a village in fief, to be provided for him perpetually.
The King mounted an elephant carriage and, shaking a bell, proclaimed his message to all; throughout the sixteen great nations and the six great cities, there was no one who did not rejoice.
At that time, he summoned the diviner named Kauṇḍinya, whose family name was Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and who was a close friend of Śāriputra.
Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent and insight, while Maudgalyāyana was most highly regarded for his noble and spirited character.
These two men were comparable in wisdom and skill, and equal in their virtuous conduct;
when traveling, they journeyed together, and when staying, they dwelt together.
From our youth until our maturity, we have been close companions, bound by a covenant that lasts from beginning to end.
Later, both weary of the world, we left the household life to study the Way, becoming disciples of a Brahmin.
We sought the gateway to the Way with sincere intent, yet after a long time no signs of realization appeared, so we questioned our teacher about it.
The teacher’s name was Śāṇakavāsin, and he replied to him, saying:
“Since I began seeking the Way, many years have passed; I do not know whether there is a fruit of the Way or not.”
"Am I not one such as they?
And yet, I too have not attained it!

On another day, when his teacher was bedridden with illness, Śāriputra stood at the head of the bed and Mahāmaudgalyāyana stood at the feet. As he breathed heavily, his life about to end, he looked upon them with compassion and smiled.
The two men were of one mind and both asked about the meaning of the smile.
The Master replied to them, saying:
"Those in the mundane world lack eyesight; they are invaded by affection and attachment."

I have seen that when the King of Kāñcanamālā died, his chief queen threw herself into the funeral pyre seeking to be in the same place as him; yet these two individuals experienced different retributions for their actions, and the places where they were reborn were utterly distinct.
At that time, the two men took down the Master’s words in writing, wishing to verify their truth or falsehood.

Later, a merchant from Kāñcanapura came from afar to the kingdom of Magadha; the two men compared his account with the notes and found it was indeed as the Master had said. They then sighed in dismay, saying:
"Are we not the ones for whom this teaching was intended?"
"Has this teacher hidden [the truth] from us?
The two of them made a vow together, saying,
"If one of us first attains the nectar of immortality, we must certainly share its flavor with the other."
At that time, after the Buddha had converted the thousand brothers of the Kāśyapa clan, he traveled through various kingdoms and arrived at Rājagṛha, where he stayed at the Bamboo Grove.
Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world, two brahmin teachers entered Rājagṛha together, desiring to obtain news of him.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Aśvajit, one of the group of five disciples. He entered the city for alms, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl.
Śāriputra, seeing that his appearance and attire were extraordinary and that his faculties were serene and silent, approached him and asked:
"Whose disciple are you?"
"Who is your teacher?

He replied, "The Prince of the Śākya clan, having become weary of the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, left the household life to study the Way and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he is my teacher."
Śāriputra said, "Tell me what your teacher has taught you!
He then replied with a verse:
"I am still young in years, and my studies have only recently begun;
how could I possibly proclaim the ultimate truth or extensively explain the meaning of the Tathāgata? Śāriputra said:
“Briefly state its essential point!
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśvajit spoke these verses:
“All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; These phenomena are explained as causes and conditions.”
"When these phenomena reach the exhaustion of their causes and conditions, the Great Teacher has spoken thus.
Having heard this verse, Śāriputra immediately attained the first stage of the Path and returned to report it to Maudgalyāyana.
Seeing that his complexion was serene and joyful, Maudgalyāyana went to meet him and said,
"Have you attained the flavor of the nectar of immortality? Tell it to me!"
Śāriputra then recited for him the verses he had previously heard.
Maudgalyāyana said,
"Recite them once more!"
He then preached the Dharma for them once more, and they also attained the first stage of the Path.
The two masters, together with their two hundred and fifty disciples, arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Seeing the two men approaching with their disciples from afar, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see these two men standing before the brahmins?
The bhikṣus replied,
"We have seen them."
The Buddha said, "These two individuals are, among my disciples, the foremost in wisdom and the foremost in supernormal powers.
The great assembly approached the Buddha in succession; having arrived, they prostrated themselves and stood to one side, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha’s Dharma.
The Buddha said:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At that moment, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord; the Dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he was fully equipped with the bowl and robes, having received the perfected precepts.
After half a month had passed, when the Buddha preached the Dharma to the brahmin Dīrghanakha, Śāriputra attained the path of Arhatship.

As for those who attain the Way after half a month, these persons shall become the masters who follow the Buddha in turning the Wheel of Dharma; they should remain on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), directly entering into all phenomena and fully knowing them in their various aspects. For this reason, they attain the path of Arhatship after half a month.
Since there are such manifold and numerous merits as these, Śāriputra, although he is an arhat, the Buddha has taught this profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā for his sake.
Question:
If that is so, why was it first taught in brief to Śāriputra, and later in detail to Subhūti?
If it were because he is foremost in wisdom that [the Buddha] should have spoken more extensively to him, for what reason was it instead spoken to Subhūti?
Answer: Śāriputra is the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in wisdom;
Subhūti is the foremost among the disciples in attaining the Samādhi of Non-contention.
The characteristic of the *araṇā-samādhi* is to constantly observe sentient beings so as not to cause their minds distress, practicing compassion extensively.
Since all Bodhisattvas fulfill great vows to deliver sentient beings, their characteristics of compassion are identical; for this reason, he was commanded to speak.

Furthermore, this Subhūti was fond of practicing the samādhi of emptiness. It was as when the Buddha, having completed the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, returned down to Jambudvīpa.
At that time, Subhūti was dwelling in a stone cave and thought to himself:
"The Buddha is descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; should I go to where the Buddha is?"
"Have they not gone to where the Buddha is?
He further thought to himself:
"The Buddha has often said:"
"If a person observes the Buddha’s Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom, they see the most excellent among Buddhas.
At that time, because the Buddha had descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the fourfold assembly gathered in Jambudvīpa; the devas saw humans, and humans likewise saw the devas.
In the assembly were Buddhas, as well as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and the great multitude of devas; the splendor of the gathering was such as had never been seen before!
Subhūti thought to himself:
"Although this great assembly is indeed extraordinary, its power will not endure for long; being subject to the law of decay, all things return to impermanence."
"By means of this initial gateway of the contemplation of impermanence, one comes to know that all phenomena are empty and devoid of reality;
when one performs this contemplation, one immediately attains the realization of the Way.
At that time, all the people desired to be the first to see the Buddha, to pay him homage, and to make offerings."

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Huase who, wishing to eliminate the ill repute associated with her female name, transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King accompanied by the seven treasures and a thousand sons. When the multitude saw this, they all vacated their seats and rose to leave.
Once the Transformation King had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he returned to his original form and was the first among the bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“It was not you who paid homage first; Subhūti was the first to pay homage to me.”
Why is this? Subhūti contemplates the emptiness of all dharmas;
this constitutes seeing the Buddha’s Dharma-body and attaining true offering—the supreme among all offerings. It is not by paying respect to the physical body that one performs an offering.
For this reason, it is said that Subhūti constantly practices the samādhi of emptiness and accords with the mark of emptiness of the prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, the Buddha commanded him to speak on the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, because sentient beings have faith and reverence for Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, the Buddha commands them to preach; thus, the assembly attains pure faith.
Since the outflows of Bodhisattvas are not yet exhausted, if they were taken as witnesses, people would not believe them.
For this reason, he speaks the Prajñāpāramitā together with Śāriputra and Subhūti.
Question:
Why is he named Śāriputra?
Is this a name given by his parents,
or is it a title established based on his practiced virtues?
He replied:
These names were given by his parents.

In Jambudvīpa, there was the most peaceful and prosperous land called the kingdom of Magadha; within it was a great city named Rājagṛha, where the king was named Bimbisāra. There lived a Brahmin master of debate named Māthara, whom the king, because of his skill in disputation, granted a fief consisting of an entire village located not far from the city.
Māthara subsequently established a household, and his wife gave birth to a daughter whose eyes resembled those of a śāri bird; she was thus named Śāri.
Next, a son was born whose knee-bones were coarse and large, and he was named Kuṭīla.

Kukīla—meaning "Great Thigh" in the language of Qin—was a brahmin who maintained a household and raised sons and daughters; he had already forgotten all the scriptures he had studied and did not pursue new learning.
At that time, there was a great brahmin master of debate in South India named Tiṣya, who was thoroughly proficient in all eighteen kinds of great scriptures.
This man entered the city of Rājagṛha with fire upon his head and his belly bound with copper plates.
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied:
"The sūtras and scriptures I have studied are so numerous that I fear my belly might burst; therefore, I bind it with these plates."
He asked again,
"Why do you carry fire upon your head?
He replied:
"Because of great darkness.
The people said, "The sun has risen and illuminates all; why do you say it is dark?"
He replied:
"There are two kinds of darkness:
first, that which is not illuminated by the light of the sun; second, the obscuration of ignorance."
"Though there is now the light of the sun, ignorance remains as dark as ever.
The people said, "It is only because you have not yet seen the Brahmin Māṭhara; if you were to see him, your belly would shrink and this light would turn to darkness."
The brāhmaṇa went straight to the drum and struck the drum of debate.
When the king heard it, he asked, "Who is this?
The ministers replied:
"In South India there was a brahmin named Tiṣya, a great master of debate, who wished to seek out a place for discussion and therefore struck the drum of debate.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately gathered the multitude, addressing them:
"Whoever is able to challenge him, let them engage in debate with him!"
Upon hearing this, Māṭhara felt self-doubt, thinking, "I have neglected my studies and have not practiced anything new; I do not know whether I am now able to debate with him.
Nevertheless, he reluctantly approached.
On the road, he saw two bulls butting each other; he thought to himself:
"This bull is I, and that bull is him. By taking this as a divination, I shall know who will be victorious."
"This ox is not my equal," he thought, and he became deeply distressed, reflecting to himself:
"With such marks as these, I shall surely be no match for him.
Just as he was about to enter the assembly, he saw a woman carrying a jar of water directly before him; she stumbled to the ground and broke the jar.
Again he thought to himself:
"This too is inauspicious.
He was deeply displeased.
Having entered the assembly, he beheld that master of treatises, whose countenance and expression were endowed with superior marks;
realizing for himself that he was inferior, and having no other recourse, he engaged him in debate.
As the debate proceeded, he immediately fell into defeat.
The King was greatly delighted and said:
"A man of great wisdom and brilliance has come from afar to our kingdom!"
He further wished to grant him a village as a fief.
The ministers deliberated, saying:

"If every clever person who arrives is granted a district, then those who have performed meritorious service will not be rewarded, while only those who engage in eloquent discourse will be favored. We fear this is not the way to ensure the peace of the state or the security of our families!"
"Now that Māthara has been defeated in debate, his fief should be confiscated and given to the victor;
should there be another who is even more victorious, it shall be given to him as well.
The king followed these words and immediately confiscated [the fief] to give it to the latter person.
At that time, Māthara said to Tiṣya:
"You are an intelligent man; I give my daughter to you as a wife and entrust my son to your care.
Now I wish to travel far to another country to seek the fulfillment of my original aspiration."
Tiṣya took his daughter as his wife.
While she was pregnant, she dreamed of a man clad in armor and holding a vajra in his hand, who shattered all the mountains and stood beside a great mountain.
Having awakened, she said to her husband, "I had such a dream.
Tiṣya said, "You shall give birth to a son who will defeat all masters of debate; he will only fail to overcome one person, and that one shall become his disciple."
Śāri was pregnant; because of her son, she too became exceptionally intelligent and highly skilled in debate.
Her younger brother, Kuṭīla, would always be defeated when debating with his sister.
Knowing that the child she carried must possess great wisdom even before birth, let alone after he was born!

He immediately abandoned his home life to pursue learning; traveling to South India, he refrained from clipping his fingernails and mastered eighteen kinds of scriptures, becoming thoroughly proficient in them all. For this reason, the people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
After his sister’s son was born, seven days later, he was wrapped in white cotton cloth and shown to his father.
His father reflected:
"My name is Tiṣya; following my name, let his name be Upatiṣya."
"Upa" means "to pursue" in the Qin language;
"Tiśya" is the name of a star. These were the names given by his parents.
Because he was born from Śāri, all people together named him Śāriputra; "Putra" means "son" in the Qin language.
