He then abandoned the casket and fled, whereupon the king ordered five men to draw their swords and pursue him.
There was yet another man who spoke words of feigned compliance while harboring a desire to cause harm;
he said to the others, "If you treat him with reason, there will be no trouble!"
The man realized this and fled for his life, arriving at an empty village.
There was a virtuous person there who skillfully addressed him:
"Although this village is empty, it is a place where bandits reside. If you stay here now, you will surely be harmed by them; be careful not to remain!"
Thereupon, he departed again and reached a great river; on the opposite bank of the river lay another country.
That land was peaceful and blissful, serene and pure, free from all calamities and hardships.

Thereupon, he gathered various grasses and woods, bound them together to form a raft, and with his hands and feet, exerted all his strength to cross over; having reached the other shore, he was at peace and free from affliction.
The king is Māra;
the chest is the human body;
the four venomous snakes are the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The five bandits with drawn swords are the five aggregates;
the one whose mouth is virtuous but whose mind is evil is defiled attachment;
the empty village is the six sense bases.
The "bandits" are the six sense objects;
the one person who takes pity and speaks to them is the virtuous teacher;
the "great river" is craving.
The raft is the Eightfold Noble Path;
the diligent crossing with hands and feet is diligence;
this shore is the world.
The "other shore" is nirvāṇa;
those who have crossed over are arhats whose outflows are exhausted.
It is the same within the Dharma of the bodhisattva: if there are three obstructions regarding giving—
To think, "I am the giver, he is the recipient, and this is the wealth bestowed," is to fall within the realm of Māra and remain subject to manifold difficulties.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving with the threefold purity, free from these three obstructions, they reach the other shore and are praised by all Buddhas; this is called Dānapāramitā.
For this reason, they are called "reaching the other shore.
These six pāramitās enable people to cross the great ocean of afflictions and attachments, such as stinginess and greed, and reach the further shore; for this reason, they are called pāramitās.
Question:
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are also able to reach the other shore; why, then, are these not called pāramitās? Answer:
The Arhat and Pratyekabuddha who have crossed to the other shore and the Buddha who has crossed to the other shore share the same name but differ in reality.
For them, birth-and-death is this shore and nirvana is the other shore, yet they are unable to cross the other shore of *dāna* (generosity).
Why is this? Because they are unable to practice giving with all things, at all times, and in all ways;
and even if they are able to give, they do so without a great mind.
One may give with an indeterminate mind, or with a tainted wholesome mind,
or with an untainted mind;
yet one lacks great compassion and is unable to give for the sake of all sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they know that this giving is neither born nor extinguished, untainted and unconditioned, possessing the characteristics of nirvana; yet they practice giving for the sake of all sentient beings—this is called dānapāramitā.
Furthermore, some say: when one gives away all things—
every kind of internal and external object— and performs such giving without seeking any karmic reward,
this is called dānapāramitā.
Furthermore, it is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) because it is inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because one knows that the object given is ultimately empty, having the same characteristic as nirvāṇa.
Because one gives to sentient beings with this mind, the retribution for such giving is inexhaustible; this is called *dānapāramitā*.
It is like a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) who hides precious jewels within a rock;
wishing to protect these treasures, he grinds diamond (*vajra*) and coats them with it so that they cannot be broken.
The giving of a bodhisattva is likewise so: by polishing and coating it with the wisdom of the true mark of *nirvāṇa*, their giving becomes inexhaustible.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva practices giving for the sake of all sentient beings, and because the number of sentient beings is inexhaustible, their giving is also inexhaustible.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva practices giving for the sake of the Buddha-dharma; since the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and boundless, the giving is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
For this reason, although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have reached the other shore, it is not called a *pāramitā*.
Question: What is meant by "fully complete"? Answer:

As previously stated, a bodhisattva is able to give away everything—whether internal or external, large or small, much or little, coarse or fine, attached or unattached, used or unused—and all such various things. He can relinquish them all without his mind harboring any attachment, bestowing them equally upon all sentient beings. He does not form such discriminations as:
"I should give to a person of high status, but not to one of low status;
I should give to those who have left the household life, but not to those who have not."
"One should give to humans, but not to birds and beasts.

To practice giving with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, to give without seeking recompense, and furthermore to realize the true nature (*dharmatā*) of giving—this is called being fully perfected.

Furthermore, one does not regard the time; there is no distinction between day and night, winter and summer, nor between auspicious and inauspicious moments. At all times, one gives with constant equanimity, the mind free from regret or stinginess, even to the point of giving away one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain without any sense of parsimony. This is what it means to be fully perfected.
Furthermore, some say:

from the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind of awakening until the thirty-four moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree, the period in between is called the fulfillment and perfection of giving.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage attains the wisdom of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, at that time they adorn Buddha-lands, transform sentient beings, and make offerings to all Buddhas. Having attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they can divide a single body into countless bodies; from each of these bodies, they cause a rain of the seven treasures, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to fall. They manifest great lamps as vast as Mount Sumeru to offer to the Buddhas and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions;
furthermore, with sublime voices they praise the virtues of the Buddhas, prostrating, making offerings, and respectfully welcoming them.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva rains down various kinds of food, drink, clothing, and coverings throughout all the infinite realms of hungry ghosts in the ten directions, causing them to be fully satisfied;
once they have attained such satisfaction, they all resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, he goes among the realm of animals, causing them to cultivate goodness and free themselves from the intent to harm one another; he removes their fears and anxieties and provides for each according to their needs until they are fully satisfied.
Having attained such fulfillment, they all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Amidst the immeasurable sufferings of the hells, they are able to extinguish the fires of hell and cool the boiling cauldrons; they cause the retribution of sin to cease and the mind to become virtuous, removing hunger and thirst so that beings may be reborn among gods or humans.
By these causes and conditions, they all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one provides wealth to those who are poor among the people of the ten directions, and bestows exquisite flavors and exquisite colors upon those who are wealthy and noble, causing them to rejoice;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, they all give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If they reach the heavens of the desire realm, he causes them to abandon the sensual pleasures of those celestial realms and bestows upon them the sublime joy of the Dharma, making them rejoice;
by these causes and conditions, they all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If they reach the heavens of the Form Realm, he removes their attachment to pleasure and delights them with the dhyāna-practices of a bodhisattva;
by these causes and conditions, they all resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In this manner, up to the tenth stage, this is called the complete fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva has two kinds of bodies:
first, the body born of karmic fetters; second, the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Within these two types of bodies, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is fulfilled; this is called being "endowed with the perfection of giving.
Question:
What is meant by the fulfillment of the perfection of giving within the body born of karmic bonds?
The answer is:

Although he has not yet attained the Dharma-body and his fetters and afflictions are not yet exhausted, he is able to give away all precious objects—his head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children—as well as everything internal and external, in total renunciation, without his mind wavering or shifting.
For example, Prince Sūdena—translated into the language of Qin as "Good-Love"—gave his two sons in alms to a brahmin, and subsequently gave his wife; yet his mind did not waver.
Furthermore, for example, King Sarvadatta—whose name means "All-Giver" in the language of Qin—was conquered by a hostile kingdom and fled into a remote forest.
There he saw a brahmin from a distant land approaching, intending to beg from him.

Thinking that his kingdom was ruined and his family lost, he had fled into hiding alone; out of pity for his hardships, [the man] spoke to the Brahmin, who had come from afar yet obtained nothing, saying:
"I am King Sarvada. The new king has issued a bounty for me, seeking me with great urgency."
Immediately, he bound himself and offered his body as a gift, sending it to the new king, thereby obtaining great wealth and goods.
This was also like the case of Prince Candraprabha, who went out for a pleasure excursion.
A leper saw him and stopped his carriage, saying:
"My body is afflicted by a grave illness; I am weary and distressed. While the Prince wanders for pleasure, does he do so alone in joy?"
"Out of great compassion and pity, we pray that you will grant us healing!
When the prince heard this, he questioned the physicians.
The physicians said:
"One must obtain the blood and marrow from a person who has grown up without anger, smear them [on the wound], and drink them; only then can it be cured.
The Prince thought to himself:
"Even if such a person existed, how could they be obtained, for they would surely cherish life and fear death?"
"Except for my own body, there is no place from which it can be obtained.
He then commanded a caṇḍāla to remove the flesh from his body, break his bones to extract the marrow to smear upon the sick man, and give him his blood to drink.
In these and various other ways, one gives away one’s body, wife, and children without stinginess, as if discarding grass and wood.

One contemplates the objects given, knowing they exist through conditions; when searching for their ultimate reality, nothing at all can be found. All things are pure, like the mark of *nirvāṇa*, until one attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is called fulfilling the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) with a body born of karmic bonds.
How does a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body fulfill the perfection of giving?

At the final stage, the Bodhisattva’s physical body attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); having relinquished the physical body, they attain the Dharma-body.
Within the six realms of the ten directions, he manifests transformations to suit the needs of sentient beings, bestowing all manner of precious jewels, clothing, food, and drink upon them all.
Furthermore, he gave away his head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children—indeed, all that he possessed internally and externally—as alms.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was once a six-tusked white elephant, a hunter lay in wait and struck him with a poisoned arrow.
The other elephants vied with one another to come and trample the hunter to death.
The white elephant shielded him with its body, protecting the man as if he were its own child, and compassionately drove away the herd of elephants.
He asked the hunter slowly,
"Why did you shoot me?
The hunter replied:
"I require your tusks! he said.
Immediately, the elephant inserted his six tusks into the hole in the stone; as his flesh and blood gushed forth, he lifted the tusks with his trunk and presented them to the hunter.
Although it is said to have the body of an elephant, since its mental activity is such as this, one should know that this elephant is not the karmic retribution of an animal.
Within the dharma of an Arhat, such a mind does not exist at all; therefore, one should know that this is a Dharma-body Bodhisattva.
At times, the people of Jambudvīpa do not know how to show reverence.
When elders of great virtue attempt to transform them through speech, they cannot be led across.
At such a time, the Bodhisattva transforms his own body, assuming the form of a kāpiñjala bird.
This bird had two friends:
one was a great elephant and the other was a monkey; they lived together beneath a pippala tree.
They asked one another:
"We do not know who among us should be the elder," they said.
The elephant replied, "In the past, I saw this tree beneath my belly; now it has grown as large as this."
Inferring from this, I ought to be the leader!
The monkey said,
“I once crouched on the ground and reached up with my hands to grasp the top of a tree.”
"Inferring from this, I ought to be the elder!
The bird said, "In the Pippala forest, I ate the fruit of this tree; the seed was excreted with my dung, and thus this tree was born."
Inferring from this, I ought to be the eldest!
The bird spoke again:
“The elder is of long-standing seniority; by custom, he should be venerated!”
Immediately, the great elephant carried the monkey on its back, and the bird perched atop the monkey, traveling about.
When all the birds and beasts saw this, they asked, "Why are you doing this?"
He replied, "I shall offer this respectful service to the Elder!
Thereupon, the birds and beasts were transformed; they all practiced ritual reverence, ceased encroaching upon the people's fields, and refrained from harming living beings.
The people were filled with wonder and marvel, for none of the birds or beasts caused them harm anymore.

When a hunter entered the forest, he saw an elephant carrying a monkey on its back, and the monkey perched atop a bird; as they moved about, they showed reverence and transformed the nature of all creatures, causing every living being to cultivate virtue.
He announced this to the people of the nation, and each person rejoiced, saying:
"The era is approaching its great peace; even birds and beasts are becoming benevolent!
The people also followed his example, and all practiced propriety and reverence.
From antiquity to the present, this transformation has flowed through ten thousand generations.
One should know that these are Dharma-body Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, in a single moment, the Dharma-body Bodhisattva manifests countless emanated bodies to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At one time, they can manifest immeasurable wealth and treasures to provide for all sentient beings;
they can, in a single moment, preach the Dharma universally to those of all superior, middling, and inferior capacities according to their respective voices;
and even sit beneath the Bodhi tree.
Such various instances as these are called the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā* by a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of giving (*dāna*):
first, the gift of material things; second, the gift of honor and respect; and third, the gift of the Dharma.
What is the gift of material things?
Precious jewels, clothing, food, head, eyes, marrow, and brain—giving away all such internal and external possessions without exception is called the gift of material things.

Generosity with reverence consists of offering gifts with pure faith, paying homage with respectful prostrations, escorting and welcoming [the recipient], praising them, circumambulating them, and making offerings—such various acts as these are called generosity with reverence.

As for the gift of Dharma: for the sake of the Way and its virtue, engaging in discourse and debate, reciting and expounding, removing doubts and answering questions, and bestowing the five precepts—such various acts performed as gifts for the sake of the Buddha-way are called the gift of Dharma.
The fulfillment of these three kinds of giving is called the fulfillment of the dānapāramitā.
Furthermore, dāna arises from three causal conditions:
first, pure faith; second, material wealth; and third, the field of merit.
There are three kinds of mental states:
compassion, reverence, and both compassion and reverence.
To give to the poor, the lowly, and to various animals is the gift of compassion.
To give to the Buddhas and the various Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body is the gift of reverence;
to give to the aged, the sick, the destitute, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas is the gift of reverent compassion.
The gift is pure: it is neither stolen nor plundered; it is given at the proper time, without seeking fame or seeking gain and sustenance.
At times, one gains great merit from the intention; at times, one gains great virtue from the field of merit; and at times, one gains great virtue from the excellence of the object.

First is that which arises from the mind; for example, the four immeasurable minds, the Buddha-recollection samādhi, and giving one's body to a tiger—such as these are called attaining great merit through the mind.
There are two kinds of fields of merit:
first, the field of merit of compassion; second, the field of merit of reverence.
The field of merit of compassion can give rise to a mind of compassion.
By revering fields of merit, one can give rise to a mind of reverence.
For example, King Aśoka—whose name means "Sorrowless" in the Qin language—offered soil to the Buddha.

Furthermore, among material gifts, there was once a woman who, being intoxicated and her mind clouded, mistakenly offered a necklace of the seven precious gems to a stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha; by virtue of that merit, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
These various kinds are called the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*). Question:
Since *dāna* (generosity) is defined as the relinquishing of wealth, why is it said that "it is fully endowed with the dharma of having nothing to relinquish"?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of dāna:
first, supramundane; second, non-supramundane.

Now, the supramundane *dāna* is explained as being signless (*animitta*); because it is signless, there is nothing to be relinquished. Therefore, it is said that "one is fully endowed with the dharma of non-relinquishment.
Furthermore, because material wealth cannot be apprehended, it is called non-relinquishment.

These things are empty in the future and the past; in the present, they are merely conceptual constructions and lack any fixed dharma. For this reason, it is said that there is nothing to be relinquished.
Furthermore, when a practitioner relinquishes wealth, the mind may think that this giving possesses great merit, and based on this, conceit, the fetter of craving, and so forth arise.
For this reason, it is said that there is nothing to be relinquished.
Because there is nothing to be relinquished, there is no arrogance; because there is no arrogance, the fetter of craving and the like do not arise.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of givers:
first, those of the world, and second, those who have transcended the world.
People of the world can relinquish wealth, but they cannot relinquish attachment;
those who have transcended the world can both relinquish wealth and relinquish attachment. Why is this?
Because both material wealth and the mind of giving are ungraspable.
For this reason, it is said that one is "fully endowed with the dharma of non-renunciation.
Furthermore, within the *Dānapāramitā*, it says:
"The three things—the object, the giver, and the recipient—cannot be apprehended.
Question: It is called *dāna* (giving) because these three things come together in combination.
Now it is said that three things are unobtainable; how then can it be called "the perfection of *dānapāramitā* being fully accomplished"?
If there is currently wealth, there is a donor, and there is a recipient, how can these three things be unobtainable?
As for the cloth that is given as a gift, it truly exists. Why is this?
Because there is the name "cloth," there must be the dharma of cloth; if the dharma of cloth did not exist, there would likewise be no name "cloth."
Because it has a name, the cloth must exist as a substantial reality.

Furthermore, the cloth has length and shortness, coarseness and fineness, and colors such as white, black, yellow, and red; it has causes and conditions, it is produced and can be destroyed, it entails karmic retribution, and it gives rise to mental states in accordance with its properties.
Ten feet is long, five feet is short;
large threads are coarse, small threads are fine;
according to the dye, there are colors.
With thread as the cause and weaving implements as the condition, it is through the conjunction of these causes and conditions that a cloth is produced.
Human effort constitutes its "making," while human destruction constitutes its "breaking.
Its function in warding off cold and heat and protecting the body is termed its "fruition."
When people obtain it, they rejoice greatly; when they lose it, they grieve greatly.
By bestowing it upon others, one gains merit that aids the Path;
yet if one steals it or robs it, they shall be executed in the marketplace and, upon death, enter hell.
For these and various other such reasons, we know that this cloth exists; this is what is called the "dharma of the cloth. How can you say that the object of giving cannot be apprehended?
[The opponent] replies:
Your claim that it exists because there is a name for it is not correct.
How is this known?
There are two kinds of names:
those that correspond to reality and those that do not.

"Unreal names" refers, for example, to a certain grass named *juli-juli*, which in the language of Qin means "thief. Although the grass neither steals nor plunders, it is not actually a thief, yet it is called a thief.
Furthermore, just as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise exist only as names and lack substantial reality,

although cloth is not non-existent in the way that rabbit horns or tortoise hair are, it exists through the convergence of causes and conditions and ceases to exist when those causes and conditions disperse.
Like a forest or an army, these all have names but lack reality.
For example, like a wooden figure, although it has the name "person," one should not seek the characteristics of a person therein.
Although the name "cloth" exists within the layers [of threads], one should not seek the true reality of the cloth.

The cloth serves as a causal condition for the arising of mental conceptions in people: upon obtaining it, one rejoices; upon losing it, one grieves. This constitutes the causal condition of mental conception.
The arising of the mind has two causes and conditions:
there is that which arises from the real, and there is that which arises from the unreal.
For example, what is seen in a dream, the moon reflected in water, or seeing a stump at night and taking it for a person—these are called cases where the mind is caused to arise from the unreal.
Since these conditions are not fixed, one should not say that because the mind arises, it must therefore exist.
If the mind exists by virtue of causes and conditions for its arising, one should no longer seek for it as a substantial reality.

It is like seeing the moon in water with the eye; the mind gives rise to the thought that this is the moon. If it were truly the moon because it arose from the mind, then there would be no real moon at all.
Furthermore, "existence" (bhāva) is of three kinds: first, relative existence (apekṣā-bhāva);
second, conventional existence (prajñapti-saṃvṛti-bhāva); and third, substantial existence (dharma-bhāva).
Regarding "mutual dependence": it is like long and short, or this and that. In reality, there is neither long nor short, nor this nor that; they exist as names only because of mutual dependence.
Length exists because of shortness, and shortness also exists because of length;
"that" exists because of "this," and "this" also exists because of "that."
If one is to the east of an object, one considers it to be to the west; if one is to the west, one considers it to be to the east.
While the single object has not changed, there arises the distinction between east and west; all such cases possess names but lack reality.
Such things as these are called "existence through mutual dependence" (*apekṣā-sat*); herein there is no real dharma, unlike [the case of] form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth.

As for that which exists as a conventional designation (*prajñapti-sat*), it is like curd having color, fragrance, taste, and touch; because of the combination of these four causal conditions, it is conventionally designated as "curd."
Although it exists, its existence is not like that of things produced by causes and conditions;
although it does not exist, its non-existence is not like that of a rabbit's horns or a tortoise's hair.
It is merely because of the conjunction of causes and conditions that we conventionally designate "curd" as existing.

It is the same for the cloth. Furthermore, because there are atoms of form, odor, taste, and touch, there are hair-fibers; due to the causes and conditions of hair-fibers, there is hair; due to the causes and conditions of hair, there is wool; due to the causes and conditions of wool, there are threads; due to the causes and conditions of threads, there is cloth; and due to the causes and conditions of cloth, there is a garment.

If there were no causes and conditions of atoms of form, fragrance, taste, and touch, there would also be no part of a hair; because the part of a hair does not exist, there is no hair; because hair does not exist, there is no wool; because wool does not exist, there is no thread; because thread does not exist, there is no cloth; and because cloth does not exist, there is no garment.
Question:

It is not necessarily the case that all things exist solely through the combination of causes and conditions; for instance, atoms are so subtle as to be partless, and being partless, they cannot undergo combination.
Because coarse objects are composed of layers, they can be broken; however, since atoms have no internal divisions, how can they be broken?
The answer is:
the ultimate atom has no substantial reality; it is merely a name applied by force.
Why is this? Because the coarse and the subtle are mutually dependent; because there is the coarse, there is the subtle, and that subtle must itself have a further subtle.
Furthermore, if there were such a thing as an ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it would necessarily possess parts corresponding to the ten directions.
If it possesses spatial divisions in the ten directions, it cannot be called an atom;
if it lacks spatial divisions in the ten directions, it cannot be called matter.
Furthermore, if atoms exist, there must be spatial boundaries for them.
If it possesses parts, it cannot be called an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Furthermore, if there were an atom, and within it there were constituent parts consisting of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—since these constitute parts of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—it could not be called an atom.
By investigating in this manner, atoms cannot be found.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whether form is coarse or subtle, whether internal or external, when viewed as a whole, it is impermanent and without self."
Not asserting that there are even subtle atoms—
this is called the emptiness of analytical division (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, there is another contemplation of emptiness:
This cloth exists according to the mind.

For example, when a practitioner of dhyāna contemplates a cloth, they may perceive it as earth, water, fire, or wind; or as blue, yellow, white, or red; or even as entirely empty, just as in the contemplation of the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*.
As the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a community of bhikṣus, he entered the city of Rājagṛha.
Along the way, he saw a great body of water; the Buddha spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana) upon the water and sat down, then addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu enters meditative absorption and attains mastery over the mind, he can cause this great water to become earth, and it will truly become solid earth."
Why is this? Because within this water there is the element of earth.
In this same way, water, fire, wind, gold, silver, and various other precious objects all become substantial.
Why is this? Because within these waters, each possesses its own portion.
Furthermore, it is like a beautiful form: when a lustful person sees it, they perceive it as pure and wonderful, and a mind of defiled attachment arises.
When one who practices the contemplation of impurity looks at it, they see various foul secretions with not a single clean spot;
when a wife sees it, she feels jealousy, anger, and loathing, her eyes unwilling to look upon it as something impure;
yet when a lustful person observes it, they regard it as pleasure.
Those who harbor envy view it as suffering;
those who practice the Way view it as attaining the Path;
and those who are indifferent view it with neither attachment nor aversion, as if looking upon earth or wood.
If this beautiful form were truly pure, then all four types of people who observe it would see it as pure;
if it were truly impure, then all four types of people who observe it would see it as impure.
For this reason, we know that beauty and ugliness reside in the mind; they have no fixed existence externally.
The contemplation of emptiness is also like this.
Furthermore, because the eighteen aspects of emptiness are contained within this cloth, when one contemplates it, it is empty; being empty, it cannot be apprehended.
Thus, through various causes and conditions, material wealth is empty and ultimately unobtainable.
Why is it that the person to whom one gives is also unobtainable?
It is like a piece of cloth which exists due to the combination of causes and conditions; yet, if one analyzes it part by part, the cloth cannot be found.

The donor is also like this: the four great elements enclosing space are called the "body"; it is the movement, coming and going, sitting and rising of this body-consciousness that is conventionally designated as a "person."
If one seeks it part by part, it likewise cannot be found.
Furthermore, within all aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the self cannot be found; because the self cannot be found, the person to whom one gives cannot be found.
Why is this? Because "I" have various names:
human, deva, male, female, giver, receiver, one who undergoes suffering, one who undergoes pleasure, animal, and so forth.
These are merely names; in reality, dharmas cannot be apprehended.
Question:
If the giver cannot be apprehended, how can there be a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
Answer:
Names exist due to the combination of causes and conditions, such as "house" or "chariot"; in reality, no such dharma can be found.
Question:
How is it that the self cannot be apprehended?
The answer is:
as has already been explained above in the section on "Thus have I heard at one time," it shall now be explained further.
The Buddha taught that there are six consciousnesses:
visual consciousness and the mental factors associated with visual consciousness together take form as their object, but they do not take houses, cities, or various names as their objects.
The ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses are also like this.

The mental consciousness and the factors associated with mental consciousness know the eye, know forms, and know visual consciousness, up to knowing the mind, knowing phenomena, and knowing mental consciousness.
These dharmas that are the objects of consciousness are all empty and without self, because they arise and perish, and because they lack autonomy.
Within unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as well, one does not conceive of a self, because neither suffering nor pleasure is experienced therein.
In this context, if there were forcibly a self and dharmas, there ought to be a seventh consciousness that cognizes the self;
yet it is not so. For this reason, we know there is no self.
Question:
How is it known that there is no self?
All people each conceive of a self within their own bodies, but do not conceive of a self within the bodies of others;
if one falsely perceives a self within one's own body where no self exists, then one should likewise falsely perceive a self within the bodies of others where no self exists.
Furthermore, if there is no self within and form and consciousness arise and perish from moment to moment, how can one differentiate and know that this form is blue, yellow, red, or white?

Furthermore, if there were no self, then the consciousness of a person in the present would arise and perish gradually, and it would also be exhausted when life and the body are severed; in that case, who would follow after and receive the various formations of merit and demerit?
Who experiences suffering and pleasure?
Who is the one who attains liberation?
It is through such various causes and conditions that we know there is a self.
The answer is:
This is a difficulty that applies equally to both sides!
If you claim that the conception of a self arises with respect to another's body, one must then ask: "Why does it not arise with respect to one's own body?"

Furthermore, because the five aggregates arise through causes and conditions, they are empty and without self. From the causal condition of ignorance, twenty types of view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arise; this is the view of a self that arises within the continuity of the five aggregates.

Because the self is produced from conditions consisting of these five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one reckons these five aggregates as the self and not as residing in another body, due to habitual conditioning.
Furthermore, if there were a permanent soul (*ātman*), then "that" and "self" could exist [as distinct entities].
You have not yet understood whether your own spirit exists or not, yet you inquire about "that" and "this"!
It is like a person who asks about the horns of a rabbit and receives an answer resembling the horns of a horse.
If the horns of a horse truly existed, they might serve as proof for the horns of a rabbit; [but since they do not, so it is with your question].
The horns of a horse have not yet been established, and yet you wish to use them as proof for the horns of a rabbit.
Furthermore, because one gives rise to the notion of a self within one's own body, one then claims that there is a deity.
Since you claim that "the self (ātman) is omnipresent," one should likewise reckon the bodies of others as one's own self.
For this reason, one should not say, "Because the notion of 'I' arises with respect to one's own body but does not arise with respect to the bodies of others, we know there is a self."

Furthermore, there are those who give rise to the notion of "self" regarding the property of others. For example, when practitioners of non-Buddhist meditation practice the earth-kasina (pathavī-kasiṇa), they see the earth as being the self, and the self as being the earth; the same applies to water, fire, wind, and space.
Due to perversion, one also conceives of a self within the bodies of others.

Furthermore, there are times when the notion of "I" arises with respect to another's body; for example, there was once a man who, having been sent on a distant mission, stayed alone overnight in an empty house.
In the middle of the night, a ghost arrived carrying a dead person and placed it before him; another ghost then pursued them, angrily scolding the first ghost:
"This dead person is my property; why have you carried him here?"
The first ghost said, "This is my property; I brought it here myself.
The second ghost said:
"This dead man was indeed carried here by me!
The two ghosts each seized one hand and contended with one another.
The ghost in front said:
"There is someone here whom you may question.
Thereupon, the ghost asked:
"Who brought this dead person here?"
The man thought to himself:

"These two ghosts possess great power; whether I speak the truth, I shall die, and whether I speak falsely, I shall also die. Since death cannot be avoided in either case, why should I speak falsely?"
The man replied, "The ghost in front brought it.

The ghost behind became greatly enraged; he seized the man's hand, pulled it out, and placed it on the ground. The ghost in front then took an arm from the corpse and slapped it onto the stump, and it immediately attached itself.
In this manner, his two arms, two legs, head, and sides—his entire body—were all exchanged.
Thereupon, the two demons together devoured the human body that had been substituted, wiped their mouths, and departed.
The man reflected:
"My mother gave birth to this body of mine, yet my eyes have seen two ghosts devour it entirely; now, this body of mine is nothing but the flesh of others.
Do I truly possess a body at all?"
Is it that there is no body?
If you consider it to exist, it is entirely the bodies of others;
if you consider it to be non-existent, yet now a body actually exists.
Reflecting in this way, his mind became bewildered and distressed, like that of a madman.

At dawn, he sought out the road and departed; upon reaching the aforementioned land, he saw a Buddhist stūpa and a community of monks. Without discussing other matters, he asked only whether his own body existed or did not exist.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Who are you? He replied:
“I myself did not know whether this was a human or a non-human.
He then related the foregoing matter in detail to the assembly of monks.
The bhikṣus said:
"This person knows for himself that there is no self; he can easily be delivered.
Then he said to him:
"Your body has been devoid of a self from the very beginning; it is not only now."
"Because it is merely a combination of the four great elements, it is reckoned as 'my body,' just like your own body, which is no different from this one.
The bhikṣus ordained him into the Way; he severed all afflictions and immediately attained arhatship.
Thus, there are times when the bodies of others are also conceived as "self.
One cannot claim that a self exists merely because of the distinction between "self" and "other.
Furthermore, the true nature of this self is absolutely unfindable.

Whether it be the characteristic of permanence or the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of sovereignty or the characteristic of non-sovereignty, the characteristic of agency or the characteristic of non-agency, the characteristic of form or the characteristic of non-form—all such various [characteristics] are ultimately unobtainable.
If there were characteristics, then there would be dharmas; if there were no characteristics, then there would be no dharmas. Since I am now without characteristics, I know that there is no self.
If the self were permanent, there should be no such thing as the sin of killing.
Why is this? The body may be killed because it is impermanent;
the self cannot be killed because it is permanent.
Question:
Although the self is eternal and thus cannot be killed, one still incurs the sin of killing when one kills the body.
Answer:
If killing one's own body constituted the offense of killing, the *Vinaya* would state:
"There is no offense of killing in suicide.
Offenses and merits arise from harming others or benefiting others; they do not exist because of nourishing one's own body or killing one's own body.
For this reason, it is said in the *Vinaya*:
"One who takes their own life incurs no offense of killing, yet bears the fault of ignorance, greed, and hatred."
"If the self were eternal, it should neither die nor be born. Why is this?
According to your doctrine, the self is eternal and omnipresent throughout the five realms of existence; how, then, could there be death and birth?"
"Death" means the loss of this place; "birth" means the emergence at that place.
For this reason, one cannot say that the self (*ātman*) is eternal.
If the self were eternal, it should likewise not experience suffering or pleasure.
Why is this? When suffering comes, there is sorrow; when pleasure arrives, there is joy. If one is transformed by sorrow and joy, then that is not permanent.
If it were permanent, it should be like empty space: rain could not moisten it, heat could not dry it, and there would be neither this world nor a future world.
If the self (*ātman*) were eternal, there would likewise be no birth in future lives nor death in this life.
If the self were eternal, one would always possess the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and thus one could not attain *nirvāṇa*.
If the self were eternal, it would neither arise nor cease, and there should be no forgetting or loss;
because there is no such self and consciousness is impermanent, there is forgetting and loss. Therefore, the self is not eternal!
Through various causes and conditions such as these, it should be understood that the self (*ātman*) does not possess the characteristic of permanence.
If the self possessed the characteristic of impermanence, there would likewise be neither sin nor merit.
If the body were impermanent and the self were also impermanent, such that both things were extinguished together, one would fall into the extreme of nihilism (*uccheda-vāda*).
If one falls into annihilationism, then there would be no one who goes to future lives to undergo retribution for sins or merit.
If it were annihilationism, then one would attain nirvana without needing to sever the fetters, nor would there be any need for the causes and conditions of sin or merit in future lives.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, it can be known that the self (*ātman*) is not impermanent.
If the self possessed the characteristics of sovereignty or agency, then one should obtain whatever one desires;
yet now, what is desired is not obtained, while what is undesired is instead obtained.
If the deity were autonomous, it should not commit evil deeds and fall into the animal realm or other evil destinies.
Furthermore, all sentient beings dislike suffering; who would delight in such things and yet further encounter suffering?
For this reason, we know that the self (ātman) is not autonomous, nor does it act.
Furthermore, just as a person practices goodness with great effort out of fear of retribution, if the self were autonomous, why would it fear retribution and exert itself to cultivate merit?
Furthermore, all sentient beings do not obtain what they desire and are constantly pulled along by the bonds of afflictions and craving.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one knows that the self (ātman) is not sovereign and does not act of its own accord.

If the self (ātman) is not sovereign and not its own creator, this constitutes the characteristic of the non-existence of a self; that which is called "I" is simply the six consciousnesses, and there is nothing else besides them.
Furthermore, if one were not the agent of these actions, why would King Yama question the sinner, saying:
"Who made you commit this sin?
To which the sinner replies:
"It was created by me myself.
For this reason, one knows that it is not the case that it was not created by oneself.
If it were a matter of physical appearance or mental characteristics, such a thing would not be so.
Why is this? Because all forms (rūpa) are impermanent.
Question:
How can people say, "Form is the characteristic of self"?
The answer is:
Some people say:
"The deity resides within the heart, as subtle as a mustard seed; its purity is called the pure form-body (*śuddharūpakāya*).
Others say it is "like a wheat grain," some say "like a bean," some say "half an inch," and others say "one inch."
At the initial moment of receiving a body, one first receives [the primary elements], which are like the skeletal frame of an image;
when the body is fully formed, it is like the image already adorned. Some say:
"It follows the size of the person; when they die and perish, this [light] also emerges first.
Such matters are not so at all! Why is that?
All forms are derived from the four great elements; because they arise from causes and conditions, they are impermanent.
If the self were form, then since form is impermanent, the self would also be impermanent.
If it were impermanent, it would be as explained above. Question:
There are two kinds of bodies:
There is the coarse body and the subtle body.
The coarse body is impermanent, while the subtle body is the self (*ātman*), which migrates eternally from lifetime to lifetime into the five destinies.
The answer is:
This subtle body cannot be apprehended.
If there were a subtle body, it should have a location where it could be found; yet when one searches among each of the five viscera and the four limbs, it is nowhere to be found.
Question:
This subtle body is so minute that it has already departed at the moment of initial death; if one is alive, it cannot be found. How then can you see it?
Furthermore, this subtle body cannot be seen or known by the five sensory faculties; only sages possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can perceive it.
The response is:
If that were so, it would be no different from non-existence.
Just as when a person dies, they relinquish these aggregates of this life and enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
At that time, the body of the present life ceases and one receives the body of the intermediate state; there is no sequence between them, for at the very moment of cessation, there is birth.

It is like a wax seal pressed into clay: the impression is received within the clay, and the seal is destroyed at that very moment; thus, formation and destruction occur simultaneously, with no sequence between them.
At that time, one receives existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and having relinquished this intermediate state, one receives existence in the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
What you call the "subtle body" is precisely this intermediate state (*antarābhava*); the body of the intermediate state has neither exit nor entry.
It is like a lamp being lit: though its arising and ceasing continue in succession, it is neither permanent nor discontinuous.
The Buddha said:
"All aggregates of form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle—are entirely impermanent."
If your "self" were of a subtle material form (*rūpa*), it too would be impermanent and subject to annihilation.
Through various such causes and conditions, one can know that it does not have the characteristic of material form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
Nor is the self without the characteristic of material form; for that which is "without material form" (*arūpin*) consists of the four aggregates (*skandha*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because the fourfold assembly is impermanent, lacks self-mastery, and is subject to causes and conditions, it cannot be the self (*ātman*).
Among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not conceive of a self, for they are devoid of anything that can be grasped.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one knows that the spirit (*ātman*) does not possess formless characteristics.
Thus, whether internal or external within heaven and earth, throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, the "self" cannot be found.

It is simply that the six consciousnesses arise from the conjunction of the twelve bases; the conjunction of these three factors is called contact (*sparśa*). From contact arise mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
Within these phenomena, through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises; because the view of a self arises, one asserts the existence of a soul (*ātman*).

This view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is abandoned upon seeing the Truth of Suffering through the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) and the subsequent inferential knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvayajñāna). At the time of its abandonment, one no longer perceives a self.
You previously asked:
"If there is no self within, and form and consciousness arise and perish from moment to moment, how can one distinguish and know colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white?"
"If you claim that the self (*ātman*) exists, it likewise cannot know independently; it must rely upon visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) to be able to know.
If this is the case, the self is useless.

Visual consciousness cognizes form (*rūpa*); the form arises and ceases, arising in similarity and ceasing in similarity. Only thereafter does a mental factor arise within the mind, which is called mindfulness (*smṛti*)."
This mindfulness has conditioned phenomena as its object; although these have ceased in the past, this mindfulness is able to know them.
Just as the power of a noble one’s wisdom can know the affairs of future worlds, so too does each moment of mindfulness enable one to know past phenomena.
If the preceding visual consciousness ceases and a subsequent visual consciousness arises, that subsequent visual consciousness becomes increasingly sharp and powerful.
Although visible forms exist only momentarily and do not abide, they can be known because the power of mindfulness is sharp.
For this reason, although things arise and perish in every moment and are impermanent, one is still able to discern and know form.
Furthermore, you say:

"The consciousness of a person in the present arises and perishes anew at every moment; when body and life are severed, it too is exhausted. Regarding all conditioned phenomena—both demerit and merit—who follows them, and who receives their results?"
"Who experiences suffering and pleasure?
Who is liberated?
Now I shall answer you:

Now, as they have not yet attained the true path, these people’s minds are shrouded by various afflictions; they perform karmic actions that serve as the causes and conditions for birth, and at the time of death, the five aggregates continue from this state to produce the five aggregates [in the next life].
It is like one lamp lighting another lamp.
Or again, it is like the growth of grain, which has three causal conditions:
earth, water, and seed.
The arising of a body in a future life is also like this.
When there is a body, there are outflowing karmas (*āsrava-karma*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*); due to these three things, a future body arises.
Among these, the body and the causal conditions of karma cannot be severed nor destroyed; only the various fetters can be severed.
When the fetters and latent tendencies are severed, although a residual body and residual karma remain, one can attain liberation.
It is like having grain seeds and soil, yet because there is no water, they do not sprout.
Thus, although there is a body and there is karma, they will not arise if moistened by the water of the fetter of craving.
This is called being without a self, and it is also called attaining liberation.
One is bound by ignorance and liberated by wisdom; thus, there is no role for a "self" to play.
Furthermore, this is a combination of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), conventionally designated as a "person."
This person is bound by various fetters; when they obtain the nail of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and loosen these fetters, at that time it is said that the person has attained liberation.

It is like a rope being knotted or a rope being unknotted: the rope itself is the knot, and there is no separate entity apart from the knot; yet in the world, one speaks of "tying a rope" and "untying a rope."
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is also like this: through the conjunction of these two factors, name and form, there is the conventional designation "person.
These fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not different from name-and-form; they are merely called the "fetters of name-and-form" and the "liberation from name-and-form."

The receiving of retribution for sins and merits is also like this: although not a single dharma constitutes a real person, because of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), one receives the fruits of sin and merit, and thus the designation "person" is applied.
It is like a cart carrying goods: if one examines each part individually, there is ultimately no real cart; yet the cart receives the designation of "carrying goods."

It is the same for a person receiving retribution for sins or merit: it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that receives the retribution for sins or merit, yet it is "the person" who receives its designation.
The experience of suffering and pleasure is likewise.
Through such various causes and conditions, a permanent self (*ātman*) cannot be found.
The self (*ātman*) is the giver, and the recipient is likewise so.
Since you regard the self as the person, for this reason, the person who gives cannot be apprehended, and the person who receives cannot be apprehended either.
Through such various causes and conditions, these things—the material object, the giver, and the receiver—are said to be unapprehendable. Question:

If, regarding all phenomena, this is their true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*)—wherein there is nothing to be destroyed, nothing to be extinguished, nothing to be produced, and nothing to be created—why do you say that "the three factors cannot be apprehended through analysis"?
Answer:

For example, when ordinary people perceive a donor, perceive a recipient, and perceive material wealth, this constitutes inverted and false views; they thereby give rise to worldly enjoyment of pleasure, but once their merit is exhausted, they turn back again.
Therefore, the Buddha wishes to cause bodhisattvas to practice the true path and attain the true fruit-retribution; this true fruit-retribution is itself the Buddha-way.
To destroy false views, the Buddha says that these three things are unobtainable, yet in reality there is nothing to be destroyed.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have been ultimately empty from the very beginning.
Through such various and immeasurable causes and conditions, they are ungraspable; therefore, it is called the fulfillment and perfection of the *dānapāramitā*.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is able to give rise to the six perfections, at that time it is called the fulfillment and completion of the perfection of giving.
How does giving give rise to the dāna-pāramitā?
Dāna is of three grades: inferior, middling, and superior;
from the inferior arises the middling, and from the middling arises the superior.
If one gives coarse things such as food and drink with a softened mind, this is called the inferior [level].
If the practice of giving increases further, such that one is able to give clothing and precious objects, this is the intermediate [level] arising from the inferior.

If the mind of giving increases even more, such that there is no longer anything held dear, and one is able to give away everything—head, eyes, blood, flesh, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children—this is the superior [level] arising from the intermediate.
When Śākyamuni Buddha first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he was a great king named Prabhāsa; seeking the path of the Buddha, he practiced giving both extensively and modestly.
He was reborn in a subsequent life as a potter, where he was able to offer bathing implements and honey syrup as alms to another Śākyamuni Buddha and his community of bhikṣus.
Thereafter, she transformed her body and became the daughter of a great elder, making an offering of lamps to the Buddha Kauṇḍinya.
Various instances such as these are called the "inferior giving" of a bodhisattva.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was himself the son of a householder, he offered his robe as a gift to the Buddha Mahāghoṣa;
after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he erected ninety stupas.
Thereafter, he again took rebirth as a great king and made offerings of a canopy of the seven treasures to the Buddha Siṃha.
Later, he again received a body as a great elder and made offerings of an excellent dwelling and exquisite flowers of the seven treasures to the Buddha Sunetra.
Various instances such as these are called the giving of Bodhisattvas.

For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was formerly a rishi, he saw that the Buddha Kauṇḍinya was upright, handsome, and exceptionally sublime; he then threw himself from a high mountain peak before the Buddha, yet his body remained safe and sound as he stood to one side.
Furthermore, as the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana did, using his own body as a lamp to make offerings to the Buddha Sūryacandraprabhāsaśrī.
In such various ways, not sparing even his own body or life to make offerings to the Buddhas—this is the supreme giving of a bodhisattva.
These are called the three kinds of giving of a bodhisattva.
If one who has first resolved to attain Buddhahood practices giving to sentient beings, it is also like this:
beginning with the giving of food and drink, as the mind of giving increases further, they are able to give even their own flesh and body.
First, one practices giving by bestowing various kinds of fine beverages; subsequently, as the mind further increases in resolve, one is able to give even one's own blood.
First, one practices giving by bestowing paper, ink, and scriptures, as well as providing the four types of offerings—robes, food, drink, and bedding—to serve the Dharma Master;
later, having attained the Dharma-body, one preaches various teachings for immeasurable sentient beings, thereby performing the gift of Dharma.
In this way, through various such means, the dānapāramitā gives rise to the dānapāramitā.
How does the bodhisattva’s generosity give rise to the śīlapāramitā?
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Because sentient beings do not practice giving, they become impoverished in future lives;
because of this poverty, the mind of robbery arises."
Because of theft, there is killing;
because of poverty, one lacks sufficient wealth;
and because of this lack of wealth, one commits sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, because of poverty, one becomes lowly and base;
being lowly and base, one gives rise to fear and speaks falsely—due to such causes and conditions as poverty, one practices the ten unwholesome paths of action.
If one practices giving, one will be born with wealth and possessions; because of having wealth and possessions, one does not engage in unrighteousness.
Why is this? Because the five sensory objects are fully provided for, and there is no lack or deficiency.
For instance, in a previous life, Devadatta was once a snake who, together with a frog and a tortoise, formed a close friendship while living in a single pond.
Thereafter, the water in the pond was completely exhausted; they were famished, destitute, and impoverished, with no one to whom they could appeal.
At that time, the snake sent the tortoise to summon the frog. The frog spoke a verse to dismiss the tortoise, saying:
"If one encounters poverty and loses their original resolve, They do not contemplate the fundamental meaning, but prioritize food."
"Carry my words to the snake and tell him: 'The frog shall never come to your side!

If one cultivates generosity, one will possess merit in future lives and lack nothing; thus one is able to maintain the precepts and be free from these various evils. This is how generosity can give rise to the *śīlapāramitā*.
Furthermore, when practicing giving, it can cause the various fetters of broken precepts to diminish and strengthen the mind of upholding the precepts, making it firm and stable;
this is how the causal conditions of giving increase one's virtue of morality.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward the recipient; they do not cling to wealth and do not begrudge their own possessions, let alone resort to robbery or theft.
How could one who possesses compassion have any intent to kill?
Such qualities as these can prevent the breaking of precepts; this is what is meant by giving giving rise to morality.
If one can practice giving to destroy the mind of stinginess, then the subsequent practices of maintaining precepts, patience, and so forth, will be easy to perform.
For example, in the distant past, many eons ago, Mañjuśrī was once a bhikṣu who entered a city to beg for food and obtained a full alms bowl of joyous sweetmeat balls of a hundred flavors.
A young boy in the city followed him, begging for [the food].
He did not give it to him immediately; instead, they went to a Buddhist monastery (*buddhastūpa*), where he took two pellets in his hand and said to the boy:
"If you can eat one pellet yourself and offer one pellet as alms to the Sangha, I shall give it to you!"
They immediately agreed with one another, each offering a single *modaka* to the assembly of monks; thereafter, they received the precepts from Mañjuśrī and resolved their minds to attain Buddhahood.
Such giving can cause those who receive it to take up the precepts and resolve to become Buddhas; this is how giving gives rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, as a result of giving, one obtains the four types of offerings, a favorable land, and excellent teachers, lacking nothing; thus, one is able to maintain the precepts.
Furthermore, the retribution for giving is that one's mind becomes harmonious and supple;
because the mind is harmonious and supple, one is able to give rise to the observance of precepts;
because one is able to give rise to the observance of precepts, one can exercise self-restraint over the mind regarding unwholesome dharmas.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) arises from generosity.
How does generosity give rise to the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)?
When a bodhisattva practices generosity, the recipient may respond with verbal abuse, or demand excessively, or demand at an improper time, or even demand what ought not to be demanded.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:
"I now practice giving with the desire to seek the Buddha-way, yet there is no one who compels me to give."
"Since I am acting for my own sake, why should I give rise to anger?
Having reflected thus, one practices patience; this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) arising from giving (dāna).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving, if the recipient becomes angry or distressed, he reflects to himself:
"I am now giving away internal and external wealth and possessions; I can relinquish what is difficult to give. How much more so, then, could I not endure empty words?"
If I am unable to endure [insults], the giving I perform will be impure.
It is like a white elephant that enters a pond to bathe, yet upon emerging, returns once more to smear its body with dust;
giving while lacking endurance is just like this.
Having reflected thus, one practices patience (*kṣānti*).
Through various such causes and conditions of giving (*dāna*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) arises.
How does giving give rise to the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*)?
When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they constantly exercise diligence. Why is this?

When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind on enlightenment, their merit is not yet great; at that time, they wish to practice the two kinds of giving in order to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings.
Because material things were insufficient, he diligently sought wealth and the Dharma to provide for them.

This was like the case of Śākyamuni Buddha in his previous existence, when he acted as a great king of physicians to treat all illnesses, not seeking fame or profit, but out of compassion for sentient beings.

The sick were so numerous that his strength was insufficient to save them all; though he grieved for all beings, his wishes were not fulfilled, and he died in deep anguish, immediately being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He thought to himself:
"Now that I have been born in heaven, I merely consume my karmic rewards; there is no further growth or benefit.
He then employed skillful means to bring about his own death and relinquish this celestial lifespan.
He was born as a dragon prince within the palace of the Naga King Pāṅgudā.

His body grew large, and his parents held him in great affection; wishing to seek death on his own terms, he went to the Garuḍa King, who immediately seized this dragon son atop a Śālmali tree and swallowed him.
The parents wailed and wept, crying out in grief and distress.
Once the dragon prince had died, he was reborn in Jambudvīpa as the crown prince of a great king, named Nengshi (Capable of Giving).
Being born with the ability to speak, he asked those around him:
"Whatever things there are in this kingdom, bring them all here to use as offerings!
The people were both astonished and terrified, and they all abandoned him and fled.
His mother, out of pity and affection, stayed by him alone.
He said to his mother, "I am not a rākṣasa;
for what reason are all these people running away?"
"In my past lives, I have always delighted in practicing generosity; I am the donor for all people.
When his mother heard these words, she told them to the crowd, and the crowd immediately returned.
His mother raised him with great care; when he reached adulthood, she gave away everything she possessed as alms.
He then went to his father, the king, and requested wealth for the purpose of giving; the father granted him his own portion, which he likewise gave away entirely.
Seeing the people of Jambudvīpa suffering in poverty and hardship, he wished to provide for them with gifts, but his wealth was insufficient;
he then wept and asked the people, "By what means can I cause everyone to be satisfied with material riches?"
The elders said, "We have heard that there exists a wish-fulfilling jewel; if one obtains this jewel, whatever one seeks according to one's heart's desire can be obtained without exception."
Having heard these words, the Bodhisattva said to his parents:
"I wish to enter the great ocean to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel upon the head of the Dragon King.
His parents replied:
"I have only you, my one son. If you enter the great ocean, it is filled with many perils difficult to overcome.
Should you once be lost, what use would we have for living?"
"There is no need to go!
Within my storehouse there are still goods; I shall give them to you!
The son said:
"The treasury has its limits, but my intention is immeasurable.
I wish to fill all things with wealth so that none shall lack anything; I pray you grant me leave to fulfill this original aspiration and bring sufficiency to all the people of Jambudvīpa!"
The parents, recognizing his great resolve, did not dare to restrain him and eventually released him to depart.
At that time, five hundred merchants, seeing that he was a man of great merit and virtue, all joyfully wished to follow him;
having learned the day of his departure, they gathered at the mouth of the sea.
The Bodhisattva had previously heard that upon the head of the Dragon King Vāsuki there was a wish-fulfilling jewel;
he asked the multitude, "Who knows the way to reach that dragon palace?"
There was a blind man named Daśa who had previously entered the great ocean seven times and possessed complete knowledge of the sea routes.
The Bodhisattva immediately commanded him to travel together with him.
He replied, "I am already old and have lost sight in both eyes; although I have entered many times before, I am unable to go now!
The Bodhisattva said to him:

"This journey of mine is not for my own sake, but for the sake of all beings universally, seeking the wish-fulfilling jewel to provide for sentient beings so that they lack nothing in their physical needs; thereafter, I shall teach and transform them through the causal conditions of the Path."
"You are a wise man; how could you decline?
My aspiration is to achieve success—could this not be through your power?
Hearing these essential words, Dāśa was filled with joy and shared his sentiment, saying to the Bodhisattva:
"I shall now enter the great ocean together with you; though I shall certainly not survive, you must place my remains upon the sandy isle of golden sand within the great ocean."
When the preparations were complete, the seventh rope was severed; the ship sped away like a galloping horse and reached the Island of Many Jewels.
The merchants vied with one another to gather the seven treasures, each taking as much as they desired until they were fully satisfied.
He said to the bodhisattva,
"Why do you not take it?
The bodhisattva replied:
"What I seek is the wish-fulfilling jewel; these are exhaustible goods, which I do not require.
Each of you should know contentment and moderation, lest the ship become too heavy and we fail to save ourselves!"
At that time, the merchants said to the Bodhisattva:
"Virtuous One!
Grant us your blessing so that we may attain peace and security!"
Thereupon, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, Dāsa said to the Bodhisattva:
"Please leave the boat behind; you should follow this separate path and go."

"Wait for seven days until the wind ceases; then sail south along the eastern shore until you reach a perilous place where there will be a sheer cliff and a jujube grove whose branches all overhang the water.
A great wind will blow the ship, and it shall be wrecked and overturned!"
"You should climb up and grasp the branches of the jujube tree; by this you may save yourself.
My body is sightless and shall perish here.
Beyond this narrow shore, there will be a sandbank of golden sand; you should place my body upon that sand."
"The purity of the golden sands is my wish!
Just as he had spoken, the wind arrived and departed.
Upon reaching the precipice, it was exactly as Dhaśa had said.
The Bodhisattva looked up at the branches of a jujube tree and managed to escape by grasping them.
He placed the corpse of Dhṛṣṭa in a secure burial place on golden ground and then departed alone.

Following his previous instructions, he floated upon deep water for seven days; he walked in water reaching up to his neck for seven days; he walked in water reaching up to his waist for seven days; he walked in water reaching up to his knees for seven days; and he walked through mud for seven days.
Seeing beautiful lotuses that were fresh, pure, and soft, he thought to himself:
"These flowers are delicate and fragile; I shall enter the *ākāśa-samādhi* (space-like samādhi) and make my own body light."
Traveling upon the lotus for seven days, he saw various venomous snakes and thought to himself, "These venom-bearing creatures are truly terrifying!

He immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) and walked for seven days atop the heads of the venomous snakes; the snakes all raised their heads and offered them to the Bodhisattva, allowing him to step over them as he passed.
Having overcome these difficulties, he saw a city made of the seven kinds of jewels with sevenfold moats; the moats were all filled with venomous snakes, and three great nāgas guarded the gates.

When the Dragon saw that the Bodhisattva’s appearance was upright and refined, his marks and signs majestic and dignified, and that he was capable of overcoming all hardships to arrive here, he thought to himself:
"This is no ordinary person; he must be a Bodhisattva, a man of great merit!"
He was immediately granted permission to proceed and entered the palace directly.
The dragon king and his wife had not long since lost their son and were still weeping in grief;
upon seeing the Bodhisattva approaching, the dragon queen, who possessed supernatural powers, recognized him as her son, and milk flowed from both her breasts.
He commanded him to sit and questioned him, saying:
"You are my son; after you left me at the end of your life, where were you reborn?
The Bodhisattva, who also possessed the knowledge of his own past lives and recognized them as his parents, replied to his mother:
“I was born in Jambudvīpa as the crown prince of a great king.
Out of compassion for the poor who suffer from hunger, cold, and toil, lacking any autonomy, I have come here desiring to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel!”
The mother said, "This precious jewel upon your father’s head serves as his head ornament; it is difficult to obtain!
He will surely take you into his various treasuries, and whatever you desire, he will certainly grant to you."
You should reply:
"I have no need for the other miscellaneous jewels; I desire only the precious gem upon the Great King's head.
If you will look upon me with compassion, I pray that you grant it to me."
"Thus it may be obtained.
He then went at once to see his father.
The father was filled with great sorrow and joy, his celebration immeasurable.

Out of compassion for his son, who has traveled far through hardships to reach this place, he points out the wonderful treasures and says, "I shall give them to you as you desire; take whatever you need."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I have come from afar, wishing to see the Great King and to beg for the wish-fulfilling jewel upon your head;
if you look upon me with compassion, you should give it to me, but if you do not grant it, I require no other thing!"

The Dragon King replied, "I have only this single jewel, which I always wear as an ornament for my head; the people of Jambudvīpa are of meager merit and lowly, and it is not fitting that they should see it."
The Bodhisattva said:

"For this reason, I have traveled far through hardships and braved death to come from afar; because the people of Jambudvīpa are of meager merit, poor, and lowly, I wish to fulfill their wishes with this wish-fulfilling jewel, and thereafter instruct them through the causal conditions of the Buddha-way."
The Dragon King gave him the pearl and made this agreement with him, saying:
"I now give this pearl to you; once you have passed away from this world, you must return it to me!
He replied:
"Respectfully obeying Your Majesty's command!
Having obtained the jewel, the Bodhisattva soared into the void and reached Jambudvīpa in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm.
When the king, his parents, and the people saw their son return safely, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; embracing him, they asked:
"What have you obtained? He replied,
"I have obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel."
He asked, "Where is he now?
and [the other] replied:
"It is within this corner of the robe.
His parents said,
"How exceedingly small it is!"
He said, "It lies in his divine virtue, not in his greatness.
He then spoke to his parents, saying:
"An edict shall be issued throughout the city, both inside and out, to sweep and sprinkle the ground, burn incense, hang silk banners and canopies, and observe the fast and receive the precepts.
At dawn the following day, a tall wooden pole shall be erected as a standard, with a pearl placed upon its top.
At that time, the Bodhisattva made this vow:
"If I am to attain the Way of the Buddha and deliver all beings, may this jewel fulfill my wishes by producing all manner of precious objects, providing everything that people require."

At that time, dark clouds spread everywhere, raining down various precious objects—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—providing everything necessary for human beings in full abundance.
This continues thus until the end of their lives, never ceasing.
Such as these are called the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence born of giving.
What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditation born of giving?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they are able to eliminate stinginess and greed.
Having eliminated stinginess and greed, they practice single-mindedness on account of this giving and gradually remove the five hindrances;
being able to remove the five hindrances is what is called dhyāna.
Furthermore, the mind relies upon giving to enter the first dhyāna, up to the dhyāna of the cessation of perception and feeling.
What constitutes this reliance?
When practicing the giving of dhyāna to others, the mind thinks to itself:
"Since this person practices meditative concentration, I have made offerings to him with a pure mind; why then should I now neglect my own practice of meditation?
Thinking thus, he immediately withdrew his mind and engaged in contemplative meditation.

If one gives to the poor, one should reflect that in past lives they committed various unwholesome deeds, failed to seek single-mindedness, and did not cultivate meritorious karma, resulting in their poverty in this life.
With this as a self-exhortation, one should practice goodness and enter meditative concentration with a single mind.

As it is said, when the noble Wheel-Turning King Priyadarśana was visited by eighty-four thousand minor kings coming to pay court, they all brought exquisite objects made of the seven treasures as offerings.
The king said:
"I have no need for these; you may each use them yourselves to cultivate merit!"
The various kings thought to themselves:
"Although the Great King is unwilling to accept it, it would likewise be improper for us to use it ourselves.
They immediately joined together to employ craftsmen to construct a palace of the seven treasures, plant rows of trees made of the seven treasures, and create bathing pools of the seven treasures.

Within the great hall, he constructed eighty-four thousand towers made of the seven precious gems; within each tower were couches and seats made of the seven precious gems, with multi-colored coverlets and pillows placed at both ends of the beds, while silk streamers, banners, and canopies were suspended above, and the ground was perfumed and anointed with fragrant unguents.
When all matters were prepared, he addressed the Great King, saying:
"I pray that you accept this Dharma-palace, the jeweled trees, and the bathing pools!
The King accepted them in silence, and thought to himself:
