"I ought not to occupy this new palace first for my own enjoyment; rather, I should seek out virtuous people—such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—and allow them to enter first to receive offerings, and only then shall I occupy it!"
He immediately gathered virtuous people and first entered the jeweled palace, where various offerings were provided in exquisite abundance.

Once the others had departed, the king entered the jeweled palace, ascended the golden pavilion, and sat upon the silver couch. He contemplated giving, removed the five hindrances, restrained the six sense faculties, and warded off the six sensory objects; thus he experienced joy and bliss and entered the first dhyāna.
Next, he ascends the silver pavilion, sits upon the golden couch, and enters the second dhyāna.
Next, he ascends the vaidūrya pavilion, sits upon the crystal-jewel couch, and enters the third dhyāna.
Next, he ascended the crystal jewel-palace and sat upon a bed of *vaiḍūrya* lapis lazuli, entering the fourth *dhyāna*.
Sitting alone in contemplation, he remained thus for a full three months.
Then the Jewel-Woman Queen, accompanied by eighty-four thousand handmaidens—each adorned with necklaces of white pearls and famous jewels—came before the Great King and addressed him:
"It has been a long time since we last met in person; I have ventured here to inquire after your welfare!
The king said to his sisters:
"Each of you should rectify your hearts; you should act as friends and not as my enemies!"
The Jewel-Woman Queen shed tears and said:
"Great King!
Why do you call me 'sister'?"
"You must have some ulterior motive; I wish to hear its meaning. Why did you instruct me, saying, 'I shall be your friend, not your enemy'?
The King told him:
"If you regard me as a worldly cause for connection and engage in acts of desire with me for the sake of pleasure, then you are my enemy."
"If one can awaken to impermanence, realize that the body is like an illusion, cultivate merit and perform good deeds, and sever all desires, this is what constitutes a true friend.
The jade maidens replied,
"We shall respectfully follow the King's command!"
Having spoken these words, he dismissed them all.
Once the women had departed, the King ascended the golden pavilion and sat upon the silver couch to practice the samādhi of loving-kindness;
he then ascended the silver pavilion and sat upon the golden couch to practice the samādhi of compassion.
Ascending the beryl tower, he sat upon a crystal couch and practiced the samādhi of joy;
ascending the crystal-jewel tower, he sat upon a beryl couch and practiced the samādhi of equanimity.
This is how a bodhisattva’s generosity gives rise to the dhyāna-pāramitā.
How does a bodhisattva’s generosity give rise to the prajñā-pāramitā?

When a bodhisattva practices generosity, they know that this generosity will inevitably have its fruit and reward, remaining free from doubt; they are thus able to destroy wrong views and ignorance. This is how generosity gives rise to the prajñā-pāramitā.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving, he is able to discern and know this:

if one who does not uphold the precepts inflicts flogging, torture, or imprisonment, and acquires wealth through the perversion of justice to perform acts of giving, they will be reborn among elephants, horses, or oxen. Although they assume the forms of animals and must bear heavy loads, endure whips and lashes, or be harnessed for riding, they will always obtain fine dwellings and excellent food, be held in high regard by others, and receive their provisions from people.

Furthermore, one should know that if a person of evil nature harbors much anger and practices giving with a crooked and insincere mind, they shall fall among the dragons, where they will obtain palaces made of the seven treasures, exquisite food, and beautiful forms.
Furthermore, it is known that those who give with a mind of anger while being full of pride fall among the garuḍas, where they always attain sovereignty.

They possess wish-fulfilling jewels as necklaces; whatever they require, they obtain at will, and nothing happens contrary to their desires. They manifest ten thousand transformations, accomplishing every task.

Furthermore, one knows that officials who oppress and corrupt the people, seizing wealth and property in violation of the laws of governance to use for acts of giving, will fall among the ghosts and spirits upon death; they become *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits, capable of various transformations and delighting themselves with the five sensory objects.

Furthermore, one knows that if a person who is prone to anger, stubborn, and perverse, or who has a fondness for wine and meat, practices giving, they will fall among the terrestrial yakṣas and pretas, where they will constantly obtain various forms of pleasure, music, food, and drink.

Furthermore, one knows that there are those who are stubborn, headstrong, and arrogant, yet capable of practicing giving; by offering carriages and horses for others' use, they fall among the *yakṣas* of the void, where they possess great power and travel as swiftly as the wind wherever they go.

Furthermore, one knows that there are those who, though possessed of a jealous mind and a fondness for contention, are able to practice generosity by giving fine dwellings, bedding, clothing, and food; therefore, they are born among the flying yakṣas in celestial palaces, where there are various means of entertainment and objects for their physical comfort.
When one is able to discern and know these various things at the time of giving, this is the bodhisattva’s generation of *prajñā* through giving.
Furthermore, by giving food and drink, one gains strength, complexion, life, happiness, and sustenance.
If one gives clothing as a gift, one will be born with a sense of shame and modesty, possessing majestic virtue and physical beauty, and enjoy peace and happiness of body and mind.
If one gives houses and dwellings, one will obtain various palaces and towers made of the seven treasures that appear spontaneously, and will delight in the five desires.
If one gives wells, ponds, spring water, and various fine beverages, wherever one is born, one will be free from hunger and thirst, and will have all the five desires in abundance.
If one gives bridges, boats, and various types of footwear, one will be born with a full complement of diverse vehicles and horses;

if one gives gardens and groves, one will attain noble and honorable status, becoming a refuge for all, receiving a handsome and upright body, and dwelling in a mind that delights in freedom from sorrow.
Among these various kinds of people, such results are obtained through the causes and conditions of giving.
If a person practices giving and cultivates merit, yet does not delight in a livelihood based on conditioned activities, they will be reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings.

If a person practices giving and further makes offerings to their parents, uncles, aunts, brothers, and sisters, remaining free from anger and resentment, not delighting in litigation, and taking no pleasure in seeing those who litigate, they will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Such various forms of conceptualized giving constitute the bodhisattva’s production of *prajñā* through giving.
If a person gives while their mind is free from attachment, feeling weary of the world and seeking the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, this is the giving of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha;
if a person gives for the sake of the Buddha-way and for the sake of sentient beings, this is the giving of a bodhisattva.
To discern and understand these various kinds of giving in this manner constitutes the arising of the perfection of wisdom from giving.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they contemplate the true reality of the three spheres as explained above.
To be able to know in this way is for generosity to give rise to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, all causes and conditions for the merit of every form of wisdom arise from generosity.

Just as when the thousand Buddhas first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they made offerings of various kinds of wealth and goods to the Buddhas—whether by offering flowers and incense, or robes, or even willow twigs—and thereby resolved their minds.
Various kinds of giving such as these constitute the bodhisattva’s giving that gives rise to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 12:
Explanation of the First Chapter, the *Śīlapāramitā*.
*The Meaning of the Śīlapāramitā*, Fascicle Twenty-One, Number Thirteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha under the decree of the Later Qin dynasty. **21. The Meaning of the Śīlapāramitā** [Sūtra] "Because neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended, one should fulfill the śīlapāramitā."
[Treatise] *Śīla* is translated in the Qin language as "inherent goodness. To delight in practicing the path of goodness and not to be self-indulgent is called *śīla*.
Whether one practices goodness after having received the precepts or practices goodness without having received the precepts, both are called *śīla*.
Regarding *śīla* (precepts), briefly stated, there are eight types of restraint of body and speech:

not harming or injuring, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct; not speaking falsely, not using divisive speech, not using harsh speech, and not engaging in frivolous speech; not drinking intoxicants; and maintaining a pure livelihood. These are called the characteristics of the precepts.
If one does not guard [the precepts] but abandons them, this is called breaking the precepts.
One who breaks these precepts falls into the three evil realms.

If one maintains the precepts to a lesser degree, one is born among human beings; if one maintains them to a middling degree, one is born among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm; and if one maintains them to a superior degree, further practicing the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions, one is born among the pure heavens of the form and formless realms.
There are three grades of upholding the precepts:

by upholding the precepts with lower purity, one attains arhatship; by upholding the precepts with middling purity, one attains pratyekabuddhahood; and by upholding the precepts with superior purity, one attains the Way of the Buddha.
Without attachment or dependence, unbroken and unimpaired, praised and cherished by the noble ones—this is called the supreme, pure upholding of the precepts.

If, out of compassion for sentient beings, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and because one also knows the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the precepts, the mind does not depend on or cling to them;
such upholding of the precepts will lead people in the future to the path of the Buddha, and this is called attaining the precepts of the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
If a person seeks great and wholesome benefit, they should firmly uphold the precepts as if cherishing precious treasures or protecting their own life. Why is this?
It is like the great earth: all things that possess form rely upon the earth to abide.
Precepts are likewise thus: the precepts are the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is like one who wishes to walk without feet, fly without wings, or cross over without a boat—these things cannot be achieved;
if one wishes to obtain good fruits without the precepts, it is exactly the same.
If a person abandons these precepts, even if they dwell in the mountains practicing austerities, eating fruit, or taking medicinal herbs, they are no different from birds and beasts.
Some may take only water as their vow, or consume only milk, or practice breath-control;
some may shave their hair, or keep it long, or leave a small tuft of hair on the crown of their head.
Some wear the saffron robe, some wear white garments, some wear clothes of grass, and some wear clothes of tree bark;
some enter the water in winter, while others roast themselves by fire in summer;
some throw themselves from high cliffs, and some bathe in the Ganges River.
If one bathes three times a day, repeatedly makes offerings to the fire,
performs various sacrifices, recites various incantations and prayers,
and practices asceticism, yet lacks these precepts, one will achieve nothing in vain.

If there are those who, though dwelling in lofty halls and great palaces with fine clothing and delicious food, are able to practice this precept, they shall be born in auspicious realms and attain the fruits of the Path.
Whether noble or base, whether small or great, those who can practice these pure precepts will all obtain great benefit.
If one breaks these precepts, then regardless of being noble or base, great or small, none shall be able to be born at will in a wholesome realm.
Furthermore, a person who violates the precepts is like a cool, refreshing pond infested with venomous snakes, unfit for bathing;
they are also like a tree of fine flowers and fruit that is covered with many thorns.

It is the same for a person who, though born into a noble family, possesses a handsome body and is widely learned and well-informed, yet does not delight in upholding the precepts and lacks a heart of compassion.
As a verse says:
"To be noble yet lacking wisdom is decline; to be wise yet arrogant is also decline.
For one who upholds the precepts to then violate them—this is total decline in both this life and the next!"
"Though a person may be poor and lowly, if they are able to uphold the precepts, they surpass one who is wealthy and noble yet violates them.
The fragrance of flowers and the scent of wood cannot be heard from afar;
but the fragrance of upholding the precepts pervades the ten directions."

One who upholds the precepts is endowed with complete peace and happiness; their fame spreads far and wide, they are revered and loved by devas and humans, and in this present life, they constantly obtain all manner of joys.
If one desires wealth, honor, long life, or rebirth among gods and humans, these are not difficult to attain;
by maintaining pure precepts, all that one wishes for will be fulfilled.

Furthermore, when a person who upholds the precepts sees those who have broken them subjected to imprisonment, torture, and various forms of suffering, they rejoice, knowing for themselves that they will forever be free from such things.
If a person who upholds the precepts sees a virtuous person obtain renown and experience the joy of fame, they think to themselves:
"Just as that person has obtained renown, I too have a share in it."

When a person who upholds the precepts reaches the end of their life, as the "sword-wind" dismembers the body and the sinews and veins are severed, they know for themselves that their observance of the precepts was pure, and their mind is free from fear.
As a verse says:
"In the midst of great and evil diseases, the precepts are the excellent medicine;
in the midst of great terrors, the precepts are the protection."
In the darkness of death, the precepts are a bright lamp;
in the midst of the evil realms, the precepts are a bridge;
in the waters of the sea of death, the precepts are a great ship.

Furthermore, one who upholds the precepts will always receive the respect and support of people in this world; their mind will be joyful and free from regret, they will lack nothing in food and clothing, they will be reborn in heaven after death, and they will eventually attain the path of Buddhahood.
One who upholds the precepts shall attain nothing that cannot be attained;
one who breaks the precepts loses everything.
It is like a person who constantly makes offerings to a deity; though this person is poor, they worship with single-minded devotion for twelve full years, seeking wealth and nobility.
The deity took pity on this person, manifested his own form, and asked him:
"What do you seek? He replied:
"I seek wealth and honor, desiring that all my heart's wishes be fulfilled!
The deity gave him a vessel called the "Vase of Virtue" (Kamandalu) and said to him:
"Whatever things you require shall emerge from this vase."
Having obtained it, that person received whatever their heart desired; there was nothing they could not attain.

Having attained their wishes, they constructed a magnificent residence, fully equipped with elephants, horses, carriages, and the seven treasures, providing for guests so that no matter what was needed, there was never a lack.
A guest asked him, saying, "Previously you were poor;
by what means have you come to be so wealthy today?
He replied:
"I obtained a divine vase; this vase can produce all these various kinds of things, which is why I am so wealthy.
The guest said, "Produce the vase and show it to me, along with the things it produces!"
He immediately brought out the jar, and from within the jar, various kinds of objects were drawn forth.
That man, becoming arrogant and intoxicated, stood upon the jar and danced; the jar was instantly shattered, and all the objects likewise vanished at once.
It is the same for one who upholds the precepts: among all manner of sublime joys, there is nothing they do not obtain through their aspiration.
If a person breaks the precepts, becoming arrogant, dissolute, and self-indulgent, they are like that person who broke the jar and lost its contents.
Furthermore, for one who upholds the precepts, the fragrance of their reputation pervades both the heavens and the human realm in this life and the next.
Moreover, those who uphold the precepts are delighted by others to give to; they do not begrudge their wealth and possessions, and though they do not cultivate worldly profit, they lack nothing.
They shall be reborn in the heavens or before the Buddhas of the ten directions, enter the path of the Three Vehicles, and attain liberation.
If one merely maintains various forms of precepts based on false views, nothing will be attained in the end.
Furthermore, even if a person does not leave the household life, if they are able to practice the dharma of the precepts, they will likewise be reborn in heaven.
If a person maintains pure precepts and practices meditation and wisdom, desiring liberation from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, this aspiration will surely be attained.
One who upholds the precepts, though lacking weapons, cannot be harmed by any evils;
no one can seize the wealth of one who upholds the precepts.
Those who uphold the precepts are close kin who do not forsake one even in death;
the adornment of upholding the precepts surpasses that of the seven treasures.
For this reason, one should protect the precepts as one protects one's own life and as one cherishes precious objects.

Those who break the precepts undergo ten thousand forms of suffering, like the poor man mentioned before who broke his jar and lost his possessions; for this reason, one should maintain pure precepts.
Furthermore, one who maintains the precepts should contemplate the transgressions of those who break them and exert themselves to maintain the precepts with a single-minded focus.
What is called the transgression of a person who breaks the precepts?
A person who breaks the precepts is not respected by others; their home is like a tomb, a place where people do not go.
A person who breaks the precepts loses all merit and virtue; they are like a withered tree, which no one cherishes or delights in.
A person who violates the precepts is like a frost-bitten lotus, which people do not delight in seeing.
A person who violates the precepts has a malevolent mind that is fearsome, like a rākṣasa.
Those who break the precepts are not sought after by others, just as a thirsty person does not turn toward a dried-up well.
Those who break the precepts are constantly plagued by doubt and regret, just as a person who has committed a crime is perpetually afraid that punishment will arrive.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a field struck by hail; one cannot rely upon them.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a bitter gourd; although its form resembles that of a sweet seed, it is unfit for consumption.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a village of thieves; one must not rely upon them.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a grave illness; people do not wish to draw near them.
One who breaks the precepts cannot escape suffering, just as it is difficult to pass through an evil path.
One who breaks the precepts should not be lived with, just as it is difficult to draw near a wicked thief.
A person who breaks the precepts is like a great pit that travelers avoid;
a person who breaks the precepts is difficult to dwell with, like a venomous snake.
One who has broken the precepts should not be approached or touched, for they are like a great fire.
One who has broken the precepts is like a wrecked ship; one cannot board it to cross over.
A person who has broken the precepts is like vomited food, which cannot be eaten again.
A person who has broken the precepts among a virtuous assembly is like a vicious horse in a herd of good horses.
A person who has broken the precepts is different from a virtuous person, like a donkey among a herd of oxen.
A person who has broken the precepts within a community of those who are diligent is like a weakling among the strong.
A person who has broken the precepts, though appearing to be a bhikṣu, is like a corpse among those who are sleeping.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a counterfeit pearl among genuine pearls.
A person who violates the precepts is like an eranda tree in a sandalwood grove.
Although such a person may outwardly resemble a virtuous one, they lack wholesome dharmas within;
though they shave their heads, dye their robes, and receive their tally-sticks in succession, they are called bhikṣus in name only, yet in reality are not bhikṣus.
If a person who has broken the precepts wears the Dharma robes, it is as if they were wrapping their body in sheets of glowing copper and iron;
if they hold an alms bowl, it is as if they were holding a vessel of molten copper;
and whatever they eat or drink is as if they were swallowing glowing iron balls and drinking hot molten copper.
If one receives offerings and provisions from others, one is being guarded by the hell-demons;
if one enters a vihāra, one is entering a great hell;
if one sits upon the beds and couches of the Saṃgha, it is as if sitting upon a bed of glowing iron.
Furthermore, a person who violates the precepts is constantly filled with fear and anxiety, like a gravely ill person who always dreads the arrival of death.
They are also like one who has committed the five heinous crimes, whose mind perpetually thinks, "I am a thief of the Buddha," and thus hides, covers themselves, and seeks out secluded corners;
like a bandit fearing others, as the months, years, and days pass, they are never at peace.
A person who has broken the precepts may receive offerings and enjoy pleasures, yet such pleasure is impure;
it is like a fool providing offerings and adornments for a corpse—when a wise person hears of this, they loathe it and do not wish to see it.
Such various and immeasurable offenses of breaking the precepts are beyond description; the practitioner should maintain the precepts with a single-minded focus.
22. The Meaning of the Characteristics of the Precepts (*Śīlākāra-artha*). *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the First Chapter, Part 22-1. Question:
Having already understood these various meritorious fruits and retributions, what is meant by the "characteristics of the precepts" (*śīlākāra*)?
Answer:

To cease evil and not commit it again—whether arising from the mind, expressed by speech, or received from others—and to bring rest to the evils of body and speech; this is the characteristic of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
What is meant by "evil"?

If one is actually a sentient being, and knowing them to be a sentient being, one gives rise to the intention to kill and takes their life, producing bodily karma consisting of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), this is called the offense of killing.
Other acts such as binding, confinement, and flogging are auxiliary methods for killing.
Furthermore, one incurs the offense of killing by killing another, not by killing one's own body.

Killing with the conscious intent that "this is a sentient being" constitutes the offense of killing; it is not like one who, seeing a person in the dark, mistakes them for a tree stump and kills them.
Therefore, one incurs the offense of killing through intentional action, not unintentionally.
One incurs the offense of killing when acting with a sense of satisfaction, not when acting out of madness or delusion.
The severing of the life-faculty constitutes the offense of killing, not merely the inflicting of a wound.
Physical action constitutes the sin of killing, not merely verbal instruction;
verbal instruction constitutes the sin of killing, not merely the arising of the thought.
Such cases as these are termed the sin of killing.
Not committing such offenses is called precept-keeping.
If a person receives the precepts and gives rise to this thought and speaks these words:
"From this day forth, I shall no longer kill living beings!"
If one neither moves the body nor speaks with the mouth, but alone in the mind makes a self-vow:
"From this day forth, I shall no longer kill living beings!
this is called the precept of non-killing.
Some say: "This precept of non-killing is either wholesome or indeterminate. He asks:
As it is stated in the Abhidharma that "all moral restraints (śīla-saṃvara) are wholesome," why is it now said that they are indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
The answer is:
as it is stated in the *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma* that all are wholesome, whereas in other Abhidharmas it is stated that the precept against killing may be either wholesome or indeterminate.
Why is this? If the precept against killing were always wholesome, then those who uphold this precept should be like those who have attained the Way and would never fall into the evil realms.
For this reason, it must sometimes be indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Because the indeterminate (avyākṛta) has no retribution, one is not reborn among gods or humans.
Question:
One does not fall into hell because of an indeterminate precept; rather, one falls into hell because of the further arising of an evil mind!
The answer is:

By not killing, one attains immeasurable wholesome dharmas; because both manifest and non-manifest merit constantly arise day and night, whereas if one commits even a slight transgression, it is limited and measurable.
Why is it that one follows what is finite rather than what is infinite?
For this reason, we know that within the precept against killing, there may be that which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, there are those who do not receive the precepts from a teacher, but instead make a vow to themselves within their own minds:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer kill!
Such abstention from killing may at times be neutral (avyākṛta).
Question:
To which realm is this precept of non-killing bound?
The answer is as stated in the *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma*:
"All observances of the restraint of precepts are bound to the desire realm.
Other *Abhidharma* texts state:
"Some are bound to the desire realm; some are unbound."
"To speak according to reality, there should be three types:
either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or untainted (*anāsrava*).
Although the act of killing belongs to the desire realm, the precept against killing should follow the act of killing and thus belong to the desire realm."
However, the non-killing of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) non-killing are true non-killing precepts because they provide a remote prevention.

Furthermore, there may be someone who has not formally received the precepts, yet from birth has had no fondness for killing; whether this state is wholesome or neutral, it is termed "neutral" (*avyākṛta*).
This dharma of non-killing is neither mind nor mental factors, nor is it associated with the mind;
it may arise together with the mind, or it may not arise together with the mind.
The *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma* states: "Non-killing is an action of body and speech;
it may be manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) or non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), and it may sometimes follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*) or not follow the mind. [The red annotation says:
"Following the mind":]
The precepts associated with meditative concentration do not follow one's own will;
the five precepts are not the karmic retribution of previous lives.
Two kinds of cultivation should be cultivated, and two kinds of realization should be realized (the *Dan* commentary states:
realization by body and realization by wisdom).
Those [defilements] to be abandoned through reflection are all acquired last within the desire realm.
It is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and abandoned by time (*kāla-prahātavya*), and is attained by both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

This is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), which may be visible (*sanidarśana*) or invisible (*anidarśana*), may be resistant (*sapratigha*) or non-resistant (*apratigha*), is a phenomenon with retribution (*savipāka*), is a phenomenon that bears fruit (*saphala*), is a contaminated phenomenon (*sāsrava*), is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), and is a superior phenomenon (*sottara*). [The annotation states:
It is "superior" because it is not ultimate; it is not a corresponding cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Such distinctions as these are called the precept of non-killing. Question:
Within the Eightfold Path, there is also the abstention from killing; why then do you speak only of the "precept of non-killing" as having retribution and being with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
Answer: Herein, only the method for receiving the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) is explained;
the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is not mentioned. Furthermore, other *Abhidharma* texts state:
The dharma of non-killing is not constantly pursued by the movements of the mind; it is neither an action of body nor speech, nor does it follow the movements of mental action.
It may have retribution or it may be without retribution;
it is a dharma dissociated from the mind, and it may be either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
"This constitutes a distinct teaching; all other aspects are the same.
Furthermore, it is said:

"The Buddhas and noble sages do not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena" (the *Danzhu* commentary states: [this refers to the fact that they do not falsely discriminate or verbally proliferate the nature of dharmas]).
Various divergent doctrines are called "playful chatter. Since living beings present before us each cherish their own lives, the Buddha said: "Do not take the lives of others;
by taking the lives of others, one shall undergo all manner of suffering and pain in life after life."
Whether sentient beings exist or do not exist shall be explained later. Question:
A person can overcome others by force, seize their kingdoms, and slay their enemies; or through hunting for their skins and flesh, the benefit provided is vast.
What benefit is gained by causing others to refrain from killing?
The answer is:
one attains fearlessness, peace, and freedom from dread.
Because I do no harm to others, they likewise do no harm to me; for this reason, I am without fear or dread.
A person who delights in killing, even if their rank reaches that of a sovereign king, cannot find peace of mind;
whereas a person who upholds the precepts may travel alone and wander solitary, yet remains free from all fear and difficulty.
Furthermore, those who delight in killing are loathsome to all living beings;
if one does not delight in killing, all sentient beings will joyfully seek to rely upon them.
Furthermore, when a person who upholds the precepts is about to end their life, their mind is peaceful and joyful, free from doubt and remorse.
Whether they are reborn in the heavens or among humans, they will always attain long life.
This serves as the causal condition for attaining the Way, leading even to Buddhahood and abiding in immeasurable longevity.
Furthermore, those who take life undergo various forms of physical and mental suffering in both this life and future lives;
those who refrain from killing do not encounter these many hardships, which constitutes a great benefit.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects:
"I cherish my own life and love my own body; others do likewise—how am I different from them?
For this reason, one should not kill living beings.
Furthermore, if a person kills living beings, they will be censured by the virtuous and envied by their enemies;
because they have taken the lives of others, they will always live in fear and be loathed by them;
at the time of death, their mind will be filled with regret, and they shall fall into hell or among the animals.
If one is reborn as a human being, one will invariably be short-lived.
Furthermore, even if one were free from transgressions in future lives, were not censured by virtuous people, and not envied by enemies, one still ought not to intentionally deprive another of life.
Why is this? It is something that those with virtuous characteristics should not even contemplate, let alone commit, for it entails sin in both worlds and results in wretched and evil retribution!
Furthermore, killing is the gravest among all sins.
Why is this? When a person faces the urgency of death, they do not spare even their most precious treasures, but prioritize saving their life above all else.

It is like a merchant who has gone to sea to gather jewels; as he was about to emerge from the great ocean, his ship suddenly wrecked and he lost all his treasures, yet he rejoiced and raised his hand, saying:
"What a great treasure you have nearly lost!
the crowd said in astonishment.
"You have lost your wealth and escaped naked; why do you joyfully say that you have nearly lost a great treasure?"
He replied:
"Among all treasures, human life is foremost;
people seek wealth for the sake of life, but do not seek life for the sake of wealth."
For this reason, among the ten unwholesome paths of action, the Buddha taught that the transgression of killing is foremost;
likewise, it is foremost among the five precepts.
If a person cultivates various kinds of merit and virtue but lacks the precept against killing, then there is no benefit whatsoever.
Why is this? Although one may be born into a position of wealth and nobility with great power and influence, if one lacks a lifespan, who can enjoy such pleasures?
For this reason, it is known that among all other transgressions, the sin of killing is the most grave.
Among all meritorious virtues, non-killing is foremost.
In the world, cherishing life is foremost.
How is this known?
All people in the world are willing to endure punishments, mutilations, and tortures in order to protect their lives.
Furthermore, if there is someone who receives the precepts and gives rise to the thought:
"From this day forth, I shall not kill any sentient being."
"Thus, among immeasurable sentient beings, one has already bestowed what is most cherished and valued; the merit thereby obtained is likewise immeasurable.
As the Buddha said:
'There are five great gifts. What are the five?'"
First, refraining from killing is the greatest gift;
likewise, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, and refraining from drinking intoxicants are also such gifts.
Furthermore, practicing the samādhi of loving-kindness brings immeasurable merit; one cannot be harmed by water or fire, nor injured by blades or weapons, and cannot be struck by any poisons.
Such results are obtained through the five great acts of giving.
Furthermore, among those honored throughout the three times and the ten directions, the Buddha is the foremost.
As the Buddha told the lay follower Nandika:
"There are ten offenses for killing; what are these ten?"
First, their minds constantly harbor venom that persists through every lifetime;
second, sentient beings detest them and take no pleasure in seeing them;
third, they constantly harbor evil thoughts and contemplate wicked deeds.
Fourth, sentient beings fear them as if seeing a snake or a tiger;
fifth, their minds are terrified while sleeping, and they remain uneasy even when awake;
sixth, they constantly have evil dreams.
Seventh, at the time of death, one undergoes a violent and terrifying death;
eighth, one plants the causes and conditions for a short life;
ninth, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the hells.
"Tenth, if one is reborn as a human, one will always have a short lifespan.
Furthermore, the practitioner reflects:
"All living beings, down to the smallest insects, cherish their own bodies; [how much more so should I do the same]."
"How can one kill sentient beings for the sake of clothing and food for oneself?
Furthermore, a practitioner should study the Dharma of the Great Beings; among all Great Beings, the Buddha is the greatest.

Why is this? Because he has accomplished all wisdom, is fully endowed with the ten powers, and is able to deliver sentient beings; he constantly practices compassion and maintains the precept against killing, thereby attaining Buddhahood himself, and also teaches his disciples to practice this compassion.
Because the practitioner wishes to learn the conduct of a Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), they must likewise refrain from killing.
A question is asked:
"If one does not encroach upon me, the intent to kill may cease; [but what of others?]"
If one is subjected to injury, robbery, or coercion, how should one act?
The answer is:
one should weigh the gravity of the situation.
If someone were about to kill oneself, one should first reflect:
"Is the benefit of the precepts more important,
or is the preservation of the body more important?"
"Is breaking the precepts the greater loss,
or is losing one's body the greater loss?
Having reflected thus, he knew that upholding the precepts is of primary importance, while preserving the body is secondary.
If one merely avoids physical harm and preserves the body, what is gained by that body?
This body is called a thicket of old age, sickness, and death; it is destined for decay and ruin!
If one loses the body for the sake of upholding the precepts, the benefit is exceedingly great.
Furthermore, he reflected:

"Throughout countless lifetimes past and present, I have repeatedly lost my body, sometimes taking the form of a wicked thief or a beast, engaging solely in unwholesome deeds for the sake of wealth and profit.

Now that I have attained the opportunity to uphold the pure precepts, I shall not begrudge this body; to sacrifice one's life to maintain the precepts is hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior to preserving one's life while violating them—beyond all comparison."
"With such a concentrated mind, one ought to sacrifice one's body to protect pure precepts.
It is like a person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna, born into a family of butchers;
as he approaches adulthood, he ought to carry on his family trade, yet he refuses to kill living beings.
The parents gave him a knife and a sheep, shut him inside a room, and said to him:
"If you do not kill this sheep, we will not let you go out, nor will you see the sun and moon, nor shall you have food or drink for your livelihood!"
The boy thought to himself:
"If I kill this one sheep, I shall end up committing this act as a habit; how could I commit such a great sin for the sake of my own body?"
He then took a knife and committed suicide.
His parents opened the door and saw the sheep standing to one side, while their son’s life had already come to an end.
At the very moment he took his own life, he was reborn in the heavens.
If one acts in this manner, it constitutes not being sparing of one's own life in order to fully protect the pure precepts.
Such meanings as these are termed the precept against taking life.

Regarding taking what is not given: knowing that an object belongs to another, giving rise to a thieving mind, taking the object and removing it from its original place so that the object comes to belong to oneself—this is termed theft.
If one does not do it, this is called non-stealing.
All other expedient means, calculations, and even grasping with the hand while the object has not yet left the ground are termed auxiliary methods of stealing.
There are two kinds of property:
that which belongs to others and that which does not belong to others.
To take property belonging to others constitutes the offense of theft.
Objects belonging to others also consist of two types:
first, those within a village; second, those in open spaces.
To take objects from these two locations with the intent to steal constitutes the offense of theft.
If an object is found in an open space, one should investigate to determine to whose country that object belongs;
since the object must have an owner, it should not be taken.
As explained in the Vinaya regarding the various forms of non-stealing, this is called the characteristic of non-stealing.
Question: What benefits are there in not stealing? Answer:
Human life is of two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.
To seize one's wealth and property is to seize their external life.
Why is this? Life depends on food, drink, clothing, and so forth for its sustenance; if these are plundered or seized, it is called the "seizure of external life.
As a verse says:
"All sentient beings sustain themselves with food and clothing;
to seize or plunder these is called 'plundering life.
For this reason, a person of wisdom should not plunder."
Furthermore, one should reflect for oneself:
"Though I may plunder others to obtain wealth and provide for myself, even if my body is satisfied, I will inevitably die;
upon death, I shall enter hell. Although my family and relatives shared in my pleasures, I alone must undergo the retribution, and they cannot save me."
Having attained this contemplation, one should refrain from stealing.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of taking what is not given:
first, theft; second, robbery.
These two together are termed "taking what is not given.
Within taking what is not given, theft is the most grave. Why is this so?
All people sustain themselves through wealth, yet some violate walls and windows to steal it; this is the most impure of acts.
Why is this? Because those who lack power and are superior men steal out of fear of death.
Among all forms of plunder, theft is the gravest offense, as the verse says:
"With body emaciated by hunger, One undergoes the most intense suffering of retribution;
The property of others must not be touched, For it is like a mass of blazing fire."
"If one steals another's property, the owner weeps in bitter affliction;
even if it were the King of Devas himself, he would likewise consider it a suffering.
Although the sin of one who kills is grave, such a person is a thief only toward the victim; however, the thief of one who steals is a thief toward all beings who possess property.
If one violates other precepts, there may be other countries where such acts are not considered offenses;
however, if one commits theft, there is no country in the world that does not punish it as a crime.
Question:
There are people in this world who praise the prowess of those who plunder; why, then, do you not engage in such plundering? Answer:
To steal what is not given is an unwholesome mark;
although there are degrees of severity among acts of robbery and theft, all are equally unwholesome.
It is like fine food mixed with poison and coarse food mixed with poison: though the quality of the food differs, the presence of the poison is no different.
It is also like the case of treading upon fire in either light or darkness; although day and night differ, the burning of the feet is one and the same.

Likewise, the foolish people of the present age do not recognize the retributions of sin and merit across two lifetimes. Lacking a heart of benevolence and compassion, when they see someone using force to encroach upon others or violently seize another's wealth, they praise that person as being "strong."
The Buddhas and worthy sages have compassion for all beings and clearly perceive that the calamities of the three periods of time do not perish;
they do not praise [such acts]. For this reason, one knows that the offenses of killing and stealing are both unwholesome, and are not practiced by those of good conduct or spiritual practitioners.
As the Buddha said:
"There are ten offenses regarding taking what is not given. What are these ten?
First, the owner of the object is constantly angry."
Second, regarding "heavy doubt," the red annotation states:
"the doubt of those who have committed grave offenses";
third, "not weighing [the situation] when it is not the proper time for action."
Fourth, they form factions with wicked people and distance themselves from the virtuous and good;
fifth, they destroy the signs of goodness;
sixth, they incur the punishment of the authorities.
Seventh, one's wealth and property will be confiscated;
eighth, one plants the causes and conditions for the karma of poverty;
ninth, after death, one enters hell.
Tenth: if one is reborn as a human and strives diligently to seek wealth, it will be shared among five parties:
kings, thieves, fire, water, or being squandered by an unloved son; even if buried in the ground, it shall be lost.
Regarding sexual misconduct: if a woman is protected by her parents, brothers, sisters, husband, sons, worldly law, or royal law, to violate her is called sexual misconduct.
If there are those who, though not guarded by a physical protector, take the Dharma as their protection;
what is meant by "protection of the Dharma"?
All women who have gone forth, or laywomen who observe the one-day precepts (upavāsa), are said to have the Dharma as their protection.
Whether by force, by wealth, or by deception;
or if one’s own wife is observing the precepts, is pregnant, is nursing an infant, or is approached through an improper orifice—if one commits such acts, it is called sexual misconduct.
In this way, through various means—even making a pact with a courtesan by means of flower garlands—to engage in such acts is called sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*).
To refrain from such various acts is called abstaining from sexual misconduct (*akāmamithyācāra*).
Question:
If one commits adultery with a person protected by another person, or violates a dharma protected by a dharma, it should be called sexual misconduct;
but when a person has their own wife, why would it be considered misconduct?
Answer: Since she has already received and accepted the one-day precepts, she has entered into the Dharma;
although she was originally a wife, she is no longer her own mistress.
If one transgresses the time for receiving the precepts, it constitutes an unlawful observance.
Furthermore, if a woman is pregnant, because her body is heavy, she will grow weary of her former practices, and moreover, it would cause injury to the fetus.
When nursing an infant, if one engages in sexual intercourse with one's mother, the milk will dry up;
furthermore, because the mind is attached to lust, one no longer protects the child.

When it occurs in an improper place—that is, not at the female organ—and the woman’s heart finds no pleasure, yet it is done by force and against reason, it is therefore called sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*).
Not committing this act is called abstaining from sexual misconduct. Question:
If the husband does not know, see, or suffer distress, what fault is there for the other?
Answer: Because it is erroneous;
since it is named "erroneous," it is not upright, and for this reason it is culpable.

Furthermore, this act entails various transgressions: the affection between husband and wife consists of two bodies sharing one essence; to seize what another loves and to shatter their fundamental heart is what defines a thief.
Furthermore, there are grave offenses: an evil reputation and a foul name, being detested by others;
little joy and much fear—fearing execution and punishment, or fearing that one's husband or associates may discover [one's transgressions];
harboring many false words, which are censured by the sages. This is the gravest among crimes. (The "Crimson Annotation" states:)
The sin of sexual misconduct is called the gravest of sins because it violates the precept against illicit lust.
Furthermore, a lascivious person should reflect to themselves:

"My own wife and the wives of others are both women; in their physical form and emotional nature, there is no difference between them. Why, then, do I give rise to perverse delusions and follow such evil intentions?"
The person who commits sexual misconduct destroys and loses the pleasures, good reputation, and virtuous fame of both this life and future lives;

they lose the peace and happiness of body and mind, which are obtained in this life, as well as the benefits of rebirth in heaven, the attainment of the Path, and Nirvana, which are obtained in future lives.
Furthermore, one should restrain the mind by exchanging one's own position with that of another, thinking:
"If he were to violate my wife, I would be filled with anger;
if I were to violate his, how would he be any different?"
"By exercising self-restraint through empathy for oneself, one ought not to commit such acts.
Furthermore, as the Buddha has said:
'A person who commits sexual misconduct will later fall into the Sword-Tree Hell, where they shall undergo all manner of suffering.'"

Having attained human birth, if one does not maintain harmony within the family and instead constantly associates with lewd women, the depraved, and the cruel, such sexual misconduct becomes a calamity—like a venomous viper or a great conflagration. If one does not swiftly avoid it, disaster will surely follow!
As the Buddha has said:
"There are ten offenses for sexual misconduct:
first, one will constantly be sought to be harmed by the husband or master of the person with whom one commits the act."
Second, husband and wife lack harmony and are constantly engaged in quarreling and strife;
third, all unwholesome dharmas increase day by day, while all wholesome dharmas diminish day by day;
fourth, failing to protect one's person, one leaves one's wife and children orphaned and destitute.
Fifth, one's wealth and property diminish daily;
sixth, one encounters various misfortunes and is constantly suspected by others;
seventh, one is not loved or esteemed by relatives and acquaintances.
Eighth, they plant the karmic causes and conditions for enmity;
ninth, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they die and enter hell;
tenth, if they emerge [from that state] as women, many men will share a single husband.
If one becomes a man, his wife will not be chaste.
Refraining from such various causes and conditions as these is called abstaining from sexual misconduct.
As for false speech: with an impure mind, desiring to deceive another, one conceals the truth and utters divergent words, thereby giving rise to verbal karma; this is called false speech.
The offense of lying arises from the mutual understanding of the sounds and signs of speech;
if there is no such mutual understanding, then even if the words are untrue, there is no offense of lying.
This offense of lying consists of claiming to know what one does not know, or claiming to know what one does know.
To say one has not seen when one has seen, or to say one has seen when one has not seen;
to say one has not heard when one has heard, or to say one has heard when one has not heard—this is called false speech.
To refrain from doing so is called abstaining from false speech.
Question: What kind of offense is there in lying? Answer:
A person who speaks falsely first deceives themselves and then deceives others;
taking the real for the unreal and the unreal for the real, they invert truth and falsehood and do not receive wholesome dharmas.
For example, just as water cannot enter an overturned jar, so too does a person who speaks falsely lack shame and remorse; they block the path to the heavens and the gate to Nirvana.
Observing and knowing this fault, one therefore does not commit it.

Furthermore, observing and knowing that truthful speech has exceedingly vast benefits, and that the benefit of truthful speech issues from oneself and is very easy to obtain—this constitutes the power of all those who have left the household life.
Such merit is a common benefit for both householders and those who have left the home life; it is the mark of a virtuous person.
Furthermore, one who speaks the truth has a mind that is upright;
with a mind that is upright, it is easy to escape suffering.
It is like dragging timber through a dense forest; that which is straight is easy to extract.
Question:
If lying carries such a transgression, for what reason do people still lie?
Answer: There are some who are foolish and lacking in wisdom; when they encounter misfortune and suffering, they tell lies in hopes of escaping it.
They do not know that once their deeds are exposed, they will incur guilt in this present life, nor do they know that there will be the retribution of great sin in future lives.
Furthermore, there are those who, although they know the sin of lying, nevertheless tell lies because their greed, anger, and delusion are excessive.
Again, there are those who, though neither greedy nor angry, falsely testify to another's crime; believing in their hearts that it is truly so, they fall into hell after death.
For example, Kokālika, a disciple of Devadatta, constantly sought out the faults of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.

At that time, after the two of them had completed their summer retreat, they were traveling through various countries when they encountered heavy rain; arriving at a potter’s workshop, they stayed overnight in a house filled with ceramic vessels.
Previously, a woman had been staying overnight in this house in the dark, unknown to the two men.
That night, the woman dreamed that she discharged impurity; in the morning, she went to the water to wash herself.
At that time, Kokālika happened to see him while walking by.
Kokālika was skilled at reading physiognomy and could discern the circumstances of people's sexual intercourse, yet he did not know whether it had occurred in a dream or not.
At that time, Kokālika looked back and said to his disciple,
"This woman had sexual intercourse with a man last night.
He then questioned the woman:
"Where did you sleep? He replied,
"I stayed overnight in the potter's house."
He asked again, "With whom? He replied:
"Two bhikṣus.
At that time, the two men emerged from the house; having seen them, Kokālika further examined their physical characteristics and concluded in his mind that the two must have committed an impure act.
Previously harboring jealousy, upon witnessing this event, he went throughout the cities and villages to proclaim it;
next, he arrived at the Jetavana and raised this evil cry.
During that interval, the Brahma King came, desiring to see the Buddha.
The Buddha entered his quiet chamber and remained in silent samādhi;
the assembly of bhikṣus likewise each closed their rooms and entered samādhi, such that none could be awakened.
He then reflected to himself:
"I have come specifically to see the Buddha, but as the Buddha has entered samādhi, I wish to return.
He then thought again:
"It will not be long before the Buddha arises from his concentration; I shall stay here for a short while."
Arriving before the door of Kokālika’s cell, he knocked on it and said:
"Kokālika! Kokālika!"
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have pure and gentle minds; do not slander them, lest you suffer for a long night!
Kuṭāḍhya asked, "Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am Brahmā, the King of Gods. He asked:
"The Buddha said that you have attained the path of an Anāgāmin; for what reason have you come?
The Brahmā King thought this in his mind and spoke in verse:
"To measure the immeasurable Dharma, One should not grasp it by means of signs."
"To try to measure the immeasurable Dharma—this is the way of the common folk who are submerged!
Having spoken this verse, he went to where the Buddha was and related the matter in detail.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
You have spoken this verse most skillfully!”
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke these verses:
"To attempt to measure the immeasurable Dharma Is not to be grasped by means of signs;
To attempt to measure the immeasurable Dharma Is the ruin of the worldly man!"
Having heard the Buddha’s discourse, the Brahma King suddenly vanished and returned to his celestial realm.
At that time, Kokālika went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha told Kokālika:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana possess pure and supple minds; do not slander them, lest you suffer for a long night!
Kokālika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not dare to disbelieve the Buddha's words; however, I have seen it with my own eyes so clearly that I know for certain that these two men have actually committed impurity.
The Buddha rebuked him thus three times, but Kokālika likewise refused to accept it three times, whereupon he rose from his seat and departed.

Upon returning to his chamber, sores broke out over his entire body; they began like mustard seeds and gradually grew as large as beans, jujubes, and pears, eventually swelling to the size of melons. Suddenly, he was consumed by a rotting decay like that of a great conflagration; wailing and howling in agony, he died that very night and entered the Great Lotus Hell.
A certain Brahmā came to the Buddha at night and said,
"Kokālika has already died.
Another Brahmā then spoke:
"He has fallen into the Great Lotus Hell.
When that night had passed, the Buddha commanded the assembly of monks to gather and addressed them, saying:
"Do you wish to know the length of the lifespan in the hell into which Kokālika has fallen?"
The bhikṣus said,
“We wish to hear it with joy!
The Buddha said:

"Suppose there were sixty *hu* of sesame seeds, and a person were to come every hundred years and take away a single seed; even when they were all exhausted, the lifespan within the Arbuda hell would still not have ended."
The lifespan in twenty Arbuda hells constitutes one lifespan in a Nirarbuda hell;
likewise, the lifespan in twenty Nirarbuda hells constitutes one lifespan in an Ababa hell;
and the lifespan in twenty Ababa hells constitutes one lifespan in an Atata hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Āpāpa hell constitute one lifespan in the Huhuva hell;
twenty lifespans in the Huhuva hell constitute one lifespan in the Utpala hell;
twenty lifespans in the Utpala hell constitute one lifespan in the Puṇḍarīka hell.
The lifespan in the Puṇḍarīka Hell is equal to one lifetime in the Mahāpadma Hell.
Kokālika has fallen into this Mahāpadma Hell; his great tongue is extended and pinned with a hundred nails, and five hundred plows furrow it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When a person is born, an axe is in their mouth;
That which cuts their own body arises from their evil words."
One should praise those who deserve rebuke, and rebuke those who deserve praise;
with mouths that accumulate all manner of evils, one shall never see happiness!
When the karma of mind and speech produces evil, one falls into the Nirarbuda hell.
For a full hundred thousand lifetimes, one shall undergo various poisonous sufferings.
If born in the Arbuda hell, for a full thirty-six [lifetimes],
and for another five lifetimes besides, one shall experience all manner of bitter poisons and pain.
"When the mind relies on wrong views and destroys the words of the noble ones,
it is like a bamboo that destroys its own form by producing fruit.
Such mental states of doubt and slander eventually lead to certainty, which is likewise false speech.
A person who speaks falsely will not even believe or accept the words of the Buddha, and their retribution for such sin is as described!
For this reason, one should not speak falsely.
Furthermore, consider the Buddha’s son Rāhula; though he was young in years, he did not yet know how to guard his speech.
Someone came and asked him,
"Is the World-Honored One here?
He spoke deceptively, saying:
"He is not present. When he was absent, people asked Rāhula,
"Is the World-Honored One here?"
He spoke deceptively, saying,
"The Buddha is here.
Someone then informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"Fetch water with this basin and wash my feet!
Having washed his feet, he said to Rāhula:
"Cover this basin!
As commanded, it was immediately covered.
The Buddha said:
"Pour water into it!
Having poured it, he asked:
"Did the water enter inside?"
He replied, "I have not entered.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"Those who lack a sense of shame and dread, whose minds are shrouded by false speech, and into whom the path of the Dharma does not enter, are just like this!
As the Buddha said:
"False speech has ten faults; what are these ten?"
First, the breath from the mouth is foul;
second, benevolent deities distance themselves while non-human spirits find an opportunity to cause harm;
third, although one speaks words of truth, people do not believe or accept them.
Fourth, they do not participate in the deliberations of wise men;
fifth, they are constantly slandered, and their foul reputation spreads throughout the world;
sixth, they are not respected by others, and even when they issue instructions, people do not accept or follow them.
Seventh, they will constantly experience much sorrow and anxiety;
eighth, they will plant the causes and conditions for the karma of slander;
ninth, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall fall into hell.
Tenth, if one is reborn as a human being, one will frequently be subjected to slander.
To refrain from such various actions is non-false speech; this is called the virtuous restraint of speech.
Regarding those who do not drink alcohol, there are three kinds of alcohol:
first, grain-based alcohol; second, fruit-based alcohol; and third, herb-based alcohol.
As for fruit-based alcohol, it refers to various types such as grape wine and wine made from the fruits of the *ariṣṭa* tree; these and others like them are called fruit-based alcohol.
As for medicinal herb wine, various medicinal herbs are blended with rice malt and sugarcane juice, which can be transformed into wine;
likewise, the milk of cloven-hoofed animals, provided it is all warm, may be used to make wine.
Briefly stated, whether dry or moist, clear or turbid—anything of this kind that can cause the human mind to become agitated and negligent is called alcohol.
"One should not drink anything [that is intoxicating]; this is called 'abstaining from liquor. Question:
"Liquor can dispel cold, benefit the body, and cause the mind to rejoice; why, then, should one not drink it?"
The answer is:
It benefits the body very little, but the harm it causes is very great; therefore, one should not drink it.
For example, it is like a delicious beverage mixed with poison. What kind of poison is it?
As the Buddha said to the lay follower Nandika:
"There are thirty-five faults of alcohol.
What are these thirty-five?"
First, one's wealth and possessions will be exhausted in this present life; why is this?
Because when a person is intoxicated by drinking alcohol, their mind lacks restraint and they spend without moderation.
Second, it is the gateway to manifold illnesses.
Third, it is the root of strife and contention;
fourth, it is nakedness and shamelessness;
fifth, it is an ugly reputation and ill repute, such that one is not respected by others.
Sixth, wisdom is obscured and submerged;
seventh, one fails to obtain what ought to be obtained and loses what has already been obtained;
eighth, one reveals all secret matters to others.
Ninth, various undertakings are abandoned and left unaccomplished;
tenth, intoxication is the root of sorrow. Why is this?
Because many errors are committed in a state of intoxication, and upon sobering up, one feels shame and distress.
Eleventh, physical strength diminishes;
twelfth, the complexion of the body deteriorates;
thirteenth, one no longer knows how to respect one's father.
Fourteenth, not knowing how to revere one's mother;
fifteenth, not revering śramaṇas;
sixteenth, not revering brāhmaṇas.
Seventeenth, they do not show respect to paternal uncles, elders, or those of superior rank; why is this?
Because they are intoxicated, dazed, and bewildered, lacking the capacity for discernment.
Eighteenth, they do not revere the Buddha.
Nineteenth, not revering the Dharma;
twentieth, not revering the Saṃgha;
twenty-first, forming factions with evil people.
Twenty-second, they distance themselves from the virtuous and good;
twenty-third, they act as those who have broken the precepts;
twenty-fourth, they lack a sense of shame and a dread of blame.
Twenty-fifth, failing to guard the six sense faculties;
twenty-sixth, indulging in sensual pleasures and being negligent;
twenty-seventh, being loathed by others and not being welcomed when seen.
Twenty-eighth, he is collectively cast out by his own kinsmen and all his acquaintances;
twenty-ninth, he practices unwholesome dharmas;
thirtieth, he abandons wholesome dharmas.
Thirty-first, one will not be trusted or relied upon by wise men and sagacious scholars; why is this?
Because of the dissipation caused by alcohol.
Thirty-second, one will be far removed from nirvana.
Thirty-third, they plant the causes and conditions for madness and delusion;
thirty-fourth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they fall into the evil realms within the hells;
thirty-fifth, even if they obtain human birth, in whatever place they are born, they shall always be insane and foolish.
Because there are various faults such as these, one does not drink.
As a verse says:
"Alcohol destroys the faculty of discernment; the complexion of the body becomes turbid and foul."
When the mind of wisdom stirs and becomes disturbed, shame and remorse are plundered away.
Losing mindfulness increases the heart of anger, and losing joy ruins one's kin.
Though such a thing is called "drinking," it is in truth drinking the poison of death.
One should not be angry when one ought not to be angry; one should not laugh when one ought not to laugh;
one should not weep when one ought not to weep; one should not strike when one ought not to strike;
one should not speak when one ought not to speak—such a person is no different from a madman.
"It robs one of all wholesome merits; those who possess a sense of shame do not drink.
Thus, refraining from these four transgressions constitutes the virtuous restraint of the body;
refraining from false speech constitutes the virtuous restraint of speech.
This is called the lay follower’s (upāsaka) discipline of the five precepts. Question:
If the eightfold discipline and pure livelihood are what constitute "precept" (śīla), [then why is this alone so designated]?
Why is it that for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), within the restraint of speech, there are not three types of restraint nor pure livelihood?
The answer is:

Laypeople living at home enjoy worldly pleasures while simultaneously cultivating merit; they cannot fully practice the entirety of the precepts. For this reason, the Buddha commanded them to observe the five precepts.
Furthermore, among the four types of verbal karma, false speech is the most grave.
Moreover, false speech arises from a deliberate intention of the mind;
the others may be either intentional or unintentional.
Furthermore, by merely mentioning false speech, three matters are already subsumed.
Furthermore, among all wholesome dharmas, truth is the greatest;
if one speaks truthful words, all four kinds of right speech are thereby fully encompassed.

Furthermore, when laypeople live in the world, they must attend to official duties, manage affairs, and labor for their households; therefore, it is difficult for them to maintain the precept of refraining from harsh speech.
As for lying, because it is done intentionally and its consequences are grave, one should not commit it.
These five precepts have five ways of receiving them, which are called the five types of upāsakas:

first, the upāsaka who practices one part; second, the upāsaka who practices a small portion; third, the upāsaka who practices a large portion; fourth, the upāsaka who practices in full; and fifth, the upāsaka who has abandoned sexual misconduct.
A practitioner of one part receives one precept among the five precepts and is unable to receive and maintain the other four;
a practitioner of few parts receives either two or three precepts;
a practitioner of many parts receives four precepts.
One who fulfills the practice observes all five precepts;
one who renounces sexual misconduct, having received the five precepts, further makes a self-vow before the teacher:
"I shall no longer engage in sexual conduct even with my own wife."
These are called the five precepts.
As the Buddha said in verse:
“Not killing, nor stealing, Nor engaging in sexual misconduct.”
Speaking truthful words, abstaining from intoxicants, And maintaining a pure mind through right livelihood—
Whoever can practice these things will have the anxieties and fears of both worlds removed.
The merit of their precepts will constantly follow them, And they shall always dwell together with devas and humans.
The flowers that bloom during the six seasons of the world manifest their radiant colors and forms;
yet these flowers of a single year are fully present in a single day in heaven.
Trees there grow spontaneously, bearing flower garlands and jeweled necklaces.
Crimson blossoms shine like lamps, their myriad colors intermingled.
Celestial robes are beyond counting, in various hues;
brilliant white reflects the light of heaven and sun, light yet dense, without gaps or seams.
Golden hues reflect upon embroidered patterns, shimmering like drifting clouds;
such garments of supreme excellence all emerge from the celestial trees.
Bright pearls adorn heavenly earrings, while precious gems illuminate their hands and feet.
According to whatever the heart desires and loves, these also emerge from the celestial trees.
With golden blossoms and lapis lazuli stalks, and diamond filaments for their stamens, they are soft, fragrant, and sweetly scented; all of them emerge from the jeweled ponds.
Lutes, harps, zithers, and lutes adorned with the seven treasures—
because these instruments are exquisite, their sounds are clear— and all of them likewise emerge from the trees.
The pārijāta tree is the king among the trees of the heavens.
In that Garden of Joy, there is nothing to compare with it.
Taking up the precepts is like tilling a field; from within it emerge the celestial trees.
From the celestial kitchens come the flavor of ambrosia, providing food and drink to dispel hunger and thirst.
The celestial maidens have no obstruction, nor do they suffer the hardships of pregnancy;
they enjoy playful and unrestrained delight, and their food brings no trouble of excrement or urine.
By maintaining the precepts and constantly restraining the mind, one attains birth in the Land of Self-Indulgence.
Without affairs and without difficulties, one’s will is always free to enjoy delight.
The devas attain sovereignty; sorrow and suffering no longer arise.
Whatever they desire arrives as soon as it is thought of, and the light from their bodies illuminates the darkness.
"Such various pleasures as these all arise from giving and ethical discipline.
If you wish to obtain this retribution, you should diligently exert yourself! He asked:
Now, while it is taught that one shall attain Buddhahood through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), for what reason is celestial merit praised?
The answer is:
The Buddha stated that these three matters will inevitably yield their fruits of retribution, and they are not in vain.
Through giving one attains great wealth; through upholding the precepts one is born in a favorable realm; and through cultivating meditative concentration one attains liberation.
If one practices ethical discipline (*śīla*) alone, one will be born in a favorable realm;
if one cultivates meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion in combination, one attains the paths of the Three Vehicles.
Now, I merely praise the merits of upholding the precepts in the present life—namely, renown and peace—as well as the rewards to be obtained in future lives, as extolled in the verses.
It is like a small child who, having been coated with honey over bitter medicine, is then able to take it;
likewise, by first praising the blessings of the precepts, people are subsequently able to uphold them.

Having been able to maintain the precepts, one establishes great vows and attains the path of Buddhahood—this is how ethical discipline (*śīla*) gives rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, all people are attached to pleasure, and among worldly pleasures, those of the heavens are supreme.
If one hears of the various pleasures in the heavens, one is able to receive and practice the *śīla*;
later, hearing that the heavens are impermanent, a sense of weary detachment arises, enabling one to seek liberation;
furthermore, hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable merits, if a mind of compassion arises, one will reach the path of Buddhahood by relying on the *śīlapāramitā*.
For this reason, there is no fault in speaking of the retribution for śīla.
Question:
For laypeople living at home, is there only these five precepts, or are there other dharmas as well?
The answer is:
There is the one-day precept; if one observes it on the six fasting days, the merit is immeasurable.
If one receives and maintains this precept from the first to the fifteenth day of each of the twelve months, its blessings are exceedingly great.
Question:
How does one receive the one-day precepts? Answer:
The method for receiving the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) is as follows: kneeling with palms joined, one should speak thus:
"I, [name], for one day and one night, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha!"
"Thus for the second time, thus for the third time, I take refuge.
I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, have completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha."
Having thus taken refuge for the second and third time:
"I, [Name], through greed, hatred, and delusion, have committed unwholesome actions of body, unwholesome actions of speech, and unwholesome actions of mind."
Whether in this life or in past lives, whatever such transgressions have occurred, I now sincerely repent them.
With body pure, speech pure, and mind pure, one receives and practices the eight precepts; this is the *poṣadha*, which in the language of Qin means "dwelling together."
"Just as all Buddhas refrain from taking life for the duration of their lives, so too shall I, [Name], refrain from taking life for one day and one night;
just as all Buddhas refrain from stealing for the duration of their lives, so too shall I, [Name], refrain from stealing for one day and one night;
just as all Buddhas refrain from sexual misconduct for the duration of their lives, so too shall I, [Name], refrain from sexual misconduct for one day and one night."
Just as all Buddhas refrain from false speech for the duration of their lives, so too do I, [name], refrain from false speech for one day and one night;
just as all Buddhas refrain from drinking intoxicants for the duration of their lives, so too do I, [name], refrain from drinking intoxicants for one day and one night;
just as all Buddhas refrain from sitting on high or large beds for the duration of their lives, so too do I, [name], refrain from sitting on high or large beds for one day and one night.

Just as all Buddhas throughout their lives do not wear flower garlands, do not anoint their bodies with perfumes, and do not wear garments scented with incense, so too shall I, [name], for one day and one night, not wear flower garlands, not anoint my body with perfumes, and not wear garments scented with incense;

just as all Buddhas throughout their lives do not personally sing, dance, or perform music, nor go to watch or listen to them, so too shall I, [name], for one day and one night, not personally sing, dance, or perform music, nor go to watch or listen to them.
Having received the eight precepts, just as all Buddhas throughout their lives did not eat past midday, so too shall I, [Name], for one day and one night, not eat past midday.
"I, [Name], receive and practice the eight precepts, following and learning the teachings of all Buddhas; this is called the *poṣadha*.
By means of the merit and reward of this *poṣadha*, I pray that in every birth I shall not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions."
I do not seek the pleasures of the world of a Cakravartin king, nor of Brahmā, nor of Śakra;
I vow that all afflictions shall be exhausted, that I shall attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and realize the path of the Buddha.
Question: How does one receive the five precepts? Answer:
Regarding the method for receiving the five precepts: kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms, saying:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Sangha!
Do this a second and a third time.
“I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
“I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of the Buddha Śākyamuni; may you bear witness that I, [Name], from this day forth for as long as life lasts, take refuge.”
The preceptor should say:
"Listen, you upāsaka!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who knows men and perceives men—has proclaimed these five precepts for upāsakas; you shall observe them for as long as you live!"
"What are the five?
'To refrain from killing living beings for as long as life lasts is a precept of an upāsaka; herein, for as long as life lasts, one should not intentionally kill living beings.
If you are able to do this, you should say, 'I agree.'"
"Throughout one's life, not stealing is a lay follower’s precept; herein, throughout one's life, one should not steal.
If you can do this, you should say 'Yes.
Throughout one's life, not engaging in sexual misconduct is a lay follower’s precept; herein, throughout one's life, one should not engage in sexual misconduct."
"If you are able to do this, you should say 'yes.
To refrain from false speech for as long as life lasts is a precept of an upāsaka; regarding this, one should not speak falsely for as long as life lasts.
If you are able to do this, you should say 'yes.'"
"To abstain from drinking alcohol for as long as life lasts is a precept of the upāsaka;
regarding this matter of abstaining from drinking alcohol for as long as life lasts, if you are able to do so, you should say 'Yes'."
"These five precepts of an upāsaka are to be observed for as long as life lasts.
