You should make offerings to the Three Jewels—
the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Bhikṣu Saṃgha Jewel— and diligently cultivate meritorious deeds in order to seek the path of the Buddha!"
Question: For what reason does one observe the eight precepts and cultivate merit on the six fasting days? Answer:
On this day, evil spirits pursue people, seeking to snatch away their lives; they cause diseases and misfortunes, bringing ill fortune upon men.
For this reason, at the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught people to observe the fast, cultivate goodness, and perform meritorious deeds in order to avoid such calamities.
At that time, the method for the fast did not involve receiving the eight precepts; rather, one simply observed the fast by abstaining from food for a single day.
Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he taught them, saying:
"You should observe the eight precepts for one day and one night, just as all Buddhas do, refraining from eating after midday. This merit will lead people to Nirvana."
As the Buddha said in the *Cāturmahārājakāyika Sūtra*:

On the six days of the fast, the messengers, the princes, and the Four Heavenly Kings descend in person to observe sentient beings. If those who practice giving, maintain the precepts, and are filial toward their parents are few, they then ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inform Śakra;
Śakra and the hearts of all the gods are then displeased, saying:
"The race of asuras is numerous, while the race of devas is few.
If there are many who practice generosity, uphold the precepts, and are filial toward their parents, the hearts of all the devas and Śakra will rejoice, and they will say:
"The hosts of devas shall increase, and the asuras shall diminish."
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, seeing the joy of the devas,
spoke this verse:
"In the month of the sixfold supernormal powers, One upholds the pure precepts."
"When this person’s life comes to an end, their merit will surely be like mine!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Śakra Devānām Indra should not have spoken such a verse."

Why is this? Śakra Devānām-Indra has not yet eliminated the three decays or the three poisons; how could he falsely claim that by observing the one-day precepts, his merit and karmic reward will surely equal mine?
"If one upholds these precepts, one will surely be like the Buddha; this is the true teaching.
Because of this cause and condition for joy, the great and honored devas shall obtain an increase in merit.

Furthermore, on these six days of fasting, evil spirits harm people and disturb all beings. In whatever villages, districts, counties, states, or towns there may be, if there are those who observe the fasts, receive the precepts, and practice goodness, by virtue of this cause and condition, the evil spirits will depart from afar, and their dwelling places will be peaceful and secure.
For this reason, observing the fast and receiving the precepts on these six days results in an increase of merit.
Question:
For what reason do the various classes of evil ghosts and spirits afflict and harm people on these six days?
The answer is:

The *Sūtra on the Original Arising of Heaven and Earth* states that at the time when the kalpa first began to form, there was a son of a Brahmā-deva king who was the father of various spirits. He practiced the ascetic austerities of a brahmacārin for twelve celestial years; during six days of this period, he cut his own flesh and drew his blood to cast them into the fire.
For this reason, malevolent spirits and ghosts suddenly gain power on these six days.
A question is asked:
Why do the fathers of these spirits cut their own flesh and blood and cast them into the fire on these six days?
Answer: Among all the deities, Maheśvara is the greatest and foremost; each deity has its own allotted day.
Maheśvara has four allotted days within a single month.
The eighth, the twenty-third, the fourteenth, and the twenty-ninth.
The remaining deities have two days each month:
the first and the sixteenth of the month; the second and the seventeenth of the month.
The fifteenth and thirtieth days belong to all the deities.
Since Maheśvara is the lord of all the deities and also possesses many days, these four days are counted as days of fasting;
the two days belonging to all the deities are likewise counted as days of fasting.
For this reason, the various ghosts and spirits always possess power and influence on these six days.
Furthermore, the fathers of these ghosts and spirits would, on these six days, cut their own flesh and draw their blood to place it into the fire;
after twelve years had passed, the Heavenly Kings would descend and say to their sons:
"What wish do you seek?
He replied,
"I seek to have a son!"
The Heavenly King said:
"The method of making offerings to a rishi consists of burning incense, sweet fruits, and various pure things;
why do you cast meat and blood into the fire as if it were a sinful practice?"
"You have destroyed wholesome dharmas and delighted in committing evil deeds; therefore, you shall give birth to evil sons who eat flesh and drink blood.
As these words were spoken, eight great ghosts emerged from within the fire; their bodies were black as ink, their hair was yellow, and their eyes were red, emitting a great radiance.
All ghosts and spirits are born from these eight ghosts.
For this reason, during these six days, one gains power by cutting flesh from one's own body and placing blood into the fire.
In the Buddha-dharma, days have neither good nor evil; however, due to worldly conditions regarding "evil days," one is taught to observe the fast and receive the eight precepts.
Question:
Between the five precepts and the one-day precepts, which is superior?
Answer: Due to specific causes and conditions, the two sets of precepts are equal;
however, the five precepts are observed for a lifetime, whereas the eight precepts are observed for one day.
Furthermore, in the case of the five precepts, the time is long while the precepts are few;
in the case of the one-day precepts, the time is short while the precepts are many.
Moreover, if one lacks the great resolve, even if they maintain the precepts for their entire life, it is not equal to a person with the great resolve who maintains them for a single day.
For example, if a weakling serves as a general, even if he leads troops for his entire life, his lack of wisdom and courage will ensure that he ultimately achieves no fame or merit;
whereas if one is like a hero who exerts himself with vigor, the calamity and chaos are settled at once, and the merit of a single day’s achievement covers all under heaven.
These two kinds of precepts are called the dharma for lay upāsakas.
There are four types of observance of the precepts by those living at home:
the inferior, the middling, the superior, and the most superior.
Inferior persons observe the precepts for the sake of happiness in this life;
or out of fear; or for the sake of praise and reputation;
or as a matter of family tradition, in order to comply with the wishes of others.
Or, because they seek to avoid forced labor and escape perilous difficulties—such various motivations as these constitute the observance of precepts by those of inferior capacity.
As for those of middling capacity who observe the precepts, they do so for the sake of wealth, honor, and pleasurable satisfaction within human life;

or they look forward to the blessings and joys of future lives, disciplining themselves and exerting effort with the thought that "the days of hardship will be few, yet what is gained will be very great. Reflecting in this way, they firmly uphold the precepts.
For example, just as a merchant who travels far and penetrates deep will surely gain great profit;
so too is the merit of observing the precepts, which causes a person to receive happiness and blessings in future lives.

The superior person upholds the precepts for the sake of nirvana, because they know that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, and because they desire to seek liberation from suffering and attain the permanence, bliss, and unconditioned state.

Furthermore, for one who upholds the precepts, the mind is free from regret; because the mind is free from regret, one attains joy and happiness; because one attains joy and happiness, one attains single-mindedness; because one attains single-mindedness, one attains true wisdom; because one attains true wisdom, one attains a mind of disenchantment; because one attains a mind of disenchantment, one attains detachment from desire; because one attains detachment from desire, one attains liberation; because one attains liberation, one attains nirvana—thus, the observance of the precepts is the root of all wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, the observance of the precepts (*śīla*) constitutes the initial gateway to the Eightfold Noble Path; entering this initial gateway to the Path inevitably leads to *nirvāṇa*. **Chapter 23:
Praising the Meaning of the Śīlapāramitā** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the First Chapter, Part Two: Praising the Meaning of the Śīlapāramitā. Question:

In the Eightfold Noble Path, Right Speech and Right Action are situated in the middle, while Right View and Right Resolve are at the beginning. Why, then, is it said here that "the precepts are the initial gateway to the Eightfold Noble Path"?
Answer: Speaking in terms of numerical order, the greatest is placed first;
since right view is the greatest, it is therefore situated at the beginning.
Furthermore, because one practices the Path, vision comes first;
because all dharmas follow a sequential order, the precepts come first.
It is like building a house: although the ridgepole and beams are large, the ground comes first.
The precepts observed by the supreme among supreme persons are for the sake of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of the Buddha-way;

because they understand all phenomena and seek the true mark, they do not fear the evil realms and do not seek personal pleasure—such various qualities constitute the observance of precepts by the supreme among supreme persons.
These four are collectively termed the Upāsaka precepts.
There are likewise four types of monastic precepts:
first, the precepts for śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs; second, the precepts for śikṣamāṇās; third, the precepts for bhikṣuṇīs; and fourth, the precepts for the bhikṣu saṃgha.
Question:

If the precepts for laypeople can lead to rebirth in the heavens, the attainment of the bodhisattva path, and even the reaching of nirvana, what further use is there for the precepts for those who have left the household life?
The answer is:
Although both may attain liberation, there is a difference between difficulty and ease.
For one living as a householder, there are various affairs regarding livelihood; if one wishes to devote oneself single-mindedly to the Dharma, household affairs will be neglected.
If one desires to focus exclusively on domestic affairs, spiritual practice will be neglected;
to neither grasp nor reject, yet act in accordance with the Dharma, is what is called difficult.
If one leaves the household life and departs from the secular world, severing all disturbances and focusing the mind single-mindedly to practice the Way, it is easy.

Furthermore, living as a householder is a state of clamor and bustle, abounding in affairs and duties; it is the root of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the repository of manifold evils—this is extremely difficult.

If one leaves the home life, it is like a person who goes out into a desolate wilderness where no one dwells and unifies their mind; being without thought or deliberation, internal perceptions are eliminated and external matters likewise depart.
As a verse says:
"Sitting in seclusion among the forest trees, Tranquil, extinguishing all evils;
Attaining single-mindedness through serenity— This joy is not the joy of the heavens."
People seek wealth, status, profit, Famous robes, and fine bedding;
Yet such pleasures are not secure, For there is no satiety in seeking gain.
Wearing patched robes and begging for food, One’s mind remains ever one-pointed in every movement and stillness.
With the eye of wisdom, he observes and knows the reality of all phenomena.
Amidst the various gateways of the Dharma, he enters them all through equal contemplation;
his mind of understanding and wisdom is tranquil, such that none within the three realms can equal it!
For this reason, one knows that for those who have left the household life, practicing the precepts and cultivating the Path is easy.
Furthermore, by leaving the household life and practicing the precepts, one attains immeasurable wholesome discipline (śīla-saṃvara), which is entirely complete and perfect.
For this reason, laypeople and others should leave the household life and receive full ordination.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, the way of leaving the household life is the most difficult to practice.
Just as when the brahmin Jambukhādaka asked Śāriputra,
"What is most difficult within the Buddha's Dharma?
Śāriputra replied:
“Leaving the household life is difficult!
He asked again,
“In what way is leaving the household life difficult?”
He replied,
“For one who has left the household life, it is difficult to find delight in the Dharma.
[The other asked,] “Once one has attained delight in the Dharma, what else is difficult?”
“It is difficult to cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, one should go forth from the household life.
Furthermore, when a person goes forth, the King Māra becomes alarmed and distressed, saying:
"This person’s fetters and latent tendencies are thin; they will certainly attain nirvana and shall be counted among the ranks of the Sangha Jewel.

Furthermore, in the Buddha-dharma, even those who have left the household life may break the precepts and fall into transgression, yet once their retribution for those sins is exhausted, they shall attain liberation.
As it is said in the *Utpalavarṇā Bhikṣuṇī Jātaka Sūtra*:
"During the time of the Buddha's presence in the world, this bhikṣuṇī attained the six supernormal powers and became an arhat."
When entering the residences of nobles, he always praised the way of renunciation, saying to the noblewomen:
"Sisters, you should leave the household life!
To which the noblewomen replied:
"We are young and our physical appearance is in its prime; it is difficult to maintain the precepts, and we might break them!
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Just go forth; if you break the precepts, then break them."
He asked, "If one who breaks the precepts shall fall into hell, how can they be broken?
He replied:
"Fall into hell! Fall right now!
The noble women laughed at him and said, "How can one fall into hell?
One must undergo punishment there."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I recall from my past lives that when I was a female entertainer, I wore various kinds of clothing and spoke old stories; at times, I even wore the robes of a bhikṣuṇī for the sake of amusement."
For these reasons, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, she was a bhikṣuṇī who, relying on her noble lineage and physical beauty, gave rise to arrogance and violated the prohibitions;
due to the sin of breaking the precepts, she fell into hell and underwent various sufferings.
When his retribution for his offenses was finally exhausted, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha, left the household life, and attained the path of an Arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers.

For this reason, one knows that although one may break the precepts after leaving home and receiving ordination, by virtue of the causal conditions of those precepts, one attains the path of an Arhat;
however, if one merely commits evil deeds without the causal conditions of the precepts, one will not attain the Path.
In the past, throughout successive lifetimes, I fell into hell; having emerged from hell, I became an evil person; when that evil person died, I returned to hell once more, gaining nothing at all.
"Now, by this evidence, one should know that although a renunciant who has received the precepts may break them, through these causes and conditions, they can still attain the fruits of the Path.
Furthermore, it was as when the Buddha was at the Jetavana; a certain intoxicated brahmin came to the Buddha's dwelling and requested to become a bhikṣu.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to shave his head and clothe him in dharma robes.
Once he had sobered from his drunkenness, he was startled and amazed to find that his body had suddenly become that of a bhikṣu, and he immediately ran away.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
"Why did you allow this intoxicated brāhmaṇa to become a bhikṣu?
The Buddha said:

"This Brahmin has had no intention of leaving the household life throughout immeasurable kalpas; now, because of his intoxication, he has briefly given rise to a faint aspiration. By reason of these causes and conditions, he shall later leave the household life and attain the Way."
Through such various causes and conditions, the benefits of leaving the household life and its merits are immeasurable.
For this reason, although a layperson may observe the five precepts, they do not equal those who have left the household life.
There are four types of this monastic discipline:
śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, śikṣamāṇā, bhikṣuṇī, and bhikṣu.
What is the method for the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs to go forth and receive the precepts?
When a layperson comes seeking to leave the household life, they should seek two teachers:
one preceptor (upādhyāya) and one instructor (ācārya).
The preceptor is like a father, and the instructor is like a mother.
Having abandoned one's biological parents, one should seek the parents of the renunciant life.
Donning the *kāṣāya* and shaving off hair and beard, one should take hold of both hands with both hands and grasp the feet of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Why does he grasp [the teacher’s] feet?
In the Indian tradition, grasping the feet is considered the foremost form of respectful offering.
The ācārya should instruct him in the ten precepts according to the ritual for receiving the precepts.
The śrāmaṇerikā is also like this, except that she takes a bhikṣuṇī as her preceptor (upādhyāyikā).
The śikṣamāṇā undergoes the six rules for two years.
It was asked:
In the case of the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras, one immediately receives the full ordination (upasaṃpadā);
why is it that within the dharma for bhikṣuṇīs, there is the stage of śikṣamāṇā before one may receive the full ordination?
The answer is:
During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was the wife of an elder who, unaware that she was pregnant, left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Later, as her body grew large and became visible, the other elders criticized and disparaged the bhikṣus.
For this reason, it was established that there is a two-year period of training in the precepts; one must receive the six rules before receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
A question is asked:
"If it is for the sake of avoiding censure, would the *śikṣamāṇā* not also incur censure?"
The answer is:
A śikṣamāṇā has not yet received full ordination; she is like a small child or a servant, so that even though she may have faults or impurities, people do not criticize or find her offensive.
This is called the śikṣamāṇā’s undertaking of the six rules.
There are two kinds of śikṣamāṇās:
first, those who are eighteen-year-old maidens undertaking the six rules; [the second being those who have previously been married].
Second, after ten years in her husband's family, she may receive the six rules of training.

If she wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), she must do so before the two assemblies of monks and nuns; she shall use five robes and an alms bowl, with a bhikṣuṇī serving as the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*) and the instructor (*ācāryā*), and a bhikṣu serving as the preceptor for the precepts (*karmakāraka*). The remainder is according to the ritual for receiving the precepts.
Briefly stated, there are five hundred precepts; extensively stated, there are eighty thousand precepts.
Upon the completion of the third *karmavācanā*, one immediately attains immeasurable restraint and becomes a fully ordained *bhikṣuṇī*.
The bhikṣu possesses the three robes and the alms bowl; with the three masters and the ten-member saṃgha, he undergoes the procedure according to the dharma for receiving the precepts.
Briefly stated, there are two hundred and fifty rules; explained in detail, they number eighty thousand.
When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, one immediately attains the dharma of immeasurable restraint (*saṃvara*).
This is collectively termed "precept" (*śīla*); this is what constitutes *śīla*.
(Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll 13)
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the First Chapter, Part Two:
The Meaning of Śīlapāramitā, Fascicle Fourteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. Question:
The characteristics of śīla have already been understood; what constitutes the perfection of śīla (śīlapāramitā)?
Answer: Some say that when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts, they would rather lose their own life than violate even a minor precept; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
As stated in the *Sutasoma-jātaka*, one should not spare even one's own body or life in order to preserve the precepts.
For instance, when the Bodhisattva was in a previous existence, he once became a powerful venomous dragon.
If sentient beings were in front of him, those with weak physical strength would die upon seeing his eyes,
while those with strong physical strength would die from the mere approach of his breath.
This dragon had received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) and, seeking tranquility, had gone out from home to meditate among the trees and forests.
After sitting for a long time, he grew weary and fell asleep.
According to the nature of dragons, when they sleep their form resembles that of a snake, with patterns upon their bodies in the various colors of the seven treasures.
When the hunter saw this, he was filled with joy and surprise, saying:
"It would be most fitting to offer this rare and hard-to-find skin to the King as a garment.
Having said this, he pressed down on its head with a staff and began to flay its skin with a knife.
The dragon thought to himself:
"My power is as I wish; to overturn this country would be as easy as turning over the palm of my hand.
This person is but a minor thing; how could he possibly trouble me?"
"Now, because I uphold the precepts, I shall not regard this body; I must follow the Buddha's word!
Thereupon, he endured it himself, closing his eyes and not looking, holding his breath and not exhaling;
out of compassion for this man and for the sake of upholding the precepts, he single-mindedly received the flaying without giving rise to a thought of regret.
Having already lost its skin, with raw flesh exposed upon the ground, and as the sun was scorching hot, it wallowed in the dust;
wishing to go toward the great waters, it saw various small insects coming to devour its body, yet for the sake of upholding the precepts, it did not dare to move again.
He thought to himself:
"Now I give this body of mine to these insects for the sake of the Buddha-way; by giving my flesh now, I satisfy their bodies;
when I later attain Buddhahood, I shall give the Dharma to benefit their minds."
Having made this vow, his body withered and his life ended, and he was immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the venomous dragon was Śākyamuni Buddha;
the hunter at that time was Devadatta and the other six teachers.
Those various small insects were the eighty thousand devas who attained the Way when Śākyamuni Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
That a bodhisattva guards the precepts, not begrudging body or life, and remains resolute without regret—such is the matter; this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts for the sake of the Buddha-way, they make a great solemn vow: "I must deliver all sentient beings!

They do not seek the pleasures of this life or future lives, nor do they act for the sake of fame, reputation, or the mere appearance of the Dharma; nor do they seek nirvana for themselves prematurely. Rather, because sentient beings are submerged in the long-flowing current, deceived by affection and deluded by ignorance, [the bodhisattva thinks]: "I shall deliver them and cause them to reach the other shore."

To maintain the precepts with a single mind is for the sake of being born in a good realm; because one is born in a good realm, one encounters virtuous people; because one encounters virtuous people, wisdom arises; because wisdom arises, one is able to practice the six pāramitās; and because one practices the six pāramitās, one attains the Way of the Buddha.
Maintaining the precepts in this manner is called the Śīla-pāramitā.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts with a mind that delights in goodness and purity—not out of fear of the evil realms, nor for the sake of rebirth in heaven, but seeking only goodness and purity—he perfumes his mind with the precepts, causing the mind to delight in goodness; this is the Śīla-pāramitā.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts with a mind of great compassion and thereby attains the path of Buddhahood, this is called śīlapāramitā.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts such that they can give rise to the six pāramitās, this is likewise named śīlapāramitā.
How does the observance of precepts give rise to further precepts? By means of the five precepts one obtains the śrāmaṇera precepts;

by means of the śrāmaṇera precepts one obtains the prātimokṣa-saṃvara precepts; by means of the prātimokṣa-saṃvara precepts one obtains the dhyāna-saṃvara precepts; and by means of the dhyāna-saṃvara precepts one obtains the anāsrava (outflow-free) precepts. This is what is meant by "precepts giving rise to precepts."
How can the observance of precepts give rise to generosity?
There are three kinds of generosity:
first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
Maintaining the precepts and self-restraint, not encroaching upon the wealth and property of any sentient being—this is called the giving of material wealth.
When sentient beings see this, they admire such conduct; furthermore, one preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain awakening.
Furthermore, he reflects to himself:
"I shall firmly uphold the pure precepts and serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings, enabling them to obtain immeasurable blessings."
Such various forms as these are called the gift of Dharma.
All sentient beings fear death; to uphold the precepts and refrain from harming them is the gift of fearlessness.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects to himself:

"I shall uphold the precepts; by the retribution of these precepts, I will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King for the sake of all sentient beings, or a king of Jambudvīpa, or a celestial king, so as to satisfy sentient beings with wealth and leave them without lack or deficiency.

Thereafter, I will sit beneath the Bodhi tree, subdue the Māra King, destroy the armies of Māra, and realize the Unsurpassed Way. I will then preach the pure Dharma for all sentient beings, enabling immeasurable beings to cross the ocean of old age, sickness, and death."
This is how the perfection of generosity arises from the causal condition of upholding the precepts.
How does upholding the precepts give rise to patience?
One who upholds the precepts reflects within their own mind, saying:
"I now uphold the precepts for the sake of upholding the mind.
If one upholds the precepts without patience, they shall fall into hell;
though one does not break the precepts, because of the lack of patience, one cannot escape the evil realms."
How can one give rein to anger and fail to restrain the mind?
It is solely because of the mind that one enters the three evil realms.
Therefore, you should exert yourself with diligence and zealously cultivate patience.
Furthermore, a practitioner who wishes to make the virtue of their precepts firm and strong should cultivate patience.
Why is this? Patience is a great power that can make the precepts solid and unshakable.
He further reflected to himself:
"I have now left the household life; my appearance is distinct from that of the laity. How could I allow my mind to run wild according to the ways of worldly people?
I ought to exert myself and discipline my mind through patience."
"If one attains patience through body and speech, the mind will also attain patience;
if the mind lacks patience, the body and speech will likewise do so.
Therefore, the practitioner should cause the body, speech, and mind to be patient, severing all anger and resentment.
Furthermore, these precepts, briefly stated, number eighty thousand; if stated in detail, they are immeasurable. How then can I possibly uphold this immeasurable body of precepts in their entirety?
One should simply practice patience, and all the precepts will be naturally attained.

It is like a person who has offended a king; the king places that offender upon a chariot drawn by blades, with sharp edges on all six sides so close together that there is no space between them. As the chariot gallops and rushes along, the driver does not choose the path.
If the offender can maintain his body and avoid being wounded by the blades, then he is as one who has been killed yet does not die.

It is the same for one who upholds the precepts: the precepts are like a sharp blade and forbearance is like the handle that holds it; if the mind of forbearance is not firm, the precepts will likewise wound the person.
Furthermore, it is like an elderly person walking at night: without a staff, they will stumble;
patience serves as the staff of precepts, supporting one to reach the Path, such that the causes and conditions for merit and happiness cannot be shaken.
Such various instances as these are called the arising of the *kṣānti-pāramitā* from upholding the precepts (*śīla*).
How does upholding the precepts give rise to diligence (*vīrya*)?

A person who upholds the precepts eliminates negligence and, through their own power, practices with earnest effort. They study the unsurpassed Dharma, renounce worldly pleasures, enter the path of goodness, and resolve to seek *nirvāṇa* in order to deliver all beings. With a great mind that never slackens, they take the seeking of Buddhahood as their foundation; this is how upholding the precepts can produce diligence.

Furthermore, a person who upholds the precepts becomes weary of the sufferings of the world—the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death—and gives rise to diligence in their heart, seeking certain liberation for themselves while also delivering others.
For example, it is like a jackal dwelling among the trees and forests, following after lions, tigers, leopards, and other beasts to seek their leftover meat for its own survival.

At times, when exhausted and destitute, it might scale a city wall at midnight and enter deep into a human dwelling; yet finding no meat, it falls asleep in a secluded spot and does not realize the night has ended.
In a state of panic and fear, it has no plan: if it flees, it fears it will not escape; if it stays, it dreads the agony of death.
He then composed his mind and feigned death on the ground.
When the crowd came and saw him, one person said:
"I need the ears of a jackal."
He immediately cut them off.
The jackal thought to himself:
“Though it is painful to have my ears cut off, it is better that my body remains.”
Next, another person said,
"I need a jackal’s tail," and he likewise cut it off.
The jackal thought again:
"Though the cutting off of my tail was painful, it was still a minor matter.
Then another person said:
"I must [hide] my jackal's teeth.
The jackal thought to himself:
"Those who take them are becoming more numerous; should they take my head, there will be no way for me to live."
He immediately rose from the ground, exerted his mental power, and with leaping bounds and strenuous effort, he straightway achieved his own deliverance.
The mind of a practitioner seeking liberation from suffering and hardship is also like this:
if old age arrives and one still remains complacent, unable to apply oneself with earnest resolve and diligence; [then one will likewise fail].
Illness is also like this: because there is still hope for recovery, one has not yet resolved to act;

but when death is about to arrive, knowing oneself to have no hope, one is able to exert oneself, becoming courageous and diligent, practicing great and refined diligence, and proceeding from the realm of death all the way to Nirvana.

Furthermore, the method of maintaining the precepts is like a person archery: first one must find level ground; once the ground is level, the mind becomes settled; once the mind is settled, one can draw the bow to its full extent; and once it is drawn fully, the arrow penetrates deeply.
Precepts are the level ground; concentration is the bow; drawing it full is diligence; the arrow is wisdom; and the enemy is ignorance.
If one can thus exert effort and apply diligence, one will surely reach the Great Way to deliver all sentient beings.
Furthermore, a person who upholds the precepts is able to use diligence to restrain the five faculties and not succumb to the five desires;
if the mind has already wandered away, they are able to gather it back.
This is what is meant by upholding the precepts being able to protect the sense faculties.
Guarding the sense faculties gives rise to meditative concentration; the arising of meditative concentration gives rise to wisdom; and the arising of wisdom leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way.
This is how the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) arises from upholding the precepts.
How does upholding the precepts give rise to dhyāna?
When a person performs various wholesome deeds through the three karmas—if the karma of body and speech is wholesome, the karma of mind naturally enters into wholesomeness;
it is like crooked grass growing amidst hemp: without being propped up, it straightens itself.
The power of upholding the precepts can weaken all the fetters (saṃyojana).
How can they be weakened?
If one does not uphold the precepts, when an occasion for anger arises, the intent to kill immediately takes birth.
If a sexual encounter were to occur, a lustful mind would immediately be formed.
However, for one who upholds the precepts, although there may be slight anger, no intent to kill arises;
and although there may be lustful thoughts, the sexual act is not carried out. This is what is meant by saying that upholding the precepts can cause all the fetters and afflictions to become weak.
When the fetters and latent tendencies are weakened, meditative concentration is easily attained.
It is like an old or sick person who has lost their strength; for them, death occurs easily.
Because the fetters and latent tendencies are weakened, meditative concentration is easily attained.
Furthermore, the human mind has not yet ceased its activity and constantly seeks ease and pleasure;
the practitioner who upholds the precepts abandons worldly blessings and keeps the mind from negligence. For this reason, it is easy for them to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, one who upholds the precepts is reborn among humans; next, they are reborn in the heavens of the six desire realms; next, they reach the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); and if they eliminate the perception of form, they reach the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
By maintaining pure precepts and severing all fetters (*saṃyojana*), they attain the path of an Arhat.
One who maintains the precepts with a great mind and takes pity on sentient beings is a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, precepts serve to restrain the coarse, while meditation serves to collect the subtle.
Furthermore, precepts govern body and speech, while meditation stills the distracted mind;
just as when a person wishes to ascend to the roof of a house, they cannot do so without a ladder—without the ladder of precepts, meditation likewise does not stand.
Furthermore, for one who breaks the precepts, the winds of the fetters (saṃyojana) are strong and scatter the mind;
when the mind is scattered, meditative concentration (dhyāna) cannot be attained.
For one who upholds the precepts, the winds of affliction (kleśa) are mild and the mind does not become greatly distracted; thus, meditative absorption (samādhi) is easily attained.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, upholding the precepts gives rise to the dhyāna-pāramitā.
How does upholding the precepts give rise to wisdom?
A person who upholds the precepts contemplates from where the characteristics of these precepts arise; they know that they arise from the absence of manifold transgressions.
If there were no transgressions, then there would likewise be no precepts.
Such is the nature of the precepts: they exist through causes and conditions; why, then, give rise to attachment?
It is like a lotus flower that emerges from the mud; though its color is fresh and beautiful, its place of origin is impure.
Awakening the mind through this, one does not allow attachment to arise; this is how upholding the precepts gives rise to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, a person who upholds the precepts reflects within themselves:
"If I were to regard upholding the precepts as noble and worth adopting, or breaking the precepts as base and worth abandoning, such a mind would be inconsistent with *prajñā*."
To weigh matters with wisdom such that the mind does not cling to precepts, neither grasping nor rejecting them—this is how the upholding of precepts gives rise to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, a person who does not uphold the precepts, though they may possess keen intelligence, will find their faculty of wisdom gradually dullened by worldly affairs and various pursuits for livelihood;
it is like a sharp blade used to cut mud, which consequently becomes a blunt tool.
If one leaves the household life and upholds the precepts, refrains from worldly occupations, and constantly contemplates the true mark of all phenomena as being markless,
then although one's faculties were dull at first, they will gradually become sharp.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, it is said that upholding the precepts gives rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this way, it is said that the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) gives rise to the six perfections.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva maintains the precepts not out of fear, nor out of ignorance, nor doubt, nor delusion; nor does he maintain the precepts for his own sake or for the sake of nirvana.
Rather, he does so solely for the sake of all sentient beings, for the sake of attaining the Buddha-way, and for the sake of attaining all the Buddha-dharmas.
Such characteristics are called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva cannot apprehend either transgression or non-transgression, at that time it is called the perfection of ethical discipline.
Question:
If abandoning evil and practicing good constitutes upholding the precepts, why do you say that "offense and non-offense are unattainable"? Answer:
This does not mean that one says "it cannot be found" through wrong views or a coarse mind;
rather, because one has deeply penetrated the characteristics of all phenomena, practices the samādhi of emptiness, and observes with the eye of wisdom, offenses cannot be found.
Since offenses do not exist, non-offenses likewise cannot be found.
Furthermore, because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, the sin of killing also cannot be apprehended;
because the sin cannot be apprehended, the precept also cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because there is the offense of killing, there is precept;
if there were no offense of killing, there would likewise be no precept.
Question:
If sentient beings currently exist, why do you say that "sentient beings cannot be apprehended"?
The answer is:
what is seen by the fleshly eye is not true seeing.
If one observes with the eye of wisdom, then no sentient being is apprehended.
As it was explained above in the section on giving—that there is no giver, no receiver, and no gift—this is also the same.
Furthermore, if there is a sentient being, is he the five aggregates?
Or is he apart from the five aggregates?
If he were the five aggregates, then since the five aggregates are five and the sentient being is one, [they would be distinct].
In this way, five may become one, and one may become five.
For example, if an object is traded at a market for a value of five bolts of cloth, it cannot be obtained by offering only one bolt.
Why is this? Because one cannot become five.
For this reason, we know that the five aggregates cannot constitute a single sentient being.
Furthermore, the five aggregates have the characteristic of impermanence through arising and ceasing;
as for the phenomena of sentient beings, they come from past lives and go to future lives, undergoing suffering and merit within the three realms.
If the five aggregates were the sentient being, then like grass and trees that arise and perish of themselves, there would be neither the bondage of sin nor liberation.
For this reason, we know that the five aggregates are not the sentient being.
If there were a sentient being apart from the five aggregates, this has already been refuted in the previous discussion on the permanence and omnipresence of the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, if one is apart from the five aggregates, the mind of self-view does not arise; if there were a sentient being apart from the five aggregates, this would constitute falling into the view of permanence.
If one falls into the view of permanence, then there would be neither birth nor death.
Why is this? "Birth" means that what was previously non-existent now exists; "death" means that what has already arisen then ceases.
If sentient beings were permanent, they would have to pervade all five realms of existence, having already existed eternally from the beginning; how then could they come to be born again now?
If there is no birth, then there is no death.
Question: Sentient beings certainly exist; for what reason do you say they do not?
Due to the causal conditions of the five aggregates, there is the phenomenon of a sentient being;
it is like how the phenomenon of a fist arises due to the causal conditions of the five fingers.
He replied:
This statement is incorrect!

If the dharma of a sentient being existed through the causes and conditions of the five aggregates, then apart from the five aggregates there would have to be a separate dharma of a sentient being; yet, such a thing cannot be found.

The eye itself sees forms, the ear itself hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue knows tastes, the body knows tangibles, and the mind knows dharmas—all of which are empty and devoid of a self.
Apart from these six matters, there are no further sentient beings.
Because of their inverted views, the various non-Buddhists claim that the eye seeing forms constitutes a sentient being,
and so on, up to the mind cognizing mental objects constituting a sentient being.
Furthermore, that which can recollect and experience suffering and pleasure is called a "sentient being.
To hold such a view alone is to fail to know the true nature of sentient beings.
For example, there was once a great elder bhikṣu of high virtue whom people took to be an arhat and offered much support and offerings.

Later, he died of illness; fearing that their offerings would be lost, his disciples stole him out at night and placed him in his usual sleeping quarters, arranging the covers and pillows so that it appeared as though the teacher were still there, lying down just as before.
Someone came to inquire after his illness,
asking, "Where is the Master?
His disciples replied:
“Do you not see the bedding and pillows on the bed?
The fool did not examine this closely; thinking the teacher was lying ill, he sent a great offering and departed. This happened more than once.
Furthermore, a wise man came and questioned them, and the disciples answered in the same manner.
The wise man said, "I do not ask about the pillow, the bed, or the bedding; I am seeking a person."
He searched for it by turning back his cloak, yet in the end no one could be found.
Apart from the six sense-bases, there is no self or person;
the knower and the seer are likewise thus.

Furthermore, if sentient beings exist by way of the causes and conditions of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), then since the five aggregates are impermanent, sentient beings must also be impermanent. Why is this?
Because cause and effect are similar;
if sentient beings were impermanent, they would not reach future lives.

Furthermore, if it is as you say that "sentient beings have existed constantly from the very beginning," then in that case, sentient beings should produce the five aggregates, and the five aggregates should not produce sentient beings.
Now, it is through the causal conditions of the five aggregates that the designation "sentient being" arises; those who lack wisdom pursue the name in search of a reality.
For this reason, sentient beings do not truly exist;
if there are no sentient beings, then there is also no sin of killing.
Because there is no sin of killing, there is likewise no keeping of precepts. Furthermore,
if one deeply contemplates these five aggregates and discerns them as empty— like what is seen in a dream or like an image in a mirror—
then if one were to kill what is seen in a dream or an image in a mirror, there would be no sin of killing.
The killing of sentient beings who are characterized by the emptiness of the five aggregates is likewise so.

Furthermore, if a person does not delight in transgression but is greedily attached to its absence, such a person will treat those who break the precepts with contempt when seeing them, yet love and respect those who uphold the precepts when seeing them;
to maintain the precepts in such a manner is itself a cause and condition for the arising of transgression.
For this reason it is said: "Because neither offense nor non-offense can be apprehended, one should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

24. The Meaning of the Perfection of Forbearance (kṣāntipāramitā). *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the First Chapter, Part Twenty-Four: The Meaning of the Perfection of Forbearance. [Sūtra] "Because the mind is unshakable, one should fulfill the perfection of forbearance."
[Treatise] Question:
What is meant by *kṣānti*? Answer:
Kṣānti, in the language of Qin, means "patience.
There are two kinds of patience:
patience toward living beings (sattvakṣānti) and patience toward phenomena (dharmakṣānti).
When a bodhisattva practices the patience toward sentient beings (sattvakṣānti), they attain immeasurable merit;
when they practice the patience toward phenomena (dharmakṣānti), they attain immeasurable wisdom.
Because they are fully endowed with these two things—merit and wisdom—they attain their aspirations as they have vowed.
For example, if a person has eyes and feet, they can go wherever they wish.

If a bodhisattva encounters harsh words and abuse, or is struck by knives and staves, they contemplate and understand that all phenomena are caused by the conditions of sinful and meritorious karma; that internally and externally all things are ultimately empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self; and that all phenomena are sealed with the three seals of the Dharma. Thus, although they have the power to retaliate, they do not give rise to an evil mind nor commit the karma of harsh speech.
At that time, the mental factors that arise are called "patience" (kṣānti).
Because one has attained this dharma of patience, the wisdom of patience becomes firm and stable;
it is like painted colors that adhere firmly once they have obtained glue. Some say:
“Wholesome states of mind are of two kinds:
there are the coarse and the subtle;
the coarse is called patience, and the subtle is called meditative concentration.”
When one has not yet attained the mental bliss of meditative concentration (dhyāna) but is able to restrain all evils, this is called patience (kṣānti);
when the mind has attained the bliss of meditative concentration and no longer engages in evils, this is called meditative concentration (dhyāna).
"This patience is a mental factor (caitta), associated with the mind and functioning in accordance with the mind.
It is not karma, nor is it the retribution of karma, yet it functions in accordance with karma. Some say:
"Bound by two realms.
Some say: "It is bound only by the desire realm, or it is unbound."
"In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are no external evils to be endured.
It is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), as it is attained by both ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
Because it obstructs unwholesome states (akuśaladharma) within one's own mind and the minds of others, it is called "wholesome" (kuśala).
Because they are wholesome, they are either abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned.
Such various categories are analyzed in detail in the Abhidharma.
Question:
What is called "patience toward beings" (sattvakṣānti)?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of sentient beings who come before a bodhisattva:
First, they may show respect, honor, and provide offerings; second, they may revile, scold, strike, or harm them.
At such times, the Bodhisattva is able to endure with a mind that neither craves the respect and offerings of sentient beings nor harbors anger toward those who inflict evil upon them.
This is called patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*). Question:
Why are respect and making offerings termed "patience"?
Answer: There are two kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*):
first, those belonging to the fetter of craving; second, those belonging to the fetter of aversion.
Although resentment does not arise when one shows respect and makes offerings, it causes the mind to become attached; this is called a "soft thief.
Therefore, one should exercise self-restraint toward these things, remaining neither attached nor craving.
How can one practice patience?
One contemplates that these [afflictions] are impermanent and are the source from which the fetters arise.
As the Buddha has said:
"The wound of gain and profit is deep; it is like cutting through the skin to reach the flesh, cutting through the flesh to reach the bone, and cutting through the bone to reach the marrow.

When a person is attached to gain and profit, they tear the skin of their observance of precepts, cut the flesh of their meditative concentration, break the bone of their wisdom, and lose the marrow of their subtle and wonderful virtuous mind."
It was as when the Buddha first traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were formerly brahmins.
Because they had maintained the sacrificial fires, their appearances were haggard;
because they had practiced asceticism through fasting, their bodies were emaciated and darkened.
King Śuddhodana thought to himself:

"Although my son’s attendants are pure and clean in heart, they lack physical beauty. I shall select those from families with many descendants; let one person from each family become a disciple of the Buddha."
Having reflected thus, he issued a decree throughout the kingdom:
"Select the sons and grandsons of the Śākya nobility; those whose bodies bear the marks [of a great man] shall all be ordained as monks."
At that time, Devadatta, the son of King Droṇodana, left the household life to study the Path; he recited sixty thousand dharma-aggregates and practiced with diligence for twelve full years.
Thereafter, for the sake of making offerings, he came to the Buddha’s presence and requested to learn the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Buddha told Kautama:
“If you contemplate the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as impermanent, you can attain the Way and also acquire the supernormal powers.”
Yet he did not explain to them the method for attaining supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
He went out in search of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and even approached five hundred arhats, but he did not explain it to any of them,
saying:
"You should contemplate the impermanence of the five aggregates; by this you may attain the Path and you may attain the supernormal powers.
Failing to obtain what he sought, he wept and was unhappy;
he went to Ānanda’s place to request instruction in the supernormal powers.
At that time, Ānanda had not yet attained the knowledge of others' minds; out of respect for his elder brother, he imparted the teachings exactly as the Buddha had spoken them.
Having received and studied these methods of supernormal power, Devadatta entered the mountains, and before long, he attained the five supernatural faculties.
Having attained the five supernormal powers, he thought to himself:
"Who shall act as my donor?
Then there was Prince Ajātaśatru, who possessed the marks of a great king.
Desiring to form a close bond with him, he went to the heavens to fetch celestial food;
returning to Uttarakuru, he took naturally grown non-glutinous rice;
and going to the Jambu Grove, he took jambu fruits, all of which he gave to Prince Ajātaśatru.
At times he transformed his own body into the form of a precious elephant or a precious horse to bewilder his mind;
at other times he became an infant sitting upon his knees, so that the prince would embrace him, kiss him, and spit upon him;
and from time to time he spoke his own name so that the prince might recognize him, employing all manner of transformations to stir his heart.

The prince’s mind was deluded, and within the Nāla Garden he constructed a great vihāra. He provided the fourfold offerings along with various miscellaneous offerings, leaving nothing unprepared to supply Devadatta;
every day he led his ministers in person to deliver five hundred cauldrons of soup and rice.
Devadatta received great offerings, yet his followers were few. He thought to himself:
"I possess thirty of the marks [of a Great Man], differing from the Buddha by only a few; it is simply because my disciples have not yet gathered.
If I were surrounded by a great assembly, how would I differ from the Buddha?"
Having reflected thus, he conceived the intention to schism the Saṃgha and gained five hundred disciples;
however, through the teaching and conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the Saṃgha was restored to harmony.

At that time, Devadatta conceived an evil intent and pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha; the Vajrapāṇi, using his vajra-pestle, hurled it from afar, and as the shattered fragments flew toward him, they wounded a toe of the Buddha’s foot.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā rebuked him, but he struck her with his fist; the bhikṣuṇī’s eyes immediately bulged out and she died, whereby he committed three ānantarya sins.
He became close friends with the wicked and heterodox teacher Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, severing all roots of goodness, his mind devoid of shame or remorse.
Furthermore, he placed a virulent poison under his fingernails, intending to injure the Buddha while prostrating before him;
however, before he could reach the city of Rājagṛha, the earth spontaneously split open, and a chariot of fire came to meet him, so that he entered hell alive.

Devadatta possessed thirty of the marks of a great man, yet he could not subdue his mind; for the sake of gain and offerings, he committed great transgressions and was reborn in hell while still alive.

For this reason, it is said that the wound of gain and honor is deep, piercing through the skin to reach the marrow; one should therefore eliminate the mind that craves those who offer worship and support.
This is the patience of a bodhisattva: a mind that does not become attached to those who provide offerings or respect.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of offerings:
first, those resulting from the merit of causes and conditions in previous lives;
second, those resulting from the virtues of the present life—namely, the cultivation of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—which lead others to respect and support one.

Third, there are those who deceive and delude others through falsehood; they lack genuine virtue within while appearing pure and upright without, using this to mislead the people of the time and obtain offerings.
Regarding these three kinds of offerings, one should reflect within one’s own mind:

"If I have obtained these offerings now due to the diligent cultivation of merit and virtue from causes and conditions in previous lives, then it is simply that I have received them by means of my own past efforts. Why, then, should I give rise to arrogance on this account?"
"It is like sowing in spring and reaping in autumn; one obtains this through one's own effort, so why should one be conceited?
Having reflected thus, he subdued his mind with patience, remaining free from attachment and pride.
If one receives offerings due to the merits of this present life, one should reflect:

"By means of wisdom, if I know the true reality of all phenomena and am able to sever the fetters, it is because of these merits that this person makes offerings; for me, there is nothing [further] to be done."
Having reflected thus, he subdued his own mind and did not become conceited;
he truly delighted in merit and did not love himself.

For example, there was a Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu from Kaśmīra who practiced the dhūta-dharmas of an araṇyaka. He arrived at a royal temple where a great assembly was being held; seeing that his robes were coarse and tattered, the gatekeeper blocked the entrance and would not let him pass.

In this manner, because his robes were worn out, he was frequently unable to advance; he therefore devised a stratagem, borrowing fine garments to come, so that when the gatekeepers saw him, they permitted him to enter without restraint.
Once he had reached the assembly, he received various kinds of excellent food, which he first gave to his robes.
The crowd asked, "Why is this so? He replied:

"I have come here many times before, yet each time I was unable to enter. Now, because of this robe, I am permitted to sit here and receive various kinds of excellent food; it is truly because of this robe that I have obtained these things, and therefore I give them back to the robe."
The practitioner, through the merit of their practice and by virtue of their observance of the precepts and wisdom, receives offerings;
they reflect to themselves: "This is due to my merit, not because of me."
Reflecting in this way, one is able to subdue one's own mind; this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If one obtains offerings through falsehood and deception, it is self-harm and must not be pursued!
One should reflect within oneself:
"If I obtain offerings through such falsehoods, it is no different from an evil thief or robber obtaining food; this constitutes the offense of deception."
Thus, among these three types of persons who provide offerings, one’s mind is neither attached nor does one become self-exalting; this is called the patience of birth (*utpattikṣānti*).
Question:

Since those who have not yet attained the Path regard food and clothing as urgent necessities, by what skillful means can one attain such patience so that the mind is neither attached to nor fond of the person who bestows gifts?
Answer:
By the power of wisdom, one contemplates the marks of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and the mind is constantly filled with weariness and aversion.

It is like a criminal about to be executed; although delicious food is placed before him and his family offers words of encouragement, because he is anxious about death, even when eating fine delicacies, he does not perceive their flavor.
The practitioner is likewise: constantly contemplating the marks of impermanence and suffering, even when receiving offerings, their mind remains unattached.
It is like a deer being pursued by a tiger that does not let it go; though the deer finds fine grass and delicious water to drink, its mind has no defiled attachment.

The practitioner is likewise: constantly pursued by the tiger of impermanence without a moment’s respite, contemplating with weariness and aversion, even when obtaining exquisite flavors, they remain undefiled and unattached.
Therefore, when among those who offer worship, the practitioner should attain self-restraint in his mind.
Furthermore, if a woman should come seeking to amuse him and deceive the Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva at that time must subdue his own mind and endure it so that it does not arise.
When Śākyamuni Buddha was beneath the Bodhi tree, the Māra King became filled with sorrow and dispatched three celestial maidens—
first named Rati, second named Arati, and third named Trṣṇā—
to manifest their bodies and display various seductive gestures, desiring to destroy the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind did not waver, nor did his eyes glance about for even a moment.
The three women thought to themselves:
"The minds of men differ; their preferences and attachments vary."

Some prefer the young, while others love those of middle age; some prefer the tall and others the short, some the dark and others the fair—among such various preferences, each has their own particular fondness.

At that time, the three women each transformed themselves into five hundred beautiful maidens, and each of these transformed maidens manifested countless variations of form as they emerged from the forest.

It is like a flash of lightning momentarily appearing amidst black clouds; or like one who raises her eyebrows and blinks her lashes, gazing with a coy and delicate look, performing various musical performances and assuming all manner of seductive postures, approaching the Bodhisattva with the intent to touch and press against him with her graceful body.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada glared at him with angry eyes and rebuked him:
"Who is this person?
How dare you, a seductive sorceress, come here to harass us!"
At that time, Guhyaka spoke a verse to rebuke him:
"You did not heed the decrees of fate, And have lost your fine appearance for a yellow beard;
The waters of the great ocean were once clear and sweet, But today they are all bitter and salty."
"You do not know that the days are diminishing, and that the Vāsava deities are falling;
fire was originally the mouth of the gods, yet now it devours all.
"You do not understand this matter, yet you dare to slight this holy man!"
At that time, the women stepped back slightly with some hesitation and said to the Bodhisattva, "These women here are of incomparable beauty;
you may amuse yourself with us. Why do you sit so upright?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"You are impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome.
Begone!"
"Do not speak recklessly!
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
"This body is a thicket of filth, A heap of decaying impurities."
"This is truly a walking latrine; how could it be sufficient to gladden the mind!
Hearing this verse, the woman thought to herself:
"This man does not know that we possess the pure celestial bodies of devas, yet he speaks such a verse."

He immediately transformed his body, restoring it to its original form; its radiance blazed forth, illuminating the forest trees, and as he performed celestial music, he spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"My body is such as this; what is there to be censured?"
The Bodhisattva replied,
"When the time comes, I shall know it myself. He asked:
"What does this mean?
He replied with a verse:
"In the gardens of the devas, There are lotus ponds made of the seven treasures."
Devas and humans enjoy themselves, yet you shall know for yourself when that time has passed!
At this moment, perceive impermanence; the pleasures of devas and humans are all suffering.
You should grow weary of sensual delights and take joy in the true and correct Path!
Having heard the verse, the woman thought to herself:
"This man possesses immeasurable great wisdom; even though celestial music is pure, he still knows its evil and cannot endure it!"
Immediately it vanished.
In this way, the Bodhisattva contemplates the pleasure of sensual desire and is able to restrain his mind, enduring it without being shaken.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates desire as being of various kinds of impurity; among all forms of decay, the decay of women is the most severe.
Swords, fire, lightning, thunderbolts, enemies, and venomous snakes may still be approached for a brief moment;
however, women characterized by stinginess and envy, anger and flattery, seductive impurity, strife, greed, and jealousy must never be drawn near.

Why is this? Women and small men have shallow minds and meager wisdom; they regard only desire and do not observe wealth, nobility, wisdom, virtue, or reputation. They are solely intent on practicing lustful evil and destroying the roots of goodness in others.
Shackles, fetters, confinement, and prisons—though said to be difficult to undo, they are still easy to open.
But when a woman’s bond binds a man, the roots of defilement are firmly established; those who lack wisdom sink into it, and it is difficult for them to attain liberation.
Among all ailments, the disease of women is the most grievous.
As the Buddha’s verse says:
"It would be better to have a red-hot iron ball / Rolled back and forth within one's eyes;"
One should not, with a distracted mind, gaze lustfully at female forms.
Whether she smiles with coquettish gestures, displays arrogance or feigned modesty,
turns her face away or casts sidelong glances, speaks sweet words or harbors jealousy and anger— [one remains unmoved].
Her gait was seductive and depraved, intended to delude men;
her net of lust was so vast that all people were submerged within it.
Whether sitting, reclining, walking, or standing, she cast sidelong glances with artful coquetry.
The foolish person of meager wisdom becomes intoxicated by this mind.
To brandish a sword against an enemy may still be overcome;
but the female thief who harms others—this cannot be restrained.
A venomous snake may still be grasped by hand;
but the passions of women delude men—these must not be touched.
A person of wisdom should not even look upon them.
If you wish to contemplate it, you should regard it as a mother or a sister.
Examine it with close attention: it is filled with impurities;
if the fire of lust is not extinguished, you will be consumed by it!
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of women: if they receive honor and hospitality, they cause their husband’s mind to become arrogant;
if their affection for such honor and hospitality is abandoned, they cause their husband’s mind to become fearful.
Women are thus: they constantly give rise to afflictions, sorrows, and fears for others; how can they be approached?
The alienation of those who are close and dear is the fault of women;
their skill in observing the vital points of others is the "wisdom" of women.
A great fire that burns people may still be approached;
a pure wind that has no form may even be grasped;
a venomous snake that harbors poison may still be touched.
The mind of a woman cannot be grasped as real.
Why is this? Because of the characteristics of a woman:
They take no account of wealth and status, physical beauty, fame, wisdom and virtue, noble lineage, artistic skill, eloquence, intimacy, or affection;
none of these enter their minds, for they regard only sensual desire—just as a dragon does not discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly, seeking only to kill humans.
Furthermore, when women are not looked after, they become distressed, sorrowful, and haggard;
yet when provided for and treated with respect, their arrogance and luxury become difficult to restrain.
Moreover, if they are among virtuous people, they harbor a mind of self-importance.
Among those without wisdom, he is viewed as an enemy;
among the wealthy and noble, he is pursued with respect and affection;
among the poor and lowly, he is viewed as a dog.
They constantly follow their desires and do not follow merit.
As it is said:
A king had a daughter named Kumuda.
There was a fisherman named Śūrpaka who, while traveling along the road, saw the princess from afar atop a high tower.
Gazing at her face through the window, he became filled with longing and attachment; his mind could not let go of her for even a moment, and as days and months passed, he was unable to eat or drink.
The mother asked him the reason for this, and he answered her with his true feelings:
"When I saw the king’s daughter, my heart could not forget her!
His mother then exhorted her son, saying:
"You are but a lowly man, while the princess is noble and honorable; she cannot be obtained!
The boy said, "My heart's longing is such that I cannot forget it for even a moment."
"If things do not go as I wish, I shall not be able to survive!
For the sake of her son, the mother entered the royal palace and constantly sent fat fish and fine meats to the princess as gifts, without taking any payment.
The princess, wondering at this, asked her:
"What boon do you seek?
Her mother replied to the princess:
"Please step aside so that I may speak of my true feelings.
I have but one son, who has come to admire your daughter with such deep devotion that his affection has turned into illness, and his life is now at its end.
I pray you will look upon him with compassion and grant him his life!"
The princess said:
"Go! On the fifteenth day of the month, stay behind the image of the deity within such-and-such a temple."
The mother returned and said to her son,
"Your wish has been granted!
She informed him as described above.
Having bathed and put on new clothes, she stayed behind the image of the deity.
When the time arrived, the princess said to her father, the king:
"I have met with an inauspicious omen; I must go to the celestial shrine to seek auspicious blessings."
The king said,
"Excellent! He immediately prepared five hundred chariots and went out to the celestial temple.
Having arrived, he commanded his attendants to stop at the gate and entered the temple alone.
The deity reflected: "This should not be so!"
"The King is the sovereign of the world; we must not allow this petty man to bring disgrace upon the Princess!
He immediately cast a spell over the man, causing him to fall into a deep sleep from which he could not wake.

Once the Princess had entered, she saw that he was sleeping so heavily that she could not rouse him by pushing him. She then left behind for him a necklace worth one hundred thousand taels of gold and departed.
After she had departed, the man regained consciousness and saw the necklaces; he questioned the people and learned that the princess had come.
His desires unfulfilled, he was consumed by grief, resentment, and anguish; the fire of lust ignited within him, burning him to death.
By this evidence, we know that the hearts of women do not discriminate between the noble and the lowly, following only their desires.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a king’s daughter who pursued a caṇḍāla and engaged in impure acts with him.
Furthermore, there were female seers who followed after lions.
In various instances such as these, the minds of women make no distinctions.
For these many reasons, one should eliminate lustful desires toward women and endure them without attachment.
How does one attain patience when encountering anger and vexation among people?
One should reflect within oneself:
"All sentient beings possess the causes and conditions for transgression, whereby they mutually harm one another."

"The affliction I now endure is also due to causes and conditions from my past conduct; though it was not committed in this present life, it is the retribution for my evil deeds in previous lives. I must now repay it and accept it with equanimity; how could I possibly resist it?"
"It is like being in debt: when a creditor demands repayment, one should joyfully discharge the debt and must not feel anger.
Furthermore, the practitioner constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness; thus, even if there are disturbances that afflict the body, they will certainly be able to endure them.
For example, the seer Kṣānti was practicing patience and cultivating loving-kindness in a great forest.
At that time, King Kali, accompanied by his court ladies, entered the forest for recreation;
having finished eating and drinking, the king fell into a brief sleep.
As the various court ladies were strolling among the flower groves, they saw this rishi; they paid him their respects with increased reverence and stood to one side.

At that time, the rishi expounded upon loving-kindness and patience for the sake of the court ladies; his words were so exquisite that those who heard them never grew weary, and they remained there for a long time without departing.
King Kali awoke and, not seeing his court ladies, drew his sword and pursued them;
finding her standing before the rishi, his arrogance and jealousy flared up, and with eyes blazing with rage, he brandished his sword and asked the rishi, "What are you doing?"
The seer replied,
"I am now practicing patience and cultivating loving-kindness here.
The king said:
"I have now tested you; I shall cut off your ears and nose with a sharp sword and sever your hands and feet. If you do not feel anger, I shall know that you have cultivated patience!"
The seer said, "As you wish!
The king immediately drew his sword, cut off his ears and nose, and severed his hands and feet, then asked him:
"Is your mind disturbed?
He replied, "I cultivate loving-kindness and patience; my mind is not disturbed."
The king said, "You are but a single person here and possess no power; though you speak with your mouth, who would believe you?
At that time, the rishi immediately made this vow:
"If I truly practice loving-kindness and patience, may my blood turn into milk!
Immediately, the blood transformed into milk.
The king was greatly astonished and joyful, and departed with his many court ladies.
At that time, the nāgas and devas in the forest caused lightning and thunderbolts for this rishi; the king was harmed by the poison and perished, never returning to his palace.
For this reason, it is said: "One can practice patience amidst affliction and disturbance."
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the mind of compassion, he considers that all sentient beings are constantly beset by manifold sufferings:
while dwelling in the womb, they are confined in a cramped space and undergo various pains;
at the time of birth, they are squeezed through a narrow passage as if their bones and flesh were being shattered, and the cold wind touching their bodies is more piercing than swords or halberds.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Among all forms of suffering, the suffering of birth is the most severe.
Since this is so for the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, as well as for various other calamities, why would a practitioner further inflict suffering upon them?
This is like adding a knife-wound to an existing ulcer!
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"I ought not to follow the current of birth and death like all other people; I shall go against the current to seek the exhaustion of its source and enter the path to nirvāṇa."
All ordinary people become angry when things diminish for them, rejoice when they increase, and feel fear in the face of danger.

As a Bodhisattva, I must not be like them; although I have not yet severed the fetters, I shall restrain myself, practice patience, feel no anger toward harm or injury, feel no joy toward honor or sustenance, and should not fear various sufferings and hardships;
rather, I shall arouse great compassion for all sentient beings!
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings coming to cause him disturbance and annoyance, he should think to himself:
"These are my close kin and friends, and they are also my teachers; I shall treat them with even greater affection and serve them with a heart of reverence."
Why is this? If they did not inflict various afflictions upon me, I would not achieve patience;
for this reason, it is said that they are my close kin and also my teachers.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s mind knows:
"As the Buddha has taught:
'Sentient beings are without beginning; the world is without limit; they come and go through the five destinies, revolving in an immeasurable cycle.'"
"I have also previously been the parents and brothers of sentient beings, and all sentient beings have likewise previously been my parents and brothers;
it shall be so in the future as well."
Inferring from this, one should not harbor malice or thoughts of anger and harm.
Furthermore, reflect thus:
"Among sentient beings, there are many seeds of Buddhahood; if I direct anger toward them, I am in fact being angry with the Buddha."
"If I were to harbor anger toward the Buddha, my purpose would already be defeated!
As it is said that even a pigeon or a bird shall attain Buddhahood, though they are currently birds, they must not be treated with contempt.
Furthermore, among all afflictions (*kleśa*), hatred is the most grave; among the retributions for unwholesome deeds, the retribution for hatred is the greatest.
No other fetters carry such grave retribution as this.
As Śakra Devānām-indra asked the Buddha in verse:
"What is it that, when killed, brings peace?"
What is it that one does not regret when killing?
What is the root of poison that swallows up all goodness?
What is it that one praises when killing?
"What thing, when killed, brings no sorrow?
The Buddha answered with a verse:
"When anger is slain, the mind is at peace; when anger is slain, the mind has no regret."
"Hatred is the root of poison; hatred destroys all that is wholesome.
The Buddhas praise the slaying of hatred; by slaying hatred, one has no sorrow.
Thus the Bodhisattva reflected:
"I now practice compassion, desiring to enable sentient beings to attain happiness.
Anger swallows and destroys all virtues and harms everything; how could I possibly commit such a grave transgression?"
If one harbors anger, one loses one's own happiness and benefit; how then could one enable sentient beings to attain happiness?
Furthermore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their foundation and emerge from it;
since anger is a poison that extinguishes compassion, it is particularly incompatible with them.
If one destroys the root of compassion, how can one be called a bodhisattva?
From what, then, would a bodhisattva arise?
For this reason, one should practice patience.
If sentient beings inflict anger and affliction upon you, you should contemplate their merits;
although this sentient being currently possesses a single fault, they furthermore possess various other sublime merits.
Because of these merits, one ought not to be angry.
Furthermore, if this person reviles or strikes me, it serves as a means of refining me;
it is like a goldsmith smelting gold: as the dross departs with the fire, the pure gold alone remains.
This case is just the same.
