*pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore."
Ordinary people of the world, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, are unable to fully practice all the pāramitās; therefore, this is not called the pāramitā of diligence.
Furthermore, such a person lacks great loving-kindness and great compassion, and abandons sentient beings;

they do not seek the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, or omniscience, nor do they seek unimpeded liberation, the immeasurable body, immeasurable radiance, immeasurable voice, or immeasurable morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
For this reason, the diligence of such a person is not called a pāramitā.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva’s diligence is unremitting and unceasing, seeking the Buddha-way with a single mind—such a practitioner is said to possess the diligence pāramitā.

It is like the Bodhisattva Good Giver (Supratidatta), who sought the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) by drawing up the waters of the great ocean; even if his sinews and bones were withered away, he never grew weary or desisted.
Having obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel, he bestowed it upon sentient beings to relieve them of their physical suffering.
That a bodhisattva is thus able to accomplish what is difficult to accomplish constitutes the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, with the power of diligence as the foremost, practices the five perfections, at that time it is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence.
For example, when various medicines are combined, they can cure a serious illness;
the diligence of a bodhisattva is likewise. If one practices only diligence but cannot practice the five pāramitās, this is not called the bodhisattva’s diligence pāramitā.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s diligence is not for the sake of wealth, profit, nobility, or power; nor is it for the sake of his own body, nor for the sake of rebirth as a celestial being, a wheel-turning king, a Brahmā, or a Śakra, King of Devas. Nor does he seek nirvāṇa for himself alone; rather, it is solely for the sake of the Buddha-way and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Such characteristics as these are called the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s diligence consists in practicing all wholesome dharmas, with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as the foremost.

Just as a compassionate father loves his son—when he has an only son who falls gravely ill, he seeks medicine with single-minded devotion to cure that illness—so too is the bodhisattva’s diligence, headed by compassion;
likewise, they rescue and heal all beings, never for a moment abandoning them in mind.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices diligence with the wisdom of the true nature as its foremost guide, performing the six pāramitās, this is called the bodhisattva’s pāramitā of diligence.
Question: The true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and without effort;
diligence (*vīrya*), however, has the characteristics of being conditioned and involving effort. How can it be said that the true mark is primary?
The answer is:

Although one knows that the true mark of all dharmas is unconditioned and uncreated, because of one's original vow and great compassion for the desire to deliver sentient beings, one employs the power of diligence within this state of non-creation to liberate all.

Furthermore, if the true mark of all phenomena (dharmas) is unconditioned and uncreated, like the mark of nirvāṇa, being neither one nor two, how can you say that "the true mark is different from the mark of diligence"?
You do not yet understand the characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, at that time, the Bodhisattva observes the sentient beings of the three realms and five destinies, each having lost their respective joys.

The devas of the formless realm, being attached to the bliss of meditative concentration, fail to perceive the exhaustion of their life-span and fall into the desire realm, receiving the forms of birds and beasts.
The devas of the form realm are likewise: falling from their pure abodes, they again undergo sexual desire and dwell amidst impurity.
The six heavens of the desire realm, being attached to the five desires, fall back into hell and undergo all manner of suffering and pain.

I see that among human beings, one obtains a human body by trading for it with the merit of the ten wholesome actions; yet the human body abounds in suffering and is scarce in joy, and when its lifespan ends, many fall into the evil realms.

I see all manner of animals undergoing various afflictions: driven by whips and staves, burdened with heavy loads over long distances, their necks pierced and torn, and scorched by glowing red-hot iron.
Due to the causal conditions of this person's past conduct— having bound sentient beings and afflicted them with whips and staves—
and for various other such reasons, they receive the forms of animals such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, roe deer, and gazelles.

With heavy lustful desires and an abundance of ignorance, one is reborn as a goose, duck, peacock, mandarin duck, pigeon, dove, chicken, waterfowl, parrot, myna bird, or other such species; among these various birds, there are hundreds of thousands of different types.

Due to the transgression of sexual misconduct, hair and feathers grow upon the body, obstructing all sensations of smoothness and softness; the beak and snout become coarse and calloused, such that one cannot distinguish between tactile sensations or flavors.
With an excess of hatred, one receives rebirth as a venomous snake, viper, scorpion, bee, or centipede—among those creatures that harbor poison.
Because of an abundance of ignorance, one receives the bodies of earthworms, moths, dung beetles, ants, termites, owls, cormorants, horned owls, and other such foolish insects and birds.
Because of an abundance of pride and anger, one receives the bodies of lions, tigers, leopards, and various other fierce beasts.
Due to the conditions of false pride, one is reborn among donkeys, pigs, and camels.
Because of stinginess, greed, jealousy, restlessness, and brevity of character, one takes the form of a macaque, a gibbon, a bear, or a brown bear.
Due to the karmic causes and conditions of perverse greed, malice, and envy, one receives the bodies of various beasts such as cats, raccoon dogs, and wildcats.
Due to the karmic causes and conditions of shamelessness, lack of remorse, and voracious gluttony, one receives the forms of various birds such as crows, magpies, owls, and vultures.
Because they treat virtuous people with contempt, they receive the bodies of chickens, dogs, jackals, and the like.
Because they practice great acts of giving while harboring anger and a crooked mind, by these causes and conditions, they receive the bodies of various nāgas.
Having practiced great acts of giving with a haughty and arrogant mind that tormented sentient beings, one receives the form of a garuḍa.
Due to various such fetters, afflictions, and karmic causes and conditions, one undergoes the sufferings of the various animals and beasts.
The Bodhisattva attains the divine eye and observes sentient beings revolving through the five destinies, circling within them:
dying among the gods and being born among humans;
dying among humans and being born among the gods.
Dying among the devas, one is born in hell;
dying in hell, one is born in the heavens;
dying in the heavens, one is born among the hungry ghosts.
Dying among the hungry ghosts, they are reborn in the heavens;
dying in the heavens, they are born among animals;
dying among animals, they are reborn in the heavens.
Dying in the heavens, one is reborn in the heavens.
It is the same for those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm.
Dying within the desire realm, one is reborn in the form realm.
Dying in the realm of form, one is reborn in the realm of desire;
dying in the realm of desire, one is reborn in the formless realm;
dying in the formless realm, one is reborn in the realm of desire.
Dying in the desire realm, one is reborn in the desire realm;
the same applies to the form realm and the formless realm.
Dying in the Reviving Hell, one is reborn in the Black Rope Hell.
Dying in the Kālasūtra Hell, one is reborn in the Saṃjīva Hell;
dying in the Saṃjīva Hell, one returns to the Saṃjīva Hell.
The same applies to the Saṃghāta Hell up to the Avīci Hell.
Dying in the Charcoal Pit Hell, they are reborn in the Boiling Excrement Hell;
dying in the Boiling Excrement Hell, they are reborn in the Charcoal Pit Hell;
dying in the Charcoal Pit Hell, they are reborn once again in the Charcoal Pit Hell.
From the Burning Forest Hell up to the Mahāpadma Hell, they likewise transmigrate and are reborn therein.
They die among the egg-born and are born among the womb-born;
they die among the womb-born and are born among the egg-born.
Dying among those born from eggs, they are reborn among those born from eggs.
The same applies to those born from wombs, from moisture, and by transformation.
Dying in Jambudvīpa, they are reborn in Pūrvavideha;
One dies in Pūrvavideha and is born in Jambudvīpa;
one dies in Jambudvīpa and is again born in Jambudvīpa.
It is the same for Aparagodānīya and Uttarakuru.
Dying in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, one is reborn among the Thirty-three Gods;
dying among the Thirty-three Gods, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
dying in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, one is reborn again in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The same applies from the Heaven of the Thirty-three up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
One may die among the Gods of Brahma’s Retinue and be reborn among the Ministers of Brahmā;
or die among the Ministers of Brahmā and be reborn among the Gods of Brahma’s Retinue.
Dying among the Brahmakāyika devas, they are reborn again among the Brahmakāyika devas.

It is likewise for the Brahmapurohita, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, and the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Dying in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, one is reborn in the Avīci Hell;
thus one wanders through birth in the five realms of existence.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion:
"I have provided no benefit to sentient beings; though I grant them worldly happiness, when that happiness reaches its limit, it turns to suffering.
I must instead benefit all beings with the eternal bliss of the Buddha-way and Nirvana."
How does one benefit others?
One must apply oneself with great diligence to attain true wisdom;
having attained true wisdom, one knows the true mark of all phenomena and, supported by the remaining perfections, brings benefit to sentient beings.
This is the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence.
Seeing those among the hungry ghosts who, due to hunger and thirst, have sunken eyes, long hair, and run hither and thither.
If one wishes to go toward water, the various spirits who guard the water strike back with iron staves;
even if there are no guarding spirits, the water naturally dries up;
or at times when it rains, the rain transforms into charcoal.
There are some hungry ghosts who are constantly scorched by fire, like when the fires break out from the mountains at the end of an eon.
There are some hungry ghosts who are emaciated and run about frantically, their hair and fur disheveled and covering their bodies.
There are some hungry ghosts who constantly eat excrement and urine, nasal mucus, saliva, vomit, and the leftover wash-water;
at times they stand by the side of latrines, waiting and seeking out impure fluids.
There are some hungry ghosts who constantly seek the blood from the womb of a woman in childbirth to drink; their bodies resemble scorched trees and their throats are like the eye of a needle.
Even if they were given water, it would not suffice for a thousand years.
Some hungry ghosts split open their own heads, taking the brains with their hands and licking them.
Others have forms like black mountains, their necks bound by iron chains; they strike their heads in supplication, seeking mercy and taking refuge in the wardens of hell.

There are some hungry ghosts who, in previous lives, committed verbal abuse and delighted in inflicting harsh speech upon other sentient beings; because those beings detested them and viewed them as enemies, these individuals fell into the realm of hungry ghosts due to this transgression.
Due to various such transgressions as these, they fall into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and undergo immeasurable suffering and pain.
They behold the eight great hells, where bitter poisons manifest in myriads of ways.

The various sinners within the Reviving Great Hell fight one another; with malicious minds and angry contention, they grasp sharp knives in their hands to slice and flay each other. They pierce one another with spears, impale one another with iron forks, strike one another with iron clubs, beat one another with iron staves, and skewer one another with iron shovels. They mince and hack one another with sharp knives, tear one another apart with iron claws, and smear themselves all over with each other’s blood.
Tormented by agonizing pain, they were so faint that they were unconscious;
then, due to the causal conditions of their past karma, a cold wind blew upon them, and the hell-wardens called out to them:
"Hey! You there!"
The various sinners return to life; for this reason, it is called the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
They immediately recover and once again undergo bitter suffering.
The sentient beings therein, due to the causal conditions of their past conduct, were fond of killing living creatures such as oxen, sheep, birds, and beasts.
For the sake of fields and estates, houses and dwellings, slaves and servants, wives and children, kingdoms and territories, and wealth and riches, they kill and harm one another.
Because of such various karmic retributions for the act of killing, they undergo these severe punishments.
He saw the offenders in the Black Rope Great Hell being constantly measured with black, glowing iron cords by evil rākṣasas, hell-wardens, and ghost-artisans.
With iron axes from within the prison, they kill and hack them:
making the tall short and the short tall;
making the square round and the round square.
Their four limbs are severed; their ears and noses are removed; their hands and feet are cut off.
With great iron saws, they are dismembered and hacked apart; their flesh is split into portions, each piece weighed out individually.

Due to the causal conditions of this person's past conduct, they slandered the loyal and virtuous; they engaged in false speech, harsh words, divisive speech, and senseless talk; they unjustly executed the innocent, or served as corrupt officials, inflicting cruel and violent harm upon others.
Because they engaged in various kinds of harsh speech,
slander, and treachery, they undergo these punishments. Within the Great Universal Convergence Hell, one sees evil rākṣasas and hell-wardens assuming various forms—

oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, deer, wild boars, foxes, dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, six-tusked elephants, great birds, eagles, vultures, and quails— approaching with the heads of such diverse birds and beasts to swallow, devour, gnaw, bite, and tear at the offenders.
Two mountains close together, and great, glowing iron wheels crush the sinners, shattering their bodies;
they are pounded in hot iron mortars until they are broken like grapes being squeezed or oil being pressed. It is like treading upon a threshing floor:
heaps of flesh pile up like mounds, heads accumulate like mountains, and pools of blood form, while vultures, eagles, tigers, and wolves all come to scramble and tear at them.

Due to the karmic causes and conditions of this person’s past lives, they frequently slaughtered oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, deer, wild boars, foxes, rabbits, tigers, wolves, lions, *ṣaḍbiḍāla* (six-tusked leopards), great birds, and various other fowl; because they so cruelly harmed such diverse birds and beasts, they now come as the heads of these very creatures to harm the sinner.
Furthermore, because they used their power and influence to oppress others and unjustly suppressed the weak, they undergo the retribution of two mountains closing together.

Because of their stinginess, greed, anger, delusion, and fear, they adjudicated matters of light and heavy gravity without following correct principles—either subverting the right path or altering the true Dharma—and thus they suffer being crushed by hot iron wheels and pounded in hot iron mortars.
The fourth and fifth are named Raurava (Screaming) and Mahāraurava (Great Screaming).

In these great hells, the sinners are pursued by rākṣasas and hell-wardens whose heads are yellow like gold, from whose eyes fire issues forth, who wear crimson robes, whose flesh and bodies are firm and tough, who run as swiftly as the wind, whose hands and feet are oversized, and who utter evil sounds from their mouths; wielding tridents, they rain down arrows like falling rain to pierce and shoot at the sinners.
The sinner, frantic with terror, struck his head in supplication, pleading for mercy and a slight reprieve.

Immediately, he was led into the Hot Iron Hell, which was a hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth; driven and beaten, he fled in haste, his feet scorched until fat and marrow flowed out like pressed ghee.
Struck by iron clubs, their heads are split open and their brains spill out like the curd from a broken jar.
Their bodies are hacked, minced, sliced, and flayed until they are mangled and putrefied.

They are then driven into iron chamber-houses where black smoke billows and stifles them; as they jostle and crush one another, they harbor mutual malice and resentment, each crying out, "Why are you pressing upon me?"
Just as he sought to escape, the gate was closed;
he cried out with a great voice, his cries never ceasing.

This was due to the karmic causes and conditions of his past conduct: he had deceived others with false measures and scales, adjudicated matters unjustly, failed to return deposits, oppressed the lowly, and tormented the poor, causing them to wail and weep.
They destroy city walls and gates, ruin human settlements, and inflict injury and plunder; families are filled with resentment and poison, and the entire city cries out in lamentation.
At times, they employ guile and deception, luring people out only to harm them.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, they undergo such retribution.
Those in the Great Screaming Hell all sit there because they killed burrowing creatures by fumigation, or imprisoned them in dungeons, or killed them by fumigating them in dark, smoky caves;
or because they threw others into wells or plundered the wealth of others.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, one undergoes the retribution of the Mahāraurava (Great Wailing) Hell.
In the sixth and seventh hells, Tapana (Heat) and Pratāpana (Great Heat), there are two great copper cauldrons:
the first named Nanda, and the second named Upananda—translated into Chinese as "Joy" and "Great Joy."
The cauldron is filled with boiling brine, and Rākṣasa demons and hell-wardens cast the sinners into it like a cook roasting meat.

The person inside the cauldron is positioned with feet up and head down; like beans being boiled until they are soft and rotten, their bones and joints disintegrate and their skin and flesh separate from one another.
Once it is known they are thoroughly cooked, they are poked out with a fork. Due to the causal conditions of their past karma, a cold wind blows upon them and they are restored to life.
Furthermore, they are cast into pits of burning charcoal or into boiling excrement, like fish taken from water and placed upon hot sand;
moreover, they are seared and boiled by thick blood.
They emerge from the charcoal pits and are cast onto flaming beds, where they are forcibly driven to sit; from their eyes, ears, noses, mouths, and all their pores, flames burst forth.

In past lives, this person troubled and disturbed their parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; they distressed those who were good people and fields of merit, causing their minds to burn with heat.
Because of these offenses, they undergo the retribution of the Hot Hell.

Some, in previous lives, boiled living cocoons; some roasted pigs and sheep alive; some impaled people on wooden stakes and roasted them alive; some burned mountains, forests, villages, Buddhist shrines, monasteries, and the abodes of deities; or some pushed sentient beings into pits of fire.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one is born within this hell.
One sees the Avīci Hell, four thousand li in length and breadth, with iron walls surrounding it; among the seven hells, its location is the deepest.
The rākṣasa wardens strike the sinners with great iron hammers, like blacksmiths forging iron; they flay their skin from head to foot.
They pin their bodies with five hundred nails, stretching them out like a hide of oxen, pulling and wrenching them against one another until they burst asunder at the touch of the hand.
Hot iron chariots crush their bodies;
they are driven into pits of fire and forced to embrace burning coals as they emerge.
They are driven into rivers of boiling excrement and compelled to enter within.
There are venomous insects with iron beaks that enter through the nostrils and emerge from the soles of the feet, or enter through the soles of the feet and emerge from the mouth.
Along the path of upright swords, they are driven to run until their feet are mangled and shredded like minced meat in a kitchen.
Sharp knives, swords, and spears fly into their bodies, falling in disarray like leaves from a tree in autumn blown by the wind.
The hands, feet, ears, noses, and limbs of the sinners were all hacked, flayed, and severed, lying upon the ground with blood flowing until it formed pools.
There were two great, wicked dogs:
one named Śyāma and the other named Śabala.
With an iron mouth and fierce determination, he tears through the sinews and bones of men; his strength exceeds that of tigers and leopards, and his ferocity is like that of a lion.
There is a great forest of thorns where he drives and coerces the offenders, forcing them to climb the trees.
When the sinner ascends, the spikes turn downward; when he descends, the spikes turn upward.
Great-bodied venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and malevolent insects vie with one another to bite him.
Large birds with long beaks pierce their heads and devour their brains.
They enter the River of Salt, drifting up and down with the current;
when they emerge, they tread upon ground of glowing iron and walk upon iron spikes.
Or they are made to sit upon iron stakes that penetrate from below.

Their mouths are forced open with tongs and molten copper is poured in; they swallow hot iron balls which scorch the mouth as it enters, rot the throat as it passes down, and set the belly ablaze, burning all five viscera until they pass straight through and fall to the ground.
They see only unpleasant sights, constantly smell foul odors, and perpetually encounter coarse and rough textures; they suffer various pains, becoming bewildered, fainting, and utterly exhausted.
At times they become狂逸 (mad and unruly) or唐突 (rash and impetuous); at times they hide and flee, or throw themselves about; at times they stumble, prostrate themselves, or fall down.

In his past lives, this person committed many great evils and the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes; he severed all roots of goodness, declaring the Dharma to be non-Dharma and non-Dharma to be the Dharma, subverting cause and effect, and harboring hatred and envy toward virtuous people.
Because of these offenses, they enter this hell to undergo the most severe punishments.
Such are the various eight great hells.
Surrounding them on the outside, there are further sixteen minor hells as their retinue:
There are eight cold hells and eight hot hells; the poisonous torments within them cannot be seen or heard.
As for the eight hot-fire hells:

first is named Charcoal Pit, second is named Boiling Excrement, third is named Burning Forest, fourth is named Sword Forest, fifth is named Blade Path, sixth is named Iron Thorn Forest, seventh is named Salt River, and eighth is named Copper Stake—these are the eight.
The eight cold hells are as follows: first, Arbuda, which has few small holes;

second, Nirarbuda, which has no holes; third, Aṭaṭa, so named from the sound of shivering; fourth, Hahava, likewise from the sound of suffering from the cold; fifth, Huhuva, also from the sound of suffering from the cold; sixth, Utpala, because the outer walls of this hell resemble blue lotuses; seventh, Padma, where sinners undergo suffering amidst red lotuses; and eighth, Mahāpadma. These are the eight.
If one violates the pure precepts of the monastic discipline, causing laypeople to despise the Buddha-way;
or if one pushes sentient beings into pits of fire, or roasts them over fires while their lives have not yet come to an end.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one falls into the Charcoal Pit Hell.
Great flames of fire and glowing coals reach up to the knees, burning the bodies of the offenders.
This also applies to those who touch the food of the *śramaṇas* and *brāhmaṇas*—the field of merit—with impure hands, or who eat it first, or who place impure things within it.
Or by pouring boiling excrement over the bodies of others, destroying their pure livelihood and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood;
through various causes and conditions such as these, they fall into the Boiling Excrement Hell.

The boiling excrement is as deep and vast as the waters of the great ocean; within it dwell insects with iron beaks that split open the heads of the sinners to devour their brains, and break their bones to eat their marrow.
If one burns grasses and trees, harming various insects, or sets fire to forests for large-scale hunting, the harm is even more extensive.
Due to such various causes and conditions as these, one falls into the Scorching Forest Hell (Kālasūtra).
Grass and trees burst into flames to burn the sinners;
or they brandish swords and blades to fight, quarrel, wound, and kill;
or they hack down trees to crush people, seeking to avenge old grudges.
If a person uses loyalty, trustworthiness, and sincerity to inform another, yet secretly brings about their ruin—
through various causes and conditions such as these, one falls into the Sword Forest Hell (*Asipatravana*).
When the offenders of this hell enter it, the wind blows the sword-leaves, which slice off their hands, feet, ears, and noses, causing them all to fall away.
At that time, there are crows, vultures, and vicious dogs in the forest that come to devour their flesh.
Whether by piercing people with sharp knives, or wounding them with stakes or spears;

whether by blocking roads, pulling down bridges, destroying the path of the True Dharma, or showing the path of unrighteousness—through various causes and conditions such as these, they fall into the Hell of the Path of Sharp Blades.
Regarding the Hell of the Path of Sharp Blades: sharp blades are erected within a narrow path along sheer cliffs, forcing the offenders to walk upon them as they pass through.

Those who have committed sexual misconduct, such as violating the wives of others or greedily seeking pleasurable touch—due to various causes and conditions such as these—they fall into the Iron Thorns Forest Hell.

There is a thorny tree one yojana high, upon which dwells a great venomous serpent that transforms itself into the body of a beautiful woman. She calls out to the offenders, "Come up here and enjoy music with me!

The wardens drive them upward; as they ascend, the thorns all turn downward, piercing and stabbing the offenders. Their bodies are mangled by the thorns, the injury penetrating to the bone and reaching the marrow.

Upon reaching the top of the tree, the transformed woman returned to her snake body; she split open his head and entered his belly, piercing holes everywhere until he was completely mangled and putrefied.
Suddenly, he revived and his body was restored to its former state.

The transformed woman again called out to him from beneath the tree; the hell-warden shot an arrow upward at him, calling for him to descend, and as he descended, the arrow pierced him once more from below.
Once they have reached that ground, the transformed female bodies turn back into venomous snakes and tear apart the bodies of the offenders.
After a long time has passed, they emerge from the forest of hot iron thorns and see from afar a river of clear, cool, and pleasant water;
they run toward it, but upon entering, it transforms into boiling brine. Within it, the offenders' skin and flesh fall away in an instant, leaving only their skeletons standing in the water.
The rakshasa wardens pull him out with pitchforks and hooks and place him upon the bank.

Due to the causal conditions of this person’s past conduct—having injured and killed aquatic creatures such as fish and turtles, or having at times pushed people and other sentient beings into the water, or thrown them into boiling water, or thrown them into ice-cold water—[he suffers this retribution].
Due to various causes and conditions of such evil karma as these, they undergo this retribution.
If they are in the Hell of Copper Stakes, the rākṣasa hell-wardens ask the sinners:
"From where have you come?"
He replied, "I am distressed and do not know where I have come from; I suffer only from hunger and thirst.
When he said he was thirsty, the hell-wardens immediately drove the sinner away and made him sit upon a hot copper stake; they forced his mouth open with iron tongs and poured molten copper into it.
If they say they are hungry, they are made to sit upon copper spikes and swallow iron balls.

When these enter the mouth, the mouth is scorched; when they enter the throat, the throat is seared; when they enter the belly, the belly burns, and the five viscera are destroyed and ruined, passing straight through until they fall to the ground.
Due to the causal conditions of this person's past conduct, they plundered the wealth of others to provide for their own sustenance.
Among those who have left the household life, some may feign illness to seek out large quantities of ghee and rock honey;
or, lacking precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they receive many offerings from others.
Or by using harsh speech to wound others—through various such causes and conditions of past karma, one falls into the Copper Stake Hell.

If a person falls into the Arbuda Hell, there is accumulated ice in that place; a poisonous wind blows upon them, causing the skin and hair of the sinners to crack and fall off, their muscles and tendons to be severed, and their bones to shatter so that the marrow flows out.
Their bodies immediately become whole and firm again, and they undergo the retribution of their sins as before.
This is due to the causal conditions of this person's past karma: in cold months, they stripped people of their clothing;
or they robbed and stole firewood and fuel from those suffering from the cold.
Some become malevolent nāgas, filled with poisonous rage and resentment, unleashing great hailstorms and rains of ice that harm and kill people;
some treat with contempt and slander the Buddha, his disciples, or those who uphold the precepts;
and some commit various grave offenses through the four karmas of speech.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, one falls into the Arbuda hell.
It is the same for the Nirarbuda hell.
In the Arbuda hell, there are few and small holes through which one may occasionally enter or exit.
The Nairañjanā hell is completely without openings or fissures, leaving no place for entry or exit.
In the three hells of Aṭaṭa, Hahava, and Huhuva, the cold winds cause such shivering that the mouths cannot be opened; these hells are named after the sounds of the cries uttered therein.
In the Utpala hell, the freezing ice is so pervasive that it resembles blue lotuses.
The Padma hell is shaped like the red lotuses found here in this world.
The Mahāpadma hell is the dwelling place of Kokālika.
A person of wisdom, hearing this, cried out in alarm:
"Alas! It is because of these factors of ignorance, hatred, and craving that one undergoes such suffering."
They emerge and re-enter, without end and without cessation!
Seeing this, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:

“These causes and conditions of suffering and karma are all produced by ignorance and the various afflictions. I shall now diligently and vigorously cultivate the six perfections, accumulate all merits, and sever the sufferings of sentient beings within the five realms of existence.”
He gives rise to great compassion and increases his vigor.

Just as one would see their own parents imprisoned in a dungeon, subjected to torture and flogging, and experience myriad forms of grief and distress, yet seek a means to rescue them without ever for a moment abandoning them;
so too does the Bodhisattva, seeing all sentient beings undergoing the sufferings of the five realms of existence, regard them as his own father.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva exerts diligence, practicing with industry throughout successive lives to seek various treasures and wealth to bestow upon sentient beings, his mind never flagging or abandoning the effort.
With whatever wealth he possesses, he is able to give it all away, his mind likewise remaining untiring.
Furthermore, with diligent effort in upholding the precepts, whether they be great or small, one is able to receive and maintain them all; one neither defiles nor violates them.
Even regarding a transgression as minute as a hair, if there is any lapse, one immediately confesses it and never conceals it for even a moment.

Furthermore, he diligently cultivates patience; whether people strike or harm him with knives or staves, revile or insult him, or treat him with respect and provide offerings, he is able to endure it all, neither grasping nor clinging to them.
Within the profound Dharma, his mind does not sink, nor does he harbor doubt or regret.

Furthermore, with single-minded diligence, he cultivates the various dhyānas and samādhis, being able to abide in and maintain them; he attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), as well as the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatana*), thereby perfecting all merits;
he also attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and the bodhisattva samādhi of beholding the Buddhas.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva diligently seeks the Dharma, never flagging in body or mind. With tireless effort, he makes offerings to the Dharma teacher, providing various forms of respect and service, never failing or falling back from his initial resolve, and not sparing even his own body or life for the sake of the Dharma.

Reciting, reading, and engaging in question-and-answer sessions during the first, middle, and last watches of the night; reflecting upon and recollecting [the teachings], weighing and discerning them, seeking their causes and conditions, and selecting between similarities and differences, desiring to know the true nature (*dharmatā*):

the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), differing characteristics, general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), particular characteristics, the single characteristic, existence and non-existence, and the reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; and the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—when the mind neither sinks nor regresses in this pursuit, it is called the diligence of a bodhisattva.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one is able to produce and accomplish all kinds of wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
The meaning of "perfection" (*pāramitā*) is as previously explained.
Furthermore, the diligence of a bodhisattva is called the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā);
the diligence of other people is not called a perfection. Question:
What is the fulfillment of diligence?
The answer is:
when a bodhisattva’s birth-body and dharma-nature body are able to be fully endowed with meritorious qualities, this is called the fulfillment of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
The meaning of "fulfillment" is as explained above.
It refers to the fact that physical and mental vigor are not abandoned or stilled.
Question:
Question: Diligence (*vīrya*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*); why, then, does the Sūtra call it "bodily diligence" (*kāya-vīrya*)? Answer:
Although diligence is a mental factor, because it arises from the power of the body, it is called bodily diligence.
Just as feeling is a mental factor, there is feeling associated with the five consciousnesses, which is called bodily feeling;
there is feeling associated with the mental consciousness, which constitutes mental feeling.

Diligence is also like this: exerting physical strength through diligent practice—whether by giving with the hand, reciting the words of the Dharma with the mouth, or expounding the Dharma—such as these are called diligence of body and speech.
Furthermore, practicing generosity and observing the precepts constitutes physical diligence;
patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom are termed mental diligence.
Furthermore, diligent cultivation of external matters is physical diligence;
internal self-concentration is mental diligence.
Gross diligence is termed physical, while subtle diligence is termed mental.
Vigor for the sake of merit is called physical vigor; vigor for the sake of wisdom is mental vigor.

If a bodhisattva, from the initial generation of the mind until the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), exerts vigor during this interval, it is termed physical vigor, because the physical body has not yet been relinquished.

Attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), relinquishing the physical body to obtain the dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), and proceeding until the attainment of Buddhahood—this is mental diligence.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva first resolves their mind on enlightenment, because their merit is not yet sufficient, they plant the causes and conditions for the three types of merit:
giving, observing the precepts, and a virtuous mind; they gradually obtain the rewards of this merit to bestow upon sentient beings.
Seeing that sentient beings were not yet satisfied, he further cultivated merit extensively and gave rise to a heart of great compassion, thinking:
"All sentient beings lack wealth and thus commit many evils; I cannot satisfy their desires with my meager riches.
If their desires remain unsatisfied, they will be unable to diligently receive instruction."
If one does not receive the Daoist teachings, one cannot attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
I shall employ great skillful means to provide them with sufficient wealth, so that they may be fully satisfied.
He then entered the great ocean to seek various extraordinary jewels;
he climbed mountains and traversed perilous heights to seek wondrous medicines;
and he entered deep stone caves to seek various rare substances, such as mineral essences and precious gems, to provide for all sentient beings.

Or they may become *sattva*s who venture onto perilous paths filled with bandits, lions, tigers, wolves, and other malevolent beasts; for the sake of bestowing gifts upon sentient beings, they diligently seek wealth and treasures without regarding such hardships as difficult.

Using medicinal herbs and incantations to transform copper into gold, and through various such transformations to acquire wealth and ownerless goods from the four quarters to provide for sentient beings—this is physical diligence.

Attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), being able to manifest transformations oneself, creating various exquisite flavors, or going to the heavens to take naturally occurring food—such as these are called mental diligence (*cittavīrya*).
To be able to gather wealth and treasures for the purpose of practicing giving is physical diligence;
to attain the Way of the Buddha through the merit of such giving is mental diligence.
When a Bodhisattva with a physical body practices the six pāramitās, this is called physical diligence;
when a Bodhisattva with a dharma-nature body practices the six pāramitās, this is called mental diligence. Before attaining the dharma-body, the mind follows the body;
once the dharma-body has been attained, the mind does not follow the body, and the body no longer burdens the mind.
Furthermore, to be able to accomplish all dharmas by not sparing one’s own body or life is physical diligence;
when seeking all meditative concentrations and wisdom, for the mind to be free from indolence is mental diligence.
Furthermore, as for physical diligence, one undergoes all manner of hardships and never slackens or desists.
As it is said:
"King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī was hunting in the wild forests."
He saw two herds of deer, each herd having its own leader; one leader had five hundred deer in his herd.
One leader’s body was the color of the seven treasures; this was the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni.
The other leader was Devadatta.
When the Bodhisattva Deer King saw that the human king’s great assembly was slaughtering his herd, he gave rise to a heart of great compassion and went straight before the king.
As the king’s men vied with one another to shoot, flying arrows fell like rain;
seeing that this deer advanced directly toward him without any fear or hesitation, the king commanded his attendants:
"Restrain your bow and arrows; do not sever their intention to come!
When the deer king arrived, he knelt and addressed the human king:
"Because of the minor matter of your amusement and pleasure, this entire herd of deer has simultaneously been subjected to the suffering of death."
"If you provide the meals, we shall arrange them in rotation, sending one deer daily to supply the King's kitchen.
The King approved of his words and granted his request.
Thereupon, the two leaders of the deer herds held a great assembly and established a rotation, such that each day one deer was sent according to the turn.
At that time, there was a pregnant doe within Devadatta’s herd who came and said to her leader:
"It is my turn today to be sent as a victim for death; however, I am pregnant, and this child is not yet due."
"I beg you to grant me this favor: let the dead receive their due, and let the living not be unjustly implicated!
The deer king spoke in anger, saying, "Who is there that does not cherish their own life?"
"Furthermore, you have come here only to depart;
how can you refuse? The mother deer reflected:
"My king is unkind and lacks the compassion of reason. He does not examine my plea but instead becomes cross and angry at random; he is not worth addressing!"
He immediately went to where the Bodhisattva-king was and reported the matter in full.
The king asked this deer,
"What did your master say?"
The deer said, "My lord is unkind;
he does not provide for me but shows me only anger.
Your Majesty’s benevolence extends to all beings, therefore I have come to take refuge in you."
"As I am today, though heaven and earth are vast, there is no one to whom I can appeal!
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"This is truly pitiable!"
If I do not attend to him, his son will be unjustly killed;
yet if he were to appoint someone other than the next in line, and that person has not yet reached their turn, how could such a replacement be sent?
There is no choice but for me to take his place.
Having thus resolved, he immediately offered himself up and sent the doe back, saying, "I shall now take your place; do not be anxious!
The deer king went straight to the king's gate; when the people saw him, they marveled at his coming of his own accord and reported the matter to the king.
The king also marveled at this and ordered him to come forward, asking:
"Are all the deer gone? Why have you come?"
The Deer King said:
"Great King, your benevolence extends to the entire herd of deer; since no one harms them, they flourish and prosper—how could there ever be an end to them?

Within my own herd, there was a doe who was pregnant. As her delivery drew near, she informed me that she would surely perish at the slaughter, and her unborn child would likewise lose its life. Out of compassion for her, I [intervened]."
To replace them with those who are unsuitable is likewise unacceptable;
yet if one returns home without providing rescue, one is no different from wood or stone.
This body will not last long; death is inevitably unavoidable.
"Compassion that rescues others from suffering and calamity brings immeasurable merit.
If a person lacks compassion, they are no different from tigers or wolves.
Upon hearing these words, the king rose immediately from his seat and spoke this verse:
"I am truly a beast, named 'the human-headed deer';
though you have the body of a deer, you are called 'the deer-headed human.
Speaking according to principle, one is not a human by virtue of physical form alone."
If one possesses compassion and kindness, though they be a beast, they are truly human.
From this day forward, I shall not eat any meat;
by bestowing upon you the gift of fearlessness, may your mind find peace!
The deer found peace, and the king attained benevolence and faith.
Furthermore, it was like the brahmin Dharmapriya, who for twelve years traveled throughout Jambudvīpa seeking the noble Dharma but could not find it;
at that time, no Buddha had appeared in the world, and the Buddha-Dharma had already vanished.
A certain brāhmaṇa said:
"I possess a single verse of the noble Dharma; if you truly love the Dharma, I shall give it to you!
He replied:
"Truly you love the Dharma!
the Brahmin said.
"If you truly love the Dharma, you should take your own skin as paper, your own bones as a pen, and write it with your own blood; then I shall give it to you!"
He then acted exactly as he had said: he broke his bones and flayed his skin, writing the verse with his blood:
"One should practice in accordance with the Dharma; That which is contrary to the Dharma should not be accepted.
In this life and in lives to come, The practitioner of the Dharma dwells in peace."

Furthermore, in the past, when a wild fire burned a forest, there was a pheasant within it who exerted its own strength and flew into the water. It soaked its feathers and wings and returned to extinguish the great fire;
though the fire was vast and the water scarce, and it grew weary from coming and going, it did not consider this to be suffering.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, came and asked him,
"What are you doing? He replied:
"I shall save this forest out of compassion for sentient beings!
This forest is a vast place of shelter and nurture, cool, refreshing, and blissful; my own kind, my kinsmen, and all sentient beings alike rely upon and look up to it."
"I possess physical strength; why should I be indolent and fail to rescue it?
The Lord of Devas asked, "How long will you continue in such diligent exertion?"
The pheasant said,
"I shall die as my appointed time!
The Lord of Devas said:
"Although your mind is thus, who can testify to it?
He then made this vow:
"If my heart is sincere and my faith is not false, may the fire be extinguished at once!"
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas, knowing the Bodhisattva’s great vow, immediately extinguished the fire.
From antiquity to the present, only this grove has always remained uniquely lush and flourishing, never being consumed by fire.

Such various deeds performed in past lives—those difficult to accomplish yet accomplished—involved not sparing his own body or life, nor his kingdom, wealth, wife, children, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, or even his head, eyes, marrow, and bones; he practiced diligent giving without weariness.

As it is said, for the sake of all sentient beings, a bodhisattva undergoes a thousand deaths and a thousand births in a single day; such is the practice within the perfections of giving (dāna), ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), meditative concentration (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā).
The various causes and conditions found within the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-jātaka-sūtra* constitute physical diligence.

To practice and take joy in all wholesome dharmas, to be free from doubt or regret and not to be indolent, and to seek the Dharma without weariness—from all the worthy and holy ones down to ordinary people—just as the ocean swallows all streams, constitutes the mental diligence of a bodhisattva.
Question:
It is not the case that the mind is never satiated. Why is this so?
If the matter sought has been accomplished and the wish fulfilled, one ought to be satisfied.
If the principle cannot be pursued and the matter cannot be accomplished, one ought likewise to abandon it; why then do you never feel weary or satisfied?
It is like a person digging a well in search of a spring: the more effort they exert, the more they find no sign of water, and thus they ought to desist.
It is also like traveling on a path: once one has reached the destination, one should not continue further. Why, then, is there such constant lack of satiety?
The answer is:

The diligence of a bodhisattva cannot be compared by means of worldly analogies. It is like digging a well: if one lacks sufficient strength, one will not obtain water, yet it is not that there is no water;
if there is no water at this spot, it must certainly exist elsewhere.
Wherever he may go, he must seek to reach Buddhahood; having reached Buddhahood, he never tires, and in instructing others, he never grows weary—thus it is said he is "tireless.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s diligence is vast and expansive in its aspiration, vowing to deliver all beings;
yet since sentient beings are inexhaustible, his diligence likewise can never be exhausted.
As for your statement that "once the task is accomplished, one should cease," this is not the case!
Although one may attain Buddhahood, as long as sentient beings are not yet exhausted, one must not rest.
It is like the nature of fire: if it is not extinguished, it will never grow cold.
The diligence of a bodhisattva is likewise: until they have entered parinirvāṇa, they never rest.
For this reason, among the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), both aspiration and diligence are constantly cultivated.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom by not dwelling in any phenomena, they do not abandon diligence; this is the diligence of a bodhisattva, not the diligence of a Buddha.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva has not yet attained the bodhisattva path, they bestow beneficial things upon sentient beings with their body subject to birth and death; yet the sentient beings, in turn, inflict unwholesome things upon them.

There may be sentient beings who, when the Bodhisattva praises them, instead revile him; who, when the Bodhisattva shows them respect, instead treat him with contempt; who, when the Bodhisattva regards them with compassion, instead seek out his faults, plotting to harm him.
These sentient beings, lacking any power or influence, come to harass the Bodhisattva.
Regarding these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva makes this great vow:
"Once I have attained the Way of the Buddha, I shall certainly deliver these multitudes of sentient beings who are the most wicked among the wicked!"
Amidst this evil, his mind remains undaunted and he gives rise to great compassion;
it is like a loving mother who, pitying her child’s illness, grieves for them without ceasing.
Such characteristics as these constitute the diligence of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), various beggars from the ten directions come seeking to obtain things; even those who should not ask come to solicit them, including objects that are cherished and difficult to relinquish. They say to the bodhisattva: "Give me both eyes;
give me your head, brain, and marrow; give me your beloved wife and children, as well as all your precious and costly treasures."

Regarding such things as these that are difficult to relinquish, even when a beggar demands them by force, his mind remains unmoved; he gives rise to neither stinginess nor anger, and no doubt arises in his sight. With a single mind, he practices giving for the sake of the Buddha-way;
he is like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be shaken by the winds blowing from the four directions.
Such various characteristics as these are called the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva’s vigor universally practices the five perfections, this constitutes the perfection of vigor.
Question:
When practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), if someone comes and begs for one's three robes and alms bowl, if one gives them away, one violates the precepts. Why is this?
Because the Buddha did not permit it.
If one does not give, then one violates the *dānapāramitā*; how then can diligence (*vīrya*) practice all five matters universally?
The answer is:
If a bodhisattva is a beginner, they cannot practice all five pāramitās simultaneously and throughout a single lifetime.
For example, when a bodhisattva practices the dānapāramitā and sees a starving tigress in desperate hunger, about to devour her cubs,
the bodhisattva then gives rise to great compassion and immediately offers his own body as a gift.
Because the Bodhisattva’s parents lost their son, they fell into grief and distress until both their eyes went blind;
yet the tiger that killed the Bodhisattva should likewise incur the fault of taking life.
However, [the parents] did not consider the sorrow and suffering of their own parents, nor did the tiger consider the karmic guilt incurred by killing.
He merely wishes to fulfill his practice of giving so as to obtain merit for himself.
It is like a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts; according to the gravity of the offense, he expels those who violate the law.
Those who are expelled feel sorrow, suffering, and distress.
They merely desire to uphold the precepts and do not take pity on the suffering [of others].
At times, they practice worldly prajñā and allow their hearts of compassion to cease.
For example, when Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was the crown prince of a great king in a previous life.
The King, his father, had a Brahmin teacher who did not eat the five grains; the people revered and trusted him, regarding him as extraordinary.
The Prince reflected:

"A person has four limbs, which must necessarily depend upon the five grains for sustenance. Yet this man does not eat them; he must surely be seeking to win over the hearts of the people, and this is not the true Dharma!"
The parents said to their son:
"This man is diligent and does not eat the five grains; he is a rarity in this world. Why are you so foolish as to fail to revere him?"
The Prince replied, "I pray you keep a close watch on this man; before long, the proof will manifest itself!
At that time, the Prince sought out his dwelling place and went among the groves of trees, where he questioned the cowherds in the forest:
"What does this man eat?
The cowherd replied, "During the night,
he consumes a small amount of ghee to sustain his life."
Having understood this, the Prince returned to the palace, intending to produce proof of his realization. He immediately took various medicinal herbs and incensed a blue lotus with them.
At dawn, when the Brahmin entered the palace and sat beside the King, the Prince took the flower in his hand and came to offer it to him;
after prostrating, he presented it to him.
The brahmin was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"The king and queen, along with all those within and without, great and small, all serve and attend to me; only the crown prince has not shown me respect or faith.
Today he has made an offering of exquisite flowers—this is most excellent and immeasurable!"
Having obtained these beautiful flowers, he respected their place of origin and held them up to his nose to smell them.
The medicinal scent from within the flowers entered his stomach; in a short while, the medicine took effect inside him, and he felt the urge to find a place to relieve himself.
The Prince said,
"Brahmin, if you do not eat, for what reason would you go to the latrine?
He then seized him urgently.
In a brief moment, he spat it out before the king; what was spat out was pure ghee.
Once this proof had been manifested, the king and his consort realized it was a deception.
The prince said:
"This man is truly a thief!
For the sake of seeking fame, he deceives the entire kingdom.
Practicing worldly *prajñā* in this manner, one seeks only to fulfill one's own wisdom, neglects the heart of compassion, and does not fear the anger of others.
At times, when a bodhisattva practices supramundane prajñā, their mind does not become attached to ethical discipline or giving.

Why is this? Because the giver, the recipient, and the gift; sin and non-sin; anger and non-anger; diligence and indolence; and the concentrated mind and the distracted mind—all these are unapprehendable.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of vigor, they understand that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither suffering nor happiness, neither empty nor substantial, neither self nor non-self, neither identical nor different, and neither existent nor non-existent;
they fully know that all phenomena are merely the conjunction of causes and conditions, existing only as names, while their true nature is ungraspable.

The Bodhisattva contemplates in this way, knowing that all conditioned phenomena are entirely false and deceptive; his mind rests in the unconditioned, desiring to extinguish the mind, and finds peace only in cessation.
At that time, out of compassion for sentient beings and mindful of his original vow, he returned to practicing the Dharma of a bodhisattva and accumulated all manner of merit.
The bodhisattva thought to himself:

"Although I know that all phenomena are empty and deceptive, sentient beings do not understand this; they undergo various sufferings within the five realms of existence. I shall now fully practice the six pāramitās."
The Bodhisattva, having attained supernormal powers as a reward for his practice, also attains the Buddha-way:

the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all-encompassing wisdom, great kindness and great compassion, unimpeded liberation, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the three types of penetration, and other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.
When this Dharma is attained, all sentient beings achieve purity of faith and are able to receive, practice, and cherish the Buddha-Dharma.
That they are able to accomplish these matters is entirely due to the power of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
This is the perfection of diligence.
As the Buddha has said:
"At that time, the bodhisattva practices diligence without perceiving the body and without perceiving the mind."
The body performs no action and the mind harbors no thought; body and mind are one and the same, without distinction.

One seeks the Buddha-way for the sake of delivering sentient beings, yet does not perceive sentient beings as this shore or the Buddha-way as the other shore, relinquishing all activities of body and mind;
like that which is done in a dream, upon awakening, there is nothing done.
This is called a "perfection" (pāramitā) because it is the quiescence of all forms of exertion.
Why is this so? Because one knows that all such exertions are ultimately false and deceptive.
Since all conditioned phenomena are false and unreal, like dreams and illusions;
and since the equality of all dharmas is what constitutes reality—
within this state of equal dharma, there should be nothing to seek or obtain— it is therefore known that all forms of diligence are likewise false and unreal.
"Although one knows that diligence is illusory, yet constantly achieves non-retrogression—this is called the Bodhisattva’s true diligence.
As the Buddha said:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have given my head, eyes, marrow, and brain to sentient beings, causing their vows to be fulfilled."
When practicing precepts, patience, and meditative concentration in mountain forests, their bodies become withered;

or by observing fasts and restricting food, or by renouncing all sensory pleasures and flavors, or by enduring the afflictions of verbal abuse, insults, swords, and staves, their bodies consequently become parched and emaciated.
Furthermore, he constantly sits in meditation, exposing himself to the elements and enduring diligent hardship in order to seek wisdom;
he recites, contemplates, interrogates, and expounds upon all dharmas;
and by means of wisdom, he discriminates between the good and the evil, the coarse and the subtle, the false and the true, and the much and the little.
I made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, diligently and vigorously seeking these merits, desiring to fulfill the five pāramitās.
At that time, I attained nothing; I did not attain the pāramitās of dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, or prajñā.

Upon seeing Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he scattered five flowers over the Buddha and spread his hair upon the mud; thereby attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the six *pāramitās* were immediately fulfilled.
Standing in mid-air, he praised Dīpaṃkara Buddha with verses and beheld the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions; at that time, he attained true diligence (*vīrya*).
Because physical diligence is equal, one attains equality of mind; because the mind is equal, one attains equality regarding all dharmas.
Such various characteristics of causal conditions are called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Dhyānapāramitā, Number Twenty-eight, Volume Seventeen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by imperial decree. 28. Dhyānapāramitā [Sūtra]: “Because it is neither distracted nor savoring, one should fulfill the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).”
[Treatise] Question:

The dharma of a bodhisattva takes the deliverance of all sentient beings as its task. For what reason does he sit idly in forests and marshes, remaining silent among the mountains, seeking only his own private perfection while abandoning sentient beings?
The answer is:

Although the Bodhisattva’s body remains far removed from sentient beings, his mind never abandons them; seeking meditative concentration in a quiet place, he attains true wisdom to deliver all beings.

For example, when one takes medicine to restore the body, one temporarily suspends household affairs; once one’s strength and vigor are restored to health, one resumes one’s work as before. It is the same with the Bodhisattva’s tranquil seclusion:

by means of the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they take the medicine of wisdom and attain the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), then return among sentient beings—sometimes acting as parents, wives, or children; sometimes as teachers, disciples, or clan elders; whether as gods or humans, down to animals—they employ various modes of speech and skillful means to guide them.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices generosity, upholds the precepts, and cultivates patience—these three matters are called the gates of merit.

Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he becomes a celestial king, Śakra Devānām Indra, a wheel-turning sage king, or a king of Jambudvīpa; he constantly bestows upon sentient beings garments of the seven treasures and whatever their five senses desire, ensuring they are fully provided for in both this life and future lives.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Wheel-Turning Sage King instructs his people in the ten wholesome actions; consequently, they are all reborn in the heavens in future lives.
From generation to generation, he benefits sentient beings, enabling them to attain happiness."
"This pleasure is impermanent; one will again suffer.
Because of this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of great compassion, desiring to benefit sentient beings through the eternal bliss of Nirvana.
This eternal and blissful nirvana arises from true wisdom; true wisdom arises from single-minded meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It is like lighting a lamp: although the lamp can illuminate, it cannot fulfill its function amidst a great wind;
yet if it is placed within a secluded chamber, its utility becomes complete.
Wisdom within a distracted mind is also like this: if there is no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a quiet room, although wisdom may be present, its function is incomplete;
once meditative concentration is attained, true wisdom arises.
For this reason, although a bodhisattva is separated from sentient beings and dwells far away in a quiet place to seek meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
because that meditative concentration is pure, wisdom is also pure; it is like how,
when the oil and the wick are pure, the light is also pure.
For this reason, those who wish to attain pure wisdom should practice this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, if one seeks even mundane, immediate matters and cannot concentrate the mind, one's undertakings will not succeed; how much more so for the profound path of the Buddha, which cannot be achieved without meditative concentration!
Dhyāna-samādhi is called the gathering of all distracted minds.
Distracted minds are as light and flighty as a goose feather;
they scatter and disperse without ceasing, racing faster than a swift wind.
It cannot be restrained; it is more restless than a monkey.
It appears for a moment and then vanishes, more swiftly than a flash of lightning.
The characteristics of the mind are such that they cannot be prohibited; if one wishes to control them, it will not be possible without meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
As the verse says:
"Dhyāna is the treasury that guards wisdom, The field of merit for all virtues;
Dhyāna is the water of purity, Able to wash away the dust of all desires."
Dhyāna is the adamantine armor, capable of warding off the arrows of affliction;
though one has not yet attained nirvana without remainder, a portion of it has already been gained.
Having attained the adamantine samādhi, one shatters the mountain of fetters and latent tendencies.
Having attained the power of the six supernormal knowledges, one is able to deliver immeasurable beings.
When the dust of worldly clamor obscures the sun in the sky, a great rain can submerge it;
when the winds of discursive thought and investigation scatter the mind, meditative concentration can extinguish them.
Furthermore, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is difficult to attain; only when a practitioner seeks it with single-minded devotion without ceasing will they obtain it.
Even the devas and immortals cannot attain it, let alone ordinary people with indolent minds!
When the Buddha was sitting in meditation beneath a nyagrodha tree, the three daughters of Māra spoke in verse, asking:
"Sitting alone amidst the forest trees, Your six sense-faculties are ever tranquil and silent.
It is as if you have lost a precious treasure; Lacking any support, you suffer the poison of sorrow."
"Your countenance is peerless in the world, yet you always sit with eyes closed;
we have doubts in our hearts—what do you seek that you are here?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"I have attained the taste of Nirvana; I no longer delight in dwelling amidst defiled attachments.
Internal and external thieves have been eliminated, and even your father has passed away.
I have attained the taste of the Deathless (Amṛta) and sit in peace within the forest."
"Sentient beings bound by affection—may I arouse a heart of loving-kindness for them.
At that time, the three daughters felt shame and said to themselves:
"This man has transcended desire; he cannot be moved."
He then vanished and was no longer seen.
A question was asked:
"By what skillful means does one attain the dhyāna-pāramitā?"
The answer is:
One sets aside the five matters and the five sense objects, eliminates the five dharmas and the five hindrances, and practices the five conducts.
What is meant by setting aside the five matters?
One should rebuke the five desires.
Alas for sentient beings!
Constantly tormented by the five desires, they nevertheless seek them without ceasing!
These five desires, when obtained, only increase in intensity, like roasting scabies with fire.
The five desires are of no benefit, like a dog gnawing on a bone.
The five desires increase contention, like birds competing for meat.
The five desires burn people like holding a torch against the wind;
the five desires harm people like treading upon a venomous snake;
the five desires lack reality, like what is obtained in a dream.
The five desires are not enduring, like a temporary loan for a mere moment.
Worldly people, deluded and ignorant, are greedily attached to these five desires; they do not abandon them until death, thereby undergoing immeasurable suffering in future lives.
It is like a foolish person who, craving delicious fruit, climbs a tree to eat it and refuses to descend in a timely manner;
when others cut down the tree, he falls as it topples over, his body and head shattered, dying in agony and distress.
Furthermore, these five desires bring but a momentary pleasure when obtained, yet become a source of great suffering when lost;
they are like a knife smeared with honey—the one who licks it craves the sweetness, unaware that it will wound the tongue.
The phenomena of the five desires are shared with the animals; those who possess wisdom recognize this and are able to distance themselves from them.
As it is said:
there was once a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who traveled far with a group of merchants to engage in trade for a livelihood.
At that time, amidst the cold snow, he lost his companions while traveling at night and stayed within a stone cave.
Then, a mountain spirit transformed into a woman and came to test him, speaking this verse:
"The white snow covers the mountains and plains; birds and beasts all hide away."
"I alone have no one to rely upon; I only pray that you will take pity on me!
The upāsaka covered his ears with both hands and replied in verse:
"Shameless and depraved man, you utter such impure words!"
Even if swept away by water or consumed by fire, I would not wish to hear your voice!
If even a wife’s heart has no desire for you, how much less would one engage in sexual misconduct?
The pleasures of desire are exceedingly shallow, while the great suffering and affliction are exceedingly deep.
All desires are insatiable; losing them is a great suffering.
Not having obtained them, one longs for them; having obtained them, one is tormented by them.
The pleasures of all desires are very few, while the poisons of sorrow and suffering are exceedingly many.
"For his sake, he has risked his very life and limb, like a moth rushing into a lamp's flame!
Having heard this verse, the mountain spirit immediately lifted the man up and delivered him back to his companions.
This is why the wise reprove desire and must not be attached to it.
The five desires are known as exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles;
those who seek meditative concentration should abandon them all.
What is meant by abandoning form?
One contemplates the afflictions of form: if a person is attached to form, the fires of all the fetters and latent tendencies blaze up intensely, burning and harming the human body.
Just as when fire burns gold and silver, or when boiling hot honey—though possessing color and flavor—burns the body and scorches the mouth, one must urgently abandon it.
If a person is attached to exquisite forms or delicious flavors, it is likewise so.
Furthermore, beauty and ugliness reside in the person; form itself has no fixed nature.
How is this known?
Just as when one sees a loved one from afar, a heart of affection and joy arises;
if one sees an enemy or a wicked person from afar, a heart of anger and malice arises;
and if one sees a neutral person, there is neither anger nor joy.
If you wish to abandon this anger and joy, you must eliminate both perverse thoughts and form simultaneously;
it is like being burned by molten gold—if you wish to remove the pain, you cannot merely desire to discard the fire while keeping the gold, for you must discard both the gold and the fire together.
For example, King Bimbisāra, for the sake of physical beauty, entered an enemy kingdom with his own body and remained alone in the chamber of the courtesan Āmrapālī.
King Udayana, due to being stained by passion for beauty, cut off the hands and feet of five hundred rishis.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, this is called the censure of form and desire.
What is the censure of sound?
The characteristic of sound does not abide; it ceases as soon as it is briefly heard.
Foolish people, not understanding that the characteristics of sound are impermanent, subject to change, and perishable, falsely give rise to attachment and delight toward sounds;
they conceive craving by recollecting sounds that have already passed.
For example, there were five hundred sages dwelling in the mountains who heard the singing of a Kinnarī bathing in a pool in the Snowy Mountains;
upon hearing her song, they immediately lost their meditative concentration, their minds became intoxicated and wild, and they could not restrain themselves.

It is like a great wind blowing through the trees of a forest; hearing this subtle and exquisite singing, which is soft and pure, they give rise to perverse thoughts. Consequently, they do not realize their minds have gone mad;
they lose all merits in this life and shall fall into the evil realms in the next!
A person of wisdom observes that sounds arise and perish from moment to moment; they do not coexist before and after, and there is nothing that can reach them.
Knowing this, one does not give rise to defiled attachment.
For such a person, even the music of the devas cannot disturb them, let alone human voices.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, this is called the "reproval of the desire for sound."
What is meant by reviling incense?
People say that applying incense involves little fault; yet, one becomes stained by and attached to the fragrance, thereby opening the gates of the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Although one may have observed the precepts for a hundred years, this [attachment] can destroy them all at once.
For instance, there was an Arhat who frequently entered the dragon palace; after he had finished eating, he handed his bowl to a śrāmaṇera to wash.
Inside the bowl were a few grains of leftover rice; when the śrāmaṇera smelled them, they were exceedingly fragrant, and upon eating them, they were most delicious.
He then employed a skillful means, entering beneath his teacher’s rope bed and grasping its legs with both hands;
when his teacher arrived, he entered the dragon palace together with the rope bed.
The dragon said, "This one has not yet attained the Way; why have you brought him here?
The Master replied:
"I do not know.

The śrāmaṇera took the food and ate it; furthermore, seeing that the dragon girl’s body was upright and her fragrance incomparably exquisite, his mind became deeply attached to her, and he immediately made this vow:
"I shall perform meritorious deeds so as to seize this dragon's place and dwell in her palace!"
The dragon said, "Henceforth, do not bring this śrāmaṇera here!
After the śrāmaṇera had returned, he practiced giving and upheld the precepts with single-minded devotion, seeking exclusively for his wish: that he might quickly become a dragon.
At that time, as he circumambulated the monastery, water welled up from beneath his feet; he knew for certain that he would become a dragon.
He went directly to the edge of the great pond where his teacher had originally entered, covered his head with his *kāṣāya*, and went in. He died immediately and was transformed into a great dragon.
Because his merit and virtue were so vast, he killed the previous dragon, and the entire pond turned crimson.
Before that had occurred, the various masters and the Sangha rebuked him.
The śrāmaṇera said:
"My mind is already settled; the characteristics of the mind have already emerged."
At that time, the teacher led the assembly of monks to the pond to observe it.
Such was the causal condition arising from the attachment to the fragrance.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was walking up and down by a lotus pond in the forest; he smelled the fragrance of the lotuses, and his mind became joyful and delighted, and as he passed by, he felt a sense of longing for them.
The deity of the pond said to him:
"For what reason have you abandoned your place of pure meditation beneath that grove to steal my incense?
Because of your attachment to this fragrance, all the latent defilements (*anuśaya*) that were lying dormant have now arisen."
At that time, another person came into the pond, gathered many of its flowers, and dug up and pulled out the roots and stalks, departing in a state of disorder;
the deity of the pond remained silent and said nothing.
The bhikṣu said,
"This man broke your pond and took your flowers, yet you said nothing at all;
but when I merely walked along the bank of the pond, you immediately scolded and reviled me, saying I was stealing your fragrance!"
The deity of the pond said:
"Evil people in this world are constantly immersed head-deep in the filth of sinful defilements; I do not speak with them.
You are a good person practicing meditation, yet you are clinging to this fragrance, which ruins your virtuous practice. For this reason, I rebuke you!"
For example, if a piece of white cotton cloth were fresh, pure, and clean, yet stained with black spots, everyone would see them;
but as for that evil person, he is like ink spots on black clothing—no one sees them, so who would question him?
Through various causes and conditions such as these, this is called the censure of desire for fragrance.
What is the censure of flavor?
One should awaken to it within oneself:
"Because I was merely attached to delicious flavors, I shall undergo manifold sufferings: molten copper poured into my mouth and swallowing glowing iron balls;
if one does not contemplate the nature of food and remains firmly attached with a craving mind, one will fall among the impure worms."

For example, there was once a novice monk who constantly craved curd. Whenever donors brought curd to the Sangha, the novice would always receive the leftovers; he became so attached to them that he delighted in them and could not let go.
After his life ended, he was reborn inside that jar of leftover curd.
