The śrāmaṇera’s preceptor had attained the path of arhatship; when the saṃgha was distributing the curd, he said:
"Be careful! Do not harm this śrāmaṇera who is so fond of curd!"
The people said, "This is a worm; why do you call it the novice who loves curd?
He replied:
"This insect was originally my śrāmaṇera; it was born within this jar solely because of his greed for the leftover curd.
When the teacher received his portion of the curd, the insect emerged from within it.
The Master said:
"O lover of curd! Why have you come?"
He immediately gave him the curd.
Furthermore, it is like a certain kingdom where there was a king named Candrabhāga.
The king had a crown prince who was attached to fine flavors, and the king’s garden keeper sent him excellent fruits every day.
In the garden there was a great tree, upon which a bird had raised its young. It would often fly to Mount Gandhamādana to gather fine fragrant fruits to nourish its offspring;
as the many fledglings vied with one another, one fruit fell to the ground. Early in the morning, the garden keeper saw it and, marveling at its extraordinary nature, immediately sent it to the king.
The king prized this fruit for its extraordinary fragrance and color; when the prince saw it, he immediately asked for it. Out of love for his son, the king gave it to him at once.
After the prince ate the fruit, he became captivated by its flavor and became deeply attached to it, desiring to have it day after day.
The king then summoned the gardener and questioned him as to its origin.
The gardener said, "These fruits have no seeds; I obtained them from the ground, and I do not know whence they came.
The Prince wept and refused to eat. The King rebuked the gardener, saying, "I rely on you to obtain these for me."
When the gardener arrived at the place where he had found the fruit, he saw a bird’s nest and realized the bird had brought it there. He concealed himself in the tree, waiting to seize it;
whenever the mother bird returned, he would snatch the fruit and send her away, doing so day after day.
The mother bird became enraged and went to Mount Gandhamādana to fetch poisonous fruits; their fragrance, flavor, and color were exactly like those of the previous ones.
The gardeners seized them and presented them to the king, who gave them to the prince to eat. Before long, the flesh of his body rotted away and he died.
The attachment to flavors is like this; it brings about the suffering of losing one's body.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, this is called the censure of attachment to the desire for flavors.
What is the censure of touch?
This contact is the primary cause for the arising of all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the very root that binds the mind. Why is this?
While the other four sense-faculties each operate within their own respective domains, this [contact] pervades the consciousness of the entire body.
Because the places of birth are vast, one frequently gives rise to defiled attachment, and this attachment is difficult to abandon.
How is this known?
For example, when a person is attached to physical form, if they contemplate the thirty-six kinds of impurity of the body, a sense of revulsion will arise.

If one becomes attached to touch, even though one knows it is impure, one craves its subtlety and softness; thus, contemplating impurity provides no benefit, and for this reason, it is difficult to abandon.
Furthermore, because it is so difficult to relinquish, one constantly commits grave offenses on its account.
If one falls into hell, there are two divisions of hells:
the first is named Cold Ice, and the second is named Blazing Fire.
Within these two hells, all undergo punishment through physical contact, with myriad forms of bitter suffering.
This contact is called the place of great darkness, a perilous and treacherous path.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Rāhulamātṛ-jātaka*:
"The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni had two wives; one was named Gopī and the other was named Yaśodharā."
Yaśodharā was the mother of Rāhula.
Gopikā was a woman of precious virtue, and therefore she did not conceive a son.
On the very night the Bodhisattva left the household life, Yaśodharā realized she was pregnant.
While the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years after leaving the household life, Yaśodharā likewise carried her pregnancy for six years without giving birth.
The Śākyas questioned her, saying:
"The Bodhisattva has gone forth; by what cause has this come about?"
Yaśodharā said, "I have committed no other transgression;
the child I carry is truly the biological offspring of the Prince.
The Śākyas said:
"Why has it been so long without producing?
He replied,
"This is not something I know!"
When the Śākyas gathered for deliberation and heard that the King intended to punish him according to the law,
Gopiyā said to the King:
"I pray that you grant him clemency!"
"I have always lived with Yaśodharā; I shall be her witness, knowing her to be without fault.
Wait until her son is born, and see whether he resembles his father or not; it will not be too late to deal with him then!"
The king immediately released him.
When the six years of the Buddha’s ascetic practice were completed and he first attained enlightenment, Rāhula was born that very night.
Seeing that the child resembled his father, the king loved him dearly and forgot his sorrows.
He said to his ministers, "Although my son has departed, I have now obtained this grandson; he is no different from my own son!
Although Yaśodharā was spared from punishment and exile, her ill repute filled the kingdom.

Yaśodharā wished to clear her ill repute; after the Buddha had attained enlightenment and returned to Kapilavastu to convert the Śākyas, King Śuddhodana and Yaśodharā frequently invited the Buddha to enter the palace for meals.
At that time, Yaśodharā took a bowl of hundred-flavored *mṛdvīkā* (joy-fruit) cakes and gave them to Rāhula, instructing him to present them to the Buddha.
Then, by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the Buddha transformed five hundred arhats so that they all appeared exactly like the Buddha’s own body, without any distinction.
With his seven-year-old body, Rāhula took the *modaka* sweets and went directly before the Buddha to offer them to the World-Honored One.

At that moment, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and the bodies of the bhikṣus returned to their former state; they all sat with empty bowls, while only the bowl of the Buddha was filled to the brim with *modaka* sweets.
Yaśodharā then said to the King:
"By this proof, I am without fault!
Yaśodharā then asked the Buddha:
“What karmic conditions have I that I have carried a child in my womb for six years?
The Buddha said,
“Your son Rāhula, in a time long past, was once a king.”
At that time, a seer possessing the five supernatural powers came into the king’s realm and said to the king:
"The King's law punishes criminals; I pray you, punish my offense!
The king said:
"What crime have you committed?
He replied, "I entered Your Majesty’s kingdom and committed the offense of taking what was not given; I drank Your Majesty’s water and used Your Majesty’s tooth-stick!"
The king said, "I gave it to you as a gift; what crime could there be in that?
Since my initial accession to the throne, I have offered water and willow branches to all beings!"
The seer said:
"Although the King has already made the offering, my mind remains filled with doubt and regret; thus, my transgression is not yet removed!
I pray that you will now provide me with a remedy, so that I may avoid future sin."
The king said,
"If you must have it so, wait a moment until I have gone in and returned!
The king entered the palace and did not come out for six days.
This seer, within the king’s garden, was hungry and thirsty for six days.
The seer reflected:
"The king is indeed treating me in this manner."
After six days had passed, the king emerged and apologized to the seer, saying:
"I have simply forgotten you; do not hold this against me!

Because of these causes and conditions, he underwent the retribution of the three evil realms for five hundred lifetimes, and for five hundred lifetimes he remained in his mother’s womb for six years each.
"By this evidence, Yaśodharā is without fault.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal and departed, Yaśodharā felt regret in her heart, thinking:
"Such a virtuous man, rare in the world, whom I have encountered, I shall now lose forever!"
When the World-Honored One sat, he gazed steadily without blinking;
when the World-Honored One departed, he followed after him with his gaze until the Buddha had vanished into the distance, whereupon he stopped.
His heart was filled with great remorse, and whenever this thought arose, he would fall to the ground and lose consciousness.
Those by his side sprinkled him with water, whereupon he regained consciousness.
He reflected alone:
"Who in the world can skillfully perform incantations to transform this mind and restore it to its original state, so that joy may return as it was before?"
He then took a famous jewel made of the seven treasures, placed it upon a golden platter, and offered it to recruit someone.
A certain Brahmin responded to him, saying:
"I can cast spells over it to cause his mind to change."

One should prepare "joy-pills" of a hundred flavors, blending them with medicinal herbs and consecrating them with incantations; thus their minds will be transformed, and they will surely come without doubt!
Yaśodharā, having received these instructions, sent a messenger to invite the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you, together with the noble assembly, would deign to manifest your majestic power!
When the Buddha entered the royal palace, Yaśodharā immediately took hundred-flavored *mudgā* (joy-pills) and placed them in the Buddha’s bowl.
After the Buddha had eaten it, Yaśodharā hoped that her wishes would be fulfilled and rejoiced as before.
Yet the Buddha’s food remained unchanged, and his mind and eyes were serene and still. Yaśodharā said:
"He who is now unmoving does so only because the power of the medicine has not yet taken effect;
when the potency of the medicine manifests, he will surely fulfill my wish!
After the Buddha had finished his meal and offered his blessing, he rose from his seat and departed.
Yaśodharā hoped that through the power of the medicine, when the sun set at the hour of *puṣya*, he would surely return to the palace.
The Buddha ate as usual, with no change in his body or mind.
On the following day at mealtime, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food; they heard this matter in full and their reverence increased.
The Buddha’s power is immeasurable and his divine mind is difficult to fathom—truly inconceivable!
Although the medicinal joy-pills given by Yaśodharā possessed immense potency, when the World-Honored One consumed them, there was no change whatsoever in his body or mind.
After the bhikṣus had finished their meal, they left the city and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Yaśodharā has not only deceived me with *modaka* cakes in this present life; in a past life as well, she deceived me with *modaka* cakes!"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the bhikṣus of a past-life因缘 (nidāna):
"In the distant past, there was a rishi dwelling in the mountains of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
In the second month of spring, while urinating into a washbasin, he saw a male and female deer mating; his lustful mind was immediately stirred, and his semen flowed into the basin.
A doe drank from it and immediately became pregnant.
When the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose form resembled that of a human, except for having a single horn on his head and feet like those of a deer.
When the deer was about to give birth, she went to the edge of the seer’s hermitage and gave birth there.
Seeing that the offspring was human, she entrusted it to the seer and departed.
When the seer came out and saw this fawn, he recalled his past karmic connection; realizing it was his own son, he took it and raised it.
When he grew older, he applied himself diligently to study and inquiry, mastering eighteen kinds of great sūtras.
He further practiced seated meditation and cultivated the four immeasurable minds, whereby he immediately attained the five supernormal powers.

Once, while ascending a mountain, he encountered heavy rain and the ground became slippery with mud. His feet being unsteady, he stumbled and fell, breaking his *piṭaka* (alms bowl) and injuring his foot.
He then became greatly incensed; taking water in his *piṭaka*, he chanted mantras to cause the rain to cease.
Due to the spiritual power of the rishi, all the dragons and spirits ceased sending rain.
Because of this lack of rain, the five grains and the five fruits failed to grow at all; the people fell into extreme poverty and were left with no means of survival.
The King of Vārāṇasī was filled with grief and distress, and he commanded his high officials to assemble for a council regarding the matter of the rain.
A wise man among them proposed:

"I have heard it said that on the Mountain of the Rishis there is a one-horned rishi; because his feet were infirm, he fell while climbing the mountain and injured his foot. In his anger, he cast a curse upon this rain, causing it not to fall for twelve years."
The King reflected, saying:
"If it does not rain for twelve years, my kingdom will come to an end, and there will be no people left!
The King immediately issued a proclamation: "To whoever can cause the seer to lose his five supernatural powers and become my subject, I shall grant half of the kingdom for them to rule."
"In this country of Vārāṇasī, there was a courtesan named Śāntā, peerless in her beauty. She came to respond to the king's recruitment and asked the people:
'Is this a human being?'"
"Is he not a human?
The crowd replied,
"He is indeed a human!"
"He was born from a seer.
The courtesan said,
"If he is such a man, I can destroy him."
Having spoken these words, she took a golden tray filled with fine jewels and said to the king,
"I shall ride upon the neck of this seer!
The courtesan immediately requested five hundred chariots to carry five hundred beautiful women.
There were five hundred deer-carts laden with various kinds of joy-pills, all compounded from a multitude of medicinal herbs and painted with various colors to resemble assorted fruits;
they also carried various potent fine wines whose color and flavor were like water.
Wearing garments of tree bark and clothing made of grass, he moved among the forest trees like a rishi;
by the side of the rishi’s hermitage, he constructed a grass hut and dwelt there.
As the Rishi Ekata was traveling along, he saw them; all the women came out to welcome him, offering him fine flowers and fragrant incense as an act of worship, which greatly delighted the Rishi.

The women all addressed the seer with pleasant words and respectful greetings; they led him into a chamber and seated him upon a fine couch and bedding. They offered him excellent, pure wine as "purifying water" and gave him *mṛdvīkā* fruits as "fruit and melons."
Having finished eating and drinking his fill, he said to the women:
"Since my birth, I have never before obtained such excellent fruit and such excellent water!
The women replied:
"Because I have practiced virtue with a single-minded heart, the devas have granted my wish, and I have obtained these excellent fruits and excellent water.
The rishi asked the women,
"For what reason is your complexion so full and radiant?"
He replied, "We eat these fine fruits and drink this delicious water; that is why we are so plump and flourishing!
The woman said to the seer:
"Why do you not dwell here? He replied,
"I could indeed dwell here!"
The woman said,
"We may bathe together!
and he agreed to this as well.
The women's hands were soft and supple; when he touched them, his heart was moved.

He then began to bathe with the beautiful maidens one after another, and as lustful thoughts arose even more intensely, they eventually engaged in sexual intercourse. Immediately, he lost his supernormal powers, and the heavens sent down a great rain.
For seven days and seven nights, they were provided with food and drink that brought them joy.

After the seven days had passed, the wine and fruit were all exhausted; they were then supplied with water from the mountains and river and fruits from the trees, which were not as delicious, so they requested the former items once again.
He replied:
"It is exhausted!
Now we must go together; not far from here, there is a place where it can be obtained."
The seer said, "As you wish!
and they immediately went out together.
Knowing that the city was not far away, the lustful woman lay down on the road and said, "I am utterly exhausted;
I can go no further! The rishi said:
"If you cannot do it yourself," she said, "mount upon my neck and I shall carry you away!
The woman first sent a messenger to inform the king:
"Your Majesty may observe my intelligence."
The king ordered his carriage to be prepared and went out to observe it.
He asked, "By what means was this achieved?"
The woman said to the king:
"By the power of my skillful means, I have now reached such a state that I can do nothing more.
He had her reside within the city, providing her with excellent offerings and respect, satisfying her five desires, and appointing her as a high minister.
Having resided in the city for only a few days, his body grew increasingly emaciated;
he turned his mind toward the joy of meditative concentration and felt weary of worldly desires.
The King asked the seer:
"Why are you not joyful?
Why has your body become so emaciated?
The seer replied to the king:
"Although I have obtained the five desires, I constantly recall the tranquility of the forest groves where the various sages dwell; they cannot leave my mind.
The King reflected to himself:
"If I forcibly oppose his will, to oppose one's will is suffering, and when suffering reaches its extreme, death follows."
"Originally he sought this to eliminate the calamity of drought; now that his purpose has been achieved, for what reason should we forcibly thwart his resolve?
He was immediately sent back.
Once he returned to the mountains, through diligent practice, he soon regained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The seer Ekaśṛṅga was my own self;
the courtesan was Yaśodharā."
"At that time, you sought to delude me with a pill of joy; because I had not yet severed my fetters, I was deluded by it.
Now, you wish again to delude me with a medicinal pill of joy, but this shall not be possible!"
For this reason, one knows that even the quality of subtle and soft touch can disturb a rishi, let alone an ordinary person.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, this is called the censure of the desire for smoothness and softness.
Thus one rebukes the five desires.
Regarding the removal of the five hindrances:
furthermore, a person who is greedy for sensual desires is very far from the Path.
Why is this so? Desire is an abode of manifold afflictions and disturbances; if the mind is attached to sensual desire, there is no way to draw near to the Path.
As it is said in the verse on removing the hindrance of desire:
"One who has entered the Way with a sense of shame and remorse holds the alms bowl to bring blessings to sentient beings;
how can they indulge in worldly desires and sink into the five sensory passions?"
One who dons armor and wields sword and staff, yet retreats upon seeing the enemy—such a timid person is held in contempt and ridiculed by the whole world.
A bhikṣu is a mendicant; he has shaved his hair and donned the kāṣāya.
Controlled by the horses of the five senses, one is mocked in just this way.
It is like a person of great wealth and nobility, who dresses in magnificent garments to adorn the body,
yet goes out to beg for food and clothing, becoming an object of ridicule for the multitude.
A bhikṣu has discarded finery and altered his appearance to restrain the mind;
yet to seek sensual pleasure once more is to invite derision in just this way!
Having already abandoned the pleasures of the five desires, he casts them away without looking back.
How can you still wish to obtain it?
Like a fool who eats his own vomit!
So it is with those who crave desire; they do not know how to contemplate their original vow.
They do not distinguish between good and evil, being maddened and intoxicated by craving.
Having utterly abandoned the qualities of shame, modesty, and reverence,
they are shunned by the wise and virtuous, yet sought after and befriended by the foolish and ignorant.
All desires are suffering when sought; once obtained, they bring much fear;
when lost, they harbor burning affliction—there is never a time of joy.
Such are the perils of all desires; by what means shall one abandon them?
Having attained the bliss of the various dhyānas, one is no longer deceived by them.
When sensual desires are clung to without satiety, by what means can they be extinguished?
If one attains the contemplation of impurity, these [desires] will naturally vanish.
Attached to desire, one is not self-aware; by what means can one awaken the mind?
One should contemplate old age, sickness, and death; only then will one emerge from the four abysses.
All desires are difficult to relinquish; how can one distance oneself from them?
If one can delight in wholesome dharmas, this desire will naturally subside.
All desires are difficult to unravel; how then can they be released?
By contemplating the body and attaining its true nature, one will no longer be bound by them.
"These various methods of contemplation can extinguish the fires of all desires;
they are like a great downpour of rain, leaving no trace of wild fire!
Through such various causes and conditions as these, the hindrance of desire is eliminated.

The hindrance of ill-will is the root that causes one to lose all wholesome dharmas, the cause for falling into the evil realms, the enemy of all happiness, the great thief of the virtuous mind, and the treasury of various kinds of harsh speech.
As the Buddha taught his disciples in a verse concerning anger:
“You should know and reflect upon the foul and grievous suffering of receiving a body and dwelling in the womb, as well as the hardships of being born!”
Having already reflected upon this meaning, yet still not extinguishing one’s anger,
one should know that such people are truly heartless!
If there were no fruit of karmic retribution for offenses, nor any censure from others, [anger would be permissible].
One should still practice loving-kindness and patience; how much more so when the fruits of suffering are so severe!
One should contemplate that regarding old age, sickness, and death, there is no one who can escape them;
one should give rise to a heart of compassion—how could one inflict evil upon others?
Sentient beings act as mutual enemies and thieves, Wounding and stabbing one another, suffering bitter poisons;
How can those who cultivate goodness In turn inflict further affliction and harm?
One should always practice loving-kindness and compassion, With a settled mind cultivating all manner of virtues.
One should not harbor ill will or inflict harm upon any being!
If one diligently cultivates the path of the Dharma, affliction and injury will not occur;
for good and evil cannot coexist, just as water and fire turn away from each other.
When hatred comes to shroud the mind, one cannot distinguish between good and foul, nor recognize profit and harm;
one knows no fear of the evil realms.
One takes no account of the suffering of others, and remains unaware of the exhaustion of body and mind.
First experience the causes of suffering for yourself, and only then extend it to others.
If you wish to extinguish hatred, you should contemplate a mind of loving-kindness;
dwelling alone in solitude and tranquility, bring affairs to rest and eliminate the conditions for suffering.
"One should fear old age, illness, and death;
by eliminating the nine kinds of anger and affliction, and contemplating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in this way, one shall extinguish the poison of hatred.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) is removed.
The hindrance of sloth and torpor can destroy three things in this present life:
sensual pleasure, beneficial happiness, and merit.
It destroys the happiness of this life, the next life, and ultimate happiness; it is no different from death, for there is nothing but the breath of life.
As one bodhisattva rebuked his disciple who was sleeping with a verse, saying:
"Arise! Do not lie there embracing this foul body, This mere collection of various impurities falsely called a 'person'!"
As if struck by a mortal illness with an arrow piercing the body, how can one sleep while all manner of agonies converge?
As the entire world is consumed by the fire of death, you should seek liberation; how can you sleep?
Like one bound and led away to execution, with disaster about to descend, how could one sleep!
While the bandit of fetters is not destroyed, harm has not been removed;
it is like sharing a room with a venomous snake, or like standing on the edge of a battle amidst white blades—at such a time, how could one sleep in peace!
Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it invades and deceives, robbing one of clarity.
When sleep covers the mind, there is no discernment; such a great loss—how can one still sleep!
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one censures the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
As for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse: the nature of restlessness destroys the mind of renunciation.
If a person cannot even maintain stability when gathering the mind, how much less so when it is agitated and scattered?
One whose mind is agitated and scattered is like a drunken elephant without a hook or a camel with its nose pierced; they cannot be restrained.
As a verse says:
"You have already shaved your head and donned dyed robes; holding an earthen bowl, you go forth to beg for food.
Why do you still delight in and cling to frivolous and restless behavior?"
"Having lost the benefit of the Dharma, one forfeits worldly happiness!

Regarding the remorse for transgressions: it is like a person who has committed a great crime, constantly harboring fear and dread; the arrow of remorse enters the heart, fixed there and impossible to extract.
As a verse says:
"To do what should not be done, And to fail to do what should be done;
Burned by the fire of regret and remorse, One falls into evil realms in future lives."
If a person can repent for their transgressions, having repented, they let them go;
with such a mind, one is at peace and should not harbor constant attachment.
If there are two kinds of regret—regret for what was not done and regret for what has been done—[one should abandon them].
To regret with an attached mind—this is the mark of a fool!
It is not by means of regretting the mind that one can undo what was not done;
once various evil deeds have been committed, one cannot cause them to become undone.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, restlessness and remorse are censured.
As for the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), because the mind is shrouded by doubt, one cannot attain a concentrated mind regarding all phenomena;
and because a concentrated mind is absent, one attains nothing at all within the Buddha-dharma.
For example, it is like a person entering a mountain of jewels; if they have no hands, they are unable to take anything.
As it is said in a verse concerning doubt:
"Like a person at a forked road, Confused and uncertain of which way to go."
Within the true reality of all phenomena, doubt is likewise thus.
Because of doubt, one does not diligently seek the true reality of all phenomena;
this doubt arises from delusion, the most wretched of evils!
Within the phenomena of good and evil, birth-and-death and nirvana, there is a determinate, real, and true dharma; do not harbor doubt therein!
If you give rise to a doubting mind, the jailers of the King of Death will bind you.
Like a lion pouncing on a deer, one cannot escape;
though there may be doubts while in the world, one should follow the sublime and wholesome Dharma.
It is like observing a forked road: one should pursue that which is beneficial and excellent!
For various reasons such as these, one should abandon the hindrance of doubt.

To cast off these five hindrances is like being released from debt, like recovering from a grave illness, like reaching a land of abundance from a place of famine, like escaping from prison, or like managing to save oneself from among wicked bandits—attaining peace and freedom from affliction.
The practitioner is also like this: having eliminated the five hindrances, their mind becomes peaceful, pure, and joyful.
For example, the sun and moon are obscured by five things—
smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and the hand-obstruction of the asura Rāhu—
and thus cannot shine brightly; the human mind is likewise, when covered by the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), it cannot benefit itself, nor can it benefit others.
If one can revile the five desires, eliminate the five hindrances, and practice the five factors—
desire, diligence, mindfulness, skillful wisdom, and one-pointed concentration—
one practices these five factors to obtain the five constituents and achieve the first dhyāna.
“Desire” means to aspire to emerge from the desire realm and to attain the first dhyāna.

“Vigor” means leaving the household life to uphold the precepts, being single-minded and untiring during the early and late watches of the night, moderating one’s food, and restraining the mind so that it does not wander or scatter.
"Mindfulness" (smṛti) means recollecting the bliss of the first dhyāna and knowing that the realm of desire is impure, delusive, and contemptible, whereas the first dhyāna is honorable and precious.

"Skillful wisdom" (kauśalya-prajñā) means observing and weighing the relative lightness or heaviness, and the gains or losses, between the bliss of the realm of desire and the bliss of the first dhyāna.
"One-pointedness of mind" means constantly binding the mind to its object so as not to allow it to become distracted.
Furthermore, it means single-mindedly seeking the first dhyāna while relinquishing the pleasures of desire;
it is like one who, suffering from an enemy, constantly seeks to eliminate that enemy and thus cannot be harmed by them.
As the Buddha said to a Brahmin attached to sensual desires:
"I have previously contemplated desire:
desire is a cause and condition for fear, sorrow, and suffering; the pleasure of desire is slight, while its suffering is vast."
Sensual desire is a net of Māra, entangling and difficult to escape from;
sensual desire is a burning heat that withers all joys, like a forest fire breaking out on all four sides;
sensual desire is like standing before a pit of fire, most terrifying to behold.
It is like being pressed by a venomous snake;
it is like a hostile thief drawing his sword;
it is like a malevolent rākṣasa.
It is like poison entering the mouth;
it is like swallowing molten copper;
it is like three rutting elephants in musth.
It is like standing on the brink of a great abyss;
like a lion blocking the path;
like a makara fish with its mouth agape.
All sensual desires are likewise thus: they are utterly terrifying!
To be attached to sensual desires brings suffering and affliction to people.
A person who clings to desire is like a prisoner in a jail, like a deer within an enclosure, or like a bird caught in a net.
It is like a fish swallowing a hook; like a jackal attacking a dog; like a crow among a flock of owls;
like a snake encountering a wild boar; like a mouse amidst cats; like a group of blind men approaching a pit;
like flies landing in hot oil; like a deaf man in the midst of battle; like a lame man caught in a fire; like entering a boiling salt river.
It is like licking honey from a razor’s edge; like a piece of meat at a crossroads; like a shallow forest of swords; like flowers covering filth;
like a jar of poison smeared with honey; like a casket of venomous snakes; like a dream that is empty and deceptive; like a borrowed object that must be returned;
like an illusion that deceives children; like a mirage that lacks reality; and like being submerged in a great flood.
Like a ship entering the mouth of a makara fish, like hail destroying grain, or like a thunderbolt falling upon a person—so too are all sensual desires:
deceptive and unreal, lacking stability or strength, with little pleasure and much suffering.
Desire acts as an army of Māra, destroying all wholesome merits; it constantly emerges to plunder and harm sentient beings.
Through various such metaphors, one censures the five desires, removes the five hindrances, practices the five dharmas, and attains the first dhyāna.
Question:

The eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana), the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni), and the various concentrations and samādhis—such diverse meditative states as these are not called pāramitās. Why, then, do you speak only of the dhyānapāramitā?
Answer: These merits of the various concentrations are all cultivated through contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
"Dhyāna" (in the language of Qin, *siwei xiu*) means cultivation through contemplation.
When one speaks of the dhyānapāramitā, everything is subsumed within it.
Furthermore, dhyāna is supreme like a king; when dhyāna is mentioned, all is included, whereas when other concentrations are mentioned, they are not so included.
Why is this? Within these four dhyānas, wisdom and concentration are equal and thus there is bliss;
in the stage of access (anāgamya) and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), wisdom is predominant while concentration is deficient.
In the formless attainments, concentration is abundant while wisdom is meager; such a state is not blissful.
It is like a chariot: if one wheel is strong and the other is weak, it will not be stable;
so it is when wisdom and concentration are unequal.

Furthermore, within these four dhyāna stages, there are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhijñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), the knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the summit dhyāna (*mūrdha-dhyāna*), the meditative concentration of mastery (*vaśitā-samādhi*), the refined dhyāna (*pariśuddha-dhyāna*),

the fourteen minds of transformation (*catur-daśa-nirmāṇa-citta*), the pratyutpanna-samādhi, and the various bodhisattva samādhis— such as the Śūraṅgama and others— which, briefly stated, number one hundred and twenty.

There are also the samādhis of all Buddhas— such as the Immovable (*Acalā*) and others— which, briefly stated, number one hundred and eight, as well as the attainment of the Way and the relinquishing of the life-span by the Buddhas.
Various such merits and sublime concentrations as these all reside within dhyāna.
For this reason, dhyāna is called a pāramitā, whereas other concentrations are not so named.
Question:
You previously stated that by censuring the five desires, removing the five hindrances, and practicing the five dharmas, one attains the first dhyāna.
By cultivating what practice and relying on what path can one attain the first dhyāna?
Answer: It relies on various gateways of meditative concentration (samādhi), such as the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-smṛti).
As it is said in the verses on the meaning of dhyāna in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*:
"Detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation,
attaining the joy and happiness born of seclusion— this person enters the first dhyāna.
Having already attained freedom from the fire of lust, they then obtain the cool samādhi."
As one suffering from great heat finds joy upon entering a cool pool,
or as a poor man’s heart is moved by great delight upon finding a treasury of jewels;
so too, when conceptualization is transformed into contemplation, one enters the first dhyāna in this same way.
Knowing these two factors disturb the mind, one should abandon them even if they are wholesome;
just as when great waters are clear and still, no ripples or waves are seen.
It is like a person who, being utterly exhausted, sleeps peacefully and soundly.
If there is the sound of calling out, the mind becomes greatly distressed and disturbed.
When withdrawing the mind to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), initial and sustained application (*vitarka-vicāra*) act as disturbances;
therefore, by eliminating initial and sustained application, one attains entry into the sphere of a single consciousness (*ekavijñānāyatana*).
Because the inner mind is pure, joy and bliss born of concentration are attained;
having entered this second dhyāna, the heart is filled with exultant delight!
With the mind gathered in the foremost concentration, it is tranquil and free from all discursive thought.
One becomes weary of joy and desires to abandon it, just as one discards applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Because of feeling (*vedanā*), there is joy; when joy is lost, sorrow arises.
Free from joy, one experiences pleasure with the body, accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and skillful means (*upāya*).
The Noble One has attained the ability to relinquish; for others, relinquishment is difficult.
If one can know the peril in pleasure and perceive the great peace of the immovable, sorrow and joy have already been eliminated, and suffering and happiness are now severed as well.
With a mind purified by equanimity and mindfulness, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
The bliss within the third dhyāna is suffering because it is impermanent and fluctuating;
in the desire realm, sorrow is abandoned, and in the first and second dhyānas, joy is eliminated.
Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said in the fourth dhyāna:
"Having already abandoned sorrow and joy, one now eliminates both suffering and pleasure.

Furthermore, with pure observance of the precepts, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, guarding and restraining the sense faculties, and practicing focused contemplation during the first and last watches of the night, one abandons external pleasures and finds delight in meditation itself.
Detached from all sensual desires and unwholesome states, one attains the first dhyāna by relying on the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya).

Regarding the first dhyāna, as stated in the *Abhidharma*: "There are four kinds of dhyānas: [the dhyāna with thought and examination, the dhyāna without thought but with examination, the dhyāna without thought and without examination, and the dhyāna that is formless]."
First, that associated with flavor; second, the pure (*śuddha*); third, the untainted (*anāsrava*); and fourth, the five aggregates obtained as retribution subsumed under the first dhyāna.
Among these, the practitioner enters the pure and the untainted.
The second, third, and fourth dhyānas are also like this.
As the Buddha has said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who, detached from all desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna."
“Various desires” refers to the five objects of desire, such as form and so forth, which one loves and clings to, and which are conceptualized and discriminated;
the censure of these desires is as previously explained.
“Evil and unwholesome states” refers to the five hindrances, such as sensual desire and so forth.
By being detached from these two matters—the internal and the external—one attains the first dhyāna.
The characteristics of the first dhyāna are:
applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā).

Regarding "with directed thought and sustained thought": because one attains within the first dhyāna wholesome dharmas and meritorious qualities never before attained, the mind is greatly awakened and stirred.
Having been constantly burned by the fire of desire, upon attaining the first dhyāna, it is as if entering a cool, refreshing pool;
it is also like a poor man suddenly finding a treasure trove.

The practitioner contemplates and discerns the faults and transgressions of the desire realm; knowing that the benefits and merits of the first dhyāna are exceedingly great, his mind is filled with great joy—this is called "with vitarka and vicāra."
Question:
Are vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) one dharma,
or are they two dharmas?
Answer: There are two factors.
The initial thought of the coarse mind is called *vitarka* (applied thought).
Subtle mental discernment is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
It is like striking a bell: the initial loud sound is called awareness (*vitarka*), while the subsequent subtle resonance is called contemplation.
Question:

As stated in the *Abhidharma*, "From the desire realm up to the first dhyāna, initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*) are associated within a single moment of mind. Why, then, do you now say that "the coarse aspect of the first moment of mind is called initial inquiry, and the subtle mental discrimination is called sustained investigation"?
The answer is:
Although these two dharmas exist within a single mind, their two aspects do not coexist;
at the time of awakening, the contemplation is not clear.
When observing at that time, awareness is not clear.
It is like the rising of the sun, when the various stars do not appear;
likewise, all mental states and mental factors receive their names according to the occasion.
As the Buddha said:
"If you abandon one dharma, I certify that you have attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
This one dharma is what is called stinginess and greed."

"In truth, one should say that by exhausting the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana), one attains the state of a non-returner (anāgāmin). Why, then, is it said that 'one merely severs a single dharma'?
It is because this person has an excessive preponderance of stinginess and greed, from which all other fetters and afflictions arise;
therefore, when stinginess is exhausted, the remaining fetters are also severed."
The designation of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) according to their respective times is likewise so.
The practitioner knows that although these *vitarka* and *vicāra* are wholesome dharmas, they nonetheless disturb the concentrated mind.
Because the mind desires to be free from them, one censures these applied and sustained thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*), forming this reflection:
"Applied and sustained thoughts disturb the meditative mind; it is like clear water which, when agitated by waves, reveals nothing.
Or again, it is like an exhausted person who, having found rest and wishing to sleep, is troubled and distracted by the calls of those nearby."
"When the mind is gathered within in meditative concentration, the agitation caused by vitarka and vicāra is likewise [to be abandoned].
For various reasons such as these, he censured vitarka and vicāra.

"With the cessation of vitarka and vicāra, there is internal purity; fixing the mind on a single point, free from vitarka and vicāra, one enters the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss."
Having attained the second dhyāna, one obtains the incomparable joy and bliss never before experienced within the second dhyāna.
As for "the cessation of vitarka and vicāra," they are ceased because one recognizes the faults and transgressions of vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding "inner purity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*): having entered deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gains faith and relinquishes the applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna. The benefit gained is significant and what is lost is minimal; since that which is acquired is vast and great, and the mind is bound to a single object, it is called inner purity.
The practitioner contemplates the faults of joy (*prīti*) in the same manner as he did for applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Wherever there is joy, there is much joy and much sorrow. Why is this so?

Just as a poor person who obtains treasure experiences immeasurable joy, yet if they lose it all at once, their sorrow is likewise profound; joy thus turns into sorrow. For this reason, one should renounce it.
“By being detached from this joy, one dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing physical bliss.
This is the bliss that the noble ones describe as ‘one who possesses equanimity and mindfulness dwells in bliss’; thus one enters the third dhyāna.”
"Equanimity" (upekṣā) means relinquishing the mind of joy and no longer feeling regret.
"Mindfulness and wisdom" (smṛti and prajñā) mean that having attained the bliss within the third dhyāna, one does not allow that bliss to give rise to affliction.
"Experiencing bodily pleasure" refers to the bliss of the third dhyāna, which is experienced throughout the entire body.

Regarding "the noble ones are able to both attain and relinquish it": this bliss is the foremost in the world and can give rise to mental attachment; thus, among ordinary persons, few are able to relinquish it.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that the fruit of practicing loving-kindness is supreme within the Realm of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
When a practitioner contemplates the faults of pleasure, it is just as when they contemplate joy; they know that the station of the immovable mind (*āniñjya*) is the most supreme.
Where there is movement, there is suffering;
because the practitioner finds movement in the bliss of the third dhyāna, he seeks the state of immovability.

"By abandoning pleasure and pain, and by the prior extinction of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness."
In these four dhyānas, there is neither suffering nor pleasure, but only immovable wisdom.
For this reason, the fourth dhyāna is described as "purity of equanimity and mindfulness."
Because the bliss of the third dhyāna is subject to movement, it is described as suffering; therefore, within the fourth dhyāna, it is said that "suffering and bliss are abandoned.
As the Buddha taught:
"Transcending all perceptions of form, not attending to perceptions of diversity, extinguishing perceptions of resistance, one enters and abides in the sphere of infinite space."
The practitioner reflects thus:
"If there were no form, then there would be no sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, or heat.

This bodily form is coarse, heavy, and wretched; it is deceptive and unreal, obtained as a retribution through the conjunction of causes and conditions from previous lives, and is the dwelling place of manifold afflictions. How can I escape the calamities of this body?"
"One should contemplate the void within this body.
Constantly contemplating the body as empty—like a cage or a steamer—one should maintain this mindfulness without abandoning it; thus, one transcends form and no longer perceives the body.
Just as the internal body is empty, so too are external forms; at that time, one is able to contemplate immeasurable and boundless emptiness.
Having attained this contemplation, there is neither suffering nor pleasure, and the mind increases further.
It is like a bird confined within a bottle; when the bottle is broken, it escapes. This is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
This space is immeasurable and boundless; if one takes consciousness as its object, then because the objects are manifold, the mind becomes distracted, which can destroy the concentration.

The practitioner contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness conditioned by space as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a thorn; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. They exist through deceptive conjunction and are not real.
Having reflected thus, he abandons the object of space and takes consciousness alone as his object.
How does he take it as an object?
He takes the present consciousness as an object, and that present consciousness takes past and future consciousnesses—immeasurable and boundless—as its objects.

This consciousness is immeasurable and boundless, like space which is immeasurable and boundless; this is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
This consciousness is immeasurable and boundless, yet if one takes that consciousness as an object, the consciousness becomes excessive and leads to distraction, thereby destroying the concentration.

The practitioner contemplates these conditioned aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a thorn; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, existing through deceptive combinations and lacking true reality.
Having observed in this way, one then destroys the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is the disparagement of the sphere of consciousness and the praise of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). By destroying all characteristics of consciousness and fixing the mind within nothingness, it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatanasamādhi*).

One contemplates feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness within the sphere of nothingness as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a thorn; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they exist through deceptive combinations and are not truly existent.
Reflecting thus, he considers the sphere of non-perception to be like an abscess; the sphere of perception to be like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a thorn;
and the supreme, sublime state to be the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question:
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there exist feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; why, then, is it called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception"?
Answer: Because the perception within this state is subtle and difficult to discern, it is called "non-perception";
yet because perception does exist, it is "not non-perception."
Ordinary beings think that attaining the true nature of all phenomena constitutes nirvana;
however, within the Buddha-dharma, although one knows that perception exists, it is called the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" based on its original name.
Question: What is this "absence of perception"? Answer:
There are three kinds of non-conception:
first, the attainment of non-conception; second, the attainment of cessation of sensation and perception; and third, the heaven of non-conception.
Ordinary persons who wish to extinguish the mind enter the attainment of non-conception.
When a disciple of the Buddha wishes to extinguish the mind, they enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
These various dhyāna-concentrations are of two kinds:
either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) is that which is practiced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as described above;
the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consists of the sixteen noble practices (*āryacaryā*).
If it is the contaminated path, one relies on the limit of a higher stage to become detached from the desires of a lower stage.
If it is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), it brings about detachment from the desires of its own level as well as those of the higher levels.
For this reason, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot achieve detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because there is no further level beyond it.

If a disciple of the Buddha wishes to abandon the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are nine types of afflictions of the desire realm to be severed through contemplation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*):

the superior, the intermediate, and the inferior—namely, the superior-of-the-superior, the superior-of-the-intermediate, and the superior-of-the-inferior; the intermediate-of-the-superior, the intermediate-of-the-intermediate, and the intermediate-of-the-inferior; and the inferior-of-the-superior, the inferior-of-the-intermediate, and the inferior-of-the-inferior.

Because these nine [categories] are abandoned, when a disciple of the Buddha seeks the first dhyāna by means of the contaminated path (*sāsravamārga*), at that time—within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantaryamārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*)—they cultivate the contaminated path in the present, while cultivating both contaminated and uncontaminated paths in the future.

In the ninth path of liberation, one presently cultivates the contaminated path of the stage of "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya), while in the future one will cultivate both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths of the stage of "not-yet-reached," as well as the contaminated path of the preliminary stage of the first dhyāna.
If one seeks to attain the first dhyāna by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), it is also like this.

If, by relying on the tainted path (sāsrava-mārga), one becomes detached from the desire for the first dhyāna, then during the nine paths of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) and eight paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) at the threshold of the second dhyāna, one presently cultivates the tainted [path] at the threshold of the second dhyāna, and in the future cultivates the tainted path at the threshold of the second dhyāna, as well as the untainted first dhyāna and its attendants.

In the ninth path of liberation, within the borderland of the second dhyāna, one presently cultivates the impure path of the borderland of the second dhyāna; in the future, one will cultivate the borderland of the second dhyāna, as well as the pure and impure paths of the first dhyāna along with their attendants, and the pure and impure paths of the second dhyāna.

If one is free from the desires of the first dhyāna by means of the untainted path, then during the nine paths of non-obstruction and the eight paths of liberation, one cultivates the untainted path of one's own stage in the present, and cultivates the tainted and untainted paths of the first dhyāna along with its attendants in the future.

In the ninth path of liberation, one presently cultivates the untainted path of one's own stage; in the future, one cultivates the tainted and untainted paths of the first dhyāna along with its attendants, as well as the pure and untainted paths of the second dhyāna.
It is the same even up to the time of becoming free from desire for the sphere of nothingness.

At the time of becoming free from desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, during the nine paths of non-obstruction and the eight paths of liberation, one cultivates only all uncontaminated paths.
In the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates the wholesome roots of the three realms as well as the untainted path—
excluding the mindless attainments.
There are two types of cultivation:
First, cultivation through attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*); second, cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation through attainment refers to that which was previously unattained and is now attained;
it is the cultivation of one's own future tasks as well as the cultivation of other tasks.
Cultivation through practice refers to that which has been previously attained and is now cultivated in the present;
it is likewise for the future, and no others are cultivated.
This constitutes cultivation among various such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there are briefly twenty-three types:
eight with flavor (*sāsvāda*), eight pure (*śuddha*), and seven untainted (*anāsrava*).
There are also six causes:

The associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and the naming cause (*nāma-hetu*).
Each of these is untainted (*anāsrava*); among the seven untainted causes, they are the similar cause;
within their own stage (*sva-bhūmi*), they increase as the associated cause and the coexistent cause.
The first flavor-concentration is the cause of the first flavor-concentration, and so on up to the last flavor-concentration being the cause of the last flavor-concentration.
It is the same for the pure [concentrations].
There are four conditions:
The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the causal condition, it is as explained above.
From the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, six kinds of concentrations arise in succession:
First, the pure first dhyāna; second, the untainted (anāsrava).
The same applies to the second and third dhyānas.
From the untainted concentration of the second dhyāna, eight kinds of concentrations arise in succession:
The pure and untainted [attainments] of their own stage;
the pure and untainted first dhyāna;
and likewise for the third and fourth dhyānas.
The untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the third dhyāna successively gives rise to ten types:
two of its own level, four of the lower levels, and four of the higher levels.
The same applies to the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
From the untainted concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nine types arise in succession:
two from its own level, four from the lower levels, and three from the higher levels.
From the untainted concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), seven types arise in succession:
From its own level, two; from lower levels, four; from higher levels, one.
From the pure state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, six minds arise in succession:
two from its own level and four from lower levels.
The various pure stages (*śuddhaka*) are also like this; furthermore, they all benefit the flavor (*āsvāda*) of their own respective stages.
Regarding the flavor of the first dhyāna, there are subsequently two kinds:
flavor and purity (*śuddhaka*).
The same applies even up to the relishing of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas take all spheres as their objects.
Relishing-dhyāna takes the relishing within its own stage as its object, and also takes the pure [dhyāna] as its object.
Because craving has no object that is untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not take the untainted as its object.
Pure and untainted fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) do not take the tainted (*sāsrava*) states of lower stages as their objects.
They are termed causes and predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*), and they apply to all [stages].
The four immeasurables, the three liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the eight spheres of totality all take the desire realm as their object.
The five supernormal powers take the desire and form realms as their objects;
the remaining [meditations] each take their respective objects according to their specific nature.
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling has no object of focus.

Within all four dhyānas there is the practice of refinement; because one refines the out-flowing (sāsrava) by means of the out-flow-free (anāsrava), one attains mastery over the mind of the four dhyānas.

One is able to refine the contaminated fourth dhyāna by means of the uncontaminated fourth dhyāna; subsequently, one refines the third, second, and first dhyānas, each using the uncontaminated version of its own level to refine the contaminated version of that same level.
Question: Why is it called "refining dhyāna"? Answer:
The noble ones delight in untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and do not delight in tainted concentration (*sāsrava*).
At the time of detachment from desire, pure tainted concentration arises spontaneously though it is not sought after;
now, because one wishes to remove its impurities, one refines it with the untainted.

For example, just as refining gold removes its impurities, so too does the untainted (*anāsrava*) refine the tainted (*sāsrava*). Arising from untainted dhyāna and entering pure (*śuddha*) dhyāna, repeating this process again and again—this is called "refining."
Furthermore, among the various dhyānas there is the dhyāna of the Peak (mūrdhan). Why is it called "Peak"?
There are two kinds of arhats: those whose dharmas are subject to regression (bhedadharman) and those whose dharmas are not subject to regression (abhedadharman).
An Arhat of the "unshakable dharma" attains mastery over all profound meditative concentrations and is able to give rise to the "summit concentration" (mūrdha-dhyāna).
Having attained this summit concentration, he can transform longevity into wealth, and transform wealth into longevity.
Furthermore, there are the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*).
As for the knowledge resulting from resolve: when one wishes to know the events of the three periods of time, one knows them according to that resolve.
This knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is subsumed under two stages:
the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the fourth dhyāna.

As for the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) are subsumed under two stages:
The desire realm and the first dhyāna;
the remaining two [sets of] distinctions are comprised within nine stages:
the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments.
The samādhi of non-contention (araṇā-samādhi) prevents the arising of contention in the minds of others; it is comprised within five stages:
the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Question:
"Are there other dharmas besides those [attained] in the various dhyānas?
He replied:
"They are also attained through the arising of attachment to meditative absorption (āsvādanasamādhi), and they are also attained through falling away from it."
Pure dhyāna is obtained at the time of birth and at the time of detachment from desire.
The untainted (anāsrava) [dhyāna] is obtained at the time of detachment from desire and at the time of falling away [from a higher stage].
There are nine stages of untainted concentration:
The four dhyānas, the three formless attainments, the threshold stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna can sever the fetters and latent tendencies.
The threshold stage and the intermediate dhyāna are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
If a person accomplishes dhyāna, they also accomplish the transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the lower stages.
For example, when the first dhyāna is accomplished, there are two kinds of transformative minds:
first, that of the first dhyāna; second, that of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The second dhyāna:
three types. The third dhyāna: [three types].
The four dhyānas are of four types;
the five [aggregates] are of five types.

When one desires to hear, see, or touch while in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, all such functions employ the consciousness of the Brahma-world; when that consciousness ceases, they likewise cease.

The four immeasurables, the five supernormal powers, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the ten totalities, the nine successive attainments, the nine perceptions, the ten conceptions, the three samādhis, the three gates of liberation, the three untainted faculties, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—all such meritorious qualities as these arise from the perfection of dhyāna; herein they should be explained in detail.
Question:
One should speak of the *dhyānapāramitā*; why, then, do you speak only of "dhyāna"? Answer:
Dhyāna is the foundation of the pāramitās.

Having attained this dhyāna, one feels compassion for sentient beings who, while possessing within their own minds various sublime joys of meditative concentration, do not seek them, but instead seek happiness amidst external phenomena that are impure and suffering.
Having observed this, he gave rise to great compassion and established a vast vow:
"I shall cause all sentient beings to attain the inner bliss of meditative concentration and leave behind impure pleasures;
having relied upon this bliss of dhyāna, I shall next cause them to attain the bliss of the Buddha-way."
At that time, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is designated as a pāramitā.
Furthermore, within this dhyāna, one does not relish its flavor, does not seek its reward, and is not reborn according to that reward; rather, one enters dhyāna for the sake of taming the mind.
By means of wisdom and skillful means (upāya), one returns to birth in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to liberate all sentient beings; at that time, dhyāna is called a pāramitā.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), no devas or humans can know the basis or the object of their mind; amidst all phenomena seen, heard, sensed, or known, the mind remains unmoved.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the method of "sitting in meditation" was explained for Śāriputra:
"Not relying on the body, not relying on the mind, and not relying on the triple world; within the triple world, neither body nor mind is apprehended—this is called sitting in meditation."

Furthermore, if a person hears that the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) surpasses the pleasures of humans and devas, and consequently abandons sensual desires to seek such concentration, this is merely seeking one's own benefit and happiness; it is not worthy of wonder.
The Bodhisattva is not like this; he acts solely for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to purify his mind of compassion and never abandoning them.
In the Bodhisattva’s dhyāna, the mind of great compassion arises throughout all states of meditative concentration.
In dhyāna there is an exceedingly sublime inner bliss, yet sentient beings abandon it to seek external pleasure.
It is like a wealthy blind man who possesses many hidden treasures, yet being unaware and unable to see them, goes about begging for alms.
The wise person takes pity on those who possess wonderful things within themselves yet, being unable to know or see them, beg for them from others.

Sentient beings are likewise: though they possess various kinds of bliss from meditative concentration within their own minds, they do not know how to bring it forth, but instead seek external pleasure.

Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva knows the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), his mind is peaceful and secure when entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and he does not cling to its flavor.

Although other non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) may enter meditative absorption, their minds are not peaceful and secure; because they do not know the true nature of all phenomena, they cling to the flavor of dhyāna.
Question:
Since both Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are equally unattached to the flavor [of meditative states], why do they not attain the dhyānapāramitā? Answer:

Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not cling to the flavor [of meditative states], because they lack the mind of great compassion, it is not called the dhyānapāramitā; furthermore, they are unable to fully practice all the dhyanas.
The Bodhisattva practices all forms of dhyāna—whether coarse or subtle, great or small, deep or shallow, with internal objects or external objects—and practices them all completely.
For this reason, within the mind of a Bodhisattva it is called the Dhyānapāramitā, whereas for others it is merely called dhyāna.
Furthermore, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas all attain meditative concentration (dhyāna).
However, within the dhyāna of non-Buddhists, there are three kinds of afflictions:
either attachment to the flavor [of the attainment], or wrong views, or arrogance.

In the dhyāna of the śrāvaka, compassion is thin; among all phenomena, they do not use sharp wisdom to penetrate the true reality (dharmatā) of all dharmas, seeking only their own solitary benefit and thereby severing the seeds of the Buddhas.

In the dhyāna of the bodhisattva, such things do not occur; because they desire to gather all the Buddha-dharmas, they do not forget sentient beings within any state of dhyāna, constantly extending thoughts of loving-kindness even to insects.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was formerly a rishi with a conch-shell topknot named Śaṅkara, he constantly practiced the fourth dhyāna;
his inhalation and exhalation ceased as he sat beneath a tree, motionless and unmoving.
Seeing this, the bird mistook it for a tree and laid its eggs within the topknot.
When the Bodhisattva arose from his meditation, he realized there were bird eggs upon his head and reflected:
"If I move, the mother bird will surely not return; [if I do not move, the chicks will perish]."
"If the mother bird does not return, the eggs will surely perish.
He then returned to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and only arose once the fledglings had flown away.
Furthermore, with the exception of a Bodhisattva, no other person can enter meditative absorption from a mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in immediate succession.
When a bodhisattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, they enter the dhyānas sequentially from the mind of the desire realm. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva has cultivated various merits throughout successive lifetimes, their afflictions are thin and their mind is supple.

Furthermore, other people attain wisdom regarding general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and are able to become free from desire, such as through the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā*), the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha*), and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*);
whereas a Bodhisattva, among all phenomena (*dharma*), is able to discern and become free from desire by means of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

For example, when five hundred rishis were flying through the air, they heard the singing voice of a kinnarī; their minds became infatuated and intoxicated, and they all lost their supernormal power of flight, falling to the ground all at once.
Just as when the Śrāvakas heard the sound of the Kinnara king Tūṇamada playing the lute and singing, praising the Buddha with the true nature of all phenomena (dharmatā),
at that time Mount Sumeru and all the trees shook;
Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples were all unable to remain composed upon their seats.
The Bodhisattva Tianxu asked Mahākāśyapa:
"You are the most senior in years and foremost in the practice of dhūta; why is it that you can no longer control your mind and abide in peace?"
Mahākāśyapa replied:

"My mind is not swayed by the various desires of humans or devas; yet this sound, which is the retribution for the immeasurable merit of a bodhisattva, and furthermore, the sound produced through the transformations of wisdom, is something I cannot endure."
If winds arise from the eight directions, they cannot cause Mount Sumeru to move;
yet when the Vairambha winds arrive at the end of the kalpa, they blow against Mount Sumeru until it is like withered grass.
For this reason, it is known that among all dharmas, the Bodhisattva attains detachment from all desires through the contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Other people merely obtain the name of *dhyāna*, but do not attain the *pāramitā*.

Furthermore, while others may know the Bodhisattva’s mind as it enters and emerges from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they cannot know the objects upon which the mind rests during that concentration or where it reaches; nor can they know the depth or shallowness of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know this, let alone other people.
It is like an elephant king crossing water: when it enters and when it emerges, its footprints can be seen;
but while it is within the water, they cannot be known.
If one attains the first dhyāna, they can know it as those who have likewise attained the first dhyāna do, yet they cannot know the bodhisattva’s entry into the first dhyāna.

If someone attains the second dhyāna, they can observe and know the mind that has attained the first dhyāna with complete clarity, yet they cannot know the bodhisattva’s mind entering the first dhyāna;
this remains the case up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, within the *samādhi* of leaping over, one arises from the first dhyāna and enters the third dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, one enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); and arising from the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The followers of the two vehicles can only transcend one level, but cannot transcend two;

the Bodhisattvas transcend with mastery: arising from the first dhyāna, they may enter the third dhyāna according to the usual rule, or at times enter the fourth dhyāna, or enter the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or enter the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling;

arising from the absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, they may enter the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of infinite space, proceeding through the fourth dhyāna down to the first dhyāna.
At times they leap over one, at times they leap over two, and so on up to nine.
Śrāvakas cannot leap over two; why is this?
Because their wisdom, merit, and power of meditative concentration are weak.
For example, there are two kinds of lions:
first, the yellow lion; second, the white-maned lion king.
Although the yellow lion is also capable of leaping, he does not equal the white-maned lion king.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one distinguishes the dhyāna-pāramitā.

Furthermore, at that time, the bodhisattva constantly enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), withdrawing the mind so that it is unmoving and free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); yet, he is also able to preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings in the ten directions using immeasurable sounds to deliver and liberate them—this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Question: As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Only after there have first been vitarka, vicāra, and reflection can one then preach the Dharma."
"When one has entered meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), there is no speech, nor are there applied or sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra); thus, one should not be able to preach the Dharma.
How can you now say, 'He constantly remains in meditative concentration, yet without giving rise to applied or sustained thought, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings'?"
Answer:

For those in the cycle of birth and death, when entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they first employ speech, applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and only thereafter preach the Dharma.

Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body are detached from the body of birth and death; they know that all dharmas are eternally abiding, and like the characteristics of meditative concentration, they perceive no disorder.
The Dharma-body Bodhisattva manifests immeasurable transformation bodies to preach the Dharma for sentient beings, yet the Bodhisattva’s mind remains free from discrimination.
It is like the lute of the asuras, which constantly produces sound spontaneously according to one's wishes, even though no one plays it;
this likewise has neither a distracted mind nor a concentrated mind, for it arises as a retribution of merit, producing sound in accordance with the inclinations of people.
The Dharma-body Bodhisattva is also like this: there is no conceptual discrimination, no distracted mind, and no characteristic of preaching the Dharma.

Due to the causes and conditions of immeasurable merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom, various sounds of the Dharma issue forth from this Dharma-body Bodhisattva in accordance with what is appropriate.
Those with many thoughts of stinginess and greed hear the sound of the teaching on generosity;

those who have broken the precepts, who are prone to anger, indolence, mental distraction, or delusion, each hear the sounds of the teachings on ethical discipline, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having heard this Dharma, they each reflected upon it and gradually attained liberation through the three vehicles.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena—whether in a state of distraction or concentration—as being characterized by non-duality.
Other people eliminate distraction to seek concentration.
Why is this? Because within the state of distraction they give rise to thoughts of aversion, while within the state of concentration they give rise to thoughts of attachment.
For example, when the seer Udraka attained the five supernormal powers, he would fly daily to the king’s palace to eat.
According to the customs of that kingdom, the king’s chief queen would grasp his feet and pay him homage.
As soon as the lady touched him with her hand, he immediately lost his supernatural powers.
He requested a chariot from the king, mounted it, and departed for his original dwelling.
Upon entering the forest, he again sought the five supernormal powers, applying himself with single-minded devotion.
Just as he was about to attain [realization], a bird on a tree cried out urgently, distracting his mind.
Leaving the tree, he went to the water’s edge to seek concentration, but again heard the sound of fish fighting and agitating the water.
This person, failing to attain meditative concentration, gave rise to anger, thinking:
"I shall kill all fish and birds!
After a long time, through reflection, he attained concentration and was reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When his life there comes to an end, he is reborn below as a flying weasel; he kills various fish and birds, commits immeasurable sins, and falls into the three evil realms.
This is the causal condition for attachment within meditative concentration.
