Such is the case with the non-Buddhists; it also occurs among the Buddha’s disciples.
There was a bhikṣu who attained the four dhyānas and gave rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), claiming he had attained the four paths.
When he attained the first dhyāna, he claimed to be a *srotāpanna*.
At the time of the second dhyāna, one considers oneself a sakṛdāgāmin;
at the time of the third dhyāna, one considers oneself an anāgāmin;
and at the time of the fourth dhyāna, one considers oneself to have attained arhatship.
Relying on this, they stop and no longer seek further progress.
When their lives are about to end, they see the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna approaching; thereupon, they give rise to false views, saying:
"There is no nirvāṇa; the Buddha has deceived me."

Because evil and false views have arisen, he loses the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna and instead perceives the intermediate state of the Avīci hell; at the end of his life, he is immediately reborn in the Avīci hell.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
“Where has the bhikṣu so-and-so, who dwelt in an araṇya, been reborn after his death?
The Buddha said:
"This person has been reborn in the Avīci Hell!
All the bhikṣus were greatly shocked and marveled,
"How could this be the consequence for one who practiced dhyāna and maintained the precepts?"
The Buddha said:
"This person was possessed of overweening pride; when he attained the four dhyānas, he claimed to have attained the four paths.
At the time of his death, seeing the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the fourth dhyāna, he gave rise to wrong views and claimed that there is no nirvāṇa."
"I am an Arhat, yet I have now been reborn; the Buddha is a deceiver.
At that moment, he beheld the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Avīci Hell; his life ended, and he was immediately reborn within the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Though one possesses much learning, upholds the precepts, and practices dhyāna, If the state of outflow-free dharma has not been attained,
Even with such merits as these, This matter cannot be relied upon!"
This bhikṣu undergoes the suffering of these evil realms. Therefore,
one knows that grasping at signs of distraction can give rise to afflictions such as anger,
while grasping at signs of concentration can give rise to attachment.

The Bodhisattva does not grasp at the signs of distraction, nor does he grasp at the signs of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because the signs of distraction and concentration are one and the same; this is called the *dhyānapāramitā*.
It is like the characteristics of the first dhyāna: being free from desire and removing the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the mind is gathered into a single point.

Because this bodhisattva observes with sharp faculties and wisdom, they neither abandon the five hindrances nor grasp at the characteristics of meditative concentration, for the characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
What is meant by "not abandoning the five hindrances"?
The hindrance of sensual desire is neither internal nor external, nor does it exist in between the two. Why is this?
If internal phenomena existed, they would not depend on external ones for their arising.
If external phenomena existed, there would be no affliction for me.
If they existed in between the two, there would be no space between them.
Nor does it come from previous lives. Why?
Because all phenomena have no coming.
For example, a young child has no desire; if such desire had existed in previous lives, it should also exist in childhood.
For this reason, one knows that it does not come from a previous life, nor does it go to a future life;
it does not come from any direction, nor does it exist eternally of itself;
it is not in a single part, nor is it throughout the entire body.
Nor does it come from the five sense objects, nor does it emerge from the five faculties.
It has no source from which it arises and no source from which it ceases.
As for this craving—whether it arises first, arises later, or arises simultaneously—none of these possibilities hold true.
Why is this? If birth were to exist first and craving were to exist later, then craving could not arise therein, because craving would not yet exist.
If birth were to exist later and craving were to exist first, then birth would have nothing from which to arise.
If they were to arise simultaneously, there would be neither one who arises nor a place of arising, because there would be no distinction between the one who arises and the place of arising.
Furthermore, this desire and the desirous person are neither identical nor different.
Why is this? Because apart from desire, desire cannot be found;
and in that which is apart from desire, desire cannot be found. It arises solely from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Phenomena arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions are themselves empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this way, desire and the desirous one cannot be found as distinct.
If they were one, there would be no distinction between desire and the desirous one.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the arising of desire cannot be found.
If a phenomenon is without arising, that phenomenon is also without cessation;
because it neither arises nor ceases, there is neither fixedness nor distraction.
When one contemplates the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) in this manner, it becomes one with dhyāna;
the same applies to the remaining hindrances.

If one attains the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, one perceives that the five hindrances are non-existent; at that time, one knows that the true reality of the five hindrances is itself the true reality of dhyāna, and the true reality of dhyāna is itself the five hindrances.

When a bodhisattva is thus able to know the five desires and the five hindrances, as well as the single characteristic of dhyāna and its factors, and enters dhyāna without any dependence, this is the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, the five pāramitās are harmoniously combined to assist its fulfillment; this is called the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, by the power of the dhyānapāramitā, the bodhisattva attains the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such that in a single thought-moment, without arising from meditative concentration, they are able to offer flowers, incense, precious jewels, and various other offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Furthermore, by the power of the dhyāna-pāramitā, the bodhisattva manifests countless bodies, entering everywhere throughout the five destinies to teach and transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters into the dhyāna-pāramitā, they eliminate all evil and unwholesome dharmas and enter the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Their minds are harmonious and supple; within each and every dhyāna, they practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
By means of these causes and conditions of loving-kindness and compassion, they extract the sins accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
Because they have attained the wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas, they are held in the thoughts of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters the dhyānapāramitā, he observes sentient beings within the five destinies of the ten directions with his divine eye:
he sees those born in the realm of form who, having tasted the bliss of meditative concentration, fall back into the realms of birds and beasts to undergo various sufferings.
Furthermore, he sees various devas of the desire realm delighting themselves with flowers and incense by the ponds of the seven treasures, only to fall later into the hell of salt-boiling excrement.

He sees those among humans who are learned and possess worldly wisdom and eloquence, yet because they do not attain the Way, they fall back into the wombs of pigs, sheep, and other beasts, having no capacity for discernment or knowledge.
In this way, through various such circumstances, they lose great happiness and gain great suffering; they lose great benefit and gain great decline; they lose nobility and gain lowliness.
Developing a mind of compassion toward these sentient beings, he gradually expands it until he achieves great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
for the sake of sentient beings, he does not spare his own body or life, but diligently practices with vigor in order to seek the path of the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is called the *dhyānapāramitā* because of being undisturbed and free from attachment.
As the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva dwells within the *prajñāpāramitā* and fulfills the *dhyānapāramitā* by being undisturbed and free from attachment.”
Question: What is meant by "distraction"? Answer:
There are two kinds of confusion:
first, the subtle; second, the coarse.
As for the subtle, there are three types:
First, those with a predominance of craving; second, those with a predominance of pride; third, those with a predominance of views.
What is meant by "predominance of craving"?
It is when, having attained the bliss of meditative concentration, one’s mind becomes attached to and relishes that flavor of pleasure.
What is meant by "abounding in conceit"?
When one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one considers it a difficult feat already accomplished and exalts oneself on that account.
What is meant by "abounding in views"?

To enter meditative concentration through views such as the view of a self, and to engage in conceptualization and grasping at signs, thinking "this is real and all else is false"—these three are called subtle disturbances.
Due to these causes and conditions, one falls back from meditative concentration and gives rise to the three poisons; this is called coarse disturbance.

Regarding "attachment to flavor" (*āsvāda*): when one first attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one becomes single-mindedly attached to it; this is what constitutes attachment to flavor.
Question:
Since all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of causing defiled attachment, why is only craving (*tṛṣṇā*) designated as "attachment to flavor"?
Answer: Craving resembles meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Why is this?
In dhyāna, the mind is gathered and firmly established; in craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is likewise single-minded attachment that is difficult to relinquish.

Furthermore, when first seeking dhyāna, the mind is focused on the desire to attain it; since the nature of craving is the longing for pleasure and the pursuit of what one desires, this desire does not contradict meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Once one has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), if one becomes deeply attached to it and refuses to let go, one will destroy that very concentration.
It is like giving away material goods while expecting immediate reward; in such a case, there is no merit.
To savor the flavor of meditation and to become passionately attached to it is likewise so.
Therefore, craving alone is designated as "taste," and no other fetters are considered taste.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seventeen;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the First Chapter: Prajñāpāramitā.
Volume Twenty-nine, Chapter Eighteen.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. 29. Prajñāpāramitā [Sūtra]: “Because of non-attachment to all dharmas, one should fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
[Treatise] Question:
What is meant by “prajñāpāramitā”? Answer:

For all bodhisattvas who, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening, seek the knowledge of all modes, the wisdom that realizes the true nature of all phenomena throughout that interval is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Question: If that were so, it should not be called a *pāramitā*. Why?
Because they have not yet reached the limit of wisdom.
The answer is:

The wisdom attained by the Buddha is the true *pāramitā*; because it is due to this *pāramitā*, that which is practiced by the Bodhisattva is also called a *pāramitā*, for the fruit is spoken of in terms of the cause.
This Prajñāpāramitā, when within the Buddha’s mind, changes its name to Sarvākārajñatā (All-Knowledge).
When a bodhisattva practices wisdom seeking to cross to the other shore, it is called pāramitā;
because the Buddha has already crossed to the other shore, it is called Sarvākārajñatā.
Question:

The Buddha has already severed all afflictions along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), and his eye of wisdom is pure; he should thus realize the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as it truly is.
This true nature of all phenomena is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva has not yet exhausted all outflows and their eye of wisdom is not yet purified, how can they attain the true reality of all phenomena?
The answer is:
this meaning shall be explained in detail in a later chapter; for now, it is only briefly stated.
It is like people entering the ocean: there are those who have just begun to enter, and there are those who reach its very source and bottom. Although they differ in depth, both are called "enterers.
It is the same with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: the Buddha has exhausted its depths;
the Bodhisattva, however, because he has not yet severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions and his power is slight, cannot penetrate deeply.
As stated in a simile in a later chapter:

it is like a person lighting a lamp in a dark room; the various objects and vessels are all clearly illuminated, and when a larger lamp is added, they become even more brightly and distinctly visible.
Thus one knows that the darkness destroyed by the later lamp coexists with the earlier lamp;
although the earlier lamp coexisted with the darkness, it was nonetheless able to illuminate objects.
If the earlier lamp were without darkness, then the later lamp would have nothing to augment.
The wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is also like this:

although the wisdom of a Bodhisattva is conjoined with the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions, it is able to realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, just as the former lamp can still illuminate objects;
the Buddha’s wisdom has exhausted all habitual tendencies of affliction and likewise realizes the true reality of all phenomena, just as the latter lamp is even more clearly luminous.
Question:
What is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena? Answer:
Each person among the multitude speaks of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, considering their own view to be the truth.
Within this context, true reality is indestructible, eternally abiding and unchanging, and devoid of any agent.
As the Buddha told Subhūti in a later chapter:

"If a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither suffering nor happiness, neither self nor non-self, neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth—and yet does not even form such a contemplation—this is called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom."

This meaning involves relinquishing all contemplation, extinguishing all verbal expression, and departing from all mental activities; it is from the very beginning neither born nor extinguished, possessing a characteristic like that of *nirvāṇa*.
The characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise so; this is called the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-stotra*:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the true dharma, free from inversion;
conceptualization and observation have been eliminated, and even the dharmas of speech have ceased.”
Countless sins are eliminated, and the pure mind is ever one-pointed;
such a noble and wondrous person is then able to see Prajñā.
Like space, it is unstained, free from conceptual play, and devoid of words or letters.
If one can contemplate in this way, this is itself seeing the Buddha.
If one contemplates the Buddha according to the Dharma, then Prajñā and Nirvāṇa—these three are of a single characteristic; in reality, they have no difference.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to benefit all beings;
Prajñā is their mother, able to give birth to and nourish them.
The Buddha is the father of sentient beings, yet it is Prajñā that can give birth to the Buddha.
This is indeed the grandmother of all sentient beings.
Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha has spoken of it by various names;
according to the capacities of sentient beings, he has established different designations for it.
If a person attains Prajñā, all discursive thoughts are extinguished;
it is like when the sun rises, the morning dew vanishes at once.
The majestic power of Prajñā can move two kinds of people:
Those without wisdom are terrified; those with wisdom rejoice.
If a person attains Prajñā, they become the master of Prajñā;
they do not cling even to Prajñā itself, much less to other dharmas!
Prajñā comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere;
though the wise seek it in all places, they cannot find it.
If one does not perceive Prajñā, then one is bound.
If a person perceives prajñā, this is also called being bound.
If a person perceives prajñā, they then attain liberation;
if one does not perceive prajñā, they likewise attain liberation.
This matter is rare and extraordinary, profound and of great renown;
like a conjured illusion, it is seen yet cannot be seen.
So too are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The path to liberation and nirvāṇa is attained entirely through prajñā.
Discourse belongs to the conventional realm;
out of compassion for all beings, one provisionally designates all phenomena with names. Though they are spoken of, they are not truly spoken of.
The Prajñāpāramitā is like a great mass of fire;
it cannot be grasped from any side, for there is no grasping and nothing to be grasped.
Having relinquished all grasping, this is called "ungraspable."
That which cannot be grasped yet is grasped—this is precisely what is called "grasping.
Prajñā has no characteristic of destruction;
it transcends all speech and has no point of reliance. Who, then, could praise its virtue?
Although Prajñā is beyond praise, I am now able to praise it;
though I have not yet escaped the realm of death, I have already attained liberation! 30.
The Meaning of the Characteristics of Prajñā. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Meaning of the Characteristics of Prajñā, Chapter Thirty. Question:
Why is it that only the *prajñāpāramitā* is called "mahā," while the other five *pāramitās* are not?
The answer is:
"Mahā" is the word for "great" in the language of Qin.
“Prajñā” means wisdom;
“pāramitā” means reaching the other shore.
Because it can reach the further shore of the great ocean of wisdom and arrive at the limit of all wisdom, exhausting its ultimate extent, it is called “reaching the other shore.”
Within all the worlds of the ten directions and the three periods of time, the Buddhas are the foremost; next are the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
These four types of great beings are all born from the Prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, it is called "Great."
Furthermore, it can bestow upon sentient beings a great fruit of retribution that is immeasurable, inexhaustible, and eternally unchanging—namely, nirvana;
the other five pāramitās cannot do so.
Generosity and the other perfections, when separated from the perfection of wisdom, can only yield worldly retributions;
therefore, they cannot be called "great. Question: What is this wisdom?
The answer is:
The Prajñāpāramitā encompasses all wisdom. Why is this so?
A bodhisattva seeking the Buddha-way should study all dharmas and attain all wisdoms—namely, the wisdom of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the wisdom of the Buddhas.
This wisdom is of three kinds:
that of the learner (*śaikṣa*), that of the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither of the learner nor beyond learning.

Wisdom that is neither of the learner nor beyond learning includes, for example, the stage of dry insight (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the four foundations of mindfulness bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-smṛtyupasthāna*), the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Knowledge of the learner (*śaikṣajñāna*) refers to the wisdom of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), up to the wisdom of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*) within the ninth path of non-obstruction on the way toward arhatship.
Knowledge of the non-learner (*aśaikṣajñāna*) refers to the wisdom of the ninth liberation of the arhat;

from this point onward, all knowledges of the non-learner, such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), constitute the knowledge of the non-learner.
The wisdom sought in the path of the pratyekabuddha is also like this.
Question:
If the path of the pratyekabuddha is also like this, how are the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha distinguished?
Answer: Although the Way is of one kind, there are differences in the application of wisdom.

If the Buddhas have not appeared and the Buddha-dharma has already ceased, such a person—due to causes and conditions from previous lives—produces wisdom alone, without hearing it from another, and attains the Way through their own wisdom.
It was as if there were a king who went out to a park to sport.
In the early morning, he saw that the trees, flowers, and fruits were lush and flourishing, exceedingly delightful.
After the king had eaten and lain down to rest, the king’s ladies and court maids all gathered to pluck flowers, thereby damaging and breaking the trees of the grove.
When the king awoke, he saw that the grove had been destroyed, and he attained self-awakening, realizing:
"All things in the world are impermanent, subject to change and decay; all are likewise thus.

Having reflected on this, the mind of the untainted Path arose within him; he severed all fetters and afflictions, attained the Way of a Pratyekabuddha, and became endowed with the six supernormal powers. He then flew at once to a secluded forest.

Through such causes and conditions as these—namely, the merit, vows, practices, and karmic retributions of previous lives—and by encountering minor causes and conditions in the present life, one accomplishes the path of a Pratyekabuddha; it is in this way that they differ [from others].
Furthermore, there are two kinds of pratyekabuddhas:
the first is called the solitary awakener (pratyekabuddha), and the second is called the one awakened through conditions (pratītyasamutpāda-buddha).
The one awakened through conditions is as described above.
The Pratyekabuddha is one who attains the Way in this present life, awakening by himself without hearing it from another; he is called a Pratyekabuddha or a Paccekabuddha.
There are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas:
first, those who were originally practitioners in training (śaikṣa) and are born among human beings;
At that time, there is no Buddha and the Buddha-dharma has perished.
This srotāpanna, having already completed seven births, should not undergo an eighth birth, as he spontaneously attains the Way.
Such a person is not called a Buddha, nor is he called an arhat; he is called a minor pratyekabuddha, who is no different from an arhat.
There may be those who are not equal to great arhats such as Śāriputra;
even great pratyekabuddhas, having cultivated merit and increased wisdom for one hundred kalpas, attain a portion of the thirty-two marks:
some have thirty-one marks, some thirty, some twenty-nine, and so on, down to a single mark.
Among the nine types of arhats, he is preeminent in the sharpness of his wisdom; he is able to penetrate the general and specific characteristics within all profound dharmas;
having long cultivated meditative concentration, he always delights in dwelling in solitude.
Such characteristics are called those of a Mahāpratyekabuddha; this is what distinguishes them.
One who seeks the Buddha-way makes a vow from the first moment of generating the mind:

"May I become a Buddha to deliver sentient beings, attain all Buddha-dharmas, practice the six pāramitās, destroy the hosts of Māra and all afflictions, attain all-knowledge, realize the Buddha-way, and even enter nirvana without remainder."

"Following the practice of his original vows, he fully knows all wisdom—both its general characteristics and its specific characteristics—from that point onward; this is called the wisdom of the Buddha-way."
These three kinds of wisdom can all be fully known, and one reaches their ultimate limit; for this reason, it is said that one "reaches the limit of wisdom. Question:

If, as you have stated, all wisdom—whether mundane or supramundane—should be entered into, why do you speak only of "reaching the limit of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles" and not mention other forms of knowledge?
Answer: The Three Vehicles are true wisdom; all others are merely false and illusory. Although the Bodhisattva knows this, he does not practice them exclusively.
It is like Mount Malaya: apart from it, nowhere else can sandalwood be found.
If there are any well-spoken words elsewhere, they are all derived from within the Buddha-dharma.
Apart from the Buddha-dharma, what seems good at first hearing will not remain excellent over time.
For example, cow’s milk and donkey’s milk are identical in color;
yet when cow’s milk is churned, it becomes butter, whereas when donkey’s milk is churned, it becomes urine.

Likewise, the words of the Buddha’s Dharma and the words of the non-Buddhists are identical in that they both advocate non-killing, non-stealing, compassion for sentient beings, mental restraint, detachment from desire, and contemplation of emptiness; yet [the results differ].
However, although the words of non-Buddhists may initially seem profound, when one exhaustively examines their ultimate destination, they prove to be false and deceptive.
All non-Buddhists are attached to the view of a self;
if a real self truly existed, it would necessarily fall into one of two categories:
Whether it be of a disintegrating nature or a non-disintegrating nature:
if it were of a disintegrating nature, it would be like cowhide;
if it were of a non-disintegrating nature, it would be like space.
In these two states, there is neither the sin of killing nor the merit of not killing.
If it were like empty space, which cannot be moistened by rain or dew nor dried up by wind or heat, then it would fall into the characteristic of permanence.
If [the self] were permanent, suffering could not afflict it and pleasure could not gladden it;
if it did not experience suffering or pleasure, one would have no reason to avoid calamity or pursue fortune.
If it were like a cowhide, it would be destroyed by wind and rain; if it were destroyed, it would fall into impermanence, and if it were impermanent, there would be neither sin nor merit.
If the words of the non-Buddhists were truly as they claim, how could it be that abstaining from killing constitutes merit and taking life constitutes a transgression?
[The opponent] asks:
"If the non-Buddhists' precepts and merit are lost in this way, what then is the case regarding their meditative concentration and wisdom?"
The answer is:
Because non-Buddhists pursue dhyāna with a self-centered mind, because they abound in craving, views, and pride, and because they do not relinquish all phenomena, they lack true wisdom.

Question: You say that non-Buddhists contemplate emptiness, and that contemplating emptiness leads them to abandon all dharmas; how then can you say, "Because they do not abandon all dharmas, they possess no true wisdom"?
The answer is:

Although non-Buddhists contemplate emptiness, they grasp at the mark of emptiness; although they know that all phenomena are empty, they do not realize their own emptiness because they are attached to the wisdom of contemplating emptiness.
Question:
The non-Buddhists have the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), in which both mind and mental factors are entirely extinguished;
because they are entirely extinguished, there is no fault of grasping signs, attachment, or [defective] wisdom.
Answer: The power of the concentration of non-conception forcibly causes the mind to cease; it is not the power of true wisdom.

Furthermore, within this state, one conceives the notion that it is nirvana, failing to realize that it is a phenomenon produced by the conjunction [of conditions]. For this reason, one falls into error.
In this state, although the mind temporarily ceases, it arises again when causes and conditions are obtained.
It is like a person who, during dreamless sleep, has no mental activity; yet upon awakening, it returns once more.
Question:

If the fault of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is thus, there is furthermore the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Within this, there is no conceptual proliferation whatsoever; nor is it like forcibly producing the attainment of non-perception to extinguish perception. Rather, within this state, there is no perception by virtue of the power of wisdom!
Answer: There is perception within this state, but because it is extremely subtle, it is not perceived.
If there were no perception, for what further reason would the disciples of the Buddha seek true wisdom?
In the Buddha-dharma, the consciousness within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception abides dependent upon the four aggregates.

Because these four aggregates belong to causes and conditions, they are impermanent; because they are impermanent, they are suffering; because they are impermanent and suffering, they are empty; because they are empty, they are without self; and because they are empty and without self, they can be relinquished.
Because you are attached to wisdom, you do not attain nirvāṇa.
It is like a measuring insect: it withdraws its hind leg and establishes it firmly before moving its front leg forward;
when the object of its movement is exhausted and there is no further place to advance, it returns.

The non-Buddhists rely upon the first dhyāna to abandon the desires of the lower stages, continuing in this manner until they rely upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to abandon the sphere of nothingness;
since there is no higher stage upon which to rely, they are unable to abandon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself.
This is because they have no further place of reliance; they fear losing their sense of self and dread falling into a state of non-attainment.
Furthermore, in the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there are permissions for killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol.
It is said that for the sake of a sacrifice to the heavens, there is no sin in killing through incantations;
and for the sake of practicing the Way, if one encounters an urgent calamity and wishes to preserve one's own life, there is no sin in killing a common person.

Furthermore, in cases of urgent distress, for the sake of practicing the Path, one may steal anything except gold to preserve one's life; later, one should eliminate the karmic retribution for this offense.
Except for the wives of one’s teacher, the consort of a king, the wife of a spiritual friend, or a maiden, engaging in sexual misconduct under circumstances of urgent distress is permissible.
Furthermore, lying is permitted for the sake of one’s teacher or parents, for one’s own life, for the sake of cattle, or for the purpose of acting as a matchmaker.
In cold regions, it is permitted to drink honey-wine;
within a deva temple, it may be permitted to taste one or two drops of wine.
In the Buddha-dharma, however, this is not the case.
One regards all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity and compassion, not even taking the life of an ant, let alone killing a human being!
One does not take so much as a single needle or a single thread, let alone many objects!
One should not even touch a prostitute who has no master with one's finger, much less a man’s wife!
One must not speak falsely even in jest, much less commit premeditated falsehood!
All types of liquor must never be drunk at any time; how much more so in cold regions or at deva temples!
You followers of external paths are as vastly different from the Buddha-dharma as heaven is from earth!
Your non-Buddhist teachings, O outsiders, are the source from which all afflictions arise;
the Buddha-dharma, however, is the place where all afflictions are extinguished—this constitutes a great difference.
The dharmas of the Buddhas are immeasurable, like a vast ocean; because they accord with the inclinations of sentient beings, they teach the Dharma in various ways.
Some say there is existence, while others say there is non-existence;
some say there is permanence, while others say there is impermanence;
some say there is suffering, while others say there is pleasure.
Sometimes he speaks of a self, and sometimes he speaks of non-self;
sometimes he speaks of diligently practicing the three karmas and gathering all wholesome dharmas, and sometimes he speaks of the mark of non-action of all dharmas.
Regarding these various differing explanations, those lacking wisdom, upon hearing them, claim they are contradictory;
however, the wise enter the three gateways to the Dharma and perceive that all the Buddha’s words are the true Dharma, without any mutual contradiction.
What are these three gates?
First, the Piṭaka gate; second, the Abhidharma gate; third, the Śūnyatā gate.
Question:
What is meant by *piṭaka*?
What is meant by *abhidharma*?
And what is meant by the "gate of emptiness"?
The answer is:
The Piṭaka consists of three million two hundred thousand words; it was composed by Mahākātyāyana while the Buddha was still in the world.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the lifespan of humans gradually decreased and their power of memory diminished, so they were unable to recite it extensively; thus, those who had attained the Way compiled it into three million eight hundred and four thousand words.
If a person enters the gateway of the Piṭaka, their discourse will be inexhaustible;
within it are various gateways, such as the gateway of following characteristics (anulakṣaṇa-mukha) and the gateway of counteractive measures (pratipakṣa-mukha).
As for the gateway of following characteristics, it is as the Buddha spoke in a verse:
"Do no evil, do good, and purify your own mind: this is the teaching of all Buddhas.

Within this [verse], all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) should have been explained; yet now, by explaining only "purify your own mind," it is known that all mental factors have already been explained.
Why is this? Because they share the same characteristics and the same objects of focus.
As the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness, within them the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, and the five powers are not separate.
Why is this? Within the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four kinds of diligence are precisely the four right efforts.
The four kinds of concentration are the four bases of psychic power;
the five kinds of wholesome dharmas are the five faculties and the five powers.
Although the Buddha does not mention other gateways, by teaching only the four foundations of mindfulness, one should know that he has already taught the other gateways.
Just as the Buddha, regarding the Four Noble Truths, sometimes taught one truth, or two, or three.
For example, the bhikṣu Aśvajit spoke this verse for Śāriputra:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; These phenomena, their conditions, and their cessation."
"My Teacher, the Great Holy King, has explained this meaning in such a way.
This verse speaks only of the three truths; one should know that the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is already included therein, for they are not separate from one another.
It is like when one person commits an offense, the entire family suffers the punishment.
These and others like them are called the "gate of following characteristics" (suxiangmen).
As for the "gate of counteracting" (duizhimen), it is as when the Buddha spoke only of the four perversions (viparyāsa):
the perversion of permanence, the perversion of pleasure, the perversion of self, and the perversion of purity.
Although the four foundations of mindfulness are not explicitly mentioned therein, one should know that their meaning is already present.
It is like when medicine is prescribed: once the illness is known, the medicine is understood; and when the illness is described, the medicine is known.
If one speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness, it should be known that one has already spoken of the four perversions;
these four perversions are themselves false characteristics.
If one speaks of the four perversions, one has already spoken of all the fetters.
Why is this? If one explains its root, then it is known that all its branches are thereby understood.
As the Buddha taught, there are three poisons within all the worlds; [by understanding the root, the branches are likewise understood].
When the three poisons are spoken of, one should know that the three divisions and the Eightfold Noble Path have already been explained.
When the three poisons are spoken of, one should know that all the poisons of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been explained.

The fifteen kinds of craving are the poison of greed; the fifteen kinds of aversion are the poison of hatred; the fifteen kinds of ignorance are the poison of delusion; and all false views, pride, and doubt belong to ignorance.
All such fetters and afflictions enter into the three poisons.
By what means are they extinguished?
By the three trainings and the Eightfold Noble Path.
If one speaks of the three divisions and the Eightfold Noble Path, it should be understood that all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have thereby been explained.
Such various characteristics as these are called the "gate of counteractive measures" (pratipakṣa-mukha).
Such dharmas as these are called the Piṭaka-gate (Kuṇḍala-mukha).
What is called the Abhidharma-gate?

It refers to when the Buddha himself explains the meaning of various dharmas, or when the Buddha himself provides the names of various dharmas, which his disciples then collect, compile, and explain in various ways.
As the Buddha said:

"If there is a bhikṣu who cannot maintain correct mindfulness regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), yet desires to attain the supreme worldly dharma (laukikāgradharma), such a thing is impossible."
If one does not attain the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) and yet wishes to enter the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), such a thing is impossible.
If one does not enter the state of certainty and yet wishes to attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*, such a thing is impossible.
It is possible for a bhikṣu who correctly recollects all conditioned phenomena to attain the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
If he attains the supreme worldly dharma, it is certain that he will enter the state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*);

having entered the state of certainty, it is certain that he will attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship (*arhat*). This is indeed possible.
The Buddha spoke directly of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) without explaining its characteristics, its connection to a realm, its cause, its condition, or its retribution.

From the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) and the various dharmas practiced by the śrāvakas, up to nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), the distinct analysis of the characteristics and meanings of each of these is called the Abhidharma gateway.
The Gate of Emptiness refers to the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena.
As stated in the *King Bimbisāra Welcomes the Buddha Sūtra*, the Buddha told the Great King:
"When form arises, it is merely emptiness that arises; when form ceases, it is merely emptiness that ceases."
When all conditioned phenomena arise, they arise as mere emptiness; when they cease, they cease as mere emptiness.

Within this, there is no self, no person, and no soul; there is no person who passes from this world to the next, other than the conventional designations of sentient beings formed through the conjunction of causes and conditions. Yet foolish ordinary people pursue these names, seeking substantial reality within them.
In such sūtras as these, the Buddha taught the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
As for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is as the Buddha said in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*:
regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, from ignorance up to old age and death, if someone says "this is old age and death," or if they say "who ages and dies," both are false views.
Birth, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance are also like this.
If someone says, "The body is the self," or if they say, "The body is different from the self"—though these two views differ, they are equally wrong views.
The Buddha said:
"To hold the view that the body is the self is a false view; such a person is not my disciple.
To hold the view that the body is distinct from the self is also a false view; such a person is not my disciple."
In this sutra, the Buddha teaches the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
If he asks, "Who ages and dies? one should know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
If he says, "This is aging and death," one should know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This applies even to ignorance, and so on.
Furthermore, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the Buddha spoke of the sixty-two views:
if someone says, "The self is eternal, and the world is also eternal," this constitutes a false view.
If one says, "The self is impermanent and the world is impermanent," this is also a false view;
to say, "The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent," or "The self and the world are neither permanent nor impermanent," are all false views.
For this reason, one knows that all phenomena are empty; this is what constitutes reality.
Question: If one says "the self is eternal," should this not be considered a false view?
Why is this? Because the nature of a self does not exist.
If one says, "The world is eternal," that too should be considered a false view.
Why is this? Because the world is in fact entirely impermanent, yet due to perversion one says it is "permanent.
If one were to say that "the self is impermanent," that too would constitute a false view.
Why is this? Because the nature of a self (*ātman*) does not exist, one should not say it is "impermanent.
If one says, "The world is impermanent," this should not be considered a false view.
Why is this? Because the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is truly impermanent.
He replied:
If all phenomena were truly impermanent, why would the Buddha say, "To claim that the world is impermanent is called a false view"?
Therefore, it can be known that they are not truly impermanent.
Question:

The Buddha has taught in various places that one should contemplate conditioned phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, so that people may attain the Path. Why, then, do you say that [the view of] impermanence falls into wrong view?
Answer: The Buddha has taught impermanence in various places and taught non-extinction in various places.
For example, when Mahānāma, the Śākya king, came to the Buddha’s presence, he said to the Buddha:
"The population of this Kapilavastu is vast and dense; should I encounter a runaway carriage, a stray horse, a mad elephant, or people engaged in combat, I might lose my mindfulness of the Buddha.
At such times, I think to myself:
'If I were to die now, where would I be reborn?'"
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Do not be afraid, do not be terrified!
At that time, you shall not be born in the evil realms; you will certainly reach a good destination."
For example, if a tree always leans toward the east, it will inevitably fall in that direction when someone cuts it down;

so too it is with a person of virtue: when the body perishes at death, because their mind and consciousness have been perfumed for a long night by faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom, they will certainly obtain benefit and be reborn in the heavens above.

If all phenomena arise and perish moment by moment and are impermanent, why does the Buddha say that "because the mind is perfumed by various merits, one will certainly attain rebirth in the higher realms"?
For this reason, we know that [the mind] is not of an impermanent nature.
Question:
If impermanence is unreal, why does the Buddha speak of impermanence? Answer:
The Buddha preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for sentient beings. To shatter the perversion of permanence, he teaches impermanence;

because people do not know or believe in future lives, he teaches that "the mind goes to future lives and is reborn above in the heavens, and the causes and conditions of one's deeds—whether of merit or demerit—are not lost for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy), not the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).
The true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Furthermore, the Buddha has taught in various places that all phenomena are empty; within the emptiness of all phenomena, there is also no impermanence.
For this reason, it is said that "the view that the world is impermanent is a false view.
Therefore, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, there was a brahmin from Vaiśālī named Vādibala; various Licchavis and others hired him with a great amount of wealth to debate with the Buddha.
Having accepted their employment, he composed five hundred difficult questions that very night. The next morning, together with the Licchavis, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and asked the Buddha:
"Is there but one ultimate path?"
"Are there many ultimate paths?
The Buddha said, "There is but one ultimate path; there are no many."
The brahmin said:
"The Buddha speaks of a single path, whereas the various non-Buddhist teachers each have their own ultimate path; thus, there are many, not one!
The Buddha said:
"Although each of these has many followers, none constitute the true path. Why is this?
Because all are attached to false views, they cannot be called the ultimate path."
The Buddha asked the brahmin,
"Has the brahmin Mṛgaśiras attained the Way?
He replied:
"Among all who have attained the Way, this is the foremost.
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu Mṛgaśiras, formerly a brahmin, was fanning the Buddha from behind.
The Buddha asked the brahmin,
"Do you recognize this bhikṣu?
The brahmin recognized him and, filled with shame, lowered his head.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses from the "Chapter on Meaning" (Arthavargīya):
"Each one claims their own view is ultimate, yet each clings to it with attachment.
Each one asserts that the other is wrong; none of these are ultimately true!"
When such a person enters a debate assembly and clarifies the principles of meaning, each side contends over right and wrong, harboring sorrow or joy regarding victory or defeat.
The victor falls into the pit of arrogance; the vanquished falls into the prison of grief.
Therefore, the wise do not follow these two extremes.
You should know, O Vātsīputrīya, that according to my disciples' Dharma, there is neither falsehood nor reality; what is it that you seek?
"You wish to refute my treatise, but in the end there is no such possibility;
the Omniscient One is invincible, and you will only bring about your own destruction!
Thus, in various places throughout the Śrāvaka sūtras, it is taught that all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the gate of emptiness in the Mahāyāna: the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty of itself; it is not empty because of being observed through wisdom and skillful means.
As the Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Form is empty of form itself; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are each empty of consciousness itself."

The twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, omniscience (*sarvajñā*), and even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all these are themselves empty.
Question: If the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty by itself, truly empty, and non-existent, how is it that one does not fall into wrong view?
For wrong view is defined as the absence of sin and merit, and the absence of this world and the next; it would be no different from this!
Answer: Those who deny both sin and merit do not say that this present life does not exist;
they merely say that there is no future life, asserting that beings are like grasses and trees, which arise and perish of their own accord.
Some believe that a person is born or a person is killed, and that this ends with the present life, with no further existence in future worlds;
yet they do not know to contemplate that all internal and external characteristics of the body are empty—this is what makes them different [from those who understand].
Furthermore, those with wrong views commit many evils and sever all wholesome deeds;
those who contemplate emptiness do not even wish to perform virtuous dharmas, let alone commit evil!
Question:
There are two kinds of wrong views:
those that negate both cause and effect, and those that negate the effect but do not negate the cause.
As you have said, the refutation of the fruit does not constitute a refutation of the cause.
To refute both the fruit and the cause means to claim that there are no causes and no conditions, and that there is neither sin nor merit; this is the refutation of the cause.
To claim that there is no present life, no future life, and no retribution for sins and merits is the refutation of the fruit.

The person who contemplates emptiness says that all things are empty; thus, sin and merit, as well as cause and effect, would all be non-existent. How does this differ from [the view you have described]?
The answer is:
the person of false views renders all phenomena empty through annihilationism.
The followers of the Mahāyāna know that all dharmas are empty and true, neither broken nor destroyed.
It is asked:
There are three kinds of false views:
First, they destroy the retribution of sin and merit, yet do not destroy sin and merit;
they destroy the fruit of causes and conditions, yet do not destroy causes and conditions;
they destroy the future life, yet do not destroy the present life.
Second, they destroy the retribution of sin and merit, and they also destroy sin and merit;
they destroy the fruit of causes and conditions, and they also destroy causes and conditions;
they destroy the future life, and they also destroy the present life, yet they do not destroy all dharmas.
Third, there is the destruction of all phenomena, asserting that they are entirely non-existent.
One who contemplates emptiness also says that true emptiness is non-existent; what difference is there between this and the third type of wrong view?
Answer: Wrong views destroy all phenomena, rendering them empty;
one who contemplates emptiness knows that all phenomena are true emptiness, which is neither destroyed nor disintegrated.
Furthermore, those with wrong views claim that all dharmas are empty and non-existent, yet they grasp at the mark of emptiness and engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Those who contemplate emptiness know that all dharmas are empty; they do not grasp at marks and do not engage in conceptual proliferation.

Furthermore, although those with wrong views verbally profess that all things are empty, they still give rise to craving toward objects of craving, anger toward objects of anger, pride toward objects of pride, and delusion toward objects of delusion, thereby deceiving themselves.
In contrast, a disciple of the Buddha truly knows emptiness; their mind remains unmoved, and the places where the fetters (saṃyojana) would arise no longer do so.
Just as empty space cannot be defiled by smoke or fire, nor moistened by heavy rain;
so too, when one contemplates emptiness in this way, various afflictions no longer adhere to the mind.
Furthermore, those with wrong views claim that nothing exists and that [things] do not arise from the causes and conditions of craving;
they assert that "true emptiness" arises from the causes and conditions of craving—this is what constitutes their difference.
Since even the four immeasurable minds and all pure dharmas do not equal the wisdom of true emptiness because their objects of perception are unreal, how much less so this false view?
Furthermore, this view is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), while the view of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
One who practices false views is a wicked person in the present life and shall enter hell in future lives;
one who practices the wisdom of true emptiness attains renown in the present life and shall become a Buddha in future lives.
It is like the difference between water and fire, or like nectar and poison; it is as if comparing the divine food *sūda* to foul excrement!
Furthermore, within true emptiness there is the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*;
whereas although wrong views regarding emptiness possess emptiness, they lack the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*.

Furthermore, one who contemplates true emptiness first possesses immeasurable merit from giving, precept-keeping, and meditative concentration; their mind is supple and their fetters and afflictions are thin, and only then do they attain true emptiness.
Within wrong views, these things do not exist; there, one merely seeks to grasp emptiness with a distorted mind through conceptualization and discrimination.
It is like a countryman who had never known salt before; seeing a nobleman put salt among various meats and vegetables while eating, he asked, "For what reason do you act thus?"
He said, "This salt can make the flavors of all things delicious.

The man then thought, "If this salt can make all things delicious, its own flavor must be abundant. He then scooped up some salt with his empty hand and filled his mouth with it to eat; it was so salty and bitter that it stung his mouth, and he asked:
"Why do you say that salt can make food delicious?
The nobleman said, "Fool!"
"One must calculate the proper proportions and blend them to make it delicious; how can one eat salt alone?

Likewise, when a person of little wisdom hears of the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), they do not practice various meritorious virtues but desire only to attain emptiness itself; this constitutes a false view that severs all roots of goodness.
These and other such meanings are called the gate of emptiness.
If a person enters these three gates, they will know that the meanings of the Buddha-dharma do not contradict one another.
To be able to understand this matter is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is unimpeded regarding all phenomena.

If one does not attain the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, entering the gate of Abhidharma leads to falling into existence; entering the gate of emptiness leads to falling into non-existence; and entering the gate of Kṣudraka-piṭaka leads to falling into both existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they know that all phenomena have a single characteristic, they are also able to know the manifold characteristics of all phenomena;
and although they know the manifold characteristics of all phenomena, they are also able to know that all phenomena have a single characteristic.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva such as this is called prajñāpāramitā. Question:
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva know the various characteristics of all phenomena?
How does one know that all dharmas have a single characteristic?
The answer is:
the Bodhisattva contemplates the characteristics of all dharmas, which are what are called "characteristics of existence."
Because this exists, the mind arises within all phenomena; thus, everything such as these exists.
Question:
How can the mind arise within that which is non-existent?
Answer: If one says "non-existent," this very statement is itself a dharma that exists.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas as having a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Just as there is no characteristic of a sheep within an ox, and no characteristic of an ox within a sheep;
so too, among all such phenomena, each lacks the characteristics of the others.
As previously stated, because of the existence of "being" (bhāva), the mind arises; yet this phenomenon is distinct from being. Because it is distinct, it ought not to exist.
If there were a thing that is a cow, then a sheep would also have to be a cow.
Why? Because the existence of the thing is not different [in either case].
If they were different, they would not exist; thus, all such things are non-existent.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as one; because this is a single dharma, the single mind arises from within all phenomena.
Each phenomenon possesses its own distinct characteristic; when these are combined as one, they are called "two" or "three.
Of these, the "one" is real, while the "two" and "three" are illusory.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena exist because they have causes for their existence, just as the human body is impermanent.
Why is this? Because it possesses the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
All phenomena are thus: they exist because they have causes.
Furthermore, all phenomena exist without having [a single] cause, just as the human body is impermanent because it arises and ceases;
it is through this arising and ceasing that one knows it is impermanent.
This cause, in turn, must have a cause; if this were so, there would be an infinite regress. If there were an infinite regress, there would be no cause.
If this cause has no further cause, then this impermanent cause is not truly a cause. In such cases, everything would be without a cause.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena possess characteristics, and that there is no phenomenon devoid of characteristics; for example:
earth has the characteristics of solidity and heaviness;
water has the characteristics of coldness and moisture.
Fire has the characteristics of heat and illumination;
wind has the characteristics of lightness and motion;
space has the characteristic of receptivity.
Discriminating and cognizing is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That there is "this" and "that" is the characteristic of direction (*dis*);
that there is "long" and "near" is the characteristic of time (*kāla*).
A turbid and evil mind that afflicts sentient beings is the mark of transgression;
a pure and wholesome mind that has compassion for sentient beings is the mark of merit.
Attachment to all phenomena is the mark of bondage.
Non-attachment to all phenomena is the characteristic of liberation.
Directly knowing all phenomena without obstruction is the characteristic of a Buddha.
All such [phenomena] each have their own characteristics.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of marks (*animitta*). These various marks arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they do not exist.

For example, "earth" is so named because of the conjunction of four factors—color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility—and it is not called "earth" because of color alone, nor because of fragrance alone, nor taste alone, nor tangibility alone.
Why is this? If only visible form were earth, then the other three would not be earth; thus, earth would lack odor, taste, and tangibility.
It is the same for odor, taste, and tangibility.
Furthermore, how can these four dharmas constitute a single dharma?
And how can a single dharma constitute these four dharmas?
For this reason, one cannot take the four as the ground, nor can one take that which is apart from the four as the ground.
Question:
I do not take the four as the earth; rather, it is because of the four dharmas that the dharma of earth arises, and this earth abides within those four dharmas!
Answer:
If the earth-element arises from these four factors, then the earth must be distinct from them—
just as a child born of parents is distinct from the parents.

If that were so, then when the eye sees forms, the nose perceives odors, the tongue perceives tastes, and the body perceives tangibles, if the earth were distinct from these four factors, there ought to be yet another distinct sense organ and a distinct consciousness to perceive it.
If there were no distinct faculties and no distinct consciousnesses to cognize them, then earth would not exist.
Question: If the previously stated definition of the characteristic of earth is flawed, one should instead state the characteristic of earth as it is taught in the Abhidharma.

Regarding the statement that the name "earth" refers to the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) composed of the four great elements, and that while the earth-element (pṛthivī-dhātu) alone has the characteristic of solidity,
"earth" itself is visible matter (sanidarśana-rūpa): the answer is that if earth were merely matter, the fault already mentioned previously would apply.

Furthermore, earth has solidity as its characteristic; yet when one sees only color with the eye—such as the moon in water, a reflection in a mirror, or the shadow of grass and trees—there is no characteristic of solidity, for solidity is known through the tactile faculty of the body.
Furthermore, if the eye sees a form that is earth, its characteristic of solidity is the earth element;
if the eye sees a form that is water or fire, its characteristics of moisture and heat are the water and fire elements.
If that were so, then wind and the element of wind should also be distinguished, yet they are not distinguished!
As it is said: "What is wind?"
The wind element;
what is the wind element? Wind.
If these were one and the same thing, there should not be two kinds of answers;
if they were not different, then earth and the earth-element (pṛthivī-dhātu) should not be distinct.
Question:
These four great elements are each inseparable from one another; within earth there are four types, and likewise water, fire, and wind each have four types.
However, because the quality of earth predominates within earth, it is named "earth";
the same applies to water, fire, and wind.
Answer: It is not so. Why is this?
If the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) were present within fire, they would all be hot, for there is no fire that is not hot.
If three of the great elements were present within fire but were not hot, they could not be called fire;
if they were hot, they would abandon their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and would all be called fire.
If it is claimed that [the subtle] cannot be known because it is subtle, then it is no different from non-existence.
If there is something coarse that can be apprehended, then one knows that the subtle exists;
if there is no coarse, there is also no subtle.
Through such various causes and conditions, the characteristic of earth cannot be apprehended;
if the characteristic of earth cannot be apprehended, the characteristics of all phenomena likewise cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, all phenomena are of a single characteristic.
Question: One should not say that there is no characteristic. Why is this?
The signlessness of all phenomena is itself their mark.
If there were no signlessness, then the marks of all phenomena could not be sublated. Why is this?
Because there is no such thing as "signlessness.
If this signlessness itself were a sign, then one should not say, "All phenomena are signless.
He replied:
One uses signlessness to dismantle the signs of all phenomena.
If there were a "sign of signlessness," one would fall into the signs of all phenomena;
if one does not enter into the signs of all phenomena, then one should not raise such an objection!
The signless destroys all characteristics of dharmas and also extinguishes its own characteristic;
it is like a fire at the front of a stack of wood: having burned all the fuel, it then naturally subsides of itself.
For this reason, the noble ones practice the signless-signless samādhi, because they destroy even the signless.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as neither conjoined nor dispersed, colorless, formless, non-obstructive, unmanifest, and ineffable; they possess a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristiclessness."
All such dharmas have but a single characteristic.
How, then, does one contemplate their various characteristics?

All dharmas are subsumed within two categories: namely, name and form; or alternatively, the dyads of form and formlessness, the visible and the invisible, the resistant and the non-resistant, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, and the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The one hundred and two dharma-gates are as explained in the "Chapter on the Thousand Difficulties.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
patience and gentleness.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
honoring with affection and making offerings.
There are two kinds of giving:
The two kinds of giving: material giving and the giving of the Dharma.
The two powers:
the power of discernment through wisdom and the power of cultivating the path.
The two fulfillments:
fulfillment of ethical discipline and fulfillment of right view.
The two characteristics:
The characteristic of integrity and straightforwardness, and the characteristic of flexibility.
Two dharmas:
concentration and wisdom.
Two dharmas:
clarity and liberation.
Two dharmas:
There are two dharmas: worldly dharma and the dharma of the ultimate meaning;
these two dharmas are mindfulness and skillful wisdom.
The two truths:
the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The two liberations:
Liberation by waiting for the opportune time (*sāmayikī vimukti*) and unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*).
Two kinds of *nirvāṇa*:
*nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Two kinds of culmination:
culmination of activity and culmination of vows.
Two kinds of views:
Knowledge and vision, and abandonment.
The two fulfillments:
fulfillment of meaning and fulfillment of expression.
Two dharmas:
fewness of desires and contentment.
Two dharmas:
Easy to nourish and easy to satisfy.
There are two factors:
the Dharma and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Two knowledges:
the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
In this manner, there are immeasurable such classifications of dual dharmas.
Furthermore, one knows the three paths:
the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
The three natures:
The nature of abandonment, the nature of detachment, and the nature of cessation.
The three cultivations:
the cultivation of ethical discipline, the cultivation of meditative concentration, and the cultivation of wisdom.
The three types of bodhi:
the bodhi of a Buddha, the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha, and the bodhi of a śrāvaka; these are names for the fulfillment of wisdom, wherein there is no further learning required.
The Three Vehicles:
the Buddha Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The Three Refuges:
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The three abidings:
the Brahma-abiding, the celestial-abiding, and the noble-abiding.
The three types of supremacy:
supremacy over oneself, supremacy over others, and supremacy over the Dharma.
The three things that the Buddhas do not need to guard against:
There is non-restraint of bodily action, non-restraint of verbal action, and non-restraint of mental action.
There are three bases of merit:
generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind.
The three staffs:
the staff of learning, the staff of detachment, and the staff of wisdom.
The three wheels:
The wheel of transformation, the wheel of manifesting others' minds, and the wheel of teaching and transforming.
The three gates of liberation:
the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
There are such immeasurable threefold dharma-gates as these.
Furthermore, one should know the fourfold dharmas:

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four noble truths, the four noble lineages, the four fruits of the śramaṇa, the four types of knowledge, the four kinds of faith, the four paths, the four means of attraction, the four reliances, the four penetrations of wholesome roots, the four paths, the four wheels of gods and humans, the four firm dharmas, the four fearlessnesses, and the four immeasurable minds—such immeasurable fourfold dharma-gates as these.

Furthermore, he knows the five groups of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the five natures of emergence, the five bases of liberation, the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the five great gifts, the five knowledges, the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), the five abodes of the Pure Abode heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*), the five paths of cultivation, the five wisdom-concentrations (*jñāna-samādhi*), the five noble branch-concentrations (*āryāṅga-samādhi*), and the five paths of speech in accordance with the Dharma—such immeasurable categories of fivefold dharmas as these.

Furthermore, he knows the six dharmas of equanimity, the six dharmas of affection and respect, the six supernormal powers, the six kinds of arhats, the six stages of the path of seeing the truths, the six conforming recollections, the six samādhis, the six concentrations, and the six pāramitās—such immeasurable dharma-gates of sixfold categories as these.

Furthermore, he knows the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven riches, the seven supports, the seven meditative absorptions, the seven sublime dharmas, the seven knowledges, the seven destinations of virtuous persons, the seven purities, the seven blessings of material wealth, the seven blessings not of material wealth, and the seven factors conducive to concentration—such immeasurable gateways of the sevenfold dharmas as these.

Furthermore, he knows the eightfold noble path, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the eight recollections of great persons, the eight kinds of diligence, the eight types of men, and the eight powers of an arhat—such immeasurable dharma-gates consisting of eights as these.

Furthermore, one knows the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*): the nine [stages] consisting of the reduction of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) starting from name-and-form down to birth-and-death; the nine untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*), which exclude conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) because they result in the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); the nine untainted stages, namely the six dhyānas and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*); and the nine stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Such are the immeasurable gateways of the ninefold dharmas.

Furthermore, he knows the ten dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the ten great grounds of goodness (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the ten powers of the Buddha—such immeasurable dharma-gates consisting of tens as these.

Furthermore, he knows the eleven factors that assist the noble path; he knows the twelvefold chain of dependent origination; he knows the thirteen methods of transcendence, the fourteen transformative minds, the fifteen minds of the path of seeing the truths, the sixteen practices of *ānāpānasmṛti*, the seventeen noble practices, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and the nineteenth stage of detachment. Within the path of contemplation, there are one hundred and sixty-two paths capable of destroying the thieves of affliction, and one hundred and seventy-eight fruits of the śramaṇa—eighty-nine conditioned fruits and eighty-nine unconditioned fruits.

In this way, he is able to know all such various and immeasurable phenomena of differing characteristics—their arising and ceasing, their increase and decrease, their gain and loss, and their defilement and purification.

Having realized these dharmas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to cause all dharmas to enter into the emptiness of their own nature, remaining unattached to any dharma. Thus, they transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and enter the rank of the Bodhisattvas.

Having entered the rank of the Bodhisattvas, out of great compassion and pity, and by the power of skillful means, they distinguish the various names of all dharmas to deliver sentient beings and enable them to attain the Three Vehicles.
It is like a skilled artisan who, by the power of medicinal substances, can cause silver to be transformed into gold and gold to be transformed into silver.
Question:
If the nature of all phenomena is empty and true, how can one differentiate the various names of these phenomena?
Why is it that one does not speak merely of the nature of true emptiness?
The answer is:
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not say that emptiness is something that can be apprehended or clung to.
If [anything] were obtainable or graspable, one should not speak of the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
That which is unobtainable is empty; it is without any obstruction.
If there were any obstruction, that would be obtainable, and thus it would not be the emptiness of the unobtainable.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the emptiness of non-apprehension, yet is still able to discern all phenomena and compassionately deliver sentient beings, this is the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To state the essential point: the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Question:
All worldly scriptures, as well as the ninety-six kinds of monastic scriptures, also speak of the true nature of all phenomena; [how does yours differ?]
Furthermore, within the Tripiṭaka of the Śrāvaka Dharma, there is also the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; why is it not called Prajñāpāramitā?
Why is it that only the true reality of all phenomena in this sūtra is uniquely named Prajñāpāramitā?
The answer is:
Within worldly scriptures, [teachings] are not real because they are for the sake of securing the state, the family, and the happiness of life and longevity.
Furthermore, those who have left home as non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) fall into states of false views; because their minds are characterized by attachment, these too are not real.

Although the Dharma of the Śrāvakas contains the Four Noble Truths, they contemplate the true nature of all phenomena through impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; because their wisdom is incomplete and not sharp, it cannot be for the sake of all sentient beings, nor for the sake of attaining the Buddha-dharma. Thus, although they possess real wisdom, it is not called Prajñāpāramitā.
As it is said:
"When the Buddha enters and emerges from various samādhis, even Śāriputra and others do not so much as hear their names, let alone be able to know them! Why is this?

When the various Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they lack great vows, they lack great kindness and great compassion, they do not seek all manner of meritorious virtues, they do not make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout the three periods of time, and they do not seek to know the true reality of all phenomena with thorough discernment;
they merely desire to escape the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.

From their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, all bodhisattvas establish vast vows and possess great compassion; they seek all merits, make offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions, and, possessing great and sharp wisdom, seek the true reality of all phenomena.

He eliminates various forms of contemplation, namely: the contemplation of purity and the contemplation of impurity; the contemplation of permanence and the contemplation of impermanence; the contemplation of pleasure and the contemplation of suffering; the contemplation of emptiness and the contemplation of reality; the contemplation of self and the contemplation of non-self.

Abandoning such contemplations based on the power of deluded views, one should contemplate only the true mark within external conditions: it is neither pure nor impure, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither empty nor substantial, and neither self nor non-self.
All such contemplations as these are neither clung to nor attained;
because they belong to the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Universally pure, indestructible and unbreakable, this is the sphere of activity of all noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*); it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
Question:
It has already been understood that the essence and characteristics of Prajñā are the dharma of signlessness and non-attainment; how, then, can a practitioner attain this dharma? Answer:
The Buddha teaches the Dharma through skillful means; if a practitioner acts according to what has been taught, they will attain it.
It is like a steep cliff or a perilous path that can be ascended by means of a ladder;
or like deep water that can be crossed by relying on a boat.

When a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening hears from a Buddha, or from a disciple, or from within the sūtras that all dharmas are ultimately empty, lacking any determinate nature that can be grasped or clung to, and that the foremost ultimate reality extinguishes all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The characteristic of nirvana is the most peaceful and secure. I desire to deliver all sentient beings; how could I alone take up nirvana?
