Because my merit, wisdom, and power of supernatural faculties are not yet complete, I am unable to guide sentient beings. I must fulfill these various causes and conditions by practicing the five perfections, such as giving:
through the cause and condition of material giving, one attains great wealth; through the cause and condition of the giving of Dharma, one attains great wisdom.
By means of these two kinds of giving, one can guide impoverished sentient beings and cause them to enter the path of the Three Vehicles.

Through the causal conditions of upholding the precepts, one is born as a noble being among humans or devas; one liberates oneself from the three evil realms and likewise causes other sentient beings to escape the three evil realms.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of patience, one obstructs the poison of anger; one attains a physical form that is upright and handsome, with supreme majesty and virtue, such that all who see it rejoice and are subdued by respectful faith—how much more so when one preaches the Dharma!

By means of the causal conditions of diligence, one is able to destroy the indolence regarding merit, the path, and the Dharma in both this life and future lives; thereby, one attains a vajra-body and an unshakable mind.
With such a body and mind, one destroys the arrogance of ordinary beings and enables them to attain nirvana.

By means of the causes and conditions of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one disperses the distracted mind and leaves behind the faults and pleasures of the five desires, thereby being able to preach the Dharma of detachment for the sake of sentient beings.
Meditative concentration is the locus upon which the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) relies; by relying on this concentration, the perfection of wisdom arises spontaneously.
As it is said in the sutra:
"A bhikṣu who is single-mindedly concentrated is able to contemplate the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
Furthermore, one knows that within the desire realm, many are obstructed from the gates of all virtues by the karmic offenses of stinginess and greed.
When practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one destroys these two matters and opens the gates to all virtues.
Because one desires these gates to remain perpetually open, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) through the ten paths of wholesome action.

Because they have not yet attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), and have not yet abandoned desire, they violate the *śīlapāramitā*; for this reason, they practice patience (*kṣānti*).
One knows that these three aforementioned matters can open the gate to merit.
Furthermore, knowing that the retribution of such merit is impermanent— experiencing pleasure among devas and humans only to fall back into suffering—
they grow weary of this impermanent merit and seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the true mark.
How can this be obtained?
It must be obtained through single-mindedness alone.
It is like the precious pearl of the Dragon King Sāgara: if one observes it with a single mind without disturbing the dragon, one shall obtain its value, which is equal to that of Jambudvīpa.

With single-minded meditative concentration, one eliminates the five desires and the five hindrances; desiring to attain mental bliss, one applies great diligence. For this reason, after patience, the perfection of diligence is taught.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The practitioner sits upright with the body straight, binding mindfulness before him, seeking concentration with single-minded diligence;
even if his flesh and bones should wither away, he shall never slacken or retreat."
Therefore, one should cultivate dhyāna with diligence.
If one possesses wealth and gives it away as a gift, it is not difficult;
likewise, fearing a fall into the evil realms and apprehensive of losing a good reputation, maintaining the precepts and practicing patience are also not difficult.
For this reason, diligence was not mentioned among the first three perfections.
Now, for the sake of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Prajñāpāramitā, one must seek concentration from within the mind; because this matter is difficult, it requires diligence.
Practicing in this way, one can attain the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Question:
Must one practice the five *pāramitās* first before attaining the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Furthermore, can one who practices only one or two pāramitās obtain the prajñāpāramitā?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of pāramitās.
First, practicing in accordance with and following one *pāramitā* while fully embodying all *pāramitās*;
second, practicing the *pāramitās* individually according to the occasion.
That which is predominant receives the name.
For example, when the four great elements are combined, although they are not separate from one another, it is named after that which is predominant.
As for "concomitance through association," within a single *pāramitā*, all five *pāramitās* are complete; thus, by not being separated from the five *pāramitās*, one attains the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding obtaining the name [of Prajñāpāramitā] according to circumstances: one may obtain the Prajñāpāramitā by means of one cause or two causes.

If a person resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practices giving, at that time they seek the characteristic of giving as being neither one nor different, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth, as explained in the section on the refutation of giving.
By means of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of giving, one understands that all phenomena are likewise so—this is called attaining the *prajñāpāramitā* through giving.
Furthermore, there may be those who maintain the precepts and do not afflict sentient beings, their minds free from regret;
yet if they grasp at signs and give rise to attachment, then contention will arise.
Although this person may not have previously felt anger toward sentient beings, they do become angry toward them because they harbor feelings of aversion and attachment toward phenomena.
Therefore, if one wishes not to afflict sentient beings, one should practice the equality of all phenomena;
if one discriminates between what is sinful and what is sinless, then one is not practicing the *śīlapāramitā*.
Why is this? Because if one hates what is sinful and loves what is not sinful, the mind becomes self-exalting and will, in turn, fall into the path of those who afflict sentient beings.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates both the sinful and the non-sinful with a mind free from hatred and attachment.
One who observes in this way is practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) alone in order to attain the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The bodhisattva reflects:
"If one does not attain the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), one will be unable to maintain constant patience."
All sentient beings can endure when they have not yet been oppressed; however, when suffering comes and cuts them to the quick, they can no longer endure it.
It is like a prisoner who, fearing the scourge of the staff, prefers the suffering of death.
For these reasons, one should give rise to the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*):
there is no one who strikes, no one who reviles, and likewise no one who receives; it is merely called "receiving" due to the causal conditions of the retributive fruits of past inversions.
At that time, one who does not discriminate between the person who endures and the phenomenon that is endured has deeply entered ultimate emptiness; this is called "dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti).
Having attained this dharma-patience, one never again becomes angry with or causes affliction to sentient beings.
The wisdom associated with the patience regarding dharmas is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Diligence is ever-present within all wholesome dharmas and is able to bring all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment.
If wisdom deliberates upon and discriminates all phenomena, thereby penetrating their true nature (*dharmatā*), at that time diligence assists in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, knowing the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of diligence—being detached from body and mind and remaining unmoved as it truly is—such diligence can give rise to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Other forms of diligence are like illusions and dreams; they are deceptive and not real, and for this reason they are not discussed.
If one gathers the mind through a profound resolve, one can perceive the true reality of all phenomena as it truly is.
The true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) cannot be attained through seeing, hearing, thinking, or knowing.
Why is this? For the six sense organs and the six sense objects are all deceptive causes, conditions, and karmic fruits.
That which is known and seen therein is likewise all deceptive.
This deceptive knowledge is entirely untrustworthy;
the only thing that can be trusted is the wisdom of the true nature (dharmatā) attained by the Buddhas over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

By means of this wisdom, relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with a single mind, one contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; this is called the arising of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) from within meditative concentration.

Alternatively, there may be those who, apart from the five perfections, merely hear, read, recite, contemplate, and deliberate upon the teachings until they penetrate the true reality of all phenomena; this is the arising of the perfection of wisdom from within the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*).
Alternatively, the *prajñāpāramitā* arises from two, three, or four *pāramitās*.
It is just as one may attain the fruit of the path by hearing the teaching of a single truth, or attain the fruit of the path by hearing the teachings of two, three, or four truths.
Because some individuals have many doubts regarding the Truth of Suffering, they attain the Path when the Truth of Suffering is taught to them;
the same applies to the other three Truths.
Furthermore, there are those who have doubts concerning all four Truths, and thus they attain the Path when all four Truths are taught to them.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you can sever desire, I guarantee that you will attain the stage of Anāgāmin.
If desire is severed, one should know that hatred and delusion are also severed.
It is likewise among the six pāramitās: in order to destroy excessive stinginess and greed, the dharma of giving is taught; one should know that by this, other evils are also destroyed.
In order to destroy various evils, all six are fully expounded.
Therefore, whether practicing each individual perfection or practicing them in combination, the six pāramitās are taught for the sake of all people universally, not for a single person alone.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva does not practice any phenomena and does not apprehend any phenomena, they attain the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this so? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty, false, and unreal; they may have faults that are proximate or faults that are remote:
for example, unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) have proximate faults and transgressions.
When wholesome dharmas undergo transformation after a long time, those who are attached to them will give rise to sorrow and suffering; this is a distant fault.
It is like fine food and coarse food, both of which may contain mixed poison.
Eating unwholesome food brings immediate displeasure, while eating wholesome food brings immediate sweetness and joy; yet because both eventually take one's life, neither should be eaten.
It is the same with all wholesome and unwholesome formations (*saṃskāra*).
Question:
If that is so, why did the Buddha speak of three types of practice:
the Brahma-conduct, the celestial conduct, and the noble conduct?
Answer: Because one practices non-practice, it is called "noble practice" (āryacaryā). Why is this?
Among all noble practices, they do not depart from the three gates of liberation.

Within the Brahma-conduct and celestial conduct, these arise because of grasping at the marks of sentient beings; thus, although there is no fault during the practice itself, there is ultimately loss in both cases.
Furthermore, even this present seeking for reality is entirely illusory;
if the noble ones (ārya) practice these two modes of conduct with a mind free from attachment, there is no fault.
If one can thus practice the dharma of non-practice such that nothing is attained, then subversion, illusion, and affliction will ultimately never arise.
Because it is pure like space, one attains the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
To attain by means of non-attainment is as taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* on Non-attainment:
"Form and other phenomena are not empty because they are made empty; rather, from the very beginning, they have always been empty of themselves."
Phenomena such as form are not unattainable because wisdom fails to reach them; rather, from the very beginning they have always been inherently unattainable.
Therefore, one should not ask, "By practicing how many pāramitās does one attain the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, speak of practice in accordance with worldly convention; this is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Question:
If there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be practiced, why does the practitioner seek it?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of "non-attainment.
First, when one seeks something in the world and it does not accord with one's wishes, this is non-attainment.

Second, within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, because a determinate characteristic of sensation cannot be apprehended, it is called "non-apprehension"; yet this does not mean that there is no increase of roots of goodness through merit and wisdom.

Just as ordinary persons perceive attainment because they conceptually differentiate worldly phenomena, so too are all virtuous merits said to be attained in accordance with the worldly mind; yet within the minds of the Buddhas, there is no attainment whatsoever.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*; it shall be explained in detail later.
From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 118, explaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within the first chapter.

Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree. **31. The Meaning of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment** [Sūtra] “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom by means of the dharma of non-dwelling, because of its non-arising, should fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”
[Treatise] Question:

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, while the six perfections are the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. For what reason are the dharmas of the śrāvakas explained within the context of the bodhisattva path?
Answer: A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should study all wholesome dharmas and all paths.
As the Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fully study all wholesome dharmas and all paths, namely, from the stage of dry wisdom up to the stage of Buddhahood.”
"In these nine stages, one should train but not realize [the fruit]; in the stage of a Buddha, one both trains and realizes.
Furthermore, where is it said that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment belong only to the Dharma of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are not the path of a bodhisattva?
In this "Mahāyāna Chapter" of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha states that the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path constitute the Mahāyāna;
nor does he state in the Tripiṭaka that these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment belong exclusively to the Hīnayāna.

Out of great compassion, the Buddha taught the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the path to nirvana; according to the vows of sentient beings and their respective causes and conditions, each attains their own path.
Those who seek the path of the śrāvaka attain the path of the śrāvaka;
those who have planted the roots of goodness for pratyekabuddhahood attain the path of the pratyekabuddha;
and those who seek the path of the Buddha attain the path of the Buddha.
According to their original vows and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, they may possess great compassion or lack it.
It is like a dragon king sending down rain that falls everywhere across the world; the rain itself makes no distinction.
Large trees and large grasses receive much because their roots are large;
small trees and small grasses receive little because their roots are small.
Question:

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), although there is no place where it is explicitly stated that these belong exclusively to the path of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and not to the path of the bodhisattva, one can know this by inferring from their meaning:
the bodhisattva dwells long in saṃsāra, wandering through the five destinies, and does not swiftly attain nirvāṇa;

yet these thirty-seven factors speak only of the dharma of nirvāṇa, do not speak of the pāramitās, nor do they speak of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For this reason, it is known that they are not the path of the bodhisattva.
The answer is:
Although a bodhisattva dwells for a long time within saṃsāra, they must also know what is the true path and what is not the true path, and what is the world and what is nirvāṇa.
Having known this, he establishes a great vow: "Sentient beings are to be pitied; I shall pull them out and establish them in the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta).
By means of these true dharmas, I shall practice the various pāramitās and be able to reach the path of the Buddha."
Although the bodhisattva studies and understands these dharmas, because he has not yet fulfilled the six pāramitās, he does not realize [nirvāṇa].
As the Buddha said:
"It is like shooting arrows upward into the air; each arrow supports the next, preventing them from falling to the ground."

The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: with the arrow of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he shoots into the void of the three gates of liberation; then, with the arrow of skillful means (*upāya*), he shoots at the arrow of *prajñā*, causing it not to fall to the ground of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, if it is as you say that a bodhisattva must dwell for a long time within birth and death and undergo various physical and mental sufferings, how could they endure such things without attaining true wisdom?

For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks the true wisdom of these factors of enlightenment, by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to transform the mundane world into the fruit of the path, which is nirvāṇa.

Why is this? All worlds within the three realms arise from conjunction; that which arises from conjunction has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty; because it is empty, it cannot be grasped. This characteristic of being ungraspable is *nirvāṇa*.

For this reason, it is said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom by dwelling in the non-dwelling of dharmas; because they do not arise, they should fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, within the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is not taught that the mundane world is itself Nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because their wisdom does not penetrate deeply into all phenomena.
Within the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, it is taught that the mundane world is itself nirvāṇa, because their wisdom penetrates deeply into all phenomena.
As the Buddha told Subhūti:
“Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form;”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves emptiness; emptiness itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Emptiness is itself nirvana; nirvana is itself emptiness.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* also states:
"Nirvāṇa is not different from the world; the world is not different from nirvāṇa.
The limit of nirvāṇa and the limit of the world are one and the same limit, for there is no difference between them."
Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained this true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), he neither loathes the mundane world nor delights in nirvāṇa;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the ground of true wisdom.
Question:
Since the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) alone are sufficient to fully attain the Path, why are thirty-seven factors mentioned?
If you argue that the four foundations of mindfulness are a brief exposition while the thirty-seven are a detailed exposition, this is not so.
Why is this? If it were extensive, it would be immeasurable!
He replied:
Although the four foundations of mindfulness are sufficient for attaining the Path, one should also speak of the four right efforts and other such dharmas. Why is this?
Because the minds of sentient beings are diverse, their fetters and afflictions are diverse, and the teachings they find pleasing and understand are likewise diverse.

Although the Buddha-dharma is of one reality and one characteristic, for the sake of sentient beings, it is explained through such distinctions as the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand clusters of teachings;
were it otherwise, the initial turning of the wheel of Dharma explaining the Four Noble Truths alone would have sufficed, and no other teachings would have been required.
Because there are sentient beings who loathe suffering and cling to pleasure, for the sake of these beings he taught the Four Noble Truths:
that all phenomena, including body and mind, are entirely suffering and devoid of pleasure;
and that the causal conditions of this suffering arise from afflictions such as craving.
This state where suffering is completely exhausted is called *nirvāṇa*;
the skillful means for reaching *nirvāṇa* is the Path.

Because there are sentient beings who have many discursive thoughts and whose minds are distracted and inverted, they become attached to this body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, thereby engaging in unwholesome conduct; it is for the sake of such people that the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are taught.
These various paths and dharmas are each taught for the sake of sentient beings.
For example, a physician cannot cure all illnesses with a single medicine; since illnesses differ, the medicines are likewise not one.
The Buddha is also like this: according to the various mental afflictions of sentient beings, he treats them with a multitude of medicines.
Or it is said that one may deliver sentient beings by means of a single dharma,
as when the Buddha told a certain bhikṣu:
"Do not take what is not yours!"
The bhikṣu said:
“I know it already,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked,
"How do you know this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"All phenomena are not mine; they should not be grasped.
Or, one may deliver sentient beings by means of two dharmas:
concentration and wisdom.
Or by means of three dharmas:
morality, concentration, and wisdom;
or by means of four dharmas:
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:

although one can attain the Path through the four foundations of mindfulness, other dharmas differ in their practice, differ in their distinctions of number and detail, and also differ in their contemplation. For this reason, one should also speak of the four right efforts and all other such dharmas.

Furthermore, because the power of faith of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is great and for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, the Buddha therein taught the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment at one time;
if other dharma-gates such as the ten perceptions are taught, they are all subsumed within these thirty-seven factors.
These thirty-seven factors are a compendium of all medicines, sufficient to cure the illnesses of all sentient beings; therefore, there is no need for further elaboration.
Just as the Buddha possesses immeasurable powers yet speaks only of the ten powers, which are sufficient for the task of delivering sentient beings.
These thirty-seven factors are rooted in ten dharmas.
What are the ten?
They are faith, ethical discipline, reflection, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, equanimity, joy, and relinquishment.
Faith consists of the faculty of faith and the power of faith.
Morality consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Diligence consists of the four right efforts, the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, and right diligence.
Mindfulness refers to the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
Concentration refers to the four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration.
Wisdom consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
When these various factors abide within the object of focus in accordance with mindfulness and wisdom, at that time they are called the foundations of mindfulness.
Because one destroys false dharmas and proceeds by way of the right path, it is called "right effort" (samyak-pradhāna).
Because one gathers the mind and establishes it in tranquility within its objects, it is called "basis of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda).
Because one attains a mind of pliant wisdom, it is called "faculty" (indriya).
Because it is attained by an intellect of sharp wisdom, it is called "power" (*bala*).
Because it functions within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
Because it functions within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
Question: One should first explain the Path. Why is this?
One must first practice the Path and only then attain the various wholesome dharmas;
it is like a person who must first travel the road before reaching their destination.
Why, then, do you now invert this order by first explaining the four foundations of mindfulness and only later explaining the eightfold noble path?
Answer: It is not a perversion.
The thirty-seven factors are the names used at the initial stage when one first desires to enter the Path.

For example, when a practitioner goes to the teacher’s presence and listens to the Dharma, they first use mindfulness to uphold this teaching; at that time, it is called *smṛtyupasthāna* (application of mindfulness).
Having upheld it, they seek the fruit from within the Dharma and thus practice with vigor; at that time, it is called *samyakpradhāna* (right effort).
Because of excessive diligence, the mind becomes distracted; by gathering and harmonizing the mind, it is called the *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power).
Once the mind has been harmonized, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is extremely profound and difficult to understand; because of the faculty of faith, one is able to believe in it—this is called the faculty of faith.
Not sparing one's body or life while seeking the Way with a single mind is called the faculty of vigor;
constantly recollecting the Buddha-way and not recollecting other matters is called the faculty of mindfulness;
constantly gathering the mind within the Way is called the faculty of concentration.
Contemplating the true mark of the Four Noble Truths is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
When these five faculties increase, they are able to obstruct the afflictions (*kleśa*), just as the power of a great tree can block water.
When these five faculties increase, one is able to enter deeply into the Dharma; this is called "power.
Having attained power, one discerns that the factors of the path consist of three parts:

the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). These three factors can cause the mind to arise when it sinks during the practice of the path.

Excluding the awakening factor of investigation, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity—these three factors, when the mind is distracted during the practice of the path, can collect and settle it.
The awakening factor of mindfulness operates in two ways: it can gather wholesome dharmas and exclude unwholesome dharmas;
it is like a gatekeeper who allows those that are beneficial to enter and removes those that are not.
When the mind sinks, one brings to mind the three factors for arousal;
when the mind is scattered, one brings to mind the three factors for concentration.
There is no awakening apart from actual awakening; because these seven matters can lead to [realization], they are called "factors" (*aṅga*).

Having attained this Dharma and being fully endowed with peace and security, one practices these various dharmas in order to enter the city of unconditioned nirvāṇa; at that time, it is called the Path.
Question: What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
Answer:
The foundation of mindfulness of the body, and the foundations of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena—these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
One contemplates these four dharmas in four ways:
One contemplates the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as non-self.
Although each of these four dharmas has four aspects, one should primarily contemplate the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as non-self.
Why is this? When ordinary persons have not yet entered the Path, within these four dharmas, they give rise to the four perversions through wrong conduct:

the perversion of perceiving purity in what is impure, the perversion of perceiving pleasure in what is suffering, the perversion of perceiving permanence in what is impermanent, and the perversion of perceiving a self in what is non-self.
Because they destroy these four inversions, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught:

to destroy the inversion of purity, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is taught; to destroy the inversion of pleasure, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings is taught; to destroy the inversion of permanence, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind is taught; and to destroy the inversion of self, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is taught.
For this reason, four are taught—neither fewer nor more.
Question:
How are these four foundations of mindfulness attained?
Answer:
The practitioner dwells in reliance upon pure precepts, practices diligence with a single-minded focus, and contemplates the five kinds of impure characteristics of the body.
What are these five?
First, impurity of the place of birth; second, impurity of the seed; third, impurity of self-nature; fourth, impurity of specific characteristics; and fifth, ultimate impurity.
What is meant by the impurity of the place of birth?
The head, feet, abdomen, spine, flanks, and ribs—this combination of various impure substances is called a female body.

Internally there are the impurities of the raw and cooked receptacles, excrement, and urine; externally there is the wind of the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma, which blows upon the seed of consciousness and causes it to enter between the two receptacles.
Whether it be the eighth or ninth month, [the body] is as if in a pit of excrement and urine.
As it is said:
"This body is foul and impure; it does not arise from amidst flowers."
"Nor does it come from the *campaka* tree, nor does it emerge from a mountain of jewels.
This is called impurity of the place of birth.

Regarding the impurity of the seed: because the parents' winds of deluded thoughts and perverse recollections fan the fire of lust, the blood, marrow, and fat flow and, through the heat, transform into semen.
Due to the causal conditions of past karmic actions, the seed of consciousness dwells within the red and white vital essences; this is called the "seed of the body.
As it is said:
"This seed of the body is impure; It is not some other exquisite treasure."
"It does not arise from purity, but issues only from the urinary tract!
This is called the impurity of the seed (*bīja-aśubhatā*).
Regarding the impurity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-aśubhatā*): from the feet to the crown of the head, within the thin skin on all four sides, it is entirely filled with impurities.
Adorned with garments, bathed with fragrant flowers, and fed with the finest delicacies and a variety of flavorful dishes, all these become impure within the space of a single night.
Even if one were to clothe oneself in celestial garments and eat celestial food, because of the very nature of the body, it would still be impure; how much more so with human clothing and food?
As it is said:
"The substances of earth, water, fire, and wind Can transform and eliminate impurity."
"Even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body, it could not be made fragrant and pure!
This is called impurity by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-aśubhatā*).

Regarding impurity by specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-aśubhatā*): this body constantly flows with impurities from its nine orifices—the eyes flow with rheum and tears, the ears produce wax, the nose flows with mucus, the mouth produces saliva and vomit, the anus and urinary tract constantly discharge feces and urine, and all the pores flow with the impurity of sweat.
As it is said:
"Various impure substances fill the interior of the body;
they flow out constantly without ceasing, like a leaking bag filled with goods."
This is called impurity by way of its own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇāśubhatā*).

As for ultimate impurity (*atyantāśubhatā*): if this body is cast into fire, it becomes ash; if consumed by insects, it becomes excrement; if left on the ground, it decays and turns into earth; if placed in water, it swells and rots, or is eaten by aquatic creatures.
Among all corpses, the human body is the most impure.
This dharma of impurity shall be explained in detail within the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*).
As it is said:
"Examine this body with careful scrutiny: it will inevitably return to the place of death.
It is difficult to restrain and lacks reciprocity; it betrays kindness like a base person.
This is called ultimate impurity.
Furthermore, at the time of this body’s birth and at the time of its death, all things that come into contact with it and all places where it rests become impure.
Just as fragrant, pure water, following the flow of a hundred rivers, turns into bitter salt once it enters the great ocean;
so too, the various delicious flavors, fine colors, pleasant fragrances, and exquisite delicacies consumed by the body turn into impurity once they enter the sea of the belly.
This body, from birth until its end, is constantly impure and is truly something to be loathed and weary of!
The practitioner reflects:
although this body is impure, it would still be tolerable if it possessed even a slight degree of permanence; yet, it is further impermanent.
Although it is impure and impermanent, even the presence of slight pleasure is better than nothing, yet it is still great suffering.
This body is the source from which all sufferings arise.
It is like water arising from the earth, wind emerging from space, and fire existing because of wood.

This body is thus: all internal and external sufferings arise from the body—internal suffering refers to old age, illness, death, and so forth; external suffering refers to swords, staves, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth. Because this body exists, these sufferings exist.
Question:
The body is not merely of the nature of suffering; there is also pleasure derived from the body.
If one were to cause the body to cease to exist, who would be there to experience the five sensory desires according to one's will?
Answer: Regarding the Four Noble Truths of suffering, the noble ones know them to be truly suffering, whereas the foolish call them pleasure;
the noble truth is truly reliable, while the delusions of the foolish should be abandoned.
This body is truly suffering; yet because it stops great suffering, one regards this minor suffering as pleasure.
It is like a person condemned to death who, upon receiving a punishment in lieu of their life, feels immense joy;
though the punishment is actually painful, because it spares them from death, they call it pleasure.
Furthermore, new suffering is experienced as pleasure, while long-standing suffering is experienced as pain.
For example, when one first sits down, there is pleasure, but after a long time, pain arises;
likewise, when one first walks, stands, or lies down, there is pleasure, but after a long time, it also becomes pain.
Bending and stretching, looking up and down, blinking and breathing—suffering constantly accompanies the body;
from the initial conception in the womb, through birth until death, there is not a single moment of happiness.
If you take pleasure in sexual desire, because the affliction of lust is so heavy, you seek the female beauty of others; yet the more you obtain it, the more severe the suffering becomes.
It is like one afflicted with scabies who rubs and scorches the skin toward a fire; though there is a slight pleasure for the moment, the great pain grows ever deeper.
Such minor pleasures also exist because they are causes and conditions for illness; they are not true happiness. One who is free from illness contemplates them and gives rise to compassion.
Likewise, one who is free from desire contemplates those who indulge in sexual lust: with pity for these deluded ones who are burned by the fire of desire and undergo manifold suffering.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, one knows the characteristics of suffering and the causes of suffering regarding the body.
The practitioner knows that the body is merely something impure, impermanent, and characterized by suffering; yet, having no other choice, one must nourish and sustain it.
It is like parents who have a child; even if the child is wicked and violent, because he was born from them, they must certainly nurture and bring him to maturity.
The body is truly without self. Why?
Because it lacks sovereignty.
For example, a person afflicted by wind-disorder cannot bend, stretch, walk, or come;
one with a constricted throat cannot speak.
For this reason, we know that the body lacks self-mastery.
Just as a person who possesses objects may take and use them as they please, the body cannot do so because it lacks autonomy; thus one clearly knows there is no self.
The practitioner contemplates this body as being thus impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, possessing such immeasurable faults and evils.
Contemplating the body in these various ways is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Having attained this contemplation of the foundation of mindfulness of the body, one further reflects: by what causes and conditions do sentient beings become greedily attached to this body?
Because of pleasant feeling.
Why is this? From the conjunction of the six internal sense bases and the six external objects, the six kinds of consciousness arise.
Within the six kinds of consciousness, three types of feeling arise:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Of these, pleasant feeling is what all sentient beings desire.
Painful feeling is what all sentient beings do not desire;
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is neither grasped nor rejected.
As it is said:
"Whether they be evildoers or those who have left the household life, whether they be devas, humans, or even crawling insects—
among all beings within the five realms throughout the ten directions, there is none who does not delight in happiness and loathe suffering."
"Because they are deluded, inverted, and lacking wisdom, they do not know the state of eternal bliss that is nirvāṇa!
When the practitioner contemplates this pleasant sensation and knows it as it truly is, there is no pleasure; there is only manifold suffering.
Why is this? What is called "pleasure" is true pleasure, free from inversion.
All worldly pleasant sensations arise from inversion; none possess reality.
Furthermore, although this pleasant feeling is sought after for its pleasure, it can bring about great suffering.
As it is said:
"If a person enters the sea and encounters a violent wind, The ocean waves surge up like black mountains; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
If one enters the midst of a great battle array, or traverses perilous paths and treacherous mountain ranges;
if a noble and wealthy elder bows his body in submission, or draws near to a lowly person for the sake of sensual desire.
"Such various great sufferings as these all arise because of attachment to pleasure and a greedy mind!
For this reason, one knows that pleasant sensations can give rise to all manner of suffering.
Furthermore, although the Buddha taught that there are three kinds of feeling, including pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), it is called suffering because the pleasure is so slight;
it is like a single *drou* of honey cast into a great river—it loses its flavor.
Question:

If worldly pleasure is suffering due to the causes and conditions of perversion, then the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) born of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the noble ones (*ārya*) should be real pleasure.
Why is this? Because this pleasure does not arise from ignorance or perversion; how, then, can it be suffering?
He replied:
This is not suffering!
Although the Buddha taught that impermanence is itself suffering, he spoke of it as suffering because it pertains to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Why is this?
Ordinary persons are attached to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); because these contaminated phenomena are impermanent and subject to destruction, they give rise to suffering.

Because the mind is not attached to uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), although they are impermanent, they cannot produce sorrow, lamentation, pain, or distress; therefore, they are not called "suffering," nor do the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) enslave them.

Furthermore, if untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) were suffering, the Buddha would not have taught the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) separately, as it would already be subsumed within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Question:
There are two kinds of pleasure:
There is tainted pleasure and untainted pleasure.
Tainted pleasure is base, inferior, and evil; untainted pleasure is sublime and excellent.
Why is it that one gives rise to attachment toward base pleasure, yet does not give rise to attachment toward sublime pleasure?

One should have much attachment toward the arising of supreme and wondrous bliss, just as one’s greedy attachment to gold, silver, and precious objects should be heavy; how could it be the same as [attachment to] grasses and trees?
The answer is:
untainted bliss is supreme and wondrous, yet wisdom is abundant; because wisdom is abundant, one is able to detach from this attachment.
Within tainted pleasure (*sāsrava-sukha*), the fetters and latent tendencies such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are numerous; craving is the root of attachment.
True wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*) is able to detach from it, and for this reason one does not become attached.
Furthermore, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) constantly contemplates all things as impermanent.
By contemplating impermanence, one does not give rise to the fetters and afflictions such as craving.
For example, just as a sheep near a tiger cannot become fat despite having access to fine grass and delicious water;
likewise, although the noble ones experience untainted bliss, because they contemplate impermanence and emptiness, the fat of defiled attachment does not arise.
Furthermore, untainted bliss is inseparable from the three samādhis and the sixteen noble practices, and it is always devoid of the mark of a sentient being;
if there were the mark of a sentient being, then a mind of attachment would arise.
For this reason, although untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*) is supreme and exquisite, one does not give rise to attachment toward it.

Through such various causes and conditions, one contemplates worldly pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as an arrow, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as having the characteristic of impermanence and decay.
In this way, one does not give rise to desire or attachment toward pleasant feeling, anger toward painful feeling, or delusion toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This is called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling.
The practitioner reflects:
"Because of pleasure, one craves the body; who is it that experiences this pleasure?"
Having reflected thus, he knows that this sensation arises from the mind; it is because the minds of sentient beings are deranged and inverted that they experience this pleasure.

He should contemplate this mind as having the characteristic of impermanence—arising and ceasing, not abiding for even a single thought-moment—and find therein nothing that can truly receive pleasure;
yet, due to inversion, people claim to receive pleasure.

Why is this? At the initial moment of desiring to experience pleasure, the mind is one thing; at the moment pleasure arises, the mind is another. Since these two do not reach one another, how can it be said that the mind experiences pleasure?

Because the past mind has already ceased, it does not experience pleasure; because the future mind has not yet arisen, it does not experience pleasure; and because the present mind abides for only a single thought-moment, its rapidity prevents one from perceiving the experience of pleasure.
Question:
The past and the future should not experience pleasure; when the present mind abides for a single moment, it should experience pleasure. Why, then, do you say "it does not experience"?
Answer: I have already stated that because the movement is so rapid,
one does not perceive the experience of pleasure.

Furthermore, because all phenomena possess the characteristic of impermanence, they have no period of abiding. If the mind were to abide for even a single thought-moment, it would likewise have to abide during the second thought-moment; this would constitute permanence, and there would be no characteristic of cessation.
As the Buddha said:
"All conditioned phenomena have three characteristics.
Within the characteristic of duration (*sthiti*), there is also the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*); if there were no cessation, it would not be a characteristic of the conditioned.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon undergoes cessation later, one should know that it has already undergone cessation from the very beginning.

For example, if a person wears new clothes and they do not become old on the first day of wearing them, they should likewise not become old on the second day; in this manner, they should remain perpetually new for ten years and never grow old, yet in reality they have already grown old.
One should know that [the sensation] co-exists with the new [object], but because it is subtle, it is not perceived;
only when the object has already come into being does one then perceive it.
For this reason, one knows that all phenomena have no duration; how, then, could the mind abide for a time and experience pleasure?
If one were to experience pleasure while remaining in non-abiding, such a thing would be impossible.
For this reason, we know that there is no real experiencer of pleasure;
it is only through the conventional dharma, by means of the continuity of various mental states, that one speaks of a single subject experiencing pleasure.
Question:
How should one know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent? Answer:
I have already explained this previously, but I shall now answer further:

all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent because they depend upon causes and conditions; they are impermanent because they did not exist before but exist now, and having existed now, they will no longer exist later.

Furthermore, because the characteristic of impermanence constantly pursues conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and because conditioned phenomena undergo neither increase nor decrease, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent due to their mutual encroachment and subjugation.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are constantly pursued by two kinds of aging:
first, the aging of approaching decay; second, the aging of destruction.
They are also constantly pursued by two kinds of death: [the first being the death of the lifespan, and the second being the death of the faculties].
First, dying by oneself; second, being killed by another.
For this reason, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent.
Among conditioned phenomena, the impermanence of the mind is the most easily perceived.
As the Buddha said:
"Ordinary people may at times understand that the body is impermanent, yet they cannot understand that the mind is impermanent.
If an ordinary person says the body is permanent, it is still a mistake; however, to regard the mind as permanent is a great delusion!"
Why is this? The body may remain for ten or twenty years;

yet this mind passes away in the briefest instant of a day, month, or season. Its arising and ceasing are each distinct, never pausing from moment to moment: that which desires to arise arises differently, and that which desires to cease ceases differently.
Like a magical illusion, its true nature cannot be apprehended.
Through such immeasurable causes and conditions, one knows that the mind is impermanent; this is called the application of mindfulness to the mind.
The practitioner reflects:
"To whom does this mind belong?
Who causes this mind to act?"
Having observed thus, he saw no owner;

because all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they lack autonomy; because they lack autonomy, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and because they lack intrinsic nature, they are without self (*anātman*).
If there is no self, who is it that impels this mind?
Question: There must be a self.
Why is this? Just as the mind can direct the body, there must likewise be a "self" that can direct the mind.
It is like a sovereign who commands his generals, and the generals command their soldiers.
Thus, there must be a self that impels the mind, and a mind that impels the body, for the sake of experiencing the pleasures of the five desires.
Furthermore, because each individual possesses the notion of "my mind," we know that a real self exists.
If there were only a body and one conceives of a self due to a perversion of the mind, why does one not give rise to the notion of a self within another's body?
Because of these characteristics, we know that each individual possesses a self.
The answer is:
If the mind impels the body, and there is a self that impels the mind, then there must be yet another who impels that self!
If there were yet another who impels that self, it would lead to an infinite regress.
Furthermore, if there were another who causes me to act, then there would be two selves.
If there is no further self, but only that "I" can cause the mind to act, then it should also follow that the mind alone can cause the body to act.
If you maintain that the mind belongs to the self (ātman), then apart from the mind, the self would have no cognition.
If it has no cognition, how could it cause the mind to act?
Furthermore, if the self possesses the characteristic of cognition, why would one need the mind at all?
For this reason, we know that because the mind alone possesses the characteristic of consciousness, it can by itself move the body without depending on a soul;
just as the nature of fire is to burn things, without requiring a person.
Question:
Although fire possesses the power to burn, it does not act without a person;
although the mind possesses the characteristic of cognition, it is not employed without a spirit (ātman).
The answer is:
All phenomena exist because they possess characteristics; this self (*ātman*) does not exist because it lacks characteristics.
Although you wish to take the inhalation and exhalation of breath, as well as suffering and pleasure, to be the characteristics of the self, this is not the case!

Why is this? Inhalation and exhalation are characteristics of the body, while the experience of suffering and pleasure are characteristics of the mind; how, then, can the body and mind be considered the characteristics of a self (ātman)?
Furthermore, at times fire is capable of burning by itself without depending on a person;
yet, merely for the sake of conventional designation, it is called "burned by a person.
Thus, your argument falls into a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Why is this? Because the self (ātman) is identical to the person; one should not use the person as an analogy for the person.
Furthermore, you have said:

"Because each person possesses their own mind, we know that there truly is a self. If it were merely the body and one falsely conceived of a self due to mental perversion, why would one not give rise to the notion of 'self' with respect to another's body?"
"You have not yet understood the existence of a self or the non-existence of a self, yet you ask why the notion of 'I' does not arise with respect to another's body.
Both one's own body and another's body originate from a self, yet that self is likewise unfindable."

Whether it be the mark of form or the mark of the formless, whether permanent or impermanent, finite or infinite, one who goes or one who does not go, one who knows or one who does not know, one who acts or one who does not act, one who possesses sovereignty or one who lacks sovereignty—such notions of a self-characteristic are all unobtainable, as explained above in the "I Have Heard" (Evam Mayā Śrutam) chapter.

Through various causes and conditions such as these, one contemplates that all dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; there is no real dharma and no self. This is called the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
These four foundations of mindfulness are of three kinds:
the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature, the foundation of mindfulness as concomitant, and the foundation of mindfulness as object.
What is the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature?
The wisdom that contemplates the body is the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
the wisdom that contemplates all sensations is called the foundation of mindfulness of sensation;
the wisdom that contemplates all minds is called the foundation of mindfulness of mind.
The wisdom that contemplates all phenomena is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
This is the foundation of mindfulness of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*). What is called the shared foundation of mindfulness (*sahagata-smṛtyupasthāna*)?
Contemplating the body as the primary gateway to the path arising through dependent origination—whether it be with outflows or without outflows—is the foundation of mindfulness of the body;

contemplating sensation, contemplating the mind, and contemplating phenomena as the primary gateways to the path arising through dependent origination—whether they be with outflows or without outflows—are called the foundations of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena.
These are the shared foundations of mindfulness.
What are the object-based foundations of mindfulness?
All material phenomena—namely, the ten bases and a portion of the base of mental objects—are called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The six kinds of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact; these are called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling.
The six kinds of consciousness:
Visual consciousness, as well as auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness, are called the foundation of mindfulness of mind;
the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the three unconditioned phenomena are called the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas.
This is called the application of mindfulness through conditions.
This is the application of mindfulness by nature; because its nature is wisdom, it is formless and invisible.
It is non-reactive (*apratigha*).
It is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*);
that which has outflows has retribution (*savipāka*), while that which is without outflows has no retribution (*avipāka*).
All are conditioned, produced by causes and conditions,
subsumed within the three periods of time,
and subsumed under names.
It is comprised within the external bases.
It is known through wisdom.
That which is with outflows is to be abandoned through knowledge; that which is without outflows is not to be abandoned through knowledge.
That which is with outflows is subject to abandonment; that which is without outflows is not subject to abandonment.
This is the dharma to be cultivated;
this is stainless.
This fruit also has a fruit;
all are non-appropriated phenomena;
they are not composed of the four great elements.
Regarding phenomena that have a superior state (*sottara*):
the contaminated foundations of mindfulness (*sāsrava-smṛtyupasthāna*) are "existent," while the uncontaminated foundations of mindfulness (*anāsrava-smṛtyupasthāna*) are "non-existent.
All of these are associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).

The four foundations of mindfulness encompass one of the six types of wholesome factors, namely the category of "practicing manifold wholesome deeds," while the category of "practicing manifold wholesome deeds" in turn encompasses the four foundations of mindfulness;
they do not mutually encompass one another among the unwholesome, the indeterminate, or the tainted factors.
There may be the four foundations of mindfulness that are not with outflows; there may be that which is with outflows but is not the four foundations of mindfulness;
there may be that which is both the four foundations of mindfulness and with outflows; or there may be that which is neither the four foundations of mindfulness nor with outflows.
Regarding "there are four foundations of mindfulness that are not with-outflows": these are the four foundations of mindfulness of the nature of being without-outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding "there are things with-outflows that are not the four foundations of mindfulness": this refers to the remaining portions of the with-outflows category, excluding those of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness that are without-outflows.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness that are also tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*): these are the four foundations of mindfulness of a tainted nature.

Regarding those that are neither the four foundations of mindfulness nor tainted phenomena: these are the remaining untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), excluding the four foundations of mindfulness of an untainted nature.
The four categories of the untainted (*anāsrava*) are also like this.

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness that are shared (*sādhāraṇa*), within these shared foundations of mindfulness, bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and verbal action (*vākkarman*) are form (*rūpa*); the remainder are non-form (*arūpa*).
All are invisible;
all are non-resistant.
Some are with outflows (sāsrava), and some are without outflows (anāsrava).
All are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The foundations of mindfulness with outflows (*sāsrava*) have retribution; the foundations of mindfulness without outflows (*anāsrava*) have no retribution.
They arise from causes and conditions.
They are subsumed within the three time periods.
Bodily and vocal karma are subsumed under form;
the remainder are subsumed under name.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are subsumed under the internal bases;
the remainder are subsumed under the external bases.
This is known through wisdom.
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is to be abandoned through knowledge; that which is without outflows (anāsrava) is not to be abandoned through knowledge.
That which is with outflows can be abandoned; that which is without outflows cannot be abandoned.
All are dharmas to be cultivated.
All are stainless.
These are results, and they also have results.
All are non-appropriated phenomena (*anupātta-dharma*).
The bodily and vocal karmas are composed of the four great elements; the remaining [karmas] are not composed of the four great elements.
All possess the higher dharma.
The tainted foundations of mindfulness are "existence," while the untainted foundations of mindfulness are "non-existence."
Bodily and vocal karma, as well as all formations dissociated from mind, are not associated causes; the remainder are associated causes.

The four foundations of mindfulness are subsumed within the five wholesome factors, and the five wholesome factors are likewise subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness; the remainder are not mutually subsumed.
Unwholesome, indeterminate, and tainted phenomena are not subsumed [within them].
There may be the four foundations of mindfulness that are not with outflows; there may be things with outflows that are not the four foundations of mindfulness;
there may be the four foundations of mindfulness that are also with outflows; and there may be things that are neither the four foundations of mindfulness nor with outflows.
Regarding "there are four foundations of mindfulness that are not with-outflows": these are the untainted (anāsrava) four foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding "there are things with-outflows that are not the four foundations of mindfulness": these are all remaining tainted phenomena (sāsrava-dharma), excluding the tainted four foundations of mindfulness.
There are four applications of mindfulness that are also with outflows; these are the four applications of mindfulness with outflows.
That which is neither the four applications of mindfulness nor with outflows consists of space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation.
There are cases where the four foundations of mindfulness are not untainted; there are cases where they are untainted but are not the four foundations of mindfulness;
there are cases where they are both the four foundations of mindfulness and untainted; and there are cases where they are neither the four foundations of mindfulness nor untainted.
Regarding those that are the four foundations of mindfulness but not untainted (*anāsrava*): these are the tainted (*sāsrava*) four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding those that are untainted but not the four foundations of mindfulness: these are the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding those that are both the four foundations of mindfulness and untainted: these are the untainted four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding "neither the four foundations of mindfulness nor the untainted": this refers to all remaining tainted phenomena, excluding the tainted four foundations of mindfulness.
These are the foundations of mindfulness as objects; among these foundations of mindfulness as objects, one foundation of mindfulness is form, while three foundations of mindfulness are not form.
Three are invisible; one should be analyzed—the foundation of mindfulness of the body:
some are visible and some are invisible;
that which is visible is one base.
That which is invisible consists of nine bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base.
Three are non-resistant (*apratigha*); one should be analyzed: the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is resistant, consisting of ten bases.
The non-obstructive [dharma] is a portion of one *āyatana*.
The mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*):
when it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it consists of ten *āyatanas* and a portion of one *āyatana*.
The untainted [factors] constitute a small portion of one entrance.
As for the foundation of mindfulness of feeling:
that which is associated with the tainted mind is itself tainted.
That which is associated with the untainted mind is itself untainted.
The same applies to the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*). As for the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*):
The aggregates of perception and formations that are with outflows (sāsrava) are "with outflows";
the aggregates of perception and formations that are without outflows (anāsrava), as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), are "without outflows.
Three of these are conditioned (saṃskṛta); one should be analyzed—the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna):
The aggregate of perception and the aggregate of formations are conditioned;
the three unconditioned dharmas are unconditioned.
The foundation of mindfulness of the body that is unwholesome, as well as the foundation of mindfulness of the body that is wholesome yet with outflows, are retributive.
The mindfulness of the body that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) are without retribution (*avipāka*).
The same applies to the mindfulness of feeling, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of phenomena.
Three arise from causes and conditions; one must be analyzed—the mindfulness of phenomena:
The conditioned arises from causes and conditions;
the unconditioned does not arise from causes and conditions.
Three are subsumed within the three time periods, while one should be analyzed—the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*):
Conditioned phenomena are subsumed within the three time periods;
unconditioned phenomena are not subsumed within the three time periods.
One foundation of mindfulness subsumes form, while three subsume name.
One foundation of mindfulness is comprised within the internal sense bases;
the foundations of mindfulness of feeling and of phenomena are comprised within the external sense bases.
One [foundation] should be analyzed—the foundation of mindfulness of the body:
They are either comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) or comprised within the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*):
the five internal bases are comprised within the internal bases, while the five external bases and a portion of one base are comprised within the external bases.
One knows this through wisdom:
that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is subject to cessation, while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is not subject to cessation;
that which is with outflows can be abandoned, while that which is without outflows cannot be abandoned.
Cultivation should be distinguished as follows: regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), that which is wholesome (*kuśala*) should be cultivated;
that which is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) should not be cultivated.
The applications of mindfulness regarding feeling and mind are also like this.
Regarding the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): conditioned wholesome phenomena are to be cultivated;
The unwholesome, the indeterminate, and analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) should not be cultivated. Regarding the defilements (mala), they should be distinguished as follows:
among the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the foundation of mindfulness of the body is "obscured" (nivṛta); this is a defilement.
It is not obscured and is not defiled.
The same applies to the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-, citta-, and dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Three of these foundations of mindfulness are both results and possess results; one must be distinguished—namely, the foundation of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Either a fruit is not possessed of a fruit, or a fruit is also possessed of a fruit, or it is neither a fruit nor possessed of a fruit.
Cessation through analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a fruit that is not possessed of a fruit;
the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are fruits that are also possessed of fruits.
Space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are neither results nor possess results.
Regarding the three types of non-sensory objects (anupādāna), one must be analyzed—namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna):
that which falls within the category of the body is "sensory" (upādāna), while that which does not fall within the category of the body is "non-sensory."
Three are not derived from the four great elements; one should be analyzed:
the foundation of mindfulness of the body consists of nine bases and a portion of two bases, which are derived from the four great elements;
a portion of one base is not derived from the four great elements.
Among the three foundations of mindfulness, one should distinguish that which is surpassable:

the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Conditioned phenomena, as well as space and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), are surpassable; nirvāṇa is unsurpassable.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are existent; if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are non-existent.
Two foundations of mindfulness are associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*); one foundation of mindfulness is a non-associated cause (*viprayukta-hetu*); one must be analyzed further.
The foundations of mindfulness of feeling and of mind are associated causes;
the foundation of mindfulness of body is a non-associated cause;
as for the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena:
The aggregate of perception and the aggregate of formations associated with it are the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*); the remaining factors are the non-associated cause (*viprayukta-hetu*).
The portion of the four foundations of mindfulness subsumes the six wholesome dharmas, and the six wholesome dharmas likewise subsume the portion of the four foundations of mindfulness.
The unwholesome category and the indeterminate category are likewise mutually inclusive according to their respective types.
The three outflows include one base of mindfulness, and one base of mindfulness also includes the three outflows.
The contaminated portion of the four foundations of mindfulness is subsumed by the contaminated, and the contaminated is also subsumed by the four foundations of mindfulness.
The uncontaminated portion of the four foundations of mindfulness is subsumed by the uncontaminated, and the uncontaminated is also subsumed by the four foundations of mindfulness.
These and other such meanings are explained in detail within the *Qian nan* (The Thousand Difficulties). Question:
What constitutes the internal body?
What is the external body?
Since both the internal body and the external body have already been fully encompassed, why is the contemplation of the internal and external body mentioned again?
The answer is:
The internal refers to one's own body, and the external refers to the bodies of others.
One's own body has two types:
first, the impurities within the body; second, the skin, hair, nails, head-hair, and so forth on the exterior of the body.

Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates a corpse that is bloated, swollen, putrefied, and decomposed; having grasped these signs, he observes his own body as being of the same nature and character, thinking: "I have not yet escaped from this condition."
A corpse is the external body; the practitioner’s own body is the internal body.
For instance, if at times the practitioner sees a beautiful woman and his mind becomes attached, he immediately contemplates her body as impure—this is the external.
He then knows that his own body is likewise so—this is the internal.
Furthermore, the five sense organs, such as the eye, constitute the internal body; the five sense objects, such as form, constitute the external body.
The four great elements constitute the internal body; the derived matter from the four great elements constitutes the external body.
That which experiences suffering and pleasure constitutes the internal body; that which does not experience suffering and pleasure constitutes the external body.
One's own body and the various sense organs, such as the eyes, constitute the internal body;
wives, children, wealth, fields, houses, and articles of use constitute the external body.
Why is this? Because all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are entirely the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When the practitioner seeks within this internal body, is there anything pure, permanent, blissful, or self?
Having examined and sought it thoroughly, it is entirely unobtainable, as previously explained regarding the method of contemplation.
Since it cannot be found through internal observation, might it perhaps exist externally? Why is this so?
External objects are the locus of attachment for all sentient beings;
yet when observing the external body, they too cannot be found.
Furthermore, one reflects as follows:
"I have not found it through internal contemplation; might it exist externally?
Having searched externally as well, he still did not find it.
He thought to himself:
"I may have erred; I shall now contemplate both the internal and external as a whole.
To contemplate the internal and the external separately is the specific characteristic (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa);
to contemplate them simultaneously is the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
When observing both collectively and individually, nothing can be apprehended; thus, the observation is complete.
A question is asked:

While the foundation of mindfulness of the body can be apprehended as internal or external, and all feelings are subsumed under the external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*), how can one distinguish between internal feeling and external feeling?
Answer: The Buddha taught that there are two kinds of feeling:
bodily feeling and mental feeling.
Bodily sensation is external; mental sensation is internal.
Furthermore, sensations associated with the five consciousnesses are external, while sensations associated with the mental consciousness are internal.
All sensations arise due to the causal conditions of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Feeling arising from the six internal bases is internal; feeling arising from the six external bases is external.
Coarse feeling is external; subtle feeling is internal.
There are two kinds of suffering:
internal suffering and external suffering.
Internal suffering is of two kinds:
There is physical suffering and mental suffering.
Physical suffering refers to the four hundred and four kinds of ailments, such as bodily pain, headaches, and so forth;
these constitute physical suffering. Mental suffering refers to grief, sorrow, anger, fear, jealousy, and doubt; such things as these constitute mental suffering.
The convergence of these two types of suffering constitutes internal suffering.
External suffering is of two kinds:

first, being oppressed and harmed by kings, those superior to oneself, wicked thieves, lions, tigers, wolves, vipers, snakes, and the like; [and second, being oppressed and harmed by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, and so forth].
Second, there are wind, rain, cold, heat, thunder, lightning, and hail;
these two kinds of suffering are called external sensations (*bāhya-vedanā*).
Pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) are likewise.
Furthermore, that which conditions internal phenomena is internal feeling;
that which conditions external phenomena is external feeling.
Furthermore, the one hundred and eight feelings are internal feeling.
The remainder is external feeling.
Question: Since the mind is subsumed under the internal sense-base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), why do you say that one contemplates the external mind?
Answer:

Although the mind is subsumed under the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), it is called "external mind" when it takes external phenomena as its object, and "internal mind" when it takes internal phenomena as its object.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the internal mind; the five sensory consciousnesses are the external mind.
A mind that has gathered itself and entered meditative absorption is the internal mind; a distracted mind is the external mind.
A mind associated with the five internal hindrances and the seven internal factors of enlightenment is the internal mind;
a mind associated with the five external hindrances and the seven external factors of enlightenment is the external mind.
Such various distinctions between the internal and the external constitute the internal and external mind.

Question: Since the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is included within the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*), why do you say that one contemplates internal phenomena?
Answer: With the exception of feeling (*vedanā*), those mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that take internal phenomena as their objects are internal phenomena;

those mental factors that take external phenomena as their objects, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), are external phenomena.
Furthermore, the phenomena that are the objects of mental consciousness are called "dharmas," as the Buddha said:
"Mental consciousness arises dependent on conditions.
Within this, with the exception of feeling (*vedanā*), the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) constitute internal dharmas.
The remaining formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are external phenomena.
There are two kinds of right exertion (*samyak-pradhāna*):
first, natural right exertion; second, concurrent right exertion.
One who is naturally diligent applies four kinds of effort for the sake of the Path: to suppress two kinds of unwholesome dharmas and to cultivate two kinds of wholesome dharmas.

When practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, if there is a mind of indolence, or if the mind is shrouded by various afflictions such as the five hindrances, or when one is separated from the five roots of goodness such as faith, one exerts diligent effort so that unwholesome dharmas already arisen may be abandoned and those not yet arisen may not arise.
One exerts diligent effort so that wholesome roots such as faith that have not yet arisen may arise, and so that those already arisen may increase.
