Because all phenomena possess characteristics, one knows they exist; just as seeing smoke and perceiving heat, one knows there is fire.
Because the five sense objects are each distinct from one another, one knows there are sentient beings.
Because of various reflections and deliberations upon all phenomena, one knows there is mind and mental factors.
Since this "self" lacks characteristics, one knows there is no self.
Question: The presence of inhalation and exhalation constitutes the characteristic of a self; [how can it be said there is no self?]
Blinking, the life-faculty, the mind, suffering and pleasure, love and hatred, diligence, and so forth—these are the marks of a self.
If there were no self, who would possess these things such as inhalation and exhalation, blinking, the life-faculty, the mind, suffering and pleasure, love and hatred, diligence, and so forth?
One should know that there is a self within, because it is that which initiates movement.
Life-force, vitality, and mind are also attributes of the self.
If there were no self, it would be like an ox without a driver.
Because there is a self, one is able to control the mind and enter the Dharma, rather than falling into negligence;
if there were no self, who would control the mind?
It is the self that experiences suffering and pleasure.
If there were no self, one would be like a tree; in that case, there should be no distinction between suffering and pleasure!
The same applies to love and hatred, as well as diligence.
Although the self is subtle and cannot be known by the five sensory faculties, its existence can be known through these characteristics.
Answer: These various characteristics are all characteristics of consciousness.
Where there is consciousness, there are inhalation and exhalation, blinking, life-span, and so forth.
If consciousness were absent when separated from the body,
then because you claim the self (*ātman*) to be eternal and omnipresent, even a dead person should possess blinking, inhalation and exhalation, and life-force!
Furthermore, inhalation and exhalation are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*); they arise and move due to the power of the wind that follows the mind.
This is a characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*), not a characteristic of a self (*ātman*).
Life-force (*jīvita*) is a formation dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), and it is likewise a characteristic of consciousness.
Question:

If, when one has entered a mindless meditative absorption or is asleep without dreaming, the breath still flows in and out and there is life, why do you say that "all these are characteristics of consciousness"?

Answer: In states such as the mindless concentrations (*acittaka-samāpatti*), although consciousness is temporarily absent, it will inevitably arise again before long because consciousness does not abandon the body.
Since the time when consciousness is present is extensive while the time without it is brief, it is therefore called the characteristic of consciousness.
Just as when a person goes abroad, one cannot say that their home is without a master;
so too, suffering and pleasure, aversion and attraction, diligence and so forth, are associated with the mind, share its objects, and follow the mind’s activity.
They exist because the mind exists, and they cease to exist because the mind ceases to exist.
For this reason, these characteristics of consciousness are not the characteristics of a self.
Furthermore, if there were a self, that self would be of two kinds:
either permanent or impermanent.
As it is said:
"If the self were eternal, there would be no subsequent body;
because that which is eternal is not born, there would likewise be no liberation!"
"There is neither delusion nor action; for this reason, one should know:
there is no agent of sin or merit, nor is there any recipient.
Having abandoned both 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' one thereafter attains nirvāṇa."
If a self truly existed, one should not abandon the notion of "I.
If the self were impermanent, it would perish along with the body;
like a great bank collapsing into water, there would likewise be neither sin nor merit.
"In this way, as for 'I' and the knower or non-knower, the agent or non-agent, it is as explained in the *Dānapāramitā*.
Because one cannot apprehend the mark of a self (*ātman*), one knows that there is no self within all phenomena (*dharma*).
If one knows that there is no self within all phenomena, then one should not give rise to the thought of 'I'."
If there is no self, nor the mind of "mine," then because one is detached from both self and what belongs to the self, there is no bondage;
if there is no bondage, that is nirvana.
Therefore, the practitioner should practice the perception of non-self.
Question:
Are these—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—one and the same thing?
Are these three matters?
If they were one matter, it would not be right to speak of three.
If they are three matters, for what reason did the Buddha say, "That which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self"?
Answer: This is a single matter, namely, the experiencing of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
Due to the distinctions made within the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanāmukha*), there are three different types:
Corresponding to the practice of impermanence is the "perception of impermanence";
corresponding to the practice of suffering is the "perception of suffering";
corresponding to the practice of non-self is the "perception of non-self."
Impermanence prevents one from entering the triple world;
suffering makes one aware of the faults of the triple world;
and non-self leads to the relinquishing of the mundane world.
Furthermore, impermanence gives rise to a mind of revulsion;
suffering gives rise to fear and dread;
and non-self uproots [the afflictions] so as to bring about liberation.
Regarding impermanence, the Buddha said, "The five aggregates of clinging are impermanent";
regarding suffering, the Buddha said, "That which is impermanent is suffering";
regarding non-self, the Buddha said, "That which is suffering is non-self."
Regarding impermanence, the Buddha showed it as the characteristic of the total extinction of the five aggregates of clinging;
regarding suffering, the Buddha showed it as being like an arrow piercing the heart;
regarding non-self, the Buddha showed it as the characteristic of relinquishment.
"Impermanence" demonstrates the severing of craving;
"suffering" demonstrates the severing of the habitual conceit of self;
and "non-self" demonstrates the severing of false views.
"Impermanence" negates the view of eternalism;
"suffering" negates the view of attaining nirvana as happiness in this present life;
and "non-self" negates attachment to a locus.
That which is impermanent is that which the world clings to as a permanent dharma;
that which is suffering is that which the world reckons to be a place of happiness;
that which is non-self is that which the world reckons to be a firm self.
These are the three characteristics of the discrimination of perception.
The perception of non-self has various objects as its conditions and encompasses all things, as explained in the section on the perception of suffering.
Regarding the "perception of revulsion toward food," one contemplates that this food arises from impure causes and conditions.
Just as flesh arises from the channels of semen and blood, it serves as the dwelling place for pus-worms;
just as ghee, milk, and curd are formed through the transformation of blood and are no different from putrid pus;
and just as the filth of a kitchen is composed of various impurities.

If it enters the mouth, the brain produces putrid saliva which flows down through two channels; this mixes with the spittle and then forms flavor. Its appearance is like vomit as it enters through the gate of the abdomen.
Earth sustains it, water moistens it, wind moves it, and fire cooks it, like porridge ripening in a cauldron; the dregs and turbidity sink to the bottom, while the clear essence remains above.
It is like brewing wine: the dregs and turbidity become excrement, while the clear liquid becomes urine.

When wind blows the oily essence through the three apertures of the waist, it disperses into the hundred vessels and combines with the pre-existing blood; through this coagulation and transformation, flesh is produced.
From the newly formed flesh, fat, bone, and marrow arise; from within these, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is produced.
From the union of the new and old flesh, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise; from the five faculties, the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) arise.
Following the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in succession, which discriminates and grasps signs, weighing the beautiful and the ugly.
Thereafter, the various afflictions such as the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," as well as various sinful karmas, arise.

One contemplates that food is thus impure in its manifold causes and conditions from beginning to end, and realizes that the four internal elements are no different from the four external elements; it is only due to the view of self that one forcibly claims them as "mine."
Furthermore, contemplate this food: it requires immense labor to plow, sow, weed, harvest, thresh, grind, wash, boil, and cook until it is prepared.
Calculating a single bowl of rice, one finds that the sweat shed by the laborers who gathered it far exceeds the amount of food itself.

The labor expended to produce this food is heavy, and its preparation involves such hardship; yet once it enters the mouth and is consumed, it immediately becomes impure, possessing no lasting value, and within a single night it transforms into excrement and urine.
Originally it was a delicious food, something people relish;
yet when it has transformed into impurity, one finds it loathsome and does not wish to see it.
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"If I were to become greedily attached to such wretched food, I would fall into hell to swallow glowing iron balls;
upon emerging from hell, I would become an animal—
a cow, a sheep, or a camel— to repay my past debts."
"Or one may become a pig or a dog, constantly devouring excrement and filth.
By contemplating food in this way, one gives rise to a sense of revulsion;
because of this revulsion toward food, one becomes weary of all five sensual desires.
For example, suppose there is a brahmin who practices the dharma of purity; due to some business matter, he arrives in an impure country and thinks to himself:
"How can I avoid this impurity?"
"One may attain purity only by eating dry food.
Seeing an old woman selling *śukra-maṇḍaka* cakes, he said to her:
"I have a reason to stay here for a hundred days; if you regularly prepare these cakes and bring them to me, I shall pay you a high price!"
The old woman made cakes every day and sent them to him;
the Brahmin, being greedily attached to them, ate his fill and rejoiced.
However, as the old woman continued to make the cakes, they initially were pure white, but later they gradually became colorless and flavorless.
He immediately asked the old woman,
"For what reason is this so?
The mother replied:
"Because the abscess has healed.
The brahmin asked, "What does this mean?"
The mother said, "My mistress had an abscess on her private parts; she treated it with flour, ghee, and licorice. When the abscess ripened and pus emerged, she mixed it with ghee to make cakes.
She did this every day, and gave these cakes to you; that is why the cakes were so good."
"Now that the lady's abscess has healed, where else shall I find one?
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin struck his head with both fists and beat his breast, wailing and sobbing:
"How could I have violated this pure dharma?"
"I have accomplished my purpose!
Abandoning the matter at hand, he galloped back to his own country.

The practitioner is also like this: attached to these foods and drinks, he delights in eating them; seeing their beautiful colors, smooth textures, fragrant scents, and delicious flavors, he does not contemplate their impurity.
Later, when one undergoes the retribution of suffering, what can regret avail?

If one can contemplate the beginning and end of food in this way, a sense of revulsion will arise; through this, one becomes detached from the desire for food, abandons all four types of desire, and completely relinquishes all pleasures within the realm of desire.
By severing these five desires, the five lower fetters are likewise severed.

When one no longer takes pleasure in or clings to various such causes and conditions of evil and transgression, this is called the "perception of repulsiveness in food" (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*). Question:

The perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self correspond to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), whereas the four perceptions beginning with repulsiveness in food correspond to tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*). Logically, the former should come first; why are they explained later?
Answer: In the Buddha-dharma there are two kinds of paths:
the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).

Within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), these three perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are employed to destroy various false views and so forth, whereby one attains the fruits of sainthood; yet, one has not yet abandoned desire.

In order to abandon desire, the four perceptions beginning with the perception of the loathsomeness of food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*) are taught in succession, through which one attains freedom from the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as sexual desire.

The first three perceptions demonstrate the path of seeing the truths; the middle four perceptions demonstrate the path of training (śaikṣa); and the final three perceptions demonstrate the path of no-more-training (aśaikṣa).
Within the initial practice of mindfulness of the body, although the perception of revulsion toward food exists, the Buddha did not mention it because its functional efficacy is slight.

Now, for the sake of those who have attained the stages of *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* and seek to transcend desire, the four perceptions—beginning with the perception of repulsiveness in food—are taught in succession.

Regarding the "perception that all the world is not to be delighted in": if one contemplates the flavors of worldly sensual desires, such as vehicles, clothing, pavilions, gardens, houses, and various other pleasant things, a perception of delight arises;
however, if one contemplates the manifold evils and transgressions of the world, a perception of revulsion arises in the mind.
What are the evil matters?
There are two kinds of evil matters:
first, sentient beings; second, lands.
Sentient beings suffer from eight afflictions:
birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from those one loves, dwelling with those one hates, not obtaining what one seeks, and, briefly stated, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.

Because sentient beings commit many sins and indulge excessively in lustful desire, they fail to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly; they do not follow the instructions of their parents, teachers, or elders; and lacking a sense of shame or remorse, they are no different from birds and beasts.

Because of an abundance of hatred, one fails to distinguish between the light and the heavy; the poison of anger erupts in madness, such that one will not even accept the Buddha’s words, has no desire to hear the Dharma, and feels no fear of the evil realms;
one inflicts punishments and whippings indiscriminately, remaining unaware of the suffering of others;
having entered the great darkness, one sees nothing at all.
Because of their great ignorance, they do not seek by means of the Path; they do not recognize the conditions of phenomena, like one who attempts to obtain milk from a horn.
Because they are shrouded by nescience, even though they are bathed in the light of the sun, they forever see nothing at all.
Because of excessive stinginess and greed, one's house is like a cemetery, and people do not approach it.
Because of excessive arrogance, one does not respect the worthy and holy, nor is one filial toward one's parents;
through such prideful indulgence, one destroys oneself and will forever lack any worth.
Because of the abundance of wrong views, one does not believe in this world or the next, nor does one believe in sin and merit;
such a person is unfit to dwell with. Because of the prevalence of these and other afflictions, one is ruined and rendered worthless.
Because their evil karma was so great, they committed crimes of immediate retribution:
either killing their parents, or harming sages and holy ones;
or, seeking honor and status at the time, slandering the loyal and upright, and cruelly harming their own kin.
Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the world, those who are virtuous are few, while those who are base and evil are many.
Sometimes there may be those with virtuous conduct, yet they are poor, lowly, and ugly;
or there may be those who are wealthy, noble, and handsome, yet their actions are not good.
Some may have a fondness for giving, yet they are impoverished and lack wealth;
others, though possessing abundant riches and treasures, are stingy and attached, refusing to practice generosity.
If one sees a person who has thoughts but remains silent without speaking, one may immediately assume they are arrogant and self-important, refusing to humble themselves to engage with others.

Conversely, if one sees someone who is kind and humble in their engagement with others, whose grace and benefits flow everywhere like moisture, one may instead assume they are deceitful, flattering, and hypocritical.
Or, seeing one who is eloquent and skilled in discourse, they immediately assume that he relies on such petty wisdom and treat him with arrogance.
Or, seeing one who is upright and good-natured, they conspire together to deceive and mock him, dragging him about and treating him with contempt.
If they see someone with a gentle and supple mind, they treat them with contempt, trampling and kicking them, rather than meeting them with propriety.
If they see one who maintains pure precepts, they claim their conduct is hypocritical and eccentric, treating them with disdain and refusing to acknowledge them.
Sentient beings such as these are corrupt and evil; there is not a single thing about them that is pleasant.

As for the wickedness of the land, in all its territories there is much decline and no auspiciousness; cold and heat, hunger and thirst, diseases, pestilence, the invasion of toxic vapors, and the fears of old age, sickness, and death exist everywhere.
Wherever the body goes, manifold sufferings follow it; there is no place from which one may escape!
Though there be fine countries that are abundant, joyful, and peaceful, they are for the most part afflicted by various defilements and thus cannot be called lands of bliss.
All things possess two kinds of suffering:
physical suffering and mental suffering; there is no country where these do not exist.
As it is said:
“There are lands where it is very cold, and there are lands where it is very hot;
there are lands without protection, and there are lands full of evil;
there are lands of constant hunger, and there are lands with many diseases.”
"There are lands where merit is not cultivated; such places are devoid of joy.
Contemplating that sentient beings and their lands possess such evils, one realizes there is not a single thing in the world worth delighting in.
Such are the evil matters of the desire realm.
When one dies or falls away from the two higher realms, the great anguish produced is even more intense than that of the lower realm;
it is like falling from a very high place, being shattered and utterly destroyed.
Question:

What is the difference between the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in, such that they are taught separately?
Answer: There are two kinds of contemplation:
general contemplation and specific contemplation.
The preceding was a general contemplation; herein is a specific contemplation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of contemplation:
contemplation of phenomena (dharma) and contemplation of sentient beings (sattva).
Previously, there was the contemplation that refutes all dharmas; here, the contemplation is on the differing sinful evils of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the former refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), while this refers to the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*).
The former is the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), while the present is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Such are their various distinctions.
They are subsumed within all stages (*bhūmi*) and take the phenomena of the three realms as their objects.
This is called "the perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds.
As for "the perception of death," it is as explained in the section on mindfulness of death.
As for "the perception of impurity," it is as explained in the section on the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of exhaustion take the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* as their object.
Because it abandons all fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), it is called the "perception of abandonment";
because it detaches from the fetters and proclivities, it is called the "perception of detachment."
Because all fetters and latent tendencies are exhausted, it is called the "perception of exhaustion. Question:
If that is so, then a single perception would suffice; why are three mentioned?
Answer: As previously stated, one dharma is explained in three ways:
that which is impermanent is suffering, and that which is suffering is non-self.
This is also like that: because the evils of all the world are so deep and heavy, there are three kinds of censures.
It is like felling a great tree; it cannot be cut down with a single blow.

The subtle and wondrous Dharma of nirvāṇa was previously unattained; therefore, it is praised in various ways as the "perception of cessation," the "perception of detachment," and the "perception of exhaustion."

Furthermore, because the three poisons are severed, it is called "severance" (prahāṇa); because craving is abandoned, it is called "renunciation" (virāga); and because all suffering is extinguished so that it does not arise again, it is called "exhaustion" (nirodha).

Furthermore, when a practitioner, through right wisdom, contemplates the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma, thereby distancing themselves from all afflictions, this is called the "perception of detachment.
When they attain the untainted path and sever all fetters and latent tendencies, this is called the "perception of abandonment.
When entering Nirvana, they extinguish the five aggregates of clinging so that they no longer continue in succession; this is called the "perception of exhaustion."
The "perception of abandonment" refers to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
the "perception of exhaustion" refers to *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
and the "perception of detachment" is the gateway to the means for both types of nirvāṇa.
These three perceptions, being both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), complete the inclusion of the ten perceptions within all stages. **38.
Explanation of the Eleven Knowledges (Ekādaśajñāna-vyākhyāna)** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Chapter One, Part Three-Eight: Explanation of the Eleven Knowledges. [The "Dan" edition states:
This section combines the meaning of the three samādhis and the meaning of the three faculties. [Sūtra] "There are eleven knowledges:"

Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin [of suffering], knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of things as they truly are.

[Treatise] "Dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) refers to the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) regarding phenomena bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the causes bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena bound to the desire realm;
the untainted knowledge regarding the path for abandoning phenomena bound to the desire realm; and the untainted knowledge within the category of dharma-knowledge.
Regarding "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*): the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) concerning the form and formless realms is also like this.

Regarding "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracitta-jñāna*): it knows the present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others bound to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as a small portion of the untainted minds and mental factors.
"Worldly wisdom" refers to all forms of tainted (sāsrava) wisdom.
"Wisdom of suffering" refers to the attainment of untainted (anāsrava) wisdom when one contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

“Knowledge of origination” (*samudaya-jñāna*) is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises when contemplating the causes of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)— namely, cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), production (*jāti*), and condition (*pratyaya*).

“Knowledge of cessation” (*nirodha-jñāna*) is the untainted knowledge that arises when contemplating cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
"Knowledge of the Path" (*mārga-jñāna*) refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that contemplates the path as the right, the practice, and the attainment at the appropriate time.

"Knowledge of Exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) refers to the untainted wisdom, vision, clarity, and awakening that arise when one reflects: "I have seen suffering; I have abandoned its origin; I have realized its cessation; I have cultivated the path."

Regarding "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*): having seen suffering, one does not see it again; having abandoned the origin, one does not abandon it again; having realized cessation, one does not realize it again; having cultivated the path, one does not cultivate it again.
When one reflects in this way, there arises untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), vision, clarity, and awakening.
"Knowledge as it truly is" (yathābhūta-jñāna) refers to the correct and unimpeded knowledge of the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena.

This is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) which takes as its object the phenomena bound to the desire realm, the causes of phenomena bound to the desire realm, the cessation of phenomena bound to the desire realm, and the path for the abandonment of phenomena bound to the desire realm.
Inference-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is also like this.
Worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) takes all phenomena as its object.
Knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) takes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*caitta*) of others as its object.
The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin take the five aggregates of clinging as their object;
the knowledge of cessation takes extinction as its object;
and the knowledge of the path takes the five untainted aggregates as its object.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) both take the four truths as their objects.
Among the ten knowledges, one is with outflows (*sāsrava*), eight are without outflows (*anāsrava*), and one should be analyzed:
the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is with outflows when it takes a mind with outflows as its object, and it is without outflows when it takes a mind without outflows as its object.

Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) comprises dharma-knowledge itself, as well as portions of other-mind-knowledge (para-citta-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is also like this.
Mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) comprises mundane knowledge and a small portion of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

The knowledge of others' minds comprises the knowledge of others' minds and a small portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), inferential knowledge, mundane knowledge, the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

The knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) comprises the knowledge of suffering itself, as well as a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
The same applies to the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna).

The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) comprises the knowledge of the path, as well as a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) comprises the knowledge of exhaustion, as well as a portion of the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is also like this:
it is associated with nine knowledges and eight faculties, excluding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is associated with ten faculties, excluding the faculty of wisdom.
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and knowledge of suffering are associated with the emptiness samādhi.
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising are associated with the signlessness samādhi.

Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising are associated with the concentration of wishlessness.

Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising are associated with the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of non-self.
Worldly knowledge (loka-jñāna) is associated with the four middle types of perception.
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising are associated with the latter three types of perception.
Some say: Mundane knowledge may be associated with the perception of separation (*viveka-saṃjñā*).
Dharma-knowledge takes nine knowledges as its object, excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Inference-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is also like this.

Worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) take ten knowledges as their objects.
Suffering-knowledge (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and origination-knowledge (*samudaya-jñāna*) take worldly knowledge and impure knowledge of others' minds as their objects.
The knowledge of cessation does not take knowledge as its object.
The knowledge of the path takes nine knowledges as its objects, excluding conventional knowledge.
The knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge possess sixteen aspects.
The knowledge of others' minds has four aspects.
Regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, each has its own four aspects.
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising both possess fourteen aspects, excluding the aspect of emptiness and the aspect of non-self.
The mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*) within the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) consists of sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).

The mundane knowledge within the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) consists of four aspects—excluding the aspect of signlessness (*animitta-ākāra*) and the aspect of turning away from signs (*vivarta-ākāra*). These were formerly termed the "sixteen noble practices" (*ārya-caryā*).
Upon first entering the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), one accomplishes the knowledge of the present life (loka-jñāna).
In the second moment of mind, the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) and the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) are added.
In the fourth moment of mind, the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is added.
In the sixth mind, the knowledge of arising (samudaya-ñāṇa) increases;
in the tenth mind, the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-ñāṇa) increases;
and in the fourteenth mind, the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) increases.
If one is free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds increases.
On the path of no-more-learning, the knowledge of exhaustion increases.
Upon attaining indestructible liberation, the knowledge of non-arising increases.
In the first untainted mind, one does not cultivate wisdom. In the second mind, one cultivates two types of wisdom in both the present and the future.
In the fourth mind, one cultivates two types of wisdom in the present and three types of wisdom in the future.
In the sixth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and two in the future.
In the eighth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and three in the future.
In the tenth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and two in the future.
In the twelfth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and three in the future.
In the fourteenth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and future.
In the sixteenth moment of mind, one cultivates two knowledges in the present and six knowledges in the future; if one is free from desire, one cultivates seven knowledges.

When a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) seeks to become free from the fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm, they cultivate seven knowledges during the seventeen moments of mind, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.
In the ninth liberation-mind, one cultivates eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

When a person liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms into one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they cultivate six knowledges within the two paths [of seeing and cultivation], excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.

When one becomes detached from the desires of the seven stages, one cultivates seven knowledges within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.

When detaching from the desire for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates six knowledges within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Within the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates seven knowledges, excluding conventional knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.

In the ninth liberation of the first moment of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), a person of non-periodic liberation (*asamayavimukta*) cultivates ten knowledges (*jñāna*) as well as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) roots of goodness.
If it is a person of periodic liberation (*samayavimukta*), they cultivate nine knowledges as well as all contaminated and uncontaminated roots of goodness.
These various categories are analyzed in detail through the gateway of the Abhidharma.
As for the analysis of the characteristics of "knowledge as it truly is," this is explained extensively in a later chapter of this *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, some say that "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) means knowing that the five aggregates of the desire realm are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; and knowing that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions—namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to birth being the condition for old age and death.
As the Buddha said to the brahmin Susīma:
“First, one employs the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) to discern all dharmas; afterwards, one employs the knowledge of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇajñāna*).

Regarding “inferential knowledge” (*anvayajñāna*): it is knowing that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) in the present are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; that the five aggregates of clinging in the past, the future, and within the realms of form and formlessness are likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
For example, just as one perceives that present fire is hot and capable of burning, one uses this to infer by analogy that fire in the past, the future, and other lands is likewise so.
"Knowledge of others' minds" refers to knowing the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings.
Question:
If one knows the minds and mental factors of others, why is it called only "knowing the minds of others"? Answer:
Because the mind is the sovereign, it is simply called "knowing the minds of others";
if one speaks of the mind, it should be understood that mental factors (caitta-dharma) have already been included.
"Worldly wisdom" is termed "conventional wisdom."

The noble ones know within the context of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dharma), whereas ordinary persons know only within the context of conventional designations (prajñapti); for this reason, it is called "conventional knowledge" (prajñapti-jñāna).
For example, when rafters, beams, and walls are called a "house," one merely knows these things without knowing their ultimate meaning; this is called "worldly knowledge" (loka-jñāna).
Regarding "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-jñāna*): it uses the wisdom of suffering to censure the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Question:

Since the five aggregates of clinging are also impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, why is it that one speaks only of "knowledge of suffering" and not of "knowledge of impermanence, emptiness, and non-self"?
The answer is:

"Knowledge of suffering" is taught for the sake of the truth of suffering; "knowledge of origin" is taught for the sake of the truth of origin; "knowledge of cessation" is taught for the sake of the truth of cessation; and "knowledge of the path" is taught for the sake of the truth of the path.
Question:

Since the five aggregates of clinging possess various kinds of evils, for what reason is only the Truth of Suffering taught, rather than the Truth of Impermanence, the Truth of Emptiness, or the Truth of Non-self?
Answer: If one speaks of the truths of impermanence, emptiness, and non-self, one does not destroy the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
However, because sentient beings are mostly attached to pleasure and fear suffering, the Buddha declares that everything in the world is suffering, desiring to cause them to renounce and abandon it.
Within impermanence, emptiness, and non-self, sentient beings do not feel great fear; therefore, these are not mentioned.
Furthermore, within the Buddha’s teaching, the five aggregates of clinging have an alternative name, namely "suffering";
for this reason, only the knowledge of suffering is taught.
This knowledge of suffering is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava):
if it occurs within the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, or the Supreme Worldly Dharma, it is with outflows;
if it enters the Path of Seeing the Truths, it is without outflows.
Why is this? Because from the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), one contemplates suffering in four ways.
The same applies to the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Furthermore, "knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-jñāna) means knowing that the characteristics of suffering are ultimately non-arising.
"Knowledge of origination" (samudaya-jñāna) means knowing that all phenomena are detached and devoid of combination.
"Knowledge of cessation" (nirodha-jñāna) means knowing that all phenomena are eternally quiescent, like nirvana.
"Knowledge of the path" (mārga-jñāna) means knowing that all phenomena are eternally pure, being neither right nor wrong.
"Knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) means knowing that all phenomena are non-existent.
"Knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna) means knowing that all phenomena subject to arising are unreal and indeterminate, and therefore do not arise.
Regarding "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*): that which cannot be known by the ten kinds of knowledge can be known through knowledge as it truly is.
Each of the ten knowledges has its own respective characteristics, its own respective objects, its own distinct differences, and its own respective modes of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-dharma*);
within this knowledge as it truly is, there are no characteristics, no objects, and no distinctions, for all modes of contemplation are extinguished, and yet there is no contemplation.

Among the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), there are the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) and the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*); within the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtajñāna*), there is only the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
The ten knowledges are shared by Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas;
the knowledge of reality as it is belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
Why is this? Because only the Buddha possesses the quality of non-deception.
For this reason, it is known that the knowledge of reality as it is belongs to the Buddha alone.
Furthermore, when these ten knowledges enter into the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna), they lose their original names and there remains only the single knowledge of reality;
it is like the flowing waters of the ten directions, which, upon entering the great ocean, relinquish their original names and are called only the "great ocean."
Thus, these various distinctions regarding the meaning of the eleven knowledges have been briefly explained herein.
[The Dan edition states:
"The eleven knowledges are concluded. [Sūtra]: "The three samādhis:"
"There is the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra, and the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
[Treatise]: All meditative concentrations that collect the mind are termed *samādhi*; in the language of Qin, this means "the sphere of correct mental activity."
This mind has come from beginningless worlds, always crooked and not upright;
once it attains this sphere of right-minded conduct, the mind becomes straight and upright.
It is like a snake that moves in constant curves, yet becomes straight when it enters a bamboo tube.
This samādhi is of three types:
in the desire realm, the threshold stage (anāgamya), and the first dhyāna, it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra" because it is associated with both vitarka and vicāra;
in the intermediate stage between the first and second dhyānas, it is called "without vitarka but with vicāra" because it is associated with vicāra alone.

From the second dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because they are not associated with *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), they are called "without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*.
Question:
There are as many as twenty mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with samādhi; for what reason are only *vitarka* and *vicāra* mentioned?
The answer is:
These vitarka and vicāra disturb samādhi; for this reason it is said that although these two matters are wholesome, they are thieves to samādhi and are difficult to abandon.
Some say: "When the mind possesses vitarka and vicāra, there is no samādhi. For this reason, the Buddha taught that samādhi with vitarka and vicāra is merely not firm;
however, when the power of vitarka and vicāra is slight, at that time one may attain samādhi."
These vitarka and vicāra can produce samādhi and can also destroy samādhi;
they are like wind, which can produce rain and can also destroy rain.
The three kinds of wholesome vitarka and vicāra can produce the first dhyāna.

Upon attaining the first dhyāna, one gives rise to great joy; however, because of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), the mind becomes distracted and the attainment is lost again.
For this reason, only vitarka and vicāra are mentioned. Question:
What is the difference between vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought)?
The answer is:
the coarse aspect of the mind is called "vitarka," and the subtle aspect of the mind is called "vicāra."

Initially, the arising of mental signs within the center of the object is called "vitarka" (applied thought); subsequently, the analytical deliberation regarding what is good or bad is called "vicāra" (sustained thought).
There are three kinds of coarse vitarkas:
the vitarka of sensual desire, the vitarka of ill-will, and the vitarka of harmfulness.
There are three kinds of wholesome thoughts:
the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harming.
There are three kinds of subtle thoughts:
The thought of relatives, the thought of country, and the thought of immortality—these six kinds of thoughts obstruct samādhi;
three kinds of wholesome thoughts can open the gate of samādhi.
If discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are excessive, one will again lose samādhi.
Just as wind can propel a ship, yet once the wind has passed, it may destroy the ship;
so too are "vitarka" (applied thought) and "vicāra" (sustained thought) variously differentiated.
Question:
The Sūtra speaks of three kinds of dharmas:
dharmas with vitarka and vicāra, dharmas without vitarka but with vicāra, and dharmas without vitarka and without vicāra;
as well as the stage with vitarka and vicāra, the stage without vitarka but with vicāra, and the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
Question: Why are only three kinds of samādhi mentioned now?
Answer: Those that are both subtle and functional are selected.

Dharmas with vitarka and vicāra are those associated with vitarka and vicāra within the desire realm, the preparatory stage (anāgamya), and the first dhyāna; these may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Dharmas with vitarka and vicāra are those associated with vicāra in the intermediate dhyāna, whether they are wholesome or indeterminate.
Dharmas without vitarka and without vicāra are those dissociated from vitarka and vicāra: all matter, all mental formations dissociated from mind, and unconditioned dharmas.
The stage with both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) consists of the desire realm, the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), and the Brahma-world.
The stage without applied thought but with sustained thought consists of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*); by skillfully cultivating this stage, one becomes a Great Brahma King (*Mahābrahmā*).
The stages without vitarka and vicāra are all the Ābhāsvara, Subhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, and all the formless (ārūpya) stages.
Among these, that which is supreme and sublime is samādhi. What is this samādhi?

From the three samādhis beginning with emptiness up to the vajra-samādhi, as well as the various samādhis of arhats and pratyekabuddhas; from the samādhi of contemplating the Buddhas of the ten directions up to the śūraṅgama-samādhi; and from the samādhi that severs all doubts up to the king of samādhis and other such samādhis of all Buddhas.
Such various classifications conclude the brief explanation of the meaning of the three samādhis.
[Sūtra]: "The three faculties:
the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has already known."
[Treatise] Regarding the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*): it is a combination of the nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

For those who practice through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who practice through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), it is termed the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,'" namely: the five faculties beginning with faith, the faculties of joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the mental faculty (*manas*).

In the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) for those who possess faith-understanding (śraddhādhimukta) or have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), these nine faculties are designated as the "faculty of knowing" (ājñendriya).
In the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), these same nine faculties are called the "faculty of having known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Question:
For what reason are only these three faculties selected from among the twenty-two faculties? Answer:
The characteristic of being sharp, clear, and sovereign in understanding is what is called a "faculty" (indriya).
As for the other nineteen faculties, because their characteristics as faculties are not fully complete, they are not included.

These three faculties are sharp and enable one to enter directly into nirvāṇa; because they are the masters among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they attain sovereignty and can surpass all other faculties.
Furthermore, the ten faculties are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and are acquired spontaneously, offering no further benefit;
the nine faculties are indeterminate, being either with-outflows or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), and for these reasons, it is not said that a bodhisattva must fully possess them.
Question: The ten perceptions (daśasaṃjñā) are both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava); for what reason is it said that they should be fully accomplished? Answer:

The ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are all factors that assist the path and seek *nirvāṇa*. Although the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are wholesome dharmas, they do not necessarily seek *nirvāṇa*.
As it is said in the Abhidharma:
"Who is endowed with the five faculties, such as faith?"
"Those who have not severed their roots of goodness.
Furthermore, if the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) become pure and transform into the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are already subsumed within the three faculties.
Within these three faculties, there must necessarily be the mental faculty (*manendriya*); among the three feelings (*trivedanā*), there must necessarily be one feeling.
For this reason, only three faculties are mentioned.
Furthermore, among the twenty-two faculties, some are wholesome, some are unwholesome, and some are indeterminate; because they are thus mixed, it is not said that one should possess them all.
These three faculties are subsumed within the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" resides in six stages; the faculty of "knowing" and the faculty of "having known" reside in nine stages.
The three faculties have the four truths as their objects and are associated with the six types of perception.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" has the [other] three faculties as its causes.
The faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) has two faculties as its cause;
the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya) has only the faculty of "having known" as its cause.
Following the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), there arises the sequence of two faculties.

From the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), there may subsequently arise either a contaminated faculty (*sāsravendriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), or the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
From the faculty of having known, there may subsequently arise either a contaminated faculty or the faculty of having known.
These and other such points are explained in detail through the gateway of the Abhidharma.

Furthermore, the faculty of "desiring to know what is not yet known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is so named because it desires to know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; thus, it gives rise to the five faculties beginning with faith.
By the power of these five faculties, one is able to realize the true reality of all phenomena.
Just as when a person first enters the womb and acquires two faculties—
the body faculty and the life faculty—
at that time they are like a lump of flesh; not yet possessing the various sense organs, they are unable to discern or know anything.
When the five faculties are perfected, one is able to know the five sense objects.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: when first resolving to become a Buddha, they have not yet fully perfected these five faculties; thus, although they possess the aspiration to know the true nature of all phenomena, they are unable to know it.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to these five faculties, such as faith, they are then able to know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

For example, the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from them is called "the eye. Although the four great elements and derivative matter exist beforehand, they are not yet termed the "eye faculty" because they have not been purified.
Likewise, although a person who has not severed their roots of goodness possesses faith, it is not termed a "faculty" because it has not been purified.

If a bodhisattva attains these five faculties, such as faith and the rest, at that time they are able to believe in the true mark of all dharmas: that they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither existent nor non-existent, neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned; that they are eternally quiescent, truly pure, like empty space, unindicatable, unspeakable, transcending the path of all linguistic expression, and surpassing all mental states and their associated factors; that their activity is like nirvāṇa—this is the Buddha-dharma.
By the power of the faculty of faith, the bodhisattva is able to receive [the teachings];
by the power of the faculty of diligence, they practice with vigor, neither falling back nor turning away;
and by the power of the faculty of mindfulness, they prevent unwholesome dharmas from entering and gather all wholesome dharmas.
By the power of the faculty of concentration, one is able to gather the mind within the true mark even when it is distracted by the five desires;
by the power of the faculty of wisdom, one attains the flavor of the meaning—whether much or little—within the Buddha’s wisdom, such that it cannot be destroyed.
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), which is the basis for the five faculties, is necessarily accompanied by feeling—whether it be joy, pleasure, or equanimity.

Relying on this faculty, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva; until the fruit of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is attained, this is called the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
In this context, because one knows the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena with perfect clarity, it is called the "faculty of knowledge" (*ājñendriya*).

From this, one attains the fruit of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), dwells in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), receives the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), and so on, until one fulfills the ten stages, sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and attains the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*). Throughout this entire interval, it is termed the "faculty of knowledge."

Having severed all habitual tendencies of the afflictions and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because the wisdom that knows all knowable phenomena is all-pervasive, it is called the "faculty of one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Dān says:
The Three Roots are concluded. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 23;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Ten Powers in the First Chapter, Number Thirty.
Volume Nine, Chapter Twenty-four.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin. 39. Commentary on the Ten Powers [Sūtra]: “Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to fully know the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered knowledges, eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion should practice the perfection of wisdom!
[Treatise] Question:

These ten powers (*daśabala*), four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth, are the unsurpassed qualities of the Buddha; they should have been explained first. For what reason are the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti*) explained first?
Answer: The six pāramitās are what the bodhisattvas employ, as has already been explained.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the three untainted faculties are the dharmas of the śrāvakas.

Because the Bodhisattva practices these six *pāramitās* and has attained power, he desires to transcend the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and also desires to transform those who incline toward the paths of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, leading them into the Buddha-way;
for this reason, he censures the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings which abandon all sentient beings and provide no benefit.
If any śrāvakas say:
"You are an ordinary person who has not yet severed the fetters and cannot practice this Dharma," they merely engage in empty reproach!
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should fulfill the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all other dharmas of the śrāvakas, because they are ungraspable.
Although he practices these various dharmas, because they are ungraspable, and because sentient beings practice wrong conduct, he practices this right conduct and never abandons it.
These dharmas are empty and ungraspable, yet one does not hastily take up the realization of nirvana.
If a bodhisattva does not understand or practice this Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) but merely reviles it, who would be willing to believe them?
For example, if Śākyamuni Buddha had not first practiced austerities for six years and then criticized them as being a non-path, no one would have believed or accepted his words!
For this reason, he personally practiced austerities exceeding those of others;
thus, when he attained the Way of the Buddha and criticized these ascetic practices, everyone believed and accepted it.
Therefore, after the six pāramitās, one practices the Dharma of the śrāvakas in succession.

Furthermore, this is not merely the Dharma of the śrāvakas; because within this Dharma one harmonizes with and does not abandon the intentions of sentient beings, fulfills all Buddha-dharmas, and employs the wisdom of non-apprehensible emptiness (anupalambha-śūnyatā), it is called the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
Question:
If a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, why does he not enter the stage of the śrāvaka?
Answer:
"Endowed" means to be fully endowed with contemplative knowledge while not yet realizing [nirvana]; because one contemplates and knows with complete clarity, it is called "endowed.
As the Buddha said:
"All fear the pain of the staff; none do not cherish their own life."
"One may use oneself as an analogy: do not let the staff fall upon living beings.

Although it is said that "all fear the pain of the staff," sentient beings in the Formless Realm have no bodies; those in the Form Realm, though possessing bodies, have no whips or staves; and within the Desire Realm, the Buddhas, the Cakravartin Kings, and those from the Yāma Heaven upward do not fear corporal punishment.
It is because they fear those who would inflict such punishment that it is said, "all."
"Being endowed" is also like this; it is not called "endowed" for the sake of seeking or becoming attached to realized dharmas.
Furthermore, I have previously said:
"By not abandoning sentient beings and by being in harmony with the wisdom of the emptiness of non-apprehension, one does not fall into the stage of the śrāvaka."
Question: From the six pāramitās up to the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), it is only said that one "should fulfill" them;
why is it that from this point onward, it is always said that "one who wishes to attain or wish to know this matter should practice the prajñāpāramitā"?
Answer: Because the Dharma of the śrāvakas is finite and limited, it is said that they "should fulfill" it;

from this point onward, these dharmas of the Buddhas are profound and immeasurable, which the bodhisattvas have not yet attained, and therefore it is said, "One who wishes to attain these matters should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Furthermore, because the teachings of the śrāvakas are easy to understand and easy to know, they are said to be "fully perfected";
whereas the teachings of the bodhisattvas and the Buddhas are difficult to understand and difficult to know, they are said to be "that which one should study."
Furthermore, the general characteristics of the Śrāvaka-dharma are:
knowing suffering, knowing the cause of suffering, knowing the cessation of suffering, and knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is like two kinds of physicians:

First, they know only a single illness, its cause, its cure, and the medicine for its cure, yet they do not know all illnesses, all causes of illness, all cures for illness, or all medicines for curing illness.
Furthermore, there are those who know only how to treat the illnesses of humans but do not know how to treat the illnesses of animals;
or those who can treat the diseases of one country but cannot treat those of other countries;
or those who can treat several dozen types of illnesses but do not fully understand the four hundred and four types of illnesses.
The causes of illness, the cure of illness, and the medicine for curing illness are also like this.
Second, among these four types, one thoroughly knows them all: one thoroughly knows the medicine and thoroughly knows the illness.
Śrāvakas are like minor physicians who cannot possess universal knowledge;
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like great physicians, for whom there is no ailment they do not understand and no medicine they do not recognize.
For this reason, one should fulfill the teachings of the śrāvakas and train in the teachings of the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the Buddha’s ten powers:
he knows, as it truly is, what is possible and what is impossible; this is the first power.

To know the various karmas and various experiences of sentient beings in the past, future, and present; to know the places where karma was created; to know the causes and conditions; and to know the retributions—this is the second power.
To know all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and concentrations, and to know their characteristics of defilement and purity as they truly are, is the third power.
To know the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings as they truly are, is the fourth power.
Knowing the various desires of other sentient beings is the fifth power.
Knowing the various and innumerable dispositions of the world is the sixth power.
Knowing the characteristics of the destinations reached by all paths is the seventh power.

He knows various past lives, including their common characteristics and common causes and conditions—through one life, two lives, up to hundreds of thousands of lives and kalpas, until the end of the first kalpa—thinking: "I was among those beings; such was my name, my food and drink, my suffering and pleasure, and the length of my lifespan.
Dying there, I was born here; dying here, I was born back there.
My name, clan, food and drink, suffering and pleasure, and the length of my lifespan in being born here were also like this. This is the eighth power.

The Buddha’s divine eye is pure, surpassing the eyes of all devas and humans; he sees beings at the time of death and the time of birth—whether they are handsome or ugly, great or small, whether they fall into evil realms or good realms—and how they receive retribution according to the causes and conditions of their karma.

These sentient beings have accomplished evil physical karma, accomplished evil verbal karma, and accomplished evil mental karma; they slander the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views.
Due to these causes and conditions, at the time of death when the body perishes, they enter the evil paths and are born within the hells.

These sentient beings have accomplished wholesome bodily karma, accomplished wholesome verbal karma, and accomplished wholesome mental karma; they do not slander the noble ones, possess right view, and have accomplished the karma of right view.
By reason of these causes and conditions, at the time of death when the body perishes, they enter a good destination and are reborn in the heavens; this is the ninth power.

Because the Buddha has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), he possesses the liberation of mind through the absence of outflows and the liberation of wisdom through the absence of outflows. Within the phenomena of the present, he personally realizes and knows: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to come has ended. This knowledge according to reality is the tenth power (*daśabala*).
Question:
These ten powers have not yet been attained by bodhisattvas, nor can they be attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
why, then, are they explained here? Answer:
Although the śrāvakas cannot attain it themselves, if they hear of these merits of the ten powers, they will think:
"The Buddha possesses such great merits," and they will rejoice, saying:
"We have gained great benefit and received no small measure of advantage; our faith has become pure, and we have entered the path that brings an end to suffering.
When the bodhisattvas heard this, they diligently cultivated the bodhisattva path, intending to attain such fruits of great merit as these ten powers.

Furthermore, there are śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who practice the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha; they do not merely mindfully contemplate the Buddha’s physical body, but should mindfully contemplate his various meritorious qualities and his dharma-body.
One should form this thought:
Because the Buddha can understand all aspects and all phenomena, he is called the "Omniscient One" (Sarvajña);
because he skillfully analyzes and explains all phenomena according to reality, he is called the "All-Seeing One" (Sarvadarśin).
Because he directly knows all phenomena, he is called "the one whose omniscient vision is unimpeded";
because he regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind, he is called "the one of great compassion";
and because he possesses great compassion, he is named "the Savior of the World."
Because he has come by way of the path of reality, he is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One);
because he is worthy of receiving all offerings from the world, he is called "Arhat" (Worthy One);
because he has accomplished non-erroneous wisdom, he is called "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One).
Because he has accomplished the wisdom of precepts, concentration, and insight, he is called "One of Clear Conduct and Practice" (*vidyācaraṇa-sampanna*);
because he has attained that from which there is no returning, he is called "Well-Gone" (*sugata*);
because he knows the general and specific characteristics of the world, he is called "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*).
Because he skillfully expounds the supramundane path of peace and security, he is called the "Unsurpassed Tamer of Men";
because he delivers sentient beings through the three types of teaching, he is called the "Teacher of Gods and Humans";
and because he is able to awaken himself and awaken others from the slumber of all worldly afflictions, he is called the "Awakened One."
Because all his aspirations are fulfilled, he is named "Possessing Virtue";
because he has accomplished the ten powers, he is named "Firm Vow";
because he has attained the four fearlessnesses, he is named "Lion among Men."
Because he has attained immeasurable and profound wisdom, he is named "Ocean of Great Merit";
because his all-encompassing proclamations are unimpeded, he is named "Like the Wind";
because he feels neither hatred nor attachment toward anything beautiful or ugly, he is named "Like the Earth."
Because he has burned away the fuel of all fetters and afflictions, he is called "Like Fire";
because he has thoroughly severed the habitual tendencies of all afflictions, he is called "Endowed with Complete Liberation";
and because he dwells in the supreme state, he is named "World-Honored One."
Because the Buddha possesses such meritorious qualities as these, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha and teaching this Prajñāpāramitā, a great assembly of the fourfold community of the Buddha’s disciples, as well as various non-Buddhists—both lay and ordained—and gods, nāgas, spirits, and other such multitudes had gathered.

The Buddha entered the Samādhirāja-samādhi and emitted a great radiance that illuminated worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the earth shook in six ways as he preached this Prajñāpāramitā, the six pāramitās, and so forth, up to the three roots of non-outflow.
Among them, there were sentient beings who had doubts:
"By what power, and by how many kinds of power, is it possible to perform such inconceivable manifestations and bring about such benefit?"
Because the Buddha knew that the minds of sentient beings harbored such doubts, he said:

"I possess the power of wisdom regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; this power is tenfold. By employing these ten kinds of wisdom, I am able to perform such miraculous transformations and manifestations, and I can even exceed what has been done."
For this reason, it is said: "One who wishes to attain the ten powers should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, although the disciples of the Buddha have planted roots of goodness throughout successive lifetimes, they may fall among the non-Buddhists due to the influence of minor transgressions.
The various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) constantly say:
"The Buddha does not possess the power of real merit; he uses the power of illusion (māyā) to deceive and delude the minds of people.
Those disciples of the Buddha who have fallen into the views of the non-Buddhists harbor doubts in their hearts:
"If that were so, the Buddha would not be a Great Being.
To extinguish this malicious slander, he said:
"I truly possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; therefore, I deliver sentient beings, and it is not a matter of illusion or deception."

Furthermore, because the practice of the bodhisattva path and the performance of ascetic deeds are difficult to accomplish and difficult to complete, bodhisattvas may wish to become weary and desist; for this reason, the Buddha said:
"By practicing these ten powers, one shall obtain immeasurable karmic retribution."
It is, for example, like a caravan leader who consoles the merchants, saying:
"Be careful not to grow weary; exert yourselves with diligent effort, and you shall reach the mountain of jewels and obtain the seven treasures and the wish-fulfilling gem."
The Buddha likewise comforted the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Do not become weary or discouraged; you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor to cultivate the bodhisattva path.
By practicing these ten powers, you shall attain immeasurable karmic rewards."
For various reasons such as these benefits, the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth are taught.
Question:
The Buddha possesses immeasurable powers; for what reason are only the ten powers mentioned?
The answer is:

Although the Buddhas possess immeasurable power, they speak of the ten powers because these are sufficient to accomplish the task of delivering sentient beings through the conditions of their salvation.
By means of the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible, they discern and deliberate upon sentient beings to determine who is capable of being delivered and who is not.

By means of the power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma, he discerns and evaluates whether this person has an obstruction of karma, this person has an obstruction of retribution, or this person is free from obstructions.

By means of the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, he discerns and evaluates whether this person is attached to the flavor [of meditative states] or is not attached to the flavor.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties, he discriminates and evaluates the extent of sentient beings' intellectual capacities.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations, he discriminates and evaluates the objects of sentient beings' preferences.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the various dispositions of beings, he discerns and evaluates the inclinations of the deep minds of sentient beings.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations, he discerns and evaluates the gates of liberation for sentient beings.
By means of the power of knowledge of past lives, he discerns where sentient beings have previously come from.
By means of the power of knowledge of birth and death, he discerns the excellence or inferiority of the places where sentient beings are born.
By means of the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*), he discerns and evaluates how sentient beings attain nirvāṇa.
The Buddha employs these ten powers to deliver sentient beings; acting with precise and unerring discernment, they all attain full completion.
For this reason, although the Buddha possesses immeasurable powers, he speaks only of these ten powers.
Furthermore, regarding the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*), one definitively knows that from such causes and conditions this retribution arises;
herein, the other nine powers are subsumed. Because he wishes to deliver sentient beings, he distinguishes nine types within this first power.

Why is this? Because the sentient beings of this world, while seeing before their very eyes that grain emerges from seed, are unable to understand it; how much less can they understand the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of the mind and mental factors?
The Buddha possesses thorough and universal knowledge of internal and external causes, conditions, and karmic retributions; therefore, this is called a "power" (*bala*).

The Buddha knows that these sentient beings are bound by the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions, and are liberated by the causes and conditions of pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and liberation.

The Buddha universally and completely knows all three types of karma and all afflictions of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—their lightness or heaviness, depth or shallowness, and coarseness or subtlety; therefore, it is called a power.

The Buddha fully and universally knows all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis of all sentient beings, as well as the causes and conditions for their liberations—whether great or small, deep or shallow; therefore, this is called a power (*bala*).

Sentient beings with dull faculties perform the causal conditions of sinful and meritorious karma for the sake of future bodies, while those with sharp faculties accumulate various karmas so that [future existence] does not arise; the Buddha fully knows these superior and inferior faculties, as well as their good and bad characteristics, and therefore this is called a "power."

Knowing the two kinds of desires of all sentient beings and the causes and conditions for their superior or inferior faculties, as well as the various distinctions between these two kinds of desires—whether wholesome or unwholesome—the Buddha knows them all completely; therefore, this is called a power (*bala*).

Because he thoroughly understands the inclinations within the deep minds of sentient beings through two kinds of causes and conditions regarding the two types of desire, it is called a "power" (*bala*).

Because all sentient beings practice two kinds of paths—namely, the wholesome path and the unwholesome path—due to various natures and causes and conditions, and because the Buddha thoroughly knows all the destinations reached through their various gateways, it is called a "power."

To possess unimpeded wisdom regarding the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of the past and future worlds is called the power of knowledge of past lives and the power of knowledge of death and rebirth.

Having known the causes and effects of the past and future, to fully know the skillful means for destroying the continuity of the characteristics of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution is called the power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The Buddha knows the two kinds of causes and conditions within the three periods of time; having discerned and weighed the faculties, desires, and natures of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the exhaustion of outflows—this is the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Question:
What is the "power of what is possible and what is impossible"? Answer:

The Buddha knows the fixed characteristics of the causes, conditions, and retributions of all dharmas; he knows that from such causes and conditions such a retribution arises, and that from such causes and conditions such a retribution does not arise.
