Why is this? As stated in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* regarding the characteristics of what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*):
it is impossible for a woman to become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Why is this? Because all women are subject to men and lack self-mastery;
since a woman cannot even become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, how much less can she become a Buddha!
If women attain liberation and nirvana, they do so because of men; there is no such thing as attaining the Way spontaneously.
It is impossible for two wheel-turning sage kings to appear in the world at the same time.
Why is this? Because the karma of enmity cannot be fulfilled.
Even two wheel-turning sage-kings do not appear in the same world, let alone two Buddhas!
It is impossible for evil karma to result in the experience of pleasant retribution;
since even worldly happiness cannot be attained through evil karma, how much less so supramundane happiness!
If one who has committed evil deeds were to be reborn in heaven, such a thing would be impossible.
If one who commits evil deeds cannot even attain birth in the heavens, how much less can they attain nirvana!
It is impossible for one whose mind is shrouded by the five hindrances and distracted to attain nirvana without cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment.
When the five hindrances cover the mind and one is removed from the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment, one cannot even attain the path of a śrāvaka, let alone the path of a Buddha!
When the mind is free from covering, the path of a Buddha can be attained, let alone the path of a śrāvaka!
Such matters as what is possible and what is impossible were spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*.
Following these words of the Buddha, various masters of discourse further expound upon what is possible and what is impossible:

that the Buddha has any deficiency or fault; that noble ones seek teachers among non-Buddhist outsiders; that noble ones claim for themselves, "I am a Buddha"; that noble ones fall into the evil realms; that the fetters severed through the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana) arise again; that noble ones conceal their transgressions; or that a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) still possesses the twenty-five states of existence—all such things are impossible.

As explained in detail within the *Āryavibhaṅga*, for those who have committed the five heinous crimes, the five kinds of eunuchs, sentient beings fallen into the four evil destinies, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, and the retinues of Māra—who are obstructed by the three hindrances—it is impossible for them to attain the Way. There is no such possibility.

One who disparages the teacher of the Dharma disparages the Dharma and disparages themselves; being one who has broken the precepts and is deluded, it is impossible for such a person to claim they have attained the full joy of the Dharma.
To claim for oneself, "I am a Buddha," yet not repent of the evils of this body and speech while desiring to see the Buddha;
or if one has committed the offense of causing a schism in the Sangha and does not repent while desiring to see the Buddha;
or to enter right concentration from wrong concentration, to enter wrong concentration from right concentration, or to enter the indeterminate from right concentration.
Apart from the Buddha-dharma, there is no other who has truly attained the Way;
it is impossible for one who should have attained the body of the Way to die [without realization].
Apart from consciousness produced through causes and conditions, it is impossible for there to be any further dharma that emerges as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is impossible for a messenger dispatched by the Buddha to fail in his mission or be obstructed.
It is likewise impossible for one who has entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (maitrī) to die due to external causes;
it is also impossible for one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or is within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) to die. These things cannot happen.
It is impossible for a Buddha or a Buddha’s mother to be harmed;
it is likewise impossible for the Wheel-Turning King’s Woman-Jewel, Elephant, Horse, Treasurer, or Military Commander to die while in the womb, or for both mother and child to perish prematurely.
That a person from Uttarakuru, a woman-jewel (strī-ratna), or the mother of a Buddha, should at the end of their life enter an evil realm in their next existence—none of these things are possible.
That conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are eternal, or that nirvāṇa is impermanent;
or that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) can sever the fetters (saṃyojana) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)—none of these things are possible.
One cultivates the Noble Path within all meditative concentrations that grasp at signs;
yet the untainted path has tainted causes.
If earth were characterized by moisture, water by solidity, fire by coldness, or wind by stability, none of these would be possible.
It is impossible that ignorance could not give rise to volitional formations, and so on, up to birth not giving rise to old age and death;
it is impossible for two minds to arise simultaneously;
and it is impossible for the group of five consciousnesses to be able to discern and grasp signs, whether with attachment or with detachment.
If the eye could give rise to bodily action (kāyakarman) or vocal action (vākkarman),
or if the eye could enter meditative concentration (dhyānasamādhi), such a thing is impossible.
It is only that the five consciousnesses (pañcavijñāna) arise in succession, without the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arising.
However, within the group of the five consciousnesses, there is the existence of a continuity;

yet it is impossible for the group of the five consciousnesses to take names as objects, to take signs as objects, or to take formless phenomena as objects; it is impossible for them to take the past or future as objects, or to take phenomena that transcend the three periods of time as objects;

furthermore, it is impossible for the group of the five consciousnesses to possess contact of increase or contact of clarity, to practice meditative concentration, to undergo wholesome or unwholesome restraints, to experience sorrow or joy, to be without vitarka and without vicāra, or to augment the faculties.
The olfactory consciousness and the gustatory consciousness possess the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta);
it is impossible for an ordinary person’s sixth consciousness to be dissociated from the notion of self.
There are immeasurable such "impossibilities" (*asthāna*).
"It is the same with 'this possibility' (sthāna).

The Buddha knows what is possible and what is impossible; he discerns and deliberates, preaching the Dharma to those who can be saved and providing the necessary conditions for those who cannot be saved—just as a skilled physician knows which illnesses are curable and which are incurable."

The knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is limited; because it is limited, they may seek to deliver those who should not be delivered, such as Śūra, or fail to deliver those who should be delivered, such as those whom Śāriputra did not deliver.

The Buddha has no such things; he cannot be defeated and cannot be surpassed because he possesses universal knowledge. This is called the "first power. Regarding the "power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma":

it refers to the actions performed by body and speech, as well as the non-actions performed in this life, the karmic effects of the precepts received, as well as evil karma, and the karma that arises day and night, which produces the karma of both sin and merit.
The Buddha briefly explains that these karmas are subsumed within three categories; this is called the characteristic of all karma.
The Buddha knows that among all sentient beings, there is karma that is past and whose retribution is also past;
there is karma that is past and whose retribution is in the present; [and so forth].
There is karma that is past, with its retribution in the future;
there is karma that is past, with its retribution in both the past and the present;
and there is karma that is past, with its retribution in both the past and the future.
There is karma that is past, whose retribution occurs in the present or the future;
there is karma that is past, whose retribution occurs in the past, the future, or the present.
The same applies to present karma.
Furthermore, within a wholesome state of mind, one experiences the retribution of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karma;
the same applies to unwholesome and indeterminate states of mind.

Furthermore, due to the causal conditions of pleasant karma, one experiences pleasant retribution; due to the causal conditions of painful karma, one experiences painful retribution; and due to the causal conditions of neither-painful-nor-pleasant karma, one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution.

Due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced in the present life, one experiences retribution in the present life; due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced upon rebirth, one experiences retribution upon rebirth; and due to the causal conditions of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, one experiences retribution in subsequent lives.

Due to the causes and conditions of impure karma, one receives retribution involving affliction; due to the causes and conditions of pure karma, one receives retribution free from affliction; and due to the causes and conditions of mixed karma, one receives mixed retribution.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of karma:
karma that must be experienced as retribution, and karma that need not necessarily be experienced as retribution.
Karmic actions that must be experienced cannot be avoided; they may be experienced by waiting for the right time, the right person, or the right place.
For example, it is as if a person is destined to share in the merit of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin):
they must wait until such a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in a favorable age before they can receive their reward; this is what is meant by "waiting for the time."
Regarding the person who receives [the retribution], that person is none other than a Cakravartin King;
regarding the place where it is received, it is the location from which a Cakravartin King emerges.

Furthermore, this is karma that must inevitably receive its retribution; it does not depend on skills or meritorious achievements, whether good or bad, but comes of its own accord without being sought.
Just as for those born in the heavens, blessings and happiness arrive of their own accord;
for those in the hells, retribution and suffering pursue them of their own accord.
They do not depend on external conditions, for these karmic actions are so profound and heavy.

Furthermore, there are karmas that must inevitably yield their retribution, such as when King Vairūḍyaka’s army killed seventy-two thousand practitioners who had attained the Way, as well as immeasurable lay followers (*upāsaka*) who observed the five precepts; even those with great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as Maudgalyāyana, were unable to save them.
For example, Bakula was cast by his stepmother into fire, boiling water, and flowing water, yet he did not die.

Likewise, when the Buddha traveled through various kingdoms, although he had left the household life to practice begging for alms and required no formal offerings of food, five hundred chariots carrying the king’s own provisions followed him; within the leaves grew non-glutinous rice, and along with the rice were a hundred flavors of soup.
Such wholesome and unwholesome karmas must necessarily be experienced;
others need not necessarily be experienced.
In the desire realm, there are three places where the retribution of karma is experienced:
There are actions resulting in pleasant feeling, actions resulting in painful feeling, and actions resulting in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
In the form realm, there are two types of locations where the retribution of action is experienced:
actions resulting in pleasant feeling and actions resulting in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
In the formless realm, there is one type of karmic retribution for feeling:
the karma of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Alternatively, regarding "depending on the object," it means that one receives the karmic retribution of feeling based upon this object.

Just as in King Puṣkarasārin’s pond, there grew a thousand-petaled golden lotus as large as a chariot wheel; because of this great assembly and its joy, many people left the household life and attained the Way.
The Buddha knows the spheres in which all sentient beings create various karmas—whether in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
within the desire realm, in which of the paths they reside;
and if in the heavenly path, in which heaven they reside.
If among humans, in which continent;
if in Jambudvīpa, in which country;
if in that country, in which city, which village, which monastery, or which territory;
If it is a city, one knows in which district, which lane, which house, and at which location it was;
and one knows at what time this karma was performed—whether in one past life, two lives, or even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of lives.
He knows how much of the retribution for these karmic actions has already been experienced and how much remains to be experienced;
how much is certain to be experienced and how much is not certain to be experienced.
He knows the objects employed for good or evil deeds—namely, weapons such as swords and staves, commands to kill, and so forth—as well as killing by one's own hand or dispatching others to kill.
All other evil karmas are likewise so;
good karmas are likewise so. One knows thus: giving, observing the precepts, and cultivating goodness.
Within giving, what is bestowed consists of lands, houses, clothing, food and drink, medicine, bedding, and the seven precious treasures.
Within the category of precepts, there are: the precept of undertaking vows, natural precepts, precepts arising from the mind, and precepts expressed through speech;
the precept of a single practice, partial precepts, majority precepts, and complete precepts;
the one-day precept, the precepts of the seven wholesome paths, the ten precepts, the full ordination precepts, and the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration.
Within the midst of wholesome merit, one cultivates the first dhyāna, the second, third, and fourth dhyānas,
as well as the minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Such are the causes and conditions of these wholesome karmas.
Whether it be stinginess and greed, anger and hatred, fear, wrong views, or evil associates—these are the various causes and conditions for unwholesome karma.
As for the causes and conditions for meritorious karma:
whether it be faith, compassion, reverence, meditative concentration, wisdom, or virtuous associates—these are the various causes and conditions for wholesome karma.

These various karmas are sovereign; among all devas and humans, there is none who can alter these characteristics of karma. Throughout hundreds of millions of kalpas, they constantly follow sentient beings without abandoning them, just as a creditor follows a debtor.
When the causes and conditions are fully assembled, they immediately yield their retribution;
it is like a seed in the earth that sprouts when the causes, conditions, and seasons harmonize.
This karma can cause sentient beings to take birth within the six realms of existence with a speed swifter than an arrow.
All sentient beings possess their respective portions of karmic retribution;
just as with the inherited wealth of parents, which all sons ought to receive their shares,
so too when the time for the fruition of this karma arrives, it cannot be obstructed, like the fire at the end of an eon.
According to the place where sentient beings are destined to be born, they are established therein, just as a great king bestows official positions upon those to whom they are suited.
At the time of a person's death, this karma comes to overshadow their mind, like a great mountain casting its shadow over objects.
This karma can produce various kinds of bodies, just as a skilled painter creates various images.
If a person acts with right conduct, it yields a favorable retribution;
if one acts with wrong conduct, it yields an unfavorable retribution.
Just as when one serves a king, one receives a reward according to the service rendered;
in this way, one should distinguish the various characteristics of karma and their retributions.
Furthermore, in the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"One who practices evil is reborn in a good realm; one who practices goodness is reborn in an evil realm.
Ānanda asked, "How can this be?"
The Buddha said:

"If an evil person’s sinful karma of the present life has not yet matured, while their wholesome karma from past lives has already matured, then by these causes and conditions, although they commit evil now, they will be reborn in a good realm."
Or, at the time of death, wholesome states of mind and mental factors may arise; by reason of these conditions, one is likewise born in a good place.

As for a person who has practiced virtue but is born in an evil place: it is because the wholesome karma of this life has not yet matured, while the unwholesome karma of past lives has already matured. By reason of these conditions, although they have performed wholesome deeds now, they are born in an evil place.
"Or at the time of death, unwholesome states of mind and mental factors arise; by reason of these conditions, one is likewise born in an evil realm.
He asked: "The meanings of 'ripe' and 'unripe' may be so; however—"
Question: How can a mind that exists for only a brief moment at the time of death overcome the power of a lifetime of practice? Answer:
Although this mind lasts for only a short duration, its mental force is fierce and sharp; like fire or poison, though small in quantity, it can accomplish great things.
Because this mind at the time of impending death is resolute and powerful, it surpasses the power of a hundred years of practice;
this final mind is called the "Great Mind" because the matter of relinquishing the body and the sense faculties is so urgent.
Just as a person who enters the ranks of battle without sparing their own body or life is called brave,
so too does an Arhat, by relinquishing attachment to this body, attain the path of Arhatship.
In this same way, one should also understand the various karmic retributions and the transformations of such retributions regarding both sins and merits.
Śrāvakas know only the retribution for the sins of evil karma and the blessings of good karma, but they cannot make such subtle distinctions;
the Buddha, however, fully and universally knows these karmas and their retributions. Because the power of his wisdom is unimpeded, inexhaustible, and indestructible, it is called the second power.

Regarding "the power of knowledge that discriminates the purity and defilement of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi": "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas. The Buddha knows these as the auxiliary dharmas for the Path, including their names and characteristics, their meanings, their sequential cultivation, whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), whether they pertain to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whether they are pure or defiled, whether they involve attachment to taste (*āsvāda*) or are free from it, and their various degrees of depth and subtlety.
Regarding the "eight liberations," they are as distinguished in the section on dhyāna.
To speak of "dhyāna" encompasses all concentrations of the form realm;
to speak of "liberation" encompasses all meditative absorptions.
The dhyāna-pāramitā is itself all liberations.
Dhyāna, samādhi, samāpatti, liberation, and dhyāna-samādhi are all termed "concentration" (samādhi); concentration is defined as the non-distraction of the mind.
"Defilement" refers to various afflictions such as craving, views, and pride;
"purity" refers to true meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), which is unmixed with afflictions such as craving, views, and pride, like genuine gold.

"Discrimination" refers to the fact that among the various meditative concentrations, there are those with single-pointed mental activity and those without; those practiced constantly and those not practiced constantly; those difficult to enter and easy to enter, and those difficult to emerge from and easy to emerge from; those involving the grasping of specific characteristics and those involving the grasping of general characteristics; and those that transform and remedy [defilements] and those that do not transform and remedy them.

Transformative treatment is as follows: for one with lustful desire, apply the mind of loving-kindness; for one who is angry, practice the meditation on impurity; for one who is deluded, contemplate the finite and the infinite;
within a mind of restlessness, use wisdom to discern all phenomena; and within a sunken mind, seek to gather the mind.
If it is not so, it is called "non-transformative treatment.
Within this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must distinguish between the proper time and the proper place:
if the body is emaciated and weak, this is not the time for practicing concentration.
For example, when a bodhisattva practices asceticism, he thinks:
"I am currently unable to give rise to meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).
Furthermore, a place with many people is not a place for practicing concentration.
Furthermore, the Buddha knows which meditative concentration leads to decline, which constitutes abiding, which leads to progress, and which leads to nirvana.

Furthermore, the Buddha knows that for certain persons, entry into concentration is difficult and emergence is difficult; entry is easy and emergence is easy; entry is easy and emergence is difficult; or entry is difficult and emergence is easy.
The Buddha knows that this person should attain such dhyāna; he knows that this person will lose their dhyāna and experience the five desires;
he knows that after experiencing the five desires, this person will regain dhyāna and, relying upon this dhyāna, attain arhatship.

All such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*), which are themselves samādhis, the Buddha fully knows through his profound wisdom; they cannot be destroyed and cannot be surpassed. This is called the "third power."
Regarding "the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings," the Buddha knows whether sentient beings possess sharp, dull, or middling faculties.
Sharp wisdom is termed "superior," while dull wisdom is termed "inferior."
By means of this power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties, the Buddha distinguishes all sentient beings as having sharp faculties, medium faculties, or dull faculties.
He knows that a person with such faculties can, in this present life, attain only the first fruit and nothing more;
or that another person can attain only the second, third, or fourth fruit.

This person can only attain the first dhyāna; this person can only attain the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; and it is the same even up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti).
This person shall realize liberation through timely application; this person shall realize liberation not through timely application.
This person shall attain preeminence among the śrāvakas;
this person shall attain preeminence among the pratyekabuddhas.
This person is fully endowed with the six pāramitās and is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having known this, [the Buddha] may bring them to deliverance through a brief exposition, or through an extensive exposition, or through both brief and extensive expositions;
he may instruct them with gentle words, or with harsh words, or with words that are both gentle and harsh.
The Buddha also discerns that this person possesses remaining faculties, and should cause them to increase the faculty of faith;
he should cause this person to produce the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
This person enters the state of certainty by means of the faculty of faith; this person enters the state of certainty by means of the faculty of wisdom.
This person possesses sharp faculties but is obstructed by the fetters and latent tendencies, such as Aṅgulimāla and others.
This person possesses sharp faculties and is not obstructed by the fetters and afflictions, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others.
There are those who possess dull faculties yet are without obstruction, such as Cūḍapanthaka;
and there are those whose faculties are dull and who are obstructed.
One knows that for this person, the faculties to be abandoned through seeing the truths are dull, while those to be abandoned through cultivation are sharp;
or that those to be abandoned through cultivation are dull, while those to be abandoned through seeing the truths are sharp.
One knows that for this person, all faculties are equally dull or equally sharp; or that for this person, all faculties are neither equally dull nor equally sharp.
This person’s prior causal power was great; this person’s present conditional power is great.
This person intended to be bound but attained liberation; this person intended to be liberated but attained bondage.
For example, Aṅgulimāla sought to kill his mother and harm the Buddha, yet he attained liberation;
whereas a certain bhikṣu who had attained the four dhyānas fell back into hell due to his overweening pride.

He knows that this person will certainly fall into the evil realms; he knows that this person will find it difficult to emerge from them, that this person will find it easy to emerge, that this person will emerge quickly, and that this person will emerge only after a long time.
Thus, he thoroughly knows the characteristics of the superior and inferior faculties of all such sentient beings; being indestructible and invincible, this is called the "fourth power."
Regarding "the power of knowing the various desires of sentient beings":
"desire" (chanda) refers to faith, preference, and inclination.
To prefer the five sensual pleasures is, for example, as in the case of Sundarananda and others.
Those who delight in fame, such as Devadatta and others;
those who delight in worldly wealth and profit, such as Sumatiśāradvatīputra and others;
and those who delight in renunciation, such as Yaśas and others.
Those who excel in faith, such as Bakula and others;
those who excel in observing the precepts, such as Rāhula and others;
and those who excel in generosity, such as Śivadatṭa (the commentary notes: [name of a donor]).
He was born of the Buddha’s paternal aunt, Amṛtā;
he delighted in dhūta practices and seclusion, like Mahākāśyapa;
and he excelled in dhyāna meditation, like Revata and others.
Those who excel in wisdom, such as Śāriputra and others;
those who excel in extensive learning, such as Ānanda and others;
and those who excel in knowing the Vinaya, such as Upāli and others.
In this way, the disciples of the Buddha each have their own preferences.
Ordinary people, likewise, each have their own inclinations:
some take pleasure in sensual desire, while others take pleasure in anger.
Furthermore, the Buddha knows that this person has much desire, much hatred, and much delusion.
Question:
What are the characteristics of having much desire, much hatred, and much delusion?
Answer: As the *Dhyāna-sūtra* explains the characteristics of the three poisons, these should be explained in detail here.

Having understood these characteristics, one who has much lust is treated by the dharma-gate of impurity; one who has much anger is treated by the dharma-gate of loving-kindness; and one who has much delusion is treated by the dharma-gate of dependent origination.
Thus, he preaches the Dharma according to what is desired: for those with wholesome desires, he teaches in accordance with their inclinations, like a boat going with the current;
for those with unwholesome desires, he instructs with words of stern admonition, like using a wedge to extract a wedge.
Within this knowledge of desire, the Buddha knows all things universally; it cannot be destroyed and it cannot be surpassed—this is called the "fifth power.
Regarding the "power of knowledge of dispositions," the Buddha knows the various distinct dispositions of the world.
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to accumulated habituation; "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) arise from nature, and "desire" (*chanda*) follows nature to produce conduct.
At times, one takes desire as nature, and by practicing desire, it becomes nature.
"Nature" is defined as the profound mind acting as the basis for affairs; "desire" is defined as arising in accordance with conditions. This is the distinction between desire and nature.
Regarding "the various diversities of the world," their respective natures and manifold natures—being immeasurable and incalculable—are called "the diversities of the world."
There are two kinds of worlds:
the world of the physical realm and the world of sentient beings.
Here, only the world of sentient beings is discussed.

The Buddha knows the nature and the inclinations of sentient beings as they are; from where they have come; whether they have accomplished roots of goodness or unwholesome roots; whether they are capable of being delivered or not; whether they are fixed or unfixed; whether they are certain or uncertain; what practices they perform; where they will be reborn; and in what stage they reside.

Furthermore, the Buddha knows the various natures and characteristics of these sentient beings; that is to say, he knows their inclinations, where they predominantly dwell, what they value, their profound mental intentions, their desires, their karma, their conduct, their afflictions, their rites, their concentrations, their deportment, their knowledge, their views, and their conceptualizations and discriminations;
as well as how many fetters have arisen and how many fetters have not yet arisen.

Following that which one is attached to, desire arises; following desire, the mind becomes defiled; following the defiled mind, one pursues [objects]; following what is pursued, one values it; following what is valued, one constantly engages in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); following applied and sustained thought, there is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); following conceptual proliferation, there is constant mindfulness (*manasikāra*); following mindfulness, one initiates activity; following the initiation of activity, one performs karma; and following the performance of karma, there is its fruit and retribution.
Furthermore, by means of this power of knowledge regarding the various dispositions (*nānādhātujñānabala*), the Buddha knows which sentient beings can be delivered and which cannot;
which can be delivered in this life and which in a future life;
and which can be delivered immediately and which at another time.
These are those who can be delivered in the present; these are those who cannot be seen by the eye as being deliverable;
this person can be delivered by a Buddha; this person can be delivered by a Śrāvaka;
this person can be delivered by both; this person is certainly deliverable; this person is certainly not deliverable.
This person can be delivered through brief exposition; this person can be delivered through extensive exposition; this person can be delivered through both brief and extensive exposition.
This person can be delivered through praise; this person can be delivered through subduing.
This person can be delivered by being welcomed; this person can be delivered by being abandoned.
This person can be delivered through subtle dharmas; this person can be delivered through coarse dharmas;
this person can be delivered through harsh words; this person can be delivered through gentle speech; this person can be delivered through both the harsh and the gentle.
This is wrong view; this is right view;
this is attachment to the past; this is attachment to the future;
this is attachment to annihilationism; this is attachment to eternalism.
This is attachment to the view of existence; this is attachment to the view of non-existence;
this is the desire for birth; this is the aversion to birth;
this is the seeking of wealth, honor, and pleasure; this is the clinging to profound false views.
This speaks of the absence of causes and conditions; this speaks of false causes and conditions; this speaks of true causes and conditions.
This speaks of the absence of karmic action; this speaks of false karmic action; this speaks of true karmic action.
This speaks of the absence of seeking; this speaks of false seeking; this speaks of true seeking.
This honors the self; this honors the five desires; this honors the acquisition of gain; this honors food and drink; this honors talk of amusements and pleasures;
this delights in crowds; this delights in clamor;
this delights in seclusion; this practices much craving; and this practices many views.
This is good faith; this is good wisdom.
This should be guarded; this should be relinquished.
This is the value of upholding the precepts; this is the value of meditative concentration; this is the value of wisdom.
This is easily awakened to; this is awakened to through exposition;
this is capable of being guided; this is understood word by word;
this is of sharp faculties, this is of dull faculties, and this is of middling faculties.
This is easy to emerge from and easy to extract; this is difficult to emerge from and difficult to extract;
this fears transgression, while this is a grave transgression;
this fears birth and death, while this does not fear birth and death.
This is much desire, this is much hatred, this is much delusion;
this is much desire and hatred, this is much desire and delusion, this is much hatred and delusion, this is much desire, hatred, and delusion;
this is thin affliction, this is thick affliction.
This is little defilement; this is much defilement;
this is wisdom that is obscured; this is wisdom that is like a garment or a basket; this is extensive wisdom;

this person well knows the characteristics of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, what is possible and what is impossible, and suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
He skillfully knows entering meditative concentration, emerging from it, and abiding within it.
Furthermore, the Buddha knows:
these are sentient beings of the desire realm; these are sentient beings of the form realm; and these are sentient beings of the formless realm.
These are the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas;
these are those born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation;
these are those with form and those without form.
This is with perception; this is without perception;
this is short-lived; this is long-lived;

this is an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned desire; this is an ordinary person who has abandoned the desires of the lower stages but has not yet abandoned the desires of the dhyānas; and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"This is the path," "this is the attainment of the fruit";
"this is the pratyekabuddha," "this is the unimpeded liberation of the Buddhas.
Such are the various distinctions [made].

The five destinies, the four modes of birth, the three groups, provisional names, hindrances, the aggregates, bases, and elements; roots of goodness and unwholesome roots; all fetters and latent tendencies; the stages, karmic fruits, those who can be delivered and those who cannot be delivered; and the analytical discernment of cessation and wisdom.
By means of such distinctions, he knows the various different natures of the world and attains unimpeded liberation.
The Buddha thoroughly and universally knows all such various differences; it cannot be destroyed and nothing can surpass it—this is called the "sixth power."
Regarding "the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations," some say that karma itself is the path.
Why is this so? Because of the causal conditions of karma, one wanders through all five realms of existence.
There is karma that can sever [the cycle], and there is karma that leads to a destination, namely, the three factors of the noble path and untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*).
For this reason, all karmas are the paths leading to all destinations.
Furthermore, some say: there are five distinct five-knowledge samādhis (the *Dan* commentary states: ...).
One dwells in the five factors of the untainted samādhi-dhyāna, accomplishing beneficial deeds in all places.
Furthermore, some say that it is precisely the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this? Because the fourth dhyāna is the destination for all meditative concentrations.
As it is said in various sūtras:
This wholesome mind, concentrated mind, undistracted mind, and collected mind all enter into the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, some say:
the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is itself the path leading to the destination; it is the root of the benefit of all paths.
Furthermore, some say:
"All noble paths (āryamārga) are [the means]; by employing these noble paths, one attains benefits according to one's wishes.
Other proponents further say:
Regarding all wholesome paths, all unwholesome paths, and all noble paths, he knows individually the destination reached by each path,
as explained in the *Loma-harṣaṇīya Sūtra*.
The Buddha knows all things universally; he cannot be defeated or surpassed—this is called the seventh power.
Regarding the "power of knowledge of past lives," there are three types of past lives:
those involving supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those involving clear vision (*vidyā*), and those involving power (*bala*).

Ordinary persons possess only supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); Śrāvakas possess both supernormal powers and clear knowledges (*vidyā*); Buddhas possess supernormal powers, clear knowledges, and powers (*bala*). Why is this so?
Ordinary persons only know the events of their past lives, but they do not understand the continuous succession of karmic causes and conditions;
for this reason, ordinary persons possess only supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) but lack true insight (*vidyā*).
Because śrāvakas understand the truth of origination (samudaya-satya), they clearly comprehend how karmic causes and conditions continue in succession;
for this reason, śrāvakas also possess supernormal powers (abhijñā) and clear knowledges (vidyā).

If a disciple of the Buddha, while still an ordinary person, attains the knowledge of past lives and, upon entering the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), understands the causes and conditions of origination, then because they have attained the eighth untainted mind (anāsravacitta) and severed [wrong] views, this supernormal power transforms into clear insight (vidyā).
Why is this so? "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) is defined as the root of vision.

If a disciple of the Buddha first attains the Noble Path and subsequently the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) arises, it also comes to be termed "knowledge" because it has been transformed through the power of the causal conditions of origination (*samudaya*).
Question:

If the Buddha, when he was originally a bodhisattva, first attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) because he had already abandoned the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) before entering the noble path (*āryamārga*), why did the Buddha say, "In the first watch of the night, I attained the first clear vision"?
The answer is:
That time was not [a time of] clear realization. If the Buddha were among the assembly, he would say, "At that time, I attained this clear realization," thereby demonstrating it to the multitude.
This was attained at the beginning of the first watch of the night.
It is like a king who, before he became king, had a son; later, when he has become king, people ask:
"When was the prince born?"
He replied, "The prince was born at such-and-such a time.
Although he had not yet become king at the time of his birth, because he is now the king, he is referred to as "the prince" by virtue of that past status. Thus it is said:
"The Prince was born at that time.
The Buddha is likewise; when the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) arose, it was not yet "clarity" (*vidyā*), but was merely called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*);
later, during the final watch of the night, because he understood the causal conditions of origination (*samudaya-pratyaya*), that supernormal power was transformed into clarity.
Later, while among the assembly, he said:
"In the first watch of the night, I attained this illumination.
Someone asked:
The meaning of "penetration" (*abhijñā*) and "clairvoyance" (*vidyā*) is as explained above. What, then, constitutes "power" (*bala*)?
The answer is:

the Buddha employs this clairvoyance to know his own body and that of sentient beings throughout immeasurable and boundless eons—the various karmic conditions and experiences of past lives—knowing them all completely and universally; this is "power."
This is called the "eighth power.
Regarding the "power of knowledge regarding birth and death," the Buddha employs his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to see the places where sentient beings undergo birth and death.
When ordinary persons employ this divine eye, they can at most see the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Śrāvakas can, at most, see a small chiliocosm by looking sideways, and they also see it completely above and below.
Question:
The Great Brahmā King is also able to see a thousand worlds; what is the difference between them?
The answer is:
When the Great Brahmā King stands in the center of a thousandfold world system, he sees everywhere;
if he stands at the periphery, he does not see other places.
The śrāvakas are not like this; wherever they dwell, they constantly see a thousand worlds.
The pratyekabuddhas see a hundred thousand worlds, and the Buddhas see immeasurable and boundless worlds.

The knowledge of the divine eye possessed by ordinary persons is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*) but not a clear vision (*vidyā*); it is likewise [limited], for they see only the phenomena themselves, but cannot see how one is born according to the causes and conditions of karma, as explained in the section on past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*).

Furthermore, Aniruddha, who is the foremost among those who have attained the divine eye, possesses a divine eye that is pure over half his head, consisting of derived matter from the four great elements of the form realm.
The Buddha’s divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is composed of the four great elements and pervasive matter (*rūpa*), and is pure throughout the head;
this constitutes the distinction.
Furthermore, when a śrāvaka dwells in samādhi and attains the divine eye, he is able to see within that very samādhi in which he dwells.
There is the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra, and the samādhi without vitarka or vicāra.
The Buddha dwells within whichever samādhi he enters; whatever he wishes to see, he sees completely.

If he attains the divine eye while relying on the samādhi without vitarka or vicāra, he is likewise able to see when entering the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, or the samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra.
Furthermore, when a śrāvaka uses this divine eye to see, while remaining in his current samādhi, his mind enters another samādhi and the divine eye then ceases.
The Buddha is not like this; although his mind may enter other samādhis, his divine eye does not cease.
This wisdom universally knows the destinies of birth and death for all sentient beings; it cannot be destroyed and nothing can surpass it—this is called the "ninth power."
Regarding the "power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*):
A question is asked:

While there are distinctions in the analytical wisdom of the [other] nine powers, the exhaustion of outflows is the same for all; what, then, is the difference between all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?
Answer: Although the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is the same, there is a great difference in the discernment of wisdom.

Even for a Śrāvaka of the greatest power, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through contemplation are severed during three stages: the stage of arising, the stage of abiding, and the stage of cessation.
The Buddha is not like this; he completely severs the fetters at the very moment of their arising.

For a śrāvaka, the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) are severed at the time they arise, while those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are extinguished over three moments;
for the Buddha, however, there is no distinction between what is abandoned through the vision of the truths and what is abandoned through cultivation.
When a śrāvaka first enters the noble path, the moment of entry differs from the moment of attainment;

for the Buddha, however, he both enters and attains within a single moment of mind. Within that single moment of mind, he realizes all-knowledge, destroys all hindrances, and attains all Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, the śrāvakas possess two kinds of liberation:
liberation from afflictions (*kleśa*) and liberation from the cognitive obstructions to phenomena (*dharmāvaraṇa*).
The Buddha possesses both complete liberation from all afflictions and complete liberation from all cognitive obstructions to phenomena.
The Buddha naturally attains wisdom, whereas the śrāvakas attain it by practicing according to the path of instruction.
Furthermore, some say:
if the Buddha uses his wisdom to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings, that wisdom neither becomes dull nor diminishes.
For example, if a red-hot iron ball is placed upon a small amount of cotton, it burns the cotton yet the heat and power of the fire do not diminish;
the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise, for while it consumes all afflictions, the power of his wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, śrāvakas only know the exhaustion of their own outflows;
the Buddhas, however, know the exhaustion of their own outflows and also know the exhaustion of the outflows of others, as it is said in the *Śuddha-sūtra*.

Furthermore, the Buddha alone knows that within the minds of sentient beings there are ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) and one hundred and ninety-six entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); apart from the Buddha, there is no one who knows this.

The Buddha alone knows that within the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*), such fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*) are severed; this is likewise true up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñāna*).
It is also the same regarding the nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The Buddha fully and universally knows all such matters concerning sentient beings;
if śrāvakas know or speak even a little, it is entirely in accordance with the Buddha’s words.
Such power and majesty of the Buddha’s wisdom that has exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) cannot be destroyed or surpassed; this is called the "tenth power."
Question:
Among these ten powers, which one is the most supreme? Answer:
Each [of these powers] is great within its own respective domain; just as water is capable of soaking and fire is capable of burning, each possesses its own specific efficacy.
Some say that the first power is the greatest, because it can encompass all ten powers.
Some say:
"The power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) is great, because the task is accomplished and nirvāṇa is attained.
The proponent says:
These ten powers all have unimpeded liberation as their root and unimpeded liberation as their sovereign condition.
Question:
If these ten powers are exclusively the deeds of a Buddha, such that no disciple in this world can attain them, for what reason does the Buddha speak of them?
Answer: It is to sever the doubts regarding the ten powers of a person; to cause those without wisdom to attain firm resolve in their minds; and to make the fourfold assembly rejoice by saying:
"Our Great Teacher alone possesses such power, which is not shared with any sentient beings."
Furthermore, various non-Buddhist practitioners say:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama dwells constantly in secluded places, and his wisdom has shriveled away.
For this reason, he utters these words of utmost sincerity:
“I am fully established and endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four fearlessnesses;
amidst the great assembly, I proclaim perfect wisdom and transform sentient beings with a lion’s roar, turning the Brahma-wheel, which no outsider, god, or human in the world is able to turn.”
To stop such slander, these ten powers (daśabala) are taught.
A question is asked:

According to the dharma of a virtuous person, one should not praise oneself even regarding a single matter of wisdom; how much less so for one who is selfless (anātman) and free from attachment (asaṅga) to praise himself for the ten powers?
As it is said:
"Self-praise and self-deprecation, praising others and deprecating others—
these four kinds of conduct the wise do not engage in!"
He replied:

"Although the Buddha is without self and without attachment, he possesses immeasurable power. It is solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings through great compassion that he speaks of the ten powers; it is not for the purpose of self-praise."
It is, for example, like a skilled merchant leader who sees various wicked bandits deceiving the merchants by showing them the wrong path;
out of compassion, the leader says to the merchants:
"I am one who speaks the truth; do not follow those who deceive you!"
Furthermore, just as when various quack physicians deceive sick people, a skilled physician takes pity on them and says to those afflicted with illness:
"I have excellent medicine that can eliminate your ailments; do not believe those who deceive you and bring suffering upon yourselves!"
Furthermore, the Buddha’s merits are profound and far-reaching; if the Buddha did not speak of them himself, no one would know of them.
By speaking of them briefly for the sake of sentient beings, the benefit is exceedingly great.
For this reason, the Buddha himself spoke of these ten powers (*daśabala*).
Furthermore, for those who are capable of being delivered, he must necessarily teach them; within that which is to be taught, the ten powers should be taught in their proper sequence.
If he were not to speak of them, they would not attain deliverance; therefore, he speaks of them himself.
For example, when the sun and moon rise, they do not form the thought:
"I shall illuminate the world, and thus I shall have a name!
Yet once the sun and moon have risen, they naturally possess names.
The Buddha is also like this: he does not think of proclaiming his own merits for the sake of having a reputation.
The Buddha’s pure speech preaches the Dharma, and its radiance shatters the ignorance and darkness of sentient beings; thus, he naturally possesses great renown.
For this reason, when the Buddha himself speaks of the ten powers (*daśabala*) and other such merits, there is no error.
"Power" (*bala*) means being able to accomplish something:
by employing these ten kinds of power to augment wisdom, one is able to defeat opponents in debate.
Because they augment their wisdom by means of these ten powers, they are able to preach the Dharma skillfully;
because they augment their wisdom by means of these ten powers, they are able to subdue those who are disobedient;
because they augment their wisdom by means of these ten powers, they attain mastery over all dharmas, just as a great sovereign attains mastery among his ministers and subjects.
This is the brief explanation of the meaning of the ten powers (*daśabala*) according to the Śrāvaka-dharma.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 24;
Explanation of the Meaning of the Four Fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) within the First Chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Volume Forty. Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. 40. The Meaning of the Four Fearlessnesses. Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*):
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge.
If there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or any deva, or Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else, who should speak according to reality, saying:"
"I do not know this Dharma," and so forth, until "I do not see even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security; I have attained fearlessness and dwell securely in the station of the Noble Lord, like a bull-king. Amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
No śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, Brahmās, or any other beings can truly turn it back;
this is the first fearlessness.
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I have exhausted all outflows (āsrava).
Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else speak truthfully thus:"
"These outflows are not yet exhausted," and so on, until he does not perceive even the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide securely in the station of the Holy Lord like a bull-king; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
No śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings can truly turn back [this wheel].
This is the second fearlessness.
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"I have taught the obstructing dharmas.
Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else speak truthfully, saying:"
"Even if one were to say, 'These dharmas that are obstacles do not obstruct the Path,' I do not perceive even the slightest sign of fear therein.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide securely in the station of the Holy Lord like a bull-king; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion's roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel."
Whether they be śramaṇas or brahmins, devas, māras, brahmās, or any other beings, none can truly turn back [this wheel].
This is the third fearlessness.
The Buddha made this solemn declaration:
"Regarding the Noble Path I have taught, which is able to transcend the world—if one follows this path, one can bring all suffering to an end.
Should there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or gods, or Māras, or Brahmās, or any other beings who could truthfully say:"
"Practicing this path, one cannot transcend the world nor can one bring an end to suffering"—even down to not perceiving the slightest sign of fear.

For this reason, I have attained peace and security, I have attained fearlessness, and I abide securely in the station of the Noble Lord, like a bull-king; amidst the great assembly, I roar the lion’s roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
No śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, brahmās, or any other beings can truly overturn these four fearlessnesses.
Question: For what reason are the "four fearlessnesses" (catvāri vaiśāradyāni) taught? Answer:
Some say: "The Buddha claims for himself all-knowledge and all-seeing;

yet the world's scriptures, arts, skills, and expedient means are exceedingly numerous and immeasurable. If it were difficult even for all sentient beings together to know all things, how much more so for the Buddha alone to possess all-knowledge!"
"There may be such matters and such difficulties; will the Buddha not have fear?
Desiring to sever this doubt and delusion, and to resolve these difficulties, the Buddha taught the four kinds of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
Furthermore, before the Buddha appeared in the world, various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) used diverse causes and conditions to deceive those seeking the Way or seeking merit.

Some ate various kinds of fruits; some ate various kinds of vegetables; some ate various kinds of grass roots; some ate cow dung; some ate only wild millet once a day; some ate once every two days, or once every ten days, a month, or two months; some sucked wind or drank water; some ate algae; they practiced such various diets as these.
As for clothing, they wore tree bark, leaves, grass garments, or deer skins, or they wore wooden planks.
Some lie on the bare ground; some lie upon pestles, branches, ashes, or thorns;
some enter the water during the cold season, or roast themselves with the five fires during the heat;
some die by entering the water, some die by entering the fire, some die by throwing themselves from cliffs, and some die by abstaining from food.
Within such various methods of ascetic practice, they seek rebirth in the heavens and seek nirvana, and they also instruct their disciples not to abandon these dharmas;
in this way, they attract sentient beings of little wisdom so as to obtain offerings.
For example, when the sun has not yet risen, a firefly can shed a small amount of light;
but once the sun rises, its thousand rays of brilliance shine forth, such that the moon and all the stars lose their luster—how much more so the firefly?
If a Buddha has not appeared in the world, the various non-Buddhist teachers illuminate the world with their minor lights and receive offerings;
when a Buddha appears in the world, he extinguishes those non-Buddhists and their disciples with the light of his great wisdom, so that they no longer receive offerings.
Because they lost the benefit of offerings, they spoke falsely to slander the Buddha and his disciples.
As stated in the *Sundarī-sūtra*, he killed Sundarī and slandered the Buddha, saying to the multitude:
"Even the base people of the world would not do such a thing; this man does not even know the worldly rules of propriety, let alone Nirvāṇa!"
Because the Buddha wished to extinguish such slanders, he himself proclaimed his actual merits and the four fearlessnesses, saying:
"I alone am the omniscient one; there is no one who can truthfully say, 'The Buddha does not know,' and I have no fear regarding this matter."
I alone have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*); no one can truthfully say, "The Buddha’s outflows are not yet exhausted," and I am not afraid of this matter.
Regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path to *nirvāṇa*, I have taught them; no one can truthfully say, "These dharmas cannot obstruct *nirvāṇa*," and the Buddha is not afraid of this matter.
The Buddha has taught that the path to the exhaustion of suffering leads to Nirvana; no one can truthfully say, "This path cannot reach Nirvana," and the Buddha does not fear this matter.
Briefly stated, the essence of these four fearlessnesses is as follows:

first, the correct knowledge of all phenomena; second, the exhaustion of all outflows along with their residual tendencies; third, the teaching of all factors that obstruct the path; and fourth, the teaching of the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering.
Among these four dharmas, if someone were to speak truthfully, saying, "I am unable to fully and universally know them," the Buddha would not fear this.
Why? Because he has perfectly and completely realized them.
The first two fearlessnesses are for the sake of being fully endowed with one's own merits;
the latter two fearlessnesses are for the sake of being fully endowed with the benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, within the first, third, and fourth fearlessnesses, wisdom (*jñāna*) is taught; within the second fearlessness, abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is taught.
Because he is fully endowed with wisdom and abandonment, his task is accomplished.
Question: The ten powers are all called wisdom, and the four fearlessnesses are also wisdom; what is the difference between them?
The answer is:
To explain the various merits of the Buddha in detail is "power" (*bala*); to explain them concisely is "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Furthermore, that which is capable of performing an action is power; that which is free from doubt and difficulty is fearlessness.
It is called "power" because wisdom is gathered; it is called "fearlessness" because all ignorance is dispelled.
It is called "power" because all wholesome dharmas are accumulated; it is called "fearlessness" because all unwholesome dharmas are extinguished.
Because one possesses intrinsic wisdom, it is called "power" (*bala*); because nothing can destroy it, it is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
Wisdom that is fierce and robust is power; being capable of withstanding questioning and debate is fearlessness.
The gathering of all wisdom is called "power" (*bala*); the outward application of this wisdom is "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).
For example, it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin-rāja*) who achieves the seven treasures;
having obtained these seven treasures, he travels throughout the four continents and there is nothing he does not subdue—this is called fearlessness.

Furthermore, just as a skilled physician who thoroughly knows medicinal formulas is said to possess power, and his compounding of various medicines and administering them to others is said to be fearlessness;
so too, benefiting oneself is called power, while benefiting others is called fearlessness.
To eliminate one's own afflictions is called power; to eliminate the afflictions of others is fearlessness.
To be incapable of being thwarted or destroyed is called power; to be neither daunted nor to retreat is fearlessness.
To spontaneously accomplish one's own virtue is called power; to be able to accomplish the virtue of others is fearlessness.
Skillful means wisdom is called power; the application of skillful wisdom is fearlessness.
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are called powers; the manifestation of all-knowledge and knowledge of all modes is fearlessness.
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) are called powers; the external manifestation of the eighteen unique qualities is fearlessness.
Thoroughly penetrating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called power;
if there are various challenges and interrogations, being able to answer them immediately without further deliberation is fearlessness.
Attaining the Buddha-eye is called power.
Having seen with the Buddha-eye, to preach the Dharma for those who can be liberated is fearlessness.
Attaining the three types of unimpeded knowledge is called power; attaining the unimpeded analytical eloquence is fearlessness.
Unimpeded knowledge is called power; the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence is fearlessness.
Mastery over all-knowledge is called power; the teaching of the Dharma adorned with various parables, various causes and conditions, and refined language is fearlessness.
Vanquishing the hosts of Māra is called power; vanquishing the various non-Buddhist teachers of debate is fearlessness.
Through such various causes and conditions, one distinguishes between power and fearlessness.
Question: What is meant by "fearlessness" (vaiśāradya)? Answer:

To attain freedom from doubt and without hesitation or difficulty, with wisdom that neither retreats nor sinks, and without one's hair standing on end, to act exactly as taught within every teaching—this is fearlessness.
Question:
How should one know that the Buddha possesses the fearlessnesses? Answer:
If one were possessed of fear, one would be unable to lead and govern a great assembly.
[The Buddha] can both restrain and release, and can either discipline with harsh severity or instruct with gentle words.
For example, at one time the Buddha dismissed Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, yet subsequently received them back with a heart of compassion.

If there are those who harbor suspicions or objections, these various masters of debate dwell upon the mountain peaks of arrogance; their minds are crazily intoxicated by external wisdom, and they all claim that in the world there is only they alone and no others.
Because they possess definitive knowledge of their own scriptures, they refute the scriptures and arguments of others, slandering them with harsh words like mad elephants that know no restraint.
Such madmen as the great masters of debate— Aṃbaṭṭha, Dīrghanakha, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, Kūṭadanta, and others— all have been subdued;
had there been anything to fear, this would not have been possible.

Furthermore, the five renunciants including Kauṇḍinya; the thousand matted-hair sages including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and others who had gone forth within the Buddha-dharma;
as well as hundreds of thousands of sons of the Śākyas;
and all the great kings of Jambudvīpa—such as King Prasenajit, King Bimbisāra, King Caṇḍapradyota, King Udayana, King Puṣkarasārin, and King Brahmadatta—all became his disciples.
All the lay brahmins possessed wisdom that transcended the entire world and were revered as teachers by great kings;
Brahmayu, Pokkharasāti, Kūṭadanta, and others all became his disciples.
There were those who attained the first path, and those who attained the second, third, and fourth paths.
There were also various great spirits,
such as the Āravakas and Vaiśvakas, and various great nāga kings.
Aparā, Elapattra, and others, as well as the wicked ones such as Aṅgulimāla, have all been subdued and brought to submission.
If one were possessed by fear, one would not be able to sit alone upon the lion throne beneath the tree.

When he was about to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the hosts of Māra’s army manifested themselves with the heads of lions, tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears; some had but one eye, others many eyes; some had but one ear, others many ears; they carried mountains and spat fire, surrounding him on all four sides.
The Buddha pressed the earth with his finger, and in the space of a single blink, they were all completely extinguished.
The devas, asuras, vaimacitris, Śakradevānām-indra, Brahmā-devaputra, and others had their minds guided so that they all became his disciples.
If one were possessed of fear, one would be unable to preach the Dharma within this great assembly;
because one is without fear, one is able to preach the Dharma for such a great multitude of devas and spirits, and is therefore called "fearless."

Furthermore, because the Buddha is the most honored and supreme among all sentient beings, having reached the further shore of all dharmas and attained great renown, he himself declares that he possesses no fear.
Furthermore, let alone these merits of the Buddha;
even among all the merits of the entire world, none can equal his, for he has already uprooted all phenomena that cause fear.
The things that cause fear are: birth into a lowly family, birth in a base place, an ugly appearance, lack of dignified deportment, coarse and evil speech, and so forth.

Regarding "birth into a lowly family," this refers to those such as the Śūdras—namely, those who carry out the dead, remove filth, raise chickens and pigs, hunt, slaughter, sell liquor, or serve in the military—these being base and humble families. If one belongs to such a family, one will experience much fear when in the midst of a great assembly.

From the very beginning, the Buddha has always been born into the lineage of Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*), such as King Mūrdhaja, King Śaṅkha, King Sagara, and King Mahādeva; having been born into such families of the Solar Dynasty, he likewise possesses nothing to fear.

As for the places where such debasement arises, they include the lands of Andhra, Śavara, and the naked nations; Tukhāra and the Lesser Yuezhi; Śūli, Anxi (Parthia), and the land of Daqin (Rome), and so forth.
Those born in these borderlands, when amidst a great assembly, experience much fear;
because the Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, the Middle Country, he has no such fear.
Regarding "ugly appearance": there are those whose physical form is withered, parched, and emaciated, whom people do not wish to behold;
even when among a great assembly, they feel fear.
The Buddha’s golden light is radiant and moist, like a fire illuminating a mountain of red gold; because he possesses such a form, he has nothing to fear.
Regarding those lacking dignified deportment: in their advancing, halting, walking, sitting, or rising, they lack human decorum and thus experience fear.
The Buddha has no such thing. Regarding coarse and evil speech:
some have harsh voices, stammering, or redundant speech that lacks order and is disliked by others; such people experience much fear. The Buddha has none of these things.
The Buddha has no such fear. Why is this?

The Buddha’s speech is true and real, gentle and supple, sequential and easy to understand; it is neither hurried nor slow, neither too brief nor too prolix, neither submerged in obscurity nor defiled by impurity, and it is free from frivolity. It surpasses the voice of the kalaviṅka bird;
its words and meanings are clear and distinct, and it does not cause harm to living beings.

Because it is free from desire, it is untainted; because it extinguishes hatred, it is unobstructed; because it removes delusion, it is easy to understand; because the joy of the Dharma increases, it is delightful; and because it precludes transgressions, it is secure.

It conforms to the minds of others and conforms to liberation; its meaning is profound and its words are sublime. Because it possesses causal conditions, its speech is reasoned; because it employs analogies, it provides excellent elucidation; because it brings matters to completion, it skillfully accords with reality.
It speaks in diverse ways because it contemplates the various minds of sentient beings; yet it is of a single flavor because, in the long run, all enter nirvana.
Because he possesses such various and immeasurable ornaments of speech, the Buddha has no fear regarding speech.
Since the Buddha has no fear even with respect to such mundane dharmas as these, how much less so for supramundane dharmas!
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha possesses four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Question:
Are these fearlessnesses included among the Buddha’s ten powers (*bala*)?
If there were fearlessnesses, they should not be said to be only four;
if there were fear, how could it be said that fearlessness is accomplished?
The answer is:
A single wisdom abides in ten locations, which is called the Buddha’s accomplishment of the ten powers (*daśabala*);
it is like one person who knows ten matters and receives a name according to each matter.
These ten powers function through four locations, which constitute the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

The power regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*) and the power regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*) constitute the first and second fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*);
although eight powers are extensively taught, these [two] correspond to the third and fourth fearlessnesses.
For this reason, although fearlessness is included within the ten powers (*daśabala*), there is no fault in explaining them separately.

As for "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*): it means knowing all phenomena without inversion, correctly and not erroneously, just as all other past Buddhas did; this is called *Samyaksaṃbuddha*.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because that which cannot be known by any in the world, whether gods or humans, the Buddha knows universally; therefore, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha."
If someone were to say,
"This dharma is not known," one asks:
Who is this person?
The answer is:
herein the Buddha says:
“If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or gods, or Māras, or Brahmās— even those who wish to debate with the Buddha”—
what dharma do they debate?
Some say: "The Buddha did not speak of the various external scriptures, such as the eighteen kinds of great treatises including the Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, and Veda."
Some say: "The weight of Mount Sumeru, the depth of the great earth, and the total number of all grasses and trees. Others say:
"The fourteen difficult questions—whether the world is eternal or non-eternal, finite or infinite—the Buddha was unable to answer. Some say:
"These dharmas include material dharmas and immaterial dharmas, visible and invisible, resistant and non-resistant, with outflows and without outflows, conditioned and unconditioned, and so forth;"
"The Buddha knows only the causes and conditions of one kind of path; as for the various causes and conditions of these diverse dharmas, the Buddha may not know them all.
"Śramaṇa" refers to those who have left the household life;
"Brāhmaṇa" refers to wise people who remain at home.
"Devas" refers to the terrestrial devas and the celestial devas;
"Māras" refers to the devas of the six heavens of the desire realm;
and "Brahmās" refers to those headed by Brahmā-devaputra, as well as all those in the form realm.
"Others" refers to persons other than these.
"According to reality" means either by means of actual facts or by means of logical reasoning based on causes and conditions.
"Not seeing even the slightest sign of fear" — here, "sign" (nimitta) refers to causes and conditions.

I do not see even the slightest cause or condition that could rightfully come to destroy me; because I see none, I speak with utmost sincerity, saying: "It is established as the dwelling place of the *āriya*—in the language of Qin, 'Noble Lord'."
The Buddha spoke these words of utmost sincerity: "I have exhausted all outflows.
If anyone were to say, "These outflows are not exhausted," he would have no fear.
What are the outflows?
"Outflows" refers to the three outflows:
the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance.
Furthermore, "outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) associated with a defiled mind that arise from within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Furthermore, as explained in detail in the *Sarvāsravāvaraṇa-sūtra*, there are seven outflows.
The dharmas that obstruct the Path refer to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma, as well as all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the karmic retribution of the evil realms;
furthermore, they include giving, observing precepts, practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, and attaining various mundane meditative absorptions for the sake of worldly ends.
In brief, whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, any dharma that can obstruct *nirvāṇa* is called a dharma that obstructs the Path.
Some say: "The Way is named by two dharmas:
noble concentration and noble wisdom."
"These two matters are equal, leading to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Some say: "There are three aggregates of the path:"
"Untainted morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Some say: "The four dharmas refer to the Four Noble Truths."
Some say: "The five supramundane faculties. Others say:
"The nature of the six perfections. Some say:
"The seven factors of enlightenment."
Some say: "The Eightfold Noble Path leads to Nirvana.
The masters of debate and others say:
"All untainted paths lead to Nirvana.
If any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others were to come and speak truthfully regarding this, saying:
"This is not so," [it would be as follows].
"Furthermore, he does not perceive even the slightest sign of fear;
because he perceives none, he speaks with sincerity:
'I am established in the dwelling place of the noble ones (ārya). "
Question: For what reason does the Buddha speak with such sincerity, saying, "He establishes the dwelling place of the noble ones (ārya)? Answer:
Having oneself fulfilled in merit, one also causes sentient beings to obtain peace, happiness, and benefit.
If a Buddha were to dwell in a state of personal peace and happiness but could not benefit sentient beings, it would not be called an "āriya dwelling.
If one were to benefit only sentient beings but did not fulfill merit oneself, that too would not be called an "āriya dwelling."
Since he himself possesses merit and also benefits sentient beings, for this reason he speaks with utmost sincerity:
"I establish the dwelling place of the *ārya*.

Furthermore, the Buddha himself extinguishes evil and also extinguishes the evil of sentient beings; because he extinguishes these two kinds of evil, he is supremely pure. Because he excellently expounds the Dharma, he establishes the dwelling place of the *ārya*.
Furthermore, because the Four Noble Truths—through their three turnings and twelve aspects—are able to turn, discern, reveal, and expound them, he spoke these words of sincerity:
"I have established the dwelling place of the noble ones."
Furthermore, because it can eliminate all doubt, regret, and false views, and because it can fully explain all profound questions and challenges, it is called the "Abode of the Ariyas.
"Ariya" means foremost, supreme, most exalted, non-retrogressive, non-repulsed, non-submerged, endowed with merit, and without deficiency; this is called the "Abode of the Ariyas."
By the power of such causes, conditions, and merits, he spoke these words of sincerity:
"I establish the dwelling place of the Arihas.
As for the phrase "lion’s roar among the assembly," "assembly" refers to the eightfold assembly:

The assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of devas, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmās.
Sentient beings aspire for wisdom regarding these eight assemblies; therefore, the sūtra mentions only these eight assemblies.
Within this context, the Buddha’s lion’s roar is also present among all assemblies;
for this reason, the sūtra states, "if there are any other assemblies."
Why is this? Those who hear the Buddha’s voice are all members of the assembly.
Furthermore, some say:
"The Buddha preaches the Dharma in private and secluded places.
For this reason, he speaks these words of utmost sincerity in the midst of the assembly:
"I possess the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses."
This is called the lion’s roar amidst the assembly.
Furthermore, the Buddha showed me this word of ultimate truth:
"I am the teacher of all the world; I am the omniscient one."
"Let all those who have doubts or lack faith come forth; I shall explain it for them.
For this reason, it is called the "Lion’s Roar among the Assembly. As for the "Lion’s Roar," it is like the lion king:
