born of a pure lineage, dwelling in deep mountains and great valleys, with square jaws and large bones, his body and flesh full and robust, his head large and eyes long, radiant and clear, his brows high and broad, his fangs sharp, white, and clean, his mouth and nose square and large, thick, solid, firm, and full, his teeth dense, even, and sharp, his tongue protruding red and white, his pair of ears high-set, his mane glossy, his upper body vast, his skin and flesh firm and well-adhered, his spine long and waist slender, his belly unprotruding, his tail long and claws sharp, his feet firmly planted, possessing a massive body and great strength.
Emerging from his dwelling, he arches his back and stretches, strikes the ground with his mouth, and manifests great majestic power;
by not eating past the proper time, he displays the signs of early morning;
he demonstrates the strength of a lion king to intimidate the deer, bear, brown bear, tiger, leopard, wild boar, and their like.
Awakening those who have long slept, subduing those who are haughty, powerful, and influential, he opens his own path and lets out a great roar.
When he roars thus, those who hear it are either filled with joy or struck with fear;

those dwelling in caves shrink back in concealment, those living in the water dive deep, and those hidden in the mountains crouch in hiding. The elephants in the stables shake their chains and break loose in wild flight, while birds in the sky take flight high and vanish into the distance.

The Buddha, the lion, is likewise: born from the six *pāramitās* and the ancient four noble lineages, he dwells within the great mountain of *nirvāṇa* and the deep, precipitous valley of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Having attained the head of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), he has gathered the various roots of goodness as his cheeks; his eyes possess the luster of cultivated, untainted right view, and his meditative concentration and wisdom are equal.
The brows are high and broad through the practice of sublime conduct; the teeth are white and sharp through the four fearlessnesses;
the mouth is endowed with unimpeded liberation; the chin is firm and full through the four right efforts; the teeth are closely set, even, and sharp through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;

the tongue is red and white, protruding through the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity; the ears are high and prominent through mindfulness and wisdom; and the hair on the head is radiant through the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Lustrous and pure white; the flesh of his upper body is firm through the three gates of liberation; his spine is straight through the manifestation of the three [trainings];
he possesses the fullness of knowledge and conduct, yet his abdomen is unmanifest; his waist is slender through the perfection of patience;

his tail is long through the practice of seclusion; he is firmly established in the four bases of power; his nails are sharp through the five faculties of one beyond training; and his ten powers are of immeasurable force.
The body fully endowed with the assembly of untainted dharmas;

emerging from the dwelling places of the Samādhirāja and other samādhis of all Buddhas; stretching forth within the stages of all dharmas through the four unhindered knowledges; and possessing a mouth of unimpeded liberation.
Relying on these ten powers, he extensively delivers sentient beings without fail, manifesting the morning signs for all the worlds of gods and humans;
he reveals the virtues of the King of Dharma, subdues the heterodox teachers, disputants, and those belonging to factions of false views;

he awakens sentient beings from their slumber within the Four Noble Truths, overcomes the power of pride in those who cling to a self and the five aggregates, and opens up the various paths of false views held by the proponents of heterodox doctrines.
Those who practice what is deviant feel fear; those who believe in what is correct rejoice; and the dull-witted are made sharp.
It comforts disciples and destroys the heterodox;
it causes the long-lived devas, who have long enjoyed celestial pleasures, to realize impermanence.
When sentient beings hear this lion’s roar of the Four Noble Truths, they all give rise to a mind of weary detachment;
through this weary detachment they attain liberation, and through liberation they enter nirvana.
This is called "roaring like a lion among the assembly."
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the lion’s roar of the Buddha and that of an ordinary lion:
when an ordinary lion roars, the various beasts are struck with terror, facing either death or the suffering of imminent death;
when the Buddha, the Lion, roars, they attain liberation from the fear of death.
The lion’s roar [of worldly beings] brings fear: the suffering of death in life after life.
The Buddha’s lion’s roar concerns only the death of this present life; there is no further suffering thereafter.
As for the lion’s roar [of worldly beings], its sound is coarse and harsh; creatures do not rejoice in hearing it, for it is the terror of birth and death.
The Buddha’s lion’s roar is soft and gentle; those who hear it never grow weary, but all find profound joy. Its sound reaches far and wide, capable of bestowing two kinds of bliss:
the bliss of rebirth in heaven and the bliss of nirvana.
This is the distinction. Question:
The Buddha’s lion’s roar also causes those who hear it to feel fear; how does it differ from the roar of an actual lion?
Answer:
Upon hearing the Buddha’s lion’s roar, one may feel slight fear at first, but later it brings great benefit.
Those who cling to the notion of a self, people who thirst for worldly pleasures, those constantly bound by perversions, and those with minds of false views give rise to fear.
As it is said in a sutra:
When the Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths, even the gods in the higher realms were all struck with fear and thought:
"We too possess the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of non-self, and the characteristic of emptiness."
Why is this? Because their minds are inverted, they are attached to the characteristics of permanence and bliss.
This is the distinction.
Furthermore, those who hear the lion’s roar are filled with fear, with the exception of those who have abandoned desire;
yet when the Buddha utters the lion’s roar, even those seeking nirvāṇa and those free from desire are struck with awe.
The lion’s roar causes both good people and bad people to fear;
the Buddha’s lion’s roar causes only good people to fear.
Furthermore, the lion’s roar inspires fear at all times.
Although the Buddha’s lion’s roar may cause slight fear in sentient beings, it reveals the evils and transgressions of the world, causing them to take no pleasure in worldly existence;
by contemplating the merits and benefits of nirvāṇa, it can eliminate the various fears of the world;
it closes off the evil realms and opens the path of goodness, enabling people to reach the city of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, for twenty reasons, the Buddha’s speech is called a "lion's roar": namely, because it relies upon the ten powers; because it does not contract; because it does not expand; because it possesses the Brahma-voice; because it is unprecedented; because it can lead the great assembly; because it causes the evil Māras to tremble with fear; because it disturbs the followers of Māra; because it causes the devas to rejoice; because it enables one to escape the net of Māra; because it severs the bonds of Māra; because it breaks the hooks of Māra; because it transcends the realm of Māra; because it increases one's own Dharma; because it diminishes the teachings of others; because its karmic retribution is non-deceptive; because its preaching of the Dharma is not in vain; because it causes ordinary persons to enter the noble path; because those who have entered the noble path attain the perfection of the exhaustion of outflows; and because it leads to the attainment of the three vehicles according to what is appropriate.
For this reason, the Buddha’s speech is called the "Lion's Roar.
This explains the general and specific characteristics of the Lion's Roar.
Regarding the phrase "turning the Brahma-wheel": it is called "Brahma" because it is pure.
The Buddha’s wisdom and the dharmas associated with that wisdom are called the "wheel";
what the Buddha has taught, which those who receive it practice in accordance with the Dharma, is called "turning."

This wheel has the four foundations of mindfulness as its hub; the five faculties and five powers as its spokes; the four bases of psychic power as its sturdy rim; right effort as its tightly joined felloe; the three doors of liberation as its linchpins; meditative concentration and wisdom as its adjustment; untainted precepts as the fragrant ointment applied to the wheel; the seven factors of enlightenment as its various flower garlands; right view as its clockwise rotation; pure faith as its delightful beauty; right diligence as its swift movement; and the fearless lion’s roar as its wondrous sound.

It can terrify the wheel of Māra, shatter the joints of the wheel of the twelve links of dependent origination, destroy the wheel of birth and death, detach one from the wheel of afflictions, sever the wheel of karma, obstruct the wheel of the mundane world, and break the wheel of suffering;
it can cause the practitioner to rejoice and be revered by devas and humans.
This wheel has no one who can turn it; this wheel sustains the Buddha-dharma, and for this reason it is called the "Turning of the Brahma Wheel.
Furthermore, the Buddha turns the Dharma-wheel just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) turns his precious wheel.
Question:
What similarities are there between the Buddha and a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin)? Answer:
Just as a king is born of a pure and unmixed lineage, achieves success through his family’s ancestral occupation, and has a body adorned with the various marks;

as one endowed with royal virtues who can turn the precious wheel, he receives the consecration with fragrant water and assumes the throne at the head of the four continents, destroying all demonic laws and ensuring that none dare to transgress.

His treasury was overflowing, and his military array was adorned with the seven treasures; he gathered sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and skillfully employed the royal laws. Entrusting the governance of state affairs to high-born ministers of the military, he bestowed exquisite and supreme jewels as gifts. His knowledge and mindfulness remained consistent from beginning to end, without any variation.
The Dharma King is likewise so.

Śākyamuni, Dīpaṃkara, Ratnapuṣpa, and other Buddhas are born into the pure lineage of all Buddhas; they possess the dignified conduct and karmic practices of former Buddhas and adorn themselves with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

These Holy Lords are fully endowed with majestic virtue and turn the true wheel of Dharma. They sprinkle the nectar of wisdom upon the heads of the wise, are honored within the triple world, and destroy all thieves of affliction. The assemblies of those in training and those beyond training rejoice, and none dare to transgress the precepts they have established.

He is fully endowed with the immeasurable treasury of the Dharma-jewels, adorned with the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment, and possesses an army of eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma. He gathers sentient beings through the four worldly means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), and knowing the skillful means, he proclaims the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths as the仪 (ritual/manner) of a Dharma King. With great generals such as Śāriputra and Maitreya who skillfully govern the Buddha-lands, he bestows the various wonderful jewels of the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Firmly resolved in his intention to deeply seek all that is wholesome for all sentient beings—this is what constitutes similarity.
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses a distinction over the wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin):
the wheel-turning sage king is not free from all afflictions (kleśa), whereas the Buddha has eternally transcended all afflictions.
The Wheel-turning Sage King has sunk into the mire of old age and death, whereas the Buddha has already emerged from it.
The Wheel-turning Sage King is a servant to affection and craving, whereas the Buddha has already transcended them.
The Wheel-turning Sage King travels upon the perilous path of birth and death, whereas the Buddha has already crossed over it.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells amidst the darkness of ignorance, whereas the Buddha abides within the supreme radiance.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King exercises sovereign power over the four continents, while the Buddha exercises sovereign power over immeasurable and boundless worlds.
The wheel-turning sage king possesses mastery over material wealth, whereas the Buddha possesses mastery over the jewel of the mind.
The wheel-turning sage king thirsts for the pleasures of the heavens, whereas the Buddha has already transcended even the bliss of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The wheel-turning sage king seeks happiness from others, whereas the Buddha generates happiness from within his own mind.
For this reason, the Buddha is the most preeminent among the wheel-turning sage kings.
Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King turns the precious wheel with his hand, it moves without obstruction through the air;
when a Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma, it moves without obstruction or hindrance among all those in the world, whether gods or humans.
Those who behold the precious wheel have all poisons extinguished;
those who encounter the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma have all the poisons of affliction extinguished.
Those who behold the precious wheel have all calamities, evils, and harms extinguished.
Upon encountering the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma, all false views, doubts, regrets, and calamities are entirely extinguished.
Just as a king governs the four continents by means of this wheel,
so too does the Buddha govern all the worlds of gods and humans with the Wheel of Dharma, causing them to attain mastery over the Dharma.
This is their similarity.
Furthermore, the Wheel of Dharma is vastly superior to the precious wheel:
the precious wheel is deceptive; the Wheel of Dharma is not.
The Wheel of Dharma is solid and substantial.
The Jewel Wheel increases the fire of the three poisons;
the Wheel of Dharma extinguishes the fire of the three poisons.
The jewel wheel is with outflows;
the Dharma wheel is without outflows.
The jewel wheel delights in the pleasures of the five desires;
The Dharma-wheel is the delight in the joy of the Dharma.
The Jewel-wheel is the locus of fetters;
the Dharma-wheel is not the locus of fetters.
The jewel wheel moves within limited realms;
the Dharma wheel moves through immeasurable lands.
The jewel wheel can be obtained in every lifetime by means of pure giving with a single-minded focus.
The Wheel of Dharma is obtained through the accumulation of the causes and conditions of all wholesome karma and wisdom over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
As for the precious wheel, it no longer turns after the king’s death;
however, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Wheel of Dharma continues to turn.
The jewel-wheel resides in a single person;
the Dharma-wheel resides in all those who are capable of being delivered.
Furthermore, "Brahma" signifies vastness; because the Buddha turns the Dharma-wheel so that it pervades the ten directions without exception, it is called vast.
Furthermore, it is called the "Brahma-wheel" because it is taught with the four Brahma-abodes in mind.
Furthermore, when the Buddha first attained the Way, the Brahma King requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma; therefore, it is called the "Brahma-wheel."
Furthermore, when the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī and Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained the Way, the sound reached as far as the Brahma Heaven; therefore, it is called the "Brahma Wheel."
Furthermore, there are those who hold the Brahmā realm in high esteem; because one wishes to cause them to rejoice, it is called the "Brahma-wheel.
For this reason, it is named the "Brahma-wheel."
Question:
The Buddha sometimes refers to it as the "Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakra) and sometimes as the "Brahma Wheel" (brahmacakra); what is the difference between them?
Answer:
It is said that the Brahma-wheel and the Dharma-wheel are not different. Furthermore, some say:
"To speak of the Brahma-wheel is to manifest the four immeasurable minds."
To speak of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) is to demonstrate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

Furthermore, that which attains the Way by means of the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa-citta) is called the "Brahma-wheel" (brahmacakra); that which attains the Way by relying on other dharmas is called the "Wheel of Dharma."
The Brahma-wheel demonstrates the four dhyānas; the Dharma-wheel demonstrates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The Brahma-wheel demonstrates the noble path of cultivating meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi); the Dharma-wheel demonstrates the noble path of cultivating wisdom (prajñā).
In this manner, the distinctions between the Brahma-wheel and the Dharma-wheel have been analyzed.
Question:
What dharmas constitute the nature of fearlessness?
Answer:
When the Buddha first attained the Way, he realized all Buddha-dharmas, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*).
Among these, the dharmas associated with the wisdom of the four fearlessnesses that are to be attained in future lives are called "fearlessness."
For example, when practicing giving, a thought associated with the dharma of relinquishment arises within the mind;
likewise, the four immeasurable minds are called the "Dharma-gate of Loving-kindness. Question:
What is the sequence among these four fearlessnesses?
The answer is:

In the first fearlessness, one demonstrates to others that one knows all phenomena; because one knows all phenomena, one’s outflows are exhausted; because the outflows are exhausted, one knows the dharmas that obstruct the exhaustion of outflows; and because one has severed these obstructing dharmas, one teaches the Path.

Furthermore, the first fearlessness is like showing a physician all medicinal herbs; the second shows the eradication of all diseases; the third is knowing what is prohibited; and the fourth shows what should be consumed.

Furthermore, in the first fearlessness, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is taught; in the second fearlessness, the absence of all afflictions and their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) is taught; in the third fearlessness, the absence of error in the teaching of the Dharma is taught; and in the fourth fearlessness, the accomplishment of what was to be done and the attainment of nirvana are taught.
Question:

Since it is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that the five aggregates up to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities are all empty, why are their characteristics now explained through differentiation?
The answer is:
Within the Buddha-dharma, there is the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), which encounters no obstruction regarding any phenomena;
it is by means of this emptiness of non-apprehension that all Buddha-dharmas and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are taught.
For example, although space is devoid of anything whatsoever, all things depend upon it to grow and flourish.

Furthermore, these ten powers and four fearlessnesses do not arise from grasping at signs or through the conceptualization of an attached mind; rather, they exist solely for the sake of liberating sentient beings, knowing that sentient beings attain liberation through these causes and conditions.
For example, medicinal herbs are used solely to cure illness, not for the sake of seeking out the characteristics of the herbs themselves.
As it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*:
"If one has faith that all phenomena are empty, this accords with the principle."
If one does not believe in the emptiness of phenomena, everything will be contradicted and lost.
If one were to claim that this emptiness does not exist, then there would be nothing to be performed;
yet karma would already exist without having been created, and there would be an agent who acts without acting.
Regarding such characteristics of all phenomena, who is able to conceive of them?
Only with a pure and upright mind, that which is spoken has no basis;
free from the views of existence and non-existence, the mind naturally ceases within.

Question: The Śrāvaka-dharma explains the ten powers (*daśabala*) and four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*) in such a manner; how, then, does the Mahāyāna distinguish the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses?
Answer:
Within these ten powers and four fearlessnesses, there is exhaustive knowledge and universal knowledge; it is within the Mahāyāna that these ten powers and four fearlessnesses are explained.

Question: In the Śrāvaka-dharma, it is also said that there is "exhaustive knowledge" (parijñā) and "universal knowledge" (sarvajñā); why then do you say that exhaustive knowledge and universal knowledge are taught in the Mahāyāna? Answer:
The various masters of treatises claim that the Buddha possesses exhaustive knowledge and universal knowledge, yet this was not spoken by the Buddha himself;
now, because the ten powers and four fearlessnesses within the Mahāyāna are being expounded, the Buddha himself declares:
"I possess exhaustive knowledge and universal knowledge."

Furthermore, for the sake of those who are śrāvakas, the ten powers and four fearlessnesses are taught; these, together with the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and other such śrāvaka dharmas, are all intended for the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Now, however, within the Mahāyāna, the ten powers and four fearlessnesses are taught together with great compassion and the true nature of all phenomena—neither arising nor ceasing.
Question:
The Buddha possesses the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; does a bodhisattva possess them as well? Answer:
There is. What is it? First, the power that is firm, deep, and solid in generating the mind of omniscience.
Second, because they are endowed with great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they possess the power of not abandoning any sentient being;
third, because they do not require any offerings, honor, or profit, they are endowed with the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);

fourth, because they have faith in all Buddha-dharmas and are endowed with the generation of all Buddha-dharmas as well as a mind that never tires, they possess the power of great vigor (*mahāvīrya*).
Fifth, because their conduct and deportment remain unimpaired through single-minded compassionate action, they possess the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*);

sixth, because they eliminate the two extremes, practice in accordance with the twelve links of dependent origination, sever all false views, and extinguish all conceptualization, discrimination, and frivolous proliferation, they possess the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*);

seventh, because they bring all sentient beings to fulfillment, undergo immeasurable births and deaths, accumulate all roots of goodness without weariness, and know that all worlds are like dreams, they possess the power of not wearying of birth and death (*saṃsāra-bala*).

Eighth, because of contemplating the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*), knowing there is no self (*ātman*) and no sentient beings (*sattva*), and through faith and understanding that all phenomena neither emerge nor arise, one possesses the power of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Ninth, because of entering the contemplation of the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—and because of knowing and seeing the liberations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one attains the power of liberation.

Tenth, because of mastery over the profound Dharma, and because of knowing the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings, one is fully endowed with the power of unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna-bala*).
These are the ten powers of a bodhisattva.
What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva?

First, because they hear and retain all things, because they have attained all dhāraṇīs, and because they remember them without forgetting, they are fearless when preaching the Dharma in the midst of the assembly.

Second, because they have attained liberation within all phenomena; because they know how to distinguish and apply the medicinal remedies for all phenomena; and because they know the faculties of all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma appropriately amidst the great assembly with fearlessness.
Third, a bodhisattva is always free from all fears and does not harbor such thoughts as:
"If someone from the ten directions comes to challenge me, I will be unable to answer."
Not perceiving such signs, he preaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly with fearlessness.
Fourth, he allows all people to come and pose difficult questions, answering each one and being able to sever their doubts; thus, he preaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly with fearlessness.
These are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva.
As for the "four unhindered knowledges" (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ):

they are the unhindered knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), the unhindered knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), and the unhindered knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
Regarding "unimpeded knowledge of meaning" (*arthapratisaṃvid*): it refers to the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena as expressed through names and language.

For instance, the characteristic of solidity: herein, the solidity of earth is the "meaning" (*artha*); the name "earth" is the "phenomenon" (*dharma*); the verbal expression "earth" is the "language" (*nirukti*); and the mastery of eloquent exposition regarding these three types of knowledge is "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
To penetrate these four matters without obstruction is called "unimpeded knowledge."

The characteristic of moisture is water; the characteristic of heat is fire; the characteristic of motion is wind; the characteristic of mental reflection is consciousness; the characteristic of impermanence is the five aggregates; the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are the five aggregates of clinging; and the characteristic of non-self is all phenomena.

In this way, the general characteristics and specific characteristics through which all phenomena are distinguished are likewise [the object of] what is called "unimpeded knowledge of meaning" (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

As for "unimpeded knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), it is the knowledge of the names for these meanings—for instance, knowing that the characteristic of solidity is called "earth. To be unimpeded within such analytical distinctions of all names is what is called "unimpeded knowledge of phenomena."
Why is this so? Because apart from names, meanings cannot be apprehended; one knows meaning necessarily by means of names. For this reason, after "meaning" (artha), there is "dharma.
Question:
Are meaning and name conjoined,
or are they separate?
If they were conjoined, then when one speaks the word "fire," it should burn the mouth.
If they were separate, then when one speaks of fire, one should obtain water!
The answer is:

they are neither conjoined nor separate. Ancient people provisionally established names to designate various phenomena; later people recognize these things by means of those names. Thus, each has its own name, and this constitutes a phenomenon (*dharma*).
Regarding these names and their meanings, how does one cause sentient beings to attain understanding?

One should employ words and phrases to analyze and adorn them so as to enable people to understand, achieving thorough penetration without obstruction; this is called "unimpeded knowledge of language" (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
To speak with reason, to expound inexhaustibly, and to attain mastery and unimpededness within all meditative concentrations—this is called "the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence."
The first and fourth unimpeded knowledges (pratisaṃvid) reside within the nine stages;
the second and third unimpeded knowledges reside in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the Brahma-heaven (brahmaloka).
The second and third unimpeded knowledges are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The first is:
The ten knowledges.
The fourth:
the nine knowledges.
This non-obstruction is of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior;
the superior belongs to all Buddhas, the middling to great Bodhisattvas, and the inferior to great Arhats.
Question: Power (*bala*), fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and unimpededness (*pratisaṃvid*) are all wisdom.
If one possesses internal power and is externally fearless, then [wisdom] is complete; why, then, is unimpededness spoken of again?
Answer: The powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) have already been analyzed.

Although some may lack fearlessness, they encounter obstacles when preaching the Dharma in the midst of a great assembly; for this reason, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are taught.
Having attained this adornment of unimpeded wisdom, one is adorned by the four fearlessnesses; being adorned by the four fearlessnesses, one is further adorned by the ten powers.
Furthermore, regarding the teaching on the fearlessnesses, some who harbor doubts may ask:
"How can a single person attain fearlessness amidst a great assembly?"
The Buddha possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*) before and the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) after; for this reason, he teaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly without fear.
Such are the distinctions regarding the four unhindered knowledges.
Question:
Are there the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) of a bodhisattva within the Mahāyāna? Answer:
There is. What is it? "Unimpeded knowledge of meaning" (arthapratisaṃvid): "meaning" refers to the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas), which is ineffable.
Meaning (*artha*), names (*nāman*), and linguistic expressions (*vyavahāra*) are not distinct from one another; this remains the same in the beginning, middle, and end.
This is called "meaning. One should not conceive of meaning as existing separately from names and linguistic expressions; because these three things are equal, it is termed "meaning."
Furthermore, to know the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*) with complete clarity and to penetrate them without obstruction is called "unimpeded knowledge of meaning" (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
As for "unimpeded knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), "phenomena" refers to the names and designations for all meanings; it is for the purpose of knowing those meanings.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters this unimpeded knowledge of dharmas, they always place their trust in the Dharma and not in persons;
they always rely on the Dharma and do not rely on what is not the Dharma.
Regarding "acting in accordance with the Dharma," there is no such thing as acting contrary to the Dharma. Why is this?
Because this person knows that all names and verbal expressions are devoid of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, by means of this unimpeded wisdom regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one discriminates the three vehicles; yet, although one discriminates the three vehicles, one does not destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Why is this so?
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has but one characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (animitta).

This bodhisattva uses such speech to teach the Dharma; knowing that speech is empty and like the nature of an echo, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings so that they may believe and know it to be identical with the nature of phenomena.
The unimpeded mastery in the names and speech that are spoken is called "unhindered knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

As for "unhindered knowledge of expression" (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), it is the use of language to explain the meanings of names; through various adornments of speech, one is able to bring about understanding according to what is appropriate.
That is to say: the languages of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, mahoragas, and other non-human beings;
the languages of world-protectors such as Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings, as well as human languages;
and languages consisting of single words, dual words, or plural words.
Whether abbreviated speech or extensive speech;
feminine speech or masculine speech;
speech of the past, future, or present—through such forms of expression, he enables each person to attain understanding.
Whether speaking of oneself or others, one neither slanders nor praises. Why is this?
Because all dharmas do not reside within speech; speech is not the true meaning.
If these words were the ultimate reality, one could not use skillful speech to speak of what is unwholesome.
They are spoken only for the sake of entering nirvana so that one may understand; do not cling to the words!
Furthermore, by means of this speech, one can cause sentient beings to act in accordance with the meaning of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because all speech enters into the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
This is called "unimpeded knowledge of language" (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding "unimpeded knowledge of eloquence" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), it means that within a single syllable, a bodhisattva can speak all syllables; within a single word, he can speak all words; and within a single dharma, he can speak all dharmas.
All that is spoken herein is Dharma, all is reality, and all is truth; it benefits each according to those who are capable of being saved.

That is to say: for those who delight in the *sūtras*, he speaks the *sūtras*; for those who delight in the *geya*, he speaks the *geya*; for those who delight in the *vyākaraṇa*, he speaks the *vyākaraṇa*; for those who delight in the *gāthā*, *udāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*, he speaks all these sūtras for them.
He teaches according to the faculties and inclinations of all sentient beings:

for those who delight in faith, he teaches the faculty of faith; for those who delight in diligence, he teaches the faculty of diligence; for those who delight in earnest mindfulness, he teaches the faculty of mindfulness; for those who delight in collecting the mind, he teaches the faculty of concentration; and for those who delight in wisdom, he teaches the faculty of wisdom.
As it is with the five faculties and so forth, so it is with all roots of goodness.

Furthermore, because there are twenty-one thousand types of faculties for those who indulge in sensual desire, the Buddha taught eighty-four thousand remedial methods as antidotes to these faculties; the Bodhisattva delights in explaining the sequence of these remedial methods in accordance with these various faculties.

There are twenty-one thousand faculties of those characterized by anger; for the sake of these faculties, the Buddha taught eighty-four thousand faculties of remedial methods. Following these various faculties, the Bodhisattva delights in explaining the sequence of these remedial methods.
There are twenty-one thousand types of faculties for ignorant persons.

For the sake of these faculties, the Buddha taught eighty-four thousand remedial dharmas; following these various faculties, the Bodhisattva delights in explaining the sequence of these remedial dharmas.

There are twenty-one thousand classifications of the faculties of sentient beings; for the sake of these faculties, the Buddha taught eighty-four thousand remedial dharmas. Following these various faculties, the Bodhisattva delights in explaining the sequence of these remedial dharmas.
This is called "the unimpeded wisdom of eloquence.

Furthermore, by means of this unimpeded wisdom, the bodhisattva may, for a kalpa or half a kalpa, adorn each and every teaching with eloquence, yet without ever violating the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

This bodhisattva may conceal his body so that it does not appear, yet he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings through all his pores, according to what is appropriate for each, without losing his fundamental practice.
The wisdom of this bodhisattva is immeasurable; no master of debate can exhaust it, nor can they destroy it.

When this Bodhisattva attains this unimpeded wisdom and undergoes rebirth by means of a transformed body, he naturally comes to know all the scriptures, incantations, wisdom, and skills of all the seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). That is to say, he knows the four Vedas, the six *aṅga* incantations, the treatises on the sun, moon, and five planets, the treatise on the origins of dreams, earthquakes, the speech of ghosts, the speech of birds, and the speech of beasts; the speech of four-legged animals and those possessed by spirits; the divination of kings' signs regarding abundance or famine; the conjunctions and conflicts of the sun, moon, and five planets; medicine, writing, mathematics, divination, song, dance, and music.

He fully understands all such crafts, technical skills, and various scriptures, his clarity and penetration surpassing that of all people and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); yet he neither exalts himself nor causes distress to others.
Knowing these to be worldly matters, one does not [strive] for nirvana.

Because this bodhisattva has accomplished the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), his physical strength and radiant light surpass those of all the Brahmās; yet while all the Brahmās revere, cherish, and honor him, his mind remains free from attachment.
He is likewise respected and honored by all such devas, yet he remains without attachment, giving rise only to the realization of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Furthermore, by means of supernormal powers, he inspires the various devas, causing their hearts to yearn with longing as he preaches the Dharma for them—teaching that is inexhaustible and indestructible, which severs doubt and regret, and establishes them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s power of the four kinds of unhindered knowledge within the Mahāyāna, by which he is able to deliver sentient beings.
This is the meaning of the four kinds of unhindered knowledge.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 25.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra),
Commentary on the Eighteen Unique Qualities within the First Chapter, Fascicle Forty-one, Number Twenty-six.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. 41. Commentary on the Eighteen Unshared Dharmas (Aṣṭādaśāveṇikadharma-vyākhyāna).
The eighteen unshared dharmas are as follows: first, all Buddhas have no failure of body; second, no failure of speech; third, no failure of mindfulness;
fourth, no divergent thoughts; fifth, no unconcentrated mind; sixth, no relinquishing without prior awareness.

Seventh, his desire does not diminish; eighth, his vigor does not diminish; ninth, his mindfulness does not diminish; tenth, his wisdom does not diminish; eleventh, his liberation does not diminish; twelfth, his knowledge and vision of liberation does not diminish;
thirteenth, all his bodily actions follow wisdom; fourteenth, all his verbal actions follow wisdom; fifteenth, all his mental actions follow wisdom;
sixteenth, his wisdom knows the past without obstruction; seventeenth, his wisdom knows the future without obstruction; eighteenth, his wisdom knows the present without obstruction.
Question:
These thirty-six factors are all factors of the Buddha; for what reason are only eighteen designated as "unique" (*āveṇika*)? Answer:
Among the first eighteen [dharmas], there is a share for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, but among the latter eighteen, they have no share.

For example, Śāriputra was able to discern all dharmas and eloquently expound upon a single phrase with unimpeded penetration; the Buddha praised him, saying, "You are well-versed in the nature of dharmas.
Aniruddha was foremost in the divine eye; such śrāvakas as these all possess a share.
Regarding those who possess a share in the four fearlessnesses: as the Buddha said that among his disciples, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja was foremost in the lion’s roar;
Śāriputra also made this vow:
"For seven days and seven nights, I am able to expound upon a single meaning so that it remains inexhaustible."
The four types of analytical wisdom possessed by the Arhats—
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Pūrṇa, Ānanda, Kātyāyana, and others— likewise know these meanings, names, phrases, and eloquent expositions.
For this reason, the preceding eighteen [attributes] are not called "unshared" (āveṇika). Question:
For what reason does the Buddha have "no failure of body" and "no failure of speech"?
Answer:
Because the Buddha has maintained pure precepts throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there is no failure in his physical or vocal karma;
whereas other arhats such as Śāriputra and others, having practiced the precepts for at most sixty kalpas and not for a long time, still have lapses.

Because the Buddha has accumulated all pure precepts throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, constantly practiced profound meditative concentration, attained all subtle and wondrous wisdom, and skillfully cultivated the mind of great compassion, he is without any fault.
Furthermore, because the Buddha has uprooted all causes and conditions for the roots of transgression, he is without fault.
There are four kinds of causes and conditions for the roots of transgression:
first, the cause and condition of greed; second, the cause and condition of hatred; third, the cause and condition of fear; and fourth, the cause and condition of delusion.
The causes, conditions, and habitual tendencies of these roots of evil have all been uprooted.
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have uprooted the causes and conditions of evil, because their habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, they may occasionally experience lapses.
Because the Buddha has always perfected all-encompassing wisdom regarding all phenomena;
if one does not know this, there will be error.

For example, Śāriputra was traveling with five hundred bhikṣus and stayed overnight at an empty monastery. It being the day for the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), he did not know the matters concerning the internal and external boundaries, and so he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one stays at a dwelling place for even a single night and then abandons it, there is no boundary.

Furthermore, on another occasion, when Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were returning with five hundred bhikṣus, they made loud and boisterous noises; therefore, the Buddha expelled them, which constitutes a verbal transgression.
Furthermore, as when Śāriputra did not know the method of eating in equal measure, the Buddha said:
"He eats impure food!
Such instances constitute faults of body and speech.
Because the Buddha has exhausted all habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), he is free from such faults.
Furthermore, because all the Buddha’s bodily and vocal actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, his body is without fault and his speech is without fault.
For various causes and conditions such as these, there is no failure of body and no failure of speech.
Regarding "no failure of mindfulness," it is because the mind has long practiced the four foundations of mindfulness;
and because the mind does not become distracted due to having well-cultivated profound meditative concentration.
He has rightly severed both craving for sensual desires and craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), because his mind is unattached toward all phenomena;
he has attained the foremost state of peace and security.
If the mind is anxious and hurried, mindfulness will be lost.
The Buddha’s mind is devoid of gain or loss; for this reason, there is no loss.

Furthermore, because the Buddha’s threefold adornments—namely, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), clear knowledge (*vidyā*), and power (*bala*)—perfect his mindfulness, his mindfulness is accomplished and without loss, as it is primarily employed with respect to the past.
Furthermore, because the faculty and power of mindfulness are boundless and inexhaustible, there is no loss of mindfulness.
Furthermore, because all of the Buddha’s mental activities proceed in accordance with wisdom, there is no loss of mindfulness;
for every single thought-moment proceeds according to his will.
Such as these are called mindfulness without lapse.
As it is said in the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Who is the person without fault?"
Who is it that does not lose mindfulness?
Who is it whose mind is always one-pointed?
It is he who is able to do what ought to be done.
“Perfectly knowing all phenomena, liberated from all obstructions, and having accomplished all virtues—there is only the Buddha alone!
Regarding “the absence of divergent thoughts,” the Buddha has no discrimination toward any sentient being; he harbors no divergent thoughts concerning distance or proximity.
It may be explained that this is for the noble and not for the lowly;
yet the light of the Buddha’s great compassion universally illumines all things, showing equal pity and delivering all equally—
whether they be respectful or disrespectful, enemies or kin, noble or lowly, [the Buddha treats] them all with perfect impartiality.
For example, there was a guest who was a dung-remover named Nanda; the Buddha transformed and delivered him, and he attained the state of a Great Arhat.
It is also like the householder Dharmapāla, who sought to harm the Buddha with a pit of fire and poisoned rice;
yet on that very day, [the Buddha] eliminated his three poisons and extinguished the fire of his false views.
In such matters, he harbors no discriminatory thoughts.

Furthermore, the Buddha feels no attachment toward those who practice in accordance with the Dharma, such as Śāriputra and Maitreya Bodhisattva; nor does he feel aversion toward Devadatta, Pūraṇa, the six heretical teachers, or those with false views.
This is because the Buddha has cultivated and perfumed his mind throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; he is a jewel among sentient beings, like pure gold that cannot be made otherwise.
Furthermore, with his Buddha-eye, the Buddha observes all sentient beings three times each day and night to see who may be delivered, so as not to let the opportune moment pass;
because he regards all sentient beings with equality, he harbors no discriminatory thoughts.
Furthermore, the Buddha praises wholesome dharmas through various causes and conditions, and censures unwholesome dharmas through various causes and conditions;

yet his mind neither increases nor decreases toward the wholesome or the evil. He makes such distinctions solely for the sake of liberating sentient beings—this is what is meant by being without discriminatory thought.

Furthermore, as stated in the *Sarvācaryāpraveśa-sūtra*: "The Buddha regards all sentient beings as his own body; having accomplished what was to be done, he is without beginning, middle, or end. This is called the absence of discriminatory thought.

Furthermore, the Buddha contemplates all sentient beings and all phenomena from their primordial origin up to the state of non-arising and non-ceasing; they are eternally pure like nirvana. This is called the absence of discriminatory thought.
Furthermore, the dharma-gate of entering non-duality is the gate of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
distinct characteristics constitute dualistic dharmas, and dualistic dharmas are the path of error.
The Buddha is one who does not practice deception; he should not employ deceptive dharmas, but constantly practices the dharma-gate of entering non-duality.
The nature of deception is precisely the characteristic of difference.
Such as these are called "the absence of the notion of difference.
Regarding "no unsettled mind": "concentration" (samādhi) means a single mind that is not distracted.
In a distracted mind, one cannot perceive reality;
it is like a face that cannot be seen when the water is turbulent, or like a lamp that cannot provide clear illumination when it is in the wind.
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha has no unconcentrated mind.
Question: It is said that "concentration" (samādhi) ranges from the stages beginning with the "unattained" (anāgamya) up to the "attainment of cessation" (nirodhasamāpatti);
while one has entered these concentrations, it is impossible to initiate bodily action (kāyakarma) or vocal action (vākkarma).

If the Buddha were always in meditative concentration and never possessed a mind not in concentration, how could he travel through various countries, maintain the four modes of deportment, and preach the Dharma for the great assembly using various causes, conditions, and parables?
Regarding such a matter, it might be possible for a mind bound to the desire realm or a mind in the Brahma-world that has not entered meditative concentration [to possess this].
The answer states:
"There is no mind that is not in concentration" (anavyupaśānta-citta); this phrase carries various meanings.
"Concentration" (samādhi) refers to dwelling within the wholesome dharmas that constantly gather the mind;
the Buddha is concentrated within the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena and never regresses from it—this is called "having no unconcentrated mind."
Furthermore, there are meditative concentrations within the desire realm; one may teach the Dharma while entering these concentrations.

For this reason, the Abhidharma states that there are such sublime qualities as the four noble lineages, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the samādhi of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge—all of which are bound to the desire realm.
Because the Buddha enters meditative concentration within the desire realm, he is said to have "no unsettled mind.
When the various śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas arise from concentration, they may enter a neutral state of mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), or a wholesome state, or even regress into a defiled state.

However, when the Buddha arises from concentration, he immediately re-enters the concentration of the desire realm; from the very beginning, there is never a moment of mental distraction. For this reason, he is said to have no unsettled mind.
Furthermore, according to the Śrāvaka-dharma, when an emanated being preaches the Dharma, the master of the emanation does not preach;
when the master of the emanation preaches, the emanated being does not preach.
The Buddha is not like this: both the emanated being and the master of the emanation are able to preach the Dharma.
The concentrated mind should also differ:
when a śrāvaka enters meditative concentration, he cannot speak;
whereas a Buddha, even while in concentration, can both preach the Dharma and travel about.
As stated in the *Guhyakapada-sutra* within the section on the Secret Mind:
"The minds of all Buddhas are always in meditative concentration, yet their minds also preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddha is entirely free from the dharmas of a distracted mind, as well as the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), such as doubt and regret.
Although Arhats have no doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths, they possess doubts in various respects concerning all phenomena;
the Buddha, however, is always certain and free from doubt regarding all phenomena, because he possesses no wisdom that is not concentrated.
Furthermore, because śrāvakas possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various afflictions and are subject to regression, they are distracted;
the Buddha, however, possesses the perfection of wisdom within the sphere of all-knowledge and is therefore undistracted.
Just as a vessel filled with water is without sound or movement, so too, the Buddha alone is called the one whose nature is non-deceptive;
among the three types of steadfast persons, he is the most supreme, and his mind remains unchanged by suffering or pleasure.

The characteristics of identity and difference, arising and ceasing, annihilation and permanence, coming and going—such characteristics of all phenomena are entirely deceptive, for they are dharmas produced by the false conjunction of conditions.
Because the Buddha is established within the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, his mind is never unsettled; because it is not unsettled, his mind does not waver.
Furthermore, among the five kinds of inconceivable phenomena, the Buddha is the most inconceivable.
These eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are the profound treasury of the Buddha; who could possibly fathom them!
For this reason, it is necessarily so that the Buddha never has an unconcentrated mind.
Although the Buddha constantly dwells in meditative concentration and lacks the coarse mind of vitarka and vicāra, because he possesses inconceivable wisdom, he is also able to preach the Dharma.

It is like celestial music that produces various sounds according to the preferences of the devas; this music likewise has no mind and no conscious cognition of dharmas, yet it exists through the causal conditions of the devas' merit and virtue.
Just as celestial music has no mind and no consciousness yet can respond to beings, how much more so would the Buddha have a mind and yet not preach the Dharma!
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha has no unconcentrated mind.
Regarding "the abandonment through full knowledge of nothing that is not known":
sentient beings have three kinds of sensation—painful sensation, pleasant sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Painful sensation gives rise to aversion; pleasant sensation gives rise to craving; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation gives rise to delusion.
These are the three kinds of feeling:
painful feeling is suffering when it arises, suffering while it persists, and pleasant when it ceases;
pleasant feeling is pleasant when it arises, pleasant while it persists, and suffering when it ceases.
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not know it as pain nor know it as pleasure.

Because other people have dull faculties, they mostly perceive painful and pleasant feelings; within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they do not perceive or know it, but instead harbor a mind of equanimity (upekṣā), being thus driven by the underlying tendency of delusion (moha-anuśaya).
The Buddha, within feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant, knows when a perception arises, when it abides, and when it ceases.
For this reason, it is said: "There is no state of mind that the Buddha has not known and then relinquished."
Question: What is equanimity (*upekṣā*) in this context?
Is it simply that which is neither painful nor pleasant?
Is equanimity (upekṣā) that which is among the seven factors of enlightenment, or is it that which is among the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) that is called equanimity?
The answer is:
that which is neither painful nor pleasant is equanimity; the equanimity in both of those states is also equanimity.

Why is this? Other people, within the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, do not perceive the arising, abiding, and ceasing moment by moment; it is only after a long time that they perceive them.
The Buddha fully understands all things within every moment of thought.
Regarding equanimity among the seven factors of awakening: when the mind is balanced, neither sinking nor agitated, it is the time to practice equanimity;
if the mind sinks, one should cultivate the perception of diligence.
When there is agitation, one practices the mental application of gathering the mind.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas sometimes mistakenly gather their minds or allow them to become agitated; before achieving equanimity, they abandon the practice.
The Buddha fully knows the coarse, subtle, deep, and shallow aspects within every thought-moment; having known them, he relinquishes them.
A question is asked:
If this is so, why did the Buddha speak to Nanda and tell the bhikṣus, "Nanda, one is aware when all sensations arise, aware when they abide, and aware when they cease"?
"All perceptions and all thoughts are also like this.
He replied:
"Thoughts are of two kinds:"

First, within the awakened mind, when a painful feeling arises, one knows that a painful feeling has arisen; when a painful feeling persists, one knows that a painful feeling persists; and when a painful feeling ceases, one knows that a painful feeling has ceased.

When a pleasant feeling arises, one knows that a pleasant feeling has arisen; when a pleasant feeling persists, one knows that a pleasant feeling persists; and when a pleasant feeling ceases, one knows that a pleasant feeling has ceased. It is the same for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
First, they are able to know these general characteristics, but cannot know their specific characteristics.
Second, within every thought-moment, they fully perceive and fully know all feelings—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
in every thought-moment, there are no mental factors that pass by without being known.
For this reason, it is said that "there is nothing the Buddha does not know before he relinquishes [his activity].
Furthermore, there are times when the Buddha relinquishes sentient beings and enters profound meditative concentration for one or two months.
Someone may have this doubt:
"The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of delivering sentient beings; why, then, does he constantly enter meditative absorption?
The Buddha said:
"I have relinquished it because I know it through various causes and conditions; it is not that I have relinquished it out of ignorance.
He asked: "What are the causes and conditions for relinquishing after having known?"
Answer: He rested briefly because he was weary from being among the great assembly.
Furthermore, throughout his successive lifetimes, the Buddha always cherished the practice of seclusion.
When the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, his mother also delighted in the practice of seclusion; she gave birth to him in the Lumbinī Grove, forty *li* from the city.
When he attained the Way, he became a Buddha while alone beneath a tree in the Uruvilvā forest.
When he first turned the Wheel of Dharma, he was likewise in the Deer Park at the abode of the sages.
At the time of entering *nirvāṇa*, [the Buddha] was beneath the twin *śāla* trees in the Śāla grove.
Because he had long practiced the joy of seclusion, the Buddha entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, because the Buddha has constantly perfected the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), he entered meditative concentration.

Furthermore, the Buddha dwells far removed from clamor and places of idle chatter; he likewise contemplates the treasury of merits of all Buddhas and experiences the foremost pure bliss, and for these reasons, he enters meditative concentration.
Furthermore, after the Buddha had preached the Dharma, he constantly instructed the bhikṣus: "You should practice dhyāna so that you shall have no cause for regret later.
What he spoke with his mouth, he also practiced with his body; therefore, he entered meditative concentration.

Furthermore, out of weariness with offerings, [the Bodhisattva], knowing those sentient beings who are ready to be delivered, enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and creates emanated beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) to go and deliver them.
Furthermore, for those sentient beings who have little concentration but much wisdom, he manifests the practice of meditation with his own body to teach and transform them.
Furthermore, because some people constantly see the Buddha, they develop a sense of weariness; therefore, he remains at a slight distance to allow them to feel a sense of hunger and longing.
Furthermore, the Buddha dwells in a secluded and quiet place because he wishes to preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas.
Furthermore, the Buddha practices dhyāna in order to establish a model for future generations.
Moreover, having himself set the wheel of Dharma in motion, he enters meditative concentration to entrust the affairs of the Teaching to his disciples.
Furthermore, he manifests two kinds of paths to gather in sentient beings:
first, meditative concentration (dhyāna), and second, wisdom (prajñā).
When the Buddha preaches the Dharma amidst the great assembly, he manifests wisdom for their sake.
Gathering the mind in a quiet place constitutes the manifestation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), sentient beings engage in three types of conduct:

seeing pleasant forms, they give rise to joy and pleasure; seeing unpleasant forms, they give rise to sorrow and suffering; and seeing forms that are neither painful nor pleasant, they give rise to a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The same applies even to mental phenomena (*dharma*).

The Buddha possesses mastery over the six sense objects; he is able to give rise to a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) toward both pleasant and painful states, as described in the "Noble Wish-Fulfilling Power" (*ārya-ṛddhi*).
For various causes and conditions such as these, he enters meditative concentration; it is not that he lacks knowledge and thus abandons it.

Regarding "the absence of decrease in aspiration": because the Buddha knows the debt of gratitude toward wholesome dharmas and constantly desires to gather all wholesome dharmas, his aspiration does not decrease.
Because he practices all wholesome dharmas with a mind that never knows satiety, his desire does not diminish.
It is like an elder bhikṣu whose eyesight had grown dim, who was sewing his saṃghāṭī robe when the needle’s thread came loose;
he spoke to the people, saying:
"Whoever desires merit, please stitch my needle for me.
At that moment, the Buddha appeared before him and said, "I am one who desires merit and is never satiated; bring me your needle."
This bhikṣu, having clearly beheld the Buddha’s radiance and recognized the Buddha’s voice, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The ocean of the Buddha’s immeasurable merit—having reached its very limits and bottom—how could you ever be satiated?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The retribution of meritorious deeds is profoundly deep; there is none like me who knows how to repay such kindness.
Although I have exhausted its very limits and depths, it was because my original desire was never satiated that I attained Buddhahood; therefore, even now I do not cease."
"Although there are no further merits to be attained, my aspiration for them does not cease!
The devas and people of the world were startled and awakened to realize that even the Buddha never tires of merit; how much less so others!
The Buddha preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus; at that time, his physical eye became clear and his wisdom-eye was perfected.
A question was asked:
"If the Buddha has already severed all desire regarding wholesome dharmas, why is it now said that 'his desires do not diminish'?"
Answer: To say "severing the desire for all wholesome dharmas" refers to the desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained, or the desire to increase what has already been obtained;
the Buddha does not possess such desire.
The Buddha is fully endowed with all merits; there is nothing he has not attained, nor is there anything further to be added.
As for the term "desire" mentioned here, it is as previously explained:
although the Buddha has fully acquired all merits, his desire-mind does not yet cease.
For example, although the horse-treasure has reached its destination, its desire to go does not cease; it continues until death.
The Buddha-treasure is also like this.
Furthermore, when the great fire at the end of a kalpa burns the trichiliocosm until nothing remains, the force of the flames does not cease.
The fire of the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it burns away all afflictions and illuminates all dharmas, yet the aspiration associated with that wisdom is never exhausted.
Furthermore, although the Buddha is fully endowed with all wholesome qualities and merits, because sentient beings are not yet exhausted, his desire to deliver them does not cease.
Question:
If the Buddha’s desire to deliver sentient beings has not yet ceased, why does he enter nirvana? Answer:
There are two ways of delivering sentient beings:
some attain deliverance while [the Buddha] is present before them, and some attain deliverance after his parinirvāṇa.
As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "The Physician prepared medicine for his children, gave it to them, and then departed," and for this reason he entered nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose faculties are dull and whose merit is meager; because they cannot accomplish the great task, they can only plant the causal conditions for merit and virtue, and for this reason, they enter nirvana.
Question:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are still those who attain arhatship; why do you say that one can only plant the causal conditions for merit? Answer:
Although there are those who attain arhatship, they are so few as to be negligible.
For instance, when the Buddha preached the Dharma even once, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings throughout the ten directions attained the Way; this was not the case after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
For example, when a great nation wages war, even if it gains a small amount, it is not considered a true victory.
For this reason, although sentient beings have not yet been exhausted, one enters nirvana.
Furthermore, it is said in the Mahāyāna *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"In the world-system Adorned, the Buddha’s lifespan lasted seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, during which he liberated sentient beings."
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha’s desire does not diminish.
Regarding “the non-diminution of diligence,” as explained in the section on desire:
the meaning of desire is itself diligence.
Question:
If that were so, the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) would not exist.
Furthermore, since "desire" (chanda) and "diligence" (vīrya) are distinct among the mental factors (caitasika-dharma), how can it be said that "desire is itself diligence"?
The answer is:
"Desire" is the initial practice; when desire increases, it is called "diligence.
As the Buddha said:
"All phenomena have desire as their root.
Desire is like a person who, being thirsty, wishes to obtain a drink; diligence is like employing skillful means and conditions to seek that drink.
Desire is the mind's longing to obtain it, while diligence is the actualization of that undertaking.
Desire belongs to the mental action (manas-karma), while diligence belongs to the three types of action.
Desire is internal, and diligence is external.
Such are their distinctions.
Furthermore, this diligence is what all Buddhas delight in; for example, by the power of his diligence, Śākyamuni Buddha transcended nine kalpas and swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, as it is said:
At one time, the Buddha told Ānanda, "Preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus;
my back aches and I wish to rest for a short while."
At that time, the World-Honored One folded his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) into four layers, spread it out, and lay down with his outer robe (saṃghāṭī) as a pillow.

At that moment, Ānanda was expounding the meaning of the seven factors of enlightenment; when he reached the factor of enlightenment of energy (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga), the Buddha suddenly rose from his reclining position and said to Ānanda:
"Are you praising the meaning of energy?"
Ānanda said, “I praise it!
This was repeated three times.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
He cultivates diligence well until he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone other paths!
For this reason, the Buddha’s diligence never diminishes; even when ill, he does not cease, how much less so when not ill!

Furthermore, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Buddha relinquishes the bliss of profound meditative concentration and employs various bodies, various languages, and various powers of skillful means to liberate them.
At times they encounter evil and treacherous paths;
at times they consume unwholesome food;
and at times they suffer from cold and heat.
At times, when encountering various heterodox challenges and difficult-to-hear words, as well as insults and abuse, he endures them without weariness.
Although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses mastery over all phenomena, he performs such deeds without giving rise to indolence.
When the Buddha had finished delivering sentient beings, he lay down between the twin śāla trees in the Śāla forest.
The brahmin Subhadra said to Ānanda:
"I have heard that the All-Knowing One shall pass into parinirvāṇa this very night; I wish to see the Buddha!"
Ānanda stopped him, saying, "The Buddha has expounded the Dharma extensively for the multitude; he is utterly exhausted!
The Buddha heard this from afar and addressed Ānanda:
"Allow Subhadra to enter; he shall be my final disciple.

Once Subhadra had entered, he questioned the Buddha regarding his doubts. The Buddha preached the Dharma according to his needs, whereby Subhadra severed his doubts and attained the Way, entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* before the Buddha himself.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly rare!”
"Even until the very end, out of compassion for the non-Buddhist brahmins, he conversed with them.
The Buddha said, "It is not only in this present life that I deliver others at the very end; even in previous lives, when I had not yet attained the Way, I delivered others at the very end."

In the distant past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a great forest teeming with many birds and beasts. A wild fire broke out and began to burn from three sides; only on one side was it separated by a body of water. The animals were driven to the brink of desperation, with no place left to escape for their lives.

At that time, I was a large-bodied, powerful deer. Spanning one bank with my forefeet and bracing the other bank with my hind feet, I allowed the various beasts to tread upon my back as they crossed over. My skin and flesh were completely destroyed, yet through the power of compassion, I endured it until death.
The last rabbit arrived when his strength was already exhausted; he exerted himself with all his might and endured it so that [the others] might pass.
Once they had passed, his back broke, and he fell into the water and died!
Thus it has been for a long time, not only now.
Those who attained deliverance previously are my current disciples;
the last rabbit was Subhadra.
The Buddha delighted in the practice of diligence throughout his successive lives, and even now he does not cease; for this reason, it is said that "his diligence does not diminish.
Regarding "no diminution of mindfulness," because his mindfulness is in accord with all wisdom regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time, his mindfulness is complete and undiminished.
Question: Previously it was stated that "mindfulness has no loss," and now it is further stated that "mindfulness has no decrease.
Are "no loss of mindfulness" and "no decrease of mindfulness" one and the same?
Are they different?
If they are one, why are they stated repeatedly now?
If they are different, what distinction is there between them?
The answer is:
"Losing mindfulness" means error;
"diminution" means falling short.
"Lapse of mindfulness" refers to losing mindfulness regarding the modes of deportment—bending, bowing, coming, and going;
"without decrease" refers to abiding in meditative concentration and supernormal powers, maintaining mindfulness of the past and present worlds with unimpeded penetration.
Question:
For what reason is the non-decline of mindfulness unique to the Buddha-dharma? Answer:
Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have skillfully cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, their mindfulness is firm;
yet, although their mindfulness is firm, it is still diminished and obstructed, failing to achieve thorough penetration.
As it is said in the "Power of Knowledge of Past Lives":
"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas recollect past lives for at most eighty thousand kalpas; in other cases, this number is reduced."
Furthermore, even within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), one cannot discern [the three marks] in every moment of thought.

The Buddha, however, discerns the three marks in every single moment of thought; there is not a single phenomenon that the Buddha’s mind does not attend to. For this reason, the Buddha alone possesses mindfulness that never diminishes.
Furthermore, regarding the power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*), the Buddha possesses the power of recollective awareness (*anusmṛti*) therein;
even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess such power of recollection, let alone other people!
Furthermore, because the Buddha possesses the mindfulness protected by the unimpeded liberation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), his mindfulness does not diminish.
For such reasons as these, the Buddha’s mindfulness is never deficient.
Regarding "no diminution of wisdom": because the Buddha has attained all-encompassing wisdom, his wisdom does not diminish.
Because his wisdom regarding the three periods of time is unimpeded, his wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, because he has accomplished the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four unhindered knowledges, his wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, it is like a lamp: when the oil and ghee are abundant and the wick is pure, the light is also brilliant;

the Buddha is likewise so. With the oil of various samādhis such as the King of Samādhis and the clarity of the wick of undiminished mindfulness, by these causes and conditions, the light of his wisdom is immeasurable and never diminishes.

Furthermore, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because he has accumulated all wisdom and because his profound resolve is for the sake of the Dharma, he practices giving by relinquishing everything internal and external—his head, eyes, marrow, and brain—and undergoes every suffering such as entering fire, throwing himself from mountains, having his skin flayed, or being nailed to a stake; yet, because he single-mindedly accumulates wisdom, his wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s wisdom is perfected through the assistance of all merits, such as the observance of precepts and meditative concentration, his wisdom does not diminish.

Furthermore, because throughout successive lifetimes he has sought out and thoroughly studied all scriptures—both worldly and Buddhist, coarse and subtle, wholesome and unwholesome—his wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, because they hear the Dharma from immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, and because they read, recite, contemplate, practice, and inquire about it, their wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, for the sake of all sentient beings, for the purpose of increasing all wholesome dharmas, and for the purpose of destroying ignorance in all places, wisdom does not diminish.
Furthermore, this wisdom truly knows that the characteristics of all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither pure nor defiled, and without action or activity;
it does not discriminate between what is wisdom and what is non-wisdom. It knows that all dharmas are of one and the same nature, pure as space, without stain and without attachment.

Because it does not rely on dualistic dharmas, it attains entry into the non-dual dharma-characteristic; this entry into the non-dual dharma-characteristic is immeasurable and boundless. For this reason, wisdom does not diminish.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, wisdom does not diminish.
Regarding "liberation does not diminish," there are two kinds of liberation:
conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation.

Conditioned liberation is called liberation associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); unconditioned liberation is called the complete exhaustion of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) without remainder.
In these two types of liberation, the Buddha never diminishes.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not exceedingly sharp and their afflictions are not entirely exhausted, their wisdom undergoes diminution;
whereas because the Buddha’s wisdom is supremely sharp and the habitual tendencies of his afflictions are forever extinguished without remainder, his liberation is without diminution.
Furthermore, as explained in the section on the "Power of the Destruction of Outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-bala*), there is a distinction between the liberation of the Buddha and that of the Śrāvakas.
Because the Buddha has attained the power of the destruction of outflows, his liberation is without diminution;
because the followers of the two vehicles lack this power, their liberation is subject to diminution.

Regarding "the knowledge and vision of liberation is undiminished": because the Buddha’s wisdom within all liberations is immeasurable, boundless, and pure, it is called the "undiminished knowledge and vision of liberation."
Question: Since the Buddha has no deficiency in any dharma, for what reason is it said that he has no deficiency only in these six matters? Answer:
Among all forms of self-benefit and benefit for others, four matters can bring them to fulfillment:
"Aspiration" is the root of seeking all wholesome dharmas;
"Diligence" is that which enables their practice.
"Mindfulness" can guard [the mind], like a gatekeeper who allows the good to enter and wards off the evil;
"wisdom" illuminates all dharma-gates and cuts off all afflictions.
By employing these four dharmas, one's task will be accomplished.
There are two kinds of retribution for these four dharmas:
first, liberation; second, the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The meaning of "liberation" (vimukti) is as previously explained.
Regarding "knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimukti-jñāna-darśana), it is indeed knowledge and vision of liberation; this knowledge consists of the two characteristics of liberation:
conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) liberation.

He knows the characteristics of all liberations, namely: liberation by time and non-time liberation; liberation through wisdom and twofold liberation; mutable liberation and immutable liberation; the eight liberations; inconceivable liberation; and unimpeded liberation, and so forth.
