For example, the Arhat Bakula offered the medicinal fruit of a single *harītakī* as a gift; for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the evil realms, enjoying the blessings and happiness of devas and humans, his body was constantly free from illness, and in his final existence he attained the path of Arhatship.
Furthermore, for example, the śramaṇa Śāriputra (Vītaśoka) built a dwelling during the Dharma-period of Vipaśyin Buddha and offered it to the community of bhikṣus;
he spread out a sheepskin and had the monks tread upon it.
By reason of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas his feet did not touch the ground, and he experienced immeasurable blessings and happiness among gods and humans.

In his final birth, he was born into the family of a great elder; his physical form was upright and handsome, and beneath the soles of his feet grew hairs two inches long, the color of blue lapis lazuli, curling to the right.
At the time of his birth, his father gave him twenty billion taels of gold.
Later, becoming weary of the five desires of the world, he left the household life and attained the Way; the Buddha declared him the foremost among bhikṣus of diligent effort.
Furthermore, there was the bhikṣu Sumana, who in a previous life saw the stupa of Vipaśyin Buddha and offered a sumana flower from his ear as a gift.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas he never fell into the evil realms, but enjoyed the pleasures among devas and humans.
When his final birth occurred, a *sumana* flower was on his ear and its fragrance filled the entire room; therefore, he was named Sumana-karṇa (Flower-Ear).
Later, becoming weary of the world, he left the household life and attained the path of Arhatship.

Through such Jātaka tales and causal conditions as these, the Bodhisattva attains great retribution from even small acts of giving; thus, he practices generosity according to whatever he possesses, whether much or little.

Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that the Bodhisattva always gives only small things; rather, he gives according to what he has—giving much when there is much, and giving little when there is little.
Furthermore, because the Buddha wishes to praise the greatness of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*, he says: "A small gift yields a great fruit; its merit is immeasurable."
Question:
If even those such as the Arhat Bakula obtained great rewards from small offerings, what is the need for the Prajñāpāramitā?
Answer:
Although those such as Bakula have attained the fruits of retribution, they are limited by the duration of kalpas and enter nirvana through the realization of the Small Vehicle;
yet because a bodhisattva employs the "skillful dedication" of *prajñāpāramitā*, even a small gift results in merit that is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Question:
What is "skillful dedication" (*upāya-pariṇāmanā*), by which one obtains immeasurable and boundless merit through even a small act of giving?
Answer:
Although their acts of giving may be small, they dedicate them all toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"By means of these roots of merit, I do not seek the sovereignty of gods or humans, nor the pleasures of the world; I seek only *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Just as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is immeasurable and boundless, so too is this merit immeasurable and boundless;
furthermore, because this merit is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, and just as sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless, so too is this merit immeasurable and boundless."
Furthermore, because this merit employs great compassion, and because great compassion is immeasurable and boundless, this merit is also immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva’s merit is in harmony with the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is pure in three aspects:
for the recipient, the giver, and the material gift are all ungraspable.
As stated at the beginning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it was said to Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva practices giving, because the giver, the receiver, and the gift cannot be apprehended, he fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
Because one practices giving with this wisdom of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), one attains immeasurable and boundless merit.

Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva contemplates all merit as having the mark of suchness (*tathatā*), the mark of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the mark of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and because suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality are immeasurable and boundless, this merit is also immeasurable and boundless.
Question:

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the true mark of all dharmas and knows suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—which are marks of unconditioned cessation (*asaṃskṛta-nirodha*)—how can they further give rise to the mind to cultivate merit?
The answer is:
Because the Bodhisattva has long practiced the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), at that time the mind of great compassion arises:
"Sentient beings do not know the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena; I shall cause them to attain this true nature."

By the power of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one returns to practicing the causes and conditions of meritorious deeds; thus, the perfection of diligence assists the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
It is like a fire about to go out which, upon encountering wind and fuel, blazes up even more intensely.
Furthermore, because he recollects his original vows, the Buddhas of the ten directions also come and say to him:
"You should recollect the time when you first resolved your mind on enlightenment!
Moreover, you have only just attained this one dharma-gate; there are immeasurable dharma-gates such as these that you have not yet all attained—you must gather all further merits!"
As it is said in the *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta* (The Gradual Preparation Sūtra) regarding the seventh stage.
Question: It may be granted that there is a measure of how much is given; however—

Within the precepts, there are the five precepts, the one-day precepts, and the ten precepts; their relative fewness or manyness can also be known because the dharmas of form (rūpa-dharma) can be distinguished.
As for the remaining four pāramitās, how is their fewness or manyness to be known?
Answer: All of these can be known.
For example, there are two kinds of patience (kṣānti):
The first is patience of the body; the second is patience of the mind.
As for patience of the body, although the body and speech do not move, the mind cannot be prevented from arising; because this is but a minor form of patience, it cannot control the mind.
As for patience of the mind, both body and mind are patient together, like a withered tree.
Furthermore, "minor patience" refers to when a person is beaten or reviled but does not retaliate;
"great patience" refers to not making distinctions between the one who reviles, the one who endures, or the act of enduring.
Furthermore, among sentient beings, patience is considered minor patience, while patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) is considered great patience.
Such is the differentiation of "minor patience.
As for "minor progress":
There are two types:
physical exertion and mental exertion.
Physical exertion is minor; mental exertion is great.
External exertion is minor; internal exertion is great.
Exertion of body and speech is minor; exertion of mind is great.
As the Buddha said:
"Because the power of mental karma is so great, when a Great Seer (maharṣi) is angry, he can cause a great kingdom to perish.
Furthermore, if one commits the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) through body or speech, the great retribution is to remain in the Avīci hell for one kalpa."

The power of mental karma is great; by it, one may be born in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with a lifespan of eighty thousand great kalpas, or likewise dwell in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions with an immeasurable lifespan.
For this reason, one knows that physical and verbal diligence are minor, while mental diligence is great.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"If the actions of body, speech, and mind are quiescent and unmoving, this is called great diligence."
"Moving" refers to having little vigor (*vīrya*).
Such instances as these are termed "little vigor. Regarding "little meditation" (*dhyāna*):
the concentration of desire (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) and the stage of access (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) are called "little" because they have not yet transcended desire.
One also contemplates the second dhyāna; therein, the first dhyāna is "small," and this continues up to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is small, while that which is without outflows (anāsrava) is great.

The meditative concentration (dhyāna) of one who has not yet attained avaivartika status or the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattikadharmakṣānti) is small; the meditative concentration of one who has attained avaivartika status or the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is great.

Up to the point of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the concentration associated with the sixteen liberations (*vimokṣa*) is considered small, while the seventeenth, the adamantine samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*), is considered great.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as eternally concentrated and without distraction—being without dependence and without conceptual differentiation—this is considered great;
all others are considered small.
Wisdom is of two kinds:
first, worldly; second, supramundane.
Worldly wisdom is minor, while supramundane wisdom is great.

The same applies to pure wisdom and mixed wisdom; wisdom of signs and wisdom of signlessness; discriminative wisdom and non-discriminative wisdom; wisdom that conforms to the Dharma and wisdom that penetrates the Dharma; wisdom for the sake of birth and death and wisdom for the sake of nirvāṇa; wisdom for one's own benefit and wisdom for the benefit of all sentient beings, and so forth.
Furthermore, wisdom derived from hearing is small, while wisdom derived from reflection is great;
wisdom derived from reflection is small, while wisdom derived from cultivation is great;
wisdom with outflows is small, while wisdom without outflows is great.
The wisdom of one who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is small, while the wisdom of practicing the six perfections is great;
the wisdom of cultivation is small, while the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*) is great;
within the various stages (*bhūmi*), the wisdom of skillful means progressively increases from small to great, up to the tenth stage.

Regarding such distinctions of quantity as these, the Buddha praised the bodhisattva’s extraordinariness: that one attains immeasurable and boundless merit from even a minor matter—how much more so, then, for a great matter!

Other people mostly give away wealth, yet they obtain little merit despite the diligent toil of their body, speech, and mind; the same applies to their observance of precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—it does not equal that of a bodhisattva, whose small acts yield great retribution.
As it was said before:
"For example, when sound is produced from the breath of the mouth, the sound does not travel far;
but when the sound enters a horn, the sound can travel far."
"In this way, although the giving and other practices are equal and slight, the merit and reward obtained by other people from performing them is small;
yet because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates [the merit] through the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) of the Prajñāpāramitā, they obtain immeasurable and boundless merit."
For this reason it is said:

“One who wishes to practice a small amount of giving, a small amount of morality, a small amount of patience, a small amount of diligence, a small amount of meditation, and a small amount of wisdom [should study the Perfection of Wisdom].
[Sūtra] “A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, and dhyānapāramitā should study the prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] The meaning of the various pāramitās is as previously explained. Question:
Are the characteristics of the five pāramitās identical to the characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā?
If this were the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there should not be a distinction among these five names!
If they were different, for what reason would it be said: "One who wishes to practice the *dānapāramitā* should study the *prajñāpāramitā*"?
Answer: It is both the same and different. As for the difference:
because the name "Prajñāpāramitā" refers to contemplating the true mark of all dharmas, it neither accepts nor clings to any dharma.
*Dāna* (giving) is defined as relinquishing all that one possesses, both internal and external.
When one practices giving with the mind of *prajñāpāramitā*, at that time, *dāna* receives the name *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, while the five *pāramitās* plant various roots of merit, *prajñāpāramitā* eliminates attachment to the mind and false views.
It is like one person sowing grain and another weeding out the various weeds, so that it may grow and the fruit be brought to fruition.
The same applies to the other four pāramitās.
Question:
How is it that "one who wishes to practice the dānapāramitā should study the prajñāpāramitā"? Answer:
There are two kinds of giving: first, pure; second, impure.
As for the impure, one gives out of pride, thinking:
Thinking, "If even an inferior person gives, how could I not be able to?
one gives out of envy, making this thought:
"Because my enemy gives, he gains renown; thus he surpasses me."
"Now I shall give extensively; I must certainly surpass him.
Giving out of a desire for reward, he thinks:
"I give a small thing, yet I shall receive a thousand-millionfold reward."
Therefore, one gives as an act of charity for the sake of reputation, thinking:
"I am now a generous donor, trusted by others, and counted among the ranks of good people."
Giving for the sake of attracting people, with the thought:
"By giving this now, people will surely come to me"—
such various forms of giving performed with entanglements are called impure.

Regarding pure giving: it is free from such entanglements; rather, with a pure mind one believes in the causes and effects of karmic retribution, respects and has compassion for the recipient, seeks no benefit in this life, and aims solely for merit in future lives.
Furthermore, there is pure giving that does not seek benefit in future lives, but merely cultivates the mind to assist in the pursuit of nirvana.

Again, there is pure giving that gives rise to great compassion; for the sake of sentient beings, it does not seek one's own self-interest or the early attainment of nirvana, but is solely for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is called pure giving.
Because they possess the mind of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to perform such pure giving.
For this reason, it is said:
"One who wishes to practice the *dānapāramitā* should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Furthermore, by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one abandons the mind that clings to all phenomena; how much more so should one abandon attachment to one's own mind!
Because one has abandoned the "I" and "mine," one regards one's body, wife, and children as mere grass and soil, having no lingering affection or regret, and gives them all away in alms.
For this reason it is said:
"One who wishes to practice the dānapāramitā should study the prajñāpāramitā.
The same applies to all the other pāramitās, because they are brought to completion through the assistance of the mind of prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, the other perfections, if they do not obtain the perfection of wisdom, do not obtain the name "perfection," nor are they firm.
As it is said in a later chapter:
"If the five perfections do not obtain the perfection of wisdom, they lack the designation 'perfection.
It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, if he lacks the wheel-treasure, is not called a wheel-turning sage king; he is not designated by the name of any other treasure."
It is also like a group of blind people who, without a guide, cannot reach their destination;
likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā guides the five pāramitās, causing them to reach sarvajñatā.
For example, a great army without a valiant general cannot accomplish its task;
likewise, even if a person’s other faculties are complete, if they lack eyes, they cannot reach their destination.
Furthermore, just as when a person lacks the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), all other faculties perish, whereas because the life-faculty exists, the other faculties remain functional;
so it is with the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): if the five perfections do not obtain the Perfection of Wisdom, they cannot increase.
Because one attains the Prajñāpāramitā, the other pāramitās attain increase and fulfillment.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"One who wishes to practice the Dānapāramitā should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Sūtra] "A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause his body in every lifetime to resemble that of a Buddha, and who wishes to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] Question:
The Śrāvaka sūtras state that after a Bodhisattva has passed through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they plant the causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks during one hundred kalpas.
Now, how can it be said that "in every lifetime one’s body is similar to that of a Buddha, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics"?
The answer is:
such a statement exists within Kātyāyanīputra’s *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*, but it is not what is taught in the Tripiṭaka.
Why is this? The thirty-two marks are possessed by others as well; how can they alone be considered noble!
For example, in a previous life, Nanda once bathed the assembly of monks and made a vow, saying:
"May I be upright, virtuous, pure, and clean in every lifetime.
Furthermore, in another life, he encountered a stūpa of a pratyekabuddha; he adorned it with colorful paintings and embellished the image of the pratyekabuddha, making this aspiration:
"May my physical form be majestic and beautiful in every lifetime."

By reason of these causes and conditions, he obtained physical marks of adornment in life after life; even in his final body, when he left the household life to become a śramaṇa, the assembly of monks saw him from afar and, thinking he was the Buddha, all rose to greet him.

If even Nanda, who cultivated only a small measure of merit within the Lesser Vehicle, still obtained this retribution, how much more so for a Bodhisattva who has established merit throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—how could his physical form from lifetime to lifetime not resemble that of a Buddha?
Furthermore, when Maitreya Bodhisattva was a layman, his teacher was named Bāvarī, who possessed three marks:
first, the mark of white hair between the eyebrows; second, the mark of a tongue that can cover the face; and third, the mark of the concealed organ.
Such as these, even those who are not Bodhisattvas possess these marks; how could a Bodhisattva only plant the seeds for the marks and signs after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas?

Furthermore, within this Mahāyāna, there are Bodhisattvas who, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never give rise to an evil mind;
in every lifetime they obtain the five supernormal powers as a karmic retribution, and their bodies resemble those of a Buddha.
Question:
Since a bodhisattva has not yet attained the path of Buddhahood, how can they possess bodily marks like those of a Buddha? Answer:

For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the Bodhisattva may manifest as the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or the body of Śakra, or the body of a Brahmā King, or the body of a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, a Bodhisattva, or a Buddha.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī himself said:
"I have returned seventy-two billion times to become a pratyekabuddha and entered parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, he manifests as a Buddha named Nāgagotra-guru;

although at that time it was not yet the destined era for a Buddha to appear, sentient beings beheld the Buddha’s body, and with hearts filled with joy and submission, they received his transformation.
Question:
If a bodhisattva is able to manifest the body of a Buddha, preach the Dharma, and deliver sentient beings, what difference is there between them and a Buddha?
Answer:

The Bodhisattva possesses great supernormal powers; dwelling in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), he is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma and remains in the world to extensively deliver sentient beings, and thus does not enter *nirvāṇa*.
He is also like a magician who manifests a transformed body to preach the Dharma for others, yet it is not the true body of a Buddha;
although he thus delivers sentient beings, there is a measure and limit to it.
Those saved by the Buddha are immeasurable and limitless.
Although a bodhisattva may manifest in the body of a Buddha, they cannot pervade the worlds of the ten directions;
the Buddha-body, however, can universally pervade immeasurable worlds, and for all those who are to be saved, he manifests in the form of a Buddha.
It is also like the moon on the fourteenth day; although it possesses radiance, it is still not equal to that of the fifteenth day.
Such is the distinction.

There may be bodhisattvas who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), possess bodies born of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-nirmita-kāya*), abide in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), dwell in the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and manifest transformed bodies like those of a Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings.

Alternatively, there are bodhisattvas who, having first resolved their minds, practice the six pāramitās; through the causes and conditions of these practices, they attain bodies resembling those of a Buddha to teach and transform sentient beings.
Question:

The thirty-two marks are the retribution for practices such as giving (*dāna*). Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent and like empty space, why is it said that "one who wishes to obtain the marks and secondary characteristics should study the *prajñāpāramitā*"?
Answer: There are two kinds of the thirty-two marks:
first, those that are fully perfected like those of a Buddha; [the second is those that are partially perfected].
Second, there is non-perfection, as in the case of the Cakravartin kings, Nanda, and others.
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is conjoined with giving, one can become fully endowed with the marks and signs like a Buddha;
other people who merely practice giving and so forth do not possess these marks in their entirety.
Question:
How do [practices] such as giving result in the attainment of the thirty-two marks? Answer:

Just as when a donor gives alms, the recipient gains five benefits for the body, such as physical form and strength, the donor thereby fulfills the mark of the wheels on the palms and soles of the hands and feet,
as explained in detail in the "Dānapāramitā" [chapter].
The same applies to morality, patience, and so forth; each is endowed with the thirty-two marks.
What are these thirty-two marks?
The first is the mark of level feet; the others are as described in the "Chapter on Praising the Bodhisattva."
Question:
By what causes and conditions does one obtain the mark of level feet? Answer:

Throughout his successive lives, the Buddha maintained the precepts with single-minded firmness and did not allow others to break them. By virtue of these karmic causes and conditions, he attained this first mark.
As for this first mark: within the Dharma, there is no one capable of moving him;
were he to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, there would be no one capable of invading his realm.
By protecting the people and those who have gone forth as śramaṇas in accordance with the Dharma, through these karmic causes and conditions, he obtains the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel;
this is the initial sign of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and if he becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he obtains the precious wheel-treasure.
By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of abstaining from taking life, one attains the mark of long fingers.
By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of abstaining from taking what is not given, one attains the mark of full heels.
By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of gathering sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one attains the mark of webbed hands and feet.
By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of making offerings of superior garments, food and drink, and bedding to one's elders, one attains the mark of soft and supple hands and feet.

By virtue of the karmic causes and conditions of increasing merit through cultivation, one attains the mark of high-arched heels, the mark of a single hair growing from each pore, and the mark of body hairs that point upward.

Because he dispatched messengers in accordance with the Dharma as a cause and condition for the harmony of merit, and because he swiftly instructed others, he attained the mark of exquisite calves, like those of the king of the eneya deer.

By giving pure things in accordance with the Dharma and not causing distress to the recipient, one attains the mark of standing upright with hands reaching below the knees and the mark of a symmetrical body like that of the nyagrodha tree.

By frequently cultivating a sense of shame and dread of blame, by abstaining from sexual misconduct, and by giving away dwellings, clothing, and coverings as acts of charity, one attains the mark of the male organ being concealed within a sheath, like that of a horse king.

By practicing the samādhi of loving-kindness, by having abundant purity of faith and mind, and by giving fine food, drink, clothing, and bedding, one attains the golden-hued mark and the mark of great radiance.
Because he always delighted in inquiring about the meaning [of the Dharma] and provided for those he revered as well as virtuous persons, he obtained the mark of fine and soft skin.

Because he adjudicated matters according to the Dharma, did not act with self-willed obstinacy, and entrusted authority to those capable of governance, he obtained the marks of an upper body like that of a lion, full armpits, and rounded shoulders.
Because he respectfully honored his elders and received them with welcoming and seeing them off, he obtained the mark of a straight and broad body.
Because his generosity was complete and full, he obtained the mark of the seven parts of the body being well-filled.
Because he practices total generosity without any sense of regret or stinginess, he attains the mark of broad and full cheeks.
Because he abstains from double-tongued speech, he attains the marks of having forty teeth, teeth that are even, and teeth that are closely set.
Because he constantly practiced loving-kindness and delighted in reflection, he obtained the mark of white, incomparable teeth.
Because he abstained from false speech, he obtained the mark of a broad and thin tongue.
Because he gave delicious food and did not distress the recipient, he obtained the mark of the supreme sense of taste among all tastes.
Because he abstained from harsh speech, he obtained the mark of the Brahma-voice.
Because he looked upon sentient beings with a virtuous mind and kind eyes, he obtained the mark of eyelashes that are deep blue-black and the mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king.
Because he reverently honored those worthy of respect, maintained his own precepts, and instructed others in the precepts, he attained the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
Because he praised those who were worthy of praise, he attained the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
This constitutes the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks according to the Śrāvaka-dharma.
Regarding the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks within the Mahāyāna,
it is asked:
The Buddhas of the ten directions and all phenomena of the three periods of time are all characterized by the mark of signlessness; why, then, do you now speak of the thirty-two marks?
If even a single mark is not real, how much less so the thirty-two?
Answer: The Buddha-dharma has two aspects:
first, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); second, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of the thirty-two marks;
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one speaks of marklessness.
There are two kinds of paths:
First is causing sentient beings to cultivate the path of merit, and second is the path of wisdom.
Because of the path of merit, the thirty-two marks are taught;
because of the path of wisdom, the signless is taught.
For the sake of the birth-body (*janmakāya*), the thirty-two marks are taught;
for the sake of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the markless is taught.
The Buddha’s body is adorned by the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
The Dharma-body is adorned with the merits of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities.
Sentient beings possess two kinds of causes and conditions:
first, the cause and condition of merit; second, the cause and condition of wisdom.
In order to guide sentient beings through the causes and conditions of merit, he employs a body endowed with the thirty-two marks;
in order to guide sentient beings through the causes and conditions of wisdom, he employs the Dharma-body.
There are two kinds of sentient beings:
first, those who know that all phenomena are merely provisional names; second, those who are attached to names.
For the sake of those sentient beings who are attached to names, the signless (animitta) is taught.
Because one seeks to know that all phenomena are merely provisional designations for sentient beings, the thirty-two marks are taught.
Question: Since these ten powers and four fearlessnesses also each possess their own distinct characteristics, why is it said that "the Dharma-body is markless"?
Answer: All untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are called "signless" (*animitta*) because they are associated with the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) and the three samādhis;
however, because the Buddha wishes to cause sentient beings to understand them, he explains them through various distinctions.
He expounds all the teachings of the Buddhas by means of the seals of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; thus, they all enter into suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality.
Yet, for those who see his physical form and joyfully resolve their minds on the Way, he manifests a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, in order to manifest supreme excellence among all sentient beings, he displays the thirty-two marks without violating the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
For example, within seven days of his birth, the Bodhisattva was wrapped in white cotton cloth and presented to various physiognomists.
The physiognomist consulted the ancient scriptures on the marks of the sages and replied to the king:

"According to my prophetic records, if a person possesses the thirty-two marks, they shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King if they remain at home, or attain Buddhahood if they leave the household life."
"Only these two possibilities exist; there is no third.
After the physiognomists had departed, the Bodhisattva went to rest.
Then there was a seer named Asita, who addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"By means of my divine ear, I have heard the devas and spirits say that King Śuddhodana has borne a son who possesses the physical marks of a Buddha; therefore, they have come to request an audience!
The King was greatly delighted, thinking, "This person is a sage and a holy one, and thus has come from afar wishing to see my son.
He then commanded his attendants:
"Take the prince out!
The attendant replied to the king,
"The prince is taking a short nap."
At that time, Asita said, "The Holy King has always invited all to partake of ambrosia; you should not sleep!
He immediately rose from his seat, went to where the Prince was, took him onto his arms, and examined his features from head to toe.
Having performed the divination, he wept profusely, unable to restrain himself!
The King was greatly displeased and asked the soothsayer,
"What inauspicious omen is there that you weep so?"
The seer replied, "Even if the heavens were to rain down great mountains of vajra, they could not move a single hair of his; how could there be any inauspiciousness!
The Prince will surely become a Buddha."
"I am now already advanced in years; I shall be reborn in the formless heavens, where I will neither be able to see the Buddha nor hear his Dharma. It is for this reason that I grieve!"
The king said:
“The various physiognomists have spoken with uncertainty regarding one matter: if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves the home life, he shall become a Buddha.”
Asita said: "The various physiognomists rely on worldly inference rather than the knowledge of the divine eye;

furthermore, the sacred treatises on physiognomy do not provide complete or universal knowledge. Observing the marks only in their general outlines, they cannot discern them with clarity and precision; for this reason, some say:..."
"If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves the home life, he shall become a Buddha.
Now the Prince’s thirty-two marks are perfectly complete, radiant and clear, profoundly deep, pure, and fully endowed; he will certainly become a Buddha, not a Wheel-Turning King!
For this reason, it is known that the thirty-two marks are the most preeminent among all sentient beings.

As for the term "the dharma of marklessness," it is spoken thus in order to shatter the marks of permanence, purity, bliss, and self, as well as the marks of male and female, birth and death, and so forth.

For this reason, although the Buddha-dharma is characterized by the mark of signlessness, it manifests the thirty-two marks to guide sentient beings, causing them to know that the Buddha is supreme and to give rise to pure faith; thus, there is no fault in speaking of the thirty-two marks.
Question:
For what reason are the thirty-two marks taught, neither more nor less?
Answer:
Whether one speaks of many or few, both positions would be subject to objection.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s body is sixteen feet tall; if one were to describe it as having fewer marks, it would not be all-encompassing and would lack full adornment;
yet if it were to exceed the thirty-two marks, it would become confused and disordered.
For example, although one may possess an abundance of pearls and gems for adorning the body, one cannot wear too many necklaces;
likewise, the thirty-two marks are neither too many nor too few, but exactly attain the proper measure.
Furthermore, if there were fewer than these, they would not be perfectly dignified;
if there were more, they would be cluttered and disordered. Question:
If the eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are required, why are they not all called "marks" (lakṣaṇa) instead of being designated separately as "secondary marks"?
The answer is:
the primary marks greatly adorn the body; if one speaks of the great, the small is already included therein.

Furthermore, the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are coarse while the refinements (*anuvyañjana*) are subtle; when sentient beings see the Buddha, they see his marks, whereas the refinements are difficult to perceive.
Moreover, the marks are shared by others, while the refinements may be either shared or unshared.
For this reason, "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "minor characteristics" (*anuvyañjana*) are explained separately. Question:

Since the Buddha has ultimately severed the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a self, and is fully endowed with the mark of the dharma of emptiness, for what reason does he adorn himself with marks as if he were one who grasps at marks?
The answer is:

If the Buddha were to adorn his mind solely with the sublime Dharma while his body lacked the primary and secondary marks, there might be certain beings to be delivered who would give rise to contempt, thinking that the Buddha’s physical characteristics are incomplete and thus unable to single-mindedly delight in receiving the Buddha-Dharma.
For example, it is like using an impure vessel to hold various delicacies; people do not find it pleasing.
Or like using a stinking leather bag to hold various precious objects; those who take them do not rejoice.
For this reason, the Buddha adorns his body with the thirty-two marks.
Furthermore, the Buddha constantly utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, saying:
"Among all sentient beings, I am the foremost in all meritorious virtues!"
If the Buddha’s physical body were not adorned with the primary marks and secondary characteristics, some might say:
"His form is ugly; what could he possibly know?

Since sentient beings still harbor such lack of faith even when his body is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, how much more so would this be the case if he were not adorned with these marks and characteristics!

Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep; because it is characterized by eternal quiescence, deluded and ignorant sentient beings do not believe in or accept it, claiming that when the body is extinguished, there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped.

For this reason, the Buddha, with his broad and long tongue, Brahma-like voice, and by emitting great light from his body, preaches the supreme and wondrous Dharma through various causes, conditions, and parables;
when sentient beings behold the physical marks and majestic virtue of the Buddha’s body and hear his voice, they all rejoice with faith and delight.
Furthermore, there are internal and external forms of adornment for beings. Such qualities as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute internal adornment;
physical marks, majestic virtue, and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) constitute external adornment.
The Buddha is fully endowed with both the internal and the external.

Furthermore, the Buddha, out of compassion for all sentient beings, appears in the world; through his wisdom and other such merits, he benefits those with sharp faculties, and through the adornment of his physical marks, he benefits those with dull faculties.
The adornment of the mind opens the gate to nirvāṇa;
the adornment of the body opens the gates to the joys of devas and humans.
Because of the adornment of the body, one establishes sentient beings in the three bases of merit.
Because of the adornment of the mind, they establish sentient beings in the three gates of liberation;
because of the adornment of the body, they extricate sentient beings from the three evil realms;
because of the adornment of the mind, they extricate sentient beings from the prison of the triple world.
For the sake of such immeasurable causes and conditions of benefit, the physical body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks.

[Sūtra] "Those who wish to be born into the family of Bodhisattvas, who wish to attain the stage of *kumārabhūta*, and who wish never to be separated from the Buddhas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Treatise] Regarding the "family of bodhisattvas": if one gives rise to a profoundly deep mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings, this constitutes being born into the family of bodhisattvas.
Just as one born into a royal family is not dared to be slighted by others, nor does one fear hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the like;

so too is it when one enters the path of a bodhisattva and is born into the family of bodhisattvas. Because they are sons of the Buddha, none among the devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or various sages dare to slight them, but instead treat them with even greater reverence.
They do not fear the evil realms or lowly states among humans and devas, nor do they fear śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhist teachers coming to obstruct their resolve.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva first resolves their mind, they single-mindedly make this vow:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer follow any evil thoughts; I desire only to deliver all sentient beings and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva can know the true mark of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, they will attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
from that point onward, they shall abide eternally in the bodhisattva path.
As previously stated in the *Cittadhāraṇī-sūtra*:
"When I beheld Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and first became fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*;
prior to that, there was no giving, upholding of precepts, or other such practices at all."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva should form this thought:
"Suppose an eon as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were made into one day and night; with such days and nights, thirty days would constitute a month, and twelve months a year.

If, after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of such years, only a single Buddha appears, and at that Buddha's place, one makes offerings, maintains the precepts, and accumulates all manner of merit;"
After encountering as many Buddhas as there are sands in the Ganges River, they will subsequently receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Throughout this process, the bodhisattvas’ minds remain untiring; they do not sink into despondency nor grow weary, but joyfully practice all these deeds.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva gives rise to compassion for those beings who are fixed in false views, those who have committed the five heinous crimes, and those who have severed their roots of goodness, leading them to enter the right path without seeking any reward for their kindness.
Furthermore, from the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they are neither obscured nor destroyed by the various afflictions.
Furthermore, although a bodhisattva contemplates the true reality of all phenomena, they do not give rise to attachment even toward the mind that performs such contemplation.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva naturally always speaks truthful words with his mouth, and does not utter false speech even in dreams.

Furthermore, whatever forms the Bodhisattva perceives are all the forms of the Buddha; by the power of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), he remains unattached even to these forms.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees all sentient beings wandering through the suffering of birth and death and amidst all forms of pleasure, their mind remains unattached; they merely make this aspiration:
"When shall I and all sentient beings be delivered?"
Furthermore, the bodhisattva does not give rise to attachment toward any precious jewels, but delights solely in the Three Jewels.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva constantly severs sexual desire, such that even the thought of it does not arise, let alone the actual act!
Furthermore, any sentient being who sees the Bodhisattva with their own eyes immediately attains the Samādhi of Loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).

Moreover, the Bodhisattva is able to cause all phenomena to become entirely the Buddha-dharma, such that there are no various distinctions between the dharmas of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary worldlings.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva discriminates all phenomena, yet within all phenomena, he gives rise neither to the notion of "phenomenon" nor to the notion of "non-phenomenon."
Through such immeasurable causes and conditions as these, this is called "being born into the family of bodhisattvas. Question:

Since one has already been born into the family of bodhisattvas from the moment the mind [of awakening] was first generated, why is it said here that "one who wishes to be born into the family of bodhisattvas should study the Prajñāpāramitā"?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of bodhisattva families:

the family of those who regress and the family of those who do not regress; the nominal family and the actual family; the pure family and the mixed family; and the family with firm faith and the family with unfirm faith.
For the sake of the family of non-retrogression, up to the family of firm faith, and because one desires to attain such families as these, it is said:
"One who wishes to be born into the family of Bodhisattvas should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

Regarding "desiring to attain the stage of *kumārabhūta*": there may be a bodhisattva who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), abandons sensual desire and constantly practices the bodhisattva path until reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called the stage of *kumārabhūta*.
Furthermore, there may be a bodhisattva who makes this vow:
"In birth after birth, may I remain a celibate youth (*kumāra*), leave the household life to practice the Way, and not receive worldly sensual desires. This is called the stage of the *kumārabhūmi*.
Furthermore, it is also like a prince named Kumāra; the Buddha is the Dharma King.
Because Bodhisattvas have entered the correct position of the Dharma up to the tenth stage (bhūmi), they are all called princes and are all destined to become Buddhas.
Just as Mañjuśrī, because he fully possesses the Buddha-activities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, dwells in the stage of Kumārabhūta and extensively delivers sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is like a youth who is over four years of age but not yet twenty; he is called a *kumārabhūta* (youth).
If a Bodhisattva is newly born into the family of Bodhisattvas, he is like an infant;

once he has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), being free from all evil deeds, this is called the stage of the *kumārabhūta*.
"If one wishes to attain such a stage, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
As for "always wishing not to be separated from the Buddhas," it means that in every lifetime where a bodhisattva is born, they always encounter the Buddhas.
Question:
Since a bodhisattva should transform sentient beings, for what reason do they always desire to encounter a Buddha? Answer:

Because there are bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the bodhisattva stage and have not yet attained the prediction of non-retrogression (avaivartika), if they distance themselves from the Buddhas, they will destroy their roots of goodness, sink into the afflictions, and being unable to save themselves, how could they possibly save others?
It is like a person riding in a boat who, when it is wrecked in midstream, wishes to ferry others across but instead sinks into the water himself;
or like a small amount of hot water poured into a great pool of ice, which, though it melts a small portion, only results in that spot freezing over all the more.

If a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stage of the fixed dharma-position (niyāma) distances himself from the Buddhas, and with meager merit and a lack of skillful means (*upāya*) attempts to transform sentient beings, although there may be some slight benefit, he will instead fall back into ruin!
For this reason, a newly initiated bodhisattva should not distance themselves from the Buddhas.
Question: If that is so, why does the text not say "not being separated from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"?
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can also benefit bodhisattvas.
The answer is:

although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the benefit of nirvāṇa, because they lack omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they are unable to instruct or guide bodhisattvas. Their resolve is great; thus, even though śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have the benefit of nirvāṇa, because they lack omniscience, they cannot teach or lead bodhisattvas.
Because the Buddhas possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to instruct and guide Bodhisattvas.
Just as an elephant that has sunk into the mud cannot emerge by any means other than another elephant, so it is with the Bodhisattva:
if one enters upon a wrong path, only a Buddha can provide salvation, for they share the same Great Path.
For this reason, it is said that a bodhisattva always desires not to be separated from the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"Because I have not yet attained the Buddha-eye, I am no different from one who is blind; if I am not guided by the Buddha, I shall have no direction and will mistakenly enter other paths."
Furthermore, even if one hears the Buddha-dharma while traveling in a distant land, one may not yet know the proper timing for teaching others or the extent of the practices to be performed.

Moreover, when a bodhisattva sees the Buddha, they obtain various benefits; their mind becomes pure upon seeing him with their eyes, and if they hear what he teaches, their mind delights in the Dharma, attains great wisdom, practices in accordance with the Dharma, and thereby achieves liberation.
Since such benefits as these are immeasurable and equal to those of encountering a Buddha, how could one not single-mindedly seek to behold a Buddha?

It is like an infant who should not be separated from its mother; like a traveler on a journey who does not leave behind his provisions; like one in great heat who cannot do without cool breezes or cold water; like one in great cold who does not wish to be parted from fire; like one crossing deep waters who should not be parted from a boat; and like a sick person who does not leave behind a skilled physician.
A Bodhisattva’s non-separation from the Buddhas exceeds all these matters.
Why is this? Because neither parents, nor relatives, nor acquaintances, nor humans, nor celestial kings can provide benefit equal to that of the Buddha;
the Buddha benefits all bodhisattvas by causing them to leave all places of suffering and dwell in the stage of the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the bodhisattva is never separated from the Buddha.
It is asked:
conditioned phenomena are deceptive and unreal; none of them are to be trusted.
How does one obtain that which accords with their wishes and remain inseparable from all Buddhas?
The answer is:
because they are fully endowed with merit and wisdom, they shall attain Buddhahood; how much more so, then, will they remain inseparable from all Buddhas!
Because sentient beings possess the karmic conditions of offenses from immeasurable kalpas, they do not attain their wishes;
although they practice merit, their wisdom is meager, and although they practice wisdom, their merit is meager, and thus their aspirations are not fulfilled.
Because Bodhisattvas seek the Buddha-way, they must practice two kinds of patience:
patience toward sentient beings (sattvakṣānti) and patience toward phenomena (dharmakṣānti).

By practicing patience toward sentient beings, they give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion among all living beings, extinguish the sins of immeasurable kalpas, and attain immeasurable merit and virtue.
Because they practice the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), they shatter the ignorance regarding all phenomena and attain immeasurable wisdom.
Because these two practices are in harmony, there is no vow that cannot be fulfilled!
For this reason, the Bodhisattva never departs from the Buddhas throughout successive lifetimes.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly delights in mindfulness of the Buddha, they encounter a Buddha in every successive rebirth after casting off one body and receiving another.
For example, if sentient beings have a heavy habituation to desire, they take the bodies of lustful birds, such as peacocks, mandarin ducks, and the like;
if their habituation to anger is particularly excessive, they are born among venomous creatures, such as malevolent dragons, rākṣasas, centipedes, poisonous snakes, and so forth.

This bodhisattva’s mind does not prize the status of a wheel-turning sage king or the blissful merits of humans and devas; rather, it contemplates only the Buddhas. Therefore, he receives a physical form according to what his mind values most.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly and skillfully cultivates the causal conditions for the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, they always encounter the Buddhas in every place of rebirth.
As it is said in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*:
"When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they immediately see Amitābha Buddha."
He then asked that Buddha:
"By what karmic causes and conditions was this land brought into being?
The Buddha immediately replied:
“Good son! Because you have constantly cultivated the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha and maintained this recollection without ceasing, you shall be born in my land. He asked:
What is the Buddha-remembrance samādhi by which one is born in that land?
The answer is:

as for "Buddha-remembrance," it means to remember the Buddha’s thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs, his golden body from which light radiates, filling the ten directions; it is like refined Jāmbūnada gold, its color bright and pure.
Furthermore, it is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, in the great ocean; when the sunlight shines upon it, its color becomes brilliantly manifest.

At that time, the practitioner has no perception of other forms whatsoever—such as mountains, the earth, trees, and so forth—but sees only the bodily marks of the Buddhas within the void, appearing like red gold manifesting from within genuine lapis lazuli.
It is also like a bhikṣu who enters the contemplation of impurity and sees only the body bloated and decaying, even until he sees only a skeleton;
this skeleton has no creator, nor does it come or go—it is seen only through the power of mental recollection and conceptualization.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, they see all buddhas in this very same way;
for they have gathered their minds and their minds are pure.
For example, it is like a person who adorns their body and looks into a clear water mirror; there is nothing they do not see.
Yet within this water or mirror there is no actual form or image; it is because of its clarity and purity that the reflection of the body is seen.

All dharmas have been eternally pure from the very beginning; because the bodhisattva has skillfully cultivated a pure mind, he beholds all Buddhas at will, inquires about his doubts, and the Buddhas answer his questions.
Hearing what the Buddha had spoken, his heart was filled with great joy;
rising from samādhi, he thought to himself:
"From where has the Buddha come?"
My body, likewise, does not go.
At that moment, he immediately realized:
“The Buddhas come from nowhere, and I, too, go nowhere.”
Again, he thought:
"All that exists within the three realms is created by the mind. Why is this so?
According to what the mind contemplates, all may be seen.
One sees the Buddha by means of the mind; one creates the Buddha by means of the mind;
the mind is itself the Buddha, and the mind is itself my own body.
The mind does not know itself, nor does it see itself.
If one grasps at the characteristics of the mind, they are entirely devoid of wisdom; the mind is likewise deceptive, arising entirely from ignorance.
By means of this mental state, one immediately enters the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is what is called "perpetual emptiness.
Having attained such samādhi and wisdom, by the power of these two practices, one proceeds according to one's wishes and never departs from the Buddhas;
just as the king of golden-winged birds (garuḍa), being fully endowed with two wings, travels freely wherever he desires through the void of space.

Because the bodhisattva has attained this samādhi and the power of wisdom, they may, in their present body, make offerings to all Buddhas according to their wishes, and at the end of their life, they shall likewise encounter all Buddhas.
For this reason it is said:
"A bodhisattva who never wishes to be separated from the Buddhas should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
— *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 29.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the First Chapter, Section Forty-Six: The Meaning of the Offerings of Roots of Goodness, Fascicle Thirty.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. 46. The Meaning of Offering with Roots of Goodness. [Sūtra] “If one wishes to offer all roots of goodness to the Buddhas, and to honor, respect, and praise them, accomplishing these according to one’s wish, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise]: Since the bodhisattva has attained non-separation from the Buddhas, they ought to make offerings to them.
If one encounters a Buddha but lacks the requisite articles for offering, it is truly a cause for great displeasure!

For example, when the Bodhisattva Sumati—which means "Wondrous Intention" in the language of Qin—encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he had no articles for making offerings and searched everywhere for them;
he then saw a girl selling flowers and purchased five stalks of blue lotuses with five hundred gold coins to offer to the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sold his own flesh and blood in order to make offerings to his teacher.
When such bodhisattvas have already succeeded in seeing the Buddha and their hearts desire to make offerings, yet lack the necessary implements for worship, their minds encounter an obstruction;
it is like a commoner who, upon meeting a sovereign, fails to present gifts of courtesy and thus acts with disrespect.
For this reason, bodhisattvas seek the requisites for making offerings to worship the Buddhas;
although the Buddhas have no need for them, the bodhisattvas’ minds achieve fulfillment.
It is like a farmer who encounters a fine, fertile field but lacks seeds; though he wishes to apply his labor, he has no means to exert his strength, and his heart is filled with great sorrow.
It is the same for a bodhisattva: having encountered various Buddhas but lacking offerings, or possessing other items that do not accord with their wishes, the mind becomes obstructed.
"Various roots of goodness" refers to the karmic fruits and rewards of those roots of goodness, such as flowers, incense, necklaces, garments, banners, canopies, and various kinds of rare treasures.

Why is this so? Sometimes the cause is spoken of as the effect, as when one says, "He eats a thousand ounces of gold in a month. Gold cannot be eaten; rather, it is because he obtains food by means of gold that one says, "he eats gold."
Sometimes the cause is described by means of the effect; for example, upon seeing a fine painting, one says, "This is a skilled hand.
Although the hand is not the painting, because the painting is exquisite, one speaks of the skill of the hand.

The karmic retribution of the roots of goodness is also like this: because of the causal conditions of the karma of the roots of goodness, one obtains the requisites for making offerings; these are called "roots of goodness. Question:
If that is so, why not speak directly of the flowers, incense, and so forth, rather than speaking of their cause?
Answer: There are two kinds of offerings:
first, material offerings; second, Dharma offerings.
If one were to speak only of offerings such as flowers and incense, then the offering of Dharma would not be included;
since we now speak of the offering of roots of goodness, it should be understood that both material wealth and the Dharma are encompassed.
"Making offerings" means that upon seeing or hearing of the merits of the Buddhas, one feels reverence and respect in one's heart;

one welcomes them and escorts them, circumambulates and prostrates, stands with body bowed and palms joined, yields one's seat to provide a place of rest, and encourages them by offering food, drink, flowers, incense, precious jewels, and the like;
and one praises in various ways their merits such as the observance of precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
To have faith in and accept the teachings as they are expounded;
such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind constitute "offering.
As for "venerable," it means that among all sentient beings, one's virtue is unsurpassed; therefore, one is called "venerable" (*bhadanta*).
The sense of awe and reverence exceeds that felt toward one's parents, teachers, or sovereigns because its benefits are so great; therefore, it is called "heavy" (*zhòng*).

As for "reverence" (*gōngjìng*): one is called "humble" (*gōng*) because of modesty and the avoidance of difficulty, while one is called "respectful" (*jìng*) because of the promotion of wisdom and virtue.
Regarding "praise" (*praśaṃsā*): to extol one's virtues is "praise" (*pra*);
because mere praise is insufficient, one further lauds them, hence it is called "extolling" (*śaṃsā*).
Regarding "accomplishment according to one's wishes": if one requires floral offerings, they arrive at will; whether sought or unsought, they are obtained.
Some emerge spontaneously, while others arise through transformation.
This applies to all implements for offering, including musical instruments and the like.
Question:
When a Bodhisattva encounters [an object] that can be used for making offerings, why does he seek it out according to his own wishes? Answer:
Merit arises from the mind; when one offers that which is most cherished and held dear, the merit obtained increases manifold.
For example, when King Aśoka was a young child, he took some soil he valued highly and offered it to the Buddha;
as a result, he became the King of Jambudvīpa and erected eighty thousand stūpas within a single day.
If a person of high status were to throw a great deal of soil into a bowl, they would obtain nothing, because it is not what is held in esteem.
If someone particularly values flowers and, out of that regard for what they hold dear, offers them to the Buddha, they will gain an increase in merit;
this is likewise true even for precious objects.
Furthermore, according to what is appropriate for the time: in cold weather, one should provide firewood, upper garments, heated rooms, bedding, and food and drink;
in hot weather, one should provide ice water, fans and canopies, cool rooms, light thin clothing, and exquisite food;
and during times of wind and rain, one should deliver the necessary offerings and requisites.
In this way, one makes offerings according to the occasion.
Furthermore, one makes offerings by providing whatever is appropriate for the local conditions and whatever is required by the recipient.

Moreover, regarding "making offerings according to one's inclination," there is the bodhisattva who knows that the Buddha has no needs, and who knows that all things are deceptive and like an illusion, having but a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless."
For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they make offerings to guide them according to what is valued in the lands where those beings dwell.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have attained profound meditative concentration and produced the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva; by means of these supernormal powers, they fly before the Buddhas of the ten directions. Whether in a Buddha-land, if it is necessary to rain down celestial flowers everywhere, they fill the three thousandfold world-system with them to offer to the Buddhas;
or they may rain down sandalwood.
In some places, it rained true pearls, their radiance vividly manifest;
in others, it rained the seven treasures;
and in others, it rained wish-fulfilling jewels as large as Mount Sumeru.
Or they may rain down female musicians whose voices are pure and exquisite;
or they may take their own bodies, as vast as Mount Sumeru, as lamp-wicks to make offerings to the Buddhas.
Such acts as these are called material offerings (*āmiṣa-pūjā*).
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās, they make offerings to all Buddhas with the Dharma.
There may be Bodhisattvas who practice the Dharma-offering to all Buddhas while on the first bhūmi, and so on, up to practicing the Dharma-offering while on the tenth bhūmi.

At times, when a bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby personally eliminating their own afflictions as well as those of sentient beings,
this is a Dharma-offering. At other times, when a bodhisattva dwells in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), by means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*),
they cause the fires of hell to be extinguished and ensure that all in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) attain full satisfaction.
Causing animals to be free from fear and leading them to birth among humans and devas;
gradually establishing them on the stage of *avaivartika*—
by virtue of such great powers of merit, it is called the "Dharma-offering."
For this reason it is said:
"One who wishes to achieve the perfection of roots of goodness should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Sūtra] "One who wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings..."
One should study the Prajñāpāramitā regarding robes, food and drink, bedding, ointments, vehicles, dwellings, couches, lamps, and candles.
[Treatise] Question:
What is the sequence for fulfilling the vows of all sentient beings? Answer:
The karma of a bodhisattva is of two kinds:
first, making offerings to all Buddhas; second, liberating sentient beings.
By making offerings to all Buddhas, one attains immeasurable merit and virtue.
Taking this merit and using it to benefit sentient beings means fulfilling their aspirations.
Just as a merchant leader enters the sea to gather treasures and returns safely to benefit his kin and acquaintances,
so too does the Bodhisattva enter the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas, obtains the treasure of immeasurable merit, and benefits sentient beings.

Just as a minor king makes offerings to a great king and is able to cause him joy, granting him his desires—such as rank, wealth, and silks—and returning him to his own country, thereby benefiting the people and removing enemies and bandits.

Because the Bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma, he receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Through the jewels of immeasurable roots of goodness, he attains inexhaustible power of wisdom and enters among sentient beings.
He is honored by virtuous people; to the poor, he gives according to their needs, and he utterly destroys the hosts of Māra’s followers, those with false views, and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This constitutes making offerings to all Buddhas, followed by fulfilling the wishes of sentient beings.
Question:
Is it truly possible for a bodhisattva to fulfill the wishes of all sentient beings?
If all the wishes of sentient beings were already fulfilled, what further benefit would there be for other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Conversely, if they were not all fulfilled, why is it said therein that "one who wishes to fulfill the wishes of all sentient beings should study the Prajñāpāramitā"?
Answer: There are two kinds of vows:
first, those that can be fulfilled; second, those that cannot be fulfilled.

Regarding "unattainable aspirations": suppose there were someone who wished to measure empty space to its very limits, or sought the boundaries of time and direction; such as a child seeking the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror—such aspirations as these are all unattainable.

Regarding "wishes that can be fulfilled": by drilling wood one seeks fire; by digging the earth one finds water; by cultivating merit one is born among humans or devas; and one may attain the fruits of Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood, even up to attaining the state of the Buddhas, the Kings of Dharma—all such things as these are called wishes that can be fulfilled.
There are two kinds of attainable vows:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
Among these, by means of the mundane vow, one fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings.
How is this known?
Because all necessary items, from food and drink to beds, bedding, and even lamps and candles, were provided to him.
He asked:
For what reason does a bodhisattva grant sentient beings wishes that are easy to fulfill, rather than those that are difficult?
The answer is:
wishes are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior.
The lower vow brings about the causes and conditions for happiness in this present life; the middle vow provides the causes and conditions for happiness in future lives;
and the superior vow provides the causes and conditions for nirvana. Therefore, one first grants the lower vow, next the middle vow, and finally the superior vow.
Furthermore, sentient beings mostly cling to present happiness and seek little of future happiness; those who seek the happiness of nirvana are even fewer still.
If one speaks of the many, the few are naturally included therein.
Furthermore, this sutra frequently discusses the path to future lives and nirvana in its earlier and later sections, while rarely speaking of the benefits of the present life.
Since the dharma of a bodhisattva consists of constantly providing all manner of benefit to sentient beings, there should be no abandonment of them.
Why is this? At the outset, he merely intends to cause all sentient beings to practice the Mahāyāna Dharma;
because they are unable to receive transformation through that, he subsequently provides them with the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
If they are still unable [to practice], one should provide them with the ten wholesome paths of action, the four Brahma-vihāras, and so forth, to cause them to cultivate merit.
If sentient beings find no pleasure in these at all, such beings should not be abandoned; rather, one should provide them with benefits for this present life, namely food, drink, and the like.

Furthermore, although ordinary persons may provide others with food, drink, and so forth to fulfill their wishes, all such instances possess causes and conditions, whether pertaining to matters of this life or matters of future lives.
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not fulfill the wishes of sentient beings due to a lack of causal conditions, the benefit they provide is very slight.

Because of the karmic causes and conditions of practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas become kings or great elders with immeasurable wealth; when sentient beings from the four quarters come to them seeking aid, they satisfy them all completely.

For instance, when the householder Bimbisāra acted as a great donor, he sat upon a grand bed made of the seven precious gems, with legs of diamond and spread with celestial rugs. A canopy of red pearls was draped above him, and eighty-four thousand attendants stood in service to his left and right, all magnificently adorned.

He opened four great gates for those who sought anything they desired; day and night, during the six periods, drums were sounded and light was emitted. Among the immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions, there were none who, upon hearing the sound of the drums or having their bodies touched by the light, did not come forth.

When those who desired various kinds of food and drink saw that the great assembly had gathered, the Elder immediately remained silent and gazed up into the void. At that moment, various foods of a hundred flavors rained down from the sky, and everyone obtained as much as they wished.
If any sentient beings did not take it for themselves, the attendants on their left and right distributed it to them until all were fully satisfied, at which point it ceased.
Food and drink, clothing and bedding, seats and mats, precious objects, and so forth—all are likewise provided.
Having allowed sentient beings to satisfy their desires, he then preaches the Dharma, causing them to transcend the four kinds of nutriment and all to abide in the stage of *avaivartika*.
By means of such powers of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*), bodhisattvas are able to fulfill the wishes of sentient beings.
A question is asked:
Even when the Buddha was in the world, there were still instances where sentient beings suffered from famine, the heavens did not send down rain, and beings were distressed and exhausted.
If even a Buddha cannot fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, how can a bodhisattva fulfill them?
The answer is:

A bodhisattva dwelling in the ten stages enters the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; within a trichiliocosm, they may at times manifest as one who has first resolved to attain enlightenment and practices the six pāramitās.
Sometimes they manifest as non-regressive bodhisattvas;
sometimes they manifest as those in their final birth before Buddhahood, preaching the Dharma to the devas in the Tuṣita Heaven;
or descending from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born in the palace of King Śuddhodana.
In some instances, they manifest leaving the household life and attaining Buddhahood;
in others, they manifest turning the wheel of Dharma amidst great assemblies to deliver immeasurable sentient beings;
or they manifest entering nirvana, where stupas made of the seven treasures are erected throughout all lands, causing sentient beings to make offerings to their relics.
At times, even when the Dharma has been completely extinguished, the bodhisattva’s benefit for beings remains thus; how much more so, then, for a Buddha!
Furthermore, there are two kinds of Buddha-bodies:
First is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and second is the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
When sentient beings behold the Buddha’s Dharma-body, there is no wish that remains unfulfilled.
The Buddha’s Dharma-body pervades all of space; its radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions, and the sound of its preaching of the Dharma likewise pervades the ten directions.

In immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the great assemblies filled therein all listened together to the Dharma; the preaching of the Dharma continued without ceasing, and within a single moment, each attained understanding and awakening according to what they heard.
Just as when a kalpa has ended, due to the causes and conditions of the karma of sentient beings, great rains pour down without interruption, which the three great elements cannot restrain;
only when the kalpa ends do winds arise from the ten directions, blowing against one another, and they are able to sustain this water.

Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body (dharmatā-kāya), with the exception of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), those of the three vehicles (triyāna) are all unable to uphold it;
only Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, through their inconceivable power of skillful means and wisdom, are able to hear and receive it in its entirety.

Any sentient beings who behold the Buddha of the Dharma-body shall be free from the three poisons and all afflictions; the sufferings of cold and heat will all be extinguished, and there shall be no unfulfilled aspiration.
If even a wish-fulfilling jewel can cause sentient beings to obtain everything according to their wishes, how much more so the Buddha!
The jewel grants all worldly wishes, whereas the Buddha grants all supramundane wishes.
If one says, "The Buddha cannot fulfill all the aspirations of sentient beings," such a statement is incorrect.

Furthermore, although Śākyamuni Buddha took birth in a royal palace and manifested the acceptance of human laws— experiencing cold and heat, hunger and thirst, sleep, enduring various slanders, and undergoing old age,
sickness, and death— his inner wisdom, spiritual virtue, true Buddhahood, and perfect enlightenment are no different [from those of other Buddhas].
If one wishes to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings, one is able to fulfill them all;

yet those aspirations that remain unfulfilled are such because, throughout countless lifetimes, one has constantly fulfilled their desires for food and clothing while they have nonetheless not escaped suffering.
Now, however, one benefits them only with the eternal bliss of nirvana, which is unconditioned.

Just as one who feels compassion for their kin would not give them delicious food mixed with poison, so too worldly aspirations give rise to various fetters and afflictions; furthermore, when separated from them, the mind experiences great suffering. Therefore, they are not to be considered essential.
Furthermore, some say:
Although Śākyamuni Buddha has already fulfilled the wishes of sentient beings, sentient beings themselves are unable to obtain them.
As it is said in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*:
"The Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the land was adorned with the seven treasures; such is my Buddha-land.
For those who are prone to anger and malice, he manifests the Buddha-land as something different."
Furthermore, it is like the rain falling from the mind of a dragon king: for humans it becomes water, yet upon the bodies of hungry ghosts (preta), it all becomes burning charcoal.
Question:
If one could fulfill the wishes of all sentient beings, then sentient beings would have an end, and there would be none who suffer the pains of hunger and cold.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings have their wishes fulfilled, for they aspire to be free from suffering and to attain happiness.
He replied:
"Universal" (*sarva*) refers to universality in name, not in reality.
As a verse in the *Dharmapada* says:
"All fear death; none do not dread the pain of the staff."
"Use yourself as a metaphor: do not kill, and do not inflict punishment!
Although it is said that "all fear the pain of the rod," for formless sentient beings there is no body, and thus they have no pain from the rod;
although sentient beings of the form realm possess bodies, they likewise have no pain from the rod.
Sentient beings in the desire realm also have those who do not suffer the pain of being struck with a staff;
yet, when it is said that "all" [beings] [suffer], this refers to those who ought to receive such punishment, and thus "all" is spoken of in this sense rather than in a literal sense.
For this reason, a bodhisattva fulfills the wishes of all sentient beings regarding that which they ought to obtain.
Yet, the mind of the bodhisattva has no limits, and the karmic fruit of their merit is likewise immeasurable;
it is only because sentient beings have been obstructed by the thick veil of sins over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas that they are unable to obtain them.

For example, there was the bhikṣu Rāhula, a disciple of Śāriputra, who was diligent in observing the precepts. After six days of begging for alms, he obtained nothing; by the seventh day, his life was nearly at its end.
