It is like the nature of water, which is inherently cold, appearing hot due to fire; once the fire is extinguished and has remained so for a long time, the water returns to its natural coldness.
The nature of all phenomena is likewise: before they arise, they are empty and non-existent, just as the nature of water is always cold.
All phenomena exist through the conjunction of various conditions, just as water becomes hot when it encounters fire.
If the conditions are deficient or absent, then no phenomenon exists, just as when the fire is extinguished, the hot water becomes cold.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The eye is empty; it is without self and without what belongs to a self. Why is this so?"
"Such is their very nature!
It is likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as for forms up to mental phenomena. He asked:

This sutra states that "self and what belongs to self are empty," which refers to the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but it does not speak of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); how, then, does it establish the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?
The answer is:
herein it speaks only of the emptiness of intrinsic nature; it does not speak of the emptiness of sentient beings or the emptiness of phenomena.
The emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) is of two kinds:
first, the absence of self and what belongs to self within the twelve bases (āyatana); second, the inherent emptiness of the characteristics of the twelve bases themselves.
"No self, no mine"—this is what is taught in the discourses of the Śrāvakas.
The Mahāyāna Dharma teaches:
"The twelve bases (āyatana) are empty because of the absence of self and mine; the twelve bases are empty because their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is non-existent."
Furthermore, if there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, one naturally attains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

Because people are mostly attached to the self and what belongs to the self, the Buddha has merely taught that "there is no self and nothing belonging to a self"; in this way, one should understand that all phenomena are empty.
If one does not yet cling even to the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self," how much less so to other dharmas!
For this reason, the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of dharmas ultimately converge on a single meaning; this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, "nature" (svabhāva) means that which exists inherently and does not depend on causes and conditions;
if it depended on causes and conditions, it would be a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) and could not be called nature.
Within all phenomena, there is no such nature.
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions; that which arises from causes and conditions is a created phenomenon.
If it does not arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is a non-phenomenon.
Because the nature of all such phenomena cannot be apprehended, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Question: Since ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is the non-existence of anything at all, it is already emptiness of nature; why then is it stated again?
The answer is:
"Ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā) means that nothing remains;
"emptiness of nature" (prakṛti-śūnyatā) means that it has always been so from the very beginning.
Just as the nature of water is cold, it becomes hot through the presence of fire, yet returns to cold when the fire is extinguished.
Ultimate emptiness is like space: eternally neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. How can you say they are the same?
Furthermore, all phenomena are ultimately empty.
Why? Because their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
All dharmas are empty by nature. Why?
Because they are ultimately empty.

Furthermore, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is primarily the sphere of practice for bodhisattvas, whereas ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is primarily the sphere of practice for the Buddhas.
Why is this? Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is only the conjunction of causes and conditions, and no real intrinsic nature exists.
Ultimate emptiness is pure throughout the three periods of time.
There are such distinctions as these.
Furthermore, the nature of all dharmas is of two kinds:
First is the general nature, and second is the specific nature.

As for the general nature, it consists of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; as well as being without arising or ceasing, without coming or going, and without entering or exiting, and so forth.
As for distinct natures: fire has the nature of heat;
water has the nature of moisture;
and the mind has the nature of consciousness.
Just as a person who delights in committing various evils is called "evil-natured," while one who enjoys accumulating virtuous deeds is called "virtuous-natured.
As it is said in the *Daśabala-sūtra*:
"The Buddha knows the various natures of the world.
These various natures are all empty; this is called the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Why is this so?
If the nature of impermanence were real, one would lose the retribution of karmic fruits. Why is this?
Because arising and ceasing pass away without abiding, the six sense organs would not receive sensory objects, nor would they accumulate the causes and conditions [for future experience].
If there were no accumulation of habitual practice, then there would be no recitation of sutras, sitting in meditation, and so forth.
For this reason, one knows that the nature of impermanence cannot be apprehended.
If even impermanence cannot be apprehended, how much less so can a mark of permanence!
Furthermore, the nature of suffering is also unapprehendable. If this suffering were truly existent, then one should not give rise to a mind of attachment toward it.
If a person feels weary of and fears painful sensations, they should likewise feel weary of and fear all pleasant sensations;
yet the Buddha would not have spoken of the three types of feeling.
There are painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings;
furthermore, one should not give rise to aversion toward the painful, attachment toward the pleasant, or delusion toward the neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
If there were a single characteristic, then aversion should arise toward pleasure, and attachment should arise toward suffering.
But such is not the case!
Thus, even the nature of suffering cannot be found; how much less could the illusory nature of pleasure be found!
Furthermore, the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) is also unapprehendable. Why is this?
If there were a characteristic of emptiness, then there would be neither sin nor merit.
Because there is neither sin nor merit, there is likewise neither this world nor a future world.
Furthermore, all phenomena exist through mutual dependence. Why is this so?
If there were emptiness, there should be reality;
if there were reality, there should be emptiness.
Since even emptiness does not exist, how much less could reality exist!

Furthermore, if there were no self, then there would be neither bondage nor liberation; nor would there be the undergoing of suffering or merit from this life to the next, nor would there be the karmic causes, conditions, and retributions thereof.
For these reasons, one knows that even the nature of non-self cannot be apprehended, let alone the nature of a self!
Furthermore, the nature of neither arising nor ceasing is also not real.
Why is this? If it were real, one would fall into the view of eternalism.
If all phenomena were eternal, there would be neither sin nor merit;
that which exists would always exist, and that which does not exist would always be non-existent;
that which does not exist would never arise, and that which exists would never perish.
Just as the nature of neither arising nor ceasing cannot be apprehended, how much less so the nature of arising and ceasing!
The same applies to all general natures, such as neither coming nor going, and neither entering nor exiting.
Furthermore, it is also not the case that the various dharmas possess distinct natures.
Why is this? For example, fire is able to burn and the derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) is able to illuminate; because these two dharmas are combined, they are called "fire."
If fire existed apart from these two factors, it would have to possess a distinct function; yet no such distinct function exists.
For this reason, we know that fire is a mere designation and lacks any substantial reality.
If the nature of fire did not truly exist, how could one say that heat is the nature of fire?

Furthermore, the nature of heat arises from a combination of conditions: internally there is the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and externally there is visible form and tangibility; through their conjunction, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises, whereby one perceives that there is heat.
When these have not yet conjoined, there is no nature of heat.
For this reason, we know that there is no fixed heat that constitutes the nature of fire.
Furthermore, if fire truly possessed the nature of heat, why is it that some people enter fire without being burned, and why does the fire within the human body not burn the body?
Why can water not extinguish fire in the air?
Because fire lacks a fixed nature of heat.
By the power of supernormal faculties, fire cannot burn the body.
Due to the causal conditions of karma, the five viscera do not become hot;
yet because of the power of the divine dragon, water cannot extinguish them.
Furthermore, if the nature of heat were distinct from fire, then fire would not be hot.
If heat and fire were one and the same, how could one say that heat is the nature of fire?
The same applies to other natures as well.
Because neither a general nature nor a particular nature exists, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, regarding "emptiness of nature," it has been empty from the very beginning.
As worldly people say:
"That which is false and impermanent is empty."
"Objects such as Mount Sumeru and diamond, as well as that which is known by the noble ones, are considered real and not empty.
To sever this doubt, the Buddha said:
"Although these possess a solid nature and endure for a long time in succession, they are all empty of intrinsic nature."
"The wisdom of the sages, though it delivers sentient beings and destroys all afflictions, is also empty because its intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, people say:
'The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are all empty;'"
"However, suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are their true nature.

Because the Buddha wished to sever this doubt, he analytically explained that the five aggregates, suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality are all likewise empty; this is called "emptiness of nature" (prakṛti-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) have three characteristics:
arising, abiding, and ceasing; unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) likewise have three characteristics:
non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing.
If even the nature of the conditioned is empty, how much more so are conditioned phenomena!
If even the nature of the unconditioned is empty, how much more so are unconditioned phenomena!
By these various causes and conditions, no intrinsic nature can be apprehended; this is called the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Regarding "emptiness of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*): all phenomena possess two kinds of characteristics—the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because these two characteristics are empty, it is called "emptiness of characteristics."
Question: What are the general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa),
and what are the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)?
Answer: General characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) are such as impermanence and so forth;

specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are that although all phenomena are impermanent, each has its own distinct characteristic, such as solidity being the characteristic of earth and heat being the characteristic of fire.
Question: Previously you spoke of nature (svabhāva), and now you speak of characteristics (lakṣaṇa);
what is the difference between nature and characteristics?
Answer: Some say:
"In reality there is no difference; it is only the names that differ."
To speak of nature is to speak of characteristics; to speak of characteristics is to speak of nature.
For example, to speak of the nature of fire is to speak of its characteristic of heat, and to speak of the characteristic of heat is to speak of the nature of fire.
Some say: "There is a slight difference between nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
'Nature' refers to its essence; 'characteristics' refers to that which can be cognized."
For a son of the Śākyas, the upholding of the prohibitive precepts is his nature;
shaving the hair and wearing dyed robes cut into patches is his mark.
For a Brahmin, personally receiving his own dharma is his nature.
Having a topknot (*cūḍā*) on the head and holding a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) are its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Just as heat is the nature (*svabhāva*) of fire and smoke is its characteristic,
so too is proximity [to the object] its nature and distance its characteristic.
Appearances are indeterminate and emerge from the body;
nature, however, speaks of reality.
For example, one may see the appearance of yellow and take it to be gold, yet internally it is copper; when burned by fire or ground on a stone, one knows it is not of the nature of gold.
When a person receives respectful offerings and worship, they appear to be a good person; this is their outward appearance (lakṣaṇa).
But when they are reviled, insulted, or humiliated, they become suddenly enraged and full of hatred; this is their true nature (svabhāva).
"Characteristics, internal and external, distant and near, beginning and end, and so forth—there are such distinctions as these.
That all these characteristics are empty is called "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
As it is said: "All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) possess the characteristic of impermanence.
Why is this so? Because they arise and perish without abiding;

because what was previously non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence; because they are dependent upon various causes and conditions; because they are deceptive and not real; because they are produced by impermanent causes and conditions; and because they arise from a combination of various causes and conditions.
For these and other such reasons, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess the characteristic of impermanence.

Because they can give rise to affliction of body and mind, they are called suffering (*duḥkha*). Because there is no moment among the four postures of the body that is not suffering, because they constitute the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), because the noble ones relinquish them and do not accept them, because there is no time when they do not cause affliction, and because they are impermanent.
Such causes and conditions as these are called the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*).

It is empty because it is free from "mine" (*mama-kāra*); it is empty because it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions; it is called empty because it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is empty because its beginning and end cannot be apprehended; it is called empty because it deceives the mind; it is called empty because the noble ones do not cling to any phenomena; it is called empty by way of the gateways of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) liberation; it is called empty because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is immeasurable and incalculable; it is called empty because it cuts off the path of all verbal expression; it is called empty because it extinguishes all mental activities (*citta-saṃskāra*); and it is called empty because the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats enter into it and do not emerge.

For such reasons as these, it is called "emptiness. Because it is impermanent, suffering, and empty, there is no self; because it lacks sovereignty, there is no self; and because it has no master, it is called "selfless.

All phenomena are without exception born from causes and conditions; because they are born from causes and conditions, they are selfless. Because they are signless and unconditioned, they are selfless; because they are merely provisional names, they are selfless; because they arise from the perversion of the view of a body, they are selfless; and because one attains the Way by severing the notion of a self, they are selfless.
By means of these various aspects, it is called "non-self.
Such as these are termed the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*): earth has the characteristic of solidity;
Fire has the characteristic of heat;
water, the characteristic of moisture;
wind, the characteristic of motion.
The basis for visual consciousness is called the characteristic of the eye; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Consciousness has the characteristic of awareness;
wisdom has the characteristic of insight.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) has the characteristic of knowledge. Equanimity is the characteristic of giving (*dāna*); freedom from regret and affliction is the characteristic of ethical discipline (*śīla*); the non-alteration of the mind is the characteristic of patience (*kṣānti*); the arousal of diligence is the characteristic of vigor (*vīrya*); the gathering of the mind is the characteristic of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); non-attachment is the characteristic of wisdom; and the ability to accomplish tasks is the characteristic of skillful means (*upāya*).
Consciousness arising and ceasing constitutes the characteristic of the world (*saṃsāra*), while the absence of consciousness constitutes the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
Such dharmas each have their own distinct characteristics.
One should know that all these characteristics are empty; this is called "emptiness of self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
The remaining meanings are as explained in the *Śūnyatā-svabhāva* [chapter], because the meanings of "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) are identical. Question:
Why does it not merely say "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), but rather "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
Answer: If one speaks of the "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), one does not speak of the emptiness of the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva-śūnyatā*);
when one speaks of the "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), that is the emptiness of the essence of phenomena.
Furthermore, because various dharmas come together, a single dharma arises; that single dharma is empty, and likewise each and every such dharma is empty.

Now, the dharmas of dependent origination through conjunction are also successively empty, and all dharmas are each empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); for this reason, it is called "emptiness of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Question:
If all dharmas are each empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), how can there still be anything to be taught? Answer:

Because sentient beings are subject to inversion, they become attached to all phenomena through such notions as single characteristics, diverse characteristics, general characteristics, and specific characteristics; it is for the purpose of severing this attachment that I have taught these things.
Based on such causes and conditions, this is called the "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

As for "the emptiness of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), "all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), and so forth.

All these phenomena enter into various gateways, namely: the characteristic of existence, the characteristic of cognition, the characteristic of consciousness; the characteristic of conditions, the characteristic of predominance; the characteristic of cause, the characteristic of fruit; the general characteristic, the specific characteristic, and the characteristic of dependence.
Question:
In what way do all phenomena possess characteristics? Answer:
All phenomena have the beautiful and the ugly, and the internal and the external;
all phenomena arise from the mind, and for this reason they are called "existent. Question:
Question: How can one speak of "having characteristics" regarding non-existence? Answer:
If non-existence were not called a "dharma," it would simply not be designated as such; it is only because it negates existence that it is called "non-existence."
If a non-existent phenomenon were to truly exist, it would be called "existent.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena have the characteristic of existence. Regarding the "characteristic of knowing":

the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of suffering can know the truth of suffering; the dharma-knowledge of origination and the subsequent knowledge of origination can know the truth of origination; the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of cessation can know the truth of cessation; and the dharma-knowledge of the path and the subsequent knowledge of the path can know the truth of the path.

Furthermore, mundane wholesome wisdom that is able to know suffering, able to know its origin, able to know its cessation, and able to know the path, as well as being able to know space and cessation not through deliberation—this is called the characteristic of knowing all phenomena.
Because it knows characteristics, it encompasses all dharmas.
Regarding "the characteristic of consciousness": eye-consciousness can know forms;
ear-consciousness can know sounds; [and so forth].
The nose-consciousness can cognize odors;
the tongue-consciousness can cognize tastes;
the body-consciousness can cognize tangibles.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to cognize phenomena (*dharma*); it can cognize the eye, cognize forms, and cognize visual consciousness; it can cognize the ear, cognize sounds, and cognize auditory consciousness; it can cognize the nose, cognize odors, and cognize olfactory consciousness; it can cognize the tongue, cognize tastes, and cognize gustatory consciousness; it can cognize the body, cognize tangibles, and cognize tactile consciousness; it can cognize the mind, cognize phenomena, and cognize mental consciousness—this is called the characteristic of consciousness.
Regarding "conditioned by signs" (*nimittālambana*): visual consciousness and the various phenomena associated with visual consciousness can take form as their object;
auditory consciousness and the various phenomena associated with auditory consciousness can take sound as their object;
olfactory consciousness and the various phenomena associated with olfactory consciousness can take fragrance as their object.

Tongue-consciousness and the various phenomena associated with tongue-consciousness can take flavors as their object; body-consciousness and the various phenomena associated with body-consciousness can take tangibles as their object; mind-consciousness and the various phenomena associated with mind-consciousness can take mental objects as their object—they can take the eye as their object, they can take forms as their object, they can take eye-consciousness as their object;

they can take the ear as their object, they can take sounds as their object, they can take ear-consciousness as their object; they can take the nose as their object, they can take odors as their object, they can take nose-consciousness as their object; they can take the tongue as their object, they can take flavors as their object, they can take tongue-consciousness as their object; they can take the body as their object, they can take tangibles as their object, they can take body-consciousness as their object; they can take the mind as their object, they can take mental objects as their object, they can take mind-consciousness as their object—this is called the characteristic of being an object-condition (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Regarding the "characteristic of predominance" (*adhipati-lakṣaṇa*): all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) each possess predominance over one another;
unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) likewise possess predominance over conditioned phenomena—this is called the characteristic of predominance.
Regarding "the characteristic of cause and effect": all phenomena each act as causes and each act as effects—this is called the characteristic of cause and effect.
Regarding "the general characteristic and the specific characteristic": within all phenomena, each possesses its own general characteristic and its own specific characteristic.
For example, "horse" is a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while "white" is a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);
likewise, "person" is a general characteristic, whereas "having lost one ear" is a specific characteristic.
In this manner, each successive instance possesses both general and specific characteristics—this is what is meant by general and specific characteristics.

Regarding "the characteristic of dependence" (niśraya-lakṣaṇa): all phenomena mutually depend upon one another, just as grasses, trees, mountains, and rivers depend upon the earth, and the earth depends upon water; in this way, everything depends on each other. This is called the characteristic of dependence.
The category of "reliance" encompasses all phenomena. In this way, various such single categories of phenomena encompass all phenomena.

Furthermore, there are two categories that encompass all phenomena, namely: form and formless phenomena; visible and invisible phenomena; resistant and non-resistant phenomena; contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; internal and external phenomena; observed phenomena and objective conditions; existent phenomena and non-existent phenomena. Such are the various characteristics of these dual categories of phenomena.
The third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and even up to immeasurable dharma-gates encompass all dharmas.
All these dharmas are empty, as explained above; this is called the emptiness of all dharmas (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
Question:
If all things are empty, why are the various names of all dharmas spoken? Answer:
Because ordinary persons, within the context of empty phenomena, grasp at signs through the inversion of ignorance, they give rise to various afflictions such as craving;
due to these afflictions, they initiate various karmas;
and because they initiate various karmas, they enter various paths.
Because they enter various paths, they receive various bodies;
because they receive various bodies, they experience various forms of suffering and pleasure.
It is like a silkworm producing silk: having no external cause, it emerges from itself and wraps itself up, thereby undergoing the suffering of being scorched and boiled.
By the power of pure wisdom, the Sage discerns that all phenomena are empty from beginning to end;
yet, because he wishes to deliver sentient beings, he speaks of the points of attachment—namely, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth.
You, however, through ignorance alone, give rise to these five aggregates and the like, creating them yourselves and becoming attached to them!
If the Sages had taught only emptiness, one would be unable to attain the Way, because there would be nothing to rely upon and nothing to be weary of.
Question:
Your statement that all dharmas are empty is not correct!
Why is this? Because all phenomena each encompass their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

For example: earth has the characteristic of solidity, water has the characteristic of moisture, fire has the characteristic of heat, wind has the characteristic of motion, the mind has the characteristic of cognition (*vijñāna*), and wisdom has the characteristic of knowing.
If all these dharmas each abide in their own characteristics, how can you say they are empty?
The answer is:

this has already been refuted within the sections on the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); now it shall be explained further.
Because their characteristics are not fixed, they should not be considered [definitive] characteristics.

For example, substances such as ghee, honey, glue, and wax all possess the characteristic of earth; yet, through contact with fire, they abandon their own characteristics and transform into the characteristic of moisture.
Likewise, gold, silver, copper, and iron, through contact with fire, also abandon their own characteristics and change into the characteristic of water.
Just as water, upon encountering cold, becomes ice and transforms into the characteristic of earth;

or as a person who is intoxicated and asleep, one who has entered the concentration of non-thought (*acittaka-samādhi*), or a fish frozen within ice—all lack mental consciousness and abandon their mental characteristics, having no perception or cognition;

so too, while wisdom is characterized by knowing, when it enters the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is no longer any perception or cognition, for it naturally abandons the characteristic of knowing.
Therefore, all phenomena have no fixed characteristics.
Furthermore, if one were to claim that phenomena possess fixed characteristics, this too would be incorrect. Why is this so?
Just as the characteristic of a future dharma should not come into the present;
if it were to reach the present, it would then abandon its characteristic of being future.
If it were to enter the present without abandoning its characteristic of being future, then the future would be the present, and there would be no future retribution.
If the present enters the past, it would abandon its characteristic of being present;
if it enters the past without abandoning its characteristic of being present, then the past would be the present.
From such faults as these, one knows that all phenomena possess no fixed characteristic.
Furthermore, if it were claimed that unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) definitely exist, they would have to possess their own distinct characteristics;
just as fire possesses its own characteristic of heat, which is not produced by anything else.
Therefore, you should know that because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are signless (*animitta*), they do not truly exist.

Furthermore, you claim that the phenomenon of cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) in the future world is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), yet it lacks the characteristics of a conditioned phenomenon.
If you claim that "the cessation through non-conditions of wisdom is the characteristic of cessation," this is also not so! Why is this?
It is called the characteristic of cessation because of impermanent cessation, not because it is the cessation through non-conditions of wisdom that it is named the characteristic of cessation.
Such various things as these have no fixed characteristic.
If they possessed a fixed characteristic, they could be made non-empty;
however, they lack any fixed characteristic.
As for that which is not empty, this is not the case.
Question: There must be truly existent dharmas that are not empty.

Why is this so? Because what is known by ordinary persons and what is known by noble ones differ: that which is known by ordinary persons is false and illusory, while that which is known by noble ones is real.
One abandons false dharmas by relying on true noble wisdom; one cannot abandon the false by relying on the false!
The answer is:
it is called "noble wisdom" because it serves to destroy what is known by ordinary people.
If there were no dharmas of ordinary beings, there would be no dharmas of the noble ones;
it would be like having no medicine if there were no illness.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Apart from the dharmas of ordinary beings, there are no further noble dharmas; the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the dharmas of ordinary beings is itself the noble dharma.
Furthermore, because the noble ones do not grasp at the marks of phenomena nor become attached to them, the noble dharma is the reality;
whereas ordinary beings grasp at the marks of phenomena and become attached to them, therefore the dharmas of ordinary beings are considered false.
Although the sages employ [these things], they do not grasp at their marks; because they do not grasp at marks, there are no fixed marks. Thus, one should not raise such an objection!
On the level of ordinary beings, they are attached to dharmas and make distinctions, thinking:
"This is the dharma of the sages; this is the dharma of ordinary beings."
If one abides in the stage of the noble ones, there is no conceptual discrimination;
yet, in order to sever the illnesses of sentient beings, one says:
"This is empty, this is real."
As it is said:
"The Buddha’s words are neither false nor true, neither bound nor liberated, neither identical nor different.
Therefore, they are without conceptual differentiation, pure as space.

Furthermore, if phenomena were not entirely empty, one should not say that "the absence of conceptual proliferation is the mark of a wise person," nor should one say that "non-acceptance, non-attachment, lack of dependence, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are called the true Dharma."
Question: If all dharmas are empty, then they are also real; why do you say they are "without reality"? Answer:
If all phenomena are empty, even if there were some phenomenon, it would already have been sublated by being included within "all phenomena.
If there is no phenomenon, one should not raise an objection! Question:
If the emptiness of all phenomena were the ultimate truth, why would the Buddha have extensively taught the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self within the Tripiṭaka?
As it is said in a sutra:
"The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:"
"I shall preach the Dharma for you, which is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning?
When the eye arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere."
"There is only karma and the retribution of karma, but no agent can be found!
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In this context, if it is said that "arising comes from nowhere and ceasing goes nowhere," it means that because a permanent phenomenon cannot be found, there is impermanence.

There are only karma and the retribution of karma, yet an agent cannot be found; this is the emptiness of the ultimate meaning within the Śrāvaka Dharma. How, then, can it be said that "all dharmas are empty"?
The answer is:
"Self" is the root of all afflictions. First, one clings to the five aggregates as "self," and subsequently clings to external things as "mine.
Because of being bound by "mine," greed and anger arise; and due to the conditions of greed and anger, various karmas are produced.
As the Buddha taught that "there is no agent," he thereby refutes the self within all phenomena;
if he says that "the eye comes from nowhere and, upon ceasing, goes nowhere," he thereby declares the eye to be impermanent;
and if it is impermanent, it is suffering, and what is suffering is neither self nor belongs to a self.
Because "self" and "what belongs to self" do not exist, the mind has no attachment toward any phenomena;
because the mind has no attachment, the fetters and afflictions do not arise;
since the fetters and afflictions do not arise, what need is there to speak of emptiness?
For this reason, within the Tripiṭaka, "impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self" are frequently taught, whereas "the emptiness of all phenomena" is not frequently taught.

Furthermore, although sentient beings hear the Buddha teach that "all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self," they still engage in conceptual proliferation regarding these phenomena;
for the sake of such people, he teaches that "all phenomena are empty."
If there is no self and no what belongs to the self, and if there is neither self nor what belongs to the self, this is precisely entering the meaning of emptiness.
Question: Why does the Buddha say that "there is karma and there is its retribution"?
"If there is karma and there is its retribution, then it is not empty.
He replied:
"The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is of two kinds:"
The first is non-self, and the second is non-dharma.
For those who cling to the view that the self is permanent, I therefore teach "the absence of an agent";
for those who cling to the view of annihilationism, I therefore teach "there is karma and there is the retribution of karma."
If a person, upon hearing it said that "there is no agent," falls further into the view of annihilationism, one explains for them that "there is karma and there is the retribution of karma.

These five aggregates can initiate karma, yet they do not pass on to a future life; rather, through the causal conditions of these five aggregates, another set of five aggregates arises to receive the retribution of karma in succession. Therefore, it is said that one receives the retribution of karma.
Just as the bodies of a mother and her child, though distinct, are linked through the continuity of causes and conditions such that when the mother takes medicine, the child’s illness is cured;

so too, although the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of this life and the next are distinct, because the causes and conditions of karma—both merit and demerit—are continuous, one receives the retribution of the five aggregates of the next life based on the causes and conditions of the five aggregates of this life.

Furthermore, there are those who seek the characteristics of all phenomena and become attached to a single phenomenon—whether it be existence or non-existence, permanence or impermanence, and so forth.
Because they are attached to phenomena, they give rise to craving for their own phenomena and aversion toward the phenomena of others, thereby committing evil karma.
For the sake of such people, it is said that "all phenomena are empty."
When all phenomena are empty, there are no phenomena.
Why is this? Those phenomena which are cherished can give rise to fetters and afflictions.
That which can give rise to the fetters (saṃyojana) is the condition of ignorance (avidyā);
if ignorance itself arises, how can it be real?
This is the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of sentient beings:
first, those attached to the mundane world; second, those seeking the supramundane.
Among those seeking the supramundane, there are three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior class has sharp faculties and seeks the Buddha-way with a great mind;
the middling class has medium faculties and seeks the Pratyekabuddha-way;
the inferior class has dull faculties and seeks the Śrāvaka-way.
For those seeking the Buddha-way, he teaches the six pāramitās and the emptiness of dharmas;
for those seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha, he teaches the twelve links of dependent origination and the dharma of solitary practice;
for those seeking the path of the śrāvaka, he teaches the emptiness of sentient beings and the dharma of the four noble truths.

Śrāvakas fear and loathe birth and death; hearing that sentient beings are empty, as well as the Four Noble Truths—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—they do not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
It is like a deer in an enclosure that, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, seeks only its release with single-minded intent and harbors no other thought.

Although a Pratyekabuddha feels aversion toward old age, sickness, and death, he is still able to contemplate the profound principle of dependent origination to some extent and can also deliver sentient beings to a small degree.
For example, just as a rhinoceros within an enclosure, though struck by a poisoned arrow, is still able to look back with longing for its calf;

so too, although a bodhisattva is weary of old age, sickness, and death, they are able to contemplate the true mark of all phenomena, exhaustively and deeply penetrate the twelve links of dependent origination, realize the emptiness of dharmas, and enter the immeasurable nature of reality.

It is like a white elephant king in the midst of a hunting encirclement; though pierced by arrows, he looks back at the hunters with no fear in his heart, and leads his retinue away with steady steps.
For this reason, the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā) is not extensively taught within the Tripiṭaka.

There may be brahmins of sharp faculties who seek the true mark of all dharmas, yet do not weary of old age, sickness, and death, and remain attached to various marks of dharmas; it is for their sake that the emptiness of dharmas is taught.
Regarding the brahmin Śreṇika, he did not say that the five aggregates are themselves reality, nor did he say that reality exists apart from the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there was another brahmin who argued forcefully; the Buddha replied to him:
"In my Dharma, neither 'existence' nor 'non-existence' is accepted. What, then, do you intend to discuss?"
"Existence and non-existence are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and the source from which the fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise.
Furthermore, the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* within the *Saṃyukta Āgama* speaks of two kinds of emptiness:
"emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) and emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)."
The *Rādha-sūtra* states:
"The aggregate of form is broken apart and dispersed, so that nothing remains.
The *Kāṣṭhāvadāna-sūtra* (Raft Simile Sūtra) states:
"One should abandon even the Dharma, how much more so that which is not the Dharma!
As stated in the *Pārāyaṇa-sūtra* and the *Arthavargīya-sūtra*:

"The wise do not accept nor cling to any phenomena (*dharma*). If one accepts and clings to phenomena, then conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) arises; if there is nothing upon which to rely, there is nothing to be proliferated."
"The noble ones who have attained the Path neither grasp at nor reject any phenomena; if there is neither grasping nor rejecting, they are able to transcend all views.
In this manner, the emptiness of dharmas is taught throughout various passages in the Tripiṭaka.
These and others like them are called the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
Regarding "the emptiness of the unapprehendable" (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), some say:

"Because within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), neither a self (*ātman*) nor a permanent phenomenon (*nityadharma*) can be apprehended, it is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambhaśūnyatā*). Some say:

"Because when seeking phenomena among various causes and conditions, they cannot be apprehended—just as a fist cannot be apprehended apart from the five fingers—it is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable."

Some say: "Because all phenomena (*dharma*) and their causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are ultimately unobtainable, it is called the emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Question:
For what reason is it called "emptiness of the unobtainable"?
Is it because it cannot be obtained due to a deficiency in the power of wisdom,
or is it because it does not actually exist that it cannot be obtained?
Answer: All phenomena are truly non-existent and thus cannot be apprehended; it is not that one’s power of wisdom is insufficient.
Question:

If that is so, it would be no different from ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); why, then, is the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) further explained?
The answer is:
if people hear that all these aforementioned forms of emptiness are entirely non-existent, their minds will harbor fear and give rise to doubt.
Now, the reason why it is empty is explained: because it cannot be found through seeking, "unfindability emptiness" is taught.
To sever this doubt and fear, the Buddha teaches unfindability emptiness.
Why is this so? The Buddha said:

"From my first generation of the mind of enlightenment until my attainment of Buddhahood, as well as for all Buddhas of the ten directions, when seeking reality among all phenomena, it cannot be found; this is called the emptiness of the unfindable."
Question: What is it that cannot be apprehended? Answer:
Because all phenomena, up to and including *nirvāṇa* without remainder, cannot be apprehended, it is called the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, when a practitioner attains this emptiness of non-apprehension, they do not apprehend the three poisons, the four floods, the four bonds, the five hindrances, the six cravings, the seven latent tendencies, the eight wrong paths, the nine fetters, the ten unwholesome actions, nor any other base, evil, defiled, or binding factors; because none of these can be apprehended, it is called the emptiness of non-apprehension.
Question:
If that is so, what benefit does one obtain by practicing this emptiness of non-apprehensibility? Answer:

One attains morality, concentration, and wisdom; one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, the five faculties, the five groups of those beyond training, the six dharmas of relinquishment, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive attainments, and the ten dharmas of those beyond training.
To attain such things as these constitutes the Dharma of the śrāvakas.
If one attains the Prajñāpāramitā, then one becomes fully endowed with the six pāramitās and all the merits of the ten stages (bhūmis).
Question:

Previously it was stated that "all dharmas, up to and including nirvāṇa, are unattainable"; why now do you say that "precepts, concentration, wisdom, and even the ten qualities of one beyond training are attained"?
Answer: Although these dharmas are attained, they are all aids to the emptiness of non-attainment, and thus are also called "unattainable.
Furthermore, because they are without reception and without attachment, they are called "unattainable."
Because they are unconditioned dharmas, they are called "unobtainable";
because they are the Noble Truths, they are called "unobtainable"; because they are the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), they are called "unobtainable.
Although the Sages attain all merits, because they enter nirvana without remainder, they do not regard them as attainment.
Ordinary people consider this a great attainment.
It is like a lion: although it performs various actions, it does not regard them as marvelous; yet when other sentient beings see them, they consider them rare and extraordinary.
These meanings are called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

There is also the emptiness of non-existent phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of existent phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existent and existent phenomena (*abhāva-bhāva-śūnyatā*).
Regarding "the emptiness of non-existence" (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), some say:
"Non-existence refers to a dharma that has already ceased; because this cessation is non-existent, it is called the emptiness of non-existence."

Regarding "the emptiness of existence" (*bhāva-śūnyatā*): because all phenomena arise through the combination of causes and conditions, there is no such thing as an existent entity. Since existent entities do not exist, it is called the emptiness of existence.

Regarding "the emptiness of non-existence and existence" (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*): the apprehension of the marks of non-existence and existence is unattainable; this is the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Furthermore, because one contemplates the emptiness of non-existence and existence, it is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the arising and ceasing of all phenomena; whether through the gate of arising or the gate of ceasing, the gate of arising gives rise to joy, while the gate of ceasing gives rise to sorrow.

When the practitioner contemplates that the dharma of arising is empty, the mind of joy is extinguished; when contemplating that the dharma of cessation is empty, the mind of sorrow is extinguished. Why is this so?

Because in arising there is nothing to be gained, and in cessation there is nothing to be lost; because it eliminates worldly greed and sorrow, this is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, among the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the first three emptinesses destroy all dharmas, and the last three emptinesses likewise destroy all dharmas.
The emptiness of existence destroys all dharmas at the time of their arising and abiding;
the emptiness of non-existence destroys all dharmas at the time of their cessation.
The emptiness of non-existence and existence simultaneously negates both arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, some say: "The emptiness of past and future phenomena is called the emptiness of non-existence; [the emptiness of present phenomena is called the emptiness of existence]."
The emptiness of present phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is called the emptiness of existing dharmas (*sad-dharma-śūnyatā*). Why is this?
Because past phenomena have ceased, perished, and returned to non-existence through transformation.

Future dharmas have not yet had their causes and conditions harmonize; they have not yet arisen, do not yet exist, have not yet emerged, and have not yet originated. For this reason, they are called "non-existent dharmas.
To observe and know that present dharmas and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas currently exist is called "existent dharmas."
Since both of these are empty, it is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Furthermore, some say: "Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) have no arising, abiding, or ceasing; this is called 'non-existence'."
"Conditioned phenomena arise, abide, and perish; these are called 'existent dharmas.
That such things are empty is called the 'emptiness of existent and non-existent dharmas' (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
This is why "a bodhisattva who wishes to dwell in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of existent and non-existent dharmas should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Thirty-One.
The Explanation of the First Chapter, Section Forty-Nine:
The Meaning of the Four Conditions. Scroll Thirty-Two.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. 49. The Meaning of the Four Conditions. [Sūtra] “Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who wish to know the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of all phenomena should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”

[Treatise] All conditioned phenomena arise from four conditions, namely: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Regarding "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*): the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the self-seed cause (*sva-bīja-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retribution cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—these five causes are termed the causal condition.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are also called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the "condition as immediate antecedent" (*samanantara-pratyaya*): with the exception of the final past and present moments of mind and mental factors of an Arhat, all other past and present moments of mind and mental factors are able to provide immediate succession; these are called the condition as immediate antecedent.
Regarding "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*), these comprise all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who wishes to know the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the four conditions should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Question: As it is stated in the Prajñāpāramitā, all four conditions (pratyaya) are unattainable. Why is this so?
If the effect already exists within the cause, this is not possible;
nor is it possible for it to be non-existent within the cause beforehand.
If it already existed, there would be no cause.
If it did not previously exist, by what would it be caused?
If that which did not previously exist could come into being, then it could likewise arise from no cause.
Furthermore, because one observes that an effect arises from a cause, it is designated as a "cause."
If the fruit does not exist beforehand, how can it be called a cause?
Furthermore, if the fruit arises from a cause, then the fruit belongs to that cause; since the cause is not self-sufficient, it must in turn belong to another cause.
If the cause is not self-sufficient, how can one say that the fruit arises solely from this cause?
If this is the case with these various [factors], one knows that there is no "conditioned cause" (hetu-pratyaya).
Furthermore, since the past mind and mental factors have all ceased and possess no functional capacity, how could they serve as the "sequential condition" (samanantara-pratyaya)?

If there is a present mind, there can be no sequence; if it were to form a sequence with a future mind that is about to arise, then since that future mind does not yet exist, how could there be a sequence?
In such cases, there would be no "condition as immediate antecedent" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Since all phenomena are thus without characteristics and without conditions, how can one speak of a "condition as object" (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
If all dharmas have no belonging, no dependence, and are all equal, why speak of "dominant conditions"?
Since these four conditions are thus unattainable, why say, "One who wishes to know the four conditions should study the Prajñāpāramitā"?
The answer is:

You do not understand the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*. For this reason, it is said that "within the *prajñāpāramitā*, the four conditions (*catuḥ-pratyaya*) are all unobtainable. The *prajñāpāramitā* neither abandons nor destroys any phenomenon; it is ultimately pure and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
As the Buddha taught that there are four conditions, those of limited wisdom become attached to these four conditions and give rise to false doctrines;
in order to destroy such attachment, it is said that all phenomena are truly empty, and there is nothing to be destroyed.

Just as mental phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions within the internal and external sense bases, this mind is like an illusion, like a dream, deceptive, and devoid of a fixed nature;
the mental factors are likewise so.
This mind arises together with mental factors (caitta), namely sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), and so forth.
Because these mental factors share the same characteristic (sabhāga) and the same object (ālambana), they are called "associated" (samprayukta).

The mind takes mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with it as its cause, and mental factors take the mind associated with them as their cause; this is called the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
As for the associated cause, it is like close friends or acquaintances who accomplish a task through harmony.
As for the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) each have their own co-arising causes; because they arise together, they mutually assist one another.
It is like brothers who, being born at the same time, support and aid each other.
Regarding the cause of one's own seeds: past wholesome seeds are the causes for wholesome dharmas of the present and future;
past and present wholesome seeds are the causes for wholesome dharmas of the future.
The same applies to unwholesome and neutral [dharmas].
Thus, for all such dharmas, each has its own specific seed-cause (*bīja-hetu*).

As for the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it refers to the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) abandoned through the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination; these are the causes of all defiled dharmas, and are thus called the pervasive cause.
Regarding the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*): because of the conditions of one's karmic actions, one obtains the retributive fruits of good or evil; this is called the cause of retribution.
These five causes are termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because the mind and mental factors arise in a continuous succession without interruption, they are called the "condition as immediate antecedent" (samanantara-pratyaya).
Because the mind and mental factors arise by taking objects as their conditions, this is called the "condition as object" (ālambana-pratyaya).
When all phenomena arise, they do not obstruct one another; this is what is meant by "absence of obstruction.
Furthermore, the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions;
the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation arise from three conditions, excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

All other formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and all matter (*rūpa*) arise from two conditions, excluding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is weak, there is nothing that arises from a single condition.
The mind and mental factors born of retribution arise from five causes;
because they are non-obscured and indeterminate and are not defiled dharmas, the pervasive cause is excluded.
All afflictions also arise from five causes, with the exception of the retribution cause.
Why is this? Because the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are obscured (*nivṛta*), whereas their retribution (*vipāka*) is unobscured (*anivṛta*); therefore, the cause of retribution is excluded.
The matter (*rūpa*) born of retribution and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) arise from four causes.
Since matter (rūpa) is neither mind nor mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), it excludes the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu);
since it is non-obscured neutral (anivṛta-avyākṛta), it excludes the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
Defiled matter and all formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) likewise arise from four causes.
Because they are neither mind nor mental factors, associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) are excluded;
because they are defiled (*sāsrava*), retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) are excluded.
All other minds and mental factors—excluding the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*)—arise from four causes, excluding retributive causes and pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Why is this so? Because they are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is excluded; because they are not defiled (*sāsrava*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is excluded.

As for all other non-associated factors—namely, the formations (*saṃskāra*) dissociated from matter and mind—if they possess their own seeds as causes, they arise from three causes, excluding the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*), the retributive cause, and the pervasive cause.
If there is no cause consisting of its own seed, then it arises from two causes:
the co-existent cause and the non-obstructing cause.
The initial untainted mind and mental factors arise from three causes:
The associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the non-obstructing cause (*anivṛtti-hetu*).
Within that first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), matter (*rūpa*) and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) arise from two causes:
the co-arising cause and the non-obstructing cause.
There is no dharma that arises from a single cause.
If it arises from six causes, these are called the four conditions.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate these four conditions in this way, and their mind remains unattached.
Although one discriminates these phenomena, one knows they are empty, all being like magical illusions;
though there are various distinctions within these illusions, the wise observer knows they have no reality and merely deceive the eye.
To discern that the dharmas of ordinary persons are all inverted, false, and devoid of reality, there are four conditions; how, then, could they be real?
The dharmas of the noble ones are also unreal because they arise from the dharmas of ordinary beings, as previously explained in the context of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is not a single dharma with a fixed nature that can be grasped; therefore, it cannot be refuted.
However, because sentient beings are attached to dharmas that are empty of causes and conditions, it is said that [the teaching] can be refuted.
It is like a child who, seeing the moon in the water, conceives an attachment and desires to grasp it; being unable to do so, he is filled with distress and sorrow.
A wise person instructs him, saying:
"Though it can be seen by the eye, it cannot be grasped by the hand."
One merely negates that which is graspable, not that which is visible!
The Bodhisattva contemplates and knows that all phenomena arise from four conditions, yet does not grasp at fixed characteristics within those four conditions.

Arising from the conjunction of four conditions, it is like the moon in water: although it is deceptive and non-existent, it necessarily arises from the causes and conditions of the water and moon, and does not exist through other conditions.
All phenomena are likewise; each arises from its own causes and conditions, and possesses no fixed reality.
For this reason it is said:

"A bodhisattva who wishes to know, as they truly are, the characteristics of the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), the sequential condition (anantara-pratyaya), the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Question: If one wishes to know the meaning of the four conditions in detail, one should study the Abhidharma;
why then is it said here that one who wishes to know the meaning of the four conditions should study the Prajñāpāramitā?
Answer:

Regarding the meaning of the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*) in the Abhidharma, a beginner may grasp them as they truly are; yet, if one pursues them too deeply, one falls into false views, as was explained by you above in your refutation of the meaning of the four conditions.
Furthermore, all phenomena arise dependent upon four conditions. Upon what, then, do these four conditions depend?
If they have a cause, there would be an infinite regress; if there is an infinite regress, there is no beginning; and if there is no beginning, there is no cause.
If that were so, all phenomena would necessarily be without cause!
If there were a beginning, that beginning would have no cause;
if something exists without a cause, then it does not depend upon causes and conditions.
If that were so, all phenomena would likewise exist without depending on causes and conditions!
Furthermore, there are two possibilities regarding phenomena arising from causes and conditions:
if they already existed within the causes and conditions beforehand, they would not depend on causes and conditions to arise, and thus they would not be produced by causes and conditions.
If [the effect] did not previously exist within the causes and conditions, then there would be no individual causes and conditions.
Because of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the four conditions, such faults as these arise.
However, in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, through the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), such errors do not occur.
Just as when people of the world perceive birth, old age, sickness, and death through their eyes and ears, these are considered to exist;
yet if one seeks their characteristics with subtle analysis, they cannot be found.
For this reason, within the Prajñāpāramitā, one merely eliminates false views without negating the four conditions.
Therefore it is said:
"If one wishes to know the characteristics of the four conditions, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know the suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality of all dharmas should study the perfection of wisdom!
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should dwell in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner.
[Treatise]: There are two kinds of suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena:
first, their individual characteristics; second, their true characteristic (*dharmatā*).
As for their respective characteristics: earth has the characteristic of solidity;
water, the characteristic of moisture;
fire, the characteristic of heat.
Wind has the characteristic of motion; in this way, when one discriminates all phenomena, each has its own characteristic.

As for the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), when one discriminates within these respective characteristics and seeks the reality, it cannot be found; yet it cannot be destroyed and is free from all faults.
As it is said in the *Self-Characteristic Emptiness* (*Svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*):
"If earth were truly characterized by solidity, why would substances such as resin and wax abandon their own nature when they encounter fire?"
A person with supernormal powers enters the earth as if it were water;
furthermore, when wood and stone are dispersed, they lose their characteristic of solidity.

Moreover, when the earth is broken down into fine dust, and that dust is further broken down by the square measure, it ultimately returns to emptiness, and thus also loses its characteristic of solidity.
When one investigates the characteristics of earth in this manner, they cannot be found;
if they cannot be found, their reality is entirely empty, and this emptiness is the true characteristic (*dharmatā*) of earth.
All distinct characteristics are likewise thus; this is what is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): as previously stated, each phenomenon is empty; that there are distinctions within this emptiness constitutes "suchness" (*tathatā*).
That they are equally one single emptiness constitutes the "nature of phenomena."
This dharma-nature also has two aspects:
first, using an unattached mind to discern all dharmas because each possesses its own nature;
second, it is called the immeasurable dharmas, namely, the true mark of all dharmas.
As stated in the *Cittadhāraṇī-sūtra*:
"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is immeasurable; although Śrāvakas have attained this nature of phenomena, because their wisdom is limited, they cannot explain it immeasurably."
"Just as a person, though having reached the great ocean, cannot take up its immeasurable waters because their vessel is small—this is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
As for the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), it is called a 'limit' (koṭi) because the nature of phenomena is realized as the ultimate reality."
Just as an Arhat is said to dwell in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). Question:
Are these three—suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the limit of reality—one and the same?
Are they different?
If they are one, why speak of three?
If they are three, you should now explain them by distinguishing them!
Answer: These three are all synonyms for the "true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Why is this so?
Ordinary worldlings lack wisdom and engage in false contemplation regarding all phenomena, namely: [viewing them as] permanent, blissful, pure, substantial, and possessing a self.
Disciples of the Buddha contemplate according to the fundamental characteristics of phenomena; at that time, they do not perceive permanence, which is called impermanence;
they do not perceive bliss, which is called suffering.
Not seeing purity is called impurity;
not seeing reality is called emptiness;
not seeing a self is called non-self.
If one does not see the permanent but sees the impermanent, this is a false view;
seeing suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity is likewise so—this is called "suchness."
That which is "as-it-is" (tathatā) remains as it was, incapable of being destroyed.

For this reason, the Buddha taught three dharmas as the seals of the Dharma (dharmamudrā): namely, the seal that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are impermanent, the seal that all phenomena (dharma) are selfless, and the seal that nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction.
Question:
These three seals of the Dharma are all dismantled within the Prajñāpāramitā.
As the Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates form as permanent, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom;
if they contemplate form as impermanent, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom."
"Suffering and pleasure, self and non-self, cessation and non-cessation are also like this.
If one asks, "In what sense, then, are these called the Seals of the Dharma (dharmamudrā)?
the answer is:
Both sutras are the word of the Buddha; for instance, in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is explained with perfect clarity.

Because some people cling to the perversion of permanence, one abandons the view of permanence and does not cling to the mark of impermanence—this is called the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*). It does not mean that abandoning permanence and clinging to impermanence constitutes the Seal of the Dharma.
It is the same for me, even unto nirvāṇa.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, one destroys attachment to views such as impermanence; it does not mean destroying the state of non-acceptance or non-attachment.

Having realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of all these dharmas, one enters into the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), extinguishing all conceptual observations and no longer giving rise to divergent beliefs, for their nature is inherently so.
It is like a small child who, seeing the moon in the water, enters the water to seek it; failing to find it, he becomes distressed.
A wise person says to him:
“The nature of things is thus; do not give rise to distress!
To enter skillfully into the dharma-nature is what constitutes the “limit of reality” (bhūtakoṭi).
Question:

Question: Why is it that in the Śrāvaka teachings this is not spoken of as suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), or the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), whereas it is spoken of everywhere in the Mahāyāna teachings?
Answer: It is also spoken of in the Śrāvaka teachings, though only rarely.
As it is said in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, a certain bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
"Regarding the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, was it created by the Buddha,
or was it created by someone else?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I did not create the twelve links of dependent origination, nor was it created by anyone else.

Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, the suchness (tathatā), the dharma-characteristic (dharmalakṣaṇa), and the fixed nature of dharmas (dharmasthititā) of all phenomena are ever-present. That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises."

Just as with ignorance as a condition there are volitional formations, and with volitional formations as a condition there is consciousness, up to old age and death as a condition there are sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress;
so too, when this does not exist, that does not exist, and with the cessation of this, that ceases.

Just as with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of volitional formations, and with the cessation of volitional formations there is the cessation of consciousness, up to the cessation of old age and death there is the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
Such is the nature of arising and ceasing; it remains ever thus whether a Buddha appears or not.
This is what is meant by "tathatā" (suchness).
As it is said in the *Śāriputra-siṃhanāda-sūtra* within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
The Buddha questioned Śāriputra on the meaning of a single phrase; though he asked three times, Śāriputra was unable to answer three times.
After the Buddha had briefly provided some instruction to Śāriputra, he entered his quiet chamber.
Śāriputra gathered the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet shown me the starting point of this matter, so I was not yet able to answer;
however, regarding this Dharma, I could expound upon its details for seven days and seven nights without exhausting it."
Again, another bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“After the Buddha had entered his private chamber, Śāriputra uttered a lion’s roar and praised himself!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
“Śāriputra’s words are true and not false.
Why is this? Because Śāriputra has thoroughly penetrated the nature of dharmas.”
"In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, contemplating the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all phenomena is termed 'Suchness' (tathatā);
extinguishing all such contemplations and attaining the true reality of all phenomena is where 'Dharmatā' is spoken of."
Question:
In this passage, only "suchness" (tathatā) and "dharma-nature" (dharmatā) are mentioned; where else is the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) mentioned? Answer:
These two matters are spoken of because they have causes and conditions;
as for the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), it is not spoken of as "the limit of reality" because it lacks causes and conditions.
Question:

The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is itself nirvāṇa; it is for the sake of nirvāṇa that the Buddha has preached the twelve divisions of the scriptures. How can you say there are no causes and conditions?
The answer is:
"Nirvāṇa" is spoken of by various names; it is sometimes called "detachment," sometimes called "sublime," and sometimes called "emergence."
Such as these are what constitute the teaching of the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi); however, because it is not expressed by means of names, it is said to be without causes and conditions.
Furthermore, the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is as follows: just as phenomena were when unarisen, so they are when arising; and once arisen and passed away, they are likewise in the present.
That all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time is called suchness.
Question: If an unarisen dharma is called "non-existent," then when a dharma has arisen and is present,
that dharma must exist and be available for use.
Because present phenomena possess the characteristic of functional activity, one recollects past events; this is what is called the "past.

Since the three periods of time are each distinct, they should not be considered as identical in accordance with reality. Why, then, do you say that "the equality of the three periods of time is called Suchness"?
Answer: Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, the three periods of time are equal and without distinction.
As it is said in the "Chapter on Suchness" (*Tathatā-parivarta*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"The suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, the suchness of the present, and the suchness of the Tathāgata are a single suchness, without distinction.
Furthermore, in the previous discussion, the dharma of arising has already been refuted;
if there is no dharma of arising, then the future and the present likewise have no arising—how then could they not be equal?
Furthermore, the past has no beginning, the future has no end, and the present has no abiding;
for this reason, the equality of the three periods of time is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Having practiced in accordance with suchness, one enters into the immeasurable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As for this "nature of phenomena," "dharma" refers to *nirvāṇa*; it is indestructible and beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called the fundamental seed-element; it is like the presence of the nature of gold within yellow stone, or the nature of silver within white stone;
likewise, the nature of nirvāṇa exists within all worldly phenomena.
The Buddhas, worthies, and sages employ wisdom, skillful means, precept-keeping, and meditative concentration to teach and guide others, enabling them to attain this Dharma-nature of nirvana.
Those of sharp faculties immediately realize that all phenomena are this very Dharma-nature;
it is like a person with supernormal powers who can transform tiles and stones so that they all become gold.
Those of dull faculties seek it through skillful means and discrimination before they attain the dharma-nature;
it is like a great smelter who must strike the ore with a hammer before he obtains the gold.
Furthermore, just as water flows downward and thus converges in the ocean, merging into a single flavor; so too does the dharma-nature manifest.
All phenomena are likewise: all general and specific characteristics ultimately return to the *dharmatā*, becoming one single characteristic, which is called *dharmatā*.
Just as a diamond at the summit of a mountain gradually pierces its way down until it reaches the diamond foundation, where it stops upon reaching its own nature;

so too are all phenomena. When wisdom has analyzed and investigated them, one arrives at suchness (*tathatā*); from suchness, one enters into their own nature. As they were originally unarisen, all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished; this is called *dharmatā*.
Furthermore, it is like a calf that, wandering in distress and lowing, stops only when it finds its mother;

all phenomena are likewise. Though they differ in various ways and involve different modes of grasping or rejecting, they cease once they reach their own nature (*svabhāva*), never exceeding it. This is called the *dharmatā*.
Regarding "the reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*):
as previously stated, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called "reality" (*bhūta*), and the point of entry is called the "limit" (*koṭi*).
Furthermore, each and every phenomenon possesses nine aspects:
First, there is substantiality;
second, each possesses its own specific function.
