For example, although the eye and the ear are both composed of the four great elements, the eye alone has the capacity to see, whereas the ear lacks the faculty of vision.
Furthermore, just as fire has heat as its intrinsic nature (dharma) and cannot moisten;
thirdly, all phenomena each possess their own power:
for example, fire has burning as its power, while water has moistening as its power.
Fourth, all phenomena each have their own causes;
fifth, all phenomena each have their own conditions;
sixth, all phenomena each have their own fruits.
Seventh, all phenomena each possess their own intrinsic nature;
eighth, all phenomena each have their own limitations and obstructions;
ninth, all phenomena each have their own skillful means for opening and penetration.
When any phenomena arise, there are nine factors: the essence of the phenomenon itself and its remaining attributes.
To know that each of these phenomena possesses its own essence and is complete with its attributes is called "the inferior suchness of the world."
To know that these nine phenomena ultimately end in transformation, exhaustion, and extinction is called "Middle Suchness.
For example, this body is born from impurity; though it may be washed and adorned, it ultimately returns to impurity.
This Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing; it extinguishes all conceptual observations and is ultimately pure.
This is called "Superior Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, some say that among these nine matters, that which possesses the Dharma is called "Suchness."

For example, the nature of earth is solidity and heaviness; the nature of water is coldness and moisture; the nature of fire is heat and illumination; the nature of wind is lightness and movement; and the nature of mind is cognition and understanding.
Such dharmas as these are called "suchness" (tathatā).
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Whether a Buddha appears or a Buddha does not appear, suchness (tathatā), the dharma-characteristic (dharmalakṣaṇa), and the dharma-position (dharmasthiti) abide eternally in the world; that is to say, the formative forces (saṃskāra) conditioned by ignorance (avidyā) always remain as they are according to their original nature."
“Dharmatā” (the nature of phenomena) refers to the nature within these nine dharmas.
“Bhūtakoṭi” (the limit of reality) refers to the realization of the fruit within these nine dharmas.
Furthermore, the true mark of all dharmas is eternally abiding and immovable.
Because sentient beings, due to ignorance and other afflictions, deviate from and distort the true nature (dharmatā);

the Buddhas and noble sages employ various skillful means to teach the Dharma, destroying ignorance and the other afflictions so that sentient beings may recover their true nature, which is no different from its original state—this is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
Because the true nature (dharmatā) is conjoined with ignorance, it undergoes transformation and is thus not pure;
if one eliminates ignorance and the like to attain its true nature, this is called "the purity of the dharma-nature."

“Reality-limit” (bhūtakoṭi) refers to entering into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Knowing that the nature of phenomena is immeasurable and boundless, and is the most subtle, such that there is no phenomenon superior to or transcending the nature of phenomena, the mind becomes satisfied and seeks nothing further; thus, one realizes it.
It is like a traveler on a journey who proceeds day after day without ceasing until he reaches his destination, at which point he no longer has the intention to go further;
the practitioner abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is likewise so.

Just as Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), even if Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for them, they could not further advance, nor would they ever again be born within the triple world.

If a bodhisattva enters into this dharma-nature and anticipates the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet has not yet fully perfected the six pāramitās or transformed sentient beings, should they realize it at that time, it would obstruct their attainment of the Buddha-way.
At that time, by the power of great compassion and diligence, the Bodhisattva returns to cultivate all practices.

Furthermore, within the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he realizes there is no dharma of permanence, no dharma of pleasure, no dharma of self, and no dharma of substantiality; he also relinquishes these very modes of contemplation.

When all such modes of contemplation are extinguished, this is the reality of all phenomena: like *nirvāṇa*, it is neither born nor extinguished, being as it was from the beginning, never having arisen.
For example, water has the characteristic of coldness, yet it becomes hot through the presence of fire;
if the fire is extinguished and the heat is exhausted, it returns to its original state of coldness.
The application of various contemplative methods is like water encountering fire.
If all methods of contemplation are extinguished, like fire being quenched or water cooled, this is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
It is suchness as it truly and eternally abides. Why is this so?
The nature of all phenomena is inherently thus.
For example, just as all material phenomena possess a constituent of emptiness, so too do all phenomena possess the nature of nirvana; this is called the dharma-nature.
Within all the various skillful means for attaining *nirvāṇa*, there exists the nature of *nirvāṇa*.
When it is realized, suchness (*tathatā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, the dharma-nature is immeasurable and boundless; it cannot be measured by the mind or mental factors—this is called the dharma-nature.
This is the ultimate excellence; it is called the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality).

[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know by calculation the atoms of the great earth and all its mountains within a trichiliocosm should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to split a single hair into a hundred parts and, with one part of that hair, lift up all the waters of the great oceans, rivers, ponds, and springs within the trichiliocosm without disturbing the nature of the water, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
“If all the fires within the trichiliocosm were to ignite simultaneously, like at the time of the conflagration at the end of an eon,
and a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to extinguish them with a single breath, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
“If great winds should arise within a trichiliocosm, wishing to blow asunder the trichiliocosm and all its Mount Sumerus as if crushing rotten grass,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to obstruct their force with a single finger so that they do not arise should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] Question:
Why does the Buddha not praise the various merits of the bodhisattvas, such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), but instead praises this great power?
The answer is:
Sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, those who delight in wholesome dharmas; second, those who delight in the retribution of wholesome dharmas.
For those who delight in wholesome dharmas, he praises all meritorious qualities;
for those who delight in the retribution of wholesome dharmas, he praises great supernormal powers.
Furthermore, some say:
"The names of the four great elements are, in reality, also boundless and inexhaustible; because they are ever-present in the world, no one can fully move them or measure their quantity.
Although people construct cities, walls, towers, and palaces, what they actually employ is very little."
"The vastness of the earth supports and nurtures all things and is most firm.
For this reason, the Buddha said:

"If one wishes to know completely the number of particles of earth and the various mountains, such as Mount Sumeru, within a trichiliocosm, and furthermore wishes to know the extent of the individual karmic causes and conditions of sentient beings within each and every particle—each having its own distinct portion—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Question: Even the minute particles of dust from a single stone are difficult to count; how much more so the number of particles of dust from the earth and all the mountains within a trichiliocosm?
"This is not to be believed!
He replied:
"If even the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know it, how much less can ordinary people!"
This matter is known to all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"For example, suppose the earth and all the mountains of a trichiliocosm were ground into dust;..."
Passing beyond a thousand worlds in the eastern direction, one deposits a single mote of dust; passing again beyond a thousand worlds, one deposits another mote of dust;
in this manner, all the motes of dust throughout the trichiliocosm are exhausted.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Can the number of these worlds, equal to the count of those atoms, be known through calculation and measurement?
The bhikṣus replied:
"It cannot be known!
The Buddha said,

"If one were to take all the lands where atoms have been placed and those where they have not, and grind them all into dust, the number of kalpas since the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū appeared in the world would be equal to that."

"In this way, the Buddhas and great bodhisattvas are able to know as many world-systems as there are atoms in immeasurable Ganges-sands; how much more so, then, a single world-system equal to a Ganges-sand!"
Furthermore, "immeasurable" is spoken according to the capacities of people's minds.

For example, the water of the great ocean is called immeasurable, yet it is eighty thousand *yojanas* deep; even for the great-bodied Rāhu, King of the Asuras, measuring its volume would not be considered difficult.
Question:
How does one practice the prajñāpāramitā to attain this wisdom? Answer:

When there is one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā, extinguishing all afflictions, false views, and conceptual proliferation, and enters the profound meditative concentration of a bodhisattva, because their mindfulness, wisdom, purity, and expansion increase, they are then able to discern all material forms down to their subtle atoms and know their quantities and numbers.
Furthermore, because the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas have attained unimpeded liberation, they do not even consider such matters difficult, let alone this one!
Furthermore, some people regard the earth as solid and stable, yet the mind has no form or substance; both are entirely illusory.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"The power of the mind is great."
Because they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they disperse this great earth into fine dust.
Since the earth possesses form, fragrance, taste, and touch, and is heavy, it has no agency of its own;
because water lacks fragrance, its activity surpasses that of the earth.
Because fire lacks scent and taste, its power surpasses that of water;
because wind lacks color, scent, and taste, its activity surpasses that of fire;
and because the mind lacks these four factors, its functional capacity is greatest.
Furthermore, because the mind is bound by many afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*), its power becomes feeble.
Although wholesome minds with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*) are free from afflictions,
their power is likewise slight because the mind grasps at the characteristics (*nimitta*) of phenomena.

Although the untainted minds of the two vehicles do not grasp at signs, because their wisdom is limited, when they emerge from the untainted path, their six sense faculties differentiate according to worldly convention and grasp at the signs of phenomena; therefore, they do not exhaust the power of the mind.
The Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas possess immeasurable and boundless wisdom; they constantly abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), making no distinction between the world and nirvana.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is in fact not different, yet there are differences in the degree of their wisdom.

Those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* are ultimately pure and free from all obstructions; in a single thought-moment, they can count the atoms within the lands, mountains, and great earths of all the trichiliocosms in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—how much more so for worlds as numerous as the sands of a single Ganges in each of the ten directions!
Furthermore, if one is separated from the Prajñāpāramitā, even if one attains supernormal powers (abhijñā), one will not be able to know as much as described above.
For this reason it is said:
"If you wish to obtain these great supernormal powers, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Furthermore, some say:
"Among all things, water is the greatest. Why is this so? Because..."
Throughout the great earth—above, below, and on all four sides—there is no place that is not filled with water.

If the World-Protecting Heavenly Lord (Lokapāla) were not to regulate the rains sent by the devas and nāgas, and if there were no water-dispelling jewels, then heaven and earth would be submerged and swept away.
Furthermore, by reason of water, all sentient and non-sentient beings in the world are able to grow and flourish; from this it may be known that water is the greatest.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to know the number of water droplets—dispersing each drop so that they lose their power—should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Again, some people say:
"Fire is the greatest. Why is this so? Because—"
This is because it excludes fragrance and flavor.
Furthermore, since there are many sources from which water emerges, fire is able to extinguish it.
By the power of a great fire, one can burn all things and illuminate all darkness.
"For this reason, it is known that fire is the greatest.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to blow out a great fire should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Question: Since fire depends on wind to burn and blaze, how can they extinguish one another? Answer:
Although they arise in mutual dependence, their defects cancel each other out.
Question:
If that is so, since fire is immeasurably great while the breath from the mouth is extremely slight, how can it extinguish it?
Answer:

When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they attain supernormal powers through meditative concentration (dhyāna). Being able to transform the body so that it becomes vast, the breath from the mouth likewise becomes vast; therefore, they are able to extinguish it.
Furthermore, by means of his supernatural power, even a slight breeze can extinguish [the fire];
it is like a small diamond that can shatter a great mountain.
For this reason, when the gods and people of the world witness this supernatural power, they all submit and take refuge in him.
Furthermore, because the scope of harm caused by fire is vast, the Bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, extinguishes it through his supernormal powers.
Moreover, as the formation of a trichiliocosm is extremely difficult, the Bodhisattva, by virtue of his merit and wisdom, possesses the power to control it.
Furthermore, some say:
"Among the four great elements, the power of wind is the greatest; because it lacks color, fragrance, and taste, its characteristic of motion is the most prominent. Why is this so?"
Just as space is boundless, so too is wind boundless;
all generation, growth, formation, and destruction depend upon wind.
With its great force, the mighty wind shatters all the mountains of the trichiliocosm.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā so that one might be able to obstruct the power of the wind with a single finger. Why is this?
The true mark (*dharmatā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable and boundless; it can cause the power of a finger to be such as this.
[Sūtra] "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to sit cross-legged and fill the space of the trichiliocosm with a single body, he should study the *prajñāpāramitā*!"
[Treatise] Question:
For what causes and conditions does the Bodhisattva sit cross-legged in this manner? Answer:
Because the Brahma King presides over the trichiliocosm, he gave rise to a mind of false views, considering himself great;
however, upon seeing the Bodhisattva sitting cross-legged, filling the entirety of space, his prideful mind was extinguished.
Furthermore, through skillful means within the power of supernormal faculties, one can become many and many can become one;
the small can become large and the large can become small.
Furthermore, desiring to manifest rare and difficult-to-attain events, he sits filling all of space.
Moreover, to prevent various ghosts, spirits, and dragon kings from harassing and disturbing sentient beings, he sits filling the entirety of space, causing all beings to dwell in peace and security.
For instance, when the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, brothers, wished to destroy the city of Śrāvastī by raining down various weapons and venomous snakes,
Maudgalyāyana sat upright, filling the entirety of space, and transformed all those harmful objects into flowers, incense, and necklaces of pearls.
For this reason it is said:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fill the space of the trichiliocosm with a single full-lotus posture should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Sūtra] "Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to lift all the kings of mountains, the Sumerus, within a trichiliocosm with a single hair and cast them beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddha-worlds in other directions, without disturbing sentient beings, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason does the Bodhisattva lift Mount Sumeru and all other mountains and transport them beyond immeasurable worlds in other directions?
Answer:
It is not that there must necessarily be someone to lift it; this merely clarifies that the power of the Bodhisattvas is capable of lifting it.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattvas were about to preach the Dharma for the Buddha, they first adorned the trichiliocosm, removing all mountains so that the ground became level and smooth.
As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"The Buddha, wishing to assemble all the emanation Buddhas, first leveled the ground.
This was also because he wished to manifest a rare and marvelous event so that sentient beings might behold it.
Why is this? A single Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand yojanas high; to lift even this one mountain would already be rare, let alone the ten billion Mount Sumerus of a trichiliocosm!

If it were already difficult to lift a hundred billion Mount Sumerus of the trichiliocosm with a single hair, how much more so would it be to hurl a hundred billion Mount Sumerus with the tip of a single hair beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds!
When sentient beings behold these rare and marvelous deeds of the Bodhisattva, they all resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thinking to themselves:
"If this Bodhisattva possesses such supernatural power even before attaining the Way of Buddhahood, how much more so once he has become a Buddha!"
For this reason, it is said thus:

[Sūtra] "If one wishes to provide a single meal as an offering to all Buddhas and their Saṃghas in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"

If one wishes to offer a single robe, flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, lamps, banners, streamers, flower parasols, and so forth, as offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise] Question:

If it is already a difficult matter for a bodhisattva to offer a single meal to a single Buddha and his Saṃgha, how much more so to offer to all the Buddhas and their Saṃghas throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
The answer is:
The merit of making offerings resides in the mind, not in the physical act.
If a bodhisattva, with a great resolve, offers even a single meal to all the Buddhas and their Sanghas throughout the ten directions, they do not allow distance or proximity to be an obstacle.
Therefore, all Buddhas see it and accept it.
Question: Because all Buddhas possess omniscience, they all see it and accept it; [but why do others not?]
The Saṃgha does not possess omniscience; how then can they see [the merit], and how can they receive it?
The answer is:
although the Saṃgha neither sees nor knows, by making offerings to them, the donor obtains merit.
For example, suppose a person sends a messenger to make an offering to another; although that other person does not receive it, the sender has already obtained the merit of giving.
Likewise, in the case of the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), although there is nothing actually bestowed upon sentient beings, the merit of the practitioner is immeasurable.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas have accomplished immeasurable and inexhaustible merits; with a single meal they make offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha of the ten directions, such that all are fully satisfied, yet the food is not exhausted—just like a gushing spring that flows forth without ever being depleted.
Just as Mañjuśrī once offered a single bowl of *mṛdvīkā* (joy-fruit) cakes to eighty-four thousand monks, and they were all fully satisfied while the food remained inexhaustible;
furthermore, when a bodhisattva here offers a single bowl of food to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the implements for food and drink appear in full abundance before each of those Buddhas.
For example, when a ghost or spirit receives a single mouthful of food from a person, it produces a thousandfold or ten-millionfold more.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they attain immeasurable gates of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and immeasurable gates of wisdom and skillful means; for this reason, there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is unimpeded, the mental activities of this bodhisattva are likewise unimpeded.
This bodhisattva is able to make offerings to as many Buddhas and their Saṃghas in the ten directions as there are sands in ten million *gaṅgā* rivers, let alone as many as one *gaṅgā* river!
The same applies to robes, flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, lamps, banners, streamers, canopies, and so forth.

[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to be fully endowed with morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and to cause them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat, even up to causing them to attain nirvana without remainder, they should study the prajñāpāramitā."
[Treatise] The meaning of the five aggregates is as previously explained.
There are two kinds of the fruit of *srotāpanna*:
first, the Buddha taught that by severing the three fetters, one attains the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Abhidharma*:
"By severing the eighty-eight fetters (*saṃyojana*), one attains the unconditioned fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Second, those who are practitioners by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and practitioners by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), abiding within the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), are those who realize the fruit of a stream-enterer.
Furthermore, "srotāpanna" (stream-enterer) refers to the stream, which is the eightfold noble path;
"āpanna" (entered) means to enter.

To enter this eightfold noble path and flow into nirvāṇa is called the first contemplation of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; one thereby attains entry into the portion of the immeasurable *dharmatā* and falls within the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).
"Śikhi" means "one," and "Gami" means "coming.
This person dies from here and is born in the heavens; having come once more to the heavens, they shall attain the end of all suffering.
"Anā" means "not," and "gāmi" means "to come"; thus, it is called the characteristic of "not-coming.
Such a person dies within the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm or the formless realm; having exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*) there, they do not return to be born again.
Question:

Regarding the Anāgāmin who attains parinirvāṇa in this life and the Anāgāmin who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava), these also do not take birth in the realm of form or the formless realm; why, then, are they called "Anāgāmin" (Non-returners)?

Answer: Anāgāmins are mostly reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life are few. Because the majority is taken as the standard, they are so named.

As for those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī), they also intend to be born in the realm of form; however, seeing that their future body will be subject to suffering, they immediately attain nirvāṇa. For this reason, they receive their name based on the majority case.
Because an Arhat has exhausted all afflictions, he should receive the offerings of all devas, nāgas, and spirits.
There are nine types of Arhats:

those subject to regression, those not subject to regression, those subject to death, those who protect [their attainment], those who abide [in their attainment], those who progress toward excellence, those of unshakable nature, those liberated through wisdom, and those liberated both ways.
The ninefold meanings are as previously explained.

Furthermore, there are the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni*), the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), and other such sublime virtues of the Arhat, as well as the attainment of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

"Nirvana without remainder" refers to an Arhat who, having relinquished these five aggregates, no longer continues to receive subsequent five aggregates; thus, the suffering of body and mind is forever extinguished.
The three subsequent fruits of the path are as explained for the first path.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while giving, he should make the following distinction:"
Giving in this way, one obtains a great reward;
giving in this way, one is born into a great clan of Kṣatriyas, a great clan of Brāhmaṇas, or a great household of householders;
giving in this way, one is born in the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

By means of this giving, one attains entry into the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By means of this giving, one is able to give rise to the eight factors of the noble path.
By means of this giving, one is able to attain the stage of srotāpanna up to the Buddha-way. One should study the Prajñāpāramitā!

[Treatise]: The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that the true nature of all dharmas is without grasping and without relinquishing, and is indestructible. While practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* that is non-apprehendable, he cultivates meritorious deeds out of great compassion;
the primary gateway to these meritorious deeds is first to practice giving (*dāna*).
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, their insight is clear and sharp, enabling them to discern the merit of giving;
although the objects given may be identical, the amount of merit varies according to the excellence or inferiority of the mind.
For instance, when Śāriputra offered a bowl of rice to the Buddha, the Buddha immediately turned it over to give to a dog and asked Śāriputra:
"You have given this rice to me, and I have given this rice to a dog; who obtains the greater merit?"
Śāriputra said, "As I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, the merit obtained by the Buddha giving to a dog is greater.

Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom among all people, and the Buddha is the supreme field of merit; yet, it is not as if the merit obtained from giving to a dog—an inferior field—is so exceedingly great.
For this reason, it is known that great merit arises from the mind and does not reside in the field [of action].
Even a hundred thousand million times the merit of Śāriputra would not equal the mind of the Buddha.
Question: As you have said, one obtains much merit because the field of merit is sublime; yet, when Śāriputra gave to the Buddha, he did not obtain great merit?
Answer:
Although a fertile field may yield much merit, it is not equal to the mind.
Why is this? Because the mind is the internal master, whereas the field is merely an external object.
Sometimes the merit of giving resides in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

For example, the Arhat Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa once offered a single flower to a Buddhist stūpa; for ninety-one *kalpas* he experienced happiness among humans and devas, and through the residual power of that merit, he attained arhatship.
Furthermore, when King Aśoka was a young child, he offered soil to the Buddha;
later, as king of Jambudvīpa, he erected eighty thousand stūpas and finally attained the Way.

The object given may be most humble and the giver’s mind may be slight; yet, because the field of merit is sublime, one obtains a great fruit and reward. One should know that great merit arises from a fertile field.
If it is the "superior within the great," all three factors are fully present:
the mind, the object, and the field of merit; all three are sublime.
As stated in the first chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
“The Buddha scatters exquisite flowers upon the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, it is like practicing the giving of the *prajñāpāramitā* mind; because there is no attachment, one obtains a great fruit of retribution.
Furthermore, giving for the sake of nirvana also yields a great reward;
likewise, giving with a mind of great compassion in order to deliver all sentient beings also yields a great reward.
Furthermore, regarding "great fruition," it is explained therein as follows:
being born into a kṣatriya family and so forth, up until attaining Buddhahood.
Question:
How does one give alms and thereby attain birth in a kṣatriya family, up to and including the attainment of Buddhahood?
The answer is:
if a person practices giving and maintains the precepts, they will obtain wealth and honor among gods and humans.
If someone, through sincere generosity and observance of the precepts, is born into a kṣatriya family—
where "kṣatriya" refers to kings and great ministers—
and if they are devoted to wisdom and sacred texts while not afflicting sentient beings, then through that generosity and observance of the precepts, they will be born into a brāhmaṇa family.
If one's practice of giving and observance of precepts is deficient, yet they take pleasure in and become attached to worldly enjoyments, they will be born into a great household of laypeople;
such a layperson is one who is of humble origin but possesses vast wealth.

If one practices giving and maintains the precepts with a degree of purity, feels weary of domestic affairs, delights in hearing the Dharma, and makes offerings to virtuous persons, one will be reborn in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Why is this? Because whatever one desires or needs there, it is all obtained as soon as the thought arises;
and because one constantly sees the worthy sages and virtuous people of this realm, the thought of making offerings arises, for that place is close to where merit is cultivated.

If one practices giving and maintains pure precepts, making offerings to one’s parents and those whom one honors, and desires with the heart to attain excellence, one will be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
If one practices giving and maintains pure precepts, while delighting in learning and possessing a gentle mind, one will be born in the Yāma Heaven.

If one practices giving and maintains pure precepts, causing these two matters to become increasingly superior; delights in extensive learning, discriminates between the beautiful and the ugly, loves and rejoices in nirvana, and fixes the mind upon merit, one will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

If one practices giving, maintains the precepts with a profound mind, possesses extensive learning, delights in study, and supports oneself through one's own efforts, one will be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).

If, at the time of practicing giving, one’s pure observance of the precepts becomes even deeper, one delights in extensive learning, harbors much self-regard, and is unable to undergo personal hardship while seeking pleasure from others, one will be reborn in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Through his contemplation and diligent application of skillful means, he manifests the five desires in the form of female beauty, seizing them for himself with sovereign mastery.
It is like a commoner who, having toiled with his own labor, has his possessions forcibly seized by another.
Furthermore, when practicing giving, one is born in the heavens due to the causal conditions of one's vows.
As the Sūtra says:

"There are people who practice giving and maintain the precepts to a small degree but do not know meditative concentration; these people hear of the existence of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and their minds constantly aspire to it."
The Buddha said:
"It is certain that when such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; this is an inevitable outcome.
It is likewise for the other heavens up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations."
"Furthermore, there are those who practice generosity and maintain the precepts. When practicing generosity, their minds attain happiness; if they give much, their happiness is likewise great.
Reflecting in this way, they abandon the five desires, remove the five hindrances, and enter the first dhyāna, continuing in this manner up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception."
The definitions of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments are as explained above.
Furthermore, there is a person who gives alms to the Buddha and his disciples and hears the Dharma from them;

because of this giving, their mind becomes supple and their wisdom sharp and keen, whereby they immediately give rise to the eight factors of the Noble Path, sever the three fetters, and attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Even up to the Buddha-way it is likewise; by means of this giving, they hear his preaching of the Dharma and immediately resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, if one gives alms without having abandoned desire, one will be reborn among humans in positions of wealth and honor, or within the six heavens of the desire realm;
if one gives alms with a mind free from desire, one will be reborn in the Brahma worlds up to the Bṛhatphala heaven;
if one gives alms with a mind free from form, one will be reborn among the formless deities.
If one gives alms detached from the three realms for the sake of nirvana, one attains the path of a śrāvaka;
if, while giving alms, one loathes clamor and disorder, delights in seclusion and tranquility, and rejoices in profound wisdom, one attains the path of a pratyekabuddha;

if, while giving alms, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion, desires to deliver all beings, and seeks the foremost, most profound, and ultimately pure wisdom, one attains the path of Buddhahood.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom while giving,

by means of the power of skillful means and wisdom, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing giving, fulfill the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā by means of the power of wisdom and skillful means?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because the giver, the receiver, and the material wealth cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the dānapāramitā;
because transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended, one fulfills the śīlapāramitā.”
Because the mind is unmoving, one fulfills the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
because body and mind are diligent and never weary, one fulfills the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
because there is neither distraction nor attachment to flavors, one fulfills the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
"Because one knows that all dharmas are unattainable, one fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
[Treatise]: The meaning of "fulfilling" has already been explained at length above.
Regarding "the skillful means of wisdom," that which is spoken of here is the so-called non-apprehension of the three things.
A question is asked:
As for the skillful means of wisdom, it is able to accomplish its task without causing destruction and has nothing further to be done.
Now, if these three things were destroyed, one would fall into the view of nihilism; how then can it be called "wisdom combined with skillful means"?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of non-apprehension.
First is "attaining the unattainable," and second is "not attaining the unattainable.
To attain the unattainable is to fall into nihilism;
if one does not attain even the unattainable, this constitutes the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñopāya*) and does not fall into nihilism.
If one practices giving without the skillful means of wisdom, one grasps at the characteristics of the three things;
if one regards those three things as empty, one then grasps at the signless.

One who possesses the skillful means of wisdom has, from the very beginning, not seen the characteristics of these three things; for this reason, one with the skillful means of wisdom does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, when practicing giving, one destroys all afflictions; this is called the skillful means of wisdom.
Furthermore, when giving while giving rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, this is called the skillful means of wisdom.

Furthermore, the merit and generosity cultivated throughout immeasurable past and future lifetimes, which are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is also called the "expedient means of wisdom."

Furthermore, to mindfully rejoice in all the merits of the Buddhas and their disciples throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, dedicating that merit toward the giving of alms and toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is called the skillful means of wisdom.
These various kinds of powers constitute the meaning of the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*).
This applies even to the skillful means of wisdom in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain the merits of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Śāstra] Question:
The merits of the Buddhas of the past have already ceased; the merits of the Buddhas of the future do not yet exist; and the merits of the Buddhas of the present cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, since the merits of the Buddhas throughout the three periods of time are all unattainable, why do you say, "One who wishes to attain the merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time should study the Prajñāpāramitā"?
The answer is:
It does not say, "one wishes to obtain the merits of the Buddhas of the three periods of time";
rather, it means that one naturally desires to possess merits equal to those of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, without any deficiency.
Why is this so? Because all the merits of the Buddhas are equal; there is neither more nor less.
Question:

If that is so, why do you say, "The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable; his radiance extends for thousands, myriads, and billions of yojanas; and he delivers sentient beings for immeasurable kalpas"?
Answer: The worlds of the Buddhas are diverse; there are those that are pure, those that are impure, and those that are mixed.
As it is said in the *Trāyastriṃśa-parivarta Sūtra*:
“The Buddha was observing the rains retreat in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
When the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrived, the fourfold assembly had not seen the Buddha for a long time; they were filled with sorrow and found no joy.
They sent Maudgalyāyana to inform the Buddha, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that you abandon these sentient beings to dwell in those heavens?
At that time, the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Observe the trichiliocosm!

By the power of the Buddha, Maudgalyāyana observed and saw some Buddhas preaching the Dharma to great assemblies, some sitting in meditation, and some begging for alms; in these various ways they performed the works of a Buddha.

Maudgalyāyana immediately prostrated himself, casting his body to the ground with all five limbs. At that moment, Sumeru, the King of Mountains, trembled violently, and all the devas were struck with great alarm and fear.
Maudgalyāyana wept and, bowing his head to the Buddha, said:
"The Buddha possesses great compassion and does not abandon any being; you perform such various deeds to transform and deliver sentient beings!"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"What you have seen is but a small portion!

Beyond what you have seen, there is a land in the eastern direction where the ground is made entirely of pure gold. The disciples of that Buddha are all arhats, possessing the six supernormal powers without obstruction."
Beyond this, to the east, there is a land whose ground is made entirely of white silver; the disciples of that Buddha all study the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Beyond this, to the east, there is a land whose ground is made entirely of the seven treasures; that land is constantly filled with immeasurable radiance.
The disciples transformed by that Buddha are exclusively bodhisattvas, all of whom have attained dhāraṇīs and the various gates of samādhi, and abide on the stage of avaivartika.
Maudgalyāyana!
You should know that those Buddhas are all my own body.

In this manner, throughout the immeasurable worlds of the eastern direction—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—whether they be adorned or unadorned, it is my own body that performs the work of a Buddha in them all.
"As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
For this reason, one should know that Śākyamuni Buddha likewise possesses pure worlds such as the land of Amitābha;
and Amitābha Buddha likewise possesses both adorned and non-adorned worlds, such as the land of Śākyamuni Buddha.

The great compassion of all Buddhas penetrates to the very marrow of their bones; regardless of whether the world is favorable or foul, they teach and transform those who are ready to be saved according to their needs.

It is like a compassionate mother who loves her child: even if the child has fallen into a latrine or privy, she diligently seeks to rescue and pull them out, never regarding it as something loathsome.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Thirty-two;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of the First Chapter, Section Fifty:
The Meaning of Pāramitā, Scroll Thirty-three.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty. 50. The Meaning of Reaching the Other Shore [Sūtra]: "Furthermore, Śāriputra,..."
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise]: “The further shore” means reaching the very limit of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
What is meant by "the other shore"?

It is to fully know and exhaustively comprehend all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) through great wisdom—understanding their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and various manifold aspects;
and within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), to thoroughly understand everything from the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to Buddhahood.
The meaning of the characteristics of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas is as previously explained.

[Sūtra] “A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know the suchness of all dharmas of the past, future, and present, the dharma-characteristics of all dharmas, and the limit of non-arising (anutpattikadharmatā), should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Śāstra] Question:
Since "suchness" (*tathatā*) has already been explained above, why is it explained again now? Answer:
Above it was stated directly that "all dharmas are suchness," whereas here it is stated that "the three periods of time are all suchness";
above it was a brief explanation, whereas this is a detailed explanation;
above it spoke of one, whereas here it speaks of three.
"Dharmalakṣaṇa" (the characteristic of dharmas) is precisely dharmatā;
"anutpādakoṭi" (the limit of non-arising) is precisely bhūtakoṭi (the reality-limit).
The suchness of past dharmas is precisely the characteristic of past dharmas.
The same applies to the future and the present.
Furthermore, the suchness (*tathatā*) of past phenomena is the very suchness of future and present phenomena;
the suchness of present phenomena is the very suchness of past and future phenomena.
The suchness of future phenomena is precisely the suchness of past and present phenomena. Why is this so?
Because the characteristic of suchness is neither one nor different.
Furthermore, as previously stated, there are two kinds of suchness (*tathatā*):
first, worldly suchness; second, supramundane suchness.
By means of this worldly suchness, the three periods of time are each distinct from one another.
By means of this supramundane suchness, the three periods of time become one.
Furthermore, "dharma-characteristics" refers to the activity of all dharmas—their functions, powers, causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions.

Just as fire has the characteristic of heat and water has the characteristic of moisture, so too among all phenomena are the causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions distinguished by their respective individual characteristics;
as explained in the "Power of Knowing What is Possible and Impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), this is called the characteristic of worldly phenomena (*lokadharma-lakṣaṇa*).
If one investigates and examines the characteristics of all phenomena and enters into the dharma of non-arising, there is nothing superior to this; this is called the "limit of non-arising."
Question:

While suchness (*tathatā*) and the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) can be distinguished as belonging to the three periods of time, the limit of non-arising (*anutpādakoṭi*) is a future phenomenon; how, then, can there be past and present?
As stated in the Abhidharma:
"Those phenomena that arise are the past and the present;
those phenomena that do not arise are the future and the unconditioned."
"How can one wish for the past and present to have non-arising?
He replied:
"As has been explained in various ways previously regarding the refutation of the dharma of arising, all dharmas are without arising; how could it be that only the future is without arising?"
As in the discussion on the meaning of "at one time," the three periods of time have already been refuted.
The single characteristic of the three periods of time is what is called "characterlessness";
thus, there is no characteristic of arising.
Furthermore, non-arising is called nirvāṇa, because nirvāṇa is neither born nor extinguished;
nirvāṇa is the ultimate finality, wherein there is no further rebirth;
yet all dharmas are themselves nirvāṇa. For this reason, the Buddha said:
"All dharmas are the limit of non-arising. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to stand before all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who wishes to serve all buddhas, who wishes to become an inner retinue of all buddhas, who wishes to obtain a great retinue, who wishes to obtain a retinue of bodhisattvas, and who wishes to obtain the pure retribution of great giving, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] Question:
If a bodhisattva has not yet attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), how can they stand before the noble ones who have destroyed the outflows? Answer:
When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they already stand before all sentient beings, let alone after practicing through the accumulation of kalpas!
Because this bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom are vast, they remain ever great throughout successive lifetimes and are able to benefit śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because sentient beings recognize the Bodhisattva’s kindness, they revere and honor him; this respect extends even to those among the animal realm.
For example, in the past, when the Bodhisattva was a deer, his coat was like gold and his antlers were made of the seven treasures; five hundred deer followed him and served him with devotion.
If among humans, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King in an auspicious age, and a Great King in a degenerate age, protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma and benefiting sentient beings.
If they leave the household life and encounter the Buddha-dharma, they will act as great teachers of deliverance for the world, causing the Buddha-dharma to flourish and manifest;
if there is no Buddha-dharma, they will become masters of external paths, practicing the four immeasurables.
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas possess untainted wisdom (*anāsrava*), their benefit to others is slight;
it is like a single *śīrṣa* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which, though pure, cannot compare with the curd from the waters of the great ocean.
Although the Bodhisattva possesses wisdom that is still subject to outflows, once it reaches maturity, its benefit is immeasurable.
Furthermore, the four types of offerings and requisites for the path provided to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are mostly obtained through the Bodhisattva.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"Mañjuśrī became a pratyekabuddha seventy-two billion times, transforming those who were pratyekabuddhas and leading them to attain the Way."
For this reason, they stand before the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to serve as attendants to the Buddhas," it is like when Śākyamuni Buddha had not yet left the household life:
Chandaka served as his attendant, Udayin was his companion in play, and Gopī, Yaśodharā, and other court ladies were his inner retinue.
During the six years of ascetic practice after his renunciation, five men served him.
At the time he attained the Way, there were Māgandiya, Rādha, Sunakṣatra, Ānanda, and the Malla Guhyapada; these are called the "inner retinue."

Regarding the "great retinue": it consists of the various sages such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Kātyāyana, Pūrṇa, and Aniruddha; as well as the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before enlightenment, such as Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Bhadrapāla. These are called the great retinue.
Furthermore, the Buddha has two kinds of bodies:
first, the body born of the dharma-nature; second, the body that conforms to the world.
The retinue of the worldly body is as previously described.

Regarding the body born of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-nirmita-kāya*), it is attended by immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before enlightenment (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).
Why is this? As stated in the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*:
"When the Buddha was about to be born, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas bound for their final birth preceded him, while the Bodhisattva emerged from behind;
it was like the moon enveloped by dark clouds."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding "the bodhisattvas who sprang forth from the earth," these are all inner retinues and great retinues.
As for "the retinue of bodhisattvas," there are Buddhas whose retinue consists exclusively of bodhisattvas;
there are also Buddhas whose retinue consists exclusively of śrāvakas.
There are Buddhas whose retinues consist of a mixture of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
For this reason, it is said:
"Those who wish to have only bodhisattvas as their retinue should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"There are three kinds of retinues:
superior, middling, and inferior—the inferior consisting solely of śrāvakas, the middling being mixed, and the superior consisting only of bodhisattvas.
Regarding 'the pure retribution of great giving,' some say:"
“A bodhisattva has accumulated much merit but has not yet eliminated the afflictions; while receiving the faithful offerings of others, they have not yet been able to repay them with purity.
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, all dharmas are empty and ungraspable; how much more so the various fetters and defilements!”

Because the Bodhisattva enters into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); for this reason, he is able to purify the karmic reward of his giving.

Furthermore, the merit of the Bodhisattva is vast; from the moment he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has desired to undergo all sufferings on behalf of every single sentient being and to bestow all his merits upon all sentient beings, only thereafter seeking the path to Buddhahood for himself.
However, because phenomena cannot be apprehended, one spontaneously attains Buddhahood and delivers all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the vow of a bodhisattva is not constrained by incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*);
it endures as long as the world, suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and space do.
The Bodhisattva’s mind dwells in the world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; likewise, it remains for a long time without end.
If such a person cannot purify the merit of the gift, who then could?

Just as parents, despite having fetters and various evils, accept the offerings of their children for the sake of benefiting them for a single lifetime, thereby enabling the children to obtain great merit;
how much more so should it be for a Bodhisattva, who is free from all fetters and dwells throughout boundless ages to benefit sentient beings—how could they not purify themselves?
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva possesses only compassion but lacks wisdom, they are still able to benefit others; how much more so when practicing the perfection of wisdom!
Question:
If a bodhisattva is free from the fetters (*saṃyojana*), how can they take birth in the world?

Answer: This has already been answered previously: the Bodhisattva attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and acquires a body born of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-ja-kāya). He manifests transformations everywhere to deliver sentient beings and adorn the worlds.
By reason of these merits, although he has not yet attained Buddhahood, he is able to purify the karmic reward for his giving.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to give rise to a mind of stinginess, a mind of breaking the precepts, a mind of anger, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, or a mind of delusion, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
[Treatise] Because these six types of mental states are evil, they are able to obscure the gates of the six *pāramitās*.
For example, when a bodhisattva practices giving (*dāna*), if a mind of stinginess arises, it renders the giving impure;
that is to say, one is unable to give excellent things, or if one gives excellent things, one is unable to give them in abundance.
If one gives external objects, one is unable to practice internal giving;
if one is able to practice internal giving, one cannot give everything away.
Both cases arise from a mind of stinginess.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that all phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self; all phenomena are empty, like dreams and like illusions.
Thus, when they give away their body, head, eyes, and marrow, it is as if they were giving away grass and wood.
Although this bodhisattva has not yet attained the Way, wishing never to give rise to such a mind of stinginess, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
As for other people, because they have abandoned desire and attained the Way, they do not give rise to a mind of breaking the precepts.
Because the Bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he does not perceive any act of breaking the precepts. Why is this?
Because the precepts are the dwelling place for all virtuous merits, just as the earth is the foundation upon which all things depend.
If one who has broken the precepts cannot even attain other paths, how much less can they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
For this reason, one should not give rise to a mind that breaks the precepts.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"The dharma of a bodhisattva is to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; if one breaks the precepts, one causes affliction and disorder for all.
For this reason, a bodhisattva does not give rise to the thought of breaking the precepts, much less actually breaking them!
Even those of the Lesser Vehicle and ordinary worldlings should not give rise to a mind of anger, let alone a Bodhisattva who has resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi!
Being a vessel of suffering, one naturally undergoes affliction;
just as a person who commits a crime brings about their own execution and must suffer the consequences of their own making, they should not harbor resentment toward others.
One should simply guard one's own mind so that evil does not arise!
It is like a person encountering foul winds, rain, cold, or heat, who feels no resentment.
Furthermore, one should think thus:
“A bodhisattva seeking Buddhahood takes great compassion as the foundation; if one harbors anger and resentment, one’s resolve and aspiration will perish.
A person who harbors anger and resentment cannot even attain worldly happiness, let alone the bliss of the Path!”
"One who harbors anger cannot obtain happiness for themselves; how then could they bestow happiness upon others!
One who is indolent cannot even accomplish the superior matters of this world, let alone attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!"
For example, if one drills for fire while counting breaths, there will be no prospect of obtaining fire.
A distracted mind is like a lamp burning in the wind; although it has light, it cannot illuminate objects.
Wisdom within a distracted mind is likewise so.
Wisdom is the root of all wholesome dharmas; if one wishes to accomplish this wisdom, one must first collect the mind, for only then can it be achieved.
For example, a person who is crazed or intoxicated is unaware of what benefits themselves or others, or of matters that are good or foul;
a distracted mind is likewise, for if it cannot even properly discern the good things of the world, how much less so the supramundane Dharma!
The minds of ignorant people cannot comprehend any matter of success or failure, let alone subtle and profound meanings!
It is like a person without eyes who may fall into a ditch or enter a wrong path;
so it is with those lacking wisdom: because they lack the eye of wisdom, they cling to false teachings and do not accept right view.
For such a person, even mundane affairs cannot be accomplished, let alone *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
By the power of practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva is able to obstruct these six obscurations and purify the six *pāramitās*.
For this reason it is said:
"If one wishes not to give rise to the six obscurations, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings in the merit of giving, the merit of ethical discipline, the merit of cultivating meditative concentration, and the merit of exhortation; and if they wish to establish sentient beings in the merit of material wealth and the merit of the Dharma, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise] Question:
What is meant by "bases of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*)? Answer:
The Abhidharma states:
"Merit" refers to wholesome, out-flowing (sāsrava) actions of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, some say:
It is non-obscured neutral. Why is this?
Because it is the fruit of retribution resulting from the causes and conditions of wholesome outflowing karma, one attains this non-obscured neutral merit.
This retribution is also called merit (*puṇya*); as people in the world say:
"One who can accomplish great matters and achieve much is called a person of merit."
This merit is briefly explained as being of three kinds:
giving, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating meditative concentration. What is giving?
If someone gives clothing, bedding, food and drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, and so forth to others, this is called *dāna* (giving).
Question:
Are things such as food and drink themselves the giving?
Is there further giving?
The answer is:

food, drink, and other such objects are not giving itself; rather, when one gives such things, a mental state arises within the mind called "renunciation" (*tyāga*), which is the opposite of the mind of stinginess (*mātsarya*). This is what is termed the merit of giving (*dāna-puṇya*).
These are either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava);
they are always wholesome;
they are mental factors (caitasika-dharma), associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta), following the mind (cittānuparivartin), and arising together with the mind (citta-sahaja).
It is formless and shapeless;
it acts as a condition;
it is associated with karma, follows the course of karma, and arises together with karma.
It is not the fruit of past karma;
it is the cultivation of attainment and the cultivation of practice;
it is realization through wisdom and realization through the body.
It is attained by ordinary persons and also by noble ones. Some say:
"The volition associated with the dharma of relinquishment is called the merit of giving."
Why is this so? Because karma is able to produce karmic retribution;
volition (cetanā) is itself karma.
Physical and verbal actions are not themselves called "karma"; they receive the name "karma" because they arise from volition (*cetanā*).
This giving is of two kinds: first, pure; second, impure.
Impure giving consists of giving merely for the sake of direct exchange;
or giving out of fear of losing one's wealth;
or giving because of the abuse or insults one has received.
One may give because it is useless;
one may give out of affection;
or one may give for the sake of seeking power, thinking that through such giving one will gain much support and influence.
Some give because they are driven by the urgency of death;
some give because they seek a good reputation;
some give because they seek to match the fame of the noble and eminent.
Or they give out of envy and jealousy;
or they give out of pride—thinking, "Even lowly, foolish, and base people still practice giving; I am a noble and great person, so why should I not give?"
Some give for the sake of incantations and blessings of merit;
some give to seek auspiciousness and eliminate misfortune;
some give to seek entry into a companionable group.
Or, if one gives without a single-minded focus, without reverence, or with contempt for the recipient;
through such various causes and conditions, giving for the sake of matters pertaining to this life constitutes giving that is contrary to purity, and is thus termed impure.
Regarding pure giving, as it is said in the sutras: one gives for the sake of disciplining the mind;

one gives for the sake of adorning the intention; one gives for the sake of attaining the supreme benefit; and one gives so as to give rise to a pure mind that is able to discern [the truth] as an aid toward nirvana.
For example, just as a fresh flower that has not yet withered is both beautiful in color and fragrant,
so too is giving with a pure mind. As it is said,
for those among the devas who give with an impure mind, the radiance of their palaces is meager.
If one gives with a pure mind, the radiance of their celestial palace will increase and expand.
This karmic act of giving is not lost even after passing through ten million lifetimes, just like a formal promissory note.
Question: How does the merit of this giving increase? Answer:
Because giving is performed at the appropriate time, one’s merit increases.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Giving during a time of famine results in a great increase of merit."

Furthermore, when one comes from a distant journey, if one gives alms on a desolate road or in a perilous pass; or if one practices constant giving without interruption; or if one constantly maintains mindfulness of giving—for these reasons, the merit of giving increases and expands.
This is as explained in the "Mindfulness of Renunciation" (*tyāgānusmṛti*) among the six recollections.

If one gives a great gift, one gains much merit; likewise, if one gives to a virtuous person, or gives to the Buddha, or because both the giver and the recipient are pure, or if one gives with a resolute mind, or gives wealth acquired through one's own effort, or gives as much as one possesses to the very end, or gives by exchanging goods, or gives gardens, fields, servants, and so forth.
Such giving can only be practiced by a bodhisattva with a profound mind.

For example, after the Bodhisattva Vairama had practiced giving for twelve years, he presented eighty-four thousand decorated milch cows, bowls made of the seven precious substances, and court ladies, each numbering eighty-four thousand; as for his other various items, such as food and drink, they were beyond counting.
Furthermore, for example, the Bodhisattva Sudāṇa descended from his excellent white elephant and gave it to his enemy, entering deep into the mountains;
he gave away his two beloved sons to twelve ugly Brahmins;
and he further gave away his wife and his eyes to a conjured Brahmin.
At that time, the earth shook violently, the heavens thundered, and flowers rained down from the sky.
It was also like King Sarvadatta, who bound his own body and gave it as an offering to a Brahmin.
For example, King Śibi, for the sake of a single pigeon, offered his own body to substitute for the pigeon's flesh.
Again, as a Bodhisattva, he once took the form of a hare and roasted his own flesh to give as alms to a rishi.
Such accounts are as described in the *Bodhisattvāvadāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, there were śrāvakas who practiced giving;

for instance, the bhikṣuṇī Sumitā, together with two of her fellow students, built a vihāra for the Buddha Kanakamuni, and thereby received the blessings of being a universal monarch (cakravartin) and a celestial king for countless tens of millions of lifetimes.
For example, there was a brahmin who offered a jar of curd to the Sangha; he enjoyed happiness life after life and has now attained arhatship, which is the foremost among all forms of happiness.
Just as Lady Mallikā, by making offerings to Subhūti, obtained the retribution of this present life as the queen of King Prasenajit;
and just as Śivā, by making offerings to Kātyāyana, obtained the retribution of this present life as the queen of King Caṇḍapradyota.
Just as the householder Ugga attained the fruit of his reward on that very day because he made offerings to Śāriputra and five hundred arhats;
and as five hundred merchants, having received their leftover food, each gave him a pearl necklace, whereby they suddenly became immensely wealthy and were subsequently called Ugga.
Generous acts such as these yield rewards in the present life.
One should know that the discourse on generosity is inexhaustible when explained.
Regarding the "meritorious sphere of observing the precepts," this refers to what the Buddha taught concerning the merit of the five precepts.
Question: What are the characteristics of the offense of killing? Answer:
Knowing this to be a sentient being, one incurs the offense of killing by taking its life intentionally, not unintentionally;
one incurs the offense of killing with a mind of peace and pleasure, not with a distracted or deranged mind;
one incurs the offense of killing by taking life, not merely by inflicting a wound.
The offense of killing is incurred once death has occurred, not while one is still alive;
it is a physical action (*kāyakarman*) that constitutes the offense of killing, not verbal action;
it is the actual bodily act that constitutes the offense of killing, not merely the arising of the intention in the mind.
To refrain from committing such offenses and not to engage in them constitutes the virtuous characteristic of the first precept.
Some may say that this refers to the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
They may be bound to the desire realm or not bound;
they are neither mind nor mental factors, not associated with the mind, and do not follow the mind;
they may arise together with the mind or not arise together with the mind.
It is not associated with karma, nor does it follow the course of karma;
it may arise from common karma or from uncommon karma;
it is not the retribution of prior karma.
Cultivation through acquisition and cultivation through practice;
realization by body and realization by wisdom;
or that which is abandoned through contemplation, or that which is not abandoned.
When one becomes free from desire for the realm of desire, one attains the knowledge of abandonment;
this is common to both ordinary persons and noble ones.
This is called the explanation of the characteristics of the precept against killing.
The remaining precepts should likewise be analyzed according to their respective meanings.
Regarding the discourses and treatises praising the various precepts, they are as explained in the "Śīlapāramitā" [chapter].

As for the "meritorious sphere of cultivating meditative concentration" (*samādhibhāvanāpuṇyakṣetra*), although the sūtras state that cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the cultivation of meritorious concentration, they also state that tainted meditative concentrations (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) capable of producing karmic retribution are included; these are collectively termed the "meritorious sphere of cultivating meditative concentration."
Because the desire realm is characterized by much anger and agitation, the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is first taught as the merit for practicing meditative concentration.

Having attained the skillful means of loving-kindness and vowing to grant happiness to sentient beings, one subsequently actually perceives them receiving that happiness; this mental factor associated with such a mind is called the "dharma of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-dharma*).
This dharma is either bound to the realm of form or unbound; this is true loving-kindness.
This is skillful means loving-kindness, which is bound to the desire realm;
it constantly follows the movement of the mind and arises together with the mind.
It is formless and without resistance;
it is a dharma that can serve as an object of cognition;
it is not karma itself, but is associated with karma, follows the course of karma, arises together with karma, and is not the maturation of prior karma.
Cultivation through acquisition and cultivation through practice;
realization through the body and realization through wisdom;
or that which is abandoned through contemplation, or that which is not abandoned.
When one becomes detached from the desire realm of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one attains the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*);

it may be accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), or without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without both applied and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*);
and it may be accompanied by joy (*prīti*) or without joy.
There may be those with breath and those without breath;
they may be ordinary persons or noble ones;
and they may be associated with pleasant feeling, or associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
First one takes as an object the sign of attainment and understanding, and subsequently takes as an object the true meaning.
Within the four fundamental dhyānas, it also transcends the four dhyānas;
that which is attained by relying upon the four dhyānas is firm and powerful.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) should be called "affection," for because it is free from enmity and contention, it is termed "affectionate";
because it takes immeasurable sentient beings as its object, it is termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*);
and because it can benefit sentient beings and bring about the departure from desire, it is termed "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*).
Other discourses on the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are as explained in the section on the "Four Immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). Question:
Among the merits of cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), why does the Buddha speak only of the mind of loving-kindness and not of the others?
Answer:
Among the four immeasurables, the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can produce great merit and virtue.
Because the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) involves sorrow, it relinquishes merit and virtue.
Because the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) dwells upon one's own merits, its merit is not profound;
because the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) relinquishes all, its merit is likewise slight.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) has five benefits, but did not speak of such for the others.
What are the five? First, blades do not wound;
second, poisons do not harm; third, fire does not burn; fourth, water does not drown; fifth, among all sentient beings who are angry and malicious, one perceives them all with joy.
The three matters beginning with compassion are not like this; for this reason, it is said that "the cultivation of meditative concentration is for the sake of loving-kindness.
The others follow as its attendants, as do all other impure concentrations capable of producing karmic retribution.

Regarding "Exhorting toward Meritorious Deeds": if a bhikṣu is unable to practice seated meditation or recite the sūtras, he should teach and exhort others to cultivate and establish meritorious deeds.

There may be a bhikṣu who is capable of practicing seated meditation and reciting the sūtras; seeing that other bhikṣus lack sufficient robes and food, he uses his strength to procure them for them and also provides exhortation and guidance.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattvas have compassion for sentient beings, they exhort and transform them by means of the causes and conditions of merit.

Moreover, if those who have left the household life were to seek wealth for themselves, they would incur a transgression of the precepts; therefore, they provide exhortation and guidance as the causal condition.
"Material fortune" refers to clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, gold and silver, carriages and horses, fields and houses, and so forth.
Question: Previously it was called "the field of merit of giving," while here it is called "material fortune. What is the difference between them?
The answer is:
Giving encompasses all forms of giving:
the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma; worldly giving and the giving of the Path.
Now I wish to distinguish between the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth.
As for the gift of Dharma: for example, because the Buddha possesses great compassion, when he first turned the wheel of Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings attained the Way;
subsequently, Śāriputra followed the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma.
Although other noble ones do not turn the wheel of the Dharma, they also preach the Dharma for sentient beings so that they may attain the Way; this is also called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Furthermore, there are the Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others, who, by means of two kinds of supernormal powers—those acquired through karmic fruition and those attained through cultivation—abide therein and, through the power of merit, skillful means, radiance, and psychic faculties, deliver sentient beings through various causes and conditions; this is also called the gift of Dharma.
When Pratyekabuddhas soar through the void and speak a single verse to guide sentient beings, causing them to plant roots of goodness, this is also called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Furthermore, when disciples of the Buddha who have not yet attained the Noble Path practice seated meditation or recite the sutras, and teach their own disciples without subverting the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), all such acts are called the gift of Dharma.
These various kinds [of giving] are called the characteristics of the gift of Dharma.
For this reason it is said:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to establish sentient beings in the six kinds of merit from giving should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to obtain the five eyes should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] What are the five?
They are the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.

The fleshly eye sees what is near but not what is distant; it sees what is before but not what is behind; it sees what is outside but not what is inside; it sees by day but not by night; it sees what is above but not what is below.
Because of these obstructions, he seeks the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Having attained this divine eye, he sees both far and near; there is no obstruction whatsoever regarding what is before or behind, inside or outside, day or night, above or below.

With the divine eye, one sees things that are conventionally designated as arising from a combination of causes and conditions, yet one does not see their true nature—that is, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing—which are the same in the beginning, middle, and end;
for the sake of this true nature, one seeks the wisdom-eye.
