To attain the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one does not perceive sentient beings; all marks of unity and difference are extinguished, one abandons all attachments, and does not grasp at any phenomena. Wisdom itself ceases within; this is called the wisdom-eye.
However, the wisdom-eye cannot deliver sentient beings!
Why is this? Because it is free from discrimination; for this reason, one seeks the Dharma-eye.

The Dharma-eye causes these people to practice this Dharma and attain this Path, knowing the various skillful means for each and every sentient being so that they may realize the realization of the Path.
However, the Dharma-eye cannot universally know the skillful paths for delivering sentient beings; for this reason, one seeks the Buddha-eye.
The Buddha-eye knows nothing that is not known; though obstructions may be dense, there is nothing it does not see or know.
What is extremely distant for others is exceedingly near to the Buddha;
what is obscure and dark for others is luminously clear to the Buddha.
What constitutes doubt for others is certainty for the Buddha;
what is subtle for others is coarse for the Buddha;
what is profound for others is very shallow for the Buddha.
This is the Buddha-eye: there is nothing it does not hear, nothing it does not see, nothing it does not know; for it there is no difficulty and no need for deliberation;
within all phenomena, the Buddha-eye constantly shines.
This will be explained in detail later in the section on the five eyes.

[Sūtra] “A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see with the divine eye all the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; who wishes to hear with the divine ear the Dharma taught by those Buddhas of the ten directions; and who wishes to know the minds of those Buddhas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise]: What is seen by the dharma of the divine eye does not exceed a trichiliocosm;
now, by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one sees the Buddhas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is neither near nor far, and there is nothing that constitutes an obstruction.
Question:
As stated in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*:
"By the power of the Pratyutpanna-samādhi, although one has not yet attained the divine eye, one is able to see the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions.
What difference is there between this Bodhisattva seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions through the divine eye [as described elsewhere] and this?
Answer: This divine eye is not obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The Pratyutpanna Samādhi can be attained by both those who have abandoned desire and those who have not yet abandoned it.
The divine eye is obtained only by those who have detached from desire.
As for the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, one sees because of constant cultivation and habitual practice through recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination.

The divine eye cultivates supernormal powers and obtains the eye composed of derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) from the four great elements of the form realm; its four sides obtain the characteristic of universal luminosity. This is the distinction between them.
The power of the divine eye is easy, like the rising of the sun, where seeing forms is not difficult;
the power of samādhi is difficult, like lighting a lamp at night, where seeing forms is not easy.
The divine ear is also like this.
Regarding the phrase "knowing the minds of all Buddhas," a question is asked:
Just as those of dull faculties on a higher stage cannot know the minds of those with sharp faculties on a lower stage,
a Bodhisattva should not even know the mind of a single Buddha, let alone the minds of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Answer: It is by the Buddha’s spiritual power that the bodhisattvas come to know this.
As it is said in the sutra:
"All sentient beings are ignorant of the Buddha-mind; yet if the Buddha were to cause them to know it through his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), even insects would be able to know it.
For this reason, by means of his supernormal power, the Buddha causes the Bodhisattvas to know the Buddha-mind.
Furthermore, the *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of non-obstruction; whether coarse or subtle, deep or shallow, foolish or holy, there is no distinction whatsoever.
The mind of all Buddhas and the mind of Bodhisattvas are one suchness (*tathatā*) without difference;
because the Bodhisattva accords with this suchness, they are able to know the minds of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is a rare and difficult matter to know that which should not be known.
For this reason, it is said:
"Those who wish to attain this should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Sūtra] “Those who wish to hear the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions, and having heard it, not forget it until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, should study the *prajñāpāramitā*!”
[Treatise] Question:
It is already difficult to uphold what has been taught by a single Buddha; how much more so to wish to remember without forgetting what has been taught by immeasurable Buddhas?
The answer is:
By the power of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, the bodhisattva is able to receive [the teachings]; by the power of the *dhāraṇī* of firm mindfulness, he does not forget them.
Furthermore, it is said here:
By the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are ultimately pure and free from attachment.

Just as the great ocean receives all streams, the Bodhisattva hears the Dharma from the Buddhas of the ten directions; because the vessel of the *prajñāpāramitā* is vast, they are able to receive immeasurable teachings, retaining them without forgetting.
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā is beyond analogy, like empty space.
Just as when the kalpa-ending conflagration has ceased and a great rain fills [the world], there is no place other than empty space that can receive this rain;

likewise, the Dharma-rain of the Buddhas of the ten directions issues from the mouths of the Buddhas, and there is no one capable of receiving it except for the Bodhisattvas who practice Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason it is said:
"Those who wish to hear the Dharma preached by all the Buddhas of the ten directions should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

51. The Meaning of Seeing All Buddha-worlds, Part One of Fifty-one. [Treatise] Explaining the First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra: The Meaning of Seeing All Buddha-worlds, Part Fifty-one, Section One. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see the worlds of the Buddhas of the past and the future, as well as the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise] Question:
If one has already seen the Buddhas of the ten directions, one has thereby already seen the worlds; why, then, does it further say, "desiring to see the worlds"?
Answer:

If a bodhisattva has not yet deeply entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), their mind will become distracted upon seeing the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the worlds in the ten directions;
therefore, they should contemplate only the Buddhas, as explained in the "Meaning of Mindfulness of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*).
The practitioner contemplates only the Buddhas, not the lands, mountains, rivers, or trees;
once he has attained the power of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), he may contemplate extensively at will.
Furthermore, because the various pure Buddha-lands are difficult to perceive, it is said:
"If one wishes to see the various Buddha-fields, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, a single Buddha has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of worlds, as previously described:
some are adorned and pure, some are not adorned and pure, and some are mixed.
Because there are worlds of ultimate purity that are difficult to see, it is only through the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* that one is able to perceive them.
It is like this: when a celestial king is in his public audience hall, outsiders can see him;
but in his inner chambers and deep palace quarters, no one is able to see him.
Question:
The worlds of the ten directions in the present can be seen; how, then, can the worlds of the Buddhas of the past and future be seen? Answer:
The Bodhisattva possesses the samādhi of seeing the past and the future; having entered this samādhi, he sees the events of the past and the future as if they were things seen in a dream.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses the *anirodhakoṭi-samādhi*. Having entered this samādhi, he does not perceive any Buddhas as undergoing extinction.
Question:
These two dharmas are not the eye; how, then, can they see?
Answer: This is wisdom, which is metaphorically named "eye";
as it is said in the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, one attains eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening regarding the Four Noble Truths.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva perceives the worlds of the Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions, they know with certainty that the worlds of all past and future Buddhas are likewise so. Why is this?
Because the merits of all Buddhas are identical, this matter is as previously explained.
Furthermore, within this Prajñāpāramitā, the present, past, and future are no different, being one suchness and one dharma-nature; for this reason, one should not raise objections.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions—

namely, the sūtras (sūtra), verses (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), stanzas (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), causal narratives (nidāna), parables (avadāna), 'thus-it-was-said' discourses (itivṛttaka), birth stories (jātaka), extensive discourses (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), and analytical treatises (upadeśa)— and desires to recite, receive, and uphold them all, whether they have been heard by the śrāvakas or not, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Treatise] Previously it was stated: "Those who wish to hear exhaustively all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions should study the Prajñāpāramitā. These "taught dharmas" refer precisely to these twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana).
Those sūtras that state matters directly are called "sūtra," namely the four Āgamas, the various Mahāyāna sūtras, and the Sūtra on the Two Hundred and Fifty Precepts;
furthermore, there are various sūtras outside the Tripiṭaka, all of which are termed "sūtra."
The verses found within various sūtras are called *geya*.
Sentient beings receive predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) within the nine paths, namely the paths of the three vehicles and the paths of the six destinies.
It may be that a person is predicted to become a Buddha after such-and-so many asaṃkhyeya kalpas, or that they are predicted to become a Buddha after such-and-so many years.
He predicts that Śrāvakas will attain the Way in this life or in future lives;
he predicts that Pratyekabuddhas will attain the Way only in future lives;
and he predicts that for those in the other six realms, they likewise all receive retribution in future lives.

Regarding the dharmas of all Buddhas, when they wish to bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon sentient beings, they first smile; then immeasurable kinds of light issue forth from their four canine teeth—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, pale green, purple, and so forth.
The light emanating from the two upper tusks illuminates the three evil realms.
From that radiance, he expounds immeasurable teachings, proclaiming that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, that all phenomena are selfless, and that Nirvana is peace and security.

Sentient beings who encounter this light and hear the teaching of the Dharma will experience peace and happiness in body and mind; they shall be reborn among humans or in the heavens, and by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall all bring an end to suffering.
That which issues from the two lower fangs shines upward upon humans and devas, reaching as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in the dhyāna realms.
Those who are deaf, blind, mute, or afflicted by insanity are all healed and restored.

The devas and humans of the six heavens of desire, as well as the asuras, who were enjoying the pleasures of the five senses, encountered the Buddha’s radiance and heard the sound of his preaching the Dharma; they all grew weary of sensual pleasures, and their bodies and minds became peaceful and secure.

When the devas of the form realm experience the bliss of meditative concentration, upon encountering the Buddha’s radiance and hearing the sound of his preaching the Dharma, they too give rise to a sense of weary detachment and come to where the Buddha is.
These rays of light further reach the ten directions, illuminating the six realms of existence everywhere; having performed the work of a Buddha, they return and circle the body seven times.
If he is to record the destiny of those in hell, the light enters through the soles of his feet;
if he is to record the destiny of animals, the light enters through his calves.
If he prophesies rebirth as a hungry ghost, the light enters through the thighs;
if he prophesies the human realm, the light enters through the navel;
if he prophesies the heavenly realms, the light enters through the chest.
If he prophesies a śrāvaka, the light enters through the mouth;
if he prophesies a pratyekabuddha, the light enters through the mark between the eyebrows;
if he prophesies that one will attain Buddhahood, the light enters through the crown of the head.
If one is about to receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa), this sign first appears, after which Ānanda and the other disciples pose their questions.
All verses are called "geya" (repetition); whether they consist of six lines, three lines, five lines, or an indefinite number of lines, they are termed both "geya" and "gāthā" (verse).
Regarding "Udāna": it refers to those teachings that the Buddha must inevitably proclaim even without anyone asking questions; thus, the Buddha briefly opens the inquiry.

For example, while the Buddha was at Śrāvastī, walking up and down in the shade of the Viśākhā Hall, he spontaneously uttered an Udāna, saying: "There is no self, and nothing belongs to a self—this matter is excellent!"
At that time, a certain bhikṣu joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self? This matter is excellent.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Ordinary people who have not yet attained the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) have their minds shrouded by inversion; therefore, they experience great terror and fear regarding that which is without self and without what belongs to a self."
"If the Buddha and his disciples hear the sublime Dharma, they joyfully practice it; because they are free from inversion, they do not need to act further.
Such passages are explained in detail within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Furthermore, as in the "Prajñāpāramitā Chapter," the devaputras praised Subhūti’s discourse, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"How rare, World-Honored One!
How difficult to encounter, World-Honored One!
This is called an udāna.

Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples collected essential verses—such as the various verses on impermanence—which they compiled into the Chapter on Impermanence, and so forth, including the verses on the brahmins which they compiled into the Chapter on Brahmins; these are also called Udānas.
Whatever collections of various wondrous matters exist are all termed *udāna*.
Such characteristics as these define the *udāna* sūtras.

As for "nidāna," it refers to the explanation of the original causes and conditions for the various teachings of the Buddha—namely, by what causes and conditions the Buddha spoke of this particular matter.
In the Sūtras, this matter is explained because someone asked about it;
in the Vinaya, this precept is established because someone committed this offense.
All matters concerning the dependent origination of the Buddha’s words are termed *nidāna*.
As for *avadāna*, these are gentle and accessible narratives that resemble worldly discourse;
such as the *Mahāvadāna-sūtra* in the *Madhyama Āgama* and the *Mahāvadāna* in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
In the *Vinaya*, there are the *Avadāna* of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and the *Avadāna* of Koṭīviṃśa;
in the *Śatapañcāśatkavarga-vinaya-sūtra*, there is one section on the *Avadāna* of Desire;
and one section on the *Avadāna* of Bodhisattvas has been extracted.
There are immeasurable *avadānas* such as these.
Regarding the "Sūtras of Thus-spoken Words" (*Itivṛttaka*), there are two types:
first, those with concluding verses, which state:
"Regarding what I previously promised to explain, I have now finished explaining it.
Second, apart from the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāyāna, there is another scripture named *Ekottarika*;
some say it is called *Muktaka*.
The *Muktaka* is said to be extracted from the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāyāna. What is it?
It is as the Buddha taught:

King Śuddhodana forcibly compelled those who had become disciples of the Buddha to leave the household life; the Buddha selected five hundred among them who were capable of attaining the Way and led them to Śrāvastī.

Why is this? Because they had not yet abandoned desire, and fearing that they might break their precepts if they remained near their relatives, he brought them to Śrāvastī and had Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others instruct them.
By remaining awake and practicing with focused diligence during both the first and last watches of the night, they attained the Way.
Having attained the Way, the Buddha returned to his native land.
It is the custom of all Buddhas, when returning to their home countries, to dwell together with a great assembly of devas in the forest of Kapilavastu seers.
This grove is fifty *li* from the city of Kapilavastu; it is a pleasure garden where the Śākyas sport.
When these Śākya sons were bhikṣus in Śrāvastī, they were so diligent and focused that they did not sleep during the first or last watches of the night, and thus they perceived the night as long.
Coming from the grove to enter the city for alms, they now perceive the distance of the road as long.
At that time, the Buddha knew their thoughts.
A lion came and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, standing to one side.
For these three reasons, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"For the sleepless, the night is long; for the weary, the road is long; for the foolish, birth and death are long, as they do not know the True Dharma!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When you had not yet left the household life, because your mind was negligent and you slept much, you did not perceive the length of the night;
now, as you diligently seek the Way during the first and last watches of the night, reducing your sleep, you perceive the night as being very long."
"In this grove of Kapilavastu, where you formerly rode in carriages for pleasure, you did not perceive it as distant;
now, wearing robes and holding alms bowls, you walk with extreme fatigue, and thus you perceive the road as long."
This Lion was a Brahmin teacher during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha. Seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma, he came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, because the great assembly was listening to the Dharma, no one spoke with him; he immediately conceived an evil thought and uttered words of abuse:
"These shaven-headed fellows—how are they any different from animals!"
"He does not distinguish between good people and he does not understand speech!
Because of this evil karma of harsh speech, from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until today, for ninety-one kalpas, he has constantly fallen among the animals;
this man should have attained the Way at that very moment, but because of his folly, he has created for himself a long duration of birth and death.
"Because your mind is now pure in the presence of the Buddha, you shall attain liberation.
Sūtras such as these are called "Expositions of Causes and Conditions.
From what source do they emerge?
Because it emerges from within the Tripitaka and the Mahāyāna, it is called "Emergent" (*niṣkrānta*).
Why is it called "causal condition" (*nidāna*)?
Because it is the root of these three matters, it is named the "Sūtra on Causal Conditions."
Regarding the *Jātaka-sūtra*: In the past, the Bodhisattva was once a lion dwelling in a forest, where he formed a close friendship with a monkey.
The monkey entrusted its two cubs to the lion.
At that time, there was a vulture seeking food who, encountering the sleeping lion, took the monkey's cubs and went away, perching upon a tree.
When the lion had awakened, he could not find the young monkeys; seeing that the vulture held them upon the tree, he addressed the vulture, saying:
"I received two children as a trust from the monkey, yet I failed to guard them vigilantly, allowing you to carry them away. Having betrayed my word and my trust, I request their return from you.
I am the king among beasts, and you are the lord among birds; our noble status is equal, so it is right that they be returned to me!"
The vulture said, "You do not know the timing; I am now famished, so why discuss similarities or differences!
The lion, realizing it would be impossible to obtain [the monkey from the vulture], used his own sharp claws to tear flesh from his own flanks to trade for the young monkey.
Furthermore, in a past age, the people suffered greatly from jaundice, edema, and fevers;
at that time, the Bodhisattva took the form of a red fish and offered his own flesh to all the sick, thereby saving them from their ailments.
Furthermore, in the past, the Bodhisattva took the form of a bird and lived in a forest. He saw a man who had entered deep water where humans do not go and was ensnared by a water spirit.
The water deity’s binding spell was such that once one was caught, it could not be undone;
however, the bird knew the method for release. It went to Mount Gandhamādana, took a medicinal herb, and placed it upon the snare; the rope immediately rotted away, and the man was able to escape.
Innumerable such Jātaka tales, which provide great benefit and salvation, are called the "Jātaka Sūtras.

As for the "Extensive Sūtras," they are known as Mahāyāna, namely: the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Ṣaṭpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Puṣpakūṭa Sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Megha Sūtra*, the *Dharmamegha Sūtra*, and the *Mahāmegha Sūtra*.
Innumerable *asaṃkhyeya* sūtras such as these were spoken for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Vaipulya" (the *lièyè* [呂夜] in the original text is a transcription;

in the Qin language it means "sūtras of unprecedented events") refers to instances such as when the Buddha manifests various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) that cause sentient beings to marvel at what has never occurred before. For example, at the time of his birth, the Buddha emitted a great radiance from his body, illuminating the trichiliocosm and its dark recesses, and further illuminating the trichiliocosms of immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
At that time, before the Mother of the Buddha, there was a pure and excellent pond for bathing the Bodhisattva;
Brahmā held a parasol, Śakra washed his body, and two nāgas spouted water.
Furthermore, at the time of birth, he did not require support as he walked seven steps; at every place where his footprints fell, lotus flowers appeared, and he uttered these words:
"I am the one who shall deliver all sentient beings from old age, sickness, and death!"
The great earth shook violently, the heavens rained down various flowers, and trees produced sounds as celestial music was played.
Such immeasurable and rare occurrences as these are called the *Adbhuta-dharma* (Marvelous Events) Sūtra.
The *Sūtra on Discussion* (*Upadeśa-sūtra*) refers to those [sūtras] that answer various questions and explain their underlying reasons,
while further elaborating upon various meanings,
such as when the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths.
What are these four?
They are the Four Noble Truths.
What are these four?
They are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
This is called "discourse.
What is the noble truth of suffering?
These are the eight kinds of suffering, beginning with the suffering of birth. What is the suffering of birth?
It refers to the various places where sentient beings are born, wherein they undergo suffering.
When such questions and answers extensively explain their meanings, this is called "Upadeśa" (Instructional Treatise).
For example, within the Mahāyāna, the Buddha taught the six pāramitās.
What are the six?
They are the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
What is the perfection of giving?
The dānapāramitā is of two kinds:
first, complete; second, incomplete. What is complete?
To be in harmony with the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including what is attained by Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), is called "complete.

That which is incomplete refers to those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) but have not yet attained the dharma of non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and have not yet entered into harmony with the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is called "incomplete."
This applies likewise up to the *dhyānapāramitā*.
One who is fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā* possesses the power of skillful means;
one who is not yet fully endowed lacks the power of skillful means.

Furthermore, the discourses on the analysis of teachings spoken by the Buddha, as well as the sūtras explained by Mahākātyāyana, and even those spoken in accordance with the Dharma by ordinary persons during the period of the Semblance Dharma, are also called *upadeśa*.
That which is not heard by the śrāvakas refers to instances where the Buddha alone preaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas, with no śrāvakas present as listeners.
Furthermore, through his supernormal powers, the Buddha manifests countless transformed bodies that travel everywhere throughout the one-vehicle worlds of the ten directions to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, when the Buddha preached the Dharma for the gods of the desire realm and the form realm, there were no disciples present; therefore, they did not hear it.
A question is asked:

If the arhats possessing the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) could see and hear with their divine ear (divyaśrotra) and divine eye (divyacakṣus) even though they were not seated there when the Buddha spoke, and if they could know past events through the power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti), why did they not hear [the teaching]?
The answer is:
It is because this is beyond the reach of the supernatural powers of the śrāvakas; therefore, they do not hear it.

Furthermore, when the Buddha preached the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* for the sake of the great bodhisattvas, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were at the Buddha’s side yet did not hear it, because they had not planted the causes and conditions for hearing such practices of the Mahāyāna dharma.

For example, when a practitioner of dhyāna enters the meditative absorption of the "all-pervading bases" (sarvatragatā-samādhi), they can cause everything to become water or fire, yet other people do not see it;
this is explained in detail in the *Acintyavimokṣa Sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "wishing to receive and uphold [it] in its entirety": hearing it and practicing it is "receiving" (*śīla*);
not losing it over a long period is "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*). *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 33;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the First Chapter: Seeing All Buddhas.
The Remainder of the Fifty-first Chapter on the Meaning of the World, Volume Thirty-four.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, after hearing the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—
whether already taught, currently being taught, or yet to be taught— to believe and uphold it all, to practice it themselves, and also to explain it to others, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise] Question:

It was previously stated that "if one wishes to remember and maintain without forgetting what is taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should study Prajñāpāramitā. Why is it now stated again that "one should believe in and uphold the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time"?

Answer: It was stated above that one "wishes to remember and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas of the ten directions," yet it was not known what those teachings were; therefore, it is said that the twelve divisions of the scriptures constitute the Buddha-dharma, including those things which the śrāvakas have not heard.

Above, it was merely stated that "the Buddhas of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" [are the object]; now it is stated that "the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, above it was only said to "uphold and not forget," without mentioning the benefits of such upholding;
now it says "to do so for oneself and also to explain it to others," and for this reason it is stated once more.
[Sūtra] “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—

who has heard what the Buddhas of the past have spoken, and who wishes to hear what the Buddhas of the future will speak, and having heard it, shall benefit both himself and others— should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] Question:
The Dharma taught by the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions can be received and upheld;
however, since those of the past have already ceased and those of the future do not yet exist, how can they be heard?
The answer is:
This point has already been addressed previously, but it shall now be explained further.

A bodhisattva possesses a samādhi called "Contemplating the Buddhas of the Three Times. When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they see all the Buddhas of the three times and hear their preaching of the Dharma.

For example, when non-Buddhist seers and immortals encounter future events that have not yet manifested signs or verbal expression, they nonetheless see and hear them by virtue of the power of their wisdom.
Furthermore, the power of the bodhisattvas is inconceivable; although in future ages there may be no forms and no speech, they are nonetheless able to see and hear them.
Whether by the power of dhāraṇīs, or by inferring past and future events through present occurrences—
for these reasons it is said:
"One who wishes to attain this should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

[Sūtra] “If one wishes to hold forth a radiance that universally illuminates the dark spaces between worlds throughout the ten directions—spaces as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, where neither the sun nor the moon shines—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”

[Treatise] When the Bodhisattva was about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, his body emitted a brilliant light that illuminated all worlds as well as the dark and hidden places of the world.
Furthermore, at the time of his subsequent birth, the pervasive illumination was likewise so.
At the time of his initial attainment of the Way, at the time of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he emitted great radiance in exactly the same manner.
Furthermore, at other times, he manifests great supernormal powers and emits great radiance.
For instance, when he wishes to preach the Prajñāpāramitā, he manifests great supernormal powers and illuminates the dark and obscure places of the world with great light.
In this manner, the supernormal powers and radiance are spoken of in various sūtras.
Question: This is the power of the Buddha; for what reason is it said to belong to the bodhisattva?
The answer is:
It is said now that if a bodhisattva wishes to attain this, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Only the great bodhisattvas possess such power.

Just as the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Jālinīprabha, Amitābha, and other Bodhisattvas possess such power that their bodies emit immeasurable radiance, capable of illuminating worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Furthermore, in the world of Amitābha Buddha, the bodies of the bodhisattvas emit a constant radiance that illuminates a hundred thousand yojanas.
Question:
By what karmic causes and conditions do the bodhisattvas obtain such bodily radiance?
Answer: Because bodily action is pure, the body attains adornment.
As it is said in a sutra:
"There was a ghost with a head like a pig's from whose mouth foul-smelling insects emerged, yet its body possessed a golden radiance.
In a previous life, this ghost was a bhikṣu who used harsh words to revile visiting bhikṣus."
"Because he maintains pure precepts with his body, his body possesses radiance;
because there are evil words in his mouth, stinking insects emerge from his mouth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Because of the superiority or inferiority of the purity of the mind, light is classified as superior, middling, or inferior:
namely, Limited Light (Parīttābha), Vast Light (Apramāṇābha), and Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara).
As for the devas of the desire realm, they possess bodily radiance because their minds are pure through generosity and the observance of precepts."

Furthermore, there are those who, out of compassion for sentient beings, light lamps in dark places; or who, for the sake of making offerings to honored images, stūpas, and monasteries, give gifts of bright objects such as luminous pearls, windows, and clear mirrors. Because of these acts, their bodies possess radiance.
Furthermore, by constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness and universally contemplating all sentient beings, one’s mind becomes pure;
and by constantly practicing the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and recollecting the radiant light and divine virtues of all Buddhas, one attains bodily radiance.
Furthermore, the practitioner constantly cultivates the fire-kasina;
moreover, by means of the light of wisdom, they teach and transform sentient beings who are ignorant, dark, and held by false views.
Due to these karmic causes and conditions, they attain the clarity of wisdom within their minds, and their bodies also possess radiance.
Through such karmic causes and conditions, one attains the purity of bodily radiance.
[Sūtra] “In as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, where there is no name for the Buddha, no name for the Dharma, and no name for the Saṅgha—
if one wishes to cause all sentient beings to attain right view and hear the sound of the Three Jewels, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”

[Treatise] When a Bodhisattva erects a stūpa in a place where there was previously no Buddha, Dharma, or monastery, through the causal conditions of this karma, they attain the perfection of power in subsequent lives;
and in places where there is no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, they praise the Triple Gem, causing sentient beings to enter into right view.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If there is a person who, in a land where no Buddha-stūpas previously existed, constructs and establishes stūpas and temples, they will attain the merit of Brahmā; 'Brahmā' being a name for immeasurable merit.
By this causal condition, they will swiftly attain meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi)."
"Because they have attained meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), they obtain immeasurable supernormal powers (abhijñā);
by the power of these supernormal faculties, they are able to travel to the ten directions to praise the Triple Gem (triratna).
As for 'right view' (samyagdṛṣṭi)': if one previously did not recognize the merits of the Triple Gem, it is through the Bodhisattva that one comes to gain faith in them."
Because of faith in the Three Jewels, one believes in the causes and conditions of karma—both transgression and merit;
because of belief in the causes and conditions of karma, one believes that the world is bondage and nirvana is liberation.
The meaning of praising the Three Jewels is as explained in the "Eight Recollections."

[Sūtra] “Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to cause the sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—by means of my power—to have those who are blind regain their sight, those who are deaf regain their hearing, those who are insane regain their mindfulness, those who are naked obtain clothing, and those who are hungry and thirsty obtain fullness, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”

[Treatise] When a Bodhisattva practices unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā*, they may either attain unimpeded liberation and achieve Buddhahood, or become a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-nature birth-body—such as Mañjuśrī and others—who abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and are fully endowed with various merits;
when sentient beings behold them, all obtain their wishes.

Just as one obtains whatever one desires through a wish-fulfilling jewel, so it is with those who behold the Buddha of the Dharma-nature-born body and the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-nature-born body: all shall obtain their aspirations.
Furthermore, from the time he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Bodhisattva has treated all sentient beings of the ninety-six types of eye diseases;
moreover, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he has personally bestowed his own eyes as alms upon sentient beings;
and furthermore, with the light of wisdom, he has shattered the darkness of false views.
Furthermore, out of great compassion, he desires that all the aspirations of sentient beings be fulfilled.
Given such karmic causes and conditions, how could it be that sentient beings see the body of a bodhisattva yet fail to perceive his eyes?
Other matters are also like this.
These various meanings are as explained in the *Prabhāsa* [Sūtra].
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—who are currently in the three evil realms—to obtain human bodies through the power of my [the Buddha’s] might, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise] Question:

One obtains a human body through the causal conditions of one's own wholesome karma; why does the Bodhisattva say, "By the causal conditions of my power, may all sentient beings in the three evil realms obtain a human body"?

Answer: It is not said that "sentient beings obtain a human body by means of the karmic causes and conditions of the bodhisattva," but rather that they "obtain it by means of the power and causes and conditions of the bodhisattva's grace."
By means of the power of their supernormal transformations and skill in teaching the Dharma, Bodhisattvas cause sentient beings to cultivate goodness and attain human birth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Two causes and conditions give rise to right view: [the instruction of others and one's own reflection]."
"First, hearing the true Dharma from without; second, possessing right mindfulness within.
It is also like grasses and trees: when there is a seed within and rain and moisture without, they can then grow.
If there were no bodhisattvas, although sentient beings possess the causes and conditions of karma, they would have no means to initiate [wholesome action].
For this reason, one knows that the benefit provided by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas is exceedingly great!
Question:
How can one cause all sentient beings within the three evil realms to attain liberation?
Even a Buddha cannot do so; how much less so a bodhisattva!
Answer: If the Bodhisattva’s mind and vow are such, then there is no fault.
Furthermore, because they have attained liberation in great measure, it is said that "all" [are liberated].

Just as the bodies of all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas emit immeasurable rays of light, from these rays of light emerge immeasurable transformation bodies that enter everywhere throughout the three evil realms of the ten directions:
they cause the fires of hell to be extinguished and the boiling water to turn cold; because the minds of the sentient beings therein have become pure, they are reborn among devas and humans;
they cause those in the realm of hungry ghosts to be satisfied of hunger and thirst, develop wholesome minds, and attain rebirth among devas and humans.
It causes those in the realm of animals to obtain food at will, to be free from all fears, to develop wholesome minds, and likewise to be reborn among devas or humans.
This is called "the liberation of all beings in the three evil realms."
Question: As other sutras state that beings are "born among devas and humans," why does this [text] say only that they "all obtain human bodies"? Answer:
Among human beings, one can cultivate great merit and likewise experience blessings and joy;
however, because those in the heavens are deeply attached to pleasure, they are unable to cultivate the Path.
For this reason, I vow that all shall attain human bodies.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not wish for sentient beings to merely receive blessings and pleasures, but desires to cause them to attain liberation and the eternal bliss of Nirvana; for this reason, he does not speak of being born in the heavens.

[Sūtra] “If one wishes, by my power, to establish the sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and to cause them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] Question:
Since these five aggregates and the fruits of the path have already been explained previously, why are they explained again now? Answer:
What was explained above pertained solely to the Dharma of the śrāvakas, from the stage of srotāpanna up to nirvāṇa without remainder;
now, the three vehicles are explained in combination:
the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and even up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to learn the majestic deportment of all Buddhas should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] Question:
What are the majestic deportments (īryāpatha) of the Buddhas? Answer:
Dignified deportment refers to the four modes of physical movement and stillness.
It is like a royal elephant that turns its entire body to look;
when walking, the feet remain four finger-widths above the ground, and although they do not touch the earth, the marks of wheels appear.
Neither slow nor hurried, his body remained unmoving;
he constantly raised his right hand to comfort sentient beings;
sitting in the full lotus posture, his body was upright and straight.
He always lay on his right side with his knees drawn up;
the grass mat upon which he slept was kept neat and orderly;
and in eating, he did not dwell on flavors, regarding the delicious and the coarse as one and the same.
If one accepts an invitation, one remains silent without opposition;
one’s speech is gentle and soothing, employing skillful means for the benefit of others without missing the proper occasion.
Furthermore, regarding the deportment of the Dharma-body Buddha: he takes a single step across worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The preaching of the Dharma with the Brahma-voice is likewise so.
The meaning of the marks of the Dharmakāya Buddha is as previously explained.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to attain the gaze of an elephant king should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
When a bodhisattva makes this vow:
"May I, when walking, remain four finger-widths above the ground so that my feet do not touch the earth;

may I be surrounded and honored by the gods of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—by immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of celestial hosts—as I proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree," they should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Treatise]: Regarding "gazing like a royal elephant," when he wishes to turn his body to look, his entire frame rotates together.
For one who possesses the marks of a Great Man, body and mind are unified;
therefore, whenever there is something to be observed, both body and mind turn together.
For example, when a lion seizes its prey, it does not alter its majestic power because the object is small;
the Buddha is likewise: whether he observes something or speaks something, his body and mind are unified and never dispersed.
Why is this so? Because from incalculable kalpas past, he has cultivated the dharma of single-mindedness;
by virtue of these karmic causes and conditions, his cranial bone and body have become one, without any separation.
Furthermore, because he has destroyed pride life after life, he does not disparage sentient beings; his observation and his action proceed in tandem.
As stated in the *Nidāna-apadāna*:
when the Buddha stroked the head of a scavenger from the city of Śrāvastī with his hand and instructed him to leave the household life, he still did not treat him with contempt.

Regarding the phrase "the feet are four finger-widths above the ground": if the Buddha were always flying, sentient beings would find it strange and suspicious, thinking that the Buddha was not of human kind, and thus would not submit to him;
yet if his feet touched the ground, sentient beings would consider him no different from ordinary people and would not give rise to a heart of reverence.
Therefore, although he walks upon the ground, his feet do not touch it by four finger-widths, yet the tracks of his wheels appear.
Question:
If the Buddha constantly emits light one zhang in length and his feet do not touch the ground, for what reason do sentient beings not all revere and follow him?
The answer is:

Sentient beings have accumulated extremely heavy sins over immeasurable kalpas, and their defilements of ignorance are profound; thus they harbor doubts toward the Buddha, claiming he is a magician who deceives people with his arts, or they say:
"His feet do not touch the ground; this is his natural disposition, just as a bird is able to fly—what is so extraordinary about it!
Furthermore, due to the karmic conditions of their heavy offenses, some sentient beings do not perceive the Buddha’s marks, regarding him merely as a śramaṇa of great majesty and virtue.
It is like a person with a terminal illness who, when offered potent medicine or fine food, perceives them all as foul and putrid; for this reason, they fail to show full respect or devotion.

"To be surrounded by the Four Heavenly Kings, up to the immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of devas of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, who respectfully encircle him as he proceeds to the foot of the Bodhi tree"—this is the constant law of all Buddhas.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One; having gone beneath the Bodhi tree, he intends to destroy two kinds of Māras:

first, the Māra of the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa-māra*), and second, the Māra of the Lord of Heaven (*Īśvara-devaputra-māra*), desiring to achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
Why, then, do these hosts of devas not pay him respectful homage and escort him?

Furthermore, throughout successive lifetimes, the devas have assisted and protected the Bodhisattva; even at the time of his renunciation, they caused the palace ladies and maidservants to fall into a deep, unconscious slumber, so that he might lift the horse's hooves and leap over the city walls.
"Today the task is accomplished; we shall together escort him to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
He asked:
"Why do you not say that immeasurable people, such as kṣatriyas and brahmins, will escort him, but speak only of 'the devas'?"
The answer is:
The Buddha sought the Bodhi tree alone in the deep forest, a place not frequented by people; for this reason, he did not speak [of it].
Furthermore, because people lack the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds, they do not know that the Buddha will attain enlightenment; for this reason, he did not speak [of it].
Furthermore, because the devas are more noble than humans, only the devas are mentioned.

Moreover, the Buddhas always delight in secluded and quiet places; since the devas are able to conceal their bodies and remain invisible, they do not interfere with such seclusion. For these reasons, it is said that only the devas follow [the Buddha].
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva saw that the five bhikṣus had abandoned him and departed, while he remained alone beneath the tree, he made this vow.
[Sūtra]: “‘I shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree with the celestial garments of the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven as my seat’—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] Question:
As it is said in the Sūtra, "The Buddha sat upon grass beneath a tree and attained the Way of Buddhahood"; why, then, does he now express the wish to "use celestial robes as his seat"?
Answer: In the Śrāvaka sūtras, it is said that grass was spread.

In the Mahāyāna sūtras, it depends on what sentient beings perceive—some see grass spread beneath a tree, while others see celestial canopies spread there; their perceptions differ according to the extent of their respective merit.
Furthermore, the *janma-kāya* Buddha gathers grass beneath a tree;
the *dharmatā-janma-kāya* Buddha uses celestial robes as a seat, or even robes superior to those of the devas.
Furthermore, when the Buddha attains enlightenment beneath the trees of a deep forest, the people within the forest see him and offer him grass.
If noble persons were to see it, they would have used their own precious garments as seats;
however, because there were no noble persons in the forest, the various nāgas, spirits, and devas each used their exquisite robes as seats.
The garments of the Four Heavenly Kings weigh two *liǎng*;
those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven weigh one *liǎng*;
and those of the Yāma Heaven weigh eighteen *zhū*.
The garments of the Tuṣita Heaven weigh twelve zhū;
those of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven weigh six zhū;
and those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven weigh three zhū.
The celestial garments of the gods in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) possess no quality of weight.
The celestial garments of the gods in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) grow from the sides of trees; they have neither threads nor weaving.
They are like thin ice, radiant and pure, and manifest in various colors.
The celestial garments of the Form Realm are of pure golden radiance, beyond measure or description.
Upon such precious robes spread as seats, the Bodhisattva sits and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Question: Why is it that only the celestial beings are said to spread out garments, while the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are not mentioned as spreading seats for the Buddha?

When the Buddha was about to attain enlightenment, all those Bodhisattvas prepared seats for him—some one *yojana* in length and breadth, others ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or even immeasurable *yojanas*.
Their height is likewise so.
These jewel thrones arise from the untainted merit of the bodhisattvas; they are invisible even to the eyes of the devas, let alone to the touch of hands!
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—how they subdue Māra, attain the Way, and perform the adornments of Buddha-works—all are clearly perceived as if in a bright mirror;
why, then, do you not speak of such a wondrous seat?
Answer: There are two kinds of Prajñāpāramitā:
first, that which is taught in common with śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and devas; second, that which is taught exclusively for bodhisattvas who have fully attained the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, it should be stated that the Bodhisattvas prepare the seat for the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the devas’ knowledge of the Buddha’s grace does not equal that of the great Bodhisattvas who have but one or two births remaining.
In this way, how could a bodhisattva not make offerings to the Buddha through the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*)?
This point is already included in the teaching for śrāvakas, and therefore it is not mentioned here.

[Sūtra]: “‘When I have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), I wish that all places where I walk, stand, sit, or lie down shall become entirely of diamond (*vajra*); one who desires this should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason is the earth entirely composed of vajra within the four modes of deportment of the Buddha? Answer:
Some say: When the Bodhisattva reached the foot of the Bodhi tree and sat there, he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
at that time, the Bodhisattva entered into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, such that no earth was able to support him.
Why is this so? Because the earth exists as a retribution resulting from the causes and conditions of the delusive karma of sentient beings; therefore, it cannot support [the Buddha].

When a Bodhisattva is about to attain Buddhahood, his body becomes the wisdom-body of true reality (*bhūtatathatā-jñāna-kāya*), and at that time, the place where he sits transforms into diamond (*vajra*).

Some say: The earth rests upon the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), and the Golden Wheel rests upon the Diamond (*vajra*). Emerging from the limit of the Diamond, it rises straight up like the pedestal of a lotus flower to support the place where the Bodhisattva sits, preventing him from sinking;
for this reason, the site of this place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is called "Diamond."
Some say: "Once one has attained the Way of the Buddha, all four modes of deportment become entirely transformed into vajra.
A question is asked:
The vajra, too, exists due to the causes and conditions of the delusive karma of sentient beings; how then can it lift up the Buddha?
The answer is:
although the vajra is composed of what is delusive, it is the most solid among all things on earth, and nothing surpasses it.
The Vajra descended into the water, and the great nāga kings offered this solid substance to the Buddha.
Furthermore, it was due to the karmic causes and conditions of the Buddha’s past lives that he obtained this established dwelling place.
Furthermore, the Buddha transforms the vajra and the four great elements into empty space; as empty space is not deceptive, so too is the Buddha’s wisdom not deceptive.
Since these two things are identical, he is therefore able to lift it up.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi on the very day he leaves the household life,
he shall turn the wheel of Dharma on that same day."
When the wheel of Dharma was turned, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, because they did not grasp at any phenomena, attained liberation of mind from all outflows (*āsrava*);
and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings attained non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One should study the *prajñāpāramitā*!

[Treatise] There are some bodhisattvas who, amidst the sentient beings of evil times with wrong views, personally undertake practices of extreme hardship and difficulty in order to eliminate the wrong views of those beings.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha was in the grove of Uruvilvā trees, he consumed only one sesame seed and one grain of rice.
The various non-Buddhists said:
"Even though our former teachers practiced asceticism, they were unable to endure such diligent suffering for six years!"
Furthermore, there are some who say that the Buddha is currently experiencing the retribution for evil karma from his previous lives.
There are also bodhisattvas who believe that the Buddha truly undergoes this suffering; for this reason, they resolve their minds [to enlightenment], thinking:
"I shall attain Buddhahood on the very day I leave the household life."

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who leave the household life during a fortunate age; like Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, they seek the path to Buddhahood and, sitting in the full lotus posture, attain buddhahood after ten minor kalpas.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva resolved, saying:
"May I attain buddhahood on the very day I leave the household life.
There are bodhisattvas who, having attained buddhahood, do not immediately turn the wheel of Dharma.
For example, after Dīpaṃkara Buddha attained enlightenment, he emitted only light for twelve years without preaching the Dharma, as no one recognized him.

Furthermore, after Susaṃtata Buddha attained enlightenment, there was no one to be transformed; thus, he manifested a transformation Buddha to remain for an eon, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, while his own body entered parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, when Śākyamuni Buddha had attained enlightenment, he did not preach the Dharma for fifty-seven days.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva made this vow: "May I, upon attaining Buddhahood, immediately turn the wheel of Dharma."

There are Buddhas who deliver sentient beings in limited numbers; for example, when Śākyamuni Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, Kātyāyana alone attained the first stage of the Path, and eighty thousand devas attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Having heard this, the bodhisattva made this vow:
"When I turn the wheel of Dharma, may immeasurable asankhyeya beings be freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena."

"When Śākyamuni Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, one bhikṣu and various devas all attained the initial stage of the Path, yet not a single person attained the path of an Arhat or a Bodhisattva.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:

'When I become a Buddha, I shall cause immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to attain liberation of mind from all outflows (āsrava) by means of the non-appropriation of all dharmas; and I shall cause immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to attain non-retrogression in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
Question: If the supernatural power, merit, and capacity to deliver sentient beings of all Buddhas are equal, why does this bodhisattva make such a vow? Answer:
A single Buddha can manifest immeasurable, incalculable bodies to deliver sentient beings; yet among worlds, there are those that are adorned and pure, and those that are not adorned or pure.

If a bodhisattva sees or hears that these Buddhas underwent ascetic practices difficult to achieve before attaining Buddhahood, or that some did not immediately turn the wheel of Dharma—such as Śākyamuni Buddha, who attained the Way after six years of ascetic practice;
or if they hear that when he first turned the wheel of Dharma, there was yet no one who had attained the path of an arhat, much less the path of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, because the Bodhisattva has not yet heard that the powers of all Buddhas are equal, he makes this vow;
however, the spiritual power and merit of all Buddhas are equal and without distinction.
[Sūtra] "When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall have an assembly (*saṃgha*) consisting of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* śrāvakas;
when I preach the Dharma but once, may they all, while still on their seats, attain the state of *arhat*—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā* for this purpose!"
[Treatise] There are Buddhas who take śrāvakas as their Saṃgha, which is numerical and limited.
For example, Śākyamuni Buddha had one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus as his Saṃgha.

In the first assembly of Maitreya Buddha, there will be nine hundred and ninety million monks; in the second assembly, nine hundred and sixty million; and in the third assembly, nine hundred and thirty million.
Such assemblies of monks under these various Buddhas each have their own specific limits and numbers, which differ from one another.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva makes the vow:
"I shall take immeasurable asaṃkhyeya śrāvakas as my Saṅgha.

There is a Buddha who preaches the Dharma for sentient beings; through one such preaching, they attain the first path, and at another time, through further preaching, they attain the second, third, and fourth paths.
For example, when Śākyamuni Buddha preached the Dharma for the five bhikṣus, they attained the first stage of the path, and on another day they attained the path of arhatship;
likewise, Śāriputra attained the first stage of the path and after half a month attained the path of arhatship;
and Mahākāśyapa, upon seeing the Buddha, attained the first stage of the path and eight days later attained arhatship.
For example, Ānanda attained the stage of Srotāpanna after twenty-five years of serving the Buddha, and only attained Arhatship after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Thus, these various Arhats did not attain the four stages of the path simultaneously.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"When I preach the Dharma even once, may all on these very seats attain Arhatship.
[Sūtra]: "I shall take immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as my Saṃgha;"
"When I preach the Dharma, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas shall all attain the stage of *avaivartika*!
[Treatise: The reason a bodhisattva makes this vow is that most Buddhas take śrāvakas as their saṃgha, and do not have a separate bodhisattva saṃgha.

Just as Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and others, because there was no separate assembly of bodhisattvas apart from Śākyamuni Buddha, entered among the assembly of śrāvakas and sat in their proper order.
There are Buddhas who teach the Dharma for the sake of the One Vehicle, with a monastic community consisting exclusively of bodhisattvas.
There are Buddhas whose monastic communities consist of a mixture of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas;
for example, in the land of Amitābha Buddha, the community of bodhisattvas is numerous while the community of śrāvakas is small.
For this reason, he vows that his Saṃgha shall consist of immeasurable bodhisattvas.
When a Buddha first turns the wheel of Dharma, there may be no one who attains *avaivartika* (non-retrogression); therefore, the bodhisattva makes this vow:
"By my single teaching of the Dharma, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings shall attain *avaivartika*."
[Sūtra] “Those who wish to attain an immeasurable lifespan and be endowed with perfect radiance should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
[Śāstra] The lifespans of the Buddhas are sometimes long and sometimes short.
For example, the lifespan of Vipaśyin Buddha was eighty-four thousand years;
that of Krakucchanda Buddha was sixty thousand years;
and that of Kanakamuni Buddha was thirty thousand years.
The lifespan of Kāśyapa Buddha was twenty thousand years;
that of Śākyamuni Buddha was one hundred years, with few exceeding it;
and the lifespan of Maitreya Buddha will be eighty-four thousand years.
For example, the constant radiance of Śākyamuni Buddha extends for one zhang, while that of Maitreya Buddha extends for ten li.
Regarding the lifespans and radiances of all Buddhas, there are two kinds:
first, concealed; second, manifest.
First is the ultimate reality, and second is its concealment for the sake of sentient beings.
Ultimate reality is immeasurable and manifest;
that which is for the sake of sentient beings is finite and measurable.
In truth, the lifespan of a Buddha should not be short. Why is this?
Because the causal conditions for the long life of all Buddhas are fully perfected.
Just as the Bhagavat, by saving the lives of the inhabitants of a village in a previous life, obtained an immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* lifespan.
While the normal lifespan in the Brahma world does not exceed half a kalpa, the lifespan of this particular Brahmā alone is immeasurable; for this reason, he gives rise to a false view, saying:
"I alone am eternal!"
The Buddha went to where he was, shattered his false views, and explained the causal conditions of his past:
"By saving a single village, his lifespan reached such a length.
How much more so for the Buddha, who throughout successive lifetimes has saved immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings!"
Whether by providing relief through material wealth or by sacrificing one's own life to save another from death, how could their lifespan not exceed a hundred years?
Furthermore, the precept against killing is the karmic cause and condition for longevity;

since the Buddha’s great compassion for sentient beings penetrates to the very marrow of his bones, he would constantly die for the sake of beings—how much more so, then, would he refrain from killing!
Furthermore, because the wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas is authentic and non-deceptive, it is also a cause and condition for long life.

Since a bodhisattva attains immeasurable lifespan by combining the perfection of wisdom with the merit of observing the precepts, how much more so must it be for a Buddha who has fulfilled all these immeasurable merits throughout successive lifetimes—how could his lifespan be limited!
Furthermore, just as among all forms the Buddha’s body is foremost,
and among all minds the Buddha’s mind is foremost,
so too, for this reason, the Buddha’s lifespan should also be foremost among all lifespans.
As worldly people say:
"In this world, human life is precious for its longevity.
Since the Buddha is the supreme among humans, his lifespan should likewise be long!
Question:
Although the Buddha possesses the karmic causes and conditions for a long life, because he was born in an evil age, his lifespan was short;
since he was able to fulfill the Buddha-work with this short life, what need is there for a long one?
Furthermore, by means of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the Buddha is able to perform all the works of a Buddha within a single day; how much more so over the course of a hundred years!
The answer is:
because this Jambudvīpa is defiled, the Buddha’s lifespan must be short.
Since other places are superior, the Buddha’s lifespan ought to be long.
Question:
If that is so, then the Bodhisattva who was born here in Jambudvīpa in the palace of King Śuddhodana, renounced the world, and attained enlightenment—this is the actual Buddha; [is he not?]
"In other places, are all Buddhas merely created through the transformative power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) in order to deliver sentient beings?
He replied:
"This statement is not correct!"
Why is this? In other parts of Jambudvīpa, each likewise says:
"In my country is the true Buddha; elsewhere they are mere manifestations."
"How is this known?
If it were in other lands, beings would know that he is a manifested Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) and would not be willing to believe in or accept his teachings and precepts.

Furthermore, if in other lands people have a lifespan of one kalpa, and the Buddha’s lifespan were but a hundred years, it would be less than a single day to them; sentient beings would then give rise to contempt and would not be willing to receive his teachings."
He regards one kalpa as the actual Buddha, and considers this [present manifestation] to be a transformation of that transformation.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"The Buddha Universal Radiance of Supernatural Powers has a lifespan of seven hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"That Buddha is my very self.
That Buddha also said:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is none other than my own body.
For this reason, it is known that the lifespans of all Buddhas are truly immeasurable; yet, for the sake of saving sentient beings, they manifest them as being either long or short.

You say: "If Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, delivers sentient beings in a manner no different from the human lifespan, then there would be no need for a hundred years; he could complete all the Buddha-works within a single day!"
For instance, at one time Ānanda had this thought:

"Just as the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, the Buddha Sarvābhibhū, and the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in auspicious ages with extremely long lifespans and were thus able to fully accomplish the work of a Buddha;
will our Śākyamuni Buddha, having been born in an evil age with an extremely short lifespan, perhaps be unable to fully accomplish the work of a Buddha?"

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Sunrise Samādhi. From his body, he manifested transformations of immeasurable Buddhas and immeasurable rays of light, which pervaded the ten directions.
Each of these manifested Buddhas, dwelling in various worlds, performed the Buddha-work:
some preached the Dharma, some displayed supernatural powers, some manifested samādhis, and some manifested meals.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, he performs buddha-work to deliver sentient beings.
Rising from samādhi, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Did you see and hear all of this?"
Ānanda said: “Indeed!
I have seen it!”
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Can the Buddha,
by means of such supernormal power, accomplish the work of a Buddha?
Ānanda replied:

"Even if the Buddha's lifespan were but a single day, and all the grasses and trees of the great earth were beings capable of being saved, he would be able to save them all; how much more so in a hundred years!
For this reason, it is known that the lifespans of all Buddhas are entirely immeasurable; it is only for the sake of saving sentient beings that they manifest lifespans of varying lengths.
For example, when the sun rises, its reflection appears in water; according to the size of the water, if the water is large the reflection lasts long, and if the water is small it quickly vanishes;
yet if it shines upon mountains of lapis lazuli or crystal, the reflection remains for a long time.
Furthermore, it is like fire burning grass and wood: if it burns a small amount, it is quickly extinguished; if it burns a large amount, it persists for a long time.
One cannot say that because there is no fire where it has been extinguished, there is likewise no fire where it is burning extensively.
The meaning of the length and brevity of light is also like this. 52.

The Meaning of Faithfully Upholding the Absence of the Three Poisons. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the First Chapter, Part Fifty-Two: The Meaning of Faithfully Upholding the Absence of the Three Poisons. [Sūtra] "When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there shall be no lust, anger, or delusion in the world, nor even the names of the three poisons."

All sentient beings who have accomplished such wisdom—who are skilled in giving, skilled in ethical discipline, skilled in meditative concentration, skilled in the holy life, and skilled in not harming sentient beings—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Treatise] Question:
If in that world there were neither the three poisons nor even the names for the three poisons, for what purpose would the Buddha be born in such a land?
Answer: Greed, hatred, and delusion are called the three unwholesome roots; they are dharmas bound to the desire realm.
If the Buddha speaks of greed, hatred, and delusion, he means these are unwholesome states bound to the desire realm.
If one speaks of defiled craving and ignorance, these pertain to all three realms.
There are Buddha-worlds consisting entirely of beings driven by desire; for the sake of such sentient beings, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"When I attain Buddhahood, my land shall be free from the three poisons, even the very names of the three poisons shall not exist."

Furthermore, there are pure Buddha-lands where there are only bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika) and born of the dharma-nature body (dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya), free from all afflictions and possessing only residual habits; for this reason, it is said that "even the names of the three poisons do not exist."
If someone were to say:
"Just as a bodhisattva vows, 'I shall deliver all sentient beings,' yet in reality not all sentient beings are delivered;

so it is with this case as well—if one wishes to cause the world to be without even the name of the three poisons, there must nonetheless actually remain some three poisons that are not yet exhausted."
If there were no three poisons, what need would there be for a Buddha?
It is like the earth: if there were no great darkness, there would be no need for the sun’s illumination.
As it is said in the sutra:
"If these three dharmas did not exist, the Buddha would not appear in the world; if these three dharmas are not severed, one cannot escape old age, sickness, and death.
These "three dharmas" refer to the three poisons, as explained in detail in the *Tridharma-sūtra*. This point should be expounded extensively herein.

Furthermore, there are worlds where sentient beings differentiate various phenomena, thinking, "This is wholesome, this is unwholesome; this is bondage, this is liberation," and so forth, giving rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within the single-marked dharma of quiescence.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"May the sentient beings in my world not give rise to the three poisons, but know that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the three poisons is itself *nirvāṇa*."
Question: When all sentient beings attain such wisdom, what kind of wisdom is it? Answer:
Wisdom is mundane right view.
Within mundane right view, it is said that there is giving, there is merit and demerit, there are this world and the next world, and there are arhats.
Because he has faith in the existence of sin and merit, he is able to practice giving well.
Because he has faith that there are arhats, he is able to maintain the precepts well, practice meditative concentration well, and cultivate the holy life well.
Because they have attained the power of right view, they are able to refrain from harming sentient beings.
Since mundane right view is the root of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), it is said that "in the land there is not even the name of the three poisons."
There are two kinds of covetousness:
first, improper covetousness; second, covetousness.
There are two kinds of ill-will:
First is perverse anger, second is anger.
Ignorance is of two kinds:
first is the ignorance of wrong views, second is ignorance.
These three kinds of beings with perverted poisons are difficult to transform and deliver, whereas the other three are easy to deliver.
"The absence of the names of the three poisons" means there is no name for the three perverted poisons.
The five matters beginning with "skillful giving" are as explained above in the "Emission of Light" chapter.
[Sūtra] "After my parinirvāṇa, so that the Dharma shall neither be extinguished nor even have the name 'extinction,' one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
[Treatise] Question:
If even the Buddha, the King of Dharma, has himself entered parinirvāṇa, why do you say that "the Dharma is without extinction"? Answer:
As stated above, these aspirations of a bodhisattva are not necessarily real.
Since all conditioned phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, how could they be permanent and not subject to extinction?
The Buddha is like the brightness of the sun, and the Dharma is like the remaining light after the sun has set. How can it be that the light remains even when the sun has set?
It is simply because it abides for a long time; since no one is able to see its extinction, it is called "non-extinction."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva observes that the duration of the various Buddhas' teachings varies—some being short and others long. For instance, the teaching of Kāśyapa Buddha remained for seven days, whereas the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha remains for a thousand years.
Therefore, the bodhisattva makes this vow, saying:
"Although the Dharma is conditioned, may it continue in succession without perishing."
"Just as fire obtains fuel, so it is transmitted without interruption.
Furthermore, the true mark of all dharmas (*dharmatā*) is called the Buddha-dharma.

This true mark of reality is neither arising nor ceasing, neither interrupted nor eternal, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going, neither receiving nor moving, neither attached nor dependent, and is non-existent, like the mark of *nirvāṇa*.
If the characteristics of dharmas are thus, how can there be cessation?
Question:
If the characteristics of dharmas are thus, then all Buddha-dharmas should likewise be non-ceasing!
Answer: As you have said, in the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas), there is no such thing as cessation.

However, some people, through recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, grasp at the characteristics of phenomena and thereby destroy their true nature; they speak in terms of dualistic dharmas, and for this reason, there appears to be cessation.
Within the reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*), there is no cessation.

Furthermore, because one practices the unimpeded dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* and accumulates immeasurable merit, the dharmas continue in succession according to their original vows; thus, no one perceives their cessation.
It is like shooting an arrow upward into the sky: although the arrow travels so far that it cannot be seen, it must inevitably fall.

[Sūtra] "When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, may all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who hear my name necessarily attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Those who wish to attain such merits as these should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Śāstra] Question:

There are those born during the time of a Buddha and dwelling within the Buddha-dharma who nonetheless fall into hell, such as Devadatta, Kokālika, and the Śākya son Khanda. Because their minds were shrouded by the three unwholesome dharmas, they fell into hell.
In this context, how can it be said that "in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges from which Buddhas have passed away, one attains the Way merely by hearing the name of a Buddha"?
The answer is:
It has already been stated above that there are two kinds of Buddhas.
First is the Buddha of the Body Born of the Dharma-nature; second is the Buddha who manifests transformations according to the superior or inferior capacities of sentient beings.
It is with reference to the Buddha of the Body Born of the Dharma-nature that it is said, "Even those who merely hear his name shall attain liberation.

It is with reference to the Buddha who manifests forms according to sentient beings that it is said, "Though they dwell together with the Buddha, some fall into hell due to the causes and conditions of their karma."
As for the Buddha of the Body Born of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya-buddha*), there is no task he does not accomplish and no aspiration he does not fulfill. Why is this?
