Because throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has accumulated all roots of goodness and merit; he is fully endowed with all wisdom without obstruction, serving as the sovereign of all sages, and is one whom even the devas and great bodhisattvas find it rare to behold.
For example, the wish-fulfilling jewel is difficult to see and difficult to obtain; yet for those who behold it, their aspirations are surely fulfilled.
It is like the medicine "Joyful to Behold"; for those who see it, all ailments are entirely eliminated.
Just as when people behold a Wheel-Turning Sage King, there are none who do not become wealthy and fulfilled;
and just as when people behold Śakra Devānām Indra, they obtain everything according to their wishes.
Just as sentient beings rely upon Brahmā Deva-king and have all their fears dispelled,
so too those who recollect the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall be completely liberated from all calamities and hardships.
If this is already so, how much more so must it be for the Dharma-nature-born body (*dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas!
Question:
Śākyamuni Buddha is also a portion of the Dharma-nature-born body; there is no difference in their essence.
Why is it that while the Buddha was in the world, there were those who committed the five heinous crimes, as well as such evils as famine and banditry?
The answer is:
It was due to the original vow of Śākyamuni Buddha.
"I have appeared in this degenerate age desiring to deliver sentient beings through the Dharma; I did not appear for the sake of wealth, status, or worldly pleasures.
If the Buddha were to employ his power, there is nothing he could not accomplish.
Furthermore, because the power of the merit of sentient beings is weak and their defilements of sin are deep and heavy, they cannot attain liberation at will.
Moreover, although the Buddha now speaks only of pure nirvana, sentient beings criticize, debate, and slander him, saying:
"Why do you keep so many disciples and convert the people?"
"This too is a phenomenon that binds.
Yet, when he was transformed by the Dharma of Nirvana alone, they still reviled and slandered him; how much more so when it was mixed with worldly pleasures!

For instance, because Devadatta wished for the thousand-spoked wheel marks to appear on his feet, he had a mold made of iron, heated it until it glowed red, and pressed it against his feet. Once it had been pressed, his feet were ruined and his body was in agony, causing him to cry out loudly.
At that time, having heard this, Ānanda wept and said to the Buddha, “My brother is about to die;
I pray that the Buddha will compassionately save him!
The Buddha immediately extended his hand and stroked his body, uttering words of supreme sincerity:
"I see that Rāhula and Devadatta are equal; therefore, his pain shall be extinguished.
At that moment, Devadatta's pain was immediately relieved.
Grasping his hand and looking at it, he recognized it as the Buddha’s hand and spoke these words:
"Prince Śuddhodana will be able to support himself with this medical skill.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you see Devadatta?"
If their mental application is such as this, how can they be delivered?
If one were a person of the world who delights in the mundane, there would be no such fault;
yet for sentient beings of this kind, they cannot be delivered by means of worldly pleasures.
The various causes and conditions for this matter have already been explained at length above.
For this reason, it is said:
"Among those who hear the name of the Buddha, there are some who attain the Way and some who do not."
Furthermore, the bodies of Buddhas are immeasurable and of various different kinds across incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas:
there are Buddhas who cause sentient beings to attain the Way by preaching the Dharma to them;
there are Buddhas who emit immeasurable light, and sentient beings who encounter it attain the Way.
There are those who attain the Way through the pointing out of their own minds by means of supernatural transformations;
there are those who attain the Way when the Buddha merely manifests his physical body;
and there are those who attain the Way upon smelling the myriad subtle fragrances emitted from every pore of the Buddha’s body.
There are Buddhas who bestow food upon sentient beings, causing them to attain the Way;
there are Buddhas whom sentient beings cause to attain the Way merely by recollecting them;
and there are Buddhas who are able to perform Buddha-work through the sounds of all grasses and trees, causing sentient beings to attain the Way.
There are Buddhas such that sentient beings who hear their names attain the Way; for the sake of these Buddhas, it is said:
"When I become a Buddha, all those who hear my name shall be enabled to cross over."
Furthermore, hearing the name does not mean that one attains the Way immediately upon hearing it;
rather, having heard it, one must cultivate the Way before one can attain liberation.
For example, when the householder Sudatta first heard the Buddha’s name, his heart was filled with wonder and joy; he went to the Buddha to hear the Dharma and was thereby able to attain the Way.

Furthermore, for example, when the brahmin Śvetara first heard the name of the Buddha from the matted-hair ascetic Kāṇeya, his heart was immediately filled with wonder and joy; he went straight to where the Buddha was, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way.
This merely speaks of hearing the names; hearing the names is the causal condition for attaining the Way, not the attainment of the Way itself.
A question is asked:
This sutra states, "Upon hearing the names of the Buddhas, one immediately attains the Way," but it does not say, "Having heard the names, one must then cultivate the Way before attaining it."
Answer: Here, we say "immediately" (*jishi*), not "within a single moment of mind" (*ekacitta*);
we simply say that there was no other intervening event between hearing [the sound] and [the realization], and thus we say "immediately."
For example, as it is said in a sutra:
"When one cultivates the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one is simultaneously cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
An objector says:

Question: "The samādhi of loving-kindness (maitrī) is with outflows (sāsrava) and takes sentient beings as its object; how can one immediately cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga)?
The respondent said:
"Having arisen from loving-kindness, one immediately cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; since there is no other intervening dharma, it is called 'immediate'."
"Immediate" (tatkṣaṇa) has two aspects:
first, simultaneity; second, although a long time may have passed, there is no other dharma [intervening].
It is precisely by means of the mind that one attains the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment; this is also called "immediate."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose merit has fully ripened and whose afflictions and mental fetters are thin; they are destined to attain the Way, and upon hearing the Buddha’s name, they immediately attain it.
Furthermore, by the power of the Buddha, they attain liberation upon hearing [the teaching];
it is like a mature abscess that, if left untreated, bursts spontaneously due to a minor cause;
or like a ripe fruit that, if no one picks it, falls of its own accord through the condition of a gentle breeze.
It is like a fresh, clean, white cotton cloth that easily takes on color.
For such people, it is said that upon hearing the name of the Buddha, they immediately attain the Way.
It is like a ghost or spirit possessing a person who, upon hearing the name of a seer’s incantation, immediately departs.
Question:
Beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who transmits this name so that they may hear it?
Answer:

By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha emitted immeasurable rays of light from every pore of his body. Upon each ray of light there was a precious flower, and upon each flower sat a Buddha. Each of these Buddhas preached the wondrous Dharma to deliver sentient beings and also proclaimed the names of all Buddhas; it is for this reason that they were heard.
As it is said in the *Prabhāsa-parivarta*:

Furthermore, because the great bodhisattvas, by virtue of their original vows, desire to go to places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist in order to proclaim the names of the Buddhas—as described in this chapter—they are thus able to hear them.
Furthermore, there are persons of great merit who hear the name of the Buddha from the midst of space, such as the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita;
others hear it from the gods, or from the sounds of trees, or within a dream.
Furthermore, because the Buddhas possess inconceivable power, they either go in person to speak or announce it by means of their voice.
Moreover, just as a Bodhisattva makes a vow to deliver all sentient beings, for this reason it is said:
"When I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who hear my name shall all attain Buddhahood."
"If one wishes to attain these, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
[The interlocutor] asks:

"Above, it was stated that one wishes to attain all merits and all aspirations; since all such matters are accomplished through the convergence of various practices, for what reason is it said only that 'one should study the Prajñāpāramitā'?"
Answer: This sutra is titled "Prajñāpāramitā. Because the Buddha wishes to explain its meaning, he praises the Prajñāpāramitā in every chapter.

Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas; among parents, the mother’s contribution is the most significant. Therefore, the Buddha takes Prajñā as his mother and Pratyutpanna Samādhi as his father.
Samādhi can only collect and sustain the distracted mind so that wisdom may be accomplished, yet it cannot contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Prajñāpāramitā can universally contemplate all phenomena and discern their true reality; there is nothing it does not penetrate and nothing it does not accomplish.
Because its merit is so great, it is called the "Mother."

For this reason, although a practitioner may practice the six pāramitās and various meritorious qualities in combination to fulfill all vows, it is said only that "one should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
Furthermore, as stated in a later chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"If there were no *prajñāpāramitā*, the other five matters would not be called 'pāramitās'."
"Although one may universally cultivate all practices, one still cannot fulfill and complete all vows;
it is like various painted colors which, if there is no glue, are not fit for use."

Sentient beings have come from a world without beginning; although they practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, once they have experienced their worldly retributions, these perfections are again exhausted.
Why is this? Because they are apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Now, by the grace of the Buddha, through the practice of the six matters via the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are named "perfections" (*pāramitā*); they bring the Buddha-way to fruition and cause the Buddhas to succeed one another without end.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they universally contemplate that all phenomena are empty, and that emptiness itself is also empty. Having extinguished all contemplations, they attain unimpeded *prajñāpāramitā* and, through the power of great compassion and skillful means, give rise once more to all meritorious deeds.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of pure karma, there is no aspiration that is not fulfilled.
Since other merits, apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, do not possess unimpeded wisdom, why is it said that "one who wishes to fulfill all vows should study the Dānapāramitā and the others"?
Furthermore, if the five perfections are separated from Prajñāpāramitā, they do not receive the name "perfection.
The five perfections are like the blind, while Prajñāpāramitā is like the eye.
The five perfections are like unbaked earthen jars containing water, whereas Prajñāpāramitā is like a matured, fired jar.
The five *pāramitās* are like a bird without two wings, whereas the *prajñāpāramitā* is like a bird with wings.
For various reasons such as these, the *prajñāpāramitā* is able to accomplish the great task; for this reason it is said:
"Those who wish to obtain all merits and vows should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll 34.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of the Chapter on Retribution (Vipākavarga), Part 2, Scroll 35.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Two: On Retribution. [Sūtra] The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā can perform such meritorious deeds, at that time the Four Heavenly Kings will all rejoice greatly, thinking to themselves:"
“We shall present these four bowls to the Bodhisattva, just as the previous heavenly kings presented their bowls to the former Buddhas.
[Treatise] Question: Since this has already been fully explained in the preceding chapter, why is it stated again here?
The answer is:
Although the Prajñāpāramitā was praised previously, the matter was not yet complete and those who heard it were not yet satiated; therefore, it is explained again.

Furthermore, while the first chapter merely praised the power of the Prajñāpāramitā, this [chapter] praises how the practitioner is able to perform such meritorious deeds, causing the Four Heavenly Kings and others to rejoice and offer their alms bowls.
Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas are able to fulfill all their vows and practices, the Buddha comforts and encourages them, saying that such karmic rewards exist and will never be in vain.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of fruits of the Prajñāpāramitā:
first, attaining Buddhahood and delivering sentient beings;

second, although not yet having attained Buddhahood, receiving worldly retributions—such as becoming a Cakravartin King, Śakra, or Brahmā Deva King who presides over the trichiliocosm—wherein all matters of worldly merit, happiness, and offerings are fully provided.
Now, these matters are explained in order to demonstrate worldly retributions to sentient beings.
Furthermore, when those in the world seek to accomplish great undertakings, there are often many obstacles and disruptions;
the Bodhisattva is not so, for once his inner mind is settled, external circumstances will correspond accordingly.
For such reasons as these, this chapter is taught.
Question:
When a bodhisattva increases the six pāramitās, for what causes and conditions do the devas and the people of the world rejoice?
Answer: All devas are born because of the ten wholesome paths of action, the four dhyānas, and the four immeasurables;
these meritorious qualities all exist because of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If a Buddha appears in the world, the hosts of devas increase and the race of asuras diminish;
if a Buddha does not remain in the world, the race of asuras becomes numerous and the devas decrease,
because their accumulated merit is mixed and impure.
If the Buddhas appear in the world, they can sever the net of doubts of the devas and accomplish great deeds.
For example, when Śakra Devānām Indra was nearing the end of his life, he harbored fear in his heart and sought the Buddha for salvation, yet could not find him anywhere.

"Even though we see those who have left the household life in secluded places such as mountains and marshes, and even though we provide them with offerings, none of us are able to sever the net of their doubts.
At that time, Viśvakarman Deva said to Śakra Devendra:
"The ascetic practice of King Śibi is extraordinary and rare in this world!"
The wise ones said:
"This person shall before long attain Buddhahood!
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"This matter is difficult to accomplish!
How do we know this?

It is like the eggs of fish, the flowers of the mango tree, and bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds: although these three things are numerous at the stage of their cause, those that bear fruit are very few."
"Now let us put this to the test!

Śakra transformed himself into a hawk, and Viśvakarman transformed himself into a dove. The dove flew into the king's arms; the king then cut the flesh from his own body, eventually placing his entire body upon the scale to substitute for the life of the dove, whereupon the earth shook.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and the others were filled with great joy; they scattered various celestial flowers and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"With such a resolute and great mind, he will attain Buddhahood before long!"
Furthermore, ordinary people possess only the fleshly eye and lack wisdom; they exhaust their bodies to seek wealth for their own livelihood.
Yet when they hear that a Bodhisattva is augmenting the six pāramitās and will soon attain Buddhahood, they still rejoice—how much more so the various devas!
Question:
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three are beset by the affliction of the asuras;
the higher heavens have no such calamity—why, then, should they rejoice?
The answer is:
Although the higher heavens are free from the affliction of asuras, if a Buddha does not appear in the world, those born in those heavens are few;
even if there are those who are born there, the five sensual pleasures are not sublime.
Why is this? It is because they have cultivated only impure merit.
The palaces, radiance, and lifespans of the various deva-heavens in the form realm are likewise so.
Furthermore, among the gods, those who possess wisdom are able to know that the flavor of dhyāna and the five desires are all impermanent;
only when a Buddha appears in the world can he cause them to attain the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa.
Because both worldly happiness and the bliss of nirvāṇa are obtained through the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one rejoices.
It is like a tree bearing sweet fruit that flourishes and reaches full maturity, causing people great joy; for the tree provides manifold benefits:
there are those who take shelter in its shade, those who use its flowers, and those who eat its fruits.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: he can use the shade of detachment from unwholesome dharmas to shield against the heat of suffering in the three evil realms, bestow the flowers of wealth and happiness upon humans and devas, and enable all noble ones to attain the fruits of the Three Vehicles; for these reasons, he rejoices.
Question:
The deities have many matters of making offerings; why do they present the bowl? Answer:
The Four Heavenly Kings offered the bowls, while the other devas made offerings.
Each of the devas' offerings followed its own established rule:

for instance, at the time of the Buddha’s birth, Śakra-devānām-indra received the Buddha’s body with celestial robes, Brahmā-deva personally held the parasol, and the Four Heavenly Kings guarded him on all four sides.
The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, wishing to inspire in the Bodhisattva a sense of weary detachment from the world, manifested the forms of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, at the time of his renunciation, the Four Heavenly Kings commanded their messengers to lift up the horse’s hooves and personally attend to and protect the Bodhisattva from all four sides.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, took the hair and erected a Hair Stūpa outside the eastern gate of his celestial city;
he also took the Bodhisattva’s precious robe and erected a Robe Stūpa outside the southern gate of the city;
and when the Buddha arrived at the foot of the tree, he offered him excellent grass.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi constantly holds the vajra to guard and protect the Bodhisattvas;
the Brahmā King requests the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Such instances each have their own constant laws.
For this reason, the Four Heavenly Kings offered the bowls.
The meaning of the four bowls is as previously explained. Question:
Question: Why does the Buddha’s single body receive four alms bowls?
Answer: Because the power of the Four Heavenly Kings is equal, he cannot accept them from one alone.
Furthermore, they were made to witness the Buddha’s supernatural power as he joined the four bowls into one; their hearts were filled with joy, faith, and purity, and they thought:
"From the time the Bodhisattva was first born until his attainment of Buddhahood, the merit we have cultivated through our offerings has not been in vain."
Question: The lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings is five hundred years, whereas a Bodhisattva becomes a Buddha only after passing through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
The Four Heavens of today are not those of the future; for what reason, then, do they rejoice?
The answer is:
Because they share the same lineage;
for example, when a noble clan’s descendants continue for a hundred generations, they do not become distinct simply because of the distance in time.
At times, when a practitioner sees a bodhisattva augmenting the six pāramitās, they make this aspiration in their mind:
"When this bodhisattva attains buddhahood, I shall offer him my alms bowl."
Thus, they are able to be born there.
Furthermore, the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings is five hundred years;
fifty human years constitute one day and night in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Thirty days constitute one month, and twelve months constitute one year;
with this reckoning, a lifespan of five hundred years equals nine million years by human calculation.
A bodhisattva who can perform such meritorious deeds may be close to attaining Buddhahood; having first been born among the Four Heavenly Kings, they will certainly be able to encounter [the Buddha].
A question is asked:
As it is said in the Mahāyāna sūtras:
There are Buddhas who take joy as their sustenance and do not consume solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

For instance, the clothing and appearance of the Buddha T’ien-wang (Devarāja) were no different from those of a layperson; he had no need for a bowl to eat from. Why, then, do you say that "the Four Heavenly Kings must certainly present him with a bowl"?
The answer is:
"As for 'fixed,' it is because [the rule] is established for those who use bowls; it does not exclude those who do not.
Furthermore, among all Buddhas, those who use bowls are many while those who do not are few; therefore, the majority determines what is fixed."
[Sūtra] "The gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations were all filled with joy, thinking to themselves:
'We shall attend upon and make offerings to the Bodhisattva, thereby diminishing the host of asuras and increasing the assembly of devas.'"
"In the trichiliocosm, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, all were filled with great joy and thought to themselves:
'We shall entreat this Bodhisattva to turn the wheel of Dharma.'"
[Treatise] Commentary:
These various devas and others made offerings by means of flowers, incense, and necklaces, prostrating, paying respect, listening to the Dharma, and offering praise;
they also formed this thought:
"When humans cultivate pure merit, the race of asuras diminishes, and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven increases; we, the gods, likewise obtain increase.
[The interlocutor] asks:

"The six classes of heavens above have already been mentioned; for what reason is it further stated that 'from the three-thousandfold world system up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they joyfully make offerings'?"
Answer: Previously, it was said that there are six heavens upon a single Mount Sumeru; here, it refers to all the devas within the trichiliocosm.
Previously, only those of the desire realm were mentioned; now, it is stated that the devas of both the desire realm and the form realm request the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Although the above described the various offerings and exhortations made by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the present request for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is of great significance.
Question:
In the Tripiṭaka, it is only stated that "Brahmā requested the turning of the Wheel of Dharma"; why is it now stated that "the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven" [made this request]?
Answer: Because the heavens of the desire realm are proximate, they were mentioned first.
Since the entire form realm is designated as "Brahmā," if one speaks of the Brahmā King inviting the Buddha, the other heavens are already included by that term.
Furthermore, Brahmā is the initial gateway to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); because he is spoken of first, the others are also mentioned by implication.
Moreover, whether a Buddha exists or not, sentient beings always recognize Brahmā; since Brahmā is regarded as the progenitor of the world, Brahmā is spoken of for the sake of worldly people.
The characteristics of the Wheel of Dharma are as previously explained. [Sūtra] “Śāriputra,
when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and augment the six perfections, various sons and daughters of good family each rejoice and think to themselves:”
"We shall act as parents, wives, children, kinsmen, and friends for such people.
[Treatise] Question:
It was previously stated that "one can perform these meritorious deeds"; why is it now stated again that "one increases the six pāramitās"?
Answer: Previously, the general characteristics were explained; now, the specific characteristics are being explained.
Furthermore, within the merits previously described in the preceding chapter, those various and immeasurable qualities might cause the listener to become weary.
Now, by briefly explaining the six pāramitās, all meritorious qualities are fully encompassed.
Furthermore, because it is taught for the sake of the devas, it says "one can perform all meritorious qualities";
because it is taught for the sake of humans, it says "one increases the six pāramitās."
How is this known?
It is known from the subsequent mention of "good sons and good daughters.
Question:

From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, why is it that the term "virtuous deva" is not mentioned, whereas among humans one speaks only of "virtuous sons and virtuous daughters"?
Answer:

All devas possess the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds; they know that [the donor] is making an offering to a bodhisattva, and therefore their virtue is not mentioned separately.
Ordinary people see with the fleshly eye and lack knowledge;
those who are virtuous are able to know how to make offerings. Because such virtuous ones are few, they are mentioned separately.
These virtuous ones hear the Dharma from the Buddha, or from his disciples or bodhisattvas.
Or, having heard that they will receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, and having heard the Buddha praise their names, one knows that they have cultivated goodness.
Question:
Why is it that only the goodness of men and women is mentioned, while the goodness of those with both sexual organs or those without any organs is not mentioned?
The answer is:
They lack the faculties; that is to say, they lack the characteristics of attaining the Path, and for this reason it is not mentioned.
It is like those who are not permitted to leave the household life in the Vinaya, because they have lost their male or female characteristics.
Their minds are not settled; they become angry over minor causes and conditions;
because their fetters and latent tendencies are numerous, they are attached to worldly affairs;
they harbor many webs of doubt and take no pleasure in the Dharma.
Although they may be able to cultivate meritorious deeds to a small extent, their wisdom is shallow and they cannot penetrate deeply;
their fundamental nature is prone to change, and for this reason it is not taught.
Such is the teaching of the Śrāvaka-dharma.
Within the Mahāyāna, it is like the great ocean, which has nothing that it cannot contain;
yet, although those without roots may occasionally cultivate goodness, it is not mentioned because such instances are so few.
What is called "few" refers to those who are the fewest among men and women; it means those who cultivate wholesome deeds are few.
It is like a person of white complexion: even though their beard, hair, and moles may be black, they are not called a "black person."
Those who possess both sexual organs have many and diverse fetters; they engage in male acts and female acts alike, their minds being crooked and perverse, making them difficult to rescue.
It is like dragging timber through a dense forest: that which is warped is difficult to extract.
Furthermore, because the minds of the asuras are not upright, they constantly harbor doubts about the Buddha, claiming that the Buddha assists the devas.
When the Buddha preaches the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), they claim there are six aggregates and do not accept the teaching of one;
if he speaks of the four truths (catuḥsatya), they claim there are five truths and do not accept the teaching of a single principle.
The same applies to those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*); because their minds are largely crooked and deviant, they are incapable of attaining the Way.
For this reason, [the sūtra] speaks only of those who are virtuous among men and women.
One with virtuous characteristics possesses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion and is able to endure malicious abuse.
As it is said in the "Chapter on Abuse" of the *Dharmapada*:
"One who can endure those who utter malicious abuse is called the foremost among men!"
It is, for example, like a fine, excellent horse fit to be the mount of a king.
Furthermore, because his mind cannot be corrupted by the five kinds of wrong speech, nor by whips, staves, beatings, injuries, or fetters, this is called a "virtuous mark."
Furthermore, his three karmas are without fault, and he delights in virtuous people;
he does not disparage the goodness of others, nor does he boast of his own virtues;
he accords with the multitude and does not speak of the transgressions of others.
Not attached to worldly pleasures, they do not seek fame or reputation, but instead find joy in the delight of the Way and its virtue;
their own karma is pure, and they do not afflict sentient beings;
their hearts value the true Dharma and look down upon worldly affairs.
He cherishes only straightforward faith and does not follow the deceptions of others;
for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain happiness, he relinquishes his own happiness;
and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to be free from suffering, he substitutes himself in their place.
Such immeasurable qualities as these are called the marks of a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*).
Since these marks are mostly found in men and women, they are referred to as "virtuous sons" (*kulaputra*) and "virtuous daughters" (*kuladuhitr*).
Question:
By what cause are sons and daughters of good family able to make such a vow? Answer:
Good sons and good daughters who know themselves to be of meager merit and scant wisdom should associate with Bodhisattvas, desiring to cross over [to liberation];
it is like a sunken stone that, though heavy, obtains passage by relying on a boat.

Furthermore, sons or daughters of good family, hearing that a bodhisattva does not attain the Way through one or two lifetimes, but rather through coming and going in birth and death for incalculable eons, will then form this thought:
"I shall become a causal condition for them."
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva has accumulated such profound merit, wherever he is born, sentient beings all come to revere and look up to him, for they receive his benefits so heavily.
If one sees a bodhisattva relinquish his life, one should then form this aspiration:
"I shall become the parents, wife, children, or kinsmen of this bodhisattva. Why is this?
One should know that associating with virtuous people increases one's merit;
it is like collecting various fragrances, whereby the scent becomes ever more abundant.

For example, in a previous life, a Bodhisattva was the crown prince of a king. Seeing the poverty of the people of Jambudvīpa, he sought the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) and entered the great ocean, arriving at the palace of the Dragon King.
Seeing the Prince’s majestic and sublime virtue, the dragon immediately rose to meet him, invited him forward to offer hospitality, and asked him:
"How have you been able to come from so far away?"
The Prince replied,
"Out of compassion for the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, I wish to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) in order to benefit them!
The dragon said:
"If you can stay in my palace and accept my offerings for one month, I shall give it to you!
The Prince then stayed for one month and praised the Dragon King’s great learning; the Dragon immediately gave him the jewel.
This wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) was able to rain down [precious things] over an area of one *yojana*.
The dragon said, "The Prince possesses the marks [of a Buddha]; before long he will become a Buddha, and I shall become his foremost disciple in learning.
At that time, the Prince again went to a dragon palace and obtained a jewel, which rained down for two *yojanas* over two months, while he praised the power of his supernormal faculties.
The dragon said, "Before long the Prince shall become a Buddha; I shall become his foremost disciple in supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
He then went to another dragon palace and obtained a pearl, which he rained down for three *yojanas* for three months while praising wisdom.
The dragon said, "It will not be long before the Prince becomes a Buddha; I shall become his foremost disciple in wisdom.
Having given the jewels to the Prince, he spoke thus:
"For as long as you live, this jewel shall be returned to me.
The Bodhisattva granted his consent.
Having obtained the jewel, the Prince returned to Jambudvīpa.
One jewel can rain down food and drink; one jewel can rain down clothing; and one jewel can rain down the seven treasures, thereby benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is like the Bodhisattva Sumati, who, upon seeing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, wished to purchase five stalks of flowers from the maiden Sujātā, but she was unwilling to give them to him.
He then obtained the five stalks of flowers for five hundred gold coins, yet the maiden still refused to part with them, demanding instead that he make a vow:
"I vow that in every lifetime I shall always be your wife; I offer myself to you!
Because the Bodhisattva was making offerings to the Buddha, he immediately granted her request.

Furthermore, when the daughter of the elder saw that the body of the Bodhisattva Wondrous Light possessed twenty-eight marks, she conceived a heart of love and reverence and stood waiting at his gate.
When the Bodhisattva arrived, the woman immediately untied a lapis lazuli bead from her neck and placed it in the Bodhisattva’s alms bowl, making this vow in her heart:
"In every lifetime, may I be the wife of this man!"
This girl had accumulated all manner of merits over two hundred and fifty kalpas;

she was subsequently born within a lotus in the garden of the courtesan Priyadarśanā, who raised her as her daughter. When she reached the age of fourteen, she was fully proficient in the arts of women and all worldly knowledge.

At that time, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Dhanapati; his crown prince was named Guṇapati, who possessed a heart of great compassion. Once, he went out from the city to enter a garden for recreation, accompanied by various courtesans who led the way with songs and praises.
Prince Guṇarāja distributed various precious objects, garments, food, and drink;
like the rain from a dragon, there was nowhere it did not reach.
When the maiden Priyadarśanā saw the prince, she composed verses in praise of him and gazed at him with eyes of love, her eyelids never blinking, as she spoke these words:
“I know all worldly affairs; with this body of mine, I offer myself to the Prince!
The Prince asked, “To whom do you belong?”
"If she has someone else to belong to,
this is not suitable for me. At that time, the courtesan Priyadarśanā replied to the prince,
"The year, month, day, and hour of my daughter's birth are all identical to yours, Prince."
"This girl was not born from my womb; early this morning I entered the garden and saw this girl born within a lotus flower. I therefore raised her and kept her as my daughter."
Do not treat this woman with contempt because of me!
This woman possesses all sixty-four arts;
she is fully proficient in feminine crafts and technical skills, as well as in the classics and medical prescriptions.
She is always mindful of shame and remorse, her inner heart is loyal and upright, she is free from jealousy, and she harbors no thoughts of illicit desire.
Since my daughter’s virtue and deportment are such as this, the Prince should certainly accept her!
Prince Virtue-Master replied to the woman, saying: "Sister!
I have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and am practicing the bodhisattva path; there is nothing I hold dear."
"Your kingdom, wealth, wife, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures—whatever anyone may seek, do not oppose their wishes.
If someone should come to ask for your sons, daughters, or even your own body, you must give it to them; do not harbor grief or regret!"
"If at some time you should abandon me to leave the household life and become a disciple of the Buddha, dwelling in pure mountain thickets,
you need not grieve! The girl Hsü-te replied,
"Even if the fires of hell were to come and burn my body to ashes, I would never regret it!"

I do not cultivate the primary and secondary marks for the sake of sensual pleasure or amorous play; rather, I serve these true men (satpuruṣa) in order to encourage and assist them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
The woman spoke again to the prince, saying:
"Last night I dreamed of the Buddha Sun-Body (Sūryagarbha) sitting beneath the Bodhi tree; you should go to behold him!

Because the prince saw that the woman was beautiful and heard that a Buddha had appeared—due to these two causes and conditions—they mounted a single carriage together and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; the prince attained immeasurable dharani-doors, and the girl attained the subduing of her mind and will.
At that time, the prince offered five hundred precious flowers to the Buddha, seeking anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
The Crown Prince said to his father, the King:
"I have been able to see the Buddha Sun-like Body (Sūryagātra), and have thereby gained great and wholesome benefit.

Upon hearing this, the father king relinquished his most cherished possessions to give to the Crown Prince; then, together with his officials and the people of the kingdom, they all proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and the king attained the *dhāraṇī* of the Lamp that Illumines All Dharmas without Darkness.
At that time, the king reflected:
"One cannot govern a kingdom according to the ways of a layman, nor can one attain the Way while indulging in the five desires!"
Having reflected thus, he established Prince Vīradatta as king and left the household life to seek the Way.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, the six treasures appeared in response, and his wife, Priyadarśanā, transformed into a jewel maiden.
As explained at length in the *Acintya-sūtra* through such causes and conditions as these,
one should know that good sons and good daughters should, in every lifetime, vow to be the parents, wives, children, and kinsmen of bodhisattvas.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven were all greatly rejoiced, each thinking to themselves:

"We shall employ skillful means to cause this bodhisattva to remain free from sexual desire; from the first moment he resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he shall always remain a celibate youth (*kumārabhūta*), and we must not allow him to encounter sensual pleasures.
If he were to experience the five desires, it would obstruct his birth in the Brahma Heaven, let alone his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!"

"For this reason, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has renounced the household life by severing sensual desire shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is not for one who does not sever desire."
[Treatise] Question:
Why do the devas make such a vow? Answer:
In the world, among the five desires, there is none that is not cherished;
yet among these five desires, touch is the foremost, for it can bind the human mind.
It is like a person who has fallen into deep mud, from which they are difficult to rescue.
For this reason, the devas employ skillful means to cause the bodhisattva to distance himself from sexual desire.
Furthermore, if one indulges in other forms of desire, one may still not lose wisdom;
however, at the time of sexual union, the body and mind become dazed and confused, devoid of discernment, leading to deep attachment and self-immersion.
For this reason, the devas cause the bodhisattva to distance himself from them.
Question: How do they cause him to distance himself?
The answer is:

When the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was in King Śuddhodana’s palace and desired to go out of the city for sightseeing, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as an old man, a sick man, and a dead man to cause his mind to feel weary of worldly existence;

furthermore, they caused him to see at midnight that the palace women and attendants were covered in foul secretions and impurities, with mucus, saliva, and drool flowing from them, and excrement and urine smeared all over.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva immediately feels revulsion and loathing.
At times, the devas cause women to harbor malicious envy, fail to recognize kindness and virtue, speak with harsh words and deceit, and lack any self-reflection;
having seen this, the Bodhisattva immediately gives rise to this thought:
"Though his body resembles that of a human, his mind is loathsome!
Thus, they abandoned him.

[The Buddha] desired that from the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, the Bodhisattva would always practice the conduct of perpetual celibacy (kumārabhūta) and never consort with sensual desire.
Why is this? Because sensual desire is the root of all fetters!
Thus spoke the Buddha:
"Rather than having sexual union with a woman, one would prefer to have one's body cut and severed by a sharp blade!
Although being cut by a blade is painful, it does not lead to rebirth in the evil realms;
whereas through the causes and conditions of lustful desire, one undergoes the sufferings of hell for immeasurable kalpas."
"If a person indulges in the five desires, they will not even be reborn in the Brahma world, let alone attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Yet some may say:
'Although a bodhisattva indulges in the five desires, because his mind is not attached to them, it does not obstruct the Path.'"
For this reason, the sutra says:
"If one indulges in the five desires, one will not even be born in the Brahma world.
In the Brahma world, all sentient beings since beginningless time have been able to be born."

If those who indulge in the five desires cannot even obtain what they ought to obtain, how much less can they obtain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which was originally unobtainable and yet they wish to obtain?
For this reason, a bodhisattva should remain as a celibate youth (*kumārabhūta*), practicing pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and shall thereby attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because a bodhisattva who practices pure conduct is unattached to the world, they swiftly accomplish the bodhisattva path;
whereas for one who indulges in sexual desire, it is like glue or lacquer—difficult to separate from.
Why is this so? Because the body experiences sensual pleasure, and the root of sexual desire is deep-seated!
Therefore, within the Dharma of renunciation, the precept against sexual misconduct is placed first and is also considered the most weighty.
[Sūtra] Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Must a bodhisattva-mahāsattva necessarily have parents, wife and children, kinsmen, and friends?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"There are some bodhisattvas who have parents, wives, children, kinsmen, and acquaintances;

there are also some bodhisattvas who, from the first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], sever sexual desire and cultivate the practice of celibacy, such that until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not transgress against sensual desire."
"Or there may be bodhisattvas who, by the power of skillful means, experience the five desires and then leave the household life to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Explanation:
These are three kinds of bodhisattvas. The first is like a worldly person who experiences the five desires, later renounces them to leave the household life, and attains the path to enlightenment.
Second, their great merit is firm: from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, they have severed sexual desire.
Such Bodhisattvas may possess either a Dharma-body or a physical body;
they may be free from desire or not yet free from desire.
Third, the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Dharma-body have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and abide in the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā).
For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they engage in the same activities as sentient beings (samānārthatā) in order to gather them in.
Sometimes he becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or a king of Jambudvīpa, a householder, or a kṣatriya, benefiting beings according to their needs.
[Sūtra] "It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, being well-versed in the arts of illusion, conjures up the five objects of desire and enjoys them together."
"What do you think?
Does this person truly experience these five desires?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“In the same way, by the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests the five desires and experiences pleasure therein, thereby bringing sentient beings to maturity.”
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is not defiled by desire; for various reasons, they disparage the five desires:
"Desire is a blazing fire; desire is foul and evil; desire is destructive; desire is like an enemy!"
Therefore, Śāriputra,
you should know that a bodhisattva accepts the five desires for the sake of sentient beings.
[Treatise] Question:
Question: Among the three types of bodhisattvas, why is a simile provided specifically for only one type?
Answer: First, it is because they are like ordinary people who do not sever their sensual desires.
Second, they constantly renounce sexual desire and cultivate pure conduct;
third, while also cultivating pure conduct, they manifest the acceptance of sexual desire—doing so as an analogy for those who do not understand.
Question:
Why are dreams, transformations, and so forth not used as analogies? Answer:
A dream is not known by the five sensory faculties; it arises solely from the recollections and imaginings of the internal mind.
That which is seen by people through the five sensory faculties undergoes transformation and loss, being impermanent, and thus can be understood [as such].
Although a transformation body is known by the five senses, those who actually see it are very few.
Because the Buddha seeks to deliver sentient beings who can be delivered, and because illusions are something everyone believes in, he uses them as a metaphor.
Just as a magician, by means of illusory arts, manifests rare wonders among the multitude to bring them joy, so too is the Bodhisattva-magician:

by means of the art of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he creates the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) among sentient beings, with whom he enjoys himself in mutual entertainment, thereby transforming and delivering sentient beings.
Sentient beings are of two kinds:
householders and those who have left the home life.
In order to deliver those who have left the home life, he manifests as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, buddhas, and various teachers of non-Buddhist paths who have left the home life.

Among sentient beings living at home, some may attain liberation upon seeing those who have left the household life, while others may be transformed by seeing those remaining at home equally experiencing the five desires.
Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva constantly uses various causes and conditions to disparage these five desires.
Regarding the phrase "desire is a blazing fire": if one has not yet lost [the opportunity], the fires of the three poisons blaze;
if one has already lost it, the fire of impermanence blazes.
Because these two fires blaze, it is called "blazing," and there is never a time of happiness.
Regarding the phrase "desire is foul and evil": it is that which all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and other those who have transcended desire, loathe and despise.
For example, when a person sees a dog eating excrement, they despise it and pity that it cannot obtain fine food but instead devours what is impure;
likewise, those who indulge in desire do not attain the bliss of inner detachment from desire, yet seek pleasure within the impurity of sensual form.

Regarding the phrase "desire acts as destruction": because of attachment to the causes and conditions of the five desires, even celestial kings, human kings, and those of great wealth and status have lost their nations and endangered their lives; there is nothing that does not arise from this!
"Desire is like an enemy" means it causes one to lose the wholesome benefits of humanity;
it is also like an assassin who appears outwardly friendly while harboring malice within the heart.
The five desires are likewise: they destroy the virtuous mind and rob one of the life-force of wisdom.
The arising of the five desires is precisely for the purpose of destroying all that is wholesome and ruining virtuous deeds; thus they emerge.
Furthermore, one knows that the five desires are like a hook catching fish, like a snare harming deer, and like a lamp incinerating moths; therefore, it is said that "desires are like enemies."
The harm caused by an enemy does not extend beyond a single lifetime;
however, due to attachment to the causes and conditions of the five desires, one falls into the three evil realms and undergoes various bitter poisons of suffering for immeasurable lifetimes.
[Sūtra] Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the word ‘bodhisattva. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that ‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom,’ nor does he perceive that ‘I am not practicing the perfection of wisdom.’”
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva and the nature of the word "Bodhisattva" are empty. Within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
yet apart from form there is no emptiness, and apart from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is also no emptiness.
Emptiness is form, and form is emptiness;
emptiness is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are emptiness.

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because there is only a name that we speak of as "bodhi"; there is only a name that we speak of as a "bodhisattva"; and there is only a name that we speak of as "emptiness."
Why is this? Because the true nature of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they neither perceive arising nor perceive cessation.
One neither perceives defilement nor perceives purity. Why is this?
Names are dharmas produced through the cooperation of causes and conditions; they are spoken of as provisional designations based solely on conceptual discrimination and recollection.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not perceive any names; because he does not perceive them, he does not cling to them.
[Treatise] Question: This matter was already asked by Śāriputra above; why is it asked again now?
The answer is:

He asked because the Buddha had previously stated, "One who wishes to know all phenomena in all their aspects should study the Prajñāpāramitā"; it was not a question posed according to his own independent intention.
Furthermore, having now heard the various praises of the merit of prajñā, Śāriputra’s heart rejoiced; out of his reverence for prajñā, he asked, "How should one practice it?
Just as a patient, upon hearing a praise of an excellent medicine, asks, "How should it be taken?"

Question: Previously, it was already asked: "One dwells in the non-dwelling dharma while practicing the *dānapāramitā*; because the giver, the receiver, and the material gift cannot be apprehended, such practices constitute the practice of *prajñā*. Why is this question about practice being asked again now?
Answer: Above, there was a general inquiry concerning all the pāramitās, whereas here the inquiry concerns only prajñā;
above, prajñā was extensively praised as the primary [pāramitā], whereas here the inquiry concerns the practice of prajñā.
Furthermore, although the Prajñāpāramitā has been extensively praised above, those present in the assembly longed for it with thirsting desire.
For this reason, Śāriputra, on behalf of the multitude, asked about "practicing the Prajñāpāramitā."
The merit of the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and inexhaustible, and the wisdom of the Buddha is likewise immeasurable and inexhaustible;
if Śāriputra did not pose his questions, the Buddha’s praises would have been endless.
If Śāriputra had not asked, there would have been no cause or condition for the discourse to conclude.
Question:
The merit of Prajñā is most venerable; if the Buddha were to praise it extensively, what would be improper about that? Answer:
If one praises Prajñā and those who hear it respond with joy and reverence, their merit and virtue will increase;
if they hear the teaching of Prajñā, their wisdom will increase.
One does not attain the Buddha-way solely through the causes and conditions of merit; it must necessarily be accomplished through wisdom.
Therefore, one need not merely offer praise.
When people hear such praise, their minds become purified, and they develop a yearning desire to obtain Prajñā.
Just as one might extensively praise and extol a fine drink for a thirsty person, yet that thirst would not be relieved unless the drink were actually given to them;
for such reasons, Śāriputra now asks about the practice of prajñāpāramitā.
Question:
Just as a person with eyes can see and thus know their destination before they are able to walk, so too it is for the Bodhisattva:
first they recollect the Buddha-way and know Prajñā; having seen it, the body should subsequently act accordingly.
Now, why do you say that one "does not see the bodhisattva and the prajñā"?
If they are not seen, how can one practice?
The answer is:
In this context, it is not said that [the Bodhisattva] never sees them; rather, it clarifies that when entering the contemplation of prajñā, one does not see the bodhisattva nor the prajñāpāramitā.
The prajñāpāramitā emerges for the purpose of enabling sentient beings to know the true dharma.
This name "Bodhisattva" is a conventional designation based on the combination of various conditions, as will be explained in detail in a later chapter.
The name "Prajñāpāramitā" is likewise; because it is a combination of various dharmas, it is conventionally designated as "Prajñāpāramitā."
Although Prajñāpāramitā is a mere provisional designation, it is able to shatter all conceptual proliferations;
because its intrinsic nature does not exist, it is said to be "unobservable."

Just as fire arises from the conjunction of various conditions and is conventionally designated as "fire"— and though it lacks substantial reality, it is nonetheless able to burn things— a question is asked:
If one does not see [the object] when entering into *prajñā*, but sees it upon emerging, which of these two states is to be trusted?
The answer is:
It may be believed that "Prajñā emerges because it is the true dharma";
however, that which emerges from the Prajñāpāramitā is not real, and therefore it cannot be believed.
Question:

If one does not see [phenomena] while "entering" into prajñā, but sees them upon "emerging" from it, then one should know that dharmas are not eternally empty; rather, they are empty by virtue of the power of prajñā!
Answer: According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), one speaks of "going" and "entering" the *prajñāpāramitā*;
however, because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have ceased through various contemplations, there is neither going out nor entering.
If the noble sages did not teach by means of names and words, they would be unable to transform ordinary people;
one should grasp the intended meaning of what is said and not become attached to the language itself!
[The interlocutor] asks:
If the Prajñāpāramitā values the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), why does it first explain the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) to refute the self?
The answer is:
when one first hears the Prajñāpāramitā, one cannot immediately be told that all phenomena are empty.

The self cannot be sought and found through the five sensory faculties; rather, it arises from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, whereby one regards what does not exist as existing.

Furthermore, within the faculty of the mind (manas), there is no fixed object; it is only due to recollection, conceptualization, and the causes and conditions of inversion that the notion of a self arises amidst the empty five aggregates.
If one hears of "non-self," it is easily understood.
Since phenomena such as form are currently seen with the eyes,
if one were to say at the outset that they are empty and non-existent, it would be difficult to believe.
Now, first the self is refuted, and next the dharmas belonging to the self are refuted;
because the self and the dharmas belonging to the self are refuted, all dharmas are entirely empty.
To be thus free from desire is called attaining the Way.
Furthermore, because the *prajñāpāramitā* has no fixed dharma, it is said:
"One does not see oneself practicing *prajñā*, nor does one see not practicing. This is because ordinary beings do not attain *prajñā* and are therefore called "not practicing";
however, the bodhisattva is not like this, for they practice only the *prajñā* of emptiness, and thus it is said that "one does not see not practicing."

Furthermore, the Buddha is the King of Dharma; he observes that other bodhisattvas possess very little wisdom and are entangled with various fetters (*saṃyojana*), such that their practice cannot be called true practice.
For example, although a king may obtain a small amount of property, it is not considered a significant acquisition;
the Buddha likewise instructs the bodhisattvas that even if they have some slight practice, it cannot be called true practice.
Furthermore, one who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* may give rise to arrogance, saying, "I possess the *prajñāpāramitā*," thereby grasping at its characteristics;
whereas one who does not practice will find their mind naturally sinking into despondency and harbor distress.
Therefore, it is said: "One does not perceive my practicing or not practicing.
Furthermore, "not perceiving that I practice the *prajñāpāramitā*" refutes attachment to the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*);
"not perceiving that I do not practice the *prajñāpāramitā*" refutes attachment to the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, by not perceiving oneself as one who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, one ceases all frivolous conceptualization regarding phenomena;
by not perceiving oneself as one who does not practice, one ceases the mind of indolence.
It is like riding a horse: if it is too fast, one restrains it; if it is too slow, one lashes it with a whip.
In this way, one discriminates between "practicing" and "not practicing.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explained the causes and conditions, namely: "The Bodhisattva and the nature of the word 'Bodhisattva' are empty."
Although in this context only the emptiness of the word "bodhisattva" is mentioned, the five aggregates are likewise empty.

Regarding the statement, "In emptiness there is no form; apart from form there is no emptiness," "emptiness" here refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Within the emptiness of phenomena, not even a single hair’s breadth of a dharma exists, let alone coarse form!
"Emptiness is also not separate from form. Why is this?
It is because emptiness exists through the disintegration of form; how then could one say it is separate from form?
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Why is this? The Buddha himself further explains the causes and conditions, saying: "There is only a name called 'bodhi,' there is only a name called 'bodhisattva,' and there is only a name called 'emptiness.'"
Question: This matter has already been explained previously; why is it being stated again now? Answer:
Previously it was stated that "one does not see the bodhisattva, one does not see the word 'bodhisattva,' and one does not see the prajñāpāramitā";

now the causes and conditions for this "not seeing" are explained, namely: "there is only a name called 'enlightenment' (bodhi), there is only a name called 'bodhisattva,' and there is only a name called 'emptiness'."
The "superior bodhisattva" and this "bodhisattva" have the same meaning.
Regarding the "term 'bodhisattva'," it is as explained in the section on "Bodhisattva.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is divided into two parts:
That which is accomplished is called "bodhi" (enlightenment); that which is not yet accomplished is called "emptiness.
Because the characteristic of arising cannot actually be apprehended, it is called "non-arising."
Why is this so? Whether birth occurs before the dharma, the dharma occurs before birth, or birth and the dharma occur simultaneously, none of these can be established, as previously explained.
Because there is no arising, there is "no cessation. If a dharma neither arises nor ceases, being like space, how could it have defilement or purity?
It is, for example, like space: even if it rains for ten thousand years, it is not moistened; even if a great fire burns it, it does not heat up; and even smoke does not adhere to it.
Why is this? Because they are fundamentally non-arising from the very beginning.
When a bodhisattva can contemplate in this way, they do not perceive anything apart from these dharmas that are neither arising nor ceasing as having birth or cessation, or defilement or purity.
Why is this? The Buddha himself explained the causes and conditions:
"All phenomena are merely conceptualizations and discriminations; because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are forcibly designated by names."
That which is ineffable is the ultimate reality; that which is expressible consists entirely of names.

When it is said, "The bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any names," this first briefly mentions names—namely, "bodhisattva" and the word "bodhisattva," as well as "perfection of wisdom" and the word "enlightenment.
Now, it is explained extensively that all names are unperceivable; because they are not perceived, one does not cling to them. Not clinging means that they cannot be apprehended.
Just as among all eyes, the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) is supreme;
the Bodhisattva, seeking everywhere with the wisdom-eye, does not see even a single subtle phenomenon, and for this reason, he is unattached.
Question:
If a bodhisattva does not cling to any phenomena, why do they not enter nirvana? Answer:
This matter has already been explained in various places; here it is stated briefly: because of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);

because of being remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions; because their original vows have not yet been fulfilled; because of the power of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*); and because of the union of the two matters of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), namely, non-attachment even toward non-attachment.
For various reasons such as these, it is said: "Although the bodhisattva does not cling to any phenomena, he does not enter nirvāṇa.
**Chapter 3: Correspondence with Practice (Śikṣā-saṃprayoga-varga)** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Three, Part One [Sūtra] The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he should reflect in this way:"
"A Bodhisattva exists as a mere name; a Buddha also exists as a mere name; and Prajñāpāramitā also exists as a mere name.
Form exists as a mere name; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also exist as mere names."

"Śāriputra! Just as 'self' exists only as a mere name, the self is eternally unapprehendable in its entirety. Sentient beings, life-spanners, individuals, living beings, nourishers, persons, human beings, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers—all these are likewise unapprehendable.
Because they are empty and unapprehendable, they are spoken of by means of names alone."

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise practices the perfection of wisdom in this way: they do not perceive a self, nor do they perceive sentient beings; they do not perceive anything up to a knower or a viewer, and even the names by which these are spoken cannot be perceived.
[Treatise] Question:
Since emptiness was already explained at the end of the second chapter, why is it stated again now? Answer:
Previously, the emptiness of dharmas was primarily taught; now, the emptiness of dharmas and the emptiness of sentient beings are taught together.

A practitioner contemplates that external dharmas are entirely empty and non-existent, yet they claim that the one who knows this emptiness is not empty. For this reason, it is further stated: "The observer, too, is empty."
This emptiness of sentient beings is frequently taught in the Śrāvaka-dharma; all disciples of the Buddha know that there is no self within all phenomena.
Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the community split into two factions:
those who believe in the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā); and—

There are those who believe only in the emptiness of sentient beings, asserting that "the five aggregates are determinately existent dharmas," yet they accept only the emptiness of the recipient of the five aggregates.
For this reason, the Buddha taught the emptiness of sentient beings as an illustration for the emptiness of dharmas.
Furthermore, the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is easy to understand, whereas the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is difficult to perceive. Why is this?

Because when one seeks the self with the five sensory faculties, it cannot be found; it is only through the power of the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) that one conceives of and discriminates it as a self.
Regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): form can be seen by the eye and sound can be heard by the ear; therefore, their emptiness is difficult to know.
Both of these things are empty within the *prajñāpāramitā*, as explained in the section on the meaning of the "eighteen kinds of emptiness."
Question:
Are the "self" up to the "knower" and the "seer" one and the same thing,
or are they each distinct?
Answer: They are all one and the same self; they differ only according to the circumstances.
Within the five aggregates, because the mind of "self" and "what belongs to self" arises, it is called "self."
Because they arise from the combination of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established, they are called "living beings" (*jīva*) and "individuals" (*puruṣa*).
It is able to initiate all things, like a father begetting a son, and is thus called the "Producer.
Through the conditions of nursing, clothing, and food, it attains growth; this is called "Nurturing."

The causes and conditions of all phenomena, such as the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus), consist of these various dharmas which possess numerical enumeration; therefore, they are called "aggregates" (gaṇa).
Because one practices these dharmas, one is called a "person" (pudgala).
Because the hands and feet are capable of performing actions, they are called the "agent" (*kartṛ*).
Because their power can employ others, they are called the "instigator" (*prayojaka*).
Because they can produce the karma of future transgressions and merits, they are called the "originator" (*utthāpaka*).
Because it causes others to give rise to karma of future retribution—both merit and demerit—it is called "the instigator.
Because one receives the fruits and retributions of merit and demerit in a future body, it is called "the recipient."
That which causes others to experience suffering and pleasure is called "the causer of experiencing.
That which beholds forms with the eyes is called "the seer.
That which cognizes through the five consciousnesses is called "the knower."

Furthermore, seeing forms with the eye, observing the five aggregates through the five false views, and observing all phenomena through mundane and supramundane right view—this is called the "seer. That is to say, the eye-faculty, the five false views, mundane right view, and the untainted view (anāsrava-dṛṣṭi) are what constitute the "seer."
The objects known by the remaining four faculties and those known by the mental consciousness are collectively termed "the knower.
All such phenomena are likewise said to be the "self" (ātman).

This deity cannot be found even by seeking it among the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, nor among all the worthy sages; it is merely a name forcibly assigned through recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination.
All phenomena are likewise: they are all empty and without substantial reality, existing merely as provisional designations.
Question:
Is this self (ātman) merely a matter of sixteen names?
Are there further names?
The answer is:
briefly stated, there are sixteen; extensively stated, they are immeasurable.

Names arise in accordance with phenomena, such as the distinctions among official titles, the skillful expertise of artisans, or the attainment of the Way by those who have left the household life. All such various names are produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions; therefore, they lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are ultimately empty.
Because sentient beings are empty, phenomena are empty; because phenomena are empty, sentient beings are also empty.

[Sūtra] “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, with the exception of the Buddha’s wisdom, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, by means of the emptiness of non-apprehension.”
Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, these dharmas of names and the objects to which names adhere are likewise unapprehendable by the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

For example, suppose Jambudvīpa were filled with bamboo, hemp, rice, and reeds, and there were as many bhikṣus as those stalks, each possessing wisdom like that of Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; yet, compared to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, their wisdom would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousandth, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas use wisdom to deliver all sentient beings.
[Treatise] Explanation:
For two reasons, the wisdom of a bodhisattva surpasses that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
first, through emptiness they know all dharmas are empty, yet they do not perceive this emptiness;
emptiness and non-emptiness are equal, one, and not different.
Second, by means of this wisdom, one seeks to deliver all sentient beings and enable them to attain nirvana.
The wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas merely contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena; they are unable to contemplate the world and nirvana as one.
It is like people escaping from prison: some merely tunnel through the wall to free themselves;
others break down the prison and destroy the locks, thereby freeing themselves while also delivering the multitude.
Furthermore, the wisdom of a bodhisattva is superior because it enters into two dharmas:
first, great compassion (mahākaruṇā); second, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
There are also another two dharmas:
First is the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, and second is skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas:
first, to dwell constantly in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and second, to be able to penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
first, being able to undergo suffering on behalf of all sentient beings; second, personally relinquishing all happiness.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
First is a mind of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will;
second is that even regarding the merits of all Buddhas, the mind remains unattached.
Because such various merits thus adorn wisdom, they surpass those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Question:
It may be appropriate to use analogies for those of dull faculties, but Śāriputra possesses sharp wisdom and keen faculties; why then provide an analogy for him?
Answer:
It is not necessary to use those of dull faculties as a metaphor; rather, metaphors serve to adorn the discourse and inspire faith and conviction.
Therefore, what is perceived by the five sensory faculties is used as a metaphor for the mental consciousness, so that one may attain awakening.
It is like ascending a tower: with a ladder, it is easy to climb.
Furthermore, all sentient beings are attached to worldly pleasures; when they hear of the Way and the attainment of nirvana, they neither believe nor find joy in it.
For this reason, one uses things seen with the eyes as metaphors for what is not seen.
For example, bitter medicine is very difficult to swallow;
if one uses honey as a vehicle for it, it becomes easy to take.
Furthermore, although Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom among the śrāvakas, compared to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, his [wisdom] has not yet been manifested.
Regarding the phrase "like Jambudvīpa": "Jambu" is the name of a tree whose groves are lush and flourishing; this tree is the largest among those in the forest.
"Dvīpa" means an island.
On this continent there is this forest;
within the forest is a river with a bed of golden sand called Jāmbūnada gold;
because of the Jambu tree, it is named "Jambudvīpa."
This continent is surrounded by five hundred minor islands, collectively named Jambudvīpa.
Question:
Since there are so many disciples, for what reason is it said that "Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others fill Jambudvīpa like bamboo, hemp, rice, and reeds"?
Answer:
Among all the disciples of the Buddha, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom, and Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernormal powers;
these two are great within the Buddha-dharma and likewise great within external teachings.
Pūrṇa, Kātyāyana, Aniruddha, and others, though great within the Buddha-dharma, were not so in the non-Buddhist teachings.
Furthermore, these two individuals constantly remained among the great assemblies to assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation and to refute the various non-Buddhists;
the bhikṣus such as Pūrṇa did not possess such merit, and for this reason they were not mentioned.
Furthermore, if one mentions Śāriputra, all those possessed of wisdom are encompassed; if one mentions Maudgalyāyana, all those accomplished in meditative concentration are encompassed.
There are two kinds of analogies:
first, analogies used figuratively; second, analogies based on actual facts.
Now, these are called metaphorical examples.
The reason other things are not used as metaphors is that these four items grow in dense clusters, are thickly packed, and belong to many different species.

Even if bhikṣus such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were to fill the entire Jambudvīpa, the combined wisdom of all such arhats would not equal even one hundredth part of a bodhisattva’s wisdom; indeed, it would be beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Question: Why do you not simply say that it "cannot be reached by calculation or analogy," but instead say that "a hundredth part, a thousandth part, does not equal one"?
The answer is:
"That which cannot be reached by calculation or analogy" is the ultimate expression.
It is like a person who has committed a grave offense; first they are beaten, bound, and subjected to cruel torture, and only then are they executed.
In the Śrāvaka-dharma, it is commonly illustrated by the metaphor that "one part does not equal sixteen";
in the Mahāyāna-dharma, however, it is said that "it is beyond even calculation or analogy."
[Sūtra] “Śāriputra! Let alone Jambudvīpa filled with those such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Suppose the entire trichiliocosm were filled with those such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;”

Setting this matter aside, even if one were to possess wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, filling worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—were it compared to the wisdom of a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, it would not equal even a hundredth part; nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor even anything reachable by calculation or analogy.
[Treatise] Commentary:
This meaning is the same as that regarding Jambudvīpa above; it differs only in that [the beings here] are numerous.
Question:
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others were equally possessed of great wisdom; why, then, is "many" used as a metaphor?
The answer is:
some people believe that what is few lacks power, whereas what is many possesses power.
For example, when water is scant, its power is also scant.
Again, it is like a man of great prowess whom a small force with few men cannot subdue, yet who submits when attacked by a great army.
Someone said, "If one Śāriputra’s wisdom is slight, he does not equal a bodhisattva; perhaps many would be able to equal him.
The Buddha said, "Even many would not equal him."
Therefore, many things are used as analogies:
