Why is this so? Because the Bodhisattva’s mind of pure compassion provides the causes and conditions for sentient beings to experience happiness and teaches them to cultivate meritorious deeds;
if sentient beings are unable to practice pure merit, what fault can there be in the Bodhisattva?
It is like a person who, with a kind heart, digs a well; if a blind person falls into it and dies, the digger is not at fault!
It is like a person who prepares excellent food to give to others; if an unknowing person eats too much and falls ill, the giver is not at fault!
Furthermore, if the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas did not teach sentient beings to cultivate the causes and conditions for merit, there would be no devas, no humans, and no asuras;
only the three evil realms would increase, and none would be able to escape from their transgressions.
Furthermore, because sentient beings delight in conditions, greed arises; because of greed, anger arises; because of anger, suffering arises; and because of suffering, transgression arises.
Now, wishing to deliver sentient beings from this fifth transgression, one therefore bestows happiness upon them.
Furthermore, it is not the case that sensual desire arises solely from the causal conditions of pleasure.
Rather, through correct mindfulness, pleasure serves as a causal condition for wholesome merit;
whereas through distorted mindfulness, sensual desire arises.
Now, for the sake of the joy of right mindfulness, he causes the conditions for the production of merit and virtue to arise.
Furthermore, only the Buddha alone is without error or failure.
Because this bodhisattva has not yet perfected the Buddha-way and has not yet attained the Buddha-eye, he teaches and transforms those beings who can be saved by means of these three kinds of joy.
The Buddhas teach and transform sentient beings solely through the bliss of liberation.

**Chapter Six: The Chapter on the Tongue-Mark** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Tongue-Mark, Number Six. [Sūtra] At that time, the World-Honored One extended his tongue-mark, covering the entire trichiliocosm.

From that tongue-mark issued forth countless and immeasurable rays of light of various colors, universally illuminating the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

At that time, in worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas, seeing this great radiance, each addressed their own Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"By whose spiritual power is this great radiance produced, which universally illumines all Buddha-worlds?
The Buddhas addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!"

In the western direction there is a world named Sahā; therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni. From his tongue-mark he emits a great radiance that universally illumines the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
He does this for the sake of teaching the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, each of those bodhisattvas addressed their own Buddha, saying:
“We wish to go to offer worship to Śākyamuni Buddha and the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and we also wish to hear the Prajñāpāramitā!”
The Buddhas said to the bodhisattvas:
"Good sons! You yourselves know the proper time!"

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, taking with them various articles of offering—immeasurable flower canopies, banners, pennants, necklaces, various incenses, gold, silver, and precious flowers—proceeded toward the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha.

At that time, the devas from the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven each took celestial divine incense, powdered incense, unguents, celestial tree incense, leaf incense, and various kinds of celestial lotuses—blue, red, crimson, and white—and approached the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was.

The various flowers scattered by these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the devas transformed into a great precious dais with four pillars suspended in the air throughout the trichiliocosm; it was of various different colors, exquisitely adorned and clearly manifest.
At that time, among the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha, there were ten trillion people who all rose from their seats, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In future ages, we too shall attain such a Dharma as this, just like Śākyamuni Buddha!
Our disciples, attendants, and great assemblies, and our preaching of the Dharma, shall likewise be so!"

At that time, the Buddha, knowing the sincere resolve of the good man, [saw] that he had attained this dharma-patience regarding all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, neither emerging nor being produced.
The Buddha then smiled, and rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition do you smile?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Within this assembly, one hundred trillion people have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas."

"These people shall, in a future age after sixty-eight billion kalpas, attain Buddhahood; that kalpa shall be named Flower Accumulation (Puṣpasaṃcaya), and all those Buddhas shall be titled Awakened Flower (Buddhābhyudgata).
[Treatise] Question:
In the first chapter, the Buddha has already manifested the mark of the tongue; why is it manifested again now?
The answer is:
This matter was not explained in a single day or a single sitting.
Previously, when the Buddha displayed the mark of the tongue, it was for the sake of the assembled great assembly and to deliver all sentient beings; Śāriputra then asked, and the Buddha answered.
Now, at this different time, it is for the sake of others;
because Subhūti skillfully explains emptiness, the Buddha commands him to explain further, and for this reason he emits the light from the mark of his tongue.
Question:
Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; what, then, was lacking in him that he had to request Subhūti? Answer:
The Buddha’s disciples are numerous; once one has spoken, he next commands another, just as when a king has many ministers, they converse with him in succession.
Question:
If that is so, since there are many such as Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and others, why did he not speak with each of them in succession? Answer:
This sutra is named "Wisdom. Since Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom, he asks this question.
Although Subhūti possesses various causes and conditions for his inquiry, two causes and conditions are particularly significant:

first, he delights in practicing the concentration of non-contention (araṇā-samādhi) and constantly maintains compassion for sentient beings; thus, although he cannot extensively deliver sentient beings himself, he always assists the Bodhisattvas by questioning the Buddha regarding Bodhisattva matters.

Second, because they delight in the profound practice of the dharma of emptiness—and since this *prajñāpāramitā* extensively expounds the dharma of emptiness—it was therefore directed that Subhūti speak on these matters.
The meanings of the "radiance of the tongue-mark," the "coming and going of the bodhisattvas," and so forth up to the "offering at the flower pedestal," are as previously explained.

At that time, sentient beings beheld this great supernatural power: namely, the Buddhas in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and because those Buddhas and Śākyamuni Buddha emitted immeasurable rays of light, the sentient beings, through the Buddhas' spiritual power, saw the mark of the tongue covering the trichiliocosm, and they heard and saw the Buddhas preaching the Dharma amidst the great assemblies. They immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and made this vow, saying:
"In future ages, our supernatural transformations shall also be like those of the present Buddha."
The Buddha, knowing that sentient beings had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), smiled.
The meaning of the "smile" and the "Buddha’s response" are as previously explained.

This person shall become a Buddha after sixty-eight billion kalpas. This person will see the bodhisattvas of the ten directions holding seven-jeweled flowers to offer as worship, which transform into pedestals made of the seven jewels.
Having seen this, their minds became pure and they attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, when they become Buddhas, the eon shall be named Flower Accumulation (*Puṣpasaṃcaya*), and all those Buddhas shall be titled Awakened Flower (*Buddhapuṣpa*).
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Fascicle Forty.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Three Designations, Fascicle Forty-one.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by Kumārajīva of Kucha under the Imperial Edict of the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Seven: The Three Provisions of Designation (Trikalpanā-varga). [Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“You should instruct the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), just as the perfection of wisdom should be accomplished by those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
At that moment, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great śrāvaka disciples, and the devas and others had this thought:
"Will the Venerable Subhūti, by the power of his own wisdom, expound the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
"Is this due to the power of the Buddha?
The venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great disciples, and the devas, said to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Whatever Dharma is taught and whatever instruction is given by the disciples of the Buddha, all is due to the power of the Buddha."
The Dharma taught by the Buddha does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena;
when these sons of good family study this Dharma and realize it, the Buddha says it is like a lamp.
“Śāriputra!
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas truly lack the power and ability to explain the prajñāpāramitā to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One, regarding what you have spoken of as ‘bodhisattva’ and the ‘name bodhisattva,’ of what dharma is the name ‘bodhisattva’ given?
Blessed One, we do not perceive such a dharma as being named ‘bodhisattva. How, then, should one teach the *prajñāpāramitā* to a bodhisattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Prajñāpāramitā is also merely a name, called 'Prajñāpāramitā';
'Bodhisattva' and the word 'Bodhisattva' are also merely names."
This name does not exist internally, nor does it exist externally, nor does it exist in between.
"Subhūti, it is like the name 'self,' which exists due to a combination of conditions; [the name of a bodhisattva is likewise]."
This which is called "self" is neither born nor extinguished; it is spoken of only by means of worldly designations.

Just as "sentient being," "life-span," "vitality," "one who is born," "nourisher," "numerical category," "person," "agent," "instigator of action," "ariser," "instigator of arising," "experiencer," "instigator of experience," "knower," "seer," and so forth—exist only because of the combination of dharmas—so too these various names are neither born nor extinguished; they are spoken of only by means of worldly designations.

The Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and even the word "bodhisattva" are likewise all existent through their combination; they too are neither born nor extinguished, but are spoken of only by means of worldly names.
“Subhūti! For example, it is like a body that exists because of a combination [of parts]; this too is neither born nor extinguished, but is spoken of only by means of worldly names. Subhūti!”

For example, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also exist through a combination of conditions; they too are neither born nor extinguished, but are spoken of only by means of worldly names.

Subhūti! Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and the designation "bodhisattva" are likewise all existent only through a combination of conditions; they are neither born nor extinguished, and are spoken of merely by means of worldly names.
“Subhūti! For example, the eye exists through a combination of conditions; it is neither born nor extinguished, but is spoken of merely by means of worldly names.
This eye is not within, not without, and not in between.”
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist through a combination of conditions; these, too, are neither born nor extinguished, and are spoken of only by means of worldly names and conventions.
The same applies to everything from form (*rūpa*) up to phenomena (*dharma*).
The eye-element exists through a combination of conditions; it, too, is neither born nor extinguished, and is spoken of only by way of worldly designations.
This applies even up to the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*).

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the bodhisattva, and the name "bodhisattva" are likewise: they exist only through a combination of factors; they are neither born nor extinguished, and are spoken of merely by way of names.
This name also does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between.
"Subhūti, it is like the internal body:
what is called 'head' exists only as a name; likewise, the neck, shoulders, arms, spine, ribs, thighs, calves, and feet exist only because of this combination."
These phenomena and their names are likewise neither born nor extinguished; they are spoken of only by means of names.
These names, moreover, do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between.
Subhūti! The perfection of wisdom, the bodhisattva, and the word "bodhisattva" are also like this: they all exist because of their conjunction, yet they are spoken of merely by way of names.
These, too, are neither born nor extinguished; they do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between.
“Subhūti! For example, external things—such as grass, trees, branches, leaves, stalks, and nodes—all these are spoken of merely by way of names.
These phenomena and their names are neither born nor extinguished; they are neither internal, nor external, nor do they abide in between.
Subhūti! Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and the name "bodhisattva" are likewise all existent only through their conjunction;
these dharmas and their names are neither born nor extinguished, and they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.
“Subhūti! For example, the Buddhas of the past exist through the combination of names; they, too, are neither born nor extinguished, being spoken of only by way of names.
Furthermore, they do not abide internally, externally, or in between.”
The Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and even the word "bodhisattva" are also like this.
Subhūti, it is as with a dream,
an echo, a reflection, an illusion, a mirage, or a magical creation of a Buddha— all these exist because of a combination of conditions and are spoken of only by way of names.
These phenomena and their names are neither born nor extinguished; they do not abide within, without, or in between.
The same is true for the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva, and the word "bodhisattva."

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should train themselves thus: regarding the designation of names, the designation of sensations, and the designation of phenomena."
[Treatise] Question:

Since the Buddha himself did not speak [of this], and since the merit, wisdom, and sharp faculties of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas surpass those of the śrāvakas, for what reason does he command Subhūti to speak?
Answer: Previously, within the section on the "characteristics of the tongue," there were already two causes and conditions that prompted Subhūti to speak.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s majestic virtue is so venerable, out of a heart of awe and reverence, he did not dare to question the Buddha, fearing he would not be able to express himself fully.
Furthermore, the Buddha knew the doubts within the minds of the assembly; yet because the people revered and held him in awe, they did not dare to pose questions. Why was this?
Because sentient beings saw that the Buddha’s body surpassed Mount Sumeru, his tongue covered the trichiliocosm, and his body emitted various kinds of immeasurable light.
At that time, the entire assembly was struck with fear and dared not ask questions;
each thought to themselves, "How shall I hear the Dharma from the Buddha?"
For this reason, the Buddha commanded Subhūti to preach the Dharma for the sake of the assembly.
He stated, "Whatever you have spoken is entirely through the power of the Buddha," as it is said in the sūtra.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of Prajñāpāramitā:
first, that which is taught in common with both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas; second, that which is taught exclusively for the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
In order to provide a comprehensive discourse, the Buddha appointed Subhūti as the leader, along with Maitreya, Śāriputra, and Śakra-devānām-indra.
At that time, when the assembly heard the Buddha appoint Subhūti to speak, their minds were filled with astonishment and doubt.
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, addressed Śāriputra and the others, saying:
"Everything spoken and known by all the śrāvakas is entirely through the power of the Buddha."
We shall, by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, speak for the sake of the multitude, like a messenger.
Why is this? Because the Dharma taught by the Buddha does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
When these disciples study this Dharma and realize it through direct experience, whatever they dare to speak is entirely through the power of the Buddha;
what we have spoken is, in fact, the Buddha’s own teaching.
Why is this? We speak now in the presence of the Buddha;
though we possess the eye of wisdom, had we not encountered the Buddha-dharma, we would have seen nothing at all.
It is like traveling by night on a perilous path: if there is no one holding a lamp, one will certainly be unable to pass through.
“The Buddha is also like this: if he did not illuminate us with the lamp of wisdom, we would have nothing to see.
He further addressed Śāriputra:
“All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas truly lack the power to explain the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas, let alone I alone!”
Why is this? The wisdom of a bodhisattva is profoundly deep, and their questions and answers are subtle and far-reaching;
it is already difficult to speak of even shallow and mundane dharmas in the presence of a bodhisattva, let alone the profound dharmas!
It is like a person who can eat one *hu* of rice, yet asks for only one *dou* from someone who has more, hoping thereby to eliminate their hunger; this cannot eliminate it.
For this reason, it is said that "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack the power to explain the Prajñāpāramitā for a Bodhisattva."
Subhūti is a greatly enlightened and noble Bodhisattva, and the Buddha likewise deems him so.
Because the Buddha wishes Subhūti to speak concerning the Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*), he says:
"Within all dharmas, a Bodhisattva cannot be found; because a Bodhisattva cannot be found, even the name cannot be found."
Because a bodhisattva and the designation "bodhisattva" cannot be apprehended, the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended.
Since these three things cannot be apprehended, how could I teach the *prajñāpāramitā* to a bodhisattva?

Question: The Buddha commanded Subhūti to explain the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas, yet Subhūti stated that "there are no bodhisattvas. This contradicts the Buddha; why then does the Buddha agree with him?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of explanations:
first, those given with an attached mind; second, those given with a non-attached mind.
Now, Subhūti speaks of emptiness with a mind of non-attachment, and the Buddha does not rebuke him.
Furthermore, Subhūti constantly practices the samādhi of emptiness because he knows that all dharmas are empty.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Since the bodhisattva is ultimately empty, Subhūti spoke in astonishment:
“What is meant by ‘bodhisattva’?
The Buddha then confirmed this:
“From the initial generation of the mind until the attainment of the Buddha-way, the bodhisattva is ultimately empty and thus ungraspable.”
"If one teaches in this manner, that is precisely teaching the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are generally two things:
first, names; second, the meaning of names.
For example, fire has the characteristics of being able to illuminate and being able to burn;
illumination is derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), while burning is the fire element (tejo-mahābhūta). The conjunction of these two factors is designated as "fire."
If fire existed apart from these two dharmas, there would have to be a third function;
yet, apart from burning and illuminating, there is no third activity.
Therefore, one knows that fire is a conventional designation for the conjunction of these two dharmas.
The name of this fire does not reside within these two dharmas. Why?
Because these dharmas are two, whereas the fire is one.
One does not become two, and two do not become one.
In meaning, these two dharmas are designated as distinct and do not conjoin. Why is this so?
If these two dharmas were conjoined, one’s mouth should be burned when speaking of fire;
if they were separate, one seeking fire should obtain water!
Through such causes and conditions, we know that [fire] does not exist within.
If fire were external to these two factors, then upon hearing the name "fire," the perception of fire should not arise within those two factors.
If it were in between the two, then it would have no locus of dependence.
All conditioned phenomena have no place of dependence;
if they were to exist in between, they could not be known!
For this reason, fire does not exist in these three places, but exists only as a conventional designation.
The "Bodhisattva" is also like this: the conjunction of two dharmas is called a Bodhisattva, namely name (nāma) and form (rūpa).
The matter of form is distinct, and the matter of name is distinct;
if there were definitively a Bodhisattva, there ought to be a third thing!
Since there is no such entity, one knows that "Bodhisattva" is a mere provisional name.
The "name Bodhisattva" is likewise: it does not exist internally, nor does it exist externally, nor does it exist in between the two.
In this regard, the Buddha spoke a parable:
"Just as the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are combined and thus designated as 'self,' yet a real self cannot be found;
so too, from sentient beings up to the knower and the seer, all are merely conventional designations produced through the causal combination of the five aggregates."
These dharmas are in reality neither produced nor extinguished; the world merely speaks of them using names.
It is the same for the bodhisattva, the name "bodhisattva," and the prajñāpāramitā: all are dharmas that are provisional designations resulting from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
In this regard, the Buddha further provides a simile. Some say:
"It is merely through the combination of the five aggregates that there is a 'sentient being'; yet the sentient being is empty, and there exist only the phenomena of the five aggregates."
The Buddha said:
"Sentient beings are empty; the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) also exist only as provisional designations due to their being a composite.
The twelve bases (āyatana) and eighteen elements (dhātu) are likewise."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who practice seated meditation; second, those who recite the sutras.

As for those who practice seated meditation, they constantly contemplate that the body is called "body" because it is a composite of various parts such as the bones. Taking what they observe as a metaphor, they say that the collection of skull-bone parts is called the "head," the collection of leg-bone parts is called the "feet," and the combination of the head, feet, bones, and so forth is called the "body."
Investigating each one in turn, none possess a fundamental basis.
Why is this so? Because these are habitual practices and habitual observations; they are used as metaphors for this purpose.
Regarding those who do not practice seated meditation, it is illustrated by the metaphors of grass, wood, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Just as the Buddhas of the past existed only as names, yet can be spoken of by means of these names.
The ten similes are likewise merely names, and the meaning of "bodhisattva" is also thus.
The meaning of the "ten similes" is as previously explained.
A bodhisattva should train in the three kinds of *paryāya* (doctrinal formulations) in this manner:
The dharmas such as the five aggregates are called "Dharma-prajñapti.

Because the five aggregates arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are termed "sentient beings"; because various bones are conjoined, they are termed "skull bone"; and just as roots, stems, branches, and leaves are conjoined, they are termed a "tree"—this is called "Upādāna-prajñapti" (designation based on appropriation).
To grasp the characteristics of two dharmas by means of these names and speak of these two kinds is called "designation by name" (*nāma-prajñapti*).

Furthermore, because various subtle dust-like dharmas combine, coarse dharmas arise; just as coarse form arises from the combination of subtle particles, this is called "designation by dharma" (*dharma-prajñapti*), because one dharma arises from [the combination of] dharmas.
These coarse phenomena arise through combination and possess names; just as when there is that which can illuminate and that which can burn, the name "fire" arises.
Because *nāmarūpa* exists, there is a "person"; *nāmarūpa* is a dharma, while the "person" is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). This is called "accepting the *prajñapti*";
because one takes up form and takes up names, it is called "acceptance" (*upādāna*).

Beyond the names of many individual things, there arise further names; just as beyond the names of beams, rafters, tiles, and so forth, the name "house" arises, and just as beyond the names of tree branches and leaves, the name "tree" arises—this is called "designation by name" (*nāman-prajñapti*).
The practitioner first destroys the designation of "names" (*nāma-prajñapti*) and reaches the designation of "sensation" (*vedanā-prajñapti*);
next, they break through the designation of "sensation" and reach the designation of "dharmas" (*dharma-prajñapti*);
having broken through the designation of "dharmas," they arrive at the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā, which is the emptiness of both all phenomena and their names.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the name of form as permanent, nor do they perceive the names of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent; they do not perceive the name of form as impermanent, nor do they perceive the names of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as impermanent;
they do not perceive the name of form as pleasant, nor do they perceive the name of form as painful;
they do not perceive the name of form as self, nor do they perceive the name of form as non-self.
One does not perceive the name of form as empty; one does not perceive the name of form as signless; one does not perceive the name of form as wishless;
one does not perceive the name of form as quiescent;
one does not perceive the name of form as defiled, nor does one perceive the name of form as pure.
One does not see the arising of the name-and-form of form; one does not see the cessation of the name-and-form of form.
One does not see the name-and-form of form within, nor does one see it without, nor does one see it abiding in between.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

"The eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the various feelings born with eye-contact as their condition, and so on up to the mind, mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the various feelings born with mind-contact as their condition, are also like this."

Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, neither the word "perfection of wisdom," nor the "bodhisattva," nor the word "bodhisattva" is perceived within the nature of the conditioned, nor is it perceived within the nature of the unconditioned.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not make any distinctions regarding these dharmas.

This bodhisattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom and dwelling within the indestructible dharma, when cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the word "perfection of wisdom," does not perceive a bodhisattva, and does not perceive the word "bodhisattva";

and so on, up until when cultivating the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, do not perceive the word "perfection of wisdom," do not perceive a bodhisattva, and do not perceive the word "bodhisattva."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they know only the true mark of all phenomena;
and the true mark of all phenomena is neither defiled nor pure.
“In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should understand that names are merely conventional designations.”
Having understood that these are merely provisional names, one does not cling to form, nor to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not cling to the eye up to the mind;
one does not cling to forms up to mental phenomena.
They do not cling to eye-consciousness, up to and including mind-consciousness;
they do not cling to eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact;
they do not cling to the feeling produced with eye-contact as its condition.
Whether it be suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure— even up to the feelings born from the condition of mental contact,
whether they be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— one does not cling to them;
one does not cling to the nature of the conditioned, nor does one cling to the nature of the unconditioned.
They do not cling to the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom;
they do not cling to the thirty-two marks, nor do they cling to the body of a bodhisattva;
they do not cling to the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva, up to and including the Buddha-eye.
They do not cling to the perfection of wisdom, nor do they cling to the perfection of supernormal powers;
they do not cling to inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
they do not cling to the maturation of sentient beings, nor do they cling to the purification of Buddha-fields, nor do they cling to the methods of skillful means.
Why is this? Because these dharmas—the one who is unattached, the dharma that is unattached, and the place where one is unattached—all do not exist.
"It is thus, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to any phenomena; thus, they increase the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. They enter the stage of a bodhisattva, attain the ground of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and become fully endowed with the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.
They travel from one buddha-field to another, maturing sentient beings, and they honor, respect, and praise all Buddhas.

To purify buddha-fields and to behold and make offerings to the Buddhas, they obtain all requisites for making offerings according to their wishes, because their roots of goodness have been perfected.

They also hear the Dharma taught by all Buddhas; having heard it, they never forget it until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they obtain all the gates of *dhāraṇī* and all the gates of *samādhi*.
"In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should know that the names of all phenomena are merely provisional designations."
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is form the bodhisattva?”
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Are form, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Are eye-consciousness, up to and including mental consciousness, the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the earth element the bodhisattva?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Are the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness the bodhisattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
What do you think, Subhūti?"
“Is ignorance the bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Is even old age and death this bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Is a bodhisattva something apart from form?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
Is even the departure from old age and death a bodhisattva? “No!”
“World-Honored One!
Subhūti, what do you think?”
“Is the mark of the suchness of form the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is even the suchness of aging and death the bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is the Bodhisattva that which is free from the suchness of form, up to and including free from the suchness of old age and death? “No,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What meaning do you perceive when you say: ‘Form is not the bodhisattva, and so on up to old age and death are not the bodhisattva;
apart from form there is no bodhisattva, and so on up to apart from old age and death there is no bodhisattva’?”
"The suchness of form is not the bodhisattva, and so on up to the suchness of old age and death is not the bodhisattva;
apart from the suchness of form is not the bodhisattva, and so on up to apart from the suchness of old age and death is not the bodhisattva"?
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!
Sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable; how much more so, then, could there be such a thing as a bodhisattva!"
Form cannot be apprehended; how much less so can a bodhisattva who is form, apart from form, the suchness of form, or apart from the suchness of form!

This applies even unto old age and death, which cannot be apprehended; how much less so can a bodhisattva who is old age and death, apart from old age and death, the suchness of old age and death, or apart from the suchness of old age and death!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom also cannot be apprehended; one should train in this way!
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Is ‘form’ the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No, [it is not].”
“World-Honored One!
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No!”
“World-Honored One!
What do you think, Subhūti?
Is ‘form is permanent’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it the meaning of 'Bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is 'form is impermanent' the meaning of a bodhisattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it the meaning of 'bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is 'the pleasure of form' the meaning of a bodhisattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the delight in feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of 'bodhisattva'?"
“No, World-Honored One!
Is ‘form is suffering’ the meaning of a bodhisattva?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is the suffering of feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Is 'form is the self' the meaning of a bodhisattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it the meaning of 'Bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it not the meaning of a bodhisattva that form is not the self?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it not the meaning of 'Bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the self?"
"No, World-Honored One!
What do you think, Subhūti?"
“Is the emptiness of form the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is it the meaning of a bodhisattva that form is not empty? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is it the case that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not empty— that this is the meaning of a bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Is the characteristic of form the meaning of a bodhisattva? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Is the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?
“No, World-Honored One.
“Is the absence of characteristics in form the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it not the meaning of 'bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are signless?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is 'form' the meaning of 'bodhisattva'?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is it the case that feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute the meaning of 'bodhisattva'?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it not the meaning of 'bodhisattva' that form is without volitional activity?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is it not the meaning of 'bodhisattva' that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without volitional action?"
"No, World-Honored One!
This applies likewise even unto old age and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Upon what basis do you say that 'form is not the meaning of a bodhisattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the meaning of a bodhisattva;
and even the non-activity of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not the meaning of a bodhisattva'?"
"Up to and including old age and death, it is also thus.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the meaning of "bodhisattva" when there is no form!
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
World-Honored One!
Form is ultimately and forever unobtainable; how much more so is the impermanence of form? This is the meaning of "bodhisattva.
It is the same for everything up to consciousness.
World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One, since the pleasure of form is ultimately unattainable, how much more so its suffering— this is the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’!
This applies likewise even to consciousness.”
“World-Honored One, form is ultimately unattainable as a self; how much more so is it that ‘form is not-self’—this is the meaning of a bodhisattva!
This applies even up to consciousness. Thus it is for all [the aggregates].
World-Honored One!
Form is ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is the emptiness of form! This is the meaning of a bodhisattva.
It is the same up to consciousness.
World-Honored One!
The characteristic of form is ultimately unattainable; how much more so is the meaning of a bodhisattva as "form being signless"!
This applies likewise up to consciousness.
World-Honored One!
"Form and its activity are ultimately unobtainable; how much more so is 'the non-activity of form' the meaning of a bodhisattva!
This applies even up to consciousness.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent! It is so, Subhūti!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of form cannot be apprehended; the meanings of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended;
even so, the meaning of non-action cannot be apprehended. In this way, one should train in the perfection of wisdom!
“Subhūti! You said:
‘I do not see any dharma named “bodhisattva.”’”
"Subhūti! All dharmas do not perceive all dharmas.
All dharmas do not perceive the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature does not perceive all dharmas."
The dharma-nature does not perceive the earth element, and the earth element does not perceive the dharma-nature;
this extends even to the consciousness element, which does not perceive the dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature, which does not perceive the consciousness element.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not perceive the eye, forms, or the nature of eye-consciousness; the eye, forms, and the nature of eye-consciousness do not perceive the nature of phenomena.

This extends up to the point where the nature of phenomena does not perceive the mind, mental objects, or the nature of mind-consciousness; the mind, mental objects, and the nature of mind-consciousness do not perceive the nature of phenomena.
Subhūti! The nature of the conditioned does not perceive the nature of the unconditioned, and the nature of the unconditioned does not perceive the nature of the conditioned. Why is this?
Apart from the conditioned, the unconditioned cannot be spoken of; apart from the unconditioned, the conditioned cannot be spoken of.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they perceive nothing among all phenomena; at that time, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid, and their mind neither sinks nor regrets."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not perceive the eye up to the mind, nor forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); they do not perceive lust, anger, or delusion; they do not perceive ignorance up to old age and death; they do not perceive a self up to a knower or a seer; they do not perceive the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they do not perceive the mind of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha; they do not perceive a bodhisattva, nor the qualities of a bodhisattva; they do not perceive a Buddha, nor the qualities of a Buddha, nor the path of a Buddha.
"Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomena, he is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not sink into despondency, and has no regret.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason does this bodhisattva’s mind not fear, not sink, and not regret?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because all mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are unobtainable and invisible; for this reason, the mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fear, does not sink, and does not regret."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Subhūti, this bodhisattva’s mind and the sphere of mind (manodhātu) are unobtainable and invisible; for this reason, he is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
Thus it is, Subhūti!”
Because all dharmas are unattainable, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Subhūti!

In all spheres of activity, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the name "bodhisattva," and does not apprehend the mind of a bodhisattva; this is precisely the instruction for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Commentary:

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they contemplate that the names of material phenomena (rūpadharma) are neither permanent nor impermanent, and so on, up to not perceiving a bodhisattva or the designation "bodhisattva" within the nature of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
This is as previously stated: "One does not form conceptualizations or discriminations regarding any phenomena."
The bodhisattva dwells within the indestructible dharma and practices the six pāramitās, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

By means of the wisdom of the true mark of all dharmas, they seek among all dharmas but do not perceive any fixed dharma—namely, the prajñāpāramitā; nor do they perceive the name "prajñāpāramitā," nor do they perceive the bodhisattva or the name "bodhisattva."
By means of this wisdom, one destroys ignorance and all other afflictions;
by means of this wisdom that neither sees nor does not see, one destroys attachment to the *prajñāpāramitā*, the name "prajñāpāramitā," the bodhisattva, and the name "bodhisattva."
The true reality of all phenomena is pure and characterized by unimpeded penetration.
When a bodhisattva attains such wisdom, whatever is seen, heard, or recollected is like a magical illusion;
whatever is heard, seen, or recollected is entirely deceptive.
For this reason, one does not cling to form and the other aggregates.
Abiding within this unimpeded wisdom, one increases the six pāramitās, enters the stage of a bodhisattva, and attains such benefits as these.
This is one section in which the Buddha himself instructs the bodhisattva to practice such contemplation.
In the subsequent section, because people might think that the Buddha frequently teaches the emptiness of all phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), he asks Subhūti in return:
"If all phenomena were not empty, would there be even a single dharma that is definitively a bodhisattva?"
"Is form the bodhisattva?
Is it even thus that there is a bodhisattva?
Subhūti had this thought:
"Since a bodhisattva exists through the combination of all dharmas, how could I say that any single dharma is definitively the bodhisattva?
For this reason, he said: "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Because Subhūti has thoroughly realized the emptiness of sentient beings, the Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent!
Because a bodhisattva knows that sentient beings are empty and unapprehendable, they should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
That "form" (*rūpa*) is the meaning of "bodhisattva," and so on, up to "non-action"; even ultimate emptiness is likewise.
Because Subhūti enters the profound emptiness of all phenomena without doubt, he is able to benefit all bodhisattvas; therefore, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"A Bodhisattva’s Dharma should be studied in this way: that all dharmas are the emptiness of non-apprehension, the Prajñāpāramitā.

As Subhūti said, "I do not see any dharma that is called 'Bodhisattva'," the Buddha replied, "It is not only the Bodhisattva who alone cannot be seen; there is, in fact, no dharma whatsoever that sees a dharma."
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is immeasurable and invisible, it is said that "all phenomena do not see the nature of phenomena.

Since all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are ultimately empty; therefore, the nature of phenomena does not see all phenomena.
The nature of form does not perceive the nature of dharmas, and the nature of dharmas does not perceive the nature of form;
this applies likewise up to the nature of consciousness.
Because the natures of the five aggregates share the same name as the nature of dharmas, they are termed "natures."
The twelve bases, the eighteen elements, conditioned phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena are also like this.
To state it briefly:
apart from the nature of the conditioned, one cannot speak of the nature of the unconditioned.
Apart from the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one cannot speak of the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because these two categories encompass all phenomena,
although this bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomena, he is not terrified.
Why is this? Where there is something seen and something not seen, there is fear;
if there is absolutely nothing seen, then there is no fear—this refers to the five aggregates up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Question: If the Buddha has already explained the causes and conditions for being free from fear, why does Subhūti ask again? Answer:
Subhūti, if one were to say that all phenomena are entirely empty and non-existent, one fears falling into wrong view.
Why is this? Because the disciples of the Buddha are called "practitioners on the path" precisely because they have attained right view; how then can it be said that "nothing at all can be seen"?
The Buddha, knowing Subhūti’s intention, said:
"Because all mental states and their associated factors are unobtainable and invisible, there is no fear."
Ordinary persons, wishing to enter into emptiness, perceive that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) can be apprehended while external phenomena cannot; therefore, they are terrified.

Bodhisattvas, however, understand that the mind and mental factors are false and unreal, being the retribution of inversion and unable to manifest actual reality to others; therefore, they are not terrified.
Because of this difference in meaning, he asks again. He asks:
"If that is so, why is there yet a third question?"
Answer: The mind and mental factors can be seen within the mental consciousness;
the mind and the mental consciousness are the root of these minds and mental factors.
Why is this? Because within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) there is much conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), fear arises;
whereas at the moment of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), the duration is so brief that no discrimination occurs.
In order to destroy the root of fear, there is no fault in asking this question again!
If a bodhisattva can practice such prajñāpāramitā, although they do not perceive four things—
the bodhisattva, the word "bodhisattva," prajñāpāramitā, and the word "prajñāpāramitā"— they [practice it].
To be fearless through these three causes and conditions is precisely to teach the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva.
If one merely understands the characteristics of the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā*, this constitutes practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is not sought from the ten directions, nor is there anyone who gives it; furthermore, it is not something obtained by striving for it like gold, silver, or precious objects.
Chapter 8: Encouraging Study The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter "Encouraging Study," Number Eight [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)!

One who wishes to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom should study the perfection of wisdom!
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know form, they should study the perfection of wisdom! ...
up to: if they wish to know consciousness, they should study the perfection of wisdom!”

If one wishes to know the eye up to the mind; if one wishes to know forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); if one wishes to know eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; if one wishes to know eye-contact up to mind-contact; and if one wishes to know the feelings produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mind-contact—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Those who wish to sever lust, hatred, and delusion should study the Prajñāpāramitā!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and all other fetters (*saṃyojana*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), should study the Prajñāpāramitā!”
"One who wishes to sever the four bonds, the four fetters, and the four inversions should study the Prajñāpāramitā!

One who wishes to know the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the samādhi of the awakening-factors (bodhyaṅga) should study the perfection of wisdom!

One who wishes to enter the six supernormal powers (abhijñā), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the transcendent samādhi (vyutkrāntakasamādhi) should study the perfection of wisdom!”
One who wishes to attain the Lion’s Play Samādhi should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
One who wishes to attain the Lion’s Rush Samādhi and wishes to attain all the gates of dhāraṇī should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Ratnamudrā Samādhi, the Suvimalacandra Samādhi,
the Candradhvajaketu Samādhi, the Sarvadharmamudrā Samādhi, the Avalokanamudrā Samādhi,
the Dharmatāparyanta Samādhi, the Niścitasthiti-lakṣaṇa Samādhi, the Vajropama Samādhi, and the entry...
The Samādhi of All Dharma-Gates; the Samādhi of the King of Samādhis; the Samādhi of the Royal Seal; the Samādhi of Pure Power;
the Samādhi of Exalted Emergence; the Samādhi of Entering All Eloquence; the Samādhi of Entering the Names of All Dharmas;
the Samādhi of Contemplating the Ten Directions; the Samādhi of the Seal of the Gates of All Dhāraṇīs; the One...
The Samādhi of Never Forgetting All Dharmas, the Samādhi of the Seal that Gathers the Multitude of All Dharmas,
the Samādhi of Abiding in Space, the Samādhi of Purity in Three Parts, the Samādhi of Non-retrogressive Supernatural Powers,
the Samādhi of Producing the Alms Bowl, and the Samādhi of the Banner-Marks of All Samādhis— if one wishes to attain such gateways to these various samādhis, [one should practice this].
One should study the Prajñāpāramitā!
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
[Treatise] Question: In the first chapter it was said:
"One who desires to attain various things should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Why is this now being stated again?
The answer is:
Previously, it was merely praised that "one who wishes to attain these various merits should practice the Prajñāpāramitā," but the Prajñāpāramitā itself had not yet been explained.
Now that one has already tasted the flavor of the Prajñāpāramitā, if one wishes to attain further merits—namely, the six pāramitās and so forth—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, although the emptiness of all phenomena has been explained through various causes and conditions above, some may say:
"The Buddha-dharma is one of annihilation; there is nothing further to be done.
To sever such doubts, it is said:
"If one wishes to attain various merits such as those of generosity, one should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If the *prajñāpāramitā* were truly empty, non-existent, and subject to annihilation, it would not be said that one should practice virtues such as generosity.
The wise say: for what reason are the beginning and the end contradictory?
Furthermore, the former was an extensive explanation, while this is a concise one;
that was spoken by the Buddha, whereas this was spoken by Subhūti.
Furthermore, because the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and subtle, it is explained again;
it is like praising the beauty of one's virtues, thus saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
Regarding the meaning of the "six pāramitās," it is as previously explained.
As for "knowing the five aggregates," it refers to seeing their impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, including both their general and specific characteristics.

The same applies to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), the six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*), and the six feelings (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*).
Of all the fetters of the world, feeling is the primary factor;
because of feeling, the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise.
Pleasurable sensations give rise to craving; painful sensations give rise to aversion; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations give rise to delusion.
From these three poisons arise all afflictions and the causal conditions for karma.
For this reason, only "feeling" (vedanā) is mentioned, while other mental factors (caitasika-dharma) are not, namely: perception (saṃjñā), mindfulness (smṛti), and so forth;

as well as the "three poisons," the "ten fetters" (saṃyojana), the "proclivities" (anuśaya), the "envelopments" (paryavasthāna), up to the "eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha" (āveṇika-buddhadharma), as previously explained.
The "Samādhi of the Awakened Mind," the "Samādhi of Transcendence," and the "Samādhi of the Lion’s Play" are among the various samādhis of a bodhisattva, which shall be explained later.
"Desiring to fulfill the vows of all sentient beings" has already been explained above.
[Sūtra] "Those who desire to be fully endowed with such roots of goodness and never fall into the evil realms;

those who desire not to be born into lowly families; those who desire not to dwell in the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; and those who desire not to fall from the summit of the Bodhisattva path—should study the Prajñāpāramitā!"
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fall from the summit?
Subhūti replied:

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās without skillful means, enters the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet neither falls into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas nor enters the rank of a bodhisattva—this is called the ‘arising of dharmas’ for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and thus they fall from the summit.”
Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"What is meant by the 'birth' of a bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Birth is called craving for dharmas.
Śāriputra asked:
"What is this craving for dharmas?"
Subhūti said: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they perceive form as empty and yet conceive attachment to it;
they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty and yet conceive attachment to them.”
Śāriputra! This is called the arising of the love for the Dharma that accords with the path in a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive form as signless and yet conceive attachment to it;
they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signless and yet conceive attachment to them.
They perceive form as unconditioned and yet conceive attachment to it.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unconditioned, yet one attends to them with attachment.
Form is quiescent, yet one attends to it with attachment;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are quiescent, yet one attends to them with attachment.
Form is impermanent, up to and including consciousness;
form is suffering, up to and including consciousness;
form is non-self, up to and including consciousness—to experience attachment to these thoughts is what is called the bodhisattva’s arising of craving for the dharmas that accord with the Path.

"This is suffering and should be known; this is the origin and should be abandoned; this is cessation and should be realized; this is the path and should be cultivated. These are defiled dharmas; these are pure dharmas. These should be approached; these should not be approached. These are what a bodhisattva should practice; these are what a bodhisattva should not practice. This is the bodhisattva path; this is not the bodhisattva path. This is the bodhisattva training; this is not the bodhisattva training. These are the bodhisattva’s dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā; these are not the bodhisattva’s dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā. This is the bodhisattva’s skillful means; this is not the bodhisattva’s skillful means. This is the bodhisattva’s maturation; this is not the bodhisattva’s maturation."

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, if they experience, attend to, or become attached to these dharmas, this is called the arising of "dharma-love" that accords with the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Question:
By what roots of goodness does one not fall into the evil destinies, nor into poverty and low status, nor into the states of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor fall from the summit?
Answer: Some say that by practicing the wholesome root of non-attachment,
the various fetters such as craving diminish and thin out, and one enters deeply into meditative concentration.
Because they practice the root of goodness that is non-anger, their various fetters and afflictions such as anger are thinned, and they enter deeply into the mind of compassion;
because they practice the root of goodness that is non-delusion, their various fetters and afflictions such as ignorance are thinned, and they enter deeply into the Prajñāpāramitā.

By the power of such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is nothing that cannot be attained, let alone these four matters!
Question: Why, among these four matters, do you ask only about falling from the summit (*mūrdhan*)?
Answer: Three matters have already been explained; because the "falling from the summit" has not yet been explained, this question is asked. Question:
"The 'Summit' (mūrdhan) is the station of the Dharma (dharmapada); this meaning has already been explained previously. Why is it stated again now?
The answer is:
"Although its meaning has been explained, the names differ."
It has already been explained that there is entry into the three gates of liberation both with and without skillful means.
Regarding "craving for dharmas" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), it provides no benefit within the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*); therefore, it is called "arising."
For example, if one eats excessively and it is not digested, it will become a source of affliction for the body if not treated with medicine.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: when first generating the mind of enlightenment, they greedily consume the food of the Dharma—namely, practicing various wholesome dharmas without skillful means—and become deeply attached to them. Regarding the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this [attachment] becomes a birth and a sickness.
Because they are attached to the love of dharmas, they also become attached to non-arising and non-ceasing.
It is like a person destined to die: although various medicines are administered, the medicine instead becomes an illness;

likewise, when this bodhisattva develops attachment within the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of the dharma of ultimate emptiness—non-arising and non-ceasing—it conversely becomes a source of affliction for them!
Attachment to the Dharma is excellent among humans and devas, yet it becomes a hindrance to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

To engage in conceptualization and discrimination within all dharmas, to contemplate their rightness and wrongness, and to feel attachment toward the Dharma according to such views—this is called "arising" (*jāti*), and it is incapable of containing the water of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
That which is contrary to "arising" is called the "maturity of a bodhisattva. Question:
These are one and the same thing; for what reason is it called "the summit," called "the stage," and called "non-arising"?
The answer is:
All dharmas that exist between the patience of compliance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*) and the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) are called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
Abiding in this Summit, one proceeds directly upward toward the Buddha-way and no longer fears falling back.
For example, within the Śrāvaka-dharma, the stage between *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *kṣānti* (Patience) is called *mūrdhan* (Summit).
Question:
If one who has attained the Summit does not fall away, why do you now speak of "falling from the Summit"?
Answer: To be on the verge of attaining [a stage] and yet lose it is called "falling" (*pāta*);
one who has attained the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) possesses stable wisdom and thus does not fear falling.
For example, it is like ascending a mountain: once the summit has been reached, one fears no longer falling;
but as long as one has not yet arrived, there is the peril of instability and the fear of falling.
When the summit is fully attained and made firm, this is called the "Stage of the Bodhisattva."

Having entered this stage, one cannot be shaken by any fetters or any of the followers of Māra; it is also called "the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Why is this so?
Because it is distinct from "birth" (*jāti*).
The mingling of craving and other fetters with various wholesome dharmas is called "birth.
Furthermore, because one lacks the fire of wisdom regarding the true nature of all phenomena, it is called "birth."
Because there is the fire of wisdom regarding the true mark of all dharmas, it is called "matured.
This person is able to believe in and accept the wisdom of the true mark of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called "matured.
It is like a fired jar that can hold water, whereas an unfired one would break and decay.

Furthermore, by relying on the wisdom of arising and ceasing, one attains freedom from inversion; by being free from the wisdom of arising and ceasing, there is neither arising nor ceasing—this is called the "Dharma of Non-arising."
Because one is able to believe, accept, and uphold [the Dharma], it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, regarding "stage" (*bhūmi*): because it uproots all contemplative dharmas such as impermanence and so forth, it is called a "stage.
If it were otherwise, this would constitute the arising of attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path.
[Sūtra] Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What is meant by the ‘non-arising’ of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Subhūti replied:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, within internal emptiness they do not perceive external emptiness, and within external emptiness they do not perceive internal emptiness;
within external emptiness they do not perceive internal-and-external emptiness, and within internal-and-external emptiness they do not perceive external emptiness;
within internal-and-external emptiness they do not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, and within the emptiness of emptiness they do not perceive internal-and-external emptiness."
Within the emptiness of emptiness, one does not see the great emptiness; within the great emptiness, one does not see the emptiness of emptiness.
Within the great emptiness, one does not see the emptiness of the ultimate meaning; within the emptiness of the ultimate meaning, one does not see the great emptiness.

Within the emptiness of the ultimate meaning, one does not see the emptiness of conditioned phenomena; within the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, one does not see the emptiness of the ultimate meaning.
Within conditioned emptiness, one does not perceive unconditioned emptiness; within unconditioned emptiness, one does not perceive conditioned emptiness.
Within unconditioned emptiness, one does not perceive ultimate emptiness; within ultimate emptiness, one does not perceive unconditioned emptiness.
Within ultimate emptiness, one does not perceive beginningless emptiness; within beginningless emptiness, one does not perceive ultimate emptiness.
Within the emptiness of beginninglessness, one does not perceive the emptiness of dispersion; within the emptiness of dispersion, one does not perceive the emptiness of beginninglessness.
Within the emptiness of dispersion, one does not perceive the emptiness of nature; within the emptiness of nature, one does not perceive the emptiness of dispersion.
Within the emptiness of nature, one does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena; within the emptiness of all phenomena, one does not perceive the emptiness of nature.

Within the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), one does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*); within the emptiness of self-characteristic, one does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena.

Within the emptiness of self-characteristic, one does not perceive the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*); within the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, one does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristic.

Within the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, one does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*); within the emptiness of non-existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of non-apprehensibility.
Within the emptiness of non-existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of existence; within the emptiness of existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence.

Within the emptiness of existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of both non-existence and existence; within the emptiness of both non-existence and existence, one does not perceive the emptiness of existence.
"Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they attain entry into the bodhisattva stage.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study the prajñāpāramitā should study in this way:

they should not attend to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they should not attend to the eye up to the mind; they should not attend to forms up to mental phenomena (dharmas); and they should not attend to the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, prajñāpāramitā, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
"So it is, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and attains this mind, he should neither dwell upon it nor be conceited."
The unequaled mind should not be contemplated, nor should it be exalted;
the great mind should not be contemplated, nor should it be exalted. Why is this?
"This mind is no-mind, because the characteristic of mind is eternally pure.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti,
"In what sense is it called 'the characteristic of mind is eternally pure'?"
Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva knows this characteristic of the mind as being neither conjoined with nor separated from lust, anger, and delusion;
neither conjoined with nor separated from the various entanglements, outflows, bonds, and all other fetters and afflictions;"
The minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are neither conjoined nor separated [from it].
Śāriputra, this is called the constant purity of the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s mind.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Does this mind that has the characteristic of being without mind exist?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Within the state of no-mind-characteristic, can a mind-characteristic or a no-mind-characteristic be apprehended?
Śāriputra replied,
"They cannot be apprehended."
Subhūti said: "If it cannot be apprehended, one should not ask whether 'this mind that has the characteristic of no-mind exists or not'!
Śāriputra asked again:
“What is the characteristic of being without mind? Subhūti replied,
“That all phenomena are neither destroyed nor differentiated— this is called the characteristic of being without mind.”
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"Is it only the mind that is neither destroyed nor differentiated, such that form (*rūpa*) is also neither destroyed nor differentiated, and so on up to the path of the Buddha (*buddhamārga*), which is likewise neither destroyed nor differentiated?"
Subhūti said:

"If one can know that the characteristics of the mind are neither destroyed nor differentiated, then this bodhisattva can also know that everything from form up to the Buddha-way is neither destroyed nor differentiated."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You are truly a son of the Buddha!

Born from the mouth of the Buddha, born from the vision of the Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma; you have taken a share of the Dharma, not a share of material wealth; you have gained confidence within the Dharma and attained realization in your own person."
As the Buddha has said:
"Among those who have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention, you are the foremost.
This is indeed as the Buddha has declared.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, and therein should also practice analytical discernment.
If a bodhisattva practices as you have described, they will not be separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti! A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to train in the stage of a śrāvaka should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, read it, recite it, correctly attend to it, and practice according to its teaching;
one who wishes to train in the stage of a pratyekabuddha should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, read it, recite it, correctly attend to it, and practice according to its teaching.
One who wishes to study the bodhisattva stages should likewise hear the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, read it, recite it, correctly bring it to mind, and practice according to its teaching.
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the three vehicles are explained in detail;
herein, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should train!
[Treatise] Commentary:
Within internal emptiness, external emptiness is not perceived; within external emptiness, internal emptiness is not perceived. Some say:
The four external great elements enter one's body through food and drink, and are therefore called "internal";
once the body dies, they return to being external.
Because all phenomena lack the characteristics of coming and going, external emptiness does not exist apart from internal emptiness.
The remaining seventeen emptinesses are also like this; because they are neither born nor extinguished, have no distinct characteristics, and neither come nor go, each does not abide within itself.

Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the bodhisattva stage, one does not conceive of any form as existing, nor does one even conceive of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) as existing.
The meaning of "not recollecting existence" is as previously explained. Question:
What is the distinction between the "bodhicitta," the "unequaled mind," and the "great mind"?
The answer is:
When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind, taking the unsurpassed path as their object and thinking, "I shall become a Buddha," this is called the "bodhicitta.
"Peerless" refers to a Buddha; why is this so?
All sentient beings and all phenomena have no equal;
this bodhicitta is similar to the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the cause resembles the fruit, it is called the "unequaled-equal mind."
This mind has no activity it does not perform; it seeks no reward and is profoundly firm and resolute.
Furthermore, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) are called the "bodhicitta."
Why is this? By reason of the *dānapāramitā*, one attains great wealth without lack;
by reason of the *śīlapāramitā*, one emerges from the three evil paths and becomes noble and honored among humans and devas.
By the power of the retribution of abiding in the two pāramitās, one establishes oneself in the ability to accomplish great deeds; this is called "bodhicitta.

The characteristics of the pāramitās of kṣānti and vīrya manifest as extraordinary feats among sentient beings: namely, when people come to cut one's flesh and extract one's marrow as if cutting down a tree, yet one regards the enemy with loving-kindness, and one's blood is transformed into milk.
This mind resembles the Buddha-mind, for within the six realms of the ten directions, it seeks to deliver every single sentient being with a profound resolve.
Furthermore, to know that all phenomena are ultimately empty, yet through great compassion be able to perform all practices—this is extraordinary!
It is like a person wishing to plant a tree in mid-air; this is truly rare.
The power and momentum of the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) such as these are similar to that which is peerless; this is called "the Peerless-Equivalent" (asama-sama).

Entering meditative concentration (dhyāna), practicing the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa), and pervading the ten directions, because it is united with great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and skillful means (upāya), it uproots the suffering of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, regarding the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena, all conceptual observations (vipaśyanā) are extinguished and all verbal expressions are severed, yet one does not fall into nihilism; this is called the "Great Mind" (mahā-citta).
Furthermore, the initial arousal of the mind is called the "bodhicitta";
practicing the six pāramitās is called the "unequaled mind" (asamasama-citta);
and entering into the mind of skillful means is called the "great mind" (mahācitta).
Each of these categories has its own distinctions.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains such great wisdom, the mind does not become arrogant, because the nature of the mind is eternally pure.
Just as the nature of space is eternally pure, yet it appears obscured and impure due to the adventitious presence of smoke, clouds, dust, and mist;
so too is the mind: eternally pure by its very nature, yet rendered impure because of the adventitious obscuration of ignorance and other afflictions.
When these afflictions are removed, it is pure as it was from the beginning.
The practitioner’s effort is slight; this purity is not something you have produced. You should not be self-exalting, nor should you dwell upon it. Why?
Because it is ultimately empty.
Question:
Śāriputra knows that the nature of the mind is eternally pure; for what reason, then, does he ask? Answer:
