Furthermore, because in previous lives the mind dwelt within the six sense organs and gave rise to various recollections and conceptual discriminations, the six sense organs and the body of the five aggregates were produced in this present life;
from the body of this present life, various fetters and afflictions arise, creating the six sense organs and the body of the five aggregates in future lives.
In this manner they proceed in succession.
Therefore it is said: "Consciousness is itself the six sense-faculties, and the six sense-faculties are themselves the five aggregates.
These dharmas cannot be apprehended within the emptiness of the internal, nor can they be apprehended up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
[Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
will bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon the Mahāyāna not be startled, terrified, or afraid upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon the Great Vehicle lacks skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom and does not encounter a virtuous friend, that bodhisattva may be startled, terrified, or afraid."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are these skillful means?”
"How is it that a bodhisattva practicing these skillful means is not startled, not afraid, and not terrified?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā, corresponding to the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and contemplates the mark of impermanence in form, yet even this [mark] is unobtainable."
To contemplate the marks of impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet to find even these [contemplations] unattainable— Subhūti,
this is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates the characteristic of suffering in form (*rūpa*); yet even this is unapprehendable. It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Corresponding to the mind of omniscience, he contemplates the characteristic of non-self in form; yet even this is unapprehendable. It is the same for feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
corresponding with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), contemplates the mark of emptiness of form (rūpa), yet even that cannot be apprehended;
feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are also like this."
One contemplates form as having the characteristic of signlessness, yet even this is unattainable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
One contemplates form as having the characteristic of non-action, yet even this is unattainable.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
One contemplates the mark of the cessation of form, yet even that is unattainable; it is the same up to and including consciousness.
To contemplate form as being free from marks, yet to find even this [contemplation] unattainable— and so it is for everything up to consciousness—
this is called the skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the mark of impermanence in form,
yet even that is unapprehendable; they contemplate the marks of suffering, non-self, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, cessation, and detachment in form, yet even these are unapprehendable."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I shall explain this dharma of impermanence for the sake of all sentient beings, yet even this [dharma] is unobtainable."

One should explain to all sentient beings the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of non-self, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of signlessness, the characteristic of wishlessness, the characteristic of cessation, and the characteristic of detachment; yet even these are unattainable.
This is called the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not, with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, contemplate that form is impermanent, nor is it apprehendable; [he contemplates it as empty].”
One does not, with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, perceive the impermanence of consciousness, for it is likewise unattainable;
one does not, with the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, perceive form as suffering, non-self, empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached, for these are likewise unattainable.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is called the śīla-pāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñā-pāramitā, he endures and delights in the fact that all these dharmas have the characteristic of impermanence, up to their being free from conceptualization; this is called the kṣānti-pāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they contemplate that the characteristic of impermanence in form (*rūpa*) is unapprehendable, and even its characteristic of detachment is unapprehendable;
the same applies to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
To accord with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), neither abandoning nor ceasing [this practice], is called the *vīryapāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor any other unwholesome thoughts; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of dhyāna.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they reflect in this way:
'It is not because form is empty that form is empty; rather, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
It is not because of the emptiness of the eye that the eye is empty; the eye itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eye.

This extends up to feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition: it is not because of the emptiness of feeling that feeling is empty; feeling itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling.

It is not by means of emptiness that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty; rather, the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the four foundations of mindfulness.

This continues up to: it is not by means of emptiness that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty; rather, the eighteen unique qualities are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eighteen unique qualities.
"In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is it that, by being protected by spiritual friends, causes a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, not to be startled, not to be afraid, and not to be terrified?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A good spiritual friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who teaches that form is impermanent and also unapprehendable; taking hold of these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s good spiritual friend.

They teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent and also unapprehendable; taking hold of these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s good spiritual friend.”

Subhūti! Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has spiritual friends who teach that form as suffering is also unapprehendable, and they teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as suffering are also unapprehendable;
they teach that form as selfless is also unapprehendable, and they teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as selfless are also unapprehendable.

It is taught that form is empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached, and yet even detachment cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached, and yet even detachment cannot be apprehended.
One upholds these roots of goodness and does not direct them toward the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but directs them solely toward omniscience.
Subhūti! These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have spiritual friends who teach that the eye is impermanent, and so on, up to the point that even its departure cannot be apprehended;
and likewise for everything up to the feeling born from the condition of mental contact, teaching that it is impermanent, and so on, up to the point that even its departure cannot be apprehended.

Taking these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge (sarvajñatā). These are called the spiritual friends of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

Subhūti! Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva has good spiritual friends who teach the dharma of cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the point that even detachment cannot be apprehended;
taking these roots of goodness, they do not direct them toward the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only toward all-knowledge.
Subhūti! These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Even when it comes to teaching the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, one cannot apprehend even the cultivation of all-knowledge.
To take these roots of goodness and not direct them toward the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but solely toward omniscience—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s spiritual friend.
[Treatise] Question:
Why does Subhūti give rise to this doubt and ask the Buddha, "Will newly resolved bodhisattvas not feel fear upon hearing this"?
The answer is:

Having heard that there is no such thing as a bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā, and that even the mere emptiness of the five aggregates cannot practice the prajñāpāramitā, for this reason doubt arises:
"Who, then, will practice the prajñāpāramitā?"
For this reason, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva lacks the internal and external causes and conditions, they will experience fear."
Regarding internal conditions: there is a lack of right mindfulness, a lack of sharp wisdom, and no profound compassion toward sentient beings; internally, one lacks such skillful means as these.

Regarding external conditions: not being born in a central land, not being able to hear the *prajñāpāramitā*, and not encountering a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) capable of severing doubts—such as these are the absence of external conditions.
Because internal and external causes and conditions do not harmonize, one gives rise to alarm, fear, and dread.
Now, Subhūti asks about this skillful means, and the Buddha replies:
"One contemplates all phenomena with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet even these phenomena are not apprehended."

Question: Since one does not feel fear because of the skillful means of contemplating various characteristics such as the impermanence of form, why is it said here only that "because the mind associated with sarvajñā contemplates all dharmas, one is neither terrified nor afraid"?
The answer is:
Previously, the bodhisattva had only contemplated the emptiness of all phenomena, but because the mind was coarse, attachment arose;
now, through recollection, conceptualization, and discernment, he contemplates according to the Buddha’s intention:
"Arising great compassion for all sentient beings, they do not cling to any phenomena; they encounter no obstruction in their wisdom, desiring only to deliver sentient beings.
By means of various contemplations such as impermanence and emptiness, they observe all phenomena, yet they do not apprehend even these phenomena."
Having thus contemplated all phenomena, he forms this thought:
"I shall deliver sentient beings by means of these dharmas, causing them to leave behind their inversions.
For this reason, his mind does not cling, and he does not perceive any single dharma as being fixed or real.
For example, it is like a physician who compiles various medicines: what is a hot medicine for one with a cold ailment is not a medicine for one with a fever.
Because among the two types of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme, this is called *dānapāramitā*.
The five pāramitās are also to be distinguished according to their meaning in this same way.
Furthermore, regarding the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva: it is not by means of the eighteen emptinesses that form (*rūpa*) is made empty.
Why is this? It is not by forcibly making it empty through the characteristic of emptiness that form is emptiness;
rather, from the very beginning, form has always been empty of itself. Because the characteristic of form is empty, emptiness is form.
Even so it is with all the Buddha-dharmas.
A virtuous friend instructs people to dedicate this wisdom toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva has previously understood various contemplations such as impermanence and emptiness; now, it is specifically "dedication" that is being taught as distinct.
[Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

What is it that causes a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom to lack skillful means, to follow evil associates, and to be startled, terrified, and fearful upon hearing this perfection of wisdom being taught?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva, separated from the mind of omniscience, cultivates the perfection of wisdom, attains this perfection of wisdom, and contemplates this perfection of wisdom;
he likewise attains and contemplates the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, apart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates form as empty internally up to its emptiness of non-existence and existence; he contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty internally up to their emptiness of non-existence and existence;

he contemplates the eye as empty internally up to its emptiness of non-existence and existence, and so on, up to contemplating the feeling produced by the condition of mental contact as empty internally up to its emptiness of non-existence and existence."
Regarding the emptiness of all dharmas, there is that which is conceptualized and that which is attained.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they depart from the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, they both conceptualize them and attain them; [this is not so]."
Even up to the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they both contemplate and attain them. Thus, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because of a lack of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), upon hearing this perfection of wisdom, they are startled, terrified, and afraid.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva follows a bad friend and, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, becomes startled, terrified, and afraid?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A bad friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva instructs them to distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom, and to distance themselves from the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.”
Subhūti! These are called the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may have evil associates who do not speak of the deeds of Māra nor of the offenses of Māra, and who do not say:
"An evil Māra may take the form of a Buddha and come to instruct a bodhisattva to abandon the six pāramitās, saying to that bodhisattva:
'O son of good family!'"
For what purpose is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
For what purpose is the cultivation of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?
"You should know that this is a bad friend (pāpamitra) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One may again take the form of a Buddha and go to where the bodhisattva is, preaching the sūtras of the śrāvakas."
If, regarding the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas, they teach, analyze, and expound such sūtras as these,
yet ultimately do not speak of the deeds of Māra or the offenses of Māra, you should know that such persons are bad friends to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra,
the Evil One, may take the form of a Buddha and approach a bodhisattva,
saying: 'Good son!'"
"You lack the mind of a true bodhisattva, nor do you abide in the stage of *avaivartika*; furthermore, you shall not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If one does not explain such demonic deeds and demonic offenses to them, you should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a wicked Māra may assume the form of a Buddha, go to where the bodhisattva is, and say to the bodhisattva:"
“Good son! Form is empty, without self and without what belongs to a self;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, without self and without what belongs to a self.”
The eye is empty, being without self and without what belongs to a self;
and so on, up to feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition, which is empty, being without self and without what belongs to a self;
the dānapāramitā is empty, up to the prajñāpāramitā, which is empty.
"The four foundations of mindfulness are empty, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty;
what use have you for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If one does not speak of or instruct regarding such deeds of Māra and such offenses of Māra, one should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Māra, the Evil One, may take the form of a Pratyekabuddha and approach the Bodhisattva, saying to him:
'Good son!'"
"The ten directions are all empty; within them there is no Buddha, no Bodhisattva, and no Śrāvaka.
If one neither speaks of nor teaches such demonic deeds and demonic offenses, one should know that this person is a bad friend to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One,
may manifest in the form of a preceptor or an ācārya and approach the Bodhisattva, instructing him to abandon the Bodhisattva path and to abandon all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
he instructs him to abandon the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."
He teaches them to abandon the *dānapāramitā*, up to and including teaching them to abandon the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*);
he teaches them to enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*),
and speaks as follows:
"O son of good family!
You cultivate mindfulness of these dharmas and attain the realization of a śrāvaka; what use is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to you?
If one does not speak of nor teach such demonic deeds and demonic offenses, know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra, the Evil One,
may take the form of a father or mother and approach the bodhisattva, saying to him: 'Son!'"
"You exert yourself with diligence for the sake of realizing the fruit of a stream-enterer, and even for the sake of realizing the fruit of an arhat; what use have you for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
One who seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* must undergo birth and death for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, having hands cut off and feet cut off, and undergoing all manner of suffering!
“Such deeds of Māra and such offenses of Māra, which he neither speaks of nor teaches, should be known as the evil associates (pāpamitra) of this bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A māra assumes the form of a bhikṣu and approaches the bodhisattva, saying to him:
"The eye is an impermanent dharma that can be apprehended, and so on up to the mind being an impermanent dharma that can be apprehended;
the eye is suffering, the eye is non-self, the eye is empty, signless, wishless, quiescent, and detached—these are dharmas that can be apprehended—and so it is for the mind as well."
"By means of dharmas that are apprehended as having existence, one speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness;
even unto by means of dharmas that are apprehended as having existence, one speaks of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Subhūti!
If one does not instruct or explain such works of Māra and such offenses of Māra, you should know that this person is a bad friend to the bodhisattva.
Having recognized this, you should keep them at a distance!
[Treatise] Commentary:

Previously, the absence of skillful means was explained briefly; now, it is to be explained in detail. This refers to practicing the perfection of wisdom apart from mental activities associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby grasping at the fixed characteristics of this perfection of wisdom.
The same applies to the five perfections and even to all the Buddha-dharmas.
This is because they themselves lack skillful means, and furthermore, because they have received the instructions of evil associates (*pāpamitra*).

Moreover, evil associates cause great loss of benefit and ruin people in various ways; because they are such a source of great evil conditions, the Buddha has further explained the characteristics of evil associates through various causes and conditions.
A bad spiritual friend (pāpamitra) teaches others to distance themselves from the six pāramitās.
Either because they do not believe in the retribution of sin and merit, they teach them to distance themselves;
or because they are attached to the prajñāpāramitā, they say:
"All phenomena are ultimately empty; what is it that you practice?
Or they may praise the Lesser Vehicle, saying:
"You merely seek to escape the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death for yourself; what concern is this to sentient beings?"
To instruct and cause others to distance themselves from such various causes and conditions in this manner is what is called an evil friend (pāpamitra).
Furthermore, an evil friend is one who does not instruct their disciples to recognize that Māra is a thief of the Buddha.
Māra is the lord of the desire realm and possesses great power; he constantly hates those who practice the Way.
Because the Buddha’s majestic power is so great, Māra is powerless against him, though he can still harm lesser bodhisattvas.
Even to the point of manifesting in the form of a Buddha to come and obstruct a bodhisattva’s practice of the six pāramitās,
or praising, explaining, and discussing the sūtras and dharmas that śrāvakas should study.
Or, manifesting in the form of a Buddha, he comes and says to them:
"You are not fit to attain Buddhahood. Or he says:
"The eye and all other dharmas are empty; what use is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Or he may manifest as a *pratyekabuddha* and say:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, those of the three vehicles are empty; those who seek the Buddha-way possess nothing but an empty name. Why do you wish to become a Buddha?"
Or they may instruct them to distance themselves from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and instead enter the three gates of liberation of the śrāvakas, saying:
"Enter these three gates and realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); thereby you shall exhaust all suffering.
Exert yourself with diligence! For the sake of attaining the four fruits of the religious life, what use have you for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Or perhaps their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), or parents might come and instruct them to distance themselves from the Buddha-way, saying:
"In vain you shall undergo the cutting off of your hands, feet, ears, nose, and so forth to give them to those who beg."
"If you do not give it, you will destroy your resolve to seek Buddhahood;
if you do give it, you will undergo this hardship.
At other times, he would appear dressed as an Arhat bhikṣu and say to him:

“The eye is definitively characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and being unconditioned; it is quiescent, detached, and so forth—even the qualities of all Buddhas are likewise.”
To teach by means of apprehension, grasping at signs, recollection, and conceptual discrimination—
such various and immeasurable demonic activities as these, which one does not instruct them to recognize and understand, is what constitutes an evil spiritual friend.
"To stay away" means that they provide no benefit.
Just as a thief who speaks with gentle words may come forward to draw near, yet once near, he harms people; an evil friend (pāpa-mitra) is even worse than this!
Why is this? A thief can only harm a single body in this present life, whereas an evil friend harms one life after life;
a thief can only take one's life and seize one's wealth, whereas an evil friend destroys wisdom, mindfulness, and the life-faculty, and robs one of the immeasurable treasures of the Buddha-dharma.
Having understood this, one should immediately distance oneself from it in both body and mind.

**Chapter Twelve: On the Meaning of Terms (Śabdārtha-varga)** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Meaning of Terms, Number Twelve. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The absence of any term-meaning is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'."
Why is this? Because within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* there is no objective referent (*artha*) nor any self;
for this reason, that which is without a referential meaning is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva.
“Subhūti! For example, just as a bird flying through the sky leaves no tracks, so too, Subhūti, the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist.”
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, that which is seen in a dream has no location; likewise, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist.

Subhūti, it is just as, for example, an illusion has no real substance, and just as a mirage, an echo, a reflection, or a magical creation of a Buddha has no real substance; likewise, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist.

“Subhūti! For example, just as suchness, the nature of phenomena, the characteristics of phenomena, the fixed position of phenomena, and the limit of reality have no referential meaning, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as a magically conjured person has no referential meaning in terms of form (*rūpa*), and a magically conjured person has no referential meaning in terms of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*);
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is non-existent.”
Subhūti! Just as a phantom person has no objective referent for the eye, and so on up to no objective referent for the mind. Subhūti!

Just as a phantom person has no referent for form, and so on up to having no referent for mental phenomena (*dharma*), and the feelings produced by the conditions of eye-contact through to mind-contact have no referent;
likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as there is no referent when an illusory person practices inner emptiness, up to and including practicing the emptiness of non-existence and existence,
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as a person created by illusion has no objective reality when practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
“Subhūti! Just as for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the referent of ‘form’ does not exist because form itself does not exist;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise non-existent.”

Subhūti! Just as for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no referential meaning (*artha*) for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness— because such consciousness does not exist— so too,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as the Buddha-eye has no locus, and so on up to the mind having no locus; just as form, and so on up to phenomena, have no locus;

and just as the feeling produced by the causal condition of eye-contact, and so on up to mind-contact, has no locus—so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as for the Buddha there is no location in internal emptiness, and so on up to no location in the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent.
Subhūti! Just as the Buddha’s four foundations of mindfulness have no locus, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities which have no locus;
likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
“Subhūti! Just as within the nature of the conditioned there is no meaning of the unconditioned, and within the nature of the unconditioned there is no meaning of the conditioned;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is non-existent.”
“Subhūti! Just as the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing has no location,
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise non-existent.”
Subhūti! Just as that which is uncreated, unarisen, unattainable, neither defiled nor pure, and without location has no existence, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" has no existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By virtue of what dharma being neither born nor extinguished is there no locus?
By virtue of what dharma being uncreated, unemerged, unattained, neither defiled nor pure, is there no locus?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because form is neither born nor extinguished, it has no location; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither born nor extinguished, they have no location; even up to being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise so."
Because the entrances (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to "neither defiled nor pure," it is likewise so.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; even up to "neither defiled nor pure," it is likewise so.

Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), because they are neither arising nor ceasing, they have no location; up to and including being neither defiled nor pure, it is likewise so. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent.
Subhūti, it is just as the pure meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness is ultimately unobtainable.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!
Just as the meaning of purity for the four right efforts, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is ultimately unattainable;
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" does not exist.
“Subhūti! Just as in purity the self cannot be apprehended because the self does not exist, so too,
up to and including, in purity the knower and the seer cannot be apprehended because the knowing and the seeing do not exist.”
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!
Just as there is no darkness when the sun rises,
so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist.
“Subhūti! For example, when the kalpa is consumed by fire, no objects whatsoever exist;
likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist.”
“Subhūti! Within the Buddha’s precepts, there is no breaking of the precepts. Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti,

it is just as there is no distracted mind within the Buddha’s concentration, no delusion within the Buddha’s wisdom, no lack of liberation within the Buddha’s liberation, and no lack of the knowledge and vision of liberation within his knowledge and vision of liberation.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Subhūti!

For example, within the light of the Buddha, the light of the sun and moon does not appear; likewise, within the light of the Buddha, the light of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, does not appear.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise non-existent. Why is this?

This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the bodhisattva, and the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have but a single mark, which is the so-called "markless."
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the unimpeded characteristic of all dharmas,
and should also know it! [Treatise] Question:
Above, the Buddha and Subhūti used various causes and conditions to deconstruct the term "bodhisattva. Why, then, does [Subhūti] now ask about the "meaning of the word 'bodhisattva'"?
The answer is:
While Subhūti deconstructed the term "bodhisattva," the Buddha did not; rather, he said:

"The word 'Bodhisattva' has been ultimately empty from its very origin; it is merely a provisional name designated among the five aggregates, yet sentient beings take this provisional name to be real."
The Buddha said:
"They are mere designations without reality; they are names formed only from the combination of various dharmas.

Furthermore, the dharmas of the Buddhas are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; Subhūti, by means of the emptiness of the name 'bodhisattva,' explains the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Now I wish to hear the Buddha explain the meaning of the term "bodhisattva," and by means of this, the *prajñāpāramitā* will be taught.

Furthermore, one should inquire into the immeasurable and boundless causes and conditions, namely that the Buddha’s voice possesses sixty kinds of adornments, which can cause even the gods to listen with single-minded devotion, let alone humans!
Merely the sound of it causes people to delight in hearing it, let alone its exposition of the meaning of great benefit!
Subhūti, having heard this matter from the Buddha, those who have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening should resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
those who have already resolved their minds but have not yet practiced the six *pāramitās* should be led to practice them.
Regarding practitioners who are not yet pure, they should be made pure;

regarding practitioners who are already pure, they should be established in the stage of *avaivartika*, brought to maturity as sentient beings, and endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, even unto the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood.

For the sake of such various and immeasurable causes, conditions, and benefits, the Buddha appointed Subhūti as the principal interlocutor and addressed all sentient beings gathered in the assembly throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The absence of any linguistic referent is the linguistic referent of a bodhisattva;
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi has no location, nor does it have a self or a name."
"In this regard, the absence of any basis for reliance is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); the absence of a 'name' for a self means there is no one who attains the Path.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti!"

If you know that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self for one who has attained arhatship, then a bodhisattva likewise has no self and nothing belonging to a self within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Just as a bird flying through the void leaves no tracks, so too is the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s term:
when practicing within the void of all dharmas, there is no place of dependence or attachment.
For this reason, it is said that there is no such thing as the "meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'.
[The interlocutor] asks:
What is this "meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'"?
Answer: According to the linguistic rules of India, words are formed by the combination of multiple syllables, and sentences are formed by the combination of multiple words.
For example, "bo" is one syllable and "di" is another syllable; if these two are not combined, there is no word.
If these are combined, it is called "bodhi," which in the language of Qin means "unsurpassed wisdom.
"Sattva" may mean "sentient being" or "one with a great mind."
Because they have generated the great resolve for the sake of unsurpassed wisdom, they are called "Bodhisattvas.
Because they vow to cause sentient beings to practice the unsurpassed path, they are called "Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, in this chapter, the Buddha and his disciples have explained the meaning of "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" through various causes and conditions.
The word "bodhi" and the word "sattva"—the combination of these two words is what is called the "meaning."
If one speaks of names, words, and phrases, they are all of one and the same thing and have no location.
Now Subhūti asks:
"By what fixed characteristic of dharmas do you define the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?"
In the language of India, it is called *pada*; in the language of Qin, it is called a "phrase" (*jù*).
This *pada* has various meanings, as explained in the subsequent section on analogies. Question:
If the meaning of the phrase can be sufficiently clarified by the analogy of "a bird flying through the void," why provide such various and extensive explanations?
The answer is:
sentient beings receive and accept teachings in different ways; some prefer the literal meaning, while others prefer metaphors.
An analogy can clarify the meaning, yet the mind may become attached to it through that analogy;
it is like a person who is naturally handsome from birth, whose splendor is further enhanced by elaborate adornment.
In these parables, the meaning is clarified through many analogies as explained below: namely, that things are like dreams, like shadows, like echoes, and like the emanations of a Buddha;

these matters are deceptive, as previously stated. The meaning of "Bodhisattva" is likewise: it can only be heard with the ears, being deceptive and without reality. For this reason, a Bodhisattva should not be self-exalting.
Terms such as "suchness," "dharma-nature," "dharma-characteristic," and "the limit of reality" have no fixed definition.
Just as an illusory person lacks the five aggregates and so forth, up to and including all the Buddha-dharmas.
Just as the Buddha has no five aggregates, nor even all dharmas;
just as there are no unconditioned dharmas within conditioned dharmas, and just as there are no conditioned dharmas within unconditioned dharmas.
Regarding unconditioned dharmas such as non-arising and non-ceasing, among all dharmas there is no characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing, nor is there any distinct characteristic;
they are like the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which possess no characteristic of purification.
Why is this? Because for some people, attachment to these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is itself a fetter.
Just as with "I" up to "the knower" and "the seer," a pure characteristic cannot be found.
Question:
How are the self, up to the knower and the seer, purified? Answer:
When one seeks in various ways for the mark of a self and it cannot be found, this is called the purity of the self;
within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither purity nor impurity.
It is like washing a stinking dead dog until its skin, hair, blood, flesh, marrow, and bones are all gone.
At that time, being neither dog nor pig, one cannot be called pure, nor can one be called impure.
It is the same for me, even regarding the knower and the seer.

By means of the wisdom of selflessness and emptiness, one seeks the mark of a self and finds it unobtainable; at that time, there is neither a self nor a non-self, just as when the sun rises, there is no darkness.
At the end of a kalpa, there are no material things whatsoever.
Just as within the five aggregates of a Buddha, transgression of the precepts cannot be found;

or just as the light of the sun, moon, stars, pearls, and the radiance of devas, ghosts, spirits, and nāga kings does not appear before the light of a Buddha, because it arises from the power of great merit and supernormal faculties.
The meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise: when one enters the light of wisdom of this Prajñāpāramitā, it no longer appears.
By means of this analogy, bodhisattvas are taught that they should train in all dharmas without grasping at their marks, because there is nothing to be apprehended.
[Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are all dharmas?”
"How should one train in, and how should one understand, the correspondence with non-obstruction regarding all phenomena?

The Buddha told Subhūti: "All phenomena are wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena; defined phenomena and undefined phenomena; mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; common phenomena and uncommon phenomena."
Subhūti! These are called all dharmas.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in and should know them within the unimpeded characteristic of all dharmas!
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are called the worldly wholesome dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Worldly wholesome dharmas consist of being filial and obedient toward one’s parents; making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; honoring and serving elders; the meritorious basis of giving;
the meritorious basis of observing the precepts; the meritorious basis of cultivating meditative concentration; and the meritorious acts of exhortation and guidance.”
Skillful means give rise to merit;
the ten paths of wholesome action in the world;
the nine meditations on repulsiveness:

The sign of bloating, the sign of blood, the sign of decay, the sign of festering pus, the sign of bluishness, the sign of being devoured, the sign of scattering, the sign of bones, and the sign of burning;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments;

mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of precepts, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of virtue, mindfulness of ānāpāna, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death.
"These are called the wholesome dharmas of the world.
"What are the unwholesome dharmas?
"Taking the life of another, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view."
"These ten unwholesome courses of action and so forth are called unwholesome dharmas.
"What are designated dharmas?
"Whether they be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, these are called designated dharmas."
“What are indeterminate phenomena?

Indeterminate bodily action, verbal action, and mental action; indeterminate four great elements; indeterminate five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements; and indeterminate retribution—these are called indeterminate phenomena.”
“What are called mundane dharmas?

Mundane dharmas are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments; these are called mundane dharmas.”
“What are called supramundane dharmas?
They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”
“The three doors of liberation: the door of liberation of emptiness, the door of liberation of signlessness, and the door of liberation of wishlessness.
The three untainted faculties:
the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known.”
“The three samādhis:
samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, samādhi without vitarka but with vicāra, and samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
Clarity, liberation, mindfulness, wisdom, and right recollection.”
“There are eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). What are the eight?
Perceiving forms while having form internally is the first liberation;”
Having no perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms is the second liberation;
realizing the liberation of the beautiful with the body is the third liberation;

by transcending all perceptions of form, by the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space—this is the fourth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation (vimokṣa).
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception; this is the eighth liberation.
The nine successive attainments:
what are the nine?

Detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome and unskillful states, with directed thought and sustained thought, born of detachment, one enters the first dhyāna, which is joy and happiness.

With the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, through internal clarity and singleness of mind, free from directed and sustained thought, born of concentration, one enters the second dhyāna, which is joy and happiness.

Through the fading away of joy, one dwells in equanimity, experiences happiness with the body, and enters the third dhyāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "One who dwells in equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily."

By abandoning pleasure and pain, and by the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses the purity of equanimity and mindfulness;
by transcending all perceptions of form, by the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space;
transcending the entire sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception.
"Furthermore, there are supramundane dharmas:

from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and all-knowledge—these are called supramundane dharmas."
"What are the phenomena with outflows (sāsrava-dharma)?

The five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha), the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana), the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu), the six kinds [of objects], the six contacts (ṣaṭ-sparśa), the six feelings (ṣaḍ-vedanā), and the four dhyānas up to the four formless attainments (catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ)—these are called phenomena with outflows."
“What are the untainted dharmas?
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the knowledge of all modes—these are called untainted dharmas.”
“What are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)?

Any phenomena that arise, abide, and cease; those belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the five aggregates up to the feelings produced by the condition of mental contact; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and omniscience—these are called conditioned phenomena.”
“What are unconditioned phenomena?

Non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing; the exhaustion of passion, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion; suchness, non-alteration, the characteristic of phenomena, the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the limit of reality—these are called unconditioned phenomena.”
“What are the shared dharmas?
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments—such as these are called the shared dharmas.”
“What are the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)?
“The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are called the unique qualities.
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not become attached to these phenomena that are empty of their own characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya), because they are immovable.”
“A Bodhisattva should also know that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-duality because they are immovable;
this is called the meaning of ‘Bodhisattva. [Śāstra] Question:
Subhūti, for what reason does he first ask about "worldly wholesome dharmas" and subsequently ask about "supramundane dharmas"?
The answer is:
he first asks about the coarse, and subsequently he shall ask about the subtle.
First one knows the characteristics of the mundane world, and subsequently one is able to know the characteristics of the supramundane.

Regarding mundane wholesome dharmas: one knows that there are transgressions and the retribution of blessings; that there are this life and future lives; that there is the mundane world and there is nirvana; and that there is the realization of the Buddhas and other noble sages regarding this life, future lives, and the true nature of all phenomena.
This refers to being filial and obedient toward one's parents and so forth, up to ten recitations.
One acquires wealth in accordance with the Dharma and provides offerings and support to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
A śramaṇa is defined as one who has left the household life to seek the Way; a brāhmaṇa is defined as one who remains at home and pursues learning.
These two individuals perform what is difficult to do in the world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; therefore, they should be honored.
"Elders" refers to paternal uncles, maternal uncles, elder sisters, elder brothers, and so forth.
Reverence and making offerings are the fundamental dharmas for practicing as a householder.
Generosity, observance of precepts, cultivation of meditative concentration, and exhortation are as explained in the first chapter.
Skillful means give rise to merit, such as repentance and sympathetic joy; requesting the Buddha to remain long in the world without entering parinirvāṇa and to turn the wheel of Dharma;
and likewise, although one practices emptiness, one does not cling to emptiness, but continues to cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds.
Through such skillful means as these, various merits and virtues are produced.
The ten paths of wholesome action up to the four formless attainments are as previously explained.
Among the ten recollections, eight matters are as previously explained.
Regarding "wholesome mindfulness": it consists of reflecting upon and discerning the causes and conditions of wholesome karma to subdue the mind.
Furthermore, nirvana is the truly wholesome dharma; constantly binding one's thoughts to nirvana constitutes "wholesome mindfulness."
Mindfulness of the body is precisely the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Those factors that are contrary to wholesome dharmas are called unwholesome dharmas.
As for indeterminate dharmas, these refer to the mind of deportment, the mind of craftsmanship, the mind of transformation, as well as the bodily and vocal actions arising therefrom.
Excluding the five aggregates that are wholesome or unwholesome, there are the remaining five aggregates, as well as space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth.
As for mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), they consist of the five aggregates:
some are wholesome, some are unwholesome, and some are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The twelve bases (*āyatana*):
eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), four are of three kinds.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*): [the same applies].
The "eight" are indeterminate, and the "ten" are of three kinds.
The ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are wholesome dharmas because ordinary persons can obtain and accomplish them;
furthermore, because they themselves cannot transcend the world, they are called "worldly dharmas."
"Supramundane dharmas" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, the three untainted faculties, and the three samādhis, as previously explained.
Clarity and liberation:
"clarity" refers to the three types of clear knowledge;
"liberation" refers to conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation.
"Mindfulness" refers to the ten recollections.
"Wisdom" refers to the eleven types of wisdom.

"Right Mindfulness" refers to contemplating according to the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), just as one contemplates the body among the factors of mindfulness, observing it as the foundation of all wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities have been explained in detail as previously set forth in the meaning of the teachings.
These four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are for the sake of taking the single mind as the path;
furthermore, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, and so forth, which ordinary persons cannot obtain, are called supramundane.
Mindfulness, wisdom, and right mindfulness are of two kinds:
mundane and supramundane; here, the supramundane is intended.
"Tainted phenomena" refers to the five aggregates and so forth, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not worldly; they consist of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), in brief, have three characteristics, namely: arising, abiding, and ceasing.

From those bound to the three realms up to the four foundations of mindfulness, and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—although these are untainted dharmas, because they are produced by volitional effort, they are conditioned dharmas.
That which is contrary to the conditioned is the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, it is the cessation of the three poisons and all other afflictions, wherein the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth do not continue in succession;

such as *tathatā* (thusness), *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena), *dharmaniyāmatā* (the fixed order of phenomena), and *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality)—these are called unconditioned dharmas.
Question:
The suchness of form is not separate from form, and suchness is not separate from form;
yet form is conditioned—how then can it be unconditioned?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of form (*rūpa*):

first, the form that ordinary persons perceive through the fleshly eye by means of recollection, imagination, and discrimination; second, the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of form as known by the minds of the noble ones, which is like *nirvāṇa*.
The form known by ordinary people is called "form";
yet this form, when entering into suchness (*tathatā*), neither arises nor ceases.

For example, although conditioned phenomena consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they possess various designations, namely the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth.

Although unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are of three kinds, they are also distinguished by various names, such as *tathatā* (suchness), *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), *dharmasthititā* (the stability of phenomena), and *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality).

Common dharmas (*sādhāraṇadharma*) refer to the places where ordinary persons and noble ones are born, as well as the places where they enter meditative concentration; because these are shared, they are called common dharmas.
Uncommon dharmas (*asādhāraṇadharma*) refer to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The Bodhisattva discriminates and knows that these various phenomena each have their own characteristics; because all these phenomena arise from the combination of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, their self-nature is empty.
The Bodhisattva abides unmoving within this dharma of non-obstruction, for by means of the gateway to the entrance into non-duality, he enters all dharmas without moving.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 44;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the "Mahāsattva" Chapter, Thirteenth, Scroll 4.
15. Created by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 13: The Mahāsattva. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is he called a ‘mahāsattva’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This Bodhisattva is the foremost among those in the assembly of the certain; therefore, he is called a Mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is the assembly of those destined for certainty (*niyata-rāśi*), of whom these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the leaders?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The assembly of those destined for certainty consists of persons of the nature-ground (*gotra-bhūmi*), the eight types of persons (*aṣṭamaka*), stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas who have first resolved [for awakening], and even bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).”
Subhūti! This is the assembly of those destined for certainty, with the bodhisattva as its leader.
Within this assembly, the bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a great mind that is indestructible like a diamond; he shall serve as the leader for this assembly of those destined for certainty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is this great mind generated by a bodhisattva mahāsattva that is indestructible like a vajra?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
'I shall, within immeasurable births and deaths, adorn myself with the great vow.'"
I ought to relinquish all that I possess;
I ought to maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
and I ought to deliver all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to enter nirvana without remainder.
"Once I have delivered all sentient beings, there shall not be even a single person who enters nirvāṇa;
I should realize that the characteristic of all dharmas is non-arising;
I should practice the six pāramitās solely with the mind of sarvajñā."
I should study wisdom so as to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena;
I should thoroughly comprehend the gateway of wisdom regarding the single characteristic of all phenomena;
I should thoroughly comprehend even the gateways of wisdom regarding immeasurable characteristics.
Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s generation of a great mind that is indestructible like a vajra.
Abiding in this mind, this bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes the foremost among all those in the assembly who are destined for certainty, because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
"I shall, on behalf of all sentient beings of the ten directions—whether they be beings in the hells, beings among animals, or beings among hungry ghosts—undergo all their sufferings and pains."

For the sake of each and every sentient being, one shall undergo the sufferings of the hells on their behalf for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, until that sentient being enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
By means of this Dharma, one undergoes all such hardships for the sake of these beings;

only after those beings have entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* will one then plant roots of goodness for oneself and, after immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! This is the great mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, indestructible like a diamond.
Abiding in this mind, he serves as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind of great joy; dwelling within this mind of great joy, he acts as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the great joyful mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to a mind of passion, a mind of anger, or a mind of delusion; he does not give rise to a mind of affliction, nor does he give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. This is called the great joyful mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Abiding within this mind, he acts as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty, yet he does not even conceive the thought that "this mind exists.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to an unshakable mind!
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by 'unshakable mind'?
The Buddha said:
“Constantly recollecting the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet not recollecting that there is such a mind—this is called the unshakable mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings.
What is meant by a "mind of benefit and happiness"?

It is to rescue and protect all sentient beings and not abandon any sentient being, yet without even thinking that one possesses such a mind; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva giving rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is the foremost among those in the assembly of the certain.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice with a mind that desires the Dharma, delights in the Dharma,
and rejoices in the Dharma. What is this Dharma?
That which is called not destroying the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is what is termed "Dharma.
What are termed "the Dharma of desire" and "the Dharma of delight"?
Faith in the Dharma, patience toward the Dharma, and acceptance of the Dharma—these are termed the "Dharma of desire" and the "Dharma of delight."
What is called "delighting in the Dharma"?
Constantly practicing this Dharma is what is called delighting in the Dharma.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to serve as the foremost among those of fixed destiny, because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, dwelling in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, he is able to act as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty; this is because these dharmas are used through non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, up to abiding in the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they are able to act as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty; this is because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the vajra-like samādhi and so forth, up to and including the samādhi of being unstained by detachment from space; therein they act as the leader among those of fixed destiny, because these dharmas are practiced through non-apprehension."
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling within these dharmas is able to act as the leader for the assembly of those destined for certainty.
For this reason, he is called a 'mahāsattva' (great being)."
[Treatise] Commentary:
Subhūti has already heard from the Buddha the meaning of "bodhisattva"; he now asks about the meaning of "mahāsattva.
"Mahā" is, in the language of Qin, "great."
"Sattva" means "mind" in the language of Qin, or alternatively, "sentient being.
Because this sentient being is the foremost and most supreme among all sentient beings in the world, he is called "Great" (Mahā).
Furthermore, because they possess the great mind that knows all dharmas and desires to deliver all sentient beings, this is called "great.
Moreover, a Bodhisattva is therefore called a Mahāsattva, and a Mahāsattva is therefore called a Bodhisattva, because they have resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, as explained in the "Chapter on Praising the Meaning of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas," this should be elaborated upon here.
Moreover, in this context, the Buddha himself explains the meaning of *mahāsattva*: sentient beings are divided into three categories;
the first is those of fixed destiny (*niyata*), who will certainly enter nirvāṇa.
Second, those of false certainty, who will inevitably enter the evil realms;
third, those of no fixed certainty.
Because they shall be the greatest among sentient beings of right certainty, they are called Mahāsattvas.
The "great assembly" refers to all other worthy and noble ones (ārya) except for the Buddha.
Regarding those called "persons of the stage of nature" (*gotrabhū*): because they are born within the nature of the noble ones, it is termed "nature."
It is like a child born into a noble family; although small and yet unable to accomplish anything, one must expect that he will surely achieve great things later.
This stage extends from the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma up to the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The "eight persons" refers to the path of seeing (darśanamārga), which proceeds through fifteen moments of mind.
Question: Why are these fifteen moments of mind called the "eight persons"?
Answer:

In the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), wisdom is predominant; in the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), insight and patience (kṣānti) are predominant, and wisdom follows along with that patience. Why is this so?
Because the power of patience is great.
Furthermore, there are two matters concerning patience and wisdom:
they are that which can sever and that which can realize.
Because one dwells within the eight stages of patience (*kṣānti*), one is called an "eight-person" (*aṣṭamaka*).
The meanings of "stream-enterer," "once-returner," "non-returner," "arhat," and "pratyekabuddha" are as previously explained.
Regarding the "bodhisattva who has first resolved [for awakening]," some say:

one who has first resolved is one who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and resolves their mind in accordance with the characteristics of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called "first resolving," and it is termed the "true resolution of the mind."
It is because one clearly knows the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) as well as the characteristics of the mind, thereby destroying all afflictions (*kleśas*);
and because it accords with the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remaining unbroken and non-perverted—this mind is called the "first resolve" (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

Some say: Although ordinary worldlings abide amidst the various fetters and afflictions, upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, they give rise to a heart of great compassion, feeling pity for sentient beings and thinking, "I shall become a Buddha."
Although this mind dwells amidst afflictions, because the mind is noble, it is revered by devas and humans.
Just as when the crown prince of a wheel-turning sage-king first conceives in the womb, he surpasses all other sons and is honored by all devas and spirits;
so too is the bodhisattva-mind: though it remains within the fetters and proclivities, it surpasses all devas and sages with supernatural powers.

Furthermore, from the time a bodhisattva first resolves their mind until they have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those who receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), enter the stage of the Dharma (*dharmatā-avasthita*), and attain the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) are called "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*).
The characteristics of an *avaivartika* will be explained in detail later.
Because such a great assembly shall act as their leaders, they are called "Mahāsattvas."
Because this bodhisattva wishes to become the sovereign of all noble ones, he has resolved upon the Great Mind and accepts all suffering, for his mind is as firm as a vajra and immovable.
"Vajra-mind" means that it cannot be moved by any fetters or afflictions, just as a vajra mountain cannot be tilted or shaken by the wind.
When various evil beings and demonic persons come, he does not act according to their whims nor does he believe or accept their words;
even if they revile and slander him with anger, strike, imprison, hack, pierce, or cut him, his mind remains unchanging.
If there are those who come to beg for their head, eyes, marrow, brain, hands, feet, skin, or flesh, he is able to give them all;
yet if the seeker remains unsatisfied and instead becomes angry and abusive, at that time his mind remains patient and unshakable.
For example, it is like a firm mountain of vajra: even if people come to dig and break it apart, or various insects come to gnaw at it, it suffers no loss or damage; this is called the "vajra mind."
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explained the "characteristics of the adamantine mind," stating that a bodhisattva should form this thought:

"I should not adorn myself with great vows for only one month, one year, one lifetime, two lifetimes, or even for ten million *kalpas*. Rather, throughout immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless lifetimes of birth and death, I shall benefit and liberate all sentient beings."
Second, I should relinquish all internal and external precious possessions.
Third, I should maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, free from hatred and attachment.
Fourth, I shall deliver all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles according to their needs.
Fifth, having delivered such sentient beings, there is in truth nothing delivered and no merit therein; in this regard, my mind shall neither regret nor sink.
Sixth, I should know that all dharmas possess such characteristics as being neither produced nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, and so forth.
Seventh, I should practice the six pāramitās with a pure and unadulterated mind, dedicating the merit toward sarvajñā (omniscience).
Eighth, I should skillfully know all activities performed in the world as well as all matters to be known regarding that which transcends the world, thoroughly penetrating and understanding them all.

Ninth, I should understand the gateway to the wisdom of the single characteristic of all phenomena; that is to say, all phenomena are ultimately empty, and one should contemplate all phenomena as having the characteristic of nirvana without remainder, free from all recollections, conceptions, and discriminations.
Tenth, I should know the gates of the two aspects, the three aspects, and even the immeasurable aspects of all phenomena, and penetrate them with clear understanding. Regarding the two aspects:
all phenomena have two kinds—either existence or non-existence, arising or ceasing, action or non-action, form or formlessness, and so forth.
The three gates are:
whether one, two, or many—anything from three upwards is termed "many";

whether existent, non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent; whether superior, middling, or inferior; whether past, future, or present; the three realms, the three dharmas, and the three categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. These are the three gates.
Regarding the four gates, the five gates, and such immeasurable Dharma-gates, he penetrates them all without obstruction.
Within this state, his mind is without regret, without timidity, and without doubt; he receives them with faith and penetrates them without hindrance.

Constantly practicing without ceasing, one extinguishes all afflictions along with their karmic retributions, and causes all obstructing matters to be utterly destroyed, just as a vajra jewel can shatter all mountains.
Abiding within this adamantine mind, one should act as the leader among the great assembly by means of the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).

As for "the emptiness of non-apprehension," if a bodhisattva gives rise to such a great mind as this adamantine mind yet conceives arrogance, their transgression exceeds that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
For this reason, it is said that one "employs non-apprehension," for all phenomena lack fixed characteristics and are like illusions or transformations.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the mind is like a vajra": for all sentient beings who have fallen into the three evil realms, I shall take their hardships upon myself;

for the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall undergo the sufferings of hell until that being emerges from the three evil realms, accumulates the roots of all virtues, and reaches nirvana without remainder, after which I shall further rescue all sentient beings.

Having thus successively delivered all sentient beings, he shall thereafter personally accumulate all merits for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before finally attaining Buddhahood; throughout this process, his mind will feel neither regret nor discouragement.

To be able to thus undergo toil and suffering on behalf of sentient beings, to personally cultivate all merits, and to dwell long within birth and death without regret or despondency—just as the vajra-ground can support the trichiliocosm and keep it from shaking—because this mind is so firm and stable, it is called "vajra-like."
Regarding "greatly joyful mind" (mahā-prasāda-citta): although one may possess a firm mind, it is not yet "greatly joyful";
it is like a horse that, though possessing great strength, is not yet "greatly swift."
Because one attains two kinds of equanimity toward sentient beings, one does not give rise to a mind of lustful attachment;
if there were partiality or favoritism, it would constitute a thief that destroys the mind of equanimity, which is the foundation of the Buddha-way.
Because one constantly practices a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, there is no mind of anger.
By constantly observing that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature, one is free from delusion;
by cherishing sentient beings more than an only child, one is free from malice;
and by not abandoning sentient beings because of the high value placed on the Buddha-way, one does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Question:
If the mind is as firm as a vajra, it is already immovable; why then do you further speak of an "immovable mind"? Answer:
At times, even though it may be firm, the mind still undergoes increase and decrease;
just as a tree, though firm, can still be shaken.
There are two kinds of such shaking:
First, movement caused by external conditions, as previously explained;
second, movement caused by internal conditions, such as various false views and doubts.
