If one constantly recollects that the Buddha-way of all-encompassing wisdom is what I shall attain as its fruit, the mind will remain unmoved.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should benefit sentient beings through various causes and conditions, using everything from food and drink up to the bliss of a Buddha to benefit them;
never abandoning sentient beings and desiring to free them from suffering is called the mind of peace and happiness (sukhacitta),
yet one does not even think that such a mind exists.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s delight in the Dharma is called "foremost.
As for "Dharma," it means not destroying the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

Not destroying the characteristics of all phenomena means that there is no dharma to which one can become attached and no dharma to be grasped; this is what is meant by "unobtainable" (*anupalabdha*).
This emptiness of the unattainable is itself nirvāṇa; to constantly believe in, accept, and endure it is called the "dharma of desire" and the "dharma of joy."
Constantly practicing the three gates of liberation is called "delighting in the Dharma.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva dwells within these eighteen kinds of emptiness and does not follow the eighteen mental activities, they do not give rise to sinful karma.

By abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and by extinguishing all afflictions and accumulating all wholesome dharmas, he is able to serve as the leader.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva enters the diamond-like samādhi and other states of mind, experiencing bliss, becoming weary of worldly pleasures, and increasing his roots of goodness, wisdom, and skillful means, he serves as the leader among the great assembly of noble ones.
If one can act as the leader for those who are great, how much more so for those who are small!
For this reason, they are called "Mahāsattvas" (Great Beings).

Chapter 14: Refuting the View of Annihilation *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Fourteen: Refuting the View of Annihilation [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, wish to explain the reason why one is called a Mahāsattva.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Speak then! Śāriputra said:

"I see the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a soul, the view of a creature, the view of a nourisher, the view of a person, the view of an agent, the view of one who causes to act, the view of one who arises, the view of one who causes to arise, the view of one who receives, the view of one who causes to receive, the view of a knower, the view of a seer; the view of annihilation, the view of permanence; the view of existence, the view of non-existence; the view of the aggregates, the view of the sense-bases, the view of the elements; the view of the truths, the view of dependent origination; the view of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the view of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the view of the Buddha-way; the view of maturing sentient beings, the view of purifying the Buddha-field; the view of a Buddha; and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma."
"To preach the Dharma for the sake of severing such views as these is called a Mahāsattva.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"For what reason is the view that form exists considered a false view?"
“For what reason is it that perceiving feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to the turning of the wheel of Dharma, is called a false view?
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they lack skillful means, they give rise to views regarding form, because they operate with the notion of something to be apprehended.”
If one gives rise to views regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even the turning of the wheel of Dharma, it is because of the grasping at something obtainable.

In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they employ the power of skillful means to sever all such views and preach the Dharma for others, doing so by way of non-apprehensibility.
[Treatise] Question:

The Buddha led five hundred great Arhats to the pool of the Naga King Anavatapta to enjoy the bliss of seclusion. Desiring to explain the karmic causes and conditions of his own past lives and those of his disciples, he found that Śāriputra was absent, so he commanded Maudgalyāyana to summon him.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana arrived at the Jeta Grove by means of his supernormal powers;
meanwhile, Śāriputra was sewing a robe and said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Wait a moment!"
"I shall depart once the sewing is finished.
Maudgalyāyana urged him to leave quickly;
then, Maudgalyāyana stroked the garment with his hand, and the garment was immediately completed.
Seeing that Maudgalyāyana prized his supernatural powers, Śāriputra immediately cast his waistband upon the ground and said to him,
"Lift this band and take it away.
Maudgalyāyana attempted to lift the band with both hands, but he could not raise it from the ground.
The Buddha immediately entered various profound meditative absorptions and lifted him up; the earth shook violently, yet his belt remained touching the ground.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions does the earth shake so greatly?"
The Buddha said:
"Maudgalyāyana entered a profound meditative concentration and exerted great supernormal power, wishing to lift Śāriputra’s belt, but he was unable to lift it.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Even Maudgalyāyana did not know the names of the meditative concentrations that Śāriputra entered and emerged from;
even Śāriputra did not know the names of the meditative concentrations that the Buddha entered.”
Question: Since Śāriputra’s wisdom is vastly inferior to that of the Buddha, why does he say, "I also delight in speaking"? Answer:
It is not because Śāriputra wishes to manifest his own wisdom or out of arrogance before the great assembly that he speaks thus.
Śāriputra is the one who follows the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma and extensively benefits sentient beings.
Because the meaning of his being a mahāsattva involves such vast benefit, after the Buddha had finished speaking, Śāriputra spoke next.
Furthermore, many people have faith in and delight in Śāriputra’s words.
Why is this? It is because of the causal conditions from past lives that many have resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva.

Because the Buddha possesses a mind of great compassion, the root of the "self" and its habitual tendencies has already been uprooted, and because his attachment to dharmas has been severed; for these various reasons, he grants permission.
Śāriputra said:

"The view of a self, the view of a knower, the view of a seer, the view of a Buddha, the view of a Bodhisattva—the views of all sentient beings and so forth—as well as false views such as existence and non-existence, or annihilationism and eternalism, and the views regarding the five aggregates up to the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas:
because this Bodhisattva is able to sever these three kinds of views, he shall preach the Dharma in the midst of the great assembly."
"These three kinds of views have been habitually clung to since beginningless time, penetrating even to the very marrow of one's bones.
Subhūti then had this thought:

"The Buddha has taught that the five aggregates and so forth, up to all the Buddha-dharmas, constitute the practice of a bodhisattva; why then does he teach the Dharma for the purpose of severing these views?"
Having formed this thought, he questioned Śāriputra.
Śāriputra replied:

“A bodhisattva who lacks skillful means and wishes to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* contemplates form (*rūpa*) seeking a mark of stability; grasping all marks of form, they give rise to views regarding form.”
That which is contrary to this is called "possessing skillful means";
such a bodhisattva, although contemplating form, does not give rise to false views, yet is able to sever all views.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I also wish to explain why one is called a mahāsattva!
The Buddha said:
"Speak then! Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!..."
This is the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unequaled mind, the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Because this mind of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned,
and because one does not even cling to this untainted and unconditioned mind of omniscience— for these reasons, one is called a Mahāsattva.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"What is the unequaled mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"
Subhūti said:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma as having arising or ceasing, increasing or decreasing, being defiled or purified."
Śāriputra!

If dharmas are without arising and without cessation, even unto being without defilement and without purity, therein there is no mind of a śrāvaka, no mind of a pratyekabuddha, no mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and no mind of a buddha.
"Śāriputra!
This is called the peerless mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra then said to Subhūti:
"As Subhūti has said:
'The mind of omniscience, the untainted mind, the unconditioned mind—within this mind there is no attachment. Subhūti!"

One does not cling to form, nor does one cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why, then, is it said that only this mind does not cling?
Subhūti said: “So it is! So it is!”
“Śāriputra!
One does not cling even to form, nor does one cling even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The minds of ordinary persons are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty;
the minds of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty."
Subhūti said: "So it is, Śāriputra!"
Śāriputra said: "Subhūti!
If form is also untainted and unconditioned, because its nature is empty;..."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is emptiness;
and so on, up to feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition, which is untainted and unconditioned, because its nature is emptiness.
Subhūti said, “So it is! Śāriputra said:
"The four foundations of mindfulness are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty;
even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty."
Subhūti said: "It is so! It is as Śāriputra has spoken."
"The minds of ordinary persons are also untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty;
even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are untainted and unconditioned, because their nature is empty."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "As Subhūti has said:
'Because it is empty and without mind, one does not cling to this mind.'"
"Subhūti! Because form does not exist, one does not cling to form;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to the feeling born from the condition of mind-contact—do not exist, one does not cling to feeling."
Because the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist, one does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness;
and so on, up to: because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, one does not cling to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti said: "So it is, Śāriputra!"
Because form does not exist, one does not cling to form;
and so on, up to: because the eighteen unique qualities do not exist, one does not cling to the eighteen unique qualities.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they do so with the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unequaled mind, and the mind not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
yet they do not think that such a mind exists, nor do they cling to this mind, because all dharmas are unattainable. For this reason, they are called a Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Commentary:
Subhūti speaks of the "unequaled mind of the mahāsattva," yet he does not even cling to this mind.

"Non-clinging" means that from the very moment the bodhisattva first resolved upon awakening, he has not perceived any dharma with fixed characteristics—whether arising or ceasing, increasing or decreasing, defiled or pure.
This mind is ultimately empty; within it there is neither the characteristic of mind nor the characteristic of non-mind, because all characteristics are ultimately pure.
For this reason, there is no mind of a śrāvaka, no mind of a pratyekabuddha, no mind of a bodhisattva, and no mind of a buddha.
Subhūti praised the bodhisattva, saying that such a mind is also sublime; yet, that the bodhisattva does not become attached to this mind is itself what makes him noble.
Śāriputra, wishing to challenge Subhūti, spoke these words:
"It is not only because the mind of omniscience is untainted and unconditioned that the bodhisattva should not be self-exalting."
Why is this? Because the minds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are likewise untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃbaddha*), for their nature is eternally empty;
just as the minds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas are untainted and unconditioned, so too is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and nature of the mind of an ordinary person empty.
The true nature of reality is empty and pure, free from attachment;
as it was previously said:
"Though clouds and mists obscure the sun and moon, they cannot defile the sun and moon."
Furthermore, the true nature of all afflictions is no different from the characteristic of the empty mind of permanence.
However, when abiding in the stage of ordinary beings, they are either defiled or pure.
When abiding in the stage of noble ones, because one cultivates the wisdom of signlessness, there is no conceptual discrimination.
However, because he has compassion for sentient beings, although he speaks, his mind remains unattached.
It is not only that the minds of ordinary people are without outflows and unconditioned; the same is true for the five aggregates up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti agreed. Then Śāriputra said:
"This mind is no-mind; because the characteristic of mind is empty, it does not cling."
"Because the characteristic of form does not exist within form, one does not cling to it; this applies even up to the Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti said, "So it is!"
For this reason, a bodhisattva is able to contemplate that the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty, an emptiness that is ungraspable, and ultimately pure.
For this reason it is said:

"The mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unequaled mind, the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—without being mindful of the existence of this mind, and without being attached to this mind, one can swiftly reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The fourteenth chapter, "The Explanation of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness," concludes.

**Chapter Fifteen: The Great Ornament** *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Great Ornament, Number Fifteen. [Sūtra] At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I, too, would like to explain why one is called a mahāsattva!
The Buddha said, "Speak then!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said: "This bodhisattva is one of great adornment;
this bodhisattva has set out upon the Great Vehicle; this bodhisattva rides upon the Great Vehicle.
For these reasons, this bodhisattva is called a Mahāsattva."
Śāriputra said to Pūrṇa:
"What is meant by the 'Great Adornment' of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Pūrṇa replied to Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell in or practice the dānapāramitā for the sake of such-and-such a number of people;
rather, he dwells in and practices the dānapāramitā for the sake of all sentient beings.”

It is not for the sake of such a limited number of beings that one dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), practices the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
rather, it is for the sake of all sentient beings that one dwells in the perfection of wisdom and practices the perfection of wisdom.
The great adornment of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not impose limits upon sentient beings by thinking, "I shall deliver so many people,
but not others," nor does he say,
"I shall cause so many people to reach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, while others shall not."
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus makes a great adornment for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he forms this thought:
"I shall personally fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to practice the dāna-pāramitā."

Having personally fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā);
having personally fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they also cause all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), all their acts of giving are conjoined with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) for the sake of all sentient beings."
Śāriputra! This is called the great adornment of the *dānapāramitā* when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *dānapāramitā*.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, they should give with a mind directed toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge), not toward the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Śāriputra! This is called the great adornment of the perfection of ethical discipline when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they give with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā); this patient acceptance, desire, and faith regarding all such acts of giving is called the great adornment of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) when practicing the perfection of giving.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he gives with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā) and cultivates it diligently without ceasing; this is called the great adornment of the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) when practicing the perfection of giving.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), he should give with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), maintaining his composure so as not to give rise to the thoughts of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is called the great adornment of the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) when practicing the perfection of generosity.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), he gives with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā). He contemplates all phenomena as like an illusion; he does not apprehend a giver, he does not apprehend the object given, and he does not apprehend a recipient. This is called the great adornment of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) when practicing the perfection of giving.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and does not grasp or apprehend the marks of the various pāramitās, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who is grandly adorned.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he gives gifts with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), sharing them with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), his faith, patience, and aspiration toward all phenomena is called the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) for that bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they cultivate it with diligence without ceasing; this is called the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; this is called the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he contemplates all phenomena as being like an illusion; moreover, he does not even conceive of the existence of this precept, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension. This is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they encompass all the perfections; for this reason, it is called the "Great Adornment."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he gives gifts with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), sharing them with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of patience."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he does not take up the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but takes up only the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta). This is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta) and exerts himself with body and mind, neither resting nor ceasing; this is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), he collects his mind in a single point; thus, even when faced with painful circumstances, his mind does not become distracted. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) while practicing the perfection of patience.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), he accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and contemplates all phenomena as empty, without an agent and without a recipient.

If there are those who revile or mutilate him, his mind remains like an illusion or a dream; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of patience.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) and gives gifts with a mind directed toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), he does not allow his body or mind to become indolent; this is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of vigor."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he maintains pure ethical discipline (śīla) from beginning to end in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta). This is called the perfection of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he practices patience (kṣānti) in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā); this is called the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva while practicing the perfection of vigor.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *vīryapāramitā*, he accords with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), collects his mind, becomes detached from desire, and enters the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). This is called the *dhyānapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *vīryapāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), he accords with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), does not grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena, and does not even cling to this non-grasping of characteristics; this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā),
they encompass all the perfections. Furthermore, Śāriputra:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they act in accordance with the mind of sarvajñatā, bestowing gifts with a concentrated mind and not allowing the mind to become distracted; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s dānapāramitā when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they maintain the precepts in accordance with the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). By the power of meditative concentration, they prevent any factors that violate the precepts from entering; this is called the śīlapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, because he is in accord with the mind of sarvajñā and abides in the samādhi of loving-kindness and compassion, he endures all harms and afflictions; this is called the kṣāntipāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, he accords with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), neither relishing nor clinging to dhyāna, constantly seeking progress from one dhyāna to the next. This is called the vīrya-pāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyāna-pāramitā.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyāna-pāramitā, he accords with the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), does not rely upon any phenomena, and is not reborn through the power of dhyāna; this is called the prajñā-pāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the dhyāna-pāramitā.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā, they encompass all the pāramitās.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they act in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), giving away all that they possess, both internal and external, without any sense of attachment or stinginess; they do not perceive a giver, a recipient, or the gift itself. This is called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he acts in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta); because he does not perceive the two things of observing precepts and breaking precepts, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he does not perceive one who reviles, one who scolds, one who strikes, or one who kills; nor does he perceive that it is by means of this emptiness that he is able to practice patience. This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he accords with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty; yet, out of great compassion, he practices all wholesome dharmas. This is called the *vīryapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he accords with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). He contemplates all dhyānas as having the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of signlessness, and the characteristic of wishlessness. This is called the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they encompass all the perfections. Śāriputra!
This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Regarding this great adornment, the Buddhas of the ten directions rejoice and, amidst the great assemblies, proclaim their names and praise them, saying:
"In such-and-such a world, such-and-such a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses great adornment; he matures sentient beings and purifies buddha-fields!"
[Treatise] Commentary:
When Pūrṇa heard the two great disciples explain the meaning of *mahāsattva*, the Buddha said:
"Excellent!"

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, who was praised by the Buddha as the foremost among the Dharma-preachers within the great assembly, wishing again to explain the meaning of *mahāsattva*, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, would like to speak on this."
The Buddha immediately granted his permission.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"Subhūti is the master who expounds the Prajñāpāramitā; Śāriputra should have questioned Subhūti. For what reason, then, does he now question Pūrṇa?"
Answer: These two individuals are both Brahmins, and both were named after their mothers;
within the Buddha-dharma, these two are both great—Śāriputra being great in wisdom.
Pūrṇa’s exposition of the Dharma was adorned with manifold embellishments and captivated the hearts of the assembly; thus, he was preeminent among those who preach the Dharma.
For this reason, these two were equal, and because they were equal, they debated together before the Buddha.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa had previously engaged in debate with Śāriputra and was able to respond skillfully, as described in the *Saptaratha-upama-sūtra*. They had already become close friends and delighted in discussing principles together;
Subhūti lacked such a background.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa has explained the meaning of "mahāsattva"; therefore, one should have questioned him. Why, then, do you question Subhūti?
The meaning of what was said regarding "mahāsattva" is that such a person is "greatly adorned."
Just as a person traveling a long distance carries ample provisions,
or as one who would defeat an enemy prepares various weapons,
so too is this bodhisattva: wishing to destroy the thieves of the afflictions that enter through Māra, he practices the six pāramitās to adorn himself.

This person has dwelt in birth and death for immeasurable kalpas, accumulating all manner of merit and wisdom as their provisions. Among the three vehicles, because they seek to proceed toward the Mahāyāna, they resolve their minds to practice the six pāramitās and thus mount this Great Vehicle.
Śāriputra asked Pūrṇa:
"Since both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also proceed toward the Way, why is it that they are not called 'Greatly Adorned,' while only Bodhisattvas are said to be 'Greatly Adorned'?"
Pūrṇa replied:

"Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice the six perfections such as giving, they do so with measure and limit; they act for their own liberation and to liberate other sentient beings who are capable of being saved. For this reason, it is not called the 'Great Adornment'."
That which a bodhisattva brings to liberation is not differentiated nor limited to a certain number of sentient beings; thus they practice giving up to wisdom without forming such thoughts as:
"I shall deliver so many people to attain the three vehicles, but cannot deliver so many others;
I shall cause so many people to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, but cannot deliver so many others."
The Bodhisattva makes such adornments so that all sentient beings may fully enter the Mahāyāna and become Buddhas.

The Bodhisattva practices the great adornment by personally practicing the *dānapāramitā* and also causing all sentient beings to practice the *dānapāramitā*, and so on, up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is likewise.
Question: What is meant by "Great Adornment" (mahāvyūha)? Answer:

For the sake of delivering sentient beings and for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, those who practice various meritorious virtues and wholesome deeds are briefly said to be practicing these six pāramitās.
As Pūrṇa explained in sequence:
if a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving for the sake of all-encompassing wisdom, this merit is shared with all sentient beings.
"Shared" means that this merit from giving is shared equally by myself and all sentient beings; I dedicate it through this toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Consecration" (pariṇāmanā) means that regarding this merit, one does not seek the pleasures of human kings, celestial kings, or worldly meditative concentrations;
nor, for the sake of sentient beings, does one even seek the bliss of nirvāṇa. One takes this karmic fruit and seeks the Buddha-dharma solely for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings.
Such characteristics as these are called the "Great Adornment of Dānapāramitā.

When this bodhisattva practices giving, if they see pratyekabuddhas or arhats manifesting great supernatural powers, attaining the destruction of outflows, and entering nirvāṇa, they feel neither greed nor attachment toward them, but single-mindedly cultivate the Buddha-way; this is called "the arising of Śīlapāramitā from Dānapāramitā."

When practicing giving, if someone reviles one with harsh words, harms one with knives or staves, or forcibly begs for what should not be given, one feels neither anger nor regret; rather, one enters into the true nature of all phenomena, which is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). This is termed "the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) arising from the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*)."

When practicing generosity, one harmonizes material goods and protects them to bestow upon others, with body and mind neither lax nor weary; this is called "the perfection of vigor arising from the perfection of generosity."
When practicing giving, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha and recollect the teachings of all Buddhas, not allowing thoughts of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to enter.
By means of this giving, one immediately enters meditative concentration; this is called "the perfection of generosity giving rise to the perfection of meditation."
When practicing giving, the bodhisattva forms this thought:

"The giver, the recipient, and the material gift arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions; therefore, they lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty, like an illusion and like a dream."
Because sentient beings are empty, there is no recipient and no giver;
because phenomena are empty, there are no material objects. This is called "the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) giving rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of omniscience, does not grasp at the marks of the various pāramitās yet is able to practice them, this is called the "Great Adornment of a Bodhisattva."
Within this, each single pāramitā fully gives rise to all the other pāramitās; the meaning of this is analyzed in detail within this sutra itself.

Because language has changed between ancient and modern times, the meaning may not be fully understood; therefore, I shall provide an auxiliary analysis and exposition to open the gateway of discourse.
The remaining five pāramitās should also be explained accordingly according to their respective meanings. Question:
Why is it that the arising of all six pāramitās is taught only within the context of dāna-pāramitā, whereas in the other pāramitās, only the arising of five is mentioned?
The answer is:
If each of the latter five pāramitās were to give rise to six [pāramitās] individually, there would be no fault.

The six pāramitās are not a phenomenon that exists at one time or in a single moment; rather, the accumulation of six kinds of merit over immeasurable kalpas, brought together in harmony, is what is called the "six pāramitās."
If the preceding [perfections] are small and the succeeding ones are middling or great, what fault is there?
All dharmas are initially small and subsequently become great; for this reason, each of the other pāramitās should likewise give rise to six.
Furthermore, when all Buddhas preach the Dharma, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) serves as the initial gateway.
As it is said in the sūtras:

"The Buddha always first teaches sentient beings about generosity, precept-keeping, and rebirth in heaven; he speaks of the flavors of the five desires, first explaining the sufferings and afflictions of the world and the benefits of the Path and virtue, and only afterwards does he teach the Four Noble Truths."
For this reason, giving (dāna) is taught first.
Question:
For what reason does the Buddha teach giving as the initial gateway?
The answer is:
In the methods for gathering sentient beings, none surpasses *dāna* (giving).
Whether they be great or small, noble or lowly, even down to animals, *dāna* gathers them all.
Even an enemy who receives a gift becomes a neutral person, and a neutral person who receives a gift becomes a close friend.
The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics of the Buddhas, as well as the perfection of all merits and the fulfillment of all aspirations, are all obtained through giving.
Just as the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi and others have seven treasures emerge from their hands to bestow upon sentient beings;
they are also able to cause sentient beings to be joyful and supple, becoming fit to attain nirvāṇa.
For these reasons, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is placed first.
Question: Why does Pūrṇa say that "within a single perfection all perfections arise as a great adornment"?
Answer: These pāramitās are each distinct, and the power of their practice is slight.
It is like soldiers who have not yet assembled; they possess no power for battle.
If a great army assembles in full array and takes up its weapons, it can defeat the enemy.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva: when the six *pāramitās* are simultaneously arrayed, they can destroy all the demons of affliction and the thieves of human beings, swiftly attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, it is said that "within a single pāramitā, all pāramitās are contained.
The "Buddhas of the ten directions praising his name," the "maturing of sentient beings," and the "purification of the Buddha-field" are as previously explained.
[Sūtra] The Venerable Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out upon the Great Vehicle?"
Pūrṇa said to Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he becomes detached from all desires and detached from all evil and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna. With a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, non-dual, immeasurable, and free from enmity, resentment, and malice, he pervades one direction, two, three, and four directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, throughout the entire world.”
The same applies to the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

When this bodhisattva enters into or emerges from dhyāna, they share all the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), and their constituent factors with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) as the setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the dhyānas and the immeasurable states of mind, forms this thought:
"I shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and, for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma."
This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), cultivates the first dhyāna and dwells in the first dhyāna—and likewise for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas—without entertaining other minds, namely those of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
This is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the various dhyānas in accordance with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they form this thought:
"I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings"; such mental inclinations, desires, and patiences [constitute this perfection].
This is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), enters into the various meditations and dedicates all roots of goodness toward omniscience, practicing with diligence without ceasing, this is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditation.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), enters the four dhyānas and their constituent factors, contemplates the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, the mark of emptiness, the mark of signlessness, and the mark of wishlessness, and dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward sarvajñā—this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva when practicing the dhyānapāramitā.
"Śāriputra! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the mind of loving-kindness, he forms this thought:"
"I shall bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings"—entering the mind of compassion;
"I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings"—entering the mind of sympathetic joy; "I shall ferry across all sentient beings."
"Entering the mind of equanimity, I shall cause all sentient beings to attain the exhaustion of all outflows.
This is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva directs these meditative absorptions and immeasurable minds neither toward the stage of the śrāvakas nor the pratyekabuddhas, but solely toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva while practicing the immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they do not covet the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but instead patiently delight in and desire *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the immeasurable minds.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), practices the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa) and practices only pure conduct, this is called the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the dhyānas and the immeasurable states of mind (*apramāṇa-citta*), he does not arise following after those dhyānas or immeasurable states of mind; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful means and *prajñāpāramitā* when practicing the immeasurable states of mind.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness in every aspect, up to and including the cultivation of the eightfold noble path in every aspect;

they cultivate the three gates of liberation in every aspect, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha in every aspect—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva in the emptiness of the internal is by way of non-apprehension;
up to the wisdom in the emptiness of non-existence and existence is by way of non-apprehension. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle."
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the wisdom that is neither distracted nor fixed amidst all phenomena is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle, they possess the wisdom that it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither real nor unreal, and neither self nor non-self; this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva setting out upon the Great Vehicle by means of non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not function in the past, does not function in the future, and does not function in the present; yet it is not that they are ignorant of the three periods of time. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Great Vehicle, by means of non-apprehension."

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has set out in the Great Vehicle possesses wisdom that does not proceed in the desire realm, does not proceed in the form realm, and does not proceed in the formless realm; yet it is not that he is ignorant of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva setting out in the Great Vehicle."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle with wisdom, they do not engage in worldly dharmas, nor do they engage in supramundane dharmas; they do not engage in conditioned dharmas, nor do they engage in unconditioned dharmas; they do not engage in tainted dharmas, nor do they engage in untainted dharmas. Yet, it is not that they are ignorant of worldly and supramundane dharmas, or conditioned and unconditioned, or tainted and untainted dharmas, for they employ the principle of non-apprehension.
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s setting out upon the Mahāyāna.
[Treatise] Question:
Among the six pāramitās, if they were explained in reverse order, one should first speak of the prajñāpāramitā and next of dhyāna;
if in direct order, one should first speak of the dānapāramitā.
Why, then, is the dhyānapāramitā spoken of as the foremost here?
The answer is:
Having donned the great armor of adornment, no sentient being is able to destroy it.
If a bodhisattva lacks meditative concentration and their mind has not yet departed from desire, then even if they practice the other perfections, they are easily destroyed.
When one practices the perfection of dhyāna and is able to enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), at that time nothing can destroy them.
As it is said:
"For one who practices the samādhi of loving-kindness, blades cannot wound them, and water or fire cannot harm them."
There is also the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) and various transformations, which can give rise to great adornments (*mahā-vyūha*).
As the Buddha said:
"A bird without two wings cannot fly."
Without the power of supernatural faculties (abhijñā), a bodhisattva cannot give rise to the great armor of adornment (mahā-saṃnāha).

By entering into the perfection of dhyāna (dhyāna-pāramitā), they are able to generate immeasurable loving-kindness (maitrī-apramāṇa) and the five supernatural faculties; therefore, nothing can harm them.
For this reason, the dhyānapāramitā is now taught as the foremost.
Question:

Within the four dhyānas there are various merits through which all six pāramitās can be practiced; why, then, is it said here that one practices the six pāramitās specifically within the four immeasurables (apramāṇa)?

Answer: The four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa) grasp the marks of sentient beings and take sentient beings as their object; the bodhisattva constantly practices the path for the sake of sentient beings.
Within these four immeasurables, there are the minds of loving-kindness (maitrī) and compassion (karuṇā), which are able to benefit sentient beings.
The other eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and so forth, do not possess such benefits.
Question:
Since a bodhisattva dwelling in the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is able to extensively benefit sentient beings, why are they not mentioned?
Answer: Great Compassion is the root of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the five supernormal powers have already been explained, and the four immeasurable minds will be explained later; since they have not yet been discussed, they are explained now.
If a bodhisattva practices only the four immeasurable minds, they are not said to have set out upon the Mahāyāna;
it is because of the integration of the six pāramitās that one is said to have "set out upon the Mahāyāna."
The four immeasurable minds give rise to the six perfections; Pūrṇa explains the causes and conditions for this himself within this section.
Question:
How does one cultivate all aspects of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
Answer: There are two types:
those of the nature of faith-practice (śraddhā-carita) and those of the nature of dharma-practice (dharma-carita).
Those of the nature of practice through faith contemplate impermanence and suffering, or they may contemplate only impermanence, or they may contemplate only suffering;
those of the nature of practice through the Dharma contemplate emptiness and non-self, or they may contemplate only emptiness, or they may contemplate only non-self.
Because Bodhisattvas deliver sentient beings, they cultivate and study all gateways.

Furthermore, those who set out in the Mahāyāna use the eighteen kinds of emptiness to dismantle the eighteen types of phenomena, and they also relinquish this wisdom of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as eternally settled, yet does not grasp at the mark of such settlement, this is called "wisdom that is neither fixed nor distracted.
Furthermore, fearing the fall into the inversions of permanence and bliss, they do not contemplate phenomena as permanent or blissful;
fearing the fall into annihilationism, they do not contemplate them as impermanent and so forth.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva’s wisdom regarding the three times and the three realms does not observe, does not engage in, and does not grasp at signs—knowing them all to be false and illusory—they do not fall into ignorance.
Furthermore, within both the mundane and the supramundane, it is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom.
It is not wisdom because it is empty, because it lacks the characteristic of emptiness, and because it is ultimately pure.
"It is not that he lacks wisdom," because he contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth, thereby entering into the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"It is not that he does not practice wisdom": "non-practice" refers to the cessation of views and the abandonment of attachment to dharmas, through detachment from all bases of reliance.
"Non-wisdom" does not exist herein, because it is free from delusion and distinct from that of ordinary worldlings.
Furthermore, since the practitioner upholds the precepts, cultivates meditative concentration, and practices various contemplations, how can one say "it is non-wisdom"?
As it is said in the *Buddhasattvārtha-sūtra*:
“The practitioner relinquishes all phenomena, Does not rely even upon wisdom, And is without any conceptual discrimination; This is definitive knowledge!”
The fifteenth chapter, "The Explanation of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise," is concluded.

Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 16: On the Vehicle of Vehicles. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Pūrṇa:
"In what way is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to 'mount' the Great Vehicle?"
Pūrṇa replied to Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he mounts the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), yet he does not apprehend the perfection of giving, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the recipient; because of this non-apprehension, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounting the perfection of giving."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they mount the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation;

they mount the perfection of wisdom as well, yet they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva, because of this non-apprehension. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounting the perfection of wisdom.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to ride upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists in practicing the four foundations of mindfulness with a mind directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because phenomena are subject to disintegration;

and so on, up to practicing the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) with a mind directed toward omniscience, because phenomena are subject to disintegration—and even these [practices] are unattainable.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this thought:
"A bodhisattva exists as a mere name, because sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
'Form exists as a mere name, because form is unapprehendable;'"
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness exist as mere names, for consciousness cannot be apprehended.
The eye exists as a mere name, for the eye cannot be apprehended;
and so it is for everything up to the mind.
The four foundations of mindfulness exist as mere names, because the four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable;
and so on, up to the eightfold noble path existing as mere names, because the eightfold noble path is unattainable.
Inner emptiness exists as a mere name, because inner emptiness cannot be apprehended;
up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which exists as a mere name, because the emptiness of non-existence and existence cannot be apprehended;
up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which exist as mere names, because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha cannot be apprehended.
The suchness of all dharmas exists as a mere name, because suchness cannot be apprehended;
the characteristics of dharmas, the nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, and the reality-limit exist as mere names, because the reality-limit cannot be apprehended.
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi and the Buddha exist as mere names, for the Buddha cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, fulfills the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers, matures sentient beings, travels from one buddha-field to another buddha-field to reverently serve, make offerings to, honor, and praise the Buddhas, and receives the teachings of the Dharma from those Buddhas— this is what is called the bodhisattva’s Great Vehicle.

This Bodhisattva, mounting this Great Vehicle, travels from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, purifying Buddha-worlds and bringing sentient beings to maturity, yet from the very beginning has no conception of a Buddha-field, nor any conception of sentient beings.
This person dwells within the non-dual Dharma and assumes a body for the sake of sentient beings; according to what is appropriate for them, they transform their own form to teach and transform them;
even until reaching all-knowledge, they never depart from the Bodhisattva vehicle.

Once this bodhisattva has attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), he turns the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, nor by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, or the people of the world.
At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, joyfully called his name and praised him, saying:
"In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, a certain Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, mounted upon the Great Vehicle, has attained all-knowledge and turns the wheel of Dharma!"
“Śāriputra! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva riding upon the Great Vehicle.
[Treatise] Explanation:
Pūrṇa clarifies the meaning of "mahāsattva" through three matters; the first two have already been explained, and now the third matter—"riding upon the Mahāyāna"—is addressed, to which Pūrṇa replies.
Some say: When a bodhisattva simply gives away internal and external things but is unable to destroy the mark of self-grasping (*ātman*), this is called "Great Adornment" (*mahā-vyūha*);

if he can destroy the mark of self-grasping and enter the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) while not yet having entered the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), this is called "Setting Out with Great Adornment."
By means of the emptiness of sentient beings, one enters into the emptiness of dharmas and practices the dāna-pāramitā, without perceiving the three things:
the giver, the recipient, and the gift. One who can act in this manner is said to be "mounted upon the Mahāyāna."
The other pāramitās are also like this.

With an unadulterated mind, free from all afflictions and the mentalities of the two vehicles, this bodhisattva practices the four foundations of mindfulness for the sake of sarvajñā (all-knowledge); yet even the cultivation of their characteristics cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
This is called "riding upon the Great Vehicle.
This applies likewise even to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are mere provisional names, and that within the conjunction of names there are yet further names;
All that is mundane or supramundane is merely a provisional designation;
this is called "riding upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva gives rise to the great armor and becomes fully endowed with the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers.
Because they are fully endowed with the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, they bring sentient beings to maturity and travel from one buddha-field to another;
in all the lands they pass through, they rain down lotuses made of the seven treasures to make offerings to the Buddhas and rescue sentient beings from the three evil realms.
They manifest countless transformations, each appearing before all the Buddhas to hear and receive the transformative teachings of the Mahāyāna;
from before the Buddhas, they proceed toward the characteristics of the Mahāyāna.
Riding upon this Mahāyāna, they travel from one Buddha-land to another, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying the Buddha-worlds.
They do not give rise to the notion of sentient beings, nor do they grasp at the signs of Buddha-fields.
Abiding in the stage of non-dual entry, they transform and deliver those among all sentient beings who are ready to be saved, taking on physical forms for the sake of sentient beings.
They constantly ride upon the Great Vehicle without ever resting.

These bodhisattvas, riding the Great Vehicle, attain buddhahood and turn the wheel of Dharma—a wheel that cannot be turned by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, let alone by other ordinary, inferior beings!
The Buddhas of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions praise this bodhisattva, saying:
"In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, a certain bodhisattva has mounted the Great Vehicle; he has attained Buddhahood and turns the wheel of Dharma."
Such characteristics as these are called "riding upon the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, the Great Vehicle is named the six *pāramitās* of ultimate purity.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva rides the Great Vehicle, he adorns himself with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Abiding within this vehicle, the bodhisattva simultaneously manifests countless bodies, traveling to the worlds of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and deliver sentient beings.
This bodhisattva never departs from the presence of the Buddhas until the attainment of the Buddha-way, always riding upon this Great Vehicle.

Chapter 17: Neither Bound Nor Liberated The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter "Neither Bound Nor Liberated," Number Seventeen [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Great Adornment: what is this Great Adornment?
What kind of Bodhisattva is able to achieve this Great Adornment?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“The great adornment of the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of the adornment of the pāramitās from dānapāramitā up to prajñāpāramitā;
the adornment of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
and the adornment of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.”
From the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities, they were adorned with all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Their manifested bodies were adorned like those of a Buddha, and their radiance shone throughout the trichiliocosm; likewise, it illuminated worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and so too did it extend to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and likewise the worlds in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
so too did it happen in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the great adornment of the Mahāyāna of the dānapāramitā, transforms this trichiliocosm into lapis lazuli;

he manifests as a wheel-turning sage king and, according to the desires of sentient beings, provides them with food when they need food, drink when they need drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, dwellings, lamps, and medicines—giving them all their various necessities.
Having given these, he preaches the Dharma for them, namely the Dharma that corresponds to the six pāramitās.
Sentient beings who hear this Dharma will never be separated from the six pāramitās, up until their attainment of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This is called the Great Ornament of the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Subhūti, it is like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people before them; to those who need food, he gives food; to those who need drink, he gives drink; and even all their various necessities, he provides them entirely.
“What do you think, Subhūti?
Does that illusionist actually have any sentient beings to whom he gives?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: he manifests as a universal monarch (cakravartin), fully endowed with all [regalia]. To those who need food, he gives food; to those who need drink, he gives drink; indeed, he provides everything they require.
Although there is giving, in reality, there is nothing given.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because the characteristics of all dharmas are like an illusion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they manifest birth in the family of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and teach and transform sentient beings through the ten paths of wholesome action. Moreover, they teach and transform sentient beings through the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma).
Those who hear these teachings will reach unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), never departing from these dharmas.

It is, for example, as if a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to conjure a great multitude at a crossroads and teach them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action; furthermore, he would teach them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Does that illusionist truly have any sentient beings whom he teaches and transforms to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!”

“Subhūti! It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva: by means of the ten paths of wholesome action, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to practice them, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha;
yet in reality, there are no sentient beings who practice the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities.”
Why is this? Because the characteristics of all dharmas are like an illusion, Subhūti!
This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the perfection of patience teaches and transforms sentient beings through forbearance.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), instruct and transform sentient beings so that they are established in the perfection of patience?
Subhūti! From the moment they first resolve their minds toward awakening, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are thus adorned with great majesty:

even if all sentient beings should come to revile them or harm them with swords and staves, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not give rise to a single thought of malice therein, and they also teach all sentient beings to practice this patience.
For example, suppose a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to create a great multitude at a crossroads by means of illusion and cause them to practice patience;
the rest is as explained above.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), teaches and transforms all sentient beings, causing them to practice the perfection of vigor. Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), teach all sentient beings to practice the perfection of vigor? Subhūti!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), exerts diligence of body and mind to teach and transform sentient beings.
It is like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude and instructs them to practice diligence of body and mind;
the rest is as explained above.
This is called the great adornment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the dhyānapāramitā, teaches all sentient beings to practice the dhyānapāramitā.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of dhyāna, teach all sentient beings to practice the perfection of dhyāna? Subhūti!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the equality of all dharmas and does not perceive any dharma as either distracted or concentrated.
Thus, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva,
dwelling in the dhyānapāramitā, teaches all sentient beings to practice the dhyānapāramitā, and until they reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they never depart from the dhyānapāramitā.
For example, suppose a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create a great multitude of people at a crossroads and instruct them to practice the perfection of dhyāna;
the rest is as explained above.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom and teaches all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom and teach all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is no dharma that attains this shore or the other shore.
Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding within the perfection of wisdom, teaches all sentient beings to practice the perfection of wisdom.
It is, for example, like a magician or a magician’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures a great multitude of people and instructs them to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Great Adornment consists of manifesting his own body as appropriate throughout worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, abiding in the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā, and likewise teaching sentient beings to practice the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā.
These sentient beings practice this Dharma until they reach unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never departing from this Dharma. Subhūti,
it is as if a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to create sentient beings at a crossroads and instruct them to practice the six pāramitās.
The rest is as explained above. Thus, Subhūti,
this is called the great adornment of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accords with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is that they do not give rise to this thought:
'I establish so many people in the dānapāramitā, and I do not establish so many people in the dānapāramitā.'"
"Even so it is with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
He does not give rise to this thought:
'I have taught so many people to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and I have not taught so many people to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness.'"
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Furthermore, they do not give rise to this thought:

"I have taught so many people so that they may attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), the path of a pratyekabuddha, or all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
"Nor do I instruct a certain number of people to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge.

Rather, I shall cause immeasurable, boundless, incalculable sentient beings to abide in the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; I shall establish sentient beings in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and I shall cause immeasurable, boundless, incalculable sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to all-knowledge."

It is, for example, like a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice who, at a crossroads, conjures up a great multitude of people and instructs them to abide in the six pāramitās, even until they attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
The rest is as explained above.
Subhūti! This is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Commentary:
The above, Pūrṇa, explained the characteristics of the Great Adornment and the Adornment of Making the Great Vow. Now, Subhūti thinks:
"Pūrṇa has not yet attained omniscience; although he speaks of the Great Adornment, there may be some error in it."
Therefore, he questioned the Buddha to seek definitive certainty.
The Buddha, for the sake of Subhūti, explained "the great adornment of the dānapāramitā, up to and including omniscience."
By virtue of the retribution of these various wholesome dharmas, they attain the great supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.

For the sake of sentient beings who delight in the path of renunciation, they manifest transformed buddha-bodies, emitting great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions and causes the great earth to tremble. They cause sentient beings to resolve their minds upon awakening and practice wholesome dharmas, preaching the Dharma to them according to their respective capacities so that they may attain the three vehicles.

For the sake of sentient beings who delight in worldly life, he becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King and transforms the three thousandfold world-system entirely into lapis lazuli so that there are no obstructions;

riding a chariot of the seven treasures, his body emits radiance and rains down all manner of precious objects, satisfying the needs of sentient beings according to their requirements, and thereafter preaches the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas for them.
The Bodhisattva, dwelling within the Mahāyāna, benefits sentient beings through two kinds of giving: namely, the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma.

Having heard this, sentient beings practice the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas), reaching unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), never departing from these dharmas until the end.
Although the bodhisattva dwells within these transformations, he does not give rise to signs of attachment toward any phenomena, nor does he become conceited.
Subhūti then had this thought:
"If a bodhisattva can perform such a great feat, yet his outflows are not yet exhausted, how is it that he attains non-attachment toward all phenomena and does not give rise to a conceited mind?"
In this regard, the Buddha himself spoke a parable:
"Suppose a magician, at a crossroads, conjures various objects by transformation and is able to give them all to people according to whatever they require."
What do you think, Subhūti?
Does that illusionist actually have anything given away?
Is there anyone who receives it, or anyone who uses it?
Subhūti said: "This is merely empty deception; in reality, nothing exists.
The Buddha said:

"The Bodhisattva is also like this: although he manifests as the body of a Buddha or a Wheel-Turning Sage King and bestows material wealth and the Dharma upon sentient beings, he is just like a magician who truly gives nothing away."
Why is this? Because the characteristics of all phenomena are ultimately empty and like an illusion.
The same applies to the other five perfections; they should be distinguished according to their respective meanings.

Furthermore, by virtue of the causes and conditions of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), one becomes wealthy and noble among humans as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin);
through the remaining perfections, one may become a Brahmā king or a Dharma-body Bodhisattva.
Question: Apart from the six pāramitās, what further dharmas are there that can serve as adornments? Answer:
All virtues are subsumed within the six pāramitās.
Some say: "There are additionally the pāramitā of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā), skillful means (upāya), and so forth."

In worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he manifests various causes and conditions and preaches the Dharma according to those who are to be saved, causing sentient beings to abide in the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, the resolute vow is called the Great Ornament (*mahā-vyūha*). This means that a bodhisattva does not form such a thought as:
"I shall deliver so many people and establish them in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), but I cannot deliver others";
and this applies likewise up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Nor does he form this thought:
"I shall cause so many people to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, and I cannot cause so many people to attain the fruit of srotāpanna";
and it is the same even up to the Buddha-way.
"I shall cause immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings to abide in all merits, from the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Establishing oneself as like a magician" is as previously explained.
This is called setting forth the great adornment.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
