According to the meaning I have heard from the Buddha, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the absence of great adornment constitutes great adornment, because all dharmas are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*). That is to say: form is empty of the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristic of consciousness.
The eye is empty of the characteristic of the eye, and so on up to the mind, which is empty of the characteristic of the mind;
form is empty of the characteristic of form, and so on up to mental phenomena, which are empty of the characteristic of mental phenomena.
Eye-consciousness is empty of the characteristic of eye-consciousness, and so on up to mind-consciousness, which is empty of the characteristic of mind-consciousness.
Eye-contact is empty of the characteristic of eye-contact, and so on up to mental-contact, which is empty of the characteristic of mental-contact;

the sensation produced through the conditions of eye-contact is empty of the characteristic of sensation, and so on up to the sensation produced through the conditions of mental-contact, which is empty of the characteristic of sensation.
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of giving is empty of the mark of the perfection of giving, and so on, up to the perfection of wisdom being empty of the mark of the perfection of wisdom.”

Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness; up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness; up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Bodhisattvas and the marks of a bodhisattva are empty,
World-Honored One!
For this reason, it should be known that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the absence of great adornment constitutes great adornment."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Subhūti!
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is not a conditioned phenomenon, and sentient beings are also not conditioned phenomena; for these sentient beings, the bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) not a conditioned phenomenon, and these sentient beings also not conditioned phenomena, yet the bodhisattva undertakes this great adornment for the sake of these sentient beings?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Because an agent cannot be apprehended, all dharmas (sarvadharma) are neither created nor arisen; likewise, these sentient beings are also neither created nor arisen.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
Form is neither created nor uncreated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither created nor uncreated.
The eye is neither an agent nor a non-agent; this extends up to the mind, which is neither an agent nor a non-agent.

Visible forms up to mental phenomena, visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, visual contact up to mental contact, and the feelings produced by conditions of visual contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mental contact, are neither agents nor non-agents.
Subhūti! I neither act nor do not act; even the knower and the seer neither act nor do not act. Why is this?
Because these dharmas are ultimately unattainable.
Subhūti, a dream is neither an act nor a non-act. Why is this?
Because they are ultimately unattainable;
illusions, echoes, shadows, mirages, and transformations are neither created nor uncreated. Why is this?
Because they are ultimately unattainable.
Subhūti! Inner emptiness is neither created nor uncreated, because it is ultimately unapprehendable;
this extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is neither created nor uncreated, because it is ultimately unapprehendable.
Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness are neither created nor uncreated, because they are ultimately unapprehendable;
this extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are neither created nor uncreated. Why is this?
This is because these dharmas are ultimately unattainable.
Subhūti, the suchness of all dharmas,

their dharma-characteristic, their dharma-nature, their dharma-abiding, their dharma-position, and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) are neither created nor uncreated, for they are ultimately unattainable.
Subhūti! Awakening (bodhi) is neither made nor unmade, because it is ultimately unattainable;
omniscience (sarvajñā) and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) are neither made nor unmade, because they are ultimately unattainable.

For this reason, Subhūti, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is neither a created nor an originated dharma, and these sentient beings are likewise neither created nor originated dharmas; for the sake of these sentient beings, the bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, World-Honored One, form is neither bound nor liberated;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Subhūti:
"Is form unbound and unliberated?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness unbound and unliberated?"
Subhūti said: “So it is! So it is!”
“Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Subhūti:
“What kind of form is neither bound nor liberated?”
“What is it that is neither bound nor liberated regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Subhūti replied:
“Just as form is like a dream—neither bound nor liberated—so too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness like a dream—neither bound nor liberated.”
“Like an echo, like a shadow, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like a transformation—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Past form is neither bound nor liberated; past feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Future form is neither bound nor liberated; future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Present form is neither bound nor liberated; present feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is there neither bondage nor liberation?
Because this form (*rūpa*) is non-existent, there is neither bondage nor liberation;
because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are non-existent, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, there is neither bondage nor liberation. "Pūrṇa!
Good form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without bondage and without liberation; [the same applies to]..."
Unwholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated;
indeterminate form is neither bound nor liberated, and indeterminate feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Worldly and supramundane, contaminated and uncontaminated form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because there is nothing that exists, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Pūrṇa!
"All dharmas are likewise neither bound nor liberated, because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen. Pūrṇa!..."
The perfection of giving is neither bound nor liberated; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom are neither bound nor liberated.
Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.
“Pūrṇa! Internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated; even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, it is neither bound nor liberated.
The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated; even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are neither bound nor liberated.”
Because it is non-existent, because it is detached, because it is quiescent, and because it is unarisen, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is without bondage or liberation; omniscience (sarvajñā) and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñā) are without bondage or liberation.
The Bodhisattva is neither bound nor liberated, and the Buddha likewise is neither bound nor liberated;
because they are non-existent, detached, quiescent, and unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.

“Pūrṇa! The suchness of all dharmas, their marks, their nature, their stability, their fixed position, the limit of reality, and unconditioned dharmas are neither bound nor liberated. Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen, they are neither bound nor liberated.”

“Pūrṇa! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which is neither bound nor liberated; likewise, the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) are neither bound nor liberated.”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of giving that is neither bound nor liberated, up to and including dwelling in the perfection of wisdom that is neither bound nor liberated;
they dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness that are neither bound nor liberated, up to and including dwelling in the knowledge of all modes that is neither bound nor liberated;
they bring sentient beings to maturity that is neither bound nor liberated, and they purify buddha-fields that is neither bound nor liberated.
Those who are neither bound nor liberated should make offerings to all Buddhas; those who are neither bound nor liberated should listen to the Dharma.

Those who are neither bound nor liberated shall never be separated from all Buddhas; those who are neither bound nor liberated shall never be separated from the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); those who are neither bound nor liberated shall never be separated from the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*).
Those who are neither bound nor liberated shall never be separated from the gateways of dhāraṇī; those who are neither bound nor liberated shall never be separated from all samādhis.
Without bondage and without liberation, one shall give rise to the knowledge of the modes of the path; without bondage and without liberation, one shall attain all-knowledge.
Without bondage and without liberation, the wheel of Dharma is turned; without bondage and without liberation, sentient beings are established in the three vehicles.
In this way, Pūrṇa!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās that are neither bound nor liberated, one should know that all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated, because they are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are quiescent, and because they are unarisen.
"Pūrṇa! This is called the great adornment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is neither bound nor liberated.
[Treatise] Commentary:
Subhūti said:
"As I have heard the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching, that which is without great adornment is itself great adornment. Why is this?
Because its own-characteristic is empty."
Question: For what reason does Subhūti speak in this way? Answer:
The Buddha has spoken on the meaning of donning the great armor; it is profoundly deep, difficult to attain, and difficult to understand.
When the sentient beings in the assembly heard this, their minds may have faltered or retreated, thinking:

"If such armor is ultimately empty, how is it that by the power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), one can simultaneously reach worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions to bring comfort to sentient beings? He said:
"This is the business of a noble king; how could we possibly know it?
For this reason, Subhūti said:
"To set forth the great adornment is neither profound nor difficult!"

Not only is the great adornment itself empty of intrinsic characteristics—making it easy to practice and easy to attain—but form and the fixed characteristics within form are likewise unattainable; this applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

If a bodhisattva can thus know that all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness and quiescent extinction, yet does not abandon their original vow or their diligent effort, for this reason it is called "donning the great armor," and it is not difficult to attain.
The Buddha validated what Subhūti had said, hence he said, “So it is.
Since all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are false and deceptive, he said:
“All-knowledge (sarvajñā) is without conditioned activity;”
"Because sentient beings are ultimately empty, there is also no phenomenon that is created.
The Buddha said:
"Because an agent cannot be apprehended, omniscience does not have the characteristic of being created."
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended;
because an agent cannot be apprehended, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) has the characteristic of being neither made nor arisen.
Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) likewise has nothing it can produce, because dharmas are empty; this applies even to the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).

Subhūti and others maintain that among all phenomena there is no fixed characteristic of action; for example, although an illusion lacks substantial reality, it possesses the characteristics of coming and going.
For this reason, the Buddha says:
"Like an illusion, like a mirage, and so forth, they lack the characteristic of action, because they are ultimately unattainable."

At that time, the listeners had this thought: "The eighteen kinds of emptiness can destroy all dharmas; thus they are functional, and thus they are real"—thereby asserting that there is something "produced."
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"From internal emptiness being without activity, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and even to the eighteen unique qualities, they are likewise without activity."
If it is argued that the eighteen kinds of emptiness are conditioned, deceptive, and without reality, and therefore may be without activity;
whereas *tathatā*, the *dharmatā*, and the *bhūtakoṭi* are true dharmas, and thus must possess activity!

Why is this? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) serve as mutual causes for one another, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) also act as causes for conditioned phenomena.
The Buddha said:
“Suchness, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, the stability of dharmas, and the fixed position of dharmas are likewise without activity.
Furthermore, it is said:
“The bodhisattva, the Buddha, and all-knowledge are real dharmas that are capable of performing functions.”
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"Because these dharmas are also ultimately empty, they are likewise without action.
This is because the characteristic of action arises from causes and conditions.
The practitioner reflects, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is most difficult!
It is most rare!"
"Since all dharmas are entirely without action, without bondage, and without liberation, how shall we be delivered from suffering?
For this reason, Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the five aggregates are without bondage and without liberation."
"If ultimate emptiness has no agent, who is bound and who is liberated?
The dharmas of ordinary beings are deceptive and unobtainable; therefore, they are not bound.
The dharmas of the noble ones are ultimately empty and unobtainable; therefore, they are not liberated.

Just as with the five aggregates that are like a dream, so it is with the five aggregates of the three periods of time, the five aggregates of the wholesome and unwholesome, and all dharmas; even up to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is likewise.
Because they are non-existent, because they are detached, and because they are unborn, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s bodhisattva path that is neither bound nor liberated.
Abiding in this path, one is not dragged down into the state of ordinary beings by the various afflictions; therefore, it is called "unbound.
Yet, because one does not destroy the afflictions by means of the various untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), it is called "unliberated."

They transform and guide sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields; even regarding the five supernormal powers, the five eyes, the various dhāraṇīs, and the gates of samādhi, they never depart from the Buddha. Furthermore, they establish sentient beings in the three vehicles, yet there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-existent, detached, quiescent, unarisen, and ultimately empty.
By such causes and conditions as these, it is called the mark of the great adornment undertaken by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely: neither bound nor liberated.
18. Chapter on the Mahāyāna. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Eighteenth Chapter, "The Mahāyāna. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
How should one know that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has set out upon the Mahāyāna?
From where does this vehicle depart?
To what destination does this vehicle go?
Where will it abide?
And who is it that shall ride upon this vehicle and depart?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "You asked:
'What is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?'"
“Subhūti! The six pāramitās are the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
What are the six? They are:”
The perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
“What is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*),

Subhūti? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), gives all that is internal and external as a gift, sharing it with all sentient beings and dedicating it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), by means of non-apprehension.”
Subhūti! This is called the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is called the śīlapāramitā?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), personally practices the ten paths of wholesome action and also teaches others to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, doing so by way of non-apprehension, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-attachment to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
“What is called the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), personally fulfills patience and also teaches others to practice patience, by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of patience.”
"What is called the *vīryapāramitā*?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to *sarvajñatā*, practices the five *pāramitās* with unremitting diligence, and likewise establishes all sentient beings in the five *pāramitās* by means of non-apprehension, this is called the *vīryapāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"What is called the dhyānapāramitā? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñatā, enters the various dhyānas through his own skillful means without being reborn according to those dhyānas, and also teaches others to enter the various dhyānas by way of non-apprehension—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dhyānapāramitā."
“What is meant by ‘prajñāpāramitā’? Subhūti,

it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to sarvajñatā, does not cling to any phenomena and also contemplates the nature of all phenomena, because they employ the principle of non-apprehension.”

Furthermore, they teach others not to cling to any phenomena and observe the nature of all phenomena through the principle of non-apprehension; this is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
“Subhūti! This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess another Mahāyāna, namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is internal emptiness?
The Buddha said:
"Internal dharmas are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The eye is empty of the eye, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?"

Such is their inherent nature. The ear is empty of the ear; the nose is empty of the nose; the tongue is empty of the tongue; the body is empty of the body; the mind is empty of the mind, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
“What is external emptiness?
External phenomena are form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects.
Form is empty of form, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.”
Why is this? Because such is their nature.

Sound is empty of sound; fragrance is empty of fragrance; taste is empty of taste; touch is empty of touch; phenomena are empty of phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called external emptiness.
“What is internal-and-external emptiness?
Internal and external phenomena refer to the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases.
Internal phenomena are empty of internal phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.”
Why is this? Because such is their nature.
External phenomena and external phenomena are empty, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
“What is the emptiness of emptiness?
All dharmas are empty, and this very emptiness is also empty, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is that?”
Its nature is thus;
this is called the emptiness of emptiness.
What is the great emptiness?
“The eastern direction, the eastern direction is empty, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.”

The south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—these directions, including the four intermediate points and above and below, are empty because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Its nature is thus of itself;
this is called the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā).
What is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?
“The ultimate truth is called nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Its nature is thus of itself;
this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
“Conditioned phenomena are called the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The desire realm is empty of the desire realm; the form realm is empty of the form realm; the formless realm is empty of the formless realm, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.”
Why is this? Because its nature is such.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned.
"What is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
Unconditioned phenomena are defined by the characteristic of non-arising, the characteristic of non-abiding, and the characteristic of non-ceasing.
Unconditioned phenomena are empty of unconditioned phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation."
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
"What is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
'Ultimate' refers to the fact that all phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately unobtainable, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this so?"
Its nature is thus;
this is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
What is beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*)?
“If a dharma’s initial point of arrival cannot be apprehended, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.”
"This is called the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?
'Dispersion' refers to the non-extinction of all phenomena, because they are neither permanent nor subject to extinction."
Why is this? Because such is its inherent nature.
This is called the emptiness of dispersion.
“What is the emptiness of nature?

The nature of all phenomena—whether the nature of conditioned phenomena or the nature of unconditioned phenomena—is a nature that was not created by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor was it created by a Buddha, nor was it created by anyone else.”
This nature is empty of nature, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
"This is called the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?

Self-characteristics are: for form (*rūpa*), the characteristic of disintegration; for feeling (*vedanā*), the characteristic of experiencing; for perception (*saṃjñā*), the characteristic of grasping; for formations (*saṃskāra*), the characteristic of conditioning; and for consciousness (*vijñāna*), the characteristic of cognizing."

Thus, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), each being empty of their own intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because such is their very nature.
"This is called the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

All phenomena refer to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; and the eye-element, form-element, and eye-consciousness-element, up to the mind-element, mental-object-element, and mind-consciousness-element."
These dharmas and all dharmas are empty, because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently so.
"This is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
"What is the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*)?
"It is that when one seeks all phenomena, they cannot be apprehended."
This is the emptiness of the unattainable, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because its nature is inherently so.
"This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (anupalambha-śūnyatā).
What is the emptiness of non-existence (abhāva-śūnyatā)?
If a phenomenon does not exist, that too is empty, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation."
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
“What is the emptiness of existing things (*bhāva-śūnyatā*)?
‘Existing things’ refers to the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) within the combination of all phenomena (*dharma*).
This emptiness of existing things exists because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.”
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*).
“What is the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?
Within all phenomena there is non-existence, yet within the combination of all phenomena there is the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
This is the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation.”
Why is this? Because its nature is inherently so.
This is called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Phenomena are empty of the characteristics of phenomena;

non-phenomena are empty of the characteristics of non-phenomena; self-phenomena are empty of the characteristics of self-phenomena; and other-phenomena are empty of the characteristics of other-phenomena."
“What is meant by ‘the emptiness of dharmas in their own nature’?
‘Dharmas’ refers to the five aggregates; that the five aggregates are empty is what is called ‘the emptiness of dharmas in their own nature.
What is meant by ‘the emptiness of non-dharmas in their own nature’?”
“Non-existence is called unconditioned phenomena; this is called the emptiness of the non-existence of non-existent phenomena.
What is called the emptiness of self-phenomena in self-phenomena?
All phenomena are empty of their own nature; this emptiness is not produced by wisdom, nor is it produced by views. This is called the emptiness of self-phenomena in self-phenomena.”
“What is meant by ‘the emptiness of other dharmas in other dharmas’?
Whether a Buddha appears or a Buddha does not appear, the dharma-abiding, the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-position, the dharma-nature, suchness, and the reality-limit remain;
that these various dharmas are empty beyond [such designations] is called the emptiness of other dharmas in other dharmas.”
“This is called the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Question:

This sutra is titled the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and furthermore, the Buddha has commanded Subhūti to explain the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the Bodhisattvas; thus, Subhūti should have asked about the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the Buddha should likewise have answered concerning the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Now, why does Subhūti inquire about the Mahāyāna, and why does the Buddha also respond concerning the Mahāyāna?
The answer is:
Prajñāpāramitā and Mahāyāna have the same meaning; they differ only in name.
If one speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā* or speaks of the Mahāyāna, there is no fault.
The Mahāyāna is named the Buddha-way; by practicing this Dharma, one attains Buddhahood—namely, the six *pāramitās*.
Among these six *pāramitās*, the foremost and greatest is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
As the Buddha explains various great causes and conditions extensively in the "Later Chapter," if he speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
it subsumes the six *pāramitās*; if he speaks of the six *pāramitās*,
it fully explains the bodhisattva path, namely from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*) up until the attainment of Buddhahood.
For example, when a king arrives, he is necessarily accompanied by a retinue; although the attendants are not explicitly mentioned, one should know they are certainly there.

The Mahāyāna is also like this: regarding the practices undertaken by a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way, the various dharmas he cultivates and accumulates, and the diverse teachings he proclaims according to the beings to be saved, are as follows:
The *Utpāda-sūtra*, the *Sarvasattva-saṃśaya-cchedana-sūtra*,
the *Kusala-hasta-sūtra*, the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Megha-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*,
the *Dharmamegha-sūtra*, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*— and other such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sūtras,
whether spoken by the Buddha, by an emanation Buddha, by great bodhisattvas, by śrāvakas,
or by various devas who have attained the Way.
The convergence of these factors is all termed Mahāyāna.
Since the Prajñāpāramitā is the greatest among all these sūtras, when Mahāyāna is mentioned, it should be understood that the Prajñāpāramitā has already been spoken of.
All other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), if not conjoined with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), cannot lead to Buddhahood.
For this reason, all factors conducive to enlightenment are themselves the perfection of wisdom. As the Buddha said to Subhūti in a later chapter:
"The Mahāyāna you describe is not different from the perfection of wisdom."
Question: If that is so, why was "Mahāyāna" not mentioned first at the beginning? Answer:
I have previously stated that the Prajñāpāramitā is the greatest; therefore, it should be explained first.
Furthermore, because the Buddha intended to expound the "Mahāprajñāpāramitā," he emitted a great radiance.
The bodhisattvas from the ten directions each asked their respective Buddha,
"Why is there this radiance now?
Each of those Buddhas replied:
"In the Sahā world there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni who wishes to preach the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thereupon, those bodhisattvas and devas came together in harmony.
Śāriputra asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know all dharmas practice the prajñāpāramitā?”
Furthermore, in the first chapter of the Buddha’s teaching, he praised the merits of the *prajñāpāramitā* in various ways:
“If one wishes to attain these, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
For these and other such reasons, one should first speak of the "Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha then commanded Subhūti:
"Explain the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas!"
Subhūti spoke humbly:
"The Bodhisattva is empty; there is only a name.
Later he said:
"To be able to understand in this way and to fully comprehend the characteristics of a bodhisattva is itself the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having understood this, one asks about the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"; next follows the meaning of "mahāsattva";
within the meaning of "mahāsattva," there are "great adornment" (*mahāvyūha*) and the "Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna*).
Just as a brave warrior, though equipped with various weapons and ornaments, can achieve nothing if he does not mount a swift horse,
so it is with this "Mahāyāna"— in the language of India, it is called "Mahāyāna."
Because the Buddhas have severed attachment to dharmas, and because they clearly understand that the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā is without distinction, the Buddha does not rebuke him.
For this reason, Subhūti again employs different names to inquire about the Mahāyāna.
Question: As stated in the introduction to the Mahāyāna:
"From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the Buddha-way, the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas for the sake of the Buddha-way is all termed Mahāyāna."
"Now, why do you say only that 'the six pāramitās constitute the Mahāyāna'?
The answer is:
as previously stated:
"The Prajñāpāramitā explains the six pāramitās;
explaining the six pāramitās encompasses all wholesome dharmas.
For this reason, one should not ask such a question:
"Since wholesome dharmas are numerous, why speak only of the six pāramitās?
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, from the initial arousal of the mind and the making of vows up to the final skillful means, these correspond to the six pāramitās;
although these various dharmas are not themselves called pāramitās, their meaning is entirely contained within the six pāramitās.
Because the power of the mind is great when first generating the resolve, making vows, and practicing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth, it is called the *vīryapāramitā*.
Because one abandons minor benefits and adopts the Mahāyāna, it is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Expedient means (*upāya*) is itself wisdom; because wisdom is pure and refined, its name is transformed into "expedient means."

The transformation and edification of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-worlds, and so forth, are all contained within the six *pāramitās*, being mutually inclusive according to their respective meanings.
Question:
If this is so, why does the text later further state that "the eighteen emptinesses, the one hundred and eight samādhis, and so forth, are called the Mahāyāna"?
Answer: The six pāramitās constitute the essence of the Mahāyāna; however, their meanings are subsequently analyzed in detail.
For instance, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the forty-two letters, and so forth, are the meaning of the prajñāpāramitā.
The one hundred and eight samādhis and so forth constitute the meaning of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
For this reason, the six pāramitās are taught at the outset.
Question:
Why is it that the six pāramitās are correctly taught—neither more nor less?
The answer is:
The Buddha is the King of Dharma; according to those beings who can be saved, he sometimes teaches them briefly as one, two, three, or four.
At times they are explained extensively, such as the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās* in the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra*.

Furthermore, sentient beings in the six realms all undergo physical and mental suffering: the suffering of torture in the hells; the suffering of mutual slaughter among animals; the suffering of hunger among hungry ghosts; the suffering of seeking desires among humans; the suffering of separation from loved ones among the gods; and the suffering of strife and contention in the realm of the *asuras*.
Because the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and desires to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings in these six realms, he generates the six *pāramitās*.
For this reason, the six pāramitās are taught—neither more nor less.
Question:

The dānapāramitā has various characteristics; why does the Buddha here speak of only five characteristics, namely: "With a mind associated with sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), one relinquishes internal and external things; this merit is shared with all sentient beings and dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by means of non-apprehension"?
Why is it that [the sūtra] does not mention "the mind of great compassion, making offerings to the Buddhas, as well as supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and giving (dāna)," and so forth?
The answer is:
within these five aspects, all forms of giving are subsumed.
"Practicing giving while conjoined with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)" means that this takes the Buddha-way as its object and relies upon the Buddha-way.
"Relinquishing the internal and external" means relinquishing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
"To share with all sentient beings" refers to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Dedication" means that by means of this giving, one seeks only the path of the Buddha and not any other retribution.

"By means of non-apprehension" means that because one has attained a portion of the Prajñāpāramitā that is the true mark of all dharmas, the Dānapāramitā is neither deceptive nor erroneous, and it is also inexhaustible.
Question:
If that is so, then the five kinds of characteristics are unnecessary; it would suffice merely to speak of "the mind associated with omniscience" (*sarvajñatā-saṃprayukta-citta*). Answer:
This matter is indeed so!
However, because sentient beings do not know the meaning of how giving should accord with the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), I therefore distinguish its meaning by means of four points.

Regarding “conforming to the mind of *sarvajñā*”: it means that with the bodhisattva-mind one seeks the *sarvajñā* of a Buddha, taking it as an object, maintaining mindfulness of it, and binding the mind to it.

Holding this practice of giving, one desires to attain the fruit of *sarvajñā*, yet does not seek the causes and conditions of this life—such as fame or gratitude—nor does one seek the wealth and nobility of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) or a celestial king in future lives.

For the sake of delivering sentient beings, one does not seek *nirvāṇa*; rather, one desires to fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas such as omniscience in order to exhaust the suffering of all sentient beings. This is called “conforming to the mind of *sarvajñā*.”
Regarding "internal and external things": "internal" refers to the head, brain, bones, marrow, blood, flesh, and so forth; these are mentioned first because they are difficult to relinquish.
"External things" refer to kingdoms, wives, children, the seven treasures, food, drink, and so forth.
“Sharing with all sentient beings” means that the fruit of the merit of giving is to be enjoyed in common with all sentient beings;
it is like a great landowner who plants grain and eats it together with others.
As for the fruit of a bodhisattva’s merit, all sentient beings come to rely upon it;
it is like a fine fruit tree to which various birds flock.
"Dedication" (pariṇāmanā) refers to the side of this merit: one seeks no other retribution, but seeks only anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Question: Previously it was said, “corresponding to the mind of sarvajñā,” and later it was said, “dedicating. What is the difference between them? Answer:
"Conforming to the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)" serves as the causal condition for generating all merits;
"dedicating" means not seeking other rewards, but seeking only the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, regarding the "mind associated with omniscience" (*sarvajñatā-saṃprayukta-citta*): one practices giving for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As stated in the previous explanation:
"Omniscience is the sovereign; all merits are for the sake of omniscience."
There are two kinds of praise for the Buddha’s wisdom:
first, the unsurpassed right knowledge called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; second, the knowledge of all modes called *sarvajñā*.
"By means of non-apprehension" means that one practices giving with the mind of *prajñāpāramitā*, conforming to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena without deception.
Such are the explanations regarding the meaning of the *dānapāramitā*.
Question:
The *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) encompasses all rules of morality, just as the great ocean gathers all streams.

Such matters as not drinking alcohol, not eating past midday, and not using sticks against sentient beings are not included within the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*). Why, then, do you speak only of the ten wholesome paths?
The answer is:

The Buddha spoke of the six pāramitās as general characteristics; the ten wholesome actions constitute the precepts of general characteristics, while there are immeasurable precepts of specific characteristics.
Not drinking alcohol and not eating past midday are included within non-greed.
Not inflicting punishment upon sentient beings and so forth constitutes entry into non-anger;
the remaining paths follow accordingly according to their respective meanings.
Precepts are termed bodily and vocal karma, and are subsumed within the seven wholesome courses of action.

Regarding the ten paths of wholesome action and their initial and final stages: for example, when one intends to kill, at that time one employs the preliminary means—such as harsh speech, whipping, binding, hacking, or stabbing—even until the victim is on the verge of death; all these belong to the initial stage.
After death, flaying the skin, devouring the flesh, cutting it up, and feeling joy—all these are termed the final stage.
Taking the life itself is the actual substance.
The conjunction of these three factors is collectively termed the unwholesome path of killing.
For this reason, it is known that the teaching of the ten wholesome paths subsumes all precepts.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion and resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he benefits sentient beings through giving, bestowing upon them whatever they require.
Maintaining the precepts means not vexing sentient beings, not inflicting various sufferings upon them, and constantly bestowing fearlessness.
The ten paths of wholesome action constitute the root; all other factors are remote causes and conditions for not vexing sentient beings.

The precepts are for the sake of attaining nirvana in this present life; therefore, although sexual desire does not afflict other sentient beings, it constitutes a grave offense because it binds the mind.
For this reason, among the precepts, sexual desire is treated as the primary transgression.
For laypeople (*avadātavasana*), the precept against killing comes first because they seek merit and fortune.
Bodhisattvas do not seek nirvana in this present life; rather, they traverse through birth and death throughout immeasurable eons, cultivating all manner of meritorious virtues.
The ten paths of wholesome action constitute the original precepts, while the remaining restraints are adventitious.
Furthermore, if a Buddha were to appear in a fortunate age, these precepts would not exist;
for example, although Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in an evil age, these precepts did not exist for twelve years [after his enlightenment]. For this reason, it is known that they are adventitious.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of precepts:
those that exist when a Buddha is present and do not exist when a Buddha is absent;
and the ten wholesome paths of action, which exist constantly whether a Buddha is present or absent.
Furthermore, regarding the precepts within the Vinaya, although they may be minute, they become pure through repentance;
however, even if one repents for violating the ten virtuous precepts, the retribution for offenses leading to the three evil realms is not eliminated.
For example, if a bhikṣu kills an animal, although he may repent, the retribution for his offense is not yet eliminated.
For various reasons such as these, only the ten paths of wholesome action are taught.
To practice it oneself and also to teach others to do so is called the Śīlapāramitā.
Regarding the ten paths of wholesome action:
seven items constitute morality (śīla), while the remaining three serve as its protection; therefore, they are collectively termed the Śīlapāramitā.
The other pāramitās are also like this, to be distinguished according to their respective meanings, as explained at length in the discourse on the "Six Pāramitās" in the first chapter.
This sūtra is named the *Prajñāpāramitā*; the name *prajñāpāramitā* signifies the characteristic of relinquishment.
For this reason, within all dharmas, one always employs non-apprehension.
A question is asked:
If it is already difficult to gather all wholesome dharmas by employing apprehension, how much more so when employing non-apprehension!
The answer is:
If one attains this wisdom of non-attainment, at that time it may obstruct wholesome conduct or give rise to false doubt;
if one does not attain this wisdom of non-attainment, at that time there is nothing to obstruct, nor does false doubt arise.
The Buddha likewise does not practice the various paths of goodness with a mind attached to or grasping at signs.
Why is this? That which dwells in the world through falsehood ultimately returns to extinction.
If one cultivates goodness with an attached mind, it is easy for it to be destroyed;
if one becomes attached to emptiness and gives rise to regret, one will lose this very path!
It is like fire arising from among the grasses: it is extinguished when it encounters water.
If fire were to arise within water, nothing could extinguish it.
A bodhisattva who is newly practicing and whose mind is attached to grasping at signs may cultivate merit, but this is like fire arising from grass; it is easily extinguished.

However, if a bodhisattva has realized the true nature of reality (dharmatā) and performs various practices with a heart of great compassion, they are difficult to overcome, like fire arising within water, which nothing can extinguish.
For this reason, although one practices all the various deeds with a mind that realizes non-attainment, the mind does not become weak, nor do doubt or regret arise.
This is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the six pāramitās.
As explained in detail in the "First Chapter," each and every *pāramitā* is fully possessed.
Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* is taught within the six *pāramitās*: it is non-attachment to all phenomena.
Why is this? It is because of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Regarding the discourse on the "Eighteen Emptinesses," as in the first chapter, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in the eighteen kinds of emptiness should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
This meaning should be explained in detail here.
Question:
Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness, it is stated after each—such as internal emptiness and the others—that they are "neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
What is the meaning of this? Answer:
If a person does not practice this emptiness, they will inevitably fall into one of two extremes: either permanence or annihilation.
Why is this? If all phenomena were substantially existent, there would be no possibility of their cessation, and thus one would fall into the extreme of permanence.
Just as when a person leaves one house and enters another, although they are not seen by the eyes, it is not said that they do not exist;
so too it is with all phenomena: as they pass from the future world into the present world, and from the present world into the past world, in this way they are not extinguished.
The practitioner regards conditioned existence as a source of affliction and uses emptiness to destroy that existence;
yet, if the mind further prizes emptiness and becomes attached to it, one falls into nihilism.
For this reason, one practices this emptiness to destroy existence, while also remaining unattached to emptiness itself.

Departing from these two extremes, one practices these eighteen kinds of emptiness by way of the Middle Way and, with a heart of great compassion, acts for the sake of delivering sentient beings. For this reason, following each of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, it is said that they are "neither permanent nor annihilated"; this is called the Mahāyāna.
If one differs from this, they are but a madman of frivolous proliferation, attaining nothing at all within the Buddha-dharma;
it is like a person who takes a crystal bead from a heap of precious jewels—though it may look good to the eye, it has no value.
Question:
If the eighteen kinds of emptiness already encompass all forms of emptiness, why are the four kinds of emptiness further explained? Answer:
Among the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the emptiness of manifestation encompasses them all.
The Buddhas have two ways of teaching the Dharma:
either beginning with brevity and ending with detail, or beginning with detail and ending with brevity.
The initial section is concise while the subsequent is detailed for the purpose of explaining the meaning;
the initial section is detailed while the subsequent is concise for the purpose of easy retention.
Alternatively, it is to provide a brief summary of the essentials for sentient beings in later assemblies, or to do so by means of verses.
Now, before the Buddha, the eighteen kinds of emptiness have been explained in detail; subsequently, the characteristics of the four kinds of emptiness will be explained briefly.
Regarding "the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmadharmalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*): within all phenomena, their characteristic marks cannot be apprehended;
just as within form (*rūpa*), the characteristic mark of form cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, because no phenomenon arises within phenomena, it is called "the emptiness of phenomena and phenomena" (*dharmadharmāśūnyatā*).
Regarding "the emptiness of non-phenomena and non-phenomena": unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are termed "non-phenomena."
Why is this? Because characteristics cannot be apprehended.
Question:
The Buddha has taught the unconditioned dharma by means of three characteristics; why then do you say it is "without characteristics"?
The answer is: Not so!

Because it subverts arising, one speaks of "non-arising"; because it subverts abiding, one speaks of "non-abiding"; because it subverts cessation, one speaks of "non-cessation. These names all exist from the perspective of the limits of arising, abiding, and cessation; there is no separate dharma of non-arising or non-cessation apart from these.
This is called "the emptiness of non-existence and non-existence.
This meaning is as explained in the section on "the emptiness of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Regarding "the self-nature of phenomena is empty of its own self-nature," "self-nature of phenomena" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Intrinsic nature is of two kinds:
first, that which is like worldly phenomena, such as the solidity of earth and so forth;
second, that which the sages know as suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality.
This dharma is empty. Why is this so?
Because there is no duality of natures known through wisdom and vision, as previously explained.
Question:
Since *tathatā*, *dharmatā*, and the *bhūtakoṭi* are already included within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, why are they mentioned again? Answer:
When observing and discerning the time, one explains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the five aggregates as the *dharmatā*,
suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); furthermore,
it is not by means of the wisdom of emptiness that they are made empty, for their nature is inherently so.
Question:
Just as form is its own dharma,
consciousness is the dharma of another.

Why is it said here that "tathatā, dharmatā, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) abide eternally whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha; beyond this is called the emptiness of other phenomena (para-dharma-śūnyatā)"?
Answer: There are those who, because they have not yet skillfully severed the fetter of views, give rise to attachment in various places.
When such people hear of this Suchness (tathatā), the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), they say, "Beyond this, there are still further dharmas."
For this reason, it is said that "even the limit of reality (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) are empty.

The samādhi that encompasses all states with contention and without contention; the samādhi that takes no pleasure in any dwelling place;

"What is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
Knowing the spheres of activity of all samādhis is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
What is called the Ratnamudrā Samādhi?"
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to seal all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Jewel Seal Samādhi (*ratnamudrā-samādhi*).
What is called the Lion’s Play Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to play among all samādhis like a lion; therefore, it is called the Lion’s Play Samādhi (*siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*).
What is called the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all samādhis like the pure moon; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon.
What is called the Samādhi of the Lunar Banner Mark?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to maintain the characteristics of all samādhis; this is called the Moon Banner Mark Samādhi (*candradhvajaketu-samādhi*).
What is called the Emergence from All Dharmas Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to bring forth all samādhis; this is called the Emergence from All Dharmas Samādhi (*sarvadharmotthāpana-samādhi*).
What is called the samādhi of observing the summit?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to observe the summit of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the samādhi of observing the summit.
What is called the samādhi of the ultimate nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one definitively knows the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); this is called the *sarvadharmatā-vyavasthāna* samādhi.
What is called the *sarvadhvajāgra-lakṣaṇa* samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to uphold the banners of all samādhis; this is called the *sarvadhvajāgra-lakṣaṇa* samādhi.
What is called the Vajra Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to shatter all other samādhis; therefore, it is named the Vajra Samādhi.
What is called the Entry into the Seal of Dharma Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enters the seals of all dharmas; this is called the "Samādhi of Entering the Seals of Dharma" (*dharmamudrāpraveśa-samādhi*).
What is called the "Samādhi of the King’s Firm Establishment" (*samādhirājavyavasthāna-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is firmly established and dwells among all samādhis like a king; this is called the "Samādhi of the King’s Firm Establishment."
What is called the "Radiating Light Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to emit light that illuminates all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Radiating Light Samādhi.
What is called the "Powerful Progress Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to exercise power and influence over all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Power-Advancement (*balavikramita*).
What is called the Samādhi of High Emergence (*udgata*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to increase all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of High Emergence.
What is called the samādhi of "certain entry into eloquence"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to eloquently expound upon all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of certain entry into eloquence.
What is called the Samādhi of Explaining Names?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to explain the names of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Explaining Names.
What is called the Samādhi of Contemplating Directions?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to contemplate the directions of all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Contemplating Directions.
What is called the Dhāraṇīmudrā Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one maintains the seals of all samādhis; this is called the Dhāraṇīmudrā Samādhi.
What is called the "Non-deceptive Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not deceive regarding any samādhis; therefore, it is called the Non-deceptive Samādhi.
What is called the "Samādhi that Encompasses the Ocean of All Dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to encompass all samādhis, just as the waters of the great ocean; this is called the "Samādhi that Encompasses the Ocean of All Dharmas.
What is called the "Samādhi that Pervasively Covers Space"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one pervasively covers all samādhis like space; this is called the "Pervasive Space Samādhi" (Gaganagañja-samādhi).
What is called the "Vajra-Wheel Samādhi" (Vajramaṇḍala-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to maintain the components of all samādhis; this is called the Vajracakra Samādhi.
What is called the Ratnavicchitti Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one cuts off the defilements of all samādhis; this is called the Ratnavicchitti Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of "Able to Illuminate"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to manifest and illuminate all samādhis with light; this is called the samādhi of "Able to Illuminate.
What is called the samādhi of "Not Seeking"?
Abiding in this samādhi, there is no dharma to be sought; this is called the "Samādhi of Non-Seeking" (*anarthābhiniveśa-samādhi*).
What is called the "Samādhi of Non-Abiding" (*anālaya-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharma abiding within all samādhis; this is called the "Samādhi of Non-Abiding."
What is called the "mindless samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind and its mental factors do not function; this is called the mindless samādhi.
What is called the "pure lamp samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one acts as a light among all samādhis like a lamp; this is called the *Vimalapradīpa* (Pure Lamp) Samādhi.
What is called the *Anantaprabha* (Boundless Light) Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one provides boundless illumination for all other samādhis; therefore, it is called the "Boundless Illumination Samādhi" (Anantaprabhāsa-samādhi).
What is called the "Able-to-Produce-Illumination Samādhi" (Prabhākara-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is immediately able to provide illumination for all samādhis; therefore, it is called the "Able-to-Provide-Illumination" (Prabhākari) samādhi.
What is called the "Universally Illuminating" (Samantāloka) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all gates of samādhi; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Illumination.
What is meant by the Samādhi of Firmly Purifying All Samādhis?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to firmly purify the characteristics of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the "Samādhi that Firmly Purifies All Samādhis.
What is called the "Stainless Radiance Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to remove the defilements of all samādhis and can also illuminate all samādhis; this is called the stainless light samādhi (*vimalaprabhā-samādhi*).
What is called the joy samādhi (*prāmodya-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to receive the joy of all samādhis; this is called the *pramuditā* (Joyful) samādhi.
What is called the *vidyut-pradīpa* (Lightning-flash) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one illuminates all samādhis like a flash of lightning; this is called the *vidyut-pradīpa* samādhi.
What is called the "Inexhaustible Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; this is called the Inexhaustible Samādhi.
What is called the "Majestic Virtue Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one’s majestic power illuminates all other samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Majestic Power (*tejo-vatī-samādhi*).
What is called the Samādhi Free from Exhaustion (*akṣaya-apagata-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; therefore, it is called the Samādhi Free from Exhaustion.
What is called the "immovable samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi causes all samādhis to be immovable and non-fluctuating; this is called the immovable samādhi.
What is called the "non-retrogressive samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able not to see the regression of any samādhis; this is called the "Non-regressing Samādhi" (Anivartana-samādhi).
What is called the "Sun-Lamp Samādhi" (Sūryapradīpa-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one emits light that illuminates all gates of samādhi; this is called the "Sun-Lamp Samādhi."
What is called the Moon-Purity Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to remove the darkness of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Moon-Purity Samādhi.
What is called the Pure-Light Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the four types of unimpeded knowledge regarding all samādhis; this is called the *Vimalaprabhā* (Pure Radiance) Samādhi.
What is called the *Prabhākara* (Able to Produce Radiance) Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to produce illumination regarding all doors of samādhi; this is called the "Able-to-Produce-Illumination" (Prabhākari) samādhi.
What is called the "Performing-Practice" (Cāritra) samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enables each of the various samādhis to perform their respective functions; this is called the samādhi of performing actions (*kārakarī-samādhi*).
What is called the samādhi of knowing characteristics (*lakṣaṇapraveśa-samādhi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives the characteristics of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of knowing characteristics.
What is called the Vajra-like Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to penetrate all phenomena, yet does not even perceive that penetration; this is called the Vajra-like Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of the mind’s abiding?
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind does not move, does not turn, and is not afflicted; furthermore, one does not even think that there is such a mind. This is called the samādhi of the mind’s abiding.
What is called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance?
Abiding in this samādhi, one universally perceives the radiance of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
What is called the Samādhi of Stable Establishment?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is firmly established and immovable among all samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Firm Establishment (*vyavasthāna*).
What is called the Jewel-Heap Samādhi (*ratnakoṭi*)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one universally perceives all samādhis as if seeing a heap of jewels; this is called the Jewel-Heap Samādhi.
What is called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to seal all samādhis; because it seals them with a non-seal, it is called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma.
What is called the samādhi of the equality of dharmas?
Abiding in this samādhi, one contemplates that all dharmas are equal and that there are no dharmas that are not equal; this is called the samādhi of the equality of dharmas.
What is called the samādhi of severing joy?
Abiding in this samādhi, one cuts off all joy regarding all phenomena; this is called the "Samādhi of Cutting Off Joy.
What is called the "Samādhi of Reaching the Pinnacle of Phenomena"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one extinguishes the darkness of all phenomena and also stands above all other samādhis; this is called the "Samādhi of Reaching the Pinnacle of Phenomena."
What is called the samādhi capable of dispersing?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to break and disperse all phenomena; therefore, it is named the samādhi capable of dispersing.
What is called the samādhi of discerning the phrases of all phenomena?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to discern the various samādhis and the phrases of all dharmas; this is called the "Samādhi of Discerning the Phrases of All Dharmas.
What is the "Samādhi of the Equal Characteristics of Names"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the equality of the names of all samādhis; this is the samādhi of the equality of names.
What is called the "samādhi of detachment from letters"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive even a single letter within any of the samādhis; this is called the samādhi of detachment from letters.
What is called the "samādhi that severs conditions"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one severs the conditions of all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi that severs conditions.
What is called the "indestructible samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the transformation of any phenomena; this is called the "indestructible samādhi" (akṣaya-samādhi).
What is called the "samādhi of the markless seed" (anānākāra-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not see the various distinctions among phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of the markless seed."
What is called the "Samādhi of Moving Without Abode"?
Dwelling in this samādhi, one does not perceive the abodes of any samādhis; this is called the Samādhi of Moving Without Abode.
What is called the "Samādhi Free from Obscurity"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is free from the subtle darkness of all other samādhis; therefore, it is called the "samādhi free from dimness.
What is called the "samādhi of no-going"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristic of going in any samādhi; therefore, it is called the "samādhi of no-going."
What is called the samādhi of non-alteration?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the marks of alteration in any samādhis; therefore, it is named the samādhi of non-alteration.
What is called the samādhi of transcending conditions?
Abiding in this samādhi, one transcends the objective spheres that serve as conditions for all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of transcending conditions.
What is called the samādhi of gathering all merits?
Abiding in this samādhi, one gathers the merits of all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi that gathers all merits.
What is called the "samādhi of abiding in no-mind"?
Abiding in this samādhi, the mind does not enter into any other samādhis; this is called the "samādhi of abiding in no-mind."
What is called the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers?
Abiding in this samādhi causes all samādhis to attain purity and excellence like flowers; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers.
What is called the bodhyaṅga-samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the seven factors of enlightenment among all samādhis; this is called the bodhyaṅga-samādhi.
What is called the apramāṇapratibhāna-samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains immeasurable eloquence among all dharmas; this is called the "Immeasurable Eloquence Samādhi.
What is called the "Unequaled Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the mark of "unequaled equality" among all samādhis; this is called the "Unequaled Equality Samādhi.
What is called the "Samādhi that Transcends All Dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one transcends all samādhis; this is called the "samādhi that transcends all dharmas.
What is called the "samādhi that discriminates all dharmas"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one discerns and perceives all samādhis and all dharmas; this is called the "samādhi that discriminates all dharmas."
What is called the Samādhi of Dispelling Doubt?
Abiding in this samādhi, one dispels doubts regarding all phenomena; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Dispelling Doubt.
What is called the Samādhi of Non-Abiding?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dwelling place for phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of non-dwelling.
What is called the "samādhi of single adornment"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one ultimately does not perceive the dual characteristics of phenomena; this is called the "samādhi of single adornment."
What is called the samādhi of the arising of formations?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the arising of any formations; this is called the samādhi of the arising of formations.
What is called the samādhi of a single formation?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the near shore or the far shore of any samādhis;
this is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi*. What is called the *anekavyūha-samādhi*?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive a single characteristic among all samādhis; this is called the *anekartha-caryā* (Non-Unity) Samādhi.
What is called the *sucarita* (Excellent Conduct) Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive dual characteristics among all samādhis; this is called the *sucarita* Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi of penetrating the bottom of all existence?

Abiding in this samādhi, one enters into all existence and all samādhis; wisdom penetrates them yet there is nothing to be penetrated. This is called the samādhi of penetrating the bottom of all existence.
What is called the samādhi of entering names and words?
Abiding in this samādhi, one enters the names and words of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of entering names and words.
What is called the samādhi of being detached from sounds, letters, and speech?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the sounds, syllables, or speech of any samādhis; this is called the "samādhi detached from sounds, syllables, and speech.
What is called the "blazing torch samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, its majestic power illuminates like a torch; therefore, it is called the Torch-Lighting Samādhi (*jvalana-dīpa-samādhi*).
What is called the Pure-Characteristic Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one purifies the characteristics of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the Pure-Characteristic Samādhi (*viśuddha-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*).
What is called the samādhi of breaking through signs?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the signs of any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of breaking through signs.
What is called the samādhi of the excellence of all modes?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is fully endowed with all varieties of samādhis; this is called the "Samādhi of All-Aspect Exquisite Fulfillment" (Sarvākāravaropeta-samādhi).
What is called the "Samādhi of Neither Delighting in Suffering nor Pleasure" (Aduḥkhasukha-anabhirata-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the suffering or pleasure of any samādhis; this is called the "samādhi of non-delight in suffering and pleasure.
What is called the "samādhi of the inexhaustible mark"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the exhaustion of any samādhis; this is called the "Inexhaustible Characteristic Samādhi" (Akṣayākāra-samādhi).
What is called the "Dhāraṇī Samādhi"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to uphold all samādhis; this is called the "Dhāraṇī Samādhi."
What is called the samādhi that encompasses all signs of the heterodox and the orthodox?

Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives neither the signs of the heterodox nor the signs of the orthodox within all samādhis; this is called the samādhi that encompasses all signs of the heterodox and the orthodox.
What is called the samādhi of extinguishing hatred and love?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive hatred or love toward any samādhis; this is called the samādhi of extinguishing hatred and love.
What is called the samādhi of the inverse and the conformable?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharmas or the opposing or conforming aspects of various samādhis; this is called the "Opposing and Conforming Samādhi" (Pratilomyānuloma-samādhi).
What is called the "Pure Light Samādhi" (Vimalaprabhā-samādhi)?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the defilements of the clarity of any samādhis; this is called the Pure Light Samādhi (*viśuddhaprabhā-samādhi*).
What is called the Firm Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any lack of firmness in any samādhis; this is called the Firm Samādhi (*dṛḍha-samādhi*).
What is called the Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon?
Abiding in this samādhi, all samādhis are fulfilled like the moon on the fifteenth day; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon.
What is called the Great Adornment Samādhi?
Abiding in this samādhi, one accomplishes all samādhis through great adornment; therefore, it is named the Great Adornment Samādhi.
What is called the samādhi that can illuminate all worlds?
Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all samādhis and all dharmas; therefore, it is named the samādhi that can illuminate all worlds.
What is called the "samādhi equal to samādhis"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of concentration or distraction regarding any samādhis; this is called the "samādhi equal to samādhis."
What is called the samādhi that encompasses all states with conflict and without conflict?

Abiding in this samādhi, one is able to cause all samādhis to be non-discriminative regarding states with conflict and without conflict; this is called the samādhi that encompasses all states with conflict and without conflict.
What is called the samādhi of not delighting in any dwelling place?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive any basis for the various samādhis; this is called the samādhi of not delighting in any dwelling place.
What is called the samādhi of abiding in suchness?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not transcend the suchness-characteristic (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all samādhis; this is called the samādhi of abiding in suchness.
What is called the samādhi of destroying the decay of the body?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of the body; this is called the "samādhi that destroys the decay of the body.
What is called the "samādhi that destroys speech so that it is like space"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one does not see the verbal karma of any samādhis as being anything other than like space; this is called the "samādhi that destroys speech so that it is like space."
What is called the "Samādhi of Non-attachment and Non-staining by Space"?
Abiding in this samādhi, one perceives all phenomena as being like space—unobstructed and unstained; this is called the "Samādhi of Non-attachment and Non-staining by Space."
“Subhūti! This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Explanation:
Above, the *prajñāpāramitā* was explained by means of the eighteen kinds of emptiness; now, the *dhyānapāramitā* is explained by means of the one hundred and eight samādhis.

Regarding these one hundred and eight samādhis, the Buddha himself explained their meaning; at that time, because people possessed sharp faculties, they were all able to attain faith and understanding.
Now it is not so; therefore, the commentator re-explains their meaning so that they may be easily understood.

The Śūraṅgama Samādhi—translated into the language of Qin as "Mighty Aspect"—is the ability to discern and know the various characteristics of all samādhis, including their number, extent, depth, and shallowness, just as a great general knows the strength and numbers of his troops.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, none of the afflictions, māras, or followers of Māra can destroy it;
it is like the military-treasure general of a wheel-turning sage king, who subdues all places he reaches.
The Jewel Seal Samādhi (*ratnamudrā-samādhi*) is able to seal all samādhis.
Among all jewels, the Dharma-jewel is the true jewel; it is able to provide benefit in this life, in future lives, and even unto nirvāṇa.
As it is said in a sutra:
"The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
'I shall preach the Dharma for you; that which is preached is what is called the Dharma-seal.'"
The Dharma-seal (dharmamudrā) is itself the Treasure-seal (ratnamudrā), and the Treasure-seal is the three gates of liberation.

Furthermore, some say that the three Dharma-seals are called the Treasure-seal Samādhi: all phenomena are without self, all conditioned things are impermanent, and nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction—these are the three Dharma-seals, which no one among gods or humans can rightfully subvert.
Entering this samādhi, one is able to contemplate all dharmas in three ways; thus it is called the "Treasure Seal" (Ratnamudrā).
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the treasure, and the samādhi associated with it is the seal; thus it is called the "Treasure Seal."
Regarding the Lion’s Play Samādhi: when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they achieve mastery over all samādhis, whether entering or emerging from them, and whether doing so slowly or swiftly.
