For example, when various beasts are at play, if they see a lion, they are all struck with terror;
yet when the lion plays, he is sovereign and free from any fear or difficulty.
Furthermore, when the lion plays among the various herds of beasts, he kills those that are strong and releases those that are subdued.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: having attained this samādhi, he breaks those among the various non-Buddhists who are strong and delivers those who have faith.
Furthermore, as for the "Lion’s Play," it is as explained in the first chapter.
When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, the earth shakes in six ways;
it causes the boiling waters of the hells in all worlds of the ten directions to become cool, and enables the blind to see and the deaf to hear, and so forth.
Regarding the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon: just as the full moon is pure and free from all obscurations, capable of dispelling the darkness of night;
so too is this samādhi. When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they are able to eliminate the darkness of ignorance, false views, and other such obscurations regarding all phenomena.
Regarding the Moon-Banner Sign Samādhi: it is like the banner of a great military commander, which is fashioned with a moon image; when people see this banner sign, they all follow it.
When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, all dharmas are penetrated without obstruction, and all things follow accordingly.
Regarding the Samādhi of Emanating All Dharmas: when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, it causes all other samādhis to flourish;
it is like seasonal rain, which makes the forests and trees grow luxuriantly.
As for the Samādhi of Observing the Summit: upon entering this samādhi, one is able to see all samādhis everywhere, just as one standing on a mountain peak can see all things below.
As for the Samādhi of the Ultimate Dharma-nature: the dharma-nature is immeasurable and non-dual, and thus difficult to grasp or maintain.
Upon entering this samādhi, one will certainly be able to attain the mark of concentration.
Just as no one can dwell within space,
yet one who has attained the power of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda) is able to abide therein.
Regarding the Samādhi of the Banner of Victory (*Vaijayantadhvaja-lakṣaṇa*): upon entering this samādhi, one becomes the most venerable among all samādhis;
it is like a military general who, having obtained the banner, displays his preeminent status.
The Vajra-samādhi is like a vajra, for there is nothing it cannot penetrate.
This samādhi is likewise: regarding all dharmas, there is nothing it does not thoroughly comprehend, causing all other samādhis to each attain their respective functions;
just as carnelian, agate, and lapis lazuli can only be pierced by a vajra.
Regarding the entry into the *dharmamudrā-samādhi*: it is like a person entering a secure country; one who possesses the seal may enter, while one without the seal cannot.
When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are able to enter into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena—that is to say, the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena.
Regarding the Samādhirāja-samādhi (King of Samādhis): it is like a great king who, dwelling securely in his main palace, summons his various ministers, all of whom obey his commands.
When a Bodhisattva enters this King of Samādhis, he emits a great radiance that invites and summons those from the ten directions, none of whom fail to assemble;
furthermore, he dispatches emanation Buddhas who travel throughout the ten directions.
Regarding "establishment": it is like a king who dwells securely in his main hall, his body and mind serene and free from all fear.

Regarding the "light-emitting samādhi": because he constantly practices the *tejokasiṇa* (fire-totality), he generates supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*) and emits various colored lights at will, according to the inclinations of sentient beings—whether hot, cold, or neither hot nor cold.
Regarding "illuminating all samādhis," there are two kinds of light:
first, the light of form; second, the light of wisdom.
Abiding within this samādhi, one illuminates all samādhis, such that there is no longer any false view, ignorance, or the like.
Regarding the samādhi of the progress of power: first, one attains the five powers, such as faith and so forth, among all dharmas; subsequently, one attains the power of mastery among all samādhis.
Furthermore, although dwelling in samādhi, he is always able to perform supernatural transformations to deliver all sentient beings.
As for the Samādhi of Exalted Emergence, when a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, all his merit and wisdom increase;
the natures of all samādhis emerge from his mind.
Regarding "one who necessarily enters the *pratibhāna-samādhi*": among the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), this is the samādhi corresponding to eloquence (*pratibhāna*).

When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they fully know the sequence of the languages of sentient beings, as well as the names of scriptures and so forth, being able to distinguish them all without impediment.
Regarding the Samādhi of Explaining Names: although all phenomena are empty, one uses names to elucidate the meanings of phenomena so that people may attain understanding.
Regarding the Samādhi of Contemplating Directions: one contemplates the sentient beings of the ten directions with a mind of equality, characterized by compassion and pity.
Furthermore, "direction" (fang) means that following the principles of reason is called "attaining direction.
Because of the power of this samādhi, one attains the principles regarding all samādhis, entering and emerging from them with mastery and without obstruction.
Regarding the *dhāraṇī-mudrā-samādhi*: one who attains this samādhi is able to discern that all samādhis possess *dhāraṇīs*.

Regarding the *a-vañcana-samādhi* (the non-deceptive samādhi): there are samādhis that give rise to craving, hatred, ignorance, false views, and so forth; yet this samādhi is entirely free from such states of delusion and confusion among all samādhis.
Regarding the Samādhi that Encompasses the Ocean of All Dharmas: just as all streams flow back to the ocean, so too do all the teachings of the Three Vehicles enter into this samādhi.

Furthermore, all other samādhis enter into this samādhi; just as the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments encompass the various liberations, the nine successive attainments, and so forth, all of which enter therein.
Regarding the Samādhi of Pervading the Void: this void is immeasurable and boundless;
by the power of this samādhi, one is able to pervade the entire void—whether sitting cross-legged, emitting light, or filling it with sound.
As for the Vajracakra-samādhi, it is like a true vajra-wheel that encounters no obstruction wherever it goes;
one who attains this samādhi encounters no obstruction in reaching any state among all dharmas.
Furthermore, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*) because it can distinguish the boundaries of various samādhis;
a wheel is a demarcation.
As for the "Jewel-Cutting Samādhi," it is like a jewel that is able to purify and refine all other jewels.
This samādhi is also like this: it can remove the defilements of all other samādhis.
While the stains of the five desires are easy to dispel, the stains of various samādhis are difficult to eliminate.
One who can illuminate samādhi attains this samādhi and is able to use ten kinds of wisdom to clearly perceive all phenomena.
For example, when the sun rises and illuminates Jambudvīpa, all things become clearly manifest.
One who seeks nothing through samādhi contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations; because craving for the three realms has been severed, they have nothing at all to seek.
Regarding the "non-abiding samādhi": this samādhi is named the non-abiding samādhi;
abiding within this samādhi, one contemplates that all phenomena are impermanent from moment to moment, with no time of abiding whatsoever.
The "mindless samādhi" refers to either the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). Why is this?
For the Buddha himself explained the causal conditions:
"When one enters this samādhi, all mental states and their associated factors do not function.
Regarding the "Samādhi of the Pure Lamp": "lamp" refers to the lamp of wisdom, while "defilements" refers to the various afflictions;
being free from these defilements, wisdom is then pure.
Regarding the Samādhi of Boundless Radiance (*Anantaprabhāsa*): "Boundless" means immeasurable and innumerable.
There are two kinds of radiance:
first, emitting light from the body for the sake of delivering sentient beings; [the second is for the sake of illuminating the Dharma].
Second, because it discerns the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, it is the light of wisdom.
Having attained this samādhi, one is able to illuminate the boundless worlds of the ten directions as well as the boundless phenomena.
The Samādhi Capable of Producing Illumination is that which can produce illumination for all dharmas, like lighting a torch in the darkness.
The Samādhi of Universal Illumination is like the precious jewel of a Cakravartin King, which illuminates one yojana on each of the four sides outside the military host;
when a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they universally illuminate the various gateways of all dharmas.
Regarding the Samādhi of Firm and Pure Samādhis: because the Bodhisattva attains the power of this samādhi, it causes all samādhis to become pure and firm.
Regarding the Stainless Radiance Samādhi: this is the samādhi associated with the three gates of liberation;
having attained this samādhi, one is free from the defilements of all samādhis, free from all ignorance, craving, and so forth, and is also able to illuminate all samādhis.
Regarding the Samādhi of Joy: when one attains this samādhi, one gives rise to joy and delight toward all dharmas.
What constitutes this? Some say:
The first dhyāna is this.
As the Buddha taught, there are four types of cultivation of concentration:
first, cultivating this samādhi to attain joy and happiness in the present;
Second, by cultivating meditative concentration, one attains knowledge and vision, seeing the birth and death of sentient beings;
third, by cultivating meditative concentration, one attains the wisdom of discernment;
fourth, by cultivating meditative concentration, one attains the exhaustion of outflows.
Furthermore, having attained this samādhi, one gives rise to immeasurable and boundless joy and delight in the Dharma.
As for the Lightning-flash Samādhi, it is like a flash of lightning that briefly appears, enabling a traveler to find their way;
one who attains this samādhi recovers the path they had lost since beginningless worlds.
Regarding the Samādhi of Inexhaustibility: having attained this samādhi, one extinguishes all marks such as the impermanence of dharmas and immediately enters into non-arising and non-ceasing.
Regarding the Samādhi of Majestic Virtue: when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are adorned with majestic virtue.

Regarding the samādhi of detachment from exhaustion: when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, the fruits of the roots of goodness and merit accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas will certainly be realized, for their retribution shall not be lost.
Regarding the "immovable samādhi" (*āniñjya-samādhi*), some say: the fourth dhyāna is immovable. It is "moved" in the desire realm because of the five sensual desires;

it is "moved" in the first dhyāna because of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); it is "moved" in the second dhyāna because of the abundance of joy (*prīti*); it is "moved" in the third dhyāna because of the abundance of bliss (*sukha*); and it is "immovable" in the fourth dhyāna because, being free from inhalation and exhalation, it lacks all signs of movement.
Some say: "The four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) are immovable because they are free from all forms (rūpa). Others say:
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is immovable because it is free from the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
Some say it is immovable because it is a samādhi associated with the wisdom that realizes the ultimate emptiness of the true nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
Having attained this samādhi, one engages in no conceptual proliferation whatsoever regarding any samādhi or any dharma.
As for the "non-retrogressive samādhi," when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any retrogression in any samādhis.
The commentator says:
When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they are constantly non-retrogressive; this is the samādhi associated with the wisdom of *avaivartika*.
"Non-retrogressive" means not falling back from the summit (*mūrdhan*), as explained in the section on the meaning of "not falling back from the summit."
Regarding the Sun-Lamp Samādhi: having attained this samādhi, one is able to illuminate all the various gateways of all dharmas as well as all other samādhis;
it is like the rising sun, which is able to illuminate the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the Moon-Purity Samādhi: just as the moon gradually wanes from the sixteenth day until it is entirely gone on the thirtieth day, so too it is with ordinary persons;
their various wholesome merits gradually diminish and are exhausted, causing them to fall into the three evil realms.
Just as the moon gradually waxes from the first day until its light becomes pure and clear on the fifteenth day, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:

having attained this samādhi, from the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, they gradually increase their roots of goodness in every lifetime, until they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, receive their prediction of enlightenment, and their wisdom becomes pure as they benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, it can destroy the ignorance within all samādhis.
Regarding the Samādhi of Pure Clarity: "clarity" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), while "defilement" constitutes an obstruction.
One who attains this samādhi encounters no obstructions regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).
For this reason, the Buddha said here:
"Abiding in this samādhi, one attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge. Question:
Why does the Buddha alone, within this context, speak of the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
The answer is:

Within meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is no mind of applied or sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); that which one delights in speaking is contrary to the state of concentration, and thus this matter is difficult to achieve.
By the power of this samādhi, one attains the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The meaning of "the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge" is as previously explained.
Regarding the "samādhi that can produce illumination," illumination is precisely wisdom; among all forms of wisdom, the wisdom of *prajñā* is the most supreme.
This samādhi associated with prajñā is able to produce illumination.
As for the "samādhi of performing practice," by obtaining the power of this samādhi, one is able to give rise to all the various samādhis previously attained.
Regarding the Samādhi of Knowing Characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna-samādhi*): having attained this samādhi, one perceives within all samādhis the characteristic of true wisdom.

Regarding the Vajra-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*): having attained this samādhi, one is able to penetrate all dharmas through wisdom, yet one does not even perceive such penetration, because there is nothing to be apprehended.
Question: Why are all three kinds of samādhi called "vajra"? Answer:
At the beginning it says "Vajra," in the middle it says "Vajracakra," and at the end it says "vajropama.
Regarding the "vajropama-samādhi," the Buddha taught that it can penetrate all dharmas, yet one does not perceive this vajropama-samādhi as being able to penetrate other samādhis.
Regarding "Vajracakra-samādhi": having attained this samādhi, one is able to uphold the wheels of all samādhis.
These are all the meanings spoken by the Buddha himself.
The commentator says:
"Vajra-like Samādhi" is that which can shatter all afflictions and fetters without exception;
it is like Śakra-devānām-indra, who, grasping a vajra in his hand, destroys the armies of the asuras.
This is precisely the final mind of the practitioner; from this mind, one successively attains the three kinds of bodhi:
the bodhi of the śrāvaka, the bodhi of the pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed bodhi of the Buddha.
“Vajrasamādhi” is that which can shatter all dharmas and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, never again to undergo existence;
it is like a true vajra, which can shatter all mountains, causing them to be utterly extinguished without remainder.
Regarding "Vajracakra" (Diamond Wheel): this samādhi is able to shatter all phenomena without obstruction or hindrance;
it is like a diamond wheel in rotation, which there is nothing it cannot break and nothing that can obstruct it.

Furthermore, first is "Vajra," second is "Vajracakra," and third is "Vajropama. Although the Buddha’s explanations of their meanings differ according to these distinctions in terminology, and commentators provide different interpretations of their underlying causes and conditions, one should not raise objections on this basis.

Regarding the samādhi in which the mind abides: the characteristics of the mind are light and swift; it wanders afar and is formless, difficult to restrain and difficult to maintain, being constantly characterized by movement.
It is like a young monkey, like a flash of lightning, and also like the tongue of a snake.
Because one attains this samādhi, one is able to gather [the mind] and cause it to abide;
even toward celestial desires, the mind does not waver, let alone human desires!
As for the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, by attaining this samādhi, one perceives the mark of radiance in all phenomena, and no longer perceives the mark of darkness.
As one sees by day, so too does one see by night;
as one sees what is before, so too does one see what is behind;
as one sees what is above, so too does one see what is below, with no obstruction in the mind.
By practicing this samādhi, one attains the supernormal power of the divine eye, universally perceiving all radiance with clarity and without obstruction.
Because one has skillfully cultivated these supernormal powers, one achieves the wisdom-eye, which universally illuminates all dharmas, seeing them all without obstruction.
Regarding the samādhi of firm establishment: one who attains this samādhi is firmly established within all merits and wholesome dharmas;
like Mount Sumeru in the great ocean, they remain established and immovable.
Regarding the Jewel-Heap Samādhi (*ratnarāśi-samādhi*): when one attains this samādhi, all lands become composed entirely of the seven treasures.
Question:
Is this something seen by the fleshly eye?
What is seen through meditative concentration?
The answer is:
both the divine eye and the fleshly eye can see it.
Why is this? Because the six external sense objects are not fixed;
the practitioner constantly cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), and therefore is able to transform their original characteristics.
Regarding the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma: "Sublime Dharma" refers to the profound merit and wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
by attaining this samādhi, one attains all such profound and sublime merit and wisdom.
Regarding the "samādhi of equality of dharmas" (dharmasamatā-samādhi), there are two kinds of equality:
equality of sentient beings and equality of dharmas.
The samādhi associated with the equality of dharmas is called the "samādhi of equality of dharmas."

The Samādhi of Severing Delight: Having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, impure, and so forth, whereby a mind of weary detachment arises;
it is the samādhi associated with the contemplation of the unattractiveness of all worlds among the ten contemplations.
Regarding "reaching the samādhi of the summit of the Dharma": "Dharma" refers here to the Bodhisattva-dharma, namely the six pāramitās;
having reached the midst of the prajñāpāramitā and attained the power of skillful means (upāya), one reaches the summit of the mountain of the Dharma.
Having attained this samādhi, one is able to abide upon the summit of this mountain of dharmas, such that no ignorance or afflictions can shake them.
As for the "samādhi that can disperse," having attained this samādhi, one is able to break and disperse all dharmas;
it is the samādhi corresponding to the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the Samādhi of Discerning the Phrases of All Dharmas: having attained this samādhi, one is able to discern all the words, phrases, and syllables of all dharmas; when preaching to sentient beings, one’s speech is without obstruction. This is the Samādhi of Corresponding Eloquence.
Regarding the Samādhi of the Equality of Letters and Signs: having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all letters and all speech as entirely equal;
whether reviled or praised, there is neither hatred nor affection.

Regarding the Samādhi of Detachment from Letters: when one attains this samādhi, one does not perceive letters within meanings, nor does one perceive meanings within letters. Regarding the Samādhi of Severing Conditions:

when one attains this samādhi, whether internally or externally, one does not give rise to joy amidst pleasure, does not give rise to anger amidst suffering, and does not give rise to a mind of equanimity amidst that which is neither painful nor pleasant.
When one remains detached and unattached to these three types of sensation, the mind returns to cessation;
if the mind ceases, its objects are also severed.

As for the indestructible samādhi, it is the samādhi associated with the ultimate emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it cannot be shattered by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor overturned by impermanence, because it has already been rendered indestructible.

Regarding the seedless samādhi (*aniñjya-samādhi*): having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive the various characteristics of all phenomena, but perceives only a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).

Regarding the samādhi of non-abiding practice (*apratisthita-caryā-samādhi*): having attained this samādhi, because one knows that the fires of the three poisons burn within the triple world, the mind does not rely upon them;
and because nirvāṇa is ultimately empty, it likewise does not rely upon it.
As for the samādhi of freedom from obscurity: having attained this samādhi, all subtle veils, ignorance, and the like are completely eliminated among all samādhis.
As for the samādhi of no going: having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of coming and going in any phenomena.

Regarding the Samādhi of Non-Transformation: when one attains this samādhi, one contemplates all dharmas as having causes that do not transform into effects, just as milk does not transform into curd;
for all dharmas abide in their own characteristics and are immovable.

Regarding the Samādhi of Crossing Over Conditions: when one attains this samādhi, all afflictions within the six sense objects are completely extinguished; one crosses the great ocean of the six sense objects and is also able to transcend the wisdom born of conditions that arises from all other samādhis.

Regarding the Samādhi of Accumulating All Merits: having attained this samādhi, one accumulates all merits from faith up to wisdom, practicing without ceasing during both the first and last watches of the night;
it is like the movement of the sun and moon, which never rest at the outset.
One who dwells in the samādhi of no-mind enters into this samādhi and does not follow the mind, but follows wisdom alone, abiding in the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Regarding the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers:
just as the blooming of tree blossoms adorns the tree, when one attains this samādhi, one opens the flowers of all merits among all samādhis to adorn oneself.

Regarding the bodhyanga-samādhi: when one attains this samādhi, it causes all other samādhis to transform into the outflow-free (anāsrava) state and become associated with the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).
It is like a single *liang* of mineral extract (*śilājatu*), which can transform a thousand *jin* of copper into gold.
The samādhi of immeasurable eloquence is precisely the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
By the power of attaining this samādhi, even a single phrase of joyful speech remains inexhaustible for immeasurable eons.

Regarding the Samādhi of the Peerless (Asamasama): having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all sentient beings as being identical to the Buddha, and contemplates all dharmas as being identical to the Buddha-dharma;
it is associated with the peerless Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the Samādhi of Crossing Over All Dharmas: having attained this samādhi, one enters the three gates of liberation, transcends the triple world, and delivers sentient beings of the three vehicles.
Regarding the Samādhi of Discerning All Dharmas: this is the samādhi associated with the wisdom of discernment.
Having attained this samādhi, one discriminates the characteristics of all phenomena— wholesome and unwholesome, with outflows and without outflows, conditioned and unconditioned, and so forth.
Regarding the "Samādhi that Dispels Doubt," some say it is the signless samādhi within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga).
The fetter of doubt is severed by the samādhi associated with the knowledge of the vision of the truths.
Some say it is the samādhi associated with the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the net of doubt regarding all dharmas was completely severed; he beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions and attained the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
Some say it is the samādhi associated with the unimpeded liberation (*asaṅga-vimukti*).
Once the Buddhas have attained this samādhi, they are free from doubt regarding all phenomena; there is nothing near and nothing far, as if they were all being observed in the palm of their hand.
This "samādhi of non-abiding" is precisely the samādhi associated with the wisdom of non-appropriation.
Having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharmas as having a fixed place of abiding.

Regarding the Samādhi of Single Adornment: having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all dharmas as being one—whether they are one because all dharmas possess marks, or one because all dharmas are non-existent, or one because all dharmas are empty; in such ways, the immeasurable are all one.
Because this samādhi is adorned with the wisdom of a single characteristic, it is called "the single adornment.

Regarding the "samādhi of producing formations": "formation" (saṃskāra) refers to contemplation. Having attained this samādhi, one is able to contemplate the various characteristics of arising, entering, abiding, and ceasing;
yet these formations are all empty and cannot be perceived.
The *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi) is a samādhi that is constantly of one practice and perfectly accords with ultimate emptiness; within it, there are no further successive practices.
It is like how, following the practice of impermanence, there is the practice of suffering, and following the practice of suffering, there is the practice of non-self.
Furthermore, in this samādhi, the bodhisattva perceives neither this shore nor the other shore.
The characteristic of entering into various samādhis is this shore, while the characteristic of emerging from them is the other shore;
the characteristic of first attaining them is this shore, while the characteristic of their cessation is the other shore.
The samādhi of non-uniform practice refers to those practices that are contrary to the aforementioned uniform practice, namely all other types of contemplative cultivation.

The samādhi of sublime practice is precisely the samādhi associated with ultimate emptiness; it extends even to the point where one does not perceive the characteristic of non-duality, such that no conceptual proliferation can destroy it.
Regarding the samādhi that reaches the bottom of all existence (*sarvabhavatalasprśa*): "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence;
"bottom" (*tala*) refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which is called the "bottom" because it is difficult to reach.

"Attainment" means that by means of untainted wisdom, one even transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters the nirvana without remainder, and the five aggregates of the three realms are dispersed and extinguished.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains this wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing, all forms of existence (*bhava*) are thoroughly penetrated and dismantled, such that none of them exist at all.

As for entering the Samādhi of Names and Words: having attained this samādhi, one recognizes the names of all sentient beings, all things, and all phenomena; moreover, one is able to transform people using these very names and words.
There is no speech whatsoever that is not understood, and all such speech possesses its proper sequence.

Regarding the samādhi of being free from sounds, syllables, and speech: having attained this samādhi, one contemplates that all dharmas are devoid of sound and speech, and are characterized by perpetual quiescence.

As for the Samādhi of Holding a Torch: just as one walking at night holding a torch does not fall into dangerous places, so too the Bodhisattva who attains this samādhi uses the torch of wisdom to remain without error or attachment amidst all phenomena.

Regarding the Samādhi of Pure Marks: having attained this samādhi, one is able to purify and fully adorn the thirty-two marks; furthermore, one can contemplate the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena according to the Dharma, and can also contemplate the purity of the marklessness of all phenomena—namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Marks."
Regarding the Samādhi of Breaking Through Characteristics: having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of any phenomena, much less the characteristics of various samādhis;
thus, one attains this signless (animitta) samādhi.

Regarding the Samādhi of the Perfect Endowment of All Modes: having attained this samādhi, one is adorned with the fullness of all merits—namely, an excellent lineage, an excellent family, an excellent body, and excellent retinues—and both meditative concentration and wisdom are entirely complete and pure.

Regarding the *asamtuṣṭi-duḥkha-sukha-samādhi*: having attained this samādhi, one contemplates that worldly pleasure has many faults and many afflictions, being illusory, inverted, and not truly desirable;
one contemplates worldly suffering as a disease and like an arrow piercing the body, such that the mind finds no delight in it.
Because all phenomena are deceptive and false, one does not seek their pleasure.
Why is this? Because they transform into suffering at another time.
If one does not even take pleasure in happiness, how much less so in suffering!
Regarding the Samādhi of the Signless Exhaustion: having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as neither decaying nor exhausted.
Question:
If that is so, why does one not fall into the extreme of eternalism? Answer:
Thus, although a bodhisattva contemplates impermanence, they do not fall into [the extreme of] annihilation;
if they contemplate non-exhaustion, they do not fall into [the extreme of] permanence.
These two characteristics are both unobtainable among all phenomena.

One practices because there are causes and conditions; that is to say, it is called "constant" because transgressions and merits are not lost, and it is called "impermanent" because of detachment from clinging.
As for the *dhāraṇī-samādhi*, by virtue of attaining the power of this samādhi, all *dhāraṇīs* such as hearing and retaining [the teachings] are naturally acquired.

Regarding the samādhi of gathering all those of wrong and right dispositions: having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive the three categories of sentient beings—namely, those fixed in the right, those fixed in the wrong, and those who are undetermined—and without abandoning any of them at all, one gathers them with a single mind.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, one does not perceive a fixed mark of correctness or a fixed mark of error, because all phenomena lack fixed marks.

As for the samādhi of extinguishing hatred and love: having attained this samādhi, one does not give rise to attachment toward agreeable phenomena, nor does one give rise to aversion toward disagreeable phenomena.
Regarding the Samādhi of Adversity and Accordance: having attained this samādhi, one gains mastery over adversity and accordance among all dharmas;
one is able to subdue sentient beings who are perverse and rebellious, and is able to accord with sentient beings who are ready for transformation.
Furthermore, because of being free from attachment, one dismantles all dharmas;
because of the growth of roots of goodness, one accomplishes all dharmas.
One does not perceive any dharmas as either contrary or conformable, nor does one perceive this very fact, because nothing exists.
Regarding the Samādhi of Pure Light: when one attains this samādhi, the stains of all afflictions within all dharmas cannot be found;
because they cannot be found, all samādhis are pure.
Regarding the "Solid Samādhi" (Dṛḍha-samādhi),
some say it is the Vajra-samādhi, because it is solid and indestructible. Others say:
It is not a vajra. Why is this?
Because even a vajra can be broken.
This samādhi associated with the wisdom of the true nature of all phenomena is indestructible like space; for this reason, it is called "firm.
As for the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon, by attaining this samādhi, one's speech becomes pure and free from all error.
Just as in autumn, when the sky is pure, the moon is full, its radiance is cool and pleasant, delightful to behold and free from anything loathsome, so too is the Bodhisattva:
because they cultivate all merits, they are like the full moon;
because they have shattered the darkness of ignorance, they are fully endowed with the radiance of pure wisdom.
Because it extinguishes the fires of craving, hatred, and so forth, it is endowed with the quality of coolness;
because it brings great benefit to sentient beings, it is delightful.

As for the Great Adornment Samādhi: one sees worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, adorned with the flowers, incense, and perfumes of the seven treasures, with Buddhas dwelling therein—such is its pure adornment.
Because one attains this samādhi, all merits are adorned simultaneously;
yet, observing that these adornments are empty and non-existent, the mind remains unattached.
As for the "Samādhi that Illuminates All Worlds," because one attains this samādhi, one is able to illuminate the three kinds of worlds:
There are the world of sentient beings, the world of dwelling places, and the world of the five aggregates.
Regarding "samādhi equal to samādhis": having attained this samādhi, one contemplates all samādhis as being of one and the same kind, namely, the characteristic of the concentrated mind.
These samādhis are all produced through causes and conditions; they are conditioned phenomena and possess no distinction of depth or shallowness.
Having attained these samādhis, they are entirely equal, and this is what is meant by "equality."

It is also equal and no different from other dharmas; for this reason, it is said in the sense-explanation that within all dharmas, the characteristics of concentration and distraction are unobtainable.

Regarding the samādhi that encompasses all that is with conflict and without conflict: having attained this samādhi, one does not perceive any dharma as having such a characteristic or as not having such a characteristic;
one does not discriminate between dharmas being with conflict or without conflict, but penetrates all dharmas with unimpeded mastery.
Among sentient beings, there is likewise no contention over beauty or ugliness; rather, one delivers and liberates them in accordance with their mental activities.
Because they have attained this samādhi, they accord with all samādhis and do not oppose them.

Regarding the *samādhi* of not delighting in any dwelling place: having attained this samādhi, one does not delight in dwelling in the mundane world, nor does one delight in dwelling in that which is non-mundane.
One does not delight [in the mundane] because of the fault of its impermanence;
as for that which is non-mundane, since it is devoid of all dharmas, it is a most terrifying place where one ought not to give rise to delight.

Just as one who dwells in the samādhi of abiding in concentration, by attaining this samādhi, knows the true mark of all dharmas as they really are, and does not perceive any dharma that exceeds this suchness.
The meaning of "as" (*tathā*) is as previously explained.
Regarding the samādhi of destroying bodily decay: because blood, flesh, sinews, bones, and so forth are combined, they are called the "body.
This body has many afflictions and is constantly in conflict with hunger, cold, chill, heat, and the like; this is called "bodily decay."
By attaining this samādhi, through the power of wisdom, one analytically deconstructs the signs of bodily decay until not even the sign of "unobtainability" is seen.
Regarding the "samādhi that destroys speech like space": speech is so named because internal winds arise and strike seven locations, thereby producing sound; based on sound, there is speech.
By contemplating the causes and conditions of such speech, one is able to destroy speech and give rise neither to the notion of a self nor to love and hatred. Some say:
"The second dhyāna is free from vitarka and vicāra; this is the samādhi that destroys speech, for the noble ones remain silent therein."
Some say: In the samādhi of the formless attainments, there is no body, because it is free from all form. Others say:

However, through the samādhis of the bodhisattvas, they are able to shatter the impure bodies resulting from the causes and conditions of karmic bonds in previous lives and receive the Dharma-body, manifesting in various forms according to the sentient beings who are to be saved.

Regarding the samādhi of being unstained by detachment from space: when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they contemplate all dharmas as ultimately empty, neither arising nor ceasing, like space, for which no worldly object can serve as a metaphor.
Bodhisattvas of dull faculties are attached to this space;
yet, because they have attained this samādhi, they are free from attachment to all phenomena such as space, and they are likewise unstained by or attached to this samādhi.
It is like a person who has sunk into the mud and is pulled out by someone else, only to have their feet bound in shackles and become a slave;
likewise, it is the same when one attains a samādhi that enables one to be free from attachment to space, yet subsequently becomes attached to that very samādhi.
This samādhi can detach from attachment to space, and it itself is also detached from attachment.
Question:
The Buddha frequently speaks of "all samādhis"; why do you speak only of "all dharmas"?
Answer: The Buddha primarily speaks of retribution (vipāka), whereas the treatise explains it by combining causes and conditions with retribution.
For example, when a person contemplates the impurity of the body, they attain the samādhi of impurity.
The body is the cause and conditions, while samādhi is the fruit.

Furthermore, it is like a person who contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and so forth, thereby attaining the samādhi of the seven factors of enlightenment, which can give rise to the eightfold noble path and the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, because the Buddha must adapt to sentient beings, he speaks of only a single dharma;
the commentators, however, explain extensively by distinguishing various matters.
For example, while all outflows (*āsrava*) are causes of suffering, the Buddha speaks only of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The cessation of all afflictions is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the Buddha, however, spoke only of the exhaustion of craving (*tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*).

Regarding these various contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*), the Bodhisattva is necessarily free from doubt; yet, because he has not yet fully mastered the various samādhis, the Buddha spoke only of samādhi.
The commentators explain that all dharmas are already contained within all samādhis.
At the conclusion of each of these samādhis, one should state that they are practiced through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), for they are identical to Prajñāpāramitā.
The harmonious integration of such immeasurable and boundless samādhis is called the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Volume 47.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Catur-smṛtyupasthāna), Number Nineteen. Volume 48.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 19: The Four Foundations of Mindfulness. [Sūtra] The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“The Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva refers to what are called the four foundations of mindfulness.”
What are the four? "Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, yet has no perception of a body, because it cannot be apprehended;..."
Contemplating the body in the external body, and in both the internal and external bodies, one likewise has no perception of a body, because it cannot be apprehended.
With diligent effort and single-mindedness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow.

Regarding internal feelings, internal mind, and internal phenomena; external feelings, external mind, and external phenomena; and internal-external feelings, internal-external mind, and internal-external phenomena—one contemplates them according to the phenomena (*dhammānupassī*), yet there is no perception of phenomena, because they are unattainable.
With diligence, vigor, and single-mindedness, one removes worldly greed and sorrow. "Subhūti,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the contemplation of the body within the internal body?"

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when walking, knows that he is walking; when standing, knows that he is standing; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; and when lying down, knows that he is lying down—just as his body acts, so does he know it.

Subhūti! In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body with diligence, vigor, and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and anxiety because [the body] is ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva comes or goes,

looks about with single-minded attention, bends or extends, looks down or up, puts on the saṃghāṭī robe, holds the robes and bowl, eats, drinks, sleeps, rests, sits, stands, wakes, sleeps, speaks, remains silent, enters meditative concentration, or emerges from meditative concentration, he is likewise always single-minded."
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom contemplates the body within the internal body, because it is ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body with single-minded mindfulness, he knows:
'When inhaling, I am inhaling; when exhaling, I am exhaling. "
When the inhalation is long, he knows the inhalation is long; when the exhalation is long, he knows the exhalation is long.
When the inhalation is short, he knows the inhalation is short; when the exhalation is short, he knows the exhalation is short.
"Just as a turner, or a turner’s apprentice, knows when the cord is long that it is long, and knows when the cord is short that it is short;
so too, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with single-minded mindfulness,
knows when inhaling that he is inhaling, and knows when exhaling that he is exhaling."
When the inhalation is long, he knows the inhalation is long; when the exhalation is long, he knows the exhalation is long.
When the inhalation is short, he knows the inhalation is short; when the exhalation is short, he knows the exhalation is short.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, with diligence, vigor, and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow because [all things] are ungraspable."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the four great elements of the body and forms this thought:
'Within the body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'"

"It is, for example, like a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice who slaughters an ox with a knife and divides it into four parts; having divided it into four parts, whether standing or sitting, he contemplates these four parts."

The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: when practicing the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the four great elements of the body in various ways—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, because [the body] is unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates the internal body from the feet to the crown of the head, seeing that it is surrounded by thin skin and filled within with various kinds of impurities.
He reflects thus:

"Within this body there are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, tendons, flesh, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, bladder, excrement, urine, filth, sweat, eyes, tears, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, bile, fat, grease, brain, and membranes."
"It is like a farmer’s granary, partitioned and filled with various kinds of grain—rice, hemp, millet, sorghum, beans, and wheat.

A person with clear vision, upon opening the granary, immediately knows which is hemp, which is millet, which is rice, which is sorghum, which is wheat, and which is beans, discerning them all with complete knowledge."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise contemplates this body from the feet to the crown of the head, surrounded by thin skin, filled within with various kinds of impurities, from hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, up to the brain and membranes.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, ardent, resolute, and single-mindedly, removing worldly greed and sorrow because [the body] is ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the body of a dead person that has been discarded for one day, two days, up to five days— swollen, discolored, and oozing with pus—
he reflects to himself: "
"My own body is also of such a nature and such a character; it has not yet escaped this dharma.

Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body with diligence, vigor, and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow because [all things] are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the discarded body of a dead person— whether after six or seven days— being torn apart and eaten by various birds and beasts such as crows, hawks, vultures, eagles, jackals, wolves, foxes, and dogs; he reflects to himself:
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet liberated from these phenomena.

In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the body within the internal body, practicing with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow, because [all things] are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the body of a dead person discarded, which has been devoured by birds and beasts, becoming impure, putrid, and foul-smelling;
he reflects to himself:"
“My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it has not yet escaped these qualities.
... [and so on] until “he removes worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees the discarded body of a dead person, with its skeleton smeared and stained with blood and flesh, the bones and sinews still interconnected, he reflects to himself:
"My own body has such characteristics and such a nature; it has not yet escaped from this condition."
"…up to the point of removing worldly greed and sorrow. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the discarded body of a dead person, where the skeleton is separated from the flesh and blood, yet the tendons and bones remain connected;"
He reflects to himself:
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet liberated from these phenomena.
Thus, he eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the discarded body of a dead person, with its skeletal remains already scattered upon the ground,
he reflects to himself:"
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet free from these phenomena.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, even unto the removal of worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the discarded body of a dead person with bones scattered upon the ground— the bones of the feet in one place, the bones of the thighs and the bones of the calves, the bones of the waist and the ribs, the vertebrae and the bones of the hands, the bones of the neck and the skull, each in a different location— he reflects to himself:"
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet liberated from these qualities.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, and so forth, until he eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the bones of a discarded dead person lying on the ground, weathered by the wind and bleached by the sun over many years until they are white like a conch shell,
he reflects to himself: "
"My body has such characteristics and such qualities; it is not yet liberated from these dharmas.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the internal body, up to the point of removing worldly greed and sorrow, because [all things] are unapprehendable.
[Treatise] Question:

Within the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), there are various modes of contemplation; why then are only twelve modes of contemplation mentioned—namely, those directed internally, externally, or both internally and externally?
Furthermore, what is internal and what is external?
Having observed the internal and the external,
why are they again explained separately as "internal" and "external"?
Furthermore, among the four foundations of mindfulness, one foundation of mindfulness is internal, subsumed within internal phenomena, namely the mind;
two foundations of mindfulness are external, subsumed within external phenomena, namely sensation and mental objects;
and one foundation of mindfulness is both internal and external, subsumed within both internal and external phenomena, namely the body.
Why are these four dharmas all said to be internal, all external, and all both internal and external?
Why does it not merely say "contemplating the body," but rather "contemplating the body by following its course"?
How is it that one contemplates the body yet does not give rise to the perception of a body?
Why is it said, "with diligent effort and single-mindedness"?
Since all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment should be described as "single-minded," why is "single-mindedness" mentioned only here?
In this context, when practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, all five hindrances should be eliminated; why then do you speak only of "eliminating greed"?
Furthermore, worldly joy can also obstruct the Path; why do you speak only of "eliminating sorrow"?
Regarding the various gateways for contemplating the body—
such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth— why is it that now one speaks only of "impurity"?
If one contemplates only impurity, why does one further attend to the four postures of the body and so on?
"This matter is easy to understand; why is it worth asking?
He replied:
"These are the twelve kinds of contemplation; through them, the practitioner attains a concentrated mind."
Previously, there were three kinds of wrong practice: internal, external, and both internal and external;
by destroying these three kinds of wrong practice, there are thus three kinds of right practice.
There are those who have great attachment to internal matters and little attachment to external matters;
for example, because of their own bodies, people are able to renounce their wives, children, relatives, and precious possessions.
There are also those who have great attachment to external matters and little attachment to internal matters.

Just as a person loses their life through greed for wealth or gives up their life for the sake of desire, so too some people are deeply attached to internal and external conditions; for this reason, the three kinds of right practice are taught.
Furthermore, one's own body is called the "internal body," while the bodies of others are called the "external body."
The nine bases of sensation (*vedanā-āyatana*) are called the internal body; the nine non-sensory bases (*avijñapti-āyatana*) are called the external body.
The five sense organs, such as the eye, are called the internal body; the five sense objects, such as form, are called the external body.
In this manner, one distinguishes between the internal and the external.

The practitioner first uses the wisdom of impurity, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, to contemplate the internal body, yet does not find any favorable characteristics in this body—
neither the characteristic of purity, nor the characteristic of permanence, nor pleasure, nor self, nor reality.
Since he could not find [such qualities] within, he further observed the external body; seeking purity, permanence, self, bliss, and reality, these too were unattainable.
Failing to find them, doubt arose in him:
"When I was observing the internal, I may have been mistaken regarding the external."
"When observing the external, one may err regarding the internal.
Now, when observing both the internal and external simultaneously, they likewise cannot be apprehended.

At this time, the mind attains right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) and realizes that this body is impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, with nine orifices flowing with filth, making it a walking latrine.
Before long, there will be signs of destruction, dispersal, exhaustion, and death;
one will be constantly surrounded by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, flogging, imprisonment, verbal abuse, revilement, old age, sickness, and other such sufferings, never attaining any autonomy.

The internal emptiness has no master, nor does it have a knower or a seer, an agent or an experiencer; rather, all phenomena exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions, arising and ceasing of themselves, without any fixed attachment, just like grass and trees. Therefore, one contemplates both the internal and the external together.
The remaining meanings regarding the internal and external are as explained in the section on the eighteen kinds of emptiness.

Regarding "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupaśyanā*): it means to investigate and follow along with observation, knowing it to be impure, subject to aging, decay, and death, a place of putrefaction and foul odor, where bones and joints rot and decay, and which, through friction and destruction, returns to the earth.
Just as this body of mine, covered with thin skin, causes people to become deluded and bewildered, giving rise to myriad forms of anxiety and fear;
for this reason, one should observe the characteristics of the body, examining its internal and external aspects from beginning to end.
Furthermore, as the Buddha taught the practice of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*):

"Not giving rise to perceptions of the body" means not grasping at the characteristics of the body as being either identical to or different from [the self], thereby giving rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Sentient beings give rise to various kinds of perceptions regarding this very body:
There are those who give rise to pure thoughts, and there are those who give rise to impure thoughts;
there are those who give rise to thoughts of anger, dwelling on the faults and transgressions of others;
and there are those who contemplate this body:
"What is the nature of the body?
Are the various parts of the body one with it,
or are they different?"
One does not give rise to such various thoughts. Why is this?
Because they provide no benefit and obstruct the path to Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, while other ordinary persons and śrāvakas grasp at the marks of the body when they contemplate the body, the bodhisattva does not grasp at the marks of the body yet is able to contemplate the body.

Regarding the phrase "diligent, energetic, and single-minded": as for the skillful means of worldly affairs, which have been constantly practiced and performed since beginningless time—just as it is easy to part from an ordinary person but difficult to part from an acquaintance;
and it is easy to part from an acquaintance but difficult to part from one's father or son.
It is easy to separate from father and son, but difficult to separate from one's own body;
it is easy to separate from one's own body, but difficult to separate from the mind.
Without single-minded diligence and vigor, this cannot be attained!

For example, when drilling wood to seek fire, if one applies oneself with single-minded diligence, without ceasing or resting, one will obtain fire; therefore, it is said: "With a single mind, exert diligent effort."
Regarding the phrase "removing worldly greed and anxiety": when greed is removed, the five hindrances are entirely eliminated;
it is like splitting bamboo—once the first node is split, the remaining nodes all fall away.

Furthermore, when a practitioner distances himself from the five desires and leaves the household life to study the Way, having already abandoned worldly pleasures but not yet attained the bliss of meditative concentration, his mind may at times give rise to sorrowful thoughts, like a fish longing for water.
The nature of the mind is such that it constantly seeks pleasant things and repeatedly dwells upon its original desires.
Practitioners frequently give rise to these two types of thoughts; therefore, the Buddha taught: "One should eliminate greed and anxiety."
To speak of "greed" is to speak of worldly delight, because they are associated.
For one who first contemplates impurity, the human body is impure because it is covered by thin skin; thus, the perception of purity arises first, followed by other perversions.
For this reason, the contemplation of impurity is taught first.
Furthermore, sentient beings are mostly attached to sensual desire and grasp at signs of purity;
since this is not the case for ill-will or wrong views, one first remedies sensual desire by contemplating impurity.
Regarding "mindfulness of the body in the four postures" and so forth: first, one wishes to destroy the thief of the body;
once one has attained single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), all that one undertakes can be successfully accomplished.

For this reason, one first investigates the body’s activities and conduct—its coming and going, lying down and waking, and sitting in meditation—observing what the body does, always with a single mind, composed, unerring, and undisturbed.
By conducting such observations, one easily attains the samādhi of impurity (*aśubha*).
Although the body is tranquil, within there may be various unwholesome thoughts and reflections that disrupt and disorder the mind;
for this reason, it is said that the sixteen stages of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) are taught to prevent such thoughts and reflections.
The meaning of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) is as previously explained.
Once the body is composed and the mind is free from confusion, one should then practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which will then become peaceful and firm.
If one first practices the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), because the distracted mind becomes deranged, the impure may conversely appear as pure.
Within the Buddha-dharma, these two methods are called the initial gateways to the nectar of immortality (amṛta).
Regarding the contemplation of impurity: it means that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the body as being no different from grass, wood, tiles, or stones.
This body consists of the four external great elements transformed into food and drink, which fill and sustain the internal body:
that which is solid is earth, that which is moist is water, that which is warm is fire, and that which moves is wind.
These four elements that enter within constitute the body.
Within these four parts, each is devoid of a self and devoid of what belongs to a self; they follow their own specific characteristics and do not conform to human will.
The same applies to the teachings on suffering, emptiness, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "whether sitting or standing": if one lies down, there is indolence; because the body does not move, the mind likewise does not move.
If one walks, the mind becomes distracted; because the body is not tranquil, the mind likewise is not tranquil.
Wishing to use what is visible to the eye as an illustration for that which is not seen, he speaks this parable:

"The ox" is the practitioner's body; "the butcher" is the practitioner; "the knife" is sharp wisdom; "taking the ox's life" is the breaking of the single characteristic of the body; and "the four parts" are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
When a butcher examines the four parts of an ox, there is no separate ox apart from them, nor is it the ox itself;
likewise, when a practitioner contemplates the four great elements of the body,
these four elements are not what is called the "body."
Why is this so? Because these four [elements] constitute a single body;
furthermore, the four great elements are the general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), whereas the body is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
If the four external great elements are not called the body, it is only when they enter within the body that they are conventionally designated as the body.
The self does not exist within the four great elements, nor do the four great elements exist within the self;
the self is far removed from the four great elements, yet through inverted and false conceptualization, one regards them as the body.

Using this wisdom of the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*), one analytically discerns the four great elements and the derived matter; subsequently, one enters the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and attains entry into the Path.
Furthermore, one contemplates this body from the feet to the hair, and from the hair to the feet, as being entirely encased in thin skin;
through repeated reflection, one finds not a single pure place.
From hair and body hair up to the brain membrane, briefly stated there are thirty-six components, but in detail they are numerous.
The granary is the body; the farmer is the practitioner; and sowing grain in the field is the causal condition for the practitioner’s bodily karma.
The ripening of the fruit and its entry into the granary represent the practitioner’s attainment of a body through the maturation of causes and conditions.
The rice, hemp, millet, sorghum, and so forth, represent the various kinds of impurities within that body.

Just as a farmer opening a granary immediately recognizes the various distinctions between hemp, millet, wheat, and beans, so too does the practitioner, through the eye of wisdom, open and behold this body-granary; they know that this body is filled with impurities, that it must inevitably decay, and that it will either be harmed by others or die of its own accord.
Within this body there is nothing but the impurities of feces and urine, various foul secretions, and the like.
Having already contemplated the impurity of the internal body, one now contemplates the decay of the external body;
therefore, two kinds of impurity are taught.
First, the already decayed; second, the not yet decayed.

One first contemplates one's own body while it is not yet decayed and still possesses consciousness; if one’s fetters are thin and one is of sharp faculties, one immediately gives rise to weariness and revulsion.
Those of dull faculties with thick fetters contemplate a dead person who has already decayed as something fearsome and loathsome.
If one dies for one day up to five days, relatives will still guard the body;

at this time, before it has been eaten by birds and beasts, it becomes livid and bloated, pus and blood flow out, the abdomen swells and bursts, the five viscera rot and decay, and the stench of excrement and urine becomes so loathsome as to be utterly detestable.
The practitioner reflects:
"This form was formerly beautiful; its gait, speech, and seductive gestures deluded the hearts of men, causing those of lustful nature to become attached.
Now, observing it, where is that beauty?"
"As the Buddha has taught, these are truly illusory phenomena that merely deceive those with ignorant eyes!
Now that this reality is revealed, the practitioner reflects:
"My body and that [other's] are equal and without distinction."
"Since one has not yet been liberated from these phenomena, why should one be attached to oneself or attached to others?
Furthermore, why should one hold oneself in high esteem while disparaging others?
Having contemplated in this way, the mind becomes subdued; one can then seek the Path and be able to eliminate worldly greed and anxiety.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"When this corpse was first dead, birds and beasts saw it and, thinking it was not a dead person, did not dare approach.
For this reason, it is said that after six or seven days have passed and the relatives have departed, crows, vultures, jackals, and their like compete to devour it."
When the skin and flesh have been completely exhausted and change day by day, for this reason it is said that there is "only a skeleton.
Seeing it thus, one gives rise to a mind of revulsion and reflects:
"In this heart, liver, skin, and flesh, there is truly no self; yet because of this body, the causes and conditions of sin and merit are gathered together, resulting in immeasurable suffering!"
He then further reflects to himself:
"My own body will not long remain; it will inevitably become like this, for I have not yet escaped this law.
At times, the practitioner sees the skeletal person on the ground, drenched by rain and water, exposed to the sun and blown by the wind, until there is nothing but white bones.
Or one may see long bones with tendons severed and joints disarticulated, scattered in various places, their color like that of a pigeon;
or they may be decayed and rotten, the same color as the earth.
First, one contemplates the thirty-six components: from the bloating of a corpse for one day up to five days, this is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
When birds and beasts come to devour it until its color becomes identical to the soil, this is the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā-bhāvanā*).
Within this, a self or what belongs to a self cannot be found; as previously stated, "because that which arises from causes and conditions lacks independence," this is the contemplation of non-self.
Contemplating the characteristics of the body in this way, one finds not a single thing to be delighted in;
if there is attachment, then sorrow and suffering arise—this is called the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*).
One contemplates the external body through the four noble practices and realizes that one's own body is likewise so, and thereafter contemplates both internally and externally together.

If the mind is distracted, one should contemplate old age, sickness, death, the sufferings of the three evil realms, the impermanence of body and life, and the impending extinction of the Buddha-dharma;
by means of such reflections, one should lash the mind into submission and bind it back to the contemplation of impurity. This is called "diligent vigor."
Because of single-minded diligent effort, one is able to eliminate greed and anxiety.
These two thieves—greed and anxiety—plunder my Dharma-treasure. The practitioner reflects thus:
"This body is impermanent, impure, and loathsome;..."
"Why do such sentient beings greedily cling to this body and give rise to various causes and conditions for transgression?

Having reflected thus, he realized that within this body there are the five sense organs and externally there are the five objects of desire; through their conjunction, the world's inverted pleasure arises!
The human mind seeks pleasure, yet it never remains for even a moment.
One should contemplate whether this pleasure is real or illusory:
if even the body, which is seemingly solid, must eventually disperse and perish, how much more so this pleasure!
This pleasure likewise has no place of abiding; it does not yet exist in the future, it has already ceased in the past, and it does not abide in the present, perishing moment by moment.
It is called "pleasure" only because it obstructs suffering; there is no real pleasure!

For example, food and drink remove the suffering of hunger and thirst and thus provide temporary pleasure; yet once this is passed, suffering arises again, as previously explained in the section on the refutation of pleasure.
Thus one knows that all worldly pleasures arise from causes and conditions of suffering and are likewise able to produce the fruits of suffering;
they deceive people for a brief moment, yet the subsequent suffering is immeasurable.
It is like fine food mixed with poison: though the food is fragrant and delicious, the poison will harm the person.
Worldly pleasures are likewise so.

Because they are poisoned by afflictions such as lustful desire, they rob one of the life-force of wisdom; the mind then becomes deranged and deluded, abandoning what is beneficial and grasping at what is ruinous—who, then, would accept such pleasure?
There is only mind-consciousness.
Contemplate this mind with discernment: because it arises and ceases moment by moment yet persists in a continuous succession, its characteristics can be grasped;
it is like the waves of water or the flame of a lamp.

A mind experiencing suffering is not a mind experiencing pleasure; a mind experiencing pleasure is not a mind experiencing suffering; a mind experiencing neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is not a mind experiencing either suffering or pleasure. Since their temporal characteristics are each distinct, for this reason the mind is impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, they lack sovereignty; because they lack sovereignty, they are non-self.
This applies likewise to perception, volition, mindfulness, and so forth.
As for the remaining three foundations of mindfulness, the characteristics of their internal and external aspects are as previously explained.
Practicing these four noble practices, one destroys the four inversions;
because the four inversions are destroyed, the gate of true reality is opened;
once the gate of true reality is opened, one feels shame for what was previously practiced.
It is like a person who eats impure food at night; others recognize his error, and he feels shame for the act.
To contemplate these four dharmas as impure, impermanent, and so forth, is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);
that the cause of this suffering consists of craving and other afflictions is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The severance of craving and all other afflictions is the Truth of Cessation;
the means for severing craving and all other afflictions is the Truth of the Path.
Observing the Four Truths in this manner, one gains faith in the path to Nirvana and the mind dwells in bliss as if it were untainted (*anāsrava*); this is called the "Dharma of Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
It is like a person drilling for fire: as long as there is warmth, one certainly expects to obtain fire.

Having gained faith in this Dharma, the mind delights in the Buddha; this Dharma is exactly as the Buddha has taught it. It is like taking effective medicine to cure an illness, whereby one knows the physician to be excellent.
Those who take the medicine and are cured of their illness are the foremost among men; this is faith in the Sangha. Thus is one’s faith in the Triple Gem.
Because merit and demerit become equal as the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) advances, it is called the "Summit" (mūrdhan).
It is like a person ascending a mountain to its peak; the distances to both sides are equal.
From the stage of *mūrdhan* (Summits) up to *kṣānti* (Patience), and even up to Arhatship, this is one path;
from *uṣmagata* (Heat) up to *mūrdhan*, this is another path.
Such is the fruit obtained by contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness within the Śrāvaka Dharma.

Regarding the Dharma of the Bodhisattva: within this contemplation, one does not forget the original vow nor abandon great compassion. First, one uses the *anupalambha-śūnyatā* (emptiness of non-apprehension) to subdue the ground of the mind; abiding in this ground, although afflictions (*kleśa*) may still exist, the mind never falls [into their power].
It is like a person who, though not yet having killed the enemy, has already been confined in a single place.
The dharma of the Bodhisattva’s summit (mūrdhan) is as explained in the previous section on the stages of the dharmas.
The stage of patience (kṣānti) and the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) constitute the Bodhisattva’s patience in accordance with the truth (anulomikī kṣānti).
The path of the srotāpanna, up to the paths of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha, is precisely the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
As the Buddha himself says later in this chapter:
“Whether it be the wisdom or the fruit of a srotāpanna, all are the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.”
Although the four right efforts and the four bases of psychic power each have their own distinct positions, they are all contained within the four foundations of mindfulness.
Because wisdom predominates, they are called the "four foundations of mindfulness";
because diligence predominates, they are called the "four right efforts."
Because concentration is predominant, they are called the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*). Question:
If that is so, why are they not called "bases of knowledge" (*jñānasthāna*) but rather "bases of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
Answer: When first practicing, one has not yet attained wisdom;
since mindfulness is the primary gateway, one constantly attends to the object. Because wisdom follows upon this mindfulness, it is named "mindfulness."
The essential substance of the four foundations of mindfulness is wisdom. Why is this so?
To contemplate the internal and external body is itself wisdom.
Because mindfulness and wisdom abide within their objects without allowing them to become distracted, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
Because they are the opposite of the ninety-six kinds of heterodox practices for seeking the Way, they are called "right efforts" (samyakpradhāna).
The various non-Buddhists abandon the five desires and subject their own bodies to hardship, yet they cannot abandon evil and unwholesome states, nor can they accumulate all wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha has two ways of severing evil and unwholesome dharmas:
he eliminates those that have already arisen, and he prevents those yet to come from arising.
Wholesome dharmas are also of two kinds:
causing wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen to arise, and causing wholesome dharmas that have already arisen to increase; this is called "right effort.
When the fire of wisdom obtains the wind of right effort, there is nothing it does not burn.
If right effort is excessive, the mind becomes distracted and the fire of wisdom grows feeble;
like fire encountering wind, that which is excessive may either be extinguished or become so weak that it can neither burn nor illuminate.
Therefore, one must employ concentration to restrain the wind of excessive diligence; thus, concentration can be attained.
There are four kinds of concentration:
concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), concentration of diligence (*vīrya-samādhi*), concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*), and concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*).

In the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, one restrains excessive wisdom; at that time, because the path of concentration and wisdom attains vigor, what is desired is accomplished according to one's wish.
Because one subsequently accomplishes these wished-for matters, they are called the "bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda).
The "feet" (pāda) are called the conditions for the fulfillment of wishes, and they are also called "limbs" (aṅga).
These twelve factors are termed "faculties" (indriya) among those of dull faculties, like a tree that has roots but not yet the power [to grow];

among those of sharp faculties, they are termed "powers" (bala), because these matters are clearly understood and one is able to accomplish things swiftly, like a sharp knife cutting through objects—hence they are called "possessing power."
Because the task is not yet accomplished, it is called the "Path" (mārga);
because the task is accomplished through contemplative cultivation, it is called "Awakening" (bodhi).
The discussion on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is as previously explained.
Question:
If a bodhisattva cultivates these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, why do they not take up nirvana? Answer:

Because their original vows are firm, because their mind of great compassion has deeply penetrated, because they clearly understand the true mark of all phenomena, and because they are protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When a Bodhisattva reaches the seventh stage, they externally contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena and internally contemplate non-self."
It is like a person who, while dreaming, binds together rafts to cross a river and awakens in midstream.
He then thinks:
"I have exhausted myself in vain; there is neither river nor raft—what was it that I crossed?"
