‘For the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall undergo diligent suffering within the hells for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, until that person attains the Buddha-way and enters nirvana.’”
"This is called enduring suffering for the sake of all sentient beings in the ten directions; this is called entering the mind of great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the teacher, and their respectful reception of instruction?"
“If a bodhisattva regards all teachers as the World-Honored One, this is called having faith in the teacher and respectfully receiving their instruction.
How does a bodhisattva diligently seek the various pāramitās?”
“If a bodhisattva single-mindedly seeks the various pāramitās without engaging in other matters, this is called diligently seeking the various pāramitās.
This constitutes the fulfillment of the eight dharmas for a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the second stage.”
"What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s insatiable pursuit of extensive learning?

To desire to hear and retain all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas—whether those spoken in this world-system or those spoken by the Buddhas in the world-systems of the ten directions—is called insatiable pursuit of extensive learning."
“What is the bodhisattva’s pure gift of Dharma?
It is when one gives the gift of Dharma even without seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone any other matter.”
"This is called the gift of Dharma that seeks neither fame nor profit.
How does a bodhisattva purify a buddha-field?
By dedicating all roots of goodness toward the purification of a buddha-field, this is called purifying a buddha-field."
“How does a bodhisattva undergo immeasurable worldly toil and suffering without becoming weary?

Because they are fully endowed with all roots of goodness, they are able to bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn the Buddha-field, even until they are perfected in *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); never tiring or wearying, this is called undergoing immeasurable toil and suffering without becoming weary.”
“How does a bodhisattva abide in a state of shame and modesty?
“To feel shame regarding the mentalities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—this is called abiding in a state of shame and modesty.”
“This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the third stage, fulfills five dharmas.
“How does a bodhisattva not abandon the forest hermitage?”
"To be able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called not abandoning the dwelling place of an araṇya.
What is the bodhisattva’s fewness of desires?"
"Even the desire for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* itself is not desired, let alone other desires;
this is called having few desires.
What is the bodhisattva’s contentment?"
"To attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is called 'contentment.
How does a bodhisattva not abandon the merit of the dhūta practices?
To contemplate the patience regarding all profound dharmas is called 'not abandoning the merit of the dhūta practices.'"
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning the precepts?
“Not grasping at the characteristics of the precepts is called not abandoning the precepts.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva loathing all desires?”
“Because the mind of desire does not arise, this is called detesting all desires.
What is the bodhisattva’s mind of world-weariness?
Because one knows that all phenomena are uncreated, this is called the mind of world-weariness.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva relinquishing all that they possess?
Because they do not begrudge any internal or external phenomena, this is called relinquishing all that one possesses.”
“How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind does not sink?
“Because the mind does not arise in the two bases of consciousness, this is called the mind not sinking.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cherish any material things?”
"Not to be attached to or to dwell upon any thing—this is called not being stingy with any thing.
These are the ten dharmas that a bodhisattva does not abandon while in the fourth stage."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva remaining far removed from intimacy with laypeople?

When a bodhisattva has gone forth, they travel from one buddha-field to another, always living as a renunciant, shaving their head, and wearing dyed robes; this is called remaining far removed from intimacy with laypeople.”
"How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from bhikṣuṇīs?
"He does not dwell together with bhikṣuṇīs; he does not even give rise to a thought toward them for as long as a finger-snap. This is called remaining far removed from bhikṣuṇīs."
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from stinginess regarding the households of others?
“The bodhisattva reflects thus:
‘I should bring happiness and peace to sentient beings; since these others now assist me in bringing them happiness and peace, why should I give rise to stinginess?’”
"This is called being far removed from stinginess regarding the households of others.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being far removed from places of useless talk?
"If there is a place of talk where the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha might arise, I shall remain far removed from it; this is called being far removed from places of useless talk."
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from ill will?
Not allowing thoughts of anger, vexation, or contention to enter—this is called remaining far removed from ill will.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from arrogance?
“It is by not perceiving internal phenomena; this is called remaining far removed from arrogance.
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from disparaging others?”
"It is said that because one does not perceive external phenomena, this is called being far removed from disparaging others.
How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from the ten unwholesome paths of action?"
"These ten unwholesome paths can obstruct the Eightfold Noble Path, let alone Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
This is called being far removed from the ten unwholesome paths."
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from great pride?
“It is when this bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomenon that could give rise to great pride; this is called remaining far removed from great pride.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from self-opinionatedness?
It is when this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that can be used for self-opinionatedness; this is called remaining far removed from self-opinionatedness.”
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from perversions?
“Because the locus of perversion cannot be apprehended, this is called remaining far removed from perversions.
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from lust, anger, and delusion?”
“Because the locus of lust, anger, and delusion cannot be perceived, this is called being far removed from the loci of lust, anger, and delusion.
This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the fifth stage remains far removed from these twelve dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva, dwelling in the sixth stage, fulfill six dharmas?
“They are the so-called six pāramitās.
All Buddhas, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwell within these six pāramitās and are able to cross to the other shore; this is called fulfilling the six dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva not give rise to the mindset of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha? [The Buddha replied:
“He forms this thought:
‘The mindset of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha is not the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
“How does a bodhisattva give gifts without giving rise to a mind of distress?
[The Buddha replied: “He forms this thought:
‘This is not the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
“How does a bodhisattva’s mind not sink when seeing someone who asks for something?
[The Buddha replied: “He forms this thought:
‘This is not the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
“What is the bodhisattva’s giving of all possessions?
When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they practice giving without saying, ‘This may be given’ or ‘This may not be given.’”
“How is it that a bodhisattva has no regret after practicing generosity?
“Because of the power of compassion.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not doubt the profound Dharma?”
“By the power of the merit of faith.
This is how a bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage remains far removed from six things.
[The Śāstra] says:

Regarding "purity of precepts": in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one practices giving (*dāna*) extensively; subsequently, one realizes that maintaining the precepts (*śīla*) is superior to giving. Why is this?
Maintaining the precepts encompasses all sentient beings, whereas giving cannot universally reach them all.
The observance of the precepts pervades the immeasurable— just as the precept against taking life bestows life upon all sentient beings,
so too, as sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless, their merit is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
Briefly stated, all matters that can destroy the Buddha-way are here termed "breaking the precepts";
being free from these stains of breaking the precepts is termed "purity.
Even the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha is still a stain upon the precepts, let alone other evils!
Regarding "knowing and repaying kindness," some say:
"I ought to have obtained this through the causal conditions of my merit from past lives.
Or they say:
"I am naturally noble and honorable; what kindness have you done for me?
To fall into such a false view, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should recognize the kindness [of others]!"
"Although sentient beings possess the causes for happiness from past lives, if conditions in the present life do not harmonize, there is no way for them to obtain happiness.
It is like a grain seed in the earth: if there is no rain, it will not sprout;
one cannot say that rain has no merit simply because the earth is capable of producing the grain."
Although the objects received were sown by one's own past karma, is the kindness of the person who offers them—with a heart of reverence and affection—not a debt of gratitude?

Furthermore, knowing gratitude is the root of great compassion and the initial gateway to wholesome karma; such a person is loved and respected by others, their fame spreads far and wide, they will be reborn in heaven after death, and ultimately attain the Way of Buddhahood.
One who is ungrateful is worse than a beast!
As the Buddha said in the *Jātaka-sūtra*:

There was once a man who entered the mountains to fell timber; he became lost and could not find his way. At that time, a torrential rain fell, and as evening approached, he suffered from hunger and cold. Malevolent insects and venomous beasts were about to come and harm him.
This man entered a stone cave, where there was a large bear; seeing it, he was terrified and fled.
The bear said to him, "Do not be afraid!"
"This dwelling is warm; you may stay here overnight.
At that time, it rained continuously for seven days, during which the bear constantly provided this man with sweet fruits and fine water.
When the rain ceased after seven days, the bear led the man and showed him the way.
The bear said to the man, "I am a sinful body with many enemies; if anyone asks about me, do not say that you have seen me!
The man replied:
"Yes! Having said this, the man went forward and saw some hunters.
The hunters asked him:
"From where have you come?
Have you seen any wild beasts?
He replied:
"I saw a great bear; this bear has been kind to me, so I cannot show it to you!
The hunter said, "You are a human being and should treat one another with human kindness; why do you begrudge the bear?"
"Now that you have once lost your way, when will you ever return?
If you show me [the bear], I shall give you a large share!
The man’s mind changed, and he immediately led the hunter to the location where the bear was.
The hunter killed the bear and gave him a large portion of its flesh.
As the man reached out his hand to take the meat, both of his elbows fell off.
The hunter said:
"What crime have you committed?
He replied, "This bear looked upon me as a father looks upon his son; that I now turn my back on his kindness—this is my crime!"
The hunter was terrified and did not dare eat the meat; he took it and offered it to the assembly of monks.
At that time, the senior elder, an Arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers, said to the junior monks:
"This is a Bodhisattva who shall become a Buddha in a future age; do not eat this meat!"
They immediately erected a stūpa to make offerings to him.
When the king heard of this matter, he issued an edict throughout the kingdom: "Let no one who is ungrateful dwell here!

Furthermore, through various causes and conditions, he praised those who recognize kindness; thus, the meaning of gratitude spread throughout Jambudvīpa, and all people came to believe in and practice it.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"If there were someone who committed an evil act toward me, I would still consider them worthy of being saved; how much more so those who have been kind to me!"
Regarding "abiding in the power of patience," it is as explained at length in the *Kṣānti-pāramitā*. Question:
Since patience has various causes and conditions as its characteristics, why is it said here only that one is "neither angry nor vexed"?
Answer: This is the essence of patience (*kṣānti*). One first gives rise to a mind of anger, and subsequently causes affliction to others through body and speech.
Because this is the initial practice of a bodhisattva, it speaks only of patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*), and not of patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*).
Regarding "experiencing joy": because the Bodhisattva sees that this upholding of the precepts results in the purity of body and speech;
because of gratitude and patience, the mind is pure;
and because the three karmas are thus purified, joy arises spontaneously.

For example, it is like a person who bathes in fragrant water, puts on fine new clothes, and adorns themselves with necklaces; looking at their own reflection in a mirror, they feel joy in their heart.
The Bodhisattva is also like this, attaining these wholesome dharmas to adorn themselves:
"Precepts are the foundation of meditative concentration and wisdom; now that I have attained these pure precepts, immeasurable and boundless merit and virtue should all be easily obtained."
He rejoices because of this.

Abiding in these precepts and forbearance, the bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to be reborn before Buddhas in other directions or to experience happiness among devas and humans;
or he causes them to attain the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha-vehicle.

Observing sentient beings’ attachment to pleasure is like an elder observing his young children playing together; he joins them in their play and gives them slightly different objects to cause them to abandon what they previously enjoyed.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to obtain the blessings and happiness of humans and devas;
he gradually leads them forward, enabling them to attain the three vehicles.
For this reason, it is said that "one experiences joy and happiness.

Regarding "not abandoning any sentient beings": because one has skillfully cultivated and accumulated the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because of the vow to deliver sentient beings, because the resolve for enlightenment is firm, because one would not be held in contempt by the Buddhas and the worthies and sages, and because one fears being in debt to all sentient beings, one does not abandon them;
it is like first promising someone an object and then failing to give it—that is the crime of falsehood!
For these reasons, he does not abandon sentient beings.
Regarding "entering the mind of great compassion," it is as previously explained.
Herein, the Buddha himself says:

"Out of the great resolve of his original vow for the sake of sentient beings—that is, for the sake of each and every individual—he undergoes the sufferings of hell on their behalf throughout immeasurable kalpas, until he causes that person to accumulate and practice merit, attain Buddhahood, and enter nirvana without remainder."
Question: Since there is no one who can take another’s place to undergo their retribution for sins, why do you make such a vow? Answer:
This Bodhisattva possesses a vast and great mind and loves sentient beings deeply; if there were someone to take his place, he would certainly do so without hesitation.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva sees that among humans there are celestial shrines where human flesh, blood, and the five internal organs are used to sacrifice to rākṣasa demons, he permits someone to take his place.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"If there should be such a representative in the hells, I must certainly act as that representative!
When the multitude hears that the Bodhisattva’s great resolve is thus, they hold him in high esteem, revere, and respect him.
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva’s profound mindfulness of sentient beings exceeds that of a compassionate mother.

Regarding the phrase “believing in the teacher and reverently receiving [instruction],” since it is through the teacher that a bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how could they fail to believe in, revere, and make offerings to the teacher?
Although one's wisdom and virtue may be lofty and brilliant, if one does not practice respect and make offerings, one cannot attain great benefit;
it is like a deep well with fine water: without a rope, there is no way to obtain the water.
If one breaks down arrogance and haughtiness, and instead honors, respects, and remains humble, then great merit and benefit will accrue to them;
it is just as when rain falls, it does not remain on the mountain peak but inevitably flows toward the lower ground.
If a person is arrogant and self-exalting, the water of the Dharma will not enter them;
if they revere a virtuous teacher, then merit will accrue to them.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that by relying on a virtuous teacher, one's observance of the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation will all increase.
For example, just as all trees that depend upon the Snowy Mountains—whether roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits—all attain lush growth.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"Among the various schools of teachers, honor them as you would the Buddha."
Question: How can an evil teacher receive offerings and be accepted with faith?
A good teacher cannot even regard him as a Buddha, let alone an evil teacher!
Why does the Buddha, in this context, state that "one should regard all teachers and venerables as the World-Honored One"?
The answer is:
a bodhisattva should not conform to worldly dharmas.
Those who follow worldly dharmas become attached to what is good and distance themselves from what is evil;

the Bodhisattva is not thus. If there is one who can expound profound meanings and unravel the knots of doubt, and who is beneficial to me, the Bodhisattva will devote his whole heart to honoring that person, without dwelling on any other faults.
It is like a worn-out bag containing jewels; one must not fail to take the jewels simply because the bag is foul.
It is also like traveling at night on a perilous path where a person of poor character holds a torch; one must not fail to accept the light simply because the person is wicked.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: having received the light of wisdom from the teacher, he does not dwell upon their faults.
Furthermore, the disciple should think:
"The teacher practices the Prajñāpāramitā with immeasurable power of skillful means; I do not know by what causes and conditions these evil matters have arisen."
Just as Sadāprarudita heard the Buddhas of the ten directions speaking from the air:
"Regarding this Dharma teacher, do not dwell on his shortcomings; always maintain a sense of reverence and awe!"
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects:
"Whether the Dharma teacher is good or bad is not my concern;
that which I seek is solely to hear the Dharma for my own benefit."

Just as clay or wooden images possess no real merit, yet one obtains immeasurable merit by conceiving of them as the Buddha, how much more so for this person who, through wisdom and skillful means, is able to preach it for others!
"For this reason, any fault lies with the Dharma Master; there is no blame for me.
As for the phrase "regarding him as the World-Honored One," I have previously stated:
"A Bodhisattva is different from worldly people."
People of the world discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly:
they are attached to what is beautiful, yet it is still not equal to the Buddha;
they treat what is ugly with contempt, regarding it as not even worth counting.
The Bodhisattva, however, is not so; he contemplates all phenomena as ultimately empty, seeing from the very beginning that they all possess the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
He views all sentient beings as if they were Buddhas, let alone those Dharma-teachers who possess wisdom and provide benefit!
Because they are able to perform the work of a Buddha, one regards them as Buddhas.
Regarding "diligently seeking the various *pāramitās*," the Bodhisattva reflects:
"These six *pāramitās* are the causes and conditions for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; I shall practice these causes and conditions with a single-minded focus."

It is, for example, like merchants and farmers who, according to the needs of the lands they visit and the seeds appropriate to those soils, diligently cultivate and procure them; thus, there is nothing they do not accomplish.

Furthermore, it is like how in this world one attains great wealth after practicing generosity, attains nobility after maintaining the precepts, and attains the Way after cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: by practicing the six pāramitās, one attains Buddhahood.
Those who diligently seek the Way should always single-mindedly and diligently seek the six pāramitās.
Why is this? If one with a weak mind progresses gradually, they will be shrouded by afflictions and destroyed by the followers of Māra.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"Strive diligently in these two stages without slackening! [The second stage concludes.

Regarding "being insatiable in extensive learning": the Bodhisattva knows that extensive learning is the causal condition for wisdom; having attained wisdom, one is then able to discern and practice the Path.
It is like a person with eyes who encounters no obstacles wherever they go.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"Whatever Dharma the Buddhas of the ten directions preach, I shall receive and uphold it all!
This is by virtue of the power of the *śrutadhara-dhāraṇī*, the power of the pure divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), and the power of the *asaṃpramoṣa-dhāraṇī*.
Just as the great ocean can receive and sustain all the waters of the ten directions,
so too the bodhisattva can receive and sustain all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding "pure Dharma-giving": it is like a field of grain from which weeds are cleared so that the crop may flourish;

the Bodhisattva is likewise. When practicing Dharma-giving, they do not seek fame, profit, or karmic rewards in future lives, nor do they seek the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle even for the sake of sentient beings. Rather, out of great compassion, they turn the wheel of the Dharma for sentient beings in accordance with the Buddha.

The characteristics of the gift of Dharma, the characteristics of adorning the Buddha-lands, undergoing immeasurable toil and suffering for the sake of the world, abiding in a state of shame and remorse, not abandoning forest retreats, having few desires and being content—these are as previously explained.
Question:
There are various causes and conditions for not feeling weary of birth and death;
why is it that only two causes and conditions are mentioned as reasons for not being weary?
Answer: Because these roots of goodness are fully perfected, the suffering and affliction within the cycle of birth and death are slight;
it is like a person with a wound who, when an excellent medicine is applied to it, finds the pain diminished.
Because the Bodhisattva has attained the purity of the roots of goodness, all present-life anxieties, envy, and malevolent thoughts are entirely stilled.

If he takes on another body, he will receive the fruit of his roots of goodness, personally enjoying blessings and happiness, while also benefiting sentient beings through various causes and conditions according to their wishes.

He purifies his own world, making it so majestic and pure that it surpasses even the celestial palaces; one can never tire of beholding it, for it is able to comfort and resolve the minds of great Bodhisattvas, let alone those of ordinary people!
For this reason, although there are many causes and conditions, only two matters are mentioned as being insatiable.
Although there are various forms of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*), the greatest among them here is the mind of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*.
A bodhisattva resolves to extensively deliver all sentient beings;
yet, upon encountering even slight suffering or affliction, they wish to personally attain nirvana alone—this is truly shameful!
For example, it is like someone who has prepared a great feast and invited many people;
yet, when a mind of stinginess arises, he eats alone by himself—this is truly shameful!

The third stage concludes with the phrase "not abandoning the dwelling in an araṇya": to dwell alone apart from the crowd. If one transcends the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, this is called "dwelling apart from the crowd."
Because all dharmas are empty through non-apprehension, one does not grasp at or cling to their marks;
even regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one does not grasp at it, because of the mind that is free from attachment.
A bodhisattva constantly accumulates all merits without ever feeling weary or satisfied; only upon attaining the Unsurpassed Way does he feel satisfied, for there is no dharma superior to it.
As for being content with food, clothing, and bedding, these are merely conditions for wholesome dharmas and are not considered essential; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Regarding "not abandoning the merit of *dhūta* practices," this is as explained later in the "Chapter on Awakening to Māra.
As for the "patience with the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), within this context, the patience with the non-arising of phenomena constitutes the *dhūta*.
The Bodhisattva abides in the patience of conformity (ānulomikī-kṣānti) and contemplates the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

These twelve dhūtas are for the sake of the purity of ethical discipline; the purity of ethical discipline is for the sake of meditative concentration (dhyāna); meditative concentration is for the sake of wisdom (prajñā);
and the dharma of the patience regarding non-arising is itself true wisdom.
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the fruit of *dhūta* practice; it is spoken of as the cause within the context of the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "not abandoning the precepts, yet not grasping at the characteristics of the precepts," this is because the bodhisattva knows the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas; since he does not even perceive the observance of precepts, how much less the breaking of them!

Although one does not break the precepts despite various causes and conditions, this is considered the greatest [virtue], for it enters the gate of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
As for "defiling desires," it is as previously explained.
In this regard, the Buddha said:
"Because one knows that the characteristics of this mind are deceptive and unreal, one does not even give rise to a thought of desire, let alone indulge in it.
As for "disgust for the world," it is as explained in the section on the characteristic of the world's lack of delight.
In this context, the Buddha speaks of the fruit of the mind of revulsion, namely, the "gate of liberation through non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣamukha*).
"Relinquishing all that one possesses" is as previously explained.

Regarding "a mind that does not sink," this has already been explained through various causes and conditions; when a bodhisattva hears of these signs of not sinking and not fearing, they do not give rise to dualistic consciousnesses.

As for "not giving rise to dualistic consciousnesses," the two bases of consciousness refer to the eye and forms, wherein visual consciousness does not arise, and so on, up to the mind and mental phenomena, wherein mental consciousness does not arise.
When a bodhisattva dwells within this gate of non-duality, they observe that all objects known by the six consciousnesses are deceptive and without reality;
they then make a great vow:
"May all sentient beings dwell within the dharma of non-duality and be free from these six consciousnesses."

Regarding the phrase "not begrudging any thing": although there are various causes and conditions among those who do not begrudge any thing, this cause and condition is the greatest—namely, that the bodhisattva knows all dharmas to be ultimately empty, does not give rise to recollections, and extinguishes all grasping at signs.
Therefore, one does not seek gratitude from the recipient and maintains no sense of superiority regarding the act of giving; in this way, one fulfills the pure *dānapāramitā*.

The fourth stage concludes. Regarding "staying far away from laypeople": the practitioner leaves the household life because it obstructs the Path; if they again associate with laypeople, they are no different from how they were before.
For this reason, a practitioner first seeks to deliver themselves and only then delivers others;
if one who has not yet delivered themselves desires to deliver others, it is like a person who does not know how to swim attempting to rescue someone drowning—the two will sink together!
This bodhisattva, by distancing himself from lay associates, is able to accumulate all pure merits;
because he deeply recollects the Buddha, he transforms his body to reach the lands of all Buddhas, where he leaves the household life, shaves his head, and dons the dyed robes.
Why is this? Because one always delights in the dharma of leaving home and does not delight in associating with laypeople.
Regarding "keeping far from bhikṣuṇīs," it is as explained in the first chapter.
Question:
Since a bodhisattva regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind, why is it that they cannot dwell together? Answer:

This bodhisattva has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and has not yet severed all outflows (āsrava); although he accumulates various merits, people become attached to him, and for this reason, one should not dwell together with him.
Furthermore, it is to avoid the slander of others, for those who slander fall into hell.
Regarding "staying far away from begrudging or coveting the households of others," the Bodhisattva reflects:
"Since I have myself renounced my own home, I do not even feel greed or attachment toward it; how then could I feel greed or attachment toward the households of others?"
The Dharma of a Bodhisattva seeks to enable all sentient beings to attain happiness; since this person assists me in bestowing happiness upon sentient beings, why should I be stingy or begrudge them?
Sentient beings have obtained these offerings through the causes and conditions of their merit from past lives, requiring little effort in this present life; why, then, should I be stingy or envious?

"Staying far away from useless talk" refers to frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). To explain matters that merely alleviate the sorrows of one's own mind or the minds of others—such as accounts of kings, bandits, the great oceans, mountain forests, medicinal herbs, precious objects, and various regions and countries—such matters are of no benefit to merit and of no benefit to the Path.

A bodhisattva takes pity on all sentient beings who are submerged in the fires of impermanence and suffering, thinking, "I must rescue them; how can I remain sitting idly and speak of things that are of no benefit?"
It is like a person whose house is on fire with flames breaking out on all four sides; how could they remain within it to discuss other matters?
In this context, the Buddha says that even to speak of the affairs of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas would be useless speech, let alone other matters!
Regarding "being far removed from ill will": that which first arises in the mind is called the mind of anger (*krodha*), because it is not yet fixed;
when the mind of anger increases and becomes fixed in action—such as striking, hacking, or killing—it is called the mind of vexation (*vyāpāda*);
speaking harshly and slandering others is called the mind of contention (*pradāśa*).
If one commits acts such as killing, beating, or binding others, this is called a combative mind.
Because a bodhisattva possesses great compassion for sentient beings, they do not give rise to such a mind;
they constantly guard against this evil mind, ensuring it does not enter.

"To remain far removed from self-conceit and contempt for others" means not perceiving internal or external dharmas—namely, the five aggregates that are grasped and the five aggregates that are not grasped.

"To remain far removed from the ten unwholesome paths" means that the bodhisattva contemplates the various causes and conditions of the faults and transgressions within the ten unwholesome paths, as previously explained.
In this regard, the Buddha said:
"The ten unwholesome paths destroy the Hīnayāna, let alone the Mahāyāna!

As for "being far removed from great pride," it means that when a bodhisattva practices the eighteen kinds of emptiness, they do not perceive any dharmas as having fixed characteristics of being either great or small.
"Being free from self-conceit" means that one has uprooted the seven kinds of pride and because one deeply delights in wholesome dharmas.
"Being free from inversion" means that within all phenomena, permanence, bliss, purity, and self cannot be found.
Regarding "being far removed from the three poisons," the meaning of the three poisons is as previously explained.
Furthermore, these three poisons have no fixed characteristics as their objects.
This concludes the fifth stage. Regarding the "six pāramitās," they are as previously explained.
In this regard, the Buddha said:
"Those of the three vehicles all reach the other shore by means of these six pāramitās. Question:
This is the stage of the Bodhisattva; why, then, is it said that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas reach the other shore?
The answer is:
The Buddha now speaks of the six pāramitās as having specific capacities; within the Mahāyāna Dharma, they can encompass the Hīnayāna, whereas the Hīnayāna cannot.
When this bodhisattva dwells in the sixth stage, they fulfill the six pāramitās;

yet, while contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas, they have not yet attained the power of skillful means and thus fear falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Because the Buddha protects them, he says:
"One should not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha."
Because the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates sentient beings, because of his great compassionate heart, and because he knows that all dharmas are ultimately empty, he has no sense of loss when giving;
upon seeing a seeker, he feels neither anger nor sorrow;
and after having given, his mind does not regret it.
Because their merit is great, their power of faith is also great; they possess deep, pure faith and reverence for all Buddhas.

They are fully endowed with the six pāramitās; although they have not yet attained skillful means, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), or the pratyutpanna-samādhi, they harbor no doubts regarding the profound Dharma, thinking thus:
"All discursive arguments contain faults and transgressions!"
"Only the wisdom of the Buddha extinguishes all conceptual proliferation (prapañca); because it is free from deficiency, he is able to cultivate all wholesome dharmas through skillful means.
For this reason, one has no doubt.
The Sixth Ground is concluded. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle Forty-nine.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the "Chapter on Setting Out" (Prasthāna-paṭala), Part Twenty, Continued;
Fascicle Fifty.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty. [Sūtra]: "How does a bodhisattva not cling to a self?
[Answer]: "Because, ultimately, there is no self."
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to sentient beings, does not cling to a life-span, does not cling to the enumeration of beings, and so on, up to a knower or a seer?
It is because these dharmas are ultimately unobtainable.”
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to the view of annihilation?
“There is no phenomenon that is annihilated, because all phenomena are ultimately unarisen.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to the view of permanence?”
“If a dharma is unarisen, it does not constitute permanence.
“Why should a bodhisattva not grasp at signs?
“Because they are free from all afflictions.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not forming views regarding causes?
It is because all views are unapprehendable.
What is meant by a bodhisattva not being attached to name-and-form?”
“Because the characteristics of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) do not exist.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), does not cling to the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu), and does not cling to the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana)?”
“Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas does not exist.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to the three realms?
“Because the intrinsic nature of the three realms does not exist.”
“How should a bodhisattva not form a mind of attachment?
How should a bodhisattva not form a vow?
How should a bodhisattva not form a basis?”
“Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas does not exist.
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not cling to the view of relying on the Buddha?
“Because one who forms a view of reliance does not see the Buddha.”
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to views based on the Dharma?
“Because the Dharma cannot be seen.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to views based on the Saṅgha?”
“Because the characteristics of the Saṃgha are unconditioned and thus cannot be relied upon.
“How does a bodhisattva not cling to reliance on views regarding the precepts?
“Because they do not cling to either transgression or non-transgression.”
"These are the twenty things to which a bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage should not be attached.
How should a bodhisattva fulfill emptiness?
By fulfilling the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena."
“What is the bodhisattva’s realization of signlessness?
“Because they do not attend to any signs.
“What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the unconditioned?”
“Because one does not create [karmic action] within the three realms.
“How is it that a bodhisattva’s three parts are pure?
“Because they are fully endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action.”
“How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with the wisdom of compassion toward all sentient beings?
“By attaining great compassion.
“How does a bodhisattva not dwell upon [the concept of] all sentient beings?”
“Because of the fulfillment of purifying the Buddha-fields.
“What is the bodhisattva’s equal contemplation of all dharmas?
“Because of neither diminishing nor augmenting any dharmas.”
“How does a bodhisattva know the true nature of all phenomena?
“Because the true nature of all phenomena is without cognition.
“What is a bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena?”
“It is because all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and are unconditioned.
“What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of non-arising?
“It is knowing that name-and-form do not arise.”
“How does a bodhisattva teach that all phenomena have a single characteristic?
“Because the mind does not engage with dual characteristics.
“How does a bodhisattva destroy the characteristic of conceptual differentiation?”
“Because all phenomena are non-discriminative.
“How does a bodhisattva transform their conceptualizations?
“By transforming the notions of small, great, and immeasurable.”
“How does a bodhisattva transform views?
“By transforming the views regarding the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“How does a bodhisattva transform afflictions?”
“Because they sever all afflictions.
“What is the bodhisattva’s stage of the equality of concentration and wisdom?
“It is the so-called attainment of the knowledge of all modes.”
“How does a bodhisattva discipline the mind?
“By remaining unmoved within the three realms.
“How does a bodhisattva attain the tranquility of the mind?”
“Because he has subdued the six sense faculties.
“What is the bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom?
“Because he has attained the Buddha-eye.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being unstained by craving?
“Because they have abandoned the six sense objects.
These are the twenty dharmas that a bodhisattva fulfills while dwelling in the seventh stage.”
“How does a bodhisattva enter into accordance with the minds of sentient beings?
“The bodhisattva, by means of a single mind, knows the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings.”
“How does a bodhisattva sport in the various supernormal powers?
“By means of these supernormal powers, they go from one buddha-field to another buddha-field, yet they do not form the notion of a 'buddha-field.'”
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate the buddha-fields?
“Abiding in their own field, they see immeasurable buddha-fields, yet they have no conceptualization of ‘buddha-fields.’”
“How does a bodhisattva adorn his own land just as he has seen the lands of the Buddhas?
“Abiding in the stage of a universal monarch (cakravartin), he adorns [himself] by reaching throughout the trichiliocosm.”
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate the Buddha’s body as it truly is?
“By contemplating the Dharma-body as it truly is.
This is the fourth dharma that a bodhisattva fulfills while dwelling in the eighth stage.”
“How does a bodhisattva know the superior and inferior faculties?
A bodhisattva, abiding in the ten powers of a Buddha, knows the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings.”
“How does a bodhisattva purify a buddha-field?
“By purifying sentient beings.
“What is a bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi?”
“Abiding in this samādhi, one can accomplish all tasks while also not giving rise to mental characteristics.
How does a bodhisattva constantly enter samādhi?”
“Because the bodhisattva has attained the samādhi of birth by retribution.
“How does a bodhisattva take on a body according to the roots of goodness appropriate for sentient beings?
“The bodhisattva takes on a body knowing the roots of goodness that should arise in sentient beings, in order to bring them to maturity.”
“This is what it means for a bodhisattva dwelling in the eighth stage to be fully endowed with five dharmas.
“How does a bodhisattva receive his portion of those to be saved in infinite worlds?”
“In the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, they liberate those sentient beings who are to be delivered according to the teachings of all Buddhas.
“How does a bodhisattva attain that which accords with their vows?”
“Because they are fully endowed with the six perfections.
“How does a bodhisattva know the languages of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas?”
“Because of the power of eloquence.
“How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection of birth from a womb?
“Because a bodhisattva is always born by transformation in every lifetime.”
“What is the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s family?
It is because they are always born into great families.
What is the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s birth?”
“Because they are born into the family of a kṣatriya or born into the family of a brāhmaṇa.
“What is meant by ‘accomplished in nature’?
“It is because one is born from the same lineage as that from which past bodhisattvas were born.”
“What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s retinue?
It is having exclusively bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as one’s retinue.
What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s birth?”
"At the time of birth, light universally illumines immeasurable and boundless worlds, yet he does not grasp at signs.
How does a bodhisattva achieve success in leaving the household life?"

"At the time of his renunciation, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of devas attended upon him as he left the household life; all these sentient beings will certainly attain one of the three vehicles.
How does a bodhisattva accomplish the adornment of the Bodhi tree?"

"This Bodhi tree has roots made of gold, with stems, nodes, branches, and leaves composed of the seven treasures; the radiance from these stems, nodes, branches, and leaves shines universally throughout incalculable trichiliocosm worlds in the ten directions."
“How does a bodhisattva bring all virtuous merits to full completion and perfection?
“A bodhisattva attains the purity of sentient beings, and the buddha-field is likewise purified.”
“This is the bodhisattva abiding in the ninth stage who fulfills twelve dharmas.
“How should it be known that the bodhisattva abiding in the tenth stage is like a Buddha?”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the six pāramitās, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha;

if they are fully perfected in the knowledge of all modes and have severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies—this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the tenth stage to be known as being like a buddha.”

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within these ten stages, by means of the power of skillful means, they practice the six pāramitās, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. They transcend the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight patiences, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva. Having transcended these nine stages, they abide in the stage of the Buddha.
These are the ten stages of the bodhisattva. Thus, Subhūti,
this is called the setting out in the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The [Treatise] author says:
We do not cling because these twenty dharmas are unattainable.
The causes and conditions for their being unattainable have been explained in various ways previously.

Views such as the view of a self up to the view of a knower or a viewer, the view of a Buddha, and the view of a Sangha—because these enter into the emptiness of sentient beings—one should not be attached to such views.
Other views, from those of annihilationism and eternalism up to the view of precepts and observances—because these pertain to the emptiness of phenomena—one should not be attached to them.
Question:
The others may be understood; what is meant by "seeing as a cause"? Answer:

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) function as causes and effects for one another; within these phenomena, to fixate the mind upon them, grasp at their characteristics, and give rise to views is called "view of cause" (*hetudṛṣṭi*). This refers to asserting what is not a cause to be a cause, or [holding] that cause and effect are identical or different, and so forth.
Regarding "perfection of emptiness": if a bodhisattva can fully practice the eighteen kinds of emptiness, this is called the perfection of emptiness.
Furthermore, if one can practice two kinds of emptiness—emptiness of sentient beings and emptiness of phenomena—this is called the perfection of emptiness.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva is able to practice ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and remains unattached within it, this is called being "fully endowed with emptiness.
Question:
If that is so, why does the Buddha here speak only of "emptiness of self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
Answer: These three kinds of emptiness are all emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Because a bodhisattva dwelling in the sixth stage possesses the merit [of that stage], their faculties are sharp; because their faculties are sharp, they differentiate all dharmas and grasp at their marks.
For this reason, in the seventh stage, the emptiness of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is considered the fulfillment of emptiness.

Sometimes the Buddha speaks of the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) as the fulfillment of emptiness; at other times, he speaks of the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) as the fulfillment of emptiness.
Regarding "realization of the signless": the signless is itself nirvana; it can be realized, but it cannot be cultivated.
Because it cannot be cultivated, one cannot say that it is "known";
because it is immeasurable, boundless, and non-discriminative, one cannot say that it is "perfected."

Regarding "knowing the unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*): although all three matters are common to this knowledge, two matters are further established by name according to their specific meanings, whereas the unconditioned possesses only the name "knowledge."
The "threefold purity" refers to the ten paths of wholesome action:
three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind; these are called the three parts.
Since the three gates of liberation have already been explained above, they will not be discussed again here.
Regarding "purity in three parts": there may be some whose physical karma is pure while their verbal karma is impure;
or whose verbal karma is pure while their physical karma is impure;
or whose physical and verbal karma are pure while their mental karma is impure.
There may be those in the world whose three types of action (trikarma) are pure, yet they have not yet abandoned attachment;
because this bodhisattva’s three types of action are both pure and free from attachment, it is called the purity of the three parts.
Regarding the phrase "possessing the wisdom of compassion toward all sentient beings," there are three kinds of compassion:
that which takes sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana*), that which takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana*), and that which is objectless (*anālambana*).
Here, it is the objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*) that is said to be "complete."

That which is called the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), up to and including the emptiness of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), is termed "unconditioned great compassion" (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*).
A bodhisattva enters deeply into the true mark and only thereafter feels compassionate concern for sentient beings;
it is like a man who has an only son and, upon obtaining a fine treasure, cherishes it with a deep heart and desires to give it to him.
"Non-recollection of all sentient beings" refers to the perfection of the purification of the world.
Question:
If one does not recollect sentient beings, how can one purify the Buddha-world?
The answer is:
A bodhisattva causes sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action in order to adorn the Buddha-land;
yet, although it is adorned, it has not yet attained unimpeded adornment.
Now, when a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, they do not grasp at the mark of a sentient being; thus, their roots of goodness and merit are pure.
Because these roots of goodness and merit are pure, this constitutes unimpeded adornment.
Regarding "the equal contemplation of all dharmas," it is as explained in the *Dharmasamatā-kṣānti*.
Herein the Buddha himself says:
"One neither increases nor diminishes any dharmas."
Regarding "knowing the true reality of all phenomena," this has been explained extensively through various causes and conditions as previously described.

As for "the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): within the true reality of all phenomena, which is without arising or ceasing, to have faith and acceptance, to attain thorough penetration, to be unimpeded, and to be non-retrogressive—this is called the patience regarding non-arising.
Regarding "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*): initially it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*), and subsequently it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
that which is coarse is patience, and that which is subtle is knowledge.
The Buddha himself said:
"Because one knows that name and form do not arise.

Regarding "explaining that all dharmas have a single characteristic": the bodhisattva knows that the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*) are all the net of Māra, deceptive and unreal; that the six kinds of consciousness arising therein are likewise the net of Māra and deceptive.
What is reality?
It is solely the non-dual dharma—neither eye nor form, up to and including neither mind nor phenomena; this is called reality.
In order to cause sentient beings to leave behind the twelve bases (*āyatana*), he constantly uses various causes and conditions to expound this non-dual dharma (*advaya-dharma*).

Regarding "destroying the marks of discrimination," it means that when a bodhisattva dwells within this non-dual dharma, they destroy the various discriminated phenomena of objects of perception, such as male and female, long and short, large and small, and so forth.
“Transforming recollections and conceptions” means destroying the internal recollections and conceptual discriminations regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).
“Transforming views” means that this bodhisattva first transforms wrong views such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and subsequently enters the Path;
now he transforms the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-dṛṣṭi*), because all phenomena lack fixed characteristics.
"Transforming toward *nirvāṇa*" means turning away from the views of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* and proceeding directly toward the Buddha-way.

"Transforming afflictions" (*kleśa*) means that because the bodhisattva possesses the power of merit and the observance of precepts, they subdue coarse afflictions and proceed on the path in peace; while only subtle ones such as craving, views, and pride remain, they now also abandon these subtle afflictions.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva, by means of true wisdom, contemplates these afflictions as being the true mark (dharmatā);
it is like a person with supernormal powers who can transform the impure into the pure.
Regarding "the stage of equal concentration and wisdom": in the first three stages, the bodhisattva has more wisdom and less concentration because they have not yet been able to collect the mind;
in the subsequent three stages, there is more concentration and less wisdom. For this reason, one does not enter the bodhisattva rank [at those intermediate points].
Now, because sentient beings are empty and phenomena are empty, and because concentration and wisdom are equal, one is able to practice the bodhisattva path with peace and security;
from the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), one gradually attains the stage of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding "disciplining the mind": this means that the bodhisattva first disciplines the mind out of compassion for sentient beings by recollecting old age, sickness, death, and the three evil realms;
now, because he knows the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he does not cling to the triple world, and because he does not cling to the triple world, he is disciplined.
Regarding "the tranquility of the mind": for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, the bodhisattva first subdues the five sensory faculties (*pañca-indriya*) among the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*);
because the mental faculty (*manas*) is difficult to subdue, it is now, while dwelling in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), that the mental faculty becomes tranquil.
Regarding "unimpeded wisdom": when a bodhisattva attains the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unimpeded amidst all phenomena, whether real or unreal.
Having attained this wisdom of the path, they lead all sentient beings to enter into the true Dharma; they attain unimpeded liberation and the Buddha-eye, becoming unimpeded amidst all dharmas.
Question: Why is it said that one attains the Buddha-eye within these seven stages? Answer:
In this regard, one should train in the Buddha-eye, being unimpeded regarding all dharmas, resembling the Buddha-eye.

As for "being unstained by craving," although this bodhisattva has attained the power of wisdom in the seventh stage, they still possess a physical body due to causes and conditions from previous lives; thus, while entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are without attachment, yet upon emerging from concentration, there remains a trace of attachment.
Following what is seen by this fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), they may feel affection for good people or become attached to the true dharmas of the wisdom of this seventh stage.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"One practices equanimity (*upekṣā*) regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), neither grasping at signs of the beautiful nor the ugly.

[The seventh stage is concluded. Regarding "entering in accordance with the minds of sentient beings": when a bodhisattva dwells within this eighth stage, they observe in accordance with the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings; observing their movements and the arising of their thoughts, they contemplate deeply and, through wisdom, discern and know them.
These sentient beings have no causal conditions for ever attaining liberation;

these sentient beings may only be liberated after the passing of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; these sentient beings may be liberated after one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to ten kalpas; these sentient beings may be liberated after one lifetime, two lifetimes, or even in this very lifetime; these sentient beings may be liberated immediately—these are those who are mature and those who are not yet mature;
this person can be liberated by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, and this person can be liberated by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
It is like a skilled physician who diagnoses an illness and knows whether the recovery will be long or near, and whether it is curable or incurable.

Regarding "sporting with the various supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*): having first attained these supernormal powers, one now attains mastery over them and can travel to immeasurable and boundless worlds.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in the seventh stage, they may wish to attain nirvāṇa;
at that time, through various causes and conditions as well as the protection of the Buddhas of the ten directions, they again give rise to the resolve to deliver sentient beings.

He possesses magnificent supernormal powers, acting with sovereign mastery at will, remaining unimpeded even throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds; he beholds all Buddha-lands, yet does not grasp at the characteristics of those Buddha-lands.

Regarding "observing the Buddha-lands": there are bodhisattvas who, by means of their supernormal powers, fly to the ten directions to observe various pure worlds, grasping their characteristics in order to adorn their own lands.
There are bodhisattvas whom a Buddha leads to the ten directions to show them pure worlds, so that they may grasp the characteristics of those pure lands and personally cultivate vows and practices;
this is like the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, who led the bhikṣu Dharmākara to the ten directions to show him pure worlds.

There may be bodhisattvas who, while remaining in their own lands, use the divine eye to see the pure worlds of the ten directions; they first grasp at the marks of purity, but subsequently, because they attain a mind of non-attachment, they relinquish them once more.
Regarding the phrase "adorn one's own land just as one has seen the Buddha-lands," it is as previously explained.
This eighth stage is called the "Cakravartin Stage.
Just as wherever the precious wheel of a Cakravartin King reaches, there is no obstruction, no hindrance, and no enemies; so it is here.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to rain down the jewels of the Dharma to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings without any hindrance; furthermore, they are able to take the characteristics of the pure lands they perceive and use them to adorn their own land.

Regarding "contemplating the Buddha's body as it truly is": one contemplates the bodies of all Buddhas as being like illusions or transformations, not comprised within the five aggregates, the twelve bases, or the eighteen elements; whether long or short, or of various colors, they are seen according to the karmic causes and conditions of sentient beings' past lives.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:
"One who sees the Dharma-body is one who sees the Buddha.
The Dharma-body is the emptiness of dharmas that cannot be apprehended.
The emptiness of non-apprehendable phenomena means that those phenomena produced through various causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature.
"Knowing the superior and inferior faculties" is as explained in the context of the Ten Powers.

The Bodhisattva first knows the mental activities of all sentient beings—whether they are dull or sharp, whether they practice much generosity or much wisdom—and delivers those according to what they have in abundance.
Regarding "purifying the Buddha-field," there are two kinds of purification:
first, the Bodhisattva purifies his own body;
second, he purifies the minds of sentient beings, causing them to practice the path of purity.
Because the causes and conditions of both self and others are pure, one obtains a pure world according to one's vows.

Regarding "entering the Illusion-like Samādhi": it is like a magician who, while staying in one place, manifests illusory phenomena that fill the entire world—namely, the fourfold army, palaces, cities and towers, food, drink, song, and dance, as well as killing and reviving, sorrow and suffering;
the Bodhisattva is also like this, dwelling within this samādhi, able to manifest transformations throughout the worlds of the ten directions, filling them all.

First, they fulfill the needs of sentient beings through the prior practice of giving and other perfections; next, they teach the Dharma to transform them and destroy the three evil realms; thereafter, they establish sentient beings in the Three Vehicles;
thus, there is no beneficial matter that they do not accomplish.
This Bodhisattva’s mind is unmoving, nor does he grasp at the characteristics of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "constantly entering samādhi": the Bodhisattva has attained samādhis such as the "illusion-like" (māyopama), whereby the mind he employs is capable of performing its functions;
now, having transformed his basis, he attains the "retribution-born" (upapatti-samādhi) samādhi, which is like a person seeing forms without exerting mental effort.
Abiding within this samādhi, one delivers sentient beings with peace and security; it excels the Illusion-like Samādhi in that matters are accomplished spontaneously without the need for exertion.
It is like a person seeking wealth: some acquire it through labor, while others obtain it naturally.

Regarding the phrase "receiving a body according to the roots of goodness appropriate for sentient beings": the Bodhisattva attains two kinds of samādhis and two kinds of supernormal powers, which are acquired through practice and acquired as karmic retribution.

He knows by what body, by what speech, by what causes and conditions, by what matters, by what path, and by what skillful means he should receive a body—even receiving the body of an animal—to transform and deliver them.

The eighth stage concludes: regarding the phrase "receiving the portion of those to be saved in boundless worlds," this refers to the bodhisattva’s teaching and saving of those sentient beings within the six realms of the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions who are destined to be liberated by his transformation.
There are three kinds of worlds:
the pure, the impure, and the mixed.
Within these three kinds of worlds, all sentient beings who are fit to be delivered and for whom there is benefit are gathered and sustained.
For example, lighting a lamp is for those with sight, not for the blind;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who acts either for those who already possess the causal conditions or for those who are beginning to create them.
Furthermore, a trichiliocosm is called one world; it arises at one time and ceases at one time.

In this manner, worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitute one Buddha-world. A number of such Buddha-worlds, equal to the sands of the Ganges, constitutes one Buddha-world-ocean. A number of such Buddha-world-oceans, equal to the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, constitutes one Buddha-world-lineage.
Such world-systems, infinite in the ten directions, are called a single Buddha-world.
Taking such a portion from among all worlds is called the portion to be delivered by a single Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "attaining as one wishes": because this bodhisattva is fully endowed with merit and wisdom, there is no wish that cannot be fulfilled.
When listeners hear that the portion of beings to be saved extends across immeasurable and boundless worlds, they may harbor doubts that such a thing is impossible;
for this reason, it is next stated that their wishes are realized according to their intent.
In this context, the Buddha himself explains that the six pāramitās are fully complete:
the five perfections constitute the fulfillment of merit, while prajñā constitutes the fulfillment of wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "knowing the languages of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas," I have previously stated that when one is complete in merit and wisdom, all that is wished for is realized as desired.
To know the various languages of others is precisely what is intended by his vow.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva has attained the purity of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he knows all languages wherever beings are born.
Furthermore, because he has attained the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), he knows the minds of those who establish names, seeing how they forcibly create various names and linguistic expressions.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva has attained the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of Sentient Beings, he is unimpeded in all speech.
Furthermore, having personally attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), he also trains in the Buddha’s four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;
for this reason, he understands the languages and sounds of sentient beings.
Regarding "accomplishment in the womb," some say that the Bodhisattva,
riding upon a white elephant and surrounded, revered, honored, and attended by immeasurable devas of Tuṣita, enters the mother’s womb.

Some say: Because the Bodhisattva’s mother has attained the power of the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), her womb becomes vast and immeasurable, allowing all the Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and spirits of the trichiliocosm to enter and exit it.

Within the womb there are palaces and towers; first, the seats are adorned, with silken banners and canopies suspended, flowers scattered, and incense burned—all of which are produced by the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s own meritorious karma. Only then does the Bodhisattva descend to take his place therein.
Furthermore, by the power of samādhi, he enters the mother’s womb while remaining as before in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Regarding "the accomplishment of birth": when the Bodhisattva is about to be born, the devas, nāgas, and spirits adorn the trichiliocosm;
at that time, a lotus throne made of the seven treasures appears spontaneously.
From within the mother’s womb, immeasurable bodhisattvas first emerged, sitting upon lotus flowers with palms joined in praise, awaiting the Bodhisattva;
likewise, the devas, nāgas, spirits, seers, sages, and celestial maidens all joined their hands in single-minded devotion, desiring to witness the birth of the Bodhisattva.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva emerged from his mother’s right side, like the full moon emerging from the clouds, emitting a great radiance that illuminated immeasurable worlds.
At that time, a great renown spread throughout the worlds of the ten directions, proclaiming:
"In such-and-such a land, a Bodhisattva has been born in his final existence."
Some bodhisattvas are born through transformation within lotus flowers;
among the four modes of birth, bodhisattvas are born either from a womb or by transformation.
Among the four classes of people, bodhisattvas are born into the two castes of Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa—being born into these two lineages because they are held in high esteem by the world.
Regarding "the accomplishment of the family": in the Brahmin family there is wisdom, while in the Kṣatriya family there is power and influence;
the Brahmin benefits future lives, whereas the Kṣatriya benefits the present life.
These two types are beneficial to the world; therefore, the bodhisattva is born among them.
Furthermore, the family of all meritorious dharmas—namely, the birth of non-retrogression—is called "birth in a noble family."

Regarding "accomplishment of lineage": when the Bodhisattva is in the Tuṣita Heaven, he observes which lineage in the world is noble and capable of gathering sentient beings, and he is then born into that very lineage.
Among the seven Buddhas, the first three were born into the Kauṇḍinya clan;
the next three were born into the Kāśyapa clan;
and Śākyamuni Buddha was born into the Gautama clan.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva’s initial profound resolve is firm and stable, this is called the lineage of all Buddhas.
Some say that attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the lineage of all Buddhas.

At that time, because they have obtained a portion of the Buddha’s *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience), they are like those on the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*) in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Regarding "perfection of retinue," these are all wise and virtuous people who have accumulated merit throughout successive lifetimes.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:
"He has exclusively bodhisattvas as his retinue.
As it is said in the *Acintya-sūtra*:
"Gopiyā is a great bodhisattva, and all her attendants are bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika);
through the power of transformation by means of skillful samādhi, she appears as men and women to serve as her retinue."
"Just as the Householder Jewel of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is a yakṣa or spirit who manifests in human form to engage in affairs with people.
Regarding "the accomplishment of leaving the home life," it is like the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, who at night within his palace saw all the court ladies appearing as if dead;
then the devas and spirits of the ten directions, bearing banners, flowers, and articles of worship, came to welcome him forth.
At that time, although Chandaka had previously received the command of King Śuddhodana, he followed the Bodhisattva’s own will and brought the horse by leading it himself;
the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings then took up and supported the horse’s hooves as they passed through the city wall and went forth.
To destroy all afflictions and the followers of Māra, he demonstrates to all people the impurity of the household life.
If even one of such great merit and noble status has gone forth from home, how much more so should ordinary and lowly beings!
Such causes and conditions as these are called the accomplishment of renunciation.
Regarding "the accomplishment of adorning the Buddha-tree," the adornment of the Bodhi tree is as previously described.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:

"This Bodhi tree has roots made of gold; its trunk, nodes, branches, and leaves are composed of the seven treasures. The radiance from its trunk, nodes, branches, and leaves shines universally throughout the countless *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-worlds of the ten directions."
Some Buddhas have bodhi-trees adorned with the seven treasures of a bodhisattva, while others do not.
Why is this? The spiritual power of all Buddhas is inconceivable; for the sake of sentient beings, they manifest various kinds of adornments.
Regarding the phrase "all virtuous merits are fully accomplished and perfected": when a bodhisattva dwells in the seventh stage, they destroy all afflictions and fulfill their own benefit;
dwelling in the eighth and ninth stages, they benefit others, namely by teaching and transforming sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields.
Because his benefit for self and others is profound and vast, he is fully endowed with all merits.
For instance, although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas place great emphasis on their own benefit, they do not possess these merits in full because their benefit for others is slight.
Likewise, although devas and lesser Bodhisattvas are able to benefit others, they too do not possess them in full because they have not yet eliminated their own afflictions.
This is called being fully endowed with merit.

The ninth stage is concluded. Regarding the phrase "one should know that he is like a Buddha": when the Bodhisattva sits beneath such a tree and enters the tenth stage, it is named the Dharma-Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Just as a great cloud pours down rain, falling continuously without interval;
so too does the mind spontaneously give rise to immeasurable and boundless pure dharmas of the Buddhas, infinite in every thought-moment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"The Māra kings of the desire realm have not yet been subdued.
He emitted a light from between his eyebrows, causing the billions of Māra palaces to be shrouded in darkness and rendered invisible.
Māra immediately became enraged and distressed, gathering his hosts of soldiers to press upon the Bodhisattva.

Once the Bodhisattva had subdued Māra, the Buddhas of the ten directions celebrated his meritorious achievement; they all emitted light from between their eyebrows, which entered through the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head.

At that time, the merit obtained through the ten stages is transformed into the Buddha-dharma; all habitual tendencies of affliction are severed, and one attains unimpeded liberation. One becomes endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four types of unhindered knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and other such immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha.
At that time, the earth shook in six ways; the heavens rained down flowers and incense, and all the bodhisattvas, devas, and humans joined their palms in praise.
Then, a great radiance was emitted, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions;
the buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans of the ten directions cried out in a loud voice:
"A certain Bodhisattva from a certain country in a certain direction, seated at the site of enlightenment, has perfected the Buddha-deeds; this is his radiance.
This is called the tenth stage, which should be known as being like that of a Buddha.

Furthermore, in this context, the Buddha further explains the characteristics of the tenth stage: namely, that by practicing the six pāramitās through the power of skillful means, the bodhisattva transcends the stage of dry wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*) up to the bodhisattva stages, and comes to abide in the stage of a Buddha.
The Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) is precisely the tenth ground.
When a bodhisattva is able to practice the ten grounds in this manner, it is called "setting out toward the Great Vehicle.
Chapter 21: Departure and Arrival *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the Chapter on Departure and Arrival, Number Twenty-one [Sutra] The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
Regarding your question, "From where does this vehicle emerge, and where does it abide?
the Buddha said:
"This vehicle emerges from within the triple world and abides within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), because it is by way of the non-dual dharma."

Why is this? The Mahāyāna and sarvajñatā—these two dharmas are together; they are neither joined nor dispersed, without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless."
"If a person wishes to cause the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*) to emerge;

if a person wishes to cause suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), or the inconceivable nature (*acintyatā*) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge."
"If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of form to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge;
if a person wishes to cause the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge."
Why is this? Subhūti!
The mark of the emptiness of form does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
The empty characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is this?

Because form is empty of the characteristic of form, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"If a person wishes to cause the emptiness of the eye to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge;
if a person wishes to cause the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge;
if a person wishes to cause even the emptiness of the feeling born of the condition of mental contact to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge."
Why is this? Subhūti!
The eye is empty; it does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Even the feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition is empty; it does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is this?

Because the eye is empty of the characteristic of an eye, and so on, up to the feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition being empty of the characteristic of a feeling produced with mind-contact as its condition.
"If a person wishes to cause a dream to emerge, that person wishes to cause a signless dharma to emerge;
