if a person wishes to cause an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, or a transformation to emerge, that person wishes to cause a signless dharma to emerge."
Why is this? Subhūti! The characteristics of a dream do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
The characteristics of an illusion, a mirage, an echo, a shadow, and a transformation likewise do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). "Subhūti!
If a person wishes to cause the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*) to emerge."

If a person wishes to cause the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to emerge, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma (animitta-dharma) to emerge.
Why is this? Because the characteristic of the dānapāramitā does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in sarvajñatā;
likewise, the śīlapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in sarvajñatā.

Why is this? Because the perfection of giving is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of giving; and because the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are each empty of the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom.

“If a person wishes to cause inner emptiness to emerge, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, that person wishes to cause the signless dharma to emerge. Why is this? Because...”

Subhūti! The characteristics of inner emptiness up to the characteristics of the emptiness of non-existence and existence do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Why is this?

Because internal emptiness is empty of the nature of internal emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence being empty of the nature of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
"If a person wishes to cause the four foundations of mindfulness to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge."
Why is this? The nature of the four foundations of mindfulness does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.

If someone wishes to cause the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
Why is this? The nature of the eightfold noble path does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
The eightfold noble path is empty of the nature of the eightfold noble path.
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it is likewise, Subhūti.
If a person wishes to cause an Arhat to arise, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to arise;
if a person wishes to cause a Pratyekabuddha to arise, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to arise;
if a person wishes to cause a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to arise, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to arise.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The nature of an arhat, the nature of a pratyekabuddha, and the nature of a buddha do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Why is this? It is because an arhat is empty of the nature of an arhat, a pratyekabuddha is empty of the nature of a pratyekabuddha, and a buddha is empty of the nature of a buddha.

If a person wishes to cause the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a buddha, and all-knowledge to emerge, that person wishes to cause signless dharmas to emerge, as explained above.

"If a person wishes to cause names, provisional designations, conceptual constructs, and characteristics to emerge as mere verbal expressions, that person wishes to cause phenomena devoid of characteristics to emerge."
Why is this? Names are empty; they do not emerge from the triple world, nor do they abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
The characteristic of names is empty of the characteristic of names; even up to the conventional designation, it is likewise.

"If a person wishes to cause a dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and unconditioned, to emerge, that person wishes to cause a dharma without characteristics to emerge."
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena—from non-arising up to the unconditioned—does not emerge from the triple world, nor does it abide in omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Why is that?
From the nature of non-arising up to the nature of non-action, they are empty of intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!
For these reasons, the Mahāyāna emerges from within the triple world and abides within omniscience (sarvajñatā), because it is of an immovable nature."
[Treatise] Question:
The Buddha already knew what Subhūti had asked; why does he now repeat it before answering? Answer:

This *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* consists of one hundred thousand verses and three million two hundred thousand words; it is equal in length to the *Four Āgamas*, and thus cannot be fully expounded in a single sitting.

Furthermore, regarding what Subhūti asked above, two matters have already been answered; because they occurred at different times and on different days, he refers to them as the third question and answers accordingly. Moreover, some say:
within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, there are no inconceivable matters, nor can everything be fully explained in a single day or a single sitting.

The Buddha possesses unimpeded liberation, and the Bodhisattva possesses inconceivable samādhi, which can cause a long duration to become a short duration and a short duration to become a long duration; furthermore, it can cause great forms to enter into small spaces and small forms to become great.
Furthermore, it is as when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached for sixty minor kalpas, yet people thought it had lasted only from morning until mealtime.
A questioner asked:
"Form has a shape that can be seen, whereas time has no shape and exists only as a name; how can the near be made to appear far, or the far be made to appear near?"
The answer is:
For this reason, it is said, "by means of inconceivable supernormal powers.
It is like a person in a dream who, having seen something in the dream, considers themselves to be awake.
Dreaming within a dream, thus proceeding in succession, constitutes a single night.
For this reason, he answers further according to his question:
"From where does this vehicle depart, and where does it abide? The Buddha replies:
"This vehicle emerges from within the triple world and abides within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Question:
Is this vehicle the Buddha-dharma?
Is this the dharma of a bodhisattva?
If it is the dharma of a Buddha, how can one emerge from the triple world?
If it is the dharma of a bodhisattva, how can one abide within omniscience (*sarvajñā*)?
Answer: This vehicle is the dharma of the bodhisattva, extending even to the vajra-samādhi;
these various merits are purified and transformed into the Buddha-dharma.
This vehicle possesses great power and is capable of proceeding until it reaches Buddhahood; since there is no further superior state to which one may go, it is said to "abide.
For example, when the fire at the end of a kalpa burns the trichiliocosm, its power is so immense that there is nothing further to burn, and thus it spontaneously extinguishes itself.

The Mahāyāna is likewise: having severed all afflictions, accumulated all merits, and reached their ultimate limit, there is nothing further to sever, nothing further to know, and nothing further to accumulate; therefore, it spontaneously returns to extinction.
"The Dharma of Non-duality" is taught in order to sever the attachments of all bodhisattvas.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself said:
"The Great Vehicle and omniscience (*sarvajñā*)—these two dharmas do not unite because they are not one, nor do they disperse because they are not different."
"Because all that is known by the six sense-faculties is entirely illusory, it is without color, without form, without resistance, and is of a single characteristic.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"Previously you said that 'because they are not one, they do not unite'; why now do you say it has 'a single characteristic'?"
The answer is:

Herein, it is said that "the single characteristic is what is called the absence of characteristics. Since there is no emergence toward the Buddha-way in the absence of characteristics, the term "single characteristic" is spoken for the purpose of guiding ordinary people.
“Reality-limit” (bhūtakoṭi) is the ultimate true mark of all dharmas, wherein there is neither emergence nor entry.
If there were a madman who wished to cause the reality-limit to emerge and reach the Buddha-way, such a person would be wishing to cause the signless dharma (animitta-dharma) to emerge.
"Suchness," "dharma-nature," and "dharma-characteristic" are as previously explained.
Regarding "inconceivable nature," some say it is identical to suchness, dharma-nature, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
because it is immeasurable and boundless, and because the mind and mental factors have ceased, it is called inconceivable.
Furthermore, some say:
to transcend the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and nirvāṇa, and further seek the true nature of all phenomena—whether they exist or do not exist—is called the inconceivable.
Furthermore, all the dharmas of the Buddhas cannot be conceived or measured; therefore, they are called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
Again, some say:
all dharmas, when analyzed and contemplated, are identical in their characteristics to *nirvāṇa*; this is what is meant by "inconceivable."
If a person wishes to cause something to emerge from empty space, that person wishes to cause something to emerge from the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
Regarding this, the Buddha himself said:

"The empty characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) cannot emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*), nor can they reach omniscience (*sarvajñā*). This is because within the five aggregates, the characteristics of the five aggregates are empty; likewise, the emptiness of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) up to the feeling produced through the conditions of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-ja-vedanā*) is also thus."
The analogies of dreams and the like are also thus:
because their own-characteristics are empty, there is neither emergence nor arrival.
If a person wishes to cause the six pāramitās to emerge, that person is wishing to cause signless dharmas to emerge.
Why is this? Because the six pāramitās arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Since bodhisattvas become attached to the six pāramitās and thereby fall into deviant paths, emptiness is taught for their sake.
The same applies to the eighteen kinds of emptiness up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Question: Among the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), there are those that pertain to the mundane and those to the supramundane; since the mundane can be clung to, it is possible to speak of their emptiness.
Since the six supramundane pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without attachment, why speak of them as empty?
Answer:

The various bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*); they practice these dharmas by the power of their merit and wisdom, or because they grasp at signs and become attached to them.
The dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are false and inverted; since these dharmas arise from the side of the dharmas of ordinary beings, how could they be real?
For this reason, the Buddha says that this too is empty, using it as a metaphor for the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*).
This Mahāyāna is itself signless; how could that which is signless have an emergence or an arrival?
All dharmas are empty; there are only names, marks, provisional designations, and linguistic expressions.
Now, these names and so forth are also empty, being used as metaphors for the signless (animitta), which cannot be apprehended within the ultimate truth (paramārtha);
yet they possess marks within conventional reality (saṃvṛti-dharma).
The meaning of conventional designations such as names and so forth is as previously explained.
By employing such dharmas, one emerges from the three realms and dwells within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
yet these are not substantial dharmas, nor is there any movement therein.
[Sūtra] “Subhūti! Regarding your question, ‘Where does this vehicle abide? Subhūti!
This Great Vehicle has no place of abiding.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas lack the characteristic of abiding.
If this vehicle were to abide, it would be abiding in that which does not abide.
Subhūti! For example, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, without origination and without activity; it neither abides nor does it not abide.
Subhūti! This vehicle is likewise: it neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
The characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), up to and including the characteristic of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*), neither abides nor does not abide. Why is this?
Because the nature of the characteristic of the nature of phenomena is empty; and so on, up to the fact that the nature of non-action and the nature of the nature of non-action are empty.
All other dharmas are likewise so,
Subhūti! For this reason,
this vehicle has no place of abiding, because it is a dharma that does not abide and a dharma that is immovable.
[Treatise] Question:
Above it was stated that "this vehicle reaches *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and there is no superior dharma to which it may go"; why now do you further say that "this vehicle has no place of abiding"?
The answer is:

It was previously stated that "one speaks of abiding because of emptiness and the non-dual dharma. Like a phantom or a dream, although there is sitting, lying down, walking, and standing, these are not actual abidings;
the Bodhisattva is also like this—although it is said that they "abide having reached sarvajñā," there is likewise no fixed abiding.
In this context, the Buddha himself says:
"All dharmas have been without the characteristic of abiding from the very beginning; why then would only the Mahāyāna have abiding?
If there were any abiding, it would abide by means of the dharma of ultimate emptiness."

For example: suchness, the dharma-nature, the dharma-characteristic, and the limit of reality neither abide nor do not abide; they are neither born nor extinguished; they are neither defiled nor pure; they neither arise nor are produced.
"Not abiding" means not abiding within self-characteristics;
"not non-abiding" means not abiding within other-characteristics.
"Not abiding" refers to the teaching of emptiness to refute existence.
"Not non-abiding" means that, as a skillful means of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is abiding.
"Non-abiding" refers to impermanence, which subverts the mark of permanence;
"not non-abiding" subverts the mark of annihilation.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:
"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty of the characteristics of the nature of phenomena. Why is this?"
"Because they are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatvāt*).
Even up to the point that all other dharmas are likewise without arising and without activity. [Sūtra] "Subhūti!"
Regarding your question, "Who will set out by means of this vehicle?", there is no person who sets out by means of this vehicle.
Why is this? Because this vehicle, the one who sets out, the dharmas employed, and the time of setting out—all these dharmas are entirely non-existent.
If all dharmas are non-existent, by means of what dharma would one emerge? Why is this?
Because a self cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to a knower or a seer, because they are ultimately pure.
Inconceivability is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
The aggregates, sense bases, and elements are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The perfection of giving is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
Even up to the perfection of wisdom, it is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
Internal emptiness is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;
even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, it is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they are ultimately pure.
The stream-enterer is unattainable, up to and including the arhat, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and Buddha, because they are ultimately pure.
The fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the Buddha, and all-knowledge are unattainable, because they are ultimately pure.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, without origination and without activity, they are ungraspable because they are ultimately pure.
In the past, future, and present, arising, abiding, and ceasing are ungraspable because they are ultimately pure.
Increase and decrease cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
Because what dharma cannot be apprehended? Because the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) cannot be apprehended;

likewise, the *tathatā* (suchness), the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality), the inconceivable nature, the *dharmatā*, the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena), and the *dharmasthititā* (stability of phenomena) cannot be apprehended.
The perfection of giving is unattainable because it is unattainable; likewise, up to the perfection of wisdom, they are unattainable because they are unattainable.
Inner emptiness is unattainable because it is unattainable; likewise, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they are unattainable because they are unattainable.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable, they are unattainable; up to and including because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unattainable, they are unattainable.
Because the stream-enterer is unattainable, he is unattainable; up to and including because the Buddha is unattainable, he is unattainable.
Because the fruit of srotāpanna is unattainable, it is unattainable; up to and including the path of the Buddha, because it is unattainable, it is unattainable.
Because non-arising and non-ceasing, up to and including non-origination and non-action, are unattainable, they are unattainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the first stage is unapprehendable, it is unapprehendable;
up to and including the tenth stage, because it is unapprehendable, it is unapprehendable—due to ultimate purity."
What are the stages from the first to the tenth? They are:

the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Buddha.
Within internal emptiness, the first stage cannot be apprehended; likewise, within the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the first stage cannot be apprehended.
Within internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The first stage is neither attained nor unattained, and so on up to the tenth stage, which is neither attained nor unattained, because it is ultimately pure.
Within inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the maturation of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure.
Within inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the purification of Buddha-fields cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure.
Within inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the five eyes cannot be apprehended,
because they are ultimately pure. Thus, Subhūti,
because all dharmas cannot be apprehended, the bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts this Mahāyāna and emerges into sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
The [Treatise] author says:

"Emergence" means that by practicing this vehicle, one reaches the vicinity of the Buddha-way and emerges; furthermore, it is called "emergence" because of its accomplishment, for through this vehicle one accomplishes *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge)—this is what is meant by "emergence."
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions for emptiness:
"The 'vehicle' refers to the six pāramitās.
The 'dharmas employed' refer to dharmas such as compassion and skillful means that are not subsumed within the six pāramitās."
"The one who emerges is the bodhisattva;
these three dharmas are all empty.
In this regard, the Buddha further explains the causal conditions:
“I cannot be apprehended, nor can anything up to a knower or a seer be apprehended, because they are ultimately empty.

The five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the *dānapāramitā* up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and from the stream-enterer up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*)—these are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. Furthermore, the three times, the three marks, increase and decrease, and so forth—this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
From "I" up to the knower and the seer, and from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the Buddha—this is called the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*). Question:
There are two kinds of unobtainability:
First, there are dharmas that cannot be attained because one’s wisdom is insufficient;
second, there are those where one possesses great wisdom yet cannot attain them through investigation.
Why is it that these are unattainable?
Answer: Because these dharmas do not exist, they cannot be apprehended.
Question:
If all phenomena (dharmas) are fundamentally and ultimately unattainable, what benefit is there for persons?
The answer is:
herein the Buddha himself says:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Regarding "ultimately":

if a practitioner relies on "non-existence" (wu) to dismantle "existence" (you), they attain purity regarding "existence," yet have not yet attained purity regarding "non-existence," because they still rely upon it.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions for non-apprehension:
all sentient beings are unapprehendable, and all dharmas are unapprehendable;
they are like suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and so forth, up to being unconditioned, unarisen, and unapprehendable.
Furthermore, because of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the dharma-nature is unattainable, up to and including its non-arising and non-acting.
Within the eighteen kinds of emptiness, there is no first stage through to the tenth stage; there is no maturing of sentient beings, no purifying of Buddha-fields, and no five eyes.
Because they are empty by virtue of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, and because they are ultimately pure, they are unattainable.
The Bodhisattva, by means of the dharma that is unobtainable, mounts this vehicle and emerges into *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 50; the explanation of the nineteenth chapter concludes here.
The twentieth chapter, "Excellence," begins. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 51.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Chapter 22: On Excellence. [Sūtra] The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Mahāyāna, the Mahāyāna, surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
World-Honored One!”
This Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Just as space accommodates immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
This Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, nor a place to which it goes, nor a place where it abides.

This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle limit; the equality of the three periods of time is this Mahāyāna.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, this vehicle is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of what are called the six pāramitās: "

The perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom—these are called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi—namely, from the Śūraṅgama-samādhi up to the Non-attachment to Space and Untainted Samādhi. This is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows:
it is the emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"As Subhūti has said:
'This Mahāyāna surpasses all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras. Subhūti!"

If the realm of desire were to possess reality, were not false, were not otherwise, were true, were not inverted, possessed permanence, possessed an indestructible nature, and were not a non-existent dharma, then this Mahāyāna could not transcend all the worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because the desire realm exists only through false recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, and as a mere combination of names and so forth—all things are characterized by impermanence and are non-existent dharmas. For this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the realm of form and the formless realm were truly existent, not false, not different, real, non-erroneous, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not non-existent, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because the form realm and the formless realm exist only as a result of false recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, and as a mere combination of names and signs—all of which are impermanent, characterized by disintegration, and non-existent—the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

“Subhūti! If form were truly existent, not false, not different, real, non-perverted, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not a non-existent dharma, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! Because form is a false conceptualization and discrimination, existing only through the combination of names and so forth, it is entirely impermanent, characterized by disintegration, and a non-existent dharma. For this reason, this Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Subhūti, if the eye up to the mind; forms up to phenomena;

eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; eye-contact up to mind-contact; and the feelings produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mind-contact were truly existent, not false, not different, real, non-erroneous, permanent, possessing an indestructible nature, and not non-existent, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to excel beyond all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! The feelings produced through the conditions of eye-contact up to mind-contact are merely false recollections, conceptualizations, and discriminations; they exist only as a combination of names and so forth. All are impermanent, characterized by disintegration, and non-existent. For this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
“Subhūti! If the nature of phenomena were an existent thing and not a non-existent thing, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras;
Subhūti!...”
Because the nature of phenomena is neither a phenomenon nor a non-phenomenon, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras; Subhūti!
Because suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature are non-entities and not dharmas;
for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
“Subhūti! If the dānapāramitā were an existent phenomenon and not a non-existent phenomenon, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras;
because the dānapāramitā is a non-phenomenon and not a phenomenon, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.”

If the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) were existent phenomena and not non-existent phenomena, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

Because the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are non-existent phenomena and not real dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all the worlds, including the gods, humans, and asuras.

“Subhūti! If the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, were a dharma that exists and not a dharma that does not exist, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to transcend all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, is a non-dharma and not a dharma, for this reason the Mahāyāna transcends all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.”

“Subhūti! If the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-existent dharmas and non-dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.”
“Subhūti! If the dharmas of the nature of persons were existent dharmas and not non-dharmas, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the dharmas of the nature of persons are non-dharmas and not dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.”

Subhūti! If the dharma of the person on the path of eight, the dharma of the srotāpanna, the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin, the dharma of the anāgāmin, the dharma of the arhat, the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharma of the Buddha were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Because the dharmas from those of the person on the path of eight up to those of the Buddha are non-dharmas and not dharmas, for this reason the Mahāyāna surpasses all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
“Subhūti! If the nature of a person were an existent dharma and not a non-existent dharma, this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the person of intrinsic nature is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma;
for this reason, the Mahāyāna excels all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti! If the eight types of persons, from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha, were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.
Because the eight types of persons up to the Buddha are non-dharmas and not dharmas, for this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

“Subhūti! If all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras, were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, this Mahāyāna would not be able to transcend all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
Because all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras, is a non-dharma and not a dharma, for this reason the Mahāyāna transcends all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.”

“Subhūti! If the various minds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening until reaching the site of enlightenment, were to be existent dharmas rather than non-existent dharmas, then this Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras;
it is because the various minds of the bodhisattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening until reaching the site of enlightenment, are non-dharmas and not dharmas.”
For this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras. "Subhūti,

if the vajra-like wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva were a dharma that exists and not a non-dharma, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva would be unable to know that all fetters and their latent tendencies are non-existent and non-dharmic, and thus could not attain all-knowledge."

Subhūti! Because the vajra-like wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, the bodhisattva knows that all fetters and their latent tendencies are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, and thereby attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). For this reason, the Mahāyāna surpasses all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras.

“Subhūti! If the thirty-two marks of the Buddhas were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, the majestic power and virtue of the Buddhas would not be able to shine forth and transcend all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras. Subhūti!”

Because the thirty-two marks of the Buddhas are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena, for this reason the majestic virtue of the Buddhas shines brilliantly, surpassing all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.

“Subhūti! If the radiance of the Buddhas were a dharma that exists and not a dharma that does not exist, the radiance of the Buddhas would be unable to universally illuminate worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
Subhūti!...”

Because the light of the Buddhas is neither a phenomenon nor a non-phenomenon, for this reason the Buddhas are able to universally illuminate worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with their radiance.

“Subhūti! If the sixty kinds of adorned voices of the Buddhas were existent dharmas and not non-existent dharmas, the Buddhas would be unable to reach throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions by means of those sixty kinds of adorned voices. Subhūti!”

Because the sixty kinds of adorned vocal sounds of all Buddhas are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena, for this reason, the Buddhas are able to cause these sixty kinds of adorned vocal sounds to pervade the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions.

“Subhūti! If the Dharma-wheel of the Buddhas were a dharma that exists and not a dharma that does not exist, the Buddhas would be unable to turn the Dharma-wheel—that wheel which no śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or other beings in the world can turn according to the Dharma;
Subhūti! [it is because it is thus that they do so].”

Because the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas is neither a phenomenon nor a non-phenomenon, for this reason the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, which no śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings in the world can turn in accordance with the Dharma.

Subhūti! When the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings, if these sentient beings were real dharmas rather than non-dharmas, they could not cause those sentient beings to attain parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder; Subhūti!

Because the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, yet these sentient beings are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas; for this reason, within *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, sentient beings have already ceased, are now ceasing, and will cease.
[The] Commentator says:
Subhūti had previously asked about the Mahāyāna by means of five matters, and the Buddha had already finished answering them.
Subhūti, filled with joy, praised [the Buddha] and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
This Mahāyāna possesses great power; having destroyed the world of humans and devas, it is able to emerge victorious therein.
It is like three people crossing a perilous path:
First, fleeing by night to escape alone and preserve one's life;
second, seeking exemption through the payment of money;
third, like a great king leading a vast army to crush rebels and save the entire host from peril, remaining free from fear or difficulty.
The three vehicles are also like this: just as an arhat cannot know all general and specific characteristics, nor can he defeat Māra, nor can he subdue non-Buddhists;
being weary of old age, sickness, and death, he proceeds directly toward nirvāṇa.

Just as a pratyekabuddha enters the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena—deeper than a śrāvaka—and possesses a slight degree of compassion, using supernormal powers (ṛddhi) to transform and deliver sentient beings;
he is able to destroy afflictions (kleśa), but cannot destroy Māra’s followers or non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

Just as a bodhisattva, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings; although they have not yet attained Buddhahood, during that interval they benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
because they definitively know the true reality of all phenomena and are fully endowed with the six pāramitās, they defeat the various māras and destroy the heterodox teachers;

they sever the habitual tendencies of afflictions, become fully endowed with the knowledge of all modes, thoroughly knowing and understanding both general and specific characteristics, and thus achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Although all three have escaped birth and death, their paths of skillful means differ.
For this reason, Subhūti praised the Mahāyāna, saying:
"It shatters everything in the world and excels above humans, devas, and asuras."
"Just as space contains all lands yet, being space, is never exhausted;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it contains all Buddhas of the three periods of time and their disciples, yet the Mahāyāna is never filled."
Furthermore, just as space is characterized by permanence and thus lacks the characteristic of entering, the characteristic of exiting, and the characteristic of abiding;
so too is this vehicle: it has no place of entry in the future, no place of exit in the past, and no place of abiding in the present.
Because it transcends the three times, the equality of the three times is called the Mahāyāna.
Question:
The Buddha ought to praise Subhūti with the words "Excellent! for what he has extolled; why then does he further speak of the Mahāyāna? Answer:

The Buddha, wishing to follow Subhūti’s praise and provide a further exposition, has thus far spoken of the Mahāyāna as being remote; now he will briefly state the characteristics of the Mahāyāna before describing it in detail.

That which Subhūti has praised as the Mahāyāna consists of the six pāramitās, the various dhāraṇī-doors, the samādhi-doors, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
As Subhūti has said, "The Mahāyāna destroys all worlds and excels above humans, devas, and asuras"—this is indeed so.

Why is this? These three realms are deceptive, like an illusion and like a dream; they exist due to the causes and conditions of ignorance and falsehood. Cause and effect have no fixed reality; all things are impermanent, subject to destruction and extinction, and are entirely characterized by emptiness.
Because the Mahāyāna is contrary to the three realms, it is able to destroy and surpass them.
If the three realms were determinately real, permanent, and non-illusory, this Mahāyāna would be unable to destroy and surpass them.
Why is this? Because their power is equal.
It is the same for the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the various feelings produced by the six types of contact.
If the nature of phenomena were an existing entity and not a non-entity, the Mahāyāna would be unable to transcend and surpass the world;
Subhūti, because the nature of phenomena is not an existing entity, the Mahāyāna is able to transcend and surpass the world.
Question: Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are said to be non-existent because they are deceptive, being produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions.

However, suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and real dharmas, and are called the "limit of reality. Why, then, do you say they are non-existent?
Answer: It is said to be non-existent because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is empty.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"Apart from the conditioned, unconditioned dharmas cannot be apprehended;
the true reality of conditioned dharmas is itself the unconditioned dharma.
Furthermore, one contemplates that these conditioned dharmas are deceptive.
Just as "suchness," "dharma-nature," and "the limit of reality" are real,
yet because people grasp at signs within dharma-nature and give rise to contention, it is said that "there is no dharma-nature."
Whether one speaks of "existence" or "non-existence," there is no fault, as each has its own causes and conditions.
It is the same with suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature (*acintyadharmatā*).
The mundane *dānapāramitā* exists because of attachment; the supramundane *dānapāramitā* is empty because it does not exist.
One says "the *dānapāramitā* exists" in order to destroy stinginess and greed, and one says "the *dānapāramitā* does not exist" in order to destroy false views.
For the sake of guiding beginners, it is said that it "exists," whereas within the minds of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is said to be "non-existent."
Just as with the *dānapāramitā*, and so on up to: if sentient beings truly existed and were not non-existent phenomena, one should not force them to cease and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Question:
From the section on the thirty-two marks onwards, why is it not stated that "the Mahāyāna excels"? Answer:
One should say that it is not explained because the direct text would be too cumbersome.
Furthermore, everything from the thirty-two marks up to turning the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings is also the Mahāyāna; it is merely a difference in names.
Furthermore, previously the Mahāyāna was described as superior in its general characteristics, but it was not known in what way it is superior;
now it is described in its specific characteristics: namely, because the Buddha’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks, he surpasses all sentient beings;
and because the Buddha’s radiance surpasses that of the sun, the moon, and all the lights of the devas.
The Buddha’s voice surpasses all musical instruments, the exquisite sounds of the world, and the Brahma-voices of the devas;
the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma surpasses the precious wheels of the universal monarchs and all the wheels of Dharma of the various non-Buddhist paths, being unobstructed and unhindered.
The benefits conferred by other wheels of Dharma are slight and shallow, lasting for perhaps one or two lifetimes, at most reaching ten million lifetimes;
the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, however, enables beings to enter parinirvāṇa without remainder forever, never again to return to the cycle of birth and death.

Furthermore, if sentient beings truly existed as substantial entities, the Buddha would not cause them to enter nirvana and forever uproot them; such a transgression would be a greater fault than killing a single body.

Because sentient beings perceive me with a perverted mind, the Buddha wishes to shatter that perversion and thus speaks of nirvāṇa; since there is no sentient being to be extinguished, there is no fault.
Because it possesses such merits, the Mahāyāna is able to surpass all the worlds.
Question:
Regarding "all the worlds," this refers to the sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions; why then do you speak only of surpassing the devas, humans, and asuras?
Answer:
Among the six realms of existence, three are wholesome paths and three are unwholesome paths.
Since the Mahāyāna is even able to transcend the three wholesome paths, how much more so the unwholesome paths!
Question: The *Nāgarāja Sūtra* states that nāgas can attain the bodhisattva path; why then is it described as an evil realm? Answer:
Sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless, yet those among them who attain the Way are few.
Furthermore, some say:
"Because great bodhisattvas manifest transformation bodies to teach and transform others, they assume the form of a dragon king."
Chapter 23: On Embracing (Saṃgraha-varga) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on Chapter Twenty-three: On Embracing [Sūtra] The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As for what you said:
'The Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is equal to emptiness.'"
"So it is! So it is, Subhūti!"
The Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. "Subhūti!
Just as space has no eastern direction, no southern, western, or northern directions, nor the four intermediate points, nor above or below;..."
Subhūti! The Mahāyāna is also like this: there is no east, no south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, nor above or below. Subhūti!
Just as space is neither long nor short, neither square nor round;
Subhūti, the Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither long nor short, neither square nor round.
“Subhūti! Just as space is not blue, not yellow, not red, not white, and not black;
so too is the Mahāyāna—not blue, not yellow, not red, not white, and not black.”
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
"Subhūti, just as space is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present;
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
“Subhūti! Just as space neither increases nor decreases, so too is the Mahāyāna; it neither increases nor decreases.”
“Subhūti! Just as space is neither defiled nor pure,
so too is the Mahāyāna neither defiled nor pure.”
“Subhūti! Just as space is without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without alteration;
so too is the Mahāyāna, without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without alteration.”
“Subhūti! Just as space is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither determinate nor indeterminate;
so too is the Mahāyāna, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, neither determinate nor indeterminate.”
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Just as space is without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, and without consciousness;
so too is the Mahāyāna—without seeing, without hearing, without cognition, and without consciousness.
"Just as space cannot be known, cannot be cognized, cannot be seen, cannot be severed, cannot be realized, and cannot be cultivated;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it cannot be known, cannot be cognized, cannot be seen, cannot be severed, cannot be realized, and cannot be cultivated."
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
"Just as space has neither the characteristic of defilement nor the characteristic of separation;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has neither the characteristic of defilement nor the characteristic of separation."
"Just as space is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm."
"Just as space has no first thought of enlightenment, nor a second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth thought;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no first thought of enlightenment, up to and including no tenth thought."

"Just as in space there is no stage of dry wisdom, no stage of lineage, no stage of the eight persons, no stage of vision, no stage of refinement, no stage of freedom from desire, and no stage of completion;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no stage of dry wisdom up to and including the stage of having completed what was to be done."
"Just as space has no fruit of stream-entry, no fruit of once-returning, no fruit of non-returning, and no fruit of arhatship;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no fruit of stream-entry, up to and including no fruit of arhatship."
"Just as in space there is no stage of the śrāvaka, no stage of the pratyekabuddha, and no stage of the Buddha;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no stage of the śrāvaka, up to and including no stage of the Buddha."
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Just as space is neither form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, neither joined nor dispersed;
so too is the Mahāyāna: neither form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, neither joined nor dispersed.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. "Subhūti!
Just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self; [so too is the Mahāyāna]."
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
“Subhūti! Just as space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, neither conditioned nor unconditioned;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, neither conditioned nor unconditioned.”
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. "Subhūti,
just as space is neither cessation nor non-cessation, neither detached nor non-detached;..."
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, neither detached nor non-detached.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
“Subhūti! Just as space is neither dark nor light,
so too is the Mahāyāna neither dark nor light.”
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. "Subhūti,
just as space is neither obtainable nor unobtainable;
The Mahāyāna is also like this: it is neither obtainable nor unobtainable.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness. "Subhūti!..."
Just as space is neither expressible nor inexpressible, so too is the Mahāyāna: it is neither expressible nor inexpressible.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
“Subhūti! For these various reasons and conditions, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
[The *Śāstra*] says:
Subhūti praised the Mahāyāna as being like space, and the Buddha then extensively explained how this was so.
Just as space has no ten directions, this Mahāyāna likewise has no ten directions;
just as space has no length or shortness, nor squareness or roundness, nor blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth, this Mahāyāna is also like this.
Question:
Space may indeed be so, for it is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), devoid of form and spatial direction;

but the Mahāyāna consists of conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and is comprised of material dharmas (*rūpadharma*), such as giving and ethical discipline. How can it be said that it is "equal to space"?
Answer: The six pāramitās are of two kinds:
mundane and supramundane.
The mundane consists of conditioned phenomena and material forms, and is therefore not the same as empty space;
the supramundane, however, because it is in union with suchness, the dharma-nature, the reality-limit, and wisdom, resembles empty space.
From the time one has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) onwards, there is no conceptual discrimination, being like empty space.
Furthermore, it is as when the Buddha, with unimpeded wisdom, contemplates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as being like empty space;
other persons are not so, because their wisdom has not yet reached ultimate purity.

Furthermore, the Buddha has taught both before and after that "all dharmas are ultimately empty, like the state of nirvana without remainder, and like space"; one should not harbor doubts regarding this.
The same applies to all other phenomena.
Even up to the point that space is neither expressible nor non-expressible, it is likewise so.
Question:
Regarding space, it would suffice to say that "nothing exists"; why, then, is it said that it lacks various characteristics?
The answer is:

Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds upon awakening become attached to the mind within the various internal and external causal dharmas. For this reason, the Buddha says that like space, it lacks these various characteristics; the Mahāyāna is also like this.
[Sūtra] “Subhūti, it is as you have said: ‘Just as space accommodates immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.’”
"So it is! So it is, Subhūti!"
Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that space does not exist;
because space does not exist, one should know that the Mahāyāna also does not exist.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is this?
Because these phenomena—sentient beings, space, and the Mahāyāna—are all unapprehendable (*anupalabdha*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the asaṃkhyeya is non-existent;
because the asaṃkhyeya is non-existent, one should know that the aprameya is non-existent."
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless is non-existent;
because the boundless is non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
These sentient beings, space, the Mahāyāna, the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless—all these dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit do not exist;
because suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit do not exist, you should know that everything up to the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) does not exist."
Because the immeasurable, the boundless, and the incalculable are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is this?

Because these sentient beings, up to and including those who know and those who see, as well as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), up to and including the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable—all these phenomena (*dharma*) are unattainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that inconceivable nature does not exist;
because inconceivable nature does not exist, you should know that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist."
Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, one should know that space does not exist;
because space does not exist, one should know that the Mahāyāna does not exist;
because the Mahāyāna does not exist, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) does not exist.
Because the *asaṃkhyeya* (incalculable) is non-existent, one should know that the *apramāṇa* (immeasurable) is non-existent;
because the *apramāṇa* is non-existent, one should know that the *ananta* (boundless) is non-existent;
because the *ananta* is non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
you should know that the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Subhūti! This is because all dharmas, from "I" up to "knower" and "seer," are ultimately unattainable.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because "I" do not exist, and because even the knower and the seer do not exist, one should know that the eye does not exist, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist;
because the eye up to the mind do not exist, one should know that space does not exist;
because space does not exist, one should know that the Mahāyāna does not exist.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the asaṃkhyeya is non-existent;
because the asaṃkhyeya is non-existent, one should know that the aprameya is non-existent;
because the aprameya is non-existent, one should know that the ananta is non-existent.
Because it is boundless and non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti,
it is because from "I" up to all dharmas, none can be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the self does not exist, and so on up to the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) does not exist; the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) do not exist.
Because the perfection of wisdom does not exist, you should know that space (*ākāśa*) does not exist."
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent;
because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable [realms] are non-existent;
because immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable [realms] are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because the self, sentient beings, and indeed all dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the self does not exist,
up to and including the knower and the seer do not exist, one should know that internal emptiness does not exist, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence does not exist."
Because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is nothingness, one should know that space is nothingness;
because space is nothingness, one should know that the Mahāyāna is nothingness;
because the Mahāyāna is nothingness, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*aprameya*), and the boundless (*ananta*) are nothingness.
Because the asaṃkhyeya, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti!
The Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the self, sentient beings, and even all dharmas are ultimately unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the self, sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, do not exist, one should know that the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist;
because the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist, [one should know] that everything up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not exist."
Because the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent;
because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent;
because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the boundless (*ananta*) are non-existent.
Because the asaṃkhyeya, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti!
This Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is this?
Because the self, sentient beings, and even all dharmas are ultimately unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the self and sentient beings do not exist, up to and including the knower and the seer do not exist, you should know that the stage of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) does not exist, up to and including the stage of having already accomplished it (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) does not exist;
because the stage of having already accomplished it does not exist, you should know that space (*ākāśa*) does not exist."
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent;
because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the boundless (*ananta*) are non-existent;
because the incalculable, the immeasurable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-existent.
For this reason, this Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings. Why is that?
Because the self, sentient beings, and even all dharmas are ultimately unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the self, sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, do not exist, one should know that the srotāpanna does not exist;
because the srotāpanna does not exist, one should know that the sakṛdāgāmin does not exist."
Because the Sakṛdāgāmin is non-existent, one should know that the Anāgāmin is non-existent;
because the Anāgāmin is non-existent, one should know that the Arhat is non-existent;
because the Arhat is non-existent, one should know that all dharmas, up to and including all phenomena, are non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings. Why is that?
"Subhūti! This is because everything from 'I' down to all dharmas is ultimately unapprehendable.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because the self, up to and including the knower and the seer, do not exist, one should know that the Śrāvaka vehicle does not exist;
because the Śrāvaka vehicle does not exist, one should know that the Pratyekabuddha vehicle does not exist;
because the Pratyekabuddha vehicle does not exist, one should know that the Buddha vehicle does not exist.
Because the Buddha-vehicle is non-existent, one should know that the śrāvaka is non-existent;
because the śrāvaka is non-existent, one should know that the srotāpanna is non-existent;
because the srotāpanna is non-existent, up to and including the Buddha, all are non-existent.
Because the Buddha is non-existent, one should know that all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-existent;
because all-knowledge is non-existent, one should know that space is non-existent;
because space is non-existent, one should know that the Mahāyāna is non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that all dharmas, even unto the very last, are non-existent.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.
Why is this? Because from "self" up to all dharmas, none can be apprehended.
"For example, Subhūti!"

Within the nature of nirvāṇa, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings are received; likewise, this Mahāyāna also receives immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
For this reason, Subhūti, just as space accommodates immeasurable,
boundless, and incalculable sentient beings, so too does this Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sentient beings.
[Treatise] Question:

Why is it not said that "space receives all things because it is vast and boundless," but rather that "space is able to receive all things and sentient beings because it is non-existent, and the Mahāyāna is likewise non-existent"?
Answer:
We see directly that space is nothingness, yet all myriad things are contained within it; because it is nothingness, it is able to receive them.
Question:
The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) likewise lack physical form; why, then, do they not receive all objects?
The answer is:

the mind and mental factors have the characteristic of cognition (*vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*), not the characteristic of receiving (*vedanā-lakṣaṇa*), and furthermore, they have no place of abiding (*sthāna*).
Whether internal or external, whether near or far, it is only through the characteristic of conceptual differentiation that one knows there is mind.
Material forms and phenomena have locations; because of these locations of form, one knows that space exists.
Because form does not receive objects, one knows that space receives objects;
since form and space are mutually exclusive, if form does not receive, one knows that space is what receives.
It is like knowing there is light because of darkness, or knowing there is pleasure because of suffering.
Because form does not exist, one speaks of the existence of space; it has no other distinct characteristic.

Furthermore, the mind and mental factors possess the further sense of "non-acceptance": for example, a mind of wrong view does not accept right view, and a mind of right view does not accept wrong view.
Space is not so, for it accommodates all things.
Furthermore, the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the mind and mental factors are dharmas that can be severed, whereas space is not so.
The mind and its mental factors, as well as space, are identical only in being formless and shapeless; yet one cannot say they are not different in every respect.
For this reason, it is said among all phenomena that space is able to accommodate everything.
Question: My previous intention in asking was not as you think!
Why do you not say that "space is immeasurable and boundless, and can receive all things," but instead say that "that which is non-existent receives all things"?
Answer: I say that space has no intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); it is spoken of as "space" only in dependence upon the characteristic of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*).
If it had no intrinsic characteristic, then space would not exist; how then could one speak of it as being immeasurable and boundless?
Question: You say that "the characteristic of sensation is space"; why then do you say it is "non-existent"? Answer:
The characteristic of sensation is itself the absence of the characteristic of form; that place where form does not reach is called space.
For this reason, there is no such thing as space.
If space were truly existent, it should have existed even before form had come into being!
If there were empty space before form existed, then empty space would be without characteristics. Why?
Because form had not yet come into being.
It is because of form that one knows there is space; because there is form, there is consequently the formless.
If form existed first and space existed later, then space would be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and a conditioned phenomenon cannot be called eternal.
If there were such a thing as a phenomenon characterized by formlessness (*animitta*), it would be unattainable; for this reason, space does not exist.
Question:
If space exists eternally, then the characteristic of space manifests because of matter (*rūpa*); only then does that characteristic reside within space.
The answer is:
If space were originally without characteristics, then later characteristics would likewise have no place to abide.
If space were originally possessed of characteristics, then those characteristics would have nothing for them to characterize.
If there were no prior marks, then the marks would have nowhere to abide.
Once one has departed from both marks and the absence of marks, the marks have no place of abiding;
if the marks have no place of abiding, then the locus where they appear likewise does not exist.
Because the locus of characteristics does not exist, characteristics themselves do not exist;
apart from characteristics and their locus, there is no further dharma.

For this reason, space is not called a characteristic, nor is it called the locus of characteristics; it is not called a dharma, nor is it called a non-dharma; it is not called existence, nor is it called non-existence. It cuts off all verbal expression, being quiescent and extinguished like *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
All other dharmas are also like this.
Question:
If all dharmas are thus, they are themselves empty space; why then is empty space used again as a metaphor?
Answer: All dharmas, whether cause or effect, are entirely false and deceptive; they exist because of ignorance and deceive the minds of sentient beings.
Sentient beings give rise to attachment toward these dharmas, yet they do not give rise to attachment toward empty space.
The dharmas of the six sense objects deceive the minds of sentient beings, yet although space is also deceptive, it is not so [in that same way].
For this reason, space is used as a metaphor; by means of coarse, manifest phenomena, subtle phenomena are refuted.
Just as space exists only as a provisional designation due to form, yet lacks any fixed dharma;
so too it is with sentient beings: because of the aggregation of the five aggregates, they exist only as provisional designations and likewise lack any fixed dharma.
The Mahāyāna is also like this: because sentient beings are empty, there is no Buddha and no Bodhisattva;
because sentient beings exist, there is a Buddha and there are Bodhisattvas.
If there were no Buddha and no Bodhisattva, then there would be no Mahāyāna.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna can accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings;
were it a finite dharma, it could not accommodate the immeasurable Buddhas and their disciples.
Question:
If space does not truly exist, how can it accommodate immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings? Answer:
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"Because the Mahāyāna does not exist, the asaṃkhyeya does not exist;
because the asaṃkhyeya does not exist, the aprameya also does not exist."
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, the boundless is also non-existent;
because the boundless is non-existent, all dharmas are also non-existent; for this reason, one is able to receive [them].
As for "asaṃkhyeya," "saṃkhyā" in the language of Qin means "number."
"A" (阿) means "non-existent" in the language of Qin.

Because sentient beings and all phenomena cannot each have a limit found, they are called "innumerable" (無數). Because the limits of the distance—near or far—of the ten directions of empty space cannot be found, it is called "innumerable."
When one analytically enumerates the six pāramitās, there is no number for the various kinds of giving, the various kinds of ethical discipline, and so forth;

when one enumerates how many sentient beings have already attained the supreme vehicle, will attain the supreme vehicle, or are currently attaining the supreme vehicle, they are incalculable—this is called "innumerable."
Furthermore, some say: the first number is one, and there is only one;
because it is one, one speaks of two, and so forth—all of these are simply one, and there is no other numerical dharma apart from this.
If all were one, then there would be no plurality. Some say:
"All dharmas exist as names through their combination; just as a wheel exists as a 'chariot' through the combination of its rim, spokes, and hub, there is no fixed, substantial dharma."
Because a single phenomenon does not exist, many also do not exist, since many presuppose the one.
Furthermore, because the objects to be counted do not exist, the counting itself does not exist.
"Immeasurable" means that just as one measures objects with a bushel or a scale, so too does one measure all dharmas with wisdom.

Because all dharmas are empty, they are innumerable; because they are innumerable, they are immeasurable and boundless. Since there is no substantial wisdom, how could one possibly attain a fixed characteristic of all dharmas?
Because it is immeasurable, it is boundless; "measure" refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while "boundary" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
"measure" denotes the beginning, and "boundary" denotes the ultimate end.
Furthermore, because the self up to the knower and the seer do not exist, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) also does not exist;
because the reality-limit does not exist, the incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) also does not exist;
because the incalculable does not exist, the immeasurable (apramāṇa) also does not exist.
Because the immeasurable does not exist, the boundless also does not exist;
because the boundless does not exist, all phenomena (*dharmas*) also do not exist.
For this reason, all phenomena are non-existent and ultimately pure.
This Mahāyāna is able to contain all sentient beings and all phenomena;
these two things are mutually dependent:
if there were no sentient beings, there would be no phenomena, and if there were no phenomena, there would be no sentient beings.
First, all phenomena were explained as empty in their general characteristics; subsequently, each phenomenon was explained as empty individually.
The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the ultimate and most subtle dharma; if this were non-existent, what need is there to mention other dharmas?
From the nature of the inconceivable up to the nature of nirvāṇa, it is also thus.
[Sūtra] “Subhūti! As for what you have said:”
"This Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, nor a place to which it goes, nor a place where it abides. "So it is! So it is!"
Subhūti! This Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, nor a place to which it goes, nor a place wherein it abides. Why is this?
Subhūti! Because all dharmas have the characteristic of immovability, these dharmas have no place from which they come, no place to which they go, and no place in which they abide. Why is this?
Subhūti! Form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! The dharma of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere;
the dharmas of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! The suchness of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere;
the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere.
Subhūti! The nature of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere;
the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! The characteristic of form comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere;
the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
“Subhūti! The eye, the nature of the eye, the suchness of the eye, the essence of the eye, and the characteristics of the eye come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere;
so too with the ear, nose, tongue, and body.”
The mind, mental phenomena, the suchness of the mind, the nature of the mind, and the characteristics of the mind come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are also like this.

“Subhūti! The earth element, the dharma of the earth element, the suchness of the earth element, the nature of the earth element, and the characteristics of the earth element come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere;
so too with the water, fire, wind, and space elements.”

The seed of consciousness, the phenomena of the seed of consciousness, the suchness of the seed of consciousness, the nature of the seed of consciousness, and the characteristics of the seed of consciousness are also like this.

"Subhūti! Suchness, the phenomena of suchness, the suchness of suchness, the nature of suchness, and the characteristics of suchness do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere."

Subhūti! The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the dharma of the reality-limit, the suchness of the reality-limit, the nature of the reality-limit, and the marks of the reality-limit come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.
Subhūti! The inconceivable, the inconceivable dharma, the inconceivable suchness, the inconceivable nature, and the inconceivable characteristic come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.

“Subhūti! The dānapāramitā, the dharma of the dānapāramitā, the suchness of the dānapāramitā, the nature of the dānapāramitā, and the characteristics of the dānapāramitā—these come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere;
so too with the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, and dhyānapāramitā.”
