Prajñāpāramitā, the dharma of prajñāpāramitā, the suchness of prajñāpāramitā, the nature of prajñāpāramitā, and the characteristics of prajñāpāramitā do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.

“Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness, the dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness, the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness, the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, and the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere;
even so it is with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva, the bodhisattva-dharma, the suchness of a bodhisattva, the nature of a bodhisattva, and the marks of a bodhisattva—none of these come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.”
“The Buddha, the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-tathatā, the Buddha-nature, and the Buddha-marks do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.”
“Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the nature and characteristics of the dharma of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.”

“Subhūti! Conditioned phenomena, the dharmas of conditioned phenomena, the suchness of conditioned phenomena, the nature of conditioned phenomena, and the characteristics of conditioned phenomena come from nowhere, go nowhere, and abide nowhere.”

Subhūti! Unconditioned phenomena, the dharma of unconditioned phenomena, the suchness of unconditioned phenomena, the nature of unconditioned phenomena, and the characteristics of unconditioned phenomena do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere, nor do they abide anywhere.
"For this reason, Subhūti,
this Mahāyāna is not seen to have a place from which it comes, nor a place to which it goes, nor a place wherein it abides."
The [Commentary] states:
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
Why do you praise only the Mahāyāna as being without coming, without going, and without abiding?
All dharmas are likewise without coming, without going, and without abiding, because the true mark of all dharmas is immovable.
Question: Since all phenomena are currently seen to have coming and going, why do you say they have the characteristic of immobility and that they neither come nor go? Answer:
The characteristics of coming and going have already been refuted; they shall now be further explained.
Within all Buddha-dharmas, because there is no self and no sentient beings, and even no knower or seer, there is neither one who comes nor one who goes.
Since there is neither one who comes nor one who goes, the characteristics of coming and going must also be non-existent.
Furthermore, when seeking the characteristic of going within the three periods of time, it cannot be found.
Why is this? There is no going in that which has already gone, nor is there any going in that which has not yet gone.
Apart from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, there is no going even in the process of going.
Question: That which possesses bodily movement is called "going"; in what has already gone and in what has not yet gone, there is no bodily movement.
For this reason, when the body moves at the time of going, there should be "going.
The answer is: Not so!
Apart from the characteristic of going, the "time of going" cannot be apprehended;
apart from the time of going, the characteristic of going cannot be apprehended. How, then, can one say that there is going during the time of going?
Furthermore, if the characteristic of going existed during the time of going, then the time of going would have to exist apart from the characteristic of going.
Why is this? Because you assert that there is going during the time of going.
Furthermore, if there is going during the time of going, there would have to be two acts of going.
First, knowing the time of going; second, knowing that which goes at the time of going.
Question:
If this is so, what fault is there?
Answer: If that were so, there would be two goers. Why is this?
The goer is devoid of the characteristic of going;
if the goer is devoid of the characteristic of going, then the characteristic of going is devoid of a goer.
Therefore, the goer does not go, and the non-goer likewise does not go.
There is no departing, no not-departing, and no act of going.
It is the same for the coming and the staying.
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"The dharmas of ordinary people are deceptive and lack reality; although they are seen with the physical eye, they are no different from those of animals, and thus cannot be trusted.
Therefore it is said:
"All dharmas have no coming, no going, no place of abiding, and no movement."
"What are these? They are: form (rūpa), the phenomena of form (rūpadharma), the suchness of form (rūpatathatā), the nature of form (rūpaprakṛti), and the characteristics of form (rūpalakṣaṇa).

'Form' refers to the object seen by the eye, prior to its differentiation as beautiful or ugly, real or unreal, or as having its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) or the characteristic of another (paralakṣaṇa)."
"Form-dharmas" (rūpa-dharma) refers to that which is impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, impure, and so forth.

"The suchness of form" (rūpa-tathatā) refers to the existence of form as a composite; it is like foam on water, lacking solidity, non-existent once dispersed, deceptive and without reality, merely deluding the human eye.
Form is thus in the present; it is likewise in the past and the future.
Just as fire is hot in the present, one infers by analogy that it was so in the past and will be so in the future.
Furthermore, just as the Buddhas contemplate the ultimate purity and emptiness of the characteristics of form (*rūpa*), the Bodhisattva should also contemplate it in this way.
Why is it that the dharma of the eye and the suchness (*tathatā*) of form are not as they are perceived by ordinary people?
Because its nature is thus of itself!
This nature is profound and subtle; how can it be known?
It can be known by means of the power of its physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
Just as fire has smoke as its characteristic, and one knows that fire exists upon seeing smoke;
so too, when one now perceives the eye and visible forms as having the characteristics of impermanence, disintegration, suffering, and coarseness, one knows that such is their nature.
These five dharmas do not go, do not come, and do not abide, as previously explained.
Even up to the unconditioned, unconditioned dharmas, suchness, nature, and characteristics—these also do not come, do not go, and do not abide; it is likewise so.
[Sūtra] “Subhūti, as for what you have said:
‘This Mahāyāna is unattainable at its prior limit, unattainable at its posterior limit, and unattainable in its middle limit; this vehicle is called the equality of the three periods of time.’”
"For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna. "So it is! So it is!"

Subhūti! This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle limit; this vehicle is called "equality across the three periods of time."
For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.
Why is that, Subhūti?

The past world is empty of the past world; the future world is empty of the future world; the present world is empty of the present world; the equality of the three worlds is empty of the equality of the three worlds;
the Mahāyāna is empty of the Mahāyāna; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!
This emptiness is not one, not two, not three, not four, not five, and not different.
For this reason, it is called the "equality of the three times" of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Mahāyāna.

Within this vehicle, because the marks of equality and inequality cannot be apprehended, defilement and non-defilement cannot be apprehended; hatred and non-hatred cannot be apprehended; delusion and non-delusion cannot be apprehended; pride and non-pride cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, which cannot be apprehended.
Within this Mahāyāna, permanence is unattainable and impermanence is unattainable;
pleasure is unattainable and suffering is unattainable;
reality is unattainable and emptiness is unattainable.
The self is unapprehendable, and the non-self is unapprehendable;
the desire realm is unapprehendable, the form realm is unapprehendable, and the formless realm is unapprehendable;
the transcendence of the desire realm is unapprehendable, the transcendence of the form realm is unapprehendable, and the transcendence of the formless realm is unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this Mahāyāna, its own intrinsic nature (svadharma) is unattainable. "Subhūti!..."
Past form is empty of past form; future and present form are empty of future and present form.
Past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
future and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of future and present feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In emptiness, past form cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because in emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can past form be apprehended within emptiness!
In emptiness, future and present form cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
Because in emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can future and present form be apprehended within emptiness!
In emptiness, past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattainable. Why is this?
Because in emptiness, even emptiness itself is unattainable; how much more so could past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be attained within emptiness!
In emptiness, future, present, and past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable. Why is this?

Because even emptiness itself is unapprehendable within emptiness; how much more so could future, present, and past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended within emptiness!

“Subhūti! The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) of the past cannot be apprehended; the perfection of giving of the future cannot be apprehended; the perfection of giving of the present cannot be apprehended; and even within the equality of the three times, the perfection of giving cannot be apprehended.”
Why is this? Within equality, the past cannot be found, the future cannot be found, and the present cannot be found.
Even within equality, equality itself cannot be found; how much less could the past, future, or present be found within equality!
The same applies to the śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
In the past, the four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha being unapprehendable in the past;
it is likewise for the future and the present."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Within the equality of the three periods of time, the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended; within the equality of the three periods of time, even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha cannot be apprehended."

Why is this? Within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the past cannot be apprehended; within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the future cannot be apprehended; and within equality, the four foundations of mindfulness of the present cannot be apprehended.
Even within equality, equality itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can the four foundations of mindfulness of the past, future, and present be apprehended within equality!
Even equality within equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can the past, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, be apprehended within equality!
The same applies to the future and present worlds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) cannot be apprehended in the past; an ordinary person cannot be apprehended in the future or the present; and an ordinary person likewise cannot be apprehended within the equality of the three times."
Why is this? Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and even the knower and the seer cannot be apprehended.

Within the past world, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended; within the future and present worlds, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended; and within the equality of the three times, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and even up to the knower and the seer cannot be apprehended.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom, they study the equal characteristics of the three periods of time and shall fulfill all-knowledge; this is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, the equal characteristics of the three periods of time.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in this vehicle, they surpass all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras, and they accomplish sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent!”
Excellent!
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas! Why is this so?
The bodhisattvas of the past attained all-knowledge by training in this Mahāyāna; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of future ages shall likewise attain all-knowledge by training in this Mahāyāna.
“World-Honored One!
Now, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions likewise train in this Great Vehicle and attain all-knowledge.”
"For this reason, World-Honored One,
this vehicle is truly the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have studied within this Mahāyāna; they have attained, will attain, and are now attaining all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
The Commentator says: Subhūti briefly praises it, saying:
"This Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended in the past, the future, or the middle; because the three periods of time are equal, it is called the Mahāyāna."
Now the Buddha extensively expounds that which Subhūti has praised.
Why are these three periods of time ungraspable?
It is because the past period is empty of the past period, the future period is empty of the future period, and the present period is empty of the present period; therefore, they are ungraspable.
The three periods of time are equal; that which is equal is empty.
The Mahāyāna is empty of itself;
the bodhisattva is empty of himself.
Within these three periods of time, the characteristics of the three periods of time are empty.
The meaning of emptiness is as previously explained.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions for emptiness, namely:

“Emptiness and the characteristic of emptiness are not one, not two, not three, not four, and not five, and so forth; they are neither different, nor joined, nor dispersed, and are without conceptual differentiation.”
Therefore, because the equality of the three periods of time is characterized by emptiness and is non-existent, these [periods] are also empty.

When a bodhisattva can thus understand that all dharmas are equal across the three periods of time, they do not become weary on account of the beginningless past, nor do they find it difficult on account of the boundlessness of the future. This is what is called the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva’s equality of the three periods of time.
In this Mahāyāna, neither the mark of equality nor the mark of inequality can be apprehended.
One attains the samādhi of the equality of the three periods of time and thereby destroys the mark of inequality.
Because inequality exists in dependence upon equality, and because inequality is ultimately non-existent, equality is also non-existent.
Whether it be desire or non-desire, up to the three realms or the transcendence of the three realms—these phenomena of mutual dependence are likewise thus.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:
"All these phenomena, because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, lack intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Furthermore, past form and the characteristics of past form are empty; the same applies to the future and the present.
As it is with form, so it is with the other four aggregates. Why is this?
Within emptiness, the characteristic of emptiness cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be the characteristics of the five aggregates across the three periods of time within emptiness!

The Bodhisattva contemplates the emptiness of the five aggregates and severs craving, entering the practice of the Path—namely, the pāramitās such as dāna—and likewise finds these five aggregates unobtainable throughout the three periods of time.
Because the three periods of time are equal, that equality is itself emptiness; within this equality, the dānapāramitā cannot be apprehended.
Question:
For what reason can the dānapāramitā not be apprehended within the three periods of time and within the equality of the three periods of time?
The answer is:
Within the equality of all dharmas, there are no three periods of time; even within this very equality, their characteristic of equality cannot be apprehended, let alone the three periods of time!
It is the same for the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas).
Furthermore, within the three periods of time, the characteristics of ordinary beings cannot be apprehended, nor can those of śrāvakas up to and including buddhas, because sentient beings are empty.

When a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they are able to train in this way—in the equality of the three periods of time as empty—and by accumulating all virtuous merits, they will then fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva can abide thus within the equality of the three periods of time, they will be able to surpass all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras."
At that time, Subhūti praised him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent!”
Excellent!
This Mahāyāna benefits all bodhisattvas. Why is this so?
"All bodhisattvas of the past who studied this Mahāyāna attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
those who have not yet attained it and those who are attaining it now are likewise. Some say:

Purity is attained without cause or condition; being defiled and stained likewise has no cause or condition. Whether large or small, beautiful or ugly, bound or liberated, none of these have a master who bestows them.
Some say that beauty and ugliness, bondage and liberation, are obtained spontaneously when the proper time arrives.
Some say: "One attains the Way of the Buddha through the fulfillment of merit. Others say:
"Only by attaining pure, true wisdom does one attain the Buddha-way.
Such statements as these all refer to non-conditions or insufficient conditions, which Subhūti does not praise.

Now the Buddha abandons non-causal conditions and also abandons incomplete causal conditions; he speaks of these complete causal conditions, namely the six pāramitās. By learning this vehicle to completion, the bodhisattvas of the three periods of time attain the path of Buddhahood.
The Buddha also endorsed what Subhūti had praised, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll 51.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Convergence of the Schools, Number Twenty-Four. Scroll 52.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 24: On the Convergence of the Schools. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Buddha has commissioned Subhūti to expound the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; why now does he instead speak of the Mahāyāna?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Would it not be that when I speak of the Mahāyāna, I am departing from the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said: "No!"
Subhūti! What you have spoken regarding the Mahāyāna accords with the prajñāpāramitā and does not depart from the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?

All wholesome dharmas that assist the path—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all these dharmas are entirely subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What are the various wholesome dharmas, the dharmas that assist the path—the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas—that are all subsumed within the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“They are what are called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities, the characteristic of being free from error, and the constant practice of equanimity.”

Subhūti! All these other wholesome dharmas that assist the path—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—are all subsumed within the prajñāpāramitā.

“Subhūti! Whether it be the Mahāyāna, or the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity;

whether it be form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; or the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the various feelings born of the causal condition of eye-contact, up to the mind, mental phenomena, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the various feelings born of the causal condition of mind-contact;”
The element of earth up to the element of consciousness;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
and the gateways to liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

And all wholesome dharmas—whether with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned; whether the truth of suffering, the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, or the truth of the path; whether belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; whether internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
the various gates of samādhi and the various gates of dhāraṇī;
and the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities.

Whether it be the Buddha, the Buddha-dharma, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), suchness (tathatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the inconceivable nature, or nirvāṇa—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive, having but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
Subhūti! For these reasons, the Mahāyāna that you have described accords with the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Subhūti! The Mahāyāna is not different from the prajñāpāramitā, and the prajñāpāramitā is not different from the Mahāyāna; the prajñāpāramitā and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.
The dānapāramitā is not different from the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is not different from the dānapāramitā; the dānapāramitā and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.
This applies even up to the perfection of dhyāna. Subhūti!

The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from the Mahāyāna, and the Mahāyāna is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.

Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are not different from the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is not different from the eighteen unique qualities. The eighteen unique qualities and the Mahāyāna are non-dual and without distinction.
"For this reason, Subhūti,
when you speak of the Mahāyāna, you are speaking of the Prajñāpāramitā. [The *Śāstra*] says:
Although Pūrṇa himself had no doubts, he asked the question because those of new learning and dull faculties did not understand that while the meaning was one, the names were different.
Subhūti then informed the Buddha of this matter, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound; could there be any error in what I have said?"
The Buddha replied:
“Your exposition of the Mahāyāna accords with the Prajñāpāramitā; it is without error.

This meaning has already been discussed previously; now the Buddha explains the causes and conditions for this accord: namely, that all wholesome dharmas subsumed within the three vehicles are gathered together and contained within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this so? Because all wholesome dharmas of the three vehicles are for the sake of nirvāṇa.
There are three kinds of gates to nirvāṇa:
All dharmas enter the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, and the gate of wishlessness.
Just as the observance of precepts can give rise to meditative concentration, and meditative concentration can give rise to true wisdom because one does not cling to the world.
What are the factors for the path of the three vehicles that are subsumed within Prajñā?

They are the so-called six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities, the characteristic of being free from error, and the constant practice of equanimity.

Among these, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation are the dharmas common to the three vehicles; the six perfections are the dharmas of the bodhisattvas; and the ten powers up to the constant practice of relinquishment are the dharmas of the Buddhas.
Some say: "The six pāramitās are either fulfilled or not fulfilled.
Those that are not fulfilled are shared with the Dharma of the Two Vehicles; those that are fulfilled are the exclusive Dharma of Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna is empty and the Prajñāpāramitā is also empty; because the meaning of emptiness is one, Subhūti conforms to it without error.
Just as the perfection of wisdom is empty, so too are the other five perfections, up to and including suchness, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, the inconceivable nature, and nirvana.

Furthermore, from the *prajñāpāramitā* down to *nirvāṇa*, all are non-conjoined, non-dispersed, formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; they possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Because they share these identical characteristics, it is said: "The Mahāyāna is the Prajñāpāramitā; the Mahāyāna and the Prajñāpāramitā are non-dual and without distinction."
25. Chapter on the Ten Absences. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Ten Absences, Number Twenty-five. [Sūtra] The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be apprehended in the past, cannot be apprehended in the future, and cannot be apprehended in the present.
Because form is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also boundless.
Form is the bodhisattva mahāsattva, yet even that is unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva mahāsattva, yet even those are unapprehendable.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
In every way and in every place, a bodhisattva cannot be found.
World-Honored One!"
"Whom, O Bhagavān, should I instruct in the perfection of wisdom?
For, Bhagavān,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as nothing more than a mere name."
As it is said regarding my name, "I" am ultimately unarisen.
As it is with me, so too are all phenomena without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
What is this form that is ultimately unarisen?
What is it that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ultimately do not arise?
World-Honored One!
That which ultimately does not arise is not called form; [it is likewise not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness].
This is ultimately non-arising; it is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
World-Honored One, if dharmas are ultimately non-arising, whom should one instruct in this Prajñāpāramitā?
Apart from that which is ultimately unborn, there is also no bodhisattva practicing for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If, upon hearing this teaching, a bodhisattva’s mind does not sink, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not afraid, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra asked: “Subhūti!
For what reason do you say that ‘the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s prior limit is unapprehendable, the posterior limit is unapprehendable, and the middle limit is unapprehendable’?”
“Subhūti, for what reason do you say: ‘Because form is boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless’?”
“Subhūti! For what reason do you say, ‘Form is the bodhisattva, yet that too is unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva, yet these too are unapprehendable’?”
“Subhūti! For what reason do you say: ‘Since a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended in any way or in any place, toward what kind of bodhisattva should one teach the perfection of wisdom?’”
“Subhūti! For what reason do you say that ‘a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as nothing more than a name’? Subhūti!”
For what reason is it said: "Just as my name is spoken, I am ultimately unarisen;
and just as I am, so too are all phenomena without intrinsic nature"?
"What kind of form is ultimately unarisen? What kind of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unarisen?
"Subhūti, for what reason is it said that 'that which is ultimately unarisen is not called form'?"
"Because that which is ultimately unarisen is not called feeling, perception, mental formations,
or consciousness. Subhūti,
for what reason do you say, "If dharmas are ultimately unarisen, whom should one instruct in this Prajñāpāramitā?"?
“Subhūti! For what reason do you say: ‘Apart from that which is ultimately unarisen, there is also no bodhisattva practicing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi’?”

“Subhūti! For what reason is it said: ‘If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, does not sink in heart, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not afraid, and if they can practice in this way, they are called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā’?”
At that time, Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Because sentient beings do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because sentient beings are empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
Because sentient beings are non-existent, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra, because form does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; [and so on for the other aggregates].
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because form is empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because form is detached, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra! Because the nature of form does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
“Śāriputra! Because the perfection of giving does not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom do not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, within emptiness,
the prior limit is unapprehendable, the posterior limit is unapprehendable, and the middle limit is unapprehendable.
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is not different from the prior limit.
Śāriputra, these dharmas—
emptiness, the bodhisattva, and the prior limit— are non-dual and without distinction.
For these reasons, Śāriputra,
the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra!

Because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is empty, because the perfection of giving is detached, and because the perfection of giving lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,

the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are empty, because the perfection of wisdom is detached, and because the perfection of wisdom lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within emptiness,
the prior limit is unapprehendable, the posterior limit is unapprehendable, and the middle limit is unapprehendable.
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is also not different from the prior limit. Śāriputra!
Emptiness, the bodhisattva, and the prior limit—these dharmas are non-dual and without distinction.
For these reasons, Śāriputra,
the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
Because internal emptiness is non-existent, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
and so on, up to: because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is non-existent, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.

Because internal emptiness is empty, because internal emptiness is detached, and because internal emptiness is non-existent in its nature—and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence being empty, detached, and non-existent in its nature—the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, because they are non-existent, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the eighteen unique qualities are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
For this reason, Śāriputra,
the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī do not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
because the doors of samādhi and the doors of dhāraṇī are empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not exist, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Because they do not exist, because they are empty, because they are detached, and because they lack intrinsic nature; because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) does not exist, because it is empty, because it is detached, and because it lacks intrinsic nature; and because the inconceivable nature does not exist, because it is empty, because it is detached, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because the śrāvaka does not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended."
Because the śrāvaka is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because the pratyekabuddha does not exist, is empty, detached, and devoid of intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because the Buddha does not exist, because he is empty, because he is detached, and because his intrinsic nature does not exist, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not exist, up to and including the non-existence of its intrinsic nature, the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not exist, and so on up to its lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Śāriputra!"
Śāriputra, in emptiness, the prior limit is unapprehendable, the posterior limit is unapprehendable, and the middle limit is unapprehendable; likewise, the bodhisattva is unapprehendable. Śāriputra!
Emptiness is not different from the bodhisattva, nor is it different from the prior limit;
emptiness, the bodhisattva, and the prior limit—these dharmas are non-dual and without distinction.
For this reason, Śāriputra!
“The prior limit of the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; the same is true for the posterior limit and the middle limit.
[Treatise] Question:
It has already been stated above that “the bodhisattva and the designation ‘bodhisattva’ cannot be apprehended,” yet for whom is the *prajñāpāramitā* being taught? Why is this stated again now?
The answer is:
One should not ask such a question!
Subhūti is foremost in the practice of emptiness and always delights in preaching emptiness.
Whatever is taught, it is always for the benefit of sentient beings through the gateway of emptiness.
Furthermore, what was briefly explained above is here analyzed in detail through ten aspects regarding the non-apprehensibility of the bodhisattva.
If a practitioner contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, they accord with signlessness and wishlessness;
because of this wishless mind, they have no desire to perform any action, such that they cannot even bring about their own benefit, let alone the benefit of others!

If a person dwells within the notion of a self, they can differentiate between the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, accumulating wholesome dharmas and abandoning unwholesome ones;
yet now the Buddha says:
"Within the Prajñāpāramitā, one should not calculate the notion of a self, nor should one differentiate among dharmas, but simply practice all manner of goodness."
"This matter is difficult.
The practitioner reflects thus:
"If there is no self, for whose sake does one cultivate merit?"
"Previously there was a self, but now because of the *prajñāpāramitā* it is non-existent; thus, a mind of sorrow and distress arises.
For this reason, Subhūti speaks again more emphatically:
"The self has been non-existent from the very beginning; it is not that it existed previously and is now non-existent."
The practitioner realizes that in this way and that way, [all things] have been originally non-existent from the beginning and are now not lost;
therefore, there is no cause for anxiety. For example, a deep-rooted great tree cannot be felled by a single blow, but requires much force from the axe to be cut down;
the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Bodhisattva is likewise—it cannot be attained through a single teaching. For this reason, it is analyzed in detail.
When Subhūti questioned the Buddha, he had this thought:
"If there were a bodhisattva-dharma that truly existed, it should exist throughout the three periods of time.
Yet, in past lives, there was no such thing as a bodhisattva."
Why is this? Because the prior world has no beginning.
The future world is likewise, for its causes and conditions have not yet arisen.
Because the preceding and succeeding depend upon one another, there is a middle; if there were no preceding or succeeding, there would be no middle.
If it is claimed that "the five aggregates are the Bodhisattva," [one must consider that] the five aggregates are limitless.

As previously explained through various causes and conditions, because the five aggregates are ultimately empty, they are immeasurable and limitless; being immeasurable and limitless, they are identical to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it were the case that Bodhisattvas were infinite, this would not be so!
For these reasons, a Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; for whom, then, would one preach?
Constantly, in all places, in every way, and at all times, one seeks a Bodhisattva and cannot find one; for whom, then, would one preach?
Just as I am ultimately unarisen, empty, and non-existent, so too are the five aggregates ultimately unarisen and non-existent.
Since there are neither sentient beings nor the dharmas of the five aggregates, how can there be a bodhisattva?
Question:
If sentient beings and the dharmas of the five aggregates are ultimately unarisen, is one who understands these dharmas a bodhisattva?
Answer:
That which is "ultimately unborn" is not called form, nor is it called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? The five aggregates are characterized by arising; within ultimate non-arising, such conceptual distinctions do not exist.
The five aggregates are ultimately unarisen and cannot be transformed through teaching;
apart from this ultimate non-arising, there is likewise no bodhisattva practicing the path—whom, then, should one teach?
That a bodhisattva hears this and is neither terrified nor afraid is what constitutes being able to practice the bodhisattva path.
A question is asked:
"I and the bodhisattva are one and the same thing; why then is the self used as a metaphor for the bodhisattva?"
The answer is:
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, all dharmas are empty; one should not explain emptiness to a beginner immediately!
First, one must distinguish between demerit and merit, abandoning demerit and cultivating meritorious virtue.
The retribution of merit is impermanent; because it is impermanent, suffering arises. Therefore, one should relinquish merit, grow weary of the world, seek the Way, and enter Nirvana.
At that time, one should form this thought:
"It is because of 'me' that various afflictions arise, yet this 'me' cannot be found when sought within the six consciousnesses; it is only due to inversion that one clings to a self."
Therefore, the understanding of non-self is easy, and it is easy for such people to be transformed.
If one says "form is empty," it is difficult to understand;
though they hear the teaching of emptiness with their ears, they constantly perceive reality with their eyes.
Therefore, one first refutes the "self" within evil transgressions, and subsequently refutes all phenomena.

Among all the disciples of the Buddha, those who have attained the Way know and realize for themselves the non-self; those who have not yet attained the Way believe in the emptiness of other phenomena, yet they cannot believe in non-self as they do [in these other phenomena]. For this reason, non-self is used as a metaphor.
In this context, Subhūti explains that all phenomena are empty; he argues that there is no bodhisattva by using the analogy of non-self.
He employs a small example to illustrate the great, just as the analogy of rock honey illustrates nectar.
Question:
Śāriputra understands the meaning of emptiness and non-self; why then does he inquire about each matter? Answer:
Subhūti is a śrāvaka whose virtue does not equal that of a bodhisattva; yet, as he speaks of the profound prajñā before the Buddha, the minds of newly initiated bodhisattvas may give rise to doubt.
Although the Buddha has stated, "What you have said regarding the Mahāyāna accords with Prajñā," it may still be thought that the Buddha is merely complying with Subhūti.
Śāriputra wishes to sever this doubt, and therefore he poses a question.
Furthermore, the Buddha wished to discourse on the Prajñā with Subhūti until its very conclusion;
for this reason, Śāriputra questioned him on every matter, causing Subhūti to skillfully analyze the profound meaning so that all people might develop reverence and faith.
For this reason, he asks:
"In past lives, a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, up to and including not being terrified or afraid.
Subhūti answers this meaning:
The self, sentient beings, and persons are all one and the same thing.
When one has not yet attained the Way, one is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
from the initial entry into the Way up to the stage of Arhat, one is called a Śrāvaka.
One who contemplates the dharma of dependent origination and realizes emptiness to a minor degree, yet feels slight compassion for sentient beings, is called a pratyekabuddha.

One who deeply penetrates the dharma of emptiness, practices the six pāramitās, and possesses great kindness and great compassion, is called a bodhisattva. Because their merits differ, their names also differ.

Just as the single entity that is the self, sentient beings, and the person is called a "seer" because it sees objects with the eye, a "knower" because it apprehends them with the mind, and an "experiencer" because it undergoes pleasure and pain.
Since it has already been explained through various causes and conditions that the self, sentient beings, persons, and so forth do not exist, the bodhisattva must likewise not exist.
For this reason, Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Because sentient beings do not exist, there is no bodhisattva within the three periods of time."
Question: Since the Bodhisattva exists through the combination of the five aggregates, the Bodhisattva should be non-existent while the five aggregates should be existent! Answer:

To refute these [notions], it is said: "There are no sentient beings; there is no self. Because there is no self, the five aggregates have nothing to which they belong; because they have nothing to which they belong, they are empty; and because they are empty, there is no bodhisattva.
Question:
If the five aggregates are empty, is emptiness itself the bodhisattva? Answer:
The emptiness of the five aggregates is not the bodhisattva either, because emptiness is non-existent and without differentiation.
The five aggregates are detached and the five aggregates lack intrinsic nature; thus, there is also no bodhisattva.
If one says there is no bodhisattva, then the three periods of time all become non-existent.
One observes that these worldly dharmas, such as the five aggregates, and these path-dharmas, such as the six pāramitās, are what is called a "bodhisattva.
Since these dharmas are empty, the bodhisattva is also empty.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"The emptiness of all dharmas is not different from the bodhisattva; the bodhisattva is not different from emptiness. The emptiness of the bodhisattva and the emptiness of the three periods of time are non-dual and without distinction."
"Because one practices these dharmas, from the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), one is called a bodhisattva;
because these dharmas are empty, the bodhisattva is also empty."
In this context, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain this emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), they are called "persons who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas";
because these persons who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are empty, it is the same for the bodhisattva as well.
[Sūtra] “As Śāriputra has said:
‘Because form is limitless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also limitless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, one should know that the bodhisattva is also limitless.’”
"Śāriputra! Form is like space; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like space. Why is this?"
Śāriputra! Just as the limit of space cannot be found and its center cannot be found—because it is neither bounded nor centered—it is merely designated by the name "space.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
The limit of form cannot be apprehended, nor can its center; because form is empty, within emptiness there is neither limit nor center.
The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness:
the limit of consciousness cannot be apprehended, nor can its center; because consciousness is empty, within emptiness there is neither limit nor center.
For this reason, Śāriputra,
because form is boundless, you should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, you should know that the bodhisattva is also boundless.
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), which are likewise so. As Śāriputra said:
"Form is the bodhisattva; this, too, is unapprehendable."
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva; these, too, are unapprehendable.

Śāriputra, form is empty of the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The perfection of giving is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of giving; this applies likewise up to the perfection of wisdom.

Inner emptiness is empty of the characteristic of inner emptiness; this applies likewise up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness; this applies likewise up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality are empty of the nature of being inconceivable and of the characteristics of being inconceivable;
the gateways of samādhi are empty of the characteristics of the gateways of samādhi; the gateways of dhāraṇī are empty of the characteristics of the gateways of dhāraṇī;

all-knowledge is empty of the characteristics of all-knowledge; the knowledge of the paths is empty of the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths; and the knowledge of all modes is empty of the characteristics of the knowledge of all modes.

The Śrāvaka vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; the Buddha vehicle is empty of the characteristics of the Buddha vehicle.

The Śrāvaka person is empty of the characteristics of the Śrāvaka person; the Pratyekabuddha is empty of the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha; the Buddha is empty of the characteristics of the Buddha.
In emptiness, form cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
For this reason, Śāriputra, form is the bodhisattva, yet even that cannot be apprehended.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the bodhisattva; yet these also cannot be apprehended.
As Śāriputra has said:
"For what reason is the bodhisattva unapprehendable in every way and in all places? To which bodhisattva should one teach the perfection of wisdom?"
"Śāriputra! Form cannot be apprehended within form;
form cannot be apprehended within sensation."
Feeling cannot be apprehended within feeling;
feeling cannot be apprehended within form;
feeling cannot be apprehended within perception.
Perception cannot be found within perception;
perception cannot be found within form or sensation;
perception cannot be found within mental formations.
Volitional formations cannot be apprehended within volitional formations;
volitional formations cannot be apprehended within form, feeling, or perception;
volitional formations cannot be apprehended within consciousness.
Consciousness cannot be apprehended within consciousness; consciousness cannot be apprehended within form, feeling, perception, or mental formations.
Śāriputra, the eye cannot be apprehended within the eye.
The eye cannot be found within the ear;
the ear cannot be found within the ear;
the ear cannot be found within the eye.
The ear cannot be found within the nose;
the nose cannot be found within the nose;
the nose cannot be found within the eye or the ear.
The nose is not to be found within the tongue;
the tongue is not to be found within the tongue;
the tongue is not to be found within the eye, the ear, or the nose.
The tongue cannot be found within the body;
the body cannot be found within the body;
the body cannot be found within the eye, ear, nose, or tongue.
The body cannot be found within the mind;
the mind cannot be found within the mind;
and the mind cannot be found within the eye, ear, nose, tongue, or body.
The same applies to the six sense bases, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, and the feelings produced by the conditions of the six contacts.

It is likewise for the *dānapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*; from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) through to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness through to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī; from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through to the *pratyekabuddha-dharmas*; from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through to the tenth stage; and all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is likewise for the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) through to the arhat, the *pratyekabuddha*, the bodhisattva, and the Buddha.
A bodhisattva cannot be apprehended within a bodhisattva;
a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended within the perfection of wisdom.
In the *prajñāpāramitā*, the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended;
within the *prajñāpāramitā*, the non-existence of that which is to be taught cannot be apprehended.
Within that which is to be taught, the non-existence of the act of teaching cannot be apprehended.
In this process of teaching and transforming, both the bodhisattva and the prajñāpāramitā do not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra, in this same way, all dharmas do not exist and cannot be apprehended.
For this reason, since a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended in any way or in any place, toward what kind of bodhisattva should one teach the perfection of wisdom?
“As Śāriputra has asked:
‘For what reason do you say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as a mere designation? Śāriputra!
Form is a provisional designation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are provisional designations.
The name "form" is not form; the names "feeling," "perception," "mental formations," and "consciousness" are not consciousness.
Why is this? Names and the characteristics of names are empty;
if they are empty, then they are not the bodhisattva.
For these reasons, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva exists only as a mere designation.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) exists only as a name;
within the name there is no perfection of giving, and within the perfection of giving there is no name.
For this reason, the bodhisattva exists only as a provisional designation.
The śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā—
the prajñā-pāramitā exists as a mere name;
within the name there is no prajñā-pāramitā, and within the prajñā-pāramitā there is no name.
For this reason, a bodhisattva exists only as a conventional designation.

Śāriputra, the emptiness of the internal exists only as a name; even up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, it exists only as a name. Within names there is no emptiness of the internal, and within the emptiness of the internal there are no names.
Why is this? Both names and internal emptiness are unapprehendable.
This applies likewise up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
For this reason, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva exists only as a mere designation. Śāriputra!
The four foundations of mindfulness exist as mere names, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which also exist as mere names;
all doors of samādhi, all doors of dhāraṇī, and even the knowledge of all modes likewise exist as mere names.
"For this reason, Śāriputra,
I say that a bodhisattva exists only as a provisional designation.
As Śāriputra has said:
"For what reason do you say that my name is ultimately non-arising?
"Śāriputra, since I am ultimately unattainable, how could there be any arising?"
Since even a knower or a seer is ultimately unattainable, how could there be arising?
Śāriputra! Since form is ultimately unattainable, how could there be arising?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unattainable; how, then, could they arise?
The eye is ultimately unattainable, and so on up to feeling produced through the condition of mind-contact, which is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could it arise?
The perfection of giving is ultimately unattainable, and even the perfection of wisdom is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be arising?
Internal emptiness is ultimately unattainable, and even the emptiness of non-existence and existence is ultimately unattainable; how, then, could there be arising?
Since the four foundations of mindfulness are ultimately unattainable, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately unattainable, how could there be any arising?
Since the various gates of samādhi and the various gates of dhāraṇī are ultimately unattainable, how could there be any arising?
Since śrāvakas up to and including buddhas are ultimately unobtainable,
how could there be any arising? For this reason, Śāriputra, I say:

"Just as my name [is merely a designation], I too am ultimately unarisen. [Treatise] Question: Because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are formless and invisible, they may be considered boundless; however, [the question remains: how can form (*rūpa*) be boundless? Furthermore, since space (*ākāśa*) is not a substantial entity (*dravya*), how can it be called "boundless"? Moreover, since the realms of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) are infinite, one might think that the Buddha’s wisdom would be exhausted by perceiving them all. How then can it be said that his wisdom is boundless? Finally, since the dharmas of the past and future are infinite, how can the Buddha’s knowledge of them be called boundless? How could he possibly know them all? If he did not know them all, he would not be omniscient (*sarvajña*). If he knew them all, his knowledge would be limited. Why? Because the number of dharmas is infinite, yet the Buddha’s lifespan is finite. If he were to know them all within that finite time, his knowledge would be limited. If he did not know them all, he would not be omniscient. Therefore, the Buddha’s knowledge cannot be called boundless. How then can it be said that he knows all dharmas? If he does not know them, he is not omniscient; if he does know them, his knowledge is limited. If one says he is omniscient because he knows all dharmas, then he must have known them all at once. If he knew them all at once, he would not be able to know the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each dharma. If he knew them sequentially, his knowledge would be limited. Therefore, the Buddha’s knowledge cannot be called boundless. If he did not know them, he would not be omniscient; if he did know them, his knowledge would be limited. Thus, the Buddha’s knowledge cannot be called boundless. How then can it be said that he knows all dharmas? Form has shape and is visible; how can it be boundless?
The answer is:
there is no place where form does not exist, and its distance, proximity, lightness, or heaviness cannot be measured.
As the Buddha said:
"The four great elements exist everywhere; therefore they are called 'great.
Their limits cannot be grasped by the five senses, nor can their quantity or weight be measured with a bushel or a scale; for this reason, it is said that 'form is boundless.'"
Furthermore, regarding this form (*rūpa*), its initial point cannot be apprehended in the past;
nor, in the future, is there any limit such that after a number of eons equal to the sands of the Ganges, form will come to an end. Therefore, it has no posterior limit.
Since the prior and posterior limits do not exist, the middle likewise does not exist.
Furthermore, "limit" (*anta*) refers to the characteristic of form (*rūpa*).
When this form is analyzed and dispersed, no limit can be found, as it lacks any fundamental characteristic.
Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are neither born nor extinguished, they are innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless.
By means of the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas, one observes that all form is empty, sharing the same characteristics as space and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless dharmas, even a single atom cannot be apprehended, let alone a bodhisattva!
Therefore it is said: "The five aggregates are boundless, and the bodhisattva is also boundless.
Just as form (*rūpa*) is boundless, so it is for everything up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); their distinctions according to their characteristics are as previously explained.
Because these five aggregates are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless, one cannot say that form is the bodhisattva;
the same applies to the other four aggregates.
Furthermore, if form were separated from the mind and mental factors, it would be like grass, wood, tiles, or stones; how then could it be called a bodhisattva?
If the mind and mental factors were separated from form, they would have no basis for support and would be incapable of any function; how, then, could they be called a bodhisattva?

Furthermore, the six pāramitās, the eighteen emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, suchness, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, the inconceivable nature, the three gates of liberation, the gates of dhāraṇī, the various gates of samādhi, omniscience (sarvajñā), the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of all modes, the three vehicles, and those of the three vehicles—if one cultivates or contemplates these dharmas, this is what is called a bodhisattva.

All these dharmas are empty because they are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*); that is to say, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of giving, and so on, up to the Buddha being empty of the characteristic of the Buddha.
"All places" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"All-knowledge" refers to the eighteen kinds of emptiness and the three gates of liberation.

When one contemplates through the Prajñāpāramitā whether things are permanent or impermanent, and so forth—entering by way of one gate, two gates, or even immeasurable gates—this is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
One cannot find a bodhisattva through seeking.
Furthermore, within one's own dharmas there are no self-dharmas, nor are there any dharmas of another.
As it is said herein:
"Form cannot be found within form;
form cannot be found within sensation.
Sensation cannot be found within sensation;"
Feeling is not to be found within form;
likewise, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of wisdom is not to be found within it;
and so on, up to and including the act of teaching and transforming others, the act of teaching and transforming others is not to be found therein.
As for the phrase "there is only a name," it means that these five aggregates are broken down, dispersed, and extinguished, no different from empty space.
This bodhisattva exists as a mere name, like a person created by illusion; within the context of provisional names, yet another name has been established.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Not only is 'Bodhisattva' a provisional designation, but all five aggregates are likewise provisional designations.
Within these provisional designations, the characteristics of provisional designations cannot be apprehended; they all enter into the ultimate truth."
"If it were empty in this way, then it would not be a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, because one practices these dharmas—from the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge—one is called a "bodhisattva";
yet these dharmas are merely provisional names, and "bodhisattva" is also a provisional name; they are empty and non-existent.
These dharmas are forcibly given names; they exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions, yet they lack any reality.
As for the statement, "The name 'self' is ultimately unarisen," this was already explained at the beginning of this chapter.
In this context, Subhūti likewise refutes the self through the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena, saying:
"The self is ultimately unattainable; even the knower and the seer are unattainable. How, then, could there be birth?"
Since the five aggregates are ultimately unattainable, how can there be sentient beings?
Even up to the feeling produced through the condition of mental contact, which is ultimately unattainable—how could there be arising?
The six pāramitās are ultimately unattainable; even the various dhāraṇī-doors, samādhi-doors, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas are ultimately unattainable—how, then, could there be any arising?
"If a phenomenon already existed prior to its arising, one could then ask about its birth;
but since the essence of a phenomenon does not exist beforehand, how can there be birth?
[Sūtra] "As Śāriputra has said:"
"Just as I am, so too all dharmas lack intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra, because all dharmas arise through a combination of conditions, they lack intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra! What is this "arising from a combination" that lacks intrinsic nature? Śāriputra!
Form arises from a combination of conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise from combinations of conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
The eye arises from a combination of conditions and lacks intrinsic nature, and so on, up to the mind arising from a combination of conditions and lacking intrinsic nature.

From form up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), from the eye-element up to the mental-object-element, from the earth-element up to the consciousness-element, from eye-contact up to mind-contact, and from the feeling produced by conditions of eye-contact up to the feeling produced by conditions of mind-contact—all these arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all dharmas are impermanent and yet do not perish.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What dharmas are impermanent yet not lost?
Subhūti replied:
“Form is impermanent yet not lost; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent yet not lost.”
Why is this? If a dharma is impermanent, it is a characteristic of movement and it is a characteristic of emptiness.
For these reasons, Śāriputra!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and yet do not perish.
Whether they be tainted or untainted phenomena, or whether they be determinate or indeterminate phenomena, they are impermanent and yet do not perish.
Why is this? If a dharma is impermanent, it is a characteristic of movement and it is a characteristic of emptiness.
For these reasons, Śāriputra!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, yet they are not lost.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to extinction."
Śāriputra asked:
“What dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to cessation?
Subhūti replied:
"Form is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why is this?
Because its nature is such."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because their nature is inherently so.
Even up to the feelings produced by the conditions of mental consciousness, they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
Why is this? Because such is their inherent nature.
For this reason, Śāriputra,
all dharmas arise through combination and lack intrinsic nature.
As you have said, Śāriputra:
“For what reason, Subhūti, do form ultimately not arise, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ultimately not arise?
Subhūti replied: “Form is not a conditioned phenomenon;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not conditioned phenomena.”
Why is this? Because an agent cannot be apprehended, Śāriputra!
The eye is not a conditioned phenomenon. Why?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
It is the same for the mind as well.
From the eye-element up to the feeling born of the condition of mind-contact, it is also thus.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All dharmas neither arise nor are created.
Why is this? Because an agent cannot be apprehended.
For these reasons, Śāriputra, form is ultimately unarisen;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately unarisen.
As you have said, Śāriputra:
"For what reason is that which is ultimately unarisen not called form?
For what reason is that which is ultimately unarisen not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?"
Subhūti said: "The nature of form is empty;
this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or changing.
The nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty; this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or changing."
From the eye up to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), their nature is emptiness; this emptiness is without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or change.
For these reasons, Śāriputra!
That which is ultimately unarisen is not called form;
that which is ultimately unarisen is not called feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
As Śāriputra has said:
“For what reason should one teach this *prajñāpāramitā* to dharmas that are ultimately unarisen?

Subhūti replied, “Ultimate non-arising is itself *prajñāpāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā* is itself ultimate non-arising. *Prajñāpāramitā* and ultimate non-arising are non-dual and without distinction.”
"For this reason, Śāriputra, when I say that ultimately there is no arising, should one teach this Prajñāpāramitā?
[The Buddha replied: "As Śāriputra has said:"
"For what reason is it that, apart from ultimate non-arising, there is no bodhisattva practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti replied:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he does not perceive ultimate non-arising as distinct from the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor does he perceive ultimate non-arising as distinct from the bodhisattva; ultimate non-arising and the bodhisattva are non-dual and without distinction."
One does not perceive the ultimate non-arising as distinct from form. Why is this?
Because this ultimate non-arising and form are non-dual and without distinction.
One does not perceive that ultimate non-arising is different from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this?
Ultimate non-arising and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and without distinction.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For this reason, Śāriputra,
apart from ultimate non-arising, there is no bodhisattva practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“As Śāriputra has said:

‘For what reason, when a bodhisattva hears this teaching, does their mind not sink, does not regret, and is not startled, terrified, or afraid? This is called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.’”

Subhūti said: “A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any phenomenon as having the characteristic of cognition; he perceives all phenomena as being like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage, like a shadow, and like a magical creation.”
Śāriputra! For these reasons, when a bodhisattva hears such a teaching, their mind does not sink, does not regret, is not startled, is not terrified, and does not fear.
The [Commentary] states:
Regarding the statement that "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature," this uses the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) to deconstruct the individual natures of all phenomena.
Herein, Subhūti speaks for himself:
"All dharmas arise through combination and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For instance, from the combination of dharmas such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and wholesome dharmas such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the name "Bodhisattva" emerges.

Since this Bodhisattva arises from conditioned dharmas and the combination of various conditions, he is not established by a single dharma; for this reason, it is said that he is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

These various phenomena also arise from the side of combination; for example, when there is the eye, visible form, light, space, and the mental intention to see, through the combination of these various causes and conditions, visual consciousness arises. Within this process, one cannot say that the eye is the seer, nor that consciousness is the seer, nor that visible form is the seer, nor that light is the seer.
If the eye, forms, consciousness, and so forth cannot each individually perceive anything, nor can they do so within their combination,
then for this reason the dharma of seeing is ultimately empty, like an illusion or a dream.
All dharmas are likewise so.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all dharmas are impermanent yet not lost": impermanence subverts the inversion of permanence, and non-loss subverts the inversion of annihilationism.
This dharma of impermanence and non-loss is precisely the gateway for entering the true mark (dharmatā). Therefore, Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Impermanence is the characteristic of movement; it is the characteristic of emptiness.
All dharmas are likewise.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that “all dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to destruction,” this is as explained in the subsequent meaning following the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
"Form is ultimately unarisen" means that among the five aggregates, an agent, a producer, or an originator cannot be found.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that the characteristic of arising cannot be found, this is as explained previously in the refutation of arising.
All dharmas are likewise thus.

As for the question, "Why is it said that if form (*rūpa*) does not arise, it is 'not-form,' and the same applies to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?"—here Subhūti himself explains:
"Form arises from causes and conditions; it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is characterized by eternal emptiness."
If a dharma has the characteristic of being eternally empty, that dharma has no characteristic of arising, no characteristic of ceasing, and no characteristic of abiding or changing.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Therefore, the dharma of non-arising is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), not a conditioned characteristic (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
It is the same for all other dharmas.

Regarding the statement, "Since they are ultimately unborn, whom should one teach with *prajñā*?"—ultimate non-arising is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, and the true reality of all dharmas is *prajñāpāramitā*. How, then, can one teach *prajñāpāramitā* by means of *prajñāpāramitā*?
If there were a bodhisattva apart from this ultimate non-arising, one should instruct them in the *prajñāpāramitā*;

yet since this bodhisattva, the *prajñāpāramitā*, and ultimate non-arising are non-dual and without distinction, how could one instruct a practitioner to practice by departing from ultimate non-arising?
The preceding section has already been explained in combination with its meaning.

Regarding the statement, "When a bodhisattva hears this, they do not sink and do not regret": within all dharmas, the bodhisattva perceives no self, no sentient being, and so forth, up to no knower or viewer; there is neither a speaker nor a listener; there is no false teaching and no correct teaching, nor is there anyone who does not teach.

Knowing that all dharmas arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions and cease when those conditions disperse—such that there is no one who causes them to arise and no one who causes them to cease—the bodhisattva is thus without fear, without terror, without sinking, and without regret.
The Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are deceptive, lacking reality and lacking fixity;
even when facing the urgency of death or falling into the Avīci hell, his mind remains unmoved—how much less would he experience terror upon hearing empty sounds!
Just as a person who sees terrifying things in a dream feels no fear upon waking, knowing that the nature of dreams can deceive the mind and that there are no real entities therein;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva: while within the dream of worldly consciousness they perceive fear, yet upon attaining the awakening to the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), they have nothing to fear;
they know that all phenomena are merely deceptive and lack any reality.
