Furthermore, it is like a magical illusion: although a wise person sees it, their mind is not deluded, for they know it to be a deceptive phenomenon.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; knowing that all phenomena are like illusions that can deceive the human mind and that therein is no reality, for this reason they feel no fear.
It is like a mirage, like a shadow, and like a magical creation; it is also thus.
[Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates all phenomena in this way, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp form, does not view form, does not dwell in form, does not cling to form, and does not say, "This is form.

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as well, they do not grasp them, do not view them, do not dwell in them, do not cling to them, and do not say, "These are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The eye is not accepted, not observed, not dwelled upon, and not clung to, nor is it said to be "this is the eye";
so too for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind— these are not accepted,
not observed, not dwelled upon, and not clung to, nor is it said to be "this is the mind."
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is not accepted, not observed, not dwelt upon, and not clung to, nor is it said to be "this is the perfection of giving.
The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā),

the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are likewise not accepted, not shown, not dwelt upon, and not clung to, nor is it said to be "this is the perfection of wisdom."
Internal emptiness is not received, not shown, not dwelled upon, and not clung to; nor is it said, "This is internal emptiness.
This applies likewise up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not accept, do not indicate, do not dwell in, and do not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, nor do they say, "These are the four foundations of mindfulness.

This extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, which they do not accept, do not indicate, do not dwell in, and do not cling to, nor do they say, "These are the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."

Regarding all gates of samādhi and all gates of dhāraṇī, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), they do not accept them, do not manifest them, do not abide in them, and do not cling to them; nor do they say, "This is all-knowledge."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive anything up to and including all-knowledge."
Why is this? Form does not arise; that which does not arise is not form.
Feeling, perception, and formations [are likewise].
When consciousness does not arise, it is not consciousness;
when the eye does not arise, it is not the eye;
[so too] the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The non-arising of mind is not mind.
The non-arising of the dānapāramitā is not the dānapāramitā;
and so on, up to the non-arising of the prajñāpāramitā, which is not the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Form and non-arising are not two and are not distinct;
likewise, up to and including Prajñāpāramitā and non-arising, they are not two and are not distinct.
The non-arising of internal emptiness is not internal emptiness;
likewise, up to the non-arising of the emptiness of non-existence and existence is not the emptiness of non-existence and existence. Why is this?
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they are non-arising, non-dual, and undifferentiated.
World-Honored One!
The four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising and are not the four foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?
The four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising, neither two nor distinct. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
This non-arising dharma is not one, not two, not three, and not different.
For this reason, the four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising, non-dual, and undifferentiated.
Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are non-arising and are not the eighteen unique qualities. Why?
Because the eighteen unique qualities and non-arising are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-arising is not one, not two, not three, and not different.
For this reason, the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) are non-arising; they are not the eighteen unique qualities.
World-Honored One!
That which is non-arising is not suchness (tathatā).
Up to and including the non-arising of inconceivability—this is not inconceivability itself.
World-Honored One!
This non-arising of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The non-arising of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is not itself all-knowledge. Why is this?
This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, up to and including all-knowledge and non-arising, are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This non-arising dharma is not one, not two, not three, and not different.
For this reason, even up to the point where all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not arise, it is not all-knowledge.
"World-Honored One!
The characteristic of the non-extinction of form is not form."
Why is this? Form and the characteristic of non-extinction are neither two nor distinct. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-extinction is neither one, nor two, nor three, nor different.
For this reason, the mark of the non-extinction of form is itself not form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness— these characteristics of non-extinction are not consciousness. Why is this?
Consciousness and non-extinction are non-dual and not distinct. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This dharma of non-extinction is not one, not two, not three, and not different. For this reason, the characteristic of the non-extinction of consciousness is not consciousness itself.

This is also true for the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*; from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); and from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). It is likewise so.
“World-Honored One!

For this reason, form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; and so on, up to all-knowledge entering into the category of non-dual dharmas.”
The *Śāstra* states:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
"When a bodhisattva can contemplate all dharmas in this manner, there are five kinds of correct contemplative practices within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)."
What is called "non-acceptance" (anupādāna) refers to the fact that within the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), there is the fire of impermanence (anityatā) capable of burning the mind.

"Non-viewing" (adarśana) means not grasping at signs (animitta); it is not merely observing faults such as impermanence, but observing these five aggregates as empty (śūnya) because one does not grasp at signs.
"Non-abiding" means not relying upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), because one fears that the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) will arrive; thus, one does not dare to dwell for long.
It is like an empty village, a place where thieves reside, where a wise person should not remain for long.

"Non-attachment" means that if there were even a single transgression among the five aggregates, one should not become attached; how much more so when the body experiences hunger, thirst, cold, heat, old age, sickness, and death, and the mind experiences sorrow, fear, envy, jealousy, and anger, leading to rebirth in the three evil realms in future lives!
All things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; they lack autonomy.
Given such immeasurable and boundless faults as these, how could one possibly become attached?

"Does not say 'this is form'" means that one does not, out of false views, describe form as either permanent or impermanent, nor does one speak of the five aggregates as having such fixed characteristics.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is this?

Because when one practices the five kinds of correct practice within form (*rūpa*), these five aggregates (*skandha*) are all characterized by non-arising; they are all of one single characteristic, and that which is of one single characteristic is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).
If there is no mark of characteristics, then the five aggregates do not exist;
this applies even up to the knowledge of all modes.
If all dharmas have the mark of non-arising, then the perfection of wisdom is neither dual nor distinct.
To attain this mind of non-arising is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
to attain the perfection of wisdom is to know that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
For this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself non-arising, neither dual nor distinct.

Furthermore, Subhūti himself explains the causal conditions, namely that these dharma-s of non-arising do not have a single characteristic, do not have a dual characteristic, are not three, and are not different.
Why is this? Because all dharmas have the single characteristic of non-arising.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
As it is with non-arising, so it is with non-ceasing.
Question: Why, at the very end, is it said that "form, up to and including all-knowledge, enters into the category of non-dual dharmas"?
The answer is:
If a bodhisattva has not yet destroyed form, they give rise to fetters such as craving and become attached to this form and so forth;
once form has been destroyed, they give rise to false views and become attached to this emptiness of form and so forth.
Now, because form and the other aggregates are empty through the wisdom of emptiness, they are all empty and of a non-dual nature.
These dharmas are deceptive and unreal; because they are comprised within the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*), they are called "duality.
From form up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), that which is free from these two is called "non-duality."
Now, Subhūti, out of compassion for sentient beings and for the benefit of all bodhisattvas, says:
"These dharmas are non-dual; they enter into the category of non-dual dharmas."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Scroll 52.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Non-Arising (Anutpāda), Number Twenty-Six, Scroll 53.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 26: On Non-arising. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and contemplates all dharmas, what is this 'bodhisattva'?"
"What is this Prajñāpāramitā?
What is this contemplation?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"As to your question,
'What is a bodhisattva?'— it is one who,
for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, has resolved upon the Great Mind; for this reason, they are called a bodhisattva."
They also know all phenomena and all their various characteristics, yet they do not cling to them;
they know the characteristics of form without clinging, and so on, up to knowing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha without clinging.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"What is the characteristic of all phenomena?
Subhūti replied:

"If one knows that all dharmas are form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; that they are internal or external; that they are conditioned or unconditioned—by means of such names, signs, and linguistic expressions one knows all dharmas; this is called knowing the characteristics of all dharmas."
"As Śāriputra asked:
'What is the prajñāpāramitā?
It is called prajñāpāramitā because it is characterized by remoteness."
What is the dharma of detachment?

It is detachment from the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases; detachment from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of meditation; and detachment from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
For this reason, detachment is called the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, because it is remote from the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and remote from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), for these reasons it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
“As Śāriputra asked: ‘What is contemplation? Śāriputra!...”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate form as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with marks nor markless, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, and neither detached nor non-detached;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.

From the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); all gateways of samādhi, all gateways of dhāraṇī, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*): one contemplates these as neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, and neither detached nor non-detached.
“Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of all dharmas when practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
[Treatise] Question:
Regarding what were called "the meaning of 'bodhisattva,' the meaning of 'prajñāpāramitā,' and the meaning of 'all contemplations,'" these were already asked above; why are they asked again now?
The answer is:
previously, the analogy of the great tree was already given—that it cannot be severed by a single blow.
Because this matter is difficult, he asks again.
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā possesses immeasurable meanings, as it is said in the "Dharmodgata-parivarta":
"The Prajñāpāramitā is like the waters of the great ocean, immeasurable; it is like Mount Sumeru, adorned with all manner of splendors."
For this reason, he asks.
Furthermore, although these questions are the same, the meanings of their answers vary in many ways.

Moreover, the Buddhas have severed attachment to dharmas; they do not establish scriptures nor do they embellish their speech, but speak solely for the sake of rescuing sentient beings, teaching according to those who are to be saved.
It is like a great, cool, and beautiful pond where immeasurable multitudes of beings come and go to drink, each departing satisfied;

the listeners are also like this. The Buddha first spoke of the Bodhisattva, Prajñā, and contemplation; those who arrived earlier attained understanding and departed, while those who arrived later had not yet heard it. For this reason, they ask again.
Regarding the term "Bodhisattva":
there are three kinds of "bodhi" (enlightenment).
There is the bodhi of an arhat, the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha, and the bodhi of a buddha.
Because the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is pure and stainless, it is called bodhi.
Although a bodhisattva possesses great wisdom, because the habitual tendencies of the afflictions have not yet been exhausted, it is not called bodhi.
In this context, only one kind is mentioned, namely, the Buddha-bodhi.
"Sattva" means "sentient beings" in the language of Qin.
These sentient beings, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, resolve their minds and practice cultivation.
Furthermore, "sattva" means "great mind.
This person has resolved upon the great mind and seeks unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), yet has not yet attained it; for this reason, they are called a "bodhisattva."
Since the Buddha has already attained this bodhi, he is not called a bodhisattva, because his great resolve is fully satisfied.
As for the remaining meanings of "bodhisattva," they have been explained extensively as before.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions herein:
"This person practices for the sake of the Buddha-way, and while knowing the characteristics of all dharmas, they do not cling to them."
Regarding "the characteristics of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*): one may know that the various dharma-gates are form, sound, and so forth.
To briefly explain the meaning of a bodhisattva:

first, one knows the respective characteristics of all phenomena—such as the characteristic of solidity in earth—and only thereafter does one know the characteristic of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, within these two kinds of wisdom, he does not cling, solely because he desires to deliver sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva attains such wisdom, he is able to remain far removed from all phenomena characterized by distinct marks.
Just as within form there is the departure from form, and this departure from form is itself the emptiness of self-characteristic;
"detachment" (*viveka*) is another name for "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
When a bodhisattva attains the *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind is detached from all phenomena.
Why is this? Because one perceives the faults and transgressions of all dharmas.
"Āramitā" (阿羅蜜) means "far removed" in the language of Qin.
"Pāramitā" means "crossing to the other shore" in the language of Qin.
Since these two sounds are similar and their meanings coincide, "Āramitā" is used as an explanation for "Pāramitā."
From what phenomena is it detached?
It is detached from the aggregates (skandha), the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), and so forth, up to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
Because it is detached from all these phenomena, it is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as the dhyāna-pāramitā can subdue the human mind, the prajñā-pāramitā can cause one to remain detached from all dharmas.
As for "contemplation," it means not contemplating whether dharmas are permanent or impermanent, as previously explained.
[Sūtra] Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"By what causes and conditions is it that the non-arising of form is not form;

that the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness; and so on, up to the non-arising of the knowledge of all modes, which is not the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti said: “Form and the characteristics of form are empty; within the emptiness of form, there is no form and no arising. For this reason, the non-arising of form is not form.

Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, as well as the characteristics of consciousness, are empty; within the emptiness of consciousness, there is no consciousness and no arising. For this reason, the non-arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.”
Śāriputra! The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty of the mark of the perfection of giving; within the emptiness of the perfection of giving, there is no perfection of giving and no arising.

This is also true for the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).

The perfection of wisdom is empty of the mark of the perfection of wisdom; within the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, there is neither perfection of wisdom nor arising. For these reasons, Śāriputra!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is non-arising; that which is non-arising is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.

It is the same for internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), for the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and for all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). For these reasons, internal emptiness is non-arising; that which is non-arising is not internal emptiness. This extends up to all-knowledge: all-knowledge is non-arising; that which is non-arising is not all-knowledge.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"For what reason do you say that 'form is non-dual and is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and are not consciousness,' and so on, up to 'all-knowledge is non-dual and is not all-knowledge'?"
Subhūti replied: "Whatever form there is, all that is non-dual;
whatever feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there are, all those are non-dual."

All these dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
This is also true for everything from the eye up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For this reason, Śāriputra, form is non-dual and is thus not form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual and are thus not consciousness; and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes, which is non-dual and is thus not the knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

“By what causes and conditions do you say that ‘this form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; and so on, up to all-knowledge entering into the category of non-dual dharmas’?”
Subhūti replied:
"Form is not different from non-arising; non-arising is not different from form; form is itself non-arising, and non-arising is itself form;
so too with feeling, perception, and mental formations."
Consciousness is not different from non-arising, and non-arising is not different from consciousness; consciousness itself is non-arising, and non-arising itself is consciousness.
For these reasons, Śāriputra!

The form aggregate enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness aggregates enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; and so it is, even up to all-knowledge.
[Treatise] Question:
At the conclusion of the superior grade, one should immediately inquire about "non-arising. Why is it inquired about here in this section? Answer:
The three great dharmas are easy to understand and benefit many sentient beings; therefore, he asks first:
"By what causes and conditions is the non-arising of form considered non-form, and so on, up to the non-arising of all-knowledge considered non-all-knowledge?"
Subhūti replied:
"Form is empty; within form there is no characteristic of form.
By means of this wisdom of non-arising, the practitioner causes form to be non-arisen."
If one attains this non-arising and the mind forms the thought, "I have now attained the true mark of form," for this reason it is said:
"The non-arising of form is non-form."
"The nature of form is eternally without arising; it is not because of the power of present wisdom that it is made non-arising.
It is like a person who breaks down a form to make it empty, yet still retains the conceptualization of its original form;
or like removing a latrine to build a house—though the latrine is no longer there, the perception of impurity still persists."
If one can know that the latrine is fundamentally non-existent and is merely a product of illusion and transformation, then the perception of a latrine will not arise;
so it is for the practitioner—if one can know that form (rūpa) has been unborn from the very beginning, then the perception of form will no longer persist.
Therefore it is said:
"Form that is without arising is non-form.
This applies likewise even to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Question: You previously stated yourself that "non-arising is itself non-duality"; why do you ask this again now? Answer:
Although the meaning is one, the meditative gateways through which one enters it differ.

What was stated above—the refutation of the existence of a result within the cause, whether it be pre-existent or non-existent, and the analysis of the identity or difference of produced phenomena, as well as whether production occurs at the initial moment or subsequently—such refutations of these modes of production are termed "non-production."
Now, because one has shattered all dualities such as eye and form, existence and non-existence, and so forth, this is called "non-duality" (advaya).
A practitioner may first enter the gate of the contemplation of non-arising and subsequently enter non-duality;
or they may first enter non-duality and subsequently enter the contemplation of non-arising.
Although the meaning is one, practitioners differentiate it.
Because they have destroyed the duality of form, it is called "non-dual"; because they have destroyed the arising of form, it is called "unborn.
What was explained above as the causal conditions for the unborn refers to "the emptiness of self-characteristics."
Now, the causes and conditions for non-duality are explained, namely: "neither conjoined nor dispersed, a single characteristic, which is to say, the characteristicless," and so forth.
Although the meaning is the same—emptiness—the former refers to the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), whereas this is the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the phrase "the form-base (rūpāyatana) is included within the category of non-dual dharmas": when the practitioner contemplates that form has the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing, at that time they discern that form has now transformed into non-arising; therefore, it is said that the non-arising of form is itself non-duality.
Why is this? The disintegration of form is itself non-arising.
As was previously analyzed regarding all phenomena, apart from form, no further arising can be found.
Now, the disintegration of form is itself non-arising; there can be no further non-arising beyond this.
For this reason, form itself enters into the category of non-dual dharmas.
After these two Arhats had finished their discussion before the Buddha, Subhūti addressed the Buddha to further explain this meaning, desiring that the Buddha would bear witness to it.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and contemplates all dharmas in this manner, at that time he perceives that form is unarisen, because it is ultimately pure;..."
One sees that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that the self is non-arising, up to and including the knower and the seer, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that the perfection of giving is non-arising, up to and including the perfection of wisdom as non-arising, because of ultimate purity.
One sees that internal emptiness is non-arising, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence as non-arising, because of ultimate purity.
They see that the four foundations of mindfulness are non-arising, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they are ultimately pure.
They see that all samādhis and all dhāraṇīs are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
and so on, up to seeing that the knowledge of all modes is non-arising, because it is ultimately pure.
One sees that ordinary beings and the dharmas of ordinary beings are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.

One sees that stream-enterers and the dharmas of stream-enterers, once-returners and the dharmas of once-returners, non-returners and the dharmas of non-returners, arhats and the dharmas of arhats, pratyekabuddhas and the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas and the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and buddhas and the dharmas of buddhas are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to the meaning of what I have heard Subhūti say, form is unarisen; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen; even up to the Buddha and the Buddha-dharmas, they are unarisen."

If that were so, one would not attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, nor the fruit of *srotāpanna*; one would not attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, nor the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; one would not attain the stage of *anāgāmin*, nor the fruit of *anāgāmin*; one would not attain the stage of *arhat*, nor the fruit of *arhat*; one would not attain the stage of *pratyekabuddha*, nor the path of *pratyekabuddha*;
one would not attain the stage of a *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*, nor the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
furthermore, there would be no distinction between the six realms of existence.
Furthermore, one cannot obtain the five kinds of bodhi of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Subhūti!

If all dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, for what reason does a srotāpanna cultivate the path to sever the three fetters; why does a sakṛdāgāmin cultivate the path to attenuate lust, hatred, and delusion; why does an anāgāmin cultivate the path to sever the five lower fetters; and why does an arhat cultivate the path to sever the five upper fetters?
Does a pratyekabuddha cultivate the path for the sake of the pratyekabuddha-dharma?
For what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform difficult practices and undergo various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings?
"For what reason has the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
For what reason does the Buddha turn the wheel of Dharma?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"I do not wish for anything to be apprehended within the dharma of non-arising.

Nor do I wish for one to attain the stage of a stream-enterer or the fruit of a stream-enterer within the dharma of non-arising, nor do I wish for one to attain the stage of an arhat or the fruit of an arhat, or the stage of a pratyekabuddha or the path of a pratyekabuddha, within the dharma of non-arising."
I also do not wish to cause bodhisattvas within the dharma of non-arising to perform difficult practices or to undergo various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not practice the path with a mind that regards it as difficult.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
one who gives rise to a mind of difficulty or a mind of suffering cannot benefit immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Now, a bodhisattva out of compassion for sentient beings regards them as his parents and brothers, and regards them as his children and even as himself; in this way, he is able to benefit immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension.
Why is this? A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should give rise to such a thought:
"Just as I cannot be apprehended in any place or in any manner, so it is with internal and external phenomena."
If one gives rise to such a conception, then there will be no mind of difficulty or suffering. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva does not accept any phenomena in any way, at any place, or in any respect.

Śāriputra! I do not wish for a Buddha to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the dharma of non-arising; nor do I wish for the turning of the wheel of Dharma within the dharma of non-arising; nor do I wish for the attainment of the Way by means of the dharma of non-arising.
The [Treatise] commentator says:
There are two kinds of contemplation on non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*):
first, the contemplation of compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); second, the contemplation of the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*).
It was previously stated that the contemplation of non-arising is the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), which is not ultimately pure;
however, by gradually practicing the contemplation of conformity and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one then becomes ultimately pure.
Question:
Since the Bodhisattva has not yet exhausted the fetters, has not yet attained the Buddha-way, and his wisdom is not yet pure, why is it said that he is "ultimately pure"?
Answer:

When this bodhisattva attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he extinguishes all afflictions, attains the bodhisattva path, and enters the stage of a bodhisattva. Although the residual traces of afflictions remain, they are exhausted at the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); because nothing can obstruct him, it is ultimately pure.
Furthermore, regarding "ultimate purity": it is ultimate purity within the path of compliance (*ānulomika-mārga*), not yet the Buddha-way.

Because of the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), from the ultimate purity of seeing that form is unarisen (*anutpāda*), up to the ultimate purity of the non-arising of both the Buddha and the Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti has explained through various causes and conditions that the characteristics of all dharmas are definitively non-arising;
on account of this matter, Śāriputra raises this objection:
"Among the noble ones, the smallest is the srotāpanna and the dharma of the srotāpanna; the greatest is the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma."

If that were so, then the noble ones would have neither greatness nor smallness, the noble Dharma would have no distinction of superior or inferior, and there would likewise be no differentiation between the six realms of existence; this constitutes the brief objection.
The subsequent question regarding the severance of the three fetters and the cultivation of the path constitutes the detailed objection.
Question:
What are these five kinds of bodhi? Answer:
First is the patience of compliance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), second is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the three types of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Among these three enlightenments, one transcends the first two and abides in the third enlightenment.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of bodhi:

first, that called "bodhi of generating the mind. Because one generates the mind for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* amidst immeasurable births and deaths, it is named bodhi—this is a case of referring to the fruit within the cause.
Second is called "Bodhi of Subduing the Mind," which subdues all afflictions and masters the mind while practicing the various *pāramitās*.

Third is called "Bodhi of Illumination," which contemplates the primary and secondary characteristics, as well as the general and specific characteristics, of all phenomena across the three periods of time; by discerning and weighing them, one attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is ultimately pure—namely, the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Fourth is called "Emerging and Reaching Bodhi. Because one has attained the power of skillful means within the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not become attached even to the *prajñāpāramitā*. One extinguishes all afflictions, beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions, attains the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), emerges from the triple world, and reaches omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

Fifth, it is called "unsurpassed enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), for by sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These are the five meanings of bodhi.
The meaning of the other noble ones (ārya) severing their fetters (saṃyojana) is as previously explained. Question:
The path of the śrāvaka extensively explains the meaning of severing the fetters; why, then, are the practices of the pratyekabuddha and the various practices of the bodhisattva not explained?
The answer is:

for the pratyekabuddha, there is no further distinct path from that of the śrāvaka; the only differences lie in their merit, their sharp faculties, and their slighter penetration into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Although the Bodhisattva path comprises various kinds of practices, it is the difficult and arduous practices that are rare and extraordinary; when sentient beings see them, they joyfully say:
"The Bodhisattva performs these deeds for our sake!"
"Although other practices are profound and subtle, they are unknown to people and cannot move sentient beings; therefore, they are not discussed.
Furthermore, as Śāriputra’s objection implies:
if all phenomena are unborn, empty, and quiescent, why is it that while all sentient beings are attached to pleasure, the Bodhisattva alone undergoes ascetic suffering?"

Furthermore, since the Buddhas always delight in seclusion and tranquility, have severed attachment to dharmas, and definitively know that all dharmas neither revolve nor return, for what reason do they turn the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings?

When Subhūti spoke of the dharma of non-arising before the Buddha, the Buddha did not rebuke or refute him; because he possessed the power of joyful ease in speech and the strength of being unimpeded, he replied to Śāriputra:

"I likewise do not wish for there to be six kinds of noble ones within the dharma of non-arising—saying 'six' excludes the bodhisattvas—and nor do I wish for the distinctions between the six realms of existence."
Why is this? Because they have attained the realization of the dharma of non-arising.
That is to say, although there are distinctions between the dharmas of the noble ones and the noble persons, within the dharma of non-arising, none of these exist at all.
Furthermore, within the dharma of non-arising, there are two kinds of faults:
"gross faults" refer to the three evil realms resulting from transgressions such as killing and stealing;
"subtle faults" refer to the three good realms resulting from meritorious acts such as giving and observing precepts performed with a mind of attachment.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of difficulty or a mind of suffering, they will be unable to deliver all sentient beings.
Just as in the world, if one finds even a minor matter difficult and regards it as suffering, one will not even accomplish that; how much more so in the case of attaining the Buddha-way!

As for the causal conditions, they consist of great loving-kindness and great compassion, regarding all sentient beings with the thought that they are one's own parents, children, or oneself. Why is this so?
Parents, children, and one’s own self naturally give rise to affection; it is not through external urging that they are loved.
Because the Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he regards all sentient beings—even enemies—with the same intent of loving-kindness and mindfulness.

This is the instrument for the benefit resulting from the retribution of great compassion; it has nothing whatsoever that it does not cherish, giving all that exists, both internal and external, entirely to sentient beings.
Herein is explained the causal condition of non-attachment, namely: "Because in all places, in all modes, and in all phenomena, nothing can be apprehended."
If a practitioner first enters the Buddha-dharma, they employ the emptiness of sentient beings to know that all phenomena are without self;
now, by employing the emptiness of phenomena, they know that all phenomena are also empty.

By virtue of these two causes and conditions—this mind of great compassion and the emptiness of all phenomena—one is able to disregard all that is internal and external to benefit sentient beings, without giving rise to thoughts of difficult practice or thoughts of asceticism, but rather with single-minded diligence and joy.
Just as a person exerts themselves in their work for the sake of themselves, or for the sake of their parents, wife, and children, without regarding it as suffering;
yet if they were to do it for another, they would have no sense of joy.

Austere practices and difficult deeds are as explained in the subsequent chapter on "The Manifestation of Transformations through Jātaka Causes and Conditions," wherein [the Buddha] intentionally assumes the forms of animals.
Because all dharmas are ultimately empty and possess inconceivable characteristics, and because all dharmas return without turning, they are not called "turning.
It is only for the purpose of destroying false and inverted views that it is called "Turning the Wheel of Dharma."
[Sūtra] Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Do you now intend that one attains the Way by means of dharmas that arise,
or do you intend that one attains the Way by means of dharmas that do not arise?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"I do not wish for one to attain the Way by means of dharmas that arise. Śāriputra said:
"Now, Subhūti, do you wish that one should attain the Way by means of non-arising dharmas? Subhūti replied,
"I also do not wish that one should attain the Way by means of non-arising dharmas."
Śāriputra said: "As Subhūti has explained, there is neither knowledge nor attainment. Subhūti said:
“There is knowing and there is attaining, yet not by way of two distinct dharmas.

Now, it is only because of worldly designations that there is knowing and attaining; it is because of worldly designations that there are those from the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, the *pratyekabuddhas*, and all the Buddhas.
Within the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no knowing and no attaining, and there are no *srotāpannas* up to no Buddhas.”

“Subhūti! If it is by way of worldly designations that there is knowing and attaining, and if the distinctions among the six realms of existence also exist by way of worldly designations rather than by way of the ultimate reality, [is this not so?]”
Subhūti said: “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! Just as there is knowledge and attainment due to worldly designations, so too do the distinctions among the six realms of existence exist due to worldly designations, and not by way of the ultimate, true meaning.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within the ultimate reality, there is no karma and no retribution; there is no arising and no ceasing; there is neither purity nor defilement.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Does a non-arisen dharma arise?
Or does an arisen dharma arise?"
Subhūti said:
"I do not wish to cause unarisen dharmas to arise, nor do I wish to cause arisen dharmas to arise.
Śāriputra said:
“What are those non-arising dharmas that one does not wish to cause to arise?
Subhūti replied:
“Form is a non-arising dharma; being empty of intrinsic nature, one does not wish for it to arise.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are dharmas that do not arise; they are empty of intrinsic nature, and one does not desire them to arise.
This extends even to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is a dharma that does not arise; it is empty of intrinsic nature, and one does not desire it to arise.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Does it arise from arising?
Or does it arise from non-arising?”
Subhūti said: “It is neither that which is produced as being produced, nor that which is produced as not being produced. Why is this?”

Śāriputra! Arising and non-arising—these two dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless."
“Śāriputra! For this reason, it is neither that which is born from birth, nor that which is born from non-birth.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Subhūti, do you delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas and the characteristics of non-arising?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“I delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas, and I also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising.”

Why is this? All dharmas—whether the dharmas of non-arising or the characteristics of non-arising, as well as the delight in discourse and speech—are all neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive, having but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of no-characteristic.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"You delight in speaking of non-arising dharmas and you also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising;
is this delight in speaking and the speech itself also non-arising?"
Subhūti said: “So it is! So it is!”
Śāriputra! Why is this? Śāriputra!
Form is unarisen; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen;
the eye is unarisen, up to and including the mind;
the earth element is unarisen, up to and including the consciousness element.
The activities of body do not arise; the activities of speech do not arise; the activities of mind do not arise;
the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) does not arise, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which does not arise.

For this reason, Śāriputra, I delight in speaking of the dharma of non-arising, and I also delight in speaking of the characteristics of non-arising; even this delight in speaking and these words are themselves non-arising.
The *Śāstra* states:
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing that Subhūti delighted in speaking without difficulty, asked:
"If all dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, how is this characteristic of non-arising realized?"
Is realization attained by means of dharmas that arise,
or is it attained by means of dharmas that do not arise?
If realization were attained by means of dharmas that arise, such arising dharmas are false and deceptive, as you have already refuted them through various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, one cannot attain liberation from the dharma of birth by means of the dharma of birth.

If one were to realize [nirvana] by means of the dharma of non-birth, since the dharma of non-birth has not yet manifested as a phenomenal characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it could not serve as a basis for realization; how, then, could realization be attained?
Subhūti does not accept either of these two dharmas, because both possess faults, as previously explained.
Śāriputra then thought:
"The Buddha’s sūtras state that all dharmas are subsumed within two categories:"
Whether conditioned or unconditioned:
that which arises is conditioned, and that which does not arise is unconditioned.
Now, Subhūti, being free from these two dharmas, how can you speak of the matter of attaining the Path?
Having had this thought, he asked Subhūti, "Is there no such thing as attaining the Way?
Subhūti was a great Arhat, foremost in the practice of the *araṇā-samādhi*;
it was solely for the sake of the Bodhisattvas that he spoke of this non-arising. [The interlocutor thought: "How can you harbor such wrong views and say that there is no one who attains the Way?"
Therefore, it is said that "there is knowing and there is attaining.
"Knowing" and "attaining" are alternative names for the realization of the fruits of the Path.
Subhūti, fearing he might contradict his previous statement, says:
It is not by way of dualistic dharmas.
It is only for the sake of worldly convention that one speaks of the existence of the srotāpanna up to the Buddha. Why is this?
All dharmas truly lack the characteristic of a self; yet, to now employ the notion of a "self" to differentiate between the *srotāpanna* and even the Buddha is a conventional (*saṃvṛti*) dharma.
Furthermore, because one has not yet attained the emptiness of dharmas, one says, "This is wholesome, this is unwholesome, this is conditioned, this is unconditioned," and so forth;
however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), since there are no sentient beings, there is no *srotāpanna* up to and including the Buddha.
Because all phenomena are empty, there is no fruit of the stream-enterer up to and including the path of the Buddha.
Since even the noble ones and the noble dharmas are illusory and lack fixed reality, how much more so the karma and its retributions of ordinary beings within the six realms!

Question: Subhūti has already definitively explained through various causes and conditions that dharmas are unarisen; why does Śāriputra now ask again whether "the unarisen dharma arises" or "the arisen dharma arises"?

Answer: Because Subhūti had previously explained the causes and conditions for attaining the Way, Śāriputra grasped Subhūti’s intention. Although Subhūti spoke of the non-arising of dharmas to refute all dharmas, he did so for the sake of causes and conditions and his mind was not attached to the dharma of non-arising; therefore, Śāriputra asked again.
Furthermore, because this Dharma is extremely profound, he asks again so that the listeners may understand it clearly.
Previously, he asked about the methods for attaining the Way; now, he asks generally how all dharmas arise.
Using the eye of wisdom, one knows that all phenomena are unarisen;
yet now we see all phenomena arising, and for this reason one asks, "How do they arise?
Subhūti replies:
Both positions are untenable.
If that which is "already arisen" were to arise, then since the dharma has already arisen, it should not arise again.
If that which is "unarisen" were to arise, then because the dharma does not yet exist, it should not arise.
If one claims that at the time of arising there is "half-arising and half-non-arising," this too is non-arising.
If it is the portion that has arisen, then it has already arisen;
if it is the portion that has not yet arisen, then there is no arising.
Therefore, Subhūti, one does not see with this fleshly eye because it lacks penetrating understanding;
rather, one does not grasp at either of these two dharmas, but simply says:
"This birth is like an illusion, like a dream; it arises from deceptive phenomena and should be abandoned and its marks should not be grasped."
Śāriputra asked:
"What dharmas are neither accepted by both [the world and the noble ones]?

Subhūti replied that, for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), he spoke of form up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as being ultimately unarisen and naturally empty in character, not wishing to allow that there is arising within ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
If birth were possible within the deceptive realm of conventional truth, such birth would be like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Herein, the cause and condition for non-arising is explained as "neither conjoined nor dispersed."
Some say: "Arising is distinct from the dharma; that is, 'arising is permanent, while the dharma that arises is impermanent.
For this reason, he asks further."
The respondent replied: "Because arising and dharmas are not different, if one speaks of arising dharmas, one has already spoken of the characteristic of arising.
Arising and non-arising are as explained above.
Having heard what Subhūti said, Śāriputra understood that Subhūti’s mind delighted in the dharma of non-arising, and so he said to Subhūti:
“You truly delight in preaching the Dharma of non-arising!
Subhūti then accepted this question, his heart feeling no shame. Why was this?
This treatise is indestructible and free from fault.
How is this known?
Subhūti himself says:
"There is no dharma that can be joined, and no dharma that can be dispersed; it is without color, without form, empty, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of non-characteristic.
If even the characteristic of emptiness is not accepted, how much less so other characteristics?
Śāriputra praised him again:
"Your delight in preaching the dharma of non-arising and your speech are both non-arising; this is truly pure!
If your delight in preaching and your speech were not themselves non-arising, but you were merely speaking of the non-arising of external objects, then it would not be pure."
Subhūti then accepted this praise and replied to Śāriputra:
"It is not only delight in discourse and language that is non-arising; from form up to all-knowledge, nothing whatsoever arises."
[Sūtra] At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Subhūti, among those who preach the Dharma, you should be the foremost!”
"Why is this? Subhūti is able to answer whatever question is asked. Subhūti said:
"Because all dharmas have no basis.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"In what way do all dharmas have no basis?"
Subhūti said: “The nature of form is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, it does not rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two.

The natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are eternally empty; they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two.”
The nature of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor the external, nor on that which is between the two.
The nature of form is eternally empty, and so on up to the nature of phenomena, which is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor the external, nor on that which is between the two.

The nature of the dāna-pāramitā is eternally empty, up to and including the nature of the prajñā-pāramitā, which does not rely on the internal, does not rely on the external, and does not rely on that which is between the two.

The emptiness of the internal is eternally empty, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which does not depend on the internal, does not depend on the external, and does not depend on that which is between the two.

“Śāriputra! The nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is eternally empty, up to and including the nature of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), which is eternally empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.
"For this reason, Śāriputra,
all dharmas have no basis, because their nature is eternally empty.
Thus it is, Śāriputra."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, they should purify form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on, up to purifying all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the bodhisattva path while practicing the six pāramitās?
Subhūti replied:
"There is the mundane perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and there is the supramundane perfection of giving;

likewise, for the perfections of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), patience (kṣāntipāramitā), vigor (vīryapāramitā), meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there are both mundane and supramundane forms."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is the mundane perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
What is the supramundane perfection of giving?"
Subhūti said:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts as a donor, able to give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and beggars—giving food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing to those who need clothing, and bedding, couches, dwellings, incense, flowers, necklaces, and medicines, as well as all kinds of necessary articles for life;
or if he gives his wife and children, his kingdom, his head, eyes, hands, feet, limbs, and joints—all internal and external things—he gives them all away."
When giving, one forms this thought: "I am the giver; he is the receiver.
I am not stingy or greedy. I am the donor; I am able to relinquish everything. I give in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)."
Having made this offering, he shares the Dharma obtained through it with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, thinking:
"By the causal conditions of this giving, may sentient beings attain happiness in the present life, and in the future, may they be led to enter nirvāṇa."
"This person's giving is characterized by three obstacles.
What are these three?
The mark of self, the mark of other, and the mark of giving."
To practice this threefold giving while remaining attached to it is called the mundane *dānapāramitā*.
For what reason is it called "mundane"?
Because it neither moves nor emerges from within the world, it is called the mundane *dānapāramitā*.
"What is called the supramundane dānapāramitā?
It is that which is pure in three respects.
What are these three?"

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving, the self is unapprehendable; he does not perceive a recipient, the object given is unapprehendable, and he does not expect a reward. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s dānapāramitā of the threefold purity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, he bestows it upon all sentient beings, yet even those sentient beings cannot be apprehended;
he dedicates this giving toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, such that he does not perceive even the subtlest mark of a phenomenon.
Śāriputra! This is called the supramundane dānapāramitā.
For what reason is it called supramundane?
Because it can move within and transcend the world, it is therefore called the supramundane *dānapāramitā*.
When the *śīlapāramitā* has a basis, it is the mundane *śīlapāramitā*;
when it is without a basis, it is the supramundane *śīlapāramitā*.
The rest is as explained in the *Dānapāramitā*.
Regarding the *Kṣāntipāramitā*, *Vīryapāramitā*, *Dhyānapāramitā*, and *Prajñāpāramitā*, that which has a basis is called mundane, while that which is without a basis is called supramundane;
the rest is also as explained in the section on *Dāna*.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, he purifies the bodhisattva path.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What is the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?
Subhūti replied:

“The four foundations of mindfulness are the path for a bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment; likewise, the eightfold noble path, the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; all gates of samādhi and all gates of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.”
"Śāriputra!
This is called the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Question:

Among the five hundred arhats, the Buddha each declared one to be foremost: Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernormal powers; Mahākāśyapa was foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities; Subhūti was foremost in attaining the samādhi of non-contention; Mahākātyāyana was foremost in analyzing the sūtras; and Pūrṇa was foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
Now, for what reason does Śāriputra praise Subhūti as being foremost among those who preach the Dharma?
The answer is:

With his Buddha-eye, the Buddha observes all sentient beings—whether they possess sharp or dull faculties—and evaluates the general and specific characteristics of all dharmas; according to the dharma each has attained, he individually designates them as foremost, without error.

Among the fourfold assembly, Pūrṇa is foremost in benefiting sentient beings by preaching the Dharma through the twelve divisions of the scriptures, various dharma-gates, and diverse causes, conditions, and parables.

Subhūti constantly practiced the samādhi of non-contention and engaged in the same activities as the bodhisattvas; he was skilled in means and delighted in expounding the single dharma-gate of the mark of emptiness, surpassing Pūrṇa.
For example, a master craftsman may possess many skills; because his capabilities are so numerous, he cannot be thoroughly proficient in all of them.
Conversely, if there is someone who specializes in a single task, they will surely bring that skill to its ultimate excellence.
Although Pūrṇa possesses great capability, he is not equal to Subhūti, who constantly delights in practicing emptiness and is thus able to skillfully expound upon emptiness.
Therefore, when Śāriputra heard Subhūti’s skillful exposition of the meaning of emptiness, he praised him, saying:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, you should be ranked as the foremost!"
Śāriputra saw that Subhūti was able to answer every question posed to him, moving like the wind through the sky without any obstruction.
At that time, Subhūti neither humbled himself nor accepted praise.
Why is this? Because they establish themselves in equanimity and reality, for they possess the characteristics of a good person.
One who possesses the characteristics of a good person neither praises nor disparages themselves, and likewise neither praises nor disparages others.
If one praises oneself, it is not the mark of a great person; to be self-exalting when not praised by others is mere vanity.
If one disparages oneself, one is a deceitful person.
If one disparages others, one is a slanderous villain.
If one praises others, that person is flatterer.
Because Subhūti speaks of the dharma of non-arising, although Śāriputra offers praise, it is not flattery.

Subhūti does not practice self-deprecation because Śāriputra’s praise is truthful; furthermore, because he has severed attachment to dharmas, his mind is not elated, nor does he harbor craving or clinging. He merely answers with the causes and conditions of being unimpeded and unobstructed:
That which is called "all dharmas have no basis" means that because they have no basis, they are unobstructed and unhindered.
The meaning of having no basis is as previously explained.
In this regard, Subhūti himself says:
"Because internal phenomena are empty, form does not rely upon the internal;
because external phenomena are empty, form does not rely upon the external."
Because there is nothing in between, form does not rely upon that which is intermediate.
As it is with form, so it is for everything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If a bodhisattva knows that all three realms are impermanent and empty, they do not rely upon anything in between.
At that time, afflictions are broken and one is able to purify the bodhisattva path.
Therefore, Subhūti said:
"A bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās should purify form, up to and including all-knowledge."
Question: Since the purification of form up to the purification of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is itself the purification of the bodhisattva path, for what reason is it asked again? Answer:
That a bodhisattva can cause form to be ultimately empty is called purity;
this matter is profound and subtle, and cannot be attained instantaneously.
For this reason, Śāriputra asked:
“How should a newly initiated bodhisattva cultivate this first path of skillful means?
Subhūti replied:
“If a bodhisattva can practice two kinds of pāramitās.”
The six pāramitās are the initial opening of the bodhisattva path;
being able to employ the emptiness of non-apprehension to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the opening of the Buddha path.
"Purity" (*viśuddhi*) is called "opening.
It is like clearing away thorns from a path; this is called "opening the path.
What are these two kinds of *pāramitās*?
The first is the mundane, and the second is the supramundane.
Regarding the mundane, Subhūti himself explained its meaning, namely: "one who needs food should be given food," and so forth.
This meaning is as explained in the first chapter. If,
at the time of giving, there is something upon which one relies— just as an old or sick person relies on the strength of others to walk or stand—
the giver relies [on such support] because they are devoid of true wisdom and their mental power is weak and meager.

Regarding "reliance": when one takes up signs within these things—the self, material wealth, and the recipient—and becomes mentally attached to them, giving rise to pride and other afflictions, this is called the mundane; it neither moves nor emerges.
"Moving" refers to the patience of compliance;
"emerging" refers to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
Within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, "moving" refers to those still in training.
The "emerging" refers to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The remaining five pāramitās are likewise.
This is called the initial opening of the bodhisattva path.
Question:
Since the path of the bodhisattva is itself the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for what reason is it asked again? Answer:
When one is a bodhisattva, there is a path;
once one has already attained Buddhahood, the path is no longer required.
Because this path is for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is called the "path to enlightenment" (*bodhimārga*).
Because Bodhisattvas practice this path, it is called the "Bodhisattva Path.
In this regard, the Buddha says:
the distant path refers to the six pāramitās, which constitute the Bodhisattva Path.
The path that is near refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣikā dharmāḥ*).
Among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), because giving, ethical discipline, and so forth are interspersed with other elements, they are distant;
whereas the thirty-seven factors consist solely of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and are therefore near.
The six pāramitās are distant because they are mixed with worldly and world-transcending elements;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, and so forth up to great loving-kindness and great compassion, are near because they are ultimately pure.

Furthermore, as for the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, from the initial generation of the resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*) up to the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), all the bodhisattva practices performed therein for the sake of enlightenment constitute the path to enlightenment.
[Sūtra] At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"What is the power of the pāramitās?
Subhūti replied, "It is the power of the prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all wholesome dharmas:
whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas.
Śāriputra! The prajñāpāramitā is able to receive all wholesome dharmas:
the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of buddhas.
Śāriputra! The Buddhas of the past practiced the prajñāpāramitā and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
the Buddhas of the future will also practice the prajñāpāramitā and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Now, in the present, the Buddhas throughout all the world-systems of the ten directions also practice this Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā and neither doubts nor finds it difficult, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the path to enlightenment.
The path of a bodhisattva consists in rescuing all sentient beings; therefore, the mind does not abandon any sentient being because of the principle of non-apprehension.
This bodhisattva should always remain inseparable from this mindfulness, namely, the mindfulness of great compassion.
Śāriputra asked again:
"If one wishes to cause a bodhisattva mahāsattva to never be separated from this mindfulness— namely, the mindfulness of great compassion—
and if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is always not separated from the mindfulness of great compassion, would it not mean that all sentient beings should become bodhisattvas?"
Why is this? Subhūti,
it is because all sentient beings likewise do not depart from various thoughts.
Subhūti said: “Excellent! Excellent!”
Śāriputra! You wish to challenge me in order to establish my own thesis. Why is this?

Because sentient beings do not exist, mindfulness does not exist; because the nature of sentient beings does not exist, the nature of mindfulness does not exist; because the phenomena of sentient beings do not exist, the phenomena of mindfulness do not exist; because sentient beings are detached, mindfulness is also detached; because sentient beings are empty, mindfulness is also empty; because sentient beings are unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.

Śāriputra! Because form (*rūpa*) does not exist, mindfulness (*smṛti*) also does not exist; because the nature of form does not exist, the nature of mindfulness also does not exist; because the dharma of form does not exist, the dharma of mindfulness also does not exist; because form is detached, mindfulness is also detached; because form is empty, mindfulness is also empty; because form is unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.
It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because the eye up to the mind, forms up to mental phenomena, the earth element up to the consciousness element, the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all doors of samādhi, all doors of dhāraṇī, all-knowledge, and all-aspect knowledge, up to and including unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), do not exist, mindfulness also does not exist;
because unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment is unknowable, mindfulness is also unknowable.
“Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this path, I desire that they not be separated from this mindfulness—namely, the mindfulness of great compassion.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
This Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—those who speak it should also speak it in this manner.”
All that you have said regarding the *prajñāpāramitā* is because you have received the Buddha’s intention.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the *prajñāpāramitā* should train exactly as you have described!
When Subhūti spoke this chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways:

it surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges; and it surged at the edges and subsided in the center.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what cause and for what reason do you smile?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Just as I am teaching the Prajñāpāramitā here in this world, so too do the Buddhas in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds to the east teach the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, they also teach this Prajñāpāramitā.”
When this chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā was being spoken, twelve nayutas of devas and humans attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the Buddhas of the ten directions spoke this Prajñāpāramitā, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings likewise gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The [Commentary] states:
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"What Subhūti has explained—the differentiation of the six pāramitās into worldly and world-transcending categories, as well as the path to bodhi—will bring great benefit to sentient beings."
Therefore, he joyfully praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
To speak of it again is the height of excellence.
Question:
"By the power of which pāramitā is this?"
Subhūti reflected thus:
"Among all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), apart from wisdom (*prajñā*), none is capable of such discernment, severing doubt, and opening the path;
among the perfections (*pāramitā*), apart from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), their own essence cannot even be accomplished, let alone be able to discern and open the path!"
Having reflected thus, he replied to Śāriputra:
"This is the power of the Prajñāpāramitā," as previously stated.
Among all phenomena, there is no self, no knower, and no seer;
it is now by this that one realizes this is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, not the power of the Buddha, nor the power of Subhūti.

Why is this? Subhūti explains the causal conditions, namely the *prajñāpāramitā*, because it is free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, as well as existence and non-existence; thus, it can give rise to all wholesome dharmas—namely, the fixed characteristics of the three vehicles and their firm, indestructible nature.
Furthermore, because the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless, it is able to receive all wholesome dharmas;
it is like the great ocean, which can receive the myriad streams and currents of all rivers.
"The wholesome dharmas of the three vehicles" refers to the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
Because the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time all practiced the *prajñāpāramitā*, they have all attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
although they also practice the other *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most honored and supreme, possessing the power of analytical penetration.
For example, when medicinal drugs are compounded, the castor bean (*bhadradāru*) possesses the greatest power;

likewise, although the *prajñāpāramitā* is combined with the other *pāramitās*, it is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* that is most supreme for destroying all afflictions, uprooting false views, and abandoning conceptual proliferation.
For this reason, it is said that "all this is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Question:
Various praises have been offered for this *prajñāpāramitā*, subtle and profound as it is; who is able to accord with and practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Answer:
There are bodhisattvas who have accumulated various merits over immeasurable lifetimes, possess sharp faculties, and have thinned out their afflictions;
although they have not yet reached the stage of *avaivartika*, upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately believe, accept, and enter deeply into it.

One who thoroughly penetrates such characteristics is able to practice the path of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is to say: to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, causing them to be free from the sorrows and afflictions of the world;
and because of their great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they do not abandon any sentient being.
A bodhisattva should never be separated from great compassion and the mindfulness of ultimate emptiness—ultimate emptiness destroys all worldly afflictions and reveals nirvana;
yet great compassion leads beings back into wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra challenged Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva does not depart from this thought of great compassion and the thought of ultimate emptiness, then all sentient beings would become bodhisattvas!"
Why is this? Because this is ultimate emptiness, signless, and without differentiation; it is not the case that it exists for the bodhisattva but does not exist for sentient beings!
If it did so exist, then all sentient beings would necessarily share in it.
"If [the dharmas] do not exist, then the Bodhisattva should also not exist. Subhūti replied:
"You wish to challenge me, yet you are actually assisting in the establishment of my meaning."
Why is this? Because the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) are ultimately empty, sentient beings are also empty;
because sentient beings are empty, even the thought of ultimate emptiness is empty.

If all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be a real emptiness of sentient beings such that you challenge me by saying, "Sentient beings do not depart from this thought, and they shall all become bodhisattvas"?
Therefore it is said:
"Because sentient beings do not exist, even the thought of ultimate emptiness does not exist;

because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, because sentient beings are detached, because sentient beings are empty, and because sentient beings are unknowable, even the thought of ultimate emptiness is ultimately empty."
The same applies to form up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Question: In this context, mindfulness is not separated from the mindfulness of great compassion; why, then, is it said to be "not separated from the mindfulness of ultimate emptiness"?
Answer: The Bodhisattva does not depart from this mindfulness and does not abandon sentient beings, because he employs the principle of non-apprehension.
Non-apprehension-emptiness and ultimate emptiness differ in name but are one in meaning.
The emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) comes first, and ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) comes last;
because ultimate emptiness is great, the arising of compassion (*karuṇā*) is likewise great.
Regarding great compassion, as stated in the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*, there are three kinds of compassion:
There are three types of compassion: that which has sentient beings as its object, that which has phenomena as its object, and that which is objectless.
Objectless compassion arises from ultimate emptiness; it is by means of this that the difficulty raised by Śāriputra is resolved.
Because the Buddha validated his statement, he praised him, saying:
“Excellent!
If one wishes to explain the Prajñāpāramitā, it should be as you have said.
At that time, the gods, humans, and bodhisattvas among the assembly had this thought:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from within it.
Subhūti, you who belong to the Lesser Vehicle—why does the Buddha praise you, saying, ‘If one wishes to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, one should do so as you have said’?”
Therefore, it is said next:
"All that Subhūti has spoken is received from the Buddha’s intention.

Even if Maitreya and other bodhisattvas, or Brahmā Devānām Indra and others, were not receiving the Buddha’s intention, they would still be unable to ask such questions; how much more so for Subhūti, who speaks with joyful spontaneity before the Buddha!
“Those bodhisattvas who wish to study the Prajñāpāramitā should also study it as you have described!

When this chapter was being spoken, the earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; at that time, many bodhisattvas within the assembly resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all were destined to become Buddhas.
The Buddha is the great sovereign of heaven and earth;
the Earth Deity rejoiced, thinking, "My Lord has now been born!
For this reason, she caused the earth to tremble greatly.

Furthermore, because it is rare and difficult to find anyone whose mind has faith in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such a person, by virtue of the causes and conditions of their merit, invokes a great wind that stirs the waters; as the waters are stirred, the earth trembles.
