Furthermore, when the great nāga kings beneath the earth wish to come and listen to the Prajñāpāramitā, they emerge from the water; because the water moves, the earth shakes.

Furthermore, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he causes the earth to tremble; for the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to see and difficult to know, and [the earthquake] is intended to guide all people so that they may increase their faith and joy.
The causes and conditions for earthquakes in other stages have been explained as before.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the cause and condition: namely, that I preach the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise preach this Prajñāpāramitā.
Twelve nayutas of devas and humans attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and entered the fixed position of the Dharma; for this reason, the earth shook.
Furthermore, sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions likewise resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path; for this reason, the earth shook.

At that time, the various devas also scattered diverse lotus flowers, various blended incenses, celestial robes, and celestial parasols; there were ten million kinds of celestial music and dance. The various dragon kings emerged from the waters of the four great oceans, along with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others, all of whom gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness, joined their palms, and praised the Buddha.
Furthermore, when the Buddha smiled, immeasurable light pervaded worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; such were the rare and wondrous events that occurred.
To state the essential point: the earth shook because he was expounding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, namely, the *prajñāpāramitā*.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 27: The Lord of Devas. [Sūtra] At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings of the Trichiliocosm, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, came together to the assembly.

The Śakras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Suyāma Kings of the Yāma Heaven, the Śakra-devānām-indra Kings of the Tuṣita Heaven, the Sunirmita Kings of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Vaśavartin Kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of billions of devas—came together to this assembly.

The Brahma Kings of the trichiliocosm, up to and including the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas, all came together to the assembly.

The radiance of the bodies born of karmic retribution belonging to all these gods, from the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, cannot equal even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a ten-thousand-billionth part of the Buddha’s constant radiance; it cannot even be compared by means of calculation or metaphor.

The World-Honored One’s radiance is most excellent, most wondrous, and the supreme first; the light resulting from the karmic retribution of the devas does not shine nor manifest in the presence of the Buddha’s constant radiance, just as a charred wick cannot compare to Jambūnada gold.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"All the devas from the Cāturmahārājika heaven up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens of this trichiliocosm have gathered together, desiring to hear Subhūti explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti! How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell within the perfection of wisdom?
What is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!..."

I shall now, in accordance with the Buddha’s intention and sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, just as it is that in which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should abide within the Prajñāpāramitā.
"O sons of the gods!
Those among you who have not yet resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should now do so.
O sons of the gods!"
If one has entered the fixed stage of the śrāvaka, such a person is unable to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because they have established a barrier between themselves and saṃsāra.
If such a person should resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I too shall rejoice in it.
Why is this? A superior person should further seek the supreme Dharma; I shall never obstruct their merit.
Kauśika! What is the perfection of wisdom?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates form as impermanent, contemplates form as suffering, contemplates form as empty, and contemplates form as selfless; he contemplates form as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, like an arrow piercing the body—painful, vexing, decaying, and destructive; it is anxiety, fear, and instability, because of non-apprehensibility.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—one contemplates them as impermanent, up to being sorrowful, fearful, and unstable, because even these are non-apprehendable.
One contemplates that form is quiescent, detached, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.

One contemplates that the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is quiescent, detached, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, because nothing is to be apprehended therein.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), contemplates how ignorance conditions the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, up to the causal accumulation of the great mass of suffering ending in old age and death; yet this is because there is nothing to be apprehended.

He contemplates that through the cessation of ignorance the formative forces cease, and so forth, up to the cessation of birth, through which old age and death cease; and through the cessation of old age and death, the great mass of suffering consisting of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair ceases; all this is because there is nothing to be apprehended."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, corresponding to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness because they are non-apprehendable;
and so on, up to cultivating the ten powers of a buddha and the eighteen unique qualities because they are non-apprehendable."
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in accordance with the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā), because of non-apprehension;

they practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), because of non-apprehension."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates in this way:

'Only dharmas and dharmas act as mutual causes and conditions for one another, moistening, benefiting, and increasing them; yet through such conceptualization and calculation, herein there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.'"
The mind of dedication does not abide within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor does the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide within the mind of dedication;
the mind of dedication cannot be apprehended within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* likewise cannot be apprehended within the mind of dedication.
"Although a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas, there is no dharma that can be apprehended; this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Śakra-devānām-indra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"In what way does the mind of dedication not abide within the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
How is it that the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not abide within the mind of dedication?
How is it that the mind of dedication cannot be apprehended within the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"How is it that the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended within the mind of dedication?
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!..."
The mind of dedication and the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are not the mind;
they are the characteristic of non-mind, and within the characteristic of non-mind, there can be no dedication.

This characteristic of non-mind is eternally the characteristic of non-mind; this inconceivable characteristic is eternally the inconceivable characteristic. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Subhūti! You shall explain the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and you shall comfort the minds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I ought to repay your kindness; I should not fail to do so.
In the past, the various Buddhas and their disciples taught the six pāramitās to all bodhisattvas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.”
The World-Honored One also studied therein at that time and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I, too, shall now expound the six *pāramitās* for the sake of all bodhisattvas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Question:
In the first chapter, the Buddha emitted a sublime radiance and the devas gathered in great numbers; why is this explained again here?
Answer: Some say,
"This is the subsequent assembly."
Some say: "This is the same assembly as before.
Because Subhūti was so skilled at expounding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the devas rejoiced.
For this reason, the Buddha smiled; his constant radiance became even more brilliant, so that the lights of the devas no longer appeared.
It was as when the sun rises, the stars, moon, lamps, and candles lose their luster;
it was like a charred wick placed beside Jāmbūnada gold.
Regarding the "Heaven of the Four Great Kings": in the east is named Tidaratha, which in the language of Qin means "Governing the State" (Zhiguó); it presides over the gandharvas and piśācas.
In the south is named Virūḍhaka, which in the language of Qin means "Increasing" (Zēngzhǎng); it presides over the kumbhāṇḍas and preta.
In the west is named Virūpākṣa, which in the language of Qin means "Variegated Speech" (Záyù); it presides over the various nāga kings and pūtanas.
In the north is the one named Vaiśravaṇa, which in the language of Qin means "Much-Hearing"; he presides over the yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Regarding "Śakra-devānām-indra":
"Śakra" in the language of Qin means "Capable."
"Devā" means "heaven" in the language of Qin;
"Indra" means "lord"—combining these, it is "Śakradevānām-indra."
"Yāma" is the name of the Heavenly King of Yāma; in the language of Qin, it means "Exquisite Goodness.
"Tuṣita" is the name of the Heavenly King of Tuṣita; in the language of Qin, it means "Exquisite Fulfillment."
“Suyāma” means “Delighting in Transformations” in the language of Qin;
“Vaśavartin” means “Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations” in the language of Qin.
Here, there is a Brahmā King named Śikhin, which means “Fire” in the language of Qin.
From the Brahma Heaven down to the "Śuddhāvāsa Heaven"—in the Qin language, the "Pure Abode Heaven"—those born through the retribution of karma possess the radiance of their own bodies.

As for the devas of the desire realm, because they have practiced giving lamps, candles, and luminous pearls, as well as the purity of generosity, observance of precepts, and meditative concentration, their bodies are constantly radiant and do not require the sun or moon.

The devas of the form realm practice dhyāna and are free from desire; because they cultivate the fire-samādhi, their bodies constantly emit wondrous light that surpasses the radiance of the sun and moon as well as the retributive light of the desire realm.
To speak briefly regarding the gods of the Heaven Free from Desire (Yāma-deva), the radiance of all these gods is obtained through the purity of their minds.
As for the "constant radiance of the Buddha," it extends one *zhang* in every direction from his face.
Although the radiance of the various devas may extend for immeasurable *yojanas*, it is eclipsed and rendered invisible in the presence of the Buddha’s light.
Seeing the power of the Buddha’s radiance, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s light can eclipse the light of all the devas; likewise, the brilliance of his wisdom shall surely shatter our ignorant darkness."
Furthermore, because the Buddha commanded Subhūti to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, it is said:
"All the devas have gathered in great assembly, desiring to hear Subhūti explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Now, the devas of great merit have all assembled, desiring to hear the meaning of Prajñā.
As for the question, 'What is this Prajñāpāramitā?', it is an inquiry into the essence of Prajñāpāramitā."
"What is the practice? asks regarding the initial entry into the practice of skillful means.
"What is the dwelling? asks regarding the profound entry into ultimate dwelling.
Subhūti accepted these words and replied as follows:
If a person who is hungry and thirsty is provided with sufficient food and drink, their gratitude will be profound;

the Bodhisattva is likewise: for one who has resolved to seek the Buddha-way, to preach the Prajñāpāramitā brings great benefit and evokes profound gratitude. For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is taught.
Those who have not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment should do so;

however, those who have already entered the Noble Path are incapable [of this task], because they have exhausted their outflows (āsrava) and will undergo no further rebirth. For such reasons as these, it is said that they are "incapable."

Question: If this person is not capable [of attaining it], for what reason do you say, "If this person should resolve their mind [on enlightenment], I too shall rejoice; I shall not obstruct their merit; the superior person should further seek the superior Dharma"?
The answer is:
Although Subhūti belongs to the Lesser Vehicle, because he constantly practices and cultivates emptiness, he does not cling to the path of the śrāvakas;
for this reason, it is said by way of metaphor:
"If one generates the thought [of awakening], what fault could there be?
In this context, Subhūti himself states two reasons:
first, that it does not obstruct the mind of merit; second, that a superior person should further seek the supreme Dharma.
For this reason, it is without fault for a superior person to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
however, if a superior person seeks inferior dharmas, that is shameful.
Because other matters were also addressed in the interim, he asks again:
"What is the *prajñāpāramitā*? This refers to that which accords with the mind of *sarvajñatā*, observing form (*rūpa*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as previously explained.
Observing that the five aggregates can give rise to all manner of afflictions, it is said they are "like a disease.
Hearing that the five aggregates are like a disease, some might consider this a minor matter; therefore, it is said they are "like an ulcerous abscess."
Some say that although an abscess is difficult to heal, it may still perhaps be cured; therefore, [the Buddha] says, "It is like an arrowhead having entered the body, which cannot be extracted.

Others say that although an arrowhead remains in the body, being deeply embedded and difficult to pull out, excellent prescriptions and wondrous techniques can still cause it to be removed; therefore, [the Buddha] speaks of constant "pain" and "affliction."

Just as a person who is afflicted by misfortune is constantly beset by inauspiciousness, so it is with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*): if a person follows after them, there is no peace or security.
Because of this "misfortune," one is perpetually filled with anxiety and fear.
These five aggregates dwell together with lions, tigers, and wolves, and thus are constantly filled with "sorrow and fear.
Because these five aggregates possess such faults as impermanence and falsity, they are always "unpeaceful."
Question:
Are there only these fifteen kinds of evils within the five aggregates, or are there further matters? Answer:
Briefly stated, there are fifteen; explained in detail, they are immeasurable and boundless;
as in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, where it is said that the five aggregates have one hundred kinds of faults and transgressions.
Question:

Why is it that impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are constantly taught, whereas at other times eight matters—such as being like a disease or an abscess—are taught, while the remaining seven matters are rarely mentioned?
Answer: People are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
For those of sharp faculties, four [truths] are taught, whereby they immediately enter into the truth of suffering.
Regarding those of medium faculties, if one speaks only of the four [truths], they are unable to give rise to a mind of revulsion;
however, if one speaks of the eight matters, such as being like a disease or an abscess, they then give rise to a mind of revulsion.

As for those of dull faculties, even upon hearing these eight matters, they still do not give rise to revulsion; therefore, one must further speak of the seven matters, such as pain and affliction, before they finally become weary and detached.
Because those of sharp faculties are easily delivered, he frequently teaches the four matters;
because there are occasionally those of dull faculties who can be delivered, he rarely teaches the other seven matters.
The first eight matters are called "Noble Practices" (*ārya-caryā*); the remaining seven matters are practiced by both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Because the first four [perfections] involve the sixteen noble practices (*ārya-caryā*), they are constantly taught within the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*;
furthermore, since the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* is taught for the sake of bodhisattvas with sharp faculties, it frequently discusses these noble practices.
Now, because the question "What is the method for the beginner? is being asked, all of this is explained herein.
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) up to the six elements (*dhātu*) and so forth should likewise be refuted in this same manner.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth should also be explained in full, yet the reciter has forgotten them. Why is this?
Because these various phenomena, such as the eighteen elements, are all specific names for the five aggregates (*skandha*); therefore, they should not be left unmentioned.

If a practitioner contemplates the five aggregates and so forth as being quiescent, detached, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and so on, this is solely for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā* and thus does not accord with the aforementioned fifteen points;
for those fifteen matters are common to all three vehicles.

Because the power of wisdom of the śrāvaka is weak, at the outset they are unable to contemplate the five aggregates as being either detached or quiescent; they can only contemplate them as impermanent and so forth.
Only upon entering the third noble truth can they contemplate quiescence.
Because the bodhisattva possesses sharp faculties, upon first contemplating the five aggregates, he immediately attains the mark of quiescence.
Regarding "using non-apprehension," it means that he constantly uses the wisdom of emptiness of non-apprehension to contemplate the marks of all phenomena.

Furthermore, Śakra-devānām-indra asked about the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*, rather than asking about the matters of weariness with and aversion toward the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); he spoke only of the characteristics of *prajñā*.
As for the "characteristics of *prajñā*": there is no nirvāṇa apart from the five aggregates, nor are there five aggregates apart from nirvāṇa;
the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates is itself nirvāṇa.

Therefore, for those of dull faculties who have first resolved their minds on enlightenment, one should first employ contemplations such as impermanence, and only thereafter contemplate the quiescence of the five aggregates and so forth.
The same applies to the twelve links of dependent origination.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is a common dharma;
that which accords with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) by way of non-apprehension is called the characteristic of prajñāpāramitā.
The six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas) constitute exclusively the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Question: One should explain the characteristics and practice of the prajñāpāramitā; for what reason is it taught in the interim?
“Do all phenomena (dharmas) mutually serve as causes and conditions for one another, moistening, benefiting, and increasing them?
The answer is:

Subhūti first previously spoke of “the faults of all phenomena, such as impermanence,” and later spoke of “all phenomena being detached, quiescent, unobtainable, and empty. Thereafter, he said, “Although all phenomena are empty, they exist due to the conjunction of causes and conditions,” followed by the explanation of “practicing the path to Buddhahood through the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
The listener thinks to themselves:
"Because it was previously stated that [all things] are detached, quiescent, and empty, one knows they are impermanent;
because it was stated that there are twelve links of dependent origination, one knows they do not cease."
"Since there is neither a knower nor a seer, who is it that practices these dharmas to attain Buddhahood?
For this reason, it is said that the Bodhisattva reflects:
"All dharmas are empty; they are without self and without sentient beings."

Yet, by reason of causes and conditions, there are the four great elements and the six consciousnesses; these ten dharmas each possess their own power, capable of producing, capable of arising, and capable of performing functions—just as earth can support, water can moisten, fire can consume, wind can cause movement, and consciousness can differentiate.
These ten factors each have their respective functions; yet because sentient beings are subject to perversion, they claim, "It is this person who acts," or "I am acting.
For example, it is through the combination of skin and bone that vocal sounds arise, yet some claim, "This is human speech."
Just as when a fire burns down a grove of bamboo, a great sound issues forth, yet there is no agent therein;
or as with a wooden man, a phantom man, or a conjured man, who can perform actions yet have no agent—these ten dharmas are likewise so.

Regarding phenomena produced earlier and phenomena produced later, there are causal conditions—whether they be co-arising conditions, associated conditions, or retributive conditions—and by constantly cultivating and accumulating these causal conditions, one causes the fruit of retribution to increase.
It is like planting fruit trees in spring and irrigating them according to the seasons, whereby their flowers and fruits flourish.
Through the discernment of wisdom, one knows that among all phenomena there is no creator.

When a bodhisattva first resolves their mind and dedicates it, this serves as the causal condition for the Buddha-mind; yet, at the time of that initial resolution and dedication, the Buddha-mind does not yet exist, nor does the Buddha-mind contain the initial mind of dedication.
Although they do not exist [simultaneously], they are nonetheless able to function as causal conditions.
Question:
If there is no bodhicitta at the time of the initial arousal of the mind and its dedication, toward what is it dedicated? Answer:

Within the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Prajñāpāramitā, all phenomena possess neither the mark of permanence nor the mark of impermanence; they possess neither the mark of existence nor the mark of non-existence. Therefore, one should not raise the objection:
"Since the mind of dedication has already ceased and is non-existent, how can it serve as the cause for bodhi?"

If all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, and yet are not non-arising and not non-ceasing, how can one raise the objection based on their being neither arising nor ceasing, asking: "Since there is no bodhicitta, what is there to dedicate?"

Furthermore, the Buddha himself has stated that the nature of bodhi is neither past, nor future, nor present; how then can you challenge this by asking, "Since there is no bodhi in the future, what is it that is dedicated?"
Furthermore, as it is said in the "Chapter on Suchness":

"The past world is not separate from the future world, and the future world is not separate from the past world; the suchness of the past world and the suchness of the future world are a single suchness, without duality."
Why is it said that "the bodhicitta is not in the mind of dedication, and the mind of dedication is not in the bodhicitta"?
It is simply that when a bodhisattva hears this praise of the Buddha-dharma, they give rise to a mind of love and joy, thinking:
"All the merits I possess shall be dedicated toward the path of the Buddha."
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of the Buddha-way, one cultivates these merits without ceasing or resting;
because they are like illusions and dreams and are non-apprehendable, this is called "the Bodhisattva’s Prajñāpāramitā.
It is the ability to know that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions as karmic retributions, yet possess no fixed characteristics.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked:
"For what reason is the mind of dedication not to be found within the mind of enlightenment,
and the mind of enlightenment not to be found within the mind of dedication?"
Subhūti does not speak according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as being like an illusion or a dream; rather, he speaks according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
"These two minds are both empty and are not the characteristics of mind."
Why is this? Because within the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, there is neither such a mind nor a non-mind.
How, then, could such a phenomenon be subject to dedication?
If there were two dharmas, there could be dedication;
it is like a carriage traveling westward that has a place to rest to the south, and thus turns the carriage toward it.
Because the carriage and the destination of the turn differ, dedication is possible.
One cannot merely speak of a vehicle while referring to dedication, for there is no difference between them.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of mind is eternally not the characteristic of mind," Subhūti’s intention is this:
"This characteristic of mind is like the eternal dwelling; it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure."
Because it is not characterized by the mind, it is not the mind; furthermore, there is neither "is" nor "is not" the mind. Therefore, it is called inconceivable.
That which is inconceivable is eternally inconceivable, and cannot be measured, deliberated upon, or grasped through signs.
For this reason, the mind that serves as the cause for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* resembles its fruit; if it did not resemble it, it could not give rise to it.
If the initial mind is impure, a pure mind cannot subsequently arise;
it would be like smelting iron that cannot become gold.
The Buddha [taught this] because Subhūti had deeply entered the *prajñāpāramitā* of dependent origination; "this" is the name of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because he was able to deeply penetrate the dependent origination of all phenomena, it was named accordingly.
Because there was no error or contradiction, he praised them amidst the great assembly, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You are a follower of the Hīnayāna, yet you are able to skillfully expound the profound Prajñāpāramitā!

Regarding "comforting the minds of the bodhisattvas," this means that by teaching the Prajñāpāramitā to all bodhisattvas, you must not allow yourselves to become weary or despondent on account of your own afflictions being未尽 (not yet exhausted) or your failure to have attained the Buddha-way.
All dharmas are unimpeded; there is no difference between the initial mind and the final mind. By merely applying diligent effort, one attains the Buddha-way.
Regarding the thought "I should repay my debt of gratitude," Subhūti reflects:

"By practicing these dharmas of the true mark (*dharmatā*), I have attained liberation from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death. How could I not contemplate the great kindness of these dharmas?"
For this reason, he always delights in preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses a heart of great compassion and delights in preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
because I have attained the Way through the Buddha’s grace, I too shall assist the Buddha in preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings—this is how one repays his kindness.
Furthermore, I know that the present World-Honored One attained the Way of Buddhahood by virtue of the Buddhas of the past; for this reason, I also love and revere the Buddhas of the past.
Just as a son loves and reveres his father, he also loves and honors his grandfather.

Furthermore, because he cherished and revered the past bodhisattvas and their disciples who were able to teach and instruct through the Dharma, the present World-Honored One was likewise brought to fulfillment by this.
Subhūti, out of deep-seated faith in the Triple Gem, said:
"I recognize the kindness of the present World-Honored One and the Dharma, as well as that of the past buddhas and their disciples."
The Dharma is the Jewel of the Dharma; the present Buddha and the Buddhas of the past are the Jewel of the Buddha; and all Bodhisattvas and disciples are the Jewel of the Sangha.
The six pāramitās are as previously explained.
"Showing" means showing people what is beautiful and what is ugly, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, and what should and should not be practiced:
that birth and death are ugly, while the peace and security of nirvana are beautiful.
"Distinguishing" refers to such things as distinguishing the three vehicles and distinguishing the six pāramitās; these are called "indications.
"Instruction" refers to instructing by saying, "You should abandon evil and practice good"; this is called instruction.
Regarding "benefit": because one has not yet attained the flavor of wholesome dharmas, the mind retreats and sinks;
therefore, the Dharma is taught to guide them out [of this state], saying:
"Do not seek the fruit during the time of the cause!"
"Although you now undergo diligent hardship, when the fruit of retribution emerges, you shall obtain great benefit!
This is called "benefit" (*li*) because it makes the mind sharp and focused.
As for "joy" (*xi*), one praises the practitioner according to their conduct, causing the mind to rejoice.
If one delights in giving, they rejoice when giving is praised; therefore, it is called "joy.
By means of these four matters, one adorns the preaching of the Dharma.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Kauśika! You should now listen to how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide and how they should not abide within the perfection of wisdom.”
Kauśika! Form is empty of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
This emptiness of form and this emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and not distinct.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; the Bodhisattva is empty. These two are non-dual and not distinct.
Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide thus within the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, the eye is empty of the eye, and so on up to the mind, which is empty of the mind; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
The emptiness of the eye up to the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and undifferentiated."
The six sense objects are also like this.
The earth element is empty of the earth element, and so on up to the consciousness element being empty of the consciousness element; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. Kausika!
The earth element is empty, up to and including the consciousness element; the bodhisattva is empty. These are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Kausika, a bodhisattva mahasattva should abide thus within the perfection of wisdom.
Ignorance is empty of ignorance, and so on up to old age and death, which are empty of old age and death;
the cessation of ignorance is empty of the cessation of ignorance, and so on up to the cessation of old age and death, which is empty of the cessation of old age and death;
the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Kauśika! The emptiness of ignorance up to the emptiness of old age and death, the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance up to the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide thus within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). This applies likewise to the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom;

from internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā); from the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma); all gateways of samādhi, all gateways of dhāraṇī; the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the buddha; and likewise for the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the buddha.
All-knowledge is empty of all-knowledge, and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva;
the emptiness of all-knowledge and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are non-dual and indistinguishable.
“Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell thus within the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
“How is it that a bodhisattva should not abide within the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!...”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell in form, because it involves apprehension;
they should not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, because it involves apprehension.

One should not dwell in the eye, nor even in the mind; one should not dwell in forms, nor even in mental phenomena (*dharma*). One should not dwell in visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, in visual contact up to mental contact, or in the feelings produced by conditions of visual contact up to the feelings produced by conditions of mental contact, because these involve apprehension (*upalambha*).
One should not dwell upon the element of earth up to the element of consciousness, because they involve apprehension.

One should not dwell upon the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, nor upon the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they involve apprehension.
One should not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry, because it involves apprehension;
likewise, one should not dwell in the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the Buddha, or omniscience, because they involve apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell on the notion that form is permanent, nor should they dwell on the notion that form is impermanent;
the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

One should not dwell upon form as being pleasant or painful, pure or impure, self or non-self, empty or non-empty, tranquil or non-tranquil, detached or non-detached, because such dwelling involves the apprehension of something to be attained.
The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not dwell upon the unconditioned mark of the fruit of stream-entry, the unconditioned mark of the fruit of once-returning, the unconditioned mark of the fruit of non-returning, or the unconditioned mark of the fruit of arhatship; nor should they dwell upon the unconditioned mark of the path of the pratyekabuddha or the unconditioned mark of the path of the Buddha."
One should not dwell on the field of merit of a srotāpanna; one should not dwell on the fields of merit of a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a buddha.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the first stage because of the apprehension of something to be attained;
likewise, they should not abide even in the tenth stage because of the apprehension of something to be attained."

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the initial resolve, they should not abide in the thought: 'I shall fulfill the perfection of giving,' nor should they abide in such thoughts up to and including: 'I shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom. They should not abide in the thought:
'Having fulfilled the six perfections, I shall enter the bodhisattva stage.
Nor, having entered the bodhisattva stage, should they abide in the thought: 'I shall abide on the stage of non-retrogression.'"
A bodhisattva should fulfill the five supernormal powers, yet should not abide in them because they involve the apprehension of something.

Having abided in the five supernormal powers, [the bodhisattva thinks: "I shall travel through immeasurable, incalculable Buddha-fields to pay homage to, revere, and make offerings to the Buddhas and listen to the Dharma;
having listened to the Dharma, I shall explain it for the sake of others."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in such a way, because it involves apprehending something as an object.

Just as the worlds of the Buddhas are adorned and purified, thinking "I too shall adorn the world" is also a state in which one should not abide, because it involves apprehending something as an object.
One should not dwell on maturing sentient beings so as to lead them into the Buddha-way;

nor should one dwell on going to the abodes of the Buddhas in immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds to honor, revere, and make offerings to them—with incense, flowers, necklaces, perfumed unguents, powdered incense, banners, flags, canopies, and hundreds of thousands of billions of kinds of precious robes—because such acts are performed with the notion of something to be attained.
"I shall cause immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*"; thus, a bodhisattva should not dwell therein.
"I shall produce the five eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye"; thus, one should not dwell therein.
"I shall give birth to all gateways of samādhi"—one should not dwell on this;
"I shall sport at will in all samādhis"—one should not dwell on this;
"I shall give birth to all gateways of dhāraṇī"—one should not dwell on this.
"I shall attain the ten powers of a Buddha"—one should not dwell on this;
"I shall attain the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas"—one should not dwell on this;
"I shall be fully endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion"—one should not dwell on this.
"I shall be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks" — one should not dwell on this, because it involves apprehension;
"I shall be fully endowed with the eighty secondary characteristics" — one should not dwell on this, because it involves apprehension.
"These eight persons—this person who practices through faith, this person who practices through the Dharma—in these ways one should not dwell;
one should not dwell in the thought that a stream-enterer will be reborn at most seven more times; one should not dwell in the thought of a 'family-to-family' [stream-enterer];
one should not dwell in the thought that for a stream-enterer, upon the end of life, defilements are exhausted."
One should not dwell on the thought that a stream-enterer enters nirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
one should not dwell on the thought that this person is heading toward the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
one should not dwell on the thought that this person, as a once-returner, enters nirvāṇa after returning to this world once more.
One should not dwell on the realization of the fruit of *anāgāmin*;
one should not dwell on the single rebirth of a *sakṛdāgāmin*;
nor should one dwell on the thought that this person, as an *anāgāmin*, will enter *nirvāṇa* in that very interval.
One should not dwell on the thought that this person is about to realize the fruit of arhatship;
one should not dwell on the thought that this person, as an arhat, will enter nirvana without remainder in this very life;
nor should one dwell on the thought that this person is a pratyekabuddha.
One should not dwell in the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, thinking,

"I shall abide in the Bodhisattva stage," for one should not dwell even in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), because that involves the apprehension of something to be attained.
Having known all phenomena in all their aspects, one should not dwell upon the severing of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies;
one should not dwell upon the Buddha’s attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and his turning of the wheel of Dharma;
nor should one dwell upon performing the works of a Buddha and leading immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings into *nirvāṇa*.
"One should not dwell in the four bases of psychic power;
one should not dwell in entering this samādhi and remaining for a lifespan equal to that of the sands of the Ganges River;
one should not dwell in the thought, 'I shall obtain a lifespan of incalculable kalpas.'"
One should not dwell on the thirty-two marks, each mark being adorned with a hundred merits;
one should not dwell on my single world being like worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions;
one should not dwell on my trichiliocosm being composed entirely of vajra.

May my Bodhi tree emit such a fragrance that any sentient beings who smell it shall be free from lust, anger, and ignorance; they shall have no thoughts of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and all such people shall surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, if sentient beings smell this fragrance, may their physical and mental ailments be entirely eliminated, and they shall not dwell [in attachment].
"One should not dwell on the thought: 'May there be no names for form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness in my world';

nor should one dwell on the thought: 'May there be no names for the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā in my world'; nor should one dwell on the thought: 'May there be no names for the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha in my world,' nor even 'May there be no names for the srotāpanna up to the Buddha,' because these involve apprehending something as an object."
Why is this? Because when the Buddhas attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, they find nothing at all among all dharmas.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
“A bodhisattva should not dwell in the perfection of wisdom, because there is nothing to be apprehended.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
“How, then, should a bodhisattva now dwell in the perfection of wisdom?”
Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, said to him:
“What do you think?
Where do the Buddhas dwell?”
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The Buddhas have no place of abiding.
The Buddhas do not abide in form; they do not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
He does not dwell in the nature of the conditioned, nor does he dwell in the nature of the unconditioned;
he does not dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he dwell in the knowledge of all modes.
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in this way within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), just as the Buddhas dwell among all phenomena—neither dwelling nor not dwelling.”
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this way:
"I shall abide by means of non-abiding."
The Treatise states:
"To abide within the Prajñāpāramitā means that the so-called five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are empty of the characteristics of the five aggregates.
That the five aggregates are empty of their own characteristics is due to the contemplation of the eighteen kinds of emptiness."
Furthermore, in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the meaning of emptiness is explained: the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are empty;

yet because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are subject to inversion, they grasp at the characteristics of the five aggregates and, within the combination of these five aggregates, they grasp at the characteristic of a bodhisattva.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the emptiness of sentient beings, one eliminates the notion of sentient beings, which is itself the absence of the mark of a bodhisattva;
by means of the emptiness of phenomena, one eliminates the five aggregates, which is the absence of the marks of the five aggregates.
The two kinds of emptiness are not distinct; therefore it is said:
"The emptiness of the five aggregates and the emptiness of the Bodhisattva are non-dual and without difference.
This is like the extinguishing of a sandalwood fire and the extinguishing of a fire of dung, grass, or wood—the nature of their extinction is no different.
Because one grasps the characteristics of the time when [phenomena] have not yet ceased and speaks of them at the time of cessation, there is a distinction;
however, within cessation itself, there is no difference.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Regarding "should not abide," this means that one should not abide within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Question: One should explain the meaning of how one abides; for what reason do you say "not abiding"?
The answer is:
If one can remain detached from the mind toward the five aggregates such that it does not dwell [upon them], this is the meaning of "dwelling.
Therefore, it is said:
"Because there is something apprehended, one should not dwell [therein].
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Previously, it was stated that "one should not dwell within the five aggregates," but it was not yet known through which gate one should not dwell; [this passage clarifies that].
Now it is said: "One should not dwell in the gates of permanence, impermanence, and so forth, up to and including 'one should not dwell in detachment. Question:
Since one should not dwell in the unconditioned characteristics (asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) such as the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), what is the sequential order [of these teachings]?

Answer: The Bodhisattva first contemplates that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; his mind then recoils, desiring to grasp at nirvana. Since nirvana is precisely the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), it is for this reason that it is now said: "One should not dwell in the unconditioned characteristics such as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*)."
If the fruit of srotāpanna were an unconditioned characteristic (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), then there would be no dharma to which one could become attached; what would there be to love?
What would there be to grasp?
If it were a conditioned characteristic (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), then since a conditioned characteristic is deceptive and lacks reality, one likewise should not abide in it.
Therefore it is said: "One should not dwell on the unconditioned mark of the fruit of srotāpanna; likewise, one should not dwell on the unconditioned marks up to that of a Buddha.
Thus, when a bodhisattva wishes to practice the path of the Buddha, they should first practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and seek out fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra).
Why is this? Because through the merit of the causes and conditions of the field of blessings, one's aspirations will be fulfilled.
It is like sowing seeds in fertile soil; then the harvest gained will be abundant.
As the Buddha has taught, the retribution for other fields of merit is limited, whereas the field of the noble ones (ārya) is immeasurable, and its retribution is likewise immeasurable.
When a bodhisattva hears that the retribution for the field of merit of the srotāpanna and others is immeasurable, he may then desire to become a srotāpanna; for this reason it is said:
"One should not dwell upon the field of merit of the srotāpanna, and so on up to the pratyekabuddha."
Question: Since the two vehicles are inferior, they should pass beyond and not abide; why then does the Buddha, the field of merit, not abide? Answer:
The Dharma of a bodhisattva should be equal toward all phenomena;
if one regards the Buddha as great and sentient beings as small, then one destroys the characteristic of the equality of phenomena.
Furthermore, because all things are empty, one should not abide in any place whatsoever.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should practice giving with an impartial mind;
if they discriminate among fields of merit, they destroy great compassion and also destroy the threefold purity of giving.
Regarding the statement "one should not abide in the first stage": if one does not relinquish the first stage, one will not attain the second stage;
therefore, because one seeks great benefit, one should relinquish minor gain.
Furthermore, one should not abide [in these stages] because of grasping at signs with a mind of attachment;
this applies even up to the tenth stage.
Question:

If the dharma of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva requires that, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should practice the six pāramitās; and because they practice the six pāramitās, they enter the stage of dharma (dharmatā); and because they enter the stage of dharma, they should abide in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika); and having abided in the stage of non-retrogression, they should give rise to the five supernormal powers and make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, as will be explained in detail later—why is it said here in all cases that "one should not abide"?
The answer is:

It does not destroy the dwelling in purity; it merely destroys the dwelling of the mind that grasps at signs through the false view of conceiving a self—just as one treats a field by removing its weeds.
Furthermore, one should not abide [in anything] in order to sever attachment to dharmas;
nor should one abide [in anything] out of a desire not to contradict the Buddhas' teaching of the wisdom of ultimate emptiness.
If one acts with skillful means and a mind free from attachment, out of compassion for sentient beings, there is no fault even if one abides [in such states].
This applies likewise even to the eighty secondary marks of excellence.

The "eight persons" refers to those who practice through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who practice through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) on the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), as well as the *srotāpanna*.
At most, a *srotāpanna* will undergo rebirth for seven more lifetimes;
yet there are *srotāpannas* who exhaust their afflictions (*kleśa*) in this very life and attain the state of an Arhat.
There is the *kulaṃkula* Srotāpanna, who undergoes three births;
having undergone these three births, he enters *nirvāṇa*.
There is the *antarāparinirvāyin* Srotāpanna, who, excluding the third birth, enters *nirvāṇa* in the intermediate state.
Those who abide within the six kinds of non-obstruction and the five kinds of liberation are all *srotāpannas* or those progressing toward the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Having severed the six types of fetters of the desire realm, they are born in the heavens; coming from the heavens to be born among humans and then entering *nirvāṇa*, they are called *sakṛdāgāmins*.
One who has severed the seventh portion of the fetters of the desire realm is called a candidate for the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

One who has severed the eighth portion of the fetters is also called a candidate for the stage of non-returner, and is further termed a "one-seed" *sakṛdāgāmin*; having died here and been born there, they enter nirvāṇa.

One who is able to sever all fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm is called an Anāgāmin; dying here, they are reborn in the form or formless realms, enter nirvāṇa, and never again return to be born [in the desire realm].

There are those who attain parinirvāṇa in this very life as non-returners; those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava) as non-returners; those who enter nirvāṇa at the very moment of birth as non-returners; those who enter nirvāṇa after having been born and having cultivated various practices as non-returners; those who enter nirvāṇa without exerting effort in various practices as non-returners; those who ascend upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven as non-returners; those who enter nirvāṇa after being born in the formless realm as non-returners; and those who attain realization through the body and enter nirvāṇa as non-returners. These are called non-returners, and they are also called those who are heading toward arhatship.
There are nine types of Arhats; when they exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*) and cast off the body, it is called entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Having transcended the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, they abide in the stage of the Bodhisattva;
through the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they know all phenomena.
Severing all afflictions along with their residual tendencies;
attaining Buddhahood and turning the wheel of Dharma;
and possessing the thirty-two marks of a great man.
They adorn the world and deliver immeasurable sentient beings;
their immeasurable lifespans are all as previously explained in the treatises.

These śrāvakas, having skillfully cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and attained the power of this samādhi, are able to remain for the duration of one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa.
The Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the four *ṛddhipāda* samādhis; if he wishes for a lifespan as long as that of the sands of the Ganges River, he likewise attains it at will.

Regarding the phrase "the trichiliocosm is entirely composed of diamond": although other worlds have diamond at their foundations, and there is diamond at the places where Buddhas walk or sit, these are absent elsewhere;
this is the vow of the Bodhisattva.
The entire world is composed of vajra.
Regarding the phrase "the fragrance of the Bodhi tree delivers sentient beings," it is as explained in the preceding section. Question:
Although the matters herein are rare, they are all credible;

however, that there are no names for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and no names for the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) up to the name of the Buddha—this is difficult to believe!
Answer:

There are worlds where those endowed with great merit and wisdom are born; in these places, the trees, the sky, the earth, the mountains, the rivers, and so forth constantly emit the sounds of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—namely, that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither pure nor defiled, empty, signless, and wishless.
As soon as sentient beings are born there, they hear these sounds and spontaneously attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In such a world, there is no need to make distinctions by naming various dharmas, such as the so-called five aggregates, twelve bases, and so forth; nor the *dānapāramitā* up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor the *srotāpanna* up to all the Buddhas.
In this world, all sentient beings have bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs, possess immeasurable radiance, and share a single path and a single fruit.
Regarding the phrase "one should not abide therein," the Bodhisattva reflects to himself:
"If I think, 'I can produce such a world,' I would give rise to a sense of superiority; for this reason, one should not take up signs and abide in them."
In this context, Subhūti himself explains the reason for non-abiding:
"When the Buddhas attain the Way of the Buddha, because they do not apprehend a fixed, real characteristic among all phenomena, what could there be for them to abide in?"
Now Śāriputra thought to himself:
"If there is no abiding whatsoever, in what place should one abide to attain the path of Buddhahood?
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra's mind, said to him:
"All Bodhisattvas are the children of the Buddhas; as children, their conduct should accord with that of their father.
The minds of all Buddhas abide nowhere among all phenomena—from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Bodhisattvas should likewise train in this way: they should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) with a mind that abides nowhere.
Just as the Buddhas do not dwell even within a mind that has no dwelling, nor do they dwell within a mind that is not non-dwelling, because it is ultimately pure;
so too should the Bodhisattvas abide in accordance with the Buddhas, because it is ultimately pure, and the Bodhisattvas should likewise learn from the Buddhas.
[Sūtra] At that time, there were among those in the assembly certain sons of gods who thought to themselves:
"The words, phrases, and expressions spoken by the yakṣas can still be understood;
yet the words, arguments, and explanations of the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by Subhūti are utterly incomprehensible!"
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"Do you not understand? Do you not know?
The sons of the gods replied:
"Venerable sirs!
I do not understand; I do not know.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"You all should not know this by nature!
I have nothing to discourse upon; I do not speak even a single syllable, nor is there anyone who hears. Why is this? "
All syllables are not the Prajñāpāramitā; within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no listener; the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is without syllables and without speech.
"O sons of the gods!

It is as if a Buddha were to manifest a transformation being, and that transformation being were further to manifest the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and that transformation being were to preach the Dharma within that fourfold assembly."
"What do you think?
In this, is there a speaker, a listener, or a knower?
The devaputras replied:
"No, Venerable Sir! Subhūti replied.
"All dharmas are like magical illusions; herein there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
O sons of the gods!
It is, for example, as if a person were to see a Buddha preaching the Dharma within a dream."
"What do you think?
In this, is there anyone who speaks, anyone who listens, or anyone who knows?
The devaputras replied:
"No, Great Virtue!
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"All dharmas are like dreams; there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
O sons of the gods!
It is as if two people were on opposite sides of a vast, deep ravine, each praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and two echoes emerged."
"What do you think, sons of the gods?
Did these two people understand each other through their conversation?
The sons of the gods replied:
"No, Great Virtue!
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"All dharmas are likewise: there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
O sons of the gods!
It is as if a skilled illusionist, at a crossroads, were to conjure a Buddha and the fourfold assembly, and therein preach the Dharma."
"What do you think, sons of the gods?
In this, is there anyone who speaks, anyone who listens, or anyone who knows?
The sons of the gods replied:
"No, Great Virtue!
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"All dharmas are like illusions; there is no speaker, no listener, and no knower.
At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"What Subhūti has spoken is intended to be easy to understand, yet it becomes increasingly profound and increasingly subtle!"
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"Form is neither profound nor subtle; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither profound nor subtle.
The nature of form is neither profound nor subtle; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither profound nor subtle."

The nature of the eye up to the nature of the mind; the nature of forms up to the nature of phenomena; the nature of the eye-element up to the nature of the mind-element; eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; eye-contact up to mind-contact; feelings born from the conditions of eye-contact up to feelings born from the conditions of mind-contact; the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī, up to all-knowledge and the nature of all-knowledge—these are neither deep nor subtle.
The sons of the gods again had this thought:
"In this teaching of the Dharma, form is not mentioned; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not mentioned;
nor are anything from the eye up to the feelings produced by the conditions of contact with the mind mentioned."
He does not speak of the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom;
he does not speak of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
he does not speak of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not speak of the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi, up to and including all-knowledge;

one does not speak of the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, nor does one speak of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor does one speak of the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—for within these dharmas, names and words are not spoken.
Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, said to them: “So it is! So it is!”
O sons of the gods!
Within this Dharma, the Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as an ineffable characteristic; herein there is neither speaker, nor listener, nor knower.
For this reason, O sons of the gods!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to abide in the fruit of a srotāpanna, or who wishes to realize the fruit of a srotāpanna, does not depart from this patience;
likewise, those who wish to abide in or realize the fruits of a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha, or the path of a buddha, do not depart from this patience.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in this manner within the prajñāpāramitā, because there is neither speaker nor listener.
[Treatise] Question:
Although the speech of the yakṣas is obscure, indirect, and improper, its subject matter is vulgar and mundane;

whereas the exposition of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, though employing conventional terminology, possesses a hidden meaning that is profound and remote. Since their subjects differ and their intents diverge, how can they be compared?
The answer is:

The various devas merely use what people do not understand to illustrate that which they themselves have not yet realized; it is not necessary for every aspect of the matter to be identical in order to serve as a metaphor. Some say:
The Heavenly Emperor has nine hundred and ninety-nine gates, each guarded by sixteen blue-clad yakṣas.
These yakṣas are deceitful in speech and inclined toward seductive flattery; the devas despise them and pay them no heed, which is why they do not understand their words.
However, their underlying intentions can be recognized without the need for verbal explanation; thus, it is said that their meaning is still easily discernible.

Now, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, the words seem within reach; yet its mysterious purport is so abstruse that the deeper one searches, the further one strays from it. Therefore, the speech of a yakṣa is used as a metaphor for its unknowability.
Furthermore, although the language of yakṣas is difficult to understand, by observing their physical expressions and transmitting their words to gauge their intentions, all can be known;
it is like a deep abyss with swift currents, which can be crossed if one obtains a boat.
The Prajñāpāramitā taught by Subhūti is the meaning of ultimate emptiness; it possesses no fixed characteristics, cannot be grasped, and cannot be transmitted or translated for the sake of awakening.

One may not say it "exists," nor may one say it "does not exist"; one may not say it "both exists and does not exist," nor may one say it "neither exists nor does not exist. Even "neither non-existence nor non-non-existence" does not apply, because all spheres of mental activity have ceased and the path of language is cut off.
Therefore, the sons of the gods were startled, filled with doubt, and bewildered.
Subhūti replied to the sons of the gods:
"As for that which you do not understand, it is only natural that you should be so!"
This Dharma cannot be spoken of as a single thing, nor can even a single syllable be spoken that might be clung to or grasped;
it is without letters and without words—this is the path of all Buddhas. Why is this so?
These names are all empty, deceptive, and without reality;
this is as explained in the analysis of form and names.
By employing names, there arises speech.
"If there were no names, there would be no speech.
The sons of the gods then thought:
"If there is neither speaking nor listening, for what purpose has this assembly gathered today?"
Subhūti, wishing to explain this meaning, clarified it through a simile.
The sons of the gods again thought to themselves:
"He wishes to bring us to understanding through a simile, yet this simile is even more profound and subtle!"
This analogy uses the coarse to illustrate the subtle and clarifies the indeterminate through determinate phenomena; yet this present analogy is likewise subtle and lacks fixed characteristics.
Subhūti, knowing that the devaputras were lost and submerged within the profound *prajñā* and unable to emerge on their own, therefore said:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is not different from the five aggregates; the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the five aggregates is itself the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Now these five aggregates are neither deep nor subtle; even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are neither deep nor subtle.

At that time, the sons of the gods deeply understood that although Subhūti spoke of form and mind, there was nothing spoken, and it was likewise even for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts of the devaputras, replied: "So it is! So it is!"
It is not only I who am thus!
When the Buddha attained Bodhi, there was likewise no speaking; in the mark of quiescence, there is truly neither speaker nor listener.
Therefore, from the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the Way of the Buddha, all exist because of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Apart from these dharmas and apart from this patience, there is no srotāpanna; it is likewise for everything up to the Buddha-way.
From the Bodhisattva’s first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, throughout that interval, all dharmas are neither spoken nor heard.

Because all observations have ceased and all speech has been cut off, it is ineffable; because it is ineffable, it cannot be heard; because it cannot be heard, it cannot be known; and because it cannot be known, there is no grasping and no attachment toward any phenomena, whereby one enters nirvāṇa.
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, Volume Fifty-Four.
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, Commentary on the Chapter on the Illusory Person Listening to the Dharma,
Number Twenty-Eight, Volume Fifty-Five.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 28: The Illusory Person Listening to the Dharma. [Sūtra] At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"By what kind of person should one listen to what Subhūti has said?"
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"Just as an illusory person listens to the Dharma, it is such a person that I should employ."
"Why is this? Because such a person has neither heard, nor listened, nor known, nor realized.
The devaputras said to Subhūti:
“Are these sentient beings like illusions and like transformations, and are those who listen to the Dharma also like illusions and like transformations? “So it is! So it is!”
O sons of the gods!
Sentient beings are like illusions, and those who hear the Dharma are also like illusions;
sentient beings are like transformations, and those who hear the Dharma are also like transformations.
O sons of the gods!
I am like an illusion and like a dream; sentient beings, up to and including those who know and those who see, are also like illusions and like dreams.
O sons of the gods!
Form is like an illusion, like a dream; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions, like dreams.

Feelings born from the conditions of contact, from the eye up to the mind, are like illusions, like dreams. Inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, are like illusions, like dreams.
"O sons of the gods!

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are like an illusion, like a dream; the fruit of a stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a dream; the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha are like an illusion, like a dream."
"O sons of the gods!
The path of the Buddha is like an illusion, like a dream.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
“You say that the Buddha-way is like an illusion and like a dream; do you also say that nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
“I say that the Buddha-way is like an illusion and like a dream; I say that nirvāṇa is also like an illusion and like a dream.”
If there were any phenomenon superior to nirvāṇa, I would say that it, too, is like an illusion and like a dream.
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
"This illusion, this dream, and nirvāṇa are non-dual and not distinct.
[Śāstra] Question:

Previously it was already stated that "like an illusion, like a dream, there is no speaker and no listener. Why is it asked again now, "By what kind of person should one listen to the Dharma according to Subhūti’s intention"?
Answer: The devaputras previously stated that "what Subhūti has spoken cannot be understood"; herein, Subhūti speaks the parable of the illusory person.
Now the sons of the gods further thought to themselves:
"What kind of person, when listening, will accord with what Subhūti has said, and be able to believe, accept, practice, and attain the fruits of the path?"
Subhūti replied:
"If it were like a person conjured by illusion who listens, then that would correspond to my teaching of the Dharma. He asked:
This emanated person has no mind or mental factors and cannot listen or receive; for what purpose, then, is the Dharma preached?
The answer is:

it is not that one intends for the emanated person to listen, but rather desires to cause the practitioner to apply the mind toward all phenomena without attachment, just like an emanated person. This emanated person neither hears nor realizes.

Sentient beings are like illusions and like dreams; listening to the Dharma is also like an illusion and like a dream. "Sentient beings" refers to those who preach the Dharma; "listening to the Dharma" refers to those who receive the Dharma.
Subhūti said:

"Not only are the speaker of the Dharma and the listener of the Dharma like an illusion and like a dream; even I, up to the knower and the seer, are all like an illusion and like a dream. Form, too, is like an illusion and like a dream; even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream—this very Dharma that is taught is like an illusion and like a dream."
"Among all sentient beings, the Buddha is foremost;
among all dharmas, nirvāṇa is foremost.
Upon hearing that these two matters are like illusions and like dreams, their minds become startled and filled with doubt."
"The Buddha and nirvāṇa are supreme and most wonderful; how can they be like an illusion or a dream?
For this reason, he asked again about the matter:
"Are the Buddha and nirvāṇa truly like an illusion and like a dream?"
“Has Subhūti perhaps spoken erroneously?
Or have we perhaps heard him mistakenly?
For this reason, they asked again to clarify.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"When I speak of the Buddha and nirvāṇa, they are exactly like an illusion and like a dream.
Although these two dharmas are sublime, they are both empty because they arise from illusory phenomena."

Why is this so? Because nirvāṇa exists due to illusory dharmas, and because a Buddha exists due to merit and wisdom; these two dharmas belong to causes and conditions and possess no fixed reality, as explained in the sections on the mindfulness of the Buddha and the mindfulness of the Dharma.
Subhūti had this thought:
"By the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, even if there were a dharma superior to *nirvāṇa*, it could be made like an illusion; how much more so, then, *nirvāṇa* itself!"
Why is this? Because in nirvāṇa, all sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are ultimately extinguished; for this reason, there is no dharma superior to nirvāṇa.
Question: If there is no phenomenon superior to nirvāṇa, for what reason is it said that "even if there were a phenomenon superior to nirvāṇa, it would likewise be like an illusion"? Answer:
The method of parables is taught according to causes and conditions, whether based on actual facts or through metaphorical assumptions.
As the Buddha said:
"If trees were able to understand what I have spoken, I would likewise declare that they have attained the stage of srotāpanna."
"However, trees have no underlying causes or conditions that can be explained; the Buddha merely employs this analogy to bring about understanding and enlightenment in people's minds.

Nirvāṇa is the ultimate and unsurpassed dharma among all dharmas, just as the great ocean is supreme among the myriad rivers and streams, Mount Sumeru is supreme among all mountains, and space is supreme among all dharmas."

Nirvāṇa is also like this: it is free from the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death; it is free from the various decays such as wrong views, greed, and hatred; it is free from the suffering of separation from the beloved; it is free from the suffering of encountering the hated; it is free from the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and all things such as impermanence, falsity, decay, and changeability are entirely absent.

In brief, nirvana is the exhaustion of all suffering and is ultimately eternal bliss; it is the destination to which the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of disciples of the ten directions return. It is a state of peace, security, and constant joy beyond compare, which can never be destroyed by Māra or his followers.
As it is said in the Abhidharma:
"Dharmas that have a superior [state] are all conditioned dharmas, as well as space and cessation not through wisdom;
dharmas that are unsurpassed are cessation through wisdom, namely, Nirvana."
Therefore, it is known that there is no dharma superior to nirvāṇa.
Subhūti, because he admires the great power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, says:
"If there were any dharma superior to nirvāṇa, that too would be like an illusion."
It is, for example, like a great red-hot iron ball placed upon a tuft of split cotton wool; it passes straight through and burns away, its heat undiminished, yet there is nothing further to burn.

So too does the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā* shatter all existent phenomena, even up to *nirvāṇa*, passing straight through without obstruction; the power of this wisdom is not diminished, for there is simply no further phenomenon remaining to be shattered.
Therefore it is said: "Even if there were a dharma superior to nirvāṇa, the power of wisdom would likewise be able to destroy it.
[Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and countless thousands of bodhisattvas asked Subhūti:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is thus profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, difficult to know, quiescent, and subtle. Who will be able to receive it?"
At that time, Ānanda said to the great disciples and the bodhisattvas:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-regressive (avaivartika) are able to receive this profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, difficult to know, quiescent, and subtle Prajñāpāramitā;
those who have achieved right view and Arhats whose outflows are exhausted and whose vows are fulfilled are likewise able to receive it."

Furthermore, good sons and good daughters who have frequently seen the Buddhas, made many offerings to the Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, associated with spiritual friends, and possess sharp faculties—such persons are able to receive it, and do not say that this is the Dharma or that it is not the Dharma.
Subhūti said: “One does not discriminate form by means of emptiness, nor does one discriminate emptiness by means of form;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
One does not discriminate form by means of signlessness or wishlessness, nor does one discriminate signlessness or wishlessness by means of form;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

One does not, by means of non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, and freedom from discrimination, regard form as such; nor does one discriminate non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, and freedom [from defilement] by means of form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
