It is the same for the feelings produced by the conditions of eye-contact up to mind-contact. From the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);

from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī; from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha;

and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—one does not differentiate omniscience by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of omniscience; one does not differentiate the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of the knowledge of all modes.
"Non-characteristic, non-activity, non-arising, non-ceasing, quiescence, and detachment are also like this.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is extremely profound; who is able to receive it?"
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be shown and no dharma that can be spoken;
since there is no dharma that can be shown and no dharma that can be spoken, even the recipient cannot be apprehended.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively explained, as well as the methods for embracing bodhisattvas—from the stage of the initial aspiration up to the tenth stage; from the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā; from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and from the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities—therein the teaching for protecting and sustaining bodhisattvas is contained."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they are always born by transformation and do not lose their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They travel through the buddha-fields, perfecting their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and whatever offerings they desire to present to the Buddhas, they obtain exactly as they wish. From the presence of those Buddhas, they hear and receive the teachings of the Dharma, which continue without interruption until they reach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Never departing from samādhi, they shall attain swift eloquence, sharp eloquence, inexhaustible eloquence, unassailable eloquence, responsive eloquence, eloquence regarding meaning, and the supreme eloquence in all worlds.
Subhūti said: “So it is! So it is!”

As Śāriputra has said, the Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds the teachings of the three vehicles and the teachings for the protection and sustenance of bodhisattvas; furthermore, it is because even the attainment by a bodhisattva mahāsattva of the most supreme eloquence in all worlds is ultimately unobtainable.

This is because I, as well as the knower and the seer, cannot be apprehended; form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence cannot be apprehended; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge, likewise cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"By what causes and conditions is it that, within the Prajñāpāramitā, the three vehicles are extensively explained yet cannot be apprehended?"
For what reason does the *prajñāpāramitā* protect and sustain bodhisattvas?
For what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain swift eloquence, up to and including the supreme eloquence in all the world, such that it cannot be apprehended?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Because of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), the three vehicles cannot be apprehended as they are extensively taught;

because of external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the three vehicles cannot be apprehended as they are extensively taught."
Because internal emptiness is unattainable, the bodhisattva’s protection and maintenance, up to the supreme eloquence of all the world, is unattainable;

because external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, is unattainable, the bodhisattva’s protection and maintenance, up to the supreme eloquence of all the world, is unattainable.
[The] Commentator says:
At that time, the great disciples such as Śāriputra said to Subhūti,
“This Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is extremely profound and difficult to understand.”
Because all dharmas lack fixed characteristics, they are "profound";
because all conceptualizations and contemplative practices have ceased, they are "difficult to see";
and because one does not cling even to the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is called "difficult to understand" and "difficult to know."
It is called "quiescence" because it extinguishes the three poisons and all conceptual proliferations;

it is called "subtle and wondrous" because, by attaining the exquisite flavor of this wisdom, one is eternally satisfied and has nothing further to seek, whereas all other forms of wisdom are coarse, harsh, and unpleasant.
The great disciples spoke thus:
"The wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound, yet the wisdom of people in the world is shallow; they merely crave the retribution of merit and do not delight in cultivating it."
If one clings to existence, the passions will be bold; if one seeks to destroy existence, the mind will become timid.
Having originally studied and habituated oneself to scriptures of false views, one clings to them tenaciously and refuses to abandon them; such a person constantly delights in worldly pleasures.
For this reason it is said:
"Who can believe and accept this profound Prajñāpāramitā?
If there were no one to believe and accept it, what would be the use of teaching it?"
Ānanda replied on his behalf:
"There are four kinds of people who can believe and accept; therefore, what the Venerable Subhūti has spoken will certainly be believed and accepted—it is not said in vain."

First, an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing; because they do not grasp at signs and have no attachments, they are thus able to receive [the prediction].

Second, as for the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted: because their outflows are exhausted, they have no attachments; they have attained the supreme unconditioned Dharma; their vows are fulfilled and they have nothing further to seek. Therefore, they constantly abide in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and because they accord with the Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to believe and accept it.

Third, there are those of the three types of trainees who have accomplished right view; although their outflows are not yet entirely exhausted, by virtue of the four powers of faith, they are also able to believe and accept it.

Fourth, there are bodhisattvas who, though not yet attained to the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), possess merit and sharp faculties, pure wisdom, and constantly follow spiritual friends; such persons are also able to believe and accept it.
The characteristic of faithful acceptance is not to say, "This dharma was not spoken by the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, or the great disciples";
even upon hearing that all dharmas are ultimately empty according to the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not, out of attachment to previously held teachings, claim, "This is not the Dharma."
Question:
From the beginning up until now, Ānanda has not engaged in any discourse; why does he now answer on behalf of Subhūti? Answer:
Ānanda is the third in the turning of the Wheel of Dharma and is capable of being a teacher for the great assembly; he is the World-Honored One’s close attendant.

Although he has attained the first stage of the Path, because his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, and although he possesses much learning and wisdom, he considers himself unskilled within the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If he were to preach the Dharma of emptiness, it would all be a matter for others, as he himself has not yet entered it; therefore, he remains silent.
At times, when discussing matters that possess substantial reality, one is able to both question and answer.
As in a later chapter, one asks the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, for what reason do you praise only the *prajñāpāramitā* and not the five *pāramitās*?"
In this context, when the questioner asked who could believe in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*—since it is not a matter of emptiness—Ānanda then replied.
Subhūti always delights in speaking of the matter of emptiness and does not rejoice in speaking of existence.
Furthermore, at that time, Ānanda’s mind was inclined toward eloquent exposition; therefore, he listened to the answer.

Because Ānanda’s afflictions were not yet exhausted, his power of wisdom was dull; however, because his power of faith was fierce and sharp, he was able to engage in questions and answers regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with the Dharma.
Question: Since the Prajñāpāramitā is non-existent and there is no fixed dharma therein, why is it said that "four kinds of people believe and accept it, and do not say it is not the Dharma"?
The answer is:
Now, Subhūti himself explains the causal conditions herein:
"One does not differentiate form by means of emptiness; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form."
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is neither lost nor destroyed;
if it is not destroyed, there is no fault or transgression, and therefore it is not said to be non-dharma.

Emptiness is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). It is not by means of the wisdom of emptiness that one destroys form to make it empty, nor does emptiness exist because of the causal conditions of destroying form; for emptiness is form, and form is emptiness.
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* destroys all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and possesses such merits, there is no reason not to believe and accept it.
The same applies to signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), non-ceasing (*anirodha*), quiescence (*śānta*), and detachment (*vivikta*).
This should be explained in detail up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Question: Since the great disciples asked about this meaning, why did Subhūti answer the devaputras?
The answer is:
The great disciples have already attained arhatship; they asked their questions merely out of personal doubt, which provides little benefit.
The devaputras, however, have resolved their minds upon becoming bodhisattvas; because their benefit is profound, [the Buddha] speaks for them.
Furthermore, although he speaks for the sake of the devaputras, he is in fact answering the great disciples.
Previously, he spoke of the "emptiness of all dharmas"; now, he speaks of the "ultimate emptiness of sentient beings within the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
For this reason, within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no speaker, much less anyone who listens or receives it!
If one can understand in this way that all dharmas are empty, and the mind has no attachment, then one will be able to believe and accept it.
At that time, Subhūti was expounding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and Śāriputra praised and supported his endeavor, saying:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is not to be received merely because of emptiness; it also extensively explains the existence of the three vehicles."
The meaning of the three vehicles is as previously explained.
Regarding "embracing the bodhisattvas," it means that through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one benefits all bodhisattvas, causing them to attain growth.
Furthermore, "comprehension" refers to the ten stages within the Prajñāpāramitā, which cause a bodhisattva to proceed from one stage to the next, up to the tenth stage.
The meaning of the ten stages, from the six pāramitās up to the meaning of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), is as previously explained.
"Birth by transformation" refers to the retribution for practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, because one is unimpeded regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), one attains "swift eloquence" (*tīkṣṇapratibhāna*).
Although some may be swift, they cannot penetrate deeply due to dull faculties; because one can penetrate deeply, it is "sharp eloquence" (*tīkṣṇapratibhāna*).
Because the true nature of all phenomena is explained as being boundless and inexhaustible, it is called "the inexhaustible eloquence of joyful speech.
Because there is no conceptual proliferation within the Prajñā, there is no one capable of posing challenges or causing its interruption; thus, it is called "the indestructible eloquence."

Because one has severed craving for dharmas, one preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for sentient beings; this is called "analytical eloquence of suitability" (*anulomika-pratibhāna*).
Because one explains the matters that lead to nirvāṇa and bring about benefit, it is called "analytical eloquence of meaning" (*artha-pratibhāna*).
To speak of that which is the foremost thing in all worlds—namely, the Mahāyāna—is called "the supreme eloquence in the world.
Subhūti affirmed his question, saying: "So it is!"
"So be it! Śāriputra then had this thought:
"Subhūti always delights in speaking of emptiness; for what reason does he accept my exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā and its detailed teaching on the three vehicles?"
"There must be further causes and conditions.
Subhūti replied:
"Although the Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds the Three Vehicles, it does not possess fixed characteristics; rather, it is taught through the integration of the eighteen kinds of emptiness."
The same applies to the bodhisattva’s grasping and the seven kinds of eloquence, because of the wisdom of emptiness.

Chapter 29: The Chapter on Scattering Flowers From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on Scattering Flowers, Number Twenty-nine. [Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods from the Four Great Kings of the trichiliocosm up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven had this thought:

“The Venerable Subhūti is raining down the rain of Dharma; we should rather manifest flowers and scatter them over the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the assembly of bhikṣus, Subhūti, and the Prajñāpāramitā!”

Śakra Devānām Indra and the devas throughout the trichiliocosm manifested flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, the community of bhikṣus, and Subhūti, thereby making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā as well.
At that time, throughout the trichiliocosm, flowers completely filled the void of space, transforming into flower pedestals that were upright, majestic, and exquisite.
Subhūti thought to himself:
"These flowers scattered by the sons of the gods are such that I have never before seen their like in the heavens."
"These flowers are conjured flowers; they are not flowers produced from trees. These flowers scattered by the devaputras are born from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), not from ordinary trees.
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what Subhūti was thinking in his mind, said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!"
"These flowers are not born of flowers, nor are they born of the wish-fulfilling tree.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!..."
You say, "These flowers are not born flowers, nor are they produced from trees of the mind.
Kausika! If these are dharmas that are not born, they cannot be called flowers.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One,
is it only these flowers that are non-arisen?"
"Is form also unarisen?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also unarisen?
Subhūti replied:
“Kauśika! It is not only these flowers that are unarisen; form (*rūpa*) is also unarisen. If it is unarisen, it cannot be called ‘form.
Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) [are likewise].”
Consciousness also does not arise; if it does not arise, it cannot be called consciousness.
The same applies to the six sense bases, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, and the various feelings produced through the conditions of those six contacts.
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is non-arising; if it is non-arising, it is not called the perfection of giving.
This extends up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is non-arising; if it is non-arising, it is not called the perfection of wisdom.
Internal emptiness is non-arising; if it were not arising, it would not be called internal emptiness.
This extends up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is non-arising; if it were not arising, it would not be called the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
The four foundations of mindfulness do not arise; if they do not arise, they are not called the four foundations of mindfulness.
This extends up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which do not arise; if they do not arise, they are not called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Up to and including the non-arising of all-knowledge; if it does not arise, it is not called 'all-knowledge.
[Treatise] Commentary:
Śakra-devānām-indra and the various devas heard the meaning of Prajñāpāramitā as expounded by Subhūti.
All phenomena are entirely the true mark (dharmatā) and are without differentiation;
although emptiness is taught, it does not negate any phenomenon, nor does it cause one to lose the karmic retribution of various actions.
Because this śrāvaka was able to expound such profound Dharma in the presence of the Buddha, Śakra Devānām Indra and the others were all filled with joy and thought:
"The Dharma taught by Subhūti is unimpeded and without obstruction, just like seasonal rain."
Suppose there is a land where irrigation for sowing and planting, as well as various uses of water, are constantly plagued by insufficiency;
yet when the seasonal rains fall universally, there is no place they do not moisten and penetrate, and nothing that does not accord with one's wishes.

The Dharma of the Hīnayāna is also like this: at the beginning, it variously praises generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and contemplations such as impermanence—all of which are finite and limited—and only at the very end does it speak of nirvāṇa.

In this context, what Subhūti elucidates—from the first generation of the mind of awakening up to the path of Buddhahood—is exclusively the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, devoid of any conceptual differentiation.
It is like a great rain that completely fills Jambudvīpa, moistening everything without exception.
Furthermore, it is like the earth: although seeds may already exist within it, they will not sprout without rain.

It is the same for the practitioner: although the causes and conditions are present, if they do not obtain the rain of the Dharma, those who have resolved their minds will regress, and those who have not yet resolved them will remain stagnant;
if they do obtain the rain of the Dharma, those who have resolved their minds will increase in growth, and those who have not yet resolved them will resolve them.
For this reason, it is said that "it rains the rain of Dharma.
Furthermore, for example, just as foul winds, dust, various heats, poisonous vapors, and the like are extinguished when rain falls;

so too is it with the rain of Dharma: the dust of evil discursive thoughts, the three unwholesome poisons, the foul wind of false views, the evil insects of false teachers, and all evil associates are entirely eliminated upon encountering the rain of the *prajñāpāramitā* Dharma.
Because people receive the seasonal rain, they make offerings to the heavens;
likewise, the various devas, having heard the rain of the Dharma which brings great benefit, desiring to make offerings, formed this thought:
"We should rather create flowers and scatter them over the Buddha, the great Bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, and Subhūti, thereby also making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā."
Because Subhūti had skillfully expounded the *prajñāpāramitā*, and out of reverence and esteem for him, [the Buddha] specifically designated him as the recipient of offerings.

Since this *prajñāpāramitā* teaches that all phenomena are empty, and because he wished to receive the Dharma as one who is like a conjured being (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*), he made offerings of conjured flowers in accordance with that characteristic.

Furthermore, when the devas were filled with joy, they made offerings according to their hearts' desire; as they could not take back what they had given, they immediately created transformed flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, Subhūti, the various bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, and the Prajñāpāramitā. Scattering the flowers upon the Buddha was an offering to the Buddha Jewel;
scattering them upon the various bodhisattvas, Subhūti, and the Prajñāpāramitā was an offering to the Dharma Jewel;
and scattering them upon the community of bhikṣus was an offering to the Saṃgha Jewel.
Having formed this thought, they manifest transformations at will to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Because they have accomplished great merit, whatever wishes arise in their minds are all fulfilled according to their desires, without seeking them from others.
Question:
By whose power is the lotus pedestal so majestic? Answer:
This is due to the power of the devas.
Because the devas possess the sovereignty of merit, the small can become great. Some say:
"This is the Buddha’s spiritual power.

Because this *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such great merit—that the cause is brief while the retribution is exceedingly vast—and because it brings about the realization of the Buddha-way, he manifests this marvel."
Subhūti immediately discerned that these were not real flowers.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that Subhūti had realized they were conjured flowers, said to Subhūti:
"Virtuous One!..."
"These flowers are not born flowers.
As for "not born flowers," it means:
"These flowers are unarisen, empty, and have no point of emergence."
Subhūti preached this Prajñāpāramitā, which is the non-arising and empty stillness of all dharmas; therefore, he made an offering of non-arising flowers.
As for the "wish-fulfilling trees," whatever the devas conceive in their minds, they obtain it.
To state it briefly: the celestial trees appear according to one's wishes; they arrive as soon as they are thought of, and are therefore called "mind-trees" (*manoratha-vṛkṣa*).
Śakra Devānām Indra questioned Subhūti, saying: "These flowers are unarisen (*anutpanna*); why then do you say that these flowers do not arise from trees?"
Subhūti countered with a question:
"If it is not produced, why is it called a flower?
Within the dharma of non-arising, there is no conceptual differentiation—namely, that "this is a flower" or "this is not a flower."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, his mind subdued, asked:
"Is it only these flowers that are unarisen, or are all dharmas also unarisen?
Subhūti replied:
"It is not only that flowers do not arise, but form (*rūpa*) also does not arise. Why is this?
If one dharma is empty, then all dharmas are empty.
If a practitioner clearly and decisively realizes emptiness within a single dharma, then they will likewise clearly understand all dharmas.
If the five aggregates do not arise, they are not the characteristics of the five aggregates.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they have no fixed nature and exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
"The true mark of the provisional designation" refers to the suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the five aggregates.
What Subhūti has said does not contradict this principle;
why is this? Because the sages know that names and designations are conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), while the true nature of reality (dharmatā) is ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Whatever is spoken follows after ordinary persons; within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is neither "this" nor "that," nor is there any contention.
This applies even to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because sentient beings are empty, up to and including the knower and the seer, the *srotāpanna* has only a provisional name; this applies likewise even to a Buddha.
[Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"This Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; without destroying provisional names, he speaks of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."
The Buddha, knowing what Śakra Devānām Indra was thinking, said to him: "So it is! So it is!"
“Kauśika! Subhūti’s wisdom is profoundly deep; he explains the true nature of all phenomena without destroying conventional designations.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Subhūti, how is it that you do not destroy conventional designations while speaking of the true reality of all phenomena?
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
“Form is merely a conventional designation; Subhūti does not destroy conventional designations when he speaks of the true reality of all phenomena.”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely provisional designations; Subhūti, moreover, does not subvert these provisional designations when he speaks of the true reality of all phenomena. Why is this?
Because this true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is neither destroyed nor indestructible, what Subhūti has spoken is likewise neither destroyed nor indestructible.
It is the same for everything from the eye up to the feelings produced by the conditions of mental contact;

it is the same for the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); it is the same for inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); and it is the same for the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).

It is the same for the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a bodhisattva, the path of a buddha, as well as all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes.

From the stream-enterer up to the arhat, pratyekabuddha, and buddha—these are merely provisional designations. Subhūti, without destroying these provisional designations, speaks of the true reality of all dharmas.
Why is this? Because the true mark of all dharmas is neither destroyed nor indestructible;
and that which Subhūti has spoken is likewise neither destroyed nor indestructible.
"In this way, Kauśika,
Subhūti speaks of the true nature of all phenomena without destroying conventional designations.
Subhūti then said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"So it is! So it is, Kauśika!"
As the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are merely provisional designations, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand this:
that all phenomena are merely provisional designations; in this way, they should train in the prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train in form, nor do they train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is that?
Not seeing form as something to be learned, and not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as something to be learned—
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are training in the non-training of the dānapāramitā.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a dānapāramitā as something that should be learned;
and so on, up to not learning the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a Prajñāpāramitā that should be studied.
To study in this manner is to not study anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive an inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, as something that can be studied.
To study in this manner is to not study the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as something that should be learned.
To train in this manner is to not train for the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Why is this? Because one does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including all-knowledge, as something that can be learned.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
“For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not see form, and so on, up to not seeing all-knowledge?
Subhūti replied:
“Form is empty of form;”
Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), all-knowledge is empty. Kausika!
The emptiness of form does not train in the emptiness of form; up to and including the emptiness of all-knowledge, it does not train in the emptiness of all-knowledge.
“Kauśika! If one does not train in emptiness in this manner, it is called training in emptiness because of non-duality.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the emptiness of form because of non-duality;”
Up to and including the training in the emptiness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they are non-dual.

If one trains in the non-duality of the emptiness of form (*rūpa*), up to and including the training in the non-duality of the emptiness of all-knowledge, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in the non-duality of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), up to and including the ability to train in the non-duality of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);

they are able to train in the non-duality of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to and including the ability to train in the non-duality of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).
Because they can study the fruit of *srotāpanna* as non-dual, and so on, up to studying all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as non-dual,
these bodhisattvas are able to study the infinite, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddha-dharmas.

"If one can study the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddha-dharmas, this bodhisattva does not train for the sake of increasing form, nor does he train for the sake of decreasing form; and so on, up to not training for the sake of increasing all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor training for the sake of decreasing all-knowledge."

If one does not train for the sake of the increase or decrease of form, and so on, up to not training for the sake of the increase or decrease of the knowledge of all modes, then that bodhisattva does not train for the sake of the apprehension of form, nor does he train for the sake of its cessation;
likewise, he does not train for the sake of the apprehension of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor does he train for their cessation.
"Even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not train for the sake of grasping, nor does one train for the sake of extinguishing.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not train for the sake of grasping form, nor does he train for the sake of extinguishing form; even up to the knowledge of all modes, he does not train for the sake of grasping, nor does he train for the sake of extinguishing?"
Subhūti said:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not train for the sake of grasping form, nor do they train for the sake of extinguishing form; and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes, they neither train for the sake of grasping it, nor do they train for the sake of extinguishing it."

“Subhūti! For what reason and by what causal conditions does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train for the sake of grasping form, nor train for the sake of extinguishing form, and so on, up to and including not training for the sake of grasping all-knowledge, nor training for the sake of extinguishing it?”

Subhūti said: "This form is not to be grasped, nor is there anyone who grasps form; even up to the knowledge of all modes, it is not to be grasped, nor is there anyone who grasps it, because of the emptiness of the internal and external."
"In this way, Śāriputra,
because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any phenomena, they are able to reach all-knowledge.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“Can a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Subhūti replied:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way can reach all-knowledge, because they do not grasp at any dharma.”
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains by neither grasping nor extinguishing any phenomena, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva reach the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti said: “When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the arising of form, nor do they perceive the cessation of form;

they do not perceive the acceptance of form, nor do they perceive the non-acceptance of form; they do not perceive the defilement of form, nor do they perceive the purification of form; they do not perceive the increase of form, nor do they perceive the decrease of form.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form.
Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as well:

one does not perceive their arising, nor does one perceive their cessation; one does not perceive them as being grasped, nor does one perceive them as not being grasped; one does not perceive them as defiled, nor does one perceive them as pure; one does not perceive them as increasing, nor does one perceive them as decreasing.
Why is this? Because consciousness is empty of the nature of consciousness.

This extends even to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is neither seen to arise nor seen to cease; it is neither seen to be received nor seen not to be received; it is neither seen as defiled nor seen as pure; and it is neither seen to increase nor seen to decrease.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge is empty of the nature of all-knowledge.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

Because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither grasped nor relinquished, neither defiled nor pure, neither conjoined nor dispersed, and neither increasing nor decreasing, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and is able to reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), for there is nothing to be studied and no destination to be reached.
[Treatise] Commentary: Śakra Devānām Indra said with joy:
"Subhūti’s wisdom is exceedingly profound; he explains the true mark of all dharmas without destroying conventional designations."
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as Śakra has said. He asked:
"For what reason does the Buddha praise Subhūti?"
Answer: This is shown so that the teacher does not become self-exalting, because the disciple receives and follows the teacher’s Dharma.
There are those who do not accept what their teacher says; [to prevent this, the teacher must not be self-exalting].
When a disciple speaks and the teacher does not listen,
it is like an ordinary person who, when preaching the Dharma in a crowd, has all their words rejected.
Because the Buddha is free from the notion of a self, he praised Subhūti, saying:
"So it is! So it is! Furthermore, out of great compassion, the Buddha, wishing to cause sentient beings to have faith and accept what Subhūti had said, praised him, saying:
"His wisdom is exceedingly profound.
When a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are merely provisional names, he should then train in the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this so?
All dharmas possess only provisional names, for they all accord with the mark of ultimate emptiness of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding the statement, "Learning in this way, one does not learn form": within these provisionally named dharmas, there is no fixed form; if there is no form, how could one "learn form"?
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva seeks form with the five eyes, they do not perceive that form as having the characteristic of a self or the characteristic of non-self;
and so it is for everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding the question, "For what reason is form not seen? the answer is:
within form, the characteristic of form is empty; because it cannot be apprehended, it cannot be seen. This is precisely the emptiness of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, regarding "not training in form": since the emptiness of form cannot itself train in the emptiness of form—because all dharmas operate through other-characteristics (*paralakṣaṇa*) and not through their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)—it is like a person riding a horse;
it is not the horse that rides the horse.
Question:
If one does not train in all dharmas in this manner, how can one "train in omniscience"? Answer:
In this regard, it is said:
"If one can have no attachment to the emptiness of all phenomena, this is truly learning the emptiness of form.
If one is attached to emptiness itself, one is destroying all phenomena while failing to destroy [the attachment to] emptiness.

If a person breaks through form (*rūpa*) yet does not cling to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then form and emptiness are neither two nor distinct; this is what it means to be able to study the emptiness of form, for by means of the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), one does not perceive emptiness.
It is the same for everything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"The immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddha-dharmas" is a praise of all-knowledge.
The aforementioned "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā) is finite and limited within the mind of a bodhisattva, whereas within the mind of a Buddha it is immeasurable and limitless.
For this reason, although it was previously stated that one studies the Buddha-dharma, it is now explained separately once more.
If one can train in this way, practicing the bodhisattva path correctly, one trains in the form-element without increase or decrease.
Regarding "without increase": if one perceives only the body as a composite formed by the four great elements and derived matter, then no attachment arises.

To give rise to notions of male and female, beauty and ugliness, long and short within this very body, and to regard them as fixed and real, thereby producing a mind of defiled attachment—this is "increase" (*ādhika*).
If one destroys form to make it empty and the mind becomes attached to this emptiness, this is "diminution.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding "neither accepting nor extinguishing": because it is empty, it is "not accepted."
Because the continuity of the causal conditions of karmic fruit does not cease, it is said to be "unextinguished.
Regarding this, Subhūti himself explains the causal conditions:
"Because form and sensation cannot be apprehended, one does not grasp them."
Furthermore, because form is empty internally and externally, one "does not accept" it; because the emptiness of the internal and external within form is itself empty, one "does not extinguish" it.
Question:
One should employ the eighteen kinds of emptiness to empty all dharmas; why, then, is only "internal and external emptiness" mentioned here?
Answer: Because there is no one who experiences form, it is called "internal emptiness"; because form cannot be experienced, it is called "external emptiness.
These internal and external emptinesses encompass the emptiness of all phenomena.
This applies even unto all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If a bodhisattva can train in this way, they will give birth to all-knowledge.

All-knowledge is characterized by non-obstruction; if a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being like space and without obstruction, they are training in all-knowledge, because cause and effect correspond to one another.
Śāriputra had this thought:
"The Dharma of a bodhisattva should extinguish all afflictions and should receive all wholesome dharmas;
yet now, he neither receives nor extinguishes them while training—how then will he emerge and reach omniscience (sarvajñatā)?"
Having formed this thought, he questioned Subhūti.
Subhūti replied:
"Because one destroys the characteristic of arising in all phenomena, they do not arise; because one destroys the characteristic of impermanence in all phenomena, they do not cease."
One does not accept because one contemplates the various faults and transgressions of all phenomena; one does not reject because one contemplates the various benefits of all phenomena.
All phenomena are undefiled because their nature is eternally pure; all phenomena are impure because they can give rise to a mind of attachment.

Although all phenomena involve conditioned and unconditioned activity, arising and ceasing, entering and exiting, coming and going, and so forth, they neither increase nor decrease, neither multiply nor diminish.
For example, the great ocean does not increase when all streams flow into it, nor does it decrease when heated by fire-jewels;
all phenomena are likewise so, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena is unattainable.

If one can train in this way, one will emerge and arrive at sarvajñā (all-knowledge), yet one does not perceive the mark of training, nor the mark of emergence, nor the mark of a bodhisattva, nor the mark of the prajñāpāramitā.
In this context, because it is stated briefly, it is said only that "there is no further training and no emergence.
[Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:
"Where should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?"
Śāriputra said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be sought within the Subhūti-parivarta.
Śakra-devānām-indra then spoke to Subhūti:
"Is it by your supernatural power that you caused Śāriputra to say, 'The Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be sought within the Subhūti Chapter'?"
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"It is not through my supernatural power.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
“By whose spiritual power? Subhūti replied,
“It is by the Buddha’s spiritual power.”
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"All dharmas are without a locus of reception; why then do you say this is the Buddha’s spiritual power?
Apart from the characteristic of being without a locus of reception, a Tathāgata cannot be apprehended."
"Apart from suchness, the Tathāgata also cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "It is so!"
"So it is, Kauśika!
Apart from the characteristic of being without a basis for apprehension, the Tathāgata cannot be found."
Apart from suchness, the Tathāgata also cannot be apprehended.
Within the characteristic of being without a locus for reception, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended; within suchness, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended.
Within the suchness of form, the suchness of the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended; within the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of form cannot be apprehended.

Within the characteristic of form-dharmas, the characteristic of the Tathāgata-dharma cannot be apprehended; within the characteristic of the Tathāgata-dharma, the characteristic of form-dharmas cannot be apprehended.
This is likewise true for the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Kauśika! The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the suchness of form; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The Tathāgata is free from the suchness of form, neither conjoined nor disjoined with it; he is free from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, neither conjoined nor disjoined with them.”
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the characteristic of form (*rūpa-dharmalakṣaṇa*); he is neither conjoined nor disjoined within the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-dharmalakṣaṇa*).

The Tathāgata is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the characteristic of form; he is neither conjoined nor disjoined apart from the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Kauśika!
Within all such dharmas, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion; this is the spiritual power of the Buddha, because he employs the dharma of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
"As Kauśika has said:
'Where should one seek the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva? Kauśika!..."
One should not seek the perfection of wisdom within form, nor should one seek the perfection of wisdom apart from form;
one should not seek it within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should one seek it apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all these dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
One should not seek the perfection of wisdom within all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor should one seek the perfection of wisdom apart from all-knowledge.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā and all-knowledge—these all dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without form, without shape, and without resistance; they have but one characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Why is this? The perfection of wisdom is not form, nor is it apart from form; it is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
and so on, up to: it is not the knowledge of all modes, nor is it apart from the knowledge of all modes.

The perfection of wisdom is not the suchness of form, nor is it apart from the suchness of form; it is not the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

The perfection of wisdom is not the dharma of form, nor is it apart from the dharma of form; it is not the dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it apart from the dharmas of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Even the suchness of all-knowledge is not [the Prajñāpāramitā], nor is it apart from the suchness of all-knowledge;
the Prajñāpāramitā is neither the dharma of all-knowledge, nor is it apart from the dharma of all-knowledge.
Why is this so? Kauśika!

All these dharmas are non-existent and unattainable; because they are non-existent and unattainable, the prajñāpāramitā is neither form nor apart from form, neither the suchness of form nor apart from the suchness of form, and neither the dharma of form nor apart from the dharma of form.

It is neither omniscience nor apart from omniscience; it is neither the suchness of omniscience nor apart from the suchness of omniscience; it is neither the dharma of omniscience nor apart from the dharma of omniscience.
[Treatise] Question:

The Buddha, Śāriputra, and Subhūti have, through various causes and conditions above, elucidated the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why does Śakra, Lord of Devas, now ask, "Where should one seek the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The answer is:
This does not inquire into the essence of *prajñā*, but rather asks about the matter of the names and words of *prajñā* that can be recited; for this reason, Śāriputra said:
"One should seek it within the chapter spoken by Subhūti."
Subhūti delights in expounding emptiness because he has constantly and skillfully cultivated emptiness;
although Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom, because he is free from the mind of self and envy and has severed attachment to dharmas, he says, "One should seek it within the chapter spoken by Subhūti."
Question:

The Buddha has taught the *prajñāpāramitā* in many places. If one were to compare it with what Subhūti has taught, it would be hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater, beyond calculation or analogy. Why, then, does he not say, "Seek it within the chapters spoken by the Buddha"?
The answer is:
Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself,
"Aside from the Buddha alone, who else is capable of explaining this well?"
For this reason, Subhūti was appointed.

Furthermore, the Buddha constantly observes sentient beings with his Buddha-eye six times throughout each day and night, so that none may fall away for failing to hear the Dharma; therefore, he teaches according to what each sentient being should understand, what they should attain, and what they should practice.
Sometimes it is taught that the *prajñāpāramitā* is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, being like a disease or an abscess, and this is called "the *prajñāpāramitā*";

sometimes it analyzes the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, or explains that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, having no agent or experiencer, and no knower or seer, and this is called "the *prajñāpāramitā*";
and at other times it teaches the emptiness of phenomena or ultimate emptiness, and this is called "the *prajñāpāramitā*."
For this reason, it is not said that "one seeks [it] within the 'Chapter on What Was Spoken by the Buddha'.
Furthermore, Śakra-devānām-indra thought to himself:
"I do not know which of these is truly the definitive characteristic of prajñā-pāramitā?"
Therefore, Śāriputra said:
“Subhūti constantly enters deeply into emptiness; all that he speaks tends toward emptiness, and even the emptiness he speaks of is itself empty.
For this reason, it is said: ‘One should seek [this] within the chapter spoken by Subhūti.’”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was filled with joy and praised Subhūti, saying:
"The great virtue’s spiritual power is truly immense!
Subhūti replied with humility:
"This is not my power; it is the supernatural power received from the Buddha.
Śakra Devānām-Indra said, "If all dharmas are entirely without that which is received, how can you say this is the supernatural power received from the Buddha?"
"If one is apart from the characteristic of non-apprehension, the Tathāgata cannot be found;
within the apartness of suchness, the Tathāgata cannot be found.
Śakra Devānām Indra then had this thought:
"All dharmas are without the characteristic of appropriation; all dharmas are empty and have no place of reliance. How then can one say that a Tathāgata definitely exists?
If there were no Tathāgata, how could there be any supernatural power to be appropriated?"
Furthermore, apart from the characteristic of non-apprehension, the Tathāgata is likewise unobtainable;
now, apart from this suchness (tathatā), the Tathāgata is unobtainable. He asked:
What is the difference between the characteristic of non-appropriation (*anupādāna-lakṣaṇa*) and suchness (*tathatā*)?
The answer is:
the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is also called non-appropriation and is also called suchness.
Among all phenomena, one cannot become attached; therefore, they are called "without grasping.
They cannot be destroyed by any conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, they are called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Now, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended within emptiness, nor can he be apprehended apart from emptiness.
Subhūti agreed with his words, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
Now, Subhūti explains this matter at length:

"In the mark of non-apprehension and in suchness, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended" means that one may designate the Buddha by the name 'Tathāgata,' or one may designate a sentient being by the name 'Tathāgata.'
As it came from a previous life, so it likewise goes to a future life; this is called the Tathāgata, and it is also called the Tathāgata-gone.
As stated in the "Fourteen Unanswered Questions":
"Regarding one who has gone after death, does he exist?"
Is it non-existent?
Is it both existent and non-existent?
Or is it neither existent nor non-existent?

Regarding the name "Tathāgata" given to the Buddha: just as Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others practiced the six pāramitās and attained the Way of the Buddha, Śākyamuni Buddha likewise came [to this state]; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Just as Dīpaṃkara Buddha and others, through their wisdom, know the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena and come from within that suchness, they are therefore called Tathāgatas;
Śākyamuni Buddha likewise comes in this manner, and is therefore called a Tathāgata.
Between these two kinds of Tathāgatas, it is here said that this refers to the Buddha-Tathāgata.
Because one understands that the Buddha-Tathāgata is non-existent, all sentient beings and all phenomena are likewise non-existent.
The meaning of "non-appropriation" and "Tathāgata" is as previously explained.
Now it shall be further explained briefly:
the characteristic of non-appropriation and the characteristic of the Tathāgata are both empty and non-existent.
Because there is no characteristic of grasping and no suchness, and because there is no fixed nature, there is no Tathāgata.
Some say: There are two ways of explaining the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:
First, the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) is real; second,

some say that because ultimate emptiness can be demonstrated and explained, it is not real, whereas the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*— which cannot be demonstrated and cannot be explained— is what is called real.
Regarding these two matters, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended within ultimate emptiness; nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended within the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that negates ultimate emptiness.
Ultimate emptiness is itself the characteristic of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*); the true mark that negates ultimate emptiness is itself Suchness (*tathatā*).
From this point onward, the two meanings are explained in detail.
Within the five aggregates up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended;
since the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, how could there be the supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) of a Tathāgata?
The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, as explained above.

These five aggregates are not the Tathāgata; apart from the five aggregates there is no Tathāgata; the five aggregates do not exist within the Tathāgata, nor does the Tathāgata exist within the five aggregates; furthermore, the Tathāgata does not possess the five aggregates.
Because the five aggregates are characterized by arising and ceasing, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, they are not the Tathāgata;
if they were the Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata would also be subject to arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, the five aggregates are five dharmas, while the Tathāgata is one. How can five dharmas constitute one?
If the five were identical to the one, then the one should likewise be identical to the five;
if that were so, all worldly and supramundane dharmas would fall into total confusion and ruin!
For these various reasons, the five aggregates are not the Tathāgata.

If the Tathāgata were to exist apart from the five aggregates, the Tathāgata would be without seeing, without hearing, without knowing, and without cognizing, nor would he experience pleasure or pain.
Why is this so? Because perception and the others are the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Question:
If it is said that the Tathāgata is able to know and see by means of the eyes, ears, wisdom, and so forth, what fault is there in this?
The answer is:
that which is able to see is the eye; it is not the Tathāgata.

If the Tathāgata were to see by means of the faculty of sight that does not possess the characteristic of seeing, then before an object has been apprehended, how could one know that it is this eye being used?
Furthermore, one might as well be able to see with the ear!
Question:
The Tathāgata, through the discernment of wisdom, knows that the eye is capable of seeing while the others are not; for this reason, he employs the eye and does not take up the other faculties.
The answer is:
Knowledge is also subject to the same faults as the eye; knowledge consists of the five aggregates and is not the Tathāgata.
If one uses knowledge to know the eye, then by what means can one know this very knowledge?
Question:
The Tathāgata uses knowledge to know the eye, and with the eye he knows forms;
if one wishes to know the Tathāgata, by what means can he be known?
If one were to know the Tathāgata by means of the Tathāgata, this would lead to an infinite regress.
The answer is:
knowledge abides within the characteristic of knowing.
If the Tathāgata were to know, that would be a characteristic of knowing;
if it were a characteristic of knowing, then he would be impermanent;
and if he were impermanent, there would be no future life!

Furthermore, if there were a Tathāgata existing apart from the five aggregates, the Tathāgata would be eternal; like the nature of space, he should not undergo transformation, nor experience suffering or pleasure, and he should likewise be neither bound nor liberated. Such would be the faults and transgressions [of this view].
Because their difference is refuted, the five aggregates do not exist in the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not exist in the five aggregates, nor does the Tathāgata possess the five aggregates.
Question:
It must be because of the causal conditions of the five aggregates that the Tathāgata exists.
If there were no five aggregates, then there would be no Tathāgata.
The answer is:
if the Tathāgata exists by means of the causes and conditions of the five aggregates, then the Tathāgata lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there is no intrinsic nature, how could it arise from another nature?
Within the five aggregates, the Tathāgata cannot be found through these fivefold searches; therefore, there is no Tathāgata.
It is only because of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that one speaks of a Tathāgata;
because conceptual proliferation has been severed, there is no Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is a phenomenon that is neither born nor extinguished; how, then, could one seek the Tathāgata through conceptual proliferation?
If one seeks the Tathāgata through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then one does not see the Tathāgata.
If one were to hold that the Tathāgata is utterly non-existent, then one falls into false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, if one seeks the Tathāgata through the conceptual proliferations of existence or non-existence, this is not the case.
The marks of the Tathāgata are the marks of all dharmas; the marks of all dharmas are the marks of the Tathāgata.
The marks of the Tathāgata are the marks of ultimate emptiness; the marks of ultimate emptiness are the marks of all dharmas.

Question: Why is it that here only these two matters are mentioned, stating: "Within the suchness of the five aggregates there is no suchness of the Tathāgata; within the suchness of the Tathāgata there is no suchness of the five aggregates"?
Answer: This is a brief explanation;
by mentioning two, all five matters are fully encompassed.
Furthermore, although the twenty kinds of self-view exist in all ordinary persons, they cannot arise simultaneously.
Now, within this assembly, these two matters may be present; for this reason, only these two matters are discussed.
As it is with the five aggregates, so it is with everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is likewise with the dharma-characteristics of the five aggregates, up to the dharma-characteristics of all-knowledge.
The suchness of the five aggregates is itself the characteristic of dharmas.
Question: If suchness is itself the characteristic of dharmas, why is it stated again?
Answer:
When the practitioner reaches the suchness of the five aggregates, their mind is startled, wondering how it is that the characteristics of dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent!
Therefore, it is said that the characteristics of the dharmas of the five aggregates are inherently so.
It is like a person who touches fire and has their hand burned; they feel no resentment because the nature of fire is inherently such.
However, if someone intentionally grasps fire and burns them, they become indignant and angry because of that deliberate act of grasping the fire to burn them.

Regarding the statement, “In the suchness of the Tathāgata’s five aggregates, and within the dharma-characteristics of the five aggregates, there is neither conjunction nor dispersion”: apart from the suchness of the five aggregates, there is no Tathāgata; this is the single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of non-existence (animitta).
Why is this? Because a single dharma has neither conjunction nor dispersion; it is because of two dharmas that there is conjunction and dispersion.
Apart from the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is likewise neither conjunction nor dispersion.
Why is this? Because apart from the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended.

The suchness (*tathatā*) and the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata and the suchness and the characteristic of phenomena of the five aggregates are non-dual and without distinction; therefore, it is said:
“Detached from the suchness of the five aggregates and the dharma-characteristics of the five aggregates, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
This applies even unto all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because one can thus know that the suchness and dharma-characteristics of all dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed, one possesses this supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*).

Regarding the question, "Where should one seek [it]?"—whereas previously the characteristics of *prajñā* were explained by means of the Buddha’s supernatural power, here it is directly stated how one should seek *prajñā*.
The commentator says:

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are deceptive and impermanent; they are originally non-existent and now exist, having existed they return to non-existence; they are like an illusion and like a dream.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the true wisdom of all Buddhas; how could it be sought among the five aggregates?
It is like seeking a precious treasure: one must seek it in the great ocean or among the mountains of jewels, and not in ditches or foul, filthy places.
Apart from the five aggregates, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither formation nor origination, and no dharma-characteristic; how, then, can anything be sought therein?

Furthermore, the five aggregates and the *prajñāpāramitā* are neither identical nor different, neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, and without resistance—possessing a single characteristic, namely, "the absence of characteristics" (*animitta*).
Question:
Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is a mental factor (*citta-saṃskāra-dharma*) of wisdom, it should be formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive;
yet among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how can the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) be said to be shapeless and non-obstructive?
Answer:
The Sage observes all phenomena with the eye of wisdom as equal, empty, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of non-characteristic;
for this reason, the aggregate of form is without shape and without resistance.
Furthermore, the forms perceived by ordinary persons are not real; their various aspects have already been refuted as before.
Furthermore, there is a reason why the Prajñāpāramitā is not identical to the five aggregates as perceived by ordinary persons:
because it refutes the five aggregates as perceived by ordinary persons, it is indeed the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, it is said that they are not separate.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*),
as previously explained regarding the characteristic of suchness and the characteristic of the dharma-characteristic.
[Sūtra] Śakra Devānām-indra said to Subhūti:
"This is the great pāramitā; this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva!
This is the immeasurable pāramitā, the boundless pāramitā; this is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva!"
All *srotāpannas* and the fruit of *srotāpatti* are accomplished through training in this *prajñāpāramitā*;

likewise, all *arhats* and the fruit of *arhatship*, all *pratyekabuddhas* and the path of *pratyekabuddhahood*, and all *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* are accomplished through training in this *prajñāpāramitā*.
The maturation of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-fields, and the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are all accomplished through training in this.
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
Kauśika! This great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva!
This immeasurable pāramitā, this boundless pāramitā, is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
From within this, one trains to realize the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*, the path of the *pratyekabuddha*, and the various *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas*;

from within this *prajñāpāramitā*, one trains to accomplish the maturation of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-fields, and the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—those who have attained it, those who are attaining it now, and those who will attain it in the future.
“Kauśika! Because form is great, the Prajñāpāramitā is also great. Why is this?
This form cannot be apprehended at its prior limit, cannot be apprehended at its posterior limit, and cannot be apprehended in its middle limit.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are great, the Prajñāpāramitā is also great.
Why is this? Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended in the past, cannot be apprehended in the future, and cannot be apprehended in the present.
This applies even unto all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
For these reasons, Kauśika,
this great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Kauśika!"
Because form is immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the measure of form cannot be apprehended.
Kauśika! Just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so too the measure of form cannot be apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, form is immeasurable.
Because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the measure of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended.
Just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so too the measure of all-knowledge cannot be apprehended.
Because space is immeasurable, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is immeasurable;
because all-knowledge is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is immeasurable.
For these reasons, this perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is immeasurable.
“Kauśika! Because form is infinite, the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is infinite. Why is this?
Kauśika! The prior limit of form cannot be apprehended, the posterior limit cannot be apprehended, and the middle limit cannot be apprehended.
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Why is this? Because the past limit, the future limit, and the middle limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable.
Furthermore, because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is boundless.
Why is this? Because the past, future, and middle limits of all-knowledge are unapprehendable.
For this reason, Kauśika!
This Prajñāpāramitā is boundless;
form is boundless, and so on, up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) being boundless.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
“Because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
“Subhūti, why is it that because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless?”
Subhūti said: “Because it takes all boundless phenomena as its object, the *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless. [The Buddha asked:
“In what way does the *prajñāpāramitā* become boundless by taking all boundless phenomena as its object?”
Subhūti said: "Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is boundless.
Furthermore, Kauśika!..."
“Because suchness is boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked:
“In what way is it that because suchness is boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless?”
Subhūti said: "Because suchness is boundless, conditions are also boundless;
because conditions are boundless, suchness is also boundless."
For these reasons, the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is boundless.
Furthermore, Kauśika,
because sentient beings are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"In what way is it that because sentient beings are limitless, the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless?
Subhūti replied:
"What do you think?
What dharma is called 'sentient being'?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"There is no dharma that is called a 'sentient being'; it is only by way of conventional designation that one speaks of a 'sentient being.
This name originally has no corresponding dharma, nor does it have any objective referent; it is merely a name applied by force."
“Kauśika! What do you think?
In this Prajñāpāramitā, is it said that sentient beings exist as real entities?”
Śakra Devānām Indra said, "No, indeed! "Kauśika!
If, within the Prajñāpāramitā, it is truly not taught that sentient beings are infinite and cannot be apprehended,
Kausika, what do you think?

“If the Buddha were to speak for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges of sentient beings and the names of sentient beings, would there be any dharma among those sentient beings that has arising or cessation?
Śakra Devānām-Indra replied, “No!”
Why is this? Because sentient beings have been eternally pure from the very beginning. For these reasons, Kauśika!
"Because sentient beings are boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
[Śāstra] Question: Śakra Devānām Indra is a person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna; how is it that he is able to inquire about the profound Prajñāpāramitā?
The answer is:
Subhūti, though he is a fully accomplished arhat, asks about the deeds performed by bodhisattvas because he seeks to benefit bodhisattvas and out of compassion for sentient beings.
Although Śakra Devānām Indra is a śrāvaka, he is the lord of all devas; because he possesses sharp wisdom and compassion for sentient beings, his inquiry regarding the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so.
Furthermore, some say:
"Within a trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Śakra-devānām-indras.
The Śakra-devānām-indra mentioned in the *Madhyama Āgama* as having attained the stage of srotāpanna is distinct from the Śakra-devānām-indra of the present."

Now Śakra Devānām Indra is a great bodhisattva; out of compassion for sentient beings, he praises the prajñāpāramitā in three ways—namely, as the mahāpāramitā, the apramāṇapāramitā, and the anantapāramitā—which is this very prajñāpāramitā.
It is because within this prajñāpāramitā one trains and accomplishes all the noble paths.
Subhūti then assented to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and extensively explained the meaning of his praise:
"Because the five aggregates are great, the Prajñāpāramitā is great."
The "greatness of the five aggregates" refers to the fact that they cannot be apprehended across the three periods of time.
Furthermore, they are called "great" because they are immeasurable and boundless.
By shattering these immeasurable and boundless five aggregates and leading all sentient beings into *nirvāṇa* without remainder, it is called the "greatness of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
It is the same for everything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) is likewise; however, it differs in that it uses space as a metaphor.
Although some phenomena may be great, they are not necessarily immeasurable; therefore, space cannot be used as a metaphor for them.

Just as Mount Sumeru, though the greatest among all mountains, is finite—measuring eighty-four thousand *yojanas*—"boundless" (*ananta*) refers to the fact that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are vast and immeasurable; thus they are called "boundless.

Furthermore, if the five aggregates were finite, they would have a beginning; having a beginning implies having an end, which would entail the fallacies of being without cause or condition, such as falling into the view of annihilationism and other such errors.
Furthermore, because the five aggregates cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time, they are said to be "boundless.
Regarding "conditions being boundless," this refers to the four conditions of all phenomena: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which gives rise to all conditioned phenomena;
[the object condition, the dominant condition, and the immediate condition].
The sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) consists of past and present mental states and their associated mental factors;
the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) consist of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Since these four types of conditions exist in all places and at all times, they are said to be "boundless conditions."
Because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Furthermore, "conditions are boundless" means that the four types of conditions are deceptive and lack substantial reality; because they are ultimately empty, they are boundless.
Furthermore, because the *tathatā* (suchness), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), and *bhūtakoṭi* (reality-limit) are boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless.
Because "suchness," "dharma-nature," and "reality-limit" are the marks of spontaneous unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*), they are immeasurable and boundless;
whereas the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are boundless only through the power of contemplation, being made boundless by force of effort.
Furthermore, regarding "sentient beings are infinite":

because sentient beings are so numerous, and because no one can know the number of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions across immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, they are said to be "infinite."
Furthermore, because it is taught therein that sentient beings are empty, it says "boundless"; this is merely a name applied by force.
As for the phrase "there is nowhere to go," it is because sentient beings have no fixed dharma toward which they can proceed;
whereas fire has a definite destination, the name "sentient being" refers to nothing real that can be reached.
"What do you think? Is it taught in the Prajñāpāramitā that there is any truly existent sentient being?
"No, Venerable Sir!"
"If sentient beings do not truly exist, how can there be limits?

For example, the Buddhas are the foremost among those who speak the truth; even if they were to speak the names of sentient beings for a lifespan as long as immeasurable Ganges-sands of kalpas, the nature of these sentient beings would not undergo birth or cessation because of such speaking. How much less so, then, could it be through the brief, inverted, and false speech of others!
Because the thought of "sentient beings" arises, there must be sentient beings.

These sentient beings are not said to be "non-existent" because they have not entered into the *prajñāpāramitā*; rather, from the very beginning they have been eternally pure and non-existent, for all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) regarding existence and non-existence have been extinguished.
Therefore it is said:
"Because sentient beings are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
A question is asked:
Question: Why is "boundless" (*ananta*) explained in detail, while "great" (*mahat*) and "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) are explained only briefly? Answer:

Because of the causal conditions of sentient beings, all ordinary persons give rise to various afflictions and commit various perverse actions within the five aggregates; because these are difficult to destroy, they are explained in detail.
If the mark of a sentient being is destroyed, all other [marks] are easily destroyed.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 55;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the "Looking Around" Chapter (Rugui-pin), Chapter 30, Scroll 56.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

Chapter 30: Looking Back and Surveying. [Sūtra] At that time, the various heavenly kings and their gods, the various Brahmā kings and their Brahmā gods, the Īśāna gods and the divine seers, together with all the goddesses, simultaneously extolled [the Buddha] three times:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!
All that the Venerable Subhūti has taught is through the causal conditions and the power of grace of the Buddha’s appearance in the world; he has thus expounded and disseminated this teaching."
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this prajñāpāramitā without departing from it, we regard such a person as a Buddha. Why is this?

Within this Prajñāpāramitā, although no dharma can be apprehended—be it form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, or even the knowledge of all modes—there nevertheless exist the teachings of the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha vehicle.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras: "So it is! So it is!"
O sons of the gods!

As you have said, although within this Prajñāpāramitā no dharma can be apprehended, there are nevertheless the teachings of the three vehicles, namely: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle.
"O sons of the gods!
If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this prajñāpāramitā without being separated from it, one should regard such a person as a Buddha, because of the principle of non-apprehension."
