Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded—namely, the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Buddha vehicles.
Within the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), a Buddha cannot be found; apart from the perfection of giving, a Buddha likewise cannot be found.
This extends even to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): within the perfection of wisdom, a Buddha cannot be found; apart from the perfection of wisdom, a Buddha likewise cannot be found.
"It is the same for inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, for the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and for all-knowledge.
The Buddha said to the devaputras:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in all these dharmas—namely, from the dānapāramitā up to all-knowledge—for this reason, one should regard this bodhisattva mahāsattva as a Buddha."
"O sons of the gods!

In the past, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, within the city of Puṣpāvatī at a crossroads, I saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma. Immediately, I attained non-separation from the practice of the dāna-pāramitā, and non-separation from the practices of śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā;

non-separation from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā); and non-separation from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."
They do not depart from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, all gateways of samādhi, and all gateways of dhāraṇī;

nor do they depart from the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four unimpeded knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and other immeasurable practices of the Buddha-dharma, because there is nothing to be attained therein.

At that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha prophesied to me: "In a future age, after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa has passed, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
At that time, the sons of the gods addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is rare!"

This Prajñāpāramitā enables all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), because they neither grasp nor reject form; because they neither grasp nor reject feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to neither grasping nor rejecting the knowledge of all modes.
[Treatise] Commentary:
When people reach the height of joy, they express their praise three times.
Therefore, when the devas heard the Venerable Subhūti preach the Prajñāpāramitā, they spoke with joy:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!

As for "Heavenly Kings," this refers to the Four Heavenly Kings in the realm of the four kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Heavenly King of the Thirty-three, and even up to the various Brahmā Heavenly Kings.
Above the Brahmā heavens, there are no further kings.
"The various devas" refers to the devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"The various Brahmās" refers to the devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
“Iśāna” refers to the Great Lord Maheśvara and his retinue.
As for “sages” (ṛṣi), there are two kinds:
either devas or humans.
Regarding the "celestial maidens," these are the celestial maidens such as Śacī, the consort of Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
The reason they extol Subhūti’s exposition of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is that they know he does so by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If one can practice this Prajñāpāramitā, we shall regard such a person as a Buddha.
Why is this? Because we revere the Dharma.
The Dharma refers to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
As for the profound Dharma: although all phenomena are ultimately empty, there is still the differentiation of the three vehicles.
Why is this so? If all dharmas were ultimately empty, one should not further cultivate and accumulate the merits of the three vehicles, for that would fall into the view of annihilationism;
yet if one cultivates the merits of the three vehicles, that constitutes a discrimination of distinctions and gradations, which should not be ultimate emptiness.

This Prajñāpāramitā, though ultimately empty, does not fall into nihilism; though it distinguishes the three vehicles, it gives rise to no mind of attachment, and between these two matters, it does not grasp at fixed characteristics.
This matter is profoundly deep and subtle; therefore, the devas were greatly delighted and exclaimed, "How wonderful!
The Buddha affirmed their praise and further explained the profound causes and conditions:
“From the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), a Buddha cannot be apprehended;
apart from these, a Buddha likewise cannot be apprehended.
It is through the causal conditions of the conjunction of all dharmas that there is a Buddha, and he possesses no intrinsic nature (svabhāva).”
If a bodhisattva can practice in this manner, one should know that this bodhisattva is indeed a Buddha.
To say "he is indeed a Buddha" is a conventional expression used within the world;
it is like a crown prince who, though not yet formally enthroned, will certainly become the king.
In this regard, the Buddha himself cites a past event as proof:
this bodhisattva has already attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), entered the rank of bodhisattvas, and beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Having heard the Buddha’s extensive elucidation of the meaning they had previously praised, the minds of the various devas became even more profound in their understanding, and they again offered praise.
Because they saw the faults and transgressions inherent in all phenomena, they did not grasp them; because they saw their beneficial utility, they did not abandon them.
Furthermore, because all phenomena are ultimately empty and neither arise nor cease, they neither grasp nor abandon them.

[Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha surveyed the fourfold assembly—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, all of whom were seated together in the assembly.
Having observed them all, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, or any sons of gods or daughters of gods—whoever hears, receives, maintains, approaches, reads, recites, explains to others, and correctly contemplates this Prajñāpāramitā, never departing from the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā)—O sons of gods!”
Such a person cannot be taken advantage of by Māra or the gods of Māra. Why is this?

Because these sons and daughters of good family have clearly realized that form is empty; emptiness cannot take advantage of emptiness, signlessness cannot take advantage of signlessness, and wishlessness cannot take advantage of wishlessness.

One thoroughly understands that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; emptiness cannot find an opening in emptiness, and even non-action cannot find an opening in non-action.
This continues until one thoroughly understands that the knowledge of all modes is empty; emptiness cannot find an opening in emptiness, and even non-action cannot find an opening in non-action.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of these dharmas cannot be apprehended; since no objective basis can be found, who is there to be afflicted?
"Furthermore, Kausika!..."
These good sons and good daughters cannot be taken advantage of by humans or non-humans.

Why is this? Because these good sons and good daughters have well-cultivated the mind of loving-kindness, as well as the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, by means of the principle of non-apprehension.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall never meet with an untimely death. Why is this?
"This is because these good sons and good daughters practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), providing for all sentient beings with an impartial mind.
Furthermore, Kauśika!"

In this trichiliocosm, among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven—among these various devas, there are those who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet heard this Prajñāpāramitā, nor have they received, upheld, or approached it. These sons of the gods should now hear, receive, uphold, approach, read, recite, and correctly contemplate it, never departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā*.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If any sons or daughters of good family hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, draw near to it, read and recite it, and maintain right mindfulness of it, never departing from the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), then these sons and daughters of good family will never experience fear, whether they are in an empty house, in the wilderness, or in a human habitation."
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family are clear regarding internal emptiness, because they have nothing to apprehend;
they are clear regarding external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, because they have nothing to apprehend.
[Treatise] Question:
In this context, after the Buddha has surveyed the fourfold assembly, why does he address Śakra Devānām Indra? Answer:
In other chapters, the essence of the *prajñāpāramitā* was primarily explained; now, wishing to praise the merit of *prajñā*, he commands Śakra Devendra.
It is like first showing a person a fine jewel and then praising the capabilities of that jewel.

Furthermore, as for "observing universally," it is because he wishes to cause the sentient beings in the assembly to each know that the Buddha is mindful of them, so that they do not disparage themselves;
because they do not disparage themselves, they are capable of listening to the Dharma, and for this reason, he observes universally.
For example, when a king casts his gaze upon his subordinates, the subordinates rejoice and congratulate themselves.
Because he speaks of merit, one should take the white-robed laypeople as witnesses;
among those in white robes, Śakra Devānām Indra is the greatest.
Those who preach the Prajñāpāramitā take renunciants as their witnesses;
among renunciants, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others are the most eminent.
Question:
Previously it was stated that "Śakra" is his name and "Devendra" means "Lord of Devas"; why does the Buddha now not say "Śakra," but instead address him as "Kauśika"?

The answer is: Formerly, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a brahmin named Māgha of the Kauśika clan. Possessing great merit and vast wisdom, he had thirty-three friends with whom he cultivated merit together. At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the second heaven atop Mount Sumeru; the brahmin Māgha became the lord of the gods, while the thirty-two others served as his ministers. Because of these thirty-three individuals, that realm is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
He is addressed by his original clan name, hence he is called Kauśika;
alternatively, he is called the Lord of Devas, or the Thousand-Eyed One, and so forth.
When addressed by a Great Being, he is thus referred to by his clan name.

What is here called "Prajñāpāramitā" refers to the words, names, and written scrolls spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, which proclaim and reveal the wisdom of the true nature of reality (dharmatā).

Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is devoid of the characteristics of conceptual observation or verbal expression; yet, it is through words and scriptures that one can attain this Prajñāpāramitā. Therefore, names and scriptures are designated as "Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha’s intention here is stated briefly:
if one can hear, receive, and uphold the *prajñā* [pāramitā] and so forth, one shall attain various merits, which will be explained extensively later.
Desiring to deliver sentient beings and to attain the Buddha-way, one makes offerings to and studies the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For such a person, neither Māra nor the gods of Māra can find an opportunity.
Question: Who is this Māra?
"Why do you harass the Bodhisattva?
How have you found an opportunity?
He replied:
"Māra" is the name for the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereign Mastery (*Īśvara*).

Although he was born there through the causes and conditions of merit, he harbors various false views; he regards the sentient beings of the desire realm as his own subjects, thinking that even as they pass through the cycle of death and rebirth, they do not leave his realm.
Furthermore, even if they are reborn above in the form or formless realms, they will eventually return to belong to him.
If there are those who attain the five supernormal powers of the non-Buddhists, they have not yet escaped my realm, and I do not consider this a cause for concern.

However, if Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear in the world, they will transform and deliver my subjects, uprooting the root of birth and death so that they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and never return again, thereby emptying my domain; for this reason, I give rise to resentment, hostility, and jealousy.
Furthermore, seeing that all people in the desire realm go toward the Buddha and do not come to seek refuge in themselves, they lose their offerings;
consequently, jealousy arises in their hearts, and for this reason, they regard the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as enemies.

When this bodhisattva enters the stage of the Dharma-position and attains the body born of the nature of reality (dharmatā-nirmita-kāya), Māra may give rise to evil, yet he cannot destroy or defeat him;
however, if one has not yet attained *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), Māra will then employ various means to cause destruction.

If a bodhisattva, with single-minded devotion, does not begrudge body or life and seeks the Buddha-way through skillful means, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the great bodhisattvas will together protect and sustain them; by these causes and conditions, they are able to achieve the Buddha-way.

If one is a bodhisattva yet remains indolent, greedily attached to worldly pleasures, and unable to seek the Buddha-way with single-minded diligence, this is to deceive oneself and to deceive the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Why is this? Because they claim, "I seek the Buddha-way for the sake of all sentient beings," yet they engage in mixed practices that destroy the Dharma of a bodhisattva;
due to this transgression, they are not protected by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, and Māra gains the opportunity to exploit them.
Why is this? All noble ones have entered the stage of certainty; with single-minded devotion they practice the Path and deeply delight in nirvana.
Mara, however, has entered the stage of error and is attached to the deviant path.

Because the heterodox and the orthodox are diametrically opposed, he harbors hatred and envy toward those who practice the right path; being mad and foolish, he exalts himself and addresses the Buddha, the Śramaṇa Gautama, by name, though the Buddha calls him by his true name: the Wicked Māra.
Because they are in opposition, they are called "enemies.
As the sutras state, there are four kinds of Māras:

first, the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*); second, the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandhamāra*); third, the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*); and fourth, the Māra of the Lord of the Gods (*devaputramāra*).
In this context, by the power of *prajñā*, the four māras cannot find an opportunity:

having attained the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, whereby the māra of afflictions is destroyed; furthermore, the celestial māra (*devaputra-māra*) likewise cannot find an opportunity;
and because one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*) and the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*) are destroyed.
What constitutes finding an opportunity?
It is when Māra and his followers come to terrify the bodhisattva, as described in the sūtras:
Māra assumes the body of a dragon and various other fearsome forms, coming at night to intimidate the practitioner.
Sometimes they manifest the five supreme sensual desires to corrupt and disturb the bodhisattva;
or they turn the minds of worldly people to cause them to make great offerings, whereby the practitioner, through attachment to these offerings, loses their virtue and conduct;

or they turn the minds of people to cause them to slight and provoke the bodhisattva, whether by reviling, beating, wounding, or harming them, so that the practitioner encounters suffering or gives rise to anger and sorrow.
In such ways, Māra follows the inclinations of a person's mind and thereby destroys them; this is called "gaining an opportunity.
This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Māra" (Māravarga).
Question:
The power of Māra is exceedingly great, while the Bodhisattva in his physical body still possesses little power from the Path; how is it that he does not find an opportunity?
Answer:
As stated above, this is because they are protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explained the causal conditions:
"This person skillfully cultivates the emptiness of all dharmas, yet does not cling to emptiness."
For one who does not cling to emptiness, how could [an affliction] find an opportunity?
It is like a person without a wound who does not receive poison;
the same applies to signlessness and wishlessness.
Furthermore, when all dharmas are observed in their true nature, they are all characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
because they are all characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there is no opportunity for attainment, nor is there anyone who receives attainment.

Therefore, emptiness should not find an opportunity within emptiness, signlessness should not find an opportunity within signlessness, and wishlessness should not find an opportunity within wishlessness, because they are of a single characteristic.
Just as fire cannot extinguish fire, but is extinguished by water because their characteristics are different;
it is asked:
when a bodhisattva dwells in the three gates of liberation, this constitutes an advantageous position, for it is contrary to all dharmas.
Emptiness is contrary to existence; signlessness is contrary to having signs; and non-action is contrary to action!
The answer is:
In this sutra, the Buddha himself says:
"The three gates of liberation have no intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, it was stated in the previous discussion:
"One should not even become attached to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
Therefore, although they abide in the three gates of liberation, Māra and his followers find no opportunity against them.
Question: In other places it is always said "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva"; why is it now said "good son or good daughter"?
The answer is:
Previously, it was stated that the wisdom of the true nature (dharmatā) is difficult to receive; because one is able to receive it, such a person is a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Now, because the discussion concerns offerings, upholding, reading, and reciting—which are mixed practices—one may be called a "good son" or a "good daughter."
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that women have five obstructions:
they cannot become Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā, Māra, a Cakravartin king, or a Buddha.
Hearing that these five obstacles prevent one from becoming a Buddha, women’s minds retreat, and they are unable to resolve their intent.
Furthermore, there may be those who preach the Dharma who do not speak of the Buddha-way to women.
Therefore, when the Buddha speaks here of "good sons and good daughters," it means that women can indeed attain Buddhahood;
it is not the case that they cannot transform their female bodies.
The "five obstructions" refer to the matters concerning a single body.
The meaning of "good sons and good daughters" has already been explained at length previously.

Regarding the phrase "people find no opportunity," "people" refers to those such as thieves, officials, or enemies who wish to vex and disturb the Bodhisattva, seeking to find an opening for such interference.
Question: Previously, when explaining the conditions for not finding an opportunity, why did you speak only of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Now, when explaining that a person does not find an opportunity, why do you speak only of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*)?
Answer: Some say that because Māra and the subjects of Māra were mentioned first, and because their enmity is great, the Dharma is likewise great; therefore, emptiness is taught.
Because the enmity is small, the dharma is also small; therefore, the four immeasurable minds are taught.
Some say that the four immeasurable minds are the constant practice of Bodhisattvas, for the purpose of accumulating all merits.
Subsequently, by means of the mark of emptiness of the Prajñāpāramitā, one causes the removal of false views, so as not to be attached to sentient beings nor to be attached to dharmas.
These two dharmas have no prior or posterior existence.

Furthermore, the superior Māras perform many acts of terror; they mostly do not manifest their true forms, but may appear as thunderclaps, or create wind and rain, or cause illnesses and the like. For this reason, one speaks of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
Because people may come to revile one with harsh words or strike and hack at one with swords and staves, one employs the four immeasurable minds (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
"Not dying an untimely death" refers to dying without transgression:
for instance, dying when one's lifespan is not yet exhausted due to administering the wrong medicine, or failing to follow the rules for taking medicine, or lacking a caregiver;
or dying prematurely from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and so forth—these are called untimely deaths.
From the first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], Bodhisattvas constantly practice the *dānapāramitā* among all sentient beings:

they provide medicine according to the illness, supplying whatever each ailment requires; they rescue the orphaned and the destitute, bestowing upon them everything they beg for; toward all sentient beings, they maintain complete equanimity and offer worship with a sincere heart;
furthermore, they also practice this *prajñāpāramitā*.
By virtue of these merits, one does not die an untimely death.

Having briefly explained these three merits herein, [the text previously] stated that among the devas within the trichiliocosm who have resolved their minds but have not yet heard the Prajñāpāramitā, sons and daughters of good family should hear, receive, uphold, and even correctly contemplate it; now, the underlying causes and conditions are being explained.
The devas possess great merit and yet still offer worship; how much more so should humans?
Although all humans and devas ought to listen to the Prajñāpāramitā, those who are able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment should listen with the deepest resolve.
Why is this so? Because Prajñā is the root of the Buddha-way.
Question:
Question: Why does this deva, having generated the aspiration for enlightenment, not hear the Prajñāpāramitā? Answer: Some say:

This person previously aroused the aspiration for enlightenment among humans, but having now been born in the heavens, they do not hear [the teaching] because their minds are shrouded by the five desires.

Furthermore, although the various devas may have aroused the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, because their five sensory faculties are sharp, the five desires are exquisite, and their attachment is deep, they forget what lies to the west while looking toward the east; thus, they are unable to seek prajñā.

Although the devas of the form realm have previously heard the Dharma and resolved their minds upon it, because they are deeply attached to the savor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are unable to seek prajñā.
For this reason, it is said that those who have not heard [the Dharma] should hear it, and those who have heard it should receive and uphold it.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that "Māra and his followers cannot find an opportunity," which refers to internal causes and conditions, namely the samādhi of emptiness and the four immeasurable minds;
now, it is further stated that they "cannot find an opportunity," which refers to external causes and conditions, namely the Buddha’s address to the devas:
"You all make offerings to and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and these sons and daughters of good family likewise uphold and make offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā."
"Because we share a common purpose, if Māra comes to disrupt you, you should protect yourself!
Furthermore, those who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā may dwell in an empty house, in the wilderness, or among people.
In an empty house, there are many ghosts, spirits, and bandits; because various evils easily approach, it was mentioned first.
Apart from human dwellings and empty houses, all remaining mountains, marshes, forests, and the like are wildernesses;
because few people travel there, they abound with tigers, wolves, lions, wicked bandits, ghosts, and spirits.
Because the places where people dwell are impure, Māras and spirits rarely come;
since various calamities are few, this is explained later.
A practitioner dwells in three locations without fear due to two causes and conditions:
First, by skillfully cultivating the eighteen kinds of emptiness; second, by virtue of the majestic power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

[Sūtra] At that time, the various devas of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and even the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens within this trichiliocosm addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"We shall always protect those sons and daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, and correctly contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā, and who do not depart from the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta)!"
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

It is because of the causes and conditions of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that the three evil realms are severed, the poverty of gods and humans is severed, and all calamities, diseases, and famines are severed.

Because of the Bodhisattva, there arise in the world the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge.

Because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas, there come to be in the world those born into the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brahmins, and the great families of householders; as well as various kings and universal monarchs (cakravartin), from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

It is because of the bodhisattva as a causal condition that there exist the srotāpanna and the fruit of srotāpanna, up to and including the arhat and the fruit of arhat, as well as the pratyekabuddha and the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas, there is the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields; thus, Buddhas appear in the world, the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs, and one comes to know the existence of the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, all the devas, humans, and asuras in the world should protect this bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra: “So it is! So it is!”
Kauśika! It is because of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that the three evil realms are severed and even the Three Jewels appear in the world.
For this reason, the devas, humans, and asuras should constantly protect, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
Kauśika! To offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is to offer worship to me.
For this reason, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always be protected, worshipped, revered, respected, and praised by gods, humans, and asuras alike.

Kauśika! Suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a grove of bamboo, or a thicket of rice, hemp, or forest trees; if a son or daughter of good family were to provide offerings, honor, respect, and praise to them, it would not equal the merit obtained by providing offerings, honor, respect, and praise to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved on awakening and does not depart from the six pāramitās.

Why is this? It is not because of the causes and conditions of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all buddhas appear in the world; rather, it is because of the causes and conditions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas appear in the world.
For this reason, Kauśika,
all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world should constantly protect, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise these bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
[Treatise] Commentary:
At that time, the devas addressed the Buddha, saying,
“We shall protect this bodhisattva, for he performs the same task as we do.”
"Furthermore, those who seek the Buddha-way are able to renounce their own bodily pleasures and desires so that all sentient beings may obtain happiness.

Regarding "the Bodhisattva cuts off the three evil paths": although the Bodhisattva has not yet abandoned desire, they are able to obstruct the ten unwholesome actions of sentient beings; thus, they cut off the three evil paths as well as the poverty of devas and humans, various calamities, afflictions, and so forth.
By practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, they open the gates to the three happy realms.
Some bodhisattvas, seeing the faults and transgressions of the five desires, are able to leave desire behind and attain the four dhyānas;
yet, by virtue of their original vows, they give rise to the four immeasurable minds.
In order to be free from the various causes and conditions of physical suffering, they give rise to the four formless concentrations.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, they cultivate the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
This Dharma is both practiced by oneself and taught to others;
through these meritorious paths of the Dharma, one teaches one another among sentient beings, remaining forever in the world.
Now I shall explain the fruits and rewards of these wholesome dharmas:
being born into a great kṣatriya clan, up to the appearance of the Three Jewels in the world;
as was explained in the previous section on the meaning.

Now this Bodhisattva, though possessing a body born of karmic bonds and existing within the realm of causes and conditions, lacks any worldly power or influence, yet is able to preach these wholesome dharmas and cause sentient beings to practice them; how could we fail to protect him?
For example, although a crown prince may be young, there are no ministers or officials who do not serve and support him.
The Buddha approved the words of the devas, recounting and confirming them:
"To make offerings to a bodhisattva is to make offerings to a Buddha. This is because *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"If one makes offerings to a bodhisattva for the sake of prajñā, then one is making offerings to the Buddha.
[The phrase] "It is not as good as making offerings to and revering a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind" means:
Question:

Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are fields of merit for all sentient beings, why are they not equal to bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment?
Answer:
They are inferior for three reasons:

first, they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*); second, they are never separated from the various merits such as the six *pāramitās*; and third, by means of this, these bodhisattvas sever the three evil realms and give rise to the three vehicles.
Relying on those of the Two Vehicles, one cannot sever the three evil paths or give rise to the Three Vehicles.

Chapter Thirty-one: On the Extinction of Disputes and Confusion *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Thirty-one: On the Extinction of Disputes and Confusion [Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How truly marvelous and rare!

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear, receive and uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly bring to mind this Prajñāpāramitā, they obtain such merits in this present life;
they also bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they shall make offerings to all Buddhas; whatever requisites they desire for making offerings, they shall obtain them at will.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall never forget it midway.
Furthermore, they shall achieve perfection in family, mother, birth, retinue, marks, radiance, eyes, ears, samādhi, and dhāraṇī.

By the power of skillful means, this bodhisattva transforms his body to appear like a Buddha and travels from one realm to another, reaching places where no Buddha resides. There, he praises the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); he praises the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*); and he praises the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

Using the power of skillful means to teach the Dharma, he delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*), namely: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle.
World-Honored One!
How wonderful! How rare!

To receive this Prajñāpāramitā is to have already comprehensively encompassed the five pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it also encompasses the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat, the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a Buddha, all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is! So it is!"
Kauśika! By receiving this Prajñāpāramitā, one has already encompassed all five pāramitās up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Furthermore, Kauśika!

As for this Prajñāpāramitā, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, approaches, reads, recites, explains it to others, and correctly brings it to mind, you should listen with single-minded attention to the merits they obtain in this present life!
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“Yes! World-Honored One!”
“I shall receive your instruction!
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām-indra: “Kauśika!

If there should be non-Buddhist brahmins, or Māras, or followers of Māra, or those with overweening pride who wish to cause discord and destroy the bodhisattva’s mind of prajñāpāramitā, as soon as these people give rise to such a thought, it shall immediately perish and never fulfill their intent.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because for a long night, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have practiced the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), and they have practiced the perfections of ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditation (dhyāna), and wisdom (prajñā).
Because sentient beings have long been addicted to greed and contention, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external things to establish them in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*);
because sentient beings have long been prone to breaking the precepts, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish them in morality;
because sentient beings have long been engaged in strife and quarreling, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish them in patience (*kṣānti*).
Because sentient beings have been indolent throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish sentient beings in diligence;
because sentient beings have had distracted minds throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish sentient beings in meditative concentration;

because sentient beings have been ignorant throughout the long night, the Bodhisattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena to establish sentient beings in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Because sentient beings have long been bound by the fetter of craving and thus wander through birth and death, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of their power of skillful means, sever the fetter of craving in sentient beings and establish them in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, and the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they establish sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.
Kauśika! These are the merits a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtains in the present life while practicing the perfection of wisdom.
As for the merits in future lives—namely, the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Bodhisattva turns the wheel of Dharma, fulfills his vows, and enters nirvana without remainder.
Kausika! These are the merits of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva in future lives.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears, receives, upholds, approaches, reads, recites, explains to others, and correctly attends to this Prajñāpāramitā, then in the place where they dwell, whether it be Māra, the subjects of Māra, non-Buddhist brahmins, or those with overweening pride who wish to disparage, challenge, or destroy the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall ultimately fail to succeed.

The evil intentions of such persons will diminish and vanish, while their merits will increase. Because they have heard this Prajñāpāramitā, they will gradually attain the exhaustion of all suffering through the path of the Three Vehicles."
For example, Kauśika, there is a medicine called Māgī.
Suppose there is a hungry snake wandering about in search of food that sees an insect and wishes to devour it;
the insect approaches the place where the medicine is, and by the power of the medicine’s fragrance, the snake is unable to advance and immediately retreats.
Why is this? Because the power of this medicine is able to overcome the poison. Kausika!
The *maghi* medicine possesses such power. If these sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, approach, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly contemplate this *prajñāpāramitā*,
then should various conflicts arise that seek to cause destruction, by the majestic power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall be swiftly extinguished at the very place where they arise.
That person will immediately give rise to a wholesome mind and increase their merit. Why is this?
Because this Prajñāpāramitā is able to extinguish all disputes and disturbances regarding phenomena.
What are these phenomena?
They are namely: lust, anger, and delusion;
from ignorance up to the great mass of suffering.
The various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);

the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), the view of impurity (*aśubha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of purity (*śubha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*)—all such views as these;
as well as stinginess and greed, violation of precepts, anger, indolence, distraction of mind, and lack of wisdom.
The perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of purity, and the perception of self—such are the modes of craving.
One is attached to form, and attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
one is attached to the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom.
They are attached to internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
they are attached to the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are attached to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes.
"Adhering to nirvāṇa,
one can completely extinguish all disputes and disturbances regarding all dharmas, preventing them from increasing.
[Treatise] Explanation:

Regarding "hearing": it means hearing the Prajñāpāramitā from the Buddha, from a bodhisattva, or from other teachers of the Dharma; this is the treasury of the Dharma-jewels of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Having heard it, one "accepts" it by means of the power of faith;
one "retains" it by means of the power of mindfulness.
Because one attains its flavor, one "draws near" by constantly coming to serve it and receiving instruction from it.
Having approached [the teacher], one either examines the text or receives it orally; hence, it is called "reading.
To ensure that it is constantly retained without being forgotten, one "recites" it.
To propagate what has not yet been heard, one "explains it to others."
The scriptures of the Sages are direct and difficult to comprehend, and thus their meanings are explained;
one observes that the Buddha-dharmas are inconceivable, and because he possesses great compassion for sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma.

One does not seek the Buddha-dharma through false views or frivolous conceptualization; as it is the intent of the Buddha, one does not cling [to it], and thus even in preaching the Dharma, one remains unattached.

Because one eliminates all wrong recollections such as the four inversions and abides in right mindfulness within the four foundations of mindfulness, doing so solely for the sake of attaining the Path and not for the sake of frivolous proliferation, it is called "right mindfulness."

Right mindfulness is the root of all wholesome dharmas; for the practitioner who begins their cultivation, it is called "right mindfulness," and because they constantly practice and thereby attain meditative concentration, it is called "cultivation."
Regarding "merit in this present life," the meaning is as previously explained.
Now, Śakra Devānām Indra further explains the merit of this present life, namely, the teaching and transforming of sentient beings, even to the point of causing them to attain the three vehicles.
First, it was stated that the *prajñāpāramitā* subsumes the three vehicles (*triyāna*) so as to cause one to understand their meaning; therefore, it is said:
"Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, the five *pāramitās* up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are subsumed."
The Buddha affirmed what had been said in order to inspire faith in others.

Regarding the phrase "Listen with single-minded attention to the merits attained in this present life": previously, the merits of this present life were explained briefly; now the Buddha wishes to explain them in detail. Because these matters are difficult to believe, he says, "Listen with single-minded attention."
Furthermore, because the fruit is great while the cause is small, it is difficult to believe; therefore, he says, "Listen with single-minded attention.
Although Śakra has accepted this with faith, others do not know it; therefore, he says:
"Yes! [I shall listen]."
“World-Honored One!
Although this Prajñāpāramitā is indestructible, the verbal expressions that proclaim its true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa) can be destroyed;
because these verbal expressions can be destroyed, the faith of those whose minds are not yet settled may also be destroyed. Therefore it is said:”
"If non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) or brahmins come, wishing to destroy the Prajñāpāramitā.
As for "brahmin," this refers to all those who have left the household life as non-Buddhists; furthermore, anyone who accepts and employs their teachings is also called a brahmin.
The brahmin was attached to his own doctrine; hearing the teaching of emptiness as the true nature of reality, he did not believe it and thus sought to destroy it.
"Māra, or the followers of Māra," is as previously explained.

Regarding the "person of overweening pride" (adhimānika): this is a disciple of the Buddha who has attained meditative concentration (dhyāna) but has not yet attained the Noble Path (āryamārga), yet claims to have attained it.

When such a person hears that there is no srotāpanna up to and including no arhat, and that there is no path and no nirvāṇa, they immediately give rise to overweening pride and a mind of resentment and vexation, desiring to destroy this true mark of emptiness (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa).
It is by the spiritual power of this Prajñāpāramitā that those evil intentions are extinguished at once, so that their vows can never be fulfilled;
it is like a person who blocks a spear with their hand—the hand alone is wounded, while the spear remains unharmed.
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas do not cling to internal or external phenomena.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have constantly clung to internal and external phenomena, and thus give rise to conflict and strife.
The Bodhisattva relinquishes attachment to internal and external objects, personally establishing himself in the six pāramitās;
he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to relinquish the contentious dharmas of internal and external things, and establishes sentient beings in the six pāramitās.

This is because of the power of merit accumulated through cultivation over immeasurable lifetimes; since the roots of strife and contention have been exhausted, even when occasions for conflict and disorder arise, they cannot find an opportunity.
It is like a venomous snake that pursues a toad with the intent to eat it;
when the toad reaches the place of the *makhī* herb, the snake, smelling the scent of the herb, finds its poison immediately neutralized.
These people who destroy the Dharma are likewise; they constantly pursue those who wish to destroy the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
However, by the power and force of *prajñā*, the poison of their anger and false views is instantly extinguished.
There are those who subdue themselves and attain the Way, those who become disciples, and those who turn back from the Way.

This Prajñāpāramitā can destroy all fetters such as ignorance, extinguish all views of annihilationism, eternalism, and heterodoxy, and can extinguish attachment to the five aggregates even unto Nirvāṇa; how much more so could it not extinguish anger, jealousy, and strife!
[Sūtra] “Furthermore, Kauśika!

Within this trichiliocosm, the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Śakras, the Brahmās, and even the devas up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven constantly protect those sons and daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, offer to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā. The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions likewise collectively protect those sons and daughters of good family who are able to hear, receive, uphold, offer to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā.”

"These sons and daughters of good family will extinguish unwholesome dharmas and cause wholesome dharmas to increase further. That is to say, the *dānapāramitā* increases further because of non-apprehension;
up to and including the *prajñāpāramitā*, which increases further because of non-apprehension;

and from the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) increasing further, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), which increases further because of non-apprehension."
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha increase further by virtue of non-apprehension;
the various gates of samādhi, the various gates of dhāraṇī, all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all modes increase further by virtue of non-apprehension.
What these good men and good women speak is believed and accepted by all.
Their friends and relatives are steadfast; they do not utter useless words.
They are not overcome by anger, nor are they overcome by arrogance, stinginess, greed, or jealousy.
This person does not kill living beings themselves, teaches others not to kill, praises the dharma of non-killing, and also rejoices in and praises those who do not kill;

they themselves distance themselves from taking what is not given, teach others to distance themselves from taking what is not given, praise the dharma of refraining from taking what is not given, and also rejoice in and praise those who refrain from taking what is not given;

they themselves do not engage in sexual misconduct, teach others not to engage in sexual misconduct, praise the dharma of refraining from sexual misconduct, and also rejoice in and praise those who refrain from sexual misconduct.
One refrains from false speech oneself, teaches others not to speak falsely, praises the dharma of refraining from false speech, and also joyfully commends those who refrain from false speech;
the same applies to double-tongued speech, harsh speech, and idle gossip.
One is not greedy oneself, teaches others not to be greedy, praises the dharma of non-greed, and also joyfully extols those who are not greedy;
the same applies to being without anger and affliction, and being without false views.

“He personally practices the dāna-pāramitā, teaches others to practice the dāna-pāramitā, praises the method of practicing the dāna-pāramitā, and also joyfully commends those who practice the dāna-pāramitā;
he personally practices the śīla-pāramitā, teaches others to practice the śīla-pāramitā, praises the śīla-pāramitā, and also joyfully commends those who practice the śīla-pāramitā;
he personally practices the kṣānti-pāramitā, teaches others to practice the kṣānti-pāramitā, praises the kṣānti-pāramitā, and also joyfully commends those who practice the kṣānti-pāramitā.”

They personally practice the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), teach others to practice the perfection of vigor, praise the perfection of vigor, and also joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of vigor;

they personally practice the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), teach others to practice the perfection of meditation, praise the perfection of meditation, and also joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of meditation;

they personally practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom, praise the perfection of wisdom, and also joyfully praise those who practice the perfection of wisdom.
"One personally cultivates internal emptiness, teaches others to cultivate internal emptiness, praises internal emptiness, and also joyfully praises those who cultivate internal emptiness;

and so on, up to personally cultivating the emptiness of non-existence and existence, teaching others to cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence, praising the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and also joyfully praising those who cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence."
"He himself enters all samādhis, teaches others to enter all samādhis, praises all samādhis, and also joyfully extols those who enter all samādhis."
He himself attains dhāraṇīs, teaches others to attain dhāraṇīs, praises dhāraṇīs, and also joyfully extols those who have attained them.
He himself enters the first dhyāna, teaches others to enter the first dhyāna, praises the first dhyāna, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the first dhyāna.
It is the same for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Having entered the state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) oneself, one teaches others to enter the state of loving-kindness, praises loving-kindness, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the state of loving-kindness.
It is the same for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

One enters the sphere of infinite space oneself, teaches others to enter the sphere of infinite space, praises the sphere of infinite space, and likewise rejoices in and praises those who have entered the sphere of infinite space.
It is the same for the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness oneself, teaches others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, praises the four foundations of mindfulness, and also rejoices in those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness."
The same applies to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

He himself cultivates the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he teaches others to cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he praises the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he also joyfully commends those who cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He himself enters the eight liberations; he teaches others to enter the eight liberations; he praises the eight liberations; and he also joyfully commends those who enter the eight liberations.

Having personally entered the nine successive meditative attainments, he teaches others to enter the nine successive meditative attainments, praises the nine successive meditative attainments, and also joyfully extols those who have entered the nine successive meditative attainments.

"He likewise cultivates for himself the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities;

he practices for himself the dharma of non-erroneousness and the dharma of constant relinquishment, teaches others to practice the dharma of non-erroneousness and the dharma of constant relinquishment, praises the dharma of non-erroneousness and the dharma of constant relinquishment, and also joyfully extols those who practice the dharma of non-erroneousness and the dharma of constant relinquishment."
He himself attains all-knowledge, teaches others to attain all-knowledge, praises all-knowledge, and also joyfully extols those who have attained all-knowledge.
"When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, having shared all his giving with sentient beings, he dedicates it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by way of non-apprehension."

Having shared all one's morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom with all sentient beings, one dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this too is because there is nothing to be apprehended.
"When these good sons and good daughters practice the six pāramitās in this way, they form this thought:

'If I do not practice giving, I shall be born into a poor family; I will be unable to bring sentient beings to maturity or purify the Buddha-field, nor will I be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).'"

"If I do not maintain the precepts, I shall be reborn in the three evil realms; I will not even attain a human body, let alone be able to bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and realize all-knowledge!"

If I do not cultivate patience, my sense faculties will be impaired and my physical form will be incomplete; I shall be unable to attain the bodhisattva’s perfect body, by the sight of which sentient beings would inevitably reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, I would be unable to use that perfect body to bring sentient beings to maturity, to purify Buddha-fields, and to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If I am indolent, I shall not be able to attain the path of a bodhisattva, nor shall I be able to accomplish the maturation of sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, or attain all-knowledge.

If my mind were distracted, I would be unable to give birth to the various dhyāna-samādhis; I would be unable to accomplish the maturation of sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, and attain all-knowledge by means of these dhyāna-samādhis.

If I were without wisdom, I would be unable to attain the wisdom of skillful means; without the wisdom of skillful means, I could not transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify the buddha-fields, and attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
“Furthermore, this bodhisattva reflects thus: ‘I must not fail to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā because of stinginess and greed;

I must not fail to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā because of transgressing the precepts; I must not fail to fulfill the kṣānti-pāramitā because of anger and hatred; I must not fail to fulfill the vīrya-pāramitā because of laziness; I must not fail to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā because of a distracted mind; and I must not fail to fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā because of a deluded mind.’”

If I were not fully endowed with the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, I would ultimately be unable to emerge and reach all-knowledge.

"In this way, good sons and good daughters who accept, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain to others, and correctly contemplate this Prajñāpāramitā, and who do not depart from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), shall obtain these merits in both the present life and future lives."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare!
"This Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and also for the sake of not giving rise to a haughty mind.
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra: "Kauśika!"

What is meant by saying, "The prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is for the sake of dedicating [merit] toward the mind of sarvajñatā, and also for the sake of not giving rise to a conceited mind"?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the worldly dānapāramitā, giving to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, as well as the poor, beggars, and travelers, that bodhisattva gives rise to a conceited mind because he lacks skillful means."
If one practices the worldly perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), saying:
"I am practicing the perfection of ethical discipline; I am able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline."
Because they lack skillful means, they give rise to a conceited mind and say:
"I practice the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation."
"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom; I am cultivating the perfection of wisdom.
Because of this worldly perfection of wisdom and due to a lack of skillful means, they give rise to a haughty mind.
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness of the mundane world, they think to themselves:
‘I am cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness; I am fully endowed with the four foundations of mindfulness.’”
Because they lack the power of skillful means, they give rise to a haughty mind, thinking:
"I cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
He thought to himself:
"I shall cultivate the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
I shall cultivate all gateways of samādhi, and thereby attain all gateways of dhāraṇī."

I shall cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity, I shall purify the Buddha-fields, and I shall attain all-knowledge.
"Because they are attached to a self and lack the power of skillful means, they give rise to arrogance.
World-Honored One!
In this way, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice worldly wholesome dharmas, they give rise to arrogance because they are attached to a self."
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices supramundane dānapāramitā, they do not apprehend a giver, they do not apprehend a recipient, and they do not apprehend the gift;
thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices supramundane dānapāramitā for the sake of dedicating it toward sarvajñā, they likewise do not give rise to a conceited mind.”
Practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), ethical discipline is unapprehendable;
practicing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), patience is unapprehendable;
practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), vigor is unapprehendable.
Practicing the dhyāna-pāramitā, dhyāna is unattainable;
practicing the prajñā-pāramitā, prajñā is unattainable;
cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness are unattainable.
Up to and including the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unattainable;
one cultivates great loving-kindness and great compassion, yet great loving-kindness and great compassion are unattainable;
up to and including the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes, the knowledge of all modes is unattainable.
World-Honored One!
Thus, this prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is for the sake of dedicating toward sarvajñatā, and also for the sake of not giving rise to a haughty mind.
[Treatise] Question:
It has already been stated that there are three kinds of people—Māra, the subjects of Māra, and others—who seek to destroy the *prajñā*. Why is this now being stated again?
The answer is:
The Buddha previously stated that there are three types of people who come: those seeking an opportunity, those driven by fear, and those wishing to cause distress.

As for those who come in the middle category, they do not intend to harm others, but merely wish to destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*. Since their wishes are not granted, they are unable to achieve such destruction.
Later, although those three types of people may wish to give rise to thoughts of destruction, these are immediately extinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the words spoken by him are all believed and accepted," this means that the Bodhisattva constantly causes unwholesome dharmas to be severed and extinguished, while wholesome dharmas—namely, from the *dānapāramitā* up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—are further increased.
Because this person has cultivated and accumulated merit and wisdom, they have attained great majestic power;
even if they were to speak falsely, everyone would believe and accept it, let alone when they speak the truth!

Regarding "steadfast toward kinsmen and friends," this person possesses a profound heart of compassion for all sentient beings, let alone toward those kinsmen and friends who have been beneficial to them!
This bodhisattva loves and reveres the Buddha-way; because he knows that body and speech are impermanent, he does not utter words that are without benefit.
Because his wholesome dharmas increase, afflictions such as anger and hatred cannot obscure his mind.
The practitioner reflects thus:
"Although the fetters and afflictions may arise, through the contemplation of wisdom, I shall not allow them to obscure the mind;
for if these fetters and afflictions arise, they will be unwholesome in this life and unwholesome in future lives, obstructing the path to Buddhahood."
Even if mental afflictions arise, one does not give rise to verbal karma;
even if verbal karma arises, it does not result in physical karma;
and even if physical karma arises, it does not reach the level of great evil as that of ordinary worldlings.
Although this bodhisattva may be lowly, base, and humble, because they practice the supreme Dharma, they are included among the ranks of the superior persons;
this is their merit in the present life.
Because this person deeply delights in the wholesome Dharma, they are able to seek the four kinds of correct practice within that wholesome Dharma.
Those of the Two Vehicles cannot fulfill the four practices because they do not deeply delight in wholesome dharmas.
That is to say, they themselves refrain from killing and practice compassion toward all beings;
yet, because their self-interest is profound, they also teach others to do the same.
Because loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the dharma of all the noble ones (*ārya*), it is constantly praised;
because this bodhisattva always desires to cause others to attain happiness, he feels joy and delight upon seeing those who do not kill.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The four types of practice mentioned above have been explained in detail; now, to speak briefly, all merits are subsumed within the six *pāramitās*, and the resulting fruits of retribution are shared with all sentient beings.

Because this bodhisattva has not yet entered the stage of certainty (samyaktvaniyāma) and his afflictions are not yet exhausted, he may at times give rise to afflictions such as stinginess. At that time, he should reflect in this way and admonish his mind with these analogies:
"If I do not practice giving, I shall personally lose four kinds of merit: namely, in a future life I will be born into poverty; being poor, I will be unable to benefit myself, let alone others!"
If one does not benefit others, then one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity;
if one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, one also cannot purify the Buddha-field. Why is this?
Because sentient beings are pure, the world is pure.
If one does not fully possess these various factors, how could one ever attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)?

To state it briefly: although those lacking skillful means may practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), they cannot internally abandon the mind of self, nor can they externally relinquish the marks of phenomena—namely, thinking, "I am the giver," "he is the recipient," and "this is the gift."
For these reasons, one cannot reach the path of the Buddha;
conversely, there is a skillful means. Question:
If worldly *pāramitās* and the like are not the true path, why did the Buddha speak of them within the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The answer is:
these are the initial gateways for practitioners, as they resemble the true path.
First practicing the similar dharmas, one subsequently attains the true Path.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 56, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Commentary on the "Chapter on the Comparative Measurement of the Jewel Stūpa," Number Thirty.
Volume Two, Chapter Fifty-seven:
The Exposition on the Measurement of the Jeweled Stūpa.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra-devānām-indra:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, accept, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, and correctly contemplate it, never departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), then when two armies are at war, because these sons or daughters of good family recite the *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall ultimately not lose their lives when entering the midst of the battle lines, nor shall they be wounded by swords or arrows."

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family have long practiced the six pāramitās, thereby removing for themselves the sword and arrow of sensual desire and also removing the sword and arrow of sensual desire from others;
they remove for themselves the sword and arrow of malice and also remove the sword and arrow of malice from others.
One removes for oneself the sword and arrow of ignorance, and also removes for others the sword and arrow of ignorance;
one removes for oneself the sword and arrow of wrong views, and also removes for others the sword and arrow of wrong views;
one removes for oneself the sword and arrow of the defilements of entanglement, and also removes for others the sword and arrow of the defilements of entanglement.
Having personally eliminated the swords and arrows of the fetters and afflictions, they also eliminate the swords and arrows of the fetters and afflictions for others.
Kausika! For this reason, these sons and daughters of good family will not be harmed by swords or arrows.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If these sons of good family or daughters of good family hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, draw near to it, read and recite it, and maintain right mindfulness of it, never departing from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), then whether they are fumigated with poisonous drugs, subjected to sorcery, cast into a fire-pit, submerged in deep water, sought to be killed by sword, or given poison—none of such evils shall be able to harm them."
Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā is the great vidyā-mantra, it is the unsurpassed mantra.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family trains in this vidyā-mantra, they will not afflict themselves, nor will they afflict others, nor will they afflict both.

Why is this? Because these good men and good women do not apprehend a self, do not apprehend sentient beings, do not apprehend a life-span, and so on, up to the knower and the seer—all of which are unapprehendable;
they do not apprehend form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to all-knowledge, which is likewise unapprehendable.
Because they are ungraspable, they do not afflict themselves, nor do they afflict others, nor do they afflict both.
By studying this Great Bright Mantra, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
observing the minds of all sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations.
Why is this? The Buddhas of the past studied this Great Mantra and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
the Buddhas of the future will study this Great Mantra and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
All Buddhas of the present have studied this great vidyā-mantra and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, if there is one who merely transcribes the scriptural volume and makes offerings to it in their home, yet does not receive, read, recite, explain, or correctly attend to it, then neither humans nor non-humans shall be able to find an opportunity to harm them in that place.

Why is this? It is because this Prajñāpāramitā is protected by the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the sons of the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven within the trichiliocosm, as well as by the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions.
Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā dwells, all the devas come to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise; having performed these prostrations, they depart.

If these sons or daughters of good family merely transcribe this Prajñāpāramitā into a volume and honor it in their home, without receiving it, reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or correctly attending to it, they will obtain such merit in this present life.
For example, whether it be humans or animals that enter beneath the Bodhi tree—whether on its periphery or within—itself;
even if humans or non-humans should come, they will be unable to find an opportunity to harm it.
Why is this? In this place, the Buddhas of the past attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the Buddhas of the future and the Buddhas of the present likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* therein.

Having attained Buddhahood, they bestow fearlessness and intrepidity upon all sentient beings, causing immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings to receive the blissful merit of gods and humans, and also causing immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

By the power of the Prajñāpāramitā, one receives respect and prostrations in this place, as well as offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, banners, parasols, and musical performances.
[Treatise] Question:
It is observed that there are those who uphold, read, and recite [the scriptures], yet when they enter into battle, they are wounded by weapons or even lose their lives.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"By the causal conditions of karma, there is no place—neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean—where one can escape.
Why, then, does the Buddha here say that "one who reads and recites the Prajñāpāramitā will not be wounded by weapons even when entering the midst of a military array, nor will they lose their life"?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of karmic causes and conditions:
first, those that must necessarily undergo retribution; second, those that do not necessarily undergo retribution.
Because one must inevitably undergo retribution, it is so stated in the *Dharmapada*;
whereas here, because retribution need not be undergone, it is said that "one who recites the *Prajñāpāramitā* shall not be harmed by weapons."
For example, a person who has committed a grave crime such as high treason and is subject to the death penalty cannot escape it despite possessing great power or wealth;

whereas another person whose crime is light, though formally categorized under the death penalty, is logically eligible for rescue and can save their life through the application of influence and resources, failing which they would die.

Good son, it is also like this: if there is no karma that must necessarily result in retribution, then even if the event of death arrives, one will attain deliverance by reading and reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā*;
if one does not read and recite it, then one cannot avoid death. Therefore, one cannot say that the *Prajñāpāramitā* lacks power and efficacy.

Furthermore, good sons and good daughters who distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas, subdue their minds, and diminish their afflictions; who single-mindedly and directly believe in wholesome dharmas without doubt or regret;

who have cultivated and accumulated merit and wisdom since time immemorial; and who possess a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, teaching and transforming them to eliminate their evil intentions.
In this way, son of good family, one will not be harmed by weapons, nor will one’s life be cut short.
As the Buddha himself spoke regarding the causes and conditions:
"Having practiced the six pāramitās throughout the long night, one removes the swords and arrows of the three poisons from both one's own body and the bodies of others."
The five pāramitās are merit, while the prajñāpāramitā is wisdom; because one extensively accumulates these two matters, one does not lose one's life prematurely.
Poisons, water, fire, and so forth are likewise [ineffective].

Furthermore, just as non-Buddhist seers and immortals, by the power of their incantations and arts, do not drown when entering water, do not suffer from heat when entering fire, and are not stung by venomous insects—how much more so is the Prajñāpāramitā, which is the incantation by which the Buddhas of the ten directions achieve their realization!
Question: What has been stated above may be accepted as credible;

however, in this present case, if one is unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, or contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, but merely transcribes it and makes offerings to it, how can such merit be obtained?
Answer: The merit obtained by this person is also the same as that mentioned above. Why is this?

Suppose there is someone who has previously heard a teacher explain the meaning of Prajñāpāramitā and has deeply entered into a state of love and joy for it; yet, because they do not know the written characters and have become separated from their teacher, they are unable to read or recite it.

Nevertheless, without begrudging their wealth or treasures, they hire others to transcribe it and provide various kinds of offerings with all their heart. Since their intention is the same as that of the one who reads and recites it, they too shall obtain merit.
That humans cannot find an opportunity against them is because they are protected by the devas.
This matter is difficult to believe, and therefore the Buddha uses the Bodhi tree as a metaphor.

By the power of *prajñā*, the Buddha attained the Unsurpassed Way beneath the Bodhi tree; because of the majestic influence of that Unsurpassed Way, that place still possesses such awe-inspiring virtue that when sentient beings enter within it, all evils cannot find an opportunity to harm them.
How much more so for the Prajñāpāramitā, which is the mother of all Buddhas—how could a son of good family who makes offerings with his whole heart have no merit?
[Sūtra] Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write out the Prajñāpāramitā and make offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, and even music;

and if another person, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, were to make offerings to the śarīra relics, or erect stūpas to offer them with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even music—with these two, which one would obtain greater merit?
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"I shall question you in turn; answer me according to your own understanding.
What do you think?"
"Just as the Buddha attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and attained this body—by training in which path did he attain this all-knowledge and attain this body?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha trained in the *prajñāpāramitā* and thereby attained all-knowledge and the body endowed with the marks and signs."
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra: "So it is! So it is!"
Kauśika! The Buddha trains in the prajñāpāramitā and thereby attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Kauśika!
