It is not because of this body that one is called a Buddha; it is because of the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) that one is called a Buddha. Kausika!
This knowledge of all modes of a Buddha arises from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
For this reason, Kauśika, this Buddha-body is the locus upon which all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) relies; it is by means of this body that the Buddha attains all-knowledge.
Good son, you should reflect in this way:
"This body is the locus upon which all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) relies.
Therefore, after my parinirvāṇa, my relics shall receive offerings.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Prajñāpāramitā, and copies it, receives and upholds it, draws near to it, reads it, recites it, and correctly brings it to mind; and if they honor, make offerings to, revere, and praise it with flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, unguents, banners, canopies, and music—then these sons and daughters of good family are making offerings to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."
For this reason, Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, or who receive, uphold, approach, read, recite, explain, correctly contemplate, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise it with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even musical instruments;

and if there are other sons or daughters of good family who, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, make offerings to the relics, erecting stūpas and revering, honoring, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even musical instruments.

If there are good sons or good daughters who write down, uphold, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this Prajñāpāramitā, and honor it with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even musical performances, the merit obtained by such persons will be vast!

Why is this? It is because within this *prajñāpāramitā* the five *pāramitās* are produced; from it arise internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), all samādhis, all dhyānas, and all dhāraṇīs—all are born from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The maturation of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-fields are both born from the perfection of wisdom;

the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva family, the accomplishment of physical form, the accomplishment of the necessities of life, the accomplishment of retinues, and the accomplishment of great loving-kindness and great compassion are all born from the perfection of wisdom;
and the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great families of householders are all born from this perfection of wisdom.

The gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; the stream-enterers up to the arhats; the pratyekabuddhas; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and all Buddhas, as well as the all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Buddhas—all these arise from this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the people of Jambudvīpa do not make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, nor revere, respect, or praise it, is it because they do not know that making such offerings brings great benefit?”
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Kauśika, what do you think?"
In Jambudvīpa, how many people have unshakable faith in the Buddha?
How many have unshakable faith in the Dharma and the Saṃgha?
And how many have no doubt regarding the Buddha?
Are you without doubt regarding the Dharma and the Sangha?
How many people have reached a definitive understanding of the Buddha?
How many have reached a definitive understanding of the Dharma and the Sangha?
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Few are the people of Jambudvīpa who possess indestructible faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; few, too, are those who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and who have attained certain understanding.”
“Kauśika! What do you think?

How many people in Jambudvīpa have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the four unhindered knowledges, and the six supernormal powers?”
In Jambudvīpa, how many people, by severing the three fetters, have attained the path of the Srotāpanna?
How many people, having severed the three fetters and further attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion, have attained the path of the Sakṛdāgāmin?
How many people have severed the five lower fetters and attained the path of Anāgāmin?
How many people have severed the five higher fetters and attained Arhatship?
How many people in Jambudvīpa seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha?
"How many people have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In Jambudvīpa, few people attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; indeed, even fewer people resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra: "So it is! So it is!"

Kauśika! Few are those who have unshakable faith in the Buddha, unshakable faith in the Dharma, and unshakable faith in the Saṅgha; few are those who have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha; few are those who have reached a definitive understanding of the Buddha, a definitive understanding of the Dharma, and a definitive understanding of the Saṅgha; Kauśika!

Furthermore, very few people attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative absorptions, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the six supernormal powers.

Kauśika! Furthermore, there are few people who, by severing the three fetters, attain the stage of *srotāpanna*; few who, by severing the three fetters and attenuating lust, hatred, and delusion, attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; few who, by severing the five lower fetters, attain the stage of *anāgāmin*; and few who, by severing the five higher fetters, attain the stage of *arhat*.

Among these, there are even fewer who seek the state of a *pratyekabuddha*; and among those, there are even fewer who resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and among those who have so resolved, there are even fewer who practice the path of a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Because these sentient beings, in previous lives, did not see the Buddha, did not hear the Dharma, and did not make offerings to the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; they did not practice giving, did not maintain the precepts, were not patient, were not diligent, were not concentrated, and lacked wisdom. They did not hear of internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; nor did they hear of or cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, they did not hear of or cultivate the various gates of samādhi or the various gates of dhāraṇī; nor did they hear of or cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) or the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Kauśika! For this reason, you should know that very few sentient beings have indestructible faith in the Buddha, indestructible faith in the Dharma, and indestructible faith in the Saṃgha;
indeed, even fewer sentient beings seek the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Among them, few sentient beings resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; among those who have resolved their minds, few practice the bodhisattva path; and among those, few attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Kauśika! With my Buddha-eye, I see immeasurable, incalculable beings in the eastern direction who have resolved their minds, practicing for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practicing the bodhisattva path.

Because these beings are far removed from the power of skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, perhaps one or two will abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), while the majority fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.”
It is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

For this reason, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should hear the Prajñāpāramitā; they should receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain, and correctly attend to it.

Having received, upheld, approached, read, recited, explained, and correctly recollected it, one should write out the sūtra scrolls and venerate, make offerings to, respect, and praise them with incense, flowers, necklaces, and even musical performances.
“Any other wholesome dharmas that enter into the perfection of wisdom should likewise be heard, accepted, maintained, and even correctly recollected.
What are these other wholesome dharmas?”
That is to say: the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation;

internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; all the gateways of samādhi and all the gateways of dhāraṇī; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
All such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as these enter into the Prajñāpāramitā; these, too, should be heard, accepted, maintained, and even correctly recollected.
Why is this? These sons and daughters of good family should reflect in this way:

"When the Buddha was originally a bodhisattva, he practiced and studied in this manner—namely, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the various gates of samādhi and the various gates of dhāraṇī; the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and great loving-kindness and great compassion."
We should also follow and study these immeasurable Buddha-dharmas such as these. Why is this?
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is what we revere, and the Dhyānapāramitā, as well as all other immeasurable wholesome dharmas, are likewise what we revere.
This is the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas; it is the Dharma-seal of all Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas.

All Buddhas, by training in this Prajñāpāramitā up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), have crossed to the other shore; likewise, all Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas have also trained in this Prajñāpāramitā up to the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and crossed to the other shore.
"For this reason, Kauśika!

Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should rely upon the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; they should likewise rely upon everything up to all-knowledge."

Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), is that upon which all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the worldlings—including devas, humans, and asuras—may rely.
[Treatise] Question:
The Buddha has already praised the merits of *prajñā* in various ways; why does Śakra Devendra now compare the quantity of the merits of the *śarīra* (relics) with those of *prajñā*?
The answer is:
Those with a predominance of the faculty of faith delight in making offerings to the śarīra;
those with a predominance of the faculty of wisdom prefer to read and recite the sūtras and the Dharma.
Therefore, the question is asked:
"If there is one person who writes out a sutra and makes offerings to it, and another person who makes offerings to the śarīra (relics), which of these constitutes more merit?
The meaning of "flowers, incense, necklaces," and so forth, is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "What do you think?", among the four types of answers, this is an answer by means of a counter-question.
Therefore, the Buddha immediately posed a counter-question to Śakra Devānām Indra.

Some people may gain greater merit by making offerings to the *śarīra*, while others may gain equally great merit by making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*; because this depends on the inclinations of individuals, the Buddha could not give a definitive answer, and therefore he asked a counter-question.
Regarding the statement, "The five perfections arise from the perfection of wisdom," the Buddha himself explains later in a subsequent chapter:
"Generosity that is dedicated through the absence of skillful means and wisdom is not called the dāna-pāramitā."

The eighteen kinds of emptiness are themselves wisdom. By reason of wisdom as their causal condition, the four foundations of mindfulness arise, continuing up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Although these are not entirely wisdom, because they share the same nature and take wisdom as their primary factor, it is said that "they are born from Prajñā."
By practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and thereby gains thorough penetration into generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth;
if one does not attain the true reality of Prajñā, one cannot achieve such penetration into generosity, ethical discipline, and the rest.
Why is this? If all phenomena are empty, then there would be neither sin nor merit; what need would there be for giving or observing the precepts?
If all phenomena truly possessed intrinsic characteristics, they should not arise from causes and conditions, because they would already exist beforehand.
If sentient beings were eternal, they would be like space, and there would likewise be no one who dies;
if they were impermanent, the spirit would perish along with the body, and there would likewise be no future retribution for sins or merit.
If there were no sentient beings, how could there be the sin of killing?
Likewise, there would be no precept against taking life and so forth.

If one realizes this reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence, but employs the Middle Way to penetrate giving, morality, and the other perfections.
Due to the retribution of such practices as this giving and upholding the precepts, there exist the great clans of the Kṣatriyas and even the Buddhas.
Question:
The people of Jambudvīpa are largely greedy for profit and merit; why do they not make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā?
Answer: Because wise people are few, it is no fault that they do not know how to make offerings to Prajñā;
it is like precious gold that a blind person does not recognize.

Since those among the people of Jambudvīpa who have faith in the Three Jewels are few, let alone those who know them and are able to practice accordingly, the Buddha wished to have Śakra Devānām Indra speak for himself; therefore, he asked in reverse:
"How many people have attained indestructible faith in the Three Jewels? and so forth.
Question:
What is the difference between unshakable faith, freedom from doubt, and definitive understanding? Answer:
Some say: there is no difference;
the Buddha’s various adornments of speech are for the purpose of awakening the minds of people.
Some say: "One attains indestructible faith within the Three Jewels.
How is this known?
Because there is no doubt.
How is it known that there is no doubt?
Because there is definitive understanding.
Question:
What is the difference between being without doubt and having definitive understanding? Answer:
Because one first places faith in the Triple Gem, there is no doubt; because wisdom is ultimate, there is definitive realization.
It is like crossing a river: entering it for the first time is being without doubt, while reaching the other shore is definitive realization.

Due to the power of the three factors of noble ethical discipline, faith is indestructible; due to the power of the four factors, there is no doubt; and due to the power of the factor of right view, there is definitive understanding.

Furthermore, within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), this is indestructible faith; within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), it is the absence of doubt; and within the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), it is definitive understanding.
Regarding these various distinctions,
what kind of retribution is obtained from these three matters?
From the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the six supernormal powers, these are conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛta-phala*).
The exhaustion of the three fetters up to the exhaustion of afflictions and their habitual tendencies constitutes the unconditioned fruit—such fruits as these are obtained.

Śakra Devānām Indra possesses knowledge of others' minds born of retribution, and he has also heard the distinctions between the various paths with his divine ear. Furthermore, because this great bodhisattva has sharp faculties and enters the samādhi that contemplates the minds of sentient beings, he knows the distinctions between the various paths; therefore, he answered the Buddha:
"Those who have deep faith are few."

From the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to those who have first resolved to seek the Buddha-way, they become fewer and fewer; because they are fewer and fewer, they do not know how to make offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why are they few?
In the cycle of birth and death throughout previous lives, they did not hear the names of the Three Jewels, nor even the name of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Buddha, wishing to testify to this matter, said:

"Now, with my Buddha-eye, I observe that among the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings in the ten directions who have resolved upon the Unsurpassed Way, only one or two abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) because they lack the power of the skillful means (*upāya*) of Prajñā."
Regarding the phrase "all other wholesome dharmas enter the prajñāpāramitā," these refer to all other sūtras, namely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*, and so forth.

Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, those whose meaning accords with the *Prajñā* are such that, although they are not specifically titled *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, their principles and meaning are nonetheless identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Question:
How is it that even a srotāpanna studies the prajñāpāramitā up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and reaches the other shore? Answer:

Among these, the six pāramitās, the three gates of liberation, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) are not exclusively the dharmas of bodhisattvas; they are common to the three vehicles, each training according to their respective capacity.
[Sūtra] “Kauśika!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, construct stūpas of the seven precious substances one yojana in height, and honor, revere, respect, and praise them with celestial incense, celestial flowers, celestial necklaces, celestial powdered incense, celestial unguents, celestial robes, celestial banners and canopies, and celestial music;”
Kauśika! What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"World-Honored One,
it is very much so!"

"Very much so! The Buddha said, "It is not equal to a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, having heard this Prajñāpāramitā, writes it down, receives and maintains it, draws near to it, and correctly recollects it, never departing from the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta), and furthermore makes offerings, shows reverence, honors, and praises it with flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, unguents, banners, canopies, and musical performances."
"The merit of these good sons and good daughters will be vast.
The Buddha said to Śakra, the devānām-indra Kauśika:
"Set aside the case of a single stūpa made of the seven treasures."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, should erect stupas made of the seven precious substances after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—filling all of Jambudvīpa, each one yojana in height—and honor, respect, and praise them, making offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music.
Kauśika! What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“World-Honored One!
That merit is exceedingly great!”
The Buddha said:
"It is not as much as the merit of these sons and daughters of good family who, as previously described, make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā; their merit is far greater."
Kauśika! Let us set aside the case of a single Jambudvīpa filled with stupas made of the seven treasures.

Suppose there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, erect stupas made of the seven treasures after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that fill the four continents, each one yojana in height, and make offerings to them as before.
Kauśika! What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family have much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Very much! Very much!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as the merit of these sons and daughters of good family who write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and who honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to it with flowers, incense, and even music; their merit is far greater."
Kauśika! Let us set aside the case of the four continents being filled with stupas made of the seven precious substances.

Suppose there were a son or daughter of good family who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erected stupas made of the seven precious substances filling a small thousand-world system, each one yojana in height, and made offerings to them as previously described.
Kauśika! What do you think?
Would that son of good family or daughter of good family have much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“Very many! Very many!”
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as the merit of those sons and daughters of good family who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, and who uphold, revere, honor, and praise it, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even music; their merit is far greater."
Kauśika! Furthermore, setting aside the case of a small thousand-world system filled with stupas made of the seven treasures;

suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erected stupas made of the seven treasures filling a medium two-thousand-world system, each one yojana in height, and made offerings to them as previously described.
It is not as meritorious as making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, for the latter’s merit is far greater. Furthermore,
setting aside the seven-jeweled stupas in two thousand medium-world systems,

suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, should erect seven-jeweled stupas after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa that fill a trichiliocosm, each one yojana in height, and provide them with offerings throughout their entire lives, including celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial necklaces, and even celestial music.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so!
It is very much so!”
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as the merit of those sons and daughters of good family who write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, and who honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to it with flowers, incense, and even music; their merit is far greater."
Furthermore, setting aside the stūpas made of the seven treasures within a trichiliocosm,

suppose every single sentient being in that trichiliocosm, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, were each to erect a stūpa of the seven treasures after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, and to honor, revere, and praise it with offerings of flowers, incense, and even music.

If there are good sons or good daughters who write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and even maintain right mindfulness of it without departing from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and furthermore honor, respect, and praise it, making offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, and even music, these persons will obtain exceedingly great merit.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
“World-Honored One!
If a person makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises this Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present!”
“World-Honored One!

If the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions were each to make offerings to a Buddha, and after that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, were each to erect a stupa made of the seven precious substances one yojana in height, and for one kalpa or less than a kalpa, were to reverently honor, respect, and praise it, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even music;”
“World-Honored One!
Would these good men and good women obtain much merit?
The Buddha said:
"Very much so!
Śakra Devānām Indra said:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā, and even correctly bring it to mind, and furthermore honor, respect, and praise it, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even music, their merit will be exceedingly great!"
Why is this? World-Honored One!

All wholesome dharmas enter into the Prajñāpāramitā; that is to say, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless concentrations, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the three gates of liberation.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the Four Noble Truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path;

the six supernormal powers, the eight liberations, and the nine successive concentrations; the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom; inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the various gates of samādhi and the various gates of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and omniscience.
“World-Honored One!
This is called the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas.
Within this Dharma, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas of the past, future, and present study this Dharma-seal and thereby attain the further shore.”
[Treatise] Commentary:
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, there are immeasurable merits in hearing, receiving and upholding, reciting, reading, and so forth.
Desiring to explain this further, he uses a present-day event as an analogy to verify it:

when people see an earthen stupa that is tall and large, they immediately conceive the thought that the merit of its patron must be exceedingly great; how much more so for a stupa made of the seven treasures, one yojana in height!
For this reason, the Buddha uses the stūpa as a metaphor.
A question is asked:
Is this stūpa real, or is it provisional?
Answer:
The Buddha wished to cause people to understand and discern the relative magnitude of merit; therefore, he employed this analogy, and one should not question its literal truth or falsity! Some say:
There are those that are real and those that are provisional.
For example, after the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a king named Kṛkin.
At that time, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
To make offerings to the śarīra, this king erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, fifty *li* in height.
Furthermore, in a past life, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Guṇendra who, in a single day, erected five hundred stūpas, each five hundred *yojana* in height.
This statement that "it fills a trichiliocosm" is a metaphorical illustration.
Some say that all these things are substantially real.
Just as a minor king builds a stūpa of the seven precious jewels according to his capacity;
a great king can build a stūpa of the seven precious jewels measuring one yojana, or even exceeding one yojana;
and a minor universal monarch (cakravartin) can build stūpas of the seven precious jewels filling the four continents.
A great Wheel-Turning King can erect stupas made of the seven treasures that exceed the four continents;

the Brahma Heaven King, who presides over the trichiliocosm, is a disciple of the Buddha who can produce transformations from his mind, erecting stupas reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven and filling the entire trichiliocosm;

or there may be bodhisattvas who have attained the gates of dhāraṇī and the various gates of samādhi, and because they have deeply practiced the six pāramitās, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they can erect stupas made of the seven treasures that fill the trichiliocosm.
"Full" (pūrṇa) is mentioned because of its abundance; it does not mean that there is no space left between them.
Later, when it says "each and every sentient being," it means that because the donors are many, their merit is great.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions for attaining merit:
"The ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are all subsumed within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
This harmonious dharma is called the Prajñāpāramitā.

Within this Prajñā, it is only the Buddhas who are produced; they alone should be venerated, let alone the fact that the Three Vehicles as well as the joys of humans and devas all exist because of the Prajñāpāramitā—how could one not venerate it?
The relics are indeterminate dharmas; because they serve as the locus upon which all wholesome dharmas rely, they can subsequently bestow retributive fruits upon people.
However, by practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, one attains the fruit immediately and also receives the retribution later.
33. Chapter on Describing Sincerity. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on Describing Sincerity, Number Thirty-three. [Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devendra:
“It is so! It is thus!”
"So it is, Kauśika!

These sons and daughters of good family who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, who take up its volumes to study them, and who draw near to it, read, recite, explain, and correctly attend to it— furthermore, those who honor it with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, banners, canopies, and music— shall obtain immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, incomparable, and boundless merit!"
Why is this? All the Buddhas’ omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are born from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) are all born from the perfection of wisdom.

From the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all are born from the perfection of wisdom.
The five eyes of all Buddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

The maturation of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-fields, the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā), the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and all the Buddha-dharmas are all born from the perfection of wisdom.
The vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the buddhas all arise from the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, Kauśika!

Good sons and good daughters who write down this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold its scrolls, draw near to it, read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate it, and furthermore make offerings of flowers, incense, and even music—these surpass the previous offering to the stupas of the seven treasures by a factor of a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy!
Why is this? Kauśika!
If the Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus will never perish.

If the Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, then the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all modes—all these appear in the world.

If the Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, then there will be in the world the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great families of householders; the gods from the Four Great Kings up to those of Akaniṣṭha; the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the fruit of Arhat; the path of the Pratyekabuddha; the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva; the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; the turning of the wheel of Dharma; the maturing of sentient beings; and the purification of Buddha-fields.
[Treatise] Commentary: Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied to the Buddha, saying:
"The merit of making offerings to Prajñā is exceedingly great."
Furthermore, because Mahādeva is not omniscient, what he says may occasionally be erroneous; therefore, the Buddha confirmed his words, saying: "So it is!"
"So it is! He asked:

"If the characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā is such that all conceptualizations are extinguished, the path of language is cut off, and it is neither arising nor ceasing, having a characteristic like empty space;"
Now, why is it said that "as long as Prajñā exists in the world, the Three Jewels do not perish"?
The answer is:
the essential nature of the Prajñāpāramitā is eternally present and indestructible, whether a Buddha exists or does not exist.

Regarding this statement, "it exists in the world," it refers to the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls that can be practiced, read, and recited; this is a case of describing the effect by way of the cause.
For example, if a well is deep and the rope is too short to reach the water, one might say the well is lost; yet the well is actually not lost.
The true nature of the Prajñāpāramitā is like the deep well, and the sūtra scrolls are called the rope. Because practitioners are unable to transcribe and practice it, they say it has perished.
Question:

If it is said that the Three Jewels encompass all virtuous persons and all wholesome dharmas, why does one further state that "as long as Prajñā remains in the world, the ten paths of wholesome action up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) exist in the world"?
Answer: These various dharmas and paths all extensively explain the meaning within the Three Jewels.
As for the Jewel of the Buddha, it consists of the five aggregates of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as encompassed by the Buddha-dharma.

The Dharma Jewel is the third truth, namely nirvāṇa; it comprises the remaining merits of pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, excluding the merits of those in training and those beyond training included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The Jewel of the Sangha consists of the five groups of those in training and those beyond training, namely the four stages of approach and the four fruits.
The remaining ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and so forth, are all merely gates of skillful means for the Path; therefore, they are mentioned separately.
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, Scroll 57.
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom, Explanation of the Chapter on Encouraging the Acceptance and Upholding,
Number 34, Scroll 58.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty. Chapter 34: Encouraging the Acceptance and Upholding. [Sūtra] At that time, all the gods from the Cāturmahārājika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven in this trichiliocosm addressed Śakra-devānām-indra, saying:
"O gods, you should accept this Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, draw near to it, read it, recite it, explain it, and maintain right mindfulness of it!"

Why is this? Because by upholding the Prajñāpāramitā and even by correctly recollecting it, all the wholesome dharmas one has cultivated and accumulated shall be fully perfected; the hosts of devas will increase, and the asuras will diminish.
O sons of the gods!
Because they uphold the *prajñāpāramitā* and even maintain right mindfulness of it, the lineage of the Buddha is not interrupted, nor are the lineages of the Dharma and the Saṅgha interrupted.

Because the lineages of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are not interrupted, there appear in the world the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*. All of them manifest in the world.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the bodhisattva path, all appear in the world;

the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha—all from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha—appear in the world.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas: “Kauśika!
You should receive this Prajñāpāramitā, uphold it, read it, recite it, explain it, and maintain right mindfulness of it!”
Why is this? Kausika, if the asuras should give rise to the thought of wishing to fight with the Trayastrimsha gods, you should at that time recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā;
the evil intentions of the asuras will then be extinguished and will never arise again.

Kauśika! If the five signs of death appear for any devaputras or devakanyās, and they are about to fall into an unfavorable rebirth, you should recite the Prajñāpāramitā before them. By the power of the merit of hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, these devaputras and devakanyās will return to their original abodes.
Why is this? Because hearing the Prajñāpāramitā brings great benefit.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there are good sons or good daughters, or various devaputras and devakanyās, who hear this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra with their ears, by virtue of this merit, they shall gradually attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Kauśika!
All the Buddhas of the past and their disciples studied this Prajñāpāramitā, thereby attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and entering nirvāṇa without remainder.

Kauśika! All Buddhas of future ages, as well as the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions and their disciples, all study this Prajñāpāramitā; they thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and enter Nirvana without remainder.
Why is this so? Kausika!
This Prajñāpāramitā encompasses all wholesome dharmas—whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the great vidyā-mantra, the unsurpassed vidyā-mantra, the peerless vidyā-mantra.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is able to eliminate all unwholesome dharmas and is able to bestow all wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “So it is! So it is!”
Kauśika! The Prajñāpāramitā is the great vidyā-mantra, the unsurpassed vidyā-mantra, the peerless vidyā-mantra. Why is this so?

Kauśika! It is because of this vidyā-mantra that the Buddhas of the past attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the Buddhas of future ages and the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present likewise attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because of this vidyā-mantra.

Because of this incantation, there come to be in the world the ten paths of wholesome action; there come to be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments; there come to be the pāramitās from dāna-pāramitā up to prajñā-pāramitā; there come to be the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; there come to be the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), suchness (tathatā), the characteristic of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the fixed course of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); there come to be the five eyes, the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the Buddha, all-knowledge (sarvajñā), and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñā).

Kauśika! It is because of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas that the ten wholesome paths arise in the world; it is because of them that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and even the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), as well as those from the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the Buddhas, appear in the world.
Just as the full moon illuminates, and the stars likewise illuminate, so it is, Kauśika!

All the wholesome dharmas and true dharmas of the world—from the ten wholesome paths of action up to all-knowledge—if the Buddhas do not appear in the world, they all arise from the bodhisattva; and these skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva all arise from the perfection of wisdom.

By means of this power of skillful means, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving up to the perfection of meditation; the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. Without realizing the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and achieve the perfection of lifespan, the perfection of the world, and the perfection of the bodhisattva’s retinue. That they attain all-knowledge—all these arise from the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Prajñāpāramitā, receives and upholds it, draws near to it, and even maintains right mindfulness of it, such a person shall obtain merits in both the present life and future lives."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What are the merits in this life and in future lives that a son of good family or a daughter of good family obtains by upholding the Prajñāpāramitā, and so forth, through to correctly recollecting it?”
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall ultimately not die from poisoning, shall not be wounded by weapons, and shall not be harmed by water or fire; indeed, they cannot be afflicted by the four hundred and four diseases, except for those resulting from the retribution of past karma."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a legal matter should arise, because this son or daughter of good family has read and recited the Prajñāpāramitā, when they go before the authorities, the officials will not reprimand them."
Why is this? It is because of the power of this Prajñāpāramitā!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family reads and recites this Prajñāpāramitā, when they go before a king, or before a prince or a minister, the king, the prince, and the minister will all joyfully greet them and speak to them with a friendly mind.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family always maintain a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings. Kausika!
If good sons or good daughters receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, they will obtain various such merits in this present life.
“Kauśika! What are the merits of these sons and daughters of good family in future lives?

These sons and daughters of good family shall never be separated from the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the six pāramitās, and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”

Such a person shall never fall into the three evil realms; their physical form will be complete and perfect, and they shall never be born into poverty or lowliness, nor among artisans, scavengers, or those who carry out the dead.
They constantly attain the thirty-two marks and are always born by transformation within the realms of all present Buddhas, never being separated from the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.
If they wish to go from one Buddha-realm to another to make offerings to the Buddhas and listen to the Buddhas' Dharma, they obtain this at will.
In whichever Buddha-realm they travel, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the Buddha-worlds, gradually attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kauśika! These are called the merits of future lives.
For this reason, Kauśika!

Good sons and good daughters should receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā; they should offer worship with flowers, incense, and even music, and never depart from the mind of sarvajña (omniscience).
These good sons and good daughters shall, until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, achieve the fulfillment of merits in both this life and future lives.
[Treatise] Commentary:
The Buddha is the Dharma King; having already praised those who receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, next Śakra, the Heavenly King, offered praise.
After Śakra had praised it, the various devas now offer praise in turn.
Because of the praise from such a great multitude, it causes people's faith to deepen further.
Thus he says:
"One should uphold this Prajñāpāramitā."
In this context, the causes and conditions for upholding [the Dharma] are explained:
"By cultivating all merits, the devas are increased and the asuras are diminished; the Three Jewels remain uninterrupted, and the six pāramitās and other such virtues appear in the world."
At that time, the Buddha, approving the praise of the devas, addressed Śakra, saying:
"You should receive and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā.
Herein, the causes and conditions are explained:
If an asura gives rise to an evil mind, desiring to fight with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, if you at that time recite the Prajñāpāramitā, that evil mind will immediately be extinguished.
If one recites the *Prajñāpāramitā* when two armies are arrayed against each other, the asuras will immediately retreat.
A question is asked:
"If that is so, why not constantly recite the *Prajñāpāramitā* so that the evil intentions of the asuras do not arise?"
"Why, then, are the two armies arrayed against one another?
He replied:

"The various devas are largely attached to the pleasures of merit and their minds are keenly stained by desire; thus, although they know that the Prajñāpāramitā possesses great merit, they are unable to recite it constantly."
Furthermore, due to the causes and conditions of impure karma, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven encounter enemies with whom they must inevitably fight.
When the life of these gods is about to end, five signs of death appear:

first, their flower garlands wither; second, sweat breaks out from beneath their armpits; third, flies come and settle upon their bodies; fourth, they see another god sitting in their own seat; and fifth, they no longer take pleasure in their original seat.

When the devas perceive these signs of death, they reflect with longing upon celestial pleasures; seeing that they are about to be born in an evil realm, their hearts are filled with the poison of sorrow.

At that time, if they hear of the true mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*—that all phenomena are deceptive, impermanent, empty, and quiescent—and they believe in this Buddha-dharma, then because their minds are purified, they return to their original place of birth.

These devas and humans do not merely return to their original places; because they have heard the Prajñāpāramitā, they receive blessings and happiness in every lifetime and gradually perfect the unsurpassed path.
The causal conditions for this are as stated in the Sūtra: "The Prajñāpāramitā is the great vidyā-mantra."
Question:
For what reason does Śakra Devānām Indra call *prajñā* "the great bright mantra"? Answer:
Various non-Buddhists and noble ones possess diverse incantations and arts that benefit the people;
by reciting these incantations, they are able to command all ghosts and spirits according to their will.
Because these sages possess this incantation, they have attained great renown and people submit to them.
Valuing incantations so highly, Śakra said to the Buddha:
"Among all incantations, the Prajñāpāramitā is the great incantation."
Why is this? Because it can constantly bestow upon sentient beings the joy of the Way and its virtue (*mārga-guṇa*).

Other incantations and arts, being causes and conditions for worldly pleasure, can give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) and, because they constitute unwholesome karma (*akuśala-karma*), lead to falling into the three evil realms.
Furthermore, other incantations can cause one to commit evil at will under the influence of greed and hatred;
this Prajñāpāramitā incantation, however, can extinguish all attachments to meditative concentration, the Buddha-way, and nirvāṇa, let alone the coarse maladies of greed and hatred!
For this reason, it is called "the Great Illuminating Mantra, the Unsurpassed Mantra, the Peerless Mantra.

Furthermore, this mantra can cause people to transcend old age, sickness, and death; it can establish sentient beings in the Mahāyāna; and it can cause the practitioner to become the greatest among all sentient beings. Therefore, it is called the "Great Mantra."
Because it is able to provide benefit in this way, it is called "unsurpassed.
Previously there were spells and incantations created by rishis, such as the spell for knowing the minds of others, called *yakṣaṇī*;
and the spell for flying and transforming, called *gāndhārī*.
The incantation capable of sustaining a lifespan exceeding ten million years is peerless among all incantations.
Within these peerless incantational arts, the Prajñāpāramitā surpasses them immeasurably; therefore, it is called "the Peerless Equal" (asamasama).
Furthermore, the name of all Buddhas is "unequaled" (*asama*); because the *prajñāpāramitā* is the cause and condition for attaining Buddhahood, it is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
Furthermore, among all sentient beings, all Buddhas are called "unequaled"; because this *prajñā* incantation was produced by the Buddhas, it is called the "incantation equal to the unequaled."

Furthermore, this sutra itself explains the causes and conditions of the three mantras, stating: "These mantras are able to abandon all unwholesome dharmas and are able to bestow all wholesome dharmas."
The Buddha, in accordance with what was thus praised, said: "So it is! So it is!"
He further elaborates on that praise, saying: "It is because of *prajñā* that the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including all Buddhas, are produced.
Since this *prajñāpāramitā* belongs to the Bodhisattvas, the Buddha provides a simile:
because the Buddhas can utterly destroy the darkness of ignorance, they are like the full moon.
Because the Bodhisattva’s destruction of darkness is not like that [of ordinary beings], he is like the constellations.
Just as whatever is seen in the night is entirely due to the power of the stars and the moon,
so too, whatever knowledge and vision exists within the night of worldly birth and death is entirely due to the power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

If there is no Buddha in the world, at that time, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; while they are immersed in the pleasures of humans and devas, he gradually causes them to attain the bliss of nirvana.
All the wisdom possessed by a bodhisattva is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, although this bodhisattva practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen kinds of emptiness, knowing that all phenomena are ultimately ungraspable, he does not realize the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; yet he is able to give rise once more to wholesome dharmas, to transform sentient beings, to purify buddha-fields, and to fulfill his lifespan—all of these are the power of the skillful means of *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a person can receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and even maintain right mindfulness of it, they will attain merits in both this life and future lives.
Regarding "merits in this life," these refer to such things as never dying from poisoning and so forth.
Question: It has already been stated previously that there is no untimely death; why is it being stated again now? Answer:
The Prajñāpāramitā has already been explained; it was not taught within a single assembly, but is now being taught again for those who have arrived later.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of swords, poisons, water, and fire:
those produced by others and those produced by oneself.
Previously, it was stated that others might inflict weapons, poison, water, fire, and so forth; now, it is for the sake of not harming oneself.
How is this known?
It is known because the four hundred and four diseases are subsequently mentioned.
Although it was stated above that "no one can find an opportunity against him," it was not said that "that person will instead revere and make offerings to him.
Regarding the "four hundred and four diseases," the four great elements constitute the body, which is constantly subject to mutual affliction.
Within each of these great categories, one hundred and one diseases arise:
two hundred and two cold diseases, arising from water and wind;
and two hundred and two hot diseases, arising from earth and fire.

Fire has the characteristic of heat; earth has the characteristic of solidity. Because of its solidity, it is difficult to digest; because it is difficult to digest, it can give rise to feverish diseases.
Blood, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and so forth, belong to the category of earth.

Regarding the phrase "except for the retribution of karma": all dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; there is no creator. Because there is no creator, one must inevitably undergo the retribution of karma, which even a Buddha cannot save, let alone Prajñā!
That one must experience the retribution of karma or need not experience the retribution of karma has already been explained previously.
As for the arising of legal disputes, by the power of reciting the Prajñāpāramitā, they are all extinguished as soon as they arise.
Question: It was previously stated that "humans cannot find an opportunity," so why is this being stated again now? Answer:

Although it was previously stated that others could not find an opportunity [to harm him], it was not said that kings, ministers, and the like—once they were unable to find such an opportunity—would instead continue to revere and make offerings to him.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas always maintain a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward sentient beings.

Regarding "merit in future lives," it means that in every birth throughout successive lifetimes they never depart from the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) and so forth; therefore, they never fall into the evil realms (*durgati*).
Because this person has subdued their evil mind, they receive a complete and perfect body and are not born into lowly or inferior families.

Because they have studied the path practiced by the Buddha, they attain a transformation body resembling that of a Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.

Regarding the phrase "constantly attaining birth by transformation in the lands of present Buddhas": wherever the mind reaches throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one makes offerings to the Buddhas, listens to and receives the various teachings, and transforms sentient beings, gradually attaining the Way of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the practitioner should hear, receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect [this teaching], never departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
In this way, one will attain merits in both the present life and future lives.

35. Chapter on the Brahmins. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Brahmins, Number Thirty-Five. [Sūtra] At that time, various non-Buddhist brahmins came toward where the Buddha was, desiring to find fault with him.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"These various non-Buddhist brahmins are coming toward the Buddha’s dwelling, wishing to seek out the Buddha’s faults;

I shall now recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā as I received it from the Buddha, so that these various non-Buddhist brahmins will ultimately be unable to create obstacles along the way or interrupt the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā."
After Śakra Devānām-indra had formed this thought, he immediately recited the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist brahmins circumambulated the Buddha from afar and returned by the same path they had come.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"For what reason do these non-Buddhist brahmins circumambulate the Buddha from afar and then return by the same way?
Knowing Śāriputra’s thought, the Buddha addressed him:

"It is because Śakra Devānām Indra recited and contemplated the Prajñāpāramitā that, for this reason, the various non-Buddhist brahmins circumambulated the Buddha from afar and returned by the way they came."
Śāriputra! I do not see even a single thought of a wholesome mind in these non-Buddhist brahmins;
these non-Buddhist brahmins come bearing only evil intentions, desiring to seek out the faults of the Buddha.
Śāriputra!

When the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, I do not see anyone in the entire world—whether among the devas, māras, brahmās, the assembly of śramaṇas, or the assembly of brāhmaṇas—who could come with malicious intent and find fault with it.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within this trichiliocosm,
the gods from the Cāturmahārājika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, as well as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all protect this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? It is because all these devas and humans are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, spirits, and others alike protect this Prajñāpāramitā.
"Why is this? It is because all these Buddhas and others are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Māra, the Evil One, thought to himself:

"Now the fourfold assembly of the Buddha has gathered before him, as have the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm; among them there must be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have received the prediction that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"I shall go to where the Buddha is and destroy his resolve.
At that time, Māra the Evil One manifested as fourfold armies and approached the place where the Buddha was.
Then, Śakra Devendra thought to himself:
"These fourfold armies are either created by Māra the Evil One, wishing to come toward the Buddha.

Why is this? These fourfold armies are so magnificently adorned that they do not resemble the fourfold armies of King Bimbisāra, nor do they resemble those of King Prasenajit; they do not resemble the fourfold armies of the Śākyas, nor even those of the Licchavis."
"This evil Māra has long sought an opportunity to harm the Buddha and intends to afflict sentient beings; I should instead recite the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra-devānām-indra immediately recited the Prajñāpāramitā. As he heard it being recited, the evil Māra gradually retraced his path and departed.

At that time, the sons of the gods from the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha heaven within the assembly manifested celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha from mid-air, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
May the Prajñāpāramitā long abide in Jambudvīpa!

Why is this? Because as long as the people of Jambudvīpa receive, uphold, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā, for that duration the Jewel of the Buddha will abide without perishing, and the Jewels of the Dharma and the Sangha will likewise abide without perishing.
At that time, the devas in worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, also scattered flowers and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Prajñāpāramitā may long abide in Jambudvīpa!”
If the Prajñāpāramitā remains for a long time, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha shall also remain for a long time, and one will also discern and know the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, wherever a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out and maintains a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, that place shall be illuminated, having already departed from all darkness.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām-Indra and the other devaputras: “So it is! So it is!”
Kauśika and all you sons of the gods!
As long as people of Jambudvīpa uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, for that duration the Jewel of the Buddha remains present; likewise, the Jewel of the Dharma and the Jewel of the Saṅgha remain present.
Furthermore, wherever a son or daughter of good family has written out and upheld a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, that place becomes illuminated, having already departed from all darkness.
At that time, the sons of the gods manifested celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women who receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, and even correctly bring it to mind, Māra or the gods of Māra shall be unable to find an opportunity against them."
"Bhagavān!
We, too, shall protect these good men and good women. Why is this?"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintains right mindfulness toward it, we regard such a person as being the Buddha himself or one next to the Buddha.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It should be known that those good men and good women who receive, uphold, and even correctly bring to mind the Prajñāpāramitā have, in previous lives, performed meritorious deeds for the Buddhas, have extensively approached and made offerings to the Buddhas, and have been protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).”
"Bhagavān!
The omniscience of all Buddhas should be sought from within the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā should likewise be sought from within omniscience!"
Why is this? The perfection of wisdom is not different from all-knowledge, and all-knowledge is not different from the perfection of wisdom;
the perfection of wisdom and all-knowledge are non-dual and undifferentiated.
"Therefore, we regard such a person as being either a Buddha or one next to a Buddha.
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra: "It is so!"
"So it is, Kauśika!
The all-knowledge of all Buddhas is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is precisely all-knowledge."
Why is this? Kauśika!
The all-knowledge of all Buddhas is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The perfection of wisdom is not different from omniscience, and omniscience is not different from the perfection of wisdom;
the perfection of wisdom and omniscience are non-dual and undifferentiated.
[Treatise] Commentary:
It was stated in the "Superior Chapter" that those who hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be taken advantage of by Māras, the followers of Māra, or non-Buddhist brahmins.
Now, desiring to provide manifest verification, he employs his majestic spiritual power to summon the various Māras and non-Buddhists.
For this reason, the non-Buddhist brahmins conceived this thought:
"The Buddha is on Vulture Peak Mountain preaching the Prajñāpāramitā, asserting that all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent, thereby attracting sentient beings from the ten directions."
"Let us go together to challenge and refute this discourse on emptiness;
if that discourse is refuted, the Buddha will naturally withdraw, and we shall return to our original state.
These non-Buddhists came only because of their false views, evil intentions, and arrogance, desiring to expose the faults and transgressions of this ultimately pure Prajñāpāramitā.
It is like a madman wishing to injure empty space; he merely exhausts himself in vain!
At that time, Śakra, following the Buddha’s instruction, upheld the Prajñāpāramitā, so that the non-Buddhists could find no opportunity to prevail.

Now, wishing to verify this reality so that people may come to believe and know it, Śakra, having accomplished immeasurable merit and possessing the sharp faculties of a deva, deeply believed in the Prajñāpāramitā; he immediately recited it, and by the power of the Prajñā, the non-Buddhists who had been circumambulating the Buddha from afar turned back and departed on their way.
Question:
Why did he not simply return directly, but instead circumambulate the Buddha before departing? Answer:
By the power of *prajñā*, they subdued [the opponent] from afar and thought:
"The Buddha and his assembly possess such immense majesty and virtue; for us to go there now would only result in self-humiliation and achieve nothing.
If we were to see him from afar and simply depart, people would say that we are cowardly and have come only to leave empty-handed."
For this reason, he feigned making offerings and circumambulating the Buddha, then departed by way of the road.

Śāriputra was originally a brahmin; seeing the various non-Buddhists departing from afar, his heart felt a slight sense of pity. Unable to enter samādhi to seek knowledge for the sake of such a minor matter, he thought to himself:
"For what cause and condition have these non-Buddhists come, only to return empty-handed without receiving deliverance?"
The Buddha said,
"This is the power of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
“The Buddha, through the *prajñāpāramitā*, leaves no matter unrescued; why then have these non-Buddhists come here empty-handed and departed?
Knowing what Śāriputra was thinking, the Buddha said to him:

“These brahmins do not possess even a single thought of a wholesome mind; they harbor only evil intentions, their minds are attached to false views, and they seek to grasp the fixed characteristics of all dharmas. For this reason, they do not pass through the middle.”
"It is like a terminal illness; even if there were a skilled physician and divine medicine, they could not provide a cure.
Śāriputra, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, it is not only this brahmin, but all people in the world who come with malicious intent that cannot find an opportunity to cause harm."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and devas constantly protect and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
For what reason?
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, and humans have this thought:
"We are all born from Prajñā.
When Māra comes wishing to challenge, question, and destroy [this teaching], it is also like this.

At that time, the sons of the gods within the assembly, having previously heard of the merit of the Prajñāpāramitā and now witnessing its actual manifestation, were filled with great joy. They manifested flowers as an offering and made this vow:
"May the Prajñāpāramitā long abide in Jambudvīpa!"
"This matter is as explained extensively below.
The Buddha then gave his approval.
The devas made a vow before the Buddha, saying:
“If a practitioner hears, receives, and even correctly recollects the Prajñāpāramitā, we shall always protect them! Why is this? Because—”
"We regard such persons as Buddhas or those next to Buddhas.

Regarding "as Buddhas," this refers to the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya), abiding in *avaivartika* [non-retrogression], attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and reaching up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "the next Buddha": it refers to a *māṃsa-kāya* (fleshly) bodhisattva who is able to expound the *prajñāpāramitā* and its correct meaning.
At that time, Śakra praises this bodhisattva by virtue of the merit and wisdom accumulated through causes and conditions in previous lives;
herein, the causes and conditions for this praise are further explained.

Regarding the statement, "The all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas should be sought within Prajñā": because the Bodhisattva, by virtue of fulfilling the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), attains Buddhahood at which time that Prajñā transforms into all-aspect wisdom; therefore, it is said that "all-aspect wisdom should be sought within Prajñā."
Because the Buddha can preach the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is said that "the *prajñāpāramitā* should be sought within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
For example, when milk transforms into curd, there is no curd apart from the milk, yet one cannot say that the milk is itself the curd;

likewise, when the *prajñāpāramitā* transforms into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is no knowledge of all modes apart from the *prajñā*, yet one cannot say that the *prajñā* is itself the knowledge of all modes.

Prajñā acts as the generative cause for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all modes acts as the explanatory cause for Prajñā; because cause and effect are inseparable, they are said to be "non-dual and undifferentiated."
36. Chapter on Ānanda’s Praise. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on Ānanda’s Praise, Number Thirty-Six. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

For what reason do you not praise the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and even the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇikadharma), but praise only the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the honored guide for the five pāramitās, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha!
Ānanda!”
"What do you think?
Without dedicating it toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge), can a gift be called dānapāramitā? "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Are morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom that are not dedicated toward *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
"No, World-Honored One!
For this reason, it is known that the Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme guide among the five pāramitās and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; therefore, it is praised."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does one dedicate the gift toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge) so that it becomes the dānapāramitā, and so on, up to becoming the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"To give with the dharma of non-duality and dedicate it to sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā);
to give by dedicating it to sarvajñā through the perspective of non-arising and non-apprehensibility is called the perfection of giving."
Even up to dedicating with the wisdom of non-dual dharmas toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*;
dedicating with the wisdom that is unborn and unattainable toward *sarvajñā*, this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that dedicating giving toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) by means of the non-dual dharma is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), and so on, up to how dedicating wisdom toward omniscience by means of the non-dual dharma is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Because form is the non-dual dharma; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the non-dual dharma; and so on, up to unexcelled perfect enlightenment being the non-dual dharma."
“World-Honored One!
What is the non-dual nature of form, and so on, up to the non-dual nature of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said:
"Form is empty of the characteristic of form. Why is this?
Because the perfection of giving and form are non-dual and not distinct."
Up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the *dāna-pāramitā*, they are non-dual and not distinct.
The same applies to the other five *pāramitās*.
For this reason, Ānanda, one should simply praise the Prajñāpāramitā;
it is the honored guide for the five pāramitās, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)!
Ānanda! It is like the earth: when seeds are scattered upon it, they arise through the convergence of causes and conditions; these various seeds depend upon the earth to grow.
In this way, Ānanda!
The five pāramitās arise depending upon the prajñāpāramitā; likewise, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), they too arise depending upon the prajñāpāramitā.
"For this reason, Ānanda,
the Prajñāpāramitā is the noble guide for the five pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha!
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Blessed One has said that for good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, and even correctly contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit is inexhaustible.”
Why is this? Because by upholding the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintaining right mindfulness of it, one receives the unsurpassed path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Why is that?
If one wishes to attain sarvajñā (all-knowledge), one should seek it from within the prajñāpāramitā;
if one wishes to attain the prajñāpāramitā, one should seek it from within sarvajñā.
World-Honored One!

Because of upholding the Prajñāpāramitā and even correctly recollecting it, the ten paths of wholesome action appear in the world; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha appear in the world.

Because they uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness of it, there exist in the world the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great families of householders, and the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Because they uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness of it, there come to be those from the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
“Because they uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness of it, the Buddhas appear in the world.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā—I do not say that they possess only such merit as that.
Why is this? Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness do not depart from the mind of sarvajña (all-knowledge); they achieve the immeasurable aggregate of morality, and they achieve the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If these sons or daughters of good family are able to receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, and do not depart from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), you should know that such persons are like the Buddha.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

The entire aggregate of morality, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation possessed by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not equal the aggregate of morality up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of these sons and daughters of good family; they do not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a ten-thousand-billionth part, nor can they be reached by any calculation or analogy!
Why is this? It is because these good sons and good daughters have attained liberation within the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and no longer seek the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who write out and uphold a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, and honor, revere, and respect it with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even musical performances, they shall likewise obtain merit in both this life and future lives.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If these sons and daughters of good family receive, uphold, and correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, remaining never apart from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā—honoring, respecting, and presenting it with flowers, incense, and even music—I shall constantly protect such persons!”
[Treatise] Commentary:
Although Ānanda was widely learned and possessed the power to discern emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because he had not yet abandoned desire, he could not penetrate it deeply;
thus, despite constantly attending upon the Buddha, he did not frequently inquire about or debate matters concerning emptiness.
Now, as the Buddha praises the *prajñāpāramitā* and also praises the practitioner, Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
why do you not praise the other *pāramitās* and all other dharmas, but praise only the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
Question: Since the beginning, the Buddha has always spoken of the names of the six pāramitās; why does Ānanda now say that they were "not mentioned"? Answer:
Although names are spoken, they are not for the purpose of praise; they are all spoken for the sake of entering into Prajñā.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), wisdom is foremost."
"Among all forms of wisdom, the Prajñāpāramitā that reaches the other shore is supreme.
It is like traveling on a road: although there may be many companions, the guide is foremost;
