so it is with Prajñā—although all wholesome dharmas each possess their own power, it is the Prajñāpāramitā alone that can provide guidance to transcend the triple world and reach the three vehicles.
If there were no Prajñāpāramitā, although one might practice wholesome dharmas such as giving, the retribution for those karmic actions would eventually be exhausted;
because it is subject to exhaustion, one could not even attain the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle, let alone the Unsurpassed Way!

If one can contemplate wholesome dharmas such as giving as being non-dual with the characteristics of the Buddha-way—neither arising nor ceasing, neither gained nor lost, and ultimately empty and quiescent—this is called "dedicating toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
The merit of this giving will constantly yield its retribution throughout successive lifetimes without exhaustion, and in the end, one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As it is with giving, so it is with the nature of all phenomena.
Question: Why does the Buddha not answer by means of the causes and conditions of non-duality (*advaya*), but instead explains it through "non-duality" itself? Answer:
Ānanda did not ask about the causes and conditions for non-duality, but rather asked, "What dharma is non-dual? Therefore, the Buddha replied:
"Because all dharmas, such as form and so forth, are non-dual."
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* enables the five things to become *pāramitās*, only the *prajñāpāramitā* is praised.
Desiring to make this meaning clear and easy to understand, the Buddha employs this analogy:
"Just as the great earth can produce all things, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*."

Regarding the phrase "able to maintain the seeds of all wholesome dharmas": from the moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment until now, it refers to all other wholesome dharmas with the exception of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This "conjunction of causes and conditions" refers to those dharmas within the Buddha-way such as single-mindedness, faith, patience, unremitting and unceasing diligence, aspiration, reception, penetration, and non-destruction.

Regarding the accomplishment of the task: this refers to the one who increases [their practice], beginning from the generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and training in the various *pāramitās*, proceeding from stage to stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of Buddhahood.
Question: For what reason does Śakra say, "The Buddha has not yet fully exhausted the description of the merits of one who practices and upholds the Prajñā"? Answer:
The Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and boundless, and its merit is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
As the teaching was not yet concluded, non-Buddhist brahmins and Māra arrived in the interim, leading to digressions on other matters; now, I wish to resume the discourse for you to hear.
Śakra, deeply cherishing the fruits of merit and fond of hearing the virtues of Prajñā, listens without ever being satiated.
Now, wishing to hear it explained once more, he himself states the causal conditions:
"World-Honored One!..."

If a person upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintains right mindfulness of it, they will receive the merit, wisdom, and the unsurpassed path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Why is this so?
"One should seek all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) within Prajñāpāramitā, and one should seek Prajñāpāramitā within all-knowledge," as stated at the end of the preceding chapter.

If a practitioner upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and resolves their mind to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they will accumulate the various merits of the Prajñāpāramitā and so forth— namely, the ten paths of wholesome action up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)— which then manifest in the world.
By reason of these wholesome dharmas, there arise great kṣatriya clans, up to and including the Buddhas.
The Buddha told Śakra Devendra:
"This person not only attains the merits mentioned above, but also attains immeasurable merits such as the aggregate of precepts."
Regarding the "multitude of precepts": when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the gift of ultimate fearlessness among all sentient beings.

The number of sentient beings throughout the ten directions is immeasurable and boundless; the number within the three periods of time is likewise immeasurable and boundless; and the various types of the six realms and four modes of birth are each immeasurable and boundless in their characteristics.

Among these immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, the bodhisattva gives that which is most cherished and beloved—namely, life itself—and thereby attains the fruit of the immeasurable multitude of precepts.
Regarding these precepts such as non-killing and so forth, if one speaks merely of their names, there are two hundred and fifty;
in the Vinaya, they are briefly explained as eighty-four thousand, and extensively explained as immeasurable and boundless.
Regarding this precept, ordinary persons may receive it for a single day, for a single lifetime, or for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes;
whereas the Bodhisattva bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings in every lifetime until they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. This is called the immeasurable aggregate of precepts.
This applies even up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; these should likewise be distinguished according to their meaning.
These merits of the five aggregates surpass those of the two vehicles and are immeasurable.
If a person transcribes and makes offerings to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they will obtain merit in both the present life and future lives.
Question:
Since the merit of the present and future lives is profound and weighty, while the acts of transcribing, upholding, and making offerings are minor, how can one obtain the merit of both lifetimes?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of offerings:
first, offering by imitation of others; second, offering with a profound mind.
By knowing the merits of Prajñā and making offerings with a profound mind, one attains the merits of both worlds.
This Prajñā has various gateways for entry: those who hear, uphold, and even correctly recollect it enter through the gateways of wisdom and diligence;
those who transcribe and make offerings enter through the gateways of faith and diligence.
If one possesses single-minded deep faith, then making offerings to the sutra scrolls is superior;
if one lacks single-mindedness, then even though one upholds them, it is not as effective.

Furthermore, there is such a thing as a wish-fulfilling jewel: it is a neutral material phenomenon (rūpa-dharma) that is without mind and without consciousness, yet it arises due to the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings; if someone makes offerings to it, it can cause that person to obtain whatever they desire at will.

How much more so for the Prajñāpāramitā, which is the unsurpassed wisdom, the mother of all Buddhas, and the foremost treasure among all the jewels of the Dharma—if a person, according to what they have heard, single-mindedly believes, accepts, and makes offerings to it, how could they not obtain the merits of both worlds?

However, it is because people do not make offerings with a single-minded devotion and because of heavy karmic offenses from previous lives that, despite making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not obtain the aforementioned merits; the fault does not lie with the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Sūtra] The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!
When these sons and daughters of good family wish to read, recite, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas will all come to hear the Dharma.”
When these sons and daughters of good family preach the Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, the devaputras augment their courage and strength.
If these Dharma-preachers become utterly exhausted and do not wish to preach the Dharma, because the devas augment their courage and strength, they are able to preach even further.

Good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect this Prajñāpāramitā, and who make offerings of flowers, incense, and even music, shall likewise attain these merits in the present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
when these sons and daughters of good family teach the Prajñāpāramitā among the fourfold assembly, their minds are free from timidity;
even if there are challenges or debates, they harbor no sense of fear."
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family are protected and sustained by the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, all phenomena (*dharma*) are also analyzed and distinguished.

Whether mundane or supramundane, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether wholesome or unwholesome, whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether the Dharma of Śrāvakas, the Dharma of Pratyekabuddhas, the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, or the Dharma of Buddhas.

Because good sons and good daughters abide in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they do not perceive anyone who can challenge the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they perceive anyone who receives such a challenge, nor do they perceive the *prajñāpāramitā* itself.
In this way, because they are protected and sustained by the *prajñāpāramitā*, no one is able to challenge or destroy them.
Furthermore, when sons and daughters of good family receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not sink, they do not fear, and they are not terrified.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family do not perceive any dharma that perishes or causes fear. Kausika!

Good sons and good daughters who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness toward it, and who offer flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies, shall likewise obtain these merits in this present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and even correctly recollects it, or writes and preserves the sūtra scrolls, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—such a person will be beloved by their parents, remembered by their kinsmen and friends, and respected by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. They will be loved and revered by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and even srotāpannas. Furthermore, they will be loved and revered by all the world, whether devas, māras, brahmās, or asuras."
This person practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), and there is no time when this perfection of giving is interrupted;

likewise, there is no time when the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is interrupted;

they practice the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) without interruption, up to and including the practice of the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*) without interruption.
They cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness without interruption, up to and including the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha without interruption;
they cultivate the various gates of samādhi without interruption, and the various gates of dhāraṇī without interruption;

they cultivate the supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas without interruption, the maturing of sentient beings without interruption, the purification of buddha-fields without interruption, up to and including the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes without interruption.
Such a person is also able to subdue difficult arguments and slanderous attacks.

Good sons and good daughters who receive and uphold the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and even maintain right mindfulness of it without departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and who copy and uphold the scriptural volumes, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies, shall likewise obtain these merits in both this life and future lives.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Wherever a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out and maintains this sūtra scroll, all the Cāturmahārājika devas within the trichiliocosm who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* will come to that place; having seen the Prajñāpāramitā, they will receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before it, and then depart."

Those from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-pariṣad, and Mahābrahmā Heavens; the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, and Ābhāsvara-svara Heavens; the Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna Heavens; and the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala Heavens—those who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all come to this place. Having seen the Prajñāpāramitā, they receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before it, and then depart.

The gods of the Pure Abodes—namely the gods of Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha—all came to this place, saw this Prajñāpāramitā, received it, read it, recited it, explained it, made offerings to it, and paid homage to it before returning.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

The various devas from the Cāturmahārājika heaven up to the Bṛhatphala heaven in the worlds of the ten directions who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and all other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, also come to behold the Prajñāpāramitā, receive it, read it, recite it, explain it, make offerings to it, and pay homage to it before returning.
These sons of good family and daughters of good family should form this thought:

"When the various devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Bṛhatphala devas in the worlds of the ten directions—who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—as well as the Śuddhāvāsa devas and all other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, come to see, receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before the *prajñāpāramitā*, I shall have already bestowed the gift of Dharma."

"Kauśika! All the Cāturmahārājika devas up to the Akaniṣṭha devas within this trichiliocosm, and even all the Cāturmahārājika devas up to the Akaniṣṭha devas throughout the worlds of the ten directions who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, shall protect these good men and good women; no evils shall find an opportunity to harm them, except for those grave karmic offenses from past lives."

Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall also obtain these merits in this present life, namely that all the devaputras who have resolved their minds on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will come to this place.
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because these sons of the gods have resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, desiring to rescue and protect all sentient beings, not to abandon any sentient being, and to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How should a son of good family or a daughter of good family know when the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven have come, as well as the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven from the worlds of the ten directions, to see, receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before this Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees a great, pure radiance, they should know for certain that great virtuous devas have come at the time when they see, receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before the Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family perceives a wondrous and extraordinary fragrance, they should know for certain that great virtuous devas have come to see, receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to, and prostrate before the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Because good sons and good daughters practice purity, the devas come to their place; having seen the Prajñāpāramitā, they receive, read, recite, explain, make offerings to it, rejoice in it, and pay homage to it."
Therein, the minor spirits immediately depart, unable to endure the majestic power and virtue of these great and venerable devas.
Because these great and venerable devas have come, these sons and daughters of good family give rise to the Great Mind.

For this reason, in the place where the Prajñāpāramitā resides, there should be no impurities on any of its four sides; one should light lamps, burn incense, scatter various famous flowers, smear the ground with various perfumes, and adorn it with various canopies, banners, and streamers.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

When a son of good family or a daughter of good family preaches the Dharma, they never experience exhaustion; they perceive their own bodies as light and their minds as joyful. They rest in accordance with the Dharma, and whether lying down or waking, they are peaceful and secure, free from all evil dreams."
In a dream, one sees the Buddhas endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics;

surrounded by a community of bhikṣus who pay them respectful homage, they preach the Dharma. Standing beside these Buddhas, one hears and receives their teachings—namely, the six pāramitās, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—and one discerns the meaning of the six pāramitās, as well as the meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities.
He also saw the Bodhi tree adorned with exquisite splendor;
he saw various bodhisattvas approaching the Bodhi tree and attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and he saw various Buddhas, having completed their enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma.

He sees hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas gathered together to discuss the Dharma and its principles, seeing that one should seek *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) in this way, should bring sentient beings to maturity in this way, and should purify Buddha-fields in this way;

he also sees countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas in the ten directions and hears their names—such as a certain Buddha in a certain direction, a certain realm, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas and hundreds of thousands of millions of śrāvakas who respectfully attend him as he preaches the Dharma;
furthermore, he sees countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas in the ten directions entering parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he saw countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of stūpas made of the seven treasures belonging to various Buddhas;
he saw offerings being made to these Buddha-stūpas, honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family, having seen such auspicious dreams, sleep in peace and awaken in peace;

the devas augment their vital strength, and they perceive their own bodies as light and agile. They do not have great craving for food, clothing, bedding, or medicine; regarding these four types of offerings, their minds remain detached.”

For example, it is like a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna who, having arisen from meditative concentration, has a mind unified with that concentration; he does not crave food and drink, and his mind is light and subtle. Why is this?
Kauśika! It is the natural law for the gods that they should augment their vital strength with the essence of all flavors.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, garuḍas, and mahoragas, likewise augment their vital strength.
"In this way, Kauśika!

A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to obtain such merits in this present life should receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā, and should likewise not depart from the mind of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."

Kauśika! Although good sons and good daughters may not be able to receive, uphold, or even correctly recollect [this teaching], they should nevertheless transcribe and maintain the scriptural volume, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even banners and canopies.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Prajñāpāramitā, and receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, correctly contemplates, and transcribes it into a volume; and if they honor, make offerings to, revere, and praise it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.

The merit of these good sons and good daughters is exceedingly great; it surpasses that of one who makes offerings to the Buddhas and their disciples throughout the ten directions, honoring, respecting, and praising them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites;

or who, after the Buddhas and their disciples have entered parinirvāṇa, erects stūpas of the seven precious substances to honor, make offerings to, respect, and praise them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.
[Treatise] Question:
Since *prajñā* exists naturally in the heavens, why does it come to the place of the Dharma-preacher to augment his courage and strength? Answer:
Although there is Prajñā in the heavens, the devas come out of compassion for sentient beings;
when the devas arrive, the evil spirits flee far away, strengthening the Dharma Master’s courage and enabling him to preach with joy.
Furthermore, they come for this reason: to cause sentient beings to increase their faith and reverence.

Some say that the flavor of the celestial nectar is so subtle and pervasive that it can enter every pore, causing the four great elements and the various faculties of the son of good family to become supple, light, and sharp, such that he delights in what he has to say.
Question:
Do all those who speak of Prajñāpāramitā obtain the nectar-like flavor of the devas, thereby causing them to delight in speaking?
Answer:

"No, indeed! If there is a practitioner who single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-way, subdues the fetters and afflictions, maintains clean and pure robes, and ensures that the place where the Dharma is preached is pure— adorned with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, with fragrant water sprinkled upon the ground and free from all impurities—
then for this reason the devas will rejoice, and it will also benefit those who listen to the Dharma."

Although the preacher of the Dharma may not have read many internal or external scriptures, because they have deeply penetrated the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā, their mind is neither timid nor weak; it does not sink, nor is it afraid, nor is it terrified.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no fixed dharma that can be grasped, challenged, or refuted.
Furthermore, within this Prajñāpāramitā, all dharmas are also explained through analytical distinction:
Whether mundane or supramundane, permanent or impermanent, wholesome or unwholesome—there is no phenomenon that does not exist.
Because all phenomena are fully present, one is neither timid nor afraid;
if there were even a single phenomenon missing, there would be much deficiency, and thus fear would arise.

When this bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, their afflictions are broken and thinned away, and because they have increased all merits which perfume the body, their majestic virtue is worthy of reverence.

Since the body is the dwelling place of merit, even if one’s physical form is ugly and incapable of much, they are still loved and esteemed by others; how much more so when one is naturally handsome and able to benefit others!
Question:
It may be so that they are loved and revered by the Buddhas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas;
but what is so worthy of praise in being loved and cherished by one's parents?
Answer: Although a person is born of one's parents, if they do not obey their parents' instructions, they will not be loved or cherished;
yet the Bodhisattva’s practice of reverence and obedience is many times more distinguished and superior.
Because they offer worship, reverence, and respect to virtue and morality, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas love and honor them;
they are upright and sincere, their speech is free from falsehood,
they deeply cherish the merit of future lives, and they do not cling to the pleasures of this world.
He nurtures those beneath him and does not exalt himself;
even when he sees others' faults, he does not speak of their reality, much less slander them!
Should he ever be compelled to do so, he ultimately does not reveal it in its entirety.
Providing relief to the orphaned and the destitute, without showing partiality toward those attached to oneself—
such matters as these are all due to the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because this person’s merit is heard of afar, they are loved and respected by both devas and worldly people.
Because they make offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*, they constantly attain the six *pāramitās* and so forth in every lifetime, without interruption.
Due to their merit, wisdom, and renown, they are able to subdue anyone who questions, challenges, or slanders them.
Furthermore, the various devas come to the place where the Prajñāpāramitā resides in order to make offerings to it.
Moreover, all the spirits of the mountains, rivers, trees, forests, lands, and cities belong to the Four Heavenly Kings;
because the Four Heavenly Kings come, they all follow along with them.

Among these spirits and deities, there are those who have not yet obtained the scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; for this reason, they come to the place where the Prajñāpāramitā is kept to make offerings, recite it, and pay homage, also for the sake of benefiting these good sons.
This is also a merit of the present life, for the various devas and benevolent spirits have come.
The Lord of Devas, in order to dispel the doubts of those with physical eyes, asked:
"How do you know that the Great Virtuous One and the devas have come?"
Answer: At that time, one sees a great radiance or perceives an extraordinary fragrance; this is also because the dwelling place is pure as previously described.
Question:
The human body is filled with impurity within; what benefit is there in cleansing the exterior?
The answer is:
by purifying one's dwelling and clothing, there will be no impurity on the outside.
Because there is no impurity outside, the devas rejoice.
It is like when a great king or a person of high status arrives, the common folk and lowly subjects flee;
when the great and virtuous devas arrive, the minor spirits depart in the same way.
Because the majestic power and virtue of the great devas are profound, the minor spirits who previously resided there flee away.
As these great devas approach, the person's mind becomes pure and expansive.
If a practitioner wishes to cause the Great Virtuous Devas to come, they should act as described in the sūtra.
Because the malevolent spirits depart to a distance, the body and mind become light and agile. Why is this so?
Associating with various evil spirits causes one's body and mind to gradually become corrupt;
it is like associating with an angry person, which tends to make others angry,
or associating with beautiful forms, which causes one to develop lustful desires.
Because this person is far removed from internal and external evil causes and conditions, they sleep in peace and awaken in peace, free from all evil dreams;
even if they dream, they see only the Buddhas, just as described in the sutras.
Question:

Since the Prajñāpāramitā resides within the body of a Buddha, if one makes offerings to a single Buddha, one is thereby making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā. Why, then, is it said that "making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as good as making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā"?
Answer: Regarding the mind of making offerings— if one makes offerings to the Buddha while grasping at the mark of a person,
since a person is ultimately unattainable, then because of this grasping at marks, although the field of merit is great, the resulting merit is meager.

One who makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā does so according to what has been heard in the Prajñā: by not grasping at the mark of a person and not grasping at the mark of dharmas. Because one makes this offering with such a mind, the merit is great.
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions and is also the teacher of all Buddhas.

That the Buddhas attain these thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary signs, immeasurable radiance, and supernormal transformations—all of these are due to the power of the Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā is superior.
By such causes and conditions as these, it surpasses making offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions; yet this is not because one does not revere the Buddhas.
Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Scroll 58.
Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Comparing Relics,
Number Thirty-Seven, Scroll 59.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 37: Weighing the Relics. [Sūtra] The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: "Kauśika!
If one portion consisted of the Buddha’s relics filling the entire Jambudvīpa, and another portion were a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, between these two portions, which would you take?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If one portion consisted of the Buddha’s relics filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa, and another portion consisted of a single scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, between these two portions, I would rather take the scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
It is not that I lack reverence for the Buddha’s relics, nor do I lack respect for them; yet...
Because the śarīra arises from the perfection of wisdom and is perfumed by the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, these śarīra receive offerings, honor, respect, and praise.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Śakra-devendra:

“Kauśika! This Prajñāpāramitā is ungraspable; it is without color, without form, and without resistance; it is of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness. How then do you wish to grasp it?”

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā does not emerge for the sake of grasping, nor does it emerge for the sake of relinquishing; it does not emerge for the sake of increase or decrease, accumulation or dispersal, loss or gain, defilement or purity.
This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons;
it does not bestow the dharmas of Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, or those in training, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons;
it does not bestow the unconditioned nature, nor does it abandon the conditioned nature.

It is not conjoined with inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; it is not conjoined with the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge; yet it does not abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons.
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! If there is anyone who knows that this prajñāpāramitā neither accords with the dharmas of the Buddhas nor abandons the dharmas of ordinary persons, and even so, neither accords with the knowledge of all modes nor abandons the dharmas of ordinary persons;
such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the prajñāpāramitā and is able to cultivate the prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā does not operate by means of dualistic dharmas; the characteristic of non-dual dharmas is the Prajñāpāramitā, and the characteristic of non-dual dharmas is likewise the Dhyānapāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Kauśika! As you have said, because the prajñāpāramitā does not operate within dualistic dharmas, the characteristic of non-dual dharma is the prajñāpāramitā; the characteristic of non-dual dharma is the dhyānapāramitā, and so on, up to the dānapāramitā.
Kauśika! If a person wishes to obtain two characteristics of the dharma-nature, that person wishes to obtain two characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Kauśika! The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are non-dual and without distinction.
This is likewise true for all the perfections up to the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).

If a person wishes to attain the two characteristics of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the inconceivable nature (*acintyadharmatā*), that person wishes to attain the two characteristics of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Why is this?
“The Prajñāpāramitā and inconceivable nature are non-dual and without distinction.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
All people of the world, as well as the devas and asuras, should pay homage to and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā! Why is this?
Because it is by training in the Prajñāpāramitā that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
I am always seated in the Hall of Good Dharma. When I am not present in my seat, the sons of gods come to make offerings to me; they pay homage to my seat, circumambulate it, and then depart.”
The sons of the gods had this thought:
"Śakra Devānām Indra is seated in this place in order to preach the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
In whatever place this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra scroll is written down, upheld, read, recited, and expounded for others;

in that place, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas will all come to pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, and having made their offerings, they will depart.

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā are born all Buddhas and all the requisites for the happiness of sentient beings; furthermore, the śarīra-relics of the Buddhas are also the causal conditions for the abiding of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
For this reason, World-Honored One,
between these two portions, I choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, World-Honored One:
If I were to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, my mind would enter deeply into the Dharma; at that time, I would see no signs of fear. Why is this?
"Bhagavān!
This Prajñāpāramitā is without marks and without appearance; it is without speech and without explanation.
Bhagavān!"
"Without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech— this is the *prajñāpāramitā*, and even this is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). World-Honored One,

if the *prajñāpāramitā* were to possess marks rather than being markless, then the Buddhas would not have realized that all dharmas are markless, without appearance, without words, and without speech, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and teaching their disciples that all dharmas are markless, without appearance, without words, and without speech."
World-Honored One!

Because the perfection of wisdom is truly without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech, the Buddhas know that all dharmas are without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech, thereby attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
for the sake of their disciples, they teach that all dharmas are likewise without marks, without appearance, without words, and without speech.
For this reason, World-Honored One,
this Prajñāpāramitā should be honored, revered, respected, and praised by all the worlds— the devas, humans, and asuras— with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even banners and canopies.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there is a person who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and who approaches it, reads it, recites it, explains it, correctly contemplates it, copies it, and makes offerings to it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—this person shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; nor shall they fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
Until they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall always behold the Buddhas."
From one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, they made offerings to all Buddhas, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Suppose one portion consists of the Buddha’s relics filling a trichiliocosm, and another portion consists of a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; between these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is from within this Prajñāpāramitā that the relics of all Buddhas are produced.
For this reason, the relics receive offerings, honor, respect, and praise.
Because these sons and daughters of good family offer worship and honor to the relics, they enjoy the blissful rewards among devas and humans, never falling into the three evil realms;
and according to their aspirations, they gradually enter nirvana by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
Whether one sees the present Buddha or sees a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, they are equal and no different. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is non-dual and indistinguishable from the Buddha.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the meaning of comparing the offering of the seven-jeweled stūpa with the *prajñāpāramitā* has already been fully established, why does the Buddha now compare the śarīra relics with the written scrolls?
Answer: Previously, it was clarified that the seven-jeweled stupa is the dwelling place of the śarīra; now, however, we clarify the śarīra alone in order to contrast it with the scripture.
Although the śarīra does not equal the Prajñāpāramitā, it fills the entire Jambudvīpa.
Because Prajñā is subtle, it clarifies only the scriptural volumes.
Furthermore, those who have left the household life mostly crave wisdom, for wisdom is the causal condition for liberation;
those who remain in the household life mostly crave merit, for merit is the causal condition for happiness.

Those who have left the household life mostly covet objects known by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whereas those who remain in the household life mostly covet objects known by the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
Śakra Devānām Indra has already realized the greatest fruit of merit and happiness and is the most honored and supreme among householders;
for this reason, the Buddha questioned Śakra Devānām Indra.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Of these two portions, I shall take the volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Herein, the causal conditions are explained of their own accord:
“World-Honored One!

I do not dare to treat the śarīras with contempt or lack reverence; I know that the merit of making offerings to even a mustard-seed amount of śarīra is immeasurable and boundless, such that it continues until the attainment of the merit of Buddhahood is exhausted—how much more so for those filling all of Jambudvīpa!”
World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva receives a body, it possesses śarīra, yet it is not esteemed by people;
when they attain Buddhahood, their śarīra is honored, revered, and made offerings to by people because it has been perfumed and cultivated by prajñā.
"Therefore, between these two parts, I shall take the superior one.
He asked: "Śāriputra knows that Śakra Devendra spoke of taking the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of conventional truth; why then do you challenge him?"
The answer is:
It is rare indeed that Śakra Devānām Indra, while still at home, bound by afflictions and shrouded by the five desires, is able to speak the Prajñāpāramitā!
For this reason, Śāriputra questioned him, wishing to cause Śakra Devānām Indra to further inquire of the Buddha regarding profound meanings;
thus he posed the challenge. Śakra Devānām Indra, complying with Śāriputra’s intention, replied: “So it is!”
Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"Among all dharmas there is no duality; one does not regard the śarīra as small, nor does one regard the Prajñāpāramitā as great."
The Prajñāpāramitā is without duality and without the characteristic of discrimination;
however, for the sake of benefiting bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, it is taught thus according to conventional truth:
"The Prajñāpāramitā can cause the minds of sentient beings to be without duality and without discrimination."
"Because of these benefits, I take up the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
Because he is able to discern all phenomena and can skillfully explain the characteristics of prajñā—namely, the characteristic of non-duality—he is thus praised.
In this context, the Buddha himself provides an analogy:

"If a person wishes to differentiate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and so forth, into two parts, that person wishes to differentiate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) into two parts."

Having personally proclaimed the Prajñāpāramitā and having further heard the Buddha’s repeated exposition of it, Śakra’s mind became pure; with deep faith and joy, he declared that it is worthy of the veneration of all the world.
In this context, Śakra himself explains the causal conditions:
"All bodhisattvas study this prajñā and thereby attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Furthermore, within this context, one's own body is used as an analogy: one's own body represents the Buddha, and the volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra represents the seat.
Some say that one's own body represents the Prajñā, and the seat represents the śarīra (relics).
"Therefore, between these two portions, I choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
When I receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, at that time I do not perceive even the appearance of fear, let alone actual fear!"
Why is this? Because all dharmas are signless, ineffable, and inexpressible.
Since the Prajñāpāramitā enables people to attain these signless dharmas, one has nothing to fear.

Those who receive, uphold, and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā will not fall into the three evil realms or the paths of the two vehicles; in every lifetime they shall never be separated from the Buddhas, and they shall constantly make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is that which all the world should honor and provide for.
Furthermore, the Buddha opened with the beginning by filling Jambudvīpa with śarīras.
Having realized the outcome of these two matters, Śakra, for the sake of all sentient beings, expanded his scope to the great trichiliocosm;
herein he himself explains the causal conditions:
"To see the Prajñāpāramitā is no different from seeing the Buddha."
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, World-Honored One,
just as the Buddha dwells in the three modes of manifestation and teaches the twelve divisions of the scriptures—
ranging from the Sūtras and Geyas up to the Upadeśas;"
Furthermore, there are good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, recite, and explain this Prajñāpāramitā; these are equal and no different. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the manifestation of the three matters and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—
from Sūtra up to Upadeśa— are produced.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The Buddhas of the ten directions abide in the manifestation of three matters and preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
from the Sūtra up to the Upadeśa;..."
Furthermore, there are those who receive the Prajñāpāramitā and explain it to others; these two are equal and without distinction. Why is this?
It is because from within the Prajñāpāramitā all Buddhas are born, and likewise the twelve divisions of the scriptures are born.
From the *sūtras* up to the *upadeśas*.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

if there were someone who made offerings to all the Buddhas in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies;

Furthermore, if there is another person who copies the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls and treats them with reverence, respect, and praise, offering flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies, their merit shall be exactly equal.
For what reason?
All Buddhas of the ten directions are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

If good sons or good daughters hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, maintain right mindfulness of it, and also explain it to others, such persons shall not fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor shall they fall into the stages of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? You should know that these sons and daughters of good family dwell correctly within the stage of *avaivartika*.
This *prajñāpāramitā* is far removed from all suffering, affliction, decay, and illness.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who write out this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra scroll, and who receive, uphold, draw near to, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise it, these people will be free from all fears."
World-Honored One!
It is like a debtor who approaches a king and serves those around him; the creditor, in turn, comes to honor and respect this person, so that the person no longer feels fear or dread.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
It is because this person relies upon and draws strength from a king.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
Because the relics of the Buddhas have been perfumed and cultivated by this Prajñāpāramitā, they receive offerings and reverence.
World-Honored One!"
One should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is like a king, while the *śarīra* relics are like a debtor;
because the debtor relies upon the king, he receives offerings, and likewise, because the *śarīra* relies upon the cultivation and perfuming of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it receives offerings.
World-Honored One!
You should know that the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas is also accomplished through cultivation and perfuming by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, World-Honored One!
Of these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
Within the Prajñāpāramitā are born the relics of the Buddhas and the thirty-two marks;

within the Prajñāpāramitā are also born the ten powers of the Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
World-Honored One!
Within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) the five perfections arise, thereby receiving the name "perfection";
within the perfection of wisdom, the all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) of all Buddhas arises.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

In whatever place within this trichiliocosm there are those who receive, uphold, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise the Prajñāpāramitā, in that place neither humans nor non-humans shall be able to find an opportunity for harm; such persons will gradually attain entry into nirvāṇa."
"Bhagavān!
The Prajñāpāramitā is of such great benefit that it is able to perform the work of a Buddha within the trichiliocosm!
Bhagavān!"
"World-Honored One, wherever there is the Prajñāpāramitā, there is a Buddha.
It is like a priceless maṇi jewel: wherever it resides, non-human beings cannot find an opportunity to cause harm."
If a man or a woman suffers from a feverish illness, by placing this jewel upon their body, the feverish illness will be immediately cured;
if they suffer from wind-related illnesses, cold-related illnesses, or combined illnesses of heat, wind, and cold, by placing the jewel upon their body, all shall be completely healed.
If it is in the darkness, this jewel can bring forth light;
in times of heat, it can bring coolness, and in times of cold, it can bring warmth.
Wherever the jewel dwells, the ground there is neither cold nor hot, and the seasons remain harmonious and temperate.
That place is also free from all other venomous stings;
if a man or woman is bitten by a poisonous snake, if one shows them this bead, the poison will be immediately eliminated.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If a man or woman suffers from eye pain, blurred vision, or blindness, and is shown this bead, it will be immediately cured."
If there is a case of leprosy or a malignant swelling, by placing the jewel upon the body, the illness is immediately cured.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
wherever this maṇi-jewel is in water, the water takes on a single color accordingly."
If one wraps a blue object and places it in water, the color of the water immediately becomes blue;
if one wraps objects that are yellow, red, white, crimson, or pale green and places them in water, the water accordingly takes on those colors—yellow, red, white, crimson, or pale green.
When various objects of such diverse colors are wrapped and placed within water, the water takes on those various colors accordingly.
World-Honored One!
If the water is turbid, when this jewel is placed within it, the water immediately becomes clear; such is the virtue of this jewel!
At that time, Ānanda asked Śakra Devānām Indra:
“Kauśika! Is this maṇi jewel a celestial treasure?”
"Is this a treasure of Jambudvīpa?
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Ānanda:
"This is a treasure of the heavens."
The people of Jambudvīpa also possess such jewels, but their marks of merit are slight and incomplete;
the jewels in the heavens are pure, light, and subtle, and cannot be compared by means of worldly analogies.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
If this maṇi jewel is placed within a casket and the bead is taken out, because the merit of the jewel has perfumed the casket, all people will love and respect it."
"So it is, World-Honored One!

In whatever place this written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra resides, that place shall be free from the afflictions of various troubles; it will be just as a place where a maṇi jewel is kept is free from all calamities."

World-Honored One! After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, that the śarīra relics receive offerings is entirely due to the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*; it is the power of these merits: from the *dhyānapāramitā* down to the *dānapāramitā*;

from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) down to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) down to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the fixed course of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature; and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is by the power of all these merits.
Good sons and good daughters form this thought:

"These relics of the Buddha are the dwelling place of all the merits of the Buddhas, including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñā*), great loving-kindness and great compassion, the severing of all fetters and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the practice of constant equanimity, and the dharma of non-erroneousness."
"For this reason, the śarīra receive offerings. World-Honored One!

The śarīra are the dwelling place of the perfection of all jewels of merit; they are the dwelling place of the perfection of neither defilement nor purity; the perfection of neither arising nor ceasing; the perfection of neither entering nor exiting; the perfection of neither increasing nor decreasing; the perfection of neither coming, nor going, nor abiding. These Buddha-śarīra are the dwelling place of the perfection of the characteristics of all dharmas."
Because these various dharmas have been perfumed and cultivated by the *pāramitās*, the relics receive offerings.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Let us set aside the relics that would fill a trichiliocosm."

If there were one portion consisting of the śarīra relics filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and another portion consisting of a written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, between these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the śarīras of all Buddhas are born;
and because it has been cultivated and perfumed by this Prajñāpāramitā, the śarīras receive offerings.
“World-Honored One!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who make offerings to the śarīras, honoring, respecting, and praising them, the karmic reward of their merit will be boundless. They shall receive the bliss and happiness of the human realm and the heavens—namely, among the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great households of householders, and from the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations.
Furthermore, by virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, they shall attain the end of suffering.”

If one receives this Prajñāpāramitā, reads it, recites it, explains it, and maintains right mindfulness of it, that person will be able to fulfill the Dhyānapāramitā and even fulfill the Dānapāramitā; they will be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness and even fulfill the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they will transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and abide in the rank of a bodhisattva;
having abided in the rank of a bodhisattva, they will attain the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva and travel from one buddha-field to another buddha-field.
This bodhisattva assumes a body for the sake of sentient beings and brings them to maturity according to what is appropriate for each:
whether as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), or as a great clan of kṣatriyas, or as a great clan of brahmins, he brings sentient beings to maturity.

For this reason, World-Honored One, it is not out of disrespect or a lack of reverence that I do not accept the śarīra; rather, it is because when a son or daughter of good family makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are thereby making offerings to the śarīra.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there are people who wish to see the dharma-body and form-body of all Buddhas currently residing in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, these people should hear, receive, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, read it, recite it, correctly contemplate it, and extensively explain it to others."
In this way, good sons and good daughters shall behold the Dharma-body and form-body of the Buddhas in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions.

These good sons and good daughters, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, should also cultivate the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) by means of the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who wish to see the Buddhas of the present should receive this Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness of it.
[Treatise] Furthermore, regarding the statement, "The Buddha dwells in three modes of manifestation and teaches the twelve divisions of the scriptures":
A question is raised:
Among all those who preach the Dharma, there is none equal to the Buddha.

The Buddha has taught the twelve divisions of the sūtras, which are complete in every respect; why then, son of good family, is it said that merely upholding, maintaining, reading, and reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā* makes one equal to the Buddha without distinction?
Answer: Herein, the Buddha wishes to praise *prajñā* as being great.
Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), *prajñā* is the most supreme.
Why is this? When this Prajñāpāramitā is taught, many give rise to the bodhicitta;
when the twelve divisions of the sūtras are taught, they give rise to the intentions of the three vehicles in a mixed manner.
One does not compare the merit of a bodhisattva with the immeasurable body of a Buddha; this refers to the Dharma-body.

Bodhisattvas teach only Prajñāpāramitā to exhort others toward the Mahāyāna, whereas Buddhas teach various doctrines to exhort others toward the Three Vehicles; therefore, they are equal and without distinction.
Furthermore, that which manifests the three matters and serves as the root of the twelve divisions of the scriptures is the so-called "Prajñāpāramitā.

If one were to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and another were to make offerings to a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the merit would be equal and no different.

In this regard, the Buddha has explained the causal conditions by which the merit of *prajñā* is superior: namely, that *prajñā* is able to destroy all suffering, affliction, decline, illness, fear, and so forth.
It is like a debtor who relies upon a king: the king is a metaphor for Prajñāpāramitā, and the debtor is a metaphor for the śarīra.
The śarīra is formed through the causes and conditions of karma from previous lives; within those causes and conditions, one ought to repay all corresponding karmic debts.

However, because it has been perfumed and cultivated by the Prajñāpāramitā, the various karmic debts resulting from past-life causes and conditions—such as hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—cannot affect it, and instead it receives offerings and veneration from gods and humans alike.
Just as a debtor who relies upon a king is, conversely, respected by his creditors,
the previous statement regarding the absence of all decline, illness, and fear clarifies the internal [protection];
now, by speaking of the *maṇi* jewel, the fact that humans and non-humans cannot find an opportunity against him clarifies the external [protection].
Because this person makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, whether in this life or in future lives, any physical decline or mental afflictions will all be completely eliminated;
furthermore, all matters of virtuous aspiration will be granted according to their wishes.
Because they have obtained this great treasure of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are free from all fears and lack nothing;
it is like a priceless jewel, through which all their wishes are fulfilled.
Question:
Among crystal, gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, vaidūrya, coral, amber, diamond, and so forth, what kind of treasure is the maṇi jewel?

Answer: Some say that this precious jewel emerges from within the brain of a nāga king; if a person obtains this jewel, poison cannot harm them and fire cannot burn them—it possesses such meritorious qualities as these.
Some say that this is the vajra wielded by Śakra, which fell and shattered upon Jambudvīpa when it was used in battle against the asuras. Others say:
The relics of all the Buddhas of the distant past, once their Dharma had been completely extinguished, transformed into these jewels to benefit sentient beings.
Some say that by virtue of the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings, these jewels naturally came to exist.
For example, due to the causes and conditions of their offenses, there naturally exist instruments for punishing offenders within the hells.

This precious jewel is named "Wish-Fulfilling" (Cintāmaṇi); it has no fixed color, is transparent, light, and exquisite, and all things throughout the four continents are reflected and manifested within it.
The meaning of the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) is as previously explained.
This jewel can constantly produce all manner of precious objects—clothing, food, and drink—granting them all according to one's every desire;
it can also eliminate all forms of decline, affliction, illness, suffering, and the like.
There are two kinds of these precious jewels:
there are wish-fulfilling jewels from the heavens, and there are wish-fulfilling jewels from the human realm.
Because the merit and virtue of the devas are profound, the qualities of their jewels are fully perfected.
Because the merit and virtue of people are meager, the qualities of this jewel are not fully realized.
Yet, wherever this jewel is placed—within a dwelling or a casket—that very place also possesses majestic power.
"Prajñāpāramitā is also like this.
Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can bestow upon laypeople the wealth and happiness of the present life according to their desires,
so too can prajñāpāramitā bestow upon those who have left the household life and seek the Way the bliss of liberation of the three vehicles according to their aspirations.
Wherever a wish-fulfilling jewel is worn, non-human spirits cannot find an opportunity;

likewise, it is with the Prajñāpāramitā: when a practitioner’s mind is in accord with it, evil and heterodox rākṣasas cannot enter their hearts to obstruct the resolve for enlightenment or seize the life-force of wisdom.
Furthermore, wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, Māra, or the followers of Māra, earth deities, yakṣas, and various malevolent spirits will be unable to find an opportunity to cause harm.
Just as a precious gem can eliminate the four hundred and four diseases— the four fundamental diseases being wind,
heat, cold, and their combination—
so too can the Prajñāpāramitā eliminate eighty-four thousand diseases, [including] the four fundamental diseases: [wind, heat, cold, and their combination].
Greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal combination.

There are twenty-one thousand types of the disease of lustful desire, twenty-one thousand types of the disease of hatred, twenty-one thousand types of the disease of delusion, and twenty-one thousand types of the disease of their equal combination.

One eliminates lust through the contemplation of impurity, hatred through a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and delusion through the contemplation of causes and conditions; alternatively, one may eliminate the diseases of the three poisons collectively by employing these three remedies—impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, or the contemplation of causes and conditions.
Just as a precious gem can dispel darkness, so too is prajñā: it can dispel the darkness of the three realms.
Just as a precious gem can dispel heat;
Prajñā is also like this: it can remove the heat of lust and anger, just as a precious gem can remove cold;
prajñā is also like this: it can remove the "cold" states of mind such as ignorance, lack of faith, lack of reverence, and indolence.

Both the sun and the moon are composed of various jewels; the sun can produce heat, and the moon can produce cold. Although both benefit sentient beings, because they cannot provide both functions simultaneously, they are not called "wish-fulfilling."
Wherever a precious jewel is located, it cannot be harmed by venomous snakes or other malevolent insects;
likewise, Prajñā cannot be afflicted by the poisons of greed and other such passions.
If someone is bitten by a venomous snake, showing them a precious jewel will cause the bite to be healed immediately;

likewise, if someone is bitten by the venomous snakes of greed, desire, and so forth, upon attaining the Prajñāpāramitā, the poison of greed and anger is immediately removed, as was the case with Nanda, Aṅgulimāla, and others.
If there is someone whose eyes are painful, blind, or sightless, and one shows them a precious jewel, their affliction is immediately cured;

the Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: if someone has had their eye of wisdom destroyed by ignorance, doubt and regret, or inverted and false views, upon attaining Prajñā, they immediately attain clarity.
Just as when a person with leprosy, sores, or abscesses is shown a precious jewel, they are immediately healed;
so too is Prajñā: the leprosy-like sins of the five heinous crimes and the like are instantly extinguished upon attaining Prajñā.
Just as a precious gem wrapped in various colored cloths takes on whichever color it is placed within, so too is *prajñā*:

because the practitioner attains the power of *prajñā*, the mind becomes supple and free from attachment, following along with faith, the five faculties, and so forth, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, regarding the stages of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, he studies them all in accordance with them, without any contradiction.
The sixth, the azure color, is the color of space.
When a practitioner attains the prajñā that contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, the mind likewise accords with it without attachment.
Such various [colors] as these enter into all phenomena, all of which are accorded with without obstruction.
Just as when water is turbid, variegated, and impure, yet becomes entirely clear and of a single color once a jewel is placed within it;

so too is it with *prajñā*: though people have various afflictions, false views, and conceptual proliferations that disturb the mind and render it turbid, upon attaining *prajñā*, it becomes pure and of a single color.
Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel possesses immeasurable merits, so too do the merits of Prajñā.
Now, I shall explain the merits of Prajñā according to their specific characteristics:
this wish-fulfilling jewel can only expel evil spirits, but it cannot destroy the Māras and devas; [whereas Prajñā can].
Prajñā can eliminate two matters:
while a jewel can cure physical illnesses,
Prajñā can cure both physical and mental illnesses.
A jewel can cure the illnesses treated by deities;
Prajñā can cure all illnesses that neither devas, nāgas, nor spirits can cure.
A jewel can cure illnesses that have been treated throughout successive lifetimes; Prajñā can cure all such things.
Prajñā can cure diseases that have never been cured since beginningless time;
such are its various distinctions.
Just as a jewel can illuminate the darkness of night wherever it is placed;

Prajñā can illuminate the darkness of ignorance associated with all afflictions, as well as the darkness of delusion—the ignorance not shared [with other afflictions]—which consists of non-comprehension regarding all phenomena.
A jewel can only dispel the heat where it resides, but cannot dispel the heat in other places;
the power of Prajñā, however, can extinguish even the great conflagration that lasts until the end of kalpas across immeasurable worlds with a single breath, let alone the heat of a single location!
A jewel can only remove the heat of physical forms, such as fire and the sun;
Prajñā can remove the mental heat of the three poisons.
A jewel can remove wind, rain, cold, and snow; [Prajñā can remove the afflictions of the mind].
Prajñā can remove the "cold" of the lack of faith, lack of reverence, and indolence of sentient beings throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.
A jewel can ward off external venomous stings, but it cannot eliminate the four great poisonous snakes;
Prajñā can ultimately eliminate both of these kinds of poison.
A jewel cannot cure the poison of wrong views;
Prajñā can remove it.
A jewel can cure the fleshly eye; [Prajñā can cure the Dharma-eye].
Prajñā can cure the eye of wisdom;
the jewel can cure the eye that sees nearby;
Prajñā can cure the eye that sees afar.
A jewel can cure the fleshly eye, yet the fleshly eye does not become the jewel;
prajñā can cure the wisdom-eye, yet the wisdom-eye becomes prajñā itself.
While a jewel can cure the fleshly eye, the disease may recur later.
Prajñā cures the wisdom-eye, making it ultimately pure.
Just as a jewel can cure leprosy, malignant sores, and swellings,
so too can Prajñā cure the leprosy of the body and the leprosy of the mind.
Question:
Since the four types of diseases encompass all illnesses, why are "eye pain," "leprosy," and so forth mentioned separately?
Answer:
The eye is the foremost among the members of the body and its function is most precious; therefore, it is mentioned separately.

Among all diseases, leprosy is the most severe; because it arises from the causal conditions of offenses committed in past lives, it is difficult to cure, and for this reason, it is further discussed.
A jewel can cause water to take on the color of whatever it encloses;
likewise, wisdom (prajñā) can accord with wholesome mental factors (caitasika-dharma).
However, a jewel cannot transform the minds of people.
Prajñā can transform the mentalities, inclinations, and desires of all sentient beings.
Just as a jewel can cause turbid water at its point of contact to become clear, yet not all water;
so too the power of prajñā can cause the turbid minds of the six consciousnesses to become pure instantly.
Furthermore, it can purify the turbid minds of greed and anger in various dragon kings, ghost kings, and human kings. Just as a jewel can cause the caskets, chests,
and dwellings in which it is placed to possess majestic power,
the power of Prajñā can deliver incalculable sentient beings across the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, causing them to possess majestic power.
The power of the jewel’s merit enters the casket, yet the casket cannot bestow its merit upon people at will;
because the śarīra has been perfumed and cultivated by Prajñā, when someone makes offerings to it, they will inevitably receive back that Prajñā and thereby attain Buddhahood.
This casket is what ordinary people value;
the relics are what both ordinary people and sages value.
The casket is what those who enjoy worldly pleasures value.
Śarīra is that which is honored by those who enjoy worldly and supramundane pleasures.
Prajñāpāramitā is the wish-fulfilling jewel, and the reliquary casket is the śarīra;
although there is no prajñā within the śarīra, it receives offerings because it has been permeated by prajñā.
Furthermore, among all the noble dharmas, Prajñā is supreme and beyond comparison;
because people of the world value this precious jewel, it is used as a metaphor for it.
When people see a wish-fulfilling jewel, all their aspirations are attained;
even if they merely see the place where the jewel resides, they still obtain some of their wishes.
It is the same for the practitioner: by attaining the meaning of this Prajñāpāramitā, one immediately enters the Buddha-way.

If one sees that by making offerings to the śarīra enshrined within Prajñā, one obtains immeasurable merit and happiness in both this life and future lives, and will certainly attain the Way after a long time;
such are the general and specific characteristics that should be known.
Question:

If Prajñāpāramitā possesses such merits as these, for what reason is it said that "the śarīra (relics) receive offerings because they are the locus where the five pāramitās, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), reside"?
Answer: It has already been stated that for all dharmas,
the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the foremost and the guiding light.
For example, when a king arrives, he is necessarily accompanied by his retinue; yet by mentioning only the name of the leader, all the others are already included.
The meaning of praising the Prajñāpāramitā has already been explained previously.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, World-Honored One,
there are two kinds of dharma-characteristics:
the characteristics of conditioned dharmas and the characteristics of unconditioned dharmas."
What is called the characteristic of conditioned phenomena?

It refers to the wisdom within internal emptiness, up to the wisdom within the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the wisdom within the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the wisdom within the eightfold noble path; the wisdom within the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities; the wisdom within wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena, contaminated phenomena and uncontaminated phenomena, and mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena—this is called the characteristic of conditioned phenomena.
What is called the dharma-characteristic of unconditioned phenomena?

It is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is without arising and without cessation, without abiding and without change, without defilement and without purity, and without increase and without decrease.
"What is meant by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena?
The non-existence of all phenomena is their intrinsic nature; this is called the characteristic of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra:
"So it is! So it is, Kauśika!"

The Buddhas of the past attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*; the disciples of those Buddhas of the past likewise attained the path of the *srotāpanna* up to the paths of the *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*.

The immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions in the future and present worlds will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*; the disciples of those Buddhas of the future and present will also attain the path of the *srotāpanna* up to the path of the *pratyekabuddha* by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the meaning of the Three Vehicles is extensively expounded by way of the dharma of signlessness, the dharma of neither arising nor ceasing, the dharma of neither defilement nor purity, and the dharma of non-action and non-origination, neither entering nor exiting, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither grasping nor abandoning.
This is according to conventional truth, not according to the ultimate truth.

Why is this? This Prajñāpāramitā is neither this nor that; it is neither high nor low; it is neither equal nor unequal; it is neither with marks nor markless; it is neither mundane nor supramundane; it is neither with outflows nor without outflows; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why is this? Kausika!
The Prajñāpāramitā does not grasp at the dharmas of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary persons.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they know the minds of all sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend a ‘sentient being,’ nor do they apprehend even one who knows or one who sees.”

This bodhisattva does not apprehend form, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; he does not apprehend the eye up to the mind, nor does he apprehend forms up to mental phenomena; he does not apprehend feelings produced by the condition of eye-contact up to feelings produced by the condition of mind-contact; he does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; he does not apprehend unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does he apprehend the Buddha-dharmas, nor does he apprehend the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā does not arise for the sake of attaining any dharma. Why is this?
“The nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent and unattainable; the dharmas employed are unattainable, and their locus is likewise unattainable!
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra:
“It is so! It is so!”
"So it is, Kauśika! It is just as you have said!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has practiced the perfection of wisdom for a long night, even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended, let alone the bodhisattva or the dharmas of a bodhisattva!
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only the prajñāpāramitā and not the other pāramitās?"
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Kauśika! A bodhisattva practices the dharmas of the six pāramitās to their full extent by means of non-apprehension.”
When practicing the dānapāramitā, one does not apprehend the giver, the recipient, or the material gift;
when practicing the śīlapāramitā, one does not apprehend the precepts, the person who upholds them, or the person who breaks them;
and so on, until when practicing the prajñāpāramitā, one does not apprehend wisdom, the person who possesses wisdom, or the person who lacks wisdom.
“Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, the perfection of wisdom acts as his guiding light, enabling him to fulfill the dānapāramitā;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices ethical discipline, the perfection of wisdom acts as his guiding light, enabling him to fulfill the śīlapāramitā.”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, the perfection of wisdom acts as a guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the perfection of patience;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, the perfection of wisdom acts as a guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the perfection of vigor;
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices meditation, the perfection of wisdom acts as a guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the perfection of meditation.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas, the perfection of wisdom acts as their guiding light, enabling them to fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
This is because all dharmas—from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—are ultimately unapprehendable.
Kauśika! For example, just as the various trees of Jambudvīpa—with their various leaves, various flowers, various fruits, and various colors—have no difference in their shade;
so too, when all the pāramitās enter into the prajñāpāramitā and reach sarvajñatā, there is no difference, because they are non-apprehendable.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the accomplishment of great merit!”
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the accomplishment of all merits!
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the accomplishment of immeasurable merit!
It is the accomplishment of boundless merit!
It is the accomplishment of incomparable merit!
"Bhagavān!

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who writes out this Prajñāpāramitā sūtra volume and reveres, makes offerings to, honors, and praises it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies, and maintains correct mindfulness as taught in the Prajñāpāramitā;
