and if there is another son of good family or daughter of good family who writes out a Prajñāpāramitā sūtra volume and gives it to others—of these two, which generates the greater merit?"
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Kauśika! I shall now question you; answer me according to your own understanding."

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who makes offerings to the relics of the Buddhas, honoring, respecting, praising, and presenting them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies;

and if there were another person who divided the relics even as much as a mustard seed and gave them to others, causing them to offer, honor, respect, and praise them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—of these two, which would have the greater merit?
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

According to the meaning of the Dharma as I have heard it from the Buddha, if there are sons or daughters of good family who personally make offerings to the śarīras, even including banners and canopies;
Furthermore, World-Honored One, if there is someone who divides the relics even as much as a mustard seed and gives them to another person to be venerated, the merit thereof is exceedingly great!
Seeing this merit and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Buddha entered the Vajra Samādhi and shattered his vajra-body into powdered relics.

Why is this? Because there are those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to the Buddha’s relics—even as small as a single mustard seed—and their meritorious reward will be boundless, until the end of suffering is reached.
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām-indra: "So it is! So it is!"

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and makes offerings to it with reverence— offering flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—

and if there is another person who writes out a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to others so that they may study it, the merit of these sons and daughters of good family will be far greater!
"Furthermore, Kauśika,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family explains the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā to others, revealing it, analyzing it, and making it easy to understand, that son or daughter of good family surpasses the merit of the former sons and daughters of good family."
From whomever one hears the Prajñāpāramitā, one should regard that person as a Buddha and also as a sublime practitioner of the holy life.
Why is this? One should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is itself the Buddha.
The Prajñāpāramitā is not different from the Buddha, and the Buddha is not different from the Prajñāpāramitā.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have studied within the Prajñāpāramitā and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

as have those of sublime and superior holy conduct—those of sublime and superior holy conduct being the avaivartika bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—who likewise study this Prajñāpāramitā and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śrāvakas also study this Prajñāpāramitā and attain the path of Arhatship;
those seeking the path of Pratyekabuddhas also study this Prajñāpāramitā and attain the path of Pratyekabuddhahood;
and Bodhisattvas also study this Prajñāpāramitā and enter the stage of a Bodhisattva.
For this reason, Kauśika,

a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to make offerings to the Buddhas of the present— honoring, respecting, and praising them with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies— should make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā!
"I perceived this benefit; when I first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I had this thought:
'Who is there whom I may offer worship, respect, honor, praise, and upon whom I may rely for my dwelling?'"
"Kauśika! Within all the worlds—whether among gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—I do not see anyone who is my equal, let alone anyone who is superior!"
I reflected to myself:
"The Dharma that I have attained has led me to become a Buddha;
I shall honor this Dharma, revering, respecting, and praising it, and I shall abide in reliance upon it, taking this Dharma as my support."
"What is this Dharma?
It is what is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Kauśika! [he said.]
I myself have made offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā, and having honored, revered, and praised it, I dwell in reliance upon it;

how much more so should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi not make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, honoring, revering, and praising it with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even banners and canopies?
Why is this? Because it is from the perfection of wisdom that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born, and from all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that all buddhas are born.
For this reason, Kauśika!

Good sons and good daughters, whether they seek the path of the Buddha, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Śrāvaka, they should all make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.
[Treatise] Question:
For what reason are the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) taught? Answer:
Śakra praised the Prajñāpāramitā as encompassing all dharmas; herein, he intends to explain the causes and conditions for this.

The characteristics of conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are what are called the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
briefly stated, these include the wholesome and unwholesome, and so forth up to the mundane and supramundane—these are termed the characteristics of conditioned dharmas.

Why is this? Because these conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛta-lakṇa) involve that which was previously non-existent now coming into being, and that which already existed returning to non-existence.
That which is contrary to the above is the characteristic of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
These two dharmas are both subsumed within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Conditioned wholesome dharmas are the sphere of practice, while unconditioned dharmas are the basis of reliance;
other indeterminate and unwholesome dharmas are not mentioned because they are to be abandoned.
This is what is studied by bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.

If they attain the power of skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* and correspondingly attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they will neither cherish the practice of dharmas nor loathe the relinquishing of dharmas; they will not be separated from conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas while possessing unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, and for this reason, they do not rely upon nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said in the sutra:
"Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the three vehicles are extensively explained by means of the dharma of signlessness (animitta), such as being without arising and without cessation."
"This is spoken thus for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
When a bodhisattva practices the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, although they can observe the minds of all sentient beings, they do not apprehend sentient beings;
although they can practice all dharmas, they do not apprehend any dharmas."
Why is this? Because they have attained the prajñāpāramitā of non-attainment.
The Buddha affirmed their praise:
“A bodhisattva constantly practices these deeds until even *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is unobtainable, let alone other dharmas!
Śakra thought to himself:
“If *prajñā* is the ultimate dharma, then a practitioner need only practice the *prajñāpāramitā*; what use are other dharmas?”
The Buddha replied:

"When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in conjunction with the dharma of non-apprehension, this is precisely the practice of the perfection of wisdom."
"If one practices only Prajñāpāramitā and does not practice the five dharmas, then one's merit will not be complete; it will neither be beautiful nor sublime.

It is like a fool who does not know the various ingredients for food and drink; hearing that salt is the sovereign of all flavors, he eats nothing but salt, thereby losing the sense of taste and bringing about affliction."
The practitioner is also like this: desiring to eliminate the mind of attachment, they practice only *prajñā*, yet instead fall into wrong views and are unable to advance in wholesome dharmas;
if, however, they harmonize with the five *pāramitās*, then their merit will be complete and its meaning and flavor will be perfectly balanced.
Although all practices are combined in harmony, Prajñā is the sovereign.
If dharmas such as giving were apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, they would possess various distinctions;
yet within the Prajñāpāramitā, they are all of one single mark and without distinction.

For example, it is like the Anavatapta Lake in Jambudvīpa, from which four great rivers flow; each great river has five hundred small streams that join it, and they all enter the great ocean, where they lose their original names and become of one single flavor, without any distinction.
Furthermore, it is like trees: their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits differ in various colors and forms, yet their shade makes no such distinction.

Question: There are indeed distinctions in the shade; when the tree is large, the shade is large, and the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits have various different shapes and sizes. How can you say there is no distinction?

Answer: Because light is obstructed, a shadow appears; that place where there is no light is what is called "shade" (*chāyā*). Shade does not take the distinction of size or shape as its defining characteristic.
Question:
To practice the Prajñāpāramitā, to receive, recite, and even maintain it through right mindfulness—this is difficult;
whereas to copy and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls and give them to others is easy. Since their merits should not even be considered equal, how can you say that one is superior?
Answer:
Although it is difficult to practice solitary recitation, chanting, and correct mindfulness, the merit is small because one may still harbor a sense of self.
To give a scripture to another, however, involves a mind of great compassion and creates the causal conditions for the Buddha-way; because there is no notion of "I" or "mine," the merit is great.
As the Buddha asked Śakra:
"If one person makes offerings to the śarīra themselves, and another person gives the śarīra to someone else to make offerings, which of these produces greater merit?"
He replied:
"It is better to give it to others so that they may make offerings and thereby gain great merit.
This is because one gives with a mind of selflessness and compassion."
Although the Buddha does not require merit for himself, because he perceives such great benefit for sentient beings, he entered the Vajra-samādhi and shattered his own body.
Question:
If merit resides in the mind, why did the Buddha crush his body into pieces the size of mustard seeds so that people might make offerings to them?
Answer:
The purity of faith arises from two causes and conditions:
first, internal correct mindfulness; second, the presence of an excellent field of merit externally.
It is like having high-quality grain seeds and fertile, excellent soil; the harvest will surely be abundant.
Therefore, although the intention of the mind may be good, one must rely upon the *śarīra* (relics) before one can obtain the great fruit of retribution.
The Buddha, approving these words, further spoke of his own accord:

"If there is one person who copies a scripture and gives it to others, and another person who extensively explains its meaning within a great assembly, the merit of the latter surpasses that of the former."
"One should regard such a person as a Buddha, or as one next to a Buddha.
The meaning of "a Buddha" or "one next to a Buddha" is as previously explained.
The Buddha, by means of two kinds of causes and conditions, realizes that the *prajñāpāramitā* is supreme:
First, the sages of the three periods of time have studied within it and thereby accomplished the holy path;
second, because of this Dharma, I have attained the state of unsurpassed holiness, and I now likewise revere and take this Dharma as my teacher.
The Dharma is the true reality of all phenomena, namely the Prajñāpāramitā. “Kauśika!

I have nothing further to seek, yet I still recommend and honor the offering to the Prajñāpāramitā; how much more so should a son of good family not offer various kinds of requisites to the Prajñāpāramitā!”
In this regard, the causal conditions are explained:

"Prajñā is the fundamental causal condition for bodhisattvas; bodhisattvas are the fundamental causal condition for all buddhas; and all buddhas are the causal condition for the great benefit and happiness of the entire world."

Therefore, if even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who wish to swiftly and peacefully enter the three gates of liberation must still make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, how much more so for a Bodhisattva!
"Requisites for making offerings" refers to listening and receiving with a single-minded focus up to correct mindfulness, as well as flowers, incense, and so forth, up to banners and canopies.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 59:
Explanation of the Chapter on Comparing the Merit of Dharma-Giving.
Volume Thirty-Eight.
Composed by the Holy One Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 38: Comparing the Gift of Dharma. [Sūtra] The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Kauśika! Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the people of a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
What do you think?”
"By reason of this cause and condition, would one not obtain much merit?
He replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as much as the merit gained by a son or daughter of good family who writes out this Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scroll, upholds it, and gives it to others so that they may read, recite, and explain it.”

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā all untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*) are extensively explained; from this, sons and daughters of good family have studied, are studying, and will study. They have entered, are entering, and will enter the stage of the true dharma (*samyaktvaniyāma*). They have attained, are attaining, and will attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
and so on up to the fruit of an arhat. Those who seek the path of a pratyekabuddha are also like this.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi enter the stage of the true dharma—having entered, currently entering, and about to enter—and they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—having attained, currently attaining, and about to attain it.
Kauśika! What are the outflow-free dharmas?

They are the so-called four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path; the four noble truths; inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; and the ten powers of a Buddha, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Sons and daughters of good family who study this Dharma shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they have attained it, they are attaining it now, and they will attain it in the future.
“Kauśika! If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct a single person so that they attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*,
the merit obtained by that person would surpass that of instructing all the people of a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Even if one were to teach the people of a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, they would still not be free from the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Kauśika! To teach a single person to attain the fruit of srotāpanna is to cause them to leave the three evil realms behind.
This applies likewise up to the fruit of arhatship and the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct the people of a single Jambudvīpa so that they attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha, it would not yield as much merit as a son of good family or a daughter of good family who instructs a single person so that they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The latter gains far more merit!
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because of the Bodhisattva that there arise those who attain the fruit of a Srotāpanna, up to and including Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because of the bodhisattvas, the Buddhas arise. For this reason, Kauśika,

you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes out a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to others, causing them to write, uphold, read, recite, and explain it, they will obtain much merit!
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all wholesome dharmas are extensively explained.

By training in these wholesome dharmas, there arise the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and the great families of householders; from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and there arise the four foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); and there arise the various Srotāpannas up to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; and there arise the Buddhas.

“Kauśika! Setting aside the people of a single Jambudvīpa, suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the sentient beings in the world-system of the four continents to practice the ten paths of wholesome action. What do you think?”
"By reason of these causes and conditions, would that person obtain much merit?
He replied, "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as this good man or good woman who writes out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another, causing them to write it, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it; the latter gains far more merit!"
The rest is as explained above.
Kausika! Let alone the sentient beings in the world-system of the four continents.
If one were to teach the sentient beings in a small thousandfold world-system to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, it would be the same.
Kausika! Let alone the sentient beings in a small thousandfold world-system.
If one were to teach the sentient beings within two thousand middle-world systems to practice the ten paths of wholesome action;

yet if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to write out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to another, causing them to write, uphold, read, and recite it—the latter would obtain far more merit!
The rest is as explained above. Kausika!
Let alone the sentient beings in two thousand medium world-systems.
If one were to teach all sentient beings within the three thousandfold world-system to practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
yet another person were to write out a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others, causing them to copy, uphold, read, and recite it—the latter person’s merit would be far greater!
Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings within a trichiliocosm,
suppose one were to instruct all the sentient beings in as many world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges River, causing them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
Furthermore, if there is someone who copies a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person, causing them to copy, uphold, read, and recite it, their merit will be even greater!
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose there is a person who instructs the sentient beings of one Jambudvīpa, causing them to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."
"What do you think?
Would the merit of these sons and daughters of good family be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to write out a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others, causing them to write it, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it; rather, the latter gains far more merit!"
Why is this? Because within this *prajñāpāramitā*, all wholesome dharmas are explained in detail.
The rest is as stated above.

Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, and further setting aside the sentient beings of the world-system of four continents, the world-system of a thousand worlds, the world-system of two thousand worlds, and the world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds.

Kauśika! Suppose there were someone who taught the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, causing them to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers. What do you think?
"Would this person's merit be great?
He replied, "It would be very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as meritorious as for a son or daughter of good family to write out a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to others, causing them to write it down, uphold it, read it, recite it, and explain it; the latter gains far more merit!”
Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, all wholesome dharmas are explained in detail.
The remainder is as stated above.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who receives this Prajñāpāramitā, writes it down, maintains it, reads it, recites it, explains it, and correctly brings it to mind, the merit of that person surpasses that of one who teaches the people of Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."

One who possesses right mindfulness receives, upholds, and draws near to the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including right mindfulness, without employing the duality of dharmas nor the non-duality of dharmas;

one receives, upholds, and draws near to the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, and *dānapāramitā*, up to and including right mindfulness, without employing the duality of dharmas nor the non-duality of dharmas;

for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one possesses right mindfulness of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), without employing the duality of dharmas nor the non-duality of dharmas.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there are good men or good women who, for the sake of others, expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, revealing it, analyzing it, and making it easy to understand.
Kauśika! What is the meaning of the prajñāpāramitā? Kauśika!

The meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* should not be viewed through dualistic characteristics, nor should it be viewed through non-dualistic characteristics. It is neither characterized by existence nor by non-existence; it neither enters nor exits, neither increases nor diminishes, neither defiles nor purifies, neither arises nor ceases, neither grasps nor relinquishes, neither abides nor does not abide, neither real nor unreal, neither joined nor dispersed, neither attached nor unattached, neither caused nor uncaused, neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither suchness nor non-suchness, and neither the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor non-limit-of-reality.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, for the sake of others, explain, reveal, analyze, and clarify the meaning of this *prajñāpāramitā* through various causes and conditions so that it is easily understood, the merit obtained by that son or daughter of good family is far greater than that of one who merely upholds the *prajñāpāramitā* themselves, or who approaches, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates it.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family personally upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, draws near to it, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates it;

and furthermore, for the sake of others, expounds the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand—then the merit obtained by this son or daughter of good family is exceedingly great!"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A son or daughter of good family should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way—revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand!”
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
“So it is, Kauśika!
These sons and daughters of good family should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, revealing it, analyzing it, and making it easy to understand.

Kauśika! When a son of good family or a daughter of good family thus expounds the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand, they shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout their entire lives, make offerings to immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions—honoring, respecting, and praising them, and providing offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies according to whatever they require;

and if there are yet other sons or daughters of good family who, through various causes and conditions, extensively expound the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* for others, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand—the merit of these latter sons or daughters of good family is far greater!
Why is this? All Buddhas of the past, future, and present have all trained in this Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained, are now attaining, and will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to practice the perfection of giving for immeasurable, boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, it would not equal the merit of this son of good family or daughter of good family who, by means of the perfection of wisdom, expounds its meaning to others, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand; the latter's merit is far greater, because they do so through the principle of non-apprehension."
What is meant by "having something to apprehend"? Kausika!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving with the notion of something to be apprehended, at the time of giving he forms this thought:
"I give, he receives, and this is the object given"—this is called attaining *dāna*, but not the *pāramitā*.
"I maintain the precepts; this is the precept."
"This is called attaining morality, but not the pāramitā;
'I practice patience, and I practice patience for the sake of this person'—
this is called attaining patience, but not the pāramitā."
"I am practicing diligence; I am diligently striving for this purpose"—this is called attaining diligence, but not the perfection (pāramitā) of diligence.
"I am cultivating dhyāna; this is the dhyāna I cultivate."
"This is called attaining dhyāna, but not attaining pāramitā;
'I cultivate wisdom, and this is the wisdom I cultivate.
This is called attaining prajñā, but not attaining pāramitā."

Kauśika! A son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices in this manner will not fully complete the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate and fulfill the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving, if they do not apprehend the giver, do not apprehend the recipient, and do not apprehend the object given, this person fulfills the dāna-pāramitā;
likewise, up to the time they cultivate the prajñā-pāramitā, if they do not apprehend wisdom and do not apprehend the wisdom being cultivated, this person fulfills the prajñā-pāramitā."
Kauśika! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā.

When a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices the prajñāpāramitā in this way, they should expound its meaning to others, revealing, clarifying, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand.
He expounds the meaning of the dhyāna-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, and dāna-pāramitā, revealing, elucidating, and analyzing them so that they may be easily understood.
Why is this? Kauśika!
In future ages there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who, wishing to expound the *prajñāpāramitā*, will instead expound a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
There are sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet having heard this counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, they lose the correct path.
Good sons and good daughters should fully expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for such persons, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying it so that it is easy to understand.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who speak of a prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension, this is a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the prajñāpāramitā with the notion of attainment, this is called a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
“Good sons and good daughters, when you say that the prajñāpāramitā which involves apprehension is a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā, and when you state that form is impermanent, saying:
‘One who can practice in this way is practicing the prajñāpāramitā,’ [you speak of the counterfeit].”
If a practitioner seeks the impermanence of form, this constitutes practicing a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To speak of the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and to say:
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*."
If a practitioner seeks the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is practicing a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is to preach the impermanence of the eye, up to the preaching of the impermanence of the mind;
to preach the impermanence of forms, up to the preaching of the impermanence of phenomena.

It is taught that the eye-element is impermanent, the form-element and the eye-consciousness-element are impermanent, and so on, up to the teaching that the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element are impermanent.
He teaches that the earth element is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that the consciousness element is impermanent;
he teaches that the eye-consciousness element is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that the mind-consciousness element is impermanent;
he teaches that eye-contact is impermanent, up to and including the teaching that mind-contact is impermanent.
He teaches that the feeling born of eye-contact conditioned by contact is impermanent, and so on, up to the teaching that the feeling born of mind-contact conditioned by contact is impermanent;
as explained in detail for the five aggregates.
He teaches that form is suffering, and so on, up to the teaching that the feeling born of mind-contact conditioned by contact is suffering.
The teaching that form is non-self, up to the teaching that feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact is non-self, is all as explained regarding the five aggregates.
When a practitioner practices the perfection of giving, [the teacher] explains to them that form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and so on, up to explaining that feeling produced by the condition of mind-contact is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
It is the same for the *śīlapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For those practicing the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), he teaches impermanence, suffering, and non-self;
for those practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), he teaches impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Even when practicing for the sake of *sarvajñatā*, one should teach them impermanence, suffering, and non-self,
giving such instruction as this:
"One who can practice in this way is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*."
“Kauśika! This is called a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika!”
If, in a future age, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should preach a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"Practice the perfection of wisdom; when you practice the perfection of wisdom, you shall attain the first stage, and so on, up to the attainment of the tenth stage.
The same applies to the perfection of meditation, and so forth, down to the perfection of generosity.
The practitioner, through a semblance of attainment and by cultivating this through general characteristics, practices this Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! This is called the semblance Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
when a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, they should speak thus:
'O son of good family, once you have practiced the Prajñāpāramitā, you shall transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.'"
This is called the counterfeit prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, good sons and good daughters who speak thus to those seeking the Buddha-way:

"After you, good sons and good daughters, have practiced the prajñāpāramitā, you shall enter the rank of bodhisattvas and attain the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);"

Having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, they abide in the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, traveling from one buddha-field to another to make offerings to the Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them.
To speak in such a manner is called a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family speaks thus to those who seek the path of the Buddha:

"O son of good family, O daughter of good family, if you study this Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate it, you shall attain immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit."
To speak in such a manner is called the counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, good sons and good daughters who seek the Buddha-way are told:

"Just as the roots of merit and virtuous foundations of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind until their attainment of Buddhahood—are all gathered together and dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"To speak in such a manner is called a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that good sons and good daughters do not speak of a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* to those who seek the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those seeking the path of the Buddha, teach the *prajñāpāramitā*:..."
"Good son, good daughter!
As you practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), do not contemplate form as impermanent. Why is this?
Form is empty of the nature of form; this nature of form is not a dharma. That which is not a dharma is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within the perfection of wisdom, form is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Why is this? Because within this, even form cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence! Kausika!
Good son or good daughter, one who speaks in this manner is said not to be speaking a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of those seeking the Buddha-way, should say:
'You, sons of good family and daughters of good family, practice the Prajñāpāramitā; regarding all dharmas, do not pass over anything, and do not dwell in anything.'"
Why is this? Within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be transcended or in which one can abide. Why is that?
All dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; that which is empty of intrinsic nature is not a dharma. That which is not a dharma is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no dharma that can enter or exit, nor any that can arise or cease.
“Kauśika! When these sons of good family or daughters of good family speak in this manner, it is called ‘not speaking a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.
As explained at length above, because it is contrary to what is counterfeit, it is called ‘not speaking a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.’”
"In this way, Kauśika!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family should expound the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in such a manner.
If one expounds the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā in this way, the merit obtained will surpass that of the former."
The [Commentary] says:
Because the Buddha further wishes to clarify the superiority of the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of another method, he asks Śakra:
"If someone were to teach the people of one Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, would their merit be great?"
As explained at length in the sūtras, this passage sets forth the superior causes and conditions:
namely, the *prajñāpāramitā*, which extensively expounds all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, brings about the paths of the three vehicles, leads to nirvāṇa, and ensures one does not return;

whereas the ten paths of wholesome action consist merely of wholesome tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, which yield worldly, impermanent blessings and joys, only for one to fall back again into suffering. Therefore, they are not equal.
Furthermore, the former are mundane dharmas and the latter are supramundane dharmas;
the former are dharmas that can produce birth and death, while the latter are dharmas that can extinguish birth and death;
the former are causes and conditions for impermanent bliss, while the latter are causes and conditions for permanent bliss.
Previously, these were dharmas common to both ordinary beings and sages; subsequently, they became dharmas belonging exclusively to sages.
Such are the distinctions among them.
As for the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), they include the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the immeasurable dharmas of all Buddhas.

In order to make this matter clear and easy to understand, he further explains the causal conditions: "To teach a single person so that they attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* yields great merit, which surpasses teaching all the people of Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action—because although one may practice the ten wholesome actions, one is not yet exempt from the three evil realms."
"It is the same even up to attaining the path of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha further spoke a parable:

"If someone were to teach the people of a single Jambudvīpa so that they attain the paths of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it would not equal the merit gained by someone who teaches a single person to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the latter person gains far more merit."
Why is this? It is because those from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha* are all born from the Bodhisattva.

Within this *prajñāpāramitā*, the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way are explained in various ways; therefore, to transcribe a scroll of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and give it to another is superior to teaching the ten wholesome paths of action to the four continents, or even to worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Furthermore, teaching the people of Jambudvīpa, and even those of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to practice the four dhyānas up to the five supernormal powers (abhijñā) is likewise so.
However, those in the four dhyānas and so forth are persons who have abandoned desire, which distinguishes them from the ten wholesome paths.

Furthermore, if someone were to instruct the people of a single Jambudvīpa, or even as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, causing them to practice the ten wholesome paths, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers, it would not yield as much merit as that person who upholds, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā; the latter obtains far more merit.
Regarding "attaining much merit": previously, it was distinguished by giving a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to others while one practiced the Prajñāpāramitā oneself;
now, there is a difference in that the ten paths of wholesome action up to the five supernormal powers are explained collectively rather than individually.
Question: Why do you not explain "receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and expounding," but instead explain only "right mindfulness"? Answer:
The merit of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining [the teachings] is great;
because right mindfulness can fulfill two matters—namely, merit and wisdom—it is therefore explained separately.
It is like a person gathering medicinal herbs; as long as they have not yet compounded and taken them, there is no benefit for the illness, but once taken, the illness is cured.
Right mindfulness is like taking the medicine that heals the illness; therefore, one should simply understand right mindfulness.
The characteristic of right mindfulness is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that is neither dual nor non-dual.
The meaning of duality and non-duality is as previously explained.
First, regarding the writing of the sūtra scrolls, they are superior to the śarīra relics;
To give a scroll of this sutra to others is superior to teaching people to practice the ten wholesome deeds or even the five supernormal powers;
now, among the acts of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it, right mindfulness regarding its reception and upholding is the most supreme.
Now, because the Buddhas have compassion for sentient beings, they explain its meaning so that it may be easily understood; this is superior to one's own practice of right mindfulness.
At that time, wishing to extensively distinguish the merit [of this teaching], the Buddha said:
"If there were someone who, for as long as their life lasts, made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, it would not be equal to explaining the meaning of the Prajñā for others."
In this context, the superior causes and conditions are explained:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time all studied this Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, "If a bodhisattva were to practice the six pāramitās for immeasurable kalpas with the notion of something to be attained, it would not equal explaining the Prajñāpāramitā for others."
"Having something to obtain" refers to grasping at signs within all phenomena by means of the self-centered mind.
Desiring further to explain the correct meaning of Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha replied to Śakra:
"When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās through non-attainment, they become fully perfected."
"Perfection is precisely the true meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Suppose there are those in a future age who speak of a counterfeit Prajñā; when the people in the assembly hear them speak of right mindfulness, they will think:
'What, then, is wrong mindfulness?'"
For this reason, the characteristics of counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* are taught.
Just as a person who knows what is the path and what is not the path is able to abandon the wrong path and proceed upon the right path.
Furthermore, out of compassion for sentient beings of future ages who will not see the Buddha and the great bodhisattvas, but will see only the written scriptures;
because of their false recollections, they will cling to the literal sound and speak a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Similar" means that while the names, words, and language are identical, the underlying mind and meaning differ.
For example, if one speaks of the five aggregates and so forth as being impermanent, up to being unarisen and unceasing, with an attached mind and by grasping at signs, this is "similar prajñā."

If one explains the impermanence of the five aggregates with a mind that is unattached and does not grasp at signs, doing so merely to destroy the perversion of permanence while remaining unattached to impermanence itself, this is true *prajñā*.

A person who teaches in this manner instructs others to abandon counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* and to cultivate true *prajñāpāramitā*; this is called teaching the correct meaning of *prajñāpāramitā*, and its merit surpasses that of the former.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa were taught and caused to attain the stage of Srotāpanna.

Would this person gain much merit?

World-Honored One!

speaking thus:
'You should train in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*; you shall thereby attain the dharma of all-knowledge.'"
If you attain the dharma of all-knowledge, you will then attain the practice of the prajñāpāramitā, increasing and perfecting it;
if you attain the practice of the prajñāpāramitā, increasing and perfecting it, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Furthermore, Kauśika,
if a son or daughter of good family were to teach the sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa and cause them to abide in the stage of avaivartika.
"What do you think?
Would that person gain much merit?
He replied:

"It is not as good as this son or daughter of good family who, for the sake of others, explains its meaning through various causes and conditions, revealing, analyzing, and making it easy to understand;
speaking thus:
'Come here!'"
"Good son!
If you receive this Prajñāpāramitā and practice even as it is taught within the Prajñāpāramitā, you shall then attain the dharma of omniscience;

Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is produced.

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Come! Receive this Prajñāpāramitā and practice according to what is taught therein;

Among these, there is a bodhisattva who will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
if any son or daughter of good family expounds the Prajñāpāramitā and its interpretive meaning for this bodhisattva, that person’s merit shall be the greatest.
"Even so it is in all worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws ever closer to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so too should they be progressively taught to practice the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā;

they should be taught inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities;
furthermore, they should be provided with offerings of robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal requisites according to their needs.
If these sons or daughters of good family provide offerings of both the Dharma and material wealth to this bodhisattva, the merit they obtain will surpass that of the former.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Kauśika! As a noble disciple, it is only right that you should comfort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are dedicated to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by benefiting them through the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth; such is the proper way of things.
Why is this? Because within the bodhisattvas, the assembly of all Buddhas and noble ones is born.
If bodhisattvas did not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these bodhisattvas would be unable to train in the six *pāramitās* up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*).
If one does not study the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas), one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
if one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then there would be no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, Kauśika,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and while training in those six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities, they attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they sever the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. In the world there then appear great clans of Kṣatriyas, great clans of Brāhmaṇas, and great families of householders; from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception. There likewise appear the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfections of morality (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Furthermore, the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas all manifest in the world.
The Commentator says:

To teach the people of Jambudvīpa, and even the people in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that they may attain the paths of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, is not as meritorious as expounding the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for others.
Herein, the causal condition is explained:
"Because all these noble ones emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā. The Prajñāpāramitā is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

one who possesses correct and universal knowledge is called a Buddha. Lesser beings are not like this—namely, the great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats—and those who follow them are even less so—namely, the Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas.
Those who cherish and make offerings to one who can know the true reality of all phenomena are the world’s people of merit, such as kings of devas and kings of men.
Therefore, it is constantly said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all the worthy sages, the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, and even all the devas."

Furthermore, to teach the unsurpassed path and lead all people from a single Jambudvīpa, up to as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, to the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) is not as meritorious as explaining the true meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā for a single person who has reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Question: It may be granted that what was said above—that the dharmas of ordinary persons and those of the Two Vehicles are inferior—is correct;

however, since it is now said that one teaches people to resolve upon the Unsurpassed Way and to attain *avaivartika* [non-retrogression], which is a matter of the Buddha-way, why is this also inferior?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas who correctly expound the meaning of Prajñā:
first, those with physical bodies born of birth-and-death; second, those with dharma-nature-born bodies who have transcended the three realms and are subject neither to birth nor death.

This bodhisattva speaks only of the matters of a bodhisattva who has transcended the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), namely: teaching and transforming sentient beings; purifying Buddha-fields; discerning the causes and conditions of the mental actions and karma of all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time; discerning the arising and ceasing, the formation and destruction, and the number of kalpas of all worlds; and the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, such as great loving-kindness, great compassion, and omniscience.

To teach the Dharma to a single person is superior to causing sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, or even as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, to resolve their minds for enlightenment and further bring them to the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
From the stage of *avaivartika* up to the path of Buddhahood, there is yet another person in between who is close to the path of Buddhahood and desires to attain it swiftly.
To teach this person the correct meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* brings the greatest merit!
Why is this? Because the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) is great, the merit (*puṇya*) is likewise great.

For example, making offerings to all the sages throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, up to Bodhisattvas about to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), is not equal to making offerings to a single Buddha.
For example, if one offends a crown prince, the transgression committed is greater than that against all other people;
likewise, if one makes offerings to a crown prince, the merit gained is superior to that of making offerings to all ordinary persons.
If one offends a king, the offense is greater than offending a crown prince;
if one makes offerings to a king, it is superior to making offerings to a crown prince.

Likewise, the merit of teaching and making offerings to Bodhisattvas who are rapidly approaching Buddhahood surpasses the merit of teaching and making offerings to as many non-regressive (*avaivartika*) Bodhisattvas as there are sands in the Ganges River.
Why is this? Because the field of merit is profound and vast, and its Dharma is able to cause sentient beings to grow and flourish.
At that time, Śakra, knowing the greatness of this Dharma-power, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As a Bodhisattva draws ever closer to the Unsurpassed Way, they should be taught and made offerings to in this manner, for their merit will increase accordingly.
At that time, Subhūti praised Śakra, saying, “Excellent!”
Excellent!
You are able to comfort and encourage those bodhisattvas who are dedicated to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the two kinds of giving: material wealth and the Dharma.
"Material giving" refers to offerings such as requisites, clothing, and food;
"Dharma giving" refers to teaching the six *pāramitās* and so forth.
Because Śakra has attained the Way, he is called a noble disciple (*ārya-śrāvaka*).
It is the duty of the noble disciples to comfort and encourage all bodhisattvas.
Regarding this, the causal conditions are explained:
"All these noble assemblies emerge from among the bodhisattvas."
Why is this? If a bodhisattva does not practice the six pāramitās and does not realize the unsurpassed path, then there would be no srotāpanna up to pratyekabuddha.
Because of bodhisattvas, the ten paths of wholesome action and even the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas appear in the world;
for this reason, the three evil realms are severed, and the great clans of kṣatriyas and even all the Buddhas appear in the world.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva explains the true meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* and instructs others to draw near to the path of the Buddha, their merit is the greatest.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 60:
Explanation of the Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication (*Anumodanā-pariṇāmanā-varga*).
Volume Thirty-Nine, Chapter Sixty-One: Rejoicing and Dedication.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who rejoice in merit and share it with all sentient beings, dedicating it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by way of non-apprehension.”
Whether it be the merit of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or the merit of all sentient beings— whether through giving, observing precepts, cultivating meditative concentration, or sympathetic joy—
the merit of this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s sympathetic joy is shared with all sentient beings and dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
that merit is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless!

Why is this? Because the giving, upholding of precepts, cultivation of concentration, and sympathetic joy of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings are for the sake of self-discipline, self-purification, and self-deliverance—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, as well as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

In contrast, the bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy in merit is dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he maintains these merits and gives rise to them for the sake of disciplining all sentient beings, purifying all sentient beings, and delivering all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

"The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring to mind the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas who have attained parinirvāṇa within the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the ten directions—the roots of goodness of those Buddhas from their first generation of the mind until they attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, up to their entry into nirvana without remainder and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma; all the roots of goodness within that interval."

It includes the six pāramitās and the roots of goodness of all śrāvakas—namely, the merit of giving, the merit of maintaining the precepts, and the merit of cultivating meditative concentration; as well as the untainted roots of goodness of those in training (śaikṣa) and the untainted roots of goodness of those beyond training (aśaikṣa); the Buddha’s aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; all-knowledge, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and other immeasurable, incalculable qualities of the Buddhas;

the teachings expounded by the Buddhas, and the study within those teachings whereby one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, enters the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and the various roots of goodness planted by other sentient beings.

All these roots of goodness, combined together with the merit of sympathetic joy, are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—the most supreme, the foremost, the most exquisite, the unsurpassed, and the peerless!
Having thus rejoiced, one takes this merit of rejoicing and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If there is a son of good family who practices the Bodhisattva vehicle and forms this thought:
"I am dedicating this mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"If a son of good family were to grasp at the marks of these thoughts, conditions, and objects and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would they be obtainable in accordance with his mental conception?"
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"When these sons of good family who practice the bodhisattva vehicle dedicate [their merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, their minds take that as an object. If these sons of good family grasp at signs, they will not obtain what they have intended."
Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

“If all conditions and all things are non-existent, yet this son of good family who practices the Bodhisattva vehicle grasps at signs—taking as his object the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the ten directions from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until the exhaustion of the Dharma, as well as the roots of goodness of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the roots of goodness of those in training and those beyond training—and unites all these merits of sympathetic joy, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
since he does so by way of signlessness, will this bodhisattva not be without inversion?”
To perceive the impermanent as permanent is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view;
to perceive the impure as pure, suffering as pleasure, and the non-self as self—these are inversions of perception, inversions of mind, and inversions of view?

Just as the conditions and the objects are, so too is unexcelled perfect enlightenment; so too is the mind of dedication; so too are the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
If that is so, what is the condition?
What is the objective entity?
And what is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"What are these roots of goodness?
What is this mind of sympathetic joy that dedicates [merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
[The Treatise] explains:
In the preceding seven chapters, the Buddha commanded Subhūti to expound the Prajñāpāramitā; meanwhile, Śakra frequently asked questions and extensively described matters concerning its merits.
Now, Maitreya follows the Buddha’s original intention, desiring once again to have Subhūti, by means of the dharma of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), expound the Prajñāpāramitā in detail.

Furthermore, Śakra, hearing that by making the aforementioned offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā with flowers, incense, music, banners, and canopies one gains immense merit, felt deep personal joy and congratulated himself, thinking: "These offering requisites are something only we [gods] can provide; they are not possessed by those who have left the household life."
Therefore, Maitreya, wishing to curb Subhūti’s feelings of self-importance, said to him:

"If a bodhisattva merely rejoices with the mind, this surpasses the merit of the giving and other such practices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings, as well as their various untainted (anāsrava) virtues; how much more so when it involves offerings of flowers, incense, and the copying of sutra scrolls!"
The meaning of "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is as previously explained.

Regarding "rejoicing in merit": without exerting physical or verbal karma to perform various meritorious deeds, one simply uses mental skillful means to see others cultivating merit and rejoices accordingly, forming this thought:
"Among all sentient beings, those who are able to cultivate merit and practice the Path are the most excellent!"
"If one is devoid of merit, humans and animals share three common activities; these three activities are:
sexual desire, food and drink, and combat.
Those who are able to practice merit and cultivate the Path are collectively respected, cherished, and revered by all sentient beings."
It is like the clear, cool full moon during the heat of summer, which all look up to with joy;
it is also like a great assembly being summoned, where musical performances and delicacies are fully prepared, and people from far and near all gather together in delight.
It is the same for those who cultivate merit.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions for the happiness of merit:
mundane and supramundane.
Regarding the supramundane, although all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas lack karmic retribution, they can generate merit; therefore, they are called "merit.
For this reason, both tainted and untainted dharmas are collectively termed "merit."
Furthermore, merit is the root of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it can fulfill all aspirations.
It is praised by all noble ones and disparaged by those without wisdom.
It is the sphere of action for the wise and is avoided by those without wisdom.

By virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, one becomes a human king, a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), a celestial king, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a Buddha, World-Honored One—possessing great kindness and great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā)—attaining sovereignty and unimpededness, all of which arise from within merit.
Regarding such various merits as these, because one has attained right view, one rejoices accordingly.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects to himself:
"I ought to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings; yet these sentient beings are able to cultivate merit for themselves. For this reason, joy arises in his heart.
Furthermore, all sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds are similar to me and are my companions; therefore, one rejoices in them.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, regarding the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings cultivating merit throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they practice giving, uphold the precepts, or cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom—generate within these merits the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), it is for this reason called "rejoicing."
One should take this merit resulting from sympathetic joy and, together with all sentient beings, dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding "together with all sentient beings": while this merit cannot itself be given to all sentient beings, its fruit and retribution can be given.
Once the Bodhisattva has obtained the karmic fruits of merit—such as clothing, food, drink, and other worldly requisites for happiness—he uses them to benefit sentient beings.

With a body and speech purified by merit, he is trusted and accepted by others; he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, enabling them to attain the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, and so forth, thereby providing them with benefits for future lives.

Finally attaining Buddhahood, he will receive the retribution of merit and virtue: his body will possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, with immeasurable radiance that never tires the beholder;

endowed with immeasurable purity, a gentle Brahma-voice, and the various Buddha-dharmas such as the unhindered liberations, he will manifest these through the three modes of manifestation to deliver immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings.
After his parinirvāṇa, his relic-sharīra will be broken into pieces and offered for worship by others, so that in the long run they may all attain the Way.
This fruit of retribution can be shared with all sentient beings; because the cause is spoken of within the context of the fruit, it is said that "merit is shared with sentient beings."
If merit could be given away, then all the merit accumulated by the Buddhas from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment could be given to others, after which they would perform it again.
However, the essence of wholesome dharmas cannot be given; rather, one now directly bestows fearlessness and freedom from affliction upon sentient beings for their use.
Regarding the phrase "because there is nothing to be apprehended," the meaning is as previously explained.

This is called the merit of rejoicing belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva; when compared to the three kinds of merit of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings, it is the most excellent, the highest, the foremost, the most sublime, the unsurpassed, and the peerless—its meaning is as previously explained.
Within this, the superior causes and conditions are explained:
"The merit of these two vehicles is entirely for the sake of self-discipline, self-purification, and self-deliverance.
Observing the precepts constitutes self-discipline;
The practitioner of dhyāna is one who purifies oneself;
the one with wisdom is one who delivers oneself.
Furthermore, self-discipline consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
"Self-purification" refers to right mindfulness and right concentration;
"self-deliverance" refers to right view, right intention, and right effort.

Furthermore, one is self-disciplined through the causal condition of giving, self-purified through the causal condition of ethical conduct, and self-delivered through the causal condition of cultivating meditative concentration.
The cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the proximate cause and condition for untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*);
untainted phenomena refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and so forth.
Generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are not explained here because they are remote causes.
The merit of a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy, though devoid of strenuous effort, is superior because it is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.
Question: In reality, one does not deliver all sentient beings; why then do you say it is "superior because it is for the sake of delivering all sentient beings"?
The answer is:
The power of the merit of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is capable of delivering all sentient beings, yet this is only because sentient beings lack the causes and conditions for union.
It is like a great fire which always possesses the power to burn; however, because the fuel does not come near it, it cannot burn, whereas if it comes near, it can indeed burn.
At that time, Subhūti, by means of the wisdom of ultimate emptiness, questioned Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"When one recollects the merit of the Buddhas, rejoices in it, and dedicates it toward the unsurpassed path, is that which is recollected as a past event exactly as it was recollected?"
Maitreya replied, "No," for two reasons:
first, because all Buddhas of the past, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, have long since entered parinirvāṇa, leaving nothing behind; [and second...]

A bodhisattva may lack the knowledge of past lives, or possess it but be unable to access it; thus, relying merely on recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination according to what has been heard, they do not act in accordance with their thoughts.

Second, all Buddhas and their merits transcend the three realms and the three periods of time; they sever the path of conceptual proliferation and verbal expression, possessing a character like that of nirvāṇa—ultimately empty and pure.
One who rejoices discriminates between the roots of goodness and merits of the Buddhas and their disciples; because this mind of dedication and the unsurpassed path are not real, it is said: "No!"
Subhūti raised an objection, saying:
"If these things do not exist, then this bodhisattva’s recollective discrimination would fall into perversion.

If these things are ultimately empty and have the characteristic of purity, then recollection is likewise so, and the merits of all past Buddhas are likewise so—without discrimination and without difference. How, then, can one rejoice in them?"
This is the summary of the meaning.

The detailed explanation is as stated in the sutra: Subhūti asks Maitreya, "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva recollects all the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa in the immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions in the past," this refers to a bodhisattva wishing to give rise to merit through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Since the Buddha is the master of merit, he therefore recollects the Buddha;
having heard the sūtras and books state the names of past Buddhas, he extensively recollects all past Buddhas by means of those names.
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment" means that at the initial production of the thought, one makes the vow:
"I shall deliver all sentient beings.
This mind is associated with the three roots of goodness:
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;

all wholesome dharmas associated with the roots of goodness, as well as the physical, verbal, and mental karmas arising from those roots of goodness—the conjunction of these factors is called merit (*puṇya*).

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, practicing the six pāramitās, entering the stage of a bodhisattva, attaining the ten stages, and even sitting at the site of enlightenment—within this process, the bodhisattva personally cultivates merit and, through its integration, attains the Buddha-way.
Even up until the entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder after final extinction, the relics and the remaining Dharma are all the result of the convergence of the Buddha’s own merits.
This is due to the merit corresponding to the practice of the six *pāramitās* by Mahāyāna practitioners.

"Corresponding" (*saṃprayukta*) means that, with the exception of the six *pāramitās* themselves, all other dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas are subsumed within them; therefore, it is said to be "in correspondence with the six *pāramitās*. Thus, they are in harmony.
If there are those seeking to become śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they plant roots of merit such as giving, observing the precepts, and practicing meditative concentration.
There are two kinds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
the first are those whose outflows are exhausted, who are termed "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Second, those who have attained the Path but whose outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted are called "learners" (*śaikṣa*).
Because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) among the various merits of these two types of persons are superior, only "roots of goodness" are mentioned.
The previous mention of "those who seek the two vehicles" includes both ordinary beings and sages;
the current reference to "those in training and those beyond training" refers exclusively to sages.

The primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) are indeterminate material phenomena (*avyākṛta-rūpadharma*) and are not virtuous merits; therefore, it is said only that "the Buddha possesses the five groups of those beyond training" (*pañca-śaikṣa-skandha*).
Great kindness and great compassion, as well as the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, are as explained in the first chapter.

Regarding the statement, "The Dharma taught by all Buddhas—by studying this Dharma, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, and so forth, until entering the stage of a bodhisattva": this refers to attaining the Way within the bequeathed Dharma after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; for this reason, it is stated again.

“Furthermore, other sentient beings plant various roots of goodness” refers to the causes and conditions for planting merit and virtue by devas, humans, and even animals, both while the Buddha was in the world and during the period of his bequeathed Dharma.

Regarding the merit of these four preceding sections, when a practitioner universally contemplates and recollects it with sympathetic joy, and dedicates it toward the pursuit of the Buddha-way, this is called "unsurpassed sympathetic joy"—it is supreme and peerless.
Question:
Why do those who seek the Buddha-way not personally cultivate merit themselves, but instead practice sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) in the minds of others? Answer:

When bodhisattvas, through the power of skillful means, are able to give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward the meritorious deeds performed with diligent effort by others, their merit surpasses that of one who performs such deeds themselves.
Furthermore, this merit of sympathetic joy is itself true merit.

Why is this so? To be mindful of the Buddhas of the past is precisely the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha), and it is also the mindfulness of the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, precepts, renunciation, and devas among the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

Because one practices the pure precepts as a cause, enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and gives rise to ultimate wisdom, through their harmonious integration one is able to give rise to correct sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Therefore, it is not merely a matter of sympathetic joy; one also practices this true Dharma.
This dedication of the mind is itself the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*).
As for the "object," it refers to that which is the object of the mind of sympathetic joy, namely, the merits performed by all Buddhas and all sentient beings.

Regarding "the object" (*vastu*): if it is the fundamental basis of what is taken as an object of focus, then merit is the locus where the qualities of that object reside. That is to say, all Buddhas and sentient beings, as well as lands, mountains and forests, and monastic dwellings, are all termed "objects."
"Can that which is conceived be obtained?
Maitreya replied, "No!"
Subhūti said to Maitreya:
"If all things and all conditions are non-existent, how is it that one does not fall into perversion?
Perversion consists of the four perversions and the three types of conceptualization."
This perversion is an analogy: to recollect and think of a Buddha when no Buddha exists is like thinking of the permanent when there is impermanence, or thinking of the pure when there is impurity.
Question:

Seeing (*dṛṣṭi*) is the root of all perversions. For instance, one who has attained the path of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) can give rise to perversions of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*), but not perversions of seeing, because the latter have been severed by the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*).
Answer: This perversion differs at the time of its arising and differs at the time of its cessation.
At the time of arising, perception comes first, followed by thought, and finally by view.
At the time of abandonment, one first abandons views, because they are abandoned through the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
The essence of all perversions (*viparyāsa*) consists of views, and thus they are abandoned through the realization of the truths.

As for the perversions of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*), when a practitioner who has not yet abandoned desire forgets their mindfulness, they grasp at the mark of purity (*śubha-nimitta*) and give rise to the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
When right mindfulness is restored, it is extinguished immediately, as illustrated by the simile in the Sūtra:
"Just as a drop of water falling upon a red-hot iron plate is extinguished at once.
