Because the error is minor, it is metaphorically termed an "inversion," but it is not a real inversion.
Therefore it is said:
ordinary persons have three kinds of inversion, while those in training have two kinds of inversion.

Furthermore, all conditions and all phenomena are ultimately empty according to reality; mindfulness is empty, awakening is empty, the mind of sympathetic joy is empty, and the *dānapāramitā* up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) are also empty.
If all dharmas have but a single characteristic, namely the characteristic of signlessness (animitta), then herein, what is the "condition" (pratyaya)?
What is the "substantial entity" (vastu)?
And what is the "mind that dedicates toward the unsurpassed path"?
[Sūtra] Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

“If bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have long practiced the six pāramitās, made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, associated with virtuous friends, and have well studied the dharma of the emptiness of self-characteristics;

these bodhisattvas take these conditions, these matters, the Buddhas, the roots of goodness, and the merit of sympathetic joy, and without grasping at signs, dedicate them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. By means of the dharma of non-duality, which is neither dual nor non-dual, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, neither an obtainable dharma nor an unobtainable dharma, neither pure nor defiled, and a dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing—this is called dedication toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

If bodhisattvas have not practiced the six pāramitās for long, have not made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, have not planted roots of goodness, have not associated with spiritual friends, and have not skillfully studied the dharma of the emptiness of self-characteristics;

then the conditions, the objects, the Buddhas, the roots of goodness, and the merit of sympathetic joy of these bodhisattvas—all those mental apprehensions of signs that they dedicate toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—are not called dedication.

“Subhūti! This meaning of the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the meaning of all-knowledge—namely, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence—should not be taught to a newly initiated bodhisattva.”
Why is this? Because all the slight faith, joy, reverence, and pure minds possessed by such a bodhisattva will be lost.

This should be explained before an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva; or to one who is protected by a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), or who has long made offerings to the Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness—for such a person, one should explain the meaning of this *prajñāpāramitā* up to the meaning of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), namely, from internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*).
When such a person hears this Dharma, they do not sink, are not startled, do not fear, and are not terrified.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate the merit of their sympathetic joy toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in this manner: namely, that the mind by which the bodhisattva rejoices in the merit and dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is itself exhausted, ceased, transformed, and departed; and those conditions, those objects, and all those roots of goodness are likewise exhausted, ceased, transformed, and departed.
Among these, what is the mind of sympathetic joy?
What are the various conditions?
And what are the various matters?
What are these roots of goodness that are rejoiced in and dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Since two minds do not coexist, and this nature of mind cannot itself be apprehended as something to be dedicated, how can a bodhisattva rejoice in a mind and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know in this way:
"This perfection of wisdom has no dharma; even the perfection of generosity has no dharma.
Form has no dharma; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, have no dharma."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus rejoice in merit and dedicate it toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one can dedicate in this manner, it is called the dedication of the merit of rejoicing toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] Commentary: Maitreya’s intention is as follows:

Because all dharmas are profoundly deep and the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*) is subtle and wondrous—namely, that while not destroying the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas, one dedicates the mind of sympathetic joy toward the Unsurpassed Way—this matter is extremely difficult!
The minds of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are rigid and stubborn, and thus they are unable to practice this Dharma.
For this reason, Maitreya replied:

"If a practitioner has long cultivated the six *pāramitās*, their various merits are so profound and thick that they remain unshakable—namely, being able to believe and able to practice; because they have made extensive offerings to many Buddhas and planted roots of goodness, they have accumulated immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits; their fetters (*saṃyojana*) are broken and diminished, and their minds have become supple. These are the causal conditions from previous lives."

In this present life, one encounters excellent teachers and virtuous companions, and personally studies the emptiness of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; because of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one does not cling to this emptiness.

For such various and immeasurable causes and conditions, although all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), one is able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*) and dedicate it toward the unsurpassed path.
For example, although iron is hard and rigid, when it enters the furnace it becomes pliant and can be fashioned into whatever vessel one desires;
the mind of a bodhisattva is likewise. Because they have long practiced the six pāramitās and are protected by spiritual friends, their minds become disciplined and supple.

Within all past Buddhas, conditions, events, and roots of goodness, they do not grasp at signs; they are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate this through non-apprehension toward the unsurpassed path.
That which is signless (*animitta*) is able to employ non-duality and non-non-duality, up to and including non-arising and non-ceasing.
That which is contrary to the above is called "unable to dedicate."
Knowing that Subhūti delighted in speaking of emptiness, Maitreya said:
"This meaning of rejoicing in the Prajñāpāramitā should not be explained before bodhisattvas who are newly trained."
Why is this? If there are those with meager merit and roots of goodness, upon hearing this dharma of ultimate emptiness, they immediately become attached to emptiness and think:
"If all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent, why should I cultivate merit?"
Thus, one loses sight of wholesome karma.

For this reason, a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment is first taught to practice sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) by grasping at signs; only when they gradually acquire the power of skillful means can they then practice signless sympathetic joy.
For example, when the wings of a fledgling bird are not yet formed, one cannot force it to soar high;
once its primary feathers are fully developed, it can fly far.
An avaivartika bodhisattva has entered the stage of the Dharma and attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti); being able to believe and practice, they may be taught.

If there are those who have long practiced the six pāramitās and have associated with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), aided by the power of internal merit and external causes and conditions, they are able to believe and practice even though they are not yet established in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
When these two kinds of people hear this, their minds become pure, and they receive it with joy and faith.
It is like one who has long suffered from hunger and thirst obtaining fine food and drink;
or like one who finds coolness in great heat or warmth in great cold—their hearts are filled with love, delight, and joy.
These two bodhisattvas were also like this; having attained this wisdom of signlessness, they thought:
"By means of this wisdom, I am able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings—how much more so, then, could there be any alarm, fear, or terror!"

"Terrifying fear arises from within my mind; since even the characteristics of all phenomena within this Dharma are empty, how much more so for a self that would definitively grasp at the characteristics of phenomena? Upon hearing that all phenomena are signless, I give rise to alarm and dread!"
This concludes the explanation of the essential nature of rejoicing (*anumodanā*). Hereafter, the aforementioned matter shall be further explained through various alternative methods.
Furthermore, "Subhūti, a bodhisattva should contemplate in this way:..."
"By means of this mind, one dedicates toward the Unsurpassed Way; yet this mind perishes, ceases, changes, and departs from moment to moment, having no time of abiding.
These are the various conditions and matters, namely the past Buddhas and all roots of goodness.
The Buddhas and all such causal conditions have long since ceased, and the mind of sympathetic joy now ceases as well;
since their cessation is no different, the sūtra says:
"One dedicates with this mind, yet this very mind is exhausted and extinguished."

In this way, because one enters the past and because one enters the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is no such discrimination as "this is the mind," "this is the condition," "this is the object," or "this is the root of goodness."
If one can dedicate in this manner, it is called correct dedication.
Furthermore, at one time two minds do not coexist; thus, at the moment of the mind of sympathetic joy, there is no bodhicitta.
Since all mental characteristics are ultimately empty, one cannot perform dedication by grasping at signs.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva knows that the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and possesses no fixed dharma.
As it is with the *prajñāpāramitā*, so it is with all dharmas, up to and including the unsurpassed path.
At that time, having severed attachment to dharmas and abandoned the mind of clinging, one dwells in emptiness without contention; this is called the bodhisattva’s correct dedication.
[Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
“When bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear these matters, will they not be startled, terrified, or filled with fear?”
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon awakening dedicate his various roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Furthermore, how does he dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not grasp at this perfection of wisdom, because it is non-apprehendable and signless; and so it is for each of the perfections, up to and including the perfection of generosity."

They have great faith and understanding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and they have great faith and understanding in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

They will always be accompanied by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who will explain the meaning of the six *pāramitās* to them, revealing and analyzing them through such instruction that they are never separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*. This continues until they enter the stage of the bodhisattva’s fixed position (*niyāma*), at which point they shall never again be separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor from the *dānapāramitā*, nor from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikadharma*).
Furthermore, he teaches about the works of Māra; having heard these various works of Māra, he neither increases nor decreases [in his resolve].
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma.
This bodhisattva is also never separated from the Buddhas until they attain the stage of a bodhisattva, during which time they plant roots of goodness;

by virtue of these roots of goodness, they are born into the family of bodhisattvas and, until they attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they never depart from these roots of goodness.

"Furthermore, a newly resolved bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the merits performed by the Buddhas of the past—in the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the ten directions—who have severed the path of birth and death, cut off all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), exhausted the [outflows], laid down the heavy burden, destroyed the thorns of the village, severed the fetters of existence, attained right knowledge, and achieved liberation; as well as the merits performed by their disciples—including those planted by the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great families of householders, and from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa deities—he unites and weighs them all together. With a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) that is supreme, foremost, most excellent, unsurpassed, and peerless, he dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"If a newly resolved bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices in the merit of the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples, which is most supreme, foremost, most exquisite, unsurpassed, and peerless, then having rejoiced, he should dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How does a bodhisattva avoid falling into perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view?"

Subhūti said: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva recollects the Buddhas and the Saṃgha, yet within that does not give rise to the notion of 'Buddha' nor the notion of 'Saṃgha,' and has no notion of 'roots of goodness';
and if they dedicate this mind toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet within that mind also does not give rise to the notion of 'mind'—[this is dedication]."
When a bodhisattva dedicates in this way, their perception is non-perverted, their mind is non-perverted, and their view is non-perverted. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however,
contemplates the roots of goodness of the Buddhas and the Sangha while grasping at signs—
and having grasped these signs, dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi— then such a bodhisattva is said to have perverted perception, a perverted mind, and perverted views.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva uses this mind to contemplate all Buddhas, the Saṃgha, and all roots of goodness;
at the time of such contemplation, they immediately know that [all things] are exhausted and extinguished.

If they are exhausted and extinguished, these dharmas cannot be dedicated. The mind used for dedication is also characterized by exhaustion and extinction, and the dharmas in the place to which they are dedicated are likewise characterized by this same mark.
If one dedicates in this manner, it is called right dedication and not wrong dedication.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate toward unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment in this way.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates] the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the past and the roots of goodness of their disciples,
as well as the roots of goodness planted by ordinary persons who heard the Dharma therein, or those of devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas..."
The *gandharvas* who hear the Dharma and plant roots of goodness, as well as those of the great Kṣatriya clans, the great Brāhmaṇa clans, the great householder families,
and those from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, who hear the Dharma and plant roots of goodness,
and give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*— all such merit as this:
Having weighed and evaluated these virtues through their harmonious convergence, one rejoices in this merit— which is supreme, foremost, most excellent,
unsurpassed, and peerless— and dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, if a bodhisattva understands that all these dharmas are utterly extinguished, and that the dharma to which they dedicate [merit] is also empty of intrinsic nature—if one can dedicate in this manner, it is called true dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva understands in this way, there is no dharma that can dedicate itself to any dharma.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty."
If one dedicates in this manner, it is called the correct dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, up to the *dānapāramitā*, they do not fall into inversion of perception, inversion of mind, or inversion of view.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva does not cling to this dedication, nor does he perceive a place where various roots of goodness are dedicated toward the mind of enlightenment; this is called the unsurpassed dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Question:
"When bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear this matter, will they not perhaps feel fear and trepidation?
This point has already been addressed in a previous question and answer; why is it asked again now?
Answer: Although Maitreya above said to Subhūti,
"One should not speak for the sake of those who have newly begun their training;"
"This may be explained to those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) and to those who have long practiced; these two types of people, upon hearing it, will be able to believe and practice.

Having already explained the causes and conditions for correct dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), he nevertheless continues to speak of the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, Śakra raises a doubt, saying:
"There are those among this assembly who have newly resolved their minds [for enlightenment]; how can you further explain this so that they do not become terrified?"
Subhūti, wishing to fulfill what Maitreya had said and desiring that those who have newly resolved their intention should practice correct dedication, replied to Śakra:

"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved his intention, although he has not long practiced the six pāramitās and has not made offerings to the Buddhas, is nevertheless capable of correct dedication due to these two causes and conditions: his sharp faculties and his acquisition of a spiritual friend."
Therefore, he said to Śakra:

“A bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening practices the perfection of wisdom, yet does not grasp this perfection of wisdom, because it is non-apprehendable and because it is ultimately empty.”
"Even the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither attained nor clung to.
This applies likewise even to the *dānapāramitā*.

Regarding 'having great faith and understanding in internal emptiness' (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*): it is because one constantly cultivates and delights in entering the meditative concentration on internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā-samādhi*) that one has faith and understanding."
This applies likewise to the extensive faith and understanding of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
The characteristics of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) are as previously explained.
Here, however, only this is clarified:
They are able to explain the meaning of the six pāramitās accordingly;

having heard this meaning, they never depart from the prajñāpāramitā until they attain entry into the bodhisattva stage—whether it be those who have long practiced and enter the bodhisattva stage, or those who have newly resolved their minds and enter the bodhisattva stage.
Furthermore, when a newly resolved bodhisattva is told about the deeds of Māra by a spiritual friend,
having heard of these deeds, they neither increase nor decrease [in their resolve], because they have skillfully cultivated the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
If Māra wishes to destroy it, he would be wishing to destroy emptiness; yet emptiness cannot be destroyed.
If there is any augmentation, it is like a phantom or a dream—what is there to be augmented?
Therefore, it is said that "there is neither increase nor decrease.

For this reason, one is never separated from the Buddhas and is always born into the family of Bodhisattvas; in every lifetime, one is not parted from roots of goodness until the attainment of the unsurpassed path.
When a newly resolved bodhisattva obtains such causes and conditions, they are no different from one who has long since resolved their mind.

Furthermore, regarding sympathetic joy and dedication: it refers to a newly resolved bodhisattva [rejoicing] in all Buddhas throughout the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions in the past—those who have severed the path [of afflictions], severed the path of birth and death, and entered nirvana without remainder.
Because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have been severed, it is said that "all conceptual proliferations are extinguished.
Because the eightfold noble path is relinquished through samādhis such as the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it is said that "the path has reached its end.
Since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are capable of producing suffering and affliction, they are the "heavy burden."
There are two kinds of relinquishment regarding the five aggregates:
first, within *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one relinquishes the causes of the five aggregates—the various afflictions;
second, upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one relinquishes the fruits of the five aggregates.
All the dwellings of laypeople are called villages.

Those who have left the household life depend on the dwellings of laypeople for their livelihood; yet these dwellings possess the thorns of the five desires. For the sake of food, they enter this forest of evil thorny fruit;
and because they seek the fruit, they are pierced by the thorns.
Just as when a person wearing wooden clogs steps on a thorn, the thorn is broken and snapped;

so too do the Buddhas, using the clogs of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), crush the thorns of the five desires, which is called the eradication and severance of the lower five fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
The exhaustion of the fetters of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is called the severance of the five higher fetters.

Because the wisdom associated with the Vajra-samādhi—the true mark of all phenomena—severs all afflictions along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), it is said that "through right knowledge, one attains liberation."
All such instances are termed "praise.
Regarding the phrase "the merits performed by the Buddhas of the past and their disciples," there are three kinds of Buddha-disciples:
Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.

Regarding the statement, "From the great clans of the Kṣatriyas up to the Śuddhāvāsa deities, one plants roots of goodness therein": these are the causes for the four kinds of fields of merit; they are the places where one plants meritorious virtue.
This merit, when combined with the mind of sympathetic joy that evaluates and weighs it, is supreme and peerless; it is dedicated toward the unsurpassed path.
This mind of dedication is correct and not erroneous.
Why is this? Now Maitreya asks Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved his mind contemplates the merits of the Buddhas and others and dedicates them toward the unsurpassed path, how is it that he does not fall into error?"
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of skillful means in the prajñāpāramitā, does not give rise to the notion of 'Buddha' regarding the Buddhas nor the notion of 'disciple,' and does not give rise to the notion of 'wholesome root' regarding any wholesome roots."

"All dharmas arise from a combination of conditions and lack intrinsic nature; therefore, there is no fixed dharma that can be called 'Buddha,' and for this reason, one does not give rise to thoughts such as 'the Buddha.'"
This mind of dedication does not even give rise to the thought of "mind.
Therefore, the bodhisattva does not fall into perversion;
were it contrary to what has been stated above, one would fall into perversion.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, with this mind, contemplates the Buddhas and all other roots of goodness, they know that as this mind comes to an end, it has ended; once the mind has ended, there is no further dedication.
Why is this? Because it undergoes transformation, loss, and destruction.
This mind likewise enters the gate of impermanence and arrives at the realm of dharmatā.

Within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no discrimination such as "this is mind" or "this is not mind," "this is a Buddha" or "this is a disciple," or "this is a root of goodness" or "this is the unsurpassed path."
The mind of dedication and the object of dedication are likewise characterized by the mark of exhaustion.
The initial mind consists of recollecting and rejoicing in the merits of the Buddhas of the past and so forth; the subsequent mind is the mind of dedication.
If one dedicates in this manner, it is called "right dedication. Question:
The initial mind and the subsequent mind possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and are therefore impermanent; [how can they be right dedication?]
The dharma toward which one dedicates [merit] is the unsurpassed path; how then can it be said that it will be exhausted and extinguished in future ages?
The answer is:
Have you not heard my previous response?
"Entering through the gate of impermanence, one arrives at the realm of dharmatā.
Herein it is not said that "all things are impermanent," but rather that "the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena is cessation."
It was previously stated:
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi transcends the three periods of time, surpasses the three realms, and is without the characteristic of grasping.
To dedicate in this manner is what constitutes right dedication.

Furthermore, there is dedication that is neither correct nor incorrect, which refers to a bodhisattva’s dedication of the roots of goodness of all past Buddhas—up to those that are unsurpassed and peerless—to the unsurpassed path.

If a bodhisattva knows that all these things are utterly extinguished, and knows that the dharmas of the objects toward which one dedicates are also empty of intrinsic nature—being able to know both extinction and emptiness—this is "true dedication."
If past phenomena are impermanent, because they are impermanent, they cannot be dedicated into phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature;
if past phenomena are empty, because they are empty, they cannot be dedicated into phenomena that are empty of intrinsic nature.
To dedicate by means of such wisdom is called "right dedication.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva knows that because all phenomena arise through causes and conditions, they lack inherent power and do not abide permanently; and since their own essential nature is immovable, how could they perform any action?
Because there is nothing to be done, among all dharmas there is no dharma that can be dedicated to another dharma; this is called "right dedication.
Thus, although a bodhisattva practices the various wholesome dharmas such as the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not fall into inversion, because they are unattached to all dharmas.

[Sūtra] "Furthermore, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that the merit produced is detached from the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); and if they also know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is characterized by detachment, and likewise that the *dānapāramitā* is characterized by detachment; and that from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is characterized by detachment; and that from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) is characterized by detachment."
In this way, the merit arising from the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of sympathetic joy is dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices in merit, they know that the self-nature of the merit of sympathetic joy is detached;
they also know that all Buddhas are detached from the nature of a Buddha.
All roots of goodness are also detached from the nature of roots of goodness;
the bodhicitta is detached from the nature of bodhicitta;
and dedication is detached from the nature of dedication.
The bodhisattva is detached from the nature of a bodhisattva;
the perfection of wisdom is detached from the nature of the perfection of wisdom;
and likewise the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline.
The perfection of giving is itself detached from the nature of the perfection of giving;
and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are themselves detached from the nature of the eighteen unique qualities.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom that is free from signs in this manner; this is called the merit of rejoicing arising within the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to dedicate the roots of goodness of all the Buddhas who have passed into parinirvāṇa in the past, they should dedicate them in this way, forming this thought:
'Just as the mark of the Buddhas' parinirvāṇa is, so too is the mark of the roots of goodness; the mark of the dharma of parinirvāṇa is likewise so.
The mark of this mind with which I dedicate is also just like that.'"

If one can dedicate in this manner, it should be known that this dedication is for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and one will not fall into inversion of perception, inversion of mind, or inversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, grasps at the marks of the Buddhas and their roots of goodness and dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is not called dedication.
Why is this? The past Buddhas and their roots of goodness do not take signs as a condition, nor do they take signlessness as a condition.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva grasps at such signs, this is not called the dedication of roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva falls into a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at the signs of the Buddhas, the various roots of goodness, or the various states of mind, this is called dedicating those roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fall into the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, or the inversion of view.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva asked Subhūti:
"How is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, without grasping at signs regarding any roots of goodness, is able to dedicate them toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said:
“For this reason, it should be known that within the Prajñāpāramitā in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains, there must be the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of the Prajñāpāramitā.”
If merit were separated from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it could not be dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Because within the perfection of wisdom, the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, the various roots of goodness cannot be apprehended, and even the mind that dedicates [merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be apprehended.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should reflect as follows:
"The bodies of all past buddhas and their disciples have perished, and their roots of goodness have also perished;

I am now grasping at signs and discriminating among those buddhas, those roots of goodness, and those mental states. To thus grasp at signs and dedicate [the merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not permitted by the buddhas."
Why is this? Because they grasp at signs and perceive something to be attained—namely, by grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions regarding the Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva wishes to dedicate all roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should not perceive attainment and should not grasp at signs.
If one performs such dedication by means of grasping or apprehending signs, the Buddhas do not say that it brings great benefit. Why is this?
Because such dedication is mixed with poison.
It is like fine food mixed with poison; although it has an excellent appearance and a pleasant fragrance, it is craved by people because it contains poison.
A foolish person eats it with joy, coveting its fine color, fragrance, and delicious taste.
When the meal is about to be digested, one undergoes suffering that is like death or equal to death.

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family does not receive [the teaching] with discernment, does not grasp its characteristics with discernment, does not recite it with discernment, and does not understand its meaning, yet instructs another, saying:
'O son of good family!'"

All Buddhas of the ten directions—past, future, and present—from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma—in the interval between these times, while practicing the *prajñā-pāramitā*, they cultivated all roots of goodness;
while practicing the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, and *dāna-pāramitā*, they cultivated all roots of goodness;

and while cultivating the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Buddha, and up to the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they cultivated all roots of goodness.
Purifying Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity by performing all roots of goodness;

as well as the various Buddhas’ assembly of precepts, assembly of concentration, assembly of wisdom, assembly of liberation, and assembly of the knowledge and vision of liberation; their omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), their unerring Dharma, and their constant practice of equanimity;

and the roots of goodness planted therein by the various disciples—along with the roots of goodness planted by the devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others who have been prophesied by the Buddhas to become pratyekabuddhas—I weigh, harmonize, and rejoice in all these merits, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This dedication, because it involves grasping at signs and attaining dharmas, is like food mixed with poison.
One who attains dharmas can never achieve true dedication. Why is this?
This is to obtain a dharma mixed with poison, characterized by signs, movement, and conceptual proliferation.
To dedicate [merit] in such a manner is to slander the Buddha; it does not follow the Buddha's teaching, nor does it accord with the Dharma discourse.

These sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way should train in this manner: regarding all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first aspiration until the exhaustion of the Dharma—as well as the roots of goodness created by their disciples when practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), as described above.
"What is the correct dedication of all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
A son or daughter of good family who seeks the Buddha-way and practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, not wishing to slander the Buddhas, should dedicate all merits in this way:
'Just as the unsurpassed wisdom known by the Buddhas perceives the characteristics and the nature of these roots of goodness, I likewise rejoice in them.'"
"Just as all Buddhas know, I likewise dedicate [these roots of goodness] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path should dedicate toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this manner.
If one dedicates in this manner, then one does not slander the Buddha; it is as the Buddha has taught and as the Buddha-dharma declares.
This dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is free from the poison of defilement.
[Treatise] Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the merit generated is detached from the five aggregates," previously only past matters were discussed; now, the merit of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) generated by oneself is being explained.

If one knows that within this merit there are no five aggregates, twelve bases, or eighteen elements, and while practicing the various dharmas such as the *prajñāpāramitā*, one also knows them to be empty and devoid of marks—such merit is called "right dedication."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva knows that within the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), the very nature of that merit of sympathetic joy is itself detached;

and if they know that the Buddhas, the roots of goodness, as well as all practices such as the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā*, are empty of intrinsic nature—this is called correct dedication.
"Rejoicing in merit" is a general description of the characteristics of all merit;
"the merit arising from rejoicing in roots of goodness" is a specific description.
When a bodhisattva, for their own sake, takes as their object the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* they seek, this is called the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the fruit of the merit of the bodhisattva’s mind of sympathetic joy; seeking only the unsurpassed path is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

Among the five aggregates, the practitioner is designated by a provisional name as a "bodhisattva," and the various dharmas such as the *prajñāpāramitā* are as explained according to the previous meaning.
Previously, it was explained that among meritorious virtues, one is detached from the five aggregates;
now, it is explained that meritorious virtue itself is empty of its own characteristics.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva contemplates the merit arising from the causes and conditions of past Buddhas, they should dedicate it in this manner:

"Just as the Buddhas of the past entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is signless, free from conceptual proliferation, and eternally quiescent by nature, so too are these merits and the mind of dedication."
Dedicating in this manner is called right dedication; it does not fall into perversion.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva takes signs and discriminates regarding the merits of all past Buddhas when dedicating, this is not called dedication.
Why is this? Having marks is one extreme; being markless is another extreme. To practice the Middle Way by departing from these two extremes is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all Buddhas.
Therefore it is said:
"The Buddhas of the past did not fall into the category of having marks, nor did they fall into the category of being markless.
If one grasps at the category of marks in this way, it is not called dedication; rather, one falls into perversion.
That which is contrary to the above constitutes not falling into perversion.
Because this matter is difficult, Maitreya asks again: namely, how can one not grasp at the marks of all phenomena and yet still be able to dedicate them?
Subhūti, finding no definitive answer to this matter, said to Maitreya:
"For this reason, a bodhisattva who studies the *prajñāpāramitā* seeks the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."
If this merit, being separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, cannot be dedicated, then among all dharmas, there is but one dharma that is real and non-deceptive, namely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is only by following this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practicing the non-deceptive path that it can be attained.
That which does not deceive the Path is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore it is said:
"Apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, this merit cannot be dedicated."
Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately empty and devoid of conceptual discrimination;
whether merit is separated from Prajñāpāramitā or not separated from Prajñāpāramitā, it cannot be dedicated.
A bodhisattva should form this thought:
"The bodies of all past Buddhas and their disciples, as well as all their roots of goodness and merit, have all ceased to exist.

For me now to grasp at signs and make distinctions—thinking 'these are the Buddhas,' 'these are the disciples,' 'these are the roots of goodness,' or 'this is the merit of sympathetic joy'—and then to dedicate [the merit] by grasping at such signs, would be improper for me!"
Why is this? Because it differs from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*);
having already received its retribution, it must eventually be exhausted after a long time.
One does not swiftly reach the Buddha-way because of having something to attain.
To engage in recollection, thought, and conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddhas of the past is a great loss!
That is to say: the Buddhas of the past are empty and non-existent, yet I engage in recollection, thought, and conceptual discrimination!
"Like food mixed with poison":
"food" refers to the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), while "poison" refers to the arising of various afflictions (*kleśa*) such as craving and views due to grasping at signs (*nimittagrāha*).
“Beautiful forms” refers to the causes and conditions of merit and virtue, by which one becomes a human king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), or a celestial king, attaining blessed happiness.
“Fine fragrances” refers to obtaining a good reputation, wealth and honor, and power.
Ordinary people who lack wisdom all greedily crave it.
"Foolish people" refers to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved [to attain enlightenment] and whose minds cling to signs.
"Rejoicing while eating" means that, due to the causes and conditions of wealth, pleasure, and merit, one experiences such wealth and pleasure among gods and humans.

"When the food is about to be digested, one undergoes suffering like death or equal to death" means that when this wealth and pleasure become impermanent, perish, or depart, one subsequently dies of grief, or else undergoes various afflictions following death.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "whether death or that which is equal to death": the loss of one's own life-force is called "death," while the loss of the objects to which one is attached is called "that which is equal to death."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "death or that which is like death": because of the abundance of suffering and affliction, the loss of the life-force of wisdom is called "death";
that which obstructs the practice of the path of goodness is called "that which is like death."
In this sutra, Subhūti himself says:
"These people of no wisdom do not receive [the teaching] with careful discernment; they do not grasp its meaning, but merely cling to the words."
"Grasping at signs without discernment" means not analyzing according to the Dharma.
"Reciting without discernment" means losing the phrasing and pauses, whether through one's own negligence or because the instruction received was incomplete.
"One who does not understand the meaning" is one who has not grasped the intent of the sutra.
Such a teacher of meager wisdom instructs his disciples:
"O son of good family!..."
To say that the Buddhas of the ten directions— past, future, and present— from their first aspiration until this dedication [are not as described],
is to slander the Buddhas, to fail to follow the Buddha’s teaching, and to fail to speak according to the Dharma.
That which is contrary to this is called "right dedication.
Furthermore, regarding right dedication, a bodhisattva should form this thought:
"Just as all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time know, I shall employ unsurpassed wisdom to understand the characteristics of all roots of goodness."
"Among all those who possess omniscience, the Buddha is the foremost and most excellent;
the roots of goodness known by the Buddha must be the true nature of reality.
Just as the Buddha knows them, I too shall dedicate these roots of goodness through their true nature."
For example, when shooting at the ground, there is no time when the arrow does not strike;
but when shooting at other objects, it may strike or it may not.
Just as the rejoicing (*anumodanā*) known by the Buddhas is like shooting at the ground—it never fails to strike; so too is this rejoicing.
If one employs other paths for sympathetic joy, it is like shooting at other objects; one may hit the mark or miss it.
To dedicate [merit] in such a manner is not to slander the Buddha.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, when sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they should dedicate their roots of goodness in this way:
Just as form is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
and that which is unbound is not called past, not called future, and not called present."
Just as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
so too, that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present.
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are also like this.
Just as the *prajñāpāramitā* is not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present.
The same applies to the dhyāna-pāramitā up to the dāna-pāramitā; the same applies to inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Just as the four foundations of mindfulness are not bound to the desire realm, not bound to the form realm, and not bound to the formless realm;
that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present.
It is the same for the eightfold noble path; it is the same for the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

It is the same for suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the characteristic of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*), the fixed position of phenomena (*dharma-vyavasthāna*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature (*acintya-dharmatā*); as well as for the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); the non-erroneous dharma; and the constant practice of equanimity.
That which is unconditioned by the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—that which is unconditioned—is not designated as past, future, or present.
This dedication, the object to which it is dedicated, and the practitioner who performs it are all likewise unattached.
In this way, the Buddhas are unattached, the roots of goodness are unattached, and the roots of goodness of these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also unattached.
That which is an unattached dharma is not designated as past, future, or present.
"If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know in this way that form is not bound to the three realms;
and that which is unbound is not designated as past, future, or present."
If a dharma is neither past, future, nor present, one cannot take it as a sign or apprehend it as a substantial dharma to dedicate toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because this form is unarisen.
If a dharma is unarisen, it is a non-dharma; and within a non-dharma, one cannot perform dedication.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

"The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the dharma of non-erroneousness, and the practice of constant equanimity are not bound to the three realms."
Unconditioned dharmas are neither past, future, nor present.
If they are not past, future, or present dharmas, one cannot take their marks as objects of attainment and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are unarisen.
If a dharma is unarisen, it is no dharma; and within that which is no dharma, there can be no dedication.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dedicate in this manner, there is no admixture of poison.

If sons or daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way take hold of signs and grasp at dharmas, dedicating their various roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this is called a perverted dedication.
If one performs wrong dedication, it is not praised by the Buddhas. By means of this wrong dedication, one cannot fulfill the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*;

one cannot fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; the ten powers of a Buddha up to the quality of being free from error and the constant practice of relinquishment;

nor can one fulfill the purification of the Buddha-field and the maturation of sentient beings. If one cannot purify the Buddha-field and mature sentient beings, then one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because this dedication is mixed with poison.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:
"As the Buddhas know how to dedicate all roots of goodness, that is true dedication;
I, too, should dedicate by means of this same characteristic of phenomena.
This is called right dedication.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
What you have done is to perform the work of a Buddha.

You have taught the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the dharma that should be dedicated, by way of signlessness, non-attainment, non-emergence, neither defilement nor purity, the nature of dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of permanence, the dharma-nature, suchness, and the limit of reality.

Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to attain the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Would those beings acquire much merit? "Very much, [World-Honored One]!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as good as when these sons and daughters of good family do not become attached in their minds to any roots of goodness, but dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to become stream-enterers, up to arhats and pratyekabuddhas; and suppose some son or daughter of good family were to provide them with offerings, honor, respect, and praise throughout their entire lives, supplying them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—whatever they required."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
By reason of this, would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
"Very much, [World-Honored One]!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not equal to when a son or daughter of good family, with a mind that does not cling to any roots of goodness, dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. And suppose that every single sentient being in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions were, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, to honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to these bodhisattvas—providing them with clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, supplying whatever they required."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
By reason of this, would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
World-Honored One!
They are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), and cannot be compared by means of analogy.
World-Honored One!
“If this merit were to have a physical form, the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, would not be able to contain it!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Excellent!”
Excellent!
It is as you have said.

Nevertheless, it is not equal to when a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a mind free from attachment toward all roots of goodness, dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is most supreme, foremost, most wondrous, unsurpassed, and peerless.

This merit of dedication free from attachment, compared to the previous merit, exceeds it a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-fold, and even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy!

Why is this? It is because these sons and daughters of good family grasp at signs and acquire dharmas; they practice the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers, all while grasping at signs and acquiring dharmas. They make offerings to stream-enterers—honoring, respecting, praising them, and providing them with their necessities such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—and even go so far as to make offerings to bodhisattvas by grasping at signs.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, together with twenty thousand devaputras, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!

The supreme dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is performed by means of the power of skillful means, by means of non-apprehension, by means of the dharma of signlessness, and by means of the dharma of non-awakening, dedicating all roots of goodness toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"By dedicating in this manner, one does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, together with countless gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and other sons of gods, brought celestial flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, celestial robes, banners, canopies, and drums, and performed divine music as offerings to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supreme dedication of merit is performed by means of skillful power, by way of non-apprehension, by way of signless dharmas, and by way of dharmas beyond conceptualization, dedicating all roots of goodness toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"By dedicating in this way, one does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

Then the Heavenly King Suyāma, together with a thousand devaputras, and the various heavenly kings of Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, each accompanied by a thousand devaputras, having made offerings to the Buddha, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s supreme dedication of merit is performed through the power of skillful means, by way of non-apprehension, by way of signless dharmas, and by way of dharmas beyond conceptualization, dedicating all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"By dedicating in this manner, one does not fall into dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Brahma Kings, together with countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of devas, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and raised their voices in a great sound, saying:
"It is unprecedented!
World-Honored One!

Because they are protected by the *prajñāpāramitā* and by the power of skillful means, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas surpass those sons and daughters of good family who previously grasped at signs and apprehended things as real.

The Ābhāsvara devas, up to and including the Akaniṣṭha devas, together with countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and with a great voice spoke these words:
“It is unprecedented!
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, being protected by the perfection of wisdom and through the power of skillful means, surpasses those aforementioned sons and daughters of good family who grasp at signs and perceive things as attainable.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras from the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha heaven:

"If all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and if all these bodhisattvas were to recollect the roots of goodness of all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present—from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the endurance of the Dharma—including all the roots of goodness therein; [if they were to recollect them all...]"

Furthermore, they rejoice in all the roots of goodness possessed by all other sentient beings—namely, giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); and the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. They rejoice in all such other immeasurable qualities of the Buddha.
Having rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet because they do so by grasping at signs and apprehending something to be attained.

Furthermore, there may be sons or daughters of good family who resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and recollect all the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as all the roots of goodness they cultivated during the interval from their first aspiration until the endurance of the Dharma;

Together with all other roots of goodness possessed by all sentient beings—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom; from the *dānapāramitā* up to the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha—all these are combined and weighed. Because they are ungraspable, because they are non-dual, because they are signless, because they are non-attached, and because they are non-conceptual, this is the supreme sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*)—the foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless sympathetic joy.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates [this merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The merit of these sons and daughters of good family surpasses that of the former sons and daughters of good family by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-millionfold, and even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy!
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One has declared that when good sons and good daughters gather all roots of goodness, weigh them, rejoice in them, and dedicate them, this is the most supreme, the foremost, the most wondrous, the unsurpassed, and the peerless.”
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘rejoicing that is supreme, even unto being without equal’?
The Buddha said:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family contemplates all dharmas of the past, future, and present—neither grasping nor rejecting them, neither thinking of them nor not thinking of them, neither attaining them nor not attaining them—and within these dharmas, there is no dharma that arises or ceases, whether defiled or pure; that all dharmas neither increase nor decrease, neither come nor go, neither unite nor disperse, neither enter nor exit;
and that the marks of the dharmas of the past, future, and present, as well as their suchness, dharma-nature, dharma-abiding, and dharma-position, are likewise so—I too rejoice in this.
Having rejoiced, I dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such dedication is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless!”

Subhūti! This dharma of sympathetic joy, compared to other forms of sympathetic joy, exceeds them a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-millionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way wish to rejoice in all the roots of goodness—from the initial generation of the mind until the Dharma remains—belonging to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as their śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and in all the roots of goodness therein, whether they be acts of giving up to wisdom, from the dānapāramitā up to the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, as well as all the roots of goodness belonging to all other sentient beings—they should rejoice in this manner!"
He forms this thought:
"Generosity is equal to liberation; morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom are equal to liberation;
form is equal to liberation, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also equal to liberation."
Inner emptiness is equal to liberation, and so on up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is also equal to liberation;
the four foundations of mindfulness are equal to liberation, and so on up to the eightfold noble path, which is also equal to liberation;
the ten powers of a Buddha are equal to liberation, and so on up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is also equal to liberation.
The aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation are equal to liberation;
sympathetic joy is equal to liberation;
and all phenomena of the past, future, and present are equal to liberation.
The Buddhas of the ten directions are equal to liberation;
the dedications of the Buddhas are equal to liberation;
the Buddhas are equal to liberation, and the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas is equal to liberation.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who are disciples of the Buddhas are equal to liberation; the parinirvāṇa of the disciples of the Buddhas is equal to liberation.

The dharmic characteristics of the Buddhas are equal to liberation; the dharmic characteristics of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are equal to liberation; and the dharmic characteristics of all phenomena are likewise equal to liberation.
I dedicate these roots of goodness, which consist of rejoicing in merit, toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for they are equal to liberation, being neither born nor extinguished.
"Subhūti! This is called the merit of the rejoicing of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless."
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva accomplishes this merit of sympathetic joy, they shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

Suppose there are good sons and good daughters seeking the Buddha-way who, throughout their entire lives, provide all that is required for the Buddhas and their disciples currently residing in the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—including offerings, respect, reverence, and praise, such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine;

and furthermore, after those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, they diligently practice day and night, offering flowers, incense, and even banners, canopies, and musical performances, yet do so because they grasp at signs and hold to the notion of attainment.
They maintain ethical discipline, practice patience, exert diligence, cultivate meditative concentration, and develop wisdom, all because they grasp at signs and seek something to be attained.

Furthermore, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who resolve to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and while practicing the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā*, they dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the skillful means of non-apprehension and the dharma of non-attainment—this merit is supreme, foremost, most wonderful, unsurpassed, and peerless; it surpasses the previous merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-billionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy!

In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, and when practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of skillful means, through the non-apprehension of signs and the dharma of non-attainment.
[Treatise] Commentary:
The Bodhisattva should reflect as follows:
"From form (*rūpa*) up to the practice of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), all these phenomena are not bound to the three realms; therefore, they are not subsumed within the three periods of time."

The Buddhas and their disciples, along with all their merits; the mind of sympathetic joy; the object of dedication; the method of dedication employed; and the one who dedicates—these are likewise [to be understood]. This is called right dedication.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If form transcends the three realms and is not subsumed within the three periods of time, it cannot be used as an object of grasped characteristics for the sake of dedication."

Why is this? This form that transcends the three realms is precisely the true mark of form; the marks of initial and subsequent arising cannot be apprehended, as explained in the "Refutation of Arising" chapter.
If dharmas are unarisen, they are non-existent; how can a mind of dedication that is non-existent dedicate itself to a bodhicitta that is non-existent?
It is the same for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the practice of constant relinquishment.
This is called the "unadulterated dedication," which is to say, the "dedication that is signless and non-attaining.

As for "adulterated with poison," this refers to that which is not praised by the Buddhas, which cannot fulfill the six *pāramitās*, and so forth, up to the point where one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Just as all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time know, so should one generate the mind, so should one reflect, so should one contemplate, and so should one dedicate; may these merits lead directly to the unsurpassed path, and I likewise rejoice in and dedicate them accordingly."
"This bodhisattva will certainly attain genuine sympathetic joy (anumodanā), and their dedication (pariṇāmanā) will not be in vain, according to the causal conditions previously explained.
This is a brief exposition of the various chapters on dedication.
There are three categories of a bodhisattva’s prostration to the Buddha:"
First is the Chapter on Repenting of Transgressions; second, the Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication; third, the Chapter on Exhorting and Entreaty to the Buddhas.
Were they explained in detail, they would be immeasurable and boundless.
"Excellent! Excellent!
You perform the work of a Buddha" means that when the Buddha first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he vowed to deliver all sentient beings.
Although Subhūti is an arhat, he is able to assist the Buddha in preaching the Dharma and elucidating the path of the bodhisattvas; therefore, it is praised, saying:
"Excellent!"
“Excellent!
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explained the causal conditions:

“To preach for the sake of all bodhisattvas the dharma that should be dedicated, by means of the signless” means that when one employs the wisdom of signlessness to harmonize and dedicate the characteristics of merit, this is called “signless,” as it is contrary to the aforementioned [characteristics].
There are three kinds of signlessness (*animitta*):
the sign of conventional designation (*prajñapti-nimitta*), the sign of dharmas (*dharma-nimitta*), and the sign of signlessness (*animitta-nimitta*).

Regarding the "sign of conventional designation": it refers to such things as a chariot, a house, a forest, an army, or a sentient being—names that further exist within the combination of various dharmas.
By the power of ignorance, one grasps at these conventional designations and characteristics, giving rise to various afflictions and karmas.
"Dharmic characteristics" refers to all phenomena such as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
Because it exists when viewed with the fleshly eye, but does not exist when viewed with the wisdom-eye, dharmas are likewise deceptive and false;
one should abandon the marks of dharmas. Having abandoned these two marks, there remains only the "mark of marklessness."

If someone grasps this mark of signlessness and pursues that grasping of marks, they will again give rise to fetters and afflictions; therefore, one should likewise not grasp the "mark of signlessness."
Because it is free from these three characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
If there are no signs, therein is "non-apprehension";
because there is no apprehension, there is "no emergence."
If a dharma is neither attained nor emerged from, it is "stainless and non-pure";
if a dharma is neither stainless nor pure, it is "the absence of dharmic nature";
if a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it is "emptiness of self-characteristic."
If a phenomenon is empty of its own-characteristic, that is the "eternal emptiness of intrinsic nature" of that phenomenon;
if a phenomenon is eternally empty of intrinsic nature, it is identical to "dharma-nature, suchness, and the limit of reality."
By means of such a harmonious union, one rejoices in the merit and dedicates it; therefore, one praises, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Furthermore, there is the causal condition for saying "Excellent," namely, the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), which brings great benefit to sentient beings and yields great fruit and retribution.
What constitutes this great benefit?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to practice the ten wholesome paths of action up to the five supernormal powers.
[Subhūti] asked:
Question: Why do the two classes of gods within the desire realm and Brahmādeva reside together with many other deities, whereas the remaining four heavens have few?
Answer: These two classes of gods rely upon the earth and are close to the Buddha; therefore, they are numerous.
Furthermore, the five desires are not equal to those of the heavens above.

When the Buddha was born, when he practiced austerities, when he subdued Māra, when he attained the Way, and when he turned the wheel of the Dharma, the gods constantly came to make offerings to him; for this reason, they are numerous.
As for the gods of the other four abodes, their palaces are situated in the void and do not belong to the earth;
because their attachment to the exquisite five desires is profound, they are unable to come in great numbers.

Furthermore, although the gods of Tuṣita Heaven possess sharp faculties and delight in the Dharma, they do not come because there is always a Bodhisattva in the stage of "next-to-be-Buddha" (kṣetra-pariśodhana) preaching the Dharma in their heaven.
Although the Brahmā heavens are distant, because they are free from desire, their longing for the Dharma is profound; and since the Buddha is the King of Dharma, many from those realms come to him.
Furthermore, the Brahmā King is the lord of the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and invited the Buddha to first turn the wheel of Dharma; therefore, he should have come accompanied by a great multitude.
All other devas of the realm of form are also designated as Brahmās.
Question: Previously, you explained right dedication through various causes and conditions, stating that right dedication is the most supreme.
Why do you ask again now? Answer:
This has been explained extensively in various places above; now it shall be explained briefly.

That is to say, one knows with certainty all phenomena of the three times and ten directions through the mind, yet within these phenomena there is neither that which arises nor that which ceases. All phenomena are unattainable and inconceivable;
because they are neither attainable nor inconceivable, one neither grasps nor abandons them, thereby entering into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
They form this thought:
"Just as the true reality of all phenomena is, so too do I dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy; I do not discriminate among phenomena, nor do I destroy the nature of phenomena."
This is called the supreme dedication.
Why? Because its karmic fruit is eternally inexhaustible.
Question:
The various dharmas such as the six pāramitās each have their own characteristics, whether they be material (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) or immaterial (arūpa-lakṣaṇa) and so forth;
furthermore, there are two kinds of liberation:
Regarding conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation, how are they both equal to liberation?
The answer is:
I have already explained this previously:
Ordinary people, because they perceive with the physical eye and the six consciousnesses through inversion, see difference;
if one uses the wisdom-eye, one perceives that all dharmas are empty and false, and that only nirvana is real.
This is conditioned liberation; because it belongs to the unconditioned and conforms to the unconditioned, it is called "liberation.

One who has attained the Path as it truly is is called a "person of the Path" (mārgajina); now, those who have not yet attained the Path are also called "persons of the Path" because their robes and their conduct conform to those who have attained the Path.

Just as in *nirvāṇa* without remainder—neither arising nor ceasing, neither entering nor exiting, neither defiled nor pure, neither existent nor non-existent, neither permanent nor impermanent—it is the mark of eternal quiescence; where the observation of mind and consciousness ceases, the path of language is cut off, and there are such marks as being neither dharma nor non-dharma, because it functions through the mark of non-existence;
so too does the wisdom-eye observe all dharmas as having this same mark. This is called "the six pāramitās and so forth being equal to liberation."
Therefore, it is said within the Buddha-dharma:
"Liberation is precious; supreme wisdom values liberation.
Within this, the Buddha makes a further distinction, saying:
"If a person practices the six *pāramitās* for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, accumulating various roots of goodness by means of a dharma that involves apprehension;
and another person, by means of the dharma of non-apprehension, simply rejoices with their mind and contemplates the merits of others, dedicating them toward the unsurpassed path—
this former person does not equal even one hundred-thousand-millionth part of the latter."
Why is this? Former merit was limited; present merit is immeasurable.
Former merit was exhaustible; present merit is inexhaustible.
Former merit was mixed with poison; present merit is free from poison.
Former merit followed along with birth and death; present merit follows toward Nirvana.
Former merit was uncertain, sometimes resulting in Buddhahood and sometimes in regression; present merit is certain to reach its goal, and one will surely and swiftly become a Buddha.
There are such distinctions as these.
Therefore, there are four kinds of persons:

those who are ordinary worldlings seeking worldly happiness; those who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas seeking the happiness of nirvāṇa; and those who are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seeking the happiness of a Buddha.
One should thus rejoice and generate merit, dedicating it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as explained in this chapter.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 61.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the "Chapter on Illumination," Scroll 40, Scroll 62.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 40: Illumination. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is this the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
The Buddha said:
“This is the perfection of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom can illuminate all dharmas because it is ultimately pure.”
"Bhagavān, one should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Bhagavān!"
“O Bhagavān, the Prajñāpāramitā does not cling to the triple world. O Bhagavān,
the Prajñāpāramitā dispels all darkness, because it eliminates all afflictions and all views.”
"Bhagavān!
The perfection of wisdom is the most supreme among all factors conducive to enlightenment.
Bhagavān!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is peaceful and secure, for it can sever all fears, terrors, and afflictions.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can bestow illumination, for it is adorned with the five eyes.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can guide sentient beings who have fallen onto wrong paths, because it is free from the two extremes.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), because it severs all afflictions along with their residual impressions (vāsanā).
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for she is able to give birth to all Buddha-dharmas.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished, because its own-characteristic is empty.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is far removed from birth and death, because it is neither permanent nor subject to extinction.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā acts as a protector for those who have no protector, because it bestows all precious treasures.
“World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is endowed with power, for nothing can destroy it.
World-Honored One!”
The Prajñāpāramitā is able to turn the wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects, because all dharmas neither turn nor return.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is able to reveal the nature of all dharmas, because of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
“World-Honored One!
How should one make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
