First, it was previously stated that "those within the two evil realms undergo suffering for a long time";
now it is further stated that "their bodies are exceedingly hideous. Some people might not believe this, and those who do not believe shall consequently endure intense suffering for a long duration.
Second, if one believes the Buddha’s words, one will experience great anxiety and fear; because of this anxiety and fear, the bodily winds are stirred up, causing one to vomit warm blood and die.
Regarding the phrase "if one dies or the like," even if one does not die, the body will remain perpetually withered and parched.
"If they do not believe, they will suffer heavy retribution in future lives; therefore, the Buddha does not speak of it.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
"Although for these two reasons you do not speak of it now, I pray that out of compassion for the people of future generations, you will speak of it."
The Buddha said:
"If there are persons with roots of goodness, a pure nature, and merit, they are sufficient as a basis for reliance.
A "pure nature" (śukla-dharmatā) is the opposite of a "dark nature" (kṛṣṇa-dharmatā).
Regarding reliance: having heard that one undergoes such suffering, one dares not commit [the offense] again.
If one does not believe, then even if it is said that the body is vast, one will still not believe;
if one does believe, then hearing that the suffering undergone above is long-lasting is sufficient for belief.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Sixty-Two.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of Chapter Forty-One:
The Remainder of "Faith and Slander," Scroll Sixty-Three.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If good sons or good daughters should properly restrain their physical, verbal, and mental actions, they will not undergo such sufferings—such as not seeing the Buddha, not hearing the Dharma, or not associating with the Sangha; or being born in a world where no Buddha dwells; or being born among humans in a family of poverty; or having people who do not trust or accept their words.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it because of the accumulation of verbal karma that there is such a grave offense of destroying the Dharma?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is because of the accumulation of verbal karma that there is this grave offense of destroying the Dharma, Subhūti."
These foolish people, having gone forth from home and received the precepts within the Buddha-dharma, will destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, disparaging it and refusing to accept it. Subhūti!
If one destroys the *prajñāpāramitā* or slanders the *prajñāpāramitā*, one thereby destroys the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the ten directions;

because omniscience is destroyed, the Jewel of the Buddha is destroyed; because the Jewel of the Buddha is destroyed, the Jewel of the Dharma is destroyed; because the Jewel of the Dharma is destroyed, the Jewel of the Saṃgha is destroyed;
and because the Three Jewels are destroyed, right view in the world is destroyed.
Because one destroys the right view of the world, one thereby destroys the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the dharma of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
because one destroys the dharma of all-knowledge, one incurs immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sins;
having incurred immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sins, one then undergoes immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable sorrow and suffering.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how many causes and conditions are there for these deluded people to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are four causes and conditions by which such foolish people revile and destroy this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
What are the four?
“Because these deluded persons are incited by Māra, they wish to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; this is called the first causal condition.”

This deluded person does not believe in the profound Dharma; lacking faith and understanding, their mind fails to attain purity. Due to this second cause and condition, this deluded person seeks to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

This foolish person associates with evil friends, his mind sinks into indolence, and he is firmly attached to the five aggregates of clinging; for this third cause and condition, this foolish person wishes to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

This foolish person frequently practices anger, exalts themselves, and disparages others; due to this fourth cause and condition, this foolish person wishes to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Subhūti! For these four reasons, these foolish people wish to revile and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
[Treatise] Question:
Question: Since verbal karma is the destruction of the Dharma, why is it said that one "restrains the actions of body, speech, and mind"? Answer:
Mental karma is the root of verbal karma; if one wishes to restrain verbal karma, one must first restrain mental karma.
Because mental action subsumes them, bodily and vocal actions are also wholesome;
because bodily and vocal actions are wholesome, mental action is also wholesome.
Regarding this, Subhūti himself explains the causal conditions:
"Do not undergo these various sufferings—such as not seeing the Buddha and so forth.
Since worldly people regard physical actions (*kāyakarman*) as weighty and verbal actions (*vākkarman*) as light, Subhūti asks:
"Is it solely through verbal action that one incurs such retribution?"
The Buddha affirmed his meaning and said:

"This foolish person has no urgent business of his own, nor does he have anyone for whom he acts, nor does he gain anything; yet, solely because of his tongue, he commits such a sin—this is truly great madness!"

This madman will, in a future age, leave the household life within my Dharma—those who leave the household life consist of the five groups, while those who receive the precepts consist of the seven groups.
These śrāvakas will become attached to the śrāvaka-dharma; after five hundred years have passed since the Buddha-dharma appeared, they will each separately divide into five schools.

From that time forward, because they sought the definitive characteristics of all phenomena, they clung to their own views; they did not understand that the Buddha taught the Dharma for the sake of liberation. Because they were stubbornly attached to words and language, when they heard it said that all phenomena are ultimately empty through the Prajñāpāramitā, it was as if their hearts had been wounded by a blade.
They all said:
"The definitive Dharma—how can you now say it does not exist?

Because they conceived notions of attainment and attachment regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is characterized by neither attainment nor attachment, they disparaged and subverted it, claiming it was not the Buddha's teaching.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Buddha taught what constitutes the path and what does not;
yet now, within this Prajñāpāramitā, both the path and the non-path are entirely of one single mark, namely, the markless (*animitta*).
Therefore, having first given rise to doubt, he subsequently fixes his mind upon the dharma of emptiness and gives birth to wrong views;
because these wrong views gain strength, he destroys the Prajñāpāramitā everywhere within the great assembly;
and because he destroys the Prajñāpāramitā, he thereby destroys all the merits of the Buddhas—the omniscience and so forth—of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Because one destroys the merit of the Buddha, one thereby destroys the Three Jewels;
because the Three Jewels are destroyed, one destroys the causes and conditions for worldly happiness, namely, worldly right view.

If one destroys worldly right view, one then destroys the causes and conditions for supramundane happiness—the supramundane right view, which consists of the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This Dharma is called the cause and condition for immeasurable and boundless merit; by destroying this Dharma, one incurs immeasurable and boundless offenses;
and because of incurring immeasurable and boundless offenses, one undergoes immeasurable and boundless sorrow, grief, and affliction.
Question:
Since the causes and conditions for the destruction of dharmas—namely, attachment to dharmas and so forth—have already been explained, why does Subhūti ask again? Answer:
What was previously discussed in the treatises is now discussed in this sutra;
what was not explained exhaustively before is now explained fully and extensively.
These are the so-called four causes and conditions:
Such a person is instigated by Māra;
whether it be Māra himself or a person acting on Māra’s behalf who enters their mind, they manipulate their body and speech, causing them to destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For example, Ānanda, when the Buddha asked three times, "Is Jambudvīpa pleasant? Is its long life also pleasant?
Māra entered his body, and thus he did not answer the Buddha on all three occasions.
Even Ānanda, having attained the first stage of the Path, was still harassed by Māra; how much more so for ordinary people!
Furthermore, there are four kinds of Māras:
the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of death, and the Māra of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

Among the four māras, because of the predominance of the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the māra of the son of a sovereign deity (*devaputramāra*), they cause one to lack faith in the *prajñā*;
due to their own attachment to dharmas, their hatred and envy of the dharmas of others, and their deluded perversion, they are able to destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Some say: the first causal condition is the demon of afflictions (kleśamāra);
the last, the fourth, is the demon of the sovereign son of heaven (devaputramāra).
Because these two types are instigated by Māra, they are called "those instigated by Māra.

Due to their stubborn attachment to false views, their craving for their own doctrines, and the dullness of their faculty of wisdom, they do not understand the Buddha’s intention; because they neither believe nor accept the profound *prajñā*, they are destroyed.
There are those with sharp faculties who are capable of faith; though Māra does not come to them, they nevertheless destroy the Prajñāpāramitā because they follow the instructions of evil teachers.
There are others who, although associated with evil associates, have thin fetters and thus exert themselves with diligence, enabling them to believe in the Prajñāpāramitā.

Therefore, these two factors combine as one: they associate with evil friends and are deeply attached to the five aggregates; their fetters and afflictions are thick, and they give rise to a mind of indolence. For these reasons, they do not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā.
Throughout successive lifetimes, this person has accumulated much anger until it became their very nature—this mark of anger is the mark of lack of faith.
This person is stubborn and arrogant, and they look down upon those who preach the Dharma, saying:
"Even I, with such wisdom and virtue, cannot understand this; how could you, who are so foolish and lowly, possibly know it!"
Because of this abundance of anger and arrogance, they destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*.
[Sūtra] Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”

"This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to believe and difficult to understand for those who do not apply diligent effort, who have planted unwholesome roots, and who possess the characteristics of evil associates.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"So it is, Subhūti!

This profound Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to believe and difficult to understand for those who do not apply diligent effort, who have planted roots of unwholesomeness, and who have obtained the company of evil friends."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is this Prajñāpāramitā so profound, so difficult to believe, and so difficult to understand?”
“Subhūti! Form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The dānapāramitā is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
The perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
The perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
The perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
The perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the dhyāna-pāramitā.
The prajñā-pāramitā is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of non-existence is the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, inner emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? The nature of non-existence is internal emptiness.
This extends up to the emptiness of non-entities and entities, which is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the emptiness of both non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.
The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the four foundations of mindfulness.
This extends even to omniscience and the knowledge of all modes, which are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Subhūti,
the nature of non-existence is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).
The original limit of form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the original limit is non-existent; that is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are neither bound nor liberated at their original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). Why is this?
Because the non-existent nature of the original limit is all-knowledge.
Subhūti! The future limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The nature of the non-existence of the posterior limit is form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge, are neither bound nor liberated at their posterior limit. Why is this?
The non-existence of the future limit is the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti,
present form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence in the present is form (*rūpa*).

Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) in the present, are neither bound nor liberated.
"Why is this? Because the non-existence of the present is omniscience.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is truly difficult to believe and difficult to understand for those who do not exert diligent effort, have not planted roots of goodness, have associated with evil friends, are indolent, lack progress, are prone to forgetfulness, and lack skillful wisdom.”
"So it is! So it is, Subhūti!"

This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to believe in and difficult to understand for those who do not exert diligent effort, have not planted roots of goodness, associate with evil friends, are under the influence of Māra, are indolent, lack progress, are prone to forgetfulness, and lack skillful wisdom.
Why is this? Because when form is pure, its fruit is also pure;
when feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, their fruits are also pure.
"Up to and including the pure fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is also pure.
Furthermore, Subhūti, because form (*rūpa*) is pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure; because the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure, form is pure."

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure; because the perfection of wisdom is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure.
The purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is itself the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the purity of the perfection of wisdom is itself the purity of all-knowledge.
The purity of form (*rūpa*) and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, without distinction, uninterrupted, and indestructible;
even so, the purity of all-knowledge and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, without distinction, uninterrupted, and indestructible.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because non-duality is pure, form is pure; because non-duality is pure, even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure. Why is this?
This is the purity of non-duality; from the purity of form up to the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is no duality and no distinction.

Because of the purity of the self (*ātman*) and the purity of sentient beings (*sattva*) up to the purity of the knower and the seer, there is the purity of form, the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the purity of all-knowledge.
Because form is pure up to and including the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the self, sentient beings, up to and including the knower and the viewer, are pure. Why is this?

Because the self, sentient beings, up to and including the knower and the viewer, and form, up to and including all-knowledge, are non-dual and undifferentiated, without interruption and without destruction.
[Treatise] Commentary:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because this Prajñāpāramitā is so profound, it is difficult to believe in due to indolence, following evil associates, and planting roots of unwholesomeness."
That which is the opposite of the above is called "faith in the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha affirmed his words.
Subhūti asked further:
“How is it that this Prajñāpāramitā is so profound as to be difficult to believe?
The Buddha replied:
“Form and all other dharmas are neither bound nor liberated.”
"The three poisons are bondage; the three gates of liberation are release.

These three poisons and all other afflictions are deceptive and unreal, arising from the causes and conditions of combination; because they lack intrinsic nature, there is no bondage, and because there is no bondage, there is no release.
Because these three poisons are destroyed, the three gates of liberation are also empty."
Furthermore, grasping at signs, attachment to phenomena, and all inverted afflictions and the like constitute bondage.
If these binding phenomena truly and definitively possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they could not be liberated;
if they truly and definitively existed, who could destroy them?
If one were to destroy them, one would immediately fall into the view of annihilationism.
Furthermore, since the various afflictions such as grasping at signs and inverted views are empty, false, and unreal, there is likewise nothing to be severed.
Moreover, all mental states and their concomitants—consisting of recollection, conceptualization, and the grasping of signs—are all bound within their respective objects.
If one enters into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one knows that they are all false and deceptive, as stated in the preceding chapter:
"The characteristic of the purity of mind is precisely the absence of the characteristic of mind."
Because this bondage is empty, liberation is also empty.
For various reasons such as these, dharmas such as form are neither bound nor liberated.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:

"Because all phenomena such as form are conditioned and produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and because they lack a fixed nature, it is said that 'the nature of non-existence is the nature of all phenomena such as form.'"
Furthermore, dharmas such as form are neither bound nor liberated within the three periods of time, as explained in the "Refutation of the Three Periods of Time.
At that time, Subhūti understood that the Prajñāpāramitā is neither profound nor not profound.
As it is said in a later chapter:
"If one thinks that the Prajñāpāramitā is profound, then one is far removed from the Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is because evil persons find the profound *prajñāpāramitā* difficult to understand, not because it is so for good persons.
Evil persons are those who do not correspond with *prajñā*, and who do not apply themselves with single-minded diligence and vigor.
They have not planted the roots of goodness for the understanding of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
they follow evil teachers who destroy the *prajñā*;
and being indolent, they are attached to worldly pleasures and do not aspire to the supramundane.
If such a person possesses diligence, it is too slight to mention;
because their mind is distracted by various afflictions, they are prone to forgetfulness.

Since they have not broken through the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, have not eliminated arrogance, and are mired in false views and frivolous discourse, they seek the true characteristic of all dharmas yet do not know how to discern the beautiful and the ugly among the characteristics of those dharmas—this is called a lack of skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
Because they possess such evil dharmas as these, this person finds it difficult to understand the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha affirmed his meaning, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"So it is! [The interlocutor] asked:
"In what Subhūti has said, there is no mention of the deeds of Māra; why then does the Buddha’s teaching add to the deeds of Māra?"
Answer: Subhūti spoke directly of the non-completion of internal and external causes and conditions; the Buddha now speaks of them in their full completion, and therefore says:
"This person is one who is instigated by Māra."
The Buddha, wishing further to explain the profound and difficult-to-understand characteristics, addressed Subhūti:
"Because all dharmas such as form are pure, their fruit is also pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are the fruit of all dharmas such as form.
Why is this? By contemplating that all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are impure, impermanent, and so forth, one attains the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The remaining applications of mindfulness are as explained above.
Among these, the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is untainted; it is pure because it severs afflictions and leads to nirvana.
Because the fruit is seen to be pure, one knows that the cause is also pure.
Question:

Previously it was stated that "by contemplating form as impure, impermanent, and so forth, one attains the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Why, then, do you say that "because the fruit is pure, one knows that the cause is also pure"?
Answer: The contemplation of impurity is the initial gateway; it is not a true contemplation, and therefore it does not enter among the sixteen noble practices.
Within these sixteen practices, one contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, but one does not contemplate impurity.
Because one gives rise to lust by purifying what is inverted, and because one speaks of "impurity" by destroying that which is perceived as pure, this is not the reality.
Therefore, impurity does not enter the sixteen noble practices; it is merely a contemplation for attaining understanding.
Within this Prajñā, one does not contemplate permanence, nor does one contemplate impermanence; one does not contemplate purity, nor does one contemplate impurity, and so forth.

The cessation of all such contemplations—permanence and impermanence, purity and impurity, emptiness and reality—and the cessation of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is the true mark of form (rūpa).
Because the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form is pure, its fruit is also pure.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions herein:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is like space; it is ultimately pure and unstained—this is the *prajñāpāramitā*."

By contemplating the true mark of all dharmas, such as form, as neither arising nor ceasing, and by practicing the six pāramitās and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, one may thus attain the prajñāpāramitā.
This Prajñāpāramitā has three kinds of causes and conditions:
right contemplation, right practice, and right cultivation.
Therefore it is said:
“Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form and all other phenomena are pure;
because form and all other phenomena are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure. Why is this so?
Phenomena such as form and the Prajñāpāramitā are, within the true mark (lakṣaṇa), neither two nor distinct;
because they are not different, not separate, not apart, and not scattered, they are neither severed nor destroyed.

Furthermore, according to my teaching, even if one searches throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, [the self] cannot be found; within the five aggregates, there exists only a provisional designation.
It is the same for sentient beings, up to and including the knower and the seer.
As I am—empty, non-existent, and pure—so too are all phenomena.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because desire is pure, form is pure, and so on up to the purity of all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because the purity of desire, the purity of form, and so on up to the purity of all-knowledge are non-dual and not distinct.
Because hatred and delusion are pure, form is pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because the purity of hatred and delusion and the purity of form, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge, are non-dual and not distinct.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because ignorance is pure, volitional formations are pure;
because volitional formations are pure, consciousness is pure; because consciousness is pure, name-and-form is pure;
because name-and-form is pure, the six sense bases are pure; because the six sense bases are pure, contact is pure; because contact is pure..."

Feeling is purified; because feeling is purified, craving is purified; because craving is purified, grasping is purified; because grasping is purified, becoming is purified; because becoming is purified, birth is purified;
because birth is purified, old age and death are purified; because old age and death are purified, the perfection of wisdom is purified;
because the perfection of wisdom is purified, even up to the perfection of generosity is purified.
Because the perfection of giving is pure, internal emptiness is pure; because internal emptiness is pure, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence is pure;
because the emptiness of non-existence and existence is pure, the four foundations of mindfulness are pure;
because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, up to all-knowledge is pure; and because all-knowledge is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure.

Why is this? Because the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the purity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are non-dual and undifferentiated, without interruption and without destruction.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure; and so on, up to: because the perfection of wisdom is pure, all-knowledge is pure.
This purity of the perfection of wisdom and this purity of all-knowledge are non-dual and not distinct.

Subhūti! Because the dhyānapāramitā is pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge; because the vīryapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, śīlapāramitā, and dānapāramitā are pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge.
Because internal emptiness is pure, up to and including all-knowledge is pure; because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, up to and including all-knowledge is pure.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because all-knowledge is pure, even up to the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
In this manner, each [point] is as previously explained.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because the conditioned is pure, the unconditioned is pure.
Why is this? Because the purity of the conditioned and the purity of the unconditioned are non-dual and undifferentiated, being neither severed nor destroyed.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the past is pure, the future and present are pure; because the future is pure, the past and present are pure; because the present is pure, the past and future are pure."
Why is this? Because present purity, past purity, and future purity are non-dual and undifferentiated, being neither severed nor destroyed.
[Treatise] Question:
The Buddha taught that "the three poisons are defilements and impurities. How, then, can it be said here that "because lust and the like are pure, form and the like are also pure"?
The answer is:
The Buddha taught:
"Because the true nature of the three poisons is pure, form and all other phenomena are also pure;
because the three poisons are pure and form and the rest are pure, they are non-dual and indistinguishable."

In order to explain in detail the purification of the three poisons and the causes and conditions for the fruit of that purification of the three poisons, it is said: "Because ignorance is pure, formative forces are also pure."
“Purity of ignorance” means that ignorance is ultimately empty, as explained in the ten similes for destroying ignorance.
This applies likewise from the twelve links of dependent origination up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, because all phenomena such as form and ignorance are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure; and because the perfection of wisdom is pure, all the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas—namely, the perfection of meditation up to the knowledge of all modes—are likewise pure.
The same applies to all dharmas such as the dhyāna-pāramitā and so forth.

Furthermore, by means of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), form (*rūpa*) and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), are empty; and because the knowledge of all modes is empty, the eighteen kinds of emptiness are also empty.

The knowledge of all modes is not separate from the eighteen kinds of emptiness, and the eighteen kinds of emptiness are not separate from the knowledge of all modes; therefore, it is said that they are "non-dual and undifferentiated."
Emptiness is itself purity.
Now, from form up to all-knowledge, whether one dharma is taken as the primary element or each subsequent dharma is taken as the primary element, they are all mutually pure.
Furthermore, because all dharmas are manifold and immeasurable, they are briefly categorized as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned dharmas is itself the unconditioned dharma.
One who knows the pure practitioner finds that permanence, bliss, self, and purity cannot be obtained among all dharmas.
If they cannot be apprehended, this is the true knowledge of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
that true knowledge of their non-apprehensibility is itself the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Therefore it is said:
"Because conditioned phenomena are pure, unconditioned phenomena are purified."
Furthermore, because of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one knows unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);
the Noble Ones, having attained these unconditioned phenomena, describe the characteristics of conditioned phenomena. Therefore it is said:
"Because conditioned phenomena are pure, unconditioned phenomena are pure; because unconditioned phenomena are pure, conditioned phenomena are pure."
Since conditioned phenomena exist within the three periods of time, it is said:
"Because the past is pure, the future is also pure; because the future is pure, the past is also pure."
Why is this so? Because the past is empty, having been destroyed, dispersed, and ceased; the future is empty, because it has not yet arisen and does not yet exist;
and since these two periods do not exist, the present likewise does not exist.
Why is this? Because there is priority and posteriority, one knows that there is the present.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena arise and perish from moment to moment; therefore, they have no time of abiding.
Because there is no duration, there is no present time.
Because the three times are empty, conditioned phenomena are empty;
because conditioned phenomena are empty, unconditioned phenomena are empty.
Emptiness is ultimate purity; it is neither broken nor destroyed, free from conceptual proliferation, and like space.
Thus, the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately pure, the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
To "break" [this] is to fall into hell, for it involves using words and letters to proclaim the Prajñā of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Question: If one who does not believe in the Prajñā falls into hell, while the believer attains Buddhahood,
then if there are those with the five heinous crimes, broken precepts, wrong views, or indolence who believe in this Prajñā, will such persons attain Buddhahood?
Furthermore, there are those who observe the precepts and exert diligence but do not believe in Prajñā; how is it that they fall into hell?
The answer is:
there are two ways in which one destroys Prajñā.
First, regarding that which was spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth, which his disciples have memorized, practiced, and written down as sutra scrolls—
foolish people slander it, saying:
"This was not spoken by the Buddha!"
"This was composed by Māra or by the followers of Māra; it is also the penwork of those with the nihilistic false view of uccheda-dṛṣṭi, spoken by one who has cultivated the power of eloquence.
Or it may be said:
"Although this is the Buddha’s teaching, here and there other people have interpolated additions."

There may be some who, with a mind attached to conceptualization and grasping at signs, speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*; though their mouths speak of the dharma of emptiness, their minds remain attached to existence.
Those who first break [this attachment] fall into the great hells, for they fail to grasp the intent of the sages in speaking of *prajñā*.
The second type of refutation is that of one who engages in debate with a mind of attachment; this is not called the refutation of Prajñā.
It is like Devadatta and Jīvaka both shedding the Buddha’s blood:
although the act is the same—shedding blood—their intentions differ, and thus one incurs sin while the other gains merit.
It is like the painting of a Buddha image: one person breaks it because the image is poorly executed, while another breaks it out of malice;
because their intentions differ, one person gains merit and the other incurs sin.
The same applies to those who destroy the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, there may be someone who destroys the *prajñā* without being angry at or disparaging the Buddha, yet personally employing their own mind to conceptualize and discriminate:
"This is a profound dharma spoken by the Omniscient One; it must contain deep and wondrous teachings. How can one say that everything is empty?"
The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a mind free from attachment for the sake of delivering sentient beings;
yet this person, with a mind of attachment and by grasping at signs, gives rise to verbal karma to revile and destroy the Prajñāpāramitā.
They are also able to give rise to physical karma, gesturing with their hands to reject and repudiate it, pointing it out as something to be destroyed and urging others to depart from it.
Because it is the opposite of two kinds of lack of faith, it is called "two kinds of faith":
first, faith that understands the true meaning of Prajñā, which attains the fruit and reward as described;
second, faith in the words, phrases, and letters of the sūtra scrolls, which attains little merit.
Because the sin of wrong view is so grave, even though one's bodily and verbal actions such as observing the precepts may be excellent, they all follow along with that wrong view and evil mind.
As the Buddha himself said in an analogy:
"It is like planting bitter seeds; although they are composed of the four great elements, they all produce a bitter taste."
It is the same for those with wrong views: although they may observe the precepts and exert themselves with diligence, all these become unwholesome dharmas.
That which is contrary to this is called right view.

For those who have committed the five heinous crimes, their evil offenses constantly shroud their minds; they harbor doubts regarding the karmic fruits of this life and future lives—how much less could they believe in the profoundly deep *prajñā*?
Even if they were to transcribe the sūtras and make offerings in hopes of escaping their evil offenses, they would remain very far removed from the Great *prajñā*.
There may be those who encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), who were diligent in previous lives and possessed the foremost merit, sharp wisdom, and faith in the Prajñāpāramitā;
through these pure causes and conditions, they are able to attain the fruits and rewards as described.

Just as King Ajātaśatru, despite the sin of killing his father, was able to eliminate that grave offense through the influence of the Buddha and the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī; he attained the fruit of Prajñā as described and received the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
42. Praising Purity. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter Praising Purity, Number Forty-Two. [Sūtra] At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This purity is profound!
The Buddha said,
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked:
"By the purification of what dharma is this purity so profound?
The Buddha said:
“Because form is pure, this purity is profound.

Because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are pure; because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, up to and including the eightfold noble path; because the ten powers of a Buddha are pure, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; because the bodhisattva is pure, the Buddha is pure, and all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes are pure—this purity is profound.”
“World-Honored One!
This is pure clarity!
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked:
“By the purity of what dharma is this purity manifest?”
The Buddha said:
"Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, it is luminous purity;
and so on, up to: because the perfection of giving is pure, it is luminous purity."
“Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge are pure, this purity is luminous.
“World-Honored One!
This purity is non-continuous!”
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Because of the non-continuity of what dharma is this purity non-continuous?
The Buddha said:
“Because form does not go and is non-continuous, this purity is non-continuous;”
“Because even up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) does not depart and does not continue, this purity is non-continuing.
“World-Honored One!
This purity is stainless!”
The Buddha said,
"Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Because what dharma is without defilement is it pure and stainless?
The Buddha said:
“Because the nature of form (*rūpa*) is eternally pure, it is pure and stainless;”
"Because even the nature of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is eternally pure, this purity is stainless.
"World-Honored One!
This purity is without attainment and without attachment!"
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“Because of the non-attainment and non-attachment to what dharma is this purity non-attainable and non-attached?
The Buddha said:
“Because of the non-attainment and non-attachment to form (rūpa), this purity is non-attainable and non-attached;”
"Because even up to all-knowledge there is neither attainment nor attachment, this purity is without attainment or attachment.
"World-Honored One!
This purity is non-arising!"
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
"Because what dharma is non-arising, is this purity non-arising?
The Buddha said:
"Because form (*rūpa*) is non-arising, this purity is non-arising; [and so on for the other aggregates]."
"Because even all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-arising, this purity is non-arising.
"World-Honored One!
This purity does not arise within the desire realm!"
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“How is it that this purity does not arise within the desire realm?
The Buddha said:
“Because the nature of the desire realm cannot be apprehended, this purity does not arise within the desire realm.”
“World-Honored One!
This purity does not arise within the form realm!
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is this purity such that it does not arise within the form realm?"
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of the form realm (rūpadhātu) cannot be apprehended, this purity does not arise within the form realm.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"This purity does not arise within the formless realm!
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is this purity such that one is not reborn in the formless realm?
The Buddha said:
“Because the nature of the formless realm cannot be apprehended, this purity does not arise within the formless realm.
“World-Honored One!
This purity is without cognition!”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“What is meant by ‘purity through non-cognition’?
The Buddha said:
“Because all phenomena are insentient, this is purity through non-cognition.”
“World-Honored One!
Form is without cognition; this is pure purity!
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is the absence of cognition regarding form the purity of purity?"
The Buddha said:
“Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, the absence of cognition in form is pure purity. [The interlocutor asked:
“World-Honored One!”
“The non-cognition of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is pure purity!
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure.”
Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is the absence of cognition regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the purity of purity?
The Buddha said:
“Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature, this non-cognition is pure purity.
“World-Honored One!
Because all dharmas are pure, this is pure purity!”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
"How is it that because all dharmas are pure, this purity is the 'purity of purity'?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are unattainable, the purity of all dharmas is the 'purity of purity'."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā neither benefits nor harms sarvajñatā.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked:
“In what way does the perfection of wisdom neither benefit nor harm omniscience?”
The Buddha said:
“Because the Dharma has the characteristic of permanence, the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms omniscience (sarvajñā).
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
"This Prajñāpāramitā is pure; it has no apprehension of any dharmas!
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked,
“In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure, such that it does not apprehend any phenomena?
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immovable, this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is pure;
it does not apprehend any phenomena. [Treatise] Commentary:
Regarding the statement "this purity is profound," there are two kinds of purity:
First is the purity of wisdom, and second is the purity of the objects of cognition.
These two things are mutually dependent: apart from the purity of wisdom there is no purity of objects, and apart from the purity of objects there is no purity of wisdom.
Why is this? All mental states and their associated factors arise from conditions; if there are no conditions, wisdom does not arise.
It is like fire that cannot burn in the absence of fuel.
Because there is wisdom, one knows that conditions are pure; without wisdom, one does not know that conditions are pure.
Herein, the purity of wisdom and the purity of conditions are mutually dependent, which is a constant law of the world.
In this context it is said:
Apart from cognition and apart from conditions, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is inherently pure.
When it becomes an object of the mind and mental factors, it becomes defiled and impure.
For example, if a hundred kinds of fine delicacies are placed in the same vessel as poison, they cannot be eaten.
The true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally pure; it is not created by a Buddha, nor by Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, or any ordinary beings.
Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, it remains eternally abiding in its indestructible nature.
Within the context of inverted, deceptive phenomena and their retributive fruits, one is defiled and impure.

This "purity" has various names: it may be called "Suchness" (*tathatā*), "Dharmatā," or "Reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*); it may be called "Prajñāpāramitā," or "the Path"; it may be called "neither arising nor ceasing," "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), "signlessness" (*animitta*), "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*), "no-knowledge and no-attainment," or "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Such names as these are immeasurable and boundless.
Śāriputra, contemplate these characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*: although they are invisible, inaudible, ineffable, and indestructible, to slander them incurs immeasurable sin;
whereas to believe, accept, and practice them correctly results in the unsurpassed fruit of retribution.
Śāriputra, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder and joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This purity is most profound!"
The Buddha replied:
“That which you perceive as rare is indeed surpassed within the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Among all phenomena, there is ultimate purity and non-attachment; even to the essence of purity itself one does not cling—this is called ultimate purification.”
Furthermore, "pure masters" refers to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
yet even these Buddhas do not cling to this purity, which is why it is said, "because of ultimate purity."

This pure prajñāpāramitā can bring about the exhaustion of all boundless suffering for all worthy ones and sages; it possesses such great benefit, yet one does not become attached even to this prajñāpāramitā.
Thus, there are immeasurable causes and conditions for this "ultimate purity," and this purity is profoundly deep!
Śāriputra asked:
"Because of the ultimate purity of what dharma is this purity so profoundly deep?"
The Buddha replied:
“Because all dharmas, such as form and so forth, are pure, this purity is profound. Why is this so?
Because all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are pure in their fundamental nature, their ultimate state, their causes, and their effects, this purity is profound.
As stated in the preceding chapter:
"Because the Bodhisattva has eliminated [defilements] through contemplative practice regarding phenomena such as form, he attains such purity."
For this reason, it is called "the purity of form and so forth.
This purity can destroy the ignorance of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within all phenomena and can bestow the light of wisdom of ultimate emptiness; therefore, it is called "pure clarity."
Because one practices the various sublime dharmas of the bodhisattvas, such as the *dānapāramitā*, one attains this "pure clarity.
Since this purity can grant *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is called "pure clarity."
Because one now attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder, it is said that "this purity is non-continuous.

Previously, by means of the three samādhis—emptiness and the others—one has relinquished all wholesome dharmas; subsequently, because one's lifespan naturally comes to an end, the five aggregates such as form do not depart nor do they continue. Therefore, "purity is non-continuous."
Because the one hundred and eight afflictions cannot obstruct, conceal, or defile its purity, it is called "pure and stainless.
Practicing this path of non-duality—the true mark of all phenomena—from the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* up to the fifteenth moment of mind is termed "attainment" (*prāpti*);
at the sixteenth moment of mind, one attains the fruit of the śramaṇa, which is termed "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*).
"Attainment" (*pratilambha*) is another name for "acquisition" (*prāpti*), meaning that once attained, one does not fall away from it.
Furthermore, practicing the six *pāramitās* up until the arising of the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*) is called "attainment";
being able to give rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and entering the stage of a bodhisattva is called "acquisition."
Within this pure dharma, by employing a mind of non-apprehension, these two things do not exist; therefore, it is called "non-attainment and non-attachment.
Practicing such a dharma, one knows that all dharmas are ultimately empty;
because they are ultimately empty, one does not grasp at signs.
Because they do not grasp at signs, they do not give rise to or perform the three kinds of karma;
because they do not perform karma, all worlds are unarisen.
"Worlds" refers to the so-called three realms.
In this context, there are two causes and conditions for non-arising:
first, because the three types of karmic activities that produce birth do not arise; second, because the intrinsic nature of the three realms cannot be apprehended.

In this context, the Buddha summarizes the causal conditions, namely that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the three realms is empty; therefore, it is said that "the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth within the three realms, cannot be apprehended."
This purity is non-cognition, because all phenomena are insentient, as explained in the superior chapter above.
The nature of all phenomena is eternally unarisen; because they are unarisen, they cannot be apprehended; and because they cannot be apprehended, they are ultimately pure.
Śāriputra has attained the *śrāvaka* pāramitā, whereas the Buddha is the Omniscient One; because of this exchange between these two, the bodhisattvas might become attached to this Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, wishing to sever their attachment, Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!"
Although the *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such merits, because it is ultimately pure, it neither benefits nor harms *sarvajñatā*.
Just as within a dream or a magical illusion there may be gain and loss, yet they neither benefit nor harm;

and just as space is ultimately pure and non-existent, yet it is through this space that things are accomplished and sustained—neither can it be said that space performs any action, nor can it be said that space provides no benefit.
The dānapāramitā performs its function because of the prajñāpāramitā; therefore, it is said that "the prajñāpāramitā neither benefits nor harms.

The prajñāpāramitā contemplates all dharmas as being flawed, impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as neither arising nor ceasing, and neither not-arising nor not-ceasing, and so forth.

Through various causes and conditions, it is praised as the cessation of all conceptualizations and proliferations, the severing of the path of speech; therefore, it is said that "the Prajñāpāramitā is pure, having no apprehension of any phenomena."

The cessation of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and the severance of the path of language is precisely the entry into the characteristics of the *dharmatā*; for this reason, it is said herein that "the *dharmatā* is immovable."
[Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, form is pure.”
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“For what reason is it that because the self is pure, form is pure and ultimately pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because the self does not exist, form does not exist and is ultimately pure.”
“World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
“By what cause and condition is it that because the self is pure, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, being ultimately pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Because the self does not exist, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist; they are ultimately pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”

Because the self is pure, the perfection of giving is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of ethical discipline is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of patience is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of vigor is pure; because the self is pure, the perfection of meditation is pure.
"World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
World-Honored One!"
“World-Honored One, because the self is pure, the four foundations of mindfulness are pure.
World-Honored One,
because the self is pure, even up to the eightfold noble path is pure.”
"World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the ten powers of the Buddha are pure.
World-Honored One!"
“Because the self is pure, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because they are ultimately pure (*atyanta-śuddha*).”
Subhūti said:
"By what causes and conditions is the purity of my dāna-pāramitā [the perfection of giving], and so on up to the purity of my eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), established?"
The Buddha said:

"Because I have nothing, the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is pure through having nothing; likewise, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (āveṇikadharma), they are pure because they have nothing."

“World-Honored One! Because the self is pure, the fruit of the srotāpanna is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the anāgāmin is pure; because the self is pure, the fruit of the arhat is pure; because the self is pure, the path of the pratyekabuddha is pure; and because the self is pure, the path of the Buddha is pure.”
The Buddha said:
“Ultimately pure. Subhūti said:

"For what reason are the purity of the fruit of srotāpanna, the purity of the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the purity of the fruit of anāgāmin, the purity of the fruit of arhat, the purity of the path of pratyekabuddha, and the purity of the path of buddhahood [established]?"
The Buddha said:
“Because their own characteristics are empty.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"Because I am pure, all-knowledge is pure.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Subhūti said: "By what cause and condition is it that because I am pure, all-knowledge is pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because it is signless and without conceptualization.
“World-Honored One!
Because of the purity of these two, there is neither attainment nor attachment.”
The Buddha said:
“Ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
"For what reason is it that, because of the purity of these two, there is neither attainment nor attachment, which constitutes ultimate purity?
The Buddha said:
"Because there is neither defilement nor purity."
“World-Honored One!
Because I am boundless, form is pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure.
The Buddha said:
“Ultimately pure. Subhūti said:
“For what reason is form pure because I am boundless? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness pure [for that same reason]?”
The Buddha said,
"Because of ultimate emptiness and beginningless emptiness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way, this is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
“By what causes and conditions is a bodhisattva mahāsattva able to know in this way? Is this called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha said:
"Because they know the seeds of the Path.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, they form this thought:
"Form does not know form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not know consciousness;
past phenomena do not know past phenomena; future phenomena do not know future phenomena; and present phenomena do not know present phenomena."
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, they do not form this thought:
'I am giving to that person;'"
I maintain the precepts, maintaining them in this way;
I cultivate patience, cultivating it in this way;
I exert diligence, exerting it in this way.
I enter meditative concentration; thus I enter meditative concentration.
I cultivate wisdom; thus I cultivate wisdom.
I attain merit; thus I attain merit.
"I shall enter the stage of the bodhisattva's dharma-position; I shall purify the Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity;
I shall attain all-knowledge. Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, they are free from all recollections and conceptual discriminations, because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the beginningless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, and the emptiness of self-characteristics.
“Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā; by the power of skillful means, there is nothing that obstructs him.
[Treatise] Explanation:
When the Buddha first commanded Subhūti to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, whatever he said should not be sought for its causes and conditions;
however, if it were spoken by anyone else, one should seek its causes and conditions.
Śāriputra has already asked about the characteristic of purity, and the Buddha has provided witness;
now Subhūti speaks of the characteristic of purity, and the Buddha likewise provides witness for it.
As for the statement, "Because the self is pure, the five aggregates are pure": just as the self ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too are the five aggregates.
Ultimate emptiness is the purity of the self and the purity of the five aggregates.

It is easy to understand the emptiness of the self, but difficult to understand the emptiness of the five aggregates; therefore, the easily understood is used as a metaphor for the difficult to understand.
It is likewise for the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and from the fruit of srotāpanna up to the path of Buddhahood; because I am pure, these dharmas are also pure.
Question:

Previously it was stated that "because the self does not exist, from form up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) also do not exist. Why is it now said that "the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) up to the path of the Buddha is empty of its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya)"?

Answer: I am born as a conventional designation based on the causes and conditions of a combination; within that which is selfless, there is the inversion of thinking "there is a self. Therefore, it is said that "the self is false and non-existent," for it does not exist due to the causes and conditions of attachment to the five aggregates.
Although dharmas such as the dāna-pāramitā are wholesome, because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and objects of attachment for bodhisattvas, it is said that "they do not exist.

The fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) and so forth are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); since unconditioned phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnya*)—meaning they are without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or change—it is therefore not said that they "do not exist," but rather that they are "empty of intrinsic characteristics."
Furthermore, because there is a preponderance of wrong practice among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they are said to be "non-existent.
Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are without arising or ceasing and lack wrong practice, they are said to be "empty of self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*).

Regarding the statement, “The purity of the self is the purity of all-knowledge,” because the bodhisattva is profoundly attached [to this], there is signlessness (*animitta*) and non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*).
Signlessness refers to the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).
One who is without thought does not even think of the signless samādhi.
Now, Subhūti, knowing that the perfection of wisdom is truly pure, said to the Buddha:
"Because of the purity of both, there is neither attainment nor attachment."
Purity is of two kinds:
first, purity by means of dualistic dharmas; second, purity by means of non-dualistic dharmas.
Purity by means of dualistic dharmas is purity of names.
That which is purified by means of the non-dual dharma is true purity.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are ultimately characterized by emptiness."
"How is it that through two dharmas there is both attainment and attachment?
To this, the causal conditions are explained: namely, that all dharmas are neither defiled nor pure.
Within the two kinds of purity, there is a distinction between what is defiled and what is pure.
Regarding the statement, "Because the self is boundless, the five aggregates are pure": just as the self is empty, and being empty it is boundless, so too are the five aggregates.
Question: It is commonly said that [all things] are "ultimately pure"; why now do you say they are "ultimately empty" and "empty from the beginningless"? Answer:
"Ultimate emptiness" is itself "ultimate purity"; because people fear emptiness, it is described as pure.
Herein it is said that "the self is boundless"; the self is none other than sentient beings, and thus sentient beings are empty.
Why is this? Because it is empty from the beginningless past.
It is said:

Regarding the statement, "To be able to know in this way is called prajñā": being able to [realize] the emptiness of sentient beings, the emptiness of phenomena, and the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas is called the *prajñāpāramitā*;
the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself ultimate purity.
The Buddha always answers with "ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā); therefore, one asks:
"If it is ultimately empty, how can you say that 'a bodhisattva who knows thus is said to possess the prajñā of a bodhisattva'?"
"It is difficult because ultimate emptiness is devoid of cognition.
The Buddha said:
"Because it knows the seeds of the Path."

Although the Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*), he wishes to cause sentient beings to attain this ultimate emptiness so that they may distance themselves from the mind of attachment.

Ultimate emptiness is taught solely for the purpose of destroying the mind of attachment; it is not a substantial emptiness. "Ultimate emptiness" is precisely the answer to "the knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgākārajñatā*).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā conceives this thought:”
"Form does not know form, and so forth.

The Buddha’s intention is that *prajñā* has no fixed characteristic; it is only through the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) that it is explained analytically. This is so that Bodhisattvas may practice *prajñā* with skillful means (*upāya*). Although phenomena are ultimately empty, one likewise knows that "form does not know the dharma of form," and so forth.

One contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately empty, and only the wisdom capable of such contemplation remains; yet one should not [cling to] ultimate emptiness itself, for one must guide sentient beings who possess attached minds so that they may enter into ultimate emptiness.
The Buddha replied:
"If a bodhisattva practices prajñā with skillful means, they are able to contemplate external phenomena as ultimately empty, such that form does not know form and so forth;
they likewise internally contemplate their own mind through the power of such skillful means. Thus, when practicing dāna, they do not form such thoughts:"
"I give this to him; he is the recipient of the gift.

Subhūti, as for the statement "form does not know form," it is because all dharmas are empty that they do not know one another. Because they do not know one another, there is no activity. This refutes two things, namely the recipient and the object given—these two things are both external.
"Now, the refutation of the giver... up to 'I cultivate all-knowledge' is also like this.
Herein, the causal conditions are explained:
"When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, because of skillful means, they do not have such conceptual discriminations."

"Because of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of self-characteristics, these thirteen kinds of emptiness exhaustively dismantle all phenomena; the final five kinds of emptiness are explained by way of their general characteristics. This is called the Bodhisattva’s state of being unimpeded."
"Unobstructed" means that these various forms of emptiness are unobstructed with respect to all phenomena.
