*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the "Chapter Praising Purity," Part 42.1.
Volume Sixty-four.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
“What, Kauśika, are the obstructing dharmas for a son of good family who seeks the bodhisattva path?
Subhūti replied to Śakra-devānām-indra: “Kauśika!”

There are sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path and grasp at mental signs; that is to say, they grasp at the sign of the dāna-pāramitā, the sign of the śīla-pāramitā, the sign of the kṣānti-pāramitā, the sign of the vīrya-pāramitā, the sign of the dhyāna-pāramitā, and the sign of the prajñā-pāramitā;
they grasp at the sign of internal emptiness, the sign of external emptiness, the sign of internal and external emptiness, up to the sign of the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
and they grasp at the signs of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the signs of the eightfold noble path.
One grasps the marks of the ten powers of the Buddha, up to and including the marks of the eighteen unique qualities;
one grasps the marks of all Buddhas, and grasps the marks of planting roots of goodness under all Buddhas.
One unifies all these merits and virtues, grasps their marks, and dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Kauśika! These are called the obstructing dharmas for good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path.
Because of these dharmas, they are unable to practice the prajñāpāramitā without obstruction.
Why is this? Kauśika! This mark of form cannot be dedicated;
the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be dedicated; and so on, up to the mark of all-knowledge, which cannot be dedicated.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens others in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should demonstrate, instruct, benefit, and gladden them in the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena."
When good sons or good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path practice the perfection of giving, they should not form such discriminations as saying:
"I give; I maintain the precepts; I practice patience; I exert diligence; I enter meditative concentration; I cultivate wisdom;
I practice internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness, up to and including practicing the emptiness of non-existence and existence."
"I have cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to: 'I practice for the sake of unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family should thus instruct, teach, benefit, and gladden others regarding unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment."

If one thus demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens others regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, being oneself free from error and acting in accordance with the Dharma permitted by the Buddha to demonstrate, instruct, benefit, and gladden them, one causes these sons and daughters of good family to remain far removed from all obstructing dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Just as you have explained the dharmas of obstruction for the bodhisattvas, Subhūti,
listen now further as I explain the subtle characteristics of obstruction.
“You, Subhūti!
Listen with a single-minded focus!
Thus the Buddha addressed Subhūti.
“Subhūti, there are sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they perceive and dwell upon the Buddhas by grasping at their signs.”
Whatever marks there may be are all obstructive marks.
Furthermore, regarding all the roots of goodness possessed by the Buddhas from their first aspiration until the endurance of the Dharma, one grasps at marks and recollects them;
having grasped at marks and recollected them, one dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! Whatever has characteristics is all a characteristic of obstruction.

Furthermore, if one grasps at the characteristics of the roots of goodness belonging to the Buddhas and their disciples, as well as the roots of goodness of other sentient beings, and dedicates them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; [this is not true dedication].
Subhūti! Whatever has characteristics is, in every case, a characteristic of obstruction. Why is this?
"One should not apprehend signs while recollecting the Buddhas, nor should one apprehend signs while recollecting the roots of goodness of the Buddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound!
The Buddha said,
"Because all dharmas are eternally detached."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
I shall pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because this Prajñāpāramitā is without arising and without activity, there is no one who can attain it. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are likewise unattainable.
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas have a single nature and not a dual nature,
Subhūti! This single dharma-nature is itself without nature."
This absence of intrinsic nature is itself the true nature; this nature neither arises nor is produced.

Thus, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena have a single nature—namely, the absence of nature, being without arising and without production—they will remain far removed from all marks of obstruction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to know and difficult to understand!”
The Buddha said: "It is as you have said.
This Prajñāpāramitā has no seer, no hearer, no knower, no cognizer, and no attainer."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable!
The Buddha said:
"As you have said:

this Prajñāpāramitā does not arise from the mind; it does not arise from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to: it does not arise from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
[Treatise] Question:
If that which is contrary to non-obstruction is called obstruction, why does Śakra ask again about obstruction? Answer:

The obstructing dharmas of the bodhisattvas are subtle and profound; they enter into the harmony of all wholesome dharmas. They are realized by those of sharp faculties, but not realized by those of dull faculties.
Because they are difficult to understand, he asks further before the Buddha.
What are obstructive dharmas? They are as follows:

when a bodhisattva discriminates between a mind of stinginess and a mind of giving, abandoning the mind of stinginess and grasping at the mind of giving—this is called "grasping at the characteristics of the mind."

To know the value of the objects of giving, and to know how to cultivate and accumulate giving so as to be able to give everything—these are the *dānapāramitā* and even the various wholesome dharmas such as taking signs in the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Although these are sublime, because one is internally attached to a self and externally attached to dharmas, one falls into the obstruction of dharmas;
it is like food that, though fragrant and delicious, causes illness if eaten in excess.
In this regard, Subhūti himself states the causal reasoning:
"Because the characteristics of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are ultimately empty, they cannot be dedicated toward the unsurpassed path."

The characteristics of obstruction were explained above; now the characteristics of non-obstruction are explained. That is to say, if a bodhisattva wishes to instruct others in the unsurpassed path, they should use the true Dharma to demonstrate, teach, benefit, and gladden them.
The meanings of "indicating, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening" are as previously explained.

Regarding "the true dharma," it refers to the cessation of all recollections and conceptual discriminations; therefore, it is said that "when practicing giving, one does not discriminate between 'I' and 'giving,' etc."
If one can provide such instruction and transformation, two kinds of benefits will be obtained:
first, one will be free from error oneself; second, one will transform others using the Dharma as realized by the Buddha.
Such infinite characteristics of obstruction as these are contrary [to it], and are therefore called the "characteristic of non-obstruction. Question:
Since the Buddha praised Subhūti by speaking of the "characteristic of non-obstruction," why does he now further speak of the "subtle characteristic of obstruction" himself?
The answer is:
The Buddha praised Subhūti on the basis of his own power, saying:
"You are one who has abandoned sentient beings, yet you are able to explain the characteristics of obstacles for a bodhisattva."
"The mark of subtle obstruction is beyond the power of Subhūti; therefore, the Buddha speaks of it himself.
Because this mark of obstruction is so subtle, you must listen with single-minded attention!"
What are these? That is to say, for a bodhisattva to employ mindfulness of the Buddhas and others by grasping at their marks is entirely an obstruction.
The markless mark is the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha emerges from within Prajñā, which is also the "markless mark.
If one takes up roots of goodness with a mind attached to marks and dedicates them, this results in worldly retribution;
because it is subject to exhaustion and mixed with poison, one cannot attain the Unsurpassed Way.

Question: Previously, regarding gross obstruction, you spoke of "grasping at signs" (*nimittagraha*); now, regarding subtle obstruction as well, you again speak of "grasping at signs. What is the difference between them?
Answer: Previously it was stated that "I am the giver and he is the recipient," and so forth; now, however, we speak only of "grasping at signs.

Furthermore, because this now discusses the "Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi of all Bodhisattvas," it involves subtle signs; these subtle signs obstruct the subtle mind within people, and for this reason they are called "subtle obstructions."
Subhūti, knowing that what the Buddha had spoken was profound and subtle, beyond his own reach, praised it by saying, "It is extremely deep.
The Buddha replied:
"Because all dharmas are eternally devoid of marks."
The Buddha said, "This Prajñā is distant from all dharmas; because it is distant from all dharmas, subtle marks cannot enter into Prajñā.
Subhūti, filled with joy, said, "I shall pay homage to Prajñā!"
Subhūti thought to himself:
"I have gained understanding of this profound characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, I have resolved to attain enlightenment. I ought to pay homage."
The Buddha said:

"Because this Prajñāpāramitā is without arising and without activity, not even the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, can obtain it; how then can you, a śrāvaka, say that you have obtained it?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
It is not only Prajñā; all dharmas are likewise without cognition and without attainment.”
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas have a single nature and no duality.
This single nature is what is called ultimate emptiness.
Non-duality means there is neither "ultimate" nor "non-ultimate.
The single dharma-nature is itself the absence of nature.
One should not be attached to ultimate emptiness, nor should one grasp its marks.
Why is this? Because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Subhūti then had this thought:
"If that which is without intrinsic nature is itself nature, because it neither arises nor acts, the suffering of future lives will not continue.
One who can thus know the Prajñāpāramitā remains far removed from all obstacles;
being far removed from all obstacles, one then freely attains the unsurpassed path."
When Subhūti heard these words, he thought to himself:
“What I considered to be attainment, the Buddha calls non-attainment;
this Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to understand and difficult to know.”
The Buddha replied:
“It is not only you who find this difficult!
Among all sentient beings, there is none who sees, none who hears, none who knows, none who cognizes, and none who attains.”
That which is not known by the ears, nose, tongue, or body, and not cognized by the mind, cannot be attained;
because this Prajñā transcends the six modes of cognition, it is said to be "difficult to understand."
Subhūti has entered into the profound *prajñā*, and because his power of wisdom has reached its ultimate limit, he says it is "inconceivable.
The Buddha said:

"This *prajñā* is not born of the mind, nor is it born of the five aggregates, nor even does it arise from the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), for it possesses the characteristic of non-arising."
Question: If it is said that [the mind] does not arise from the mind, why then speak again of the "five aggregates" (pañcaskandha)?
Among the five aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is precisely the mind.
Answer: To first speak of the mind is a brief explanation;
to subsequently speak of the five aggregates and so forth is an extensive explanation.
The five aggregates, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, can serve as causes and conditions for prajñā, yet they cannot give birth to prajñā;
it is like a fierce wind that disperses clouds and enables the sun and moon to appear, yet cannot create the sun and moon themselves.

Chapter 43: The Reality-Characteristic of Non-action The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Reality-Characteristic of Non-action, Number Forty-three. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This Prajñāpāramitā is without action.”
The Buddha said:
“Because an agent cannot be apprehended, form cannot be apprehended, and so on, up to all dharmas being unapprehendable.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, how should they practice?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with regard to form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
even not practicing with regard to the knowledge of all modes is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to form as being permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, not practicing with regard to everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as being permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to form as being either suffering or pleasure is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, not practicing with regard to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) as being either suffering or pleasure is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing the notion that form is self or not-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, not practicing the notion that even all-knowledge is self or not-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to the purity or impurity of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, not practicing with regard to the purity or impurity of anything up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because this form has the nature of non-existence; how could it have permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure, self or non-self, purity or impurity?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have the nature of non-existence; how could they have permanence or impermanence, up to and including purity or impurity?
Since even the non-existence of all-knowledge is itself non-existent, how could there be permanence or impermanence, up to and including purity or impurity?
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with the thought that form is incomplete; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
They do not practice with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are incomplete; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
This extends even to not practicing with the thought that the knowledge of all modes is incomplete; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? That which is not fully endowed with form is not called "form";
likewise, when one does not engage [with it], this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
That which is not fully possessed of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not called "consciousness";
likewise, when one does not engage [with them] in this way, that is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, if one does not practice even up to the point where all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not fully perfected, that is not called all-knowledge;
likewise, practicing in this manner is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented!
World-Honored One, you have skillfully explained the characteristics of hindrance and non-hindrance for good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path.”
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
Subhūti! The Buddha has skillfully explained the characteristics of obstruction and non-obstruction for good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice by way of non-obstruction regarding form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice by way of non-obstruction regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with the eye and being unimpeded is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with the ear, nose, tongue, or body and being unimpeded is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with the mind and being unimpeded is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
To practice the perfection of giving without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of ethical discipline without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of patience without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
To practice the perfection of vigor without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of meditation without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice the perfection of wisdom without obstruction is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Even to the point of not practicing so as to be unimpeded by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they know that form (*rūpa*) is unimpeded; they know that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are unimpeded; and even up to knowing that the knowledge of all modes is unimpeded.

He knows that the fruit of srotāpanna is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of anāgāmin is unobstructed; he knows that the fruit of arhatship is unobstructed; he knows that the path of the pratyekabuddha is unobstructed; and he knows that the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is unobstructed.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
"This profound Dharma neither increases nor decreases when it is taught, nor does it increase nor decrease when it is not taught.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is!"
It is so! This profound Dharma neither increases nor decreases when it is taught, nor does it increase or decrease when it is not taught.

It is like the Buddha, throughout his entire life, either praising or disparaging space; when he praises it, it neither increases nor decreases, and when he disparages it, it likewise neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti! It is like a phantom person: when praised, it neither increases nor decreases; when reviled, it likewise neither increases nor decreases;
it feels no joy when praised and no sorrow when reviled.

“Subhūti, the characteristics of all dharmas are also like this: whether they are spoken of, they remain as they were originally and do not differ; whether they are not spoken of, they remain as they were originally and do not differ.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is most difficult for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas to accomplish!
While practicing this Prajñāpāramitā, they are neither sorrowful nor joyful, yet they are able to train in and practice the Prajñāpāramitā, and they do not turn back from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
To cultivate the perfection of wisdom is like cultivating empty space.

Just as in empty space there is no perfection of wisdom, no perfection of meditation, no perfection of vigor, no perfection of patience, no perfection of ethical discipline, and no perfection of generosity;

just as in empty space there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; nor are there the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; nor are there the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities; nor are there the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat; nor is there the path of a pratyekabuddha, nor is there unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā is also like this,
World-Honored One!
One should pay homage to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to perform such great adornment.
“World-Honored One!
This person exerts great diligence as a great adornment for sentient beings, just as one exerts great diligence as a great adornment for empty space.
World-Honored One!”
This person wishes to deliver sentient beings as if wishing to deliver empty space.
World-Honored One!
This great adornment of these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is a great adornment for sentient beings who are equal to empty space.
“World-Honored One!
This person’s great adornment, in their desire to deliver sentient beings, is like lifting up empty space.
World-Honored One!”
World-Honored One, it is by the power of great diligence that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to deliver sentient beings, resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The great adornment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is that, desiring to deliver sentient beings, they resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess great heroic valor; for the sake of delivering sentient beings who are as infinite as space, they resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with Buddhas, as densely as a grove of bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, hemp, or thickets; and suppose these Buddhas were to preach the Dharma for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, such that each and every Buddha brought immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings across to enter nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
This nature of sentient beings neither decreases nor increases. Why is this?
Because sentient beings do not exist and because sentient beings are detached [from inherent existence].
This applies even to all the sentient beings being delivered by the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions; it is likewise so for them.
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, I say this:
"This person, wishing to deliver sentient beings, has resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is like wishing to deliver empty space."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who spoke these words:
“I shall pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā!

Although within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no dharma that arises and no dharma that ceases, therein exist the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; therein exist the various srotāpannas, the various sakṛdāgāmins, the various anāgāmins, the various arhats, and the various pratyekabuddhas; therein exist the Buddhas, and the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; and therein exists the turning of the wheel of Dharma.”
[Treatise] Commentary:
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching that the *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of being without arising and without activity, Subhūti now speaks before the Buddha, saying:
“The *prajñāpāramitā* performs no action.”
If there were no agent, one would be unable to sever the various afflictions and unable to cultivate and accumulate the various wholesome dharmas.
Regarding this, the Buddha explained the causal conditions:
"From the agent down to all dharmas, because they are unapprehendable."
"If even the knower does not exist, how much less the agent?
Subhūti said:
"If there is no agent, and the Prajñāpāramitā has nothing that it can do, how should one practice it, and how should one attain the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva does not practice any dharmas and does not apprehend any dharmas—namely, whether they are permanent or impermanent, and so on, up to whether they are pure or impure—this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom."
"All dharmas" refers to everything from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); these are the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva.
Within these dharmas, those who lack wisdom practice the view that all dharmas are permanent and so forth; those with wisdom practice the view that all dharmas are impermanent and so forth.
Because this Prajñāpāramitā reveals the ultimate true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), it does not speak of phenomena as permanent or impermanent.

Although [the teaching of] impermanence and so forth can destroy such inversions as permanence, these dharmas are not accepted within Prajñā, because they are capable of giving rise to a mind of attachment.
Upon reflection and deliberation, one finds that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence cannot be established as fixed or real.
Question:
While phenomena such as form (*rūpa*)—which are subject to defilement—can be contemplated as impure and suffering, how can other wholesome phenomena be contemplated as impure and suffering?
Answer: These names refer to impurity and suffering.
Just as phenomena that are at ease and agreeable according to one's wishes are called pure and blissful; [so too are their opposites].
That which is not to one’s liking and is not a state of security is called impure and suffering.
Among wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*), that which is cherished and finds approval is regarded as pure and pleasant;
that which is loathed and disliked is regarded as impure and suffering.
Subhūti had this thought:
"If one is separated from all dharmas of contemplation, will it not be that the bodhisattva path is incomplete?
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"If one does not practice by way of the non-perfection of form and so forth, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Regarding "perfection of form," some say that the conceptualization and discrimination of permanence,
impermanence, and so forth within phenomena such as form is called "perfection."

Regarding "incomplete": herein, one uses the contemplation of impermanence and so forth to subvert permanence and so forth; this is called "incomplete," because it is deficient in permanence and the like.
Now, one does not even practice [notions such as] impermanence regarding form; therefore it is said:
"Not practicing the non-perfection of form is the practice of the perfection of wisdom."
Furthermore, some say: "To be 'complete' means that a Bodhisattva in his final birth (caramabhavika) can contemplate form as it truly is, up to and including all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
this is called being complete, while others are incomplete."
If a bodhisattva does not practice the non-perfection of form and so forth, this is precisely practicing the perfection of prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the non-perfection of form is not form, for form does not possess the characteristic of impermanence.
The Buddha said:
"To deliver sentient beings from permanence and to cause them to dwell in non-existence by following the sounds of speech—therefore it is said:
'Thus, even that which is truly pure is not practiced; this is the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
Because he has skillfully explained what is the path and what is not the path, Subhūti said:
“It is marvelous!
That which is obstructed is not the path; that which is unobstructed is the path.

The Buddha observed that the minds of those in the assembly were largely inclined toward emptiness; knowing that the *prajñāpāramitā* possesses the characteristic of non-obstruction, he therefore said:
"To not practice with regard to the non-obstruction of form and so forth—this is the practice of *prajñāpāramitā*."
"One who can practice in this way is unimpeded regarding phenomena such as form.
Although Subhūti was unable to exhaustively realize the principle of ultimate emptiness, he constantly delighted in speaking of it;
for this dharma of emptiness is rare and stands in opposition to all worldly dharmas.
The Buddha affirmed what Subhūti had said:
"Whether one speaks or does not speak, there is neither increase nor decrease.
This is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; even if one were to attempt to destroy it through physical action, one could not cause it to change, let alone by means of verbal expression!"
Because it is eternally characterized by non-arising.
Just as with space, space is the *prajñāpāramitā*;
the illusory person is the practitioner.
Although the practitioner’s karmic causes and conditions for offenses are deceptive phenomena, because they are united with the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no difference between them;
it is like various colors reaching the vicinity of Mount Sumeru, all becoming the same golden color.
This true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) is unknowable and ineffable;
therefore, whether it is spoken or not spoken, it remains no different from its original state.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"If all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent, like space, to the extent that they possess not even the slightest characteristic;
yet a bodhisattva is able to cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas and attain the unsurpassed path—this matter is difficult to believe and difficult to accept!"
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The deeds performed by the bodhisattvas are most difficult!
They are able to accomplish what is hard to do; therefore, they should be venerated, for they are able to bring about great adornment."
Subhūti spoke with a mind of rare aspiration:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is a great adornment for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; all devas and humans should pay him homage.”
Question: How is it known that this is the Great Ornament? Answer:
Subhūti, herein he himself provides an analogy:
"Just as if there were someone who, for the sake of empty space, would practice with diligent vigor and make great adornments for its benefit;
so too is it for a bodhisattva who practices with diligent vigor for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
If there were someone who wished to cross over empty space, it would be the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to deliver sentient beings. He asked:
Question: Why is a single matter stated twice? Answer:

Regarding "benefit," it refers to those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, but are instead enabled to obtain wisdom, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and other forms of happiness in both this life and future lives.
Those who wish to be delivered shall be enabled to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), accomplish the path of the Three Vehicles, and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Just as space is without arising or ceasing, without suffering or pleasure, without bondage or liberation, and because it is devoid of anything possessed, so too are sentient beings.
Therefore it is said:
"World-Honored One!
You have made the Great Adornment in order to deliver sentient beings who are like empty space."
"Just as space is without color and without form, it would be difficult for anyone to wish to lift up space;

so too are the dharmas of sentient beings ultimately empty. Yet, the Bodhisattva wishes to lift up all sentient beings of the triple world and place them within nirvāṇa. For this reason, it is called the Great Adornment."
Subhūti further praised him, saying:

"Because this bodhisattva possesses the power of great diligence and does not follow a mind of false doubt, although he has not yet attained the Buddha-way and has not yet extinguished all fetters, he is able to be greatly courageous and can thus practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of sentient beings, even though sentient beings are also empty."
It is, for example, like wishing to paint the void with various colors.

In this context, the Buddha explains the causal conditions for the emptiness of sentient beings: that is to say, even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to teach the Dharma to sentient beings through their supernormal powers for immeasurable eons, and each Buddha were to deliver immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of sentient beings into *nirvāṇa*, even if this were so, there would be no decrease whatsoever among sentient beings.
If sentient beings truly existed and there were a true decrease in their number, then the Buddhas would incur the fault of diminishing sentient beings.

However, since sentient beings are truly empty and exist only as provisional designations through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they possess no fixed characteristics; therefore, however many sentient beings the Buddhas deliver, there is in reality no decrease whatsoever.
If they are neither saved nor increased,
for this reason the Buddhas bear no fault of failing to save sentient beings!
Therefore it is said:
“A bodhisattva who wishes to deliver sentient beings wishes to deliver empty space.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, hearing this mark of ultimate emptiness, spoke with wonder and joy:
“I shall pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā!”
"In Prajñā, there is no dharma that possesses a fixed, real mark; yet there exist the aggregate of precepts and so forth, as well as various karmic fruits.
[Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), what dharma is he practicing?"
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Kauśika! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he is practicing emptiness."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, approaches, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā, how should I provide protection for them?”
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika, do you perceive any such dharma that can be guarded or protected?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No, Subhūti!"
“I do not see any dharma that ought to be protected.
Subhūti said: “Kauśika!...”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices as it is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā, that itself constitutes protection; namely, they are never separated from the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught.

Neither humans nor non-humans shall find an opportunity to harm these sons or daughters of good family; one should know that these sons or daughters of good family do not distance themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika! If a person wishes to protect a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, they wish to protect empty space. Kauśika!
"What do you think?
Are you able to protect dreams, mirages, reflections, echoes, illusions, and magical transformations?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"One cannot protect them.
"If anyone wishes to protect bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, it is likewise in vain; they will only exhaust themselves in suffering."
Kauśika! What do you think? Is it possible to protect that which has been conjured by the Buddha?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"One cannot protect them.
"If a person wishes to protect those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, it is also like this."
Kauśika! What do you think?
Is it possible to protect the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), suchness (tathatā), and the inconceivable nature?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"I cannot protect them.
"If anyone wishes to protect bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom, it is also like this."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, know and see all phenomena as being like a dream, like a flame, like a shadow, like an echo, like an illusion, and like a transformation?”

Because the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive and know things as they truly are, they do not conceive of a dream, they do not conceive of "this is a dream," they do not conceive of using a dream, and they do not conceive of "my dream."
"Flames, shadows, echoes, illusions, and transformations are also like this. Subhūti said, "Kauśika!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not conceive of form, do not conceive of "this is form," do not conceive of the use of form, and do not conceive of "my form. This bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise able not to conceive of a dream, not to conceive of "this is a dream," not to conceive of the use of a dream, and not to conceive of "my dream"; this extends even to not conceiving of a transformation, not to conceive of "this is a transformation," not to conceive of the use of a transformation, and not to conceive of "my transformation.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he does not conceive of omniscience, does not conceive "this is omniscience," does not conceive of employing omniscience, and does not conceive "I am omniscient.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise able not to conceive of dreams, not to conceive "this is a dream," not to conceive of employing a dream, and not to conceive "I have a dream";
up to and including emanations (*nirmāṇa*), it is also thus.
In this way, Kauśika,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas are like a dream, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an echo, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation.
[Treatise] Commentary:
At that moment, Śakra asked:
"Regarding this profound *prajñā* heard from the Buddha and Subhūti, what dharma is it that one practices?"
Subhūti said: "Because all dharmas, after a long time, ultimately return to nirvāṇa, one should practice the emptiness of all dharmas; for this reason it is said:
'One who wishes to practice prajñā should practice emptiness.'"
Śakra, the King of Devas and Lord of Men, who possesses sovereignty over the world and can provide whatever is required, vowed to act as a protector.
Upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, he joyfully addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should I do to protect it?"
"Whatever they may require, I shall give it all to them.
Subhūti and a certain bhikṣu merely paid their respects according to the monastic dharma;
yet evil spirits constantly harassed these people, and Māra, or the followers of Māra, constantly harassed the practitioner.
Therefore, he asked the Buddha:
"By what means should I provide protection?
Whether by guarding myself, or by dispatching my sons and younger brothers, or by sending my officials and attendants to serve as guards—I shall follow the Buddha’s instructions."

Subhūti, knowing that prajñāpāramitā possesses immeasurable power and further understanding that the Buddha intended for the prajñāpāramitā to be held in high esteem so that one would not regard it as a favor received, spoke to Śakra: “Kauśika!...”
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, all things are empty, like illusions and like dreams. Do you perceive any dharma whatsoever that can be guarded?
Śakra replied, "No!"
If it were visible, it could not be called the *prajñāpāramitā* that is ultimately empty;
if it is invisible, how can one say, "I shall perform such-and-such an act to protect it"?
Furthermore, "Kauśika!
If a practitioner abides in the Prajñā as it has been described, this is itself protection.

If a bodhisattva, as taught in the Prajñā, single-mindedly accepts it with faith, contemplates it, maintains right mindfulness, enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), observes the true mark of all phenomena, attains the wisdom of ultimate emptiness, corresponds to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and enters the stage of a bodhisattva—such a person does not spare even their own body or life, much less external things!
Such a person requires no protection.
Protection means to ward off all suffering and affliction so that one may attain peace and happiness.
Since this person has transcended all worldly dharmas, they possess neither sorrow nor suffering and affliction.
To neither rejoice upon attaining worldly matters nor to grieve upon losing them, is what is called never being separated from the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught.
If a person should practice for a short time and later lose it, they must guard it;
however, if they never depart from the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been described, then there is no need for guarding.
For example, when the yakṣa Gāla struck Śāriputra on the head with his fist, Śāriputra had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and did not feel the pain of the blow.
The constituent element of the Prajñāpāramitā is precisely this absorption of cessation; therefore, neither humans nor non-humans can find an opportunity to harm it.
Briefly stated, there are two causes and conditions for which one need not provide protection, such that neither humans nor non-humans can find an opportunity:
first, from the body up to all phenomena, one feels weary of and detached from them;
because they are without self and without what belongs to a self, one has no attachments whatsoever.
First, like cutting down grass or trees, one does not give rise to sorrow or anxiety.
Second, because one has attained the most sublime Dharma, one is protected by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as by the devas.
Furthermore, it is like a person who wishes to protect empty space.
Empty space cannot be destroyed by rain, nor can it be dried up by wind or sun, nor can it be harmed by swords, staves, or the like;
if there is someone who wishes to protect empty space, they will only exhaust themselves in vain, for it provides no benefit to the space.
If one wishes to protect a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, it is also like this.
To make this matter clear, he asks:
"Are you able to protect emptiness, or a person seen in a dream, or a reflection, an echo, or a magically conjured person?"
He replied, "No!
"This phenomenon merely deceives the eye and mind; having appeared for a moment, it perishes. How can it be guarded?"
The Bodhisattva practicing *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this: he contemplates the five aggregates as being deceptive, like dreams and so forth.

Just as with unconditioned phenomena—suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the inconceivable nature (*acintyadharmatā*)—there is no one who can protect them, nor is there anything to be benefited by them.
A bodhisattva practicing prajñā knows that the body is suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and does not engage in discrimination;
when receiving offerings and benefits, they do not rejoice, and when meeting with ruin or loss, they do not grieve.
"Since such a person has no need for protection,
why then would there be a need for it? At that time, Śakra, coveting and valuing this wisdom that is like a dream and so forth— whereby a bodhisattva, having attained the power of this wisdom,
requires no external protection— therefore asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva know that these dharmas, such as dreams, are empty?
"As for 'not dwelling upon dreams and so forth according to what is known and seen,' the metaphor of dreams and so forth refers to the five aggregates."
The five aggregates are that which people cling to; they do not cling to dreams and the like.
Because one wishes to cause them to abandon clinging to things, the state of non-clinging is used as a metaphor, so that they may contemplate the five aggregates as being like a dream.
One also gives rise to attachment even toward dreams; for this reason, Śakra asks about "being like a dream," yet he does not become attached even to that dream.

Ordinary people, using the metaphor of a dream for the five aggregates, immediately become attached to the dream itself, saying, "There must certainly exist a dharma of dreaming that arises during sleep. This is called "recollection of a dream."
To discriminate thus, "This dream is bad; this dream is good," is called "recalling the dream.
When one obtains a favorable matter in a dream, the mind becomes elated; when one obtains an unfavorable matter, the mind becomes sorrowful.
Furthermore, by using this analogy of a dream, one attains the true wisdom that all things are like a dream; this is called "recalling the application of the dream.
Upon hearing this analogy, one realizes through this dream that all phenomena are like a dream; this is called "recalling my own dream."
The other metaphors are also like this.
At that time, Subhūti replied to Śakra:

"If a practitioner does not bring to mind form—whether it be the form of a human, the form of a non-human, the form of a tree, the form of a mountain, or the four great elements, or the forms derived from the four great elements, and so forth."
One does not contemplate whether this form is permanent or impermanent, and so forth; one does not give rise to arrogance on account of form.
One does not contemplate that form is "mine" or "not mine," but enters the gate of non-self and proceeds directly into the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This person is able not to think of the dream, nor to think of it as a dream;
by using such analogies as the dream, they break attachment to the five aggregates.
Because they have broken such attachment, they do not err even within a dream.
If one cannot break through attachment to form, that person is mistaken regarding form and is likewise mistaken regarding dreams.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes.
It is the same with illusions, mirages, echoes, shadows, transformations, and so forth.
Bodhisattvas know all dharmas to be like dreams, yet they do not even dwell upon the dream.

[Sūtra] At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, all the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, and so on up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven—within this trichiliocosm—all these gods scattered celestial sandalwood from afar over the Buddha. They approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the gods of the Four Great Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Brahmā Devānām Indra, and even the gods of the Pure Abodes, beheld in the eastern direction a thousand Buddhas preaching the Dharma. They were all of the same appearance and the same names, and they were teaching this chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā;
all the bhikṣus were named Subhūti, and those who questioned and debated the chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā were all named Śakra Devānām Indra.
In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, a thousand Buddhas likewise appeared in each direction.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place."
Just as when the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, by what marks, by what causes, and by what meanings will he explain this meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he shall preach the Dharma thus: ‘Form is neither permanent nor impermanent;
he shall preach the Dharma thus: ‘Form is neither suffering nor happiness; form is neither self nor non-self; form is neither pure nor impure.’”
Form is neither bound nor liberated; one should teach the Dharma in this way.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent, and so on, up to being neither bound nor liberated; one should teach the Dharma in this way.
Form is not of the past, form is not of the future, and form is not of the present; one should teach the Dharma in this way.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Form is ultimately pure; one should preach the Dharma in this way.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure; one should preach the Dharma in this way.
This continues up to omniscience, which is ultimately pure; one should preach the Dharma in this way.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is pure.”
The Buddha said:
“Because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
How is it that because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?”
The Buddha said:
"If form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, this is called the purity of form;

if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, this is called the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because space is neither born nor extinguished, it is pure; the perfection of wisdom is likewise."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
because form is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that because form is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
Why is it that because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Just as space cannot be defiled, so space is pure. [He asked:
“World-Honored One!”
"How is it that space is pure because it cannot be defiled?
The Buddha said, "Space is pure because it cannot be grasped; because space is pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space can be described, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
“How is it that because space can be described, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because two sounds arise within space, and the perfection of wisdom is likewise pure because it can be described as being like space.”
“Subhūti! Because space is inexpressible, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One!”
"How is it that because space is inexpressible, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said,
"Just as space is inexpressible, so the perfection of wisdom is pure."
"Furthermore, because space cannot be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
"World-Honored One!
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because space cannot be apprehended?"
The Buddha said:
"Just as space has the characteristic of being ungraspable, so too the prajñāpāramitā is pure because it, like space, has the characteristic of being ungraspable."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
“How is it that because all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure?
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are ultimately pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure.”
[Treatise] Commentary:
Although all aspects of this Prajñāpāramitā are profoundly deep, it is in this chapter that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is explained with complete clarity.
Therefore, the devas throughout the trichiliocosm, bearing various articles of offering, came to make offerings to the Buddha and stood to one side.
A question was asked:
"Are these the same devas who previously came?"
Answer: Some say that because an event has lasted for a long time, it departs, only to return once again.
Some say: "There are even new heavens that come into being.
In order to inspire faith in the Prajñāpāramitā, a thousand Buddhas appear in each of the ten directions.
Due to the causal conditions of this person’s merit, they ought to see a thousand Buddhas;
yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, all those in the assembly see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
What humans and devas perceive is limited; were it not for the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, there would be no way for them to see those various Buddhas.
Those who preached the Dharma before the Buddha were all named Subhūti;
those who posed difficult questions were all named Śakra-devānām-indra. There were one thousand individuals who shared these same names.
At that time, Subhūti and Śakra both spoke with joy, saying,
"It is not only we who are able to speak and to ask.
Because the Buddha wished to authenticate this matter, he extensively cited the relevant events and said:
“Maitreya and the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa shall here, at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, the capital of the kingdom of Magadha, expound the Prajñāpāramitā.”
As it is said in the sūtra:

"The Bodhisattva Maitreya, leading a great assembly to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, opened the summit of the mountain with his toe. There emerged Mahākāśyapa’s skeletal body, wearing his saṃghāṭī robe, holding a staff and carrying an alms bowl."
Maitreya spoke to the great assembly, saying:

"In the past, there was a Śākyamuni Buddha when the human lifespan was one hundred years. This person was foremost among the disciples who practiced the dhūta austerities with few desires and contentment; he possessed the six supernormal powers and attained the three insights.
Because he constantly felt compassion for and benefited sentient beings, he used his supernormal power to cause this skeletal body to remain until now."
"Therefore, even those with small bodies obtain such benefits; how much more so for you who possess large bodies and are born in a fortunate age—how can you not benefit yourselves?
At that time, Maitreya, on account of this matter, extensively expounded the Dharma, causing immeasurable sentient beings to reach the end of suffering.
By this matter, one knows that Maitreya is preaching the Dharma on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
This Prajñāpāramitā was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it should be faithfully accepted.
Subhūti asked:
“By what marks, by what causes, and by what Dharma-gates does the Bodhisattva Maitreya teach?
The Buddha said:
"As I have said":
that form and all other phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither bound nor liberated, and so forth, as previously explained.
Furthermore, one does not speak of form as past, future, or present.

Just as nirvāṇa transcends the three periods of time, so too are all phenomena such as form; as was previously stated, "all dharmas have the same characteristic as nirvāṇa," so it is with that which Maitreya has spoken.
At that time, Subhūti joyfully addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the foremost purity.”
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas, such as form and so forth, are pure;
because cause and effect are analogous."

Regarding the purity of dharmas such as form: because dharmas such as form do not lose their causal conditions for karma, and because one cannot apprehend any fixed or real characteristic of arising in these dharmas, they are neither born nor extinguished;
and because the characteristics of all dharmas are eternally unpolluted, they are neither defiled nor pure.
An analogy is provided here in order to clarify this matter:
just as dust and water do not adhere to space because its nature is pure, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is eternally pure because it is neither born nor extinguished.
Just as space cannot be defiled, so too is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā):

although it may be subject to the conceptual proliferations (prapañca) of false views, it cannot be defiled; weapons and staffs, or other harmful things, cannot destroy it. Because it is formless and shapeless, it cannot be grasped; because it cannot be grasped, it cannot be defiled.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattvas abide in the unimpeded wisdom of eloquence and joyful exposition, they preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand clusters of dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; yet all these are but the single matter of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which they explain by means of differentiation.
Therefore it is said: "Because the *prajñāpāramitā* can be explained, it is as pure as space."
"Due to space and mountain valleys, a human voice issues forth from the void of the mouth; because this sound issues forth, it is called an echo.
Just as the echo is empty, so too is the voice from the mouth. Both these sounds are deceptive and unreal, yet people take the voice to be real and the echo to be unreal."
Prajñā is also like this: all dharmas are ultimately empty, like illusions and like dreams; both the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the noble ones are deceptive.
Lesser bodhisattvas regard the dharmas of ordinary beings as deceptive and the dharmas of the noble ones as real.
Question:
Both of these are false and deceptive; for what reason does a small bodhisattva regard the dharmas of ordinary persons as false and the dharmas of the noble ones as true?
Answer:
The Noble Dharma is established as real because it is accomplished through the cultivation and accumulation of merit based on ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
In contrast, the dharmas of ordinary beings exist spontaneously, like an echo that arises naturally; they are not produced through intentional effort and are therefore considered unreal.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to this body; therefore, they take the sound emerging from the body to be real.
Lesser bodhisattvas, because they deeply delight in wholesome dharmas, likewise take it to be real.
Furthermore, just as there is nothing that can be spoken in empty space because it lacks the characteristics of sound or speech;
these sounds and speeches are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whereas empty space is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: its foremost profound meaning is ultimate emptiness, which is beyond verbal expression, for all paths of language are cut off.
Furthermore, just as space has the characteristic of being ungraspable— neither existence nor non-existence can be found—
if there were such a thing as "signlessness," it would be refuted in the same manner as the previously analyzed characteristics of space;
yet if it does not exist, it is because of this space that immeasurable activities are performed!
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it is pure because its marks of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā arises from the correct mindfulness of all dharmas.
Regarding right mindfulness: because it is ultimately empty and pure, all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure.
