*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter 40, "The Reality-Mark of Non-action."
Part Three, Volume Sixty-five.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, draw near to, and correctly recollect this Prajñāpāramitā, they shall never suffer from eye disease; nor shall their ears, noses, tongues, or bodies ever suffer from disease. Their bodies shall not be maimed or deformed, nor shall they become decrepit with old age, and they shall never meet an untimely death.”
Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devas—from the Cāturmahārājika devas up to the Śuddhāvāsa devas—all followed along to listen and receive [the teaching].
On the six fast days—the eighth, twenty-third, fourteenth, twenty-ninth, fifteenth, and thirtieth days of the month—the assemblies of the devas gather.
Noble son, wherever a Dharma teacher expounds the Prajñāpāramitā, all shall gather there.
When these noble sons and noble daughters teach this Prajñāpāramitā within the great assembly, they shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, inconceivable, and unfathomable merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

If these sons or daughters of good family, on the six fast days—the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth day of the month—expound this Prajñāpāramitā before the assembly of devas, those sons or daughters of good family will obtain immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), inconceivable, and unfathomable merit.
Why is this? Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā is a great and precious treasure.
What is this great treasure?

It is the Prajñāpāramitā, which can extract beings from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and human poverty; it can bestow [status upon] the great clans of Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas, and the great households of householders; it can bestow [rebirth in] the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and it can bestow the fruit of Srotāpanna, the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of Anāgāmin, the fruit of Arhat, the path of Pratyekabuddha, and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments are extensively taught; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are extensively taught; the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence are extensively taught; and the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge are extensively taught.
From this one learns, giving birth to the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brahmins, and the great households of householders;
it gives birth to the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, and the Brahmapurohita Heaven.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven; the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābhā Heaven, the Apramāṇābhā Heaven, and the Ābhāsvara-svabhāva Heaven;

the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven,
the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven,
the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana Heaven, and the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven.

Training in this Dharma, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; one attains the path of the pratyekabuddha, and one attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the perfection of wisdom is called a great treasure.
Within this treasure-perfection, there is no dharma to be found that can be produced or extinguished, defiled or purified, grasped or relinquished.
In the Jewel Perfection, there is likewise no dharma—whether wholesome or unwholesome, worldly or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned.
For this reason, Subhūti,
this is called the precious perfection of non-apprehension. Subhūti!
This is the jewel-like perfection (ratnapāramitā), which no dharma can defile. Why?
Because the defiling dharmas cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti! For this reason, it is called the "stainless jewel pāramitā. Subhūti!

If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they likewise do not know, likewise do not differentiate, likewise do not apprehend, and likewise do not engage in conceptual proliferation (prapañca), this is called being able to practice the perfection of wisdom;
and they are also able to pay homage to and visit the Buddhas, traveling from one buddha-field to another buddha-field to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to those Buddhas;
and they roam through the buddha-fields to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the buddha-lands.

“Subhūti! This prajñāpāramitā has no power regarding all phenomena, nor does it have a lack of power; it neither receives nor bestows; it is neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”

This pāramitā is neither past, nor future, nor present; it does not abandon the desire realm nor abide in the desire realm, it does not abandon the form realm nor abide in the form realm, and it does not abandon the formless realm nor abide in the formless realm.

This Prajñāpāramitā does not associate with the Dānapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Śīlapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Kṣāntipāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Vīryapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Dhyānapāramitā, nor does it abandon it; it does not associate with the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does it abandon it.
It does not associate with internal emptiness, nor does it abandon it, up to and including its non-association with the emptiness of non-existence and existence, nor does it abandon it.
It does not associate with the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does it abandon them, up to and including its non-association with the eightfold noble path, nor does it abandon it.
He neither bestows nor relinquishes the ten powers of a Buddha; likewise, he neither bestows nor relinquishes even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He neither bestows nor relinquishes the fruit of a stream-enterer; likewise, he neither bestows nor relinquishes even the fruit of an arhat.
He neither bestows nor relinquishes the path of a pratyekabuddha; likewise, he neither bestows nor relinquishes even all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the dharmas of an Arhat nor does it abandon the dharmas of an ordinary person;
it does not bestow the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha nor does it abandon the dharmas of an Arhat;
it does not bestow the dharmas of a Buddha nor does it abandon the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha.
This Prajñāpāramitā neither joins with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) nor abandons conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Why is this?

Whether there are Buddhas or no Buddhas, the characteristics of these dharmas remain eternally constant and unchanging; the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-abiding, and the dharma-position are eternally constant, for they are neither erroneous nor lost.
[Treatise] Question:
If there are still many afflictions even when one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and maintains right mindfulness, why do you say that one will ultimately never suffer from eye diseases and the like?

Answer: This matter has already been explained in detail above in the "Chapter on Merit and Hell," namely, that it is not necessarily karma that must be experienced as retribution; therefore, there are no manifold afflictions.
Furthermore, because one constantly upholds, correctly recollects, and practices according to the teachings of the *prajñā*, there are no afflictions.
It is like a potent medicine that can eliminate all diseases;
if it cannot cure the ailment, it is not the fault of the medicine, but rather due to a failure to apply it properly.
Furthermore, it is like a person with impaired vision who, despite possessing sharp weapons, is unable to withstand danger; this is not the fault of the weapons.

In the same way, when a practitioner fails to attain the power of *prajñā* due to heavy sins from previous lives or because they do not act according to the teachings in the present life, this is not the fault of *prajñā*.
Question:
Since the Prajñāpāramitā also exists in the heavens, why do the devas seek to hear the Prajñā on the six fast days by following after the impure human body?
The answer is:
There are sutra scrolls in the heavens; such is what has been heard by tradition, yet they were not spoken by the Buddha.
If they did exist, they would have to exist in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or the Tuṣita Heaven.
Why is this? When the asuras were fighting with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Buddha commanded Śakra:
"You should recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā."
"In the Tuṣita Heaven, there is always a Bodhisattva in his final birth who preaches for the sake of the devas; therefore, it may exist there.

As for the devas of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), their bodies and clothing are so subtle and light that they do not even possess the weight of two units; they constantly delight in tranquil seclusion and experience the flavor of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi). For this reason, there should be no physical scriptures there."
The devas are attached to two kinds of pleasure—
the pleasure of desire and the pleasure of meditative concentration— and thus cannot diligently transcribe, uphold, or study the Prajñāpāramitā with arduous effort. The people of Jambudvīpa, however,
are able to apply themselves with diligence to transcribing, upholding, studying, and correctly recollecting it.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The people of Jambudvīpa surpass those of the heavens and those of Uttarakuru for three reasons:
first, they are able to sever lustful desire; second, they possess powerful power of mindfulness and recollection; third, they are capable of diligent and courageous exertion."

Because the people of this Jambudvīpa can write it down, read it, recite it, and uphold it, for this reason the devas descend to pay homage to the volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, or they wish to hear it being expounded.
Furthermore, some say:

"If there are scriptural volumes in the heavens, one should come from afar to make offerings to them; thus merit and virtue will increase, and one shall never grow weary in seeking the Prajñāpāramitā."

There are bodhisattvas whom the devas desire to cause to be honored for their prajñā; thus they descend from above, wishing to increase the faith and reverence of sentient beings, thinking: "If even the devas come, how much more so should we!"
If a practitioner smells a fragrant scent or sees a radiance, because of such rare occurrences, they will develop deep faith and joy in the *prajñā*.
Furthermore, for those who have not yet abandoned desire, evil spirits and the subjects of Māra constantly pursue them, seeking an opportunity to cause them to fall into evil realms;
however, when the great powerful devas from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven arrive, these minor spirits flee away.
The Bodhisattva was able to give rise to the pure great mind as described in the preceding chapter; for this reason, he followed after the Dharma Master.
On the six fast days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), the various devas come to observe the minds of human beings; on the fifteenth and thirtieth days, they report [their findings] upward to the higher devas.
Furthermore, these six days of fasting are ill-omened days that cause people to suffer decline and misfortune;

yet, if on such days one receives the eight precepts, observes the fast, practices giving, and listens to the Dharma, the devas will rejoice, the minor spirits will find no opportunity to harm them, and the practitioner will receive benefit.
On this day, the Dharma Master ascends the high seat to preach the Dharma; for various causes and conditions such as these, all the devas come.
The preacher of the Dharma extols the immeasurable, boundless, and unsurpassed Dharma—namely, the Prajñāpāramitā—and likewise attains immeasurable and boundless merit.
If one explains this to humans, because those humans have dull faculties and meager merit, they obtain little merit;
whereas the devas have sharp faculties, abundant merit, and superior fields of merit, and thus they obtain much merit.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"When a practitioner recites the Prajñāpāramitā on an upoṣadha day before the devas and the great assembly, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.

In this passage, the Buddha endorses what Subhūti has said and further explains the causes and conditions for immeasurable merit, namely: "The Prajñāpāramitā is the most precious jewel of all perfections (pāramitās)."
Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can satisfy all the wishes of people,
so too this Prajñāpāramitā can fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings— namely, that they may be free from suffering and attain happiness.
Regarding the removal of suffering, the Prajñāpāramitā can uproot sentient beings from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and human poverty;
regarding the bestowal of happiness, it can grant them birth into great kṣatriya clans and even lead them to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

These wholesome dharmas that are the causes and conditions for happiness are explained in detail within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, namely the ten paths of wholesome action up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Just as a wish-fulfilling gem can produce clothing, food and drink, gold, silver, and so forth, according to whatever is required by one's wishes;
so too is the *Prajñāpāramitā*: it enables the attainment of everything from the ten paths of wholesome action up to all-knowledge, and from the great clans of the *kṣatriyas* up to Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is called the "Jewel Perfection" (*ratnapāramitā*). Furthermore, regarding the "Jewel Perfection":
it is like a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); they obtain whatever they require according to their wishes, and if they lose it, they suffer distress.
This Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished; it is never lost, bestowing happiness upon sentient beings in every lifetime, and finally causing them to attain the Buddha-way.

Just as when a person obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel, their mind becomes conceited and they look down upon others—this being a cause and condition for decline—so too is it with one who attains worldly *prajñāpāramitā*.

If they likewise engage in such discrimination, becoming attached to various wholesome dharmas and rejecting various unwholesome dharmas, giving rise to a sense of superiority and despising others, they open the gates to all transgressions.

Within this precious Prajñāpāramitā, the supramundane Prajñāpāramitā, one does not differentiate between the wholesome and the unwholesome; this is called the Great Precious Pāramitā, which is able to benefit sentient beings and ultimately brings freedom from sorrow.
This treasure-like *pāramitā* cannot even be defiled by wholesome dharmas, let alone by unwholesome ones!
As it is said here, "In this way, one does not know," just as the characteristics of *prajñā* were explained above: one neither forms such knowledge nor acts as a knower;
one does not grasp at marks nor give rise to attachment; one does not engage in discrimination, and does not apprehend a fixed characteristic.
This is called "being without faults, being without attachment to dharmas, and severing all conceptual proliferation.

Such a person is able to truly practice the *prajñāpāramitā*; because they honor the Buddha through the Dharma and personally attain the benefit of the true Dharma, they are able to benefit sentient beings;
because they can personally distance themselves from evil and cause sentient beings to distance themselves from evil, they attain a pure Buddha-field.

By means of the power of the skillful method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-upāya*), one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) possess the characteristic of ultimate quiescence (*atyanta-śānta-lakṣaṇa*), yet for the sake of sentient beings, one is able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas.
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately pure, it possesses neither power nor lack of power;
it is like space (*ākāśa*), which, though devoid of any dharma, allows for the accomplishment of activities by virtue of space.
There is not a single dharma with a fixed characteristic to which one can become attached;

therefore, [in that state] there is no power. Yet, upon attaining the true nature of all dharmas, one is unimpeded regarding all wholesome dharmas, even unto the subduing of Māra and the attainment of Buddhahood; it is not that there is no power.
"Neither receiving nor giving," "neither arising nor ceasing," and so forth, up to "neither abandoning conditioned phenomena nor bestowing unconditioned phenomena," are likewise.
In this regard, the causal condition is explained:
"Whether a Buddha exists or does not exist, the nature of all phenomena (dharmatā) eternally abides in the world.
The nature of all phenomena is precisely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one seeks the true reality of all phenomena by means of permanence, impermanence, and so forth, these are all errors;
if a person enters into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to seek it, then there will be no error or delusion.
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternal, it is not lost.

[Sūtra] At that time, the sons of the gods stood in the sky, raising a great sound and leaping for joy; they scattered *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers over the Buddha, speaking thus:
"We behold the turning of the second wheel of Dharma in Jambudvīpa."
Within this, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This turning of the wheel of Dharma is neither the first turning nor the second turning."
"This Prajñāpāramitā does not arise for the sake of turning away, nor does it arise for the sake of returning, because of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why is it that, because of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the Prajñāpāramitā does not proceed nor does it return?
The Buddha said, "The Prajñāpāramitā is empty of the characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā; even so, the Dānapāramitā is empty of the characteristic of the Dānapāramitā."

Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness; up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence, which is empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence and existence;

the four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness; up to and including the eightfold noble path, which is empty of the characteristic of the eightfold noble path;

the ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the characteristic of the ten powers of a Buddha; up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The fruit of srotāpanna is empty of the characteristics of the fruit of srotāpanna; the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin is empty of the characteristics of the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin; the fruit of anāgāmin is empty of the characteristics of the fruit of anāgāmin; the fruit of arhat is empty of the characteristics of the fruit of arhat; the path of pratyekabuddha is empty of the characteristics of the path of pratyekabuddha;
and the knowledge of all modes is empty of the characteristics of the knowledge of all modes.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the mahāpāramitā!”

Why is this? Although all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics, it is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet there is no dharma that can be apprehended.
Turning the wheel of Dharma, there is no dharma that can be turned, nor any dharma that can be returned;
within this Mahāprajñāpāramitā, there is likewise no dharma to be perceived.
Why is this? Because these dharmas cannot be apprehended, whether in their progression or their return, for all dharmas are ultimately unarisen. Why is this?
This mark of emptiness cannot be turned back nor returned; this mark of signlessness cannot be turned back nor returned; this mark of wishlessness cannot be turned back nor returned.

If one can thus speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*, teaching, illuminating, opening, demonstrating, analyzing, manifesting, explaining, and making it easy to understand—if there is one who can teach in this way, this is called the pure exposition of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
There is no speaker, no recipient, and no one who realizes;
if there is no speaking, no receiving, and no realizing, then there is also no one who brings about cessation, and within this teaching of the Dharma, there is likewise no fixed field of merit.
[Treatise] Commentary:
When the devas hear the Prajñā, they experience great joy and leap for gladness.
The bodies of the devas are light and their faculties are sharp; yet because they discriminate and cling to marks, they perceive that there is lightness and heaviness.
Having heard that the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately pure, the equal and true mark of reality, and brings great benefit to sentient beings such that none can surpass it, they leap for joy and rejoice.
Rising from their seats, they took up offering implements such as lotuses and made offerings to the Buddha, saying:
"We have witnessed the turning of the second wheel of Dharma here in Jambudvīpa."

Question: When the first teaching of the Dharma causes people to attain the Path, this is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma. Why, then, is it now said that "the second turning of the wheel of the Dharma" occurs?
If that which is spoken by the Buddha is called "turning the wheel of Dharma," then all such teachings are the wheel of Dharma; why limit it to the second [turning]?
The answer is:

the first teaching of the Dharma is definitively and substantially the one wheel of Dharma; because it was first turned, everything up until the exhaustion of the Dharma is collectively termed "turning."
These devas, seeing that many within this assembly had resolved upon the unsurpassed path and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas,
and perceiving this benefit, praised it by saying, "The second turning of the wheel of Dharma."

When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, eighty thousand devas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and Ājñātakauṇḍinya alone attained the first stage of the Path;
now, immeasurable devas have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, and for this reason it is said that the second turning of the Wheel of Dharma occurs.
The turning of the wheel of Dharma now seems like the first turning.
Question:
At the first turning of the wheel of Dharma, few attained the Way, whereas at this turning, many have attained the Way; how can you use the great to illustrate the small?
The answer is:
The deeds of the Buddhas are of two kinds:
first, the secret; second, the manifest.
When he first turned the wheel of Dharma, eighty thousand śrāvakas and one person were seen to attain the first stage of the Path.

The Bodhisattvas see countless asaṃkhyeya beings attaining the path of the śrāvakas; countless beings planting the causal conditions for the path of the pratyekabuddhas; countless asaṃkhyeya beings generating the mind for the unsurpassed path; countless asaṃkhyeya beings practicing the path of the six pāramitās and attaining various profound samādhis and dhāraṇī-gates; immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings dwelling from the first stage up to the tenth stage; immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings attaining the state of being in their last birth before Buddhahood (ekajāti-pratibaddha); immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); and hearing this Dharma, swiftly attaining the path of Buddhahood—such inconceivable manifestations as these are called the characteristics of the secret turning of the wheel of Dharma.
For example, when it rains heavily, a large tree receives much water while a small tree receives little.
For this reason, one should know that the first turning of the wheel of Dharma was also great; thus, using the later as a metaphor for the earlier is without fault.

Regarding the statement that "the turning of the wheel of Dharma is neither one nor two," this is spoken thus for the sake of ultimate emptiness and the nirvana that is the fruit of turning the wheel of Dharma; it is, therefore, a case of speaking of the fruit within the cause.
The Wheel of Dharma is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā;
since this Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of neither arising nor acting, it neither turns forward nor turns back.
As it is said in the [teaching on] the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination:
Because ignorance is ultimately empty, it cannot truly give rise to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth;
because ignorance is false, inverted, and lacks any real stability, there is no dharma that can be extinguished.
Because it speaks of the phenomena of worldly arising, it is called "turning";
because it speaks of the phenomena of worldly cessation, it is called "returning.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, these two things do not exist; therefore, it is said that there is no turning and no returning.
"Because of the emptiness of non-existence and existence"—the absence of turning is the "emptiness of existence," and the absence of returning is the "emptiness of non-existence.
Question: Why does Subhūti ask this question: "Because of the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the Prajñāpāramitā issues forth neither for the sake of turning nor for the sake of returning"?
Yet the Buddha replies with emptiness?
The answer is: Some say:
All phenomena have four kinds of characteristics:
first, they are said to exist; second, they are said not to exist; third, they are said to both exist and not exist; and fourth, they are said to neither exist nor not exist.
In this regard, because of wrong mindfulness, there are four kinds of wrong practice; because one is attached to these four dharmas, they are called the "wrong path.
In this regard, because of right mindfulness, there are four kinds of right practice; because one is not attached to them, they are called the "right path."
In this context, because it refutes both non-existence and existence, it is called "the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.
The Buddha taught that by refuting even non-existence and existence, there is "no turning forward and no returning."
There are two ways to refute "neither existence nor non-existence":
first, by using the preceding three propositions to refute it; second, by using the true reality (*dharmatā*) of *nirvāṇa* to refute it.

Although Subhūti knows that the Buddha uses *nirvāṇa* to dismantle existence and non-existence, therein there may be bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and, due to error, employ three propositions to refute "neither existence nor non-existence," thereby giving rise to false views even within the emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas.

For this reason, the Buddha says, "Existent dharmas and non-existent dharmas are also empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*)," and thus he says, "The *prajñāpāramitā* has no turning forward and no returning."
Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no characteristic of *prajñāpāramitā*, because all dharmas are without characteristics;
this applies likewise even to the *dānapāramitā*.
It is likewise for everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the characteristics of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, Subhūti and the great assembly rejoiced and praised the *prajñāpāramitā*, saying:
"The great *pāramitā* is what is called the *prajñāpāramitā*."

"Great Perfection (Mahāpāramitā) means that although all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, the Prajñāpāramitā is able to benefit the bodhisattva, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
yet even though it is attained, there is nothing attained;
and even though the wheel of Dharma is turned, there is nothing turned."
Question:
If all dharmas are empty, the prajñāpāramitā is empty, and anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is also empty, one should not praise prajñā as the mahāpāramitā.
The answer is:

Because it is taught herein that all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), and within this emptiness of intrinsic nature there is also no emptiness of intrinsic nature; for this reason, it is called the Mahāpāramitā.
If there were no characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should not raise such an objection.
Because it is ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*), there is nothing that obstructs it; yet, through the practice of various wholesome dharmas, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is according to worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) and is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Although the Buddhas preach the Dharma to enable others to attain the Way and destroy their afflictions—moving from this state to that—they are said to "turn" [the wheel].
Now, our various afflictions are deceptive, inverted, false, and lack any fixed characteristic;
if they have no fixed characteristic, what is there to be severed?
If there is nothing to be abandoned, there is neither progression nor regression; therefore it is said, "Although the wheel of Dharma is turned, there is neither turning nor returning. Why is this?
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be seen by the five eyes as either revolving or returning, because all dharmas have been ultimately unborn from the very beginning.
This is emptiness of intrinsic nature and ultimate emptiness; it is neither a phase of transformation nor a phase of return.
It does not transform for fear of falling into permanence, and it does not return for fear of falling into annihilation;
it does not transform for fear of falling into existence, and it does not return for fear of falling into non-existence.
Because they fear attachment to the world, they do not turn back; because they fear attachment to nirvāṇa, they do not return.
Thus, the immeasurable emptinesses—such as intrinsic emptiness, ultimate emptiness, and the eighteen emptinesses—are the gate of liberation of emptiness, which neither turns back nor returns;
the same applies to signlessness and wishlessness.
Entering these three gates of liberation and abandoning the mind of "I" and "mine" is called attaining liberation.
Being able thus not to grasp at signs and not to cling with the mind, one explains the *prajñāpāramitā*, teaching, illuminating, and so forth.
"Explanation" refers to either consulting the written text or receiving oral transmission.
"Instruction" refers to praising the Prajñāpāramitā for others, causing them to receive, uphold, read, recite, and maintain correct mindfulness of it.
"Shining" (zhào) is like a person holding a lamp to illuminate objects;
if one does not know prajñā, it uses the light of wisdom to illuminate it so that one may come to know it.
"Opening" (kāi) is like a treasure store whose door is closed; although there are fine things within, they cannot be obtained.
If one opens its door, then one may take whatever one desires.
Likewise, for those who doubt and do not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā, if they open the gate of false doubt and break the bolt of ignorance, such persons may then take whatever they desire.
"Indicating" means, for example, like a person whose eyesight is unclear pointing out what is beautiful or ugly;
or like one who possesses little faith and little wisdom being shown what is the path and what is not the path, what is beneficial and what is a loss, and so forth.
"Differentiation" means to differentiate all phenomena as being wholesome or unwholesome, sinful or meritorious, mundane or nirvāṇic.
The sūtras provide brief explanations that are difficult to understand and difficult to believe;
one is able to explain them extensively through differentiation so that others may attain faith and understanding.

Regarding "manifestation": for the sake of various sentient beings, the Buddha teaches various dharmas; at times he disparages wholesome dharmas or assists unwholesome dharmas, solely to lead sentient beings toward understanding.
"Expounding the Dharma" means explaining the Buddha’s intended meaning in accordance with sentient beings, so that they may understand the characteristics of what is weighty and what is light.
"Explaining" means that it is like precious objects within a bag: if the opening is tied shut, people do not know of them;
but if one unties the bag of the sutra for others, one explains its principles and meanings.
Furthermore, it is like a heavy object that is split apart to make it light;
through various causes, conditions, and parables, the beginning and end are explained so that they may be easily understood.
"Shallow and easy" means that just as deep water is difficult to cross, if someone disperses this water to make it shallow, then all who would cross will find it easy.

The Prajñāpāramitā is as profoundly deep as water; yet, through the power of skillful means in its exegesis, it is explained in various ways so that it may become shallow and easy to access, such that even those of limited intelligence can believe and understand it.
To be able to expound the profound meaning by means of these ten [categories] as the foremost is called the pure exposition of the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is in fact nothing that is spoken, because it is ultimately empty; because there is "no speaking," there is "no receiving"; because there is "no receiving," there is "no realization"; and because there is "no realization," there is "no extinction of afflictions. If there is no extinction of afflictions, then there is "no field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
"Receiving" refers to receiving with faith, reading, and reciting.
To practice this Dharma and thereby attain the fruits of the śramaṇa and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is called "realization."
At the time of realization, all afflictions are extinguished, and one attains *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).
Because one has attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one is a field of merit that is definitively fixed (*niyata*).

"Definitively fixed" means that all phenomena share the nature of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder); therefore, it is said that there is no field of merit that is not definitively fixed.
44. Chapter on the Perfections. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Perfections, Number Forty-four. [Sūtra] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"The boundless *pāramitā* is this *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is like space, which is boundless."
"World-Honored One!
The perfection of equality is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas are equal.
Second: “World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is free from [all things].”
The Buddha said:
"Because it is ultimately empty.
[Third: "World-Honored One!"
“The perfection of non-destruction is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
“Because all dharmas are unattainable.”
"World-Honored One!
The perfection that has no further shore is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is nameless and bodiless.
5. “World-Honored One!
The perfection of the element of space is the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said:
“Because inhalation and exhalation cannot be apprehended.
6. “World-Honored One!
“The perfection that is ineffable is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said,
“Because mental application and discursive thought are unapprehendable.”
"7. 'World-Honored One!
The nameless perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:"
“Because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended.
8. “World-Honored One!
The non-departing perfection is the perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said:

[Treatise] Explanation:
Regarding "the boundless *pāramitā*," Subhūti, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the meaning of the great jewel *pāramitā*, consequently praised Prajñā as the *mahāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, having entered deeply into various dharma-gates through wisdom, he contemplates the prajñāpāramitā as being like the waters of the great ocean—immeasurable and boundless;
knowing deeply the merits of the prajñāpāramitā, he gives rise to great joy;
desiring to praise the prajñāpāramitā through various causes and conditions, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The boundless *pāramitā* is this *prajñāpāramitā*.
” Regarding the meaning of “boundless,” from the beginning of this chapter to its conclusion, it is entirely the meaning of being boundless.
This is explained briefly because it would obstruct the discussion of other matters; if explained extensively, it would be immeasurable.

Furthermore, permanence is one extreme and impermanence is another extreme; self and non-self, existence and non-existence, the world being finite or infinite, and sentient beings being finite or infinite—such dharmas as these are called the extremes of false views.
Upon attaining the Prajñāpāramitā, these various extremes no longer exist; therefore, it is called "boundless" (*ananta*).
Furthermore, for example, the point where a substance is exhausted is called a "limit" (anta); because space is without color and without form, it is limitless.
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately pure, it has no limit, no exhaustion, no place of grasping, and no place of reception;
therefore, the Buddha replied:
"Just as space is boundless, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā* boundless.

When a bodhisattva attains the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), they contemplate all dharmas as entirely equal; therefore, because it is said that all dharmas are equal, it is called the "equality *pāramitā*."
The Bodhisattva, by means of the mind of ultimate emptiness, is free from all afflictions and also free from all dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Detachment.
By means of this Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva seeks all dharmas through their general and specific characteristics, yet does not find even a hair’s breadth of a fixed characteristic.
Because nothing can be found, the mind does not cling to any dharma.

If there are those with false views and frivolous conceptualization who, using their attachment to false views, desire to destroy this bodhisattva, that bodhisattva cannot be destroyed because they have no attachments; this is called the "perfection of being unbreakable" (akṣayapāramitā).
This shore is called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); the other shore is called *nirvāṇa*. Between them lies the great river of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
All those who have left the household life desire to abandon this shore and cling to the other shore;
yet the Prajñāpāramitā has no "other shore. That other shore is *nirvāṇa*, which is without form and without name. Therefore it is said:
"Because it is without form and without name, it is called the 'Perfection of No-Further Shore' (apārapāramitā).
Where there is space, there are inhalation and exhalation; these inhalations and exhalations all arise from the causes and conditions of deceptive karma.
That which goes out is not that which comes in, and that which comes in is not that which goes out; arising and ceasing moment by moment, their true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) cannot be apprehended."
Because breath cannot be apprehended, all dharmas also cannot be apprehended;
because they cannot be apprehended, it is called the "Perfection of the Element of Emptiness.
Because all dharmas possess the characteristic of emptiness and quiescence, there is no need for vitarka and vicāra.
Because vitarka and vicāra are absent, there is no verbal expression;
because there is no verbal expression, it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* cuts off the path of language. For this reason, it is called the "Ineffable *Pāramitā*."
Two dharmas encompass all dharmas, namely name (nāma) and form (rūpa).
The four great elements and derived matter are subsumed under form;
the four aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā) are subsumed under name.
Those who analyze all phenomena say:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of wisdom; therefore, it is subsumed under the category of names.

However, in reality, form is not separate from names, and names are not separate from form. Since this *prajñāpāramitā* lacks the characteristic of cognition, it is said that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable"; thus, it is called the "nameless *pāramitā*."
Because all dharmas neither come nor go, it is called the "Perfection of No Departure" (Agatipāramitā).

The Prajñāpāramitā is the treasury of the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time and the ten directions; it is sealed with the Three Dharma Seals and cannot be destroyed by any deva or human, and is therefore called the "Perfection of No Shifting" (Ananyathāpāramitā).
All conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment and have no time of abiding.
If this is so, then past phenomena do not exhaust, future phenomena do not exhaust, and present phenomena do not exhaust because they do not abide;
since the exhaustion of the three periods of time cannot be apprehended, it is called ultimate exhaustion.
Because it is ultimately exhausted, it is called the "perfection of exhaustion" (*kṣayapāramitā*).

Because the arising of all phenomena cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time, they are unarisen; because they are unarisen, it is called the "perfection of non-arising" (*anutpādapāramitā*).
The "perfection of non-extinction" is also like this.
There are two kinds of activity:
first, the activity of sentient beings; second, the activity of dharmas.
The "sentient being as agent" refers to acts such as giving and observing precepts;
the "dharma as agent" refers to things such as burning by fire or rotting by water, which are known by the mind-consciousness.
Because sentient beings are empty, there is no agent.
All dharmas are dull because they do not give rise to the characteristic of activity; thus, dharmas themselves do not act.
Because these two are without action, it is called the "Perfection of Non-action."
The "Perfection of Non-Cognition" is also like this: because all dharmas are insentient, there is nothing to be known.
While the divine eye perceives birth and death, the eye of wisdom of emptiness perceives that birth and death cannot be apprehended;

because birth and death cannot be apprehended, when beings of the present life die, none go on to a future life. It is merely that the five aggregates arise in continuous succession due to the causes and conditions of prior karma; therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Non-Arrival."
The Prajñāpāramitā does not lose the true mark of all dharmas, and it can also cause all dharmas not to lose their true mark;
apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, all dharmas are lost.
By contemplating the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one attains the *prajñāpāramitā*; for this reason, it is called the "non-failing *pāramitā*.

(43) [Treatise] Explanation:
Subhūti praised the Prajñāpāramitā, showing sentient beings that the world is empty like a dream.
The Buddha said:
"Because even a dream cannot be apprehended, it is called the 'Dream Pāramitā.'"
So it is with echoes, shadows, mirages, and illusions.
The human mind regards sound as real and the echo as unreal;
it regards the face and the mirror as real and the reflected image as unreal.
In a mirage, wind, dust, and sunlight are taken as real while water is taken as unreal;
in an illusion, the incantation is taken as real while that which is produced by the incantation is taken as unreal.
Subhūti praised *prajñā* by means of metaphors as being empty, and the Buddha stated that both metaphors and fundamental events (*nidāna*) are all empty.
Because all fundamental entities are empty, this analogy is also empty.
This Prajñāpāramitā is stainless and is able to sever and extinguish all stains.
The Buddha said:
All afflictions have been eternally non-existent from the very beginning; what, then, is there to be severed now?
For this reason, it is called the "Stainless Perfection" (*vimala-pāramitā*).
The "Pure Perfection" (*viśuddha-pāramitā*) is also like this.
The absence of afflictions is "purity.
Lust, hatred, and other such afflictions are called "defilements";
this Prajñāpāramitā is not defiled by any such impure dharmas.

The six sense faculties are the locus of all afflictions; yet, since neither the six sense faculties nor any phenomena can be found as the causal conditions for, or the dwelling place of, any afflictions, it is called the "unsoiled pāramitā."
Having attained this Prajñāpāramitā, all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), recollection, and discrimination are extinguished; therefore, it is called the "Non-proliferation Pāramitā.
Because all phenomena are ultimately empty, they are without the characteristics of recollection or mindfulness;
because they lack the characteristics of recollection and mindfulness, it is called the "Non-mindfulness Pāramitā."
A Bodhisattva who abides in the *dharmatā* cannot be defeated by any disputants, nor can they be obscured by any fetters (*saṃyojana*) or false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Although all phenomena are impermanent and subject to destruction, their mind gives rise to no sorrow.
For such reasons, it is called the "Immovable Perfection" (*akṣobhya-pāramitā*).
All dharmas are false conceptions; they are not merely objects of attachment and defilement, and for this reason it is called the "Perfection of Non-attachment.
Conceptualization and discrimination are the root of all fetters (saṃyojana);
when there are fetters, one can give rise to karma that leads to future rebirths.

Knowing that conceptualization, recollection, and discrimination are illusory, and because all karmic actions leading to rebirth in future lives will no longer arise, this is called the "perfection of non-arising."
Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not grasp at the characteristics of the fires of the three poisons; therefore, it is called the "perfection of quiescence.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only that the characteristics of the three poisons are quiescent, but because the characteristics of all dharmas are unattainable."
"This Prajñāpāramitā does not even crave among wholesome dharmas, let alone other desires!
The Buddha said:
'Desire has been unobtainable from the very beginning.'"
Greed is deceptive and its intrinsic nature is unattainable; therefore, it is called the "perfection of desirelessness.
It is not because of being separated from desire that it is called desireless.
Because the nature of anger is ultimately non-existent, it is called the "Perfection of Non-Anger";
it is not that one is called non-angry because of being separated from anger.
Because the darkness of ignorance is destroyed within all phenomena, it is called the "Perfection of Non-Delusion."
It is not that one is called "without delusion" simply because delusion has been extinguished.

Regarding the "perfection of being without afflictions," because the bodhisattva has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), all afflictions are extinguished.
The Buddha said:
"Recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination are the root of afflictions;
since even recollection and conceptualization do not exist, how much less so the afflictions!"
Therefore, it is called the "Perfection of No Afflictions.
Because Prajñā can destroy the perversion of perceiving a sentient being where there is no sentient being, it is called the "Perfection of No Sentient Beings."
The Buddha said:
"These sentient beings have been unborn and non-existent from the very beginning; therefore, they are called 'non-sentient beings.
Subhūti thought to himself:
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* can sever all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), it is called the "Perfection of Severance" (*chedanapāramitā*).
The Buddha said:
All phenomena do not arise, are not born, and are without activity; because all phenomena possess the characteristic of being naturally severed, they are called "severed."

The two extremes refer to what are known as self and non-self, annihilation and non-annihilation, phenomena subject to cessation and phenomena not subject to cessation, permanence and extinction, existence and non-existence—such are the immeasurable pairs of extremes.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, none of these extremes exist; therefore, it is called the "Pāramitā Free from the Two Extremes."
The Buddha said:
"These various extremes have been non-existent from the very beginning; they are merely adhered to due to falsehood and inversion.
Because Bodhisattvas seek the reality of things, they depart from these inverted extremes."
Because this Prajñāpāramitā has but a single characteristic—emptiness—it cannot be destroyed.
The Buddha said:
"Not only is Prajñāpāramitā thus; all dharmas likewise lack any fixed or distinct characteristics."
If one does not depart from the cause, the cause does not depart from the fruit;
conditioned phenomena do not depart from unconditioned phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena do not depart from conditioned phenomena;
the Prajñāpāramitā does not depart from all dharmas, and all dharmas do not depart from the Prajñāpāramitā.
The true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is itself the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, it is called the "indestructible *pāramitā*.
That which is "destroyed" refers to the various phenomena being individually dispersed and separated.
All dharmas possess the faults of being permanent, impermanent, and so forth;
therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā does not grasp at any dharma.
The Buddha said:
One does not even grasp at any phenomena, including the supramundane pure dharmas of the two vehicles; therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Non-Grasping.
To differentiate and give rise to a mind based on the characteristics of grasping is deluded conceptualization;
because the Prajñāpāramitā is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), such deluded conceptualization does not exist therein.
The Buddha said:
"Because of conceptualization and discrimination, there is the discrimination of existence and non-existence;
yet this present conceptualization and discrimination has been non-existent from the very beginning. Therefore, it is called the 'Perfection of Non-discrimination.'"
The Prajñāpāramitā gives rise to the four immeasurables; therefore, it is called the "Immeasurable Pāramitā.
Furthermore, because ultimate emptiness attains the immeasurable dharmas of nirvāṇa, it is called "immeasurable."
Furthermore, that which the limits of wisdom cannot reach is called "immeasurable.
This refers to that which is calculated and measured by the six sense faculties;
yet this Dharma is empty, signless, and without arising or ceasing, and thus cannot be measured by the six sense faculties.
"Why is this? Because the substance is great while the measuring vessel is small.
The Buddha said:
It is not only that the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable; because all dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are ungraspable, they are all immeasurable.
Just as space is without color, without form, and incapable of performing any action, so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only that space is non-existent; all dharmas, such as form and the rest, are likewise non-existent. Therefore, it is called the 'Perfection of Space.'"

The perfection of the Buddha-dharmas is this Perfection of Wisdom."
The Buddha said:
“Because it transcends all dharmas.
87. “World-Honored One!”
"One who speaks according to reality speaks of the perfection that is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because all speech is according to reality."
"World-Honored One!
The perfection of spontaneity is the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Because of mastery over all dharmas.
89. "World-Honored One!
The Buddha-pāramitā is this prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said:
"Because of knowing all dharmas and the knowledge of all modes, [it is] ninety.
[Treatise] Explanation:
Within the *prajñāpāramitā* there is the noble practice of impermanence; therefore, it is called the "Impermanence *Pāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only within *prajñā* that there is impermanence; because one contemplates all phenomena as impermanent, it is called the 'Impermanence *Pāramitā*.'"
Question: Previously it was stated that "the dharma-nature of Prajñāpāramitā is eternally abiding," yet why is it now said to be "impermanent"? Answer:
The Prajñāpāramitā is wisdom; it contemplates that phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and because they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they are impermanent.

The objects of focus for the Prajñāpāramitā—suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), and therefore they are permanent.
Subhūti speaks of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) prajñā; therefore, he says that the *prajñāpāramitā* is impermanent. Question:

If this is so, why does the Buddha say, "All phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely subject to destruction and impermanence, whereas unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena have no characteristic of destruction"?
Answer: All dharmas are called the six sense-faculties; both internal and external are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because they are conditioned phenomena, they necessarily revert to the characteristic of disintegration.
Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there are no unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), nor is there any further characteristic of phenomena;
it is because of the characteristic of conditioned phenomena that one speaks of unconditioned phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are of two kinds:
first, the "all" of names; second, the "all" of reality.
Because all conditioned phenomena are subject to disintegration, they are called "all-impermanent."
The same applies from "suffering" up to "the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Subhūti praised the Prajñāpāramitā by describing the characteristics of all dharmas, and the Buddha responded by citing all dharmas.

The correct contemplation of the four dharmas, such as the body and so forth, arises from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The four foundations of mindfulness are the initial gateway to the Four Noble Truths; the Four Noble Truths are the initial gateway to the four fruits of the śramaṇa; and the differentiation of the fruit of arhatship constitutes the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The four foundations of mindfulness are explained in various ways at length within the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:
"Because these four kinds of dharmas as objects of focus have been unobtainable from the very beginning, they are called the 'Pāramitā of Mindfulness.'"
The same applies from the "four right efforts" up to the "perfection of wisdom.
Question:
Other dharmas may be used to praise the perfection of wisdom; why, then, is the perfection of wisdom itself used to praise the perfection of wisdom?
Answer: There are two kinds of prajñā:
first, eternally abiding prajñā; [second, adventitious prajñā].
Second, there is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* in conjunction with the other five *pāramitās*, which possesses utility.
Subhūti praised this useful *prajñāpāramitā*, noting that it can destroy the darkness of ignorance and bestow true wisdom;
for this reason, the Buddha said:
"Because one abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither delusion nor wisdom can be apprehended.

When a bodhisattva practices this *prajñāpāramitā*, they first attain the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a bodhisattva and subsequently attain the ten powers of a Buddha; for this reason, it is called the "power-perfection" (*balapāramitā*).
The Buddha said:
"Not only is the One Possessing the Ten Powers indestructible and unsubduable, but the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena is likewise indestructible and unsubduable."
The Buddha’s intention was this:
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he spoke of the power of the Buddhas of the ten directions as being immeasurable and boundless;
just like the power of a Buddha, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is likewise invincible, and is therefore called the "Perfection of the Ten Powers" (*daśabala-pāramitā*).
When a bodhisattva attains this power of the prajñāpāramitā, they are able to preach the Dharma and engage in debate before the Buddha, let alone in other places!
They do not even fear the Māra King, let alone non-Buddhist outsiders!
Therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Fearlessness.
The Buddha said:
"Because the knowledge of the aspects of the path does not sink."
The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is called the Dharma-eye; it knows by which paths all sentient beings attain *nirvāṇa*.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is the mark of eternal quiescence and is ineffable;
yet, by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, this bodhisattva guides sentient beings and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

Because the knowledge of the aspects of the path increases, one does not sink; being fearless and without self-conceit regarding the thought "I possess these dharmas," it is called the "perfection of fearlessness."
Having heard this from the Buddha, Subhūti’s fearlessness deepened further; thus he praised the *prajñāpāramitā*, calling it the "unimpeded *pāramitā*.
The Buddha said:

"It is not merely the four kinds of unimpededness; because all dharmas enter into suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they all possess the characteristic of being unimpeded."

Because a bodhisattva, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, is able to gather all the Buddha-dharmas—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and great loving-kindness and great compassion—it is called the "Buddha-dharma *pāramitā*."
The Buddha said:

"The Dharma of the Śrāvakas is superior to the Dharma of ordinary persons; the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas is superior to the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; and the Dharma of the Buddhas is the most supreme among all dharmas."
Just as space is vast among all forms, so too is the Buddha-dharma supreme, beyond compare, beyond analogy, and transcending all phenomena; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-dharma Pāramitā."

Just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the six *pāramitās* and attained the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, so too does the present Buddha practice the six *pāramitās* and attain the path of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata-pāramitā."
"Tathāgata" may be called "Tathāgata," or "One who speaks according to reality," or "One who knows according to reality."
In this regard, the Buddha said:

"It is not only that which the Buddha speaks that is called 'speaking according to reality'; all speech is in accordance with reality. Therefore, it is named the 'Perfection of Speaking According to Reality' (bhūtavāda-pāramitā)."
When this *prajñāpāramitā* is perfected, one spontaneously becomes a Buddha in a subsequent life; therefore, it is called the "spontaneous *pāramitā*.
"Spontaneous" refers to the Buddha;
because it was spoken by the Buddha, it is called the "spontaneous *pāramitā*."
Furthermore, this *prajñāpāramitā* is naturally so in its true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and does not arise through the agency of another; therefore, it is called "natural" (*svayambhū*).
The Buddha said:
Because the Buddha has attained the power of mastery over all dharmas, it is called the "natural *pāramitā*."

Being fully endowed with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), attaining the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), turning the wheel of Dharma, and beating the drum of Dharma, one awakens sentient beings who are sleeping in the darkness of ignorance within the world; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-pāramitā."
"Buddha" is translated in the Qin language as "the Awakened One" or "the Knower.
What does this mean?
It refers to one who correctly knows all phenomena (dharmas) in all their aspects; therefore, he is called "Awakened."
"All dharmas" refers to the so-called five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), and so forth.
Furthermore, "all dharmas" also includes the scriptures of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), technical arts, meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so on;

briefly stated, there are five kinds, namely: the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of Buddhas.
The Buddha’s concise knowledge consists of two kinds of characteristics, namely general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
furthermore, there are the characteristics of differentiation and the characteristics of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
His extensive knowledge comprises all modes (*sarvākāra*), wherein "all modes" refers to all immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates.
For this reason, it is called the "Buddha-pāramitā";
it is not called the Buddha-pāramitā because of the Buddha's body, but solely because of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Sixty-Five;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter Praising Faith and Practice, Number Forty-Five,
Scroll Sixty-Six.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 45: Praising Faith and Practice. [Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra had this thought:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should merely hear the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with their ears, such a person must have performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and associated with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); how much more so if they receive, uphold, draw near to, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and practice according to the teaching!"
It should be known that these sons and daughters of good family have frequently drawn near to many Buddhas; they are able to hear, receive, practice according to the teachings, question, and answer.

It should be known that because these sons and daughters of good family have, in previous lives, frequently made offerings to and drawn near to many Buddhas, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.

It should be known that such persons have also, throughout immeasurable billions of eons, practiced the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, are not startled, not terrified, and do not fear it; and having heard it, they receive, uphold, draw near to, and practice it as taught—then one should know that these good sons and good daughters are like Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are irreversible (avaivartika).”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep!

If, in previous lives, one did not practice for long the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā, one will ultimately be unable to believe in and understand the profound prajñā-pāramitā.
"Bhagavān!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that these persons also reviled the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their previous lives."

Why is this? When these sons or daughters of good family hear the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they lack faith and lack joy, and their minds are not pure. One should know that these sons or daughters of good family did not, in previous lives, inquire of or question the Buddhas and their disciples:
"How should one practice the *dānapāramitā*, the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
How should one cultivate internal emptiness, up to and including how should one cultivate the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
How should one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including how should one cultivate the eightfold noble path?
"How should one cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on, up to how should one cultivate the eighteen unique qualities?
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:

"Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if there are sons or daughters of good family who have not long practiced the *dānapāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and *prajñāpāramitā*; who do not practice the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; who do not practice the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; who do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and who do not practice the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities—then it is no cause for wonder that such persons do not believe in or understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*!"
Venerable Śāriputra!
I pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā!
To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: “So it is! So it is!”
Kauśika! To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to omniscience (sarvajñatā). Why is this?
Kauśika! All the omniscience of the Buddhas arises from the perfection of wisdom; omniscience itself is the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters who wish to abide in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) should abide in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If good sons and good daughters wish to give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), they should practice and cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*) along with their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they should practice and cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Sons and daughters of good family who wish to turn the wheel of Dharma should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Sons and daughters of good family who wish to attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), or the fruit of arhatship should practice the perfection of wisdom;
those who wish to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha should practice the perfection of wisdom.

If one wishes to teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha, one should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to instruct sentient beings so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, or wishes to gather and sustain the saṅgha of bhikṣus, they should practice the prajñāpāramitā.
[Treatise] Commentary:

Śakra Devānām Indra is the lord of all devas; because his faculties are sharp, his wisdom is superior, and he has faith in the Buddha-dharma, he increases and prospers even further—just as fire, when it encounters wind, burns with even greater intensity.
Hearing Subhūti praise the *prajñāpāramitā* through various causes and conditions, the Buddha validated his praise by means of profound principles.
Śakra, conceiving a sense of rare wonder, thought to himself:

"If a son or daughter of good family hears this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, such a person must have made extensive offerings to many Buddhas and performed great meritorious deeds in previous lives; they must have encountered excellent teachers, fellow students, and other spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in this present life."
Because of having made offerings to the Buddhas in previous lives and due to the presence of spiritual friends in this present life, one is able to believe in the Prajñāpāramitā upon hearing it;
how much more so for those who read, recite, contemplate, maintain right mindfulness, cultivate meditative concentration, and analyze its meaning and intent to accomplish their tasks!

It should be known that this person has heard the meaning of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Buddhas of the past and their disciples; having received it with faith, they are neither terrified nor afraid.

Why is this? Because these persons have practiced the six pāramitās and other meritorious virtues for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, although they have not yet attained the stage of avaivartika, they harbor neither doubt nor regret regarding the profound Dharma.
It is like newly split dry wool that drifts east and west with the wind;
yet moist wool, being tightly woven, cannot be moved.

A bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment is also like this: having not long cultivated virtue and having meager merit, they follow the words of others and are unable to believe in or accept the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one has long cultivated merit and does not follow the words of others, then one can believe in and accept the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without being startled or terrified.
When Śakra, Lord of Devas, contemplated that the *prajñāpāramitā* possesses immeasurable merit, Śāriputra, knowing what Śakra was thinking, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Good sons and good daughters, although they have not yet entered the stage of a bodhisattva, if they are able to believe in and accept the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without being startled or terrified, and practice according to what is taught, then because of their great merit, wisdom, and power of faith, you should know that they are no different from those who are *avaivartika*.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is profound!
It has no marks that can be grasped, believed, or received."
If one can believe and accept this, it is truly rare!
It is as difficult as a person planting seeds in mid-air!
When all ordinary beings attain the supreme Dharma, they then abandon their former basis.

Just as one who has attained the bliss of meditative concentration abandons the pleasures of the five desires, and even one relying on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) abandons the merits of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
one cannot abandon anything without having something upon which to rely.

It is like a climbing insect seeking a branch: it secures its front foot, then advances its hind foot; having reached the very top of the tree, it has no further place to rely upon, so it returns to its original position.

In this same way, a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the Way, while having no place of reliance within the *prajñāpāramitā*, is nevertheless able to cultivate merit and renounce the five desires—this is truly rare!
In this regard, the causal conditions are explained:
"This person, in previous lives, believed and accepted [the teachings], long practiced the six pāramitās, and accumulated a great mass of merit.
Contrary to such faith, they then revile the prajñāpāramitā.
Just as those with great merit have accumulated it over a long period,
so too has the lack of faith and the practice of disparagement been cultivated over a long time.
It is asked:
If one has reviled and slandered others in previous lives and should thus fall into hell, by what cause can they further hear the Prajñāpāramitā?
The answer is: some say that—
When this person has finished expiating the sins that led to their fall into hell, they return again to revile [the Dharma]; this does not refer to subsequent lifetimes. Some say:
when the accumulation of karma is dense and heavy, it is then able to yield its retribution.
Although this person did not have faith in their previous life, their accumulated karma was not yet sufficient to yield its fruit;
thus, they were born among humans due to residual merit, yet they continue to lack faith.
Furthermore, some say: regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), one must necessarily undergo retribution in the very next life;
other offenses are not like this, as their retribution may occur either in the next life or in a much later life.
At that time, Śakra addressed Śāriputra:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound because it is ultimately empty and non-existent.

It is not at all surprising that a bodhisattva who has not long practiced meritorious deeds would have a mind that clings firmly and weak power of faith, such that they do not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including omniscience."
Śakra reflected and deliberated:
"The merit of one who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable, while the transgression of one who lacks faith is profound and heavy.
Out of deep love and reverence for the Prajñāpāramitā, he spoke these words:
"I shall pay homage to this Prajñā!
Why is this? To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)."
"To pay homage to the Omniscient One is to pay homage to all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions.

At that time, the Buddha approved these words and further spoke in praise of the causes and conditions of the *prajñāpāramitā*, saying: "The all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas is born from within the *prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, it is said:
'If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to abide in omniscience, and even to encompass the entire community of bhikṣus, they should practice and cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.'"
[Sūtra] Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, how is it that they are said to abide in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?”
How does one dwell in inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
How does one dwell in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers?
"How does one dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one dwell in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities?
World-Honored One!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom, up to the perfection of generosity, and the emptiness of the internal, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Kauśika! That you are able to joyfully inquire about this matter is entirely due to the Buddha’s spiritual power! Kauśika!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not abide in form, this constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The same applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; and likewise to the eye-element up to the consciousness-element.
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide within the perfection of wisdom, it is for the sake of practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not abide within the perfection of meditative concentration, it is for the sake of practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
Not abiding in the perfection of vigor is the practice of the perfection of vigor;
not abiding in the perfection of patience is the practice of the perfection of patience;
not abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline.
Not dwelling within the dānapāramitā is for the purpose of practicing the dānapāramitā.
In this way, Kauśika,
it is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva not dwelling in the prajñāpāramitā while practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! Not dwelling in internal emptiness is the practice of internal emptiness;
likewise, not dwelling in anything up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence is the practice of the emptiness of non-existence and existence.
Not dwelling in the four dhyānas, one practices the four dhyānas;
not dwelling in the four immeasurable minds, one practices the four immeasurable minds;
not dwelling in the four formless attainments, one practices the four formless attainments.
Not abiding in the five supernormal powers is the practice of the five supernormal powers;
not abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness is the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness;
and so on, up to not abiding in the eightfold noble path is the practice of the eightfold noble path.
Not dwelling in the ten powers of a Buddha, one practices and cultivates the ten powers of a Buddha;
and so on, up to not dwelling in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one practices and cultivates the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Kauśika!
This bodhisattva does not apprehend form as a place where one may dwell or practice.
