...up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), one cannot obtain the eighteen unique qualities as a place where they can be dwelled upon or practiced.
Furthermore, Kauśika,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice form (*rūpa*), if he does not practice form, this is called practicing form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is this?
Because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, the prior limit of form cannot be apprehended, its middle limit cannot be apprehended, and its posterior limit cannot be apprehended.
"Even up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas), it is also thus.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound!
The Buddha said:
"Because the suchness of form is profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profoundly deep, the Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep;
this applies likewise even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to fathom!”
The Buddha said:
"Because form is difficult to measure, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to measure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are difficult to measure, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to measure."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable!
The Buddha said:
“Because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not practice the profundity of form, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if he does not practice the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? Because the profound characteristic of form is non-form;
the profound characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are non-unique qualities.
To practice in this manner of non-practice is to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing the idea that form is difficult to fathom is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing with regard to sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to not practicing with regard to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that are difficult to fathom—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because the immeasurable characteristic of form is non-form;
the immeasurable characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are non-unique qualities.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice the immeasurability of form, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice the immeasurability of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because form has immeasurable characteristics and is therefore not form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, have immeasurable characteristics and are therefore not the eighteen unique qualities.
Śāriputra said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound; its profound characteristics are difficult to see, difficult to understand, and inconceivable. It should not be spoken before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.”

Why is this? Because bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, may become startled and terrified, giving rise to doubt and regret, failing to believe it, and failing to practice it.
This profound Prajñāpāramitā should be taught before the irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas;

when these Bodhisattvas hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they will not be startled, nor terrified, and their minds will be free from doubt or regret, whereby they are able to practice it with faith.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to preach this profound Prajñāpāramitā in the presence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly resolved their minds, what fault would there be?"
Śāriputra replied to Śakra Devānām Indra:

“Kauśika! If this profound Prajñāpāramitā were spoken in the presence of bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, they might become startled and terrified, disparage it, and lack faith; such a possibility exists for bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.”
If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and disparages it or lacks faith, they plant the karma for the three evil realms;
by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, it will be difficult for them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for a long time.
[Treatise] Explanation:
At that time, having heard from the Buddha the praise of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) being complete, Śakra now asks the Buddha:
"How does a bodhisattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom, [proceeding] from the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇikadharma)?"
The Buddha praised him, saying, “Excellent!
Excellent! This was because Śakra Devānām Indra, as the lord among the gods, is one whose words are necessarily trustworthy.
By inquiring into this matter, he resolved the doubts of the great assembly, attained unimpeded penetration, and was able to bring about great benefit; therefore, [the Buddha] spoke thus.
"Excellent! Excellent!

Furthermore, because Śakra was able to renounce the five supreme and wondrous sensual desires, the seven treasures, and his palaces, and was able to question the Buddha regarding the conduct practiced by the noble sages, the Buddha said, "Excellent! By the Buddha's spiritual power, you are able to joyfully inquire about this matter. Within this, there are even more supreme and wondrous devas who contemplate the Buddha’s immeasurable spiritual virtues.
Now, that Śakra is able to inquire about the Buddha’s affairs amidst the great assembly is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
As stated in the *Cittadhāraṇī-sūtra*:
"The Buddha’s radiance enters into his body, enabling him to inquire about the Buddha’s affairs."
The Buddha answered Kauśika:

"If a bodhisattva does not dwell in form and so forth, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). This means that because the bodhisattva perceives the faults of form—such as its impermanence and suffering—he does not dwell in form;
if he does not dwell in form, he is thereby able to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Because ordinary persons perceive forms and become attached to them, they give rise to perverted afflictions and lose this path of the Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, it is those who do not abide [in such perceptions] who are able to practice and cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.
The five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements are also like this.
Question:
For what reason do they not abide in the six perfections, each practicing its own respective conduct?
The answer is:
These six pāramitās and so forth are all practices of wholesome dharmas; for this reason it is said:
"Not abiding in the six perfections, etc. means that one practices each of these individually.
The aggregates, elements, and sense bases constitute the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one does not become attached to these phenomena, then attachment is severed;
because attachment is severed, one practices purity within all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*).

In this context, it is explained that there is no abiding in causes and conditions; that is to say, one does not find a place of abiding for dharmas such as form, nor does one find a place of cultivation for dharmas such as form.
Furthermore, because this matter is difficult to understand, the Buddha further explains the causes and conditions:
"Not cultivating form" means that because the bodhisattva perceives the faults of form, they do not abide within form.
Because they do not abide, they do not practice.
"Practicing form" means grasping the characteristics of form, such as whether it is permanent or impermanent, and so forth.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly practices wholesome dharmas—such as right speech and right action—and accumulates these until they are pure and profound, it is called "practicing form."
Now, because the bodhisattva wishes to practice *prajñā*, he disperses and destroys this form (*rūpa*) and does not cultivate it. Why is this?
Because past form has already ceased and future form does not yet exist, it cannot be cultivated.
Because form arises and ceases simultaneously in the present, it does not abide; if there is no cultivation even for a single moment when it abides, how much less so when it ceases moment by moment?
Therefore, it is said herein that one does not cultivate the causal conditions of form:
"Form of the three periods of time cannot be apprehended."
This applies even up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

If one can thus contemplate all phenomena as being dispersed and disintegrated, and does not grasp at their marks, this is called "being able to practice the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena such as form."
At that time, having heard this teaching from the Buddha, Śāriputra was filled with joy; he entered deeply into the wisdom of emptiness and addressed the Buddha:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is profound!"
The Buddha affirmed this, validating their praise:
"Form and all other phenomena are as they are, profoundly deep.
The Buddha said:
"It is not merely that the eye perceives forms as profound; rather, it is because one discerns form through the *prajñāpāramitā* and enters into its suchness (*tathatā*) that it is profound.
Just as individual drops of rain are not called profound, but when they converge with the various streams and enter the great ocean, they are then called profound."
Form and the other aggregates are likewise.
The divine eye and the fleshly eye see what is shallow but not what is deep;
if one observes with the wisdom-eye, then it is so profound as to be unfathomable.
Because it is profoundly deep, it is difficult to fathom; only the Buddhas can reach its very bottom.
Because it is profoundly deep and immeasurable, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
There is no wisdom capable of grasping the true nature of form and so forth—whether as permanent or impermanent—because such deliberation involves error and fault.
At that time, Śāriputra and all the listeners had this thought:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable and limitless; how, then, should a bodhisattva practice it?"
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound nature of form and so forth, he loses the prajñāpāramitā;
if he does not practice the profound nature of form, this is the attainment of the prajñāpāramitā."
Ordinary beings have dull faculties, and therefore it is said to be "profound";
however, for those who possess single-mindedness, merit, and sharp faculties, it is not profound.
It is like the depth of water, which is not fixed: what is deep for a small child is shallow for an adult.
Even as the great ocean is deep for humans but shallow for Rāhu, the king of the asuras,

so too is it extremely profound for ordinary persons, those who have newly resolved [for awakening], and those who are indolent, yet shallow for those who have long accumulated merit and are irreversible (avaivartika).
The Buddhas are like Rāhu, the King of the Asuras; regarding all dharmas, there is nothing profound for them, because they have attained unimpeded liberation.

For this reason, it should be known that they distinguish between the profound and the shallow only for the sake of sentient beings, according to the timing, their faculties of sharpness or dullness, whether it is the beginning or long practice, and their indolence or diligence.
It is likewise immeasurable and without limit.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:
"The profound characteristic of dharmas such as form is non-form."
Why is this? Because of fear, mental despondency, and doubt and regret, one regards form as profound; yet the characteristic of form is not profound, as previously explained.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound; its profound characteristics are difficult to see and difficult to understand.”
Question: Previously it was stated that "a bodhisattva does not practice the profound; this is practicing the prajñāpāramitā. Why does Śāriputra now again speak of the "profound"?
Answer: Śāriputra did not speak of the profound with a fixed mind; rather, having grasped the Buddha’s intention, he spoke of the profound for the sake of others.
Therefore, it is said here:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā should not be taught before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; for when such novice bodhisattvas hear of this profound wisdom, their hearts will sink.”
"This should be spoken before an avaivartika bodhisattva; because the wisdom of an avaivartika is profound, they will believe it and not sink into despair.
It is like deep water: one should not allow small children to cross it, but should instruct adults to cross it.
Śakra asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to explain this to bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, what fault would there be?
Śāriputra replied:

“Those who have newly resolved their minds do not believe and their hearts sink; because their hearts sink, they give rise to doubt, regret, and fear, thinking: ‘If one accepts all dharmas as empty, how shall I not fall into annihilation?’”
"If one does not accept it, how could one not accept the Dharma taught by the Buddha!
For this reason, fear arises and doubt and regret are produced.
If the mind is fixed, then evil and heterodox views and slander will arise.
The retribution for disparagement is as explained in the "Chapter on Hell.
To summarize it here:
"By planting the causes and conditions for the three evil realms, one will find it difficult to attain the unsurpassed path for a very long time."
[Sūtra] Śakra Devānām-indra asked Śāriputra:
“Is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment], who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, would not be startled or terrified?”
Śāriputra said: "So it is, Kauśika!"

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, is neither startled nor terrified, you should know that this bodhisattva will receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before long, after no more than one or two buddhas.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has long since resolved their mind [on awakening], practiced the six pāramitās, and made extensive offerings to many buddhas; thus, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, they are not startled, not terrified, and do not fear it. Upon hearing it, they immediately receive and uphold it, practicing in accordance with what is taught within the prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to speak a parable.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeking the bodhisattva path practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in their dreams—entering meditative concentration, exerting diligent effort, perfecting patience, guarding the precepts, practicing generosity, and cultivating inner emptiness and outer emptiness, up until sitting at the site of enlightenment—one should know that such a son or daughter of good family is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

How much more so for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practices the *prajñāpāramitā* while awake—entering meditative concentration, exerting diligent effort, perfecting patience, guarding the precepts, and practicing generosity—and yet does not swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and sit at the site of enlightenment! This is simply impossible.
“World-Honored One!
When good sons and good daughters have accomplished roots of goodness and are able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, and even practice it as taught;

one should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have long since resolved their minds, planted roots of goodness, made extensive offerings to various Buddhas, and associated with spiritual friends.”
If this person is able to receive, uphold, and even correctly recollect the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this person is close to receiving the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

It should be known that these sons and daughters of good family are like *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are immovable and irreversible from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and are able to attain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having attained it, they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly bring it to mind.
“World-Honored One!
It is as if a person wishing to cross a wilderness path of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred yojanas first sees various signs—
such as herdsmen, boundary markers, or groves— and by these signs, they know that a city, town, or village is near.”
Having seen these signs, that person will think:
"According to the signs I see, one should know that a city, town, or village is not far away."
"Their minds will attain peace and stability, and they will not fear robbers, evil insects, hunger, or thirst.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: if they obtain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it, one should know that they are close to receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long; one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva need not fear falling into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."
These are the preliminary signs, namely, because one has heard, seen, received, and even correctly recollected this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
“If you have further things you wish to say, then speak.
“World-Honored One!

It is like a person who wishes to see the great ocean; having resolved to go toward it, they see neither the signs of trees nor the signs of mountains. Although this person has not yet seen the great ocean, they know that the great ocean is not far away.”
Why is this? Because the great ocean lies level, being without the appearance of trees and without the appearance of mountains.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receives, upholds, and even correctly recollects it, although they have not yet received a prediction of their lifespan before a Buddha—whether for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, or hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas—that bodhisattva knows for themselves that they will soon receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because I have heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and have received, upheld, read, recited, and even correctly contemplated it.
"World-Honored One!..."
It is like early spring, when the old leaves of all the trees have fallen; one should know that new leaves, flowers, and fruits will appear before long. Why is this?
Because by observing these preliminary signs of the trees, one knows that the leaves, flowers, and fruits will soon emerge.
At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa, seeing these preliminary signs of the tree, were all filled with great joy.
World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and even correctly contemplates it and practices according to its teaching, one should know that this bodhisattva has perfected their roots of goodness and has made extensive offerings to many Buddhas.
This bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Pursued by the roots of goodness from previous lives, I am heading toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, I have been able to see and hear this profound prajñāpāramitā, and I receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it, practicing according to what is taught."
Among them, those devaputras who had previously seen the Buddha were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to themselves:

"The former bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also had such preliminary signs when they received their prediction; now it will not be long before this bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“World-Honored One!

It is, for example, like a woman who is pregnant; her body becomes heavy and painful, her gait is unsteady, she is uneasy when sitting or rising, her sleep and food diminish, she takes no pleasure in speech, and she grows weary of her former habits because she suffers from pain.
When another woman observes these preliminary signs, she knows that childbirth will not be long in coming.”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having planted roots of goodness, made extensive offerings to the Buddhas, practiced the six pāramitās for a long time, and associated with virtuous friends, their roots of goodness reach fulfillment. They then hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it, practicing according to what is taught;
other Bodhisattvas also know that this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva will soon receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Whatever you delight in expounding is entirely through the power of the Buddha.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare!
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have well entrusted the affairs of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to bring peace and security to many sentient beings, to cause immeasurable sentient beings to attain happiness, and out of compassion for all devas and humans, to bring them peace, joy, and benefit."

When these bodhisattvas practice the bodhisattva path, they gather immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings through the four means of attraction— namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—
and they also bring sentient beings to maturity through the ten paths of wholesome action.
He himself practices the first dhyāna and also teaches others to practice the first dhyāna;
likewise, he himself practices up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and also teaches others to practice up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One practices the dāna-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the dāna-pāramitā;
one practices the śīla-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the śīla-pāramitā;
one practices the kṣānti-pāramitā oneself and also teaches others to practice the kṣānti-pāramitā.
They personally practice the perfection of vigor and also teach others to practice the perfection of vigor;
they personally practice the perfection of meditation and also teach others to practice the perfection of meditation;
they personally practice the perfection of wisdom and also teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom.

This bodhisattva, having attained the perfection of wisdom, uses the power of skillful means to teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, yet he himself does not realize it within;
he teaches sentient beings so that they may attain the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, yet he himself does not realize them within;
he teaches sentient beings so that they may attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, yet he himself does not realize it within.
They personally practice the six pāramitās and also instruct immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas to practice the six pāramitās.
They themselves abide in the stage of avaivartika and also teach others to abide in the stage of avaivartika.
He purifies his own buddha-field and also teaches others to purify their buddha-fields;
he brings sentient beings to maturity himself and also teaches others to bring sentient beings to maturity.
Having personally attained the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, they also teach others to attain the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.
Having personally purified the gateways of dhāraṇī, they also teach others to purify the gateways of dhāraṇī.
They themselves possess the eloquence of joyful speech and also teach others to possess the eloquence of joyful speech.
They themselves experience the perfection of form and also teach others to experience the perfection of form.
They themselves accomplish the thirty-two marks and also teach others to accomplish the thirty-two marks.
They themselves accomplish the stage of youthful purity (*kumārabhūmi*) and also teach others to accomplish the stage of youthful purity.
Having personally accomplished the ten powers of a Buddha, they also teach others to accomplish the ten powers of a Buddha.
Having personally practiced the four fearlessnesses, they also teach others to practice the four fearlessnesses.
They personally practice the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and also teach others to practice the eighteen unique qualities.
They personally practice great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*), and also teach others to practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Having personally attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they also teach others to attain all-knowledge.
Having personally become free from all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they also teach others to become free from all fetters and their residual tendencies.
"Having turned the wheel of Dharma myself, I also teach others to turn the wheel of Dharma.
[Treatise] Commentary:
At that time, Śakra asked Śāriputra:
“Is there any bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment] who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, would not be startled or terrified?
Śāriputra replied, “There is no one who,
without having received a prediction, could hear the prajñāpāramitā and believe it.”

"If there should be one who at any time is able to have faith, you should know that they are about to receive their prediction; after seeing no more than one or two Buddhas, they shall immediately obtain their prediction.
The Buddha approved of Śāriputra’s words.
When Śāriputra heard that the Buddha approved of what he had said, his heart was filled with joy;
wishing further to clarify and make this matter perfectly understood, he spoke a parable, saying:
"In a dream, because the mind is shrouded by sleep, it is not produced by the true mind."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while in a dream, resolves their mind to practice the six pāramitās and even sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), you should know that this person’s merit is slight, and they are close to receiving the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

How much more so for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, while awake, with a sincere mind, has resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practices the six pāramitās—how could such a person not draw near to receiving the prediction of enlightenment?
"Bhagavān!

If a person who wanders through the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence should at some time hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and maintain right mindfulness of it, one may know for certain that this person will before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Just as a fish that has swallowed a hook, though it may still sport within the pond, should be known to be on the verge of emergence before long;
so too is the practitioner who possesses deep faith and delight in the *prajñāpāramitā*, for they will not remain long in saṃsāra."
In this context, Śāriputra himself provides a simile: "If a person wishes to cross a perilous path.
Here, the "perilous path" refers to the world.

"One hundred yojanas" refers to the desire realm; "two hundred yojanas" refers to the form realm; "three hundred yojanas" refers to the formless realm; and "four hundred yojanas" refers to the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, "four hundred yojanas" refers to the desire realm; "three hundred yojanas" refers to the form realm; "two hundred yojanas" refers to the formless realm; and "one hundred yojanas" refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"One who wishes to go forth" refers to a person who faithfully accepts and practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"First seeing the characteristics of all phenomena" means seeing that the great bodhisattvas renounce worldly desires and pleasures, and with a profound mind delight in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Boundaries" refers to the differentiation of all dharmas—these are the dharmas of the śrāvakas, these are the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and these are the dharmas of the Mahāyāna;
likewise, such small benefit belongs to the śrāvaka, while great benefit belongs to the bodhisattva;
the realm of Māra is birth and death, whereas the realm of the Buddha is the *prajñāpāramitā*, the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, the place of immortality.
“Gardens and groves” refers to the bliss of the Buddha-way’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth;
such are the characteristics of immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

“Villages” refers to the patience of compliance with the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharma-kṣānti*); “market towns” refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and “cities” refers to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding "attaining peace and security": when a bodhisattva hears this Dharma, they contemplate and deliberate upon its practice, thinking:
"I have attained this Dharma, and my mind is at peace; I shall surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Robbers” refers to our sixty-two types of false views.
“Vicious insects” refers to the various afflictions such as craving and hatred.
"Not fearing thieves" means that humans find no opportunity against him.
"Not fearing evil insects" means that non-humans find no opportunity against him.
"Not fearing hunger" means he does not fear being unable to attain the true wisdom of a sage.
"Not fearing thirst" means not fearing that one will be unable to obtain the flavor of the Dharma-joy of dhyāna, liberation, and so forth.
Herein, he himself states the causal conditions:
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva obtains the prior signs, it will not be long before he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Not fearing falling into the evil realms or dying of hunger" means not fearing falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha approved of this analogy, using the coarse to illustrate the subtle, and the worldly to illustrate the supramundane.
The remaining three metaphors should also be explained through analysis as above.
"The waters of the great ocean" represent the unsurpassed path;
"the level ground without trees or mountains" represents the volumes of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and so forth.
"The fruit of the tree" is the unsurpassed path; "the flower of the tree" is the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

"The withered leaves fall in springtime and new leaves grow again" signifies that all afflictions, false views, doubts, and the like are extinguished, whereby one is able to obtain the scrolls of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and other such works.
"The woman" is the practitioner; "the pregnant body" is the unsurpassed path; "the signs of impending birth" are the Bodhisattva’s long cultivation of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
"disgust for what was formerly practiced" is the weariness with the pleasures of worldly lust, no longer taking delight in or being attached to them.
The Buddha praised what he had said, exclaiming, "Excellent!

At that time, Subhūti, hearing the Buddha affirm Śāriputra’s words and praise them as excellent, understood that the Buddha’s intention was one of profound respect for these bodhisattvas; therefore, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How most rare!
You have well entrusted the affairs of a bodhisattva.
Regarding "the affairs of a bodhisattva," these are the path of emptiness and the path of merit.

Furthermore, just as the Buddha has taught through various general and specific characteristics, entrusting [this teaching] to Ānanda, Maitreya, and others, you should personally uphold and propagate these instructions after my entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, benefiting sentient beings and ensuring that no errors occur!
The Buddha spoke on the causes and conditions for the excellent entrustment:
"All bodhisattvas resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding 'bringing peace and security to many sentient beings,' among all sentient beings—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*)—there is none except a Buddha who can calculate or know them."
Those who have obtained benefit from the Buddha are beyond counting; therefore, they are called "many.
As for "peace and security": for sentient beings who are attached to permanence, he teaches impermanence;
for those attached to pleasure, he teaches suffering.
To those attached to substantiality, he teaches emptiness;
to those attached to a self, he teaches non-self—such as these are called "peaceful.
When ordinary people hear this, although they may not find joy at the time, after a long period they will extinguish all afflictions and attain peaceful bliss.
It is like taking bitter medicine: although it is painful at the time, it later brings about the removal of illness.

Regarding the phrase "immeasurable sentient beings obtain happiness," when a bodhisattva seeks the *prajñāpāramitā* and has not yet achieved its fulfillment, they benefit sentient beings with the happiness of both this life and future lives, as described in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-jātaka-sūtra*.
If one attains the Prajñāpāramitā, having already severed all afflictions, one benefits sentient beings with both worldly happiness and supramundane happiness;
when one attains the Unsurpassed Way, one benefits sentient beings solely with supramundane happiness.
Regarding "peaceful happiness and benefit": they bring about peaceful happiness and benefit solely out of a heart of compassion.
As for "benefit" (饒), it refers to providing great benefit to devas and humans;
it is not mentioned regarding other realms because the benefit therein is slight.
"Beneficial actions" refers to the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
One attracts sentient beings through two kinds of giving: material giving and the giving of the Dharma.
"Affectionate speech" is of two kinds:
First, speaking with agreeable words according to their wishes; second, preaching the Dharma according to the teachings they love.
Although these bodhisattvas have not yet attained the Path, out of compassion for sentient beings, they personally break their own pride and preach the Dharma according to their inclinations.
If one attains the Way, one preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for those to be saved:
for those with haughty minds who are wealthy, one praises generosity, because such people are able to obtain the benefits of others' property, as well as fame and merit;

if one were to praise the observance of precepts or disparage the breaking of them, their hearts would not find joy—thus, in such cases, one preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.
"Benefit" is also of two kinds:
first, benefiting in this life and the next by preaching the Dharma, sustaining one's livelihood through the Dharma, and diligently cultivating beneficial matters;

second, causing those who have not yet believed to believe, causing those who break the precepts to uphold them, causing those with little knowledge to become learned, causing those who do not practice giving to practice generosity, and teaching wisdom to those who are deluded—through such means as these, one benefits sentient beings with wholesome dharmas.
"Sameness of purpose" means that when a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to practice wholesome dharmas, he acts in accordance with what they do;
even when the bodhisattva possesses a virtuous mind while sentient beings possess an evil mind, he is able to transform their evil so that it becomes identical to his own virtue.

This bodhisattva causes sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); this is the detailed explanation of the meaning of the four methods of attraction.
Among the two types of giving, it is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
To preach the Dharma according to their inclinations is the foremost among pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).
Sentient beings cherish their own lives; by causing them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action, they shall obtain long life.
Regarding benefit, among all forms of benefit derived from precious things, the benefit of the Dharma is supreme—this is what constitutes true benefit.
Among those who share the same purpose, practicing wholesome dharmas together is supreme;
this Bodhisattva personally practices the ten wholesome paths of action and also teaches others to do so.
Someone says:
Subsequently practicing the ten wholesome paths of action oneself constitutes the fourth point of commonality; therefore it is said:
"One practices the ten wholesome paths oneself and also teaches others to do so.

"One practices the first dhyāna oneself and also teaches others to practice it": since the first dhyāna and its equivalents involve the same freedom from desire and the same observance of precepts, they are thus mutually inclusive in name and substance.
Because they mutually encompass one another, they are gradually able to deliver others by means of the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This continues up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where it is likewise so.
They personally practice the six pāramitās and also teach them to others.
By means of *prajñā*, they cause sentient beings to attain a portion of *prajñā*, namely the attainment of the stage of *srotāpanna* and so forth;
yet, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), they themselves do not realize [the ultimate fruit].
Because their merit and the power of their wisdom have increased, they instruct immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodhisattvas to abide in the six *pāramitās*.
Abiding oneself in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and so forth, one also instructs others therein;
even turning the wheel of Dharma oneself, one also instructs others to turn the wheel of Dharma.
For this reason, it is out of a heart of compassion that I properly entrust these matters to the bodhisattvas, and not out of attachment.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Sixty-six.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of the Chapter on Praising Faithful Practice,
Part Fourty-five Continued, Scroll Sixty-seven.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare!
World-Honored One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished great merit, namely, practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all sentient beings, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive a mark of increase in form, nor do they perceive a mark of decrease in form;
they do not perceive a mark of increase in feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor do they perceive a mark of decrease in them;
and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes, they do not perceive a mark of increase, nor do they perceive a mark of decrease."
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive this as a dharma or a non-dharma; they do not perceive these as past dharmas, future dharmas, or present dharmas; they do not perceive them as wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, determinate dharmas, or indeterminate dharmas; they do not perceive them as conditioned dharmas or unconditioned dharmas; they do not perceive the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they do not perceive the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom; and so on, up to not perceiving the knowledge of all modes.
In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully practices the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are signless;
because all phenomena are empty, deceptive, and not solid; and because they lack a cognizer and lack a life-principle.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
What the World-Honored One has spoken is inconceivable!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form is inconceivable, that which is spoken is inconceivable;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, that which is spoken is inconceivable."
Because the six pāramitās are inconceivable, that which is taught is inconceivable;
up to and including because all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is inconceivable, that which is taught is inconceivable.

Subhūti! If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they perceive that form is inconceivable, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, up to and including perceiving that the knowledge of all modes is inconceivable, then this bodhisattva will not be able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
as for this profound Prajñāpāramitā, who will be able to believe and understand it?"
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has long practiced the six pāramitās, planted roots of goodness, extensively attended upon and made offerings to the Buddhas, and associated with virtuous friends, such a bodhisattva is able to believe in and understand the profound prajñāpāramitā."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long practiced the six pāramitās, planted roots of goodness, extensively attended upon and made offerings to the Buddhas, and associated with virtuous friends?”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not discriminate form, does not discriminate the characteristics of form, and does not discriminate the nature of form;
and does not discriminate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, does not discriminate the characteristics of consciousness, and does not discriminate the nature of consciousness."
The same applies to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; and to the eye-element up to the consciousness-element.
They do not differentiate between the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; they do not differentiate the characteristics or natures of these three realms.

They do not differentiate the *dānapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*, the emptiness of the internal through to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness through to the eightfold noble path, or the ten powers of a Buddha through to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); they do not differentiate the characteristics or natures of these eighteen unique qualities;
nor do they differentiate the path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*), its characteristics, or its nature.
One does not discriminate omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor does one discriminate the characteristics of omniscience, nor does one discriminate the nature of omniscience. Why is this?
Subhūti! Form is inconceivable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable; and so on, up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), which is inconceivable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has long practiced the six pāramitās, planted roots of goodness, frequently attended upon and made offerings to the Buddhas, and associated with virtuous friends.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Because form is profoundly deep, the Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep."
"Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound, and even because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound, O Bhagavān."

This Prajñāpāramitā is a treasury of jewels, because it contains the jewel of the fruit of srotāpanna; because it contains the jewels of the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat; because it contains the jewel of the path of the pratyekabuddha and of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi;

because it contains the jewels of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers; and because it contains the jewels of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities, omniscience, and the knowledge of all modes.
World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is a mass of purity.
Because form is pure, the prajñāpāramitā is a mass of purity;

"Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is a mass of purity.
[Treatise] Commentary:
"This Bodhisattva has accomplished great merit" refers to what was previously stated:
"Practicing it oneself and also teaching others.

Furthermore, regarding those with many merits: although sentient beings are not one's kin and one has no personal gain or profit from them, one diligently practices the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of these beings and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva having a great share of grace; therefore, they are said to possess great merit.
The characteristics of practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* have been explained through various causes and conditions in the preceding chapter;
now, the question concerns the characteristics of the perfection of practicing *prajñā*.
The Buddha said:
Just as with the cultivation of prajñā, so it is with the fulfillment of the marks. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva does not perceive the increase or decrease of dharmas such as form (rūpa), this is called fulfillment.
Although this bodhisattva has attained the ten stages and sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), at that time they fully cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
it is like a dream or an illusion, neither increasing nor decreasing, explained as such because of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva does not discriminate among all phenomena as being "this is the Dharma" or "this is not the Dharma," then they are all entirely the Dharma;
just as the waters of the great ocean, though fed by hundreds of rivers and myriad streams, all merge into a single taste.
At that time, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is complete.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva enters into the emptiness of phenomena and does not perceive phenomena as having the three periods of time, nor as being wholesome or unwholesome, and does not perceive the six perfections up to all-knowledge, at that time the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is complete.
Why is this? "The signlessness of all dharmas" is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). If one discriminates among dharmas, these are all marks of false views.
Because of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, they are called "the emptiness of all dharmas."
All dharmas arise through the combination of causes and conditions and thus exist; when those conditions disperse, they are destroyed, and are therefore "deceptive.
Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are impermanent and lack substantial reality, they are called "unstable."
"There is no one who experiences suffering or pleasure" because sentient beings are empty; thus, "there is no experiencer," meaning they do not perceive suffering or pleasure.
"There is no life-span" (jīvita); "life-span" refers to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Some say: "This life-faculty (jīvitendriya) possesses the mark of a self; therefore, life-span is the self.

However, within the emptiness of sentient beings, this has already been refuted through various causes and conditions. Consequently, there is no one who performs dharmas, nor is there anyone who receives dharmas.
If one contemplates that all phenomena are empty—both the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena—one thus fully cultivates the prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Subhūti was filled with wonder and joy, unable to remain composed, for the prajñāpāramitā he had described was inconceivable.
The Buddha said:
"Because form and all other dharmas are inconceivable, they are inconceivable. Why is this so?
Because cause and effect are similar.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva knows that phenomena such as form are also inconceivable, yet dwells within this inconceivability, they do not fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they grasp at the mark of inconceivability.
Therefore it is said:
"If a bodhisattva perceives that dharmas such as form possess an inconceivable nature, then they do not fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Subhūti found no place of reliance within the *prajñāpāramitā*, like one submerged in a great ocean; therefore, he addressed the Buddha:
"This profound *prajñā* is inconceivable; since even the inconceivable is itself inconceivable, who could possibly believe and understand it?
If even that which is merely inconceivable is difficult to believe, how much more so that which is inconceivable and yet further inconceivable!
The Buddha replied:
"If a bodhisattva has long practiced the six pāramitās, long planted roots of goodness, long made offerings to and attended upon the Buddhas, and long associated with virtuous friends;
by these causes and conditions, their faith is firm and they are able to believe in and accept the profound prajñāpāramitā."

In other chapters it was said that "even those who have newly resolved their minds can believe in the profound Prajñāpāramitā," whereas now the Buddha says that "it is because they have long resolved their minds that they can believe.
For this reason, Subhūti asks:
"What is meant by one who has long resolved their mind?"
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva clearly understands the characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā and does not differentiate any dharmas—namely, 'not differentiating form,' which includes the four great elements or the form derived from the four great elements."
"Non-discrimination of the characteristics of form" means not discriminating that form is visible or sound is audible;
nor does it mean discriminating whether this form is beautiful or ugly, short or long, permanent or impermanent, suffering or pleasure, and so forth.
Regarding "not discriminating the nature of form": one does not perceive form as a permanent phenomenon, such as the solidity of earth and so forth.
Furthermore, the true nature of form is called the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), because it is ultimately empty;
this Bodhisattva does not discriminate the *dharmatā*, for the *dharmatā* is characterized by indestructibility.
This applies even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Question:
Earth has the characteristic of solidity; why then do you speak of its "nature" (*svabhāva*)?
Answer: These marks are formed by the accumulation of habitual practice;
for example, if a person repeatedly practices anger day after day without ceasing, it becomes their evil nature.
In some cases, the characteristic and the nature are distinct, as when one perceives smoke and knows there is fire; smoke is a characteristic of fire, yet it is not fire itself.
In other cases, the characteristic and the nature are not distinct, as heat is both a characteristic of fire and the very nature of fire.
In this regard, the Buddha spoke of the causal conditions:
"All phenomena, such as form and so forth, are inconceivable.
This inconceivability is precisely ultimate emptiness; it is the true mark of all phenomena, which is eternally pure.
Subhūti said:
"Although a bodhisattva has not been [in this state] for many months, years, or ages, if they can practice in such a manner, this is called 'long-standing'.
Having heard the Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti attained even deeper benefit and therefore addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is profound because form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are profound.
The characteristics of the profundity of form and the others are as previously explained.
“World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is a treasury of rare jewels. As for “rare jewels,” this refers to the fruit of *srotāpanna*, which can extinguish the poisonous venom of the three fetters;
and so on, up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which can extinguish all afflictions along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*) and fulfill all vows.
These various fruits, based on the meditative concentrations up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), are spoken of as the union of cause and fruit; this is called the "Heap of Jewels.
This perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is a pure heap, because all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are pure.
"Practicing correctly within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) without deviating is called 'purity' (*viśuddhi*), being free from all faults and afflictions;
even not clinging to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and not clinging to the inconceivable (*acintya*), it is therefore called the 'mass of purity' (*viśuddhi-rāśi*)."
At that time, Subhūti should form this thought:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is a collection of rare jewels; it can fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, namely: the happiness of the present life, the happiness of future lives, the happiness of nirvāṇa, and the happiness of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Foolish people further wish to destroy this pure accumulation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel is free from blemishes, and just as space is free from dust and defilement, the *prajñāpāramitā* is an ultimately pure accumulation.
Yet people, by their own arising of the causes and conditions of false views, desire to create obstacles and bring about destruction;
it is like a person with cataracts in the eyes who, upon seeing a wondrous and precious jewel, calls it impure.
Having formed this thought,
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"It is truly strange!
When this Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, there will be many obstacles.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is, Subhūti!"
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* encounters many obstacles.
For this reason, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to write down this *prajñāpāramitā*, they should write it down swiftly;
likewise, when reading, reciting, contemplating, explaining, correctly recollecting, or practicing it, they should also practice it swiftly.

Why is this? It is because when this profound Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, contemplated, explained, correctly recollected, or practiced, one does not wish for various obstacles to arise.
Good sons and good daughters, if you can complete the transcription in one month, you should diligently transcribe it;
if it takes two months, three months, four months, five months, six months, seven months, or even a year to complete the transcription, you should likewise diligently transcribe it.
As for reading, reciting, contemplating, explaining, correctly recollecting, and practicing it—if you achieve mastery in one month or even in a year, you should diligently achieve such mastery.
Why is this? Subhūti,
it is because many difficulties arise regarding such precious treasures.
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!

Because Māra, the Evil One, delights in creating obstacles within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he prevents it from being written down, and prevents it from being read, recited, contemplated, explained, correctly recollected, and practiced."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although Māra may wish to create obstacles to this profound *prajñāpāramitā* so that it cannot be written, read, recited, contemplated, explained, correctly recollected, or practiced, he will be unable to destroy this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s writing of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to its practice."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By whose power is it that the evil Māra is unable to obstruct a bodhisattva mahāsattva from copying the profound *prajñāpāramitā* up to its practice?”
The Buddha said:
"It is by the power of the Buddha that Māra, the evil one, is unable to obstruct or hinder a bodhisattva mahāsattva in writing the profound Prajñāpāramitā, or even in practicing it."

Śāriputra! It is also by the power of all the Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions, and because those Buddhas protect and keep this bodhisattva in mind, that Māra is unable to obstruct or hinder the bodhisattva-mahāsattva so as to prevent them from copying, completing, or even practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the present immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas protect and keep in mind this Bodhisattva who writes out the profound Prajñāpāramitā and even practices it;
such is the nature of the Dharma, and none can create obstacles!
Śāriputra! Good sons and good daughters should form this thought:
"That I write out this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and even practice it, is entirely through the power of the Buddhas of the ten directions."
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who write out this profound Prajñāpāramitā, or even practice it, all of this is due to the power of the Buddha; one should know that such persons are protected by all the Buddhas.”
The Buddha said: “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! You should know that if there are good men or good women who write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā and even practice it, all of this is due to the power of the Buddha; you should know that they are likewise protected by all the Buddhas.
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!

The present Buddhas of the ten directions—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable in number—all recognize and all behold with their Buddha-eyes these good men and good women while they write out the profound Prajñāpāramitā, up to the time they practice it.”
The Buddha said: “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! All the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions all recognize and, with their Buddha-eyes, behold these good sons and good daughters while they write out the profound Prajñāpāramitā and even while they practice it.
Śāriputra!

Among these, if good sons and good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, and practice it as taught, you should know that such persons are close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long.
Śāriputra!

If good men and good women write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and receive, uphold, read, recite, and even correctly contemplate it; if these persons possess the mark of faith and understanding in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and furthermore make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with flowers, incense, necklaces, and even banners and canopies—
Śāriputra! All Buddhas recognize these good men and good women, and all see them with their Buddha-eye.
"The merit of these good men and good women making offerings shall result in great benefit and a great karmic reward."

Śāriputra! By virtue of these causes and conditions of making such offerings, these sons and daughters of good family shall never fall into the evil realms; furthermore, until they reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), they shall never be separated from the Buddhas.

Śāriputra! By virtue of these roots of goodness, these sons and daughters of good family shall, until they reach unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), never be separated from the six pāramitās; they shall never be separated from inner emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā); they shall never be separated from the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) up to the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga); and they shall never be separated from the ten powers of a Buddha (buddha-daśabala) up to unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
[Treatise] Commentary:
Obstacles refer to demonic activities and the like that destroy the causal conditions for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The Buddha affirmed what Subhūti had said:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to write down this Prajñāpāramitā, they should write it down with great speed;
likewise, when correctly recollecting it and practicing according to the teaching, they should practice with great speed."
The reason it is said to be "swift" is that conditioned phenomena are unreliable and many obstacles arise.

These Prajñāpāramitā sections and sūtra scrolls are numerous or few, and categorized as superior, middling, or inferior—namely, the *Prasphullapraśaṃsā*, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*.

Among those who transcribe [the scriptures], there are those who write slowly and those who write quickly; there are those who transcribe with single-minded diligence and those who are indolent and lack application.
Human life is impermanent, and conditioned phenomena are not to be relied upon.
Because Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in an evil age, there are many obstacles; therefore it is said:
"If it can be finished in one month, you should diligently complete the transcription without interruption, for fear of encountering obstacles;
this applies even up to a year."
"As with writing, so it is even up to the practice of cultivation.
According to whether a person's faculties are sharp or dull, there may be slowness or swiftness [in progress].
Herein, the Buddha further explains the causes and conditions:
“In the world, because of rare treasures, many thieves appear;
because the Prajñā is a great treasure, there are many obstacles.
As for these obstacles, although there are illnesses, hunger, and so forth, it is because the deeds of Māra are so great that they are specifically termed "deeds of Māra."

Whether it be Māra, the subjects of Māra, or malevolent spirits who create evil conditions, they may enter into a person's body to disturb their physical and mental faculties and destroy the written Prajñāpāramitā;
or they may cause the scribe to become weary and discouraged, or cause disturbances to arise within the country, or prevent the scribe from receiving offerings, and so forth.
When reciting and chanting, the teacher and disciples are not in harmony.
While preaching among the great assembly, someone may come forward to speak of the Dharma Master’s faults and transgressions, or say:
"If one cannot practice according to what has been taught, why is it worth listening to or receiving? Or they say:
"Even if one can maintain the precepts, if their faculties are dull and they do not understand the profound meaning, there is no benefit whatsoever in listening to what they say."
Or it is said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is empty and non-existent; it extinguishes all dharmas, leaving no place for practice.
It is like a naked person who says to himself:"
"I am wearing celestial garments.
Through such obstacles, he prevents them from speaking.
To those who lack right mindfulness, Māra manifests as a beautiful body, or in the form of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), or in the guise of a respected and trusted śramaṇa, and says to them:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is empty and possesses nothing; although the names 'sin' and 'merit' exist, they lack any underlying principle.
Or it is said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is empty; one may immediately attain nirvāṇa therein."
Such matters as these destroy the right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) for practicing the Buddha-way.
When bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear of these things, their hearts are greatly terrified:

"We possess bodies subject to birth and death; Māra is the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and his power and majesty are exceedingly great. How can we practice the *prajñāpāramitā* and attain the unsurpassed way?"
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"Although the evil Māra may wish to create obstacles, he cannot destroy [this practice]. Why is this?
Because the great can overcome the small:

just as one who is free from desire always triumphs over one possessed by greed, one who possesses loving-kindness and compassion always triumphs over one possessed by hatred, and the wise person always triumphs over the ignorant.
The Prajñāpāramitā is true wisdom, and its power is exceedingly great;
the works of Māra are deceptive and false.
Although this bodhisattva has not yet fully attained the Prajñāpāramitā, because they have attained a portion of its essence, Māra cannot destroy them.
For these reasons, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
"By whose power is Māra unable to destroy it?
The Buddha replied:
"It is by the power of the Buddha.
Just as among evil people Māra is the greatest, and among good people the Buddha is the greatest;
among those who are bound Māra is the greatest, and among those who are liberated the Buddha is the greatest.
Among those who encounter obstacles, Māra is the greatest; among those who have attained penetration, the Buddha is the greatest.
When the "power of the Buddha" is first mentioned, it refers to Śākyamuni Buddha;
when the "present Buddhas of the ten directions" are subsequently mentioned, they refer to other Buddhas.
Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and others are like a bandit who is assisted by other evildoers;
the teachings of all Buddhas are likewise: for the sake of all sentient beings, whenever there is one who resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they immediately provide protection.
Why is this so? The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions; if anyone wishes to obstruct or destroy it, they must necessarily protect it.

One should know that those who write it down, read it, or even maintain right mindfulness toward it do so entirely through the power of the Buddhas of the ten directions, for the power of these obstacles is great.
Śāriputra said:
"If there are those who write it down, uphold it, or even practice it, they shall all be protected by the Buddhas.
The Buddha approved these words.
Śāriputra spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Do all the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions behold, know, and keep in mind those good sons and good daughters who write, uphold, and so forth [this sutra] with their Buddha-eye?”
The Buddha may say, "So be it!
When an evil Māra first arrives intending to cause destruction, the Buddhas of the ten directions provide protection so that he cannot thwart or ruin [the endeavor].

Now, with the Buddha-eye, I see these sons and daughters of good family; I know that the merit of such persons is rare, for they are able to perform this great task of the *prajñāpāramitā* even before having broken the net of Māra.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions, with their Buddha-eyes, see, know, and keep these persons in mind.
Question:
Is it seen with the divine eye (divyacakṣus) or is it seen with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus)?
If one sees with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), why is it said here that one sees with the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*)?
If one sees with the Buddha-eye, sentient beings are deceptive; how, then, can one see them with the Buddha-eye?
Answer: There are two kinds of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*):
first, that which is subsumed under the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*), and second, that which is not so subsumed.
Those not encompassed by the Buddha-eye see present sentient beings as finite and measurable;
those encompassed by the Buddha-eye see sentient beings of the three periods of time as infinite and immeasurable.
When the Dharma-eye enters the Buddha-eye, one perceives only all phenomena and does not perceive sentient beings;
when the Wisdom-eye enters the Buddha-eye, one does not perceive phenomena but perceives only ultimate emptiness.
Question:
Is the divine eye (divyacakṣus) subsumed within the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus) real,
or is it false?
If it were false, the Buddha would not perceive it as such;
if it were real, then sentient beings would be empty—for if present sentient beings are not even real, how much less so those of the future and the past?
Answer: That which is encompassed by the Buddha-eye is entirely real.
Sentient beings are illusory in relation to nirvana, but that which is perceived within the world is not illusory.
If a person grasps at fixed characteristics regarding sentient beings, they speak of them as false; it is not for the sake of conventional truth that they speak of them as false.
For this reason, the divine eye, which is subsumed within the Buddha-eye, perceives sentient beings.
Question:
If that is so, why does one not see sentient beings with the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) subsumed within the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus)? Answer:
Because the wisdom-eye is beneficial for being signless (*animitta*).
The wisdom-eye is always in constant association with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness, and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); it does not observe sentient beings in between. Why is this?
The five aggregates come together and are conventionally designated as "sentient beings.
It is like a small child who may be whipped with a small cane, but not with a large one.
Herein, the praise of the Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken for the sake of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and not from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Question:
Since the future world does not yet exist, it is already difficult to know it through recollection; how much more so to see it with the eye?
Answer:

Just as past phenomena, though extinguished and non-existent, can still cause one to remember past events and exhaustively know one's former lives through the power of mindfulness within the mind and mental factors;
so too it is with the Noble Ones: possessing the power of noble wisdom, they are able to know and see even that which has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, within this prajñā, there is no discrimination among the three periods of time; the future, past, and present are not different.
If one perceives the present, one should also perceive the past and the future;
if one does not perceive the past and the future, one should likewise not perceive the present.
Question:

In the northern region during the age of the final dharma, sentient beings have not yet exhausted their outflows and fetters; they are people of evil deeds. For what reason does the Buddha perceive, know, and keep them in mind? Answer:
The Buddha’s mark of great compassion penetrates to the very marrow of his bones;
this Bodhisattva is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings.
The Buddha observes that these dharmas will flourish most intensely at the end of the age, and that after his parinirvāṇa, this person will assist the Buddha-dharma; thus he knows and remembers this.

Furthermore, people at the end of time in the northern region will be born in borderlands during an evil age when the three poisons are rampant and the kalpa of weapons prevails; in such times, sages and holy ones are rare.

These people do not know for themselves the causes and conditions of various karmas of sin and merit, yet merely by hearing from others or reading the sutras, they are able to believe with joy, make offerings, and swiftly draw near to the unsurpassed path before long—this is indeed difficult!
If the Buddha were present in the world, it would not be difficult for one to become an *avaivartika* and practice the perfection of wisdom with faith.
For various and immeasurable reasons such as these, the Buddha ought to see, remember, and know [the bodhisattva].
Because this person’s faith and understanding are vast, they are able to make offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The requisites for offering, such as flowers and incense, are as previously described.
By virtue of these offerings, one obtains a great reward.
Just as those who disparage [the Dharma] undergo great suffering, so too does one who attains the great fruit—such as a *srotāpanna*—never fall into the three evil realms.

This Bodhisattva, who with single-minded faith and understanding makes offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*, likewise cherishes all Buddhas; because they constantly practice the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, they never depart from the presence of the Buddhas.
Until they reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), they teach and transform sentient beings; apart from the Buddhas, there is no fault in this.
It is like a small child who does not leave his mother, fearing that he might fall into various perils.
Because they always deeply cherish and love the wholesome dharmas, they will never depart from the six pāramitās and so forth until they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
They thus obtain such great fruits and rewards in both this life and future lives.
[Sūtra] “Śāriputra!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* shall, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, reach the lands of the south. There, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen shall write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and they shall receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, explain, correctly attend to, and practice it.”
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall never fall into the evil realms, but will instead experience the joys of the heavens and among humans;
they will further increase the six pāramitās, and will make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise all Buddhas;
and they will gradually attain nirvāṇa by means of the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.

“Śāriputra! This profound *prajñāpāramitā* shall proceed from the south to wherever it reaches in the west. There, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen shall write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and they shall receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, explain, correctly remember, and practice it.”
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall never fall into the evil realms, but will instead experience the pleasures of the heavens and among humans;
they will increase the six *pāramitās* and make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise all Buddhas;
and they will gradually attain *nirvāṇa* by means of the vehicles of the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and Buddhas.

“Śāriputra! This profound *prajñāpāramitā* shall be transmitted from the west to wherever it reaches in the north. There, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen shall write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and they shall receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, explain, correctly attend to, and practice it.”
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall never fall into the evil realms, but will instead experience the pleasures of the heavens and among humans;
they will increase the six pāramitās, and will make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise all Buddhas;
and they will gradually attain nirvāṇa by means of the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas.
Śāriputra! At that time, this profound Prajñāpāramitā shall perform the work of a Buddha in the northern direction. Why is this?
Śāriputra! When my Dharma flourishes, there is no mark of extinction. Śāriputra!
I have already kept in mind those sons and daughters of good family who uphold this profound Prajñāpāramitā and even practice it;

I have also kept in mind those sons and daughters of good family who are able to write down this Prajñāpāramitā, and who honor, make offerings to, revere, and praise it with flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies.

Śāriputra! By reason of these roots of goodness, these sons and daughters of good family shall never fall into the evil realms, but will instead experience the pleasures of the heavens and among humans;
they shall increase the six pāramitās and offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to all Buddhas.
They gradually attain nirvana by means of the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
With my Buddha-eye I see this person; I also praise and extol them.
In the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas likewise see this person with their Buddha-eyes, and likewise praise and extol them.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
will this profound Prajñāpāramitā be widely practiced in the northern region in the future?”
The Buddha said: “So it is! So it is!”
Śāriputra! This profound Prajñāpāramitā shall later be widely practiced in the northern region. Śāriputra!

In the future, in the northern region, if these sons of good family or daughters of good family hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it, explain it, correctly bring it to mind, and practice according to its teaching, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family have long since set their minds upon the Great Vehicle, have made offerings to many Buddhas, have planted various roots of goodness, and have long associated with spiritual friends.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future, how many sons of good family and daughters of good family will there be in the northern direction who seek the path of the Buddha, copy the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and even practice it according to the teaching?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
