"In the future, although there will be many sons and daughters of good family in the northern direction who seek the path of the Buddha, there will be few sons and daughters of good family who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will not sink, be startled, be terrified, or be afraid."

Why is this? Because such a person has extensively approached and made offerings to the Buddhas and has extensively questioned the Buddhas; such a person will certainly be able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), and the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā); they will fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni), and so on, up to fulfilling the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).

Śāriputra! Because the roots of goodness of these sons and daughters of good family are pure and profound, they are able to bring great benefit to sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? It is because I now teach the Dharma corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) for these sons and daughters of good family; likewise, the Buddhas of the past also taught the Dharma corresponding to omniscience for these sons and daughters of good family.

By reason of these causes and conditions, when this person is born in future lives, they will continue to attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and they will also preach the Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to others.

These sons and daughters of good family are all united in one mind; neither Māra nor the followers of Māra can thwart their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, let alone those who practice evil or disparage those who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* being able to destroy their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!

Śāriputra! These sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, obtain great joy in the Dharma and bliss in the Dharma; they also establish many others in roots of goodness for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Treatise] Commentary:

Regarding the statement, “This profound *prajñāpāramitā*, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, shall reach the lands of the south,” it means that the Buddha appeared in the east and there preached the *prajñāpāramitā*. Having defeated Māra and his followers, as well as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and having delivered immeasurable sentient beings, he subsequently entered parinirvāṇa beneath the twin *śāla* trees at Kuśinagara.
Thereafter, the *prajñāpāramitā* proceeded from the east to the south.

Just as the sun, the moon, the five planets, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions constantly proceed from the east to the south, from the south to the west, and from the west to the north, circling Mount Sumeru.
Furthermore, just as when making offerings to the eternal Dharma by circumambulating it clockwise, one universally delivers the people of Jambudvīpa;
by virtue of these causes and conditions, [the light] proceeds from the east to the south, and from the south to the west.
Just as the Buddha, because his mind is free from attachment, does not remain fixed in one place;
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā, not abiding fixedly in one location.

From the western direction to the northern direction, sentient beings in these two directions who delight in making offerings, copying, reading, and even practicing it—using flowers, incense, and even banners and canopies—will receive great rewards, as described in the sūtras.
Subsequently, it will be transmitted in succession until it reaches the north.
The karmic fruit obtained from making offerings therein shall be as described above. "Śāriputra!
"This Prajñāpāramitā shall perform the work of a Buddha in the northern direction.
Within this, the causal conditions are explained:
"While the Buddha was in the world, he was able to sever the doubts of the multitude; the Buddha-dharma flourished, and there was no fear of its extinction."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, five hundred years will have passed and the True Dharma will gradually perish; at that time, performing the Buddha’s work will become increasingly difficult.
At that time, those of sharp faculties will read, recite, and maintain right mindfulness, and will also make offerings of flowers and incense;
those of dull faculties will copy [the scriptures] and make offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth.
"These two kinds of people shall both eventually attain liberation; therefore, it is said that 'they shall perform the work of a Buddha.
The Buddha said:
'These sons and daughters of good family—I and all the Buddhas of the ten directions behold them with the Buddha-eye, keeping them in mind, knowing them, and praising them.'"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Will this profound *prajñā* be widely practiced in the northern region?
[The phrase] "widely practiced" refers to its extensive prevalence in the northern part of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, in the northern lands there is the Snowy Mountain (Himavat). Because the Snowy Mountain is cold, its medicinal herbs can neutralize all poisons;
the rice and grains consumed there cannot cause the three poisons to erupt violently.
Because the three poisons do not erupt violently, sentient beings are gentle and supple, and their five faculties, such as faith, all attain strength.
For such reasons as these, the *prajñāpāramitā* is widely practiced in the northern region.

When people hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and copy it, uphold it, and even maintain right mindfulness of it and practice according to its teaching, one should know that these people have long since resolved upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), have made many offerings to the Buddhas, have planted roots of goodness, and have associated with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Therefore, they are able to copy, uphold, believe and accept, and even practice according to the teaching within this degenerate age.
Śāriputra asked:
"In the northern direction, how many people, having heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā, are able to write it down, read it, recite it, and even practice it according to the teaching?"
The Buddha replied:

"This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to know and difficult to practice. Although many people may resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path and receive the name of 'bodhisattva,' few, upon hearing this *prajñāpāramitā*, will have their minds penetrate it without being startled or discouraged."
Regarding the characteristics of mental penetration—being neither startled nor terrified—the Buddha himself explains herein:

"This person has frequently drawn near to many Buddhas. As for "drawing near to many Buddhas," it means that throughout immeasurable lifetimes, one constantly beholds the Buddhas, paying them respect and making offerings.
Regarding "questioning and challenging" (*paripṛcchā*): to directly inquire about a matter because one's doubts are not resolved, and to ask repeatedly in various ways, is called "challenging.
This person has, throughout successive lifetimes, questioned and challenged the Buddhas regarding the matters of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Although the karmic fruit of this person's merit has not yet been realized, one should know that this person is fully endowed with the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Because these merits have reached full maturity, they bring great benefit to sentient beings; that is to say, by virtue of the causes and conditions of the *dānapāramitā* and the *śīlapāramitā*, one is born into a wealthy and noble family, personally practicing giving and teaching others to give.

By means of the causes and conditions of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), they cause immeasurable sentient beings to leave the household life, receive the precepts, and resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
In this regard, the Buddha explains the causal conditions:
"This person has heard from me and from the Buddhas of the past the Mahāyāna Dharma corresponding to *sarvajñatā*; therefore, in future births, they do not lose this mind;
furthermore, this person also teaches others, speaking of such matters."
"Just as when one lamp is lit, it is passed on until they are all lit, so too this person’s afflictions are thin;
because they are free from stinginess, greed, envy, and anger, they do not slander one another and always remain harmonious with a single mind.
For this reason, neither Māra nor the followers of Māra can thwart or destroy them."
If a person makes even a slight error, Māra seizes the opportunity;
it is like a person with an open sore receiving poison.
Māra is the lord of the desire realm, yet he cannot thwart or destroy such a person—how much less so one who practices evil!
There may be those whose conduct is evil yet who are not truly evil, such as noble ones (ārya) who have not yet abandoned desire;
for this reason it is said:
"One who reviles the *prajñāpāramitā* while practicing evil conduct thereby destroys the bodhisattva."

Furthermore, sons and daughters of good family who, throughout immeasurable ages, have loved the Buddha-dharma and been deeply attached to the true Dharma, possess great power of faith and power of wisdom; because they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and attain the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they cause sentient beings to enter the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to their capacities, or cause them to obtain the causes and conditions for *prajñā*, namely, the various roots of goodness such as giving and observing the precepts.

The phrase "for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" means that because these good men and good women seek the unsurpassed path, they instruct others to cause them to abide in all roots of goodness and merit.
[Sūtra] "These sons and daughters of good family made a vow before me:

'When I practice the bodhisattva path, I shall deliver countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, until they reach the stage of *avaivartika* and receive their prediction [of enlightenment].'"
I know their minds, and I likewise rejoice in them.
These sons and daughters of good family also made a vow before the Buddhas of the past:

"When I practice the bodhisattva path, I shall deliver countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, until they reach the stage of *avaivartika* and receive their prediction."
The Buddhas of the past also knew their minds and rejoiced in them. “Śāriputra!

These good sons and good daughters have great resolve; the forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects they receive are also great, and they are likewise able to practice great giving.”
Having been able to practice great giving, one plants great roots of goodness;
having planted great roots of goodness, one attains great retribution.
For the sake of gathering in sentient beings, one takes on a body and is able to relinquish all internal and external possessions among those beings.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he makes a vow to be born in other worlds where the present Buddhas are currently preaching the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* before those Buddhas, he likewise demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings there, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare,
World-Honored One!”

Regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present, there is no phenomenon that the Buddha does not know; there is no characteristic of knowing that he does not know; and regarding the conduct of sentient beings, there is nothing he does not know.

Now the Buddha fully knows all past Buddhas, as well as their bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; he also knows the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the worlds of the present Buddhas throughout the ten directions; and he likewise knows all future Buddhas, as well as their bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
“World-Honored One!

In future ages, will there be good men and good women who diligently seek the six pāramitās, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and even practicing them, such that some succeed and others do not?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If good sons and good daughters seek with single-minded diligence, they shall obtain the various sūtras corresponding to the six pāramitās.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If good men and good women practice with such diligence, will they attain these profound sūtras that correspond to the six pāramitās?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“These sons and daughters of good family shall obtain these profound sūtras corresponding to the six pāramitās. Why is this?

Good sons and good daughters, for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they preach the Dharma to sentient beings, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing them to abide within the six pāramitās.
For this reason, these sons and daughters of good family will, in their subsequent lives, easily obtain profound sūtras corresponding to the six pāramitās;

having obtained them, they will practice as taught in the six pāramitās with diligent and unceasing effort, until they purify buddha-fields, bring sentient beings to maturity, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] Commentary:
The Buddha said:
"Good sons and good daughters shall make a vow before me and before the Buddhas of the past:..."

"As I practice the bodhisattva path, I shall cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings to resolve upon the unsurpassed path; I shall instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden them, so that they may attain the prediction of non-retrogression."
“I and the Buddhas of the past know that this good man’s mind is great and capable of accomplishing what must be done; therefore, we rejoice.
When good men and good women hear that the Buddha knows their minds, they give rise to joy and, reflecting upon the vows they made in the past, redouble their diligent progress.
Regarding "the great mind": the minds of all sentient beings delight in taking the six sense objects as their conditions.
There are those who practice mixed merit; that is to say, when performing meritorious deeds, their minds give rise to doubt and regret.
Although they obtain wealth and status as the karmic fruit of such merit, they are unable to use it properly, nor can they give it to others.
Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, their faculties are dull and dark, and they cannot distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.

When these sons of good family have not yet attained the Way, because of their pure merit and virtue, they obtain the five supreme sensual pleasures; they are able to enjoy them to their heart's content and can give them away as they wish—whether to those who are impoverished or to plant them within fields of merit.

If one encounters a virtuous friend and hears the Buddha-dharma, the mind’s attachment to desire ceases; out of compassion for sentient beings and for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one practices all forms of giving—both internal and external—without any sense of stinginess or attachment.

If one maintains the precepts, practices the ten paths of wholesome action universally, and is endowed with the discipline of the precepts, one acts together with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
It is the same for all other wholesome dharmas: they are all practiced by oneself with a profound mind, as well as leading others to practice the paths of wholesome action.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of merit, they do not seek worldly pleasures—the status of celestial kings, human kings, or positions of wealth and nobility;
rather, upon hearing that there is a place where a present Buddha resides, they vow to be reborn there.
Because this bodhisattva knows the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), he does not delight in birth;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he takes birth before the Buddhas of the ten directions to hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having heard this, he brought immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to spiritual maturity, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed path.

Śāriputra, who does not possess all-knowledge, having heard the account of the vows and practices of the bodhisattvas of the three periods of time, was struck with wonder and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
The Buddha knows all phenomena throughout the three periods of time;
there is nothing he does not know regarding suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality;
and as for the mental activities, karmic deeds, retributions, and causal conditions of all sentient beings, there is no matter he does not know.
He fully and universally knows all the present Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the Buddhas of the past and future worlds, their disciples, and the deeds they perform.
"The Buddha’s omniscience is of such great power that it is inconceivable!
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"We are both renunciants, and we both seek the Prajñāpāramitā; for what reason is there one who attains it and another who does not?"
The Buddha replied:

"If a bodhisattva always seeks the six pāramitās with a single mind, not begrudging body or life, this is because that person possesses a virtuous heart within and is protected and assisted by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and devas without."
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Even though he is diligent, the Buddha is no longer in the world and the power of Māra is great; how can this bodhisattva obtain such a profound sūtra as this Prajñāpāramitā?"
For this reason, he asked again:
"Have you obtained these profound sūtras that correspond to the six pāramitās?
The Buddha said:
"It is attained.

Herein, the causes and conditions for attainment are explained: namely, "If good men and good women, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, preach the Dharma to sentient beings, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing them to abide in the six pāramitās and opening the way to the Buddha-path."
Because of the retribution of this karma, when he changes bodies, he easily obtains profound sūtras corresponding to the six pāramitās;

having obtained them, he is able to quickly receive and uphold them, practicing according to what is taught with diligence and without abandoning it, never being separated from them throughout successive lives.
By means of the fruit and retribution of the six pāramitās, he purifies Buddha-fields, brings sentient beings to maturity, and proceeds even unto the unsurpassed path.
"If one is stingy with the Dharma, one will constantly be born in remote borderlands where the Buddha-Dharma does not exist.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 67;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on Mara’s Deeds, Chapter 46, Scroll 68.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 46: On the Deeds of Māra. [Sūtra] The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These good men and good women have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practice the six *pāramitās*, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify Buddha-fields; the Buddha has already praised and spoken of their merits.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that good sons and good daughters who seek the Buddha-way encounter various obstacles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If eloquence for joyful exposition does not arise immediately, one should know that this is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is it that the eloquence of joyful speech does not immediately arise? This is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, it is difficult for them to fully complete the six pāramitās."
For these reasons, if eloquence for joyful exposition does not arise immediately, this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if eloquence for joyful exposition arises abruptly, you should know that this too is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is it that the sudden arising of the eloquence of joyful speech is also the work of Māra?
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, they become attached to the joy of preaching the Dharma;
because of these causes and conditions, a sudden burst of eloquence in joyful preaching arises—this should be known as a work of Māra for that bodhisattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
when copying this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, if one is deceitful and arrogant, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When copying this sutra, if one is distracted by laughter and jesting, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If, while copying this sutra, one laughs lightly and shows disrespect, you should know that this is the work of Māra toward a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if, while copying this sutra,
the mind is distracted and unsettled, you should know that this is the work of Māra toward a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When this sutra is being written, if there is mutual discord, you should know that this is the work of Māra for the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a son or daughter of good family thinks,
"I do not find any flavor in this sutra," and then abandons it and departs,
you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when one upholds,
reads, recites, explains, or correctly contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā, if one becomes haughty and arrogant, you should know that this is the work of Māra for that bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if,

while upholding the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, drawing near to it, and correctly recollecting it, they instead mock and deride one another, you should know that this is the work of Māra for these bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
reads it, recites it, correctly contemplates it, and practices it, if they treat one another with contempt, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
If, while upholding, reading, reciting, or even correctly reflecting upon the Prajñāpāramitā, one’s mind becomes distracted, one should know that this is the work of Māra for that bodhisattva.
If, while upholding the Prajñāpāramitā, reading, reciting, or even correctly reflecting upon it, the mind becomes discordant, one should know that this is the work of Māra for that bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has said:”
"Good sons and good daughters may form this thought:
'I do not find the flavor within these sutras,' and they then abandon them and depart;
you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason and by what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva fail to find the flavor within the sutras and then abandon them?
The Buddha said:

"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva did not practice the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity for long in previous lives. Upon hearing this exposition of the perfection of wisdom, he rises from his seat and thinks to himself:
'I am not designated within the perfection of wisdom.'"
"With a mind that is not pure, he then rises from his seat and departs; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"For what reason do they not receive a prediction [of enlightenment], but rather rise from their seats and depart when this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being taught?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva has not yet entered the stage of the fixed position (*niyāma*), the Buddhas do not grant them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
when the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, a bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I have no name within it."
"If their mind is not pure, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti asked: "By what cause and condition is the name of this bodhisattva not mentioned within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha said:
"For bodhisattvas who have not yet received their prediction, the Buddhas do not proclaim their names.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Within this Prajñāpāramitā, there is no name for the place of my birth, whether it be a village or a city."

If such a person does not wish to hear the Prajñāpāramitā and rises from the assembly to depart, at every moment of that thought, they shall be set back by one kalpa; they must then once again diligently apply themselves with vigor to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] Commentary:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) each possess sovereignty (*adhipati*).
Sovereignty is mutually contradictory, and contradiction is itself an enemy or thief.

Just as water extinguishes fire when it gains superior power, and fire consumes water when it gains superior power, even down to grasses and trees which each harm one another—how much more so for sentient beings!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses a heart of great compassion; although he does not act as an enemy toward sentient beings, sentient beings act as enemies toward the Bodhisattva.
Because the Bodhisattva’s body is composed of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is capable of creating obstacles.

The Buddha has previously spoken of the merits of the bodhisattva—namely, that they are protected by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and devas—but he had not yet described the characteristics of their enemies and robbers.
Out of compassion, the Buddha had previously explained this matter only briefly;
now, at the request of Subhūti, the Buddha explains in detail the matters concerning obstacles and hindrances.

Although the Buddha’s mind is equal toward all sentient beings and all phenomena, because this bodhisattva is able to bring great benefit to the world, he speaks of the characteristics of the beautiful and the ugly, the beneficial and the harmful, what is the path and what is not the path, and matters of obstacles.
The Buddha does not cause practitioners to destroy, harm, or obstruct others; rather, he causes them to awaken to and recognize these things so that they do not follow after them.
What are these "enemies and robbers"?
Briefly stated, they are any phenomena pertaining to sentient beings or non-sentient beings that can thwart or destroy a bodhisattva’s mind set upon the unsurpassed path.
Non-sentient beings refer to such things as illness, hunger and thirst, cold and heat, being beaten and oppressed, falling, and so forth.

Sentient beings refer to Māra and his followers, evil spirits, those with perverse doubts and lack of faith, those who have severed their roots of goodness, those fixed in the notion of attainment, those who truly and definitively differentiate all phenomena, those deeply attached to worldly pleasures, as well as enemies, robbers, officials, lions, tigers, wolves, predatory beasts, venomous insects, and the like.
There are two kinds of thieves among sentient beings:
those that are internal and those that are external.

The internal ones arise from within one's own mind, such as sorrow and distress from failing to obtain the flavor of the Dharma, and the arising of wrong views, doubt and regret, lack of faith, and so forth.
As for "external," it is as explained above.
Such various difficult circumstances, the Buddha collectively names "Māra.
There are four kinds of Māra:
The demon of afflictions, the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of death, and the demon of the son of heaven.
As for the demon of afflictions, it refers to the one hundred and eight afflictions and the eighty-four thousand varieties of afflictions that are conceptually distinguished.
Regarding the five groups of Māras: through the causal conditions of the conjunction of afflictions and karma, this body is obtained.
The four great elements and the derivative matter of the four great elements, as well as the physical forms such as the eye-faculty and so forth, are called the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
The conjunction of the one hundred and eight afflictions and other sensations is called the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
The aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) consist of the conceptualization and synthesis of notions such as small, large, immeasurable, and non-existence.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of those mental factors—both associated and dissociated—that arise from a mind perceiving beauty or ugliness, and which give rise to states such as greed and hatred.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) refers to the six consciousnesses produced through the conjunction of the six sense organs and the six sense objects; it is the differentiation of these six consciousnesses that synthesizes the infinite and boundless mind.

As for the Māra of Death: because of the conditions of impermanence, it destroys the continuity of the five aggregates and the life-span; by exhausting and separating from the three factors—consciousness, warmth, and vitality—it is called the Māra of Death.

The Devaputra Māra is the lord of the desire realm who is deeply attached to worldly pleasures; because he perceives things as having substantial existence, he gives rise to false views and harbors hatred and envy toward all the noble ones, the path to nirvāṇa, and the Dharma. This is called the Devaputra Māra.
*Māra*—in the language of Qin, it means "one who can snatch away life.

Although the *mṛtyu-māra* (the demon of death) truly can snatch away life, the others are likewise able to create the conditions for snatching it away; they also snatch away the life of wisdom. For this reason, they are called "killers."
Question:
Since the five classes of Māras subsume the three types of Māras, why are four mentioned separately? Answer:
In reality, there is but one Māra; it is by distinguishing its meanings that there are four.

As for the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), people die because of greed and hatred, and these can also act as the conditions for the taking of life; they are mentioned separately because they are proximate causes for the taking of life.

The Devaputra Māra possesses great power and influence due to his mixed roots of merit and karmic conditions; yet, because of the power of his false views, he can seize the life-force of wisdom and also act as a cause for death. For this reason, he is mentioned separately.
The power of impermanence and death is great; since no one can escape it, it is spoken of separately because it is so utterly terrifying and loathsome.
Question:
Why does this Māra disturb and harass those who practice the Path?
Answer: This has already been explained at length.
Within this chapter, all four types of Māra are present, though they are discussed according to their respective contexts.
Furthermore, the three Māras do not exist apart from one another:
if there are the five aggregates, then there are afflictions;
if there are afflictions, then the celestial Māra finds an opportunity.
Because of the conjunction of the five aggregates and the afflictions, there exists the celestial Māra.
For this reason, Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"Having previously praised and spoken of the merits of the bodhisattva, why is it that now these works of Māra arise for the bodhisattva?"
The Buddha replied:

"If eloquence for joyful exposition does not arise immediately, this is the work of Māra. This means that if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, ascends a high seat to preach the Dharma, yet the eloquence for joyful exposition does not arise.
The listeners were distressed, thinking:
"We have come for this very purpose, yet the Dharma Master does not preach.
Or they thought thus:
"The Dharma Master cannot preach because of fear," some said;
others said, "He does not preach because he does not know."

Some do not speak because they consider their own transgressions to be too grave; some are unwilling to speak because they believe they will not receive offerings; some do not speak because they think we hold them in contempt; and some do not speak because they are habituated to pleasure.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the minds of the listeners are disturbed; therefore, not delighting in speaking is called an activity of Māra.

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva comes out of compassion for sentient beings wishing to preach the Dharma, and the listeners wish to hear it, yet the Dharma master’s mind desires to speak while his mouth is unable to utter a word.
This is seen as the work of Māra; for example, when Māra entered Ānanda’s mind, the Buddha asked him three times and he did not answer until after a long time.
In this context, Subhūti asks the World-Honored One:
"By what causes and conditions does eloquence not arise immediately?"
The Buddha replied,
“When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, it is difficult to fully complete them. Why is this?”
Due to causes and conditions from previous lives, this person has dull faculties and is indolent, allowing Māra to find an opportunity;
because they do not practice the six pāramitās with single-minded devotion, the eloquence of joyful speech does not arise immediately.
Question:
If eloquence in joyful exposition does not arise immediately, that may indeed be the work of Māra;
but now, since this eloquence in joyful exposition arises suddenly, why is it also the work of Māra?
The answer is:

This Dharma-master loves the Dharma and clings to the Dharma; because he seeks fame and reputation, he speaks at will and with delight, yet it lacks any principle or reason, like a runaway horse difficult to restrain, or like a great flood in sudden spate where all manner of filth is turbidly mixed together.
Therefore, in this context the Buddha himself says:
"When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās yet becomes attached to the joy of preaching the Dharma, this is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the purpose of destroying pride.
Furthermore, those who copy this sutra may give rise to thoughts of self-importance and arrogance;
because of such arrogance, their bodies become haughty—meaning they are insolent and overbearing.
When copying this Prajñāpāramitā, they may employ a mind of contempt, anger, derision, or a lack of reverence.
Furthermore, this Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to obtain even when one has a single-minded or concentrated mind; how much more so when writing it with a distracted mind!
Whether receiving the words from another's mouth at the time of writing or copying from a manuscript, it can be attained if there is single-minded harmony;
however, if the teacher does not grant permission, or due to various other such causes and conditions, there will be a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, when one contemplates this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, every chapter is empty and there is nothing therein to be delighted in;
one then forms this thought: "I find no flavor in this sūtra!"
He then abandons it and departs.
Since the Prajñāpāramitā is the root of all happiness, that this person does not experience its flavor is the work of Māra.

Furthermore, when receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, or correctly recollecting [the teachings], one may be indolent, mockingly smile, have a distracted mind, or lack harmony, as described above.
Regarding "mutual contempt": when receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, or correctly recollecting [the teachings] from others, the teacher and disciple mutually despise one another.
However, when copying the sūtras, they merely abandon the task and depart; there is no mutual contempt.
Question: Among the various matters mentioned above, why do you ask only about "not obtaining the flavor within the sūtras" and not about the others? Answer:
The Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the noble ones differs from that spoken by ordinary people; therefore, ordinary people do not obtain its flavor.
Subhūti’s thought was:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is a collection of pure, precious jewels that can benefit sentient beings and is free from fault or evil; why then would these people not obtain its flavor?"
The Buddha replied:
"Because this person did not practice the six pāramitās for long in previous lives, their five faculties—faith and the others—are weak.
Because they are weak, they cannot believe in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-reliance; thus, a disturbed mind arises, and they speak these words:"
"Why does the Buddha, who possesses all-knowledge, not grant me a prediction of enlightenment?
Having said this, he departed.
The remainder is easy to understand and therefore is not questioned.
Subhūti asked:
"If that is so, for what reason have they not been granted a prediction [of enlightenment]?
The Buddha possesses great compassion; he ought to take pity on them, protect their minds, and prevent them from falling into evil states!"
The Buddha said:
"To those who have not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-position, the Buddhas do not bestow a prediction of enlightenment. Why is this so?"

Although the Buddhas fully know the long-distant affairs of sentient beings, there are five-attainment seers and devas who, seeing that this person lacks the causal conditions of wholesome karma to warrant a prediction of enlightenment, might—if they were to receive a prediction—disbelieve and slight the Buddha, thinking:
"There being no causal conditions, how can he grant a prediction?"
Therefore, those who have entered the stage of the Dharma receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
This applies equally to their names and the villages where they dwell.
If such a person rises from their seat and departs, for as many thoughts as they entertain during that departure, for each and every thought, one *kalpa* is subtracted.
When the retribution for their offenses has been fully expiated, they will regain a human body; yet they must once again practice for that same number of kalpas.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva studies other sūtras while abandoning the Prajñāpāramitā, they will ultimately never reach sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
"Good sons and good daughters who abandon the roots to grasp at branches and leaves—know that this, too, is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What are those other sūtras that a son or daughter of good family studies which cannot lead them to omniscience (sarvajñatā)?
The Buddha said:

“They are the sūtras to be practiced by the śrāvakas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.”

When sons or daughters of good family abide in this, they attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat; these are called the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas, and they cannot reach sarvajñatā.
In this way, noble sons and noble daughters abandon the *prajñāpāramitā* and draw near to these other sūtras.
Why is that? Subhūti!
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born, and they accomplish mundane and supramundane dharmas. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the perfection of wisdom, they also study mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Subhūti, it is as if a dog does not seek food from its master, but instead begs from the laborers.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead cling to the branches and leaves—the sūtras to be practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. You should know that this is a work of Māra for bodhisattvas.
Subhūti! It is as if there were someone who, wishing to see an elephant, having seen it, instead examines its footprints. Subhūti!
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
Subhūti replied:
"It is not wise," the Buddha said.

"It is likewise with those sons and daughters of good family who seek the path of the Buddha: they obtain the profound Prajñāpāramitā, yet they abandon it and instead take up the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Subhūti! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Subhūti!
It is like a person who wishes to see the great ocean; having seen it, they instead seek water in a cow’s footprint and think:
"Can the water of the great ocean be equal to this?"
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise?"
Subhūti said: “It is not wise.
The Buddha said:

"In the future age, there will be sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way and will likewise do so: having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will abandon it and instead take up the sūtras practiced by *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. You should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Subhūti! It is as if, for example, a master carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice, wishing to construct the magnificent palace of Śakra Devānām Indra, were instead to take the palaces of the sun and moon as their model.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti said, “It would not be wise. “So it is, Subhūti!”

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family with meager merit who seek the Buddha-way; having obtained this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they will reject it and instead seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) within the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti said: “It is not clever.
The Buddha said:
“You should know that this, too, is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

Subhūti, it is as if there were a person who wished to see a universal monarch (cakravartin), but having seen him, did not recognize him; later, seeing various minor kings, he took their physical characteristics and said:”
"How does this differ from a Wheel-Turning Sage King? Subhūti,
what do you think?"
"Would this person be considered wise?
Subhūti replied,
"He would not be wise."

“Subhūti! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family with meager merit who seek the Buddha-way; having obtained this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they will abandon it and instead take up the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, holding to them in their quest for sarvajñatā.”
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti said: "It is not wise. [The Buddha said:
"You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
Subhūti! It is as if a hungry person, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, were to cast it aside and instead eat sixty-day-old grain porridge. Subhūti!
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
Subhūti replied:
“It is not wise,” the Buddha said.

“Suppose there were good men and good women seeking the path of the Buddha in a future age who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, would cast it aside and instead take up the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, holding them to seek *sarvajñatā*. What do you think?”
"Would such a person be wise?
Subhūti replied, "He would not be wise."
“You should know that this, too, is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Subhūti,
it is like a person who, having obtained a priceless maṇi jewel, instead compares it to a crystal gem.”
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti said, “It is not wise.
The Buddha said:

"In a future age, if there are sons or daughters of good family seeking the Buddha-way who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, abandon it and instead take up the sūtras practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, holding them to seek *sarvajñatā*—would such people be wise?"
Subhūti said: “It is not wise.
“One should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when these sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, if they take pleasure in speaking of things that are not in accordance with the Dharma, they will not succeed in writing the *prajñāpāramitā*."

That is to say: delighting in speaking of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; delighting in speaking of the precepts, meditative concentration, and the formless attainments; delighting in speaking of the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; and delighting in speaking of the four foundations of mindfulness up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Subhūti,
within this prajñāpāramitā there is no characteristic of delight in discourse.

Subhūti! The Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being inconceivable; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being neither defiled nor pure; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being neither distracted nor dispersed; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being ineffable; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being without words or meaning; the Prajñāpāramitā has the characteristic of being non-apprehensible.
Why is this? Subhūti,
within this prajñāpāramitā, these various marks do not exist.

Subhūti! If there are good sons or good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path who, while copying this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, do so with a distracted mind regarding these dharmas, you should know that this, too, is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can this Prajñāpāramitā be written down?”
The Buddha said:
"It cannot be written down. Why is this?"

Because the *prajñāpāramitā* lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because the *dhyānapāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *śīlapāramitā*, *dānapāramitā*, and even up to the *sarvākārajñatā* lack intrinsic nature;
if there is no intrinsic nature, it is not called "nature," and one cannot write down a non-existent dharma with a non-existent dharma.
Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeking the bodhisattva path should think:
"The dharma-less is this profound prajñāpāramitā."
"You should know that this is precisely a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"World-Honored One!
When good sons and good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path write the Prajñāpāramitā using written characters, they think to themselves:"
"To write down this Prajñāpāramitā"—
to attribute the letters to the Prajñāpāramitā— should be known as yet another work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is without letters; the Dhyānapāramitā, Vīryapāramitā, Kṣāntipāramitā, Śīlapāramitā, and Dānapāramitā are likewise without letters.
World-Honored One!
Form has no words; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no words; even up to all-knowledge, there are no words.
World-Honored One!

If good sons or good daughters seeking the bodhisattva path become attached to the letterless Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including becoming attached to the letterless knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), you should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Reading, reciting, explaining, correctly reflecting upon, and practicing according to the teaching are also like this.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons or daughters of good family seeking the Buddha-way are transcribing the Prajñāpāramitā, there may arise thoughts of countries, thoughts of villages, thoughts of cities, or thoughts of regions; or thoughts may arise upon hearing slander or defamation of their teacher; or they may think of their parents, brothers, sisters, or other kinsmen; or they may think of thieves, or outcasts (caṇḍāla), or of crowds of women, or of prostitutes—such various and diverse distracting thoughts and obstacles as these."
The Māra further reinforces his intent to destroy the writing of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and to destroy its copying, reciting, explaining, correct mindfulness, and practice according to the teaching.
Subhūti, you should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti:

When sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way receive fame, respect, gifts, and offerings—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine for illness, and various articles of pleasure—if, while writing, receiving, reading, reciting, or even correctly contemplating this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, those sons and daughters of good family become attached to these things and fail to complete the writing of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, or fail to proceed through to its correct contemplation, you should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way write out the *prajñāpāramitā* and even practice it as taught, Māra the Evil One may employ skillful means to provide these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with various other profound sūtras.
Those who possess skillful means should not greedily cling to those other profound sūtras given by Māra the Evil One."
Why is this? Because this sutra cannot cause people to reach sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
In this regard, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who lack skillful means, upon hearing these other various profound sutras, will then abandon the profound prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti! Within this Prajñāpāramitā, I have extensively expounded the path of skillful means for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should seek it from herein.

Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeking the bodhisattva path abandons this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seeks the way of skillful means within the profound sūtras given by Māra concerning the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, you should know that this, too, is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
[Treatise] Commentary:

Regarding those who study other sūtras while abandoning the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth: there are some who receive the precepts and study the Dharma within the Śrāvaka teachings, yet from the beginning have not heard the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Or, having perhaps heard of it elsewhere at some time, they remain deeply attached to the teachings they previously studied; thus, they abandon the *prajñāpāramitā* and seek *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) within those previously studied teachings.

There are śrāvaka disciples who first obtain the Prajñāpāramitā, yet do not understand its underlying meaning or grasp its essential flavor, and thus practice the bodhisattva path by means of the śrāvaka sūtras.
Suppose there is a person who is a disciple of the Śrāvakas and obtains the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, desiring to believe and accept it;
yet other Śrāvakas discourage and undermine their resolve, saying:
"This sūtra is inconsistent from beginning to end and lacks any fixed characteristic; you should abandon it!"
Within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, what is there that does not exist?
The six *pāda* Abhidharmas and their commentaries, which analyze the characteristics of all phenomena, are themselves the Prajñāpāramitā;
the eighty sections of the Vinaya are themselves the Śīlapāramitā.
In the Abhidharma, the detailed analysis of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis constitutes the dhyāna-pāramitā;
in the Jātaka tales of the Tripiṭaka, the praise of liberation, generosity, patience, and diligence constitutes the [other] three pāramitās.
For various reasons such as these, they abandon the *prajñāpāramitā* and seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) within the *śrāvaka* sūtras.

It is like a person who, wishing to obtain solid and excellent wood, discards the roots and trunk to take the branches and leaves; although these are still called "wood," they are of no practical use.
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the root of the Three Piṭakas;
having attained the Prajñāpāramitā, one speaks of other matters for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and these are called "branches and leaves."
Furthermore, although the characteristics of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena are taught in the *Śrāvaka* sūtras, they are not clearly manifest;
in the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, however, they appear with distinct clarity, being easy to perceive and easy to attain.
Just as a person who clings to branches and leaves falls, whereas one who grasps the trunk remains firm;
so too, if one adheres to the sūtras of the śrāvakas, one falls into the Lesser Vehicle,
but if one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, it is easy to attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Therefore it is said:
"Abandon the roots and trunk; take the branches and leaves. Question:

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation are also found within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*; for what reason, then, are they now designated solely as the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Answer:

Although these dharmas exist within the Mahāyāna, they are conjoined with ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), such that the mind has no attachments. They are taught for the sake of all sentient beings because of not abandoning *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) and the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*);
the Śrāvaka sūtras are not so, as they are for the sake of the realization of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he is able to accomplish both mundane and supramundane dharmas;
therefore, if a bodhisattva seeks buddhahood, he should study the perfection of wisdom.
For example, when a dog guards for its master, it should seek food from the master, yet instead seeks it from the servants or guests;
so it is with the bodhisattva.
The dog is a metaphor for the practitioner, and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is a metaphor for the master.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā there are manifold benefits, yet people abandon it to seek other sūtras.
Because the Buddha wishes to make this clear and easy to perceive, he employs parables.
It is the same with the elephant, the great ocean, the palace of Śakra, the wheel-turning sage king, and the priceless jewel.
Question:
The five desires give rise to the five hindrances; because these five hindrances shroud wisdom, one should not delight in speaking of them.
Why then do you delight in speaking of the other six pāramitās, up to the unsurpassed path, while saying that [speaking of the five desires] is not in accordance with the Dharma?
The answer is:
"Not in accordance with the Dharma" means not in accordance with the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within the true mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no dharma of fixed characteristics; how, then, could it be joyfully expounded?
If there were fixed characteristics, the mind would become attached to the joy of eloquent discourse.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great compassion, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without attachment to words;
employing the dharma of non-apprehension, they reveal to sentient beings the Prajñāpāramitā, which is the characteristic of ultimate emptiness.

Because this person writes, reads, recites, and so forth with a mind of attachment, grasping at the characteristics of the six sense objects up to the Unsurpassed Way, it is said that they do not act according to the Dharma. Question:
If the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately empty and devoid of any existent phenomena, it cannot be written, read, or recited.
If this is so, then there should be no work of Māra?
He replied:
Ultimate emptiness and non-existence are also not the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā; why, then, would they be the work of Māra?
In this regard it is said:
If a person knows that "non-existence" is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that is the work of Māra.
If one writes down the *prajñāpāramitā* using written characters, yet [simply] thinks to oneself:
"To write the Prajñāpāramitā"—
to have such a mind of attachment is itself the work of Māra.
If a person knows the characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā, they will not write, read, or recite it with a mind of attachment.
If there should be anyone who comes to destroy it, this constitutes the destruction of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, due to the two conditions of the internal demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the external demon of the deva-sons (*devaputramāra*), the *prajñāpāramitā* is ruined during the time of copying it or even while practicing it.
As for the arising of thoughts, it refers to thinking that this land is not peaceful and secure, while that land is abundant and joyful;
the same applies to villages, cities, and regions.
Or, hearing that their teacher has been slandered or disparaged, they wish to assist their teacher by eliminating his ill repute;
or, hearing that their parents are ill or involved in legal affairs;
or, thinking of the terror of bandits, they wish to resolve to go elsewhere.
It is the same with the caṇḍāla.
By living together with thieves and caṇḍālas, anger arises;
by living together with many courtesans, the mind of lust arises.
Through various causes and conditions such as these, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is destroyed;
the bodhisattva, being aware of this, should neither dwell upon it nor speak of it.
Or, when writing the perfection of wisdom, those of dull faculties may become attached to matters of much reverence and offerings, thinking to themselves:
"Because I am able to write and able to practice accordingly, this exists.
To be attached to such gain and honor is the work of Māra.
Or, in the case of those with sharp faculties, Māra may think:

"This bodhisattva does not cling to worldly pleasures and single-mindedly receives the Prajñāpāramitā; this person cannot be thwarted or destroyed. I shall now use the profound sūtras of the śrāvakas to transform his mind and cause him to become an arhat."
The Buddha said:
"Although the sūtras of the śrāvakas are profound, one should not be greedily attached to them.
It is like a glowing, heated gold ball; though its color is exquisite, it must not be grasped."

If a bodhisattva lacks skillful means and does not possess sharp faculties, yet upon obtaining this sutra feels great joy, thinking: "This is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it exhausts the root of suffering—what could possibly surpass this!"
To then abandon the Prajñāpāramitā is also the work of Māra.
Why is this? For herein the Buddha explains the causal conditions:

"In the Prajñāpāramitā, the path of skillful means for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is explained in detail; that is to say, they contemplate the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without realizing them, because they practice the three gates of liberation with a mind of great compassion."
It is like a person who mixes ghee with poison; the potency of the poison is then neutralized and cannot harm them.
Prajñā is likewise: for a bodhisattva, it is easy to attain the unsurpassed path by seeking it within Prajñā, whereas in other sūtras it is difficult, being like taking poison alone.
Therefore, one should not seek the bodhisattva path from the sūtras of the śrāvakas. 47.
Chapter on the Lack of Concord, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Lack of Concord, Number Forty-seven. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The person who wishes to hear the Dharma desires to write down, uphold, read, recite, inquire about the meaning of, and correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā;
yet the person who expounds the Dharma is indolent and unwilling to explain it for them.
Subhūti, you should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there may be a person who preaches the Dharma who is untiring and does not fall into negligence, desiring to cause others to copy and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā; yet [the listener] may still harbor doubts. This too is a deed of Māra.
If the listener does not wish to receive the Dharma,
and the two minds are not in harmony, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If the recipient of the teaching wishes to write down, uphold, read, recite, or even correctly contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā,
while the teacher of the Dharma intends to go to another region.
One should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, there are those who preach the Dharma who desire to cause others to write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā; [yet they do not themselves practice it].
If the listener of the Dharma wishes to go to another region,
and the two minds are not in harmony, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Dharma-preacher values offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities of life;
the Dharma-hearer has few desires and is content, practices seclusion, maintains mindfulness with diligence, and possesses single-minded wisdom.

If the two do not harmonize, one will be unable to write, receive, uphold, read, recite, inquire about the meaning of, or correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this constitutes the work of Māra.
Subhūti! The Dharma-preacher has few desires and is content, practices the conduct of seclusion, maintains mindfulness with diligence, and possesses single-minded wisdom;
yet the listener values the offering of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities of life.

When the two are not in harmony, one will be unable to write down, uphold, read, recite, inquire about the meaning of, or maintain right mindfulness of the Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The teacher of the Dharma observes the twelve dhūtas:

first, dwelling in an araṇya; second, always begging for food; third, wearing robes made of rags; fourth, eating in one sitting; fifth, moderation in eating; sixth, not drinking liquids after midday; seventh, dwelling among tombs; eighth, dwelling at the foot of a tree; ninth, dwelling in the open air; tenth, always sitting and never lying down; eleventh, begging for food in sequence; twelfth, possessing only the three robes."
If the person listening to the Dharma does not accept the twelve dhūtas, from not dwelling in an araṇya up to not accepting only the three robes, there will be no harmony between the two;
they shall not be able to write, uphold, read, recite, inquire about the meaning of, or correctly attend to the Prajñāpāramitā. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! Suppose there is a listener of the Dharma who observes the twelve dhūtas, dwells as an araṇya-dweller, and so forth, up to accepting only the three robes;
yet the teacher of the Dharma does not observe the twelve dhūtas, does not dwell as an araṇya-dweller, and so forth, up to not accepting only the three robes.

When the two do not harmonize, one will be unable to write down, uphold, read, recite, inquire about the meaning of, or maintain right mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this constitutes the work of Māra.
[Treatise] Commentary:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions; when the various conditions are separated, they cease to exist.
It is like seeking fire by drilling wood: with both the drill and the fire-drill base present, fire is obtained through these two causal conditions.

The same applies to the transcription of the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to its correct recollection: it arises through the conjunction of internal and external causes and conditions. That is to say, because the teacher and disciple share the same intention and the same task, the transcription is successfully completed.
For this reason, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the listeners have given rise to the five roots of goodness, such as faith, they desire to write down, uphold, and even correctly contemplate the Prajñā;
whereas because the Dharma-preachers have their minds shrouded by the five hindrances, they do not wish to preach it."
Question: If you do not wish to speak because your mind is shrouded by the five hindrances, why do you act as a teacher? Answer:

This person is attached to worldly pleasures and does not contemplate emptiness or impermanence; although they can understand it with their mind and speak of it with their mouth, they cannot practice it themselves.
Although the disciple certainly wishes to practice, they are unable to know how; because they cannot know, and having no other recourse, they must consult this person.
At times, because the teacher’s heart of compassion has been stirred, he desires that the disciple write down and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā;

yet because the disciple’s five roots of goodness, such as faith, are dull and fail to arise, and because they are attached to worldly pleasures, they do not wish to receive, write down, uphold, or even correctly bring it to mind.
Question:
If one does not wish to receive and uphold [the teaching], why is such a person called a "listener of the Dharma"? Answer:
If one listens to, receives, reads, and recites [the teachings] only to a small or limited extent, and is unable to achieve ultimate accomplishment, it is merely called "listening to the Dharma.
If two people share a common virtuous mind, they can attain the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if their minds do not accord, they cannot attain it—this is called the work of Māra.
When internal afflictions arise or external devas, the Māras, act as causal conditions, one becomes separated from this Prajñāpāramitā;
the Bodhisattva should recognize these as demonic activities and guard against them so that they do not arise.
If one has lost [the teachings] oneself, one should restore them to full completion;
if a disciple has lost them, one should instruct them so that they may attain them.
Furthermore, it may be that the teacher’s heart of compassion is thin, and he abandons his disciples to go to another region.

Whether due to unsuitability of the local water and soil, disharmony of the four great elements, lack of increase in wholesome dharmas, unfavorable conditions of flood or drought, or the desolation and turmoil of the land;
for various causes and conditions such as these, one may go to another region, and the disciples likewise,
for various causes and conditions, are unable to follow.
Those who value gain and honor are those whose minds are covered by the five hindrances as described above.
Furthermore, both of these individuals possess faith and precepts; however, one person adorns their precepts with the twelve dhūtas, while the other cannot.
Question:
For what reason is one person unable [to do so]? Answer:
The precepts established by the Buddha are to be received and upheld by his disciples.

The twelve dhūtas are not termed "precepts" per se; if one is able to practice them, they serve as the adornment of the precepts, but if one cannot practice them, it does not constitute a violation of the precepts.
For example, regarding the practice of giving: one who is able to practice it gains merit, while one who is unable to practice it incurs no fault.
It is the same with the dhūta practices.
Therefore, when these two do not harmonize, it is the work of Māra.
Regarding the twelve dhūtas: because the household life brings much disturbance and confusion, the practitioner abandons parents, wife, children, and kinsmen to leave home and practice the Way;
yet, when teachers, disciples, and fellow students again become mutually attached, the mind becomes disturbed once more.
Therefore, one should undertake the practice of the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) to keep the body far removed from bustle and dwell in seclusion.
As for being "far removed," even three *li* is the minimum; the further, the better.
Having attained this physical seclusion, one must likewise cause the mind to be far removed from the five desires and the five hindrances.
Whether it be a meal received through an invitation or a meal provided by the Sangha, these give rise to the causes and conditions for the outflows (āsrava). Why is this?
Regarding one who receives a meal through an invitation, if they obtain it, they form this thought:
"I have obtained this because I am a person of merit.
If he does not obtain it, he harbors resentment toward the host, thinking:
"That person lacks discernment; he has invited those who should not have been invited and failed to invite those who should have been invited."
Or, one may despise oneself, becoming distressed and self-reproachful, thereby giving rise to sorrow and suffering.
These qualities of greed and sorrow can obstruct the Path.

Regarding those who eat the food of the Saṃgha: when entering among the assembly, they must follow the rules of the community; whether adjudicating matters, expelling individuals, managing monastic affairs, making assignments, or performing tasks, their minds will become distracted, hindering and causing them to neglect the practice of the Way.
Because of such disturbances and afflictions, one adopts the practice of constant alms-seeking;
due to the pursuit of fine clothing, one wanders in all directions and falls into wrong livelihoods.
If one receives fine robes from others, attachment will arise;
if one does not become attached, the donor will feel resentment.
If robes are obtained within the Sangha, the faults regarding the assembly are as explained above.
Furthermore, fine clothing is a source of greedy attachment for those who have not yet attained the Path.
With fine clothing as a cause and condition, one invites the danger of bandits, even to the point of losing one's life.
Because there are such afflictions as these, one undertakes the practice of wearing coarse rag-robes.
The practitioner reflects thus:
"Seeking even a single meal already presents many obstacles; how much more so for morning, midday, and afternoon meals!
If one does not diminish these, one will lose half the day's effort and be unable to practice the Way with a single mind."
"The Buddha-dharma is for the purpose of practicing the Path and not for the benefit of the body, such as feeding horses or pigs.
For this reason, one abandons frequent eating and accepts the practice of eating only once a day.

Although some may eat only one meal a day, they may consume excessively out of greed, causing their bellies to swell and their breath to become stifled, thereby obstructing and abandoning their practice of the Path; for this reason, they receive the rule of eating in measured portions.

Regarding moderation in eating: briefly stated, one should eat according to what one can consume and set aside one-third of that portion. Thus, the body will be light and stable, food will be easily digested without ailment, there will be no harm to the body, and one’s practice of the Path will not be interrupted.
As Śāriputra said in the Sūtra:
"If I eat five or six mouthfuls and supplement them with water, it is sufficient to sustain my body.
In the food of the people of Qin, this would amount to about ten mouthfuls.

Although some may practice moderation in their food intake, if they take pleasure in and become attached to drinking liquids after midday—seeking various kinds of drinks such as fruit juices and honeyed syrups—their desire for them will never cease;
thus, they are unable to cultivate wholesome dharmas with a single-minded focus.
Just as a horse that is not fitted with a bridle and bit will graze on grass to the left and right and refuse to advance on the path;
yet if it is fitted with a bridle and bit, it ceases its grazing and resolves its intent, following wherever the person’s will leads it.
For this reason, one should not drink even water after midday.
The contemplation of impermanence and emptiness is the gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma; it enables one to cultivate weary detachment from the three realms.

In the charnel ground, there are constant sounds of lamentation and wailing, and corpses lie scattered about. One sees impermanence with one's own eyes: later, they may be consumed by fire or devoured by birds and beasts, soon to be utterly extinguished.
By means of this contemplation of the corpse, one easily attains the mark of impermanence and the mark of emptiness among all phenomena.

Furthermore, dwelling in a cemetery, if one sees a corpse that is putrid, rotting, and impure, one easily attains the contemplation of the nine marks; this is the primary gateway for transcending desire.

Therefore, having practiced the rule of dwelling in cemeteries and being able to cultivate contemplations such as impurity and impermanence, one accomplishes the task of attaining the Path and proceeds to dwell under a tree;
or, for one who has not yet attained the Path, the mind is not yet sufficiently weary of the world, so they take up these signs and practice reflection beneath a tree.
Just as when the Buddha was born, when he attained enlightenment, when he turned the wheel of Dharma, and when he entered parinirvāṇa, he was always beneath a tree;
the practitioner, following the example of all Buddhas, should constantly dwell beneath trees.
For such reasons as these, one undertakes the practice of sitting under a tree.
A practitioner may perceive the space beneath a tree as no different from half a house—providing shade, coolness, and comfort—and thus develop attachment, thinking:
"My dwelling is excellent; that other tree is not as good."
Because such things give rise to taints (*āsrava*), he went to stay in the open air and reflected thus:
"There are two kinds of faults under a tree:
first, the dampness and cold from leaking rain; second, being defiled by bird droppings and inhabited by venomous insects."
"Since there are such faults as these, an open space is free from such afflictions.
Dwelling in the open air, one may put on or take off clothes at will with ease and joy;
the moonlight shines everywhere, and the sky is bright and pure, making it easy for the mind to enter the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.
Among the four modes of physical deportment, sitting is foremost; food is easily digested and the breath is harmonized.
For one seeking the Way whose great task remains unfinished, the various thieves of affliction constantly watch for an opportunity; thus, reclining in peace is unsuitable.
If one walks or stands, the mind is restless and difficult to collect, and these postures likewise cannot be maintained for long.
Therefore, one should adopt the practice of sitting constantly.
When drowsiness arises, one should not let the side of the body touch the mat.
Because the practitioner does not cling to flavors, does not disparage sentient beings, and possesses a mind of equal compassion, they should beg for food by successive rounds.
Because one does not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy, one undertakes the practice of alms-round by sequential begging.

Because the practitioner has few desires and is content, and because their robes serve merely to cover the body—neither more nor less than necessary—one undertakes the practice of possessing only the three robes.
Because laypeople seek pleasure, they accumulate many kinds of clothing;
some non-Buddhists, due to their ascetic practices, go naked without shame.
Therefore, the disciples of the Buddha abandon these two extremes and practice the Middle Way.
Regarding dwelling places and food, these matters are frequent and common;
as for clothing, it need not be sought day by day, and thus it is explained briefly.
These twelve *dhūta* practices were praised by the Buddha because he intended for his disciples to follow the Path and renounce worldly pleasures. Thus, he extolled the twelve *dhūtas*.
This is the Buddha’s intention: he always takes *dhūta* (ascetic practices) as the foundation;
it is only due to specific causes and conditions that he is compelled to permit other matters.
For example, when the Wheel of Dharma was being turned, the five bhikṣus first attained the Path and said to the Buddha:
"What kind of robes should we wear?
The Buddha said,
"You should wear robes made of discarded rags (pāṃśukūla)."

Furthermore, regarding the method of receiving the precepts: wearing patched robes for as long as life lasts, begging for food, dwelling under trees, and using discarded medicine—among the four ancient noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), these constitute three of the ascetic practices (*dhūta*).
The Buddha-dharma takes wisdom alone as its foundation, rather than making suffering its priority.
Because these teachings all assist the Path and accord with the Path, the Buddhas constantly praise them.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Volume Sixty-Eight.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of the Chapter on the Non-Harmony of the Two, Part Four of the Remainder of Chapter Forty-Seven. Volume Sixty-Nine.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
[Sūtra] “Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there is a teacher of the Dharma who possesses faith and virtue, and desires to write down, receive, and even correctly recollect the profound Prajñāpāramitā;”

If those who listen to the Dharma lack faith, violate the precepts, and engage in evil conduct, and do not wish to write down, receive, or even maintain right mindfulness of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! If the listener possesses faith and virtue, while the speaker lacks faith and engages in broken precepts and evil conduct, these two will not be in harmony;
you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there may be a teacher of the Dharma who is able to give everything away, with a mind free from stinginess,
while the listener of the Dharma is miserly and does not relinquish anything."
"You should know that this is the work of Māra. Subhūti!
As for the listener of the Dharma, they are able to give everything and their mind is not stingy."
If the teacher of the Dharma is stingy with the Dharma and does not bestow it,
and the two do not harmonize, such that they are unable to write down, uphold, or even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
suppose the listener wishes to provide the teacher with offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities of life;
yet the teacher does not wish to accept them."
One should know that this is the work of Māra.
