Subhūti, it may be that the teacher of the Dharma wishes to provide the listener with clothing and even all other necessities of life; yet—
If the listener does not wish to receive it,
and the two do not reach harmony, such that they are unable to write down, uphold, or even maintain right mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if the one who preaches the Dharma is easy to awaken, while the person who listens is dull-witted,
you should know that this is the work of Māra."
Subhūti! If the listener of the Dharma is quick to understand while the speaker of the Dharma is dull-witted, these two will not be in harmony.
Consequently, they will be unable to write down, uphold, or even maintain right mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there may be a teacher of the Dharma who understands the sequential meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures— from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*—
while the listener of the Dharma does not understand the sequential meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures."
One should know that this is the work of Māra:
the listener understands the sequential meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, while the speaker does not understand the sequential meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
"When the two are not in harmony, one will be unable to write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If the teacher of the Dharma has accomplished the six pāramitās, but the listener of the Dharma has not accomplished the six pāramitās, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will be unable to write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā or even maintain right mindfulness of it; one should know that this is the work of Māra.
If the listener possesses the six pāramitās while the teacher lacks them, the two will not be in harmony;
they will be unable to write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā, nor even maintain right mindfulness of it. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
it may be that the teacher of the Dharma possesses skillful means regarding the six pāramitās, while the listener of the Dharma lacks skillful means regarding the six pāramitās."
When the two do not harmonize, such that one is unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
It may be that the listener possesses the power of skillful means regarding the six *pāramitās*, while the teacher lacks the power of skillful means regarding the six *pāramitās*.
"When the two are not in harmony, one will be unable to write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If the teacher of the Dharma has attained dhāraṇī while the listener of the Dharma lacks dhāraṇī, these two will not be in harmony;
they will be unable to write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā, nor even maintain right mindfulness of it. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
If the listener attains dhāraṇī while the speaker lacks dhāraṇī, these two will not be in harmony;
they will be unable to write out the profound Prajñāpāramitā, nor even maintain right mindfulness of it. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
it may be that the teacher of the Dharma desires to have the Prajñāpāramitā written down, maintained, and even correctly recollected;
yet the listener of the Dharma does not desire to have the Prajñāpāramitā written down, maintained, read, recited, or even correctly recollected."
When the two do not harmonize, such that they are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness of it,
you should know this to be the work of Māra. It may be that the listener wishes to write, read, recite, or explain the *prajñāpāramitā*,
while the speaker does not wish them to write the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even wish them to explain it.
"When two people do not harmonize, they will be unable to write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā, nor even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The teacher of the Dharma is free from sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt; the listeners of the Dharma, however, possess sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
One should know that this is the work of Māra:

while the listener is free from sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, the speaker of the Dharma is possessed of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
"When the two do not harmonize, one will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
While one is writing out this profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even when one is maintaining right mindfulness, someone may come and say:
"The suffering within the three evil realms is extreme; why do you not bring an end to suffering with this very body and enter *nirvāṇa*?"
"What is the use of this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Because these two do not harmonize, they will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even to maintain right mindfulness of it; you should know that this is the work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when one is writing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, or correctly contemplating it, someone may come and praise the gods of the Four Great Kings, praise the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmā heavens, up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; or they may praise the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, saying:
'Good son!'"

In the realm of desire, one experiences the pleasures of the five desires; in the realm of form, one experiences the bliss born of meditative concentration; and in the formless realm, one experiences the bliss of tranquility.
These things, too, are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they possess the characteristics of transformation, exhaustion, dispersal, detachment, and cessation.
Why do you not, within this very body, realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, or the path of a pratyekabuddha?
"What is the use of seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by undergoing various sufferings within this worldly cycle of birth and death?
Because these two do not harmonize, they will be unable to write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even maintain right mindfulness; one should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the one who preaches the Dharma is alone, without entanglements, free and unimpeded;
yet the one who listens to the Dharma brings along a large multitude of people."
When the two are not in harmony, they will be unable to write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness; you should know that this is the work of Māra.
The listener has no entanglements and is free and unimpeded, yet the Dharma-preacher leads a large multitude of people.
"When two people do not harmonize, they will be unable to write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā, let alone maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The teacher of the Dharma speaks thus:
"If you can comply with my wishes, I shall give you the Prajñāpāramitā so that you may write it, read it, recite it, explain it, and correctly attend to it;
if you do not comply with my wishes, then I shall not give it to you."
"When these two do not harmonize, one will be unable to write, read, recite, explain, or correctly attend to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there may be a listener who wishes to follow [the teaching] according to their own inclination,
yet the speaker of the Dharma does not listen."
"When the two are not in harmony, one will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If the teacher of the Dharma, for the sake of seeking wealth and profit, provides the Prajñāpāramitā and causes others to copy, uphold, and even correctly contemplate it;
yet the listener of the Dharma, because of these very conditions, does not wish to receive it from him.

When the two parties do not reach an agreement, such that they are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness of it, one should know this to be the work of Māra.
It may be that the listener desires to write, read, recite, and explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of wealth and profit,
while the speaker, for that very reason, is unwilling to grant it.
"When the two do not harmonize, one will be unable to write, read, recite, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If the teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another region where life is in danger, but the listener of the Dharma does not wish to follow him,
and because these two are not in harmony, they are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even to maintain right mindfulness— know that this is the work of Māra.
If the listener wishes to go to another region where life is in danger, while the teacher of the Dharma does not wish to go,
and because these two do not harmonize, they are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness, one should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

suppose the teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another region that is plagued by famine, high grain prices, and a lack of water, while the listener of the Dharma does not wish to go along with him."
When the two do not reach accord, such that they are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness, one should know this to be the work of Māra.
Or, the listener wishes to go to another region where there is famine, high grain prices, and a lack of water, while the teacher of the Dharma does not wish to go.
"When the two are not in harmony, they will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Dharma-preacher wishes to go to another land that is prosperous and joyful, and the listeners wish to follow him there.
The Dharma-preacher says:
"O sons of good family!..."
"You have followed me for the sake of gain; reflect well for yourself, so that whether you succeed or fail, you shall have no cause for regret!
Because of these minor circumstances, the two were not in harmony.
When those who listen to the Dharma hear it, their hearts become weary, and they think:
"This person opposes me; he does not wish to accompany me.
They then stop and do not go on.
"When the two are not in harmony, one will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Dharma-preacher wishes to cross a wilderness, fearing bandits, outcasts, hunters, and fierce beasts or venomous snakes;
the listener wishes to follow after him.
The Dharma-preacher said: "Good son!
To what end would you go there?"
"In that place there are many fears—the fear of bandits, and so on, up to the fear of venomous snakes.

When those who listen to the Dharma hear this, they know that [the teacher] does not wish to write down, uphold, or even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*; their minds become weary, and they do not wish to follow him.
Because of these minor causes and conditions, the two will not be in harmony; you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the one who preaches the Dharma may have many donors who frequently visit him to inquire after his health. For this reason, he says to the listener of the Dharma:
"I have a matter to attend to and must go there.
When those who wish to hear the Dharma perceive this intention, they stop.
Because the two parties do not harmonize, they are unable to write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even to maintain right mindfulness; one should know that this is the work of Māra.
[Treatise] Question:
It may be that some people write down, uphold, read, and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā*, yet fail to practice it and instead violate the precepts; this might indeed be possible.
But if they lack faith, how can they receive the Dharma from it?
The answer is:
This person does not believe in the Prajñāpāramitā, which is called ultimate emptiness; they merely read, recite, and explain it extensively out of a desire for fame.
They are like a disciple of the Buddha who, while having no faith in the scriptures of non-Buddhists, nevertheless preaches them to others.
Furthermore, one is called "faithless" because they are unable to believe in and delight in the Prajñā with a profound mind; it does not mean that they lack faith altogether. Question:
According to the dharma for disciples, they ought to make offerings to their teacher and present him with all they possess; why then do you say that the teacher cannot give?
The disciple replied: "I thought to myself:
'If my teacher cannot relinquish even a small thing, how much less could he relinquish his own body!'"
"Though one may praise and speak of giving, this is a deception!
For this reason, they do not harmonize.
A disciple wishes to provide for his teacher with the four requisites of support.
Because the teacher has few desires and is content, he does not accept; or, out of shame, as if it were like selling the Dharma, he does not accept.
Alternatively, the teacher possesses great knowledge and extensive learning, lacking for nothing, and is thus able to provide for his disciples.
The disciple thinks to himself:
"People will say that I received the Dharma merely because I was greedy for my teacher's food and clothing.
Or he may think that his own virtue is too slight to be worthy of what has been bestowed upon him.
Although this mind is good, because it cannot bring about the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is also the work of Māra.
A teacher of dull faculties is a teacher who merely recites the sūtras, not a teacher who explains their meaning.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures are also the masters of recitation.
Furthermore, regarding a master who possesses the six *pāramitās*, he reflects thus:
"My disciples are sinners with dull faculties; they are unable to practice the six *pāramitās* and are attached to worldly affairs. They possess only the name of 'disciple,' but lack the reality."

This teacher does not realize that his disciple, having heard the Prajñāpāramitā, will later accomplish the Great Matter; he merely refuses to provide instruction because the six pāramitās are not present before him.
The disciple also thinks:
"As for the meaning of the six pāramitās, I too am able to practice them;
my teacher can only speak of them with his mouth, but cannot cultivate them through practice."

Not knowing that the turning of the teacher’s body would constitute a momentous event, nor knowing that there were other beneficial causes and conditions for recitation and study, they did not harmonize with one another.
Furthermore, the disciple has straightforward faith and is attached to wholesome dharmas,
whereas the teacher is unattached to dharmas and practices the six pāramitās through skillful means; thus,
the disciple thinks that the teacher does not deeply delight in the six pāramitās.
How is this known?
At times the Teacher praises the six pāramitās;
at other times, in order to sever people's attachments, he dismantles and disperses the six pāramitās.
It is the same for a disciple who possesses skillful means.
A question is asked:
"If the disciple has attained dhāraṇī while the teacher lacks dhāraṇī, how can he be considered a teacher?"
Answer: There are various kinds of dhāraṇīs.
There are disciples who attain the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining; they are able to maintain and recite it, but cannot understand its meaning.
The teacher may be able to provide explanations,
yet the disciple may be able to attain the meaning of the *dhāraṇī* of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena but be unable to recite them in sequence;

or the teacher may have attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining [the teachings], yet because he has not attained great compassion, he treats the disciple with contempt and is unable to instruct him.
Question:
It may be that a disciple wishes to receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, yet the teacher does not grant it;
how could it be that the teacher wishes to give the Dharma, yet the disciple is unwilling to receive it?
Answer: As previously answered:
because the disciple perceives faults in the teacher, he does not wish to receive the Dharma.
Furthermore, the teacher wishes to transform and instruct the person before him as a disciple;
however, because that person possesses wrong views and various evil conditions, they are unwilling to accept the teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas practiced by all sentient beings, those who are alike form a harmonious union;
yet if one person is free from the five hindrances while another is not, they will disparage one another, and because of this mutual disparagement, they do not harmonize.
All supreme dharmas are like this.

Furthermore, when one is copying, reciting, or even correctly contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā, if one person reviles the three evil realms while another praises the various heavens, this matter is as previously answered.
Although he cannot entirely destroy their virtuous conduct, he nonetheless subverts their Mahāyāna and bestows upon them the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, while the teacher has few desires and is content, taking no pleasure in large assemblies,
the disciples have many followers.
The teacher thought to himself:
"Although these disciples are worthy of being converted, they have brought a great multitude with them.
Deeply attached to the wholesome Dharma, the teacher abandoned his disciples.
The disciple’s own person is also like this.
Furthermore, the intention of the Dharma-preacher is as follows:
if the disciple acts according to his will—whether going or staying, or inquiring after his well-being at the appropriate times—and so forth.
Those who listen to the Dharma desire only to seek the benefits of the Dharma and are unable to perform these various tasks;
this constitutes a lack of harmony.
Or, at times, those who listen to the Dharma may proceed or stop according to their own whims, or engage in inquiries and the like.
The Dharma-preacher does not listen, thinking to himself:
"What is the use of this?
It diminishes my merit!"
The listener thinks the teacher holds them in contempt and does not feel affection or joy toward them;
this is a lack of harmony.
Furthermore, the teacher desires to give the Dharma for the sake of gain and offerings.
The disciple’s mind will then lack respect for the teacher, thinking:
"Why does he wish to sell the Dharma of the sutras?
The disciple is likewise so disposed; they recite the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of wealth and gain, rather than with a pure mind.
When the teacher knows that the disciple’s mind is thus, he treats him with slight and disdain and does not grant [the teachings].
Therefore, they do not harmonize.
Furthermore, the teacher wishes to travel to another region, and the path passes through dangerous and difficult terrain.
Because the disciples cherish their own bodies and lives, they are unable to follow; they think to themselves:
"Only after I have a body can I seek the Dharma.
It is the same when the disciples wish to depart.
It is the same in cases of famine, high grain prices, or places lacking water.
Furthermore, when a teacher wishes to go to a place of abundance and prosperity,
a disciple may wish to follow the teacher but feel ashamed or reluctant to go along.
Either the disciples were accustomed to comfort and unable to endure long journeys;
or the distance was vast;
or the teacher was already familiar with that country.
The disciples did not understand fully, thinking that the teacher’s praise of that country was not necessarily true;
at times they even suspected him, thinking he had gone there because of a craving for food and drink.
For various reasons such as these, the teacher said to his disciples:
"What you have heard concerning that land need not be entirely as it was described; deliberate well for yourself!
If you wish to go, then go, but do not go because of its wealth and abundance. Once you arrive there, you may not obtain your desires; do not harbor resentment!"
The teacher further said to him:
"You have gone because you heard that his land is prosperous and pleasant, not for the sake of the Dharma; therefore, you need not follow me.
The teacher, with good intentions, sought to stop his disciple, unaware that he was creating the conditions for the destruction of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When the disciple heard these words, he was unable to respond out of reverence and awe for his teacher, so he simply stopped and did not go on.
Thus, they were not in harmony.
The teacher further desired to travel to a distant country, which was filled with various tigers, wolves, bandits, and thieves.
He said to his disciple, "There are many hardships there; you need not go!
Having heard this, the disciple stopped.
The Master merely knew that his disciple had encountered difficulties and stopped him from proceeding, but he did not realize it was an occasion for the destruction of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
[The disciple] asked:
"If there are many hardships in a distant land, why should I go there myself?"
Answer: Some say:
Because the Master was born in that country, he has become accustomed to its customs and is thus able to protect himself.
Some say: He went because he possessed excellent teachers and scriptures, and did not begrudge his own life or body.
The teacher thought to himself:
"I would rather die myself; how could I wrong another?
For reasons such as these, he stopped his disciples and did not allow them to depart.
Furthermore, the teacher had many acquaintances who were donors (*dānapati*), and his mind became attached to them with pleasure.
The disciple has few desires and is content, and does not become attached to the donors.
The teacher constantly inquires after the donors' welfare at appropriate times;
the disciple, however, seeks only the Dharma and takes no pleasure in such matters.
The Master, knowing his intention, said to him:
"I have certain circumstances that prevent me from preaching the Dharma for you.
Having heard this, the disciple was displeased.
"To value worldly connections rather than the Dharma is to lack harmony.
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Māra will come in the guise of a bhikṣu and employ skillful means to destroy this Prajñāpāramitā, so that it may not be written down, upheld, read, recited, explained, or correctly recollected.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

for what reason and by what causes and conditions does Māra, the Evil One, assume the form of a bhikṣu and employ skillful means to destroy the Prajñāpāramitā, so that it may not be written down, upheld, or even correctly recollected?”
The Buddha said:
"An evil Māra may come in the guise of a bhikṣu to corrupt the minds of good sons and good daughters, causing them to distance themselves from the Prajñāpāramitā, and say:
'The sūtras that I have spoken are the Prajñāpāramitā; this sūtra is not the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
"Subhūti! When the bhikṣus are thus being divided, bodhisattvas who have not yet received their prediction will fall into doubt.
Because they fall into doubt, they do not write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā, nor do they receive it, uphold it, or even bring it to right mindfulness."
If they are not in harmony and are unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or even to maintain right mindfulness of it, you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A māra, having assumed the form of a bhikṣu, approaches the bodhisattva and speaks thus:

"If a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), he will attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha!"
Because these two are not in harmony, they will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness; you should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva speaks this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, many demonic activities (*mārakarman*) arise that obstruct the *prajñāpāramitā*; these are demonic activities."
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should awaken to this; having known it, they should remain far removed from it.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"What are the demonic deeds and obstacles that a bodhisattva should recognize, and having recognized them, should distance himself from?
The Buddha said:

'Demonic deeds resembling the perfection of wisdom arise; demonic deeds resembling the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity arise. A bodhisattva should recognize them, and having recognized them, should distance himself.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Those sūtras that should be practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—these a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize as the work of Māra and remain far removed from them."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the gates of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
it is by means of these dharmas that one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha."
In such sutras as these, Māra assumes the form of a bhikṣu and employs skillful means to provide them to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Because of this discordance, they will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even to maintain right mindfulness of it; one should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One may manifest in the form of a Buddha with a golden body and a fathom-wide radiance, and approach the bodhisattva.
That bodhisattva becomes greedily attached; because of this attachment, their *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is diminished."
Because of this lack of harmony, one will be unable to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even maintain right mindfulness of it;
you should know that this is the work of Māra. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
Māra manifests in the form of a Buddha and a community of bhikṣus and approaches the bodhisattva;
the bodhisattva then gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment and thinks:
"In a future life, I too shall likewise preach the Dharma for a community of bhikṣus."

Because this bodhisattva is greedily attached to the body of Māra, their omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is diminished; they will be unable to write out, complete, or even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Māra the Evil One may manifest as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, practicing the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom, and point them out to sons and daughters of good family."

When good sons or good daughters, having seen it, become attached to it, they diminish their *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) because of that attachment; they will not be able to write down the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even maintain right mindfulness of it. You should know that this is the work of Māra.

Why is this? Because within this profound Prajñāpāramitā, there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to and including no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti! If this prajñāpāramitā were devoid of form, up to and including being devoid of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then within it there would be no Buddha, no śrāvaka, no pratyekabuddha, and no bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When good sons and good daughters write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and when they receive, read, recite, explain, and correctly contemplate it, many obstacles will arise.
Subhūti! For example,
among the precious treasures in Jambudvīpa—
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, coral, and other such gems— they are many and difficult to obtain, and there are many thieves.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When good sons and good daughters write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā, or even when they maintain right mindfulness of it, many thieves and many obstacles will arise.
Subhūti said to the Buddha: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The precious treasures within Jambudvīpa—
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, agate, coral, and so forth— are beset by many thieves and many perils.
World-Honored One!

It is likewise for good sons and good daughters: when they write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā, or even when they maintain right mindfulness of it, many thieves, many obstacles, and many demonic affairs will arise.

Why is this? Because these foolish people are incited by Māra; when good sons and good daughters write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness of it, they cause it to be destroyed and cause them to be estranged from it.
“World-Honored One!

These foolish people possess little knowledge and little wisdom; when these good sons and good daughters write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā* or even maintain right mindfulness of it, they destroy it and cause them to be estranged from it.”

These deluded people do not delight their minds in the Great Dharma; for this reason, they do not write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they accept, read, recite, correctly attend to, or practice it as taught.
Furthermore, they cause others to be ruined, preventing them from writing down the profound *prajñāpāramitā* up to practicing it as taught.
The Buddha said: “So it is! So it is!”

Subhūti! Because those sons and daughters of good family who have newly resolved upon the Mahāyāna are incited by Māra, have not planted roots of goodness, have not made offerings to the Buddhas, and do not follow spiritual friends, they do not write out the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—up to and including failing to correctly recollect it—and thus create obstacles.

These sons and daughters of good family possess little wisdom and little insight, and their minds do not delight in the Great Dharma; for this reason, they are unable to write out this profound Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including its correct recollection, because the work of Māra has arisen.

Subhūti! If good sons or good daughters are able to write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and even maintain right mindfulness of it, then demonic activities will not arise; they will be able to fulfill the *dhyānapāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, and they will be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Subhūti! You should know that it is by the power of the Buddha that these sons and daughters of good family are able to write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and even correctly recollect it; they are also able to fulfill the *dhyānapāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the ten powers of a Buddha up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Subhūti! The immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions also assist these good sons and good daughters, enabling them to write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā and even to maintain right mindfulness of it.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten directions who have attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) also protect, guard, and assist these good sons and good daughters as they write down the profound Prajñāpāramitā and even maintain right mindfulness of it.
[Treatise] Commentary:
Māra assumes the form of a great śramaṇa, possessing profound majesty and virtue, causing people to accept his words;
carrying many scriptural volumes and accompanied by a multitude of disciples, he speaks to the bhikṣus:
“The Prajñāpāramitā, as I have explained it in my sutras, is the true word of the Buddha;
that which you previously heard was not real, nor was it spoken by the Buddha.”
He reviles the previous sutras and in various ways praises what he himself has spoken.
Bodhisattvas of dull faculties believe and accept these words, giving rise to wrong views;
those of sharp faculties who have not yet received a prediction of enlightenment give rise to doubt.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas are ultimately empty and signless, and their wisdom is difficult to comprehend; therefore, they do not enter into union.
At times, Māra may say to the bodhisattva:
"The Prajñāpāramitā and the three gates of liberation are extensively explained as being merely emptiness;
you have constantly practiced this emptiness and attained realization therein.
If you had not attained realization, how could you become a Buddha or establish the Buddha-dharma?"
Having previously practiced giving, observing the precepts, and so forth, one cultivates the merit for the thirty-two marks;
it is only when sitting at the site of enlightenment that one then employs emptiness.
Whether the bodhisattva has faith or doubt, they are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Question:
In what way do things resembling the six pāramitās constitute the work of Māra? Answer:
It is as explained in the *Sādharmya-prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, practicing the six *pāramitās* with an attached mind is called "semblance.
The sūtras of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* lack compassion; they do not seek the Buddha-way, but desire only their own deliverance.
Although this is a good thing, it destroys the bodhisattva path; therefore, it is called a demonic deed (*mārakarman*). Question:
If a bodhisattva beholds the Buddha’s body, their faith becomes pure; why then is this called a demonic deed?
The answer is:
All afflictions and the grasping at signs are the works of Māra.

This minor bodhisattva has not yet attained the vision of the Buddha’s body; thus, Māra assumes the exquisite form of a Buddha, and the bodhisattva’s mind becomes attached to it, practicing the Path for the sake of such a beautiful body.

Just as a person who has not yet abandoned desire, upon seeing the form of a celestial maiden, becomes deeply attached in his heart; unable to endure the celestial desires, he dies in a state of delirium and distress.
Thus, Māra’s wish is fulfilled.
Although a bodhisattva may attain a slight degree of pure mind, they lose the wisdom of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*);
it is like a person holding a precious gem who is deceived by another with a small amount of gold, causing them to discard the high-value jewel and take a base object—this is called depletion.
Māra assumed the form of a Buddha and led the bhikṣus to show them many bodhisattvas practicing the six pāramitās, as described above.
In this context, the Buddha explained the causal conditions:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, is empty."
Furthermore, the assembly gave rise to doubt:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is the unsurpassed Dharma and brings manifold benefits; why is it that some people harbor hatred and envy toward it?"
For this reason, the Buddha spoke this parable:
"Just as gold, silver, and other such treasures in Jambudvīpa appear because there are many enemies and many thieves, and not because of common things like tiles or stones."

The Prajñāpāramitā is a wondrous jewel within the treasury of the Buddha-dharma; it is subtle, sublime, and profoundly deep. Those who are indolent and of dull faculties do not understand it, and for this reason they revile it.
"Because Māra causes sentient beings to enter nirvāṇa by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, Māra acts as an enemy and a thief.
Subhūti joyfully received the Buddha’s teaching and recounted what had been said regarding those who disparage and destroy the *prajñā*:
"World-Honored One!"
These deluded and foolish people are driven by Māra and lack self-mastery; because their wisdom is meager, they cannot penetrate the Buddha’s intent.
These individuals possess no great resolve and do not know the flavor of the pure Dharma;
they know only three things—craving for flavors, lust, and anger—which are like the nature of beasts, creating obstacles for the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha affirmed what Subhūti had said and addressed him:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva writes down the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, up to correctly recollecting it, and no demonic activities arise, you should know that this is due to the power of the Buddha, and also because they are protected by all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions;
furthermore, that they are able to fulfill the five *pāramitās* up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is also due to the power of the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions.”
Why is this? Māra is the lord of the desire realm; he possesses worldly merit and wisdom, and he is the very root of birth and death in the world.
Although the devas of the form realm possess wrong views, because they constantly enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), their minds are supple and cannot cause any destruction.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because there is no physical form and the mind is subtle, it is incapable of performing any action.
Because the lower devas lack power and majesty, they are unable to cause such destruction.
This is due to the power of the karmic causes and conditions from that Māra’s previous lives;
furthermore, it is due to the conditions of his dwelling place where others seize what he has made. Within this context, the chief of thieves is called Māra.
This is the mark of Māra, which destroys wholesome deeds.

Because the merit and wisdom of a bodhisattva who has first resolved on enlightenment are slight, they cherish their own body; if the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions did not protect and assist them, they would be unable to achieve success.
Therefore, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and devas act to destroy the works of Māra;
yet this bodhisattva may either perceive them or not perceive them—just as when bandits surround a city, an adult guards it while a child remains unaware.
Thus have the deeds of Māra been briefly described; were they explained in detail, they would be immeasurable and boundless.

Nevertheless, since the Buddha’s intention is solely to enable the practitioner to accomplish the great task of Prajñāpāramitā, teacher and disciple should remain in harmony, and all evil matters should not be dwelt upon or even considered.
Chapter 48: The Mother of Buddhas The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Mother of Buddhas, Chapter Forty-Eight [Sūtra] The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Suppose, for example, there is a woman who has five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand sons.
If the mother falls ill, the sons each diligently seek medical treatment, thinking:
"How can we cause our mother to find peace, free from all afflictions, suffering, and unpleasant things?"
"Wind and cold, heat and chill, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, and vipers afflict our mother's body; this is our sorrow!
Thus, those sons constantly sought articles of pleasure to provide for their mother.
Why is this? Because they have given birth to us and shown us the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Buddha constantly beholds this profound Prajñāpāramitā with his Buddha-eye.
Why is this? Because this profound Prajñāpāramitā is able to reveal the characteristics of the world.
The Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions also constantly behold this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with their Buddha-eyes. Why is this?
Because this profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas, can bestow upon all Buddhas omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and can reveal the characteristics of the world.
For this reason, the Buddhas always behold this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with the Buddha-eye.

Furthermore, because the *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to the *dhyānapāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*; can give rise to internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); can give rise to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); and can give rise to the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddhabala*) up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
In this way, the perfection of wisdom can give birth to srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas.

Subhūti! All Buddhas who have already attained, are now attaining, or will attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, all do so by reason of the causal conditions of profound prajñāpāramitā.

Subhūti! If sons or daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and even maintain right mindfulness of it, the Buddhas will always look upon these people with their Buddha-eye.

Subhūti! These sons and daughters of good family who seek the bodhisattva path are constantly protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions, so that they do not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has taught, the Prajñāpāramitā is able to give birth to all Buddhas and is able to reveal the characteristics of the world."
World-Honored One!
How is it that the prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas?
How is it that it can reveal the characteristics of the world?
"How is it that all Buddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom?
How is it that all Buddhas explain the characteristics of the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* are born the ten powers of a Buddha, up to the eighteen unique qualities, and the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti!
Because one attains all these dharmas, one is called a Buddha.
Subhūti, for this reason,
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas.
"Subhūti! The Buddhas declare that the five aggregates are the characteristics of the world. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
How are the characteristics of the five aggregates explained within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
How are the five aggregates demonstrated within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”

“Subhūti! The Prajñāpāramitā does not demonstrate the breaking of the five aggregates, nor does it demonstrate their disintegration; it does not demonstrate arising, nor does it demonstrate cessation; it does not demonstrate defilement, nor does it demonstrate purity; it does not demonstrate increase, nor does it demonstrate decrease; it does not demonstrate entering, nor does it demonstrate exiting; it does not demonstrate the past, nor does it demonstrate the future, nor does it demonstrate the present.”

Why is this? Because the characteristic of emptiness is neither broken nor destroyed; the characteristic of signlessness and the characteristic of wishlessness are neither broken nor destroyed; and the dharmic nature of non-arising dharmas, non-birth dharmas, and non-existent dharmas is neither broken nor destroyed. Such is the demonstration of these characteristics.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Buddha has said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the characteristics of the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddhas fully know the mental activities of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.

Subhūti! Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there are no sentient beings and no names of sentient beings; there is no form and no name of form; there is no feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness, and no names of feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness; there is no eye up to no mind; there is no eye-consciousness up to no mind-consciousness; there is no eye-contact up to no mind-contact; and so on, up to no all-knowledge and no name of all-knowledge.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom is able to reveal the characteristics of the world. Subhūti!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā does not indicate form, nor does it indicate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it does not indicate anything up to and including all-knowledge.
Why is this? Subhūti, within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, even the *prajñāpāramitā* itself does not exist; how much less so form, and so on, up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
As for all categories of sentient beings—whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
whether in this world or throughout the worlds of the ten directions—the Buddha knows as they truly are the concentrated minds and the distracted minds of these sentient beings."
Subhūti! How does the Buddha know the characteristics of the concentrated mind and the distracted mind of sentient beings?
He knows them by means of the characteristic of dharmas.
By what characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) is this known?
Subhūti, within these characteristics of phenomena, there is not even the characteristic of the characteristic of phenomena; how much less could there be a concentrated mind or a distracted mind!
Subhūti! By means of these characteristics of phenomena, the Buddha knows the concentrated minds and the distracted minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Buddha knows whether the minds of sentient beings are concentrated or distracted.
How does he know this? Subhūti!

One knows by means of the characteristic of exhaustion; one knows by means of the characteristic of non-defilement; one knows by means of the characteristic of cessation; one knows by means of the characteristic of abandonment; one knows by means of the characteristic of tranquility; and one knows by means of the characteristic of detachment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha knows the concentrated minds and the distracted minds of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha knows the defiled minds of sentient beings; he knows defiled minds as they truly are.
He knows minds of anger and minds of delusion as they truly are.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does the Buddha know the defiled minds of sentient beings, knowing the defiled mind as it truly is?”
“How does one truly know an angry mind and a deluded mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In the true mark of a defiled mind, there is no mark of a defiled mind.”

Why is this? Because within the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), neither the mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*) can be apprehended; how much less could one apprehend a defiled mind or a non-defiled mind! Subhūti!
The true mark of anger and delusion is that they possess neither the mark of anger nor the mark of delusion. Why is this?

Because within the true mark, even mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) cannot be apprehended; how much less could one apprehend a mind of anger or a mind free from anger, or a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion!
In this way, Subhūti,
by means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha knows the defiled mind of sentient beings as it truly is— a defiled mind;
he knows the angry mind and the deluded mind as they truly are— an angry mind and a deluded mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, as it truly is, that sentient beings have no defiled mind;
he knows, as it truly is, their lack of a defiled mind. He knows, as they truly are, their lack of a hateful mind and their lack of a deluded mind."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one truly know, as it really is, that a sentient being’s mind is unstained when it is unstained?”
“Does one truly know a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred?
Does one truly know a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In this state where the mind is without the characteristic of defilement, neither the characteristic of defilement nor the characteristic of non-defilement can be apprehended.
Why is this? Subhūti!...”
Because two minds do not coexist.
Thus, Subhūti, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, that sentient beings have no defiled mind as being a mind without defilement.
Subhūti! Within this mark of a mind free from hatred and a mind free from delusion, neither a deluded mind nor a non-deluded mind can be apprehended. Why is this?
Because two minds do not coexist.
In this way, Subhūti,
by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, that sentient beings have no mind of hatred and no mind of delusion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, as it truly is, that these sentient beings have expansive minds.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Buddha, by means of the perfection of wisdom, knows the expansive mind of these sentient beings as it truly is—an expansive mind? “Subhūti!”
The Buddha knows that the characteristics of the minds of all sentient beings are neither broad nor narrow, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither coming nor going;
because the characteristics of the mind are detached, this mind is not broad, and so forth, up to neither coming nor going.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mind is non-existent, who could make it vast, who could make it narrow, or even cause it to come and go?
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, as it truly is, that these sentient beings have expansive minds; he knows their expansive minds as they truly are.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, as it truly is, that these sentient beings have great minds; he knows their great minds as they truly are."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how does the Buddha,
by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, truly know the great minds of these sentient beings as great minds?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“By means of the prajñāpāramitā, a Buddha does not perceive the characteristic of coming or the characteristic of going of sentient beings' minds; he does not perceive the characteristic of arising, the characteristic of ceasing, the characteristic of abiding, or the characteristic of change of sentient beings' minds.”
Why is this? Because these minds have no inherent nature, who comes and who goes?
Who is born, ceases, abides, or changes?
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha knows this great mind of sentient beings as a great mind, in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
“By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha knows the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are— immeasurable minds.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"How does the Buddha, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, truly know the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as immeasurable minds?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows the minds of these sentient beings, neither seeing them as abiding nor seeing them as not abiding."
Why is this? Because these immeasurable mental states have no basis; who could abide in a place that is not a place of abiding?
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, as they truly are, the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as immeasurable minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the Buddha knows, as they truly are, the invisible minds of sentient beings as invisible minds."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how does the Buddha,
by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, truly know the invisible mind of sentient beings as an invisible mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The minds of sentient beings are signless; the Buddha knows them as they truly are to be signless, because their own-characteristics are empty.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings, which cannot be seen by the five eyes.
Thus it is, Subhūti:
by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, that the minds of sentient beings are invisible and that they are invisible minds.
[Treatise] Commentary:
It was stated above that "the Buddhas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas protect the Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including its correct recollection, so that Māra may find no opportunity."
When those in the assembly heard this matter, some thought to themselves:

"The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas is a mark of quiescence; toward all phenomena and sentient beings, it is without hatred and without affection. For what reason, then, does it protect those who write down, uphold, and even correctly recollect the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
For this reason, the Buddha told Subhūti and spoke a parable:
"Just as a son, out of gratitude, protects his mother, so too is Prajñāpāramitā the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Therefore, if there are obstacles such as Māras who wish to destroy the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas—though they abide in the mark of quiescence—out of compassion for sentient beings and because they recognize their debt of gratitude, constantly keep those who practice Prajñā in mind with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, and always behold them with the Buddha-eye, protecting these practitioners so that they may attain increase and not lose the path to Buddhahood."
In this regard, the Buddha spoke of the causal conditions:
"All noble ones and the dharmas of the noble ones are born from within Prajñā. Question:
Subhūti asked about four matters, yet why did the Buddha answer with only three points instead of stating that "all Buddhas are born from Prajñā"?
The answer is:
that Prajñā gives birth to all Buddhas and that all Buddhas are born from Prajñā—these meanings are not different.
Some say that because all dharmas are combined, they can give rise to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and the *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to all Buddhas;
others say that by practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* and various other practices, one attains Buddhahood.
The first refers to the agent, and the second refers to the phenomenon.
If one says, "The falling branch killed the person," or if one says, "The falling tree killed the person," because these cases are identical,
no distinction is made in the response.
If it is said that "the Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas," this means that "all Buddhas are born from Prajñā.
Question: As other sūtras state:
"Because the five aggregates are subject to disintegration, they are called 'the world.
Why, then, does this [text] state that 'the Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the five aggregates have no disintegration, nor arising or ceasing,' and so forth?"
The answer is:
That refers to the matters of the Hīnayāna, while this refers to the matters of the Mahāyāna.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, impermanence is frequently expounded; in the teachings of the Mahāyāna, the emptiness of phenomena is frequently expounded.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, impermanence is taught first and the emptiness of phenomena is taught later;
in the teachings of the Mahāyāna, the emptiness of phenomena is taught from the very beginning.
In the Hīnayāna, the teaching on impermanence is intended to cause sentient beings to feel awe and trepidation.
In the Mahāyāna, however, it is not so; therefore, it is said that there is no destruction and so forth.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself stated the cause and condition:
"Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are ultimately neither broken nor destroyed."
The Prajñāpāramitā reveals such characteristics of the world as these.

Furthermore, the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are called the "world"; the physical form and color of sentient beings' bodies are easy to know, whereas the other mental factors (caitasika-dharma), being formless, are difficult to know.
Therefore, the Buddha said to Subhūti:
"The mental activities of immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings are all known.

Although within profound prajñā there are no sentient beings, nor dharmas such as form, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, one is nevertheless able to know the mental activities of sentient beings through the power of the skillful means of prajñā.
Because this *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), it does not manifest dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding this, the Buddha explains the causal condition:
"Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, even the mark of *prajñā* itself does not exist, let alone dharmas such as form!"
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the world," this refers to all sentient beings, whether they possess form (*rūpin*) or are formless (*arūpin*).
Those with form are the sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
those who are formless are the sentient beings of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Those with perception are all others except for the Heaven of Non-perception and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception;
those without perception are the non-percipient beings;
and those who are neither with nor without perception are the gods of the Peak of Existence.
"This world" refers to this trichiliocosm;
"pervading the ten directions" refers to all other immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds.
Within the six realms of this world, the Buddhas fully know the concentrated minds and distracted minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Having heard this, Subhūti felt doubt and wonder, thinking:

"The Buddhas always delight in practicing the emptiness of all dharmas through quiescence; how is it that they now universally know the concentrated and distracted minds of sentient beings who have been without beginning and are boundless?"
"The Buddha's mind is one, while the minds of sentient beings are of immeasurable kinds; how then can he know the minds of all sentient beings simultaneously?
For this reason, he asked:
"How does the Buddha know?"
The Buddha replied:
"By means of the wisdom of the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas), one knows whether the minds of sentient beings are concentrated or distracted.
Subhūti asked:
"What is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?
He replied: "It is what is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)."
"This is ultimate emptiness; even the nature of ultimate emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone a concentrated mind or a distracted mind!
[The interlocutor] asks:
"In the ultimate emptiness of the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are no discriminating minds or mental factors (*citta-caitta*); how then does the Buddha know their minds?"
The answer is:
In this context, the Buddha himself says:
"The nature of the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is also unattainable; yet by means of this wisdom, one knows the concentrated minds and distracted minds of sentient beings."
Why is this? If emptiness were apprehendable, there would be an objection;
since emptiness is not apprehendable, how can one raise an objection?

Now, the Buddha has transcended all conceptualizations, discriminations, and false dharmas, and abides securely in the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, he knows the minds of all sentient beings as they truly are;
because the minds of sentient beings abide within false dharmas, they are unable to know the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are.

First, "knowledge of others' minds" was briefly explained; next, the concentrated and distracted minds of sentient beings were distinguished—namely, those possessing the three poisons and those free from them—as well as their vastness, magnitude, immeasurability, invisibility, emergence and disappearance, contraction and expansion, and so forth.
Subhūti asked about each matter in turn. Initially, the answer was given by means of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, whereby one knows the concentrated mind and the distracted mind.
Subsequently, it was known by means of their exhaustion, non-defilement, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and detachment.
"Exhaustion" refers to the wisdom of impermanence;
when a bodhisattva practices this mind of the wisdom of impermanence, they remain detached from all worldly defilements.
Using the mundane path to suppress and extinguish the fetters and latent tendencies is called "cessation."
Because it is severed by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), it is called "severed.
Having severed all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*), one contemplates the quiescence and signlessness of nirvāṇa.
By these causes and conditions, one attains the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
By means of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one knows that both the concentrated mind and the distracted mind of others are themselves the true reality.
Furthermore, this mind arises and ceases moment by moment; because it does not exist in the future, it cannot be known [as such];
because it ceases moment by moment in the present, it cannot be known [as such] since there is no duration.
Ordinary people grasp at signs and engage in discrimination; within the three periods of time, they harbor recollections and false views, claiming to know the thoughts of others.
By observing through the gateway of exhaustion (*kṣayamukha*), these are seen as ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*);

because they are ultimately empty, there is no attachment. At that time, one attains the Way and knows the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. When one no longer engages in false conceptualization or discrimination regarding any phenomenon, one then knows the minds of others as they truly are.
Regarding the defiled mind: all phenomena enter into the dharma-nature and are thus entirely pure. Therefore it is said:
"The true reality of the defiled mind is that within it there is no defiled mind."
Why is this? Because within reality as it truly is, there is no mind and no mental factors; how much less so a defiled mind!
The same applies to the mind of hatred and the mind of delusion.
Within the characteristic of the undefiled mind, there is no characteristic of a defiled mind therein, because a defiled mind has been non-existent from the very beginning;
nor is there an undefiled mind, for the undefiled mind is the characteristic of quiescence, free from all discrimination.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the cause and condition: "Subhūti,
it is because two minds do not coexist."
Regarding the phenomena of sentient beings, minds arise in succession one after another; when there is no defiled mind, then there is no defiled mind.
Why is this? Because past defiled minds have already ceased, future ones do not yet exist, and in the present there is no defiled mind—thus, there is no defiled mind.
Since there is no defiled mind, there is likewise no non-defiled mind, because they are mutually dependent phenomena.
Therefore, within the true reality (dharmatā) that is devoid of defilement, there is neither a defiled mind nor a non-defiled mind.
It is the same for a mind without hatred and a mind without delusion.
Minds that are broad or narrow, increasing or decreasing, are all the conceptual discriminations of sentient beings grasping at signs.
The Buddha does not know in such a way.

Why is this? Because this mind is without color or form, has no place of abiding, and perishes moment by moment; thus, it is devoid of distinctions such as expansion or contraction, increase or decrease.
Within this, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:
"Because the characteristics of the nature of mind do not exist, breadth, narrowness, and so forth cannot be apprehended.
The meanings of breadth and narrowness, increase and decrease, and large and small are as explained in the section on the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Regarding "immeasurable mind" (*apramāṇacitta*): a broad mind and a great mind are themselves immeasurable.

Furthermore, it is called immeasurable because it takes immeasurable sentient beings as its object; it is called immeasurable because it takes the immeasurable dharmas of *nirvāṇa* as its object; and it is called immeasurable because the characteristics of the mind cannot be grasped.

Just as visual consciousness arises due to the conditions of the eye and visible forms, this consciousness does not abide in the eye, nor in visible forms, nor in between them; it is neither here nor there, and therefore has no place of abiding.
If there were truly no place of abiding, how could there be any action—whether good or foul?
Such things are like what is seen in a dream; one cannot seek their actual, fixed characteristics.
The mind is also like this: because it has no basis, it lacks a fixed characteristic, and is therefore called "immeasurable.
The terms "vast" and "great" should likewise be explained by distinguishing them according to their respective meanings.
Question:
If it is understood that the mind cannot be seen, for what reason does the Buddha say, "knowing the unseeable mind as it truly is"? Answer:
There is a practitioner of dhyāna who, through recollection and conceptualization, perceives this mind as being like a thread within a pure jewel;
while observing a skeleton, he perceives the mind arising in successive succession;
or at times, he perceives the mind as residing within the body.
Or one may perceive them as existing within conditions, such as in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), where one perceives only consciousness as immeasurable and boundless.
To refute such false conceptions, the Buddha said:
"One knows the minds of sentient beings as they truly are; because the self-characteristic of the mind of a sentient being is empty, it is characterized by signlessness."
Furthermore, the Buddha observes this mind with the five eyes and finds it ungraspable: the fleshly eye and the divine eye do not see it because they take form as their object;
the wisdom-eye does not see it because it takes nirvāṇa as its object.
The initial awakening of the Dharma-eye involves the analytical knowledge of all phenomena as wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, and so forth;
yet when this Dharma-eye enters into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is no longer any such differentiation, as it was previously stated:
"In all phenomena, there is no knower and no seer."
Therefore, it should not be seen. Because the Buddha’s eye contemplates the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), it does not see.
As for the minds of sentient beings, to "see" is to see according to reality (*yathābhūta*).
It is not as seen through the conceptualization and discrimination of ordinary people.

Furthermore, the five eyes arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are all conditioned phenomena, deceptive and unreal. The Buddha does not believe in them nor employ them; therefore it is said:
"One does not see with the five eyes."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Sixty-nine;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Explanation of the "Mother of the Buddha" Chapter, Part Fourty-eight, Continued;
Scroll Seventy.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.

[Sūtra] “Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha knows, in accordance with reality, the emergence and submergence, the contraction and expansion, of the mental activities (*citta-saṃskāra*) of sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!
How does the Buddha, by means of the perfection of wisdom, know as they truly are the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion, of the mental activities of sentient beings?”
The Buddha said:
"The arising, subsiding, contracting, and extending of all sentient beings' mental factors all arise in dependence upon form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."

Subhūti! Within this, the Buddha knows the mental states of sentient beings as they emerge and subside, contract and expand—namely, the view that "the self and the world are eternal" is the truth and all else is false, which is a view based on form;
and the view that "the self and the world are impermanent" is the truth and all else is false, which is a view based on form.
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false"—this view is based on form.
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is clinging to views.
"The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is clinging to views.
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is clinging to views.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view dependent on feeling.
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view dependent on perception.
"The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this is a view dependent on perception.
“The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false”—this is a view based on perception.
“The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false”—this is a view based on perception.
“The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false”—this is a view based on mental formations.
"The self and the world are impermanent; this is the truth, and all else is false"—this is a reliance on views.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this is the truth, and all else is false"—this is a reliance on views.
"The self and the world are neither permanent nor impermanent; this is the truth, and all else is false"—this is a reliance on views.
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this view is dependent upon consciousness.
"The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this view is dependent upon consciousness.
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—this view is dependent upon consciousness.
“That the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite is the truth, and all else is false; this view is based on consciousness.
“That the world is finite is the truth, and all else is false; this view is based on form.
That the world is infinite is the truth, and all else is false; this view is based on form.”
"The world is finite" is the truth, and all else is false—this view is based on form;
"the world is neither finite nor infinite" is the truth, and all else is false—this view is based on form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"The self is identical to the body"—this view is based on form;
"the self is distinct from the body"—this view is based on form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"That the Tathāgata exists after death—this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view is based on form.
"That the Tathāgata does not exist after death—this is the truth, all else is falsehood"—this view is based on form.
That after death there is a "going forth" (Tathāgata) or that there is no "going forth" is a factual truth, and all else is false speech; this view is dependent upon form.
That after death it is neither the case that there is a "going forth" nor that there is no "going forth" is a factual truth, and all else is false speech; this view is dependent upon form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness. "In this way, Subhūti,
by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha knows the emergence and submergence, the contraction and expansion of sentient beings, as they truly are."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha knows the characteristics of form (*rūpa*).
How does he know the characteristics of form?
As suchness is indestructible, non-conceptual, signless, without recollection, without proliferation, and without attainment, so too is the characteristic of form, Subhūti.
The Buddha knows the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
How does he know the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?

Just as the characteristic of suchness is indestructible, non-conceptual, signless, without recollection, without discursive proliferation, and without attainment, so too are the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Buddha knows the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the arising, ceasing, contracting, and expanding of the mental factors of sentient beings.
The suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of all conditioned phenomena are themselves the suchness of all dharmas.
What is the suchness of all dharmas?
It is the suchness of the six pāramitās; the suchness of the six pāramitās is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness. The eighteen...
The suchness of emptiness is the suchness of the eight liberations; the suchness of the eight liberations is the suchness of the nine successive concentrations;
the suchness of the nine successive concentrations is the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers;
and the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers is the suchness of the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
Up to and including the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities is itself the suchness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
the suchness of all-knowledge is itself the suchness of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas,
worldly and world-transcending dharmas, and out-flowing and non-out-flowing dharmas— namely, the suchness of non-out-flowing dharmas.
The suchness of marks is the suchness of past, future, and present dharmas;
the suchness of past, future, and present dharmas is the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas;
the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas is the suchness of the fruit of srotāpanna; [the suchness] of the srotāpanna...
The suchness of the fruit is itself the suchness of the fruit of the once-returner; the suchness of the fruit of the once-returner is itself the suchness of the fruit of the non-returner;
the suchness of the fruit of the non-returner is itself the suchness of the fruit of the arhat;
the suchness of the fruit of the arhat is itself the suchness of the path of the pratyekabuddha; [the suchness of] the pratyekabuddha...
The suchness of the Way is the suchness of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
the suchness of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the suchness of all Buddhas;
and the suchness of all Buddhas is the single suchness—non-dual, undifferentiated, inexhaustible, and indestructible. This is called the [suchness] of all phenomena.
The Dharma is the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).

It is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Buddha attains this nature of suchness; for this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the characteristics of the world.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Buddha knows all dharmas as they are in their suchness (*tathatā*); they are not otherwise than suchness, nor are they different from suchness.
Because he has realized this suchness, the Buddha is named Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This suchness of all dharmas is not non-suchness; it is a profound state of non-differentiation!”
"Bhagavān!
It is by means of this suchness that all Buddhas preach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of beings.
Bhagavān!"
Who is able to believe and understand this?
Only the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas, those endowed with right view, and the arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*). Why is this so?
“Because this Dharma is extremely profound.
“Subhūti! This Suchness is profound because its characteristic is inexhaustible.”
Subhūti asked: "By virtue of what dharma being of an inexhaustible nature is it profound?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are inexhaustible.
In this way, Subhūti,
having realized the suchness of all these dharmas, the Buddha teaches them for the sake of sentient beings."
[Treatise] Explanation:

The Buddha fully knows all that sentient beings do and practice, including the sixty-two types of false views and other such heterodox views, as well as the ninety-eight fetters and other such afflictions. Therefore it is said:
"The Buddha knows the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion, of the minds and mental factors of sentient beings."

Those who live at home are said to be "immersed" because they are submerged by various afflictions such as craving; those who have left the home life among the ninety-six kinds of heterodox views are said to be "emerged."
Furthermore, because one is constantly attached to worldly pleasures, it is called "sinking";
alternatively, because one realizes impermanence, feels fear, and seeks the Path, it is called "emerging."
Furthermore, because those who receive the teachings of the ninety-six types of paths cannot attain the Right Path, they sink back into the world.
"Bending" refers to not being free from the realm of desire; "stretching" refers to being free from the realm of desire.
The same applies to the separation from and non-separation from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
It is like a person standing by a clear pond who sees fish:
