It is the same for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).

They personally realize the path of a pratyekabuddha but do not themselves become a pratyekabuddha; they also instruct others to enter the path of a pratyekabuddha, praise the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha path, and joyfully extol those who have attained the path of a pratyekabuddha.

Having himself entered the stage of a bodhisattva, he also teaches others to enter the stage of a bodhisattva; he praises the dharma of entering the stage of a bodhisattva, and he joyfully extols those who have entered the stage of a bodhisattva.

They themselves purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; they also teach others to purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; they praise the methods for purifying Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity; and they rejoice in and praise those who purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.

They themselves give rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, and they also teach others to give rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva; they praise the method of giving rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva, and they joyfully praise those who give rise to the spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.

They themselves give rise to all-knowledge, and they also teach others to give rise to all-knowledge; they praise the dharma that gives rise to all-knowledge, and they joyfully praise those who give rise to all-knowledge.

He himself severs all fetters and habitual tendencies, and he also teaches others to sever all fetters and habitual tendencies; he praises the dharma of severing all fetters and habitual tendencies, and he joyfully extols those who have severed all fetters and habitual tendencies.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice in this way!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should themselves take up the accomplishment of longevity, teach others to take up the accomplishment of longevity, praise the method for accomplishing longevity, and joyfully extol those who have accomplished longevity.

He himself abides in the dwelling of the accomplishment of the Dharma, teaches others to abide in the dwelling of the accomplishment of the Dharma, praises the dharma of abiding in the accomplishment of the Dharma, and joyfully extols those who abide in the accomplishment of the Dharma.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice in this way and should likewise train in the power of skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā.

When this bodhisattva trains in this way and practices in this way, they shall attain unimpeded form; they shall attain unimpeded feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and even attain the abiding in unimpeded phenomena.

Why is this? Because from the very beginning, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not apprehended form, nor have they apprehended feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all modes.
"Why is this? Because that which does not grasp form is not form; and so on, up to: that which does not grasp all-knowledge is not all-knowledge.
When this "Chapter on the Practice of Bodhisattvas" was being spoken, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
[Treatise] Commentary: Subhūti asked:
"How should a bodhisattva who wishes to accomplish the unsurpassed path practice?"
The Buddha replied:
"One should give rise to an impartial mind, without partiality toward any sentient beings.
The five aggregates are harmoniously combined and conventionally designated as 'sentient beings,' just like a chariot or a forest."
"All sentient beings" refers to the entirety of the six realms throughout the ten directions, without exception.
Regarding the nature of all sentient beings, each is categorized into three groups:
enemies, kin, and neutral persons.

The Buddha now teaches the bodhisattvas to maintain an impartial mind, regarding all sentient beings with thoughts of kinship and affection; do not give rise to thoughts of enmity, nor thoughts of indifference.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of sentient beings:
those who are loved and those who are hated.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding all sentient beings, one should be free from these two states of mind; do not give rise to hatred or attachment.
Attachment is craving, a defiled state of mind, and should not be practiced."
One should practice a heart of loving-kindness.
According to worldly conventions, one cherishes and loves one's wife, children, cattle, horses, and so forth, while harboring hatred and malice toward enemies and thieves.
A Bodhisattva transforms these worldly ways and practices only a heart of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding "equanimity of mind": the bodhisattva gives rise to the joy of the Dharma and desires that all sentient beings may reach the Buddha-way;
the bodhisattva personally relinquishes feelings of aversion and attachment, and likewise relinquishes the aversion and attachment that sentient beings direct toward themselves.
In the world there are three kinds of people:
the evil, the greatly evil, and the most evil among the evil;
the good, the greatly good, and the best among the good.
"Evil" refers to when someone inflicts harm upon oneself and one retaliates with harm in return.
The Dharma of all Buddhas maintains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; one should not give rise to evil thoughts, let alone engage in evil actions of body or speech!
A great evil is, for example, when one inflicts harm upon others even though no one has harmed oneself.

An evil among evils is, for example, when someone provides for another with a kind heart and compassionate thoughts, yet the other person instead responds with a malicious mind to destroy and injure them; such evils as these are called "evils among evils."
"Good" refers to when a person treats one with kindness, and one repays them with goodness in turn.
"Greatly good" refers to when a person has done no good for oneself, yet one benefits them with kind deeds.

The best among the good is as follows: when someone harms one with evil deeds, yet one responds by providing offerings of good deeds—even at the cost of one's own body and life—this is called the best among the good.
The Bodhisattva abandons these three evils and transcends these two kinds of goodness, practicing the sixth mind toward all sentient beings.
Question:
This Bodhisattva has not yet attained the Dharma-body; how can he practice this mind?
The answer is:
This bodhisattva seeks the unsurpassed path and should practice the unsurpassed Dharma; only by undergoing such difficult and arduous ascetic practices does he accomplish the unsurpassed path.
For example, it is like a merchant who, having endured all manner of sufferings on a perilous road, finally attains great profit.

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva hears the true essence of the Buddha’s Dharma—namely, ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), the absence of self and what belongs to a self, and the lack of any fixed, real dharma—and understands that all that is seen, heard, and known is deceptive, like an illusion or a dream;
because he has deep faith in these teachings, he is able to offer his own body and life as an act of worship even to hostile robbers.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva knows that this body arises from the causes and conditions of sinful karma, afflictions, and inversions; all that is seen and heard is fundamentally false, deceptive, and the root of defilement.
If someone comes wishing to inflict harm upon me, I should joyfully accept it, for by means of this wretched body I shall attain the benefit of the Unsurpassed Way—why should I not give it?

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva resolves upon the path, out of deep love for sentient beings and the desire to benefit them, he personally offers his own body as an offering to enemies and robbers, wishing to cause sentient beings to emulate his conduct;
because there may be sentient beings who, when taught the Dharma by others, are unwilling to accept it, he uses his own body as a teaching to inspire their faith and acceptance.
Furthermore, there are many who speak of seeking the unsurpassed path while their physical conduct does not correspond to their words;
for this reason as well, the Bodhisattva instructs them through his own example, causing them to fortify their resolve and perform these difficult deeds.
"Those who seek the unsurpassed path should practice the most excellent of all wholesome dharmas; only by undertaking such difficult tasks can it be attained.
For these and countless other reasons, he offered his own body and life as an offering to his enemies and robbers."
Question:
What is the difference between an impartial mind (*upekṣā-citta*) and a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*)? Answer:
"Equal mind" refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), while "loving mind" (*maitrī-citta*) refers to one specific immeasurable mind. Some say:
initially abandoning the distinction between enemy and friend is equal mind; subsequently adding compassionate concern is loving mind.
Furthermore, some say:

"Equanimity" means observing all sentient beings as suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because these dharmas are all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and immeasurable, they are equal.
To cherish and care for sentient beings is called the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).

The reason compassion (*karuṇā-citta*) is not mentioned here is that when one contemplates sentient beings with a compassionate mind and accumulates this state of mind, the mind may become despondent and sink.
Furthermore, there are some sentient beings who do not appreciate a bodhisattva’s compassionate concern, saying:
"Why do you not worry about your own body instead of thinking of others?"
The mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) does not involve such matters; because it easily gathers in sentient beings, only the mind of loving-kindness is mentioned.
Question:
If there are three kinds of sentient beings:

Since a bodhisattva has accumulated merit and wisdom of superior, middling, and inferior degrees, they ought to be a great person; why then do you say that they should "give rise to a lowly mind toward all sentient beings"?
The answer is:
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"All phenomena are impermanent; all sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—all return to destruction. Within this, what could be considered 'great'?"
"What is small? People perceive 'large' and 'small' based on worldly conventions.
Furthermore, largeness and smallness are not fixed; what is considered large in one country may be considered small in another.
What is great here may be small there;
one who is lowly and base in this life may become a celestial king in a future life.
Through such karmic causes and conditions, beings revolve in the world, where nobility and baseness, greatness and smallness, are without fixed status.
Just as water and fire, or the noble and the humble, vary according to the time, their use or abandonment is not fixed.

Furthermore, although a bodhisattva possesses merit, they know that this merit is ultimately empty, like an illusion, and like a dream; thus they do not cling to this merit, nor do they perceive it as having magnitude or smallness.
Furthermore, among all sentient beings, only a Buddha can know those who possess the causes and conditions for the path to Buddhahood.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"If I were to disparage sentient beings based on their physical appearance or talents—disparaging them for such matters—I would be disparaging future Buddhas."
"If one slights the Buddha, it constitutes a definitive transgression.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"I have vowed to deliver all sentient beings;"
"If sentient beings have nothing to attain, then I would be failing them.
It is like a host who invites guests; he should honor the guests while humbling himself.
If there is nothing provided for them, then he is guilty of failing his guests.
Furthermore, because of a mind of self-importance, one takes pleasure in giving rise to anger;
arrogance is the root of anger, and anger is the root of all grave offenses.
If a bodhisattva maintains a humble attitude toward sentient beings, they will harbor no resentment even if those beings revile or strike them;
it is like when a master beats a slave, the slave does not dare to feel anger or hatred.
If a bodhisattva exalts himself and looks down upon sentient beings, he will become enraged when those beings harm him;
it is like a servant who becomes angry when striking his master.
Because subduing the mind brings about such various benefits as these, a bodhisattva should practice it.

"The mind of peace and security" bestows happiness in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate state; it is not like the happiness provided by parents or friends, which pertains only to the present life.

When a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings with an impartial mind, a mind of loving-kindness, and a humble mind, if there should be an ungrateful person who comes to disturb the bodhisattva, disbelieving their practice and claiming it is deceptive, done for the sake of seeking fame and devoid of reality;
or if they are sent by Māra to disturb the bodhisattva—being the worst among the wicked and ignorant of the bounds of gratitude.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is equanimous, and he attains unimpeded penetration therein.
Having attained this unimpeded mind, even though sentient beings may have great sins and great transgressions, he desires only to benefit them and does not give rise to a mind of vexation.
The mind of loving-kindness is peaceful, unimpeded, and free from affliction.

It is, for example, like a filial son who loves and respects his parents as he would an elder brother, a younger brother, a sister, or his own children; it gives rise to love, respect, and compassionate mindfulness, devoid of any lustful desire.
Worldly people are only able to love and respect those close to them, whereas Bodhisattvas extend this to all beings.
To attain such a supple, pure, and benevolent mind is called "patience toward sentient beings" (*sattvakṣānti*); it is the initial gateway to the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
Next, one practices the ten paths of wholesome action.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, these ten paths of wholesome action are always present in the world; they are the teaching of wholesome dharmas.
A bodhisattva first practices these ten paths of wholesome action through forty modes of conduct.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas deeply contemplate wholesome dharmas and maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings.
There are twelve matters regarding the dharma of ordinary persons who have abandoned desire, which are also practiced through forty-eight kinds of conduct.
The six pāramitās up to the endurance of the Dharma (dharmasthiti) are adventitious dharmas; when there is a Buddha who teaches them, there is the practice of the bodhisattva.
Thus far, both the original dharmas and the adventitious dharmas have been fully explained from beginning to end. Now, having attained wholesome dharmas in this life, one’s wisdom is unimpeded;

by relinquishing the physical body, one attains the unimpeded Dharma-body and travels at will to the ten directions to transform sentient beings, cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas before the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Regarding the statement, "When this Dharma was heard, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)," it means that in this chapter, the subtle and profound Dharma is explained, as well as the practice with effort; thus, both the gate of skillful means and the gate of wisdom are fully perfected through these two practices.
If one speaks only of the Dharma of suchness, the benefit is slight;
if one speaks only of the Dharma of existence, the benefit is likewise slight.
Now, by speaking of both the dharmas of existence and non-existence in their completeness, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Just as one can reach a destination because both wheels are complete, so too,
because the two truths were well-expounded herein, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Seventy-two.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Avaivartika,
Number Fifty-five, Scroll Seventy-three.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 55: On the Non-Retrogressive. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"By what conduct, what category, and what characteristics is one known to be an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to know the stage of ordinary persons, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of buddhas;"
These stages, within the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), are neither dual nor distinct; they are neither conceptualized nor discriminated.
Entering into this suchness, upon hearing these matters, one passes directly through them without doubt.
Why is this? Because within suchness there is neither the characteristic of oneness nor the characteristic of duality.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not engage in useless speech, but speaks only words that correspond to what is beneficial, and does not look upon the long and short [faults] of others.
“Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, by what practices, categories, and characteristics can one know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can contemplate all dharmas as being without activity, without category, and without characteristics, it should be known that this is called an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are without activity, without category, and without characteristics, in what dharma does a bodhisattva turn such that it is called ‘not turning’?”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns away from form, and turns away from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called a bodhisattva who does not turn back."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns within the *dānapāramitā* up to turning within the *prajñāpāramitā*; turns within emptiness of the internal (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); turns within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to turning within the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); and turns within the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha up to turning within unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*), you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn."
Why is this? Subhūti,
since the nature of form does not exist, where could a bodhisattva abide?
"Furthermore, Subhūti, even up to the point where the nature of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is non-existent,
in what would that bodhisattva abide? Moreover, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe the countenances, appearances, or speech of the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of external paths, nor does he form such thoughts:"
"These non-Buddhists—whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—truly know and truly see.
If one speaks of right view, such a thing does not exist!

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give rise to doubt, does not cling to the grasping of precepts, and does not fall into wrong views. Nor does he seek worldly auspiciousness as a means to purification, nor does he worship or make offerings to other deities with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, or music."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that one is named an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is never born into a low-born family, nor is he ever born into any of the eight unfavorable conditions; he never again receives a female body.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly practice the ten paths of wholesome action:
they themselves refrain from killing, do not instruct others to kill, praise the dharma of refraining from killing, and rejoice in and praise those who refrain from killing; and so on, up to:
they themselves refrain from wrong views, do not instruct others in wrong views, do not praise the dharma of wrong views, and do not rejoice in or praise those who practice wrong views.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the ten unwholesome paths even in dreams.
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is called an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, and so on, up to practicing the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Whatever dharmas a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives, reads, recites, explains, and correctly attends to—namely, from the *sūtras* up to the *upadeśas*.
When this bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma, they form this thought:
"By means of these causes and conditions of the gift of Dharma, may the vows of all sentient beings be fulfilled.
Through the merit of this gift of Dharma, I share it with all sentient beings and dedicate it toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not doubt or regret the profound Dharma.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"For what reason does a bodhisattva have no doubt and no regret regarding the profound Dharma?

The Buddha said, "This non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma as a basis for giving rise to doubt—whether it be form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), or even unsurpassed complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). He does not perceive any such dharma as a basis for giving rise to doubt or regret."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The physical, verbal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are supple.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of loving-kindness. Subhūti!"
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell together with the five hindrances:
sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva has no attachment whatsoever in any place.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters or exits,
goes or comes, sits or lies down, walks or stands, he should always maintain single-minded mindfulness.

Whether entering or exiting, going or coming, sitting or lying down, walking or standing, lifting or lowering his feet, he should move with stability and composure, always maintaining single-minded mindfulness, and walk while looking at the ground."
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that one is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Subhūti, the clothing and bedding used by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are not loathsome or foul-smelling to others; they delight in purity and cleanliness, and they suffer little from illness. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
In the bodies of ordinary people, there are eighty thousand families of worms that consume their flesh; however, the body of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no such worms. Why is this?
The merit of this bodhisattva transcends the mundane world; for this reason, this bodhisattva has no such "door-insects.
As the merit of this bodhisattva increases, in accordance with that merit, they attain purity of body and purity of mind.
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that one is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain purity of body and purity of mind?
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, according to what they have attained, increase their roots of goodness and eliminate mental crookedness and mental perversity.
Subhūti! This is called the purity of body and the purity of mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Because their body and mind are thus purified, they are able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the rank of bodhisattvas.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, you should know that such a person is named an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not prize gain and offerings; although he practices the twelve dhūtas, he does not prize the dharma of the araṇya, nor even the dharma of possessing only the three robes.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never give rise to a mind of stinginess or greed; they do not give rise to a mind of broken precepts, a mind of agitation through anger, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, a mind of delusion, or a mind of jealousy.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mind abides immovably and his wisdom penetrates deeply; with single-minded attention, he listens and receives whatever Dharma he hears as well as all worldly matters, all of which are in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any worldly activity that does not enter into the nature of phenomena;
he perceives all such things as being in union with the prajñāpāramitā.
"For these reasons, Subhūti,
this is called the mark of an avaivartika bodhisattva.
[Śāstra] Question:
Question: Since the characteristics of the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) have been explained in various places above, why is this asked again? Answer:
Although they have been briefly explained in various places above, they are now intended to be explained in detail.
Since most of what is contained herein consists of the characteristics of an *avaivartika*, it is titled the "Chapter on the Characteristics of the *Avaivartika*.
Furthermore, while the preceding section explained the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the subsequent section explains the causes and conditions by which Māra subverts the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Now, it is said that those who believe and accept the *prajñāpāramitā* are *avaivartika*. Subhūti asks because he wishes to describe their characteristics.

Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions practiced by a bodhisattva from the first generation of the mind of awakening onward, as well as the fruits and rewards obtained—these constitute the state of being *avaivartika*, whereby one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that one will certainly become a Buddha.
It is like a person who, upon receiving an office, has already obtained the official seal and thus no longer harbors any doubt;
or again, it is like the various practices undertaken by a śrāvaka, all of which are for the sake of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The stage of *avaivartika* is a ground of certain security; having transcended the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one does not enter the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Although one has not yet attained the Buddha-way, one is able to serve as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the world.
Because this matter is subtle and difficult to attain, Subhūti asks about its practice and characteristics.
Since the Buddha had originally commanded Subhūti to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti asks:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the practices, categories, and characteristics of an avaivartika?
He asked: "What is the difference between these three things?"
Answer: Some say that these three matters all have the same meaning;
by means of this, one knows whether someone is an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) or not an *avaivartika*.

Some say: "Practice" refers to the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of an avaivartika bodhisattva, which differ from those of others; by means of these practices, one manifests the profound wisdom of the avaivartika.
"Category" refers to the discerning knowledge that distinguishes which bodhisattvas are irreversible (*avaivartika*) and which are not.
"Signs" refers to the various causes and conditions—excluding conduct and category—by means of which one may know the characteristics of irreversibility.
The Buddha explained the underlying meaning:

if a bodhisattva can fulfill the five pāramitās and enter deeply into the prajñāpāramitā, by the power of skillful means (upāya), they do not become attached to the prajñāpāramitā, but merely contemplate suchness (tathatā)—that is to say, the true mark of all dharmas (dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam).

At that time, the bodhisattva does not regard the stages of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles as lowly, nor does he regard the stage of a Buddha as noble; he enters into all dharmas as they truly are.

Within the suchness of all phenomena, there is no differentiation between two dharmas; one simply enters suchness by means of suchness, with nothing else remaining, nor does one differentiate or grasp at signs.
Why is this? Because it is equal.
One who can enter in such a manner enters the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
The mind does not give rise to doubt and further seeks the definitive characteristic of all phenomena.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"From the stage of ordinary beings up to the stage of Buddhahood, within the nature of suchness, there is neither duality nor distinction.
To attain such a Dharma is called the conduct, category, and characteristics of an avaivartika.
Furthermore, to state this meaning briefly:
because of the suchness of all dharmas—namely, ultimate emptiness—the bodhisattva relinquishes all worldly affairs, yet does not dwell even in ultimate emptiness.
Why is this? Because they have attained the ultimately pure true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
If a bodhisattva hears this teaching on the dharma of non-reliance, their mind will be free from doubt or regret, and they will not think of relying upon anything.
From the aforementioned matters upward, these constitute the essential body of the *avaivartika*;
from this point downward, all are the fruits of the practice of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Because one has attained ultimate emptiness, the mind is matured in the mark of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) and does not utter speech that is without benefit.
What he says is always the Dharma, never what is not the Dharma;
what he says is entirely truthful, never false speech;
and what he says is gentle, never coarse or harsh.
All were spoken with a mind of compassion, not with a mind of anger;
what was taught was timely and always seized the opportune moment, as he observed the minds of others and accorded with their local customs.
Now, to briefly explain the words concerning benefit herein:
whether it be teaching the Buddha-way, the two vehicles, or the paths of humans and devas; whether it be attaining non-reproachful happiness in this present life;

because one constantly remains far removed from the four verbal evils, because one possesses great compassion toward sentient beings, and because one is further able to suppress and thin out one's own afflictions—for these reasons, one can speak various beneficial words through manifold causes and conditions.
Question: A śrāvaka proceeds directly toward nirvāṇa and may not concern himself with others;
however, a bodhisattva regards sentient beings as his own children and constantly desires to transform them through teaching—why, then, would he not observe their strengths and weaknesses?
The answer is:
If there are sentient beings who cannot be subdued or broken, nor can be transformed and delivered, do not observe such as these. Why is this?
If one instructs with a benevolent heart, the other considers it jealousy, as if a knife were piercing their heart;
since it provides no benefit and only increases their transgressions, one therefore does not consider whether they are superior or inferior.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"Even though the Buddhas possess all-knowledge and have exhausted the habitual tendencies of afflictions, they are still unable to deliver all sentient beings completely;
how much more so for me, who have not yet attained the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva nor unimpeded wisdom—how could I possibly observe all sentient beings universally?"
Among those who are *avaivartika*, there are some who have attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and some who have not;
having attained the state of *avaivartika*, they must cultivate the path of the supernormal powers separately before they can obtain them.
If one has previously attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet they are not fully perfected, one cannot observe [all things] universally.
A question is asked:

Why did the Buddha not immediately answer Subhūti’s initial inquiry regarding practice, characteristics, and categories by saying "there is no practice, no characteristics, and no categories," but instead explain this only now?
The answer is:

When the initial question was asked, sentient beings had not yet become attached to the marks of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression); therefore, the Buddha’s response sometimes spoke of the mark of emptiness and sometimes of the mark of existence.

Now, because sentient beings are attached to the marks of *avaivartika* and wish to enter the stage of *avaivartika* from the state of ordinary beings, the Buddha says: "All things are without activity, without category, and without characteristics."
Subhūti asked again:
"If all dharmas are entirely empty, why speak of 'turning' or 'not turning' with respect to any dharma?
One should turn away from the stage of an ordinary person and not turn away from the stage of a Buddha!"
The Buddha replied:

"If a bodhisattva can contemplate that all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are empty and non-existent, and thereby turns away from all clinging minds, they will not turn back from the path of the Buddha."

Form and other dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; because the Bodhisattva knows the faults and transgressions of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), he should not abide within them.
Because all dharmas are empty, he is able to turn away the mind of attachment; because he turns away the mind of attachment, it is called "non-turning."
Furthermore, because an avaivartika bodhisattva has entered the stage of certainty, their mind is resolute and free from doubt:
"There is no true wisdom among any of the non-Buddhist paths!"
"If one possesses true wisdom, they are not called a non-Buddhist.
Such is what is called the mark of an *avaivartika*. Question:
Now, "not giving rise to doubt" is taught first, and later, "not doubting the profound Dharma" is taught; what is the difference between these two forms of non-doubt?
The answer is:
the non-doubt mentioned now refers to that which is abandoned by a Srotāpanna within the context of the Four Noble Truths.
"Having no doubt later" means that one has no doubt regarding the profound Dharma known by the Buddha.
Because of the power of this bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom, although they have not yet become a srotāpanna and have not yet become a buddha, they are able to be free from these two doubts.
The term "precepts" refers to the precepts of non-Buddhists;
by practicing these non-Buddhist precepts, one cannot attain nirvana.
The remaining four views are all termed wrong views.

Because they have deep faith in the causes, conditions, and retributions of karma, they do not seek auspicious matters, nor do they make offerings to celestial deities with flowers, incense, and the like.
Because they seek the Way and destroy the root of arrogance, they never take birth in lowly or inferior families.
Because they do not obstruct the merits of others and constantly practice exhortation and assistance, they are not born in the eight difficult states.
Because they have subdued and thinned their lustful desires and remain far removed from a deceitful mind, they do not receive a female body.
Furthermore, although other people may practice the ten paths of wholesome action, they might do so only once, twice, or thrice, and are unable to fulfill all four types;
this bodhisattva, because of his great compassion and deep love for wholesome dharmas, practices all four types in their entirety.
Because they constantly cultivate and accumulate the ten paths of wholesome action, they do not engage in the ten unwholesome paths even in their dreams.
The merit cultivated by other people is for themselves alone;
although small bodhisattvas act for the sake of sentient beings, they also act for themselves.
Whatever merit an avaivartika bodhisattva performs is entirely for the sake of sentient beings and not for their own sake.
If that merit could be given away, they would give it all to sentient beings and then cultivate it themselves once more;
however, it is simply impossible to give it away.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva uses the twelve divisions of the scriptures to teach and transform sentient beings, they do so solely for the sake of sentient beings and not for their own benefit.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva’s five faculties—faith and the others—are sharp, they are able to have faith in all dharmas even though they have not yet become Buddhas.
In this context, the Buddha further explains the causes and conditions for emptiness:
"Because the bodhisattva does not perceive dharmas such as form, there is no basis for the arising of doubt.

Furthermore, because this bodhisattva constantly practices a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, their mental karma is supple; because their mental karma is supple, they achieve the compassionate actions of body and speech.
Question: Non-Buddhists also possess a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; why, then, is this said to be a mark of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva? Answer:

Although non-Buddhists possess [compassion], it is not profound; they cannot universally contemplate all sentient beings, nor is it constant, because it does not arise from union with the true nature of all phenomena (dharmatā).
It is not so for the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva rebukes the five desires and eliminates the five hindrances, entering the first dhyāna with its five factors, remaining unaccompanied by the five hindrances.
This is because the five hindrances, when they shroud the mind, can exhaust and diminish wisdom, destroy the path of the Buddha, and open the way for Māra.

This bodhisattva knows that all conditioned phenomena are false and unreal, like illusions and dreams; and that unconditioned phenomena are empty, non-existent, and characterized by quiescence. For this reason, they have no attachment or clinging toward anything whatsoever.
Among sentient beings, one does not cling even to the Buddha;
among phenomena, one does not cling even to nirvāṇa.
As for hatred, it is a gross offense that has already been severed by a small bodhisattva, and therefore it is not mentioned here.
Attachment is profound and subtle, difficult to sever; therefore, it is discussed here now.
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva has entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he protects all sentient beings;
because he protects all sentient beings, he constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness and does not afflict them.
Because he does not break the precepts, his coming and going, entering and exiting, and so forth, are composed and single-minded.
As for "lifting and setting down the feet while walking while looking at the ground," it is for the sake of protecting sentient beings and avoiding a distracted mind.

Furthermore, because this bodhisattva has long cultivated and accumulated immeasurable and boundless wholesome dharmas, there are no eighty thousand families of worms within his body, and he suffers little from illness; consequently, his robes, bedding, and other requisites are always clean and free of defilement.
Because of the power of roots of goodness such as attaining the true nature of all phenomena, there are no eighty thousand families of parasites within the body.
Because the mind is pure, the body, speech, and so forth are also pure;
because one is free from the base afflictions of falsehood, deceit, crookedness, and the like, the mind is pure.
Because these two matters are pure, although they act within the world, they remain free from all oppressive afflictions;
because their minds do not become weary or despondent, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because this bodhisattva values the Buddha-way, he does not value gain and offerings;
although he practices the dhūtas, he does not value these dharmas, for these dharmas are but a small portion of the causes and conditions for the ultimate path, and are not the ultimate path itself.
This is called the practice, category, and characteristic marks of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. Question:
Since this bodhisattva has not yet attained the Buddha-way and has not yet severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), how is it that he never gives rise to evil thoughts such as stinginess and greed?
Answer:

When an avaivartika bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they sever all afflictions (kleśa), though not yet their residual habits (vāsanā).
If these were not severed, how could they constantly remain free from the arising of obstacles to the path, such as stinginess and greed?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"From the srotāpanna up to the arhat, these are precisely the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Furthermore, some say:

Because the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās and deeply cultivates and accumulates all merits, all afflictions are broken and thinned; since they do not arise within the mind, this is called "constant non-arising."
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva has practiced the dhyāna-pāramitā for immeasurable eons, his mind dwells immovably;
and because he has accumulated and cultivated prajñā, he penetrates deeply into wisdom.
Because this bodhisattva knows the subtle and wondrous flavor of the Dharma, they listen to and receive the Dharma from others with single-minded attention;

because their longing for the Dharma is profound, whether the teachings they hear pertain to the Triple Vehicle, to non-Buddhist paths, or to worldly dharmas, they—due to the excellence of their own minds—harmonize them all with Prajñā-pāramitā, without destroying the characteristics of the dharmas.
It is like a robust man free from illness, for whom there is no food that cannot be digested;
or like the Buddha, who possesses the mark of the supreme sense of taste (*rasāgra-lakṣaṇa*), such that even bitter, pungent, or unpalatable food becomes a supreme flavor within his mouth;
or like when rock honey is being boiled until it is nearly finished, where all various substances placed within it turn into rock honey because its wondrous flavor and power are so potent.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: because the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* is so preeminent, they are able to cause all various dharmas to merge with *prajñā* into a single flavor, free from all faults and transgressions.
Furthermore, regarding worldly matters, all the physical and verbal actions undertaken by a bodhisattva are for the sake of compassionately delivering sentient beings;
this compassionate mind enters the initial gateway of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, regarding all worldly affairs and conditions—even in sitting, rising, walking, eating, drinking, and speaking—he constantly maintains mindfulness of bringing peace and security to sentient beings.
These phenomena of coming and going all enter into the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), as explained in the "Refutation of Coming and Going.
The same applies to matters of worldly livelihood.
This is called the mark of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive bodhisattva).
[Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti, if an evil Māra,

before an avaivartika bodhisattva, conjures up eight great hells, and within each hell there are thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas all being burned and boiled, undergoing various bitter and poisonous sufferings, and says to that bodhisattva:
'These bodhisattvas are all avaivartikas who have received the prediction of the Buddha, yet they have fallen into the great hells.'"
"If you have been granted by the Buddha the prediction of *avaivartika* [non-retrogression], you shall enter this great hell;
since the Buddha has granted you the prediction of hell, it would be better for you to abandon the Bodhisattva mind, so that you may avoid falling into hell and instead attain birth in the heavens."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, upon seeing or hearing such things, their mind remains unmoved, without doubt or alarm, and thinks:
'It is absolutely impossible for a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive (avaivartika) to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts! "
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Māra transforms himself into the appearance of a bhikṣu and approaches the Bodhisattva, saying to him:

"Regarding what you previously heard—that one should thus purely cultivate the six pāramitās, and so forth, up to practicing in such a way as to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—quickly repent and abandon these matters!"

Furthermore, you must quickly relinquish those roots of goodness that you previously cultivated in the presence of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from their initial aspiration until the endurance of the Dharma—including your acts of sympathetic joy and your dedications toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You must let go of them as well!
If you will quickly abandon [these views], I shall tell you the true Buddha-dharma.
What you have previously heard is none of the Buddha-dharma and none of the Buddha’s teaching; it is merely a compilation of literary embellishments!
"What I have spoken is the true Dharma of the Buddhas.

If, upon hearing this statement, a bodhisattva’s mind is startled, doubtful, or regretful, it should be known that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas and has not yet become firmly established in the nature of *avaivartika*.

If a bodhisattva’s mind is unmoving, unstartled, free from doubt, and free from regret; if they accord with and rely upon the dharma of non-action and non-arising; if they do not believe the words of others nor follow the conduct of others;
and while practicing the six pāramitās, they do not follow the words of others—up to and including when practicing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—they likewise do not follow the words of others.

Subhūti! For example, it is like an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted: he does not rely on the words of others nor follow the conduct of others; having directly perceived the true reality of all dharmas, even Māra the Evil One cannot turn him away from it.
In this way, Subhūti, it is also thus for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible: those who seek the path of śrāvakas or the path of pratyekabuddhas are unable to destroy or subdue their mind.
Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva definitely dwells in the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and does not follow the words of others;
he does not even accept the words of a Buddha with blind faith, much less the words of those seeking the state of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or of evil Māras, externalists, or brahmins!
This is absolutely impossible! Why is that?

Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma to be followed with faith—whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor form-tathatā up to consciousness-tathatā; nor even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), let alone the tathatā of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that such a person is named an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
A Māra, having assumed the form of a bhikṣu, came to where the Bodhisattva was and said to him:
"That which you practice is the dharma of birth and death; it is not the path to sarvajñā (omniscience). You should now, in this very body, realize the exhaustion of suffering!"

At that time, Māra the Evil One, for the sake of the bodhisattva, teaches what appear to be the dharmas of the path by means of worldly practices. These dharmas that appear to be the path are bound to the three realms; they consist of the contemplation of the skeleton, or the first dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He says to the son of good family:
"By employing this path and practicing these deeds, you shall attain the fruit of srotāpanna, and so on, up to the fruit of arhat."
"By practicing this path, you shall bring an end to suffering in this present life;
why then do you continue to undergo the various afflictions within the cycle of birth and death?
Even this body composed of the four great elements should not be accepted, let alone accept a future body!"
"Subhūti! If the mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is not startled, does not doubt, and does not regret, and he thinks:
'This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has taught me a dharma that resembles the Path.'"

If one practices these dharmas that resemble the Path, one cannot attain the realization of the fruit of Srotāpanna, nor can one attain the realization of the path of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, let alone attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva becomes even more joyful and thinks to himself:
"This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has explained to me the dharmas that obstruct the path."
"I know these factors that obstruct the path, yet they do not obstruct one's training in the paths of the three vehicles.
At that time, the evil Māra, knowing that the bodhisattva was joyful, spoke these words:
"O son of good family!
Do you wish to see this bodhisattva mahāsattva making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life;

and also practicing the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and also drawing near to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to inquire about the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?

How does he practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom; and how does he practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to great loving-kindness and great compassion?”
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells, acts, and practices exactly as the Buddha has taught.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva, through such instruction and such training, does not even attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, nor does he attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), how much less could you possibly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon hearing these matters, does not change his mind and is not startled, but instead becomes even more joyful and reflects:
"This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has explained to me the dharmas that obstruct the path;
by means of these dharmas that obstruct the path, one cannot attain the stage of srotāpanna, nor can one attain the stages up to arhat or pratyekabuddha, let alone attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!"
At that time, the evil Māra, knowing that this bodhisattva’s mind did not sink and was not startled, immediately manifested as many bhikṣus at that spot and said to the bodhisattva:
"All these are bodhisattvas who have resolved to seek the Buddha-way, yet they all now abide in the stage of arhatship;
even such as these cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how then could you possibly attain it?"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should think:

"This is Māra, the Evil One, speaking of a counterfeit practice of the path; a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should not turn back from the mind set on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor should they fall into the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
Again, he forms this thought:

"It is impossible that one who practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, and so forth up to all-knowledge, should not attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, you should know that this is called an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

"If a bodhisattva can act as the Buddha has taught, not departing from the mind of the prajñāpāramitā up to the knowledge of all modes, that bodhisattva will ultimately never regress from anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If a bodhisattva recognizes these works of Māra, they shall not lose their *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By such conduct, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called the mark of an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
in regard to what dharma does ‘turning’ become called ‘not turning’?”

The Buddha said: “It is by turning away from the characteristics of form; by turning away from the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; by turning away from the characteristics of the twelve bases and the eighteen elements; by turning away from the characteristics of lust, hatred, and delusion; by turning away from the characteristic of false views; by turning away from the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the characteristics of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and even the characteristics of a buddha—for these reasons, it is called the mark of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Why is this? Because these *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the stage of bodhisattvahood by means of these dharmas that are empty of self-characteristics; they attain the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Since not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, and because it cannot be apprehended, they do not act; because they do not act, there is no arising. This is called the patience regarding non-arising.
"By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Commentary:
When Māra clearly knows that this bodhisattva is irreversible, he no longer attempts to obstruct or destroy them.
If they do not yet possess clear understanding, then various causes and conditions will test and destroy them.
He may manifest the eight great hells and conjure countless bodhisattvas being burned and boiled therein, saying to those [real] bodhisattvas:
"These are all those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) and have received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas."
"If you receive a prediction [of enlightenment], it will be a prediction of hell. He asked:
"For what reason does the evil Māra say that 'one who practices good receives a prediction of hell'?"
The answer is:

Because this bodhisattva wishes to undergo suffering on behalf of all sentient beings, the evil Māra says that he has received the prediction of rebirth in hell; [Māra argues] that if you were to cultivate merit and be born in heaven, you would be acting only for your own sake and would have no concern for the affairs of sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing these matters, experiences mental agitation, doubt, or regret, or if they believe and accept the words of Māra, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
If a bodhisattva hears these matters and does not doubt, is not shaken, and is not startled, but reflects thus:
"Because an avaivartika has attained the true reality of all dharmas, they do not cling to any dharma; they do not even give rise to a minor offense, let alone the offenses of the three evil realms!"
"It is as impossible as for water to exist within fire, or for fire to arise from within water!
Furthermore, there was a Māra who, disguised in the robes of a bhikṣu, came and said to the Bodhisattva:

"The teachings on the practice of the six pāramitās that you previously heard from your former teacher are all false; even the merit of the mind of sympathetic joy that you have accumulated is deceptive."
"What you have previously heard is all false and deceptive, merely ornamental and not true; it was not spoken from the mouth of the Buddha.
What I am now speaking for you is truly the Buddha-dharma."
"Quickly abandon this!
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this, experiences agitation, anger, or doubt, one should know that the Buddhas have not yet conferred upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
It is like counterfeit gold: when subjected to fire, grinding, and hammering, if it turns black, red, or white, one knows it is not genuine.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this, feels neither anger nor doubt, but follows that which is without arising or ceasing, and without production or formation;
and while practicing within the characteristics of the six pāramitās, knows for himself and does not follow the words of others—then it should be known that he is a true *avaivartika*.
For example, because an Arhat has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), no demonic activities can destroy him.
A Bodhisattva who is irreversible (*avaivartika*) is likewise: none can subdue him, because he personally realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena before his own eyes;
even if Māra were to appear in the form of a Buddha and speak things that contradict the characteristics of the Dharma, he would not believe or accept them.

For example, it is like a dog wearing a lion’s skin; although all other beasts are terrified upon seeing it, they recognize it as a dog as soon as they hear its voice—how much more so when it merely transforms into some other body!
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:
"Since this bodhisattva perceives that dharmas such as form are empty, who would follow the words of another?
Furthermore, an evil Māra may come in the guise of a bhikṣu and say to the bodhisattva:
"These six pāramitās are all paths of saṃsāra:
by virtue of the causes and conditions of merit such as giving, one experiences blissful rewards within the desire realm;
by virtue of the causes and conditions of the dhyāna-pāramitā, one experiences bliss within the form realm."
Because this Prajñāpāramitā has no fixed characteristic, it is called a deceptive dharma; revolving within the five destinies, one cannot emerge from them oneself—this is the path of birth and death.
People may deceive you by saying,
"This is the path to omniscience.
I now speak the truth:
“Attain nirvāṇa and bring an end to suffering in this very life!
If the bodhisattva remains silent, Māra will then preach to him a counterfeit dharma:

“If you contemplate the thirty-six kinds of impurity, or contemplate a skeleton, or the inhalation and exhalation of breath, through this path you shall attain the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions.”
"By means of this meditative concentration, you may attain the stage of a stream-enterer up to that of an arhat.

This present body of yours was produced through the causes and conditions of transgression; the Buddha has said that one should not even praise the taking on of another body for as long as it takes to snap one's fingers, let alone dwelling for a long time within the cycle of birth and death!"
When an avaivartika bodhisattva hears this matter, his heart rejoices and he thinks:
"This bhikṣu has greatly benefited me by explaining to me a dharma that resembles the Path;
having obtained this dharma that resembles the Path, I shall immediately know the true Path."
"Just as a traveler who knows a wrong path thereby comes to know the right path,
so it is with that which obstructs the Way.
Because he is a great man, being highly esteemed and honored, the Avaivartika does not engage in contentious speech with this bhikṣu."
Seeing that the Bodhisattva remained silent, Māra was delighted and said,
"This person has accepted my words!
He then spoke to the Bodhisattva:

“Good son! There were immeasurable bodhisattvas who made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, inquiring about and practicing the six pāramitās and the dharmas of the bodhisattva path; they received the Buddha’s teachings face-to-face and fully practiced all the bodhisattva conducts, yet even so they did not attain the Unsurpassed Way, but have now all become arhats. Do you wish to see them?”
Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva remained silent.
Thereupon, Māra manifested as countless Arhat bhikṣus at that spot and said to the Bodhisattva:
"All these bhikṣus have long practiced the unsurpassed path, yet they have all now attained Arhatship; why do you alone now wish to become a Buddha?"
The *avaivartika* [bodhisattva] then rejoiced, thinking:
"This bhikṣu has explained to me the dharmas that resemble the Path and those that obstruct the Path.
This bodhisattva truly practices the merits of the six pāramitās and is certainly not subject to falling back into the two vehicles."
"As the Buddha has taught, it is impossible that one who never departs from the mind of the six pāramitās and other such merits should fail to attain the Unsurpassed Way.
If a bodhisattva recognizes this as the work of Māra, they will gain great benefit and suffer no loss.
"For this reason, the bodhisattva’s mind does not waver or shift; this is called the mark of an avaivartika.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In what phenomena does it turn so as to be called 'non-turning'?
The Buddha said:
"It turns back from within phenomena such as the characteristics of form (*rūpa*)."
The above was a brief explanation; now it is explained in detail.

If a bodhisattva is able to transform all marks such as form, this is called practicing the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas, attaining the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and entering the stage of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): since even the most subtle dharma cannot be apprehended, how much less so a great one!
This is called "non-arising.
Having attained this non-arising of dharmas, one does not perform or give rise to any karmic activities; this is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
A Bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is called an avaivartika.
Such immeasurable practices, categories, and characteristics as these are the marks of an avaivartika.
56. Chapter on Turning and Not Turning: Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Chapter Fifty-Six, "Turning and Not Turning. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
An evil Māra approaches the Bodhisattva and seeks to corrupt his mind, saying:
"All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is equal to space and has no marks of existence;
all dharmas are likewise equal to space, empty and devoid of marks."
Within the emptiness and signlessness of all phenomena, such as space, there is no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there anyone who does not attain it.
"All these dharmas are like space, characterized by non-existence; you have undergone toil and suffering in vain!
That which you have heard regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is entirely the work of Māra and was not spoken by the Buddha;
you should relinquish this vow, lest you undergo for a long night such insecurity, sorrow, and suffering, and fall into the evil realms!"
When these good sons and good daughters hear this rebuke, they should think:
"This is the work of Māra; it seeks to destroy my resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Although all dharmas are like space—non-existent and empty of intrinsic characteristics—sentient beings do not know, see, or understand them.

I too, adorned with the great vow that all things are like space, non-existent, and empty of intrinsic characteristics, have attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and preach this Dharma for sentient beings so that they may attain liberation, and realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Subhūti! From the moment a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon awakening, upon hearing this Dharma, they should make their mind firm, unshakable, and irreversible."
By means of this firm mind, an unswerving and immovable mind, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās and shall enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is one called ‘non-retrogressive’ (avaivartika) because of not turning back?”
"Is it because he turns back that he is also called an *avaivartika*?
The Buddha said, "He is called an *avaivartika* because he does not turn back; he is also called an *avaivartika* because he turns back."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Why is it that one is called *avaivartika* because of non-retrogression, yet is also called *avaivartika* because of retrogression?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not turn back toward the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, for this reason he is called 'one who does not turn back'."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns away from the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, for this reason they are also said to be "non-retrogressive.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, one should know that these are the marks of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive (avaivartika).
By virtue of these practices, categories, and characteristics, evil Māras will be unable to corrupt their resolve or cause them to turn away from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the first dhyāna, the second, the third, or the fourth dhyāna, up to and including the dhyāna of cessation, he enters them immediately."
Furthermore, Subhūti,

if an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, or the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, up to the five supernormal powers, he is able to cultivate them immediately.
Although this bodhisattva cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the five supernormal powers, he does not receive the fruit of the four foundations of mindfulness;
although he cultivates the various dhyānas, he does not receive the fruits of those dhyānas, nor does he receive the fruit of the dhyāna of the meditative absorption of cessation;
he does not realize the fruit of a srotāpanna, nor does he realize the path of a pratyekabuddha.
This bodhisattva intentionally takes on a body for the sake of sentient beings, benefiting them according to what is appropriate for each.
Subhūti, by these practices,
categories, and characteristics, you should know that this is called an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly recollects anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
because he never departs from the mind of sarvajñatā, he does not prize form, nor does he prize marks."
One does not value the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; one does not value the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, or prajñāpāramitā;
nor does one value the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, or the four formless attainments.
He does not value the five supernormal powers; he does not value the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
he does not value the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities;
he does not value purifying buddha-fields, nor does he value bringing sentient beings to maturity, nor does he value seeing the Buddha, nor does he value planting roots of goodness.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics; one does not perceive any phenomenon that is worthy of esteem, nor anything that can give rise to a mind of esteem. Why is this?
All these dharmas are equal to space; they are non-existent and empty of intrinsic characteristics.

Subhūti, this is the mind accomplished by an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva, who, amidst the four modes of physical conduct—coming and going, sitting and lying down, walking and standing—remains single-mindedly without distraction.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva lives as a householder, he employs the power of skillful means to benefit sentient beings by partaking in the five desires;

he bestows gifts upon sentient beings, giving food to those who need food and drink to those who need drink, and providing clothing, bedding, and all other necessities of life to them in their entirety.

This bodhisattva personally practices the dāna-pāramitā, teaches others to practice the dāna-pāramitā, praises the method of practicing the dāna-pāramitā, and joyfully extols those who practice the dāna-pāramitā;
it is the same for the śīla-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā.

Subhūti! When an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva is living as a householder, he is able to bestow upon sentient beings treasures filling Jambudvīpa, and even provide sentient beings with treasures filling a trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, he does not act for his own sake, but constantly cultivates the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), never treating others with contempt or plundering them to cause them distress. Subhūti!
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that such a person is called an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Vajradhara Śakra-devendra King constantly follows the bodhisattva mahāsattva who is irreversible (avaivartika), making this vow:
'When this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), I shall always follow him.'"
"Furthermore, the five classes of Vajradhara deities will constantly follow and protect them.

For this reason, whether they be devas, māras, Brahmās, or other powerful beings in the world, none can destroy this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s resolve for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Subhūti! This is called the mark of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always fully possess the five bodhisattva faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; this is called the mark of an avaivartika.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is a superior person, not an inferior person.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
who is a superior person?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with a single-minded resolve for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta without distraction, they are called a superior person."
By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called the mark of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) Bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, an *avaivartika* Bodhisattva always mindfully contemplates the Buddha-way with a single mind; he does not perform incantations or compound medicines, nor does he invoke spirits or deities to possess men and women so as to inquire about their fortune or misfortune, their status and fortune, or the length of their lifespan."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*) and do not perceive the marks of any dharmas, they practice pure livelihood (*pariśuddhājīva*).
"Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is called the mark of an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva.
[Treatise] Explanation:
Furthermore, there is another mark of an avaivartika bodhisattva:
if a wicked Māra should say,
"All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is equal to space."
The term *sarvajñā* has various names:

it is sometimes called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*), sometimes called "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñā*), sometimes called "unsurpassed path," sometimes called "the immeasurable dharmas of a Buddha," and sometimes called "bodhi"; these are all names for *sarvajñā*.
In this context, when "sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) is mentioned, one should know that it refers to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (unexcelled, perfect enlightenment).
All bodhisattvas aspire to attain sarvajñā.
When Māra comes wishing to destroy [his resolve], he speaks thus:
"This omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is empty and non-existent; it is merely that various teachers have deceived you!
Just as space is non-existent, without color, without form, and unknowable;"
"All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is also like this.
Therefore, it is said to be equal to space.
"All phenomena" refers to the six perfections and other factors conducive to enlightenment that lead toward all-knowledge.
These dharmas are also empty.
Even *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is empty and lacks any mark of substantial existence; these dharmas exist merely as names, without any real entity.
Within this, there is no one who attains *sarvajñā*, no one who proceeds toward *sarvajñā*, and no one who assists on the path; you have endured toil and hardship in vain!
Your teacher constantly instructs you to remain free from the works of Māra; yet omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) itself is a work of Māra. Why is this?
Because it involves abandoning nirvāṇa and grasping at saṃsāra.
"The sutras you have previously heard, as well as the meanings of the six pāramitās, are not the Buddha-dharma; they were all created by humans.
You must now quickly repent and abandon this heterodox mind;
if you do not abandon it, you will suffer the pains of the three evil realms for a long night."
When an avaivartika bodhisattva hears this matter, he immediately recognizes it as the work of Māra:
"This Māra disparages sarvajñatā, desiring to cause me to distance myself from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Although all dharmas are empty and non-existent, ordinary beings have their minds shrouded by inversion; thus they do not know and do not see them.
I, too, shall adorn myself with the emptiness of self-characteristics to attain all-knowledge and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
If all dharmas are empty, yet I adorn them with reality, this is inconsistent;
if all dharmas are empty and adornment is also empty, then they are in accord.
Preaching the Dharma for sentient beings is also like this.
"Causing sentient beings to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*" refers to two kinds of *srotāpanna* fruits:

first, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit, which is the severance of the three fetters; second, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) fruit of *srotāpanna*, which is associated with the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Both of these are empty:
within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they are empty because of the three gates of liberation;
within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), they are themselves empty because they possess the characteristics of non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing.
It is the same even up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
