"By reason of these sentient beings' acts of giving, up to and including the bodhisattvas' acts of giving, when they later attain Buddhahood, there will be no one in their land who is poor; whatever arises in their minds will be obtained at will, just like all the objects found in the sixth heaven of the desire realm."
Because the Bodhisattva has thus accumulated the merit of the dānapāramitā for as long as it takes, he fulfills all things. Why is this?

All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) depend upon causes and conditions; because the causal conditions for practicing virtue are fully complete, one obtains their fruit and retribution according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, because sentient beings have violated the *śīlapāramitā*, they suffer from short lifespans, many illnesses, and a lack of majestic power (*tejas*).
The Bodhisattva makes this vow:
"I shall personally fulfill the observance of the precepts, and I shall also teach sentient beings to observe the precepts."
The remaining vows are also to be understood in this way, distinguished according to their respective meanings.
The meaning of the final vow is not clear; it shall now be briefly explained.
Having made these supreme vows, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of weariness and fatigue:
"The Buddha-way can only be attained after practicing all manner of meritorious virtues for immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas;

yet even the number of years in a single kalpa cannot be calculated, so the Buddha uses analogies to show it to people—how much more so when one undergoes the various sufferings and afflictions through birth and death for immeasurable, boundless, and asankhyeya kalpas!"

Sentient beings are likewise immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of analogy or calculation; yet, if even the sentient beings equal in number to the atoms within a single trichiliocosm are already difficult to deliver, how much more so those equal in number to the atoms within the infinite worlds of the ten directions!
Because of these matters, the mind may become discouraged or retreat; this is called wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-manasikāra*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught this bodhisattva right mindfulness (*samyak-manasikāra*):
"Though saṃsāra is long, all these things are empty—like space, like what is seen in a dream. They are not truly long-lasting, and one should not give rise to a mind of weariness."
Furthermore, the future world is also an object of a single thought-moment and is not something remote.
Moreover, by virtue of the power of immeasurable merit and wisdom, a bodhisattva is able to transcend immeasurable kalpas.
For various reasons such as these, one should not give rise to a mind of weariness.
Herein, the Buddha speaks of the great causal conditions, namely:
"Birth and death are like space; sentient beings are also thus."
Although sentient beings are numerous, there is no fixed or real entity that constitutes a "sentient being.

Just as sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless, the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise immeasurable and boundless; thus, delivering them is not difficult. For this reason, a bodhisattva should not give rise to a mind of weariness or exhaustion.
Chapter 59: Gaṅgadevā. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Fifty-nine, Gaṅgadevā. [Sūtra] At that time, there was a woman named Gaṅgadevā sitting among the assembly.
The woman rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall practice the six pāramitās and take hold of a pure buddha-field; I shall practice everything exactly as it is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā.”

At that time, the woman scattered golden and silver flowers, as well as flowers grown on land and in water, various articles of adornment, and two layers of cloth woven with gold thread over the Buddha;
having scattered them, they transformed in the air above the Buddha’s head into a four-pillared jeweled pavilion, upright, magnificent, and beautiful.
This woman takes these merits and shares them with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the causes and conditions of this woman’s profound mind, immediately smiled.

Just as the various colored lights of all Buddhas issue from their mouths—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and violet—they illuminate the infinite and boundless Buddha-lands of the ten directions; they then return, circle the Buddha three times, and enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"For what cause and condition does the Buddha smile?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not smile without a cause or condition."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sister Gaṅgādevā shall become a buddha in a future age; the kalpa will be named Nakṣatra, and the buddha’s name will be Suvarṇapuṣpa."
Ānanda! This woman, having finished her female existence, will receive a male form and shall be born in the land of Abhirati of the Buddha Akṣobhya, where she will purely cultivate the holy life.
Ānanda! This bodhisattva shall also be named Golden Flower in that land.
When this Bodhisattva Golden Flower passes away from there, he will again go to a buddha-land in another direction.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, he never departs from the presence of the Buddhas.
It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, from one palace to another, from birth until the end of his life, never sets foot upon the ground.
Ānanda! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Golden Flower is also like this: from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, until he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he has never failed to see a Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"When this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvarṇapuṣpa later becomes a Buddha, the assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas at that time should be known as being like an assembly of Buddhas."
The Buddha, knowing what was in Ānanda’s mind, addressed him, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
At the time of that Buddha Golden Flower, the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be known as being like an assembly of Buddhas. Ānanda!
The bhikṣu-saṃgha of that Buddha Golden Flower will be immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and beyond counting—numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
"Ānanda!
When this Bodhisattva Golden Flower becomes a Buddha, there will be none of these various evils in his land as described above.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From where did this woman plant the foundations of merit and sow the roots of goodness?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This woman planted roots of goodness in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and first resolved her mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. By virtue of these merits, she dedicated them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
she also scattered golden flowers over Dīpaṃkara Buddha, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Ānanda! Just as I scattered five flowers upon the Buddha Dīpaṃkara at that time, seeking anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
knowing that my roots of goodness were perfected, conferred upon me the prediction of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Upon hearing my prediction, this woman resolved her mind, saying:
"In a future age, may I also be like this bodhisattva and receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Ānanda! You should know that this woman first resolved her mind on enlightenment in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This woman has long practiced for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is! This woman has long practiced for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
[Treatise] Question:
Since this great assembly has heard the teaching on the practice for attaining a pure land, why is it that only one woman has taken the vow to attain a pure land?
The answer is:
There are many who have made vows to attain a pure land but do not speak of them;
however, because women are by nature fickle and fond of competition, and due to the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) cultivated over successive lifetimes, they speak of them.
Furthermore, some say: "Great beings possess the factors for attaining the Way, whereas others do not.
The Buddha-dharma is not thus; it depends upon the karmic causes and conditions of sentient beings.
It is like a fine medicine that treats all illnesses without discriminating between the noble and the lowly.
Although a woman may possess shallow wisdom, if she is destined by the causal conditions of her past karma to receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*),
and her mind gives rise to the desire to speak, the Buddha permits her to speak for herself.
Furthermore, if the Buddha were to grant a prediction of enlightenment while remaining silent, people would give rise to doubt, wondering:
"For what cause and condition does he alone grant this girl a prediction?"
For this reason, the Buddha granted him a prediction of enlightenment because he had spoken of it himself.
Question: Why is he named "Gaṅgadevā"?
Answer: All things possess names for the sake of cognition; why, then, is it necessary to seek their underlying meaning? Some say:
The parents of this girl made offerings to the goddess Gaṅgā; because they obtained this girl [from her], she was called Gaṅgadevī.
Gaṅgā is the name of a river, and Devī means "goddess."

By virtue of her merit and its causal conditions, this woman was born into a wealthy family; because she heard the Buddha-dharma and believed in it with joy, she was able to offer to the Buddha above gold, silver, and precious flowers, as well as upper and lower garments woven with golden threads, along with the necklaces and ornaments that adorned her own person.
The Buddha granted her a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and, observing the conduct of this woman in her past lives, smiled.
The meaning of his smile is as previously explained.
Here, because a great matter arises from a minor cause, the Buddha smiles.
Question:
This woman’s merit should have caused her to transform out of her female body long ago; why is it that she only transforms her female body now in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya? Answer:

The five desires of the world are difficult to sever; because women are deeply attached to desire and possess much passion, even though they practice various merits throughout successive lifetimes, they cannot obtain a male body.
Now that you have received this prediction, your various afflictions have been broken and thinned; therefore, it is only in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha that you shall finally obtain a male body.
Some say: Because many people in past lives had disparaged women, this woman vowed that her own body should receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Through such causes and conditions, she received the prediction without transforming her female body.
Furthermore, the sutra speaks of the five obstacles for women, but it does not say that they cannot receive a prediction of enlightenment; therefore, one should not raise such an objection.

When Ānanda heard that this woman had, throughout immeasurable kalpas, traveled from one buddha-field to another to extensively accumulate merit, and would in the future attain a pure buddha-field wherein all bodhisattvas would possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, as well as immeasurable radiance, he marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, saying:
"To be able to purify a buddha-field in such a manner is indeed equivalent to being in the assembly of a Buddha."

After the Buddha had affirmed her words, Ānanda and the others were filled with doubt regarding this rare woman who, having heard but a small portion of the Dharma, attained such a great fruit of retribution; therefore, they asked:
"From where did this woman plant the roots of all these virtues?"
The Buddha replied,
“When Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed the prediction upon me, this woman scattered golden flowers over the Buddha and made this vow:
‘When this person later attains Buddhahood, he shall likewise bestow a prediction upon me.’”
"From planting those roots of goodness, one now obtains this retribution.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 75,
"Explanation of the Chapter on Learning Emptiness without Realizing [Nirvana]," Number Sixty.
Fascicle Seventy-Six.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Sixty: Training in Emptiness Without Realization. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, how should they train in the samādhi of emptiness?
How should they enter the samādhi of emptiness?”
What is training in the signless and wishless samādhi?
How does one enter the signless and wishless samādhi?
What is training in the four foundations of mindfulness?
How does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?
Up to: how does one train in the eightfold noble path?
How does one cultivate the eightfold noble path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that form is empty, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; they should contemplate that the twelve bases and eighteen elements are empty, and even contemplate that the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are empty.”
When practicing this contemplation, one must not allow the mind to become distracted.
If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind is undistracted, then they do not perceive these dharmas;
if they do not perceive these dharmas, then they do not realize them.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied the emptiness of self-characteristics; thus there is no remainder and no parts, for neither the realization of the Dharma nor the one who realizes it can be perceived.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize the emptiness of dharmas.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva dwells within the dharma of emptiness yet does not realize it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, fully contemplating emptiness, first makes this vow:
'I should not now realize the dharma of emptiness;
this is my time for training, not my time for realization.'"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not single-mindedly concentrate the mind by binding it to an object; therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor do they realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Subhūti! It is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus accomplished in such great, virtuous, and sublime dharmas. Why is this?
Abiding in this emptiness, one forms this thought:
"Now is my time for training; it is not yet my time for realization. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:
"When I am training in the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), this is not the time for realization;

when training in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā); and when cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) up to the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), this is not the time for realization."
When practicing the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness, it is not the time of realization;

when practicing the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion, it is not the time of realization.

When I now train in the knowledge of all modes, it is not the time for attaining the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, nor even the realization of the paths of arhatship or pratyekabuddhahood.
"In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they study the contemplation of emptiness and abide in emptiness;
they study the contemplations of signlessness and wishlessness and abide in signlessness and wishlessness."

He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness but does not realize the four foundations of mindfulness; likewise, he cultivates up to the eightfold noble path but does not realize the eightfold noble path.

Although this bodhisattva studies the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he does not realize the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the path of a pratyekabuddha.

“Subhūti! It is like a strong man, powerful, courageous, and robust, skilled in military strategy and the sixty-four arts, who firmly grasps his weapons, stands steady and immovable, is adept in various technical skills, upright and pure, loved and respected by others, and who, with little effort in his undertakings, gains great rewards.”
For these reasons, he is revered, honored, and praised by the multitude;
seeing others show him such respect, his joy redoubles.
On rare occasions, when he must travel elsewhere, he leads the elderly and the weak across dangerous and terrifying places.
He comforted his parents and instructed his wife, saying:
"Do not be afraid!
I shall pass through this; there will certainly be no suffering."

"In that perilous and difficult path, there are many hostile bandits lying in ambush to plunder and harm; because that person is fully endowed with wisdom and strength, they are able to cross the evil way and return to their original place, meeting no harm from the bandits, and remaining joyful and at ease."
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: among all sentient beings, they fully satisfy the mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the four immeasurable minds, fulfills the six pāramitās, yet does not realize the exhaustion of outflows;
he studies all-knowledge and enters the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva does not follow any signs, nor does he realize the samādhi of signlessness;
because he does not realize the samādhi of signlessness, he does not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a winged bird that soars through the void without falling; though it is in the air, it does not dwell in the air.”

Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: they train in the gate of liberation of emptiness, and they train in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, yet they do not realize them.
Because they do not realize them, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

They have not yet fully acquired the ten powers of a Buddha, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the immeasurable qualities of all Buddhas, and the knowledge of all modes; nor do they realize the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

“Subhūti! It is as if there were a strong man who has studied the various methods of archery and is skilled in the art of shooting. He shoots upward into the air, then shoots a subsequent arrow at each preceding one, so that the arrows support one another and do not fall, remaining under his control as he wishes.
If he desires for them to fall, he simply stops shooting subsequent arrows, and they then fall to the ground.”

Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*: by the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as long as their various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are not yet fully perfected;
once the roots of goodness are accomplished, at that time they then realize the limit of reality.
For this reason, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) in this manner!
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do is exceedingly difficult!”

Why is this? Although they study these characteristics of all phenomena, study the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), study suchness (*tathatā*), study the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and study ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), up to and including studying the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the three gates of liberation, they never fall away midway.
“World-Honored One!
This is most rare!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva makes such a vow because they do not abandon all sentient beings.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:..."
"I ought not to abandon all sentient beings!
Sentient beings are submerged in the dharma of non-existence; I must deliver them!
At that moment, he immediately enters the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness.

Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished the power of skillful means; although he has not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he practices these gates of liberation and does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to contemplate these profound dharmas— namely, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the three doors of liberation— at that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
'These sentient beings have for a long night practiced with the mark of a self, up to the marks of a knower and a viewer, and are attached to the attainment of dharmas.'"
‘In order to sever these various marks for the sake of sentient beings, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preach the Dharma.

At that time, the bodhisattva practices the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; yet he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Because he does not realize it, he does not fall into the fruit of a srotāpanna, nor even into the path of a pratyekabuddha.”

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to bring these roots of goodness to fulfillment with such a mind, he does not realize the limit of reality midway; he does not lose the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes all factors conducive to enlightenment, such that they never diminish until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Because this bodhisattva possesses the power of skillful means, they constantly increase wholesome dharmas, and their faculties become so sharp and penetrating that they surpass those of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
'Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the four inversions:'"
They harbor perceptions of permanence, perceptions of pleasure, perceptions of self, and perceptions of purity;
for the sake of these sentient beings, they seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), I shall preach for them the dharma of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self.

This bodhisattva, having accomplished this mind, practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means; yet they do not attain the samādhi of a Buddha, nor do they fully possess the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor do they realize the limit of reality.
At that time, the Bodhisattva cultivates the gate of liberation through non-action; although he has not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor does he realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

'Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the attainment of dharmas—namely, the self, sentient beings, and so forth up to the knower and the seer; that this is form, this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are the sense bases, these are the elements; these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments.'"
"I shall practice in such a way that when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, sentient beings will have no such attainment of dharmas.

When a bodhisattva has accomplished this mind, they practice the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means; yet, until they are fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities, they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
At that time, the bodhisattva fully cultivates the samādhi of emptiness. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"Sentient beings have long practiced various signs—namely, the sign of male, the sign of female, the sign of form, and the sign of the formless.
I shall practice in such a way that when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, sentient beings will be free from these faults of signs!"

With this mind thus accomplished, he practices the perfection of wisdom through the power of skillful means; until he has fully perfected the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities, he does not realize the limit of reality.
At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully cultivates the signless samādhi.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the six pāramitās; studies inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; studies the four foundations of mindfulness up to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and studies the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
When such wisdom is accomplished, it is impossible for one to compose dharmas or dwell within the three realms!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the factors conducive to enlightenment and practice the factors conducive to enlightenment, they should be tested with this question:
"How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi study these dharmas so that they contemplate emptiness without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?"
Because they do not realize [these stages], they do not fall into the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the path of a pratyekabuddha;
contemplating the signless, the unconditioned, the unarisen, the unborn, and the non-existent, they do not take realization as a goal, yet they practice the perfection of wisdom.
One should ask in this way:
“Subhūti! If, when various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are being tested with questions, a bodhisattva should answer in this manner:”
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should only contemplate emptiness; they should only contemplate signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should not study emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence; they should not study these factors conducive to enlightenment.”
"Subhūti! You should know that these bodhisattvas have not yet been granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by the Buddhas. Why is this?
Such a person cannot describe the characteristics of what an avaivartika bodhisattva studies, nor can they demonstrate them or answer questions regarding them.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to describe, demonstrate, and answer concerning the characteristics of what an avaivartika studies, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already practiced and studied the bodhisattva path and entered the stage of attenuation (*tanubhūmi*), possessing the characteristics of avaivartika as found in other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are avaivartika.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
could there be bodhisattvas who have not yet attained *avaivartika* [irreversibility] that are able to answer in such a manner?"
The Buddha said: “There is, Subhūti.”
Whether this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has heard or not heard of the six pāramitās, he is able to answer in such a manner like an avaivartika bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

There are many bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha-way, but few bodhisattvas are able to answer in this manner, as do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika) within the path of training and the path beyond training.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
Such bodhisattvas are very few!
Why is this? Because there are but few bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having received such a prediction, practice the stage of wisdom of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
"If there are those who have received the prediction [of enlightenment], such people can answer in this way.
Their roots of goodness are clear and manifest, and cannot be destroyed by gods or worldly people.
[Treatise] Question: Why is this so?
What is the difference between studying emptiness and entering emptiness?
The answer is:
the former is called studying emptiness, while the latter is entering emptiness.
The cause is the study of emptiness, and the fruit is the entry into emptiness;
the skillful means is called the study of emptiness, while the attainment is called the entry into emptiness.
Such are these two paths.
The signless, the wishless, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are also like this.

These three gates of liberation and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the path to nirvana for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the Buddha commands that bodhisattvas should practice this path.
Subhūti had this thought:
"This is the path to nirvāṇa; how is it that a bodhisattva practices these dharmas of the path yet does not realize the proof of nirvāṇa?
The Buddha answered:
“The Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena, such as form and so forth, as empty.

Because this Bodhisattva has deeply entered meditative concentration, their mind cannot be disturbed, and because they have attained the power of sharp wisdom, they do not perceive these empty phenomena;
because they do not perceive them, there is nothing to be realized.”
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas sever the notion of self and abandon attachment, proceeding directly toward nirvāṇa.

This bodhisattva, however, has skillfully studied the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*); within material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), not even a subtle particle remains, nor is there any minute residue left behind;
within non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*), not even a single thought-moment remains."
He enters directly into ultimate emptiness, such that he does not even perceive this dharma of emptiness as something that can be realized as a fruit of enlightenment.
Although the Buddha has answered, Subhūti has not yet grasped the Buddha’s intention and asks again:
"As the Buddha has said, a bodhisattva should not realize the dharma of emptiness as a fruit of enlightenment; [how then is it to be understood?]"
"Now that you have entered into emptiness, why do you not realize it?
The Buddha replied:
"Because of their profound penetration, they are able not to realize it."
To be "fully endowed" is to enter deeply.
It is like grasping a blade of *śara* grass: if one holds it loosely, the hand will be injured;

if one holds it tightly, there is no injury. The Bodhisattva is likewise: because he enters deeply into emptiness, he knows that emptiness itself is empty and that nirvāṇa is also empty; therefore, there is nothing to be realized.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva has not yet entered into emptiness, they reflect thus:
"I should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena universally; I must not realize the realization while my knowledge remains incomplete."
Therefore, one does not enter dhyāna by single-mindedly concentrating the mind and binding it to the object of emptiness.
Why is this? If one single-mindedly binds the mind to the object of emptiness, the mind becomes so supple that it cannot emerge from emptiness on its own.

Question: Previously it was said, "One enters deeply into meditative concentration so as not to allow the mind to become distracted"; why is it now said that one does not "single-mindedly concentrate"? Answer:
Now, as for the statement "not single-minded," this refers to the initial stage of entry, when one is unable to emerge from it on one's own;

whereas the previous statement "profoundly entered" means that having already entered deeply, one realizes that even emptiness is empty, and thus does not allow the mind to dwell on other matters—hence it is called "undisturbed."
Furthermore, this bodhisattva should reflect:
"I have not yet perfected the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary signs, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses of a Buddha; how could I realize the attainment of nirvana?"
Now is my time for study; with afflictions thinned, I shall transform sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-way.
When I have fully accomplished the work of a Buddha, at that time I shall realize the fruit of enlightenment.
Therefore, although the bodhisattva enters the three gates of liberation, he does not realize them as a final attainment.

Regarding this, a parable is given: "The strong man" represents the bodhisattva; "parents and kinsmen" represent the sentient beings who are to be delivered; "the perilous path" represents the cycle of birth and death within the triple world; "the wicked bandits" represent the demonic hordes and various afflictions (*kleśa*); "the weapons" represent the bodhisattva’s five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and various other skillful means (*upāya*); "returning to his original place" represents the path practiced by the bodhisattva; and "standing firm and unmoving" represents the bodhisattva abiding in ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), employing the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) to transport the deliverable sentient beings to the state of peace and happiness that is *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, those present in the assembly had doubts, thinking:
"Since there is nothing at all in the air, how can it be traversed?
For this reason, the Buddha spoke the parable of the bird:
"Just as a bird flying through the void has no place of reliance, yet soars far away without falling.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva, while not yet having fulfilled the dharmas of the path and not yet having reached the Buddha-way, does not realize [nirvana] in the interval;
like a bird that has not yet reached its destination, it never stops midway.
One studies these dharmas of emptiness for the sake of severing one's own afflictions and for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Furthermore, for the sake of clarity, the analogy of a skilled archer is given:
it is like a person who is highly proficient in the art of archery.
The "bow" is the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration; the "arrow" is wisdom; "space" is the three gates of liberation; and the "ground" is nirvāṇa.

This bodhisattva shoots the three gates of liberation with the arrow of wisdom into the void; furthermore, by the power of skillful means, he shoots a subsequent arrow at the preceding arrow so as not to let it fall to the ground of nirvana.
Until the ten powers and other buddha-activities are fully perfected, he never takes final realization.
Subhūti, filled with joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The deeds performed by the bodhisattvas are exceedingly difficult and truly rare!
That is to say, they practice emptiness yet do not realize it as a final attainment."
The Buddha replied:

"This bodhisattva’s original vow was to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation from suffering. Because he is sustained by this original vow and by his great compassionate mind, although he practices emptiness, he does not realize it as a final attainment."
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva forms this thought:
"All sentient beings dwell in suffering, bound by inversions, and submerged in non-existence."
At that time, they immediately practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
It should be known that this bodhisattva possesses the power of skillful means; while practicing these three gates of liberation, they do not abandon sentient beings.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wishes to contemplate the profound dharmas—namely, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the three gates of liberation—they should first form this thought: "Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the mark of a self."

If a practitioner directly contemplates the profound Dharma alone, they may either attain the path of a śrāvaka or fall into wrong views; this is because, lacking a mind of compassion, they are unable to penetrate deeply into the emptiness of self-characteristics.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva wishes to contemplate these phenomena, they first give rise to a mind of compassion, thinking: "Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the self and the 'mine,' as well as to all afflictions.
"Long night" refers to a vast duration;
since immeasurable kalpas past, a "self" is absolutely unobtainable, yet because of emptiness, vanity, deception, and inversion, they undergo all manner of sorrow and distress.
Having seen this, the bodhisattva makes a vow:
"I shall attain the path of Buddhahood for the sake of all sentient beings and sever their attachment to the self and their inverted views.
At that time, he practices the three gates of liberation, such as emptiness, yet does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Through the fulfillment of these roots of goodness, the bodhisattva does not take realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor do they lose the various merits such as the four dhyānas.
Because the bodhisattva penetrates deeply into emptiness, their faculties are sharp and keen, surpassing those of the two vehicles.
The meaning of destroying the four inversions is also as explained above.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:

"It is impossible for sentient beings, who have been attached to the attainment of dharmas throughout the long night—namely, to the notions of 'self' and 'sentient beings,' and even to the notion of attaining dharmas or dwelling within the triple world—to remain so."
The meaning is that in both cases one contemplates emptiness without realizing it.
A question is asked:
How is it known that this bodhisattva has not yet attained the Path, yet is able to practice this profound emptiness?
The answer is:
The sutra itself explains the causes and conditions:
"This bodhisattva should ask an investigative question:..."
"How should a bodhisattva train in emptiness without realizing it?
If the bodhisattva replies:
"One should simply maintain mindfulness of emptiness and practice it with single-minded devotion;"
"Just as with the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is not merely a matter of learning and knowing them.
This applies even up to the states of non-arising and non-existence; it is likewise so.
One should know that this bodhisattva has not yet been granted a prediction by the Buddhas. Why is this?
Because they contemplate emptiness without having explained the learning of skillful means.
If a bodhisattva’s response differs from the one above, it should be known that this is an avaivartika who has already trained and entered the stage of thinness (*tanubhūmi*).
"Training" means having previously studied and realized emptiness.
The "thinning of the defilements" refers to the thinning of all afflictions within the stage of the *avaivartika*.
Having heard the characteristics of the *avaivartika* and the characteristics of those who are not *avaivartika*, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is there perhaps a bodhisattva who, though not yet attained to the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika),
could answer in such a manner? The Buddha said, "There is."
Whether a bodhisattva has heard of the six pāramitās or not, they are able to answer as an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva would.
If they have heard them, it is merely from a teacher, for they themselves have not yet fully perfected the bodhisattva stages;

if they have not heard them, through their own reflection and correct mindfulness, although they have not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), they are able to seek the characteristics of all phenomena and answer as an avaivartika bodhisattva does.
Subhūti said:
“Many people seek the path of the Buddha, but few are able to answer in this way as do those bodhisattvas who are irreversible (avaivartika) within the stages of training and beyond training.”

"Not having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is called the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi); having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is called the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa-bhūmi).
The Buddha said: “Few.”
Why is this? There are few bodhisattvas who have received predictions from the Buddhas.
Only those who have already received predictions from the Buddhas are able to answer in such a manner.
Why is this? The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena can only be fully known by a Buddha;
because the Buddha knew that this person was able to answer in accordance with the Dharma, he granted him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) in advance.
Although these bodhisattvas are few in number, their roots of goodness are clear and manifest; they are able to bring vast benefit to sentient beings, and none can destroy them.
Chapter Sixty-one: Not Realizing [Enlightenment] in a Dream. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Sixty-one: Not Realizing [Enlightenment] in a Dream. [Sūtra] The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not crave the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor does he crave the three realms; and if he contemplates all dharmas as being like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a mirage, and like a transformation, yet does not realize them as such."
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream the Buddha preaching the Dharma to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and kiṃnaras;
having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, they immediately understand its inner meaning and practice in accordance with that Dharma.
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva’s irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

In a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, emitting a great radiance and soaring in the void, preaching the Dharma amidst a great assembly of bhikṣus;
manifesting great supernormal powers, he creates emanated beings who travel to other lands to perform the work of a Buddha.
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s irreversibility.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dreaming, sees the outbreak of war, or the destruction of a village, or the destruction of a town or city; or when a fire breaks out; or sees fierce and predatory beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions; or sees someone coming to behead him; or sees the death of his father or mother, or the death of his brothers, sisters, and various kinsmen, friends, and associates.
Seeing such various matters of sorrow and suffering, he was neither startled nor terrified, nor did he feel any distress;
having awakened from the dream, he immediately reflected:
"The three realms are illusory; they are all like dreams!"
"When I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, I too shall preach to sentient beings that the three realms are like a dream. Subhūti,
you should know that this is the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva's irreversibility.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
how should one know that when this irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, there will be no three evil realms in his land?"
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts in a dream, he should form this thought:
"I shall apply myself with diligent vigor so that when I attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, there will be no three evil paths whatsoever in my land."
Why is this? Because this dream and all phenomena are non-dual and without distinction, Subhūti!
"You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees in a dream the fires of hell burning sentient beings, he makes this vow:"
"If I am truly an *avaivartika*, this fire shall be extinguished!
As soon as he said this, the fire was immediately extinguished.
If the fires of hell are extinguished, that is the mark of an *avaivartika*.
"Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees a city or town fire breaking out during the day, he forms this thought:
'In my dreams, I have seen the conduct, characteristics, and signs of an avaivartika; since I truly possess these now, I make this vow:
"This fire shall be extinguished!"'"
"If the fire is extinguished, you should know that this bodhisattva has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and dwells in the stage of *avaivartika*."
If the fire does not go out, it burns one house and leaves another, burning one village and leaving another.

Subhūti, you should know that the causes and conditions for the karma of destroying the Dharma have been thickly accumulated by those whose houses are burned; for this reason, one house is burned while another is left. These sentient beings are burned because they are currently undergoing the remaining retribution for their past destruction of the Dharma.
“Subhūti! By these causes and conditions, you should know that these are the marks of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall now further explain for you the conduct, categories, and signs of an *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva. Subhūti!
If a man or a woman is possessed by a non-human spirit, at that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:"

"If I have been granted a prediction by the Buddhas of the past, and my mind is pure as I seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practicing the pure right path, remaining far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and far removed from the thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then I shall surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is not that I shall not attain it.

Throughout the lands of the ten directions, the present immeasurable Buddhas know nothing that they do not know, see nothing that they do not see, understand nothing that they do not understand, and realize nothing that they do not realize.
"The Buddhas know my profound mind and have determined that I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By virtue of this sincere vow, if any man or woman is possessed by non-human spirits or afflicted by non-human spirits, those non-humans shall depart far away!

Subhūti! If a non-human being does not depart despite such a vow made by this bodhisattva mahāsattva, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas of the past.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes such a vow and non-human beings depart, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas of the past.
Subhūti! By these practices, categories, and characteristics, one should know that this is the mark of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva’s irreversibility.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from the six pāramitās and the power of skillful means, and does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness for long, nor practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness for long, and has not yet entered the bodhisattva stage, such a bodhisattva will be harassed by Māra the Evil One."
The Bodhisattva made this vow:
"If it is true that I have received the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas, then these non-human beings shall depart.
At that moment, the evil Māra employed a skillful means and commanded the non-human beings to leave.
Because the Māra possesses power that surpasses all non-human beings, those non-humans immediately departed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought:
"It is by the power of my vow that these non-humans have left."
Not realizing this was the power of Māra,
and relying on that realization, they treated other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision, saying:
"I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas, whereas you have not yet attained it."
Because they rely on such empty vows and lack the power of skillful means, they give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Due to this matter, they distance themselves from *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) and distance themselves from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment).
Subhūti! You should know that such a person falls into two stages—either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
It is because of these causes and conditions of their vow that demonic activities arise.

Because this person does not associate with or rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and does not inquire about the characteristics of non-retrogression (avaivartika), they become increasingly and firmly bound by Māra.
Why is that? It is because this bodhisattva has not practiced the six pāramitās for long and lacks the power of skillful means, Subhūti!
"You should know that this is a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva. Subhūti,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet practiced the six pāramitās for long, and who has not yet entered the bodhisattva stage, is harassed by evil Māras?"
Subhūti! Māra, the Evil One, manifests various forms and says to the bodhisattva:
"You have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddhas."
Your name is so-and-so; your father’s name is so-and-so; your mother’s name is so-and-so; your brothers and sisters’ names are so-and-so; such are the names of your ancestors for seven generations;
you were born in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a city, in such-and-such a village.
If he sees that a bodhisattva’s nature and conduct are gentle and mild, he says to that bodhisattva:
"In your previous lives, you were likewise gentle and mild.
If he sees one who is quick-tempered and violent, he then says:
"You were also like this in your previous lives.
If one sees a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of an araṇya-dweller, one says:
"In your previous lives, you also practiced the conduct of an araṇya-dweller."

If they see a bodhisattva begging for food, wearing patched robes, not drinking liquids after midday, eating in a single sitting, eating from a single bowl, dwelling among corpses, dwelling in the open air, dwelling at the foot of a tree, always sitting without lying down, using only a mat as a seat, accepting only the three robes, or being of few desires, contented, dwelling in seclusion, not anointing the feet, or speaking little, they will say to that bodhisattva:
"In your previous lives, you also practiced these deeds."
"Why is this? Since you now possess these merits of *dhūta* practice, you must have certainly possessed them in previous lives as well.

When that bodhisattva hears of these matters concerning his past lives and his name and clan, and hears the current praise of his *dhūta* merits, he immediately feels joy and gives rise to a mind of arrogance and pride.
At that time, Māra spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Since you possess such merit and such marks, you have indeed received from the Buddhas the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Subhūti! Māra, the Evil One, may appear before a bodhisattva wearing the robes of a bhikṣu, or in the form of a layperson, or in the body of their father or mother, and speak thus:
'You have already received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
Why is this? Because you possess all these marks of the qualities of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva in their entirety.
Thus spoke Subhūti.
"Subhūti, that person lacks entirely the actual conduct, characteristics, and signs of an avaivartika that I have described!
You should know, Subhūti, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed by Māra."

Why is this? Because such a person lacks forever the conduct, characteristics, and signs of an *avaivartika*; yet, because they have heard these names, they give rise to a mind of arrogance, treating others with contempt, mockery, and disdain.
Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva being possessed by Māra; you should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not long practiced the six pāramitās does not know the characteristic of names, nor does he know the characteristic of form, nor does he know the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
A māra comes and says:
"When you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age, you shall have such-and-such a name.
According to his original thought, he proclaims that name.
These bodhisattvas, lacking wisdom and skillful means, think to themselves:

"I too previously had this thought regarding the name by which I shall become a Buddha; since this person speaks exactly as I thought, and what they say accords with my original thought, I must certainly have received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas."

"Subhūti! The practices, categories, and characteristics of non-retrogression that I have described are entirely absent in such a person; they merely use empty names to mock, deceive, and despise others.
Because of this, they remain far removed from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has distanced himself from the *prajñāpāramitā*, lacks the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), is far removed from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and associates with evil friends (*pāpamitra*), he falls into one of two levels: either the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

If, after wandering for a long time through birth and death (*saṃsāra*), he subsequently relies once more upon the *prajñāpāramitā* and encounters a spiritual friend whom he constantly follows and attends to, he will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If this person does not immediately repent within this very body, they shall fall into one of two stages: either the stage of an Arhat or the stage of a Pratyekabuddha. Subhūti!

For example, if a bhikṣu violates even one of the four grave prohibitions, he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya; such a person shall not attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in his present body.

Subhūti! The mind of this bodhisattva who clings to the mere name of "emptiness" is likewise; because he treats others with contempt, mocks them, and slanders them, you should know that his offense is more grave than the four pārājika offenses of a bhikṣu.
Subhūti! Setting aside these grave offenses, their sin exceeds even that of the five heinous acts.
Because they have received this title, they give rise to arrogance, treating others with contempt, mockery, and disdain.
If one gives rise to such a thought, you should know that its transgression is extremely grave!
A bodhisattva should be aware of such subtle demonic activities as these names and so forth.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva dwells in a secluded mountain, marsh, or remote wilderness, Māra comes to where the bodhisattva is and praises the dharma of seclusion, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"What you practice is the dharma of seclusion praised by the Buddha.
Subhūti! I do not praise this kind of seclusion, which consists merely of dwelling in empty, secluded places such as mountains, marshes, or remote wildernesses.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If dwelling in empty, quiet mountains, marshes, or remote wilderness were not the dharma of seclusion, what other form of seclusion could there be?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwelling in empty, secluded mountains, marshes, or remote wildernesses— this is the dharma of seclusion permitted by the Buddha.”
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice this dharma of seclusion; practicing this dharma of seclusion day and night is called a bodhisattva who practices seclusion.
Subhūti! If the Māra speaks of the dharma of seclusion as being in empty, quiet places, mountains, forests, or remote wildernesses,

yet the mind of this bodhisattva remains in turmoil— meaning he does not distance himself from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and does not diligently cultivate the prajñāpāramitā— then this bodhisattva mahāsattva will be unable to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This bodhisattva practices the dharma of seclusion as taught by an evil Māra; his mind is not pure, yet he looks down upon other bodhisattvas who dwell near cities, whose minds are pure, who are free from the clamor of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who lack all other various defiled thoughts, and who are fully endowed with meditative concentration, liberation, wisdom, and supernormal powers.

Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom and lacks skillful means, even if they dwell for one year, or for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, or millions of billions of years, or even beyond that, in a desolate wilderness a hundred yojanas away—a place inhabited by birds, beasts, spirits, and rākṣasas—will not recognize this method of seclusion: namely, that it is through this method of seclusion that bodhisattvas, with a profound resolve, set their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practice without distraction.
This bodhisattva practices amidst turmoil, yet relies upon and becomes attached to this dharma of seclusion.
Such conduct as this is not permitted by the Buddha! Subhūti!
Regarding the true dharma of detachment that I have taught, the bodhisattva does not abide within it, nor does he perceive the characteristic of detachment. Why is this?
Because he practices only this emptiness of detachment.
At that time, Māra the Evil One came and stood in the air, praising him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!
This is the Dharma of true seclusion taught by the Buddha; if you practice this seclusion, you will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva becomes attached to this seclusion and treats other bhikṣus seeking the purity of the Buddha-way with contempt, regarding them as noisy distractions. He perceives what is noisy as not noisy, and what is not noisy as noisy; he fails to show respect where respect is due, and shows respect where it is not due.
This bodhisattva says:
"Non-humans have thought of me and come to praise me; that which I practice is true seclusion.
As for those who dwell near a city, who would ever praise you?"
For these reasons, they hold other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in contempt.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person is called a "caṇḍāla" among bodhisattvas; they defile all bodhisattvas.
Such a person is a mere semblance of a bodhisattva; in reality, they are a great thief among devas and humans, and a thief within the robes of the śramaṇas!
Those who seek the path of the Buddha should not associate with such a person, nor should they offer them worship or respect.
Why is this? Subhūti,
you should know that such a person has fallen into overweening pride.

For this reason, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes not to abandon all-knowledge, wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, single-mindedly seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and wishes to benefit all sentient beings, they should not associate with such a person, nor honor or make offerings to them.
The dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that one should always diligently seek self-benefit, feel weary of and distressed by the world, and keep the mind perpetually detached from the triple realm;
toward such persons, one should give rise to the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, thinking:
"I practice the bodhisattva path; I should not give rise to such faults or transgressions."
"If it arises, it must be swiftly extinguished! Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should skillfully awaken to this matter and skillfully extricate himself from within it.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a profound mind, desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, should draw near to, revere, and make offerings to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who are the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All Buddhas are the good spiritual friends of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise the good spiritual friends of bodhisattvas.”
Subhūti! Arhats are also good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva; these are the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The six pāramitās are also the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha are also the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends.
Subhūti! Suchness, the limit of reality, and the nature of phenomena are also the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends. Subhūti!

The six pāramitās are the World-Honored One; the six pāramitās are the Path; the six pāramitās are the Great Illumination; the six pāramitās are the Torch; the six pāramitās are Knowledge; the six pāramitās are Wisdom; the six pāramitās are the Rescue; the six pāramitās are the Refuge; the six pāramitās are the Island; the six pāramitās are the Ultimate Path; the six pāramitās are the Father and the Mother.
The four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are also thus.

Why is this? The six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*) are the parents of the Buddhas of the past; the six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are also the parents of the Buddhas of the future and the present throughout the ten directions.
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is because within the six pāramitās and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions are born.
For this reason, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, to purify buddha-fields, and to bring sentient beings to maturity, should study the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*) in order to gather in sentient beings.
What are the four?
They are generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation. Subhūti!
Because of these benefits, I have said:

"The six perfections and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the World-Honored Ones for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the path, the great illumination, the torch, knowledge, wisdom, salvation, the refuge, the island, the ultimate path, the father, and the mother."

"Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes not to abide according to the instructions of others, who wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, and who wishes to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, should study this Prajñāpāramitā!"
Why is this so? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā all dharmas are extensively explained; this is the place where the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train.
[Śāstra] Question:
Question: Since the characteristics of an *avaivartika* have already been explained in detail within the "Chapter on the *Avaivartika*," why are they being explained again now? Answer:

All the meanings of the *prajñāpāramitā* that have been taught are characteristics of an *avaivartika*. However, while the "Chapter on the *Avaivartika*" primarily discusses these matters, the characteristics of an *avaivartika* are also mentioned here and there in other chapters; it is simply not presented in a systematic sequence.
Some say: [The Buddha] spoke of the characteristics of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) using different terminology for the sake of future sentient beings. Others say:
There are two kinds of *avaivartika* [bodhisattvas]:
first, those who have already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), and second, those who have not yet received the prediction.
There are two kinds of receiving the prediction:
First is the prediction in the presence [of the recipient], and second is the prediction in the absence [of the recipient].
There are two kinds of predictions in the absence:
first, those in which the causes and conditions for the prediction are complete; and second, those in which the causes and conditions for the prediction are not yet complete.
Those who possess the causes and conditions for full prediction (vyākaraṇa) know the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena and are fully endowed with the six pāramitās;

those who do not possess the causes and conditions for full prediction merely know the true reality of all phenomena and have attained a portion of the prajñāpāramitā, but the remaining pāramitās are not yet complete.
"This bodhisattva is able to answer as an avaivartika bodhisattva. This refers to the avaivartika mentioned at the end of the preceding chapter; therefore, it is explained in sequence:
"In dreams, one does not crave the two stages; although one has not yet fully perfected the dharmas of avaivartika, one is nevertheless called avaivartika."
In order to explain such characteristics of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva, they are set forth in sequence within this chapter.
Because this bodhisattva constantly practices and cultivates emptiness during the day, he does not crave the three realms even in his dreams at night.
Because this person constantly practices a mind of compassion toward sentient beings and deeply delights in the Buddha-dharma, they do not crave the two vehicles.
Whether dreaming or awake, they contemplate all phenomena as being like dreams, like illusions, and so forth.

Although this bodhisattva has not yet received a manifest prediction of enlightenment and other qualities are not yet fully perfected, they are nonetheless said to possess the marks of an *avaivartika*. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva may regress from two points:
The first is turning away due to attachment to worldly pleasures; the second is turning away due to grasping at the two vehicles.

Because this bodhisattva’s resolve is firm and they have deeply entered into emptiness and the mind of compassion, they do not crave the three realms or the two vehicles even in their dreams, let alone while awake!
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva dreams of the Buddha preaching the Dharma to a great assembly of devas and humans— namely, the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—
and the bodhisattva understands this meaning, their mind becomes unified with that Dharma.

Furthermore, there are the secret dharmas of all Buddhas that a bodhisattva may perceive within a dream; namely, seeing the Buddha’s body as immeasurable, surpassing Mount Sumeru, with a complexion like Jāmbūnada gold, adorned by the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, emitting immeasurable light;

preaching the Dharma with a Brahma-voice, and from the pores of his body, immeasurable transformation Buddhas emerge to the ten directions, performing buddha-work through various powers of skillful means to deliver and liberate sentient beings.

At that time, because this bodhisattva has seen the supernatural power of the Buddha, his profound mind becomes pure as he inquires about the Buddha-dharma and attains the true reality of all dharmas; this is called *avaivartika*.

Because this bodhisattva constantly practices ultimate emptiness, afflictions such as the notions of "self" and "mine" are worn thin; he does not even begrudge his own body, let alone other relatives!
For this reason, even if one sees in a dream—
whether it be oneself, one's parents and so forth, or the causes and conditions for being killed or dying, as well as the destruction of a village— one does not feel sorrow, affliction, or fear.
Having awakened, he reflected:
"Just as in a dream one sees death though not dead, and sees fear though not afraid, so it is with all the three realms; how much more so in a dream!"
"When I become a Buddha, I shall preach to sentient beings that all dharmas are ultimately empty and are all like dreams.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva plants the causes and conditions for a pure buddha-field, they make this vow:

"Having accumulated the practices for a pure buddha-field for such a long time through the cultivation of this mind, if I should see sentient beings in the three evil realms within a dream, I shall immediately attain this thought:"
"When I become a Buddha, may my land be such that even the names of the three evil realms do not exist.

Furthermore, because this bodhisattva constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, when he sees sentient beings being burned by the fires of hell in his dreams, he makes a vow, and the fires immediately extinguish.
Having awakened, he grasps this sign; if he sees a real fire burning the city walls, he thinks:
"I was able to extinguish the fire in my dream; this fire, too, can certainly be extinguished!"
Why is this so? Because the Buddha has taught that there is no difference between dreaming and waking.

Since this bodhisattva has cultivated and accumulated merit over immeasurable eons and has realized the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), spirits, nāga kings, and others assist in extinguishing this fire.

Among these, there are those that do not perish, burning one house while leaving another intact; this is because of the heavy transgressions of sentient beings. When the power of a bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom cannot extinguish such heavy transgressions, they are what are called the karmic retribution for destroying the Dharma.
The Dharma is the Prajñāpāramitā;
no other dharmas provide benefit equal to that of the Prajñāpāramitā, and for this reason, the transgression of one who destroys it is grave.

By the power of the Bodhisattva’s vow, the fires do not burn in succession; however, those whose offenses are so grave that they cannot be saved are not rescued. This does not contradict the marks of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) Bodhisattva.
Being sustained by non-human beings is also like [extinguishing] fire with incantations.

There are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); because they hear this incantation for the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*), the spirits depart, and they then assume it is their own incantation.
These bodhisattvas themselves lack power; it is because Māra has sent forth the ghosts and spirits that they falsely rely upon [the incantation], taking it to be their own power.
Because such faults exist, the Buddha reveals them so that they may be understood.
Furthermore, before a bodhisattva has entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*), Māra assumes various forms and, according to the bodhisattva’s thoughts, manifests and says:
"You have already received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); you possess these marks; it is only because of your fleshly eyes (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) that you do not recognize them."
For these reasons, they give rise to overweening pride and look down upon others.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva has not attained the true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) and does not understand that beyond the mere combination of the five aggregates, such as form, there exists further conceptual characteristics of names.
When a Māra comes and bestows a prediction upon him,
saying, "You shall become a Buddha, and your name shall be such-and-such," that bodhisattva reflects:
"I originally possessed this recollection of my name; what has now been spoken accords with my own aspirations, and must surely be the prediction of enlightenment granted by the Buddhas.
For this reason, arrogance arose in his heart, and he looked down upon other great bodhisattvas.
For this reason, they distance themselves from the unsurpassed path;
once their retribution for these offenses is exhausted, they fall into the two vehicles.

If, however, they repent while still in this very body, they shall repay their debts for a long time until they are finished, after which they will again rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā and attain Buddhahood.
Why is this? If one repents only after changing lives, the transgression will be so grave that it cannot be extinguished, and one shall not become a Buddha.
Because the mind clings to these empty names and incurs a heavy offense, the Buddha spoke of the four grave prohibitions as a parable:
Having violated this grave prohibition, one shall not attain the fruits of the four paths in this present body. Why is this?
Because among these four prohibitions, one falsely claims, "I am an Arhat," by means of lying.

In this context, "attachment" refers to receiving a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) by declaring for oneself, "I shall become a Buddha"; for this reason, one treats the four grave prohibitions with extreme gravity.
Regarding the transgression that exceeds the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), it is as explained in the "Hell Chapter" concerning the sin of destroying the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding "subtle demonic activities": "subtle" means not opposing their intentions, but rather following their original thoughts and assisting in the fulfillment of their minds.
This occurs when a bodhisattva has not yet attained the state of *avaivartika*, yet Māra deceives them by saying they have already attained it.
This is a subtle work of Māra; a bodhisattva of sharp faculties should recognize and distance themselves from it!
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in a secluded place, Māra comes and praises them, saying:
"You are able to distance yourself from your kinsmen and fellow students, dwelling alone in deep mountain forests for the sake of the Buddha-way; this is the true practice of the bodhisattva path."
Because of this, that bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of arrogance and looks down upon other bodhisattvas dwelling among the assembly.
Due to this matter, they distance themselves from the Buddha-way and fall into the two vehicles.
Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha rebukes these bodhisattvas as being thieves and outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), as stated in the sūtras: "One should not associate with them.
What the Buddha calls "detachment" is to have the mind detached from the two vehicles and the three realms; this is called true detachment.
As explained at length in the sūtras regarding such subtle demonic activities (*mārakarman*), one should recognize them and remain far removed from them.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva desires to attain the unsurpassed path with a profound resolve"—a profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) refers to a single-minded and earnest resolve; it is a deep love for the Buddha-way that transcends all worldly pleasures.
One should draw near to spiritual friends. Why is this?
Because there are two causes and conditions by which one attains the unsurpassed path.
The first is the internal, and the second is the external.
The internal refers to right mindfulness, which consists of contemplating and deliberating upon all phenomena;
the external refers to virtuous spiritual friends.
Since the Buddha has described the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in various ways on other occasions, Subhūti asks the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
who are the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends?"
The Buddha replied:
“All Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas are the bodhisattva’s spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Furthermore, all dharmas—from the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), as well as suchness (tathatā), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—are also spiritual friends.”
Because the Dharma can accomplish that task, the various dharmas such as the six pāramitās are called "spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
These three types of noble beings cause bodhisattvas to practice these six pāramitā dharmas so that they may attain Buddhahood;
therefore, both the Dharma and the person are collectively termed "spiritual friends."
Question:
Since the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the six *pāramitās* can bring a bodhisattva to fulfillment, they should be considered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
However, since the path of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is different, how can it serve as a spiritual friend?
The answer is:

There are followers of the Hīnayāna who, because they sought the Buddha-way in previous lives, possess sharp faculties. Although they belong to the Hīnayāna, they possess a heart of compassion; observing those who are destined to achieve the Mahāyāna, they preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for them. This is because they know how to repay the Buddha’s kindness and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.

For example, although Śāriputra sought the Buddha-way for sixty kalpas and subsequently regressed to become an arhat, he possessed sharp faculties and wisdom, enabling him to expound the Mahāyāna for the sake of all bodhisattvas.

Subhūti constantly practices the samādhi of non-contention and always maintains a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward sentient beings; therefore, he is also able to teach and transform bodhisattvas in the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Just as Mahākāśyapa, by means of his supernormal powers, maintains this body until the appearance of Maitreya in the world, emerging from Mount Navaśaila to serve as the causal condition for the great assembly to attain the Way.
There are many such categories. Question:
