“What are the profound dharmas of equal mind and so forth that constitute the bodhisattva’s sphere of training?
The Buddha replied:
“From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of self-characteristic—these are called the dharmas of equality.”
There are two kinds of equanimity (samatā-kṣānti):
the superior grade was explained in the previous chapter as equanimity toward sentient beings; this chapter explains equanimity toward dharmas.
Just as when the two ends of a scale are balanced and equal, so too are the various emptinesses, such as internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) and others, equal among all dharmas.
Just as internal phenomena have various distinctions, when one attains internal emptiness, they are all equally non-existent dharmas;
even up to the emptiness of self-characteristics, the characteristics of all dharmas are themselves empty, at which time the mind is equanimous.
When a bodhisattva dwells within these states, they are able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti asked again:
"Is it for the sake of the exhaustion of form and so forth that one trains in sarvajñā?"
"One contemplates that form and so forth are impermanent, ceasing moment by moment, and do not abide. If one attains this contemplation, the mind then becomes detached from form;
because the mind is detached from form, all afflictions are extinguished;
and because the afflictions are extinguished, one attains the state of non-arising."
Subhūti asked:
"Is training in this manner training for sarvajñā (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha反问ed Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Is the suchness of all phenomena, such as form, and the suchness of the Tathāgata—this suchness something that can be exhausted, extinguished, or severed?
Subhūti replied:
"No! Since this Suchness has been, from the very beginning, neither accumulated nor compounded, how could it have an end?
Since it is originally unarisen, how could it have cessation?
These dharmas are from the very beginning empty and deceptive, lacking any fixed characteristic;
how could they be severed? "Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in suchness in this way, he trains in sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
This suchness is eternal, cannot be realized, cannot be extinguished, and cannot be severed;
this exhaustion, detachment, and severance are practices undertaken to eliminate inversion, and are not the ultimate.
In this context, the ultimate matter is explained, whereupon the Buddha praised:
"One who trains in this way, though not training for the sake of any single dharma, trains for the sake of sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
If one trains in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that is training in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and so forth;
if one can train in the six perfections and so forth, this constitutes reaching the ultimate limit of all training.
If one exhausts the limits of all training, because such a person is fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom, neither Māra nor the followers of Māra can subdue them.
By training correctly in this way, they proceed directly to the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Training in this way is training in the path practiced by the Buddhas.
Training in this way is protected by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as by the great Bodhisattvas, devas, and virtuous persons.

One who can train in this manner will be free from false views and have a mind without attachment; toward all sentient beings, they will be able to give rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Because of this great loving-kindness and great compassion, they are able to teach and transform sentient beings.
Because the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-realm is pure.

Once the Buddha-realm is purified, he attains the Way of the Buddha and turns the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, delivering immeasurable sentient beings by means of the Three Vehicles.
Because he delivers sentient beings by means of the Mahāyāna, he does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas;

because he does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas, he constantly opens the gateway to the nectar-like Dharma in the world and constantly reveals to sentient beings the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The unconditioned nature refers to suchness, the dharma-nature, the reality-limit, and nirvana.
Ambrosia is the unconditioned nature;
the gate refers to the three gates of liberation.

Those who are inferior are called indolent and negligent; they take no delight in the Buddha-dharma, do not practice the Way with a single mind, and engage in a mixture of sinful and meritorious deeds.
Such as these are unable to study this Dharma.
Why is this? Those who are inferior think thus:
"My own body and my relatives are what I ought to protect; why should I concern myself with other sentient beings by giving them my head, eyes, marrow, and brain so that they may obtain happiness?"
"All people employ skillful means to seek happiness; why should I now abandon happiness to seek suffering?
Or, giving rise to wrong views, they further think:
"Sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless; it is impossible to deliver them all."
If they could be fully delivered, then there would be a limit and a boundary, and a single Buddha would be able to deliver them all.
Or one might think:
“The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are empty, neither arising nor ceasing; what, then, is there for me to deliver?”
"Whether seeking the Buddha-way or not seeking the Buddha-way, all are equally like illusions and dreams.
Such inferior persons, due to various false views and the causes and conditions of greed and desire, are unable to study this Great Dharma.

At times, there appears a Great Being in the world who deliberates upon and contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—namely, that they are neither eternal nor impermanent, neither finite nor infinite, neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth.
Practicing such a path, he destroys inverted views;
then, relinquishing even this path, he enters directly into the *dharmatā* and dwells eternally within this pure *dharmatā*.

Because all sentient beings do not know this matter, he gives rise to great compassion; thereafter, he cultivates and accumulates the various merits such as the six pāramitās, the Buddha’s supernormal powers, wisdom, and unimpeded liberation, attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and extensively delivers sentient beings through various doors of skillful means.
Such a person is truly rare.
It is asked:
As it was previously stated that "sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless," yet it is also said:
"If sentient beings are empty, what is there to deliver?
How, then, can there be anything to be delivered?
The answer is:
This is what is spoken by inferior persons; how can it be sufficient as proof?
Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated:

due to the causes and conditions of wrong views and craving, inferior persons conceive such thoughts as "sentient beings are finite" or "infinite," or that "all dharmas are empty and non-existent," or that "all dharmas are eternal and real"—all of these are subsumed within the sixty-two wrong views.

The Great Being is free from desire; through reflection and deliberation, he remains aloof from such faults and transgressions, abiding in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and giving rise to great compassion.
For example, it is as when a Great Being gives wealth to others solely with a mind of generosity, yet does not take a price for it.
A person of greedy desire gives because they seek a cause and condition;
a person of wrong view acts based on views such as finitude or infinity, never performing any deed that is without benefit.
For example, it is like a petty person in the marketplace who gives only when seeking profit.
Furthermore, the Great Being Bodhisattva has no desires of his own, yet he is able to give his head, eyes, and so forth to sentient beings; the karmic rewards he thereby obtains he also gives away.
With a mind that relies on nothing regarding all phenomena, he is able to accumulate all merits.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Those who wish to uproot all sentient beings submerged in birth and death should train in this way.
Furthermore, because a bodhisattva who trains in this manner always possesses a heart of compassion and pity, and does not afflict sentient beings, they do not fall into the hells.
Because they constantly contemplate the true nature of all phenomena arising from causes and conditions, they do not give rise to ignorance and thus do not fall among the animals;
because they constantly practice giving and destroy the mind of stinginess and greed, they are not born among the hungry ghosts.
Because they never begrudge the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s teachings or the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, they are not born in the borderlands.
Because they constantly make offerings to their elders and virtuous people, thereby destroying arrogance, they are not born among the lowly classes such as the Caṇḍālas.
Because they love sentient beings with a profound mind and fully carry out deeds that benefit them, they receive a complete and perfect body.
Because they transform sentient beings through many wholesome dharmas, their retinue is accomplished, and they never suffer from loneliness or destitution.
Because they deeply love and delight in the *śīlapāramitā*, they do not engage in the ten unwholesome paths of action nor in wrong livelihood.

Being devoid of the notion of a self, they act solely for the benefit of sentient beings and not for their own sake; therefore, they do not associate with evil people or those who have broken the precepts.
An "evil person" is defined by evil of mind; one who violates the precepts is defined by evil of body and speech.
Furthermore, practicing the three unwholesome paths is called being an evil person, while practicing the seven unwholesome paths is called violating the precepts.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva who, while living as a householder, gathers in evil persons is called an "evil person"; one who, having left the household life, gathers in evil persons is called "one who breaks the precepts.
Question:
A bodhisattva appears in the world for the sake of delivering evil persons, just as a skilled physician treats all manner of diseases; for what reason, then, does he not gather in evil persons?
Answer: Among evil persons and those who have broken the precepts, there are those who can be transformed and those who cannot; here, only those who cannot be transformed are discussed.
If one were to take them in and live with them, one would ruin one's own path and provide no benefit to them.
For example, it is like one who attempts to rescue someone drowning while being unable to swim oneself; both will fail to escape danger.
Therefore, it is said that one should distance oneself from evil persons.
Because the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) abounds in evils, one gives rise to a heart of compassion and is thus born within the realm of desire.

Although he practices dhyāna, his mind is harmonious and supple; yet, by the power of skillful means, at the time of death he is not reborn according to that dhyāna, as explained at length in the sūtra: “Subhūti!...”
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they attain purity regarding all dharmas—namely, the purification of the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This "purity" is the relinquishing of the *Vimalakīrti*, non-existence, and ultimate emptiness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas have been empty and pure from the very beginning, why do you say that 'a bodhisattva who trains in this way attains purity among all dharmas'?"
The Buddha approved Subhūti’s words and explained the causal conditions for him:
“If a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas have been empty and pure from the very beginning, his mind will neither sink nor recoil within them.”
Not sinking is called being without doubt and not giving rise to false views.
To be thoroughly penetrating and not contending with emptiness—this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
All ordinary persons do not know or see such pure dharmas; for the sake of these people, one practices the six *pāramitās* and other auxiliary dharmas of the path.

It is the duty of a Bodhisattva to teach and transform these sentient beings; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of purity within all dharmas. That is to say, by relinquishing the inversions of the triple world and transcending the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they attain the power of pure wisdom regarding all dharmas.

Because they have attained these merits, they are able to fully know the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as the various causes and conditions of the karmas arising from their mental activities.
Having known them, they preach the Dharma and provide instruction according to what is appropriate for each.
All such benefits as these are obtained by studying Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, it is said that one reaches the ultimate limit of all learning.
Few are able to study in this manner; such persons are rare!
The Buddha, wishing to make this meaning clear, therefore provides analogies such as gold, silver, and the karma of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva studies this *prajñā*, thoughts of stinginess and the like do not arise.
Regarding "not giving rise to thoughts of stinginess and so forth": because the bodhisattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, they suppress all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although these afflictions have not yet been completely exhausted, they are rendered incapable of functioning; therefore, it is said that they do not arise.

When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, they know that the characteristics of all dharmas are entirely false and unreal; therefore, they do not grasp at the characteristics of form, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause others to fall into the views of existence or non-existence; rather, one proceeds directly upon the Middle Way, accumulating the practices of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, they do not apprehend any dharma; because nothing is apprehended, there is no dharma for which a mark can be grasped—whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise."
If a bodhisattva can train in this way, they encompass all the pāramitās.

The various pāramitās, such as dāna and the rest, do not depart from the prajñāpāramitā; by the power of the prajñāpāramitā, it causes the other pāramitās to be freed from all false views and attachments, so that each may attain growth.
Because the Buddha wished to make this meaning clear, he spoke a simile:
"It is like the view of self, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and so forth.
He was asked:
Question: The view of self and the various views each have their own distinct characteristics; how can they be subsumed within the view of self?
Answer: Although they have distinct characteristics, the view of self is the fundamental basis.
Because people have ignorance as a causal condition, they give rise to the view of a self within the empty five aggregates;
because they give rise to this view of a self, they say, "When this body dies, it goes [to another world], or it does not go."
If one holds that there is a going forth, this is the view of eternalism;
if one holds that there is no going forth, this is the view of annihilationism.
If one asserts total extinction—enjoying pleasure in the present, being attached to the five desires, and regarding unwholesome dharmas as supreme—then one gives rise to the grasping of views.
If one asserts permanence, then practicing the path as a renunciant—observing the precepts and engaging in asceticism—gives rise to the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Alternatively, seeing that both the view of annihilation and the view of permanence possess faults, one might then claim that there are no causes, conditions, or karmic retributions, thereby giving rise to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Abiding within these five views—such as the world being eternal or non-eternal, the prior limit and the posterior limit, and so forth—one gives rise to fifty-seven views.
Therefore, it is without fault to say that "the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) subsumes the sixty-two views."
Through various causes, conditions, and parables such as these, one knows that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost among all dharmas;
because the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost among all dharmas, the bodhisattva who studies this *prajñā* is the foremost among all sentient beings.
The Buddha, wishing to skillfully transform sentient beings through this matter, spoke a parable:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Are there many sentient beings in a trichiliocosm?
and so forth, up to: "When a bodhisattva trains in this way, it should be known that they are non-retrogressive, far removed from the two vehicles, and drawing near to the Buddha-vehicle."
Furthermore, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva should form this thought:
'This is the prajñāpāramitā.'"
"This Prajñāpāramitā demonstrates the characteristics of Prajñāpāramitā—whether as existent or non-existent—and [the states of] seeing Prajñā, attaining Prajñā, and becoming attached to Prajñā."
As for my attaining all-knowledge through this *prajñāpāramitā*, it is the "Bodhisattva" that exists as a conventional designation based on the harmony of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The Bodhisattva follows after these conventional names and conceives of them as a self; it is by means of this *prajñā* that there is anything performed.

Prajñāpāramitā is characterized by non-attachment; yet, if someone says that prajñāpāramitā has characteristics, that person follows after conventional designations and gives rise to the notion of a self.
Prajñāpāramitā is characterized by non-action; yet this person wishes to employ prajñā for the sake of some action, saying: "By means of this prajñā, I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"One who forms such thoughts is not said to be practicing prajñā.
If one does not form such thoughts, it is called practicing the prajñāpāramitā."
Question:
Since the matter is already concluded by the thought having been formed or not formed, why is there yet a third explanation? Answer:
The first is the characteristic of wrong practice; the second negates wrong practice.
Since the characteristic of right practice has not yet been explained, the third explains the characteristic of right practice.
Furthermore, the first is the grasping of signs by means of an attached mind.
The second [section] refutes attachment to signs, but does not explain what the characteristics of all phenomena are;
the third [section], while refuting false attachments, also explains the true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"In all places, one does not manifest the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
nor does one give rise to the thought 'I' or 'I am using the *prajñāpāramitā* to perform some action.

Rather, one knows that all phenomena eternally abide within suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and within suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality, one does not engage in contention."
Therefore, the third [explanation] is stated, which is without fault.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 77;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on Aspiration and Delight, Chapter 64, Scroll 78.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 64: On Aspiration and Delight. [Sūtra] At that time, Śakra Devendra had this thought:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of generosity, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they already surpass all sentient beings; how much more so when they attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment!"

If these sentient beings hear of this omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and have faith in it, they obtain the excellent benefit among humans and the most supreme within their lifespan; how much more so for those who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
“Those sentient beings who are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, other sentient beings should aspire to emulate them.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra scattered heavenly *mandārava* flowers over the Buddha and spoke these words:
“By this merit, may whoever seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* be endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, endowed with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and endowed with the self-arisen Dharma.”
If there are those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, I shall cause them to be fully endowed with the dharmas of a śrāvaka.
World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall never give rise to even a single thought to cause them to turn back; nor shall I ever give rise to even a single thought to cause them to turn back and fall into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Bhagavān!

I vow that all bodhisattvas shall redouble their diligence toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; seeing the various sufferings and afflictions within the birth and death of sentient beings, they desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras.
With this mind, they make this vow:"
"Since I have already crossed over myself, I shall also cross over those who have not yet crossed;
since I have already been liberated myself, I shall liberate those who are not yet liberated;
since I have already attained peace myself, I shall bring peace to those who have not yet attained it."
“Once I have attained parinirvāṇa, I shall cause those who have not yet entered parinirvāṇa to attain it.
World-Honored One,
how much merit does a son of good family or a daughter of good family obtain through a mind of sympathetic joy toward the merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain awakening?
How much merit is obtained from a mind of sympathetic joy toward the virtues of a bodhisattva who has long since resolved [for enlightenment]?
How much merit is obtained from a mind of sympathetic joy toward the virtues of a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*)?
“With a mind of sympathetic joy toward the merits of a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood, how much merit does one obtain?
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!
The four continents of this world-system may be weighed and their weight known, but the merit of this mind of sympathetic joy is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
This trichiliocosm may all be weighed and its weight known, but the merit of this mind of sympathetic joy is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

Suppose the waters of the great trichiliocosm were filled to the brim; if one were to take a single hair, split it into a hundred parts, and use one such part to draw up a drop of that seawater, the number of drops could be known, yet the merit of this mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*) cannot be calculated or known.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If sentient beings do not rejoice in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in their hearts, they are all the retinue of Māra."
Those whose minds do not rejoice [in this] have come from among the māras. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
These bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [on awakening] are born for the purpose of shattering the realm of Māra.
Therefore, those who desire to love and revere the Triple Gem should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
having given rise to sympathetic joy, they should dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, by virtue of the characteristic that is neither one nor two.
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
Kauśika! If there is anyone who can thus rejoice in and dedicate the merit of a bodhisattva, they will always encounter the Buddhas;

they shall never see unpleasant forms, never hear unpleasant sounds, never smell unpleasant odors, never taste unpleasant flavors, never touch unpleasant textures, and never follow unwholesome thoughts.
They shall never be separated from the Buddhas, traveling from one Buddha-field to another, drawing near to the Buddhas and planting roots of goodness.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family, for the sake of the roots of goodness of immeasurable, incalculable bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, rejoice in them and dedicate them; and for the sake of the roots of goodness of immeasurable, incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the second stage, the third stage, up to the tenth stage, and those in their final birth before Buddhahood, they rejoice in them and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By virtue of these roots of goodness as causes and conditions, they will swiftly draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Once these bodhisattvas have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will deliver immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.

Kauśika! For this reason, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should, with respect to the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva who has first resolved [for awakening], rejoice and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, neither as mind nor apart from mind;

and with respect to the roots of goodness of those who have long since resolved, those who are irreversible (*avaivartika*), and those in their last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they should rejoice and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, neither as mind nor apart from mind.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This mind is like an illusion; how can it attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do you perceive this mind as being like an illusion?"
"No, World-Honored One! I do not perceive illusion,
nor do I perceive the mind as being like an illusion."
“Subhūti, what do you think? If there were no illusion,
nor a mind that is like an illusion, would you perceive such a mind?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti! "
What do you think?
Apart from illusion and apart from the mind which is like an illusion, do you see any other dharma that attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"No, World-Honored One!
I do not see any dharma apart from illusion, or apart from a mind that is like an illusion, by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"World-Honored One!
I do not see any other dharma whatsoever that could be said to exist or not to exist.
Because the characteristic of this dharma is ultimately detached, it does not fall into existence and does not fall into non-existence."
If dharmas are ultimately detached, they cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
nor can a dharma that is non-existent attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
All dharmas are non-existent; therein there is neither that which is defiled nor that which is pure.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached; the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity are ultimately detached; and even up to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment, it is also ultimately detached.
If a dharma is ultimately detached, then it should neither be cultivated nor destroyed.
When practicing the perfection of wisdom, there is likewise no dharma that can be apprehended, because it is ultimately detached.
World-Honored One!
If the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached, how can one attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment by means of the perfection of wisdom?
“Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is also ultimately detached; within these two forms of detachment, how could there be anything to be attained?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Excellent!”
Excellent!

This perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached; the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity are ultimately detached, even unto the knowledge of all modes, which is ultimately detached.
Subhūti! If the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached, and even up to all-knowledge is ultimately detached, it is for this reason that one can attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! If the perfection of wisdom were not ultimately detached, and even if the knowledge of all modes were not ultimately detached, it would not be called the perfection of wisdom, nor would it be called the perfection of meditation, up to and including the knowledge of all modes.
Subhūti! If the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is ultimately detached—for this reason, Subhūti!

It is not that one attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment without relying on the perfection of wisdom; nor is it that one attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment by means of detachment through detachment, while not relying on the perfection of wisdom. It is not that one does not rely on the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The meaning of what the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice is exceedingly profound!”
The Buddha said: "So it is, Subhūti!"
The meaning of the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is extremely profound. Subhūti!
These bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult to do: namely, practicing this profound meaning while not realizing the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to the meaning I have heard from the Buddha, what the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice is not difficult.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend this meaning as something to be realized, nor does he apprehend the prajñāpāramitā as something to be realized, nor is there anyone who realizes it.
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are unattainable, what is this meaning that can be realized?
What is this Prajñāpāramitā that can be realized?”
"Who is it that realizes this?
Having realized it, who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
World-Honored One?"
This is called the practice of non-apprehension of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
When a bodhisattva practices this, they attain clear understanding of all dharmas.
"World-Honored One!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound Dharma, does not become startled, does not sink into despondency, does not tremble, and does not fear, this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that "I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," nor does he perceive this perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that "I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts as:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is near to me."
“World-Honored One!
It is as if space does not form this thought:
‘There are dharmas that are distant from me, and there are dharmas that are near to me.’”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because space is without discrimination.
"Bhagavān!
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not form such a thought as:
'The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is near to me.'"
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā there is no discrimination.
World-Honored One!
For example, a conjured person does not think:
"The illusionist is near to me; the spectators are far from me. Why is this?
Because an illusory person is without discrimination, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom likewise does not form this thought:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is near to me."
"World-Honored One!
It is, for example, as if a reflection in a mirror does not think:
'That which is its cause is near to me; the rest are far from me.'"
Why is this? Because an image is without discrimination.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom likewise does not form such a thought:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me; sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is near to me. Why is this?
Because within the prajñāpāramitā there is no discrimination.
"Bhagavān!
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom has neither attachment nor aversion. Why is this?"
"Because the intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended.
World-Honored One!
It is, for example, as if the Buddha has neither attachment nor aversion."
It is the same for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) who has neither attachment nor aversion. Why is this?
Because within the perfection of wisdom, there is neither aversion nor attachment.
World-Honored One!
For example, the Buddha has severed all conceptual discriminations;
so too is it for a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, who has severed all conceptual discriminations because of ultimate emptiness.
“World-Honored One!
It is as if a person conjured by the Buddha does not form this thought:
‘The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me; anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me.’”
Why is this? Because a person conjured by a Buddha is without discrimination.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is also like this; they do not form such a thought:
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me; anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me.
World-Honored One!
It is like a transformation created for a specific purpose; the work performed by that transformation is without discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā is also like this: for whatever purpose it is practiced, that purpose is accomplished, yet the prajñāpāramitā itself remains without discrimination.
World-Honored One!

It is like a craftsman or a craftsman’s apprentice who, for some purpose, fashions a wooden figure—whether male or female, an elephant, a horse, an ox, or a sheep. This creation is also capable of performing actions, yet it is devoid of discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā is also like this: although it is said that these matters are accomplished for the sake of some purpose, the prajñāpāramitā itself is without discrimination.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Is it only the perfection of wisdom that is without discrimination, or are the perfections from the perfection of meditation down to the perfection of generosity likewise without discrimination?”
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“The dhyānapāramitā is without conceptual discrimination; even the dānapāramitā is likewise without conceptual discrimination.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“Is form non-conceptual, and so on, up to consciousness which is also non-conceptual?
Are the eye, and so on, up to the mind non-conceptual?
Are forms, and so on, up to mental phenomena non-conceptual?”
Is there no conceptual discrimination regarding eye-consciousness-contact through to mind-consciousness-contact?

Is there likewise no conceptual discrimination regarding feelings produced by the causal conditions of eye-contact through to feelings produced by the causal conditions of mind-contact; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness through to the eightfold noble path; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities, anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the unconditioned nature?

Subhūti! If form is without discrimination, and even the unconditioned nature is without discrimination, and if all dharmas are without discrimination, how can one discriminate the cycle of birth and death within the six realms—namely, "this is hell," "this is the realm of hungry ghosts," "this is the animal realm," "this is the deva realm," "this is the human realm," or "this is the asura realm"?
“How does one distinguish between the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddhas?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:

“Because of the causes and conditions of the perversions of sentient beings, they perform actions of body, speech, and mind; according to their fundamental karma and desires, they receive bodies in the six realms as retribution.”
The bodies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, devas, and asuras.
As you have asked:
"How is it that there is a distinction between the stage of a srotāpanna up to the path of a Buddha?"

"Śāriputra! The srotāpanna exists because it is non-conceptual; the fruit of srotāpanna also exists because it is non-conceptual. This extends even to the arhat, the fruit of arhatship, the pratyekabuddha, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the Buddha, and the path of the Buddha—all of these exist because they are non-conceptual."
Śāriputra! The Buddhas of the past also exist because they are non-conceptual and have severed conceptualization.
For this reason, Śāriputra!
One should know that all dharmas are without discrimination and possess an indestructible characteristic, because they are suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality.
Śāriputra, in this way,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice non-discriminative prajñāpāramitā.
"Having practiced non-conceptual *prajñāpāramitā*, one then attains non-conceptual *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[The Commentary] explains:
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and all those present in the assembly were filled with joy.
Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:
"When this bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, his merit already surpasses that of all sentient beings; how much more so when he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!"
Sentient beings are of two kinds:
first, those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment], and second, those who have not yet resolved their minds.
A bodhisattva who has resolved their mind surpasses all those who have not yet resolved their minds.

Why is this? Because these people plant the causes and conditions for immeasurable and unsurpassed Buddha-dharma, desiring to deliver all sentient beings so that they may leave suffering behind and attain happiness;
whereas other sentient beings merely seek their own happiness and wish to inflict suffering upon others.
For such reasons as these, the one who generates the thought [of enlightenment] is superior.
Question:
Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and those with the five supernatural powers are persons who have abandoned desire; [how then can they be surpassed?]
Regarding the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), it may be asked: "How can one who has not yet abandoned desire, yet merely generates the mind, attain superiority?
The answer is:
this matter has already been answered in various ways in the preceding chapter.
Although Arhats and others have exhausted their outflows, they are not equal to a Bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment.
For example, although the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is still within the womb, he already surpasses all other sons;
likewise, although the crown prince of a king has not yet ascended the throne, he surpasses all ministers who possess rank, wealth, and nobility.
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas who resolve their minds [on enlightenment]:
first, those who practice the bodhisattva path such as the various pāramitās; second, those who merely resolve their minds on it in an empty manner.
Herein, the text speaks of "those who practice the bodhisattva path."
Although this person’s task is not yet accomplished, they are able to surpass all sentient beings; how much more so once it is accomplished!
It is like the kalaviṅka bird within its egg: even before it has uttered a sound, it can surpass all other birds, how much more so once it is fully developed!

The Bodhisattva is also like this: although he has not yet attained Buddhahood, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, he utters the sounds of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena to shatter the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the various non-Buddhists and the followers of Māra; how much more so once he has attained Buddhahood!
Some say: If there is one who can give rise to a single thought of resolve, saying,
"I shall become a Buddha and extinguish the suffering of all sentient beings."
"Although they have not yet severed the afflictions nor performed difficult deeds, because their mental and verbal karma is so weighty, they surpass all other sentient beings.
All sentient beings seek happiness for themselves alone; for the sake of their own bodies, they cherish those who are dear to them.
Although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not crave worldly pleasures, they seek the bliss of Nirvana merely to extinguish their own suffering, and thus cannot act for the sake of sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva’s arising of the thought and utterance of speech are for the sake of delivering all beings; therefore, they are superior.
It is like a certain Arhat possessing the six supernormal powers who, taking a śrāmaṇera with him, had him carry his robes and bowl as they traveled along the road.
The śrāmaṇera reflected:
"By which vehicle shall I enter nirvāṇa?
He then gave rise to this thought:
"The Buddha is the World-Honored One, most supreme and most wondrous; I shall enter nirvana by means of the Buddha-vehicle.
The Master, knowing his thought, immediately took up his robes and bowl to carry them himself, and pushed the śrāmaṇera to walk in front.
The śrāmaṇera reflected again:
"The path of the Buddha is extremely difficult; dwelling long in birth and death, one undergoes immeasurable suffering. For now, I shall enter nirvana early by means of the Hīnayāna."
The teacher again gave his robe and bowl bag back to the śrāmaṇera, telling him to carry it and follow behind.
This happened three times.
The śrāmaṇera then said to the teacher:
"The Master is old and senile; his behavior is like that of a child at play!
He has just now placed me in front, and already he has placed me behind again—how can this be so hasty?"
The teacher replied:
"The very first thought you conceived to become a Buddha is a precious mind; thus, you abide within the path of my teacher.
Such a person as this should be venerated even by Pratyekabuddhas, let alone by Arhats!"
For this reason, I have placed you in front.
Your mind has turned back in regret and you wish to take up the Hīnayāna, yet you have not yet attained it; you are far removed from me, and for this reason I have placed you behind.
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera was startled and awakened to realization:
"My teacher can know my mind!
My single resolve already surpasses that of an arhat; how much more so its fulfillment!"
Thus, one immediately establishes oneself firmly in the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Furthermore, being "superior" does not necessarily mean being superior in all matters; rather, it is simply this: "to resolve once to become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings"—this is what constitutes superiority.
Since other states such as meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) have not yet been attained, how can they be said to be superior?
For example, if one speaks in terms of flying, birds surpass humans.
As for the merit that will be attained in the future, this matter is not discussed here.
The followers of the Hīnayāna say:
"Even a Bodhisattva in his final birth is not superior to a young novice who has attained immeasurable discipline.
In the Mahāyāna treatises, some may say:
"One who has resolved upon the Great Vehicle, even if they are among base and wicked people, is still superior to those of the Two Vehicles who have attained liberation."
These are called the two extremes.
To be free from these two extremes is called the Middle Way.
The meaning of the Middle Way is as explained above.
Because it possesses the reality of principle and truth, it should be accepted.
Therefore, it is said:
"At the moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one surpasses all sentient beings; how much more so when one attains Buddhahood!"
"One who hears of and believes in omniscience (sarvajñatā) attains the excellent benefits among humans.
Some say: "The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are these benefits."
Some say: "The fruit and retribution of the six pāramitās are benefits, namely those of the wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin), Śakra and Brahmā, human kings, and Dharma kings."
Some say: "One who has attained *avaivartika* does not fall into the evil realms, but is always reborn among humans and devas in places of wealth and honor. Others say:

“A bodhisattva, dwelling in the supernormal powers of karmic fruition, travels to the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and teaches and transforms sentient beings through various skillful means;
by causing sentient beings to believe and accept dependent origination, they teach and transform them, thereby attaining such great benefits as these.”
Regarding "the foremost among those with life-span," sentient beings have two kinds of life:
first, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); second, the life-span of wisdom.
Because this person has attained the life-span of wisdom, it is said that they are "foremost among those with life-span."
How much more so for one who has resolved their mind!
One who has resolved their mind is worthy of reverence and esteem. Why is this?
As previously stated regarding the causes and conditions:
"One is able to relinquish one's own happiness to give happiness to others;
one does not grieve over one's own suffering because one grieves over the suffering of others."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to manifest a sign of joy, scattered heavenly mandārava flowers over the Buddha, as described at length in the sutra.
A question is asked:

"Since merit and demerit cannot be transferred to another, and even if one wished to transfer them, it would be impossible—why does Śakra Devānām Indra say, 'By this merit, may those who seek the Buddha-way be fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas'?"
Answer: Although it cannot be given away to others, it nevertheless causes one’s own mind to become favorable.
Furthermore, this is Śakra Devānām Indra manifesting that merit is not clung to; therefore, he gives it with a mind of sympathetic joy to those who seek the Buddha-way.
It is the same with the śrāvakas.
Śakra Devendra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have attained the path of a śrāvaka, I would not give rise to even a single thought of causing a bodhisattva to turn back toward the mind of the two vehicles."
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas see that sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death undergo various kinds of suffering; wishing to benefit the entire world, they make this vow:
"I shall equally deliver those who have not yet been delivered."
At that time, there were beings in the assembly who thought to themselves:

"If, as has been said above, there is merit in rejoicing, what is the difference between rejoicing for one who has first resolved their mind and rejoicing for one who has long since resolved their mind?"
Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to resolve the doubts of the assembly, asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
how much merit does one obtain by rejoicing in the virtues of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind toward enlightenment?”
As explained at length in the sutra:
this merit is immeasurable and boundless because it is planted within immeasurable and boundless fields;
since people are unable to calculate or know its extent, the sutra provides analogies to facilitate understanding, as explained in detail therein.
Although the merit of sympathetic joy is immeasurable and boundless, for those who are close to the path of Buddhahood, the merit of sympathetic joy becomes even greater.
At that time, Śakra, out of great joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Those who, upon hearing of these merits, do not rejoice are the subjects of Māra; they have come from the realm of Māra.
Why is this? Because, dwelling within the sphere of Māra, they have accumulated evil intentions and therefore do not rejoice.
The causal conditions for this are explained as follows:
"A mind of sympathetic joy can destroy the realm of Māra.

Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way and desire to love and revere the Triple Gem without forsaking it should dedicate their merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a mind of sympathetic joy."

Regarding the characteristic of neither one nor two: because one does not perceive that any phenomena possess a fixed characteristic that is not subject to causes and conditions, it is called "not one.
Because one does not conceptually differentiate between the mind of sympathetic joy and the mind of dedication—since they are ultimately empty—it is called "not two."
Having affirmed the intention of Śakra, the Buddha further proclaimed the merit of sympathetic joy:
"Because this person constantly recollects and rejoices in the merits of the Buddhas of the ten directions, they will swiftly attain the vision of the Buddhas."

Furthermore, with a profound mind, they desire to cause all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness; for this reason, though they come and go within the cycle of birth and death, their six sense faculties do not initially receive any defiled objects.
"They shall never be separated from the presence of the Buddhas who have arisen, because they do not sever the seed and continue to see the practice of the Buddhas.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"Because this person rejoices in all bodhisattvas from those who first resolve their minds throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, up to those bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) who are immeasurable, they obtain the aforementioned rewards, swiftly attain the Buddha-way, and deliver immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
This bodhisattva dedicates this merit according to the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Within that true nature, no mind can be apprehended; therefore it is said: 'it is not the mind, yet it is not apart from the mind.'"
As explained above regarding the meaning of "neither one nor two," it is further expounded because of the diversity of phenomena.
Having heard this, Subhūti, grasping at this emptiness and the absence of mental characteristics, challenged the Buddha:
"This mind is no-mind; it is empty, non-existent, and like an illusion. How can it attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
The Buddha asked Subhūti in return:
"Do you see this mark of the samādhi of the empty mind as being like an illusion?
Subhūti had this thought:
"If the mind is empty like an illusion, how can it be seen?
If it can be seen, then it is not empty.
To this, he replied:
"No," the Buddha said.
"If the mind is empty and non-existent, do you perceive within it any conceptual proliferation regarding existence or non-existence?"
He replied, "No.
[The Buddha asked:
"Apart from this mind that is empty, non-existent, and like an illusion, do you see any other dharma that can attain the unsurpassed path?"
He replied, "I do not see it.
Since it is neither seen nor obtainable, how could there be any dharma that either exists or does not exist?
Because all dharmas are ultimately detached and ultimately empty, they do not fall into existence nor do they fall into non-existence;
if a dharma does not fall into either existence or non-existence, it is then ultimately non-existent, and thus one should not be able to attain the Unsurpassed Way.
For this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately characterized by detachment, because both the views of existence and non-existence are seen to be errors.
From the *dhyānapāramitā* up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is likewise ultimately characterized by detachment.
If a dharma is ultimately detached, it cannot be seen, cannot be cultivated, cannot be abandoned, and cannot be realized;
practicing this dharma results in nothing further to be attained, because it is ultimately detached.
“World-Honored One!
Now, the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately detached, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is ultimately detached; how can that which is ultimately detached attain that which is ultimately detached?”
"If even a single dharma that is ultimately detached cannot be apprehended, how much less so two that are detached!
It is like using a finger to touch space; because space has no tangibility, the finger cannot touch it, let alone two things both lacking tangibility!"
It is also like space and nirvāṇa.

Since the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached and unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is ultimately detached, how can one attain detachment by means of that which is itself detached?
Knowing that Subhūti was speaking in accordance with the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Buddha approved his words, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
He then explained the causal conditions: "Subhūti!
If the perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is ultimately detached, it is by these causal conditions that [enlightenment] can be attained."

Why is this? If a single dharma were to possess a fixed characteristic that was not empty, it would be a permanent dharma with the characteristic of non-arising; it would proceed from the future to the present, and from the present to the past.

If there were no real characteristic of arising, there would be no characteristic of cessation; if there were no arising or cessation, there would be no Four Noble Truths; if there were no Four Noble Truths, there would be no Jewel of the Dharma; because the Jewel of the Dharma would be absent, there would also be no Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—for the Jewel of the Dharma is itself Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If there were no Jewel of the Dharma, there would be no Jewel of the Buddha; if there were no Buddha-Dharma, there would be no Jewel of the Saṅgha; and if there were no Three Jewels, there would be no all-encompassing dharmas. Because such faults as these would follow, [the view that dharmas arise from conditions is untenable].
Being ultimately free from marks, one then attains unimpeded penetration.
If one speaks of ultimate detachment, one should know that this is also detached from emptiness;
if one is not detached from emptiness, it cannot be called ultimate detachment.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately detached, it can attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
although one does not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi apart from the Prajñāpāramitā, nor does one attain detachment through a duality of detachments."
Because it is ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), one should not raise objections.
Subhūti, knowing the profound characteristics of what the Buddha had taught, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the profound meaning."
The Buddha affirmed his words:
"This bodhisattva is able to perform a difficult task—being able to practice such profound meaning without realizing the two vehicles."
"Why is this? It is because it is difficult for a bodhisattva, with a single-minded focus on the wisdom of benefit, to enter deeply into emptiness without realizing nirvāṇa.
Subhūti said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, this is not difficult.

Why is that? Because such a person does not apprehend this profound meaning as a fixed characteristic that can be realized; they do not apprehend the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they apprehend one who realizes it. Who, then, could realize the profound meaning?"
If one does not realize this profound meaning, who could ever attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-attainment.
"By practicing this path, one illuminates all dharmas.
He asked: "The Buddha said it is 'difficult,' yet Subhūti says it is 'not difficult.'"
The meaning of teacher and disciple should be the same; why then do they contradict one another?
The answer is:
The Buddha speaks according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), whereas Subhūti speaks according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The Buddha said that a bodhisattva attains this profound meaning, yet Subhūti said that a bodhisattva does not even attain this profound meaning.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha spoke through Subhūti, saying:
"There are those who, upon hearing of difficult matters, give rise to the resolve for enlightenment; therefore, difficult matters are spoken of."
"There are those who, hearing of difficult matters, withdraw and retreat; therefore, it is said that there are no difficulties.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-attainment;
abiding in this practice, one penetrates all phenomena without obstruction.
Subhūti said:

"If, upon hearing such a teaching—that there is ultimate detachment, that there is no dharma to be realized, no one who realizes it, and likewise no prajñā or anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—a bodhisattva is not startled, does not become despondent, and penetrates this without obstruction, this is called practicing the prajñāpāramitā."
"One who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* is said to practice truly and practice deeply.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not perceive the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they perceive themselves practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*; they do not perceive *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor do they perceive any dharma by which *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* can be attained; they are entirely without conceptual discrimination."
Because this bodhisattva dwells securely within the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena, they do not make such discriminations as saying:
"The two vehicles are far from me; the Buddha-way is near to me."
In this context, analogies such as space are taught; these various analogies are intended to clarify the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Although the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, if there is something cultivated within it, one can accomplish the task at hand.
"Even as a wooden puppet, whatever task it is made to perform, it can accomplish.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
'Is it only that prajñā is without discrimination, or are all the pāramitās also without discrimination?'"
If only prajñā were empty and without discrimination, while the other pāramitās possessed signs, then the bodhisattva path would be differentiated and unequal.
Furthermore, it was stated in the first chapter:
"When practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), there is no giver, no receiver, and no gift.
How can it now be said that these are distinct?
"If these five things are all empty, then there is no discrimination, no six names, and nothing that can be practiced.
Subhūti said:
"The five pāramitās are also empty and without discrimination."
Those who have first resolved their minds but have not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas possess conceptual discrimination.
It is, for example, like the four rivers which have distinct names before they merge into the great ocean; once they have entered the great ocean, there is no longer any distinction.
So it is with the Bodhisattva: within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) there is distinction, but in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there is no discrimination.
Śāriputra asked:
"From form up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even up to the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), is there likewise no conceptual differentiation?"
"If these dharmas are empty and without distinction, how can there be the distinctions of the six realms of existence?
How can there be the distinctions from the stage of a *srotāpanna* up to the path of a Buddha?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:

"Although all phenomena are ultimately empty and without differentiation, sentient beings, with their deluded and inverted minds, give rise to actions of body, speech, and mind; according to these actions, they receive bodies and the karmic retributions thereof."
"Greed is the root; however, being oppressed by desire, one gives rise to a mind of attachment. All phenomena have no fixed characteristics.
As for the retribution of karma, it refers to the six realms of existence."
Therefore, one should know that emptiness and non-discrimination are its true foundation;
it is only because of inversion and unreality that the distinctions of the six realms of existence arise.

Furthermore, the noble ones such as the srotāpannas are also born from the dharma of ultimate emptiness and non-discrimination; that is to say, the dharma of severing the three fetters is called the fruit of srotāpanna.

The three fetters are themselves inversions; awakening to these inversions and removing them is called "abandonment. Therefore, the dharma of abandonment is itself emptiness, devoid of discrimination.
From the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one is conventionally designated as a "person," and because they have attained this dharma, it is called the fruit of srotāpanna;
therefore, one should know that both the person who is a srotāpanna and the fruit are ultimately empty and without differentiation.
This applies even unto the Buddha and the Buddha-way as well.
Herein the causal conditions are explained:

"It is not only that there is no discrimination in the present; because all discriminations of the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have been severed, they have entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, such that there is not the slightest fixed characteristic of a dharma that can be discriminated."
"All dharmas are ultimately empty because they enter through the gateways of suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality.
For this reason, it is said that "the dharma of causes and conditions is profound," because one enters through the gateway of this samādhi.

A bodhisattva should practice the non-conceptual *prajñāpāramitā* in this way; by practicing the non-conceptual *prajñāpāramitā*, they attain the non-conceptual Dharma, which is to say, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Chapter 65: Praising [the Perfection of Wisdom] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter "Praising," Number Sixty-Five [Sūtra] Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, is he practicing the true dharma?"
"Is it that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the dharma of non-reality?
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he practices the dharma of non-reality."
Why is this? Because this *prajñāpāramitā* lacks reality, and even up to the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-knowledge) lacks reality.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, even "lack of reality" cannot be apprehended, let alone "reality"!
"Even when practicing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), no truly real dharma can be apprehended; how much less so a 'true reality'!
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms had this thought:

"Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practice the equality of dharmas according to the meaning taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—they are worthy of our prostration!"
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"For bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it is not difficult not to realize the stage of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha within the state of equality."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are adorned with the great vow:
"I shall deliver immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.
To know that sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable and yet to deliver them—this is indeed difficult!
"O sons of the gods!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* make this vow:
'I shall deliver all sentient beings.'"
"Sentient beings are in truth unobtainable; for this person who wishes to deliver sentient beings, it is like wishing to deliver empty space.
Why is this? Because empty space is detached, one should know that sentient beings are likewise detached."
Because space is empty, one should know that sentient beings are also empty;
because space lacks solidity, one should know that sentient beings also lack solidity;
because space is deceptive, one should know that sentient beings are also deceptive.
O sons of the gods!
For this reason, you should know that the deeds performed by a bodhisattva are difficult.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings who do not exist, they undertake great adornment; such a person makes a vow for the sake of sentient beings, as if wishing to battle with empty space.
Once this bodhisattva has made the vow, they do not apprehend a sentient being while making the vow for the sake of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are detached, one should know that the great vow is likewise detached.
Because sentient beings are deceptive, one should know that the great vows are also deceptive.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this teaching and their mind is neither startled nor discouraged, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? The detachment from form is itself the detachment from sentient beings;
the detachment from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself the detachment from sentient beings.
The detachment from form is the detachment from the six pāramitās;
the detachment from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the detachment from the six pāramitās.
Up to and including the detachment from all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), this is the detachment from the six pāramitās.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing that all these dharmas are devoid of marks, is not startled, does not sink, is not terrified, and does not fear, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"For what reason does the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind not sink within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent, it does not sink; because the *prajñāpāramitā* is detached, it does not sink; because the *prajñāpāramitā* is quiescent, it does not sink.”
World-Honored One!
For this reason, the bodhisattva’s mind does not sink within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?
This Bodhisattva cannot be submerged, cannot meet with destruction, and cannot find a place of submersion, because all these dharmas are ultimately unobtainable.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this Dharma, is not startled, does not sink into despondency, is not terrified, and is not afraid, it should be known that this bodhisattva is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? Because the one who perishes, the act of perishing, and the place of perishing—all these phenomena are unattainable.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, all the devas, including Śakra Devendra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and the world-protector devas, pay him homage.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Not only do Śakra-devānām-indra, the various devas, Brahmā-rāja, and the various devas, as well as the lords of the world and their respective devas, pay homage to this bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā; beyond these, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas all likewise pay homage to this bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Subhūti! The immeasurable Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions also keep in mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom.
You should know that such a bodhisattva is like a Buddha.

Subhūti! If all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were each to become a Māra, and each of those Māras were further to manifest as Māras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—even all these Māras together could not obstruct a Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
[Treatise] Commentary:
At that time, having heard the aforementioned Dharma of non-discriminative characteristics, Śāriputra was filled with great joy and asked Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, is he practicing the true Dharma?"
"Is it that one practices a dharma that lacks reality?
A "real dharma" is that which is definitively established and unchanging; such is what can be grasped and clung to.
If it is not real, it is false and deceptive speech.
Subhūti constantly delights in practicing profound emptiness, and his mind is free from hindrances; therefore, he replied:
"One who practices Prajñā is practicing that which has no reality."
Why is this? Because the prajñāpāramitā is empty, lacks fixed characteristics, and is without discrimination.
This applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

When a bodhisattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, even those conditioned phenomena that are deceptive—which they previously practiced and clung to within saṃsāra—cannot be apprehended; how much less can one apprehend the prajñāpāramitā, which arises from deceptive causes and conditions and is a phenomenon to which one does not cling?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates all worlds as unreal and does not cling even to this Prajñāpāramitā.
It is said to be real only from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), reality itself cannot be apprehended, let alone unreality!
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms spoke with joy:
"All those who have resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva should be honored and revered!
They are able to perform what is difficult to do; they are able to practice the foremost, profound meaning without realizing it as a final fruit."
"The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is itself the dharma of equality; it is merely spoken of by different names.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"It is not difficult for a bodhisattva not to realize the dharma of equality."
For a bodhisattva who wishes to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet finds that sentient beings are ultimately non-apprehendable—this is indeed difficult! Why is this?
To wish to deliver sentient beings is to wish to deliver empty space.
"Because space is detached, sentient beings are also detached;
because space is deceptive and unreal, sentient beings are also deceptive and unreal.
[The interlocutor] asked:
One does not realize the equality of dharmas, yet one delivers sentient beings who are ultimately empty; since both of these are ultimately empty, why say that one is difficult and the other is not?
Answer: Sentient beings, being deceptive and merely provisional designations, are the objects of attachment;
the dharma of equality, being unconditioned, is not an object of attachment.
Sentient beings arise from the conventional designations of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is difficult to remain unattached to that which is the locus of inverted attachments;
it is not difficult to remain unattached to that which is already a state of non-attachment.
For this reason, it is said thus:
"Because sentient beings are empty, the great adornment is also empty;
if the great adornment is empty, yet one is able to resolve to attain enlightenment, that is difficult."

If a bodhisattva hears this meaning of the foremost equality—that the deliverance of sentient beings and the great adornments are all ultimately empty—and yet their mind is neither startled nor discouraged;
It is like a well-trained horse that is not startled upon seeing its own reflection. Why is this?
Because it knows that the reflection arises from its own body.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: knowing ultimate emptiness because [all things] arise from the false conjunction of conditioned phenomena.
When the Bodhisattva hears these matters, they are not startled and do not sink into despondency; this is called practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because phenomena such as form are detached, sentient beings are also detached.
This detachment is called emptiness.
If sentient beings were empty while phenomena were not empty, there would necessarily be fear.
If phenomena are also empty, there is no basis for the arising of fear.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing that all these phenomena are devoid of characteristics, does not feel fear, this is also called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Previously, having heard that sentient beings are empty, one was not afraid; now, having heard that dharmas are empty, one is not afraid.
If, upon hearing these two kinds of emptiness, one is not afraid, this constitutes the true practice of Prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding the passage, "The Buddha asked Subhūti: 'For what reason does the bodhisattva’s mind not sink?
A questioner asks:
Since the Buddha is the Omniscient One, why does he inquire about his disciple’s state of mind—specifically, why it is neither startled nor sinking?
The answer is:
Because those in the assembly had doubts, yet out of reverence and awe they did not dare to ask; therefore, the Buddha questioned them.

Furthermore, this meaning of the foremost equality is extremely profound and difficult to attain; since it should have been submerged within the depths [of their understanding] but was not, he thus tested Subhūti with a question.
Furthermore, the Buddha has appointed Subhūti as the master of the Dharma discourse; according to the proper method for listeners, one should pose questions and challenges. He asks:
Since the Buddha is omniscient, why does he not act as the master of the discourse himself, but instead causes Subhūti to speak?
He replied:

"There are people among the assembly who, because the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and boundless while our own intellectual power is limited, do not dare to voice their doubts when they have them."
For the sake of these people, he commands Subhūti to speak.
A question is asked:
"If that is so, why does he not command the great bodhisattvas to speak?"
The answer is:
The wisdom of the great bodhisattvas is also vast and inconceivable; because their majestic virtue is so profound, one does not dare to pose difficult questions to them.
Furthermore, some say:
Because Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas have eternally exhausted all traces of ignorance bound to the three realms without remainder, they are able to preach the Dharma according to reality;

whereas although Bodhisattvas have extensively accumulated merit, because their outflows are not yet exhausted, they may sometimes be untrustworthy, and for this reason they are not commanded [to preach].
Question:
If that is so, why were Śāriputra, who is foremost in wisdom, and the other great disciples not summoned? Answer:
This matter has already been answered previously: namely, that Subhūti delights in the practice of emptiness and is particularly skilled at explaining it;
because the *Prajñāpāramitā* explains emptiness, it causes Subhūti to speak.

Subhūti addressed the Buddha: “All dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent; because they are non-existent, they are devoid of self-characteristics; because they are devoid of characteristics, they are eternally quiescent; because they are eternally quiescent, there is no recollection or conceptual discrimination. Therefore, a bodhisattva should neither be startled nor sink into despondency—for the one who sinks, the place of sinking, and the dharma of sinking are all unobtainable.”
"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing these matters, is neither startled nor discouraged, this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Having replied thus, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To practice in such a manner is also called practicing the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva can practice in this way, all the devas, Śakra, and the lords of the world pay homage to that bodhisattva; the earth deities, the deities in the void, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Trāyastriṃśa devas, with Śakra as their leader, all together pay homage to this bodhisattva.”
The Brahmā King is the lord of sentient beings in the Brahma-world within the first dhyāna;
as for the "lords of the world," these are the other celestial kings of the desire realm.
Because many sentient beings have faith in the existence of these heavens, Subhūti says that one should pay homage.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas relinquish their own happiness in order to benefit sentient beings,
whereas these three kinds of devas seek only their own happiness.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It is not only these three classes of devas who pay homage; all the devas of the Pure Abodes, such as those of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, who possess pure single-mindedness, likewise pay homage."
"The devas of the desire realm, because their minds are largely attached to sensual desires, find it insufficiently noble to pay homage;
the devas of the first dhyāna have the distraction of vitarka and vicāra, so it is likewise not considered marvelous.
As for the devas of the higher realms, their minds are pure, yet they pay homage to the Bodhisattva because of his great merit; therefore, this is truly difficult."
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva can practice prajñā in this way, they will be held in the thoughts of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions.
The causes and conditions for the Buddhas’ mindfulness are as previously explained.

Now the Buddha says that this is the fruit of retribution for being mindful of these bodhisattvas by all Buddhas; that is to say, one should know that such a bodhisattva is like a Buddha, because they will certainly reach the path of Buddhahood without falling back.
Why is this so? Because even Māras as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot destroy this bodhisattva, as explained at length in the sutra.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 78.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Praise,
Part Sixty-Five (Continued), Fascicle Seventy-Nine.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
[Sūtra] “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes two dharmas, Māra cannot destroy him.”
What are these two?
Contemplating that all phenomena are empty, yet not abandoning any sentient beings. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these two dharmas, Māra cannot destroy them.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are another two dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes, such that Māra cannot destroy them."
