What are these two?
Acting according to what one says, and being kept in mind by all Buddhas.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these two dharmas, Māra cannot destroy them.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices in this way, all these devas come to where the bodhisattva is, drawing near, inquiring, exhorting, and consoling him, saying:
"O son of good family!"
"You shall soon attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without long delay.
Son of good family!
You should constantly practice these modes of conduct: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."

Why is this? Good son! By practicing this conduct, you shall act as a protector for those beings who have no protector; you shall act as a refuge for those beings who have no refuge; you shall act as a savior for those beings who have no savior; you shall act as the ultimate path for those beings who lack the ultimate path; you shall act as a home for those beings who have no home; you shall act as an island for those beings who have no island; you shall provide illumination for those in darkness; and you shall act as eyes for those who are blind.

Why is this? When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, the immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions, while preaching the Dharma amidst great assemblies, praise and extol the names and clans of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"The bodhisattva named so-and-so has accomplished the merit of the perfection of wisdom."
"Subhūti! Just as I now, while preaching the Dharma, personally extol the names of the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa and the Bodhisattva Śikhin;

furthermore, there are other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā and purely cultivate the brahma-faring within the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha—I likewise extol the names and clans of those bodhisattvas."

Subhūti! It is also as when the Buddhas currently residing in the eastern direction are preaching the Dharma; therein there may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have purely cultivated the brahma-faring, and the Buddha likewise rejoices and personally extols and praises these bodhisattvas.
It is the same for the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, from their first aspiration to fulfill the Buddha-way, proceed until they attain all-knowledge;
when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they also joyfully proclaim and praise these bodhisattvas.
"Why is this? Because the conduct of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly difficult; they practice so as not to sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do the Buddhas praise and extol when they preach the Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they praise and extol the *avaivartika* bodhisattvas.
Subhūti asked: “What kind of *avaivartika* bodhisattva is praised by the Buddhas?”
The Buddha said:
“Just as the practices and studies undertaken by the Buddha Akṣobhya when he was a bodhisattva, so too do all bodhisattvas train;
these non-retrogressive bodhisattvas are joyfully praised by all Buddhas when they preach the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and have faith-understanding that all phenomena are unarisen, yet they have not yet attained the dharma of the patience regarding non-arising;
they have faith-understanding that all phenomena are empty, yet they have not yet attained the dharma of the patience regarding non-arising."
They believe and understand that all dharmas are deceptive, unreal, and insubstantial, yet they have not yet attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Subhūti, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these rejoice and praise themselves, extolling their own names and clans.

Subhūti! If any bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, rejoice and praise themselves, these bodhisattvas will extinguish the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and shall receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, rejoices and praises themselves, that bodhisattva shall abide in the stage of avaivartika;
having abided in this stage, they shall attain sarvajñā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, has a mind that is clear and sharp, free from doubt and regret, and thinks:
'This matter is just as the Buddha has taught it. "
This bodhisattva shall also hear this Prajñāpāramitā extensively from Akṣobhya Buddha and the various bodhisattvas, and shall also have faith and understanding;
having attained faith and understanding, they shall abide in the stage of avaivartika, just as the Buddha has taught.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Merely hearing the Prajñāpāramitā brings great benefit; how much more so when one has faith and understanding!
Having attained faith and understanding, one dwells as taught and practices as taught.
"Having thus explained dwelling and practice, one dwells within omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If the Buddha says that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells as described and practices as described, thereby abiding in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
yet if a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no dharma that can be apprehended, how can they abide in omniscience?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the suchness of all dharmas, dwelling in sarvajñā. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Apart from Suchness, no other dharma can be apprehended;
who, then, dwells within Suchness? Having dwelt within Suchness, who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Who, abiding in suchness, shall preach the Dharma?
Since even suchness cannot be apprehended, how much less can one abide in suchness to attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi!
Who, abiding in suchness, shall preach the Dharma?
"It is impossible!
The Buddha told Subhūti: "As you have said:"
"Apart from suchness, there is no other dharma; who, then, could abide within suchness?
Having abided within suchness, how could one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Who, abiding in suchness, shall preach the Dharma?
Since even suchness itself cannot be apprehended, how much less can one abide in suchness to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Who, then, abiding in suchness, shall preach the Dharma?
"It is impossible!
The Buddha said, "It is so!"
"So it is, Subhūti! Apart from suchness, there is no other dharma to be found; who, then, could abide within suchness?"
Having dwelt within suchness, will one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Who, dwelling within suchness, shall preach the Dharma?
Since suchness itself cannot be apprehended, how much less can one dwell within suchness and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Who dwells within suchness and teaches the Dharma?
Why is this? Because within this suchness, arising is unapprehendable, cessation is unapprehendable, and abiding or alteration are unapprehendable.
If the arising, ceasing, and alteration of abiding of phenomena cannot be apprehended, then who therein would abide in suchness?
And who, having abided in suchness, would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Who could abide in suchness and preach the Dharma?
Such a thing is impossible!
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is most difficult for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to do; they seek to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the profound prajñā-pāramitā.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
There is no one who dwells within suchness, nor is there anyone who shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there anyone who preaches the Dharma.
"In this matter, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is not startled, does not sink, is not terrified, does not fear, does not doubt, and does not regret.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"As Kauśika has said:"

"It is most difficult for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas to act thus; within this profound Dharma, their minds are not startled, do not sink, are not terrified, do not fear, and have neither doubt nor regret."
"Kauśika! In the emptiness of all dharmas, who is startled and who sinks?
Who is terrified and who is afraid?"
"Who doubts? Who regrets?
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra said to Subhūti:
"What Subhūti has spoken concerns only emptiness; it is without any obstruction."
"Just as when one shoots upward into the air, the arrow travels without obstruction;
so too is Subhūti’s teaching of the Dharma without obstruction.
[Treatise] Explanation:
The assembly wondered:
"By what causes and conditions has the Bodhisattva attained such power that Māra cannot destroy him?
The Buddha replied:
"There are two causes and conditions by which Māra cannot destroy them:
first, contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena; second, not abandoning any sentient beings."
"By reason of the sun and the moon, all things are moistened and brought forth.
If there were only the moon and no sun, then all things would become damp and decay;
if there were only the sun and no moon, then all things would be scorched and withered."
Because the sun and moon harmonize, all things reach maturity.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva, who possesses two paths:
first, compassion; second, emptiness.
With a compassionate heart, one feels pity for sentient beings and vows to deliver them;
yet when the mind of emptiness arises, it extinguishes this heart of pity.
If there is only the heart of pity without wisdom, the mind sinks into the inversion of perceiving sentient beings where no sentient beings exist.
If one possesses only the mind of emptiness and abandons the compassionate resolve to deliver sentient beings, one falls into the extreme of nihilism.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that these two matters must be employed together: although one contemplates the emptiness of all things, one does not abandon sentient beings; and although one feels compassion for sentient beings, one does not abandon the emptiness of all things.
Contemplating that all phenomena are empty, one does not cling to emptiness because emptiness itself is empty; therefore, this does not hinder one’s compassion for sentient beings.

Contemplating compassion for sentient beings, one likewise does not cling to sentient beings nor grasp at the marks of sentient beings, but simply feels compassion for them and guides them into emptiness. Thus, although one practices compassion, it does not hinder emptiness.
Although one practices emptiness, because one does not grasp at the mark of emptiness, it does not hinder the mind of compassion; these two are like the sun and moon, which require one another.

The various devas and spirits despise those who speak falsely; if a bodhisattva does not act according to what they have said, then the five kinds of Vajradhara deities will abandon them and no longer provide protection, allowing evil ghosts to find an opportunity.
Such a person delights in giving rise to evil thoughts; because of these evil thoughts, they produce evil karma; because they produce evil karma, they fall into the evil realms.
A bodhisattva who is not held in the mindfulness of the Buddhas will have their roots of goodness decay and wither;
it is like fish eggs that, if not attended to by their mother, rot and fail to hatch.
Therefore it is said:
"Acting as one speaks, and being mindful of by all Buddhas—
because these two qualities are attained, one cannot be destroyed."

"If a bodhisattva can thus truly practice the perfection of wisdom, Māra cannot destroy them; their merit and wisdom increase, and the devas come to attend upon them, inquire of them, comfort them, and encourage them, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
"You shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before long.
For this reason, you should constantly practice the conduct of emptiness. He asked:
Question: Since the various devas have not yet attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), how can they bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon a bodhisattva? Answer:

The devas possess long lifespans; having heard from past buddhas that such conduct leads to receiving a prediction, they now see that the bodhisattva possesses such conduct and thus speak of it. This is because one knows the fruit by seeing the cause.

The devas see that this bodhisattva practices the seal of the three gates of liberation and also concurrently cultivates a heart of compassion toward sentient beings; for this reason, they say, "He will become a Buddha before long."
"The meaning of 'you provide protection for those beings who have no protection, and you provide refuge for those who have no refuge,' and so forth, is as previously explained.

If a bodhisattva can practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, the immeasurable Buddhas currently teaching the Dharma in the ten directions will proclaim and praise that person’s name, just as I now proclaim the names of the Bodhisattva Ratnalakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Śikhin, and the bodhisattvas in the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha."
Furthermore, when the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Dharma, they extol the various sublime practices of Bodhisattvas.

When a Bodhisattva is able to accord with the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as it has been taught, the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise use that Bodhisattva as an analogy while preaching the Dharma, saying:

"In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a world, although this Bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, he is able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner; therefore, his merit is rare and marvelous."
"Just as a great king has a great general who does not spare his own life or limb, who possesses skillful means to defeat enemies, and is constantly praised by the king;

so too is the Bodhisattva: observing ultimate emptiness, he does not spare his own body, he destroys the thieves of the afflictions, and possessing skillful means, he does not realize [nirvana] prematurely, but teaches and transforms sentient beings, being praised by all Buddhas."

Although the Buddhas possess no mind of attachment and no discrimination between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, they regard all arhats and non-Buddhists with neither hatred nor affection; yet, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they praise virtuous people, extol wholesome dharmas, and censure what is unwholesome.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to cause sentient beings to rely upon virtuous persons, so that their minds may follow wholesome dharmas and enable them to transcend the world.
Question:
In which sūtras is it stated that two bodhisattvas were praised by the Buddha?
The answer is:
the Buddha’s sūtras are immeasurable.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, kings of evil and false views will arise, burning the sūtras and the Dharma, destroying stūpas and monasteries, and harming the śramaṇas.

Five hundred years later, during the impure period of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), because Arhats and bodhisattvas with supernormal powers will be difficult to encounter, and because there will be few practitioners and recipients, the profound sūtras will no longer remain entirely in Jambudvīpa; the devas, nāgas, and spirits will take them away.
Question:

Why is it that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others are not praised, while only these two bodhisattvas are extolled?
The answer is:
These two bodhisattvas have not yet attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), yet they are able to act in a manner resembling that patience.
Such a thing must certainly exist; they cannot be destroyed by any of the followers of Māra, and for this reason, the Buddha praised them as rare and marvelous.

Furthermore, these two bodhisattvas possess pure great vows and practices, as well as profound and vast compassion; they do not expect to quickly become Buddhas for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Because they possess such merits as these, the Buddha praises them.
Furthermore, the merits of Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Avalokiteśvara are extremely great, and these are known to all;
however, the merits of these two bodhisattvas [in this context] are not yet known by people, and therefore they are being extolled.
The bodhisattvas in the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha all emulate Akṣobhya Buddha; from the time they first resolved their minds, they have practiced pure conduct free from admixture.
The bodhisattvas born there all emulate his practice; for this reason, it is said that the bodhisattvas of Akṣobhya Buddha’s world praise his virtue.
Furthermore, just as the Buddhas of the ten directions also extol the sublime Bodhisattvas of all worlds, so too did Śākyamuni Buddha extol these two Bodhisattvas.

What are they? From the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the tenth stage, the Buddha praises these bodhisattvas for performing what is exceedingly difficult: they are able to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
In this context, Subhūti asks:
"Which bodhisattvas does the Buddha, when teaching the Dharma, praise and extol by mentioning their names? He asks:
The Buddha has already spoken previously; why does Subhūti ask again?
The answer is:
at first the Buddha spoke of "great bodhisattvas," and later he referred to "all bodhisattvas, from the initial generation of the mind up to the tenth stage."
For this reason, Subhūti questioned the Buddha:
"Whom among the bodhisattvas does the Buddha praise by mentioning their names?
The Buddha replied:
"Although the Buddha loves and cherishes all bodhisattvas equally, he proclaims the names of those among them whose virtue and conduct are preeminent.
Which bodhisattvas are praised by the Buddha?

Just as when the Buddha Akṣobhya first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he practiced pure conduct without ceasing or resting until he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; such bodhisattvas as these are praised by the Buddha.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and have not yet entered the bodhisattva stage; yet, by the power of practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they constantly contemplate and deliberate, seeking the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. They are able to believe in, understand, and endure that all phenomena possess the mark of non-arising, are empty, deceptive, and lack solidity.
The Buddha names and praises those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who possess such characteristics as these.
That which is deceptive, unreal, and insubstantial—all such things are gateways to impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
That all dharmas are empty is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*).
That all dharmas are unarisen is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas, which extinguishes all conceptualizations.
Furthermore, that they are deceptive, unreal, and not solid is the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
The emptiness of all phenomena is the gate of liberation of emptiness;
the non-arising of all phenomena is the gate of liberation of signlessness.
Such are the three distinctions.

This person has emerged from the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*) but has not yet attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); they have emerged from the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) but have not yet entered the dharmas of the noble ones (*ārya*). Yet, they are able to believe in and accept the dharmas of the noble ones, appearing as one who has attained the state of a noble one; therefore, this is rare.
Just as the Buddha praises the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva who is able to sever the two stages and receive the prediction of enlightenment,
so too is this person praised by the Buddha in the same way.

A person with such characteristics, although not yet having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), is praised by name by all Buddhas due to the power of their wisdom;
now, because the power of their faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is preeminent, the Buddha likewise praises them by name.
What are they? Namely:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound prajñā, has a mind that is clear and sharp, free from doubt or regret, and forms this thought:
"This matter is just as the Buddha has taught."
Question: Since this bodhisattva has already attained faith and understanding in the *prajñāpāramitā*, why does he still hear it from Akṣobhya Buddha and the various bodhisattvas?
The answer is:
This person hears of the pure conduct practiced by Akṣobhya Buddha when he was a bodhisattva;
having heard this, they wish to emulate the conduct of Akṣobhya Buddha.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Because this person has attained the power of faith in this regard and the power of wisdom in that regard, they shall abide in the stage of *avaivartika*."

Although this person has not yet attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), by the power of wisdom they attain a state like that of an *avaivartika* and are praised by all Buddhas;
by the power of faith they attain a state like that of an *avaivartika* and are praised by all Buddhas.

If merely hearing the Prajñāpāramitā yields such benefits, how much more so for those who believe and accept it, and practice according to what is taught, gradually abiding within all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)!
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"Since all dharmas are empty in nature and unattainable, how does a bodhisattva abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha said:
"Abiding as it is.
"As it is" (tathatā) is precisely emptiness.
When a bodhisattva abides in this ultimate emptiness, it is called abiding in sarvajñā (omniscience).
In this context, Subhūti asks the Buddha:
"Apart from suchness (tathatā), no other dharma can be apprehended; who, then, abides within suchness?
This continues until he says, "Such a thing is impossible," as explained at length in the sūtra.
The Buddha affirmed what Subhūti had said and explained that suchness (*tathatā*) is also empty by way of causes and conditions, saying:
"In this suchness, arising, ceasing, and abiding-change cannot be apprehended. If a dharma lacks these three characteristics, it is ultimately empty; how, then, could it abide?"
"If one were to dwell within this and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and then preach the Dharma, such a thing is impossible!

Śakra Devānām-indra, wishing to grasp a fixed characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *prajñā*, heard the Buddha and Subhūti speaking of the signless (*animitta*) and its non-apprehensibility; therefore, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare!..."
World-Honored One!
This Prajñā is profound, and what these bodhisattvas undertake is extremely difficult, as they desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?

This Suchness is ultimately empty; apart from Suchness, there is no bodhisattva who dwells within this Suchness and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma called "Buddha. Those who preach the Dharma and the sentient beings they deliver do not depart from Suchness, nor is there a place of extraction called nirvana, for all dharmas eternally abide in the characteristic of Suchness.
When a bodhisattva hears these matters, their mind feels no doubt or regret; this is what makes it difficult!
Although they believe that all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet they desire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, practicing with diligence without ceasing or resting—this is what is difficult.
Subhūti said to Śakra:
"If all phenomena are ultimately empty and non-existent, from what could doubt arise?
What difficulty could there be?"
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, was delighted in his heart and thought:
"Subhūti truly delights in expounding the dharma of emptiness;
whatever Subhūti explains, he explains entirely as matters of emptiness."
"Although other matters such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are spoken of, their meaning all tends toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
if there is any challenge or question, it cannot create an obstruction, because emptiness itself is empty.
If someone challenges emptiness, Subhūti has already deconstructed emptiness; thus, within both existence and non-existence, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
It is like shooting an arrow upward into the air.
Space is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), and the arrow is the wisdom of Subhūti.
What he has spoken is like an arrow moving unimpeded through space; when its momentum is exhausted, it falls of its own accord, yet this does not mean that space itself has been exhausted.
Subhūti ceased his preaching because the purpose for which he had set out to teach the Dharma was accomplished; it was not because the Dharma itself has come to an end.
It is like a person who, though possessing a sharp arrow, cannot penetrate a wall with it;
likewise, though a person possesses sharp wisdom, if they harbor wrong views and are attached to existence, they will be obstructed and unable to pass through.
For this reason, Subhūti speaks of the dharma that is unobstructed and unimpeded.
Chapter Sixty-Six: Entrustment *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter Sixty-Six: Entrustment [Sutra] At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"When I speak and answer in this way, does it accord with the Dharma?
Is it a correct answer?
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
“Kauśika! What you have said and what you have answered are indeed entirely in accordance [with the truth].
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!

Everything that Subhūti delights in expounding is for the sake of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it is for the sake of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.”
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
"When the bhikṣu Subhūti practices emptiness, even the pāramitā of giving (dāna-pāramitā) cannot be apprehended, let alone one who practices the pāramitā of giving!"
Even the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended, let alone the one who practices the perfection of wisdom!
Even the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended, let alone the one who cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness!
Even the eightfold noble path cannot be apprehended, let alone one who practices the eightfold noble path!
Even dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and concentrations cannot be apprehended, let alone one who practices dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and concentrations!
The ten powers of a Buddha cannot be apprehended, much less the one who cultivates the ten powers of a Buddha!
The four fearlessnesses cannot be apprehended, much less the one who can give rise to the four fearlessnesses!
The four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) cannot be apprehended, much less one who can give rise to the four unhindered knowledges!
Great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) cannot be apprehended, much less one who practices great loving-kindness and great compassion!
The eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) cannot be apprehended, much less one who gives rise to the eighteen unique qualities!
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) cannot be apprehended, much less one who attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment!
All-knowledge is unattainable, how much less so one who attains all-knowledge!
A Tathāgata is unattainable, how much less so one who shall become a Tathāgata!
The dharma of non-arising is unattainable, how much less so one who realizes the dharma of non-arising!
The thirty-two marks cannot be apprehended, let alone one who possesses the thirty-two marks!
The eighty secondary characteristics cannot be apprehended, let alone one who possesses the eighty secondary characteristics!
Why is this? Kausika!
The bhikṣu Subhūti practices the detachment from all dharmas, the non-apprehension of all dharmas, the emptiness of all dharmas, the signlessness of all dharmas, and the wishlessness of all dharmas.

Kauśika! This is the practice of the bhikṣu Subhūti; if one were to compare it to the practice of the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it would not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor ten-thousand-millionth part, nor indeed could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

Why is this? Excluding the practice of the Buddhas, this practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the prajñāpāramitā is the most honored, the most wondrous, and the most supreme among all the practices of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to become the most supreme among all sentient beings should practice this conduct of the prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Kauśika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā, they transcend the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the rank of bodhisattvas, are able to fulfill the Buddha-dharmas, attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies, and become Buddhas.
In this assembly, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven scattered celestial mandārava flowers over the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

At that time, eight hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats, scattered flowers over the Buddha, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms, placed their right knees upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"We shall practice this supreme conduct, which cannot be practiced by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas!
At that time, the Buddha, knowing the mental activities of the bhikṣus, smiled.
Just as is the nature of all Buddhas' dharmas,

various colored lights— blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and pale green— issued from his mouth, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm, circling the Buddha three times, and then re-entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition do you smile?"
"The Buddhas do not smile without cause or condition. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These eight hundred bhikṣus shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi during the Star-Constellation Eon (Tārakā-kalpa). Their buddha-names shall all be the same, 'Scattering Flowers' (Puṣpavikiraṇa); their assemblies of bhikṣus, their worlds, and their lifespans shall all be equal. Each shall pass ten thousand years before leaving the household life and becoming a buddha. At that time, five-colored celestial flowers will constantly rain down upon all those worlds."
"For this reason, Ānanda,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the supreme practice should practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.

"If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that these bodhisattvas have died among humans and been reborn here, or have died in Tuṣita Heaven and come to be born here;
they have extensively heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* either among humans or in Tuṣita Heaven."
Ānanda! I see that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice this profound prajñāpāramitā. Ānanda!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive, uphold, read, recite, draw near to, and correctly contemplate it, and furthermore teach and practice the Bodhisattva path through the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that these Bodhisattvas have personally heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Buddha, and so on up to drawing near to it; they have likewise planted roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas.
Good sons and good daughters should form this thought:
"We have not planted roots of goodness under śrāvakas, nor have we heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā from śrāvakas."

"Ānanda! If there are good sons or good daughters who receive, uphold, read, recite, draw near to, and practice in accordance with the meaning and the Dharma this profound Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that these good sons and good daughters are seeing the Buddha face to face."

Ānanda! If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, possess pure faith that cannot be thwarted or destroyed, you should know that these good men and good women have in the past made offerings to the Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, and associated with virtuous friends.

“Ānanda! Although planting roots of goodness in the field of merit of the Buddhas is never in vain, one must attain liberation by becoming a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a buddha; therefore, you should practice the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) with profound clarity!”

Ānanda! If a bodhisattva thoroughly and clearly practices the six pāramitās up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), it is impossible that such a person should abide in the path of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you! Ānanda!
If you should receive and uphold all other dharmas, with the exception of the Prajñāpāramitā, and should forget or lose them, the fault would be minor; there would be no great transgression.
Ānanda! If you receive and uphold the profound Prajñāpāramitā and should forget even a single phrase, the fault thereof will be exceedingly great! Ānanda!
If you were to receive and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and later forget it, the transgression would be exceedingly great!
For this reason, Ānanda,
I entrust it to you!
"You should properly receive, uphold, read, and recite this profound *prajñāpāramitā* so that it becomes sharp! Ānanda,

if any son of good family or daughter of good family receives and upholds the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are thereby receiving and upholding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."

Ānanda! If good sons or good daughters now make offerings to me, honoring, respecting, and praising me with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, robes, banners, and canopies, they should likewise uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, reading, reciting, explaining, drawing near to, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even with banners and streamers.
Ānanda! To make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā is to make offerings to me, and it is also to have made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, develop pure faith, reverence, and affection, they have thereby already developed pure faith, reverence, and affection for all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda! Since you love and delight in the Buddha and do not abandon him, you should likewise love and delight in the Prajñāpāramitā and not abandon it! Ānanda!
The profound Prajñāpāramitā, even down to a single phrase, must not be lost! Ānanda,
I have spoken of many causes and conditions for this entrustment, but now I shall speak only briefly:
Just as I am the World-Honored One, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā the World-Honored One.
For this reason, Ānanda,
I entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you through various causes and conditions.
Ānanda! Now, among all the assemblies of humans, devas, and asuras in this world, I entrust you with this matter.

Those who do not wish to abandon the Buddha, nor the Dharma, nor the Saṅgha, nor the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—be careful never to abandon the prajñā-pāramitā.
Ānanda! This is the Dharma by which I have taught and transformed my disciples. Ānanda!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, and correctly contemplates this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and further extensively expounds its meaning for others—revealing, elucidating, and analyzing it so that it is easy to understand—then these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and swiftly draw near to Sarvajñā.
Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is born. Ānanda!

The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past and future arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*; likewise, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas currently present in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir also arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, Ānanda,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should train in the six pāramitās!
Why is this? Ānanda!
The six pāramitās are the mother of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for they give birth to all bodhisattvas.
Ānanda! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who study these six pāramitās, they shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Ānanda, I entrust these six pāramitās to you again and again with redoubled earnestness.
These six pāramitās are the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
Ānanda! All the Buddhas of the ten directions who are currently preaching the Dharma have emerged from the Dharma-treasury of the six pāramitās.
The Buddhas of the past likewise trained in the six pāramitās and thereby attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddhas of the future will also train in the six pāramitās and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

the Buddhas of the present also train in the six pāramitās and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and the disciples of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present all train in the six pāramitās and attain nirvāṇa—having attained it, attaining it now, and attaining it in the future.

“Ānanda! If you were to teach the Dharma to the śrāvakas so that all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm attained the realization of the fruit of arhatship, it would still not constitute the duty of my disciple.

However, if you were to teach even a single phrase associated with the Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, that would indeed be the duty of my disciple; I would rejoice in this more than if I had taught all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to attain the fruit of arhatship.”
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Suppose all the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm were to simultaneously, at one and the same time, all attain the realization of the fruit of arhatship;
and suppose these arhats were to practice the merit of giving, the merit of observing the precepts, and the merit of meditative concentration—would that merit be great?
Ānanda said, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
It is not as meritorious as for a disciple to teach the Dharma associated with the Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even for a single day; the latter’s merit is far greater!”
Setting aside one day, let it be but half a day;
setting aside half a day, let it be but the duration of a single meal;
setting aside the duration of a single meal, let it be spoken of for but a brief moment—the merit thereof would be great!
Why is this? Because the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva surpass those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva, desiring for himself to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, also demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens others, causing them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Ānanda! When a bodhisattva thus practices the six pāramitās, practices the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to practicing the knowledge of all modes, increasing their roots of goodness—if they were not to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, such a thing is impossible!

When this "Prajñāpāramitā Chapter" was being spoken, the Buddha, amidst the fourfold assembly and before the great multitude of devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, manifested miraculous transformations through his supernormal powers:
the entire assembly beheld the Buddha Akṣobhya, surrounded by a saṃgha of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma;
the assembly was like the waters of the great ocean, all of them arhats.
With outflows exhausted and free from afflictions, they have all attained mastery and achieved excellent liberation—excellent liberation of mind and excellent liberation through wisdom;
their minds are tamed and supple like great elephants;
having accomplished what was to be done and realized their own benefit, they have ended the fetters of existence and attained liberation through right knowledge.
He has attained mastery over all minds and mental factors, as well as the accomplishment of the immeasurable merits of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), so that the entire assembly no longer saw Akṣobhya Buddha, the śrāvakas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or their world; they were no longer within the range of their vision.
For what reason?
Because the Buddha had withdrawn his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"In this way, Ānanda!
All phenomena do not confront the eye; phenomenon does not see phenomenon, and phenomenon does not know phenomenon.
Thus it is, Ānanda!"
Just as the Buddha Akṣobhya, his disciples, his bodhisattvas, and his world do not come before the eye;
so it is, Ānanda!
All dharmas do not come before the eye; dharma and dharma do not know one another, nor do dharma and dharma see one another.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are without cognition, without vision, without action, without movement, ungraspable, and inconceivable; they are like a phantom person who has no sensation, no perception, and no reality.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and yet do not cling to any phenomena.
Ānanda! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, it is called training in the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to attain the various pāramitās, one should study the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Studying in this manner is called the foremost study, the supreme study, and the subtle and wondrous study.
Training in this way, one brings peace, happiness, and benefit to the entire world, acting as a protector for those who have no protector; this is what all Buddhas have trained in.
Abiding within this training, the Buddhas are able to lift the trichiliocosm with their right hand and place it back in its original location, yet no sentient being therein would perceive it.
Why is this? Ānanda!
By training in this Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas attain unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda! Just as the perfection of wisdom is the most honored, the foremost, the most subtle, and the unsurpassed among all trainings,
so it is, Ānanda!
If anyone wishes to attain the limit of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they wish to attain the limit of empty space.
Why is this? Ānanda!
The *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable; from the beginning, I have never spoken of a measure for the *prajñāpāramitā*.
While the collection of names, the collection of phrases, and the collection of syllables are measurable, the *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is the Prajñāpāramitā immeasurable?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible, it is immeasurable; because the Prajñāpāramitā is detached, it is immeasurable."
Ānanda! All Buddhas of the past attained liberation by training in the Prajñāpāramitā, yet this Prajñāpāramitā is therefore not exhausted.
All Buddhas of the future will likewise attain liberation by training in this Prajñāpāramitā, and thus this Prajñāpāramitā is not exhausted.

All the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present have attained liberation by studying this Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible—it was inexhaustible in the past, is inexhaustible in the present, and will be inexhaustible in the future.
Ānanda! To wish to exhaust the *prajñāpāramitā* is to wish to exhaust space.
The *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be exhausted; it was not exhausted in the past, is not exhausted in the present, and will not be exhausted in the future.
The dhyāna-pāramitā, up to and including the dāna-pāramitā, are inexhaustible; they were inexhaustible in the past, are inexhaustible in the present, and will be inexhaustible in the future;
even so it is with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Why is this? Because all these phenomena are without arising;
if a phenomenon is without arising, how could it have an end?
At that time, the Buddha extended his tongue to cover his face and said to Ānanda:
"From this day forward, you shall extensively expound, reveal, and analyze the Prajñāpāramitā among the fourfold assembly; you must ensure it is clear and easy to understand."
Why is this? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the characteristics of all phenomena are explained in detail.
Those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or those seeking Buddhahood, should all train therein.
Having studied it, each shall attain accomplishment. Ānanda!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā is the gateway to all syllables.
Practicing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one is able to enter the gates of *dhāraṇī*;
by studying these gates of *dhāraṇī*, all bodhisattvas attain the eloquence of unhindered speech.
Ānanda! The Prajñāpāramitā is the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
For this reason, Ānanda!

I shall explain this clearly for you: if there is anyone who receives, maintains, reads, recites, and draws near to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, that person will be able to uphold the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"Ānanda! I say that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the feet of the practitioner.
Because you uphold this dhāraṇī of the perfection of wisdom, you will be able to uphold all dharmas."
[Treatise] Question: Why did Śakra Devānām Indra doubt what he had said himself, asking,
"Am I in accord with the Dharma and have I given the correct answer?"
He replied:

"Śakra Devānām Indra is not an omniscient person. Although he has attained the first stage of the path, his three poisons are not yet exhausted, and he still possesses errors. He thus reflects to himself:

'Although I am the lord of the gods by virtue of my merit and conditions, and although I have tasted the flavor of the noble path, I do not yet possess omniscience. Because all outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted, what I say may be erroneous, and I do not realize it myself.'"
For this reason, he asks.

Furthermore, within the assembly there are many *avaivartika* bodhisattvas, arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*), and various devas who have abandoned desire. When these people see Śakra Devānām Indra engaging in debate with the Buddha and Subhūti, their minds do not become timid or weak, and they think:
"This Śakra Devānām Indra has not yet exhausted his outflows; how can he engage in debate and reach the ultimate limit of all phenomena?"
Śakra Devānām-indra questioned the Buddha regarding this matter.

Furthermore, Śakra Devānām-indra, knowing that the characteristics of all dharmas he had described were free from contradiction or error, sought the Buddha’s confirmation so that listeners would believe and accept them; therefore, the Buddha approved his words.
Question: Why did the Buddha permit Śakra Devānām Indra to speak? Answer: [The Buddha permitted it] because...
(text continues)
Although Śakra Devānām Indra is not omniscient, he constantly hears from the Buddha; because his power of recitation is strong, what he says is reasonable, and the Buddha accordingly approves it.
The Buddha taught that there are three kinds of wisdom:
the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Because some individuals possess clear and lucid wisdom of hearing and reflection, they are able to engage in debate with those who possess the wisdom of cultivation.
It is like riding a boat downstream; without exerting one's own strength, one travels faster than by land.

Thus, although Ānanda has not yet abandoned desire nor attained profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he is able to engage in debate with the Buddha and the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*), following the Dharma without contradiction.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Subhūti delights in expounding emptiness and is skillful in expounding emptiness; among all the disciples, he is the foremost.”

Whatever is spoken all tends toward emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; that is to say, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—all these dharmas are explained as being in harmony with ultimate emptiness.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
“Subhūti is one who practices ultimate emptiness; he has cultivated and accumulated this merit life after life, not merely in this present lifetime.
This person enters the Way by means of the gate of liberation that is emptiness, and likewise teaches and transforms sentient beings through this very gate.”
"If such a person, upon entering the profound dharma of emptiness, cannot even apprehend the dharma, how much less can they practice this dharma!
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The *dānapāramitā* cannot be apprehended, how much less the one who practices giving!"
"Up to and including the eighty minor marks, they cannot be apprehended; how much less could one obtain the eighty minor marks!
Subhūti’s practice of emptiness, when compared to the bodhisattva’s practice of emptiness, does not equal even a hundredth part of it.
Question:

Since both the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) have been explained, what further deficiency remains such that one says, "it does not equal even one hundredth part"? Answer:

In this context, the Buddha himself says: "Except for the Buddha, none among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas can equal him. Regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there are various names:

it is sometimes called emptiness (*śūnyatā*), sometimes called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), sometimes called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and sometimes named unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
In this context, the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-caryā*).
Just as among all the śrāvaka disciples, Subhūti’s practice of emptiness is supreme;
so too, with the exception of the Buddha, the practice of emptiness of the bodhisattvas surpasses that of the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because wisdom discriminates between the sharp and the dull, and there are varying depths in one's entry [into reality], all are said to have attained the true mark of all dharmas; it is only those of sharp faculties who attain it with complete clarity.
It is like lighting a lamp to dispel darkness; if there is yet another, larger lamp, the illumination becomes even more superior.
One should know that although the first lamp shone, it did not exhaust the subtle darkness;
had it exhausted it, the subsequent lamp would have been useless.
It is the same for those who practice emptiness: although they all attain the Way, because their wisdom is either sharp or dull, their ignorance is either exhausted or not exhausted;
only the Buddha-wisdom can exhaust all ignorance.

Furthermore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack the mind of great compassion; they lack the mind to deliver sentient beings; they lack the purification of buddha-fields; they lack the vows for immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; they lack the turning of the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings; nor do they have the vow to enter nirvana without remainder or to deliver sentient beings through their bequeathed teachings. They lack the mind to deliver sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—namely, during the stage of being a bodhisattva, at the time of becoming a Buddha, and at the time of parinirvāṇa. It is not merely because of practicing emptiness that they are equal to bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the two vehicles attain emptiness with divisions and limitations;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain it without divisions and without limitation.
It is like a thirsty person drinking from a river: they do not exceed their own sufficiency. How can one say that because both practice emptiness, there should be no difference between them?
Furthermore, it is as impossible as comparing the space within a single pore to the space of the ten directions; such a principle does not exist!
Therefore, when compared to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [the merit of the former] falls short by a factor of thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions.
Having distinguished these practices of emptiness, the Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra:
"If you wish to be supreme among all sentient beings, you should practice the Prajñāpāramitā."
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"Because the bodhisattva trains in this practice of the emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not grasp at the mark of emptiness, he transcends the two stages, attains the dharma of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and enters the rank of a bodhisattva;
by entering the rank of a bodhisattva, he becomes fully endowed with the buddha-dharmas."
The Buddha-dharma is the path of the bodhisattva; because the bodhisattva path is fully perfected, one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because one attains all-knowledge, one is called a Buddha—one who has severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
All these matters have the practice of emptiness as their foundation.
Question: Nirvāṇa is immeasurable; why then do you say that "what is attained by the two vehicles is finite"?
The answer is:
When it is said that "wisdom has divisions and limits," it is not meant that "the dharma-nature of all phenomena has limits.
Have you not heard the analogy of the great body of water?
The vessel has a measure; it is not that the water has a measure.
Furthermore, "measure" and "immeasurable" are relative concepts.
What is immeasurable for ordinary people is all measurable for a Buddha.

Such a portion constitutes the *srotāpanna*, and so on up to such a portion constituting the *arhat*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and the *bodhisattva*; that which remains, when the dharma-nature is fully exhausted, is the Buddha.
At that time, the various devas in the assembly scattered celestial *mandārava* flowers upon the Buddha and others, as described in the sūtra.
A question is asked:
"When flowers are offered to both the Buddha and the Saṃgha, why did these eight hundred bhikṣus take [only] those to offer to the Buddha?"
The answer is:

When the flowers scattered by the devas fell upon the robes that the bhikṣus had received as their allotted shares, they saw that their colors and fragrances were most exquisite. Consequently, they resolved to make offerings to the Buddha and said:

"From this day forward, we shall practice this supreme path—namely, ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, just as the Buddha has taught, which is beyond the reach of the two vehicles."
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
The meaning of his smile is as explained in the "Gaṅgādevā" chapter.

These eight hundred bhikṣus were all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); their practices were identical and their minds were equal because they had together cultivated and accumulated merit throughout successive lifetimes. Therefore, they shall simultaneously become Buddhas, all bearing the same name.
Because they made offerings to the Buddha with five-colored celestial flowers, five-colored celestial *mandārava* flowers constantly rained down upon the world.
On account of this matter, the Buddha praised the Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"Ānanda!..."
"One who wishes to practice the supreme bodhisattva path should practice the Prajñāpāramitā. Ānanda!
If there is a son of good family who can practice this profound Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this person has come from the human realm, or has come from the Tuṣita heaven."
Why is this? Because within the three evil realms, the suffering of karmic retribution is so great that one cannot practice the profound *prajñā*.
Furthermore, the devas of the desire realm are attached to the five pure and subtle sensual pleasures; their minds are thus deranged and deluded, and they are unable to practice it.
The devas of the form realm are deeply attached to the flavor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and thus cannot practice it;
those of the formless realm lack physical form, and thus cannot practice it;

and those in the realm of ghosts and spirits possess sharp faculties such as the eye-organ, yet their minds are shrouded by various afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus they cannot single-mindedly practice the profound *prajñā*.

Within the human realm, suffering differs from that of the three evil paths, yet happiness does not equal that of the various heavens; the faculties such as the eyes are turbid and heavy, and the body consists largely of the earth element; therefore, one is able to control the mind regarding both suffering and pleasure and practice Prajñā.

In the Tuṣita Heaven, there is always a Bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood; the devas therein constantly hear the teaching of Prajñā, and although the five desires are numerous, the power of the Dharma prevails.
Therefore, it is said that they come from two places:
either from the Buddha-worlds of other directions, or from this very place where the Prajñāpāramitā resides.
Furthermore, "Ānanda!..."

If there are those who seek the Buddha-way and are able to inquire about it, believe in it, receive and uphold it, and even maintain right mindfulness toward it, you should know that the Buddha constantly beholds these people with his Buddha-eye.
They should form this thought:

"We have received instruction directly from the Buddha's presence; we have resolved our minds upon enlightenment and planted roots of goodness under the Buddha, not having resolved our minds through the two vehicles."

"Ānanda! If there are those whose faith is pure and indestructible, you should know that such persons have, in previous lives, made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and have been protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); therefore, they are able to receive and uphold [this teaching]."
Question: The Buddha is also called a "jewel" and is also called the "unsurpassed field of merit";
if a person plants roots of goodness with the Buddha, they will certainly enter nirvana through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, never in vain.
As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"If there are people who offer even a single flower or a small amount of incense to the Buddha, or even those who once utter the name 'Namo Buddha,' all such persons shall become Buddhas."
"If that is so, some may think: 'One should simply practice the five pāramitās and contemplate emptiness only when one wishes to become a Buddha;
what need is there to constantly practice the prajñāpāramitā, which involves the difficult-to-know and difficult-to-attain practice of emptiness?'"
The answer is:
For this reason, the Buddha himself replied to Ānanda:

"Although one may not be deceptive regarding the field of merit of the Buddha and will certainly attain entry into nirvāṇa through the three vehicles, one must practice the six pāramitās with complete clarity; because one practices even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) with complete clarity, one will swiftly attain the Buddha-way and will not long remain subject to the suffering of birth and death."
"Because the Prajñāpāramitā possesses such benefits and merits as these, one should practice it. Ānanda!
Because the Prajñāpāramitā possesses such merits and benefits, I entrust it to you."
Question: The Buddha has nothing to crave;

he does not even crave the all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), the Buddha’s unimpeded liberations, or the various pure and subtle Buddha-dharmas. For what reason, then, does he so earnestly entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to Ānanda, as if he were craving or begrudging it?
The answer is:

The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; they manifest the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, immeasurable radiance, and supernatural transformations—all for the sake of sentient beings.
There is nothing that benefits sentient beings more than the Prajñāpāramitā, for it is able to exhaust all suffering.
The meaning of this Prajñāpāramitā can be understood through language, writing, and phrases; therefore, the Buddha earnestly entrusted the Prajñā Sūtra scrolls to Ānanda.
Furthermore, some people, seeing that the Buddha earnestly entrusted [the Dharma] to them, said:
"The Buddha’s great task is accomplished, yet he still holds the Prajñā in such high esteem; therefore, this Dharma must surely be honored and must surely be sublime!"

"It is, for example, like a wealthy elder who, when his life was about to end, gave various treasures to his children, but specifically and earnestly entrusted him with a wish-fulfilling jewel, saying:
'Do not fail to protect this jewel because it has no fixed color of its own, its substance is like empty space, and it is so subtle and wondrous as to be difficult to recognize!'"
"If other treasures are lost, it may be tolerated, but this treasure must not be lost!
The Great Wealthy Elder is the Buddha; he entrusts the Prajñāpāramitā to Ānanda, saying:
"You must receive and uphold it well, guarding it so that you do not forget or lose it!"
"Except for the Prajñāpāramitā, even if one were to forget all twelve divisions of the scriptures, the fault would still be minor;
however, if one loses a single phrase of the Prajñāpāramitā, the fault is far too great!"
Why is this? This profound treasury of Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; it enables people to swiftly reach the path of Buddhahood.

As stated in the sutras: "All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained [enlightenment] through Prajñā," and even down to "preaching the Dharma for the sake of śrāvakas"—all such passages therein are praises of the matters concerning Prajñā.
Question:
If one were to preach the Dharma so that all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm attained arhatship, why would this not be as effective as teaching a single phrase of Prajñā to a bodhisattva?
Answer: Although this matter has been answered previously, it shall now be briefly restated:
although all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to attain arhatship and deliver themselves, they would not be fit to become Buddhas.
If one speaks even a single phrase of Prajñā, those who hear it will attain Buddhahood.
It is like a person planting many fruit trees; this is not as good as a single person planting one wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), which can grant all desires according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, within the teachings for śrāvakas, there is no great compassion;
whereas in the Mahāyāna teachings, even a single phrase, though brief, contains great compassion.
In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, all is for one's own sake;
in the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is extensively for the sake of sentient beings.
In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, there is no desire for the broad knowledge of all dharmas, but only the desire to swiftly leave behind old age, sickness, and death.
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, one seeks to know all phenomena with complete clarity.
In the Śrāvaka Dharma, the merits are limited;
in the Mahāyāna Dharma, one seeks to exhaust all merits without exception.
Such are the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
For example, although a diamond is small, it can surpass all other jewels; one cannot say that because it is small, it is inferior to those that are large.

The merit of all the Arhats within a trichiliocosm is vastly surpassed by the merit of a single word of instruction in the Prajñāpāramitā given to a Bodhisattva for even a single day, or even for a mere moment.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:
"This person desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for themselves and also teaches others to attain it;
they personally practice the merits of the six *pāramitās* and also explain them to others."
"It is impossible that a Bodhisattva, having accumulated merit in two places, should fail to attain the Way of the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha, wishing to clarify this matter, cited scriptural evidence; furthermore, wishing to testify that all dharmas are empty, yet not being attached to this emptiness of dharmas, he entrusted [the teaching] out of mere compassion for sentient beings.
Just as the Buddha Akṣobhya, his great assembly, and his adornments do not confront the eye, so too all dharmas do not confront the eye.
That which is seen by the fleshly eye and the divine eye is entirely a conditioned phenomenon—deceptive and unreal.
The wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye are all signless and unconditioned dharmas;
therefore, they cannot be seen. If they cannot be seen, they also cannot be known.
The same applies to non-action and so forth.
The assembly of the Buddha Akṣobhya that one perceives is like an illusion and like a dream;
to be able to contemplate all phenomena in this way is called a bodhisattva practicing prajñā, and it is called being without attachment.
Even that which the Buddha entrusts to me is without attachment; it is solely out of great compassion that I praise this Prajñāpāramitā.
Although all dharmas possess an inconceivable nature, I praise them for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, saying:
"Ānanda!..."
"To train in this manner is to train in the *prajñā*;
if one wishes to attain all the *pāramitās*, one should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Such points are explained at length as in the sutra.
The Buddha praised Prajñā with immeasurable words:
"If the wisdom of a Buddha is inexhaustible, then the merit of Prajñā is likewise inexhaustible. Why is this?"
Because the Prajñāpāramitā has immeasurable characteristics, it is designated by various words, phrases, and chapters;

yet the number of fascicles is finite. For instance, the chapters and phrases of Prajñāpāramitā sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* (Small Version), the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* (Emitting Light), and the *Saptaśatikā* (Praise of Light) have limits and measure;
however, the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable.
Ānanda asked:
"In what way is the Prajñāpāramitā immeasurable?
The Buddha replied:
“The characteristic of the prajñāpāramitā is itself detached.
Because it is detached, from the very beginning it has neither arisen nor accumulated; because it has neither arisen nor accumulated, it is neither exhausted nor extinguished.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas and their disciples used this Prajñāpāramitā to illuminate the ten directions and deliver immeasurable sentient beings, all of whom together entered nirvana without remainder; yet, because of the Prajñāpāramitā, it was not exhausted.
It is the same for the future and the present."
For example, it is as if someone wished to exhaust space; yet space cannot be exhausted.

The same is true for the various merits such as the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*): they have not been exhausted now, they have not been exhausted in the past, and they will not be exhausted in the future.

There are those who know that the past is inexhaustible, yet believe that the future and the present are exhaustible; for this reason, it is said that "the three periods of time are inexhaustible. Why is this?
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; how could they ever be exhausted?
The Buddha knows that Prajñāpāramitā is truly inexhaustible, yet because names, words, phrases, and collections [of teachings] are subject to exhaustion, he entrusts [this teaching] to others.
It is like a person who entrusts a jar of fragrant oil to their children; although they do not begrudge the jar itself, it is for the sake of preserving the fragrant oil within.
Likewise, words can preserve meaning: if the words are lost, the meaning cannot be attained.
At that time, so that people might have faith in and accept the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha extended his tongue until it covered his face and addressed Ānanda:
"I now entrust this Prajñāpāramitā to you among the fourfold assembly. You should explain, reveal, and analyze it for the sake of sentient beings, making it easy for them to understand."
The reason for manifesting the mark of the tongue is that, according to the conventional laws of the world, the ability of the tongue to cover the nose is a sign of non-falsehood;

how much more so when it covers the entire face! Therefore, the Buddha shows sentient beings: "I was born from my parents with this physical body, and I possess this mark of the tongue. I wish to cause you to believe and understand through the Prajñāpāramitā;
because you have not yet attained all-knowledge and cannot know everything, I desire to inspire your faith. This was not manifested through the power of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi*).

The Buddha does not even cling to the profound and wondrous Dharma, wisdom, or meditative concentration; how much less would he engage in falsehood for the sake of the eight worldly concerns or the gain of offerings!

Within all dharmas, you shall be like a bird flying through space, encountering no obstruction; yet, because you have vowed by your original aspiration to deliver sentient beings and out of your great compassion that pities all, I earnestly entrust this foremost, beneficial Prajñāpāramitā to you.
Furthermore, "Ānanda!
One who practices this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to enter all *dhāraṇīs* of syllables.
Because one enters ultimate emptiness through a single syllable, this is called the *dhāraṇī* of syllables.
As stated in the aforementioned *dhāraṇī*,
all dharmas of written characters are obtained through the *prajñāpāramitā*;
likewise, other *dhāraṇīs* such as the "retention of what is heard" (*śrutadhāraṇī*) are also all obtained from training in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Once the Bodhisattva has attained the various dhāraṇīs, he attains manifold eloquence in joyful exposition; for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he could never exhaust the explanation of the meaning of a single phrase.
This is called the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
there is no other dharma besides it. Furthermore, Ānanda, Prajñāpāramitā is the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
"Just as in a city with a single gate, those coming from the four directions have no other entrance but that one.
Ānanda, I shall now explain this to you clearly: "
"If there is anyone who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not merely uphold my Dharma; such a person upholds the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas of the three periods of time."
"Ānanda! This Prajñāpāramitā, which I have taught in various places, is the 'foot' of the practitioner. Why is that? Because..."
When a bodhisattva attains this prajñā, they are able to practice the bodhisattva path. "Ānanda!
Because you have attained this Prajñāpāramitā dhāraṇī, you are able to uphold all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas."

Question: Since one is able to uphold [the teachings] by the power of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, why do you say that "by attaining *prajñā*, one is able to uphold all the Buddha-dharmas"?
Answer:

The *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining can maintain dharmas that have number and measure; such things exist even in the world, as for example the non-Buddhist practitioner Śuśima also attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
Although such a person attains it for a short time, they eventually forget and lose it after a long period.
From *prajñā* one attains *dhāraṇī*, whereby one extensively upholds all dharmas and never forgets them.
This constitutes the distinction.
Question:
If Prajñā is itself a pāramitā, why is it called a dhāraṇī?
The answer is:
the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is Prajñā; because it can provide manifold benefits and is cherished by sentient beings, it is given various names.
Just as the Buddha possesses the ten titles and other such designations,
so too is the Prajñāpāramitā:
because it can reach the limit of all wisdom, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
When a Bodhisattva practices Prajñā and attains Buddhahood, it is designated as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
if it is within the mind of the Lesser Vehicle, it is merely called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation;
if there are those who wish to hear it and not forget it, within their minds it is called *dhāraṇī*.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke the analogy of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), which changes its name according to the color of the object it encounters.
In this way, the Buddha has explained in various ways the great merit of *prajñā*.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Seventy-nine;
The Mahāprajñāpākaramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Inexhaustible Expedient Means,
Scroll Eighty.
Composed by the Holy Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Sixty-Seven: On Inexhaustible Expedient Means. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of these Buddhas is profoundly deep; I should question the Buddha regarding it."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Is this Prajñāpāramitā inexhaustible?"
The Buddha said:
“Because space is inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"How should one generate the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"Because form is inexhaustible, one should generate the perfection of wisdom."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth.
Because the dānapāramitā is inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth;
because the śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā are inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should be brought forth. Moreover, Subhūti,
because the emptiness of delusion (*moha-śūnyatā*) is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of wisdom should be brought forth."
Because the emptiness of formations is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom should be generated;
because the emptiness of consciousness is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom should be generated;
because the emptiness of name-and-form is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom should be generated.
Because the emptiness of the six sense bases is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated;
because the emptiness of the six contacts is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated;
because the emptiness of sensation is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated.
Because the emptiness of craving is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated;
because the emptiness of grasping is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated;
because the emptiness of existence is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be generated.
Because the emptiness of birth is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth;
because the emptiness of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā should be brought forth.
Thus, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be brought forth. Subhūti!
These twelve links of dependent origination are the unique teaching of the Bodhisattvas; they are able to eliminate all extremes and inversions.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, one should contemplate in this manner, and shall thereby attain the knowledge of all modes.

Subhūti! If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by means of the inexhaustible nature of space, practice the prajñāpāramitā and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, they do not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but abide in anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! Those who seek the bodhisattva path but turn back do so because they have abandoned mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Such persons do not know how to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*; they should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination through the dharma that is inexhaustible like space.

Subhūti! Those who seek the bodhisattva path but turn back do so because they have not attained this power of skillful means; thus, they turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is entirely because they have attained this power of skillful means.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustible nature of space; they should give rise to the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustible nature of space.

"In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, he does not perceive any phenomenon arising without causes and conditions; he does not perceive any phenomenon as permanent or indestructible;
and he does not perceive any phenomenon as having a self, a person, a life-span, a soul, a sentient being, a knower, or a seer."

One does not perceive phenomena as impermanent, one does not perceive phenomena as suffering, one does not perceive phenomena as selfless, nor does one perceive phenomena as either cessation or non-cessation.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in this way.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner, at that time they do not perceive form as either permanent or impermanent, as suffering or happiness, as self or non-self, or as cessation or non-cessation.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Subhūti, at that time,
