Chapter 71: The Tree of the Path. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound, World-Honored One!
That the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, not apprehending a sentient being, yet seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings— this is most difficult!"
"World-Honored One!
It would be extremely difficult, for example, for a person to wish to plant a tree in empty space!
World-Honored One!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: for the sake of sentient beings, they seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet sentient beings themselves cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

The deeds performed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are exceedingly difficult; for the sake of sentient beings, they seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in order to deliver those beings who are attached to a self and held in the inversion of views.

Subhūti! It is like a person who plants a tree; though they do not recognize its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits, they cherish and water it. Gradually it grows large, and when the flowers, leaves, and fruits are fully formed, they can all be put to use.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they gradually practice the six pāramitās, attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), and become the tree of enlightenment, benefiting sentient beings with its leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Subhūti! What is the "leaf-like benefit" for sentient beings?
It is that sentient beings attain liberation from the three evil realms by means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is the leaf-like benefit for sentient beings.
What is meant by "benefiting sentient beings through blossoming"?

It refers to the fact that because of the Bodhisattva, one is born into the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, the great clans of the Brahmins, the great households of the householders, or from the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the abode of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; this is what is meant by benefiting sentient beings through blossoming.
What is the benefit for sentient beings as a result?

This bodhisattva attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and causes sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha. These sentient beings gradually attain parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*) by means of the three vehicles; this is the benefit for sentient beings as a result.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the real dharma of sentient beings, yet he delivers sentient beings, causing them to be free from the perverted attachment to a self. He forms this thought:
"Within all dharmas there are no sentient beings; for the sake of sentient beings, I seek all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), yet these sentient beings are in reality unapprehendable."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You should know that this bodhisattva is like a Buddha.”

Why is this? Because by reason of these bodhisattvas, all seeds of the hells are severed, all seeds of the animal realm are severed, and all seeds of the hungry ghost realm are severed; all calamities are severed, all paths of poverty and low birth are severed, and all realms of desire, form, and formlessness are severed.
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is like a Buddha. Subhūti!

If Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas did not resolve their minds to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there would be no Buddhas of the past, future, or present in the world; nor would there be Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, or Srotāpannas in the world;
furthermore, the three evil realms and the three worlds would never cease to exist.
Subhūti! As for what you have said:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as being like a Buddha."
"So it is! So it is! Subhūti!"
You should know that this bodhisattva is truly like a Buddha.
Why is this? It is because of suchness (*tathatā*) that one speaks of a Tathāgata; it is because of suchness that one speaks of pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and all noble ones (*ārya*).
Because of suchness, they are called form, and so on, up to consciousness; because of suchness, all dharmas are called such, even up to the conditioned nature and the unconditioned nature.
These various suchnesses are, in reality, without difference; for this reason, they are called "suchness."
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study this suchness (tathatā) and attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), they receive the name Tathāgata.
For this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be known as Buddhas by virtue of the characteristic of suchness.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the suchness of the prajñāpāramitā!
When a bodhisattva trains in the suchness of the prajñāpāramitā, they are then able to train in the suchness of all dharmas.
By studying the suchness of all dharmas, one attains the full realization of the suchness of all dharmas;
having fully realized the suchness of all dharmas, one dwells in the suchness of all dharmas and attains mastery;
having attained mastery while dwelling in the suchness of all dharmas, one skillfully knows the faculties of all sentient beings.
Having thoroughly understood the faculties of all sentient beings, they know the fulfillment of the faculties of all sentient beings;
having known the fulfillment of the faculties of all sentient beings, they also know the karmic causes and conditions of all sentient beings;
having known the karmic causes and conditions of all sentient beings, they attain the fulfillment of the wisdom of vows.
Having attained the perfection of the knowledge of vows, one purifies the wisdom of the three periods of time;
having purified the wisdom of the three periods of time, one benefits all sentient beings;
having benefited all sentient beings, one purifies the Buddha-lands.
Having purified the Buddha-fields, one attains all-knowledge;
having attained all-knowledge, one turns the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, one establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles and causes them to enter nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain all merits for their own benefit and for the benefit of others should resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught should be paid homage by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught; all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—should pay homage to them.
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of sentient beings, how much merit does this bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind obtain when seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If all sentient beings within a thousand lands were to each give rise to the aspiration for the state of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, what do you think?"
"Would that merit not be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be exceedingly great and immeasurable!"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“That merit is not equal to that of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind [on awakening]; it does not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.”

Why is this? Those who give rise to the aspiration for the stage of Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha all emerge because of the Bodhisattva; a Bodhisattva never emerges because of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
It is likewise in the two-thousandfold world system and the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
Let alone those who dwell on the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
"If all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to abide on the stage of dry wisdom, would their merit be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be exceedingly great and immeasurable!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred million-fold, or even to the extent that no calculation or analogy can reach."

Setting aside those beings who abide on the stage of dry wisdom, suppose all the beings in a trichiliocosm were to abide on the stage of the nature-ground, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of seeing, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha. All these merits, when compared to those of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment, would not approach even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part; they would be beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

Subhūti! If there were Bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds toward enlightenment within a trichiliocosm, they would not equal even one Bodhisattva who has entered the stage of the Dharma-position (dharmatā-avasthita) by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions, billions of millions, or even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy.

If there were Bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of the Dharma-position within a trichiliocosm, they would not equal a Bodhisattva who is directed toward the Buddha-way by even a hundred thousand million times, a hundred trillion times, or even to the extent that calculation and analogy cannot reach.

If all the bodhisattvas in the three-thousandfold world system who are directed toward the Buddha-way were compared to the merit of a Buddha, they would not equal it by a hundred thousand million times, nor by a billion trillion times, nor even by any calculation or analogy could they reach it.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what dharmas should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening keep in mind?”
The Buddha said:
“One should bring to mind all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Subhūti said:
“What is ‘all-aspect omniscience’ (sarvākārajñatā)?
What is its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)?
What is its dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)?”
“What are its practices?
What are its characteristics?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-existent, without conceptualization, without recollection, without arising, and without demonstration.
As Subhūti has asked:
'What is the objective condition (ālambana) of all-knowledge?'"
What is its predominance?
What is its practice?
What is its characteristic?
“Subhūti! The knowledge of all modes has non-dharmas as its object; mindfulness is its predominance, tranquility is its practice, and signlessness is its characteristic. Subhūti!”
"This is called the object-condition, the dominant condition, the activity, and the characteristic of the knowledge of all modes.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If all-knowledge is a non-existent dharma, are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also non-existent dharmas?
Are internal and external dharmas also non-existent dharmas?

Are there no dharmas—the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path; the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, the samādhi of wishlessness; the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities; great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the first supernormal power, the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth supernormal powers; nor even the conditioned marks, the unconditioned marks? Or are there no dharmas at all?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Form is also non-existent; even the marks of the conditioned and the marks of the unconditioned are non-existent. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!

For what cause and condition is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) non-existent as a dharma, and why are form (rūpa), and so forth, up to conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) and unconditioned characteristics (asaṃskṛtalakṣaṇa), also non-existent as dharmas?”
The Buddha said:
"Because the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not exist, if a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it is called 'non-existent.
This is also true for form (*rūpa*) up to the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
“World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do all phenomena lack intrinsic nature?
The Buddha said:
“Because all dharmas arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If there is no intrinsic nature, they are called ‘non-existent dharmas.
For this reason, Subhūti!...”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; for this reason, one should know that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are without intrinsic nature, by what power of skillful means can a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening practice the dānapāramitā, purify the buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity?”

Can one practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); practice the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; practice the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) up to the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*); practice the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); practice internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); practice the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); practice the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), and the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*); practice the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*), the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddha-daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); and can one practice the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), purify Buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, and is also able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; knowing that both worlds and sentient beings likewise lack intrinsic nature is precisely the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).”

Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving while training in the Buddha-way; practices the perfection of ethical discipline while training in the Buddha-way; practices the perfections of patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom while training in the Buddha-way; and even practices the knowledge of all modes while training in the Buddha-way, yet he also knows that the Buddha-way is without intrinsic nature.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās and train in the Buddha-way, until they have fully accomplished the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes—this is what it means to train in the Buddha-way, whereby they are able to fulfill the causal conditions for the Buddha-way.
Having fulfilled the causal conditions for the Buddha-way, they attain the knowledge of all modes through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment.
At that time, all afflictions and habitual tendencies are forever exhausted, because they do not arise.
At that time, observing the trichiliocosm with the Buddha-eye, even non-existent dharmas cannot be apprehended, let alone existent dharmas!
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the prajñāpāramitā of non-nature.
Subhūti, this is called the power of skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Even non-existent dharmas cannot be apprehended, let alone existent dharmas! Subhūti,
when this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, even the act of giving non-existent dharmas cannot be apprehended, let alone existent dharmas!
Regarding the recipient and the mind of the bodhisattva, they do not even know non-existent dharmas, let alone existent ones!
Even regarding the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—the attainer, the dharma attained, and the place of attainment—they do not even know non-existent dharmas, let alone existent ones!
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is thus.
It was not made by a Buddha, nor made by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor made by anyone else; for all phenomena are without a creator.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are all phenomena separated from the intrinsic nature of phenomena?”
The Buddha said, “So it is! So it is!”
"All phenomena are devoid of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
"World-Honored One!

If all phenomena are devoid of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, how can a phenomenon that is devoid [of nature] know another phenomenon that is devoid [of nature], whether it exists or does not exist?"
Why is this? A non-existent dharma cannot know a non-existent dharma, and an existent dharma cannot know an existent dharma;
a non-existent dharma cannot know an existent dharma, and an existent dharma cannot know a non-existent dharma.
World-Honored One!
Since all these dharmas have the characteristic of non-existence, how can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva make such distinctions as to whether a dharma exists or does not exist?

The Buddha said, “A bodhisattva-mahāsattva shows sentient beings that things exist or do not exist by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), but not by way of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). [The interlocutor asked:
“World-Honored One!”
“Are there differences between the conventional truth and the ultimate truth? “Subhūti,
there is no difference between the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.”
Why is this? The suchness (*tathatā*) of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is identical to the suchness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Because sentient beings do not know or see this suchness, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva indicates it through conventional truth as either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
because sentient beings have attachments to the five aggregates of clinging, they do not know that there is nothing whatsoever.
For the sake of these sentient beings, I demonstrate both existence and non-existence, so that they may come to know the purity of non-existence.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom.
[Treatise] Explanation:
Having heard from the Buddha that non-attainment is itself attainment, Subhūti marveled at this unprecedented teaching and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep!"
As explained at length in the sutras, the tree serves as a metaphor:
the leaves, flowers, and fruits develop from thinness to thickness.
Just as the shade of a tree provides cool relief during the heat;
Sentient beings, by virtue of the shade of the Bodhisattva’s path-tree, are able to escape the heat and suffering of the three evil realms. Why is this?
Because it obstructs evil.
Just as a flower is beautiful in color, pure in fragrance, and soft to the touch;
so too, because sentient beings are taught by Bodhisattvas through the practices of giving and ethical discipline, they receive the blessings and happiness of the realms of humans and devas.
Just as a tree fruit possesses color, fragrance, flavor, and potency,
so too do sentient beings, by reason of the Bodhisattva, attain the fruits of the various noble paths,
such as the stage of Srotāpanna. Upon hearing this, Subhūti spoke with joy:
"This bodhisattva is no different from a Buddha.
Regarding this, he himself explains the causal conditions:
"It is because of the bodhisattva that the evil realms, such as the hells, are brought to an end."
The Buddha affirmed his meaning and further explained the causal conditions: "Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva does not resolve to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, [the cycle of existence] would continue until the three realms are no longer severed."
Furthermore, because one has realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, one is called a Tathāgata, and so on, up to being called a Srotāpanna;
it is by virtue of this suchness that form (*rūpa*) and even the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*) are spoken of.
This suchness of all phenomena is entirely one and without difference.
When a bodhisattva studies this suchness (tathatā), they will certainly attain omniscience (sarvajñā); therefore, it is said that they are no different from a Buddha.

It is not because of a mind of attachment or a desire for the prestige of being a bodhisattva that one says they are like a Buddha; rather, it is because they have attained suchness that they are said to be like a Buddha.
This "suchness" (tathatā) exists both in the Buddha and in the bodhisattva because they share a single characteristic; for this reason, the bodhisattva is said to be "like the Buddha.
Apart from suchness, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that does not enter into suchness.
Question:
If one is called a "Bodhisattva like a Buddha" because they share the same suchness (tathatā), and since this suchness also exists even among animals, why are they not called "like a Buddha"?
Answer:

Although animals also possess suchness, because the causal conditions have not yet arisen, they are unable to benefit sentient beings and are unable to practice suchness until they reach sarvajñā (omniscience).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva should train in this suchness of the prajñāpāramitā; because a bodhisattva trains in this suchness of the prajñāpāramitā, they are able to fulfill the suchness of all dharmas.
To be fully endowed with this is called attaining the true mark of all dharmas, whereby one can enable sentient beings to attain understanding through various gateways.
Because of this full endowment, one attains mastery over all dharmas;
having attained such mastery over these dharmas, one is able to skillfully know the faculties of sentient beings.
Because they are able to skillfully know the faculties of sentient beings, they can discern which faculties sentient beings possess in their entirety.
As for these "faculties," they refer to the five wholesome faculties, such as faith and so forth, which each person of the three vehicles possesses.
They are able to discern that a certain person possesses [wholesome roots] while another does not, and that a certain person has attained power while another has not.
"Endowed" means being fully possessed of the roots of goodness such as faith; such a person is able to transcend the world.
When the faculty of faith gains power, one is able to decisively accept and uphold [the teachings] without doubt;
by the power of diligence, although one has not yet seen the Dharma, one seeks the Path with a single mind, not sparing body or life, neither resting nor ceasing;

by the power of mindfulness, one constantly recollects the teacher’s instructions, allowing wholesome dharmas that come to enter while not allowing unwholesome dharmas that come to enter, like a gatekeeper.
By the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gathers the mind to a single point without movement, thereby assisting wisdom;
by the power of wisdom, one is able to contemplate the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) as they truly are.
There are two kinds of attainment of the faculties (*indriya*):
First, within the bodies of those with great resolve, it becomes the faculty of a bodhisattva;
second, within the bodies of those with small resolve, it becomes the faculty of the Hīnayāna.
When one attains these perfected faculties, they can then be delivered.

However, there may be bodhisattvas who see that although a person has attained the five faculties such as faith, they cannot yet be delivered because their heavy karmic offenses from previous lives remain. For this reason, it is said: "He knows the karmic causes and conditions of all sentient beings."
If one wishes to know the karmic causes and conditions of incalculable eons, one must attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
having known them, one then explains to sentient beings the causes and conditions of their past transgressions.
Because sentient beings do not fear due to these past transgressions, they seek the wisdom of aspiration, desiring to know the events of the three periods of time;
having known them, they shall explain to sentient beings the causes and conditions of their future karmic offenses, which will lead them to fall into hell.
When sentient beings hear this, they conceive fear;
once they are fearful, their minds become submissive and easy to deliver.
If sentient beings wish to know the causes and conditions for the retributive blessings of future lives, once these have been explained to them, they will rejoice and be ready for deliverance.
Therefore, it is said that once one has understood the causes and conditions of karma, the wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) becomes perfected.
Because the wisdom of aspiration is perfected, one attains the purity of insight into the three periods of time, achieving unimpeded penetration:

knowing the good and evil karma of the past, knowing the good and evil retributions of the future, and knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings in the present; thereafter, one preaches the Dharma to transform and teach them, bringing great benefit without fail.
For the sake of bringing great benefit to sentient beings, one is able to purify Buddha-fields;
having purified the Buddha-fields, one attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
and because of attaining all-knowledge, one turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles and leads them into nirvana without remainder.
Such benefits all arise from training in suchness; therefore, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to attain all merits for their own benefit and the benefit of others should resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having heard that the merit of this bodhisattva was so vast, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All the world should pay homage to a bodhisattva who is able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to these teachings.”
As explained at length in the sutra, the merits of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*) were analyzed.
At that time, Subhūti, knowing that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) and is not something attainable by a beginner, asked the Buddha:
"In what dharmas should a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening take mindfulness?"
The Buddha replied:
"One should bring to mind all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
All-knowledge is precisely *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, *sarvajñatā*, the Buddha-dharmas, and the Buddha-way; these are all synonyms for all-knowledge.
Question: Why did the Buddha answer by saying, "Mindfulness of all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*)? Answer:

A bodhisattva who has first resolved on enlightenment has not yet attained profound wisdom; because they have already renounced the pleasures of the five worldly desires, the Buddha teaches them to bind their minds in mindfulness of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
They should form this thought:
"Although I have renounced minor and mixed pleasures, I shall attain pure and great bliss."
Abandoning the pleasure of inverted and deceptive states, one attains true pleasure;
abandoning the pleasure of bondage, one attains the pleasure of liberation;
abandoning the pleasure of solitary goodness, one attains the pleasure of goodness shared with all sentient beings.
Because they obtain such benefits as these, the Buddha taught those who have first resolved their minds to constantly keep *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) in mind.
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One!”
Is this knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) an existent phenomenon (bhāva),
or is it a non-existent phenomenon (abhāva)?
What are its conditions (pratyaya)?
What is its predominance?
What is its practice?
What is its characteristic?
The Buddha replied:
“Subhūti, all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-existent.”
That which is non-existent is called "non-dharma"; it is without arising and without cessation.
All dharmas are as they truly are, and their conditions likewise do not exist; mindfulness is supreme, tranquility is the practice, and signlessness is the characteristic.
Question: Since all things are ultimately empty, why do you specifically say that mindfulness is "preeminent"? Answer:
All dharmas each possess their own power, yet the Buddha’s wisdom is ultimate emptiness;
it is suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality—signless, which is to say, the mark of quiescent extinction.

The Buddha has attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and no longer engages in deliberation; for him there is no longer difficulty or ease, nor distance or proximity. Whatever he intends, he attains it; therefore, it is said that mindfulness is preeminent.
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One,
is it only that all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is non-existent as a dharma, or are dharmas such as form (rūpa) also non-existent as dharmas?”
The Buddha replied:
"All dharmas, such as form and so forth, are likewise non-dharmas.
He then explained the causes and conditions himself:
"If a phenomenon arises from the combination of causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature;
if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it is an empty, non-existent thing.
For these reasons, one should know that all phenomena have no inherent existence."
Subhūti asked:

"By what skillful means does a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening practice the perfection of giving up to the knowledge of all modes, thereby purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings?"
The Buddha replied:

"One trains within the nature of phenomena which is non-existent; even while entering meditative contemplation, one is able to accumulate all merits, transform sentient beings, and purify the Buddha-fields—this is the power of skillful means."

Because the two dharmas of existence and non-existence can be practiced simultaneously—namely, ultimate emptiness while accumulating all merits—when this person practices the six pāramitās, they also cultivate the Buddha-way.
Just as the Buddha’s mind does, they practice the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) by means of ultimate emptiness and the dharma of non-existence.

When these bodhisattvas practice this path, they are able to fulfill the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
While practicing the bodhisattva path, one fulfills these dharmas.
Seated at the site of enlightenment, by means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
it is like a person who has lost a string of pearls in the night and immediately recovers them when a flash of lightning momentarily appears.
The afflictions and their residual tendencies are forever exhausted and will never arise again.
Having attained Buddhahood, he observes all worlds throughout the ten directions with the Buddha-eye; therein, he does not perceive even a single non-existent thing, let alone an existent one!

Ultimate emptiness can destroy perversions and enable bodhisattvas to attain buddhahood; yet even this matter cannot be apprehended, let alone the existence of any dharma of perversion belonging to ordinary beings!
Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-existence; this is called "the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
Even emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone existence!
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence.

When this bodhisattva practices this *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence, if they give a gift, they immediately know that the object given is empty and non-existent, and that both the recipient and the bodhisattva’s own mind are likewise non-existent.

Up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), even the attainer, the dharma attained, and the place of attainment—since they do not exist as dharmas, they are not even known; how much less so could they exist!
The "attainer" is the bodhisattva;
the "dharma attained" is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To employ the Dharma in this manner is the path of a bodhisattva.
They know that all these dharmas are non-existent. Why is this?
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is thus; it does not differ because of wisdom.
It is not created by ordinary beings, nor is it created by the noble ones; all phenomena are uncreated, for there is no creator.
Subhūti thought to himself:
"If all dharmas are characterized by non-existence, who is it that knows this non-existence?
For this reason, he questioned the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are detached from the intrinsic nature of dharmas. How can a dharma that is detached know another dharma that is detached, whether it exists or does not exist? Why is this so?”
Non-existence cannot know existence, and existence cannot know existence;
non-existence cannot know existence, and existence cannot know non-existence!
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are thus characterized by non-existence, how can a bodhisattva make such distinctions as ‘this dharma exists’ or ‘this dharma does not exist’?
The Buddha replied:
"Because Bodhisattvas act according to conventional truth, they teach sentient beings that things either exist or do not exist; this is not the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If 'existence' were truly existent, then 'non-existence' would likewise have to be truly existent."
"If there is that which is unreal, how could that which is non-existent be real?
Subhūti asked:
"Is there a difference between the conventional and the ultimate truth?"
If they were different, it would destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); therefore, the Buddha said:
"They are not different.
The suchness of the conventional is itself the suchness of the ultimate (*paramārtha*)."
Because sentient beings do not know this suchness (*tathatā*), they speak in terms of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) as either "existence" or "non-existence.

Furthermore, because sentient beings have attachments within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), the Bodhisattva speaks of "non-existence" so that these beings may abandon what exists and attain non-existence.
According to conventional dharmas, he discriminates among all phenomena, desiring to lead sentient beings to understand that these are non-existent.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should train in the *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence. Chapter 72:
The Practice of the Bodhisattva The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Practice of the Bodhisattva, Number Seventy-Two [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has spoken of the bodhisattva practice; what, then, is this bodhisattva practice?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva practitioner who practices for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is said to be engaged in the bodhisattva practice.
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the emptiness of form, practices the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
practices the emptiness of the eye up to the mind, and practices the emptiness of forms up to phenomena (dharmas);..."
He practices the emptiness of the eye-element up to the consciousness-element;
he practices the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom;

he practices internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence.

They practice the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyāna; they practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they practice the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path;
they practice the samādhi of emptiness, and the signless and wishless samādhis.
They practice the eight liberations and the nine successive concentrations;
they practice the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities; they practice great loving-kindness and great compassion;
they practice the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings.
They practice all forms of eloquence; they practice entering into the absence of letters through the use of letters; they practice all the gates of dhāraṇī;
they practice the nature of the conditioned and the nature of the unconditioned, just as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not constitute duality.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, this is called the practice of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the World-Honored One speaks of a ‘Buddha,’ for what reason is he called a ‘Buddha’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One is called a Buddha because of knowing the true meaning of all dharmas.
Furthermore, one is called a Buddha because of attaining the true mark of all dharmas."
Furthermore, he is called a Buddha because he has thoroughly realized the true meaning.
Furthermore, he is called a Buddha because he knows all phenomena as they truly are. Subhūti said:
"In what sense is it called bodhi? Subhūti! The meaning of emptiness is the meaning of bodhi;
the meaning of suchness, the meaning of the dharma-nature, and the meaning of the limit of reality are the meaning of bodhi."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Names, signs, and verbal expressions constitute the meaning of bodhi. Subhūti!
The true meaning of bodhi is that which cannot be destroyed and cannot be differentiated; this is the meaning of bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the true mark of all dharmas is that which is non-deceptive and non-alterable; this is the meaning of bodhi.
For this reason, it is called bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
this bodhi is called bodhi because it belongs to all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
because the Buddhas possess right and universal knowledge, it is called bodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās for the sake of this bodhi, up to practicing all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), regarding all dharmas, what is gained and what is lost? What increases and what decreases? What arises and what ceases? What is defiled and what is pure?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, up to and including practicing all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), they neither gain nor lose anything regarding all phenomena; there is no increase and no decrease, no arising and no ceasing, and no defilement and no purification."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not set out for the sake of gain or loss, increase or decrease, arising or ceasing, or purity or defilement.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and does not set out for the sake of gain or loss, nor even for the sake of purity or defilement, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the prajñāpāramitā so as to be able to take up the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā?”
How does one practice inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and existence?
How does one practice the dhyānas, the immeasurable minds, and the formless attainments?
How does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path?
How does one practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one practice the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion?
“How does one practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
How does one transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the rank of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom by means of dualistic dharmas; nor do they practice even up to the knowledge of all modes by means of dualistic dharmas."
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā* without relying on dualistic dharmas, and practices up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) without relying on dualistic dharmas, how do the roots of goodness of this bodhisattva increase from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If one practices with respect to dualistic dharmas, one's roots of goodness will not increase. Why is this?"
All ordinary beings rely on dualistic dharmas and thus cannot increase their roots of goodness.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the non-dual dharma; from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought, throughout that interval, they increase their roots of goodness.

For this reason, no devas, humans, or asuras in any world can subdue a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor can they destroy their roots of goodness and cause them to fall to the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha;

nor can any various evils or unwholesome dharmas restrain the bodhisattva from practicing the dāna-pāramitā and increasing their roots of goodness, and so it is likewise for all the pāramitās up to the prajñā-pāramitā.
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way.
“World-Honored One!”
“Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of roots of goodness?
The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā neither for the sake of roots of goodness, nor for the sake of what are not roots of goodness.
Why is this? Subhūti!

By the nature of things, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not made offerings to the Buddhas, who has not perfected the roots of goodness, and who has not obtained true spiritual friends, cannot attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva make offerings to the Buddhas, fulfill roots of goodness, and, by relying on true spiritual friends, attain all-knowledge?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes offerings to all Buddhas.

Regarding the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by those Buddhas—from *sūtra* up to *upadeśa*—this bodhisattva hears them, retains them, recites them, masters their benefits, contemplates them with the mind, and thoroughly understands them.”
Because of thorough comprehension, one attains dhāraṇī;
because of attaining dhāraṇī, one is able to give rise to unimpeded wisdom;
because of giving rise to unimpeded wisdom, in whatever place one is born, one will never forget this Dharma, up until the attainment of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
They have also planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas and are protected by these roots of goodness, such that they never fall into the evil realms or the various difficulties.
By virtue of these roots of goodness as their cause and condition, they attain purity of the profound mind;
because they attain purity of the profound mind, they are able to purify Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity.

Because they are protected by their roots of goodness, they are never separated from true spiritual friends—namely, the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and the Śrāvakas who are able to praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should make offerings to the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, and draw near to spiritual friends.
[Treatise] Explanation:
In the superior section, Subhūti asks the Buddha:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is frequently spoken of; for what reason is it named *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha answers with various causes and conditions.
For this reason, within this chapter, it is asked of the Bhagavān once more:
"You frequently speak of the bodhisattva-caryā; what is this bodhisattva-caryā?
Thus, Subhūti asks concerning the bodhisattva-caryā.
Question:
If all dharmas are subsumed within the *prajñāpāramitā*, and furthermore, *prajñā* itself is the practice of the bodhisattva, for what reason is this question asked again?

Answer: All paths of the bodhisattvas are called "bodhisattva practices," while the wisdom that universally and thoroughly knows the true reality of all phenomena is called "prajñāpāramitā"; this is the distinction between them.
If the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* and the "Bodhisattva Practices" (*bodhisattvacaryā*) are mutually inclusive, they are not different.
Furthermore, some say:
"The practices of a bodhisattva" refers to all that is performed by a bodhisattva through the actions of body, speech, and mind; all such deeds are termed "bodhisattva practices."
For this reason, Subhūti asks solely with the intention of distinguishing the "correct practice of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha replies:
"The practice of a bodhisattva consists of all wholesome deeds for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the correct practice of a bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva practices wholesome dharmas with unwholesome, indeterminate, or attached states of mind, it is not the bodhisattva practice;
however, when one acts for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through compassion and the wisdom of emptiness, this is called the bodhisattva practice.
What is the practice of purity?

It is the practice of the emptiness of form; the practice of the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and even the practice of the emptiness of conditioned nature and unconditioned nature.

Thus, regarding all phenomena, one does not discriminate between what is empty and what is real, nor even between what is conditioned and what is unconditioned; as in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, where conceptual proliferation is extinguished and there is no duality of marks—this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
There is nothing that can destroy it, nor is there any fault in it.
Having heard this practice of the bodhisattva, Subhūti asked with joy:
"If a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood as the fruit and retribution of their practice;..."
“Since you frequently speak of the Buddha, what is the meaning of ‘Buddha’?
The Buddha replied,
“One is called a Buddha because of knowing the true meaning of all phenomena.”
Question: If that is so, then Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and great Bodhisattvas also know the true meaning of all phenomena; for what reason are they not called Buddhas?
The answer is:
The "analogy of lighting a lamp" has already been explained above.
It is real for ordinary beings, but it is not real for the Buddha.
Because it is shrouded by the habitual tendencies of afflictions, it is not called "real.
Because one cannot attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and sever doubts and regrets regarding all phenomena, it is not called "correct knowledge" or "the true meaning."
As analyzed above, it is asked: What is the difference between these four—

knowing the true meaning of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-bhūtārtha*), attaining the true characteristic of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-bhūtalakṣaṇa*), penetrating the true meaning, and knowing all phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta*)?
Answer: Some say that the meaning is not different, only the names are different.
Some say: There is a distinction.
The meaning of "Dharma" is the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmasatyatā*); it is neither arising nor ceasing, its dharma-characteristics are eternally abiding, just like *nirvāṇa*.
Because he knows this meaning, he is called a Buddha.
Within this meaning, he is eternally awakened and free from error;
regarding this meaning, he employs various names, signs, and teachings to enable sentient beings to understand the supreme ultimate reality.

Therefore, among the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) and the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) are specifically mentioned.
There are two causes and conditions why some people, although they have attained the true meaning of all phenomena, are unable to penetrate it thoroughly:
first, their afflictions (*kleśa*) have not been exhausted; second, they have not yet attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Just as the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin cannot penetrate [reality] because they have not yet severed their afflictions;

and although the arhat, pratyekabuddha, and great bodhisattvas have exhausted their afflictions, they cannot penetrate it because they have not yet attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, it is said: "Because he has thoroughly realized the true meaning, he is called a Buddha.

One who knows all phenomena as they truly are understands both the aforementioned three matters as well as their meaning and their phenomena; because he clearly and fully knows whether all phenomena exist or do not exist, as explained in the section on the meaning of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*):
he knows both the characteristic of quiescence and the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, "Bodhi" means wisdom, and a "Buddha" is one who possesses wisdom.
Because he has attained this wisdom, he is called a "wise one.
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One! What is bodhi?
The Buddha replied:
"Emptiness, suchness, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are called bodhi.
The wisdom of the true mark associated with the emptiness samādhi takes suchness, the nature of phenomena, and the limit of reality as its object; thus, bodhi is defined as true wisdom.
Those on the path of the three trainings have not yet severed the afflictions; therefore, although they possess wisdom, it is not called bodhi.
As for those of the three stages beyond training, because their ignorance has been forever exhausted without remainder, their wisdom is called bodhi.
Because the two types of those beyond training do not attain omniscience—the correct and universal knowledge of all phenomena—they cannot be called "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Only the wisdom of the Buddha alone is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, it is called *bodhi* because it consists of names, marks, speech, and written characters.
The true meaning of bodhi cannot be conceptualized or destroyed.
Furthermore, bodhi is suchness (*tathatā*), non-differentiated, eternal, and not deceptive. Why is this so?
The wisdom of all sentient beings becomes increasingly superior until it reaches that of a Buddha, beyond which there is nothing more superior;
likewise, all phenomena become increasingly superior, such that what precedes is false while what follows is true, until one reaches Bodhi, beyond which there is nothing more real.
Therefore, bodhi is called "reality.
Furthermore, just as one is called a Buddha because of attaining bodhi, now bodhi is so named because it is attained by the Buddha.
Moreover, some say:
The knowledge that birth has been forever exhausted is called bodhi.
Some say that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called bodhi.
Some say: Unimpeded liberation is called bodhi. Why is this?
Having attained this liberation, one penetrates all dharmas.
Some say that the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are bodhi.
Why is this? The Buddha’s knowledge of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is "unimpededness regarding meaning" (*artha-pratisaṃvid*);
his knowledge of the distinctions between the names and characteristics of all phenomena is called "unimpededness regarding phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
To discern various forms of speech so that sentient beings may attain understanding is called "unimpededness in expression" (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*);
to preach the Dharma for the sake of teaching and transforming others inexhaustibly and without end is called "unimpededness in eloquence" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Because one fully benefits sentient beings by means of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it is called bodhi. Some say:

the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)—all such immeasurable Buddha-qualities are collectively termed bodhi.
Why is this? Because wisdom is great, all dharmas are termed bodhi. Some say:

True enlightenment (bodhi) refers to the Buddha’s ten untainted knowledges (anāsrava-jñāna). The feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with these ten knowledges, as well as bodily and vocal karma and all formations dissociated from the mind, are all termed enlightenment.
Because they share the same conditions, arise together, and mutually assist one another, they are all called bodhi.
Furthermore, some say:
the meaning of bodhi is immeasurable and boundless; only a Buddha can know it in its entirety, while others know but a small portion of it.

For example, among the various treasures within the treasury of a wheel-turning sage king, no one is able to distinguish or know their value; yet when the sage king brings forth these treasures to bestow them upon others, it is precisely those who receive them who can know their worth.
In this context, after Subhūti had questioned the Buddha regarding the characteristics of bodhi, he further asked the World-Honored One:
"If bodhi is ultimately empty and its characteristic is indestructible, what kind of roots of goodness does a bodhisattva increase when practicing the dharmas of the six pāramitās?"
The Buddha replied:
"If a bodhisattva practices this true nature of bodhi, they do not add anything to any dharma, let alone to roots of goodness! Why is this?"
"The Prajñāpāramitā does not emerge for the sake of gain or loss, nor even for the sake of defilement or purity, because it is ultimately pure.
The Buddha affirmed his meaning.
He then asked again:
"If there is neither increase nor decrease, how does a bodhisattva practicing *prajñā* take up the various bodhisattva practices such as the *dāna-pāramitā*?
The Buddha replied:
"Although a bodhisattva practices these dharmas, they do not practice by means of dualistic dharmas."
"Because they proceed in union with ultimate emptiness, one should not raise such an objection.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva does not practice dualistic dharmas, how can they increase their roots of goodness from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final moment of mind?
The Buddha replied:
“If a person practices dualistic dharmas, this is a perversion; such a person cannot increase their roots of goodness.”
"Just as a person in a dream may acquire great wealth but ultimately gains nothing,
whereas what one acquires after waking is truly called 'gain.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:"
"Because all ordinary people are attached to dualistic dharmas, they are unable to increase their roots of goodness.

The Bodhisattva practices the true mark of all dharmas, which is the so-called non-dual dharma; from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought, he increases his roots of goodness without error."
Therefore, no devas, humans, or asuras can destroy the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness and cause them to fall into the two vehicles, nor can any other evils destroy them.
"Other evils" refers to afflictions such as stinginess and greed, which destroy the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and other wholesome dharmas.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the bodhisattva practice prajñā for the sake of roots of goodness?
The Buddha replied,
“One practices prajñā neither for the sake of what is wholesome nor for the sake of what is unwholesome.”
Question: It may be granted that one practices *prajñā* not for the sake of unwholesome roots; however, how can it be said that one practices "not for the sake of wholesome roots"?
The answer is:

Herein, the Buddha’s intention is that because he values *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, although one practices various roots of goodness, one does so merely to accomplish a task and does not regard them as valuable in themselves.
As stated in the *Kāṣṭhaka-upama-sūtra*:
"Even wholesome dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so unwholesome dharmas!
Wholesome roots are the dharmas that assist the path to Buddhahood.
If a person does not cross for the sake of the raft, but crosses for the sake of reaching the other shore,
the Buddha explains the causal conditions therein:
"A bodhisattva who has not yet made offerings to the Buddhas and has not yet attained true spiritual friends cannot attain all-knowledge."
"Therefore, although one plants roots of goodness, one does not regard them as precious, but does so solely for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti asked:
'How is it that a bodhisattva, though not acting for the sake of roots of goodness, is able to make offerings to all Buddhas and even attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)?'"
The Buddha replied:
"Since first generating the mind of enlightenment, the bodhisattva has made offerings to all Buddhas," as it is said in the sutras.

Because the offering to the Buddha is of great significance, when it says "only the Buddha," one should know that this already includes making offerings to the pratyekabuddhas and even those dwelling on the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā).

Ordinary people, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, receive the twelve divisions of the scriptures from those from whom they hear them; because they cannot always have a teacher, they must all uphold them;
and because they are prone to forgetfulness, they should recite them until they are proficient.
As for mental contemplation: one should constantly bind the mind to the sutra scrolls and recollect them in sequence.
First, one proclaims the meaning through speech; subsequently, upon attaining thorough mastery, one immediately acquires dhāraṇī.
There are two kinds of dhāraṇīs:
first, the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining; second, the dhāraṇī of attaining the true mark of all phenomena.
By reading, reciting, practicing, and constantly mindfulness [of the teachings], one attains the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.
Because they have attained mastery over the meaning [of the teachings], they obtain the *dhāraṇī* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Abiding within these two gates of *dhāraṇī*, they are able to give rise to unimpeded wisdom;
and for the sake of preaching the Dharma to sentient beings, they become fully endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*).
Question:
If a bodhisattva possesses unimpeded wisdom, how does it differ from that of a Buddha? Answer:
There are two kinds of unimpededness:
first, true unimpededness; second, nominal unimpededness.
Among these, with the exception of the Buddha’s unimpededness, the others correspond to the unimpededness attained by bodhisattvas.

Because of causes and conditions such as this Bodhisattva’s reading of scriptures and so forth, in whatever place he is born, up until the attainment of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), he shall never forget or lose [what he has learned]. Why is this?
Because they have deeply studied and recited all dharmas, their afflictions are broken and thinned.
Because they are protected by roots of goodness, they will never fall into the evil realms or various calamities;
just as a blind person, being led and protected by one with sight, will never fall into a ditch or a ravine.
Because one has accumulated roots of goodness and merit, one attains purity of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
One whose profound mind is pure loves all sentient beings; even toward those who are enemies or thieves, one does not inflict evil, such as taking their lives and so forth.

Furthermore, because wisdom and merit are gathered in great abundance, afflictions are slight and cannot completely shroud the bodhisattva’s wholesome mind. Furthermore, as for the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*):

it is the attainment of a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, non-abandonment, and the resolve to deliver sentient beings; it is the attainment of the realization of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and ultimate emptiness regarding all phenomena; and even with respect to the Buddha, one does not give rise to the notion of "Buddha" or the notion of "nirvāṇa. This is called the purity of the profound mind.
Because their profound resolve is pure, they are able to teach and transform sentient beings.

Why is this? Because their afflictions are thin, they do not give rise to arrogance, self-centeredness, or anger; thus, sentient beings cherish and delight in them, and they believe and accept their words, thereby being taught and transformed.
Because of teaching and transforming sentient beings, one attains a pure Buddha-field;
as it is said in the "Buddha-land Chapter" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
"Because sentient beings are pure, the world is pure."
Because they are protected by roots of goodness, they never part from spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Spiritual friends are the Buddhas, the great Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats.
To briefly describe the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra): one who is able to praise the Triple Gem.
Such a bodhisattva should make offerings to the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, and draw near to spiritual friends.
Why is this? It is because a sick person should seek out a skilled physician and medicinal herbs;
the Buddha is the skilled physician, the various roots of goodness are the medicinal herbs, and those who attend to the sick are the spiritual friends.
Because the patient possesses these three factors, the illness is cured;
likewise, the Bodhisattva also possesses these two factors, and because he extinguishes all afflictions, he is able to benefit sentient beings.
Chapter 73: On the Planting of Roots of Goodness. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter 73: On the Planting of Roots of Goodness. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not make offerings to the Buddhas, does not fulfill the roots of goodness, and does not obtain true spiritual friends, will they attain sarvajñā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If even the all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) is difficult to attain for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has made offerings to the Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, and obtained true spiritual friends, how much more so for one who does not make offerings to the Buddhas, does not plant roots of goodness, and does not obtain true spiritual friends!"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have made offerings to all Buddhas, planted roots of goodness, and obtained true spiritual friends, for what reason is it difficult for them to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the power of skillful means; he has not heard the power of skillful means from the Buddhas; the roots of goodness he has planted are incomplete; and he does not constantly follow the instructions of spiritual friends."
“World-Honored One!
What is this power of skillful means, by practicing which power the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains all-knowledge?
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the perfection of giving while corresponding to the mindfulness of omniscience (sarvajñatā), and bestows gifts upon Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, humans, or non-humans, at that time he does not give rise to the notion of 'giving' nor the notion of a 'recipient'."

Why is this? Because one contemplates that all dharmas are empty of self-characteristic, unarisen, devoid of fixed characteristics, and subject to no transformation; thus one enters the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, which is to say, the characteristic of all dharmas being without action and without origination.
By means of this power of skillful means, the bodhisattva increases their roots of goodness;
by increasing these roots of goodness, they practice the perfection of giving, purify buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity.
One practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) by bestowing gifts without seeking worldly retribution, but solely with the desire to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) in accordance with the mindfulness of omniscience (sarvajñatā), while observing the precepts they do not fall into lust, anger, or delusion; nor do they fall into any afflictions (kleśa), fetters (paryavasthāna), or unwholesome factors that destroy the path—such as stinginess and greed, breaking the precepts, malice, laziness, distracted mind, or folly; nor pride, extreme pride, conceit, self-pride, overweening pride, inferiority pride, or false pride; nor the mind of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all dharmas as empty of self-characteristic, unarisen, without fixed characteristics, and without transition; they enter into the true reality of all dharmas, which is to say, the characteristic of all dharmas being without action and without arising.
Because the Bodhisattva accomplishes this power of skillful means, he increases his roots of goodness;
because he increases his roots of goodness, he practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), purifies Buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity.
One upholds the precepts not for the sake of receiving worldly retribution, but solely because of the desire to rescue and deliver all sentient beings;
thus one practices the śīlapāramitā. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), in accordance with the mindfulness of omniscience (sarvajñatā) and through the accomplishment of the power of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya). Thus, he practices the path of seeing the truths (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), yet he does not take up the fruit of stream-enterer (srotāpanna), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returner (anāgāmin), or arhat.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), unborn, without fixed characteristics, and without anything that can be transmuted; thus, although they practice these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor and enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, as well as the four immeasurable minds and the four formless attainments; although they enter and emerge from these various meditative concentrations, they do not undergo their karmic retribution.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has accomplished the power of such skillful means that he knows all dhyānas and samādhis are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), unarisen, devoid of fixed characteristics, and without transition; thus he purifies buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity.
One practices the *vīrya-pāramitā* because one does not seek worldly retribution through diligence, but desires only to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dhyānapāramitā while maintaining mindfulness of sarvajñā; he enters the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments, yet he does not realize the fruit of srotāpanna, nor does he realize the fruits up to arhatship.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics, unarisen, without fixed characteristics, and without anything that can be transformed.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, training in the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique dharmas, great loving-kindness, and great compassion; until they have attained all-knowledge, purified the buddha-field, and matured sentient beings, they should practice in this manner throughout that interval.

Why is this? Because, Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), unarisen, without fixed characteristics, and without anything that can be transformed. Subhūti!
This Bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, without receiving its karmic retribution.
[Treatise] Question:

Why does Subhūti pose such a blunt question—“If one does not make offerings to the Buddhas, does not fulfill the roots of goodness, and does not encounter true spiritual friends, will one still attain *sarvajñatā*?”
Answer: Some say:
"If all dharmas are of a non-existent nature and are ultimately empty, then within ultimate emptiness, there is no difference between planting roots of goodness and not planting them."

"If that were so," [someone] asked, "could one not attain *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) without making offerings to the Buddhas, without planting roots of goodness, and without encountering true spiritual friends?
Furthermore, another person doubted, saying:
"There are various other gateways for attaining *sarvajñā*; it may not be necessary to plant roots of goodness and so forth."
For this reason, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha replied:
"If even making offerings to the Buddhas, planting roots of goodness, and encountering true spiritual friends are difficult to achieve, how much more so is it for those who do not!"
Subhūti asked:
"Since within ultimate emptiness there is neither merit nor non-merit, why is it that one attains [enlightenment] solely by means of merit?
The Buddha replied:
"It is because merit exists within the conventional truth that one attains it.
Subhūti asked this because sentient beings were attached to the notion of non-existence; the Buddha answered by not adhering to any dharma, saying:
"If even the merit cultivated through diligent effort cannot be apprehended, how much less so that which is not cultivated!"
Suppose a mendicant monk arrives at a village and goes from house to house begging for food, but receives nothing.
He sees a starving dog lying down in hunger and strikes it with a staff, saying:
"You ignorant beast! Even though I have sought food from house to house through various means, I am still unable to obtain any; how much less can you expect to get anything while simply lying there!"
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One,
since there are such causes and conditions as making offerings to the Buddhas and so forth, for what reason does one not obtain their karmic fruit?”
The Buddha replied:
“Because they are devoid of skillful means (upāya).
Skillful means refers to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Although they see the form bodies of all Buddhas, they do not see the dharma body with the eye of wisdom;
although they plant a few roots of goodness, they do not bring them to fulfillment;
and although they encounter spiritual friends, they do not draw near to them to seek instruction or receive their teachings.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explained the causes and conditions, saying:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the bodhisattva practices the dānapāramitā with both a mind that exists and a mind that does not exist.

That which is 'with a mind' refers to practicing giving while corresponding to the mind of sarvajñā (omniscience), recollecting the various immeasurable merits of all Buddhas, and practicing giving out of compassion for sentient beings.

One who is "without mind" does not give rise to the three perceptions—namely, the giver, the recipient, and the gift—when making an offering to anyone from the Buddha down to an ordinary person. Why is this?
All phenomena, such as the objects of giving and so forth, are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*) and have been eternally unarisen from the very beginning.
They possess no fixed characteristics—whether of identity or difference, permanence or impermanence, and so on—because these phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics;
they cannot be altered, for they abide within suchness (*tathatā*).
Observing in this way, one enters the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, which is characterized by non-action and non-arising.
All phenomena are incapable of acting; they do not give rise to conceit, nor do they harbor any expectations.
By means of such skillful power, they are able to increase their roots of goodness and eliminate unwholesome roots, transforming sentient beings and purifying Buddha-worlds.
Whether their giving is much or little, they do not accept worldly retribution, desiring only to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva’s giving to sentient beings is finite and limited, they form this thought:
"In my past lives, I did not practice profound merit; therefore, I am currently unable to give extensively to sentient beings."

I shall now deeply and truly practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) extensively; having obtained this karmic fruit, I will be able to fully provide benefit by widely bestowing it upon immeasurable sentient beings—whether for their benefit in this life, their benefit in future lives, or the benefit of the Path and its virtue.

"Without such skillful means, even if a bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, plants roots of goodness, and encounters true spiritual friends, they will still not attain it; how much less so if they do not make offerings!"
The same applies to the other five pāramitās.

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of Chapter 70: "Universal Training."

Chapter 74: On Universal Study Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, based on the work of the Holy Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished great wisdom; though he practices this profound dharma, he does not receive its karmic retribution.
The Buddha told Subhūti, “So it is!”
Thus it is!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished great wisdom and practices this profound prajñāpāramitā, they likewise do not receive its karmic retribution. Why is this?
"This is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva is immovable within the nature of all phenomena.
"World-Honored One,
within what nature of what phenomena is he immovable?"
The Buddha said:
"One does not move within the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not move within the nature of form, nor does he move within the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

He does not move from the nature of the *dānapāramitā*; he does not move from the nature of the *śīlapāramitā*, the *kṣāntipāramitā*, the *vīryapāramitā*, the *dhyānapāramitā*, or the *prajñāpāramitā*.

He does not move from the nature of the four *dhyānas*, he does not move from the nature of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and he does not move from the nature of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
He does not move from the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to and including the nature of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
They do not waver from the samādhi of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless, nor even from the nature of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The nature of these dharmas is precisely non-existence.
Subhūti, by means of a dharma that is non-existent, one cannot obtain a dharma that exists.
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
