can any dharma obtain any dharma?"
The Buddha said: "No. [He replied:
"World-Honored One!"
“Can all dharmas attain the dharma of non-existence?
The Buddha said, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
Can a non-existent dharma attain a non-existent dharma?
The Buddha said:

"No, World-Honored One! If that which is non-existent cannot attain that which exists, that which exists cannot attain that which exists, that which exists cannot attain that which is non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot attain that which is non-existent, then would it not be the case, World-Honored One, that you have not attained the Way?"
The Buddha said:
"There is attainment, but not by means of these four phrases.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'attainment'?
The Buddha said,
"Neither existing nor non-existing, free from all conceptual proliferation— this is called attaining the Way."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates form as either permanent or impermanent, this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent is conceptual proliferation.
To contemplate form as either suffering or pleasure, or feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either suffering or pleasure, is conceptual proliferation.”
To contemplate form as self or as not-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self or as not-self;
form as tranquil or as not tranquil; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as tranquil or as not tranquil—this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

To say that the noble truth of suffering should be seen, the noble truth of origination should be abandoned, the noble truth of cessation should be realized, and the noble truth of the path should be cultivated—this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To say that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments should be cultivated—this is conceptual proliferation.

To say that one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path is conceptual proliferation;
to say that one should cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness is conceptual proliferation;
to say that one should cultivate the eight liberations and the nine successive absorptions is conceptual proliferation.

To think, "I shall transcend the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, and the path of the pratyekabuddha," is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall fulfill the ten stages of a bodhisattva"—this is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall enter the rank of a bodhisattva"—this is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall purify the buddha-fields"—this is conceptual proliferation.
To think, "I shall bring sentient beings to maturity," is conceptual proliferation.
To think, "I shall give birth to the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas," is conceptual proliferation;
to think, "I shall attain all-knowledge" (sarvākārajñatā), is conceptual proliferation.
"I shall sever all habitual tendencies of affliction"—this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because form (*rūpa*)—whether permanent or impermanent—is beyond conceptual proliferation, one should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding it; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*)—whether permanent or impermanent—are beyond conceptual proliferation, one should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding them; and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is beyond conceptual proliferation, one should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding it.
Why is this? One does not conceptualize existence through existence, nor does one conceptualize non-existence through non-existence;
apart from existence and non-existence, no further dharma can be apprehended—namely, the one who conceptualizes, the dharma that is conceptualized, or the locus of conceptualization.
For this reason, Subhūti, form is without conceptual proliferation;
feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even up to all-knowledge are without conceptual proliferation.
It is thus, Subhūti.
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the non-conceptualizing (*niṣprapañca*) perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Why is it that form cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation, and so on, up to why all-knowledge cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The nature of form does not exist, and so on, up to the nature of all-knowledge does not exist."
Subhūti! If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-existent, it is without conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca).

For this reason, form (rūpa) cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), which also cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the non-conceptualization of the prajñāpāramitā in this way, at that time they enter the bodhisattva stage.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if all dharmas have no intrinsic nature, by what path does a bodhisattva practice to enter the bodhisattva stage?”
Is it by means of the path of the śrāvaka?
Is it by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha?
Or is it by means of the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"One does not enter the stage of a bodhisattva by means of the path of the śrāvaka, nor by means of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor by means of the path of the Buddha; rather, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the stage of a bodhisattva by training thoroughly in all paths."

Subhūti! It is as if an *aṣṭamaka* first studies all the paths and then enters the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*); before attaining the fruit, he first gives rise to the path to that fruit. So it is with the Bodhisattva:

having first universally studied all paths, he then enters the Bodhisattva stage; yet, even before attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he first gives rise to the Vajra-like Samādhi. At that time, through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, he attains all-knowledge.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train thoroughly in all paths in order to enter the bodhisattva stage, then the path of the person practicing for the fruit of srotāpanna and the attainment of srotāpanna; the path of the person practicing for the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin and the attainment of sakṛdāgāmin; the path of the person practicing for the fruit of anāgāmin and the attainment of anāgāmin; the path of the person practicing for the fruit of arhat and the attainment of arhat; as well as the path of the pratyekabuddha and the path of the Buddha—these various paths are each distinct.”
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva must study all paths exhaustively before entering the bodhisattva stage, then if this bodhisattva gives rise to the eightfold path, they should become one of the eight persons (aṣṭamaka)!
If one is born into the Path of Seeing, one should become a Srotāpanna!
If one is born into the Path of Cultivation, one should become a Sakṛdāgāmin, an Anāgāmin, or an Arhat!
"If one were to give rise to the path of a pratyekabuddha and become a pratyekabuddha—
World-Honored One!—
it would be impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to become an 'eightfold person' and subsequently enter the bodhisattva stage."
It is impossible that one could attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) without entering the stage of a bodhisattva!
It is also impossible that one could enter the stage of a bodhisattva only after having become a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to a pratyekabuddha!
"It is impossible, World-Honored One, that one could attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) without entering the stage of a bodhisattva!
World-Honored One,
how should I understand how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully studied all paths, enters the stage of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to become one of the eight persons, attain the fruit of srotāpanna, and so on up to attaining the fruit of arhat, or attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, and only thereafter enter the stage of a bodhisattva—such a thing is impossible!
"It is impossible that one who has not entered the stage of a bodhisattva should attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)!
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the six perfections and contemplates them with wisdom, they transcend the eight stages."
What are the eight stages?

They are the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of thinness, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
By means of the knowledge of the modes of the path, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva;
having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, one uses the knowledge of all modes to sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies. Subhūti!
Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of these eight types of persons, this is the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha—each and every instance of their wisdom or abandonment is the patience of the bodhisattva.
The bodhisattva trains in this way in the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), he enters the stage of a bodhisattva.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, by means of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), he eradicates all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and attains the Buddha-way.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully trained in and perfected all the dharmas, should attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he shall benefit sentient beings with its fruit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the path spoken of by the World-Honored One:”
“Regarding the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha—what is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the paths?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to the pure knowledge of all aspects of the paths.”
Subhūti! What is the pure wisdom of the aspects of the path?
It is that which a bodhisattva should correctly know regarding the characteristics and the dharmas that can be manifested by those characteristics.
Having attained right knowledge, they expound and reveal it for others, enabling all sentient beings to attain understanding.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should master all sounds and languages; using these sounds to preach the Dharma, they fill the trichiliocosm, like the nature of an echo.
For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should first fully train in all paths.

Once they have perfected the knowledge of paths, they should discern and know the deep intentions of sentient beings—namely, that for beings in the hells, they should know the hellish path, the causes of hell, and the fruits of hell, and they should obstruct them;

for those in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, they should know the paths of animals and hungry ghosts, the causes of animals and hungry ghosts, and the fruits of animals and hungry ghosts, and they should obstruct them.
One should know and should obstruct the various realms of the nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and asuras, as well as their causes and effects.
The path, cause, and fruit of the human realm should be known; the paths, causes, and fruits of the various celestial realms should be known:

the path, cause, and fruit of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven should be known;

the paths, causes, and fruits of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception should be known.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—their causes and fruits should be known.

The gate of liberation through emptiness, the gate of liberation through signlessness, and the gate of liberation through wishlessness; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion—their causes and fruits should be known.
By means of this path, the bodhisattva causes sentient beings to enter the path of srotāpanna up to the paths of arhat, pratyekabuddha, and even anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s pure knowledge of the aspects of the path.
Having trained in this knowledge of the aspects of the path, the bodhisattva enters into the characteristics of the deep minds of sentient beings.
Having entered, he teaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings as appropriate, and his words are not in vain. Why is this?

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas skillfully know the characteristics of the faculties of sentient beings, and they know the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, as well as the destinies of their births and deaths.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Why is that?
All wholesome dharmas that assist the path enter into the Prajñāpāramitā; it is what all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should practice.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

If the four foundations of mindfulness up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed, formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; they have but one characteristic, which is so-called ‘characteristiclessness.’”
"Bhagavān!
How can these factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) take hold of anuttarasamyaksambodhi?
Bhagavān!"

This is neither conjoined nor dispersed; it is formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive. It is a single characteristic, namely the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*). It is without anything to be grasped and without anything to be relinquished, just as space is without grasping or relinquishing.
The Buddha said: "So it is! So it is!"
Subhūti! All dharmas are empty of their own characteristics; there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be abandoned. Subhūti!

There are sentient beings who do not know that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics; for the sake of these beings, he reveals the factors conducive to enlightenment that can lead to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Furthermore, Subhūti!
All form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
all the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration...”
The *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā*, all forms of emptiness from internal emptiness and external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence,
the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path,
the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments.

The ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the knowledge of all modes, and all such dharmas—within these noble dharmas, they are all neither conjoined nor dispersed;
they are formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; they have but a single characteristic, which is to say, "non-existence."
These characteristics are taught for the sake of sentient beings by means of conventional truth so that they may understand; it is not by means of the ultimate truth, Subhūti.
Regarding all these phenomena, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should train in accordance with the Dharma through wisdom and vision;
having so trained, they should discern which phenomena are applicable and which are not.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
Which dharmas, having been analyzed by a bodhisattva, should he apply and which should he not apply?”
The Buddha said:
"The dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, though known through analytical discernment, should not be employed;
the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), known through analytical discernment, should be employed."
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom within these noble dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are they called ‘noble dharmas’?
What are these noble dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Regarding all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the Buddhas, they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with desire, hatred, and delusion; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, or doubt; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with sensual passion, ill will;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with passion for the realm of form, passion for the formless realm, restlessness, pride, or ignorance.”

From the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
from internal emptiness up to great compassion, the conditioned nature, and the unconditioned nature, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed.

Why is this? Because all these dharmas are without color, without form, and without resistance; they have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).

A dharma without color does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma without color; a dharma without form does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma without form; a dharma without resistance does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma without resistance; a dharma with a single characteristic does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma with a single characteristic; and a dharma without characteristics does not conjoin with nor disperse from a dharma without characteristics.
Subhūti! This Prajñāpāramitā is formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; it is of a single mark, namely, the markless. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study it;
having studied it, they do not apprehend the marks of any dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train in the marks of form?”
Does one not train in the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Does one not train in the characteristics of the eye up to the mind, nor in the characteristics of forms up to phenomena,

nor in the characteristics of the earth element up to the consciousness element, nor in the characteristics of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) or the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*)?
The characteristics of the perfection of giving, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom;
the characteristics of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence;
the characteristics of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; and the characteristics of loving-kindness up to equanimity—one does not study these.
One does not study the characteristics of the boundless emptiness up to the characteristic of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
one does not study the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the characteristics of the eightfold noble path;

one does not study the characteristics of the emptiness samādhi, the signless, or the wishless samādhis; and one does not study the characteristics of the eight liberations or the nine successive attainments.

One does not study the characteristics of the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, or great loving-kindness and great compassion;
one does not study the characteristics of the noble truth of suffering, nor the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path;
one does not study the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination in direct or reverse order; and one does not study conditioned phenomena.
"Are they the characteristic of nature, or the characteristic of the unconditioned?
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not study the characteristics of all dharmas, how can he study the characteristics of all dharmas—whether conditioned or unconditioned—and having so studied, transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
If one does not transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, how can one enter the bodhisattva stage?
If one does not enter the bodhisattva stage, how will one ever attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)?
If one does not attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), how can one turn the wheel of Dharma?
If one does not turn the wheel of Dharma, how can one deliver sentient beings from birth and death by means of the three vehicles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If all dharmas truly possessed marks, then a bodhisattva should train in those marks. Subhūti!”
Because all dharmas truly have no marks; they are without color, without form, and without resistance, having but a single mark, which is to say, no mark.
For this reason, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not train in signs, nor do they train in signlessness.
Why is this? Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, all dharmas have a single characteristic: their nature is eternally abiding.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas possess neither marks nor lack marks, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the prajñāpāramitā?”
If one does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
if one does not transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one cannot enter the rank of a bodhisattva;
and if one does not enter the rank of a bodhisattva, one will not attain the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
If one does not attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, one cannot obtain the supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas;
if one does not obtain the supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas, one cannot purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity;
if one does not purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity, one cannot attain all-knowledge.
If one does not attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one cannot turn the wheel of Dharma;

if one does not turn the wheel of Dharma, one cannot cause sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship, nor can one cause them to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha, nor can one cause them to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Furthermore, one cannot cause sentient beings to obtain the merit of giving, nor can one cause them to obtain the merit of observing the precepts or cultivating meditative concentration.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"All dharmas are without marks; they are neither of one mark nor of different marks.
To cultivate the absence of marks is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that practicing the signless is practicing the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"To cultivate the disintegration of all phenomena is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“World-Honored One,
how is it that cultivating the disintegration of all phenomena is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha said:
"To cultivate the destruction of form is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
To cultivate the destruction of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-objects is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the contemplation on impurity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of the first dhyāna, and the destruction of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of cessation, and mindfulness of the destruction of ānāpāna is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

To cultivate the mark of impermanence, the mark of suffering, the mark of non-self, the mark of emptiness, the mark of origination, the mark of cause, the mark of arising, the mark of condition, the mark of obstruction, the mark of cessation, the mark of excellence, the mark of emergence, the mark of the path, the mark of correctness, the mark of the track, and the mark of detachment until they are destroyed—this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

To cultivate the destruction of the twelve links of dependent origination, to cultivate the destruction of the marks of a self, a sentient being, and a life span, and even to cultivate the destruction of the marks of a knower and a seer—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the marks of permanence, bliss, purity, and self—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the eight liberations and the nine successive concentrations while remaining detached from them is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, the concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, and the concentration with neither directed thought nor sustained thought while remaining detached from them is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds is to cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To cultivate the destruction of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is to cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*;

to cultivate the destruction of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.

To cultivate the destruction of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the destruction of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the path of the pratyekabuddha, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To cultivate the destruction of all-knowledge is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the destruction of the eradication of all habitual tendencies of affliction is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

what is meant by ‘cultivating the destruction of form’ up to ‘cultivating the destruction of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies through abandonment,’ which is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not to conceive of the existence of dharmas of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

not to conceive of the existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including not to conceive of the existence of the dharma that destroys all habitual tendencies of affliction—this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? One who possesses the notion of dharmas does not cultivate the prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti!

Those who possess the notion of dharmas do not cultivate the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Such a person is attached to dharmas and does not practice the dāna-pāramitā, up to and including the prajñā-pāramitā.
For one who clings in this way, there is no liberation, no Path, and no nirvāṇa.

One who possesses the notion of dharmas does not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path; they do not cultivate the samādhi of emptiness, nor even up to the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes.
"Why is this? Because such a person is attached to dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is existence? What is non-existence?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Duality is the existence of dharmas; non-duality is the non-existence of dharmas.
[Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!"
"What are these two? The Buddha said: "The characteristic of form is duality;

the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are duality. The characteristic of the eye up to the characteristic of the mind is duality; the characteristic of forms up to the characteristic of phenomena is duality. The perfection of giving up to the characteristic of a Buddha, the characteristic of unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and the characteristics of the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned—all these are duality."
Subhūti! All marks are dualistic, and all duality consists of existent dharmas;
as soon as there are existent dharmas, there is birth and death; and as long as there is birth and death, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.

For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that for those who possess these two marks, there is no perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; there is no path and no fruit, even up to the absence of the patient acceptance of conformity—how much less could they perceive the mark of form, up to the perception of the mark of all-knowledge!

If there were no cultivation of the path, how could one attain the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the eradication of all habitual tendencies of afflictions?
[Treatise] Commentary: The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they do not receive worldly retribution."
Subhūti marveled at what had never before occurred and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas have accomplished great wisdom; practicing this profound Dharma, they are able to act as causes without receiving their results.”
"This bodhisattva, for the sake of great benefit, does not accept a small reward.
Having affirmed his meaning, the Buddha further explained the causal conditions himself, namely:
"The bodhisattva remains unmoved within the nature of all phenomena."
The nature of all phenomena is non-existent, ultimately empty, suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality.
The bodhisattva’s concentrated mind abides therein, unwavering.
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One,
in what nature does one remain unmoved?”
The Buddha replied:
“One does not move within the nature of form, nor does one move within the natures of [the other aggregates] up to great compassion and so forth. Why is this?

"The nature of these phenomena, because they arise from a multitude of causes and conditions, is not independent and lacks a fixed characteristic; because it lacks a fixed characteristic, it is non-existent.
"All phenomena" refers to phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Because of these phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is spoken of; therefore, even the unconditioned phenomenon does not exist. Why is this?
Because one cannot obtain an existent phenomenon by means of a non-existent phenomenon.
Subhūti said:
"If that which is non-existent cannot attain that which is existent, how could one possibly attain an existent dharma by means of an existent dharma?
The Buddha replied:
"No. Why is this? Even for non-existent dharmas—which are praised by all noble ones and wherein they dwell—one cannot obtain anything; how much less so for existent dharmas!
“Can all dharmas attain non-existence?
The Buddha said, “No.”
Why is this? Because both "existence" and "non-existence" entail faults, it is said "no.
Can non-existence be attained by means of non-existence?
The Buddha said, “No. Why is this?

Since all phenomena possess the characteristics of arising and abiding, and because they are deceptive and illusory, they cannot be apprehended even as such; how much less can that which is non-existent and ultimately empty from the very beginning be apprehended!
In this regard, Subhūti asks further:
"World-Honored One!
If none of the four propositions can be apprehended, will there then be no path and no attainment of the fruit?"
The Buddha replied:
"There truly is a dharma for attaining the Way, but it is not by means of these four propositions. Why is this?"
Because the four propositions entail the aforementioned faults.
If one is free from the conceptual proliferation of these four propositions, that is the Path.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s conceptual proliferation?
The Buddha replied:
"If form and so forth are either permanent or impermanent, this is the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
If they were permanent, they would neither arise nor cease, and there would be no demerit or merit, nor beauty or ugliness.
Impermanence is likewise not tenable. Why?
Because impermanence is predicated upon permanence; since permanence cannot be found, how much less so impermanence!
Furthermore, if impermanence were the fixed and true nature of form and the other aggregates, there would likewise be no such thing as karma, causes, conditions, or karmic retribution.
Why is this? Because all phenomena, such as form, perish and vanish from moment to moment.
If the retribution resulting from the causes and conditions of karma were to perish, it could not be termed the characteristic of impermanence.
For various reasons such as these, impermanence is not the true characteristic of form and the other aggregates, as was explained previously in the "Refutation of Impermanence."
Even to form the thought, "I shall sever all habitual tendencies of affliction," is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

All phenomena, such as form and so forth, are beyond conceptual proliferation; yet ordinary persons proliferate regarding these phenomena. A bodhisattva, with respect to that which is beyond conceptual proliferation, does not proliferate in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? An intrinsic nature cannot engage in conceptual proliferation regarding its own intrinsic nature. Why is that?
Since intrinsic nature arises from causes and conditions, it exists only as a provisional designation; how then could it engage in conceptual proliferation?
If intrinsic nature cannot engage in conceptual proliferation, how much less so that which lacks intrinsic nature!

Apart from existence and non-existence, there is no third dharma that can be the object of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). As for what is called "conceptual proliferation"—namely, the proliferated phenomena and the locus of proliferation—all such dharmas are unattainable.
“Subhūti! Dharmas such as form are characterized by being beyond conceptual proliferation; thus, a bodhisattva should practice the non-proliferated perfection of wisdom.”
Furthermore, the Buddha himself explained the reasons why there can be no frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*):
"Phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are by definition beyond frivolous conceptual proliferation."
“If a bodhisattva can practice this non-conceptualizable (*aprapañca*) prajñā, they shall enter the bodhisattva stage.
Subhūti thought:
“Since the absence of conceptual proliferation is the path of the three vehicles, by what path does a bodhisattva enter the non-conceptualizable bodhisattva stage?”
The Buddha answered, and they all said, "No. Why was this?
Because a bodhisattva is a follower of the Mahāyāna, they should not employ the path of the two vehicles;
and because the six pāramitās are not yet perfected, they cannot employ the path of the Buddha.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:
“A bodhisattva should thoroughly study all paths in order to enter the bodhisattva stage.
Regarding this, a simile is given:

“It is like the person of eight stages (*aṣṭamaka*) within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), who previously studied all paths and entered the state of correctness (*samyaktvaniyāma*), yet has not yet attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).”
The Bodhisattva is also like this: having first extensively studied all paths and entered the stage of a Bodhisattva, he has not yet attained the fruit of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);
however, when the Bodhisattva abides in the Vajra-samādhi, through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, he attains the fruit of omniscience.
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva must fully study all paths before entering the bodhisattva stage, then these various paths are each distinct from one another.”

If a bodhisattva studies all these paths universally, if they give rise to the path of the eightfold [noble ones], they are an "eight-person" (aṣṭamaka); up to and including giving rise to the path of a pratyekabuddha, they are a pratyekabuddha.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva were to become one of the eight persons, or even a pratyekabuddha, and only thereafter enter the stage of a bodhisattva, such a thing is impossible!
If they do not enter the stage of a bodhisattva, yet attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), such a thing is also impossible!”
"How should I understand how a bodhisattva universally trains in all paths and enters the stage of a bodhisattva?
After the Buddha had affirmed his meaning, he further explained the causes and conditions himself:
"When a bodhisattva first resolves upon the mind and practices the six pāramitās, they observe and enter the eight stages with wisdom-vision, passing through them directly."
Just as when a person has a relative imprisoned, they enter to visit them but do not themselves put on the shackles; so too,

because the bodhisattva wishes to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path, they enter the bodhisattva stage— entering the bodhisattva stage by universally observing all paths— and having entered the bodhisattva stage,
they attain the knowledge of all modes and sever the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
The Buddha showed Subhūti:

"Those of the two vehicles obtain but a small portion of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, whether it be the knowledge or the abandonment of the 'eight persons,' up to the knowledge or the abandonment of the pratyekabuddha, all are the bodhisattva's patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
"Wisdom" refers to the eight knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*); for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it may be nine or ten.
"Abandonment" refers to the abandonment of the ten kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely the ten fetters of the higher and lower realms.
The *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin*, briefly stated, have abandoned the three fetters; in detail, they have abandoned eighty-eight fetters.
The *anāgāmin*, briefly stated, has abandoned the five lower fetters; in detail, he has abandoned ninety-two.
An Arhat, in brief, is one who has exhausted the three outflows; in detail, it refers to the abandonment of all afflictions.
This is called knowledge and abandonment.
Both knowledge and abandonment constitute the patience of a bodhisattva.
Śrāvakas attain the Way through the Four Truths, whereas Bodhisattvas enter the Way through a single truth.
The Buddha says that these four truths are all one truth; they are four only because of analytical differentiation.
These four truths and the wisdom and abandonment of the two vehicles are all contained within this single truth.

The Bodhisattva first dwells within the patience of compliance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), training in neither arising nor ceasing, nor that which is neither non-arising nor non-ceasing; he departs from the views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, extinguishes all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the Buddha himself explains in a later chapter:
"Even until one attains Buddhahood, one never gives rise to an evil mind; therefore, it is called the patience of non-arising."
The commentator says:

To attain this patience (*kṣānti*), one contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately empty (*atyanta-śūnya*), severs conditions, and the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) do not arise; this is called the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, it is said:
that which can transcend the wisdom of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The wisdom of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas contemplates the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, such as form; their minds become weary, they become free from desire, and they attain liberation.
When a bodhisattva contemplates arising and ceasing with great merit and wisdom, their mind does not experience fear as do those of the Lesser Vehicle.
With the eye of wisdom, the bodhisattva seeks the true, fixed characteristics of arising and ceasing and finds them unobtainable, as was explained previously in the "Chapter on Refuting Arising."
It is only with the coarse mind of the fleshly eye that one perceives impermanence, arising, and ceasing.

Ordinary persons cling to the notion of permanence regarding all phenomena; yet these very phenomena to which they cling eventually revert to impermanence, causing sentient beings to experience sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to be free from sorrow and suffering, do not contemplate the mark of permanence!"

This [teaching on] impermanence is for the purpose of subverting the perversion of permanence; it is not taught for the sake of attachment to impermanence. Therefore, the bodhisattva abandons the contemplation of arising and ceasing and enters into the state of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Question:
If one enters into that which is neither arising nor ceasing, then that which is neither arising nor ceasing is itself eternal; how, then, can one be free from the inversion of permanence? Answer:
Regarding impermanence, there are two kinds:
first, destroying the perversion of permanence while not clinging to impermanence;
second, clinging to impermanence and giving rise to conceptual proliferation.
The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is also like this:
first, although one has destroyed arising and ceasing, because one does not cling to non-arising and non-ceasing, one does not fall into the inversion of permanence;
second, because one clings to non-arising and non-ceasing, one falls into the inversion of permanence.
True non-arising means the cessation of all contemplations and the severance of the path of language; one contemplates all phenomena as having the characteristic of nirvana.
From the very beginning, they have always been non-arising by their own nature; it is not through the application of wisdom in contemplation that they are made non-arising.
Having attained this state of neither arising nor ceasing, which is ultimately pure, one does not even grasp at the contemplation of impermanence, let alone [grasp at] arising and ceasing!
Such characteristics as these are called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because they have attained this patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), they immediately enter the stage of a bodhisattva;
having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, they sever the afflictions along with their habitual tendencies by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
through various causes and conditions, they deliver all sentient beings, like a fine fruit tree that brings great benefit to many.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the path?”
The Buddha replied:
"A bodhisattva abides in the dharma of the patience of non-arising and attains the true mark of all dharmas.

Arising from this true mark, they take up the names, marks, and language of all dharmas; having themselves attained excellent understanding, they explain them for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to attain awakening."

By virtue of the causes and conditions of a bodhisattva’s merit, they understand the sounds and languages of all sentient beings; with these sounds they pervade the trichiliocosm, yet they do not cling to these sounds, knowing them to have the characteristic of an echo.
This voice is precisely the mark of the Brahma-voice.

For this reason, a bodhisattva should know all paths and universally observe the minds of sentient beings, understanding their origins and ends; he benefits them with wholesome dharmas and restrains unwholesome dharmas, as explained at length in the sūtras.

Because the Bodhisattva first knows the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he enters and emerges from the paths of the two vehicles with mastery; having observed them, he passes directly through and enters the stage of a Bodhisattva.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, he gives rise to the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*).

Desiring to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they understand the languages and sounds of all sentient beings and preach the Dharma with the Brahma-voice—namely, to block the evil paths and open the way to the wholesome paths.
The evil paths refer to the three evil destinies;
the good paths refer to the three good destinies:
humans, devas, and asuras.
Through various causes and conditions, he censures the evil paths and praises the wholesome paths.
That which obstructs the evil paths refers to the path of hell, the causes of hell, and the fruits of hell.
The hells are as previously described.
The path of the hells is the superior unwholesome path.
The causes of the hells are the three poisons:

The increase of greed gives rise to the unwholesome path of covetousness and envy; the increase of hatred gives rise to the unwholesome path of malice and resentment; the increase of delusion gives rise to the unwholesome path of wrong views.
The three poisons are the causes of the three unwholesome paths;
the three unwholesome paths are the causes of the seven unwholesome paths.
Regarding the fruit of hell: because of these causes, one receives a hellish body and experiences various kinds of physical and mental suffering and affliction; this is called the fruit.
A bodhisattva should manifest the retribution of the hells to sentient beings, and only then preach the Dharma for them, causing them to sever the path to hell as well as its causes and effects.
Regarding the ten unwholesome paths of action, there are superior, middling, and inferior grades:
the superior grade results in the hells;
The middling [result] is the realm of animals;
the inferior is the realm of hungry ghosts.
The ten paths of wholesome action likewise have superior, middling, and inferior [levels]:
The superior are the heavens;
the middling are human beings;
and the inferior are ghosts and spirits.
Abiding in the ten paths of wholesome action, one is able to leave behind desire and be born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), or leave behind form and be born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Since one constantly undergoes suffering within the three evil realms, it is said that "one should know [them] and should prevent [them]."
Among devas and humans, there are causes and conditions for attaining the Way for the sake of nirvana; yet at times these should be obstructed. Because they are not fixed, they are not spoken of.
As for the other factors that assist the Path, one should not speak of obstructing them, up to and including *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Once the Bodhisattva has made such distinctions, he knows that those sentient beings who should be delivered by the Hīnayāna Dharma are delivered by the Hīnayāna Dharma;
and those who should be delivered by the Mahāyāna Dharma are delivered by the Mahāyāna Dharma.

This bodhisattva knows the various matters within the deep minds of sentient beings as well as the causes and conditions of their past lives; he also knows the causes and conditions for the retributive fruits of future lives, and he knows the proper timing for converting sentient beings as well as the appropriate locations.
He fully knows all other causes and conditions for delivering them; therefore, what he says is not in vain.

In this way, the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are entirely subsumed within *prajñā*. Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice the *prajñā* that is the wisdom of the path.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If these factors conducive to enlightenment and awakening are all neither conjoined nor dispersed, formless, shapeless, and non-resistant, having but a single characteristic, which is to say, the characteristic of being without characteristics."
These factors that assist the path are all empty; how, then, can they grasp at *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Since these dharmas are empty and non-existent, there should be neither grasping nor abandoning;
it is like space, which, because it is devoid of dharmas, has neither grasping nor abandoning.
Because Subhūti speaks what is true with an unattached mind, the Buddha may say: "So it is! So it is!"
He further explained the causal conditions:

"Because there are sentient beings who do not know that all such dharmas are empty of their own characteristics, they engage in conceptual discrimination, thinking that these factors conducive to enlightenment can bring about the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Subhūti! Not only are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment empty, neither conjoined nor dispersed; all things from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*) within the noble Dharma, neither conjoined nor dispersed.
"Neither conjoined nor dispersed" is the meaning of ultimate emptiness;
as it is said therein:
"The single characteristic is what is called the absence of characteristics."

"Although these dharmas are empty, they are taught to sentient beings by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) with the desire to cause them to enter the noble Dharma; they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Within this, bodhisattvas should all train in these dharmas through knowledge and vision."
The initial stage of knowing is called "knowledge" (jñāna), while the subsequent deep penetration is called "vision" (darśana);
knowledge refers to that which is not yet fully understood, whereas vision refers to that which is already fully understood.
Question:
What is the difference between knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*)?
The answer is: some say:

There is that which is knowledge but not vision; there is that which is vision but not knowledge; there is that which is both knowledge and vision; and there is that which is neither knowledge nor vision.

Regarding that which is knowledge but not vision: the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), with the exception of mundane right view and the five views, all other wisdom (*prajñā*) is termed "knowledge"; this wisdom is not vision.

Regarding "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) as distinct from "knowledge" (*jñāna*): the five views, mundane right view, and the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing the truths—these are views but not knowledge.
All other untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is called both knowledge and view.
Apart from these views and cognitions, other dharmas are neither view nor cognition.
Furthermore, some say:
a concentrated mind is called "view," while both concentrated and unconcentrated minds are collectively termed "cognition."
As it is said in the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra*:
"Having known the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one should see it; having known it, one discerns:
'This dharma should be seen; this is the truth of suffering.'"
Those phenomena that should be abandoned are the truth of origination;
those phenomena that should be realized are the truth of cessation;
those phenomena that should be cultivated are the truth of the path.
Alternatively, knowing the abandonment of afflictions is called "vision," as in the case of the nine knowledges of abandonment (*navaprahāṇajñāna*).
Having heard that Prajñā has other names, namely "Noble Dharma" (*āryadharma*), Subhūti asks:
"What is this Noble Dharma?"
The Buddha replied:
"In the Noble Dharma, all the noble ones—whether Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas—regard all phenomena such as desire as neither conjoined nor dispersed."
Regarding "not joining": all afflictions are called perversions, and what is perverted is non-existent;
if it is non-existent, how can it be joined?
If there is no attachment, how could there be aversion?
Because of non-attachment, one does not look down upon ordinary people; because of non-aversion, one does not exalt oneself.
Thus, toward all sentient beings, one feels neither hatred nor love.
Furthermore, within this context, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions for neither-conjunction-nor-disjunction, saying:
"These dharmas are all formless, shapeless, and non-obstructive; they have a single characteristic, which is the so-called 'characteristic-less'."
Formless phenomena and formless dharmas neither conjoin nor disperse; even so, signless phenomena and signless dharmas neither conjoin nor disperse. Why is this?
Because all these dharmas are of a single nature, self-nature does not conjoin with self-nature.
This is called the single-character, signless Prajñāpāramitā, which Bodhisattvas should study;
having studied it, they will find no dharma that possesses a mark.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva not train in the marks of form?"
"Does this mean that one does not even study the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

World-Honored One, if one does not study the characteristics of these dharmas, why does the sūtra say: 'The bodhisattva first studies the characteristics of all dharmas, and subsequently transcends the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha'?"
"If one does not transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, how can one enter the bodhisattva stage?
This is explained at length in this passage.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If all dharmas truly possessed characteristics, one should train in those characteristics.
Subhūti, however, all dharmas are truly without characteristics; therefore, a bodhisattva should not train in characteristics.”
"One should not even train in signlessness, because of grasping at signs.
The matter of destroying signs is as explained in the "Chapter on Inquiring about Signs.
Whether Buddhas appear or do not appear, all dharmas are eternally abiding in a single mark, which is so-called signlessness.
Having heard from the Buddha that all dharmas are signless, Subhūti now asks the Buddha in return:
“World-Honored One,
if all dharmas are neither with signs nor without signs, how does a bodhisattva cultivate prajñā?”

"If there were characteristics, one could cultivate prajñā by means of those characteristics; but now, since both characteristics and the absence of characteristics are both non-existent, by means of what thing can one cultivate prajñā?"
If one does not cultivate prajñā, one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, nor can one even establish oneself in the three fields of merit.
The Buddha affirmed these words, saying: "So it is!"
"So it is! He further explained the causes and conditions for cultivating prajñā, saying:
"A bodhisattva does not cultivate prajñā by means of signs; this is the cultivation of prajñā."
“Because one cultivates signlessness, this is the cultivation of prajñā.
He asked again,
“World-Honored One!”
"How is it that cultivating the signless is the cultivation of prajñā?
If there is no sign, how can it be cultivated?
The Buddha replied:
"To cultivate the disintegration of all dharmas is to cultivate prajñā.
Because all dharmas are disintegrated, even the characteristic of signlessness is disintegrated.
It is, for example, like the characteristic of a chariot being extinguished when its parts are disintegrated.
Furthermore, just as the characteristic of a wheel ceases when its parts are destroyed, so it is even down to the finest atom.
"World-Honored One,
what are those phenomena that can be destroyed?"
The Buddha replied:
"To cultivate the destruction of the dharma of form is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
even unto cultivating the destruction of the abandonment of all habitual tendencies of affliction is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“How is it that the cultivation of the destruction of form, up to the cultivation of the destruction of all habitual tendencies of afflictions, constitutes the cultivation of prajñā?
The Buddha replied:

“When a bodhisattva, with a single-minded focus on omniscience (*sarvajñā*), out of compassion for sentient beings, desires to attain the correct practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not conceive of form as an existent phenomenon;
practicing in this way is the cultivation of *prajñā*.
Because form is a fixed reality, it possesses the fault of having characteristics. Why is this so?
For the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions herein:
"One who perceives signs does not cultivate prajñā; within prajñā, even non-existent dharmas do not exist, let alone existent dharmas!
Such a person does not cultivate the prajñāpāramitā, nor do they cultivate the five pāramitās;
such a person is attached to the conceptual proliferation of existent dharmas and does not cultivate giving and the other perfections."
For one who clings in this way, there is no liberation, no Path, and no Nirvāṇa:

because the three gates of liberation are absent, it is said there is no liberation; because the empty dharmas of the noble ones are absent, it is said there is no Path; and because there is no Path, it is said there is no Nirvāṇa.
Question: For what reason is there no Path? Answer:

This person engages in conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena; because they do not weary of old age, sickness, and death, and because they are attached to phenomena, they give rise to wrong views.
Due to these wrong views, they are unable to contemplate the body as impure and so forth according to reality.
Because they cannot contemplate the body, they do not cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Because they do not cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of the body, they cannot cultivate the foundations of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena;
because they do not cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, they cannot cultivate anything up to and including all-knowledge.
Why is this? Because they are attached to the existence of dharmas.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What is that which exists?
What is that which does not exist?”

Ordinary people may conceive the notion of non-existence regarding things that exist, or the notion of existence regarding things that do not exist; wishing to distinguish these matters, they ask this question.
The Buddha replies:
"The two characteristics are existence; the characteristic of non-duality is non-existence."
He asked again,
"What are these two characteristics?
The Buddha replied:
"To grasp the characteristics of form is duality.
As it was said in the previous chapter:
"Apart from form there is no eye; apart from the eye there is no form."
"Up to and including the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned. Why is this?
Apart from the conditioned, one cannot speak of the unconditioned; apart from the unconditioned, one cannot speak of the true mark of the conditioned."
Therefore, these two dharmas cannot be separated from one another;
ordinary people claim they are two, and for this reason they are deluded.
The Buddha briefly explains their two characteristics as follows:
"To grasp at signs within all dharmas is duality; all dualities are existence.
As soon as there is existence, there is birth and death. Why is this so?

From existence arises the mind of attachment; with the mind of attachment as a condition, various afflictions arise; with afflictions as a condition, one wanders through birth and death; and with birth and death as a condition, there arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.
Therefore it is said:
"As soon as there is a phenomenon (dharma), there is birth and death; with birth and death, one cannot escape old age, sickness, grief, and suffering. "Subhūti!"
By this you should know that for such persons of dualistic marks, there is no dānapāramitā, up to and including no *anulomikī kṣānti*;
how much less could they see the true mark of form, or even see the true mark of the knowledge of all modes!

If this person does not perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena such as form and so forth, then there is no cultivation of the path; how, then, could there be the fruit of a *srotāpanna* up to the severance of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies?
The six pāramitās are of two kinds:
mundane and supramundane.
Because this person lacks the supramundane six pāramitās, it is said:
“Those who possess marks do not have the six pāramitās.
If they were to have them, they would only have mundane pāramitās; mundane pāramitās are not what is being discussed here.
If even the fruits of the Śrāvaka path do not exist, how much less could there be the Buddha-path!
Question: What kind of "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti) is this?
The answer is:
This is the "patience in conformity" (anulomikī kṣānti) of the Hīnayāna.
If even the patience in conformity of the Hīnayāna does not exist [in such a state], how much less so that of the Mahāyāna!
Question:
Since one is already incapable of falling back once the stage of the Summits (mūrdhan) has been attained, why is it said "up to the stage of Patience" (kṣānti)? Answer:

In the Śrāvaka-dharma, falling from the summit (*mūrdha-pāta*) is also taught; in the Mahāyāna, falling from the summit is likewise taught. Why do you say that "the stage of the summit does not fall"?
Some say: although one does not fall from the stage of the summit, it is not said [to be secure] because it is not firm and cannot be certain.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is long-enduring; having already entered right concentration, although one has not yet attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it is equivalent to the outflow-free.
It is called "patience" because it accords with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmanidhyānakṣānti*);
because one has never before seen this dharma, one is able to endure upon seeing it, and for this reason it is called patience.
Such a person is small compared to the Buddhas and noble ones, yet great compared to ordinary beings.
There are two ways of seeing form:
first, seeing the true mark (*dharmatā*) of form with perfect clarity; second, it is called "seeing" because one has severed the afflictions bound to all forms.
As it is with form, so it is with everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the traces of all afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).

If, for a person, even the seeing of form and the cultivation of the path do not exist, how much less could they attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) or eradicate the traces of affliction!
75. Chapter on Gradual Training: Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Chapter Seventy-Five, "Gradual Training. [Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
If there were any marks of dharmas, one would not even attain the patience of conformity (anulomikī kṣānti), let alone attain the Way!
World-Honored One,
if there are no marks of dharmas, would one then attain the patience of conformity?

Whether it be the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Buddha—if there is the cultivation of the path, will afflictions be severed by means of this cultivation of the path?
Because of these afflictions, one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha to enter the bodhisattva stage;
if one does not enter the bodhisattva stage, then one cannot attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā);
and if one does not attain all-knowledge, then one cannot eliminate the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of all afflictions.
World-Honored One!
If there were no dharmas, then these dharmas would not arise;
if these dharmas do not arise, then one cannot attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"If there were no dharmas, then there would be the patient acceptance that accords with reality, up to and including the severing of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, is there any characteristic of dharmas?

That is to say: the characteristic of form up to the characteristic of consciousness; the characteristic of the eye up to the characteristic of the mind; the characteristic of forms up to the characteristic of phenomena; the characteristic of the eye-element up to the characteristic of the consciousness-element; the characteristic of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the characteristic of all-knowledge;

whether it be the characteristic of form or the characteristic of the cessation of form, up to the characteristic of consciousness or the characteristic of the cessation of consciousness—the same applies to the twelve bases and the eighteen elements.

Whether it be the characteristic of ignorance or the characteristic of the cessation of ignorance, up to the characteristic of grief, lamentation, sorrow, and despair, or the characteristic of the cessation of grief, lamentation, sorrow, and despair;

whether it be the characteristic of desire or the characteristic of the cessation of desire, the characteristic of hatred or the characteristic of the cessation of hatred, the characteristic of delusion or the characteristic of the cessation of delusion, the characteristic of suffering or the characteristic of the cessation of suffering, the characteristic of origination or the characteristic of the cessation of origination, the characteristic of cessation or the characteristic of the cessation of cessation, the characteristic of the path or the characteristic of the cessation of the path, up to the characteristic of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the characteristic of severing the habitual tendencies of all afflictions.
The Buddha said: "No, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas; this is precisely the bodhisattva’s patience in accordance with truth (ānulomikī kṣānti).
If there is neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas, this is itself the cultivation of the path, and it is also the fruit of the path.
Subhūti! For a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the existence of dharmas constitutes the bodhisattva path, while the non-existence of dharmas constitutes the bodhisattva fruit.
By this causal condition, one should know that all dharmas are of the nature of non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have the nature of non-existence, how does the Buddha, by knowing that all dharmas have the nature of non-existence, attain buddhahood and achieve sovereign power over all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
All dharmas are of the nature of non-existence.

When I formerly practiced the bodhisattva path and cultivated the six pāramitās, I was free from all desires and free from evil, unwholesome dharmas; with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joy and bliss, I entered the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding these dhyānas and their factors, I grasped their characteristics but did not think, "I have these dhyānas"; I did not relish the flavor of the dhyānas, nor did I grasp at them as being dhyānas. Without defilement, I practiced the four dhyānas in purity, and I did not accept the karmic retribution of these dhyānas.
Abiding in the four dhyānas, one gives rise to the five supernormal powers:
the power of the body, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the power of recollecting past lives, and the realization of the divine eye;

yet regarding these supernormal powers, one does not grasp at their signs, does not dwell on the thought that "these are supernormal powers," does not relish the flavor of the supernormal powers, and does not conceive of attaining them, thinking, "I am practicing without discrimination regarding these five supernormal powers."

Subhūti! At that time, by means of the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment, I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—namely, that "this is the noble truth of suffering," "this is the noble truth of its origin," "this is the noble truth of its cessation," and "this is the noble truth of the path"—and I accomplished the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion; thus I became a Buddha and distinguished the three groups of sentient beings:
those fixed in the right, those fixed in the wrong, and those who are not fixed.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it, World-Honored One, that within the non-existence of all dharmas you give rise to the four dhyānas and the six supernormal powers, and yet, though there are no sentient beings, you differentiate them into the three groups?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If all desires, evil, and unwholesome dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature of their own or an extrinsic nature—then when I was formerly practicing as a bodhisattva, I would not have been able to contemplate the non-existence of all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas and enter the first dhyāna.

Because all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas lack an intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature of their own or an extrinsic nature—all are of the nature of non-existence; therefore, when I formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, I detached from all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas and entered the first dhyāna, up to and including the fourth dhyāna."

Subhūti! If these supernormal powers possessed an intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature of their own or an extrinsic nature—I would not have been able to realize that these supernormal powers are devoid of any nature and thereby attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti! Because supernatural powers have no intrinsic nature—whether an intrinsic nature or an extrinsic nature, they are all of the nature of non-existence—for this reason, the Buddhas, regarding supernatural powers, know them to be of the nature of non-existence and thereby attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[Treatise] Question:
Since all dharmas have the single meaning of emptiness, for what reason does Subhūti ask again with various causes and conditions?
Herein, he asks:

"One who perceives the characteristics of phenomena cannot attain the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*); even if one does not give rise to these phenomena, one still cannot attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
He replied:
"The meaning of the ultimate emptiness of all these phenomena is extremely profound and difficult to understand!"
To explain this is already difficult, let alone for those who receive it or practice it!
Therefore, as the *Prajñāpāramitā* was nearing its conclusion, Subhūti questioned repeatedly through various causes and conditions, fearing that many people might harbor doubts and confusion.
Furthermore, although the meaning of what is asked is the same, the basis for the inquiry differs.
For instance, one might ask:
"World-Honored One!..."
"If all dharmas are empty, how can one differentiate the five destinies?
Or it may be asked:
"If all things lack any characteristic of existence, how can one differentiate the three vehicles?"
Someone asked:
"World-Honored One!
Since one who possesses signs cannot even attain the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti), how can they contemplate the eighth stage and enter the rank of a bodhisattva?"
Through such various questions, the meaning is differentiated according to their diverse approaches, for Prajñā has no fixed characteristic.
The Buddha affirmed Subhūti’s intent: “So it is!”
"So it is! Previously, when Subhūti asked about "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti), he was referring to the conformity-patience of the Lesser Vehicle;
now, Subhūti asks about the dharma of the conformity-patience of a bodhisattva.
"If, when a bodhisattva practices prajñā, is there any characteristic of dharmas?
The Buddha replied:
"When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, there is no characteristic of the arising of dharmas, whether they be existent or non-existent."
Why is this? Because seeing both existence and non-existence entails faults; this is the Bodhisattva’s conformative patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*).
Not giving rise to the mark of existence within all phenomena is itself the cultivation of the path.
“Subhūti! ‘Existence’ (bhāva) is the bodhisattva path; ‘non-existence’ (abhāva) is the fruit.
Existence refers to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), while non-existence refers to unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
By practicing the eightfold noble path, which is conditioned, one severs all afflictions and attains the unconditioned fruit.
Furthermore, some say that the five perfections are called "conditioned dharmas" and constitute the bodhisattva path;
Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately empty, there is no dharma; this is the fruit of the bodhisattva.
Some say: the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is wisdom, and because it is a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛtadharma*), it constitutes the Path (*mārga*).
Suchness (tathatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are called "fruits" because they do not arise from causes and conditions and are eternally present.
Such categories as these constitute the distinction between existence and non-existence.
