By means of the knowledge of others' minds, this bodhisattva knows the minds of all Buddhas of the ten directions as well as the minds of all sentient beings, and is thus able to benefit all sentient beings.
By means of the knowledge of past lives, this bodhisattva knows the causes and conditions of all past karmas;
because these karmic causes and conditions do not perish, he fully knows the places where these sentient beings have been born throughout their various existences.

By means of this knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, this bodhisattva enables sentient beings to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship and the path of pratyekabuddhas; wherever they may be, he is able to lead sentient beings into wholesome dharmas.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the śīla-pāramitā by means of all dharmas being signless, unobtainable, and unconditioned.
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are signless, unconditioned, and unattainable, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can fulfill the perfection of patience?”

“Subhūti! From the time a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon awakening until they sit at the site of enlightenment, if all sentient beings were to come during that interval and strike this bodhisattva with tiles, stones, knives, or staves, the bodhisattva would not give rise to a mind of anger, nor even produce a single thought of it.”
At that time, a bodhisattva should cultivate two kinds of patience:
first, when all sentient beings revile them with harsh words or strike them with knives, staves, tiles, or stones, they do not give rise to a mind of anger;
second, the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena, which is the realization that all phenomena are unarisen.
If a bodhisattva is encountered by someone who comes to revile him with harsh words, or strikes him with tiles, stones, swords, or staves, at that time the bodhisattva should reflect thus:
"Who is it that reviles me?"
Who is it that reviles?
Who is it that strikes and hurls?
Who is there that receives?
Immediately, the Bodhisattva should contemplate the true nature of all phenomena, which is so-called ultimate emptiness: there are no phenomena and no sentient beings;
since even phenomena cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be sentient beings!
When observing the characteristics of all phenomena in this way, one sees neither the one who reviles nor the one who cuts and dismemberes.
When this bodhisattva observes the characteristics of all phenomena in this manner, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
What is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
It is knowing that the characteristics of all dharmas are eternally unarisen, and that all afflictions have likewise been eternally unarisen from the very beginning.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these two patiences, they are able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
This bodhisattva, dwelling in these noble, untainted, supramundane dharmas—which are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—perfects the noble supernormal powers.

Having dwelled in the noble supernormal powers, one sees the Buddhas of the eastern direction with the divine eye; this person attains the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), which shall never be interrupted until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
With the divine ear, this bodhisattva hears the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions; as he has heard it, he teaches it to sentient beings.

This bodhisattva also knows the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions and knows the thoughts of all sentient beings; having known them, he teaches the Dharma to them in accordance with their minds.

By means of the knowledge of past lives, this bodhisattva knows the roots of goodness of all sentient beings in their previous existences, and he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to rejoice.
By means of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, this bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings, enabling them to attain the three vehicles.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, uses the power of skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity, fulfills all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and turns the wheel of Dharma.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the perfection of patience within the state that is signless, unobtainable, and non-conditioned.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the pāramitā of vīrya while all dharmas are signless, unconditioned, and unattainable?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they achieve physical vigor and mental vigor, entering the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, and receiving various supernormal powers; they are able to divide one body into many bodies, even reaching out with their hand to touch the sun and the moon.”

Because they have accomplished physical diligence, they fly to the eastern direction, passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds, making offerings to the Buddhas of food and drink, clothing, medicine, bedding, flowers, incense, necklaces, and all manner of necessities; even until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the fruit of their merit will never be exhausted.

When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, all the gods and humans of the world will diligently provide offerings of clothing, food, and drink; furthermore, even after he has entered nirvana without remainder, his relics and disciples shall receive such offerings.

Furthermore, by virtue of this power of supernormal knowledge, they go to the abodes of all Buddhas to hear and receive their teachings; until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never fail or lose them.
When this bodhisattva cultivates the knowledge of all modes, he purifies the buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom accomplishes physical diligence and is able to fulfill the perfection of vigor.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva accomplish mental diligence and thereby fulfill the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā)? Subhūti!”

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mental diligence is noble and untainted; through this mental diligence, he enters the diligence of the eightfold noble path, not permitting unwholesome karma of body or speech to enter.

Furthermore, one does not grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena—whether they be permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self, conditioned or unconditioned; whether they belong to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; whether they are of the nature of outflows or without outflows; whether they be the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; whether they be loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, or equanimity; whether they be the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; whether they be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path; or whether they be emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness; or even the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities.

One does not grasp at signs—whether they be permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self; nor the fruit of a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat; nor the path of a pratyekabuddha, the path of a bodhisattva, or unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); nor whether one be a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat; nor whether one be a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a buddha.

Not grasping at signs, one realizes that because this being has severed the three fetters, they have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; because this being’s three poisons are attenuated, they have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; because this being has severed the lower fetters, they have attained the stage of *anāgāmin*; because this being has severed the upper fetters, they have attained the stage of *arhat*; because this being follows the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, they become a *pratyekabuddha*; and because this being practices the knowledge of the modes of the path, they are called a *bodhisattva*—yet they do not grasp at the signs of any of these dharmas.
Why is this? Because one cannot grasp characteristics by means of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for such intrinsic nature does not exist.
By means of this mental diligence, the bodhisattva extensively benefits sentient beings, yet he does not apprehend those sentient beings; this is the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the *vīryapāramitā*.
Because the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas, the purification of Buddha-lands, and the maturation of sentient beings are ungraspable.
"Because this Bodhisattva has accomplished physical vigor and mental vigor, they embrace all wholesome dharmas;
yet they do not cling even to these dharmas."
Traveling from one Buddha-land to another for the benefit of sentient beings, he exercises his supernatural powers without hindrance according to his will:

whether raining down various flowers, or various famous incenses, or performing music, or shaking the great earth, or emitting radiance, or manifesting lands adorned with the seven treasures, or appearing in various forms, or emitting the radiance of great wisdom to cause them to know the Noble Path and to lead them to abandon everything from taking life up to wrong views;

or benefiting sentient beings through generosity, or through the observance of precepts, or by having his body dismembered, or by giving away his wife and children, or his kingdom, or even his own person—employing whatever skillful means are appropriate to benefit sentient beings.
In this way, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, within all dharmas that are signless, unconditioned, and unattainable, by exerting effort of body and mind, they are able to fulfill the perfection of vigor.
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwelling within the dharmas that are signless (*animitta*), unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and ungraspable (*anupalambha*), manage to fulfill the *dhyānapāramitā*?”
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva can fully accomplish all other dhyanas and samādhis, with the exception of the various dhyānas and samādhis of a Buddha.”

This bodhisattva, detached from all desires and from evil, unwholesome states, enters the first dhyāna— accompanied by applied and sustained thought and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion—
and continues in this manner up to entering the fourth dhyāna.
With this mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he pervades one direction, and so on until he pervades all worlds throughout the ten directions.
This bodhisattva, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters the sphere of infinite space;
and so on, up to entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This bodhisattva, dwelling within the dhyāna-pāramitā, enters the eight liberations and the nine successive concentrations in both forward and reverse order; he enters the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; at times he enters the lightning-flash-like samādhi, at times the noble and correct samādhi, and at times the vajra-like samādhi.

“This bodhisattva, dwelling within the dhyāna-pāramitā, cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. By means of the knowledge of the modes of the path, they enter all meditative concentrations and transcend the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of nature, the stage of the eight persons, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha;
having entered the rank of a bodhisattva, they become fully endowed with the stage of a buddha.”
Practicing within these stages up until *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not prematurely realize the fruits of the path.

Abiding in this *dhyāna-pāramitā*, these bodhisattvas go from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to the Buddhas, planting roots of goodness under those Buddhas, and purifying the buddha-fields.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they benefit sentient beings.

They gather in sentient beings through giving, or through ethical discipline, or through meditative concentration, or through wisdom, or through liberation, or through the knowledge and vision of liberation;
they teach sentient beings so that they may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha.
Whatever wholesome dharmas can cause sentient beings to attain the Way, he teaches them all so that they may attain them.

Abiding in this dhyāna-pāramitā, this bodhisattva is able to give rise to all dhāraṇī-doors, attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and obtain supernormal powers as a result of his retribution.
This bodhisattva never again enters a mother’s womb, never again experiences the five desires, and is neither born nor unborn;
though he takes birth, he is not defiled by the phenomena of birth.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas perceive all conditioned phenomena as being like illusions, yet they benefit sentient beings; furthermore, they neither apprehend sentient beings nor any phenomena, teaching sentient beings to attain the state of non-apprehension.
This is because it is a conventional phenomenon, not the ultimate reality.
Abiding in this dhyānapāramitā, one practices all forms of meditation, concentration, liberation, and samādhi, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, never departing from the dhyānapāramitā.
When this bodhisattva practices such knowledge of the aspects of the path, they attain the knowledge of all aspects and sever all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies;
having severed them, they benefit themselves and also benefit others;
having benefited themselves and others, they become a field of merit for all the world—gods, humans, and asuras.
In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the signless perfection of meditation.
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, abide within the dharmas that are signless, unconditioned, and unobtainable, and thereby cultivate and fulfill the perfection of wisdom?”
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any fixed or real characteristic in any phenomena.
This bodhisattva perceives that form is not fixed and is not a real characteristic, and so on, up to perceiving that consciousness is not fixed and is not a real characteristic.”
One does not see the arising of form, nor even the arising of consciousness;

if one does not see the arising of form up to the arising of consciousness, then regarding all phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows—one does not see their place of coming, their place of going, nor their place of accumulation.

When observing in this manner, one does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form, nor even that of consciousness; one likewise does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of phenomena that are with outflows or without outflows.
When this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they have faith and understanding that all dharmas are characterized by non-existence.

Having thus attained such faith and understanding, one practices inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; one remains unattached to any phenomena, whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This Bodhisattva practices the non-existent Prajñāpāramitā and is able to fulfill the Bodhisattva path, namely the six pāramitās, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.

“This bodhisattva dwells within the pure Buddha-way of emptiness—namely, the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation—and benefits sentient beings through these dharmas:
those who should be gathered through giving, he teaches to practice giving;
those who should be gathered through ethical discipline, he teaches to maintain ethical discipline;”

Those who should be gathered through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), he teaches and instructs them to cultivate meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Those who should be taught through the various paths of the Dharma, he teaches and instructs them to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), and the path of the pratyekabuddha.

Those who should be transformed through the Buddha-way, he teaches and instructs them to attain the bodhisattva path and fulfill the Buddha-way. In such ways, he teaches and transforms them according to their respective appropriate stages of the path, causing each to obtain what they require.

When this bodhisattva manifests various supernormal powers, they traverse immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, liberating sentient beings; according to their needs, they transform and provide for them all, causing each to be fully satisfied.
Traveling from one land to another, he beholds pure and wondrous lands, thereby adorning his own Buddha-field.
It is like the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), where all necessities of life arrive spontaneously according to one's wish;
likewise, it is like those pure Buddha-fields, which are free from the pursuit of desire.

By means of these, this person obtains as a karmic reward the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, dhyānapāramitā, and prajñāpāramitā; they obtain as a karmic reward the five supernormal powers, practice the bodhisattva-path of the knowledge of all modes, accomplish all merits, and shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"At that time, this bodhisattva does not grasp at form-dharmas up to consciousness; he does not grasp at any dharmas—whether wholesome or unwholesome, worldly or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned. Thus, he does not grasp at any such dharmas whatsoever."
When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all things for the sustenance of life within that land shall have no owners.
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva practices by not grasping at any phenomena, for they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
“Within the signless dharma, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to fulfill the prajñāpāramitā.
[Śāstra] Question: Both the questioner and the respondent speak of “non-existence”; how can one distinguish and know which is the question and which is the answer?
The answer is:
Although the Dharma spoken of is one, the minds [of those involved] differ—the questioner asks with a mind of attachment, while the respondent answers with a mind free from attachment.
Subhūti’s intention was as follows:
One should not resolve to attain enlightenment within the state of non-existence.
Subhūti asks this question because he perceives that the listeners might become attached to their minds.

Within the emptiness of all phenomena, one does not see a bodhisattva who resolves to attain enlightenment, nor does one see sentient beings who are to be benefited, nor does one see unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, he raises an objection regarding the dharma of non-existence:
“If all dharmas are of a non-existent nature, for what benefit does a bodhisattva resolve their mind [on awakening]?
Subhūti has no doubt regarding bodhisattvas, sentient beings, or *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; he asks only about dharmas that are non-existent.
The Buddha replied:
"It is precisely because of non-existence and emptiness that one is able to resolve upon the mind [of enlightenment].
If there is non-existence and emptiness, then the bodhisattva, sentient beings, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are likewise all empty and non-existent; how then can you raise this objection?"
If sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* were apart from non-existence and emptiness, this objection would hold.
As previously stated:
"Ultimate emptiness encounters no obstruction among all phenomena; what hindrance could there be to the arousal of the mind?"
The Buddha, in turn, refuted Subhūti’s question by means of non-existence and emptiness.
He further explained the causal conditions himself, saying: “Subhūti!...”
"Those whose minds are attached find it difficult to attain liberation.

These people have come from beginningless birth and death; because of all their afflictions, they are deeply attached to all phenomena. Hearing that there is existence, they are attached; hearing that there is emptiness, they are also attached;
and they are attached to both gain and loss. Such sentient beings are difficult to extricate.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva resolves upon the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment; he adorns his own body with the primary and secondary marks, attains the Brahma-voice, and possesses great majestic virtue. Knowing the fundamental nature of the minds of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, he uses various supernormal powers, causes and conditions, and parables to preach the dharma of non-existence and the gate of liberation through emptiness, thereby guiding their minds.
When sentient beings witness such rare and marvelous events, their minds immediately become supple, and they place faith in the Buddha and accept the Dharma.
Therefore, the sutra says:
"Those who are attached to existence find it difficult to attain liberation; [whereas those who are detached easily attain it]."
"For those who have something to attain, there is no path, no fruit, and no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti asked:
"World-Honored One!"
If there were something to be attained, would there be no Path, no fruit, and no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
For one who has nothing to attain, is there a Path and is there a fruit?
The Buddha replied:
“Non-existence itself is the Path, it is the Fruit, and it is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If a person does not discriminate between that which is attained and that which is unattained, entering into the ultimate emptiness of the true mark of all dharmas, this too is unattainable; it is the Path, it is the Fruit, and it is Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, because it does not destroy the true mark of all dharmas.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is precisely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Subhūti’s thought was this:

since the nature of phenomena is eternally indestructible regardless of whether one practices correctly or incorrectly, why does the Buddha say that "the indestructible nature of phenomena is the Path and the Fruit"?
The Buddha replied:
“Although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be destroyed, it is called ‘destruction’ because sentient beings engage in perverse conduct.
It is like space: although it cannot be defiled by clouds, mist, soil, or dust, it is nonetheless called ‘impure.’”
It is as if a person truly wished to defile space; such a person would wish to defile the *dharmatā*, for that is impossible.
The Buddha spoke this parable:
"If a person wishes to destroy the *dharmatā*, it is as if they wish to attain the Path, attain the Fruit, or attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within a state where nothing exists."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"If non-existence itself is the Path, how can there be the ten stages and other such dharmas of the bodhisattvas?
This is as explained at length in the sūtra.
Question: This matter has already been answered by the Buddha previously, namely:
"If all phenomena are empty, for what purpose does the bodhisattva resolve his mind [on awakening]?"
Now it is asked:
"If all phenomena are empty, how can there be the first stage and so forth?
Since the Buddha has answered everything by means of emptiness, why does Subhūti ask again?
Answer: Because the minds of sentient beings are attached and difficult to liberate, he asks again.

Within this assembly, there are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds; upon hearing that the true mark of all dharmas is emptiness, they immediately give rise to a mind of attachment. The Buddha shatters their attachment, yet they also become attached to the very dharmas that were shattered.
For the sake of these people, Subhūti asks again.
The Buddha answers Subhūti:
"Because there is nothing to be attained, there is the first stage (bhūmi), up to and including the attainment of offerings for the relics after parinirvāṇa."
If one were attached to anything therein, it would be impossible to speak of the first stage and its various merits.

Furthermore, because of the condition of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), there is no distinction from generosity up to the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); since there is no distinction, one should not raise objections!
Subhūti asked again:
"In what way are there no distinctions between the giving that is without acquisition and even the various supernormal powers?
The Buddha replied:

"From the moment a bodhisattva first generates the mind of awakening, they resemble the mark of quiescence of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Their giving is ultimately empty; that is to say, they practice giving without apprehending a giver, a recipient, or material wealth. Thus, within such giving there is no discrimination.
This extends even to the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without apprehending *bodhi*; it is likewise so."
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the prajñāpāramitā of non-apprehension.
Practicing this prajñāpāramitā of non-apprehension, Māra or the gods of Māra cannot destroy them.
Regarding "practicing the six pāramitās in a single thought-moment":
A question is asked:
Why does Subhūti ask about "practicing the six pāramitās and all other meritorious qualities in a single thought-moment"?
The answer is:
Subhūti has heard from the Buddha that the *prajñāpāramitā* possesses the mark of profound non-existence and the mark of non-obstruction among all phenomena;

if this is so, then there is nothing he cannot do and no task he does not perform—how then can a bodhisattva, within a single thought-moment, encompass the six *pāramitās* up to the eighty minor marks?
When first resolving to attain enlightenment, because the mind was still heavily attached to existence and non-existence, one proceeded through the stages gradually and in succession;
now, having completely relinquished both existence and non-existence, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished—therefore, this question is asked.
The Buddha replied:

“Because a bodhisattva does not depart from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* when performing meritorious deeds such as giving, they are able to practice them within a single thought-moment, owing to the absence of obstacles.”
"If one is separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, then one proceeds gradually and by stages.
Subhūti asked:
"What is meant by 'not being separated'?"
The Buddha replied:
“A bodhisattva does not practice giving and so forth by means of dualistic signs.
He asked again:
“How does one not employ dualistic characteristics?
The Buddha replied:
“When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, desiring to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, they encompass all wholesome dharmas within a single moment of giving.”
As previously stated:
What is this "single thought-moment"?

It refers to when a bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), severs all afflictions (*kleśa*), eliminates all recollections and conceptual discriminations, abides in the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), and practices giving to all.
The untainted mind is the markless mark.
When a bodhisattva dwells within this mind, they do not perceive who gives, who receives, or what object is given; they practice giving with a mind free from all marks.
They do not perceive a single dharma, and they do not even perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, let alone any other dharma!
This is called the mark of non-duality.
This applies likewise even up to the eighty minor marks of excellence.
Subhūti then asked about this meaning by means of another illustration:
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are signless, unconditioned, and unarisen, how can one fulfill the dānapāramitā and so forth, up to the eighty minor marks?”
The Buddha replied:
"Because a bodhisattva does not grasp at signs within the signless and unconditioned Dharma, they practice giving with an unobstructed mind, providing food to those who need food, and so forth."
This has already been explained in detail within the sutra.
Furthermore, it was also extensively discussed in the preceding chapter; therefore, it will not be further explained here.
There are two kinds of the six *pāramitās* that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and signless (*animitta*):

First is the practice of Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); second is the practice of Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.
The practice of Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is as described herein.
Why is this? Because one practices various dharmas such as giving while abiding in a mind that is signless and untainted.
Question:
Because Bodhisattvas in their physical bodies have not yet eliminated greed and attachment, the pain of being cut and dismembered is extreme; thus, this is difficult.

For a Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is like the actions of a conjured person: there is no pain from being cut and dismembered. What benefit, then, would there be?
The answer is:
For a Bodhisattva who has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), practicing these six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) is difficult! Why is this so?

Having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and a mind of quiescence, one ought to enjoy the bliss of nirvāṇa; yet, forsaking this bliss of quiescence, one enters among sentient beings to undergo various forms of existence—whether as lowly persons or as animals—and this is indeed difficult!
Bodhisattvas in their physical bodies have not yet eliminated craving; because they are attached to the Buddha-body, they give away their own bodies as an act of charity.
This is done out of expectation and is not a pure gift; therefore, it is inferior.
Furthermore, when one practices the six pāramitās that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and signless (*animitta*), at that time they can be brought to fulfillment;
however, when they are tainted (*sāsrava*) and characterized by signs (*sanimitta*), they cannot be brought to fulfillment.
Therefore, those who are able to fulfill [this practice] possess a great share of grace.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 87:
Explanation of the Chapter on the Six Similes, Number Seventy-seven.
Fascicle Eighty-eight.
Composed by the Venerable Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter Seventy-seven: The Six Similes. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does one fully cultivate the six pāramitās—namely, the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā—within all dharmas that are signless, undifferentiable, and empty of self-characteristic?”
World-Honored One!
How is it that within the dharma of non-differentiation you analytically explain different characteristics?
And how does the Prajñāpāramitā encompass giving (dāna), ethical discipline (śīla), patience (kṣānti), diligence (vīrya), and meditation (dhyāna)?
"How can one practice dharmas of diverse characteristics and yet attain the fruit through a path of a single characteristic?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the five aggregates as being like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation; dwelling therein, he practices giving, maintains morality, cultivates patience, exerts diligence, enters meditative concentration, and cultivates wisdom."
One knows that these five aggregates are truly like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation;
the five aggregates are signless, like a dream, up to being signless, like a transformation.
Why is this? Dreams lack intrinsic nature; echoes, reflections, mirages, illusions, and transformations all lack intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, that phenomenon lacks characteristics.
If dharmas are without marks, these dharmas have but a single mark,
namely, the markless. For this reason, Subhūti,
you should know that when a bodhisattva practices giving, the gift is markless, the giver is markless, and the recipient is markless.

To be able to know giving in this way is to be able to fulfill the *dānapāramitā* up to the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*; to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; to fulfill internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; to fulfill the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; to fulfill the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the five supernormal powers, and the five hundred *dhāraṇī* gates; and to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Abiding in this state of untainted dharmas obtained as a result of maturation, this bodhisattva flies to immeasurable lands in the eastern direction, making offerings of robes, food, and drink, and even providing whatever else they require to all the Buddhas.
They also benefit sentient beings: those who should be gathered through giving, they gather by means of giving;
those who should be gathered through ethical discipline, they teach them to observe ethical discipline;

those who should be gathered through patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they teach them to practice patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, thereby gathering them.
Even those who should be gathered through various wholesome dharmas, he gathers by means of those various wholesome dharmas.
This bodhisattva, having accomplished all these wholesome dharmas, assumes a worldly body yet is not defiled by worldly birth and death;
for the sake of sentient beings, he undergoes noble and wealthy happiness among gods and humans, and by means of this noble and wealthy happiness, he gathers in sentient beings.

Because this bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are signless, he knows the fruit of srotāpanna and does not abide therein; he knows the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat, and does not abide therein; he knows the path of the pratyekabuddha and does not abide therein.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva, having known all phenomena through the knowledge of all modes, shall attain the knowledge of all modes, which is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has realized that all dharmas are signless, they realize that the six pāramitās are signless, and so on, up to realizing that all buddha-dharmas are signless.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the five aggregates as being like a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a magical transformation, they are able to fulfill the signless perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
This precept is unimpaired, unbroken, unmixed, and unattached; it is the outflow-free precept praised by the noble ones, which enters into the factors of the Eightfold Noble Path.

Abiding within this precept, one upholds all precepts, namely: the precept of name, natural precept, restraint precept, active precept, non-active precept, dignified conduct precept, and non-dignified conduct precept.
This bodhisattva, having accomplished all the precepts, does not make such a vow as:

"By reason of these precepts, may I be born into a great clan of kṣatriyas, a great clan of brāhmaṇas, a great household of householders, or a minor royal family; or may I be born into the family of a wheel-turning sage-king; or may I be born in the abode of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
They do not make such a vow as this:
"By reason of my upholding the precepts, I shall attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha."
Why is this? All dharmas are signless, which is to say they have but a single mark.
A signless dharma cannot obtain a signless dharma, and a dharma with signs cannot obtain a dharma with signs.
A signless dharma cannot obtain a dharma with signs, and a dharma with signs cannot obtain a signless dharma.
In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the signless perfection of ethical discipline and enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Having entered the stage of a bodhisattva, they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas;
they practice the knowledge of the paths and attain the five supernormal powers as a result of their retribution;
they abide in five hundred dharani-doors and attain the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they make offerings to all buddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify buddha-fields.
Although they enter among the five destinies, the karmic retributions of birth and death cannot defile them.

Subhūti! For example, it is like a magically conjured wheel-turning sage king who, though sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, is seen neither to come from anywhere, nor go anywhere, nor abide, sit, or lie down anywhere; yet he is able to benefit sentient beings, while not apprehending any sentient beings.
A bodhisattva is also like this.

Subhūti! For example, when the Buddha Susaṃtata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he turned the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the three vehicles, yet there was no one among them who received a prediction of bodhisattvahood;
having manifested a transformation Buddha, he relinquished his body and life-span and entered nirvana without remainder.
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva:
when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
having fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline, they gather all wholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the five aggregates as being like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation, thereby fulfilling the signless perfection of patience."
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the signless perfection of patience? “Subhūti!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in two types of patience, they are able to fulfill the pāramitā of kṣānti.
What are these two patiences? They are patience toward sentient beings (janma-kṣānti) and patience toward dharmas (dharma-kṣānti).

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening, throughout this interval, even if all sentient beings should come to revile him with harsh and abusive language, or should strike this bodhisattva with tiles, stones, swords, or staves, because this bodhisattva desires to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), he does not give rise to even a single thought of malice.
This bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"Who is it that reviles me?
Who is it that harms me?"
"Who is it that addresses me with harsh words, or harms me with tiles, stones, swords, or staves?
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has attained the patience of signlessness (animitta-kṣānti) regarding all phenomena; how, then, could they entertain such a thought?
"Does this person revile me or harm me?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they can fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Because they have fulfilled this perfection of patience, they attain the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?”
"What is eliminated by this patience?
What is known by it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"To attain the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), such that not even the slightest unwholesome dharma arises—therefore it is called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).
That all afflictions severed by all bodhisattvas are exhausted is called 'severing';
that one uses wisdom to know that all dharmas do not arise is called 'knowing'."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is the difference between the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas of the bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the srotāpannas is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the sakṛdāgāmins is called the patience of a bodhisattva.”
Whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of an Anāgāmin, this is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of an Arhat, this is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
whether it be the wisdom or the abandonment of a Pratyekabuddha, this is called the patience of a bodhisattva.
This is the distinction, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes this patience surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Abiding within such fruition-attained non-arising forbearance (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one practices the bodhisattva path and is able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*);

because of fulfilling the knowledge of the aspects of the path, one is never separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) and the three samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and is never separated from the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*);
because of not being separated from the five supernormal powers, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
Having brought sentient beings to maturity and purified the Buddha-fields, one shall attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
It is in this way, Subhūti,
that a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the signless perfection of patience (*akṣobhya-pāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the five aggregates that are signless— like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation— and practices physical vigor and mental vigor."
Through physical diligence, one gives rise to supernormal powers;
by giving rise to supernormal powers, one reaches the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and benefit sentient beings;
through the power of physical diligence, one teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Three Vehicles.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is able to fulfill the signless perfection of diligence.
This bodhisattva, through mental diligence and noble, untainted diligence, enters into the eightfold noble path and is able to fulfill the pāramitā of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

This perfection of vigor encompasses all wholesome dharmas, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments; as well as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When this bodhisattva practices these dharmas, they should fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
having fulfilled all-knowledge, they sever all afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), fully perfecting the thirty-two marks, and their body emits incomparable and immeasurable light;
having emitted this light, they turn the wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions.
Because the Wheel of Dharma was turned, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and its radiance illuminated the entire trichiliocosm;
all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm who heard the sound of the preaching of the Dharma were all delivered and liberated by means of the Three Vehicles.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, is able to bring great benefit and is able to fulfill all-knowledge.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva dwells in the five aggregates as being signless— like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a transformation— they are able to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā."
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, dwelling in the five aggregates as being like a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation, fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā?”

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; enters the immeasurable states of mind—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; enters the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; enters the samādhi of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless samādhi; enters the samādhi like a flash of lightning, the samādhi like a vajra, and the noble right samādhi.
With the exception of the samādhis of the Buddhas, all other samādhis—whether those shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—he realizes and enters them all.”
Nor does he experience the flavor of samādhi, nor does he experience the fruit of samādhi. Why is this?

Because this bodhisattva knows that this samādhi is signless and of a non-existent nature; how could he experience the flavor of a signless dharma within a signless dharma, or experience the flavor of a non-existent dharma within a non-existent dharma?
If one does not relish the flavor [of meditative attainment], one will not be reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm by the power of dhyāna-concentration. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva does not perceive these two realms, nor does he perceive this dhyāna, nor does he perceive the one who enters dhyāna, nor does he perceive the dharmas used to enter dhyāna.
If one does not apprehend these dharmas, one is then able to fulfill the signless dhyāna-pāramitā.
By means of this dhyāna-pāramitā, the bodhisattva is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva, by being fully endowed with the signless dhyāna-pāramitā, is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva skillfully studies internal emptiness, skillfully studies external emptiness, and so on up to skillfully studying the emptiness of non-existence and existence;

regarding these various forms of emptiness, there is no dharma in which one may abide—whether it be the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, or even up to all-knowledge.”
"These various emptinesses are also empty.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these various emptinesses in this manner, they are able to enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
What is that which is not a stage?”
“Subhūti! All that is attained is not the stage of a bodhisattva; all that is unattained is the stage of a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is that which is apprehended?
What is that which is non-apprehended? "Subhūti!"

If form is apprehended as an object, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are apprehended as objects; if the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), are apprehended as objects—this is not the stage of a bodhisattva.
Subhūti! As for the stage of a bodhisattva, all dharmas therein cannot be demonstrated and cannot be spoken of.
What dharmas cannot be demonstrated and cannot be spoken of?
Whether it be form, or even up to all-knowledge.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The nature of form is unindicatable and inexpressible, and so on up to the nature of all-knowledge, which is unindicatable and inexpressible. Subhūti!
This is called the stage of a bodhisattva.

When a bodhisattva enters this stage, they are fully endowed with all dhyānas and samādhis; yet they do not even arise by the power of these dhyānas and samādhis, let alone dwell in lust, anger, or delusion to give rise to sinful karma within them.
The bodhisattva dwells solely within dharmas that are like illusions to benefit sentient beings, yet neither grasps at sentient beings nor at dharmas that are like illusions.
When there is nothing to be apprehended, at that time, he is able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the buddha-fields.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the dhyāna-pāramitā that is signless, up to and including the ability to turn the wheel of Dharma—namely, the wheel of Dharma that is ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that all phenomena are like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a shadow, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know that all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical transformation?”

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive a dream, nor do they perceive one who dreams; they do not perceive an echo, nor do they perceive one who hears an echo; they do not perceive a reflection, nor do they perceive one who sees a reflection; they do not perceive a mirage, nor do they perceive one who sees a mirage; they do not perceive an illusion, nor do they perceive one who sees an illusion; they do not perceive a transformation, nor do they perceive one who sees a transformation.”
Why is this? Because these things—the dream, the echo, the shadow, the mirage, the illusion, and the transformation—are all inverted phenomena of foolish ordinary beings.
Arhats do not see dreams, nor do they see those who see dreams; likewise, they do not see transformations, nor do they see those who see transformations.
Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all Buddhas likewise do not see dreams, nor do they see those who see dreams; they do not even see emanations, nor do they see those who see emanations.
Why is this? Because all dharmas have the nature of non-existence, are unarisen, and are indeterminate.

If dharmas have the nature of non-existence, are unarisen, and are indeterminate, how should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) therein by grasping at signs of arising or signs of determinacy?
This is not the case.
Why? If dharmas possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature, arising, or fixedness, it could not be called the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Thus it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not cling to form, nor even to consciousness; he does not cling to the realms of desire, form, or formlessness; he does not cling to the dhyānas, liberations, or samādhis; he does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even to the eightfold noble path; he does not cling to the samādhi of emptiness, the signless, or the wishless; and he does not cling to the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.
Because they do not cling, they are able to fulfill the first stage of a bodhisattva, yet within that first stage they likewise give rise to no clinging.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas do not apprehend this stage; how then could they give rise to greedy attachment?
It is the same up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
This bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), yet does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom.

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, because he does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, at that time he sees that all phenomena enter into the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not apprehend those phenomena either.
Why is this? Because these dharmas and the prajñāpāramitā are non-dual and without distinction. Why is this?
“Because all dharmas enter into suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality, they are without discrimination.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena are without marks and without conceptual differentiation, how can one say that they are wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, worldly or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned?
“Subhūti, what do you think?

Within the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena, is there any dharma that can be said to be wholesome or unwholesome, or even conditioned or unconditioned; or is there anything that is the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?”
“World-Honored One!
It is ineffable! “Subhūti!
For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas are signless, non-conceptual, unarisen, undetermined,
and inexpressible.

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, there was likewise no dharma that possessed an intrinsic nature to be apprehended—whether it be form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; or even anything conditioned or unconditioned; from the fruit of stream-entry up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should skillfully study the nature of all dharmas;
because they skillfully study the nature of all dharmas, this is called the path to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Practicing this path, one is able to fulfill the six pāramitās, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify the buddha-fields;
abiding within these dharmas, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, yet remains unattached even to the three vehicles.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study the prajñāpāramitā by means of the signless dharma.
[Śāstra] Question:
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"If all dharmas are without marks and without differentiation, how can you distinguish and speak of the six pāramitās?
The Buddha replied in turn:
“A bodhisattva dwelling within these five aggregates, which are like a dream, is able to fulfill the six pāramitās.
Subhūti asks by means of emptiness, and the Buddha answers by means of emptiness; how can this dialogue be considered distinct?
The answer is:
Subhūti asked,
"If all dharmas are empty, how is it that we now see with our own eyes a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās and becoming a Buddha?"
The Buddha replied:

"Ordinary beings are far removed from true wisdom; they grasp at signs and see the Bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās to become a Buddha. Because they are attached to these dharmas of emptiness, it is difficult for them [to understand]."

Although a bodhisattva dwells within the five aggregates, they dwell within these five aggregates as being like an illusion, like a dream, and as empty phenomena; furthermore, they practice giving with an empty mind. Therefore, although they practice all dharmas and fulfill the six pāramitās, this does not obstruct their realization of emptiness.
For example, like clouds and mist, which are visible when viewed from afar but disappear when one approaches them, so it is with ordinary beings:
because they are distant from the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they perceive the various Buddhas.
Because the Bodhisattva is close to the true mark (*dharmatā*), he perceives all things as empty; therefore, there is no obstruction.
Because there is no obstruction, he is able to fully practice all wholesome dharmas within a single thought-moment of the *dānapāramitā*.

Because this person constantly cultivates the untainted (anāsrava) and pure pāramitās, when they undergo a transformation of their physical existence, they receive as a karmic retribution the attainment of the untainted pāramitās.
This is called "attainment through retribution" because it is acquired spontaneously without further cultivation;
it is, for example, like the faculty of sight obtained through retribution, which naturally enables one to perceive forms.

Having attained this retributive, untainted perfection (*anāsrava-pāramitā*), one is able to transform a single body into immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* bodies, fully hearing the profound teachings of all Buddhas in the ten directions from those Buddhas, liberating sentient beings throughout the ten directions, gradually purifying Buddha-worlds, and becoming a Buddha according to one's vows.
Question:
If all dharmas are empty and signless, how can they be differentiated?
How can it be known that when practicing the *dānapāramitā* and so forth, each is fully endowed with the remaining *pāramitās*?
The answer is:

Although the practitioner does not himself make such distinctions, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas describe his practice of *dāna* (giving) and his practice of *śīla* (ethical discipline), as he fulfills all the various practices.
Just as when a śrāvaka enters the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga) into the untainted, signless, and non-conceptual dharmas, other noble ones also enumerate the dharmas they have entered:
knowing the true mark of all dharmas—namely, the mark of signlessness—is called right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi);
once right view has gained power, it is called right practice (samyak-caryā).
At that time, not afflicting sentient beings and committing no evil is called right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
At that time, although there is nothing spoken and nothing performed, these are nonetheless termed right speech and right action.
Why is this? These are called profound and subtle right speech and right action, because they consist in ultimately not afflicting sentient beings.
Within this, to resolve the mind and engage in purposeful activity is called diligence;
To bind one's mindfulness to its object is called right mindfulness;
to collect the mind in a single point is called right concentration.
To perceive the true nature of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena is called the "four foundations of mindfulness."
This applies likewise up to the seven factors of enlightenment.
Within the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as within the eightfold noble path, they are likewise counted among the noble ones.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: by practicing this signless *dānapāramitā*, they are able to fulfill all wholesome dharmas such as the *śīlapāramitā* and the others.
Just as it is with the *dānapāramitā*, so it is with the *śīlapāramitā* and the others in encompassing all wholesome dharmas.

Question: In the superior section, it was stated that a single pāramitā encompasses all pāramitās; here, it is said that signlessness encompasses all dharmas. What is the difference between these two?
The answer is:

The former [section] holds that one can fully possess all the pāramitās within a single thought-moment; this [section] differs in that it maintains one can fully possess all the pāramitās despite the fact that all dharmas are empty and signless.

78. Chapter on the Four Means of Integration (*Catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*). *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Four Means of Integration, Number Seventy-Eight. [Sūtra] Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”

If all dharmas are like dreams, echoes, shadows, mirages, illusions, and transformations—lacking substantial reality, having no intrinsic nature, and being empty of self-characteristics—how can one differentiate between wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas, outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas? How can one distinguish those dharmas that enable the attainment of the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat; or those that enable the attainment of the path of a pratyekabuddha, or the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Ordinary foolish people experience dreams and see those who dream, and even experience emanations and see those who emanate; they give rise to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate karma of body, speech, and mind; they give rise to meritorious karma, or sinful karma, or perform karma that leads to the imperturbable.”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, abides in two kinds of emptiness—ultimate emptiness and beginningless emptiness—and preaches the Dharma to sentient beings, saying:
"O sentient beings!..."
This form is empty and non-existent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and non-existent;
the twelve bases and the eighteen elements are empty and non-existent.
Form is a dream; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are dreams.
The twelve bases and the eighteen elements are dreams.
Form is an echo, a reflection, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
The twelve bases and eighteen elements are a dream, an echo, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a magical creation.

Within them there are no aggregates, bases, or elements; there is neither dream nor one who dreams, neither echo nor one who hears the echo, neither shadow nor one who sees the shadow, neither mirage nor one who sees the mirage, neither illusion nor one who sees the illusion, and neither magical creation nor one who sees the magical creation.

All dharmas are without fundamental reality and are non-existent; yet you perceive aggregates where there are no aggregates, perceive sense-bases where there are no sense-bases, and perceive elements where there are no elements.

All these phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they originate from a perverted mind and belong to the retribution of karma. Why, then, do you grasp at the mark of a fundamental essence within phenomena that are empty and without root?

"At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā through the power of skillful means, draws sentient beings out from midst of stinginess regarding the Dharma and teaches them to practice the Dānapāramitā;
by means of the merit of this giving, they obtain great rewards of fortune."
He draws them out from great karmic rewards and instructs them to uphold the precepts;
through the merit of upholding the precepts, they are born in noble and exalted places in the heavens.
He draws them out once more and causes them to dwell in the first dhyāna.
The merit of the first dhyāna leads to rebirth in the Brahma heavens;

the same applies to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Sentient beings practice this giving and its fruit, upholding the precepts and their fruit, meditative concentration and its fruit; through various causes and conditions, they are extracted [from suffering] and established in *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and the path to nirvāṇa—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; the gate of liberation of emptiness, the signless, and the wishless gates of liberation; the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities. Thus they bring peace and security to sentient beings, causing them to abide in the noble, untainted dharmas—the formless, formless-shape, and non-obstructive dharmas.
For those who are capable of attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna*, he teaches them with peace and security, causing them to abide in the fruit of *srotāpanna*;

for those capable of attaining the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*, he causes them to abide in the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, the fruit of *arhat*, or the path of a *pratyekabuddha*;
and for those capable of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he likewise teaches them with peace and security, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is truly rare and difficult for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be able to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, wherein all dharmas are of a non-existent nature, ultimately empty, and empty from the beginningless past; yet they can still distinguish that these dharmas are wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, and even conditioned or unconditioned.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and difficult to equal, for they are able to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, wherein all phenomena are of the nature of non-existence, ultimately empty, and empty from the beginningless past, yet they still discern all phenomena.

Subhūti! If you understand that this is the rare and difficult-to-attain dharma of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, then you will know that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot repay it, let alone other people!
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is this marvelous and extraordinary dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which is not possessed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Listen attentively with a single-minded focus!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, dwelling in the six pāramitās obtained as a result of maturation, as well as in the five supernormal powers and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment obtained as a result of maturation; dwelling in various dhāraṇīs and the various unhindered knowledges, they go to the worlds of the ten directions and, for those who can be saved through giving, they gather them in by means of giving.”
Those who can be delivered through the observance of precepts, he gathers by means of observing precepts;
those who can be delivered through patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom, he gathers according to what is appropriate for each.
Those who can be delivered by the first dhyāna, he gathers them through the first dhyāna;

those who can be delivered by the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, or by the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he gathers them accordingly as is appropriate for each.

Those who can be delivered by means of the minds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), he gathers them through these minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Those who can be delivered by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he gathers them according to those respective means.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva benefit sentient beings through giving? “Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they give in charity whatever is required—food and drink, clothing, vehicles and horses, incense and flowers, necklaces, and all manner of necessities—providing them all completely.
If one makes offerings to Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, anāgāmins, sakṛdāgāmins, srotāpannas, and so forth, there is no difference;
likewise, if one gives to those who have entered the right path as well as to ordinary people, down even to birds and beasts, there is no discrimination, for it is all one and the same act of giving.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-different and non-discriminative.
Having practiced giving without difference or distinction, this bodhisattva shall obtain the retribution of the non-discriminative dharma, which is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing a beggar, gives rise to this thought:
"The Buddha is a field of merit; I should make offerings to him;"
"Wild birds and beasts are not fields of merit; they should not be venerated.
This is not the Dharma of a bodhisattva. Why is this so?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not form such thoughts as:
"This sentient being should be benefited by means of giving; that one should not be given to."

"By reason of these sentient beings' causes and conditions of giving, they should be born into great kṣatriya clans, great brāhmaṇa clans, or great householder families; and furthermore, by means of these causes and conditions of giving, I shall deliver them through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles and cause them to enter nirvāṇa without remainder."
If sentient beings come to beg from a bodhisattva, they do not give rise to a discriminatory thought, thinking:
"I should give this to one, but I should not give that to another. Why is this?
This bodhisattva has generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of these sentient beings;

yet, if they engage in conceptual discrimination and selection, they fall into a place of reproach by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, those in training and those beyond training, and all the gods and humans of the world, who will say:
"Who requested you to save all sentient beings?"

Since you are a shelter for all sentient beings, a protector for all sentient beings, and a refuge for all sentient beings, why do you engage in discrimination and selection regarding what should and should not be given?

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, if a human or a non-human being comes seeking to beg for the limbs and members of the Bodhisattva’s body, at that time he should not give rise to two thoughts:
'Should I give them?'"
"If they do not give it?
Why is this? This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has taken on a body for the sake of sentient beings; when sentient beings come to take from him, how could he not give it?
"I have received this body for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; if sentient beings do not ask, I should give to them of my own accord, how much more so when they do ask!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this way."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a beggar, he should give rise to this thought:
'In this matter, who is it that gives? Who is it that receives? "
What is it that is given?
It is that the self-nature of all phenomena is ultimately unapprehendable because they are absolutely empty;
in phenomena characterized by emptiness, there is neither giving nor taking away.
Why is this? Because it is ultimately empty;
because it is internally empty; because it is externally empty, both internally and externally empty, great empty, emptiness of the ultimate truth, and emptiness of self-characteristic.
Dwelling in these various forms of emptiness while practicing giving, one at that time fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Because the perfection of generosity is fulfilled, when cutting off internal or external phenomena, one forms this thought:
"Who is it that cuts me?"
"Who is it that cuts me?

Furthermore, Subhūti, with my Buddha-eye I see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who enter the great hells and cause the fires to be extinguished and the boiling water to turn cold, teaching them through three things: [the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Saṃgha]."
First, supernormal powers; second, knowledge of others' minds; third, preaching the Dharma.
By means of his supernormal powers, this bodhisattva causes the fires of the great hells to be extinguished and the boiling water to turn cold;
he knows the minds of others.
With loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations.
These sentient beings give rise to a pure mind toward the Bodhisattva, thereby attaining liberation from hell and gradually reaching the end of suffering through the three vehicles of the Dharma.
It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions,
and the zenith and nadir. Furthermore, Subhūti,

with my Buddha-eye I observe the worlds of the ten directions and see bodhisattvas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges serving as attendants to the Buddhas, making offerings to the Buddhas, and honoring them with joy and devotion according to their wishes.
"If one is able to receive and uphold everything spoken by all Buddhas, without ever forgetting it until reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

With my Buddha-eye, I behold the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in lands throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who, for the sake of animals, relinquish their lives, have their bodies cut and mangled, and are scattered in all directions.
All sentient beings who eat the flesh of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will all come to love and revere the bodhisattvas;

because of this love and reverence, they shall immediately escape the realm of animals, encounter the Buddhas, hear the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma, and practice according to what is taught. Gradually, by means of the three vehicles—the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha—they shall enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

The benefit brought about by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly great—they teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to practice according to the teaching, and even to enter parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I see the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who eliminate the suffering of hunger and thirst for all hungry ghosts. Because these hungry ghosts love and revere the bodhisattvas, they are able to leave the realm of hungry ghosts;

they encounter the Buddhas, hear the Buddhas preach the Dharma, and practice according to those teachings. Gradually, by means of the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha-vehicle—they attain parinirvāṇa, even up to the nirvāṇa without remainder."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the mind of great compassion.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preaching the Dharma in the heavens of the Four Great Kings; they preach the Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Hearing the bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, the devas gradually attain parinirvāṇa by means of the three vehicles.

Subhūti! Among these hosts of devas, there are those who are attached to the five desires. To them, this bodhisattva manifests the breaking out of fire that burns their palaces, and preaches the Dharma to them, saying:
"O devas!..."
"All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent; who could find peace therein?

Furthermore, Subhūti, with my Buddha-eye I behold the worlds of the ten directions and see the Brahmā devas in lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges clinging to false views. These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas instruct them to distance themselves from such false views, saying:
"How is it that you give rise to false views regarding these empty-characteristic, illusory dharmas? In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a mind of great loving-kindness and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti! This is the rare and difficult-to-attain dharma of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
