Likewise, when one has left the household life, neither the followers of Māra nor malevolent spirits can cause them to waver or be defeated.
The meaning of the forty-two letters is as explained in the Mahāyāna.
As for how a single letter completely enters into all letters: it is like how two ones combined become two, three ones become three, four ones become four, and so on up to ten million.
Furthermore, just as the letter *a* serves as the basis for meditative concentration, it transforms into *ra*, and also transforms into *pa*;
in this manner, all [letters] enter into the forty-two letters.
As for the forty-two letters entering into the one letter, the forty-two letters all possess a portion of *a*, and that portion of *a* in turn enters back into *a*.
Because one skillfully knows characters, one skillfully knows the names of all phenomena;
because one skillfully knows the names of all phenomena, one skillfully knows the meanings of all phenomena.
The absence of characters is precisely the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Why is this so? Because within the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*), all phenomena are without names.
Subhūti asked:

"If all dharmas are ultimately empty and devoid of names, how can a bodhisattva, dwelling in the six supernormal powers as a result of their retribution, preach the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings?
If there are ultimately no sentient beings, then there are no dharmas either!"
The Buddha affirmed Subhūti’s words: “So it is!

Because of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, all phenomena are unapprehendable; from self and sentient beings up to the knower and the seer, and even the Buddha and the bodhisattva, one should know that they are all empty.”
Having understood this, he preaches this Dharma of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings.
If sentient beings were existent and he were to preach emptiness for them, that would be impossible;
rather, because sentient beings are empty and exist only through inversion, the Bodhisattva does not lose sight of emptiness while preaching the Dharma.
"Not losing" means not to treat all phenomena as empty while asserting that what is spoken of is not empty;
for if one asserts that what is spoken of is not empty, one loses the characteristic of emptiness.
Furthermore, if one speaks of emptiness with the mouth but maintains the notion of existence in the mind, this too constitutes a loss.
In this regard, the Buddha himself said:
"It is non-dual, because it does not destroy the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa).
To clarify this matter, he provides an analogy:

"Just as a Buddha might manifest an emanated being and preach the Dharma to them regarding the various merits of observing the precepts and practicing generosity—if one preaches the Dharma through such skillful means, there is no fault;
for it is able to pull sentient beings out of their inversions, because there is neither bondage nor liberation."
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is only according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) that there is bondage and liberation.
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explained the causal conditions:
"Form is neither bound nor liberated."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither bound nor liberated, there is no characteristic of form.
This applies likewise, up to and including consciousness.
In this way, because the bodhisattva does not abide by means of non-abiding dharmas, they dwell within the dharma of emptiness and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
yet sentient beings cannot be apprehended, because both sentient beings and all dharmas are unapprehendable.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions: namely, that a dharma of non-existence does not abide in non-existence, just as space does not abide in space;
and that a dharma of intrinsic nature does not abide in a dharma of intrinsic nature, just as fire does not abide within fire.

A phenomenon characterized by other-nature does not abide within a phenomenon characterized by other-nature; for example, there is no nature of fire within the nature of water, and furthermore, because other-nature is not fixed.
If one can thus preach the Dharma with such purity, that bodhisattva will be without fault before all Buddhas, worthies, and sages.
Why is this? The Buddhas and the worthy sages do not cling to any phenomena, and those who preach the Dharma likewise do not cling to any phenomena.
The Buddhas and the worthy sages take ultimate emptiness and the mark of universal quiescence as the sphere of their mental activity; those who preach the Dharma are also like this.
The Buddhas and the worthy sages enter the three gates of liberation and attain the true nature of all phenomena, which is called nirvana without remainder;
because the teacher of the Dharma follows this Dharma, there is no fault.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"After the Buddhas and noble sages have attained this Dharma, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, yet they do not alter the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), because the nature of phenomena is empty and signless."
Subhūti asked:
"If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not undergo transformation, are form and the other phenomena different from the nature of phenomena?
The Buddha replied:
"No, it is not so. Why is this? Because the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena, such as form and the rest, is itself the dharma-nature (dharmatā)."
The Buddha’s intention was that when a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, they likewise do not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Subhūti then asked:
"Form and all other phenomena are also not different from the *dharmatā*; for what reason, then, is only the *dharmatā* esteemed?
Because the Buddha replied that "form is not different from the *dharmatā*," Subhūti raised an objection:
"If they are not different, how can there be distinctions such as good and evil, white and black, or the various fruits beginning with the *srotāpanna*?"
The Buddha replied:
"Although dharmas such as form are not separate from the dharma-nature, they are differentiated by way of conventional truth; in the ultimate sense, however, there is no differentiation."

Why is this? Because those who have attained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) are sages who do not engage in conceptual discrimination; they do not rejoice upon hearing that there is something to be attained, nor do they grieve upon hearing that there is nothing.
Having realized emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*), they do not even grasp at the marks of subtle phenomena, let alone discriminate between good and evil!
Those who have not yet attained the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) engage in conceptual discrimination because they desire to attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Regarding this, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:

"This Dharma is beyond verbal expression; it is devoid of dharmas such as arising and ceasing, or defilement and purity—namely, it is ultimate emptiness (atyantaśūnyatā) and beginningless emptiness (anavarāgraśūnyatā)."
Question: Why is it that here only the two kinds of emptiness are spoken of as "dharmas"? Answer:
All that exists—
whether phenomena or sentient beings—
if one says they are ultimately empty, then one destroys all phenomena.
If one says that beginningless emptiness exists, then one destroys sentient beings.
Once these two dharmas are destroyed, all dharmas are completely destroyed.
In this context, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, by means of the two kinds of emptiness, he destroys these two things.
Although there are other forms of emptiness, they are not as profoundly exhaustive as ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Other forms of emptiness are like wood burned by fire, where ashes and embers still remain;
ultimate emptiness has neither ash nor embers.
Some say: "If one speaks of the eighteen emptinesses, there is no fault; however, because it is a brief exposition, only two emptinesses are mentioned. Subhūti said:

"If one were to distinguish between good and evil, white and black, as well as the various fruits of sainthood, on the basis of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), then in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) ordinary persons would possess such fruits as those of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and so forth!"

Why is this? If one were to distinguish the existence of various noble ones (ārya) within the false context of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), then in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) would have to become noble ones.
Subhūti distinguishes between the true nature (*dharmatā*) and ordinary beings as being different.
The Buddha said:
"The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) has but a single characteristic."
For this reason, Subhūti said:
"Ordinary worldlings should be noble ones!
At that time, the Buddha replied:

"If ordinary persons knew that discrimination was the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and this was conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), then ordinary persons would possess the various noble fruits such as stream-entry (srotāpanna).

Since ordinary persons truly do not know the Way, do not know how to discriminate the Way, and do not know how to practice or cultivate the Way, how much less could they attain the fruits of the Way!"
The Buddha said:
"Because the noble ones are able to make such distinctions, they speak of these fruits of the noble path.
At that time, Subhūti, realizing he had made an error, said:
Within the state that is immeasurable, signless, and immovable, how could I grasp at signs to attempt to measure immeasurable dharmas?
How could I forcibly take ordinary, mundane dharmas to be the fruit of the noble ones?

At that time, having received the Buddha’s words and understanding that those who practice the Path attain the fruit while those who do not practice the Path do not attain the fruit, he addressed the Buddha:
“Does one attain the fruit by practicing the Path?”
The Buddha said, "No. He asked:
The Buddha previously spoke of the analytical cultivation of the path and the attainment of its fruits; why does he now say "no"?
The answer is:
what the Buddha spoke of before was not with a mind of attachment.
Now, Subhūti asks with an attached mind, desiring to produce a fruit from within the Path, like extracting oil from sesame seeds.
If that were so, then both the Path and its fruit would be equally false and deceptive; therefore, he says "no."
The listeners conceived this thought:
"If it cannot be attained through cultivation, then one should attain it without cultivation!
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If even through cultivation one does not attain it, how much less so without cultivation!
It is like two people who wish to reach a certain destination:
one remains stationary and does not travel; [the other travels].
Second is losing the path;
in both cases, one does not arrive.
If one does not cultivate the path, there is not even the slightest joy of mental composure, let alone the fruit of the path!
If one cultivates the path while the mind grasps at signs, although there may be the bliss of meditative concentration through the gathering of the mind, there is no fruit of the Path;
if one cultivates the path without grasping at signs or becoming attached in the mind, then there is the fruit of the Path.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Because a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not discriminate between the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned, there is a distinction between the path and its fruit."
At that time, Subhūti asked:
"If that is so, for what reason does the Buddha speak of severing the three fetters to attain the stage of a srotāpanna, and why are there such distinctions?"
The Buddha answered with a counter-question:
"What do you think:
Do you consider the fruit of stream-entry and so forth to be conditioned or unconditioned?"
Subhūti said, "This is unconditioned.
The Buddha said:
“If that is so, is there any distinction among unconditioned phenomena? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
If there is no conceptual discrimination, how can you raise an objection?
He then asked Subhūti again:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family penetrates all phenomena as having a single characteristic—namely, the characteristicless—and, abiding within the three gates of liberation, realizes nirvana, at that time, is there any conceptual differentiation of phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned?"
He replied, "No!
The Buddha’s intention was:
Only this mind is real; all else is at all times false and deceptive. How can you raise such an objection?

When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not discriminate among any phenomena (*dharma*), dwelling within the various emptinesses such as internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*); this is great purity.

They themselves do not cling, and they also teach sentient beings to be without clinging—namely, from the *dānapāramitā* up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within the path of the bodhisattva, they teach them all to remain unattached.

For example, when a person created by a Buddha practices giving and so forth, they do not discriminate regarding giving and so forth, nor do they receive the karmic retribution for the dharmas of giving and so forth; it is solely for the purpose of benefiting and delivering sentient beings.
The bodhisattva’s mind is also like this.
Why? Because it skillfully penetrates the nature of all phenomena.
One who has skillfully attained thorough penetration does not grasp at the characteristics of the dharma-nature, nor does he dwell within the dharma-nature;
without doubt or despondency regarding the dharma-nature, he expounds the Dharma without obstruction, hindrance, or impediment—this is the thorough penetration of the dharma-nature.
Chapter 79: Skillful Mastery The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on Skillful Mastery, Number Seventy-nine [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva who has thoroughly mastered the characteristics of all dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“For example, it is like a person created by transformation (nirmāṇapuruṣa) who does not engage in lust, anger, or delusion; who does not engage in form up to consciousness; who does not engage in internal or external dharmas; who does not engage in the various afflictions (kleśa) or fetters (saṃyojana); who does not engage in out-flowing (sāsrava) or non-out-flowing (anāsrava) dharmas, mundane or supramundane dharmas, conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, nor even in the fruits of holiness.”
“The Bodhisattva is also like this: such a thing does not exist, nor does he discriminate that this is a dharma; this is called being well-versed in the characteristics of all dharmas. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”
"How can a transformed person cultivate the path?
The Buddha said,
"When a transformed person cultivates the path, it is neither defiled nor pure, nor does it abide within the cycle of birth and death in the five realms."
Subhūti, what do you think?
Does a person conjured by a Buddha have any fundamental reality, or any defilement or purification?
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One!
A person conjured by the Buddha has no fundamental reality; he is neither defiled nor pure, and he does not abide within the cycle of birth and death in the five realms."
“Thus it is, Subhūti! It is in this same way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly penetrates the characteristics of all phenomena. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Are all forms like an illusion?
Are all feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses like an illusion?”
The Buddha said:
“All form is like an illusion; all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an illusion.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”

If all form is like an illusion, and all feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions, and all phenomena are like illusions—if an illusory person has no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if they have neither defilement nor purity, neither the cycle of birth and death in the five realms nor any place of liberation—then what function or efficacy does a bodhisattva possess?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva originally practiced the bodhisattva path, did he perceive any sentient beings who were liberated from the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, humans, or gods?"
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said: “So it is! So it is!”
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive sentient beings as being liberated from the three realms. Why is this?
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives and knows all phenomena to be like illusions and like transformations.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives and knows all phenomena to be like illusions and like transformations, for what purpose do they practice the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to practicing great loving-kindness and great compassion, purifying buddha-fields, and bringing sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If sentient beings themselves knew that all phenomena are like illusions and like transformations, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would never practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of sentient beings throughout incalculable eons."

Subhūti! Because sentient beings themselves do not know that all dharmas are like illusions and like transformations, for this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, bringing sentient beings to maturity, purifying buddha-fields, and attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are like dreams, like echoes, like shadows, like mirages, like illusions, and like transformations, in what place do sentient beings abide so that the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās to deliver them?"

“Subhūti! Sentient beings dwell only within names, marks, and false conceptualizations; therefore, the bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā pulls sentient beings out from within these names, marks, and falsehoods.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘name’?”
“What are these characteristics? The Buddha said: “These are called artificial and conventional designations, namely:

‘this is form,’ ‘this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness’; ‘this is male,’ ‘this is female’; ‘this is large,’ ‘this is small’; ‘this is hell,’ ‘this is the animal realm,’ ‘this is the realm of hungry ghosts’; ‘this is a human,’ ‘this is a deva’; ‘this is conditioned,’ ‘this is unconditioned’; ‘this is the fruit of stream-entry,’ ‘the fruit of once-returning,’ ‘the fruit of non-returning,’ ‘the fruit of arhatship,’ ‘the path of the pratyekabuddha,’ and ‘the path of the Buddha.’”
Subhūti! All phenomena that arise through combination are merely provisional designations; one grasps at all phenomena by means of names, and for this reason they are called "names.
All conditioned phenomena possess only names and characteristics, yet foolish ordinary people give rise to attachment within them.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, they instruct [beings] to distance themselves from names and say:
"O sentient beings!..."
This is called a mere empty name, arising from false recollection and conceptual discrimination; you should not cling to such false recollections!
This matter is non-existent from beginning to end, for its intrinsic nature is empty; thus, it is that which the wise do not cling to.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom uses the power of skillful means to teach the Dharma to sentient beings."
Subhūti! This is what is called "name. What is "mark"?
Subhūti! There are two kinds of characteristics upon which ordinary persons become attached. What are these two?
First is the mark of form, and second is the mark of the formless. Subhūti,
what is called the mark of form?
Whatever forms there may be—whether coarse or subtle, beautiful or ugly—all are empty.
Within this dharma of emptiness, the mind that gives rise to recollection, conceptualization, and attachment is called the mark of form (*rūpa-nimitta*).
What is the characteristic of the formless?

Regarding all formless phenomena, because one gives rise to conceptualization and discrimination, and grasps at characteristics with an attached mind, afflictions are produced; this is called the characteristic of the formless.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, instructs sentient beings to distance themselves from these signs and to abide within the dharma of signlessness, so that they do not fall into dualistic dharmas—namely, "this is a sign" and "this is signlessness."
In this way, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they teach and transform sentient beings so that they distance themselves from signs and cause them to abide within the nature of signlessness.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are merely names and signs, how can a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom benefit themselves and also teach others so that they may attain wholesome benefits?”
“How does a bodhisattva fulfill the stages, proceeding from one stage to the next, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they attain the three vehicles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If the fundamental essence of all dharmas truly existed and were not merely names and signs, then when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he would be unable to benefit himself, nor could he benefit others.”

Subhūti! All dharmas have no fundamental reality; they exist merely as names and signs. Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is able to fulfill the perfection of meditation because it is signless;
likewise, he fulfills the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, because they are signless.

They are fully endowed with the perfection of the four dhyānas, because they are signless; they are fully endowed with the perfection of the four immeasurables, because they are signless; they are fully endowed with the perfection of the four formless attainments, because they are signless;
they are fully endowed with the perfection of the four foundations of mindfulness, because they are signless;
and so on, up to being fully endowed with the perfection of the eightfold noble path, because they are signless.
They are fully endowed with the perfection of internal emptiness because it is signless;
up to being fully endowed with the perfection of the emptiness of non-existence and existence because it is signless;
and they are fully endowed with the perfection of the eight liberations because they are signless.
They fulfill the perfection of the nine successive meditative concentrations because they are signless;
they fulfill the perfection of the ten powers of a Buddha because they are signless;
and so on, up to fulfilling the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha because they are signless.
Because they are signless, this bodhisattva personally fulfills these wholesome dharmas and also teaches others to fulfill wholesome dharmas, because they are signless. Subhūti!

If any characteristic of phenomena were to exist in reality even to the extent of a hair’s breadth, then when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they would be unable to know that all phenomena are signless and free from recollection, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor could they teach sentient beings to attain the outflow-free dharmas.
Why is this? Because all untainted dharmas are signless and beyond recollection.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom benefits sentient beings through untainted dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If all dharmas are signless and beyond recollection, how can one enumerate them as the dharma of śrāvakas, the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of bodhisattvas, or the dharma of buddhas?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Is the dharma of signlessness different from the dharma of the śrāvakas?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Are the dharma of signlessness different from the dharma of Pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of Bodhisattvas, and the dharma of Buddhas?"
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Are the dharma of signlessness the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the dharma of pratyekabuddha, the dharma of bodhisattva, and the dharma of buddha?”
Subhūti said: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that all dharmas are signless. Subhūti!”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas study the signlessness of all dharmas, they attain the increase of wholesome dharmas, namely: the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because for a bodhisattva, no other dharma is considered essential as much as the three gates of liberation, namely: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Why is that?
All wholesome dharmas enter the three gates of liberation. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics; this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.
All phenomena are signless; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness.
All phenomena are without volitional activity and without the characteristic of arising; this is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the three gates of liberation, at that time they are able to train in the characteristics of the five aggregates, the characteristics of the twelve bases, and the characteristics of the eighteen elements; they are able to train in the four noble truths and the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination; they are able to train in internal emptiness, external emptiness, and so forth up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence; they are able to train in the six pāramitās, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth up to the eightfold noble path; and they are able to train in the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) learn the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the characteristic of form, they know the arising and ceasing of form, and they know the suchness of form."
How does one know the characteristics of form (*rūpa*)?
One knows that form is ultimately empty; its internal components are distinct, void, and without reality;
it is like foam on water, lacking any solidity. This is what is meant by knowing the characteristics of form.
How does one know the arising and ceasing of form?
When form arises, it comes from nowhere; when it passes away, it goes nowhere. If it neither comes nor goes, this is knowing the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of form.
How does one know the suchness of form?
This suchness of form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure; this is what it means to know the suchness of form.

Subhūti! As "suchness" (tathatā) is according to reality and not false—just as it is in the beginning, so it is in the end and in the middle, always without change—this is what is meant by knowing the suchness of form (rūpa-tathatā).
"How does one know the characteristic of feeling?
How does one know the arising and ceasing of feeling?
How does one know the suchness of feeling?"
The Bodhisattva knows that the characteristics of all sensations are like bubbles on water, arising and ceasing one after another; this is knowing the characteristics of sensation.
Knowing the arising and ceasing of sensation means knowing that this sensation comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; this is knowing the arising and ceasing of sensation.

To know the suchness of sensation is to know that this suchness is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither defiled nor pure; this is what is meant by knowing the suchness of sensation.
“How does one know the characteristics of perception?
How does one know the arising and ceasing of perception?
How does one know the suchness of perception?”

To know the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*) is to know that this perception is like a mirage: water cannot be found there, yet one falsely gives rise to the perception of water; this is knowing the characteristic of perception.
To know the arising and ceasing of perception is to know that this perception comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; this is knowing the arising and ceasing of perception.

To know the suchness of perception (*saṃjñā*) means that the suchness of all perceptions is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, and does not deviate from the true nature (*dharmatā*); this is what is meant by knowing the suchness of perception.
"How does one know the characteristics of formations?
How does one know the arising and passing away of formations?
How does one know the suchness of formations?"

Regarding the characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*): formations are like a plantain tree; when one peels away layer after layer, no solid core is found. This is called knowing the characteristic of formations.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of formations: all formations arise from nowhere and go nowhere. This is called knowing the arising and ceasing of formations.

To know the suchness of all phenomena is to know that all conditioned things are neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither defiled nor pure; this is what it means to know the suchness of phenomena.
"What is the characteristic of consciousness?
What is the arising and ceasing of consciousness?
What is the suchness of consciousness?"
Regarding the characteristic of consciousness: it is like a magician who conjures four kinds of troops through illusion;

they have no reality, and consciousness is likewise. Regarding the arising and ceasing of consciousness: when this consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere. This is what is meant by the arising and ceasing of consciousness.

As for the suchness of consciousness: consciousness is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; this is the suchness of consciousness.
"How does one know the sense bases?
The eye is empty of the nature of the eye, and so on up to the mind, which is empty of the nature of the mind;
forms are empty of the nature of forms, and so on up to phenomena, which are empty of the nature of phenomena."
“How does one know the elements?
The eye is empty of the element of the eye; forms are empty of the element of forms; eye-consciousness is empty of the element of eye-consciousness;
and so on, up to the element of mind-consciousness, which is likewise.”
"How does one know the Four Noble Truths?
When knowing the Noble Truth of Suffering, one remains far removed from two dharmas; knowing that the Truth of Suffering is neither dual nor distinct is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
It is the same for Origination, Cessation, and the Path."
How does one know the suchness of suffering?
The noble truth of suffering is itself suchness, and suchness is itself the noble truth of suffering.
It is the same for the truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
"How does one know the twelve links of dependent origination?
To know that the twelve links of dependent origination have the characteristic of non-arising—this is called knowing the twelve links of dependent origination.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, as they analytically discern each and every dharma, will they not, by means of the nature of form, destroy the nature of dharmas, and so on, up to destroying the nature of dharmas by means of the nature of all-knowledge?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there were any dharma existing apart from the nature of dharmas (dharmatā), it would destroy the nature of dharmas.
Since no dharma can be found apart from the nature of dharmas, it is therefore not destroyed."
Why is this? Subhūti,

because the Buddha and his disciples know that no phenomenon can be found outside of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they do not say that there is any phenomenon outside of the nature of phenomena.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in the dharma-nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the dharma-nature, is it that there is nothing to be trained in?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies the dharma-nature, they study all dharmas.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions are all dharmas identical to the dharma-nature?”
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas enter into the nature of signlessness and unconditionedness. For this reason, by training in the dharma-nature, one trains in all dharmas."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature, why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity?”
Why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the first dhyāna, and the second, third, and fourth dhyānas?
Why do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
Why study the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Why study the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?
Why study the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Why study the eight liberations, the nine successive concentrations, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities?
Why study the six supernormal powers?
Why study the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics?
Why study birth into great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, or great families of householders?

Why do they train to be born in the abodes of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven?
Why should one study the abodes of the Brahmā-pārṣadya devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, the sphere of non-perception, and the Śuddhāvāsa devas?
Why do they give birth to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Why study the stage of the initial resolve, and the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages?
Why study the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharma-position of the bodhisattva?
Why study the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields?
Why study the various dhāraṇīs?
Why study the delight in preaching the Dharma?
Why study anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so that having studied it, one may attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and know all phenomena?
"Bhagavān!
Within the dharma-nature of all dharmas, there is no such discrimination!
Bhagavān!"
Could it be that a bodhisattva has fallen into a non-path?
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no such conceptual discrimination.

Within the nature of phenomena, there is no form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; yet the natures of all phenomena are not separate from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Form itself is the nature of phenomena, and the nature of phenomena itself is form.
“Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus; all dharmas are likewise.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so!”
So it is! It is as you have said:
"Form is itself the dharma-nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the dharma-nature."

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they perceive any phenomenon as existing outside of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they are not seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know that the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having known that all phenomena are the nature of phenomena, they express through names and signs that which is without name or sign—namely, "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and so on, up to "this is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Subhūti! It is as if a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to stand in a crowded place and conjure through illusion various forms and colors:

men and women, elephants and horses, magnificent gardens and groves, as well as various lodgings, flowing springs, bathing pools, clothing, bedding, perfumes, flowers, necklaces, delicacies, food and drink, and perform various musical entertainments to delight the multitude.”
Furthermore, he creates illusory persons and causes them to practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the cultivation of wisdom.

This illusionist further creates illusory members of the great Kṣatriya clans, the great Brāhmaṇa clans, and the great householder families; he manifests the abodes of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three on Mount Sumeru, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven to show to the multitude. He further creates illusory beings from the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven, and he further creates illusory Śrotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas.

From the first generation of the thought of enlightenment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). Practicing from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, they enter the rank of a Bodhisattva, sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify Buddha-lands. They sport with the various dhyānas, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis; they practice the ten powers of a Buddha (*buddha-bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and great loving-kindness and great compassion. They fully manifest the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s body and the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) to demonstrate them to all people.
Among them, those who lack wisdom praise him, saying: "How marvelous!

This person is highly capable and skillful in performing all manner of tasks, providing entertainment for the multitude through various forms and colors, even adorning the Buddha’s body with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics."
Among them, a wise person reflected, saying: "How extraordinary!
There is no substantial reality herein;

yet by means of dharmas that are non-existent, he entertains the multitude, causing them to perceive forms where there is no substance, and signs where there is no sign, and characteristics where there are no characteristics."
"Thus it is, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any phenomenon as existing apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). By means of skillful power, although they do not apprehend a sentient being, they personally practice giving, teach others to give, praise the dharma of giving, and rejoice in and praise those who practice giving;
they themselves maintain the precepts and also teach others to maintain the precepts."
One practices patience oneself and also teaches others to practice patience;
one practices diligence oneself and also teaches others to practice diligence;
one practices meditative concentration oneself and also teaches others to practice meditative concentration.
One cultivates wisdom oneself and also teaches others to cultivate wisdom; one praises the practice of the Dharma of wisdom and joyfully lauds those who cultivate wisdom.

One practices the ten wholesome paths oneself and also teaches others to practice the ten wholesome paths; one praises the practice of the Dharma of the ten wholesome paths and joyfully lauds those who practice the ten wholesome paths.

One personally undertakes and practices the five precepts, and also teaches others to undertake and practice the five precepts; one praises the dharma of the five precepts and joyfully extols those who undertake and practice them.

One personally observes the eightfold precepts and fast, teaches others to observe the eightfold precepts and fast, praises the dharma of the eightfold precepts and fast, and joyfully commends those who practice the eightfold precepts and fast.
One practices the first dhyāna oneself, up to and including the fourth dhyāna.
One practices loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity oneself.
One practices the sphere of infinite space, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and also teaches others to practice them.
They personally practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

they personally practice the three gates of liberation, the ten powers of a Buddha, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They also teach others to practice the eighteen unique qualities, praise the eighteen unique qualities, and joyfully praise those who practice the eighteen unique qualities.

Subhūti! If the nature of phenomena were different in the beginning, the end, or the middle, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would be unable to manifest the nature of phenomena through the power of skillful means and bring sentient beings to maturity.

Subhūti! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without difference in the beginning, middle, or end, this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and traverses the bodhisattva path for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
[Treatise] Question:
In every chapter, the Buddha has spoken of "thoroughly penetrating the characteristics of all dharmas. Why does Subhūti now ask again? Answer:
This Prajñāpāramitā has no fixed characteristic because it is beyond verbal expression; thus, even though it has been heard many times, it is not yet sufficient, and for this reason he asks again.
For example, although a calf may be large, it does not cease drinking from the fine milk of its excellent mother;

the Buddha’s great compassion is like the excellent mother, the Prajñāpāramitā is like the fine milk, and Subhūti is like the calf—though he has repeatedly heard the characteristics of all dharmas, he is still not satiated.

Furthermore, only the Buddha’s all-encompassing wisdom can penetrate the true nature of all phenomena; although others may attain some understanding, they cannot exhaustively fathom it. For this reason, he asks.
"How can other bodhisattvas who have not yet become Buddhas attain such thorough penetration? The Buddha answered with a simile:

"It is like a person created by illusion (māyāpuruṣa), who possesses neither the three poisons nor the fetters and afflictions (kleśa-saṃyojana). He has no mind (citta) or mental factors (caitasika-dharma); he is not subsumed within internal or external phenomena, nor among those that are outflowing (sāsrava) or non-outflowing (anāsrava). He does not fall into the category of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), nor does he fall into the fruits of the noble ones (āryaphala); one cannot say of him that he is a srotāpanna, and so forth."
It can also manifest the good and evil thoughts of others' minds; whatever transformative acts it performs will certainly bring them to fulfillment.
These transformations are, in reality, neither defiled nor pure, and are not subsumed within the six realms of existence.

The body of a bodhisattva is also like this: it is free from afflictions such as the three poisons. Knowing that this mind and its mental factors are all produced through the causes and conditions of false, deceptive, and inverted dharmas from previous lives, they do not believe in them and do not follow after them.
To be able to practice in this way is to have skillfully mastered the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

At that time, although Subhūti well understood emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because he held the Buddha’s Dharma in high esteem and respect, and could not measure the extent of the Buddha’s Dharma, he asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"Are all phenomena, such as form and so forth, empty and like illusions?
The Buddha replied, "All phenomena,
such as form and so forth, are like illusions."
"Because you hold the Buddha-dharma in high esteem, you do not dare to speak of emptiness;
because I possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), I am able to declare that all phenomena are empty.
It is like other people who prize the strength of a lion, while the lion himself does not prize his own strength."
At that time, Subhūti said:

"If all dharmas are ultimately empty and all are like magical illusions, for what reason does the Buddha praise the merits of bodhisattvas in various ways—claiming that because of bodhisattvas, the three evil realms are eliminated and they are able to deliver sentient beings so that they may attain nirvāṇa?"
The Buddha questioned Subhūti in return:
"What do you think?
When a bodhisattva originally practices the bodhisattva path, does he perceive any truly existent sentient beings whom he can extract from the five realms of existence?"
Subhūti replied,
“No. The Buddha affirmed his meaning:
"So it is! So it is! Why is this?
"When a bodhisattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they know and see all phenomena as being like illusions and like transformations.
Subhūti said: "If that is so, for what purpose does the bodhisattva practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and so forth?"
The Buddha replied:
"If sentient beings themselves were to know that all dharmas are empty and like an illusion, then the bodhisattva would have no task.
Furthermore, if all dharmas were definitively characterized by emptiness, then the bodhisattva would have no task.
It causes all phenomena to be neither real nor empty, transcending the path of all language, characterized by ultimate emptiness and quiescent extinction.
Because sentient beings do not know this matter, they give rise to the notion of "self," produce evil and sinful karma, and undergo immeasurable suffering;
for this reason, the Bodhisattva, knowing the true reality of all phenomena, gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
It is like a householder who has a son that is blind and drinks poison; the householder, knowing the boy will surely die, employs various skillful means to prevent him from drinking it.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: seeing that these sentient beings drink the three poisons because they are blinded by the ignorance of perversion, he gives rise to great compassion and, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, cultivates the six *pāramitās*, purifies Buddha-lands, and transforms sentient beings.
Having heard this, Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are empty and without root, like dreams and like illusions, in what place do sentient beings abide so that the bodhisattva may extract them?"
Subhūti’s thought was:
“It is as if a person who has sunk into deep mud were to be pulled out.
The Buddha answered:
"Sentient beings dwell only within names, marks, deceptive recollections, and conceptual discriminations.
The Buddha’s intention is this:
among all phenomena, there is nothing that is determinate or real; it is only because of their delusion that ordinary people become attached to them.
It is like a person who, seeing what appears to be a human figure in the darkness, mistakes it for a real person and gives rise to fear;

or like a vicious dog that, standing at a well, barks at its own reflection—the water contains no dog, yet there is only its semblance—and thus conceives an evil mind, throws itself into the well, and dies.

Sentient beings are also like this: because the four great elements are combined, they are called a "body"; consciousness arises due to causes and conditions, and through their combination, there is movement and speech.
Ordinary people give rise to the notion of a "person" within this, producing attachment and aversion, committing sinful karma, and falling into the three evil realms.

When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, out of compassion for sentient beings, they teach them through various causes and conditions, enabling them to understand the dharma of emptiness and thereby deliver them from suffering.
They speak thus:

"All these dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent; yet because sentient beings are deluded and false, they perceive them as if they were real. They are like transformations, like illusions, like a city of the *gandharvas*—they have no substantial reality and merely deceive the human eye."
Furthermore, all phenomena arise merely from the combination of names; there are yet other such names.
For example, because the head, feet, belly, and spine are combined, they are conventionally designated as a "body";
because hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin, and bones are combined, they are conventionally designated as a "head."
Because various hairs are combined, they are called "hair";
because they are combined part by part, they are conventionally named "hairs";
because various atoms are combined, they are called "hair-parts."
Furthermore, because it is a combination of various parts, it is called an atom (*paramāṇu*).
[The opponent] asks:

Since an atom is the most subtle thing, it cannot be divided into parts; and since it has no parts, there can be no combination. This is a fixed reality (*niyata-dharma*); therefore, one cannot say that "all things are empty and there is no fixed reality."
Answer: If atoms were form, they would necessarily have parts. Why is this?
All forms exist within empty space and all possess the ten directions.
If a minute particle were form, it would possess ten parts;
if it possessed ten parts, how could it be an ultimate atom?
If, as you say, atoms have no parts, then they are not matter (rūpa).
Why? Because they lack the characteristics of matter.
Furthermore, form is that which can be apprehended by the five sense faculties; if atoms were not apprehended by the five sense faculties, how could it be known that they are form?
Therefore, atoms exist as nothing more than a mere empty name.
Even coarse forms seen by the eye can still be analyzed until they become empty; how much more so those that are invisible and intangible!
Question:
Because atoms are subtle, they cannot be apprehended by the five sensory faculties; however, when a sage attains the divine eye, he sees them.
Answer: Although that which is seen by the divine eye is subtle, because it is a form-characteristic (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), it must possess parts;
if it had no parts, it would not be form, and if it were not form, the divine eye would not see it.
For this reason, even the divine eye is a deceptive and false vision;
therefore, when the Noble Ones observe the world with the wisdom-eye, they attain the Way.
As previously stated, atoms exist only as names and have no reality.

Because atoms do not exist, all dharmas are merely combinations of names; thus there are further provisional designations that lack any real or fixed substance, yet sentient beings falsely give rise to greedy attachment.
Due to the causes and conditions of greed and anger, they initiate evil karma and undergo suffering in the three evil realms for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

If all phenomena were truly fixed, one should not even give rise to the causes and conditions for the offenses of greed and hatred; how much less so when they are empty, deceptive, and without reality!
If one can abandon deceptive names and signs and remain unattached to dharmas that are empty, then one will attain the eternal bliss of nirvana.
Question:
What is the difference between name (nāma) and appearance (nimitta)? Answer:
"Name" refers to the designation for a collection of things, such as the name "fire" for that which is hot.
"Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is like knowing it is fire by seeing smoke; heat is the essence (svabhāva) of fire.
Furthermore, within the combination of the five aggregates, "man" and "woman" constitute the name;
the physical appearance by which man and woman can be distinguished constitutes the mark.
Because one perceives these marks, one applies names, calling them "man" or "woman."
Question:
If that is so, then names and characteristics would be no different! Why is this?
"One obtains the name because of seeing the characteristic; one obtains the characteristic because of knowing the name.
[The opponent] asks: "Do you not understand what I have said?"
First one perceives the appearance of a male or female, and subsequently designates them as "male" or "female.
The marks are the root, while the names are the branches.
Furthermore, it is like a person who sees a form with their eyes and, selectively grasping at the marks they find pleasing, gives rise to attachment; this is not the case for other people.
Because it can give rise to a mind of defiled attachment, it is called a "mark" (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, in this context, the Buddha himself explains the discrimination between name (*nāman*) and mark:
"Name is a provisional designation; by means of names, one grasps all phenomena."
As explained at length in the sutra,
Subhūti asked:
"If all dharmas are merely names and signs, how does a bodhisattva benefit themselves and benefit others?"
The Buddha replied:
"If all dharmas were fundamentally existent, then when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they would be unable to benefit themselves or others."
Why is this? If the nature of all phenomena were fixed and truly existent, it would be non-arising. Why is this?
Because their nature would already be determinately existent.
If a phenomenon arises from the combination of causes and conditions, it possesses no determinate nature.
If its nature were determinately existent, it would not require the combination of causes and conditions.
If that were so, there would be no arising; because there is no arising, there is no cessation; and because there is no cessation, there is neither demerit nor merit.
It is by knowing impermanence that one abandons demerit and cultivates merit;
if things were permanent, there would be neither bondage nor liberation, neither the mundane world nor nirvana, and so forth.
Therefore, the Buddha told Subhūti:

"If dharmas were fixedly existent and not merely names and signs, the bodhisattva would not practice the perfection of wisdom for his own benefit and the benefit of others, nor would he practice the perfection of meditation and so forth for his own benefit and the benefit of others."
Because they are signless, this Bodhisattva personally fulfills these wholesome dharmas and also benefits sentient beings through those wholesome dharmas, by virtue of their being signless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If any dharmas were to exist in reality even to the extent of a single hair’s breadth, then when a Bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he would be unable to contemplate all dharmas as empty, signless, and non-existent, and thus could not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Nor can they benefit sentient beings by means of this dharma.
Why is this? Because when these bodhisattvas sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they contemplate all dharmas as the foremost reality.
If there were even a slight error, one would not be able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
nor could one expound this dharma of emptiness and signlessness for the sake of sentient beings.
Why is this? If dharmas were definitively existent, how could the Buddha deceive sentient beings by saying, "All dharmas are without outflows, without marks, and without recollection"?
Question:

Among the Four Noble Truths, three truths all possess characteristics—the Truth of Suffering has the characteristic of suffering, the Truth of Origination has the characteristic of origination, and the Truth of the Path has the characteristic of the path;

only the Truth of Cessation is without characteristics, yet it still possesses mindfulness, for it is the signless Nirvana. Why do you say that "all untainted dharmas are without characteristics and without mindfulness"?
Answer: The Mahāyāna dharma differs from the Śrāvaka dharma.
Within the Mahāyāna dharma, it is taught:
"All untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are signless (*animitta*) and without recollection (*asmṛti*).
Furthermore, that which possesses signs and recollection is entirely deceptive and unreal;
if it is deceptive and unreal, it is precisely the outflows of the afflictions (*kleśāsrava*). How, then, could it be untainted?
Furthermore, these three truths all follow the truth of cessation: upon seeing suffering, one abandons it; upon seeing its origin, one cuts it off—neither being spoken of as ultimately fixed;
and because one sees the path as the means for proceeding toward cessation, one likewise does not abide within that path;
cessation is the sovereign.
This is the dharma of cessation, signless and objectless; how could there be recollection?
Recollection consists entirely of attachment to signs and dharmas as objects.
Therefore, all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are signless and without recollection.
Subhūti thought:

"If untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are the foremost reality, being without marks (*animitta*) and without recollection (*asmṛti*), then the nature of all dharmas should likewise be without marks and without recollection;
it is only because ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are subject to inversion (*viparyāsa*) that there are marks and recollections."
Therefore, he asked the Buddha:
"If all dharmas are without marks and without recollection, how can one enumerate them as the dharma of śrāvakas, the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, the dharma of bodhisattvas, or the dharma of buddhas?"
The Buddha then asked Subhūti in return:
"Are the dharmas of the three vehicles different from the dharma of signlessness?
Subhūti replied:

The cessation of all afflictions is itself abandonment; abandonment is itself the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). One also knows that the truths of cessation and the path are themselves untainted (*anāsrava*) and signless (*animitta*). Therefore, it is said:
"The three vehicles are not different from the signless dharma."
The Buddha asked again:
"Are those from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha not themselves the signless dharma?
He replied:
"It is so. For this reason, you should know that all dharmas are without marks (animitta).
If they are without marks, how can you raise the objection that there are various paths?"
"Precisely because they are signless, there are the various paths of the three vehicles.
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva can train in the dharma of signlessness in this way, they will be able to increase all wholesome dharmas, namely the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the cause and condition:
"A bodhisattva dwells solely in the three gates of liberation and does not take other dharmas as essential. Why is this so?
The three gates of liberation are the ultimate dharmas; although other dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness are also real, they are all taught as skillful means.
The three gates of liberation are proximate to nirvāṇa and can also encompass all truly wholesome dharmas; for this reason, it is said that a bodhisattva should study them.
Question:

If a bodhisattva trains in these three gates of liberation, they are training in the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth. These three gates of liberation are all empty, signless, and without conceptual differentiation, whereas these dharmas of the five aggregates are all dharmas with signs and with conceptual differentiation. How can one train in these other dharmas by virtue of training in the three gates of liberation?
Answer:

When a bodhisattva studies these three gates of liberation, they transcend the triple world and exhaust the three outflows; thus, among all phenomena, they attain true wisdom that penetrates everything without obstruction.
Previously, among the five aggregates, all were false and characterized by perverse conduct;
now, because one has attained these three gates of liberation, one attains correct penetration.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:

"When a bodhisattva practices these three gates of liberation—the dharma of signlessness—they know the arising of form, they know the cessation of form, and they know the suchness of form; this applies likewise up to consciousness."
As explained at length in the sutra,
Subhūti asked again: “As the Buddha has said,
a bodhisattva knows the characteristics of form and so forth, knows the arising of form and so forth, knows the cessation of form and so forth, and knows the suchness of form and so forth.”
"If one discriminates in this way, will it not destroy the nature of form (rūpa-dharmatā)?
The Buddha replied:
"If there were any dharma that transcended the nature of dharmas (dharmatā), then the nature of form would indeed destroy the nature of dharmas."
The true mark of all phenomena is called the *dharmatā*; therefore, all phenomena enter into the *dharmatā*.
The true mark of the nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself the *dharmatā*, being of one and the same nature; how, then, could the nature of form destroy the *dharmatā*?
The Buddha further explained the causal conditions:
"The Buddhas and noble sages do not perceive any dharma that transcends the dharma-nature; because they do not find such a thing, they do not speak of it.
Since the Buddhas and noble sages are the most trustworthy of beings, the bodhisattva should train in the dharma-nature in this manner.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“If a bodhisattva trains in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this constitutes having nothing to train in. Why is that?”
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without intrinsic nature.
The Buddha replied:
"If a bodhisattva studies the nature of phenomena that is without intrinsic nature, they are studying all phenomena."

If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were to possess a distinct nature of its own, or if being "without nature" were itself a nature, then one should study only the nature of phenomena and not all phenomena;
however, since the nature of phenomena actually has no distinct nature and is also not "without nature," one must study all phenomena universally.
However, the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the dharma-nature; therefore, by attaining the true reality, one correctly and universally studies all phenomena.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!...”
If all dharmas are themselves the dharma-nature, for what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the six pāramitās, up to and including the gates of dhāraṇī?

Why is this? The true mark of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*) is precisely the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). If all phenomena are themselves the dharma-nature, what further would a bodhisattva have to seek?
Furthermore, within the dharma-nature there is no discrimination such as these six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) up to the dhāraṇīs.
"Now, when a bodhisattva discriminates and practices these dharmas, will they not fall into perversion?
The Buddha, affirming Subhūti’s intention, replied:
"If a bodhisattva were to emerge from the dharma-nature and perceive the existence of dharmas, they would not seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? That which exists apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is a constant perversion and ignorance; it cannot be transformed into reality. How, then, could one sever ignorance within all phenomena and thereby attain Buddhahood?
The Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are ultimately empty, characterized by perpetual quiescence, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and devoid of names;

yet, out of compassion for sentient beings, through the power of skillful means, he teaches them by means of names and signs, saying: "This is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and so on, up to "unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
As stated in the sūtras regarding the analogy of illusion:
the illusionist is the bodhisattva, and the illusory phenomena are the dharmas such as the six pāramitās.
Although they practice these dharmas, they possess a mind free from attachment.
Just as a magician, though conjuring various objects through illusion, knows they lack reality and thus does not become attached to them,
so it is with the wise— the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas— whereas the ignorant—
the ordinary people and those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment— are filled with great joy and exclaim, "This is unprecedented!"

When a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, although they emerge from the dharma-nature, they do not perceive any further dharmas, nor do they perceive any fixed sentient beings; yet they bring great benefit to themselves and to all beings.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"This bodhisattva personally practices giving and so forth, and also instructs others; he praises the dharma of giving and rejoices in praising those who practice giving."
"Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), it is also thus.
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"If the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) were non-existent before and existent after, a bodhisattva would be unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor could they teach by means of skillful power (*upāya-bala*)."

Why is this? If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were previously non-existent and later came to be, arising from causes and conditions, it would be no different from the common dharmas of ordinary worldlings.
If the nature of phenomena were previously existent and later ceased to be, then sentient beings and all phenomena would fall into annihilationism.
Because the nature of all phenomena is empty from the beginning, it is likewise so in the middle and at the end; it is not made empty by the power of wisdom.
Sentient beings and all phenomena are not empty only upon entering nirvana without remainder; they have been eternally empty from the very outset.
The Bodhisattva instructs sentient beings:
"Why do you not contemplate their true nature and instead cling to perversions?
If you contemplate the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, you will know that they have been eternally empty from the very beginning, and there is nothing to be lost now."
“A bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner is thus able to benefit and bring aid to sentient beings.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 89.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Explanation of the Chapter on the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), Fascicle 80 (Fascicle 90).
Composed by the Holy Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eighty: The Reality-Limit (Bhūtakoṭi). [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If sentient beings are ultimately non-apprehensible, for whose sake does the bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Subhūti,
if the limit of reality were different from the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*), the bodhisattva would not practice the perfection of wisdom.”

Subhūti! The limit of reality and the limit of sentient beings are not different. For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they establish sentient beings within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) by means of the non-differentiation of the reality-limit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is itself the limit of sentient beings, then the bodhisattva would be establishing the limit of reality within the limit of reality.”
World-Honored One!
If one establishes the limit of reality within the limit of reality, then one establishes self-nature within self-nature.
World-Honored One!
"One cannot establish self-nature within self-nature.
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, establish sentient beings in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The limit of reality cannot be established upon the limit of reality; intrinsic nature cannot be established upon intrinsic nature. Subhūti!”
Now, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, they establish sentient beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, the limit of reality is not different from the limit of sentient beings; the limit of reality and the limit of sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the power of skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”

By means of this power of skillful means, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he establish sentient beings in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without destroying the characteristic of the limit of reality?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, he establishes sentient beings in giving."
Having established this, he explained the characteristics of the prior and posterior limits of giving, saying:
"Such giving is empty at its prior limit, empty at its posterior limit, and empty in its middle limit as well; the giver is empty, the reward of giving is empty, and the recipient is also empty."
"O sons of good family!

Within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all these dharmas, nothing can be apprehended; you should not conceive of the gift as distinct, the giver as distinct, the reward of the gift as distinct, or the recipient as distinct."

If you do not conceive of the gift as distinct from the giver, the reward for the gift as distinct, or the recipient as distinct, then at that time, the gift can take up the flavor of the deathless and attain the fruit of the flavor of the deathless.
"O son of good family!
Because of this giving, do not be attached to form; do not be attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is that?

This giving and the characteristic of giving are empty; the giver and the giver are empty; the reward of giving and the reward of giving are empty; the recipient and the recipient are empty. Within emptiness, giving cannot be apprehended, the giver cannot be apprehended, the reward of giving cannot be apprehended, and the recipient cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because these dharmas are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, they teach sentient beings to uphold the precepts, saying to them:
"O son of good family!
One abandons the practice of killing, up to and including abandoning wrong views. Why is this?
O son of good family!
Regarding the phenomena as you have discriminated them, these phenomena do not possess such a nature.
You, son of good family, should reflect carefully:
what is this "sentient being" that one would seek to deprive of life?
"By what means do they take life?
This applies even up to wrong views. Subhūti!
In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva brings sentient beings to maturity through the power of skillful means.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva then teaches sentient beings the fruits of giving and the fruits of maintaining ethical discipline; yet he knows that the self-nature of these fruits of giving and maintaining ethical discipline is empty.
Having realized that the self-nature of the fruits of giving and maintaining ethical discipline is empty, he does not become attached to them.
Because they do not cling, the mind is not distracted, and thus they are able to give rise to wisdom;
by means of this wisdom, they sever all fetters and afflictions and enter nirvana without remainder.
This is a conventional dharma, not the ultimate reality. Why is this so?
Because within emptiness there is no cessation, nor is there anyone who causes cessation.
That all dharmas are ultimately empty is itself nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings with minds of anger and affliction, he instructs them, saying:"
“O son of good family!
Come, practice patience; become a person of patience, and you should delight in patience.
This is because that which you are angry at is empty of intrinsic nature.”
Come here,
son of good family!
Reflect in this way:
"In what phenomena am I angry?
Who is the one who is angry?
And who is the object of my anger?"
"All these dharmas are empty; this nature of emptiness is such that there is no time when it is not empty.

This emptiness was not made by the Buddhas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas, nor by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. It was not made by devas, yakṣas, nāga kings, asuras, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas; nor by the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven; nor by the gods from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; nor by the gods from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception."
You should reflect in this way:
"Against whom is there anger?
Who is the one who is angry?"
"What is the object of anger? [The Buddha replied:
"All these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; within dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature, there is nothing toward which one can feel anger.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of these causes and conditions, they establish sentient beings in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, gradually and successively instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is a conventional dharma, not the ultimate reality.
Why? Because within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no attainer, no dharma to be attained, and no place of attainment.
Subhūti! This is called the reality-limit, the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
For the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this dharma, yet even those sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are free from the mark of a sentient being.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, seeing sentient beings who are indolent, he instructs them to cultivate physical diligence and mental diligence, saying:
"O sons of good family!
In the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, there is no phenomenon of indolence, no one who is indolent, and no matter of indolence;
the nature of all these phenomena is entirely empty, and nothing exceeds this emptiness of nature.
"You all must exert physical vigor and mental vigor; for the sake of producing wholesome dharmas, do not be indolent!

Good sons, whether it be giving, or ethical discipline, or patience, or vigor, or meditative concentration, or wisdom; whether it be the various dhyānas, liberations, or samādhis; whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gates of signlessness and wishlessness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—within these, do not be indolent!"
"O sons of good family!

Within the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, you should know that there is the characteristic of non-obstruction; within this dharma of non-obstruction, there is neither one who is indolent nor any dharma of indolence."
"In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they teach sentient beings to abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, so that they do not fall into dualistic dharmas."
Why is this? Because this nature is empty, non-dual, and without distinction; since this dharma is non-dual, there is no basis for anger.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they instruct sentient beings to be diligent, saying:
"O sons of good family!
