Exerting diligent effort—whether it be giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; whether it be the dhyānas, liberations, or samādhis; whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; whether it be the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness; whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, or great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Regarding these dharmas, you should not conceive of them as having dual characteristics, nor should you conceive of them as having non-dual characteristics. Why is this?

Because the nature of these dharmas is entirely empty; regarding dharmas whose nature is empty, one should not employ the thought of dual characteristics, nor should one employ the thought of non-dual characteristics.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom brings sentient beings to maturity through the power of skillful means."

Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he gradually instructs them so that they may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, and the stage of bodhisattva, leading them ultimately to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, seeing sentient beings with distracted minds, he employs skillful means for the sake of benefiting those beings and says this:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You should cultivate meditative concentration!
Do not give rise to distracted thoughts; you should give rise to a single-minded focus. Why is this?"
This dharma-nature is entirely empty; within this emptiness of nature, there is no dharma to be found, whether it be distraction or single-mindedness.
You should abide in this samādhi, and whatever actions you perform—whether of body, speech, or mind;
whether practicing giving, maintaining precepts, exercising patience, or applying diligent effort—[you should do so].
Whether practicing meditative concentration or cultivating wisdom; whether practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

whether practicing the various liberations, the successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, or great compassion—
The thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; whether it be the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, or the path of the Buddha;
or the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or all-encompassing knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Whether it be maturing sentient beings or purifying Buddha-fields, you shall all obtain these according to your vows,
because the nature of practice is emptiness.

"In this way, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the power of skillful means in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the end, they never grow weary or desist; they constantly seek wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings.

From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they make offerings to all buddhas and hear the Dharma from them. Through successive relinquishing of bodies and receiving of new bodies, until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they never forget or lose it."
This bodhisattva constantly attains all dhāraṇīs and is endowed with all faculties—namely, the faculty of body, the faculty of speech, and the faculty of mind. Why is this?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly cultivates the knowledge of all modes;
because they cultivate the knowledge of all modes, they cultivate all paths:
whether the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the supernatural powers of the bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva who practices the supernormal powers of the divine way constantly benefits sentient beings and never forgets this.
Abiding in the supernormal powers obtained as a result of maturation, this Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings and enters the five paths of birth and death without ever being diminished.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom dwells in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and benefits sentient beings through meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he benefits sentient beings through the power of skillful means,
saying to them: 'You sons of good family!'"
Contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is empty!
Sons of good family,
you should perform all actions— whether physical, verbal, or mental— to take up the flavor of ambrosia and attain the fruit of ambrosia.
In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no dharma that regresses.
Why is this? Because the emptiness of intrinsic nature does not regress, nor is there anyone who regresses.
"Because emptiness by nature is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, how could there be any falling back within these dharmas that are non-existent? Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should thus instruct sentient beings so that they never grow weary or desist.
This bodhisattva personally practices the ten wholesome paths of action and also teaches others to practice them;
the same applies to the five precepts and the eight precepts.
He personally practices the first dhyāna and also teaches others to practice the first dhyāna.
This applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
One constantly practices the mind of loving-kindness oneself and also teaches others to practice the mind of loving-kindness;
this applies likewise up to the mind of equanimity.
One practices the sphere of infinite space oneself and also teaches others to practice the sphere of infinite space;
this applies likewise up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He practices the four foundations of mindfulness himself and also teaches others to practice the four foundations of mindfulness;
this extends up to the eightfold noble path, and likewise for the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighty minor marks of excellence.

One gives rise to wisdom within the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) oneself, yet does not dwell therein; one also teaches others to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and so on up to the fruit of arhatship, which is likewise.
One generates wisdom within the path of a pratyekabuddha oneself, yet does not abide therein, and also teaches others to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha.
One generates the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi oneself, and also teaches others to attain the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"In this way, Subhūti,
because of the power of skillful means in practicing the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva never becomes indolent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the nature of all dharmas is eternally empty, and within this eternal emptiness sentient beings cannot be apprehended, nor can dharmas or non-dharmas be apprehended, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seek the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
As you have said:
"The nature of all phenomena is empty; within emptiness, sentient beings cannot be apprehended, nor can phenomena or non-phenomena be apprehended. Subhūti!

If the nature of all phenomena were not empty, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva would not rely on the emptiness of nature to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor would he preach the dharma of the emptiness of nature for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti! The nature of form is empty; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they teach the dharma that the five aggregates are empty of intrinsic nature, and they teach the dharma that the twelve bases and eighteen elements are empty of intrinsic nature.
He teaches the nature-emptiness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

he teaches the nature-emptiness of the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics;

he teaches the nature-emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the all-knowledge that severs the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Subhūti! If the emptiness of the internal were not empty, or if the emptiness of the external, up to the emptiness of non-existence and existence, were not empty, then one would destroy emptiness.
This intrinsic emptiness is neither eternal nor discontinuous. Why is this?
Because this intrinsic emptiness has no place of abiding; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Subhūti! This is called the characteristic of the stability of dharmas (*dharmasthitilakṣaṇa*).

Within this, there are no dharmas; there is no accumulation and no dispersion, no increase and no decrease, no arising and no cessation, no defilement and no purity. This is the characteristic of all dharmas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within this and gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not perceive any dharma that is being produced; there is neither production nor dwelling. This is called the characteristic of the abiding of dharmas.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they see that the nature of all dharmas is empty, and thus they do not turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not perceive any dharma that can act as an obstacle; how, then, could doubt arise?
This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one cannot find sentient beings, cannot find a self, cannot find a person, cannot find a life-span, and cannot find a vital principle; even up to, one cannot find a knower or a seer.

Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, form is unattainable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unattainable; even up to, the eighty minor marks of physical excellence are unattainable.
Subhūti! It is as if a Buddha were to manifest four assemblies—
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— and constantly preach the Dharma for these assemblies for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas without ceasing.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Will these transformed beings attain the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, or the fruit of an arhat; will they receive the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because these manifested beings have no fundamental reality.

All dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and likewise lack any fundamental reality; what, then, is this "sentient being" who attains the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat, or who receives the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“Subhūti! It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva:

he teaches the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature to sentient beings, yet these sentient beings are in reality unapprehendable. Because sentient beings have fallen into perversion, the bodhisattva extracts them and establishes them in non-perversion.”
Perversion is itself non-perversion;
although perversion and non-perversion share a single characteristic, perversions are many while non-perversions are few.
In the midst of non-perversion, there is no self and no sentient beings, and even no knower or seer.

In the state free from inversion, there is neither form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there are no twelve bases, and so on, up to and including no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within this and practices the perfection of wisdom, they pull sentient beings out from among the inversions regarding the marks of sentient beings; that is to say, they pull them out from the mark of "sentient beings" where there are no sentient beings, and so on, up to pulling them out from the marks of "one who knows" and "one who sees."

Within the formless, they extract sentient beings from the perception of form; within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they extract them from the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is the same for the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and even all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

“Subhūti! There are also various untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakpradhāna), the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).”
Although such dharmas as these are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not accord with the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The characteristic of the ultimate truth is non-activity, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), unborn, signless, and ineffable; this is called the ultimate truth, and it is also called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*), and it is also called the path of all Buddhas.
Within this, one cannot find sentient beings, nor can one find a knower or a seer;
one cannot find form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor can one find even the eighty secondary marks of physical excellence.

Why is this? It is not for the sake of the dharmas of the Path that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; rather, it is for the sake of the true mark of all dharmas—the emptiness of intrinsic nature—that he seeks Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This nature is empty; the prior limit is also empty by nature, the posterior limit is also empty by nature, and the middle limit is also empty by nature;
it is eternally empty by nature, and there is no time when it is not empty by nature.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this Prajñāpāramitā of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path in order to extract sentient beings who are attached to the mark of a sentient being.
When seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), one traverses all paths—whether the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the bodhisattva.

This bodhisattva, having perfected all paths, delivers sentient beings from their attachments to false conceptions; and once the buddha-field has been purified, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* according to his lifespan.

Subhūti! The nature of the path of all Buddhas of the ten directions in the past is empty of intrinsic nature; the paths of all Buddhas of the ten directions in the future and present are likewise empty of intrinsic nature.
Apart from this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no path in the world, nor is there any fruit of the path.
"One must approach the Buddhas, hear that the nature of all these dharmas is emptiness, and practice these dharmas so as not to lose *sarvajñā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How most rare!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, yet they do not destroy the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature—namely, that form is different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
World-Honored One!

Form itself is the emptiness of nature, and the emptiness of nature is itself form; and so on, up to and including unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—unsurpassed perfect enlightenment itself is the emptiness of nature, and the emptiness of nature is itself unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

If form were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and even if unsurpassed perfect enlightenment were different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not be able to attain all-knowledge.
Subhūti! Now, form is not different from the emptiness of nature, and so on up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, which is not different from the emptiness of nature.
For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, knowing that all dharmas are empty by nature, resolves his mind to seek unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because within these there is no dharma that is real or permanent; it is only that ordinary beings are attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Ordinary beings grasp at the characteristics of form, and they grasp at the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Because one possesses a mind that clings to internal and external things, one undergoes the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of future bodies; for this reason, one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, and continues to wander through the five realms of existence.

For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they do not destroy the characteristics of phenomena such as form, whether they be empty or non-empty.
Why is this? Because the nature of form is empty and does not destroy form—that is to say, "this is form" and "this is emptiness.
It is like space not destroying space: internal space does not destroy external space, and external space does not destroy internal space.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Form does not destroy the mark of emptiness, and the mark of emptiness does not destroy form. Why is this?
These two dharmas have no inherent nature that can be destroyed—namely, "this is emptiness" and "this is not emptiness"—and it is the same even up to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty and without differentiation, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, makes this vow: ‘I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi’?”
World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are without discrimination, how is it that a bodhisattva generates the thought, saying, "I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"?
“World-Honored One!
If one discriminates among all dharmas, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with dualistic characteristics, there is no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If one discriminates by making a duality, there is no *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one does not dualize and does not discriminate among all phenomena, that is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Enlightenment is characterized by non-duality and indestructibility.

Subhūti, this enlightenment does not operate within form; it does not operate within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; indeed, even enlightenment does not operate within enlightenment itself.
Why is this? Form is itself awakening, and awakening is itself form; they are non-dual and without distinction.
This applies likewise even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"This bodhi is not practiced for the sake of grasping, nor is it practiced for the sake of abandoning.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices for awakening neither by way of grasping nor by way of relinquishing, where, then, does the bodhisattva mahāsattva practice awakening?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think?”
"Where does a person created by the Buddha travel— is it by taking up the middle way,
or by abandoning the middle way?
Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is not practicing in the midst of grasping, nor is it practicing in the midst of abandoning.
The Buddha said:
“The bodhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: it does not proceed by way of grasping, nor does it proceed by way of relinquishing.
Subhūti, what do you think?”
"Where does the Bodhi of an Arhat move within a dream— is it by taking up the middle way,
or by abandoning the middle way? "No."
World-Honored One!
It is neither practicing in the midst of grasping nor practicing in the midst of abandoning.
World-Honored One!
“An Arhat never sleeps at all; how, then, could there be a dream in which awakening is practiced through either grasping or abandoning? “Subhūti!

The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: it does not proceed by way of grasping, nor does it proceed by way of abandoning—namely, it proceeds within form, and so on, up to proceeding within all-knowledge.
“World-Honored One!

Could it be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without practicing the ten stages, without practicing the six pāramitās, without practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, without practicing the fourteen kinds of emptiness, without practicing the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, and without practicing the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighty minor marks, abiding in the five superknowledges, purifying buddha-fields, and maturing sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Although a bodhisattva now practices in the absence of a locus for awakening, if they do not fully complete the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the ten powers of a buddha (*daśabala*) up to the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), the quality of constant relinquishment, and the quality of non-erroneousness—if they do not fully complete all these dharmas, they will ultimately never attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within the marks of form, dwelling within the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even dwelling within the mark of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, is able to fulfill the ten stages and eventually attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This mark is eternally quiescent; there is no dharma that can increase or decrease, arise or cease, be defiled or purified, attain the Path, or attain the fruit.
It is by way of conventional truth that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, not by way of the ultimate reality. Why is this?
In the ultimate sense, there is no form, nor anything up to and including unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nor is there anyone who practices for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
All these dharmas are spoken of by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Subhūti, from the moment a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon awakening until they practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, awakening does not increase and sentient beings do not decrease; likewise, the bodhisattva neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti, what do you think? When a person first attains the Way,

abiding in the *anupādāya-samādhi* (uninterrupted samādhi) and obtaining the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and if they realize the fruit of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*, at that time, do you perceive anything obtained— whether it be a dream, a mind, a path, or the fruit of the path?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
it cannot be attained!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"How should one know those who have attained the path of an arhat? [Subhūti replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"It is by way of conventional truth that one discriminates and names it the path of an Arhat.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"It is by way of conventional truth that one speaks of a 'Bodhisattva,' and speaks of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
In this awakening (*bodhi*), there is no dharma to be found that either increases or decreases, because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas is empty.

Since even the intrinsic emptiness of all dharmas cannot be apprehended, how much less could one apprehend the mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the mind of the tenth stage, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), or even any of the Buddha-dharmas? That such things should be apprehended is impossible!
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and brings benefit to sentient beings.
[Treatise] Commentary:
In the "Superior Chapter," Subhūti raises various objections based on causal conditions, asking:
"If all dharmas are empty, how can there be the five destinies of birth and death, or wholesome and unwholesome dharmas?"
Now, some difficult-to-convert beings speak thus:
"World-Honored One!
If sentient beings are ultimately unobtainable, for whose sake does the bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?"
Previously, he questioned the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; now, he questions sentient beings for the sake of the Dharma.
The Buddha replied:
"For the sake of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
Subhūti thought to himself:
"The bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
The Buddha’s intention was:
Sentient beings are merely conventional designations, deceptive and ultimately unfindable;
yet the bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of all real dharmas.
Real dharmas are precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Question: All Bodhisattvas perceive the suffering and affliction of sentient beings; for the sake of delivering these beings, they give rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Why, then, is it now said that this is for the sake of the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
Answer: A bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment generates the mind of great compassion solely for the sake of extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings.
This "suffering" refers to old age, sickness, death, and so forth, as well as the decline and affliction of body and mind.
How is this suffering extinguished?
One seeks the causes and conditions of suffering; because it arises from birth, as the Buddha said in the discourse on the twelve links of dependent origination:
"By what causes and conditions do old age, sickness, and death exist?"
"Because there is birth. He asked:
"All sentient beings know that the causal conditions of birth are suffering; what is so extraordinary about the Bodhisattva?"
The answer is:
Sentient beings do not know that suffering arises from birth; when they encounter suffering, they merely harbor resentment toward others and fail to regulate themselves, never blaming birth itself.
For this reason, they increase their fetters (*saṃyojana*) and further give rise to the phenomena of birth, remaining ignorant of the true cause of suffering.
There are those who, though free from whips, staves, weapons, and all manner of sorrowful afflictions, still undergo the suffering of death;
from where does this death come? It comes from birth.
Furthermore, whips, staves, weapons, grief, and affliction all exist because of birth.
While other phenomena may be either painful or painless, this phenomenon of birth is necessarily accompanied by suffering.

Even for those of great wisdom and the various devas, where there is birth there must be death; where there is death there must be suffering. Therefore, one knows that "birth is certainly the root of suffering."
Just as grass and trees, because they possess birth, can certainly be burned;
if they were not to be born, then even with fierce fires and great winds, there would be nothing to burn or harm.
Having already understood the causal conditions for suffering, the bodhisattva further investigates the causal conditions for birth.
As for the causal conditions for birth, they are "existence" (bhava).
There are three kinds of existence:
There are existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm.
Attachment to these three forms of existence gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma; this is the cause of birth.
As for the cause of existence, it consists of the four kinds of clinging.
Regarding the "condition of grasping" (*upādāna*), it refers to the various afflictions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
When they are minor and have not yet been able to initiate karma, they are called "craving";
when they increase and are capable of initiating karma, they are called "grasping."
Due to grasping at sensual desire, views, precepts and observances, and the doctrine of self—by clinging to these four things—one is able to give rise to various types of karma.
With craving as the condition, there are three kinds of feeling.
Regarding the condition of sensation (*vedanā-pratyaya*), it refers to the six types of contact (*sparśa*) involving the eye and so forth.
"Contact" is the name for the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) such as sensation and others.
Because of the conjunction of the three factors—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness—mental factors such as sensation arise within the mind.

Although the fundamental factors are three, contact arises from their conjunction; because they serve as the locus of support for the six sense faculties, only the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are mentioned.
The causal condition for the six sense bases is name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

Although the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are themselves part of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), when they are fully developed they are designated as the "six sense bases," and when not yet fully developed they are designated as "name-and-form.
When the aspect of form is fully developed, it is designated as the "five sense bases," and when the aspect of name is fully developed, it is designated as the "one sense base" (the mind-base).
This is the sequence of conditions during the time in the womb:
name-and-form has consciousness as its condition;
if consciousness were not to enter the womb, the embryo would perish at the very beginning.
"Consciousness" refers to the five aggregates within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Because these five aggregates are subtle, they are designated simply as "consciousness.
If consciousness were not to enter [the womb] for the embryo to be formed, then whenever all conditions were assembled, an embryo should be formed in every case!
Question:
By what causes and conditions does consciousness enter the womb? Answer:
The causal condition of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Formations are the three types of karma from the past; this karma leads consciousness (*vijñāna*) into the womb.
It is like a flame blown by the wind that travels through the air; the flame then depends upon the wind for its support.
Because one burned the six consciousnesses while in a human body in previous lives, at the time of death, karma leads the consciousness into the womb.
Question: Why is superior karma called "existence" (*bhava*)?
Question: Why is karma now called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*)? Answer:
Above, it was stated that "present-life karma, because it serves as the cause for future existence, is therefore called 'existence' (*bhava*)."

Now, "karma that has already ceased and been exhausted in past lives, which exists as a mere name, is called 'formations' (saṃskāra). In the language of India, this is *saṅkhāra*; in the language of Qin, it is "formations."
The causal conditions for these formations are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Although all afflictions serve as the causal conditions for past karma, they are designated simply as "ignorance" because ignorance is their root.
In the present life, because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are predominant, they are designated by those names;
in past lives, because these were the locus of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), they are designated simply as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now we have identified the root of all suffering and affliction: it is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Question:
Since beginningless birth and death have proceeded in succession for an exceedingly long time, why is [the root] restricted solely to ignorance?
Answer: This matter has already been answered previously.
The Bodhisattva reflects that, for the sake of liberating beings from suffering, he seeks the causes and conditions of suffering.
The sufferings of old age, death, and so forth that sentient beings have experienced in the past and are currently undergoing cannot be eliminated;
rather, in order to eliminate the suffering of old age and death in future lives, one must sever the continuity [of existence] so that it does not arise again.
It is like a skilled physician: a disease from the past cannot be cured, nor can a present disease be cured;
taking medicine can only treat the disease that is currently arising, neutralizing its cold or heat so that it does not arise again.

Furthermore, it is like a house on fire: one does not strive to extinguish the fire for the sake of what has already passed, nor does one strive to extinguish it for the sake of the fire currently present; rather, one strives to extinguish it solely so that the future fire shall not burn again.
A skilled physician or one who extinguishes a fire exerts diligent skillful means that are not in vain.
It is the same for a bodhisattva in extinguishing the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings:
past suffering has already been extinguished and can no longer be acted upon.
The suffering and affliction of the present cannot be averted because it is accomplished by causes and conditions from previous lives;
however, by destroying the causes and conditions for old age, death, and other sufferings in future lives,
these phenomena of birth are destroyed, and old age, death, and other sufferings naturally and eternally cease.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to extinguish the causes and conditions for the arising of old age, death, and other sufferings in future lives, attains the eight present causes and conditions,
the first of which is called "outflowing karma" (*sāsrava-karma*).
The second refers to the afflictions of the present life, namely the four graspings and craving.
These two types of afflictions arise from two mental factors: sensation and contact.
Contact (*sparśa*) is able to give rise to all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); because it arises prior to sensation (*vedanā*), contact is designated as the causal condition for sensation.
Although sensation can give rise to the three poisons, among all sentient beings, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the fundamental affliction.
The condition for contact consists of the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*), as previously explained.
Although the six external bases exist, if the six internal bases are absent, mental factors such as contact do not arise; therefore, the six internal bases receive their name.
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the causal condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), as explained herein.
At the initial moment of entering the womb, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the causal condition for name-and-form.

While consciousness and name-and-form exist within the womb, although the six sense bases are present therein, they have not yet been fully formed and are not yet functional; therefore, they do not yet receive their designation.
Once born as an infant, one is unable to perform any actions; there is only the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
As one grows larger, the six contacts (*ṣaṭsparśa*) arise.
It is like a small child treading on fire or walking on ice: there is only contact, but they do not yet know suffering or pleasure.
They undergo great suffering and pleasure in turn, yet they have not yet developed deep attachment.
Just as a small child, though capable of anger, is unable to initiate evil karmas such as killing;
and though capable of joy, is unable to initiate wholesome karmas such as giving.
Upon reaching adulthood, one gives rise to aversion when encountering suffering and attachment when encountering pleasure.
Because of the pursuit of the means to obtain pleasure, one grasps at the four types of clinging, such as sensual desire.
At the time of grasping, one is able to initiate wholesome and unwholesome karma.
If one knows the causes and conditions of ignorance and karma from a previous lifetime, then one can know them for hundreds of millions of lifetimes;
it is just as when fire is hot in the present, so too was it in the past and will it be in the future.

If one seeks further for the root of ignorance as its causal condition, it becomes infinite; this constitutes falling into an extreme view and losing the path to Nirvana. Therefore, one should not seek it.
To seek further would be to fall into frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), which is not the Buddha-dharma.
Because the Bodhisattva wishes to sever ignorance, he seeks the essential nature and characteristics of ignorance;
at the moment of seeking, he enters ultimate emptiness. Why is this?
The Buddhist sutras state:
"The characteristic of ignorance is not knowing internal phenomena, not knowing external phenomena, and not knowing both internal and external phenomena."
The Bodhisattva contemplates internal phenomena through internal emptiness, and internal phenomena are themselves empty;
he contemplates external phenomena through external emptiness, and external phenomena are themselves empty;
he contemplates both internal and external phenomena through internal-and-external emptiness, and both internal and external phenomena are themselves empty.
All such things as these are the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*), as explained in detail in the previous chapter of the *Śrīmatī-sūtra* under the section "Destroying Ignorance.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva seeks the essence of ignorance, it is at that very moment illumination (*vidyā*); this so-called true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is termed the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

One contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations; yet due to the causes and conditions of sentient beings' inversions, they give rise to various afflictions, commit evil and sinful deeds, transmigrate through the five destinies, and undergo the suffering of birth and death.
For example, it is like a silkworm that produces silk to entangle and bind itself, only to enter boiling water and be scorched by fire.
Ordinary sentient beings are just like this: at the time of their initial birth, they possess no afflictions; yet later, they themselves give rise to various afflictions such as greed and hatred.
Due to these afflictions as causes and conditions, true wisdom is obscured, and when they undergo rebirth, they suffer being burned and boiled in the fires and cauldrons of hell.
The Bodhisattva knows that these dharmas are empty from beginning to end; it is only because sentient beings are deluded and mistaken that they undergo such suffering.

The Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings, and desiring to shatter this delusion, seeks the true Dharma, practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, and penetrates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Through various causes and conditions, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to abide in the limit of reality.
Therefore, abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is without fault.
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras:
"If sentient beings were different from the limit of reality, the bodhisattva should not practice the *prajñāpāramitā*."
As for their difference: the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is ultimate emptiness, whereas the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) is definitively existent.
If this were so, one should raise the following objection:
"If the characteristic of the limit of reality of all phenomena is empty, how can a bodhisattva cultivate this limit of reality for the sake of sentient beings?"

If sentient beings were ultimately empty while the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) were definitively existent, then in the absence of sentient beings there would be nothing to benefit; for whose sake, then, would one practice the limit of reality?
Now, since the realm of sentient beings is in truth not different from the limit of reality, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One practices the perfection of wisdom in order to awaken ordinary beings who are deluded, confused, and inverted;
one causes sentient beings to abide within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without destroying that limit of reality.
At that time, Subhūti asked again:
"If the limit of sentient beings (*sattvakoṭi*) and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) are not different, how can one be attached to the reality-limit by means of the reality-limit?
A self-nature should not abide within a self-nature, just as a fingertip cannot touch itself."

The Buddha approved of his intention: "By means of skillful means, the bodhisattva establishes sentient beings in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Just as sentient beings and the limit of reality are not different, even 'one' cannot be apprehended."
If they were one, then the characteristic of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) would be destroyed. Why is this?
Because it would result in the attainment of a single nature.
The Bodhisattva knows that these two dharmas are neither one nor two, yet neither not-one nor not-two; they are ultimately quiescent, devoid of the characteristics of conceptual proliferation.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of great compassion and teaches and transforms sentient beings solely because he wishes to pull them out from their inverted views.
He was asked again:
"What is meant by 'expedient means' (upāya)?"
The Buddha said:

“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful power, he establishes sentient beings in generosity (dāna), explaining that this generosity is empty of a prior limit, a posterior limit, and likewise of a middle limit.”
As explained at length in the sutra,
the bodhisattva who realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) reaches the very limits of sentient beings,
as previously stated in the "Chapter on Generosity" (Dānaparivarta).
Having heard this, sentient beings resolve their minds, weaken their afflictions, and become deeply attached to giving.
The Bodhisattva feels compassion for these beings, thinking:
"I have pulled them out from stinginess, yet now they are again attached to giving."
If sentient beings accept gifts, their merit will be exhausted and they will undergo various sufferings;
furthermore, due to the causes and conditions of wealth and status, they may commit great transgressions and consequently fall into hell.

Therefore, out of compassion for these sentient beings who obtain only a brief moment of happiness while suffering for a long duration, the Bodhisattva explains to them the true nature of giving, which is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), saying:
"This giving has already passed and ceased; it cannot be seen, it cannot be apprehended, and it cannot be used; it can only be recollected, no different from what is seen in a dream.
Because the future has not yet arisen, it likewise does not exist and is ultimately empty."
"Because this giving has no prior limit or posterior limit, it likewise has no middle limit.
As it is said in the refutation of the six sense-objects, specifically within the refutation of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*):
"Although present giving is seen with the eyes, if one breaks it down part by part until even the finest atom (*paramāṇu*) is reached, nothing can be found."
"Generosity is empty of the three periods of time; the giver, the receiver, and the karmic fruit are likewise so.
The Bodhisattva says to the giver:
'The dharmas such as generosity are the initial gateway into the Buddha-dharma.'"
Within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), even the characteristic of the reality-limit does not exist, let alone giving!
You must not think of or be attached to dharmas such as giving.

If one gives without thinking of or being attached to the essential nature or characteristics of giving, then such a giver shall obtain the flavor of the deathless (*amṛta*) and the fruit of the deathless.
"The flavor of ambrosia" refers to the eightfold noble path;
"the fruit of ambrosia" refers to nirvana.
Although the bodhisattva dwells within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), by means of the power of skillful means, he delivers sentient beings through the gateway of giving.
The other pāramitās are also like this, as explained in detail in the sūtra.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If the nature of all dharmas is emptiness, and within the emptiness of nature there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, nor even a sentient being, how can a bodhisattva dwell within this emptiness and seek all-knowledge?
The Buddha replied:
"Because the Bodhisattva is established within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he is able to practice these dharmas such as giving.
He asked again:

"If the emptiness of intrinsic nature exhaustively destroys all phenomena without remainder, how can a bodhisattva, dwelling within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, practice the various wholesome dharmas such as giving?
The Buddha affirmed Subhūti’s intention and explained the causal conditions:
"The bodhisattva knows the true mark of all phenomena; dwelling therein, he is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is precisely their emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

If the nature of all phenomena were not empty, a bodhisattva would not abide in this emptiness of the nature of all phenomena to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having attained it, would not preach the Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the sake of sentient beings—namely, that the nature of form (*rūpa*) is empty, the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) is empty, and so on, up to preaching for sentient beings the Dharma of the emptiness of the nature of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).
Furthermore, "Subhūti!
If the eighteen kinds of emptiness were not empty by nature, this would constitute a destruction of the essence of emptiness. Why is that?"
The eighteen kinds of emptiness can cause all phenomena to be empty; if they themselves were not empty, they would be deceptive.
Furthermore, if they were not empty, one would fall into the extreme of eternalism and become attached, thereby giving rise to afflictions.
Its nature is empty and lacks any real place of abiding; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. This is called the characteristic of the eternally abiding dharma.
The characteristic of the eternally abiding dharma is another name for the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and it is also called the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Within these marks there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither increase nor decrease, neither defilement nor purity.

When a bodhisattva dwells within this, they see that the nature of all phenomena is empty, and thus they do not regress, do not doubt, and do not regret their progress toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive any phenomena that can act as obstacles; yet, by means of the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), they deliver sentient beings.
As for the power of skillful means: ultimately there are no phenomena and no sentient beings, and yet they deliver sentient beings.
Question:
If sentient beings and phenomena have been non-existent from the very beginning, for whom is skillful means (upāya) created,
and whom does it deliver?
The answer is:
Since the emptiness of intrinsic nature is called "emptiness" and that very emptiness is also non-existent, why do you grasp at the characteristic of this emptiness to raise an objection?
If there were a characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, then one should indeed raise an objection!

Furthermore, one who attains the true mark of all phenomena knows that their nature is empty; such a person knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty—there are no phenomena and no sentient beings.
Because ordinary beings have not yet attained the true mark of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), they engage in various recollections,
conceptions, and discriminations; like a madman who falsely perceives things and takes them to be real,
[the Buddha] speaks thus for the sake of delivering ordinary beings who are like madmen:

"In the dharmas of madness that I teach for the sake of sentient beings, there is this conceptual differentiation of all phenomena; however, within the reality of true dharmas, such differentiation does not exist.
Because the Bodhisattva wishes to fulfill his original vow and yet remains unattached to the emptiness of intrinsic nature, he brings sentient beings across to liberation.
In this regard, one should not raise such an objection.
Furthermore, in this sutra, the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions:

"In the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), sentient beings cannot be apprehended; the knower and the seer cannot be apprehended either, and so it is even for the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*)."
The Bodhisattva establishes these dharmas and teaches them to sentient beings; because they are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are not real.
Regarding this, the Buddha speaks a parable:

"Suppose a Buddha were to create an emanation person (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*), and that emanation were further to create the fourfold assembly and preach the Dharma to them—could any among them attain the Way?"
Subhūti said: "No, it is not so. Why is that? Because..."
Since there is no fixed, fundamental reality, how could there be anyone who attains the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the attainment of Buddhahood?
The Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is also like this:
sentient beings have no fixed reality; he merely wishes to pull sentient beings out from within their delusions and establish them in the state beyond delusion.
The non-perverted dharma has no location; within it there are no sentient beings, nor even any knower or seer.
Although emptiness is of a single characteristic, perverted views are many while non-perverted views are few;
therefore, one values this non-perverted dharma of the emptiness of nature.
When a bodhisattva abides therein, they only destroy the false conceptualizations of sentient beings, not the sentient beings themselves.

Furthermore, although the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), up to and including the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), are untainted, because they are subject to arising and ceasing, they do not equal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
“Subhūti! This is the emptiness of intrinsic nature; for all Buddhas, there is only this path, and no other path. Why is this so?”

All Buddhas seek true wisdom, which is an indestructible and non-differentiated dharma; although they possess various distinct dharmas such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, these are not called the "One Way."
Why is this so? Because all these are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), subject to transformation and impermanence.
Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), there are no sentient beings, nor are there any phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest.
A bodhisattva does not seek anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of the bodhisattva path, but solely for the sake of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā).
Question: What is this emptiness of intrinsic nature?
What is the bodhisattva path?
The answer is:
in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no conceptual differentiation; in the conventional sense (saṃvṛti), there is conceptual differentiation.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); other practices, from generosity up to the eighty minor marks of excellence, constitute the bodhisattva path.
Although one practices these dharmas, it is not for the sake of these dharmas, but for the sake of seeking emptiness of nature. Therefore, it is said:
"One does not practice for the sake of the bodhisattva path."
"This nature is empty; it was empty of its very nature in the past, and it is empty of its nature in the middle and at the end.
It has been eternally empty from the very beginning, and there is no agent who makes it so.
It is not made empty by the power of merit, nor is it made empty by the power of wisdom; it is simply that its nature is thus."

By means of the power of great merit, wisdom, and skillful means, the Buddhas and holy sages shatter the inversions within the minds of sentient beings, causing them to realize that their nature is empty.
It is like space, whose nature is eternally pure and unattached to defilement or darkness;
yet when at times it is obscured by wind, clouds, and gloom, people of the world say:
"The sky is impure.
Then, when a fierce wind blows away the clouds and mist, one says:
"The sky is pure."
Yet, space is in reality neither defiled nor pure.

The Buddhas are likewise: by means of the fierce wind of preaching the Dharma, they blow away the clouds and veils of perversion to bring about purity, yet the nature of all phenomena is eternally and inherently neither defiled nor pure.
Because this bodhisattva knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty, they are able to practice all various paths to deliver sentient beings;
they fulfill all paths to purify buddha-fields and transform sentient beings;
and when they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their lifespan is according to their will.

Regarding those who control their own lifespan: Bodhisattvas who have attained the dharma of the forbearance of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) enter the illusory path of a bodhisattva; they are able to simultaneously manifest transformations into thousands of billions of bodies, pervading the ten directions and fully practicing all bodhisattva paths.
In every land, they assume forms according to the length of the lifespans of sentient beings.
Just as Śākyamuni Buddha has a lifespan of one hundred years in this land, his lifespan in the Land of Adornment is seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Among the five inconceivable things, the Dharma of the Buddha is the foremost inconceivable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The nature of all dharmas is empty; this is the true dharma of all Buddhas!
If one attains this dharma, one is called a Buddha."
If one speaks of this Dharma, it is called "delivering sentient beings.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time do likewise.
Apart from this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is neither the Path nor the fruit.
The Path consists of the eight factors of the noble path;
the fruits consist of the seven kinds of fruits. Why is this so?

If there were fixed dharmas existing apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one would grasp at their characteristics and become attached; because of this attachment, there would be no freedom from desire, and because there is no freedom from desire, there would be no fruit of the Path.

If one is apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, then although one practices giving and maintains the precepts, or practices loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, by the power of these wholesome dharmas, one may indeed avoid falling into the evil realms; yet, once the fruit of rebirth in heaven is exhausted, one falls back into the evil realms, no different than before.
To practice the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, yet not to be attached even to that emptiness of intrinsic nature, is itself nirvāṇa.
To practice other dharmas while giving rise to a mind of attachment leads to regression and loss;
if one practices this dharma, there will be no regression or loss.
Subhūti, filled with joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How truly rare!
A bodhisattva practices this dharma of the emptiness of nature, yet does not destroy the characteristic of the emptiness of nature.”
The Buddha replied:
"If dharmas such as form were different from the emptiness of their own nature, the bodhisattva would not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?..."
If there were a phenomenon of emptiness, it could not be separated [from things]. Subhūti!
Now, the true nature of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, is empty.
Once the Bodhisattva has realized these dharmas, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this? Because within this [reality], there is not a single dharma that is definitively permanent;

it is only because ordinary beings give rise to the notion of "self" that they become attached to internal and external dharmas, failing to escape birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices this emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), unifying the six *pāramitās*, without destroying the characteristics of all dharmas such as form—namely, whether they are empty, or not empty, or both empty and not empty, or neither empty nor not empty.
Not manifesting the characteristics of phenomena in such a manner is called "non-disintegration.
Why is this? The true characteristic of form is its very emptiness of intrinsic nature; how could that which is empty of intrinsic nature ever disintegrate its own emptiness of intrinsic nature?
"Even up to bodhi, it is likewise.
In this regard, the Buddha spoke a parable:
"Just as internal space does not destroy external space, because they are of the same essence."
Subhūti asked:
“World-Honored One!
If the nature of all dharmas is empty and without distinction, in what place does a bodhisattva attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha affirmed his meaning, saying: "It is so!
If one discriminates between two characteristics, then one cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is called true wisdom; it does not function within the realm of form, meaning that it neither clings to nor is defiled by it.
Why is this? Because this wisdom does not function for the sake of grasping form; therefore, it does not function within form.
Subhūti asked again:
"If awakening neither proceeds by way of grasping nor proceeds by way of relinquishing, in what place should it proceed?
Grasping is termed "substantial phenomena," and relinquishing is termed "empty phenomena."
To grasp at names is called "clinging to practice"; to relinquish names is called "non-clinging practice.
To grasp at duality is called "dualistic practice"; to relinquish names is called "non-dual practice.
Such are the distinctions.
The Buddha asked Subhūti in return:
"What do you think?
Where does a person created by a Buddha go?"
Subhūti said: "This emanated person acts nowhere, because an emanated person has no mind and no mental factors;
awakening is also like this."
He asked again:
"What do you think?
Where does the awakening of an arhat move within a dream?"
Subhūti said: “Even an Arhat does not sleep, much less could there be any sphere of activity for awakening within a dream! He asked:
There are three kinds of bodhi:
the bodhi of an arhat, the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha, and the bodhi of a buddha.
The bodhi of an arhat does not function within a mind that is subject to outflows (sāsrava) or within a neutral (avyākṛta) mind; rather, it functions only within a mind free from outflows (anāsrava).
Why does the Buddha ask, "In what place does the bodhi of an arhat move within a dream?
The answer is:

An arhat is a noble one who has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and thus has no dreams; the Buddha asks because such a place necessarily does not exist, intending to clarify that there is necessarily no movement of dharmas.
Question:
Even the Buddha still experiences sleep; how is this known?
The Buddha once commanded Ānanda:
"Spread out your four-fold folded *uttarāsaṅga* robe; I wish to sleep for a short while, and you shall preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus.
Furthermore, the Nirgrantha Saccaka asked the Buddha:
"Does the Buddha himself ever fall asleep during the day?"
The Buddha said, “At the end of spring and the beginning of summer, one sleeps briefly because of the heat; this is to remove the affliction caused by food.
Saccaka the Nirgrantha addressed the Buddha:
Others have said: "Sleeping during the day is a sign of delusion.
The Buddha said:
"Set that aside!
You do not distinguish the characteristic of delusion (*moha*).

That which causes the various outflows (*āsrava*) to give rise to the continuity of future existence without interruption is called the characteristic of delusion; even though one is constantly awake, this too is delusion."
"If these outflows (āsrava) are forever extinguished without remainder, one is not called 'deluded' even while asleep.
Such passages are found throughout the sūtras.
Why, then, does Subhūti say that "even an arhat does not sleep"?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of sleep:
first, sleeping and dreaming; second, sleeping without dreaming.

An Arhat does not sleep for the sake of seeking security or attachment to pleasure; rather, as one who possesses a body composed of the four great elements, he must naturally experience eating, breathing, sleeping, and waking. Therefore, resting for a short duration is called "sleeping," but it is not a sleep characterized by dreaming.
Therefore, Subhūti said:
"Even an Arhat does not sleep. Some say:

"One who has abandoned desire attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) enter into their body, and because their body and mind experience joy and bliss, they have no sleep.
An Arhat liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), however, does not have the four great elements of the realm of form enter into their body; therefore, such a person experiences sleep."
Therefore, Subhūti said:
“Even an arhat does not sleep.
Thus, there are arhats who sleep and those who do not sleep.
The Buddha, through the power of skillful means, manifests sleep in order to deliver sentient beings and to conform to human ways.
Subhūti asked again:
"If he does not practice, how can a bodhisattva proceed from the first stage to the tenth stage, and even attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
The Buddha affirmed his meaning:
"Although awakening has no place where it proceeds, if one has not yet fulfilled the various dharmas of the six pāramitās, one will ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This bodhisattva dwells within the marks of form, and so on, up to dwelling within the mark of awakening; thus they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They do not abandon dharmas such as form, nor do they cling to the mark of awakening; they know that dharmas such as form are themselves awakening, eternally quiescent, with no dharma that increases or decreases, is defiled or pure, attains the path, or attains the fruit.

"It is only according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) that we say a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no form, nor anything up to and including bodhi."
Wishing to clarify this matter, the Buddha asked Subhūti in return:
"What do you think?
When you severed the afflictions and attained the Way, was there anything obtained?"
“Are these so-called five aggregates— which are like a dream— and whether it be the path or the fruit of the path, determined to be a single dharma?
Subhūti replied,
“They cannot be so found.”
Why is this? Subhūti’s thought was:
"If one enters the Way by abiding within the gate of signlessness (animitta), how could one grasp at signs?"
The Buddha said,
"If you do not perceive even the slightest subtle dharma, how can you say that you are an arhat?
Subhūti replied:
"Because of the phenomena of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), one speaks of 'Arhat';
within the inverted phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is gain and loss, and there are sentient beings and dharmas."
The Buddha said:
"Awakening is also like this. Because it is a phenomenon of worldly convention (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of a bodhisattva, one speaks of form and so forth, even up to awakening;
yet within awakening, there is no fixed dharma, nor is there a sentient being, nor is there awakening."
The Bodhisattva contemplates these dharmas of awakening as being neither increasing nor decreasing.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all dharmas.

The Bodhisattva likewise does not apprehend the nature of these dharmas; how much less could there be anything to be apprehended regarding the initial generation of the mind up to the ten stages, the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, or even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha!
This is impossible! Why is that?

Since the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is the root of all phenomena, cannot even be apprehended, how much less could the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and such—which are conditioned phenomena—possess any fixed reality!
"It is so! When a Bodhisattva practices these natures of all dharmas and attains Buddhahood, he is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
— *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle 90.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the "Chapter on Illumination," Fascicle Eighty-one (Ninety-first),
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 81: Illumination. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, yet does not fulfill the bodhisattva path, they will be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the bodhisattva path so as to be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of giving by means of skillful means—neither apprehending the gift, nor apprehending the giver, nor apprehending the recipient, yet not being separated from these dharmas while practicing the perfection of giving—this is what illuminates the bodhisattva path."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva fulfills the bodhisattva path;
having fulfilled it, they are able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"It is the same for morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and even the eighteen unique qualities.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means, they do not destroy form, nor do they follow after form."
Why is this? Because the nature of form does not exist, it is neither destroyed nor followed; this applies likewise up to consciousness. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by means of the power of skillful means, they do not destroy nor do they follow the dānapāramitā. Why is this?
"Because the nature of the perfection of giving does not exist,
and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, it is likewise.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas have no intrinsic nature that can be destroyed or followed, how is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice the perfection of wisdom, which is the place where bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train?”
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not study the prajñāpāramitā cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "As you have said:
'If a bodhisattva does not study the prajñāpāramitā, they cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"It can be attained because one does not depart from the power of skillful means. Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom were to find even a single dharma that could be apprehended, they should grasp it."
If they cannot be apprehended, what is there to be grasped?

That is to say: "This is the perfection of wisdom," "this is the perfection of meditation," "this is the perfection of vigor," "this is the perfection of patience," "this is the perfection of ethical discipline," "this is the perfection of generosity," "this is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and so on, up to "this is unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Śāriputra! This Prajñāpāramitā is without a mark that can be grasped; even all the dharmas of the Buddhas are without marks that can be grasped. Śāriputra!
This is called not grasping at the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the Buddha-dharmas; this is what a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, even the characteristic of training cannot be apprehended, let alone the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha-dharmas, the bodhisattva-dharmas, the pratyekabuddha-dharmas, the śrāvaka-dharmas, or the dharmas of ordinary persons!
Why is this? Śāriputra, among all phenomena,
there is not a single phenomenon that possesses an intrinsic nature.
Since all phenomena are thus devoid of intrinsic nature, what are ordinary persons, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas?
If these noble and holy ones did not exist, how could there be dharmas?
It is because of these dharmas that one distinguishes and speaks of ordinary persons, srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have no nature, no reality, no root, and no basis, how can one know who is an ordinary person and so forth, up to who is a Buddha?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Regarding the form (rūpa) in which ordinary persons are attached, does it have an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or is it real?
“No, [it does not],” [he replied].
World-Honored One!
It is solely because of the perverted mind.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are also like this.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by the power of skillful means, because they see that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and lack a fundamental basis, they are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by means of the power of skillful means, seeing that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature and without a fundamental basis, he gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any fundamental basis of phenomena within which they might dwell and then fall back or give rise to a mind of indolence."

Śāriputra! The root of all dharmas is truly without self, without anything possessed, and its nature is eternally empty; it is only because of inversion and delusion that sentient beings cling to the aggregates, the bases, and the elements.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives that all dharmas are non-existent, their nature eternally empty, and their self-nature empty, they practice the prajñāpāramitā and establish themselves like a master illusionist to preach the Dharma for sentient beings:

for those who are stingy, they preach the Dharma of giving; for those who break the precepts, they preach the Dharma of upholding the precepts; for those who are angry, they preach the Dharma of patience; for those who are indolent, they preach the Dharma of diligence; for those with distracted thoughts, they preach the Dharma of meditative concentration; and for those who are ignorant, they preach the Dharma of wisdom.
He causes sentient beings to abide in generosity up to wisdom, and thereafter preaches for them the noble Dharma that can bring about escape from suffering;
by means of this Dharma, they attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the path of a pratyekabuddha, and even attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes that these sentient beings do not exist, he instructs them in giving, precept-keeping, and so forth up to wisdom; only then does he preach the noble Dharma capable of bringing them out of suffering.”
"By means of these dharmas, one attains the fruit of srotāpanna up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is no fault of 'attainment'."

Why is this? Śāriputra, when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend a sentient being; it is only because of the continuity of empty phenomena that they are called "sentient beings."
Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell within the two truths and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings:
the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.

Śāriputra! Although sentient beings cannot be apprehended within the two truths, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings by means of skillful power.
When sentient beings hear this Dharma, even the "self" of the present life cannot be found; how much less could they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or the dharmas used to attain it!
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of skillful power.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is vast and expansive!”
There is no dharma that can be apprehended—whether as a single characteristic, a different characteristic, or a distinct characteristic—that is able to be thus adorned with such a great vow.

Because of this adornment, one is not born in the desire realm, not born in the form realm, and not born in the formless realm; one does not perceive the nature of the conditioned, nor does one perceive the nature of the unconditioned, yet one delivers sentient beings from within the three realms, while also not apprehending any sentient beings.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are neither bound nor liberated;
because sentient beings are neither bound nor liberated, they are neither defiled nor pure.
Because there is neither defilement nor purity, there is no differentiation of the five destinies;
because there is no differentiation of the five destinies, there is neither karma nor afflictions;
because there is neither karma nor afflictions, there should likewise be no retribution, for it is by means of such retribution that one is born within the triple world.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
If sentient beings existed previously and later ceased to exist, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault.
It is the same for all phenomena and the cycle of birth and death within the five realms; if these existed previously and later ceased to exist, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault.

Śāriputra! Whether there is a Buddha in the world now or not, the characteristics of all dharmas remain eternally constant and unchanging. Within these dharma-characteristics, there is no self, no sentient being, and no life-span; even up to there being no knower and no seer—how much less could there be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
If these dharmas did not exist, how could there be the coming and going of the five destinies, or the place from which sentient beings are pulled out? Śāriputra!
The nature of all these dharmas is eternally empty; for this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard this mark of dharmas from past buddhas, resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Within this, there is no dharma that I shall attain, nor is there any dharma to which sentient beings are fixedly attached such that they could not emerge from it; it is only because of the perversions of sentient beings that they are attached.
For this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes the adornment of the great vow and never retreats from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This bodhisattva does not doubt:
"Shall I not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I will benefit sentient beings with the true Dharma and cause them to emerge from perversion."

Śāriputra! It is like a magician who conjures hundreds of thousands of millions of people by means of illusion, provides them with various kinds of food and drink until they are full, and joyfully proclaims:
"I have attained great merit!"
"I have attained great merit!
What do you think?
Would anyone among them be satiated by eating and drinking?
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Śāriputra!

From the first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path; the fourteen emptinesses, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They fulfill the Bodhisattva path, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify Buddha-fields, yet there is no dharma of a sentient being to be delivered."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
