It is the same here: if one observes various distinct phenomena, many attachments will arise;
however, if one observes all phenomena as having a single characteristic—such as impermanence, suffering, or emptiness—at that time afflictions do not arise.
Because attachment is minimal, this "one" is frequently employed.
Within the ultimate sense, even "one" is not employed;
if one clings to "one," that itself becomes a fault.
Furthermore, because distinctness does not exist, "one" cannot be apprehended either, for things exist only in mutual dependence.
It is only because they do not dwell with attachment and do not grasp at a single characteristic that it is said there is no fault.
Since the one [Buddha] is not real, the Bodhisattva cannot be identical to the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Buddha now further answers Subhūti, personally explaining the causal conditions:

"Although bodhi has the characteristic of quiescence, the bodhisattva is able to fulfill all merits such as the six pāramitās, abide in the vajra-samādhi, and through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, one who possesses mastery over all phenomena is named a Buddha.
Although a bodhisattva knows that the path and enlightenment are not different, because they have not yet fulfilled all merits, they are not called a Buddha.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s various activities are ultimate and his vows and practices are fulfilled, he is not called a bodhisattva.
"Attainment" refers to the Buddha; "Dharma" refers to bodhi; and one who seeks bodhi is a bodhisattva.

Having heard from the Buddha the characteristics of bodhi and the characteristics of the path, and having brought sentient beings to maturity, Subhūti now asks about the matter of purifying buddha-fields.
Since the arhats and pratyekabuddhas lack the power to know the matter of purifying buddha-fields, he asks about it.
Question: What is the purification of a Buddha-field? Answer:
A buddha-field consists of ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, and ten billion heavens such as those of the Four Great Kings; this is called a trichiliocosm.
An immeasurable and boundless number of such trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems is called one buddha-field.
Within this, the Buddha performs buddha-works; throughout the day and night—three periods by day and three periods by night—he surveys all sentient beings with his buddha-eye:
"Who is capable of planting roots of goodness?"
"Who has perfected their roots of goodness and should have them further increased?
Who has perfected their roots of goodness and should be delivered?
Having seen this, he employs his supernormal powers to teach and transform beings according to what he perceives.
When the minds of sentient beings follow external conditions and obtain what they desire, they do not give rise to anger or vexation;
when they encounter conditions such as impurity and impermanence, they do not give rise to afflictions such as craving;
and if they encounter conditions of non-existence and emptiness, they do not give rise to ignorance or any other afflictions.
Therefore, bodhisattvas adorn buddha-fields in order to make it easy for sentient beings to be delivered.
Because there is no sense of "mine" within those lands, afflictions such as stinginess, greed, and anger do not arise.

There are buddha-lands where all trees constantly produce the sounds of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—namely, "neither arising nor ceasing," "neither originating nor conditioned," and so forth;
sentient beings hear only these sublime sounds and no other sounds, and because their faculties are sharp, they immediately attain the true reality of all phenomena.
Such adornments of buddha-fields as these are called "pure buddha-fields," as described in various sutras such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*.
The Buddha replied:

"From the time a bodhisattva first resolves on enlightenment, they personally purify their coarse actions of body, speech, and mind, and also teach others to purify their coarse actions of body, speech, and mind."

Question: If a bodhisattva purifies a buddha-field, it is only after that bodhisattva has attained the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and dwells in the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā) that they are able to purify a buddha-field;
why, then, is it said here that "from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, one purifies coarse actions of body, speech, and mind"?
Answer: The purification of the three karmas is not merely for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field; rather, all paths of the bodhisattvas are purified by it.
First, these three karmas purify the actions of body, speech, and mind, and subsequently they serve to purify the Buddha-field.
One purifies oneself and also purifies others. Why is this?
It is not merely a single person; all those born within the land together create the causes and conditions.
Internal dharmas act as causes and conditions for external dharmas, whether they be wholesome or unwholesome:
because of much karma of harsh speech, thorns grow from the earth;
because of a crooked mind of flattery and deception, the ground becomes uneven with highs and lows.
Because stinginess and greed abound, floods and droughts become irregular and the earth produces sand and gravel.
Because one does not commit the aforementioned evils, the earth becomes level and upright, and precious treasures abound;
just as when Maitreya Buddha appears, all people practice the ten wholesome deeds, and thus the earth abounds in precious treasures.
Question:
If various wholesome dharmas such as giving result in the retribution of a pure Buddha-field, why is it said that one purifies only the three karmas? Answer:

Although one knows that all dharmas of good and evil are the causes and conditions for suffering and pleasure, among all mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma), wisdom is supreme at the time of attaining the Path;
concentration is supreme within the collected mind;
and volition is supreme at the time of performing an action.
Having attained this mental karma (*cetanā-karma*), one gives rise to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
In acts such as giving (*dāna*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), volition is primary;
it is like using a needle as the guide when sewing a garment.
When receiving the retributive fruits of future lives, the power of karma is paramount.
For this reason, it is said that the three types of karma encompass all wholesome dharmas:
within mental karma, all mind and mental factors are fully included; through bodily and verbal karma, all material dharmas are included.
When human beings practice the three kinds of conduct and are fully endowed with merit, the land becomes pure.
Because internal phenomena are pure, external phenomena are also pure;
it is like how when the face is clean, the reflection in the mirror is also clean.
As it is said in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*:
"Because they do not kill living beings, all people are long-lived," and so forth.
Question:
Coarse actions of body, speech, and mind are easy to understand; why, then, does Subhūti ask?
The answer is:
because coarse and subtle are not fixed.
For example, among those seeking the Way, giving is a coarse goodness, whereas for laypeople it is subtle.
Likewise, within the Hīnayāna, unwholesome karma is coarse while wholesome karma is subtle;
yet within the Mahāyāna, grasping at the characteristics of wholesome dharmas—even up to Nirvāṇa—is all termed coarse.
The question was asked because of the uncertainty regarding what is coarse and what is subtle.
The Buddha then explained the characteristics of coarse karma in successive order: namely, taking life, up to and including wrong view.
These three types of bodily karma, four types of verbal karma, and three types of mental karma are all termed "coarse."
Furthermore, the factors that destroy the Bodhisattva’s six *pāramitās*—such as stinginess and greed—are all termed "coarse.
Question:
Since stinginess and greed were already subsumed within the previously mentioned ten unwholesome paths (*daśākuśala-mārga*), why are they stated separately here?
The answer is:
These six dharmas do not enter into the ten unwholesome paths; the ten unwholesome paths are all dharmas that afflict sentient beings, whereas these six dharmas do not merely afflict sentient beings.
Just as with a mind of stinginess, which merely cherishes one's own wealth without troubling sentient beings, there are two kinds of greedy minds:
first, that which merely covets the wealth of others without yet troubling sentient beings; [the second is that which actually troubles them].
Second, when greed increases and one seeks but does not obtain, one then desires to harm; this is called a path of action (*karmapatha*), because it is capable of initiating karma.
It is the same with hatred: that which is slight is not called a path of action, but because it leads toward evil destinations, it is termed a "path."
Therefore, there is no fault in explaining the six dharmas separately. Question:
Since morality has already been discussed among the six pāramitās, why is it now mentioned again under the heading of "impurity of morality"?
Answer: The dharma of breaking the precepts consists of gross offenses such as killing;
the impurity of the precepts consists of subtle offenses that do not afflict sentient beings.
Drinking alcohol and the like do not constitute the ten unwholesome paths of action.
Furthermore, violating the precepts of the five groups of practitioners is called "breaking the precepts.

However, not breaking the precepts one has received while constantly having one's mind shrouded by the three poisons, failing to maintain mindfulness of the precepts, dedicating them toward heavenly rebirth, or observing the precepts with wrong views—such cases as these are called "impurity of the precepts."

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva’s mind distances itself from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, and the three gates of liberation, this is called coarse karma. Why is that?
In this state, the mind contemplates only real dharmas, following toward nirvana and not following the world;
if one departs from dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness, the mind becomes distracted.
For example, a snake’s natural disposition is to be curved; yet if it enters a bamboo tube, it becomes straight, and upon exiting the tube, it returns to its curvature.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva craves the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), this is considered coarse.
For example, when a person hears the Buddha say, "The fruit of srotāpanna does not lead to rebirth in the three evil realms;
it exhausts immeasurable suffering like the water in a pond fifty yojanas wide, leaving behind only one or two drops," they will give rise to a mind of craving.

Because their minds are not firm—having originally sought to become Buddhas for the sake of sentient beings, yet now desiring to realize realization for their own sake alone—they deceive the Buddha and betray sentient beings; therefore, this is called "coarse."
It is like a person who invites guests, intending to provide them with food and drink, but ultimately fails to give anything; this is a lie that wrongs the guests.

It is the same for a bodhisattva: having first resolved to attain Buddhahood and vowed, "I shall deliver all sentient beings," yet craving the stage of *srotāpanna*, they thereby wrong all sentient beings.
As it is with craving for the fruit of *srotāpanna*, so it is likewise for craving even up to the path of a *pratyekabuddha*.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 92;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on Chapter 80, "Purifying the Buddha-field."
Part Two, Scroll Ninety-three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva grasps the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the characteristics of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the characteristics of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; the characteristics of male and female; the characteristics of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the characteristics of wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; and the characteristics of conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas—this is called the coarse activity of a bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all far removed from such characteristics of coarse karma.

They practice giving themselves and also instruct others to give; they provide food to those who need food and clothing to those who need clothing, even bestowing all manner of necessities for life, and they likewise instruct others in various forms of giving.
One shares this merit with all sentient beings and dedicates it toward the purification of Buddha-lands.
The same applies to the observance of precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva may take precious jewels filling the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system and offer them to the Triple Gem, making this vow:
'By means of these roots of goodness, may my own land be composed entirely of the seven treasures.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva delights the Buddhas and their stūpas with celestial music and makes this aspiration:
'By the causal conditions of these roots of goodness, may celestial music be constantly heard within my buddha-field.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva fills the trichiliocosm with celestial incense to make offerings to the Buddhas and their stūpas, making this vow:
'By means of these roots of goodness, may there always be celestial incense within my own buddha-field.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives food of a hundred flavors to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, making this aspiration:
'By means of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field obtain food of a hundred flavors!'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives celestial fragrances and fine, smooth textures to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
making this aspiration: 'By reason of these roots of goodness, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field experience celestial fragrances and fine, smooth textures!'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives the five objects of desire according to their wishes to the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and all sentient beings, making this aspiration:
'By means of these roots of goodness, may the disciples and all sentient beings within my buddha-field obtain the five objects of desire according to their wishes!'"
This bodhisattva dedicates the five objects of desire according to their wishes, together with all sentient beings, toward the purification of a Buddha-land, making this vow:
"When I attain Buddhahood, may the five celestial desires appear in that land at will, arriving exactly as the mind intends!"
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he makes this vow:

'I shall personally enter the first dhyāna, and I shall also teach all sentient beings to enter the first dhyāna, as well as the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity; and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment shall be treated in the same way.'"

When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall cause all sentient beings not to be separated from the four dhyānas, and even not to be separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to purify a buddha-field.
For as long as that bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, they fulfill these various vows."
This bodhisattva personally accomplishes all wholesome dharmas and also causes all sentient beings to accomplish wholesome dharmas;
this bodhisattva receives an upright and handsome body, and the sentient beings whom they transform also attain such uprightness and handsomeness.
Why is this? Because the causes and conditions of their merit are profound. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should purify a buddha-field in this manner:
"In that land, there shall not even be the names of the three evil realms; nor shall there be the names of wrong views, the three poisons, or the two vehicles—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

One’s ears shall not hear the sounds of impermanence, suffering, or emptiness; nor shall there be the names of 'mine' or anything belonging to a self, up to and including the names of all fetters and afflictions; nor shall there be the names for the various [karmic] fruits of discrimination."

When the wind blows through the trees of the seven jewels, sounds issue forth according to those who are to be saved—namely, the sounds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), which are the sounds of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena: "Whether a Buddha appears or not, all phenomena and all characteristics of phenomena are empty; in emptiness there are no signs, and in the absence of signs there is no wishful activity. Such sounds of the Dharma issue forth, so that whether by day or night, whether sitting, lying down, standing, or walking, they constantly hear this teaching.
When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, the Buddhas throughout the lands of the ten directions will praise him;
and when sentient beings hear this Buddha’s name, they will surely reach unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.

When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment and preaches the Dharma, there shall be no sentient beings who, upon hearing it, do not believe and instead give rise to doubt, saying:
"Is this the Dharma?"
"Is this not the Dharma?
Why is this? Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything is the Dharma; there is nothing that is not the Dharma.

Those individuals of meager merit who have not planted roots of goodness toward the Buddhas and their disciples, who do not follow virtuous friends, and who are submerged in the view of a self, even unto being submerged in all manner of various views, fall into extreme views—either of annihilationism or eternalism.

Because such people hold wrong views, they call what is not the Buddha "the Buddha" and call the Buddha "not the Buddha"; they call what is not the Dharma "the Dharma" and call the Dharma "not the Dharma.
Because such people destroy the Dharma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the evil realms and the hells.

When the Buddhas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they behold these sentient beings wandering through the five destinies; they cause them to leave the assembly of the heterodox and establish them within the assembly of those fixed in the right path, so that they shall never again fall into the evil realms.
"In this way, Subhūti,
within the buddha-field purified by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, sentient beings have no defiled or impure minds—
whether regarding worldly dharmas or supramundane dharmas, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether conditioned or unconditioned."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, all sentient beings within that buddha-field shall ultimately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This, Subhūti,
is the purification of the buddha-field by a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
[Treatise] Commentary: Furthermore, there is coarse karma:

grasping at signs within the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas and giving rise to a mind of attachment. This refers to grasping at the sign of form, the signs of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the signs of the eye up to the sign of the mind; the signs of visible objects up to the signs of mental phenomena (*dharma*); the signs of male and female; the three realms; the wholesome and unwholesome; and the signs of the conditioned and the unconditioned, and so forth.
Question:

While it may be true that the marks of male and female are illusory and unreal, if one does not grasp at the marks of other things such as form, or of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, how can one cultivate revulsion toward form and the like, and accomplish wholesome dharmas?
Answer: Within the Buddha-dharma there are two kinds of emptiness:
first, the emptiness of sentient beings; second, the emptiness of phenomena.
One uses the emptiness of sentient beings to破除 (shatter) the marks of sentient beings, namely the marks of male, female, and so forth;
one uses the emptiness of phenomena to破除 (shatter) the false marks within phenomena such as form, as explained in the section "The Emptiness that Shatters All Phenomena."

When one can contemplate that dharmas such as form and wholesome qualities are like illusions and transformations, and does not grasp at them as having a fixed, real nature, one attains a mind of weary detachment; thus, one abandons conceptual proliferations such as permanence and impermanence—this is not called "grasping at signs."
Furthermore, because form and other phenomena, as well as wholesome dharmas, all practice the emptiness of the nature of conditioned conjunction, no afflictions arise.
Question:
Since all conditioned dharmas are merely conventional designations of conjunction, they should not be grasped.
Unconditioned dharmas are the true dharmas—namely, suchness, the dharma-nature, and the limit of reality. Why are they not grasped?
The answer is:
because non-grasping of marks is the unconditioned dharma; the absence of marks is called the gate of the unconditioned dharma.
If one grasps at signs, this is conditioned.
All such things are empty, deceptive, grasped as signs, and unreal.
One should remain far removed from coarse actions of body, speech, and mind.

A bodhisattva who wishes to practice the purification of a buddha-field should distance themselves from such coarse actions of body, speech, and mind; they should personally practice the six pāramitās and also teach others to do so.
Through these shared causes and conditions of purity, the buddha-field becomes pure.
The former is a general explanation; the latter is a specific explanation.
Suppose this bodhisattva fills a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gives them as a gift to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, making this vow:
"By means of these causes and conditions of my giving, may my buddha-field be adorned entirely with the seven treasures."
Question: If one were to fill the trichiliocosm with precious jewels, from where would they be obtained?
Furthermore, since the Buddhas and noble sages have few desires and are content with little, who would accept such things?
If ordinary beings were never satisfied, how could they possibly receive the wealth of the three thousandfold world system?
The answer is:

this bodhisattva possesses a body born of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-nirmita-kāya) and dwells within the perfection of fully accomplished supernatural powers (abhijñā-pāramitā). For the sake of making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, he offers treasures equal in value to those of the three thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, these precious objects are produced through the power of supernormal faculties; they are so light and subtle that they cause no obstruction.

It is like the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven in the Third Dhyāna, where sixty people may sit upon the head of a single needle to listen to the Dharma without hindering one another; how much more so for the precious objects produced by Great Bodhisattvas who have deeply entered into supernormal powers!

There may be bodhisattvas who transform their bodies to be like Mount Sumeru and extend them before the Buddhas of the ten directions to serve as lamp wicks, making offerings to the Buddhas or to Buddha stūpas and temples, and making this vow:
"May my land always possess radiance, requiring neither sun, moon, lamps, nor candles."
Some bodhisattvas rained down various flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and necklaces as offerings, and further made this vow:
"May the sentient beings in my buddha-land be as upright as these flowers, their physical forms majestic and pure, free from any ugliness."
Through various causes and conditions such as these excellent forms and colors, there are further bodhisattvas who entertain the Buddha or his stūpas with celestial music.

These bodhisattvas may, at times, produce celestial music through their supernormal powers; they may produce the music of celestial kings or universal monarchs (cakravartin), or provide offerings of celestial music performed by asura deities, nāga kings, and others—vowing that within their own lands, fine sounds shall be heard constantly.
Question:
Since the Buddhas and noble sages are persons who have transcended desire, they have no need for music, song, or dance; why, then, do we offer them worship with musical performances?
Answer:

Although the Buddhas have no attachment in their minds toward any phenomena and have no need whatsoever for worldly things, they appear in the world out of compassion for sentient beings; thus, they accept offerings from those who wish to make them, so that such donors may obtain merit according to their aspirations.

Just as offerings of flowers and incense are not what the Buddha requires—for the Buddha’s body is always possessed of a sublime fragrance that surpasses even that of the devas—he accepts them solely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
This bodhisattva seeks excellent sounds for the sake of purifying the buddha-field—desiring that the sentient beings within that land hear these excellent sounds so that their minds become supple;
because their minds are supple, they are easily transformed.
Therefore, one makes offerings to the Buddhas through the condition of vocal sounds.

There may be bodhisattvas who fill the trichiliocosm with incense as an offering to the Buddhas or their stupas—root incense, stem incense, leaf incense, powdered incense, whether celestial incense, transformed incense, or incense born of the karmic fruition of bodhisattvas—making this vow:
"May my land always possess excellent fragrances, which are not produced by any agent."
There may be a bodhisattva who makes offerings of a hundred flavors to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
Someone might say:
"To be able to offer a hundred kinds of things is what is meant by 'a hundred flavors'."
Some say: there are five hundred varieties of cakes, and their flavors number one hundred; this is called "hundred-flavored. Others say:
One hundred kinds of medicinal herbs and fruits are made into "joy-pills" (ānanda-guḍa);
this is called the "hundred flavors.
Some say that food, drink, soup, and cakes together constitute the hundred flavors.
Some say: Because food and drink are provided in every variety and abundance, they are called "a hundred flavors.
Since humans consume food and drink, there are a hundred flavors; however, the food and drink of the devas possess hundreds of thousands of kinds of flavor.

The food produced as the karmic fruit of a bodhisattva’s merit, as well as the food manifested through the power of their supernormal transformations, possesses immeasurable flavors; it can transform the minds of people, causing them to leave behind desire and attain purity.

Regarding these four kinds of food, because the bodhisattva provides offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha according to causes and conditions, there naturally arise foods of a hundred flavors within that land.
Alternatively, some bodhisattvas offer celestial unguents and perfumes.
In the land of India, it is hot and the body has an odor; therefore, they apply fragrances to their bodies as an offering to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, may the sentient beings of my own land receive celestial, subtle, and smooth sensations.
Question:
From the śrāmaṇera precepts up to the one-day precepts (upavāsa), one does not even anoint the body with incense; why then offer incense to the Buddha and the Saṅgha?
The answer is:
This bodhisattva uses his own precious possessions to make offerings whenever they are needed, whether by smearing them on the ground, on the walls, or at places for walking and sitting.
Furthermore, he offers the five objects of sensory pleasure at will to the Buddhas, the Sangha, and other sentient beings.

With fine chariots, horses, wives and concubines, musicians, banners and canopies, gold and silver, clothing, and precious jewels—things that those who have left the household life do not accept—the Bodhisattva gives them to all sentient beings, making this vow:
"May the sentient beings in my land always obtain the five objects of sensory pleasure according to their wishes."

Question: These five desires have been described by the Buddha as being like fire, like a pit, like a wound, like a prison, like an enemy, and like a thief; they are able to strip away a person’s roots of goodness. Why, then, does the Bodhisattva vow to enable sentient beings to obtain these five desires?

Furthermore, the Buddha taught that his disciples should wear robes made of discarded rags, practice begging for food, and sit beneath forest trees; why then does a bodhisattva seek to provide the five desires for sentient beings?
The answer is:
the five desires among gods and humans are the karmic fruits and rewards of merit.
Whether in this life or in future lives, those who are impoverished and of meager merit, unable to sustain themselves, will commit robbery and theft;
they may be harmed by their masters for the sake of goods, or kill others for the sake of wealth;
or, when interrogated, they will falsely claim not to have done it.
In this way, the successive commission of the ten unwholesome actions is all performed because of poverty.
If a person is fully provided with the five desires, then their wishes are fulfilled according to their intent, and they will not commit the ten unwholesome actions.

When the sentient beings in a Bodhisattva’s land are prosperous, joyful, and self-sufficient, lacking nothing, they are free from all evils; there remain only mild fetters and latent tendencies, such as craving and pride.
If one hears what the Buddha has spoken, or what his disciples have spoken, because the mind is supple, one can easily attain the Way upon hearing the Dharma;
even if one is attached to many things, because of sharp faculties, one immediately attains the Way upon hearing of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth.
For example, when a garment stained with grease and oil is soaked in ash-water and left overnight before being washed with water, the stains are all removed at once.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva does not wish to cause sentient beings to become attached by giving them the five desires; rather, he gives them these only because he wishes for them to renounce them all at once.
As you previously stated:
"The disciples of the Buddha wear patched robes and beg for food.
Due to the causal conditions of past offenses, they are born in an evil age with many defiled attachments; if they obtain fine clothing or delicious food, their attachment becomes deep.
Furthermore, for the sake of seeking fine clothing and food, one might neglect and abandon the practice of the Way.

However, because these Bodhisattvas have purified their Buddha-lands and achieved immeasurable merit, they regard the five desires as equal; thus, they no longer value or cling to them, nor do they seek them further. Therefore, there is nothing that can hinder them.
Furthermore, if a practitioner abandons the five desires to practice asceticism, then hatred increases;
moreover, if they dwell upon the five desires, afflictions arise, at which time there is no direction toward which one can turn.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Abandoning both suffering and pleasure, one employs wisdom and abides in the Middle Way.
For this reason, there is no hindrance to purifying the Buddha-land while bestowing the five desires.
Question: If that is so, why does a certain bhikṣu say in the Vinaya:
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; it does not hinder the Path to enjoy the five desires"?
"That bhikṣu should be rebuked; if he does not desist even after being admonished up to three times, he shall be expelled.
He replied:
"The Buddha-dharma has two kinds:"
The Lesser Vehicle and the Greater Vehicle.
Within the Lesser Vehicle, those of meager merit have an excess of the three poisons.
As the Buddha said in the *Vatsa Sūtra*:

"My lay disciples are not merely one or two, but even as many as five hundred, who have anointed their bodies with red sandalwood and received fine incense and flowers; though they sleep together with their wives and children and employ servants and slaves, they have severed the three fetters and attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
having exhausted the three fetters and attenuated the three poisons, they have attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin."
When the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa heard this matter, he immediately said:
"Even while enjoying the five desires, it does not obstruct the Path!
He did not know for whom the Buddha had spoken these words.
The Buddha spoke this for the sake of laypeople; however, this bhikṣu applies it within the context of the monastic dharma.
Those such as the srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin do not say:
"For as long as life lasts, I shall not commit sexual misconduct!"
Because the remaining three poisons still exist within them, they occasionally forget the Path and give rise to lustful thoughts.
When a renunciant is among the Sangha, they must personally vow:
"For as long as I live, I shall not commit sexual misconduct!"
The Buddha said:
"If one who has left the household life commits sexual desire, he shall be expelled.
This bhikṣu made a vow and yet committed the offense; this constitutes one transgression.
To knowingly violate that which has been prescribed by the Buddha constitutes two offenses.
Because this bhikṣu saw that laypeople could attain the Way, he identified himself with them; for this reason, he falls into an offense.
There are two kinds of sentient beings who purify Buddha-fields:
those who have left the household life and those who remain at home.
As for those at home, although they experience the five desires, they commit no offense and encounter no hindrance.
Just as the devas of Tuṣita and the people of Uttarakuru, though they enjoy the five desires, do not give rise to grave offenses;
so too, for those who have left the household life, there is no fault in enjoying the five desires permitted by the Buddha for the sake of renunciation.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, this was spoken for the sake of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa;
it is because those of meager merit and heavy transgressions have much remorse in their hearts.

As for those who purify Buddha-lands, they habitually practice the six pāramitās and the three gates of liberation throughout successive lifetimes; thus, although they may encounter the five desires, they remain unstained by them.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he forms this thought:
'I shall personally enter the first dhyāna, and I shall also teach and transform sentient beings so that they enter the first dhyāna;
[the same applies to] the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and even up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.'"
This bodhisattva makes this vow:
"When I become a Buddha, I shall fully practice the four dhyānas up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Because of such merit, although sentient beings experience the five desires, they cannot cause any hindrance.
This bodhisattva makes immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya vows; for as long as he practices the path, he brings these vows to complete fulfillment.
This bodhisattva achieves all wholesome dharmas, as well as the beings whom he has brought to maturity.
Because all wholesome dharmas are accomplished, one attains a handsome body that those who see it never tire of;
furthermore, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment, enabling them to attain such physical excellence. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva should purify the buddha-field in this manner.
Furthermore, as for purifying the buddha-field, it should be such that even the names of the three evil states do not exist, let alone the actual existence of the three evil paths!
Question:
The Buddhas appear in the world out of great compassion for the sake of suffering sentient beings;
if there were no three evil realms, whom would they have pity for?
Answer:

The Buddha appears in the world for the sake of delivering sentient beings; however, those in the three evil realms cannot be delivered [in the ultimate sense], but can only be caused to plant roots of goodness. For this reason, the Buddha is called the "Teacher of Gods and Humans."
If there were no devas or humans, but only the three evil realms, then it would be appropriate to raise an objection and pose this question:
"The Buddha has compassion for sentient beings; why, then, are there no sentient beings of the three evil realms within his purified buddha-field?"
Answer: Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he regards them with equality and without distinction;
herein it is explained that because of the causes and conditions of pure karma, there are no three evil realms within this land.
Furthermore, the Buddha does not reside in only a single land; rather, there are lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Among these, some are pure lands, while others are mixed lands.
In impure lands, all five destinies are present;
in pure Buddha-lands, there may be a distinction between humans and devas, or there may be no such distinction between humans and devas.
Just as in the land of the past Buddha Devendra, only the World-Honored Buddha served as the Dharma King; for this reason, he was named Devendra Buddha.
Furthermore, there are lands where the three poisons and false views do not exist.
Question:

The Buddhas appear in the world solely for the purpose of eliminating the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings. Since false views and the three poisons are themselves afflictions, if there were no afflictions, for what purpose would they appear?
Answer: Some say that because of the causes and conditions of great merit within this [state], wrong views and the three poisons do not arise; therefore, it is said that they do not exist.
Furthermore, some say:

"The bodhisattvas herein have all attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); they constantly cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and other meritorious qualities; they constantly roam through the ten directions to deliver sentient beings; and in the presence of the Buddhas, they practice the samādhis of the Buddhas.
They excel in teaching and transforming countless śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they also excel in teaching and transforming bodhisattvas who are irreversible (*avaivartika*)."
Bodhisattvas who bring sentient beings to maturity and bodhisattvas who purify Buddha-lands bring even greater benefit because they are close to the Buddha-way.
Regarding the statement, "In this land, there is not even the name of the two vehicles":
Question:
Other Buddhas employ the teaching of the three vehicles; how could this [Buddha] alone be inferior? Answer:
The Buddha appears in the world of the five turbidities and divides the single path into three vehicles.
Question:
If this is so, why do the Buddhas such as Amitābha and Akṣobhya—who are not born in an age of the five turbidities—also have three vehicles?
The answer is:
When the Buddhas first resolve their minds toward enlightenment, they see that the Buddhas deliver sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, and they themselves make this vow:
"I, too, shall deliver sentient beings by means of the three vehicles."

Furthermore, there are no such names as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self; rather, because sentient beings are deeply attached to the inversions of permanence, bliss, and so forth, [the Buddha] preaches the dharmas of suffering, such as impermanence.
Because there are inversions such as [perceiving] permanence and pleasure within this [reality], there is no need for impermanence or suffering;
just as one who is not ill has no need for medicine,
so too there is no "mine," and even the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) are likewise non-existent.
Because there are no two vehicles, there are likewise no fruits such as those of the *srotāpanna* and so forth; rather, one is solely intent upon the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Those who have previously attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) obtain various *samādhis* and *dhāraṇī* gates, and further increase their merits, such as those pertaining to the stages (*bhūmi*).

When the wind blows through the trees made of the seven treasures, producing sounds according to those who are to be delivered, it is because the Bodhisattva desires that sentient beings may easily hear the Dharma; thus, the trees of the seven treasures emit the sounds of the Dharma.
Because jeweled trees fill the entire land, sentient beings hear the Dharma immediately upon birth; no other thoughts arise, but only the thought of the Dharma.
A question is asked:

Since the Buddhas possess immeasurable and inconceivable powers of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*), why do they not manifest immeasurable bodies to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings?
"Why is there no need for the sounds of trees?
He replied:

"Sentient beings are exceedingly numerous. If the Buddha were to manifest his body in various places, sentient beings would not believe him; they would say it is a magical illusion and their minds would not be respectful."
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma from humans, do not attain awakening in their minds;
yet if they hear the Dharma from an animal, they immediately believe and accept it.
As stated in the *Jātaka-sūtra*:
When a bodhisattva assumes the body of an animal, they preach the Dharma for the sake of humans;
because such a thing is rare, no one fails to believe and accept it.
Furthermore, it is said that the minds of animals are straightforward and not deceitful.
Some say that animals, being sentient beings, all possess the capacity for deception;
yet when trees, which lack consciousness, produce sounds, people accept them as true.

That which is called emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—whether a Buddha exists or does not exist—all phenomena are eternally empty. Because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they are wishless and without arising.
Such dharmas as these constantly emerge day and night.
While other lands rely on supernatural powers and the power of speech for various transformations, here there is always this spontaneous sound.
Purifying the Buddha-lands is constantly praised by all Buddhas; because one performs great meritorious deeds, one is able to attain such a pure land.
If one hears the name of a Buddha of a pure land, one will certainly become a Buddha.
Question:

If other Buddhas taught the Dharma through various forms of diligent effort and hardship, yet sentient beings still did not attain the Way, why is it that merely hearing the name of a Buddha allows one to attain the Way?
Answer:
In other places, the Buddha teaches the Dharma in various ways, and sentient beings may attain the Path or acquire roots of goodness; his teachings are never in vain.
However, if one hears this Buddha’s name, they will ultimately reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), though it is not said that they attain it immediately.
Question:

Regarding all Buddhas, if a person hears their names with a sincere mind, they shall all attain Buddhahood; as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether one's merit is great or small, all shall become Buddhas.
Why is it that only the Buddha of the Pure Land is mentioned?
The answer is:
when people hear the names of other Buddhas, they say:
“His birth is no different from that of ordinary people; he differs only in that he has attained the Way through omniscience.
Because their minds lack reverence, even though they plant roots of goodness, they cannot do so deeply.

Among these, this is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*). The Buddha-body is immeasurable and boundless; its radiance and the sound of its preaching of the Dharma pervade the lands of the ten directions. The sentient beings within those lands are all those who draw near to the Buddha-way. He preaches the Dharma amidst a multitude spanning immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* yojanas.

His radiance surpasses that of immeasurable billions of *asaṃkhyeya* suns and moons, constantly issuing from his body. If sentient beings are permitted by the Buddha to see it, they shall see it; if he does not permit it, they do not see it.

From each and every pore of this Buddha, there constantly emerge immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas; each of these Buddhas is identical and without distinction, and from the side of each emanation Buddha, others emerge in succession.
Although the manifestations of the Buddha appear as superior or inferior according to the capacities of those to be saved, the fundamental, true Buddha has no distinction of large or small.
Thus, whether one sees him, hears his name, or hears of such merits, because of one's deep faith and reverence, how could the roots of goodness planted thereby not lead inevitably to Buddhahood?
Furthermore, when this Buddha preached the Dharma, there was no one who harbored doubt, nor even a single person who said:
"This teaching was not spoken from the mouth of the Buddha!"
"All of these are the Dharma.
He asked:
"Among people, are there many who hear the Dharma from Śākyamuni Buddha and give rise to doubt?"
The answer is:
In this context, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions:
"There are those who, having little merit and not having planted roots of goodness, fail to encounter virtuous friends and thus give rise to doubt."

Because they are shrouded by various afflictions such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), they claim that what is not the Buddha’s word is the Buddha’s word, and that what is the Buddha’s word is not the Buddha’s word.

Having failed to deeply plant roots of goodness and having failed to follow virtuous teachers, the three poisons and false views arise simultaneously; having no one to rely upon or follow, they act according to their own whims and self-indulgence—when they encounter false views, because they accord with their own inclinations, they declare them to be the vision of omniscience;
yet when the Buddhas teach ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), it does not accord with their inclinations, so they immediately declare it to be not the Buddha’s word.

To speak of what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and of the Dharma as not the Dharma—such people give rise to much doubt regarding the Buddhas; because they give rise to much doubt, their minds feel regret.
In this Pure Buddha-land, there are no such sinful persons, and therefore no doubt arises.
The Buddha said:
“Such a sinner, because they have destroyed the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, will die and fall into the evil realms of hell!

When bodhisattvas attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they see these sinners wandering through birth and death; by means of their Buddha-empowerment (*abhijñā*), they pull out sentient beings and cause them to dwell within the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), so that they do not fall into the three evil destinies. This is called purifying a buddha-field.”
"In this Buddha-field, there are none of these faults. There is nothing that is not complete;

among the mundane and supramundane, the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*), the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth, there is no obstruction—namely, the land consists of the seven treasures, the bodies of sentient beings are upright and handsome, adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they possess immeasurable radiance, they constantly hear the sound of the Dharma, and they are never separated from the six *pāramitās* up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*) of a Buddha."
The sentient beings herein shall all ultimately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Question: Previously it was said that "upon hearing the Buddha’s name, one is destined to reach Buddhahood," whereas here it is said that "being unimpeded regarding all dharmas, one will certainly become a Buddha. What is the difference between these two?
The answer is:

Because the sentient beings herein constantly see the Buddha, constantly hear the Dharma, deeply plant roots of goodness, and extensively accumulate the Buddha-dharmas, they quickly attain Buddhahood;
those who merely hear the name, although equally destined for ultimate certainty, are slightly inferior.
Such as these are called the characteristics of a pure land, as described in the section on "Adorning the Bodhi Tree" within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Chapter 83: Determination (*Niścaya*) From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the commentary on the Chapter on Determination, Number Eighty-three. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Is this bodhisattva mahāsattva one who is destined for certainty,
or one who is not destined?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who is fixed in destiny,
not one who is unfixed. “World-Honored One,
in what respect are they fixed?”
Is it within the path of the śrāvaka?
Is it within the path of the pratyekabuddha?
Or is it within the path of the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva is not fixed within the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, he is fixed within the path of the buddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds destined for certainty?
Or are it bodhisattvas in their final existence who are destined for certainty?”
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment is also fixed; a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive (avaivartika) is also fixed; and a bodhisattva in their final existence is also fixed.”
“World-Honored One!
Do bodhisattvas who are fixed in certainty fall into birth within the evil realms? “No!”
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would those who are on the path of the eight persons, or those who are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas, be born within the evil realms?
"No, World-Honored One! It is so, Subhūti!"

From the time a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they practice giving, maintain morality, exercise patience, exert diligence, cultivate meditative concentration, and develop wisdom, thereby severing all unwholesome karma.

It is impossible that such a person would fall into the evil realms, or be born among the long-lived devas, or fail to find a place to cultivate wholesome dharmas, or be born in a borderland, or be born into a family of evil or heterodox views, or a family with the view of non-action—places where the name of the Buddha does not exist, the name of the Dharma does not exist, and the name of the Saṃgha does not exist. Such a thing cannot happen!
Subhūti! It is impossible for a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to practice the ten unwholesome paths with a deep resolve.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such roots of goodness and merit as you yourself have described in your own accounts of past lives where they experienced unwholesome retributions—at that time, where were those roots of goodness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, a bodhisattva mahāsattva assumes a body in accordance with their needs, and by means of that body, he benefits sentient beings.”

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born as an animal, he possesses such power of skillful means that if an enemy or bandit comes to kill him, he gives up his body with unsurpassed patience and unsurpassed compassion, without causing any distress to the enemy;
you śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess such power.
For this reason, Subhūti,
you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to fulfill great compassion and out of pity and for the benefit of sentient beings, intentionally take on the bodies of animals.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
in what roots of goodness do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide to receive such bodies as these?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, there is not a single root of goodness that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring to fulfillment during this interval;
having brought them to fulfillment, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
For this reason, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the fulfillment of all roots of goodness;
having trained in these roots of goodness, they shall attain all-knowledge and sever all habitual tendencies of affliction.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such pure and untainted dharmas, is born among the animals in the evil realms?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Has the Buddha accomplished the pure, untainted dharmas?"
Subhūti said: “The Buddha has accomplished all pure, untainted dharmas. [The Buddha said: “Subhūti!”
"If the Buddha himself transforms into the body of an animal to perform the work of a Buddha and deliver sentient beings,
is he actually an animal? Subhūti replied, "No!"
The Buddha said:

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this; having accomplished pure and untainted dharmas, he assumes the body of an animal for the sake of delivering sentient beings, using that body to teach and transform them.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If an arhat were to manifest a transformation body, would he be able to cause sentient beings to rejoice?
Subhūti replied:
"Yes! the Buddha said. "It is so!"
"So it is, Subhūti!

By means of these pure, untainted dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva takes on a body according to the beings he seeks to deliver; with this body he benefits sentient beings, yet he does not undergo suffering."
Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose a magician were to conjure various forms— such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, women, and so forth— and display them to the multitude.
“Subhūti! Do these elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, women, and so forth have any reality?
Subhūti replied:
"It is not so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes pure, untainted dharmas; because he manifests various bodies to show them to sentient beings, he benefits all with these bodies and yet does not undergo any suffering."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By the power of the great skillful means of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having attained noble, untainted wisdom, they manifest in various forms according to the bodies of the sentient beings who are to be saved, in order to deliver them!”
[Treatise] Question:
In the preceding "Chapter on the Irreversible" (Avivartika-paṭala), it was stated:
"Such characteristics are those of the irreversible; such characteristics are not those of the irreversible."
"Avivartika (non-retrogressive) is itself definitive certainty; why then does Subhūti ask again?
The answer is:
this Prajñāpāramitā has various gateways and various paths.
The term "avaivartika" (non-retrogressive) was explained from one perspective;
now, having asked about certainty, we ask again from another perspective.
Furthermore, within the Buddha’s mind, all sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely certain.
Because people’s wisdom is insufficient, they are said to be "not definitively fixed.
The Buddha knows those who, despite having accumulated great merit over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, will inevitably regress and become followers of the Lesser Vehicle;
yet he also knows that even a minute insect, though it has not yet given rise to a virtuous mind, will after such a number of kalpas resolve to attain enlightenment and subsequently become a Buddha.
One definitively knows that all dharmas are thus: from this cause, this fruit is obtained; for this reason, one is called a Buddha.
Because one has attained definitive knowledge, there is no obstruction regarding any dharma.
Furthermore, Subhūti heard it said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"If one performs even a small amount of merit for the sake of the Buddha—even if it is merely a single invocation of 'Namo Buddhāya' in jest—one will gradually and inevitably become a Buddha."

Furthermore, I have heard that within the "Chapter on Non-Retrogression" there are both those who regress and those who do not; yet I have also heard that all śrāvakas shall become buddhas—if this is so, there should be no regression.
As it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they are fixed, while other sūtras state that there are those who regress and those who do not, I now ask: are they fixed or unfixed?
For various reasons such as these, the question was asked regarding certainty and uncertainty.
The Buddha replied:
"The bodhisattva is one who is definitively destined for enlightenment."
Subhūti, because his mind was fixed upon entering *nirvāṇa*, he asked:
"In which path is one fixed?
The Buddha replied:
"It is not that they are fixed in the two vehicles, but rather that they are fixed within the Mahāyāna.
Since those who seek the Buddha-way are of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, he asks:
"Are you one who has first resolved [to attain enlightenment]?"
"Are they *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive),
or are they those in their final body who are fixed [in liberation]?
Subhūti’s intention was that those from the stage of *avaivartika* upward are "fixed in dwelling within the Buddha-way."
The Buddha replied:
"Bodhisattvas of all three types are destined for certainty.
To be "destined for certainty" means that they will inevitably become Buddhas.
Question:

As stated in the preceding chapter, "The Buddha, with his Buddha-eye, beholds the bodhisattvas of the ten directions seeking Buddhahood like the sands of the Ganges; those who attain *avaivartika* status are but one or two.
Why, then, is it now said that "the three kinds of bodhisattvas are all entirely destined"?

Answer: I have already stated previously that the profound Prajñā has immeasurable gateways. In some places it is said that "bodhisattvas may regress and are not fixed," while in other places it is said that "bodhisattvas are fixed and do not regress."
As in the "Chapter on the Avaivartika," Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"When a bodhisattva regresses, from what does he regress?
Is it from form, or from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to the eighteen unique qualities?"
"Because they are ultimately empty, all dharmas do not regress.
Why does the Buddha further speak of non-regression here?
Question:
Regarding these two meanings, which one is the reality?
The answer is:
both matters are real.
There is nothing that the Buddha’s spoken words do not accord with reality.
For instance, the Buddha may sometimes say, "All dharmas are empty and non-existent," or he may say, "Generosity, the observance of precepts, and so forth, do exist."

For those who have newly resolved their minds on enlightenment, he teaches that "all phenomena exist"; for those who have long practiced and are attached to wholesome dharmas, he teaches that "all phenomena are empty and non-existent."

Those who are indolent regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and lack firm resolve are such that they ought to attain liberation through the path of the *śrāvaka*, yet they do not seek it; consequently, they suffer for a long time within *saṃsāra*. For this reason, it is said: "Though those who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment] are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, those who attain *avaivartika* status are but one or two."
When sentient beings have heard this, those who are able to endure various sufferings will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
if they are not so able, they will take up the path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
There are those who are capable of attaining Buddhahood, yet their great compassion is slight and their attachment to their own bodies is heavy.
When such persons hear that Buddhahood is difficult to attain, many of them regress and think:
"I may not be able to attain Buddhahood; it would be better for me to enter parinirvāṇa early rather than undergo such toil and suffering life after life."

For the sake of such people, it is said that all bodhisattvas, from the first generation of the mind of awakening onward, are all destined for certainty (*niyata*), as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Question:
If all bodhisattvas are destined for certainty, why does the Buddha in various ways rebuke the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) and not permit bodhisattvas to realize the fruits of the two vehicles?

The answer is: One who seeks the Buddha-way should thoroughly know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because such a person fears old age, sickness, and death, they realize only a small portion of the nature of phenomena and then cease their efforts; they abandon the Buddha-way and do not deliver sentient beings. Thus, they are rebuked by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:

"Though you wish to depart, you shall ultimately not escape [the cycle]. When you attain the realization of an Arhat, you will not seek the profound samādhis of the Bodhisattvas, nor will you extensively transform sentient beings. This is a detour that causes you to linger on the Buddha-way."
Question: Since the body received by an Arhat as a result of causes and conditions from previous lives must necessarily perish, in what state does he abide to fulfill the path to Buddhahood? Answer:
When they attain arhatship, the causes and conditions of all outflows within the three realms are exhausted, and they will no longer be reborn in the three realms.

There are pure buddha-fields that transcend the three realms, where even the name of affliction does not exist; in those lands, at the presence of a Buddha, they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and fully perfect the path to buddhahood.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"There are arhats who, if they have not heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, consider themselves to have attained nirvāṇa;
I shall proclaim this matter to them in other lands, and you shall all become buddhas."
Question: If an Arhat goes to a pure Buddha-land and receives a Dharma-nature body, they should thus quickly attain Buddhahood; why, then, do you say it is circuitous and delayed?
The answer is:
This person is attached to the causes and conditions of the Hīnayāna; they abandon sentient beings and abandon the Buddha-way, yet falsely claim to have attained the Way.

For these reasons, although they do not undergo the sufferings of birth and death, their faculties as a bodhisattva are dull and they cannot swiftly accomplish the Buddha-way, unlike the bodhisattvas who proceed directly.
Furthermore, among the five inconceivable things, the Buddha-dharma is the foremost; that "an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted may yet become a Buddha" is something known only by a Buddha.
Those who engage in formal debate may indeed discuss it, yet its true nature cannot be fathomed; therefore, one should not engage in frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Only when one attains Buddhahood will one be able to fully comprehend it;
for others, it is merely something to be trusted, not something that can be known.

Regarding the question of whether a bodhisattva destined for enlightenment could fall into the three evil realms: having heard the Buddha’s account of immeasurable past lives (*jātaka*)—in which he underwent various sufferings as an elephant, a deer, a tortoise, a pigeon, a peacock, a parrot, and so forth—Subhūti asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"If Bodhisattvas receive such bodies as those of animals, how can it be said that all Bodhisattvas are 'fixed' (niyata)?
To be fixed means to be *avaivartika*;
one who is *avaivartika* does not fall into the three evil destinies."
The Buddha replied with a counter-question: "What do you think?
Do noble persons such as those on the eight stages of realization fall into the three evil realms?"
Subhūti reflected:
"Because these noble ones have entered the noble path, they lack the causes and conditions for falling into the three evil realms.
Having reflected thus, he replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"The Bodhisattva is also like this; because the causes and conditions for falling into the three evil realms have been exhausted, how could he fall into the three evil realms?"
The causes and conditions for falling into the three evil realms are what are known as all unwholesome dharmas.

Since this bodhisattva, from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, has practiced wholesome dharmas such as generosity and ethical discipline, and has severed the ten unwholesome paths beginning with killing;
it is impossible that such a person should fall into the three evil realms!
Why is this? Because it extinguishes all unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas.
The unwholesome paths are of three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
Those of the highest grade fall into hell; those of the middle grade fall among animals; and those of the lowest grade fall among hungry ghosts.
Since these three types [of obstacles] have been completely exhausted by this bodhisattva, and because he possesses a profound mind of compassion for sentient beings, he does not fall.
Question:
If that is so, one may indeed not be born in the three evil realms;
however, since this bodhisattva possesses such great merit, why is he not born among the long-lived devas?
The answer is:
This bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, practices the six pāramitās;

although he is able to enter the dhyāna-pāramitā and harmonize it with the practice of loving-kindness and compassion, he does not become attached to the flavor of dhyāna. When his life is about to end, because he keeps the dharmas of the desire realm in mind, he withdraws from the path of dhyāna.

Because there is no suffering or affliction therein, and because they are deeply attached to the flavor of dhyāna, it is difficult for them to be delivered; therefore, one is not reborn in the heavens of long life.
Because borderlands are obstructive and one cannot cultivate wholesome dharmas there, one is not reborn there either.
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas have uprooted the very foundation of stinginess regarding the Dharma;
due to the causes and conditions of such stinginess, they are born in borderlands where the Dharma is not known.
Furthermore, because this bodhisattva always delights in the Middle Way and abandons the two extremes, he is not born in a borderland.

A borderland is so called because there the names of the Triple Gem do not exist, the seven classes of followers are unknown, and people value only the immediate affairs of this life rather than the path of merit and the Dharma; thus it is named a borderland. It is not merely because one is born in such a country that it is called a borderland.

If one recognizes the Three Jewels, understands the causes and conditions for the continuity of sin and merit, and comprehends the true nature of all phenomena, such a person is not considered to be living in a borderland even if born outside of Jambudvīpa, let alone if born within Jambudvīpa!

This bodhisattva constantly delights in preaching the Dharma for others and, because they also deeply cherish the wholesome Dharma, they attain rebirth together with sentient beings who are amenable to their will, namely, in a central land.
A person is not born into a family of wrong views in the central lands. Why is this?

Because such a bodhisattva, throughout successive lifetimes, has always practiced right view themselves, taught right view to others, praised the Dharma of right view, and rejoiced in those who practice right view; for this reason, they are not born into a family of evil and wrong views.
Question:

This Bodhisattva possesses the power of great merit and wisdom; he ought to be born in borderlands or into families with wrong views in order to transform them. Why, then, does he fear such births and not take them?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who have accomplished great power; second, those who have newly resolved their minds [for enlightenment] due to causes and conditions.
Great Bodhisattvas assume bodies according to the needs of sentient beings for the sake of their deliverance, not shunning frontier regions or heterodox views;

however, if a Bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon enlightenment were born in such places, they would be unable to save others and would instead bring about their own ruin; therefore, they do not take birth there.
For example, just as pure gold remains undestroyed even when in the mud,
whereas copper and iron are ruined;
so it is with those of wrong views— namely, the view of non-action (akriyā-dṛṣṭi).
Although all sixty-two types of views are false views, the view of non-action is the most grave. Why is this?
The view of non-action asserts that one should not cultivate merit nor seek nirvana.
Whether one claims that [the world] was created by a god or that it has existed from the very beginning, although these are wrong views, they do not preclude the performance of meritorious deeds.
Because one does not commit great evils, one will not be reborn [in the lower realms].
Furthermore, it is impossible for a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment to deeply take pleasure in practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action. Why is this?
Because such a bodhisattva single-mindedly dedicates themselves toward awakening, cherishing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while not valuing worldly dharmas.
Because this person has not yet abandoned the causes and conditions of desire, although they may give rise to various afflictions, they ultimately do not commit evil with a deep-seated intent;
even if subjected to flogging and whippings, they will never take another's life, nor seize another's property to cause them to lose their life.

Because this bodhisattva abandons all unwholesome dharmas and cultivates and accumulates all wholesome dharmas, they are not born in the eight unfavorable states of existence and always attains the eight favorable states.
Subhūti asked:
"If a bodhisattva has accomplished such roots of goodness, why did he take birth through past causes and conditions as a deer, a horse, and so forth?
The Buddha replied:

"Bodhisattvas truly possess the accomplishment of merit and roots of goodness; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they assume the forms of animals, yet they do not incur the transgressions of animals."
In this regard, the Buddha himself explains the causes and conditions, saying:
"When a bodhisattva dwells among animals, he feels compassion for his enemies and plunderers; such a thing does not exist even among arhats or pratyekabuddhas."

"Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, even when harmed by enemies and robbers, may refrain from retaliating, yet they are unable to feel love and compassion for them or provide them with offerings and sustenance.
For example, when the Bodhisattva was in a previous life as a six-tusked white elephant, a hunter struck him in the chest with a poisoned arrow!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva elephant encircled the hunter with his trunk so that no other elephants could harm him, and said to the female elephant:
"You are the wife of a Bodhisattva; for what reason have you conceived such an evil thought?"
The hunter’s transgression lies in his afflictions, not in the fault of others!
Once I have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall extinguish those afflictions and transgressions;
it is like a person possessed by a ghost: when a master of incantations arrives, he treats only the ghost and does not harbor anger toward the person.
"Therefore, do not seek his fault!
He then asked the hunter gently,
"Why did you shoot me?"
He replied, "I require your tusks.
The elephant immediately went to a crevice in the rock, pulled out his tusks, and gave them to him; though both flesh and blood flowed forth, he felt no pain.
Providing them with food and showing them the way—
such acts of compassion do not exist among Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
With such a benevolent heart, how could one receive the body of an animal?
One should know that this is a transformation-body for the purpose of delivering sentient beings.
A question is asked:
Why does he not assume a human body to preach the Dharma, but instead takes the form of this beast?
Answer:

There are times when sentient beings do not believe or accept [the teaching] upon seeing a human body, yet they give rise to faith and joy, and receive its transformative instruction, upon hearing the Dharma preached from the body of an animal.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wishes to fulfill the mind of great compassion and desires to practice its actual deeds,
sentient beings who see them are filled with wonder and joy, and all are enabled to enter the Way.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Scroll 93.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on "Certainty" (Niścaya), Part Eighty-three, Continued; Scroll Ninety-four.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] “World-Honored One!
In what pure and white dharmas does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide, such that he is able to exercise such power of skillful means without being defiled?”
The Buddha said:

"By means of the power of skillful means through the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings in lands throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet they do not become greedily attached to this body."
Why is this? Because the one who clings, the object of clinging, and the locus of clinging—these three phenomena are all unattainable, for their intrinsic nature is empty.
Emptiness does not cling to emptiness; within emptiness there is no one who clings, nor is there any locus of clinging.
Why is this? Subhūti,
within emptiness, the characteristic of emptiness cannot be apprehended.
"This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
Dwelling in this emptiness, a bodhisattva is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
“Does a bodhisattva attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by abiding solely within the prajñāpāramitā, and not by abiding in other dharmas? “Subhūti!
"Is there any dharma that does not enter into the perfection of wisdom?
"World-Honored One,
if the perfection of wisdom is empty of intrinsic nature, how can all dharmas enter into the perfection of wisdom?"
"Bhagavān!
In emptiness, there is no dharma that either enters or does not enter. "Subhūti!"
“Are all phenomena and the characteristics of all phenomena empty?
“World-Honored One,
they are empty.”
“Subhūti! If all dharmas and the characteristics of all dharmas are empty, why do you say that all dharmas do not enter into emptiness?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, dwelling within the emptiness of all phenomena, is able to give rise to the *abhijñāpāramitā*?

And how, dwelling within this *abhijñāpāramitā*, does he go to lands in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to make offerings to the Buddhas currently residing there, hear the Dharma preached by those Buddhas, and plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates that these lands in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all empty. The Buddhas within those lands are also empty of intrinsic nature; they exist merely as provisional designations. Furthermore, the provisional designations by which those Buddhas manifest their bodies are also empty."
If the lands of the ten directions and the natures of all Buddhas were not empty, then emptiness would be partial;
because emptiness is not partial, all phenomena and all characteristics of phenomena are empty.
For this reason, all phenomena and the characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they employ the power of skillful means to give rise to the perfection of supernormal powers;

abiding within this perfection of supernormal powers, they manifest the divine eye, the divine ear, the bases of psychic power, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of past lives, thereby knowing the birth and death of sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva is far removed from the perfection of supernormal powers, they will be unable to bring benefit to sentient beings, nor will they be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This supernormal power perfection (abhijñā-pāramitā) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the path to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Why is this? By means of this divine eye (divya-cakṣus), they personally perceive all wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma) and also instruct others so that they may attain these wholesome dharmas; yet they do not become attached even to these wholesome dharmas, because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all wholesome dharmas is empty.
Emptiness is without attachment; if one were attached, one would experience its flavor, yet within this emptiness there is no flavor.
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are able to produce such a divine eye, and with this eye they contemplate all phenomena as empty.
Seeing that these phenomena are empty, they do not grasp at signs nor do they perform karmic actions.
They also preach this Dharma for others, yet they do not apprehend the characteristic of a sentient being, nor do they apprehend the name of a sentient being.

Thus, by means of the dharma of non-apprehension, the bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the perfection of supernatural powers (ṛddhipāramitā); by means of this perfection of supernatural powers, they are able to perform whatever is to be done through supernatural power.
"By means of the divine eye, which transcends that of humans, this bodhisattva sees the lands of the ten directions;
