having seen them, he flies to the ten directions to benefit sentient beings—either through giving, or through ethical discipline, or through patience, or through diligence, or through meditative concentration, or through wisdom, he benefits sentient beings;

or by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, or by means of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, or by means of the teachings of the śrāvakas, or by means of the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, or by means of the teachings of the bodhisattvas, or by means of the teachings of the Buddhas, he benefits sentient beings."
"For those who are stingy, he preaches the Dharma in this way:
'O sentient beings!
You should practice giving. Poverty is a state of suffering and affliction; if a person in poverty cannot even benefit themselves, how could they possibly benefit others?'"
For this reason, you should diligently practice giving; by doing so, you will attain happiness for yourselves and enable others to attain happiness as well.
Do not, out of poverty, devour one another, lest you fail to escape the three evil realms.
He preaches the Dharma for those who have broken the precepts, saying:
"O sentient beings!
The dharma of breaking the precepts brings great suffering and affliction!"
One who has broken the precepts cannot benefit themselves; how then could they benefit others?
The karmic retribution for breaking the precepts is to suffer in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.
If you fall into the three evil realms, you will not even be able to save yourselves; how then could you save others?
For this reason, you should not follow a mind that breaks the precepts, lest you have cause for regret at the time of death.
If there are those who are quarreling and contending with one another, he preaches the Dharma to them in this way:
"O sentient beings!
Do not harbor mutual anger toward one another!"
Those whose minds are agitated by anger do not accord with wholesome dharmas.
If you now harbor mutual anger and agitation in your hearts, you may fall into hell, or among the hungry ghosts and animals.
"For this reason, you should not give rise to even a single thought of anger, much less many!
For the sake of indolent sentient beings, I preach the Dharma to enable them to attain diligence;
for distracted sentient beings, I enable them to attain meditative concentration."
It is likewise for deluded sentient beings, enabling them to attain wisdom.
For those who engage in sexual desire, I cause them to contemplate impurity;
for those who harbor anger and hatred, I cause them to contemplate loving-kindness.
For sentient beings who are deluded, they cause them to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
For sentient beings who travel by non-pathways, they cause them to enter the right path—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha.
For the sake of these sentient beings, he preached the Dharma in this way:

"The dharmas to which you are attached are empty of intrinsic nature; within dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature, attachment cannot be found. This absence of attachment is itself the mark of emptiness."
"In this way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide within the perfection of supernormal powers and bring benefit to sentient beings."
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva is far removed from the supernormal powers (abhijñā), they cannot skillfully teach the Dharma in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
For this reason, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should give rise to the supernormal powers. Subhūti,
it is like a bird that cannot soar high into the sky if it lacks wings.
Without supernormal powers, a bodhisattva cannot teach and transform sentient beings according to their wishes.
For this reason, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should give rise to the various supernormal powers.
Having aroused the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if he wishes to benefit sentient beings, he is able to benefit them according to his will.
This bodhisattva, using the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), sees lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, as well as the sentient beings within those lands;

having seen them, he travels to their locations by means of his supernormal power, knows the minds of sentient beings, and preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each—whether preaching on generosity (*dāna*), or ethical discipline (*śīla*), or meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or even up to the Dharma of nirvāṇa.
With the divine ear, this bodhisattva hears two kinds of sounds:
those of humans and those of non-humans.
Using the divine ear, they hear the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and are able to receive and uphold it all.
He preaches to sentient beings the Dharma as he has heard it, whether it be the teaching on generosity up to the teaching on nirvāṇa.

This bodhisattva purifies his knowledge of others' minds; using this knowledge of others' minds, he knows the thoughts of sentient beings and preaches the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate, whether it be the teaching on generosity up to the teaching on nirvāṇa.
This bodhisattva, through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), recollects various places of former births, both his own and those of others;
using this knowledge of past lives, he remembers the names of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples in every place where he has been in the past.

To those sentient beings who have faith and delight in the knowledge of past lives, he manifests the events of past lives and preaches the Dharma to them—whether it be the teaching on giving (*dāna*) or even up to the teaching on nirvāṇa.

By means of the power of supernormal knowledges at will, they travel to various and immeasurable Buddha-lands to make offerings to the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness under those Buddhas, and then return to their own lands.

This is the Bodhisattva’s realization of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; by means of this realization of the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, he preaches the Dharma to sentient beings according to their needs, whether it be the teaching on generosity or even up to the teaching on nirvana.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should thus give rise to the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
By cultivating these supernormal powers, the bodhisattva assumes a body at will, remaining untainted by suffering or pleasure.
For example, it is like a person conjured by a Buddha who performs all manner of tasks yet remains unstained by suffering or pleasure.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they should likewise sport with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), being able to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not purify the buddha-fields and does not bring sentient beings to maturity, they will be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Why is this? Because the requisite conditions are not fulfilled, one cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the causes and conditions that, once fully perfected by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, lead to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All wholesome dharmas are the causes and conditions for a bodhisattva’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What are these wholesome dharmas, by means of which wholesome dharmas one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, the dāna-pāramitā is the causal condition for these wholesome dharmas; herein there is no discrimination that ‘this is the giver’ or ‘this is the recipient,’ because their nature is empty.”
By means of this dānapāramitā, one is able to benefit oneself and also benefit sentient beings, drawing them out from birth and death and causing them to attain nirvāṇa.
All these wholesome dharmas are the causes and conditions for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
By practicing this path, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cross over birth and death.

The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*); the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*); the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*); the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpattayaḥ*), and the doors of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa tathāgatabalāni*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmāḥ*)—all such merits as these constitute the path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! These are called wholesome dharmas.
Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with these wholesome dharmas, he shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
"Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), one shall turn the wheel of Dharma;
having turned the wheel of Dharma, one shall deliver sentient beings.
[Treatise] Explanation:
At that time, Subhūti asked:
"By abiding in what roots of goodness is one able to receive such a body?
The Buddha replied:
“The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Thereupon, Subhūti, filled with great joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By the power of the accomplishment of the great skillful means of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in what noble, untainted dharmas does he abide that he is able to receive this body without being defiled by the nature of an animal’s body?”
"It is like a magician, or like a magical transformation.
Abiding in what kind of pure and white dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) is one able to perform such skillful means (*upāya*)?
The Buddha replied:

"By the power of the prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva is able to accomplish such skillful means (upāya) as to manifest various bodies to benefit sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions, yet he does not crave these bodies."
In this context, the Buddha explains the causal conditions:
"This bodhisattva cannot apprehend three things:
first, the body of this bodhisattva; second, the deer and horses he has manifested; and third, the dharmas he employs."
Why is this? Because all these phenomena are empty by nature.
Emptiness itself does not cling to emptiness, and within emptiness there is no attachment.
Because dharmas do not exist, sentient beings do not exist; because sentient beings do not exist, dharmas also do not exist.
Regarding this, the Buddha spoke of dependent origination:
"In emptiness, emptiness itself cannot be apprehended."
Because it is unattainable, how could a bodhisattva be attached to this wisdom?
This is called the *prajñāpāramitā* of the emptiness of non-apprehension; dwelling within this, a bodhisattva is able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because it is free from obstruction, it is easily attained.
Subhūti asked:

"If a bodhisattva dwells in the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharmas), why is it said now that one attains [them] only by dwelling in the prajñāpāramitā of non-apprehension?"
The Buddha replied:
“Subhūti! What dharma does not enter into the Prajñā?”
"All dharmas enter into the Prajñāpāramitā;
if one abides in the Prajñāpāramitā, then one abides in all dharmas.
He asked again:
"If the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, how can all phenomena enter into it?
In this regard, Subhūti himself explains the reason:
"Within the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, there is no phenomenon that emerges and no phenomenon that enters."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Are all phenomena and the characteristics of all phenomena empty? [Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"Emptiness.
"Subhūti! If all dharmas and the characteristics of all dharmas are empty, then all dharmas should enter into emptiness. Why do you say that within emptiness there are no dharmas that enter or exit?"
At that time, Subhūti bowed his mind in submission and accepted the teaching;
having heard that these bodhisattvas manifest emanations to deliver sentient beings, he now asked:
"World-Honored One!..."

How does a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the emptiness of all phenomena, manage to give rise to the perfection of supernatural powers (ṛddhipāramitā) and travel to buddha-fields throughout the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to make offerings to the Buddhas, listen to the Dharma, and plant profound roots of goodness?
"Roots of goodness" are the foundation for all dhāraṇīs, gates of samādhi, and unimpeded liberations.
Subhūti’s thought was:
"The nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is emptiness; how can a bodhisattva, while abiding in this *pāramitā* of the nature of emptiness, practice these supernatural powers which are phenomena?"
The Buddha said:
"Because it is empty, one is able to practice. Why is this so?"

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices prajñā, they contemplate that the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, are all empty, and that the Buddhas of those lands are also empty.
Question: If the buddha-field is empty, then the Buddha should also be empty; why then do you speak of them separately? Answer:
The Buddha attained this body through immeasurable, incalculable, and real merits; with a single toe, he can shake the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, throughout successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva has deeply cherished and revered the Buddha, and thus cannot quickly contemplate him to realize his emptiness.
For this reason, it is not spoken of in conjunction with the lands.
Herein, the Buddha himself states the causal conditions:
"If the lands of the ten directions and the various Buddhas were not empty, then emptiness would be partial."
There is a partiality in naming some things empty and others non-empty;
now, in reality, there is no such partiality, and therefore all dharmas and all dharma-characteristics are empty.
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are unimpeded regarding all dharmas.
Observing forms with the fleshly eye, one's vision is obstructed:
one sees what is above but not what is below; one sees what is before but not what is behind; one sees through what is open but cannot see what is blocked; one sees by day but not by night.
Knowing that the power of the fleshly eye is limited, one employs skillful means to further seek the divine eye.
As for the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), it causes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of other realms to enter into one's own body.
The application of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is as previously explained.

One gives rise to the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhipāda*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), thereby knowing the destinies and rebirths of sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva lacks supernormal powers (abhijñā), they cannot bring benefit to sentient beings.
Why is this? If one lacks supernormal powers, how can one cause many sentient beings to resolve their minds toward enlightenment?
Even though Bodhisattvas possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are still unable to cause all sentient beings to resolve their minds toward enlightenment; how much less so when they lack them!
Therefore, the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) is the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattva personally perceives wholesome dharmas and also enables others to perceive wholesome dharmas, yet he does not cling to these wholesome dharmas.
Why is this? Because the nature of these dharmas is entirely empty.
Question:
The divine eye can perceive visible forms; how then can it perceive wholesome dharmas?
Furthermore, you say that it perceives the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas.
Answer: This is to speak of the fruit within the cause.

By means of the divine eye, one sees one's own body and the sentient beings of the ten directions; thereafter, one employs the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of past lives to seek their roots of goodness in this life and future lives.
These roots of goodness and their karmic fruits have long since been worn away; because they are worn away, one perceives emptiness.

These roots of goodness are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty. Because they are empty, they cannot be clung to, nor can their flavor be relished. Because their flavor cannot be relished, there is no clinging.
For example, a fly alights on everything except the flames of a fire.

The attachment of sentient beings is likewise: they cling to all things, whether wholesome or unwholesome dharmas, even clinging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; thus, they cannot enter nirvāṇa.
Only the fire of the emptiness of intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* can they not cling to.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* and the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā* are empty.
If the *prajñāpāramitā* were not empty, it would constitute a flavor, and thus a point of attachment.

Abiding in this wisdom, the bodhisattva does not give rise to outflowing karma; he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, while also knowing that sentient beings are merely provisional names and are ultimately ungraspable.
Abiding within this prajñāpāramitā of non-apprehension, one is able to fulfill the activities of the supernormal powers;
if a bodhisattva does not attain this unobstructed prajñā, they will be unable to attain unimpeded supernormal powers.

Having attained this unimpeded emptiness supernatural power (*abhijñā*), the Bodhisattva flies to the lands of the ten directions to benefit sentient beings, as extensively explained in the sutras—whether by means of giving (*dāna*), or by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and so forth.
For those who are stingy, he explains the meaning of the six pāramitās, such as generosity, as the Buddha himself has explained extensively herein.
As an analogy is given here:
it is like a bird that cannot fly because it lacks wings.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: without the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), he cannot transform and guide sentient beings.
By means of the divine eye (divyacakṣus), the Bodhisattva perceives the lands of the ten directions, all Buddhas, and all sentient beings.
By means of the power of the divine ear, they hear the Dharma from all Buddhas.

By means of the power of supernormal feats of will (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), they emit great radiance, or manifest water and fire, performing various transformations and displaying extraordinary wonders to cause sentient beings to give rise to a sense of rare wonder and reverence.

By means of the power of knowing the minds of others, he knows the mental states and their concomitants of others—what they are attached to and what they weary of; who can be saved and who cannot; who is sharp-witted and who is dull-witted; whose roots of goodness are perfected and whose are not yet perfected. Thus, by knowing the minds of other sentient beings in such ways, he gathers in those whose roots of goodness are perfected.
For those who are capable of being delivered, he observes their origins and ends through the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of birth and death:
"From where have they come?
What roots of goodness have they planted?"
What are his inclinations and what are his practices?
From here, where will he ultimately be reborn?
And when shall he attain liberation?
Having thus deliberated and reflected, he knew the past karmic causes and conditions and the future worldly retributions of those who could be saved.
Furthermore, by means of his supernormal powers, for those who should be saved through fear, he showed them the hells, saying:
"You shall be born within these."
For those who should be delivered through joy, he shows them the heavenly realms;
seeing this with their own eyes, they feel both awe and joy, and develop weary detachment toward the world.

At that time, by means of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, he taught the Dharma of the exhaustion of outflows; sentient beings, hearing this Dharma, shattered their clinging minds and attained nirvana through the three vehicles.

For example, when a white heron wishes to catch a fish, it carefully gauges its advance and retreat; not missing the opportune moment and knowing that the prey can be obtained, it immediately seizes it, never failing in vain.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: by means of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), he observes the beginning and end of sentient beings, their conditions for being delivered, their lands, and the proper seasons; knowing that their faculties such as faith have increased and sharpened, and that all necessary causes and conditions are complete, he preaches the Dharma for them, and thus his teaching is not in vain.
Therefore it is said:
"A bodhisattva who is devoid of supernormal powers cannot benefit sentient beings,
just as a bird without wings."
Regarding his other supernormal powers, as the Buddha himself has said:
"With the divine eye, he perceives the birth and death of sentient beings in the ten directions; he also knows the minds of sentient beings and preaches the Dharma according to their inclinations."
"Furthermore, having thoroughly cultivated the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhibala*), he takes on a body for the sake of sentient beings, yet remains untainted by suffering or pleasure.

This bodhisattva, among sentient beings, may act as a father or a son, a teacher or a disciple, a master or a slave; he may become an elephant or a horse, or one who rides an elephant or horse; at times he is wealthy, noble, and powerful, and at other times poor and lowly—yet amidst all these circumstances, he is not defiled.
He is like a person conjured by a Buddha, who performs all manner of tasks without being stained by suffering or pleasure.
"Regarding all matters": this refers to previously manifesting various kinds of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodies to deliver sentient beings.
"Untainted by suffering or pleasure" means not giving rise to attachment amidst pleasure nor giving rise to aversion amidst suffering;
it is unlike the sentient beings of saṃsāra who give rise to afflictions wherever they encounter circumstances.
A bodhisattva should thus sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.
Question: Since the bodhisattva’s supernatural powers perform specific tasks, why are they called "sporting"?
Answer: "Play" (līlā) refers to the various transformations manifested by a magician;
the various manifestations and transformations produced by the supernatural powers (abhijñā) of a Bodhisattva are called "play."
Furthermore, among the three samādhis in the Buddha-dharma, emptiness (śūnyatā) is called the "superior practice. Why is this?
Because it resembles nirvāṇa in being without attachment and without attainment.
All other dharmas of practice are termed "lowest of the low," like small children.
Therefore, it is said that the power of supernormal faculties (abhijñā) is called "playful sport" (vikrīḍita), for it is of the utmost utility in maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields.
Regarding the maturation of sentient beings, it is stated in this [text]:
"Purifying the Buddha-field, they cultivate roots of goodness together. Question:
Why is it necessary to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings and purify the Buddha-lands?
The answer is:
The Buddha himself explained the causes and conditions:
"If one does not bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the Buddha-fields, one cannot attain the Unsurpassed Way. Why is this?
Because if the causes and conditions are not fully assembled, one cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Conditions" refer to all wholesome dharmas.

From the initial generation of the mind of awakening through the practice of the *dānapāramitā* up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), within these practiced dharmas, there is no recollection or conceptual discrimination such as:
"this is the giver," "this is the material object," or "this is the recipient."
This applies likewise even to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

If a bodhisattva practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) up to the eighteen unique qualities with a mind free from attachment and without conceptual discrimination, this constitutes the causal condition for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By means of this path, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and is able both to deliver oneself and to deliver sentient beings.
Question: If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind of attachment, what fault is there such that it is not called "complete"?
If one practices giving with an attached mind, the gratitude owed by the recipient becomes heavy.
The answer is:
although there may be small benefit, there is great fault.
It is like fine food mixed with poison; although it possesses excellent benefits, one loses one's life because of it.
Question: What is the fault here?
The answer is:
If one gives with an attached mind, then when things do not go as desired, anger arises;
if the recipient does not acknowledge the kindness, resentment and dislike are formed.

If one makes offerings to virtuous people with a mind of attachment, and encounters even slight misfortune or decline, one will then resent that the giving did not bear fruit and regret what was bestowed.
If the mind that gives is followed by regret, the karmic retribution received will not be pure.

Furthermore, one who practices giving with an attached mind is deeply covetous of wealth and property; if someone were to seize or plunder it, they would immediately inflict harm upon them, thinking to themselves:
"I have gathered this wealth for the sake of merit and virtuous deeds; why do you seize and plunder it?"
Previously, out of greed for wealth and goods, one practiced giving for the sake of this life; yet for the sake of future lives, one’s attachment deepens further.
Because of this defiled clinging, if there is any infringement or seizure, it can lead to grave offenses;
due to the causal conditions of these grave offenses, one undergoes the suffering of the three evil realms.
Furthermore, due to the causes and conditions of attachment, anger arises; due to the causes and conditions of anger, one employs blades and staves;
through this killing with blades and staves, one undergoes various sufferings and afflictions.

Furthermore, when a person gives rise to the karma of delusion, there is great lack of peace and security; because they engage in these deceptive and unreal matters, they will inevitably encounter great calamity later on.
All Buddhas of the ten directions proclaim the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*); that all phenomena are characterized by the mark of signlessness is the reality.
If a person grasps at these material objects as having the characteristics of being deceptive and unreal, and subsequently becomes mentally attached to them;
because of this mental attachment, they expect a great karmic reward and are thus able to give them away.
For example, it is like a person who, desiring a large harvest, uses a great quantity of grain seeds.

Likewise, giving with an attached mind results in meager and impure rewards that ultimately come to an end; one will undergo unspeakable sorrows and afflictions, all because of grasping at signs. Such are the faults that arise from this.
If one practices giving according to the true nature of reality, such faults do not exist;
throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of birth and death, one will experience various blessings and joys without exhaustion, until finally attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, if a person practices wholesome dharmas with a mind of attachment, and upon hearing that all dharmas are ultimately empty, immediately abandons the dharmas they were practicing to become attached to this dharma of emptiness, grasping at its signs and regarding it as real while deeming their former practice to be false and deceptive—
such a person loses two kinds of dharmas:
they lose their previous wholesome dharmas and fall into wrong views.
Those who harbor attachment have such faults;
it is like a person with a grave illness who, despite having many medicines, finds that although they treat him, there is no improvement, and the medicine itself becomes an illness.
When one practices various meritorious virtues with a mind of attachment, there are faults such as these.
A bodhisattva abandons the mind of attachment and does not grasp at the characteristics of emptiness;
they view suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the same way they view the dharmas of giving and so forth.
One dedicates [the merit] for the sake of all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they form this thought:

"Just as the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time possess ultimate pure wisdom that knows the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they likewise know the characteristics of this giving."
"I also dedicate by means of this very nature.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva does not employ or practice within all five sense-faculties or within the mental states and mental factors, because they are unable to know the characteristics of dharmas.
All these phenomena arise from conditions and are deceptive, for they lack intrinsic nature;
I now wish to know the true reality of all phenomena through dedication, wherein all these deceptions enter into the true reality without any distinction.
Because I have not yet attained the pure, true wisdom regarding all phenomena, I engage in discrimination between what is false and what is real.
When one knows through pure wisdom, all things are seen as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
having entered into the ultimate truth, all are pure and without distinction.
Thus, one dedicates acts such as giving all the way until the path of Buddhahood is reached.
Therefore it is said:
"The mind that is free from discrimination is able to practice giving and other virtues; this is called the true path of a Bodhisattva."
Chapter 84: The Four Noble Truths. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Commentary on the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths, Number Eighty-Four. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what then are the dharmas of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding your question, 'If these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what then are the dharmas of a Buddha?'—Subhūti!"
The Dharma of a bodhisattva is also the Dharma of a Buddha.
If one knows all modes [of existence], one attains the knowledge of all modes; having severed all afflictions and their habitual tendencies, the bodhisattva shall attain this Dharma.
Once the Buddha has known all dharmas through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! This is the distinction between a bodhisattva and a buddha.
It is like the difference between one who is on the path and one who has attained the fruit; both are noble ones (ārya).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices within the path of non-obstruction, he is called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva";
when there is no longer any darkness or obscuration within the path of liberation, he is a Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty of their own marks (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), how can there be distinctions and differences within these dharmas that are empty of their own marks—such as ‘this is a hell-being,’ ‘this is a hungry ghost,’ ‘this is an animal,’ ‘this is a deva,’ ‘this is a human,’ ‘this is a person of the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*)’, ‘this is a person of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka*)’, ‘this is a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*)’, ‘this is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)’, ‘this is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)’, ‘this is an arhat’, ‘this is a pratyekabuddha’, ‘this is a bodhisattva’, or ‘this is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’?”
“World-Honored One!
Just as these persons cannot be apprehended, so too the causes and conditions of karma cannot be apprehended, and the retribution of fruit cannot be apprehended!
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is! As you have said, within phenomena that are empty of self-characteristics, there are no sentient beings, no causes and conditions of karma, and no retributive fruits."
Subhūti! Sentient beings do not know that these dharmas are empty of their own characteristics; yet they perform karmic actions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Due to the causes and conditions of such sinful karma, they fall into the three evil realms.
By reason of meritorious karma, one is born among humans or devas;
by reason of immovable karma, one is born in the realm of form or the formless realm.
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving up to the eighteen unique qualities, they fully undertake and practice all these factors conducive to enlightenment.
By means of the vajra-like samādhi, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
having attained it, one benefits sentient beings.
Because this benefit is never lost, one does not fall into the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
after the Buddha has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does he still attain the cycle of birth and death within the five realms?”
The Buddha said: "It is not so, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there karma that is black, or white, or neither black nor white?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One! If these are not attained,
how can you speak of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, devas, srotāpannas, up to arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas?"

“Subhūti! If sentient beings knew that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not seek unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, nor would they deliver sentient beings from the three evil destinies, nor from the cycle of birth and death involving wandering through the five realms of existence.”
Subhūti! Because sentient beings truly do not know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the five realms.
These bodhisattvas, having heard from the Buddhas that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, resolve their minds to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti! All dharmas are not as they are grasped by ordinary people.

Within these dharmas that do not exist, sentient beings, through inverted false conceptualization and discrimination, apprehend dharmas—where there is no sentient being, they perceive the mark of a sentient being; where there is no form, they perceive the mark of form; and where there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they perceive the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Even though all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are non-existent, by means of a mind of inverted false conceptualization, one creates the causes and conditions for the karma of body, speech, and mind, thereby wandering through the births and deaths of the five destinies without attaining liberation.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they internalize all wholesome dharmas within the perfection of wisdom, practice the bodhisattva path, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he shall preach the Four Noble Truths—suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—to sentient beings, revealing, elucidating, and analyzing them.

All wholesome dharmas that assist the path to enlightenment are subsumed within the Four Noble Truths; it is by means of these wholesome dharmas that assist the path that the Three Jewels are distinguished.
What are the three?
“The Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel.
Because they do not believe in and instead reject these Three Jewels, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is one delivered by means of the Noble Truth of Suffering?
Or is one delivered by means of the knowledge of suffering?”
Is one delivered by means of the noble truth of the origin [of suffering]?
Is one delivered by means of the knowledge of the origin?
Is one delivered by means of the noble truth of cessation?
Is one delivered by means of the knowledge of cessation?
Is one delivered by means of the noble truth of the path?
Or is one delivered by means of the knowledge of the path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One does not attain liberation through the noble truth of suffering, nor through the knowledge of suffering;
likewise, one does not attain liberation through the noble truth of the path, nor through the knowledge of the path."
Subhūti! Because these four noble truths are equal, I say they are themselves nirvāṇa;

one does not attain nirvāṇa by means of the noble truth of suffering, nor by the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path, nor by the knowledge of suffering, nor by the knowledge of origination, cessation, or the path.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the equality of the four noble truths?”

“Subhūti! If there is no suffering and no knowledge of suffering, no origin and no knowledge of the origin, no cessation and no knowledge of cessation, and no path and no knowledge of the path—this is called the equality of the four noble truths.”
Furthermore, Subhūti, the suchness, non-alteration,

dharma-characteristic, dharma-nature, dharma-abiding, dharma-position, and reality-limit of these four noble truths remain ever-present as dharma-characteristics whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, for they are non-deceptive and non-perishing.
"When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of penetrating the true reality.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the sake of penetrating the ultimate truth, by means of that penetration of the ultimate truth, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but enter directly into the rank of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives all dharmas as they truly are;
having perceived them, he attains the dharma of non-existence;"

Having attained the dharma of non-existence, one perceives that all dharmas are empty—both those dharmas subsumed within the Four Noble Truths and those not subsumed within the Four Noble Truths are all empty.
If one contemplates in this way, at that time, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva;
this is called the bodhisattva abiding in the stage of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-bhūmi), from which there is no falling back from the summit.
Because of such a fall from the summit, one would fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

This bodhisattva, dwelling within the stage of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), is able to give rise to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Dwelling in this initial stage of determination, this bodhisattva discriminates all dharmas and penetrates the Four Noble Truths:
they know suffering, yet do not give rise to a mind that takes suffering as its object.
Even up to the point of knowing the Path, they do not give rise to a mind that takes the Path as its object;
rather, they accord with the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and contemplate all dharmas according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
“World-Honored One!
How does one contemplate all dharmas according to their true mark?
The Buddha said:
“Contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena.
“World-Honored One,
what is emptiness?”
The Buddha said:
"Their intrinsic nature is empty.

This bodhisattva uses such wisdom to contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena; there is no nature of dharmas that can be seen, nor is there any abiding within such a nature through which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Because the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

it is not something produced by the Buddhas, nor produced by the *pratyekabuddhas*, nor produced by the *arhats*, nor produced by those on the path, nor produced by those who have attained the fruit, nor produced by the bodhisattvas.

However, because sentient beings do not know and do not see the true reality of all phenomena as it is, for this reason, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, employs the power of skillful means to preach the Dharma for these sentient beings.
[Śāstra] Question:
There is a great difference between the Buddha-dharma and the Bodhisattva-dharma:
the Buddha is omniscient (*sarvajña*), whereas the bodhisattva is not yet omniscient.
Subhūti, for what reason did he give rise to doubt and ask the Buddha:
"What are the dharmas of the bodhisattvas?
What are the dharmas of the Buddhas?"
He replied:
"In this context, the Buddha taught that a bodhisattva should practice the six pāramitās and so forth, up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), in accordance with the conduct of a Buddha."
Therefore, Subhūti asked:
"If one practices in the same manner as the Buddha, how does one differ from the Buddha?
The Buddha affirmed his point, stating that it was appropriate to ask in this way.
The spheres of activity for all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are the same; the only difference lies in the sharpness or dullness of one's wisdom.
Herein, the Buddha himself explains the cause and condition:
"Although a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās according to reality, they are not yet exhaustive, nor have they entered all gates; therefore, they are not called a Buddha."

If a bodhisattva has already entered the gateway of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) and entered into the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena, attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, severing all afflictions and habitual tendencies, and attaining sovereign power over all phenomena—at that time, he is called a Buddha.
"Just as on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month, although both are equally 'the moon,' the moon on the fourteenth day cannot cause the tides of the great ocean;

so it is with the Bodhisattva: although they possess true wisdom and purity, because they have not yet fully perfected all the Buddha-dharmas, they cannot move all sentient beings throughout the ten directions."
Just as the waters of the great ocean are made to rise in tide when the moon is at its full brilliance on the fifteenth day, so too is it when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood:
he emits a great radiance that can move the sentient beings of the lands throughout the ten directions.
In this regard, the Buddha himself provides an analogy:
"Just as those who are on the path and those who have attained the fruit are both noble ones (*ārya*), yet there is a distinction between them.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva: one who practices is called a Bodhisattva from the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) until the attainment of the Vajra-samādhi.
The Buddha has already attained the fruit, severed all doubts regarding all phenomena, and has nothing he does not fully understand; therefore, he is called "Buddha.
Subhūti asked again:

"Within phenomena that are empty of self-characteristics, no distinctions can be found—namely, those from hell up to the heavens, those who are ordinary persons or those on the eight stages, and those from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha!"
World-Honored One!
Just as sentient beings in the hells and other realms cannot be apprehended, the causes and conditions of karma should likewise be unapprehendable. Why is this so?
The agent cannot be found;
because the action cannot be found, the retribution also cannot be found.
Why, then, does the Buddha say there is a distinction between a Buddha and a bodhisattva?
The Buddha affirmed Subhūti’s intention and replied to him with the very question he had asked:
"Because sentient beings do not know that the nature of phenomena is empty, they are able to give rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma."
As explained at length in the sutras:
"Sentient beings" refers to ordinary worldlings who have not yet entered the state of certainty;
these people possess the inversion of a self-centered mind and, due to the causes and conditions of their afflictions, give rise to various karmas.
Karma is of three kinds:
bodily, verbal, and mental.
These three types of karma are further divided into two kinds:
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, whether with outflows or without outflows:
due to unwholesome karma one falls into the three evil destinies; due to wholesome karma one is born among gods or humans.
Wholesome karma is further divided into two types:
first, that which is bound to the desire realm; second, that which is bound to the form and formless realms.
Karma that leads to birth in the form and formless realms is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*); because it is immovable karma, one is born in the form and formless realms.

If sentient beings were to know for themselves that the nature of all phenomena is empty, they would immediately not give rise to a mind of attachment. Because a mind of attachment does not arise, karma would not be produced, and they would not even be reborn in the realms of form or formlessness.
Because they do not truly know [the nature of things], they arise.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas fully undertake and practice the dharmas beginning with giving up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), without loss and without deficiency;
even by means of the Vajra-like Samādhi, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and bring great benefit to sentient beings.
Because sentient beings obtain these benefits, they no longer undergo the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Subhūti asked again:
"When the Buddha attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, did he truly attain these five realms?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted. He asked:
The Buddha previously stated that "because of great benefit, one does not fall into the five realms of existence," yet now he says "one does not attain. How is this so?
The answer is:
to definitively grasp at signs is wrong view; thus one falls into wrong view.

The cycle of birth and death within the five destinies cannot be found; it is merely that ordinary people, through the conditions of inversion, give rise to karma, and thus there is a conventional designation of the birth and death of the five destinies, though in reality they are like illusions and dreams.
He asked again:
"Are the four kinds of karma—the black, the white, and so forth—attained?
The Buddha said:
"No. 'Black karma' refers to unwholesome karma;
its retribution consists of places of suffering, such as the hells."
Among these beings, because they are utterly oppressed by great suffering and distress, it is called "black.
The place where one experiences the retribution of wholesome karma refers to the various devas;
because they experience pleasure according to their will with clarity and mastery, it is called "white karma."
This karma belongs to the heavens of the three realms;
it is the sphere where the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma are experienced, namely the eight classes of beings such as humans and asuras.
Because one experiences both pleasure and suffering in these places, it is called "white-and-black karma."

"Outflow-free karma" (*anāsrava-karma*) can destroy unwholesome karma with outflows (*sāsrava-karma*) and can uproot sentient beings, causing them to leave behind the retributions of both good and evil.
Question: Since outflow-free karma should be white, why is it said to be neither white nor black?
Answer:

Although untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are pure and stainless, because they are characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they are devoid of conceptual discrimination; thus, one cannot say they are "white."
Black and white are relative phenomena; since there is no relativity herein, one cannot speak of "white.

Furthermore, untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is able to extinguish all things. Because black and white exist through conceptual differentiation within various contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), and because there is no such contemplation herein, there is no "white."
Subhūti asked again:
"If these four kinds of karma cannot be apprehended, how can one differentiate between the hells and so forth up to arhatship?
If there is no black karma, how can one speak of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts?"
If there were no white karma, how could one speak of gods and humans?
If there were no black or white karma, how could one speak of the path of the asuras?
If there were no karma that is neither white nor black, how could one speak of those from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat?
The Buddha replied:

"If all sentient beings were to know for themselves that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, Bodhisattvas would not give rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor would they pull sentient beings out from within the six realms of existence."
Why is this? Because if sentient beings themselves knew that the nature of all phenomena is empty, there would be nothing to deliver;
it is like not needing medicine when one is without illness, or not needing the light of a lamp when there is no darkness.

Subhūti! Because sentient beings today do not truly know that the dharmas of self-characteristic emptiness, they follow their minds to grasp at signs and give rise to attachment. Because of this attachment, they become defiled; because of defilement, they pursue the five desires; because they pursue the five desires, they are shrouded by greed. Due to the causes and conditions of greed, there arise stinginess, deception, jealousy, anger, and strife. Because of anger, they commit various sinful karmas, remaining without any discerning knowledge.

Therefore, at the end of their lives, they are born in those places according to the causes and conditions of their karma; they continue to perform the karma of birth and death, constantly wandering through the six realms of existence without end.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva hears from the Buddhas and their disciples the teaching that all phenomena are empty, they feel compassion for sentient beings, thinking:

"Sentient beings give rise to attachment due to madness, folly, and inversion; I shall become a Buddha, shatter the inversions of sentient beings, and cause them to understand the empty nature of all phenomena."
Why is this? All phenomena are not as they are grasped by ordinary people. Sentient beings and phenomena have no fixed reality;
it is merely that within what is non-existent, they engage in recollection, imagination, and discrimination, hoping to find something to be attained.

In that which is devoid of sentient beings, they give rise to the perception of sentient beings; in that which is devoid of form, they give rise to the perception of form; and in that which is devoid of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they give rise to the perception of consciousness.
Because of such madness and inversion, these people are able to produce karma of body, speech, and mind, and are unable to escape from the cycle of birth and death within the six realms.
If one merely gives rise to the notion of sentient beings and phenomena, the fetters are still light and it is easy to attain deliverance.
However, if one gives rise to greed and hatred, thereby committing various grave karmas therein, this constitutes a heavy fetter;
once one undergoes the retribution of these karmic fruits, it is difficult to attain deliverance—just as when fine dust accumulates to form a mountain, it is difficult to move.

For the sake of these sentient beings, the bodhisattva wishes to destroy the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of birth and death; therefore, within the *prajñā*, he encompasses all wholesome dharmas, practices the bodhisattva path, and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For the sake of sentient beings, he preached the Four Noble Truths—namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—revealing and expounding them through various causes and conditions.
Question:

The Buddha has practiced the subtle and wondrous Dharma for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—namely, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), up to the unimpeded liberations and all profound karmic activities. Why, then, does he speak only of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
Answer: Among all that which sentient beings fear and find urgent, nothing surpasses suffering;
only after eliminating suffering does one then show them the Buddha-way.
It is like a person with a grave illness who first makes the removal of the disease their urgent priority;
only afterward do they adorn their body with precious objects and clothing.
As for suffering: the body, which consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), is the root of all suffering, for its very nature is suffering.
Briefly stated, this suffering consists of birth, old age, sickness, and so forth, as explained extensively in various places throughout the sutras.
As for the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*), it refers to craving and other afflictions (*kleśa*).

Craving is a long-standing condition within the mind; for this reason, the Buddha said, "Craving can produce future existence, and is therefore the cause of suffering. This cause of suffering is precisely the origin.
If a person wishes to abandon suffering, they must first sever craving; when craving is severed, suffering is extinguished, for the severing of craving is itself the extinction of suffering.

The extinction of suffering is the Path. One contemplates these various causes and conditions of the five aggregates, as well as the faults and evils of suffering and its origin—namely, that they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, being like a disease, like a wound, like an enemy, and like a thief—and so forth. Within the eightfold noble path, this constitutes right view, while the remaining seven factors assist in its realization and initiation, enabling one to sever craving within all phenomena;
it is like using wine to activate medicine.
This person has no further craving for anything in all the worlds; having attained liberation from the fire of suffering, the Buddha then reveals the sublime Dharma to them.
Furthermore, herein the Buddha himself explains the causal conditions, namely:
"Within the Four Noble Truths, all wholesome dharmas are subsumed."
Someone asks:
"Why does the Buddha speak only of the four dharmas, such as suffering?
For this reason, the Buddha says:
"All wholesome dharmas that assist the Path are subsumed within the Four Noble Truths.
Due to the causes and conditions of these wholesome dharmas that assist the Path, the Three Jewels are distinguished.
Because sentient beings do not have faith in the Three Jewels, they are unable to escape the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
Question: Why does Subhūti pose such a coarse question, saying:
"Is it by means of suffering that there is cessation, or by means of the knowledge of suffering that there is cessation?"
"By the cessation of what accumulation, and by the cessation of what knowledge of accumulation? He replied:
"This is no coarse question!"
Now I ask:
"Is it because one perceives the essence of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, that [defilements] are extinguished?
Or is it by means of wisdom that they are extinguished?"
Because afflictions such as craving have been extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa with remainder*.
If one were to attain the Way by means of the Truth of Suffering alone, then all sentient beings—even cattle, sheep, and the like—should also attain the Way!
If one attains the Path by means of the knowledge of suffering, then when one is free from suffering, there is no such knowledge;
being free from the knowledge of suffering, it is not called the "Truth of Suffering," but is simply called "suffering."

Because the Truth of Suffering arises through the conjunction of suffering and the knowledge of suffering, one cannot say that it is "extinguished by suffering alone" or "extinguished by knowledge alone.
This applies likewise up to the Truth of the Path.
The Buddha replied:
"It is not extinguished by the truth of suffering, nor is it extinguished by the knowledge of suffering; this applies likewise up to the truth of the path and the knowledge of the path. I say:"
"This equality of the four truths is itself cessation;
it does not cease by means of the truth of suffering, nor does it cease by means of any up to the truth of the path. Why is this so?

These four dharmas, beginning with suffering, are all produced from conditions; they are false and unreal, and because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are not called real. Since they are unreal, how could they be extinguished?
Question:
The two truths are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and are phenomena practiced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); therefore, they may be deceptive and unreal.

However, the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is an outflow-free phenomenon (*anāsravadharma*) and is free from attachment; although it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, it is not deceptive.
Furthermore, the Truth of Cessation is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and does not exist by way of causes and conditions.
How then can it be said that "all four dharmas are false and deceptive"?
The answer is:
Upon first attaining the Way, one knows that the two truths are deceptive.

When about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one likewise realizes that the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is deceptive; thus, through the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi* and other such concentrations, one relinquishes the truth of the path, as illustrated by the analogy of the raft.
The truth of cessation is likewise not a fixed dharma.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Apart from the conditioned, there is no unconditioned; it is because of the conditioned that the unconditioned is spoken of."
The cessation of suffering is like the extinguishing of a lamp; one should not engage in frivolous conceptualization to seek its location.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Cessation is not attained by means of suffering, nor even by means of the Path."
Subhūti asked the Buddha,
"What is the equality of the Four Noble Truths?
The Buddha replied:
If there were no locus for the eight dharmas—namely, the Four Noble Truths and the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths—that would be equality.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Four Noble Truths are suchness, non-deceptive, and unchanging; they are suchness, the dharma-nature, the dharma-characteristic, the dharma-abiding, and the limit of reality. Whether a Buddha exists or not, these dharma-characteristics abide eternally; they do not depend upon the mind, mental factors, or various contemplations, but exist solely so as not to deceive sentient beings.

All other dharmas that abide therein are inverted, for they arise from the false attachment to inverted retributions; although they can bestow joy and bliss upon humans and devas, they are all ultimately empty, false, and subject to change over time.
There is, however, but one dharma—namely, the true mark of all dharmas—which, because it is non-deceptive, abides eternally and is never extinguished.
In this way, the bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and penetrates the true reality (*bhūtārtha*) of all phenomena.
Subhūti asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva penetrate and attain the true reality, thereby transcending the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha and entering the rank of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha replied:

"If a bodhisattva contemplates, deliberates, and seeks all dharmas, not a single dharma can be found with a fixed characteristic; he sees that all dharmas are empty—whether they pertain to the Four Noble Truths or do not pertain to the Four Noble Truths."
Those that are not among the Four Truths are space and cessation not through deliberation;
the remainder are contained within the Four Truths.
If one contemplates such dharmas as empty, at that time, one enters the stage of a bodhisattva.
Question: Why is it not said that "one enters the stage of a bodhisattva by means of the contemplation that emptiness is also empty"? Answer:
There is no need for such an explanation. Why?
Because if one says that all dharmas are empty, that very emptiness is itself empty; emptiness is also empty.
If it were both empty and not empty, it could not be called "all-empty.
Therefore, by practicing this emptiness, one attains entry into the stage of the bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva dwells within this stage of nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), they do not fall from the summit.
The "stage of nature" (dharmatā-bhūmi) refers to the fixed position of the bodhisattva-dharma.
Just as in the Śrāvaka-dharma, the stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) are called the stage of nature.
Because these dharmas accord with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), they are called "nature" (*gotra*); one who dwells therein must expect to attain the Path.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva: dwelling securely within this stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*), he must expect to become a Buddha.
He is able to give rise to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless concentrations.

This bodhisattva, dwelling within the stages of dhyāna, collects his mind and discriminatively contemplates and deliberates upon all dharmas, thereby penetrating the Four Noble Truths—namely, knowing and seeing suffering, yet not giving rise to a mind that takes suffering as its object-condition.
One knows that suffering arises because ordinary people receive a body and become attached to the causes and conditions of suffering, thereby undergoing various anxieties and afflictions;
these bodies are all like thieves and like enemies, being impermanent, empty, and so forth.

Having attained this, he immediately relinquishes it; he does not grasp at the characteristic of suffering, nor does he take the truth of suffering as an object, due to the power of the bodhisattva’s stage of dharma-position (*dharmatā-avasthā*).
This applies likewise even up to the truth of the path.
One should simply direct the mind single-mindedly toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Knowing that these Four Noble Truths are like medicine applied to a disease, one should not become attached to them; rather, one should contemplate all phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), without engaging in the fourfold conceptual discrimination.
Subhūti asked:
"How does one contemplate all phenomena as they truly are?
The Buddha said:
“Contemplate emptiness,
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva can contemplate all phenomena— whether great or small— as empty, this is called contemplating according to reality.”
He asked again,
"By means of what emptiness?
The Buddha replied:
"By means of the emptiness of self-characteristics. Question:
Among the eighteen kinds of emptiness, why does the Buddha speak only of the emptiness of self-characteristics?
Answer: This is the emptiness of the Middle Way.

Internal and external emptiness and so forth are minor emptiness; ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of non-apprehension and so forth are profound emptiness; and the emptiness of self-characteristics is middle emptiness.
Because their own-characteristics have been refuted through reasoning, their minds do not sink, and they are able to enter the profound emptiness.

Having attained such a dharma, these bodhisattvas contemplate all dharmas as empty; they do not perceive even a single dharma possessing an intrinsic nature in which they might abide, yet they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One contemplates all phenomena as being like *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* itself is empty of intrinsic nature;
it is not made by a Buddha, nor made by great Bodhisattvas, nor made by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas; it is a state of perpetual quiescence, free from the proliferation of conceptual discourse.

Sentient beings are unable to know or see things as they truly are; therefore, the Bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and, through the power of skillful means, preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Regarding the power of skillful means: the bodhisattva attains the dharma of the forbearance of non-arising, enters the stage of a bodhisattva, and penetrates the bodhisattva’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
He contemplates these marks of the path as profoundly deep and subtle, characterized by neither attainment nor relinquishment;
since they cannot be apprehended even by sublime wisdom, how much less can they be expressed through speech!
With a heart of great compassion, he reflects deeply:
"Sentient beings fall into the three evil realms because of empty matters, undergoing intense and grievous suffering;
if I were to preach this Dharma directly, they would neither believe nor accept it, and by destroying the Dharma, they would fall into hell!"

I shall now accomplish all wholesome dharmas and adorn my body with the thirty-two marks; I shall guide sentient beings, give rise to the immeasurable and boundless supernatural powers of all Buddhas, attain the Buddha-way, become the sovereign among all assemblies, and achieve mastery over all dharmas.
"If sentient beings would still accept even when evil dharmas are praised, how much more so when the true Dharma is taught!
Thus, this bodhisattva practices according to his aspirations and reflects accordingly, preaching for the sake of sentient beings to cause them all to attain liberation.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Scroll Ninety-four.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter on the Seven Similes, Number Eighty-five;
Scroll Ninety-five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 85: The Seven Similes. [Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the nature of all phenomena is non-existent, and is not created by Buddhas, nor created by Pratyekabuddhas, nor created by Arhats, nor created by Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, or Srotāpannas; nor created by those on the path, nor by those who have attained the fruits, nor by Bodhisattvas—how can one differentiate between the various distinctions of phenomena, such as: "this is hell," "this is the animal realm," "this is the realm of hungry ghosts," "this is a human," "this is a deva," and so forth, up to "this is the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception"?
By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows there are those born in the hells;
by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows there are those born among animals or hungry ghosts;

and by reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one knows there are those born among human beings, or born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, up to and including birth in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
It is by reason of these karmic causes and conditions that one knows there are those who attain the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha;
it is by reason of these karmic causes and conditions that one knows these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
and it is by reason of these karmic causes and conditions that one knows the tathāgatas, arhats, and samyaksaṃbuddhas?
“World-Honored One!
Within dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, there is no karmic activity.

It is due to the causes and conditions of performing actions that one falls into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm; or is born among humans and devas, up to being born in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.”
By reason of these karmic causes and conditions, one attains the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha;

and when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the bodhisattva path, they shall attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), and by attaining all-knowledge, they are able to pull sentient beings out from within birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
Subhūti, dharmas that lack intrinsic nature have neither karma nor karmic retribution.

Ordinary persons do not enter the noble Dharma; because they do not know that all dharmas are without the characteristic of intrinsic nature, and due to their perversion and delusion, they give rise to various causes and conditions of karma.
These sentient beings receive bodies according to their karma:

whether a body in hell, a body as an animal, a body as a hungry ghost, a human body, or a celestial body—whether the body of a deity in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, up to the body of a deity in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
These phenomena that lack intrinsic nature have neither karma nor karmic retribution; that which lacks intrinsic nature is eternally without intrinsic nature.
As Subhūti has said:
"If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, how is it that from the stream-enterer up to the Buddhas one attains the knowledge of all aspects?"
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the path without intrinsic nature?"
“Is the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the all-aspect omniscience of all Buddhas,
devoid of intrinsic nature? Subhūti replied,
“World-Honored One, it is.”
“The Path has no intrinsic nature; the fruit of srotāpanna also has no intrinsic nature, and so on up to the omniscience of all Buddhas, which likewise has no intrinsic nature. “Subhūti!
“Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature attain a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature? “No,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Can a dharma that has intrinsic nature obtain a dharma that has intrinsic nature?
“No, [Blessed One].”
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Subhūti!

The dharmas of non-nature and the Path—all these dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are without color, without form, without resistance, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness.”
Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the prajñāpāramitā, they employ skillful means to see that sentient beings, due to their inversions, are attached to the five aggregates:
perceiving permanence in the impermanent, pleasure in suffering, purity in the impure, and a self in the non-self; thus they are attached to that which is non-existent.
"By means of skillful power, this bodhisattva draws sentient beings out from within non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
Is there anything real about that which ordinary people are attached to, such that it is not different [from reality]?
Because of attachment, they give rise to karma;
because of the conditions of karma, they fail to escape from birth and death within the five realms of existence?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In the basis for the arising of karma upon which ordinary persons are attached, there is not even as much as a hair’s breadth of a real thing; it is merely due to inversion.”
Subhūti! I shall now speak a parable for you, for the wise gain understanding through parables. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Is there a real dwelling place for the person seen in a dream who experiences the pleasures of the five senses?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Even a dream is illusory and unobtainable; how much more so for one who dwells within a dream to experience the pleasures of the five desires!
“What do you think?”
“Among all phenomena—whether they be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—is there any that is not like a dream?
“World-Honored One!
Among all phenomena—whether they be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—there is none that is not like a dream.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
In a dream, is there the coming and going through birth and death within the five realms of existence?"
“World-Honored One,
there is not. “What do you think?”
“In a dream, one practices the path; by means of this practice of the path, does one become defiled or does one attain purity?
“No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because these dream-phenomena have no substantial reality;
they cannot be described as either defiled or pure. "What do you think?"

Does the reflection in a mirror possess a real entity that can serve as the causal condition for the arising of karma? By means of such karmic conditions, would one fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm; or would one become a human or a deva—from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-perception?
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!”

This image has no substantial reality; it merely deceives small children. How could there possibly be karmic causes and conditions in such a thing? By what karmic causes and conditions could one fall into the hells, or even reach the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“What do you think?
Does this reflection in a mirror have a path of cultivation? By means of that path of cultivation, would it become defiled or would it attain purity?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"This image is empty and lacks any substantial reality;
it cannot be described as either defiled or pure. "What do you think?

Suppose there is an echo in a deep ravine. Does that echo have karmic causes and conditions? By virtue of those karmic causes and conditions, would it fall into hell, or even be reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!”

Since these things are empty and lack any real sound, how could there be karmic causes and conditions? How could one, by means of such karmic causes and conditions, fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“What do you think?
Does that echo possess a path of cultivation, such that by means of this path of cultivation it would either become defiled or attain purity? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
This matter is without reality; it cannot be said to be either defiled or pure.
“What do you think?”

Just as a mirage is not water despite having the appearance of water, nor is it a river despite having the appearance of a river—does that mirage possess any karmic causes and conditions? And by means of those karmic causes and conditions, could it fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
"No, World-Honored One!

Water in a mirage is ultimately unobtainable; it merely deceives the eyes of the ignorant. How could there be karmic causes and conditions, by which one would fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
"What do you think?
Does this flame have a path of cultivation? By means of such a path of cultivation, would it become defiled or would it attain purity? "No, sir!"
“World-Honored One!
This mirage has no substantial reality; it cannot be described as either defiled or pure. “What do you think?

Regarding a city of the gandharvas: when a city of the gandharvas is seen at sunrise, an ignorant person perceives a city where there is no city, perceives a palace where there is no palace, and perceives a garden where there is no garden.”

Does this city of the gandharvas have any karmic causes and conditions? By means of such karmic causes and conditions, could one fall into hell or even be reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
"No, World-Honored One! This city of the Gandharvas is ultimately unobtainable;

it merely deceives the eyes of the foolish. How could there be karmic causes and conditions, and by means of such karmic causes and conditions, fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
“What do you think?
Does this city of the gandharvas have a path of cultivation, by means of which path of cultivation one might become defiled or attain purity?”
"No, World-Honored One!
This city of the Gandharvas has no substantial reality; it cannot be described as either defiled or pure."
“Subhūti, what do you think?
If a magician were to conjure various things by magic— whether an elephant, a horse, an ox, a sheep, a man, or a woman— what do you think?”

“Does this illusion have karmic causes and conditions? By means of these karmic causes and conditions, does it fall into the hells or even take birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? “No, it does not.”
World-Honored One!

Since these illusory dharmas are empty and lack substantial reality, how could there be karmic causes and conditions? By means of such karmic causes and conditions, how could one fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“What do you think?
By means of this illusory cultivation of the path, or by means of that cultivation of the path, would one become defiled or would one attain purity? “No, indeed!”
“World-Honored One!
These dharmas have no substantial reality; they cannot be described as defiled or pure.
“Subhūti! [the Buddha replied.]
What do you think?

If there were a person created by a Buddha through transformation, would that transformed person have karma as a causal condition, and by means of that karmic causal condition, fall into hell or even be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
"No, World-Honored One! This emanated person has no substantial reality;
