Regarding the "Samādhi Like a Vajra": just as a vajra can shatter all mountains, so too does this samādhi;
it can shatter all obstacles to the dharmas of the six pāramitās, leading directly to the path of Buddhahood.
Regarding "the samādhi of not fearing attachment to forms": one who attains this samādhi does not even become attached to celestial forms, let alone other forms!
Regarding "the samādhi of attaining victory": whatever one wishes to accomplish, one is always able to achieve victory and never suffer defeat.

Regarding the "Samādhi of Turning the Eye": one who attains this samādhi causes Māra and his followers—who wish to see faults in the Bodhisattva—to turn their views and instead perceive him as virtuous.
Regarding the "Samādhi of the Ultimate Dharma-nature": one who attains this samādhi perceives that all dharmas ultimately enter into the dharma-nature.

Regarding the "Samādhi Capable of Bestowing Peace and Security": one who attains this samādhi, although wandering through the six realms of rebirth, knows for themselves that they will certainly become a Buddha, remaining peaceful, joyful, and free from sorrow.
Regarding the "Lion’s Roar Samādhi": those who enter this samādhi are all able to subdue all māras and followers of external paths, such that none dare to oppose them.
Regarding "the Samādhi of Surpassing All Sentient Beings": having attained this samādhi, one is most supreme among all sentient beings.
There are two kinds of "all": first, all in name; second, all in reality.

Because he excels among those ordinary beings who have minds attached to the three realms, as well as among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those who have newly resolved to attain awakening but have not yet attained this samādhi, it is said that he surpasses "all."

Regarding the "Flower Adornment Samādhi": one who attains this samādhi sees the Buddhas of the ten directions seated upon lotus flowers made of the seven precious jewels; from the midst of space, precious lotus flowers rain down upon those Buddhas.
Regarding "the samādhi of severing doubt": one who attains this samādhi is able to sever all the doubts of sentient beings, even though they have not yet attained Buddhahood.
Regarding "the samādhi that accords with all that is firm": the true mark of all dharmas (*dharmatā*) is called "firm";
one who attains this samādhi accords with the true mark of all dharmas and does not accord with other dharmas.

Regarding "Emerging from all dharmas to attain the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and samādhi": one who attains this samādhi transcends all dharmas of ordinary beings and attains the six supernormal knowledges, the ten powers (*bala*), and the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva.

Regarding "the samādhi that can penetrate all dharmas": one who attains this samādhi penetrates and does not dwell within the suchness, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit of all dharmas, up to the equality of all dharmas.
Regarding "the Samādhi of the Seal of the Wealth of All Dharmas": "Wealth" refers to wholesome dharmas, and "seal" refers to their characteristic mark.
Just as when a person obtains a seal or ribbon, no one dares to treat them with contempt or alter them;
so too, when a Bodhisattva obtains the seal of the wealth of wholesome dharmas, none can create obstacles or difficulties for them.
Regarding "the samādhi of non-discriminative vision of all dharmas": if one discriminates among dharmas, then feelings of aversion and attachment arise;
one who attains this samādhi perceives all dharmas without making such discriminations.

Regarding "the samādhi of being free from all views": as for "views," they refer to the sixty-two false views, as well as the grasping at signs within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), up to and including views of the Buddha, views of the Dharma, views of the Saṃgha, and views of nirvāṇa—all of these are termed "views."
Why is this? Because grasping at signs gives rise to a mind of attachment.
"The Samādhi of Detachment from All Signs" is precisely the samādhi associated with the gate of liberation through signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).
Regarding "the samādhi of being detached from all attachments": because one is detached from all marks (*nimitta*), one does not cling even to all phenomena (*dharma*).
Regarding "the samādhi of removing all indolence": one who attains this samādhi, as described herein, may remain for up to seven years without sitting or lying down.
When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are always free from a mind of indolence, continuing until they attain Buddhahood without ever ceasing.
Regarding "the attainment of the Samādhi of Profound Dharma-Illumination": "profound dharma" refers to all the Buddhas' dharmas, their universal wisdom, and so forth;
because the bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are able to see the Buddha-dharmas from afar, contemplate and deliberate upon them, and know them to be profoundly subtle and peerless.
Regarding "the samādhi that cannot be taken away": one who attains this samādhi practices the Dharma of a bodhisattva such that no one can thwart their resolve.

Regarding "the samādhi that destroys Māra": by the power of attaining this samādhi, although Māra is the lord of the desire realm, the bodhisattva is able to destroy Māra’s activities while in a human body.

Regarding "the samādhi of non-attachment to the three realms": having attained this samādhi, although the body remains within the three realms, the mind constantly dwells in nirvāṇa; therefore, it is unattached.
Regarding "the Samādhi of Emitting Radiance": one who attains this samādhi can emit immeasurable light that illuminates the ten directions.

Regarding "the Samādhi of Beholding All Buddhas": one who attains this samādhi, although not yet having attained the divine eye or the divine ear, is able to see all Buddhas of the ten directions and hear the Dharma preached by those Buddhas of the ten directions, thereby inquiring about whatever doubts they may have.

While Sadāprarudita dwelt within such samādhis, he immediately beheld immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions amidst great assemblies, teaching the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Scroll Ninety-Seventh. 3.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Explanation of the Sadāprarudita Chapter, Eighty-Eight, Part Two. Scroll Ninety-Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions comforted the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent, noble son!
When we formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, we sought the prajñāpāramitā and attained these various samādhis, just as you have now attained them.
We have attained these various samādhis, skillfully entered the Prajñāpāramitā, perfected the power of expedient means, and abide in the stage of avaivartika.

We contemplate the nature of these samādhis and do not see any dharma that emerges from or enters into samādhi; nor do we see anyone who practices the Buddha-way, nor anyone who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā, which means not to harbor thoughts that these various dharmas exist. Good son!"

We abide in the dharma of non-conceptualization, having attained this golden-hued body, the sixteen-foot radiance, the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor signs, inconceivable wisdom, unsurpassed precepts, unsurpassed samādhi, and unsurpassed insight; we are fully endowed with all meritorious virtues.
Because he is fully endowed with all merits, even a Buddha cannot grasp their characteristics and describe them exhaustively, let alone śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any other beings!
For this reason, son of good family!
Within this Buddha-dharma, you should redouble your reverence and affection, giving rise to a pure mind;
and toward spiritual friends, you should conceive the thought that they are the Buddha.
"Why is this? Because they are protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), Bodhisattvas quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:
"What are those who are my spiritual friends whom I should approach, serve, and make offerings to?
The Buddhas of the ten directions said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and brought you to maturity for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata protects you and instructs you in the prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means—he is your virtuous friend.
If you were to serve and honor the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for one eon, or two eons, or three eons, or even for more than a hundred thousand eons—carrying him on your head with reverence;

and if you were to offer all manner of articles of pleasure, including every exquisite form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch found within the triple-thousandfold world system as your entire offering—you would still not have repaid even a moment’s worth of his kindness.

Why is this? It is because of the causal conditions provided by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata that you have attained such samādhis as these, as well as the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
After the Buddhas had thus instructed and comforted the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, causing him to rejoice, they suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita arose from his samādhi; no longer seeing the Buddhas, he thought to himself:
"From where have these Buddhas come?"
"Where have they gone?
Because he did not see the Buddhas, he was again filled with sorrow and unhappiness, thinking:
"Who will sever my doubts?"
Again, he thought to himself:

"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has for a long, long time practiced the Prajñāpāramitā, attained the power of skillful means and various dhāraṇīs, and achieved mastery within the bodhisattva-dharmas. Having made offerings to many past Buddhas, he has been my teacher life after life and has constantly benefited me. I shall ask the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata: 'From where do all the Buddhas come?'"
"Where have you gone?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita conceived a mind of reverence, affection, and respect for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and he thought to himself:
"With what shall I make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata?"

Now I am poor and destitute; I have no flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, fragrant unguents, robes, banners, or canopies, nor gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, or amber—I lack such things as these with which to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Dharma-preacher, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
"It is not right for me to go to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata empty-handed; if I were to go empty-handed, the heart of joy would not arise.
I should sell my body to obtain wealth, and for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā, make an offering to the Dharma-master, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."

Why is this? Throughout my countless lifetimes, I have lost my body innumerable times within the beginningless cycle of birth and death—whether through death, or being sold, or due to the causes and conditions of desire. In life after life, I have endured immeasurable suffering and affliction in the hells, yet I have never sacrificed my body for the sake of the pure Dharma, nor for the sake of making offerings to a teacher of the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita entered a great city along the way and went to the marketplace, where he cried out in a loud voice:
"Who needs a person?"
"Who desires a person?
Who wishes to buy a person?
At that time, the evil Māra had this thought:

"Because this Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma, he wishes to sell his own body in order to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā, so that he may correctly inquire about the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means:
'How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?'"
They shall become endowed with great learning, like the waters of the great ocean; at that time, they shall be indestructible, fully possessing all merits, and benefiting all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
For the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall transcend my realm and likewise teach others to transcend my realm, so that they may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"I shall now ruin his undertaking!
At that time, the evil Māra concealed all the brahmins and householders so that they would not hear her voice as she offered herself for sale;
however, he was unable to conceal one daughter of an elder.
At that time, Sadāprarudita was unable to sell his body; filled with grief and weeping, he stood to one side and said through his tears:
"I am a person of great transgression, for I cannot sell my body."
"I have sold myself for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā* in order to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra had this thought:
"This Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma so much that he has sold his own body for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*, desiring to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
"I shall test him to see whether this son of good family truly abandons his body out of a deep-seated love for the Dharma.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra transformed himself into the body of a brahmin and walked beside the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, asking:
"O son of good family!..."
"Why are you sorrowful and weeping, with such a withered and emaciated countenance, standing to one side?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
I cherish and revere the Dharma; I wish to sell my own body for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā and to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Now, as I seek to sell my body, there is no one to buy it. I reflect that I am of little merit and possess no wealth or treasures; though I wish to sell my body to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, there is no buyer.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Good son! I do not require a person;
however, I now wish to perform a sacrifice to the gods, for which I must have human heart, human blood, and human marrow. Are you able to sell these to me?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I have obtained a great benefit; I have obtained the foremost benefit!
For I have now found one who will purchase my heart, blood, and marrow, thereby enabling me to fulfill the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, his heart was filled with great joy and delight, free from all sorrow;
with a gentle and mild mind, he spoke to the brahmin, saying:
"Whatever you require, I shall give it all to you!"
The brahmin said: "Good man!
What price do you require?"
He replied, "Give it to me as you wish! Immediately,
Sadāprarudita took a sharp knife in his right hand, pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut the flesh from his right thigh, and was about to break the bone to extract the marrow.
At that time, there was the daughter of a householder who, seeing from atop her terrace the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita cutting his own body and disregarding his life, thought to herself:
"For what cause and condition does this son of good family thus afflict his body?"
"I shall go and ask him.
The daughter of the elder then descended from her chamber, went to where Sadāprarudita was, and asked:
"Noble son!..."
"For what reason do you afflict your body with such hardship?
What will you do with this heart, blood, and marrow?
Sadāprarudita replied:
"I have sold myself to this Brahmin for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā, in order to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
The daughter of the elder said,
"Noble son!..."
By selling oneself in this way, desiring to offer one's own heart, blood, and marrow as an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, what kind of merit and benefit will be obtained?
Sadāprarudita replied, "O virtuous woman!
This person has well studied the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means; this person shall explain to me what a bodhisattva ought to do and the path a bodhisattva ought to travel."
I shall study this Dharma and study this Path so that, when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I may serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.

I shall obtain a golden-colored body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, great radiance, and immeasurable light; great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, and the six supernormal powers; inconceivable pure morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieved unimpeded omniscient vision regarding all phenomena, I shall distribute the supreme treasure of the Dharma to all sentient beings.
"May I obtain such merits and benefits as these from him.

At that time, having heard this sublime and wondrous Dharma of the Buddha, the daughter of the elder was filled with great joy; her heart was stirred and her hair stood on end as she spoke to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
"How most rare!
What you have spoken is subtle and difficult to encounter!
For the sake of each and every one of these meritorious dharmas, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Why is this? What you have spoken is most profound and subtle!
O son of good family!

Whatever you now require, I shall give it all to you—gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, coral, and other such rare treasures; as well as flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, burning incense, banners, canopies, robes, musical instruments, and other articles for making offerings, to offer to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
"O son of good family!
Do not afflict your body with such hardship!

I, too, wish to go to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata dwells, so that together with you we may plant various roots of goodness, for the sake of attaining such a subtle and wondrous Dharma as you have described."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra resumed his original form and praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! You have firmly accepted this matter, and your mind remains unshakable.
When all the Buddhas of the past practiced the bodhisattva path, they likewise sought the prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means, thereby attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Good son!
I truly do not need human hearts, blood, or marrow; I have merely come to test you.
What is it that you wish for? I shall grant it to you."
Sadāprarudita said,
"Grant me *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!
Śakra-devendra replied:
"This is not something that can be accomplished by my own power; it is the domain of all Buddhas.
I must certainly make offerings to you, but please seek another boon. Sadāprarudita said:
"If you lack the power for this, you must certainly provide offerings so that this body of mine may be restored to its former state.
At that moment, Sadāprarudita’s body was immediately restored; it was free of any scars or blemishes, remaining no different than it had been originally.
Having fulfilled his vow, Śakra Devānām Indra suddenly vanished.
At that time, the daughter of the elder spoke to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
When you come to my house, whatever you may require, ask it of my parents; they shall give it all to you.
I, too, shall take leave of my parents and go together with these handmaidens to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
Immediately, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the merchant’s daughter went together to her house and stood outside the gate.
The merchant’s daughter entered and said to her parents:

“Give me various exquisite flowers and incense, as well as necklaces, ointments, burning incense, banners, canopies, robes, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, and all manner of musical instruments and articles for making offerings.”

May it also be permitted that my own person and five hundred maidservants previously assigned to me attend together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata resides, for the sake of making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall preach the Dharma for us; we shall practice according to what he says, and we shall attain the teachings of all Buddhas.
The girl's parents said to her:
"Who is this Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita?"
The woman said:
"This person is now outside the gate.
This son of good family seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi with a profound mind, desiring to deliver all sentient beings from the immeasurable suffering of birth and death."
For the sake of the Dharma, this son of good family sells his own body to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā—the Prajñāpāramitā being the path studied by bodhisattvas.
In order to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to honor the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, he cried out in a loud voice in the marketplace:
"Who needs a person?"
"Who needs a person?
Who wishes to buy a person?
Having failed to sell himself, he stood to one side, weeping in sorrow and distress.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a brahmin and came to test him, asking: "Good son,
why do you stand weeping with a sorrowful face?"
He replied, "Brahmin!
I wish to sell my body in order to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; however, being of little merit, I have been unable to find a buyer for my body."
The brahmin said to this son of good family:
"I have no need for a person; I wish to perform a sacrifice to the gods, and I require human heart, human blood, and human marrow. Can you sell these to me?"
At that time, this son of good family was no longer distressed; his mind was harmonious and joyful, and he spoke to the brahmin, saying:
"Whatever you require, I shall give it all to you."
The brahmin asked,
"What price do you require?
He replied:
"Give it to me as you wish.

At that moment, this son of good family took a sharp knife in his right hand, pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut the flesh from his right thigh, and further intended to break the bone to extract the marrow.
From atop my pavilion, I saw this event from afar;
at that time, I thought to myself:
"For what reason does this person afflict his body with such hardship?"
"I shall go and ask him.
I immediately descended from the pavilion and went to inquire:
"O son of good family!..."
"For what reason do you afflict your own body with such hardship?
This son of good family replied to me,
"Sister!"
"For the sake of the Dharma, I wish to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, who preaches the Dharma.
Yet I am poor and possess nothing; I have no gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, crystal, or pearls, nor do I have flowers, incense, or music."
"Sister!
For the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, I have sold my own body.
Now that I have found a buyer, they require human heart, human blood, and human marrow."
"I shall use this price to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the teacher of the Dharma.
I then asked that son of good family:
"Now that you have offered your own body, heart, blood, and marrow, desiring to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, what merit will you obtain?"
That son of good family said:

“The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall explain to me the perfection of wisdom and the power of skillful means; this is what a bodhisattva should study, what a bodhisattva should practice, what a bodhisattva should abide in, and the path that a bodhisattva should travel.”
I shall study this path so that, having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I may become a refuge for all sentient beings.

I shall attain a golden body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, great radiance, and immeasurable light; great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the ten powers of a Buddha, the eighteen unique qualities, and the six supernormal powers; as well as inconceivable pure morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall obtain unimpeded omniscient vision regarding all phenomena.
"I shall distribute this unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma to all sentient beings.
Such subtle and wondrous great Dharmas as these, I shall obtain from him.
Having heard of these subtle and inconceivable merits of the Buddhas and having heard of their great vows, my heart was filled with joy, and I thought to myself:
"This is pure, subtle, most great, and rare!
For the sake of even a single such dharma, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Now this good man, for the sake of the Dharma, is able to undergo ascetic practices and difficult tasks, namely, not sparing his own body or life;
I possess many exquisite treasures—why do you not conceive a wish and diligently seek such a Dharma, making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata?
Having reflected thus, I said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!

Do not afflict your body with hardship. I shall speak to my parents and provide you with much gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, parasols, and various musical instruments, to offer in worship to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the teacher of the Dharma."

I too shall seek my parents and, together with all the handmaidens, go with you to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata as he preaches the Dharma; together with you, we shall plant various roots of goodness in order to attain such subtle, wondrous, and pure dharmas as you have described.

"Father and mother, you have now granted me permission; please also allow me to take with me the five hundred handmaidens previously assigned to me, as well as various exquisite flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, powdered perfumes, robes, banners, canopies, musical instruments, and offerings of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli, so that I may go together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Dharma-preacher Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, for the sake of attaining such pure and subtle qualities of the Buddhas."
At that time, the parents replied to their daughter:
"What you have praised is rare and difficult to equal!

To speak thus of this son of good family’s diligence for the sake of the Dharma, his great delight in the characteristics of the Dharma, and these inconceivable qualities of all the Buddhas—which are the most supreme in all the world and the cause of joy for all sentient beings!"
This son of good family has made great adornments for the sake of this Dharma; we permit you to go and see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, to attend upon and make offerings to him.
Since you have resolved upon the Great Mind and exert such diligence for the sake of attaining all Buddha-dharmas, how could we not rejoice in your merit?
"Then, having been granted permission to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the girl said to her parents:
'We also rejoice in this heart; I shall never sever the causes and conditions for the wholesome dharmas of others.'"

At that time, the daughter of the elder adorned five hundred carriages made of the seven precious gems; she and her attendants, along with various precious objects and articles for offering, took with them various flowers grown on land and in water, as well as gold, silver, and jeweled flowers, robes of many colors, fine incense, powdered incense, unguents, necklaces, and various kinds of flavorful food and drink. Together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, they each mounted one carriage with five hundred attendants, respectfully surrounding him as they gradually proceeded toward the east.
He saw the city of Saṃghāṭa adorned with the seven treasures, surrounded by sevenfold enclosures;
its moats of the seven treasures and its rows of trees of the seven treasures were likewise sevenfold.
The city was twelve yojanas in length and breadth, prosperous, peaceful, and most delightful, with a vast and flourishing population.

The city extended for hundreds of thousands of *li*, with streets and alleys aligned in perfect symmetry, as magnificent as a painting; its bridges and ferries were as level as the ground, vast and pure.

From afar he beheld the City of Universal Fragrance (*Saṃghāṭa-nagara*). Having entered the city, he saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon a high dais at the Dharma-seat, surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of beings as he preached the Dharma.

When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, his heart was immediately filled with joy, like that of a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna and attained a state of collected and peaceful mind.
Having seen him, he thought:
"Our deportment does not permit us to approach the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata while riding in a carriage."
Having formed this thought, he descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot.
The daughter of the elder, along with her five hundred handmaidens, likewise descended from their carriages.

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and the five hundred handmaidens—adorned with various jewels, surrounded by them, and paying him respectful homage—arrived together at the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata had a pavilion made of the seven precious gems, adorned with red ox-head sandalwood. A net of pearls covered the top of the pavilion, and at each of its four corners hung maṇi jewels to serve as lamps. Furthermore, four precious incense burners constantly burned famous incenses for the sake of making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā."
Within that terrace was a great bed of the seven treasures and a small bed of four treasures, layered one upon the other;
upon the small bed was placed the *Prajñāpāramitā* written on golden tablets, adorned with various banners and canopies draped over it.

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the women saw this wondrous pavilion adorned with various jewels, and they saw Śakra Devendra together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devas scattering celestial māndārava flowers, powdered sandalwood, and ground fragments of various precious gems upon the pavilion, while playing celestial music in the air to delight the pavilion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita asked Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!

For what cause and condition do you, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of devas, scatter celestial māndārava flowers, powdered sandalwood, and ground fragments of various jewels upon this terrace, and play celestial music in the void to delight this terrace?"
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Do you, son of good family, not know?
This is the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; it is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, capable of giving birth to all buddhas and sustaining all bodhisattvas."
“A bodhisattva who trains in this perfection of wisdom accomplishes all merits and attains the buddha-dharmas and the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was filled with joy and delight, and he asked Śakra Devendra: “Kauśika!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; she gives birth to all Buddhas and sustains all bodhisattvas.
When bodhisattvas study this Prajñāpāramitā, they accomplish all merits, attain the Buddha-dharmas and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Where is it now?
Śakra Devānām Indra said: "Good son!
Within this pavilion there is a great bed made of the seven treasures, upon which smaller beds made of four jewels are layered."
The *Prajñāpāramitā* was written on golden tablets and placed upon a small couch.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has sealed it with seals made of the seven precious gems; we are unable to open it to show it to you.

At that time, Sadāprarudita, together with the elder’s daughter and five hundred female attendants, took the articles for offering—flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, and canopies—and divided them into two portions:
one portion to offer to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the other portion to offer to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata upon the Dharma-seat.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with five hundred women, took flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, music, and various precious jewels; having made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, he then proceeded to where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.

Having arrived, he saw the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata seated upon the Dharma-throne; for the sake of the Dharma, he scattered various flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, fragrant ointments, gold, silver, precious blossoms, banners, canopies, and jeweled robes over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata as an offering.
At that time, the various flowers, incense, and precious robes transformed in the air above the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata into flower pedestals;
the powdered sandalwood, precious powders, gold, silver, and precious flowers transformed into a jeweled canopy;
and upon the jeweled canopy, the various precious robes scattered there transformed into a jeweled parasol, with precious banners hanging from its four sides.
Sadāprarudita and the women, seeing the miraculous transformations performed by the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, were all greatly delighted and thought to themselves:
"How unprecedented this is!"
The divine virtue of the Great Master Dharmodgata is indeed such as this!
When he was practicing the bodhisattva path, his supernormal powers were already able to manifest in this way; how much more so when he has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!

At that time, the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women, with pure faith and deep reverence for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow:

"Just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained the various profound dharmas of a bodhisattva; just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata makes offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*; just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata expounds and reveals the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* within the great assembly; and just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has attained the *prajñāpāramitā*, the power of skillful means, accomplished the supernormal powers, and attained mastery in the deeds of a bodhisattva—may we also become thus."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women, having made offerings of flowers, incense, and precious objects to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, joined their palms in reverence, and stood to one side.
Having stood to one side, he addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"In the past, when I was seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I heard a voice in the sky while in a secluded forest, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
"You should go east from here, and you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having received these words, I traveled east. After traveling for a short while, I had this thought:
"Why do I not ask the voice in the sky: [where I should go]?"
"Where shall I go? How far is that place?
And from whom shall I hear it?"
At that time, I was filled with great sorrow and wept; I remained in that place for seven days and seven nights. Because of my grief, I did not even think of food or drink, but thought only:
"When shall I be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
While I was thus sorrowful, as I focused my mind single-mindedly on the *prajñāpāramitā*, I saw the Buddha’s body in the midst of the sky, who spoke to me, saying: “Good son!
Do not abandon this mind of great desire and great diligence!

With this mind of great desire and great diligence, proceed eastward from here; five hundred yojanas from here, there is a city named Saṃghagandha. Within it dwells a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Dharmodgata, from whom you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
"In every lifetime, this Bodhisattva has been your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and has constantly protected you.
Having received these instructions from the Buddha, I set out toward the east with no other thought in mind, thinking only:
"When shall I see the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, who will explain the Prajñāpāramitā to me?"

At that time, as I stood upon the middle way, I attained unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, and various samādhis such as the "Contemplation of the Equality of All Phenomena" manifested before me;
having abided in these samādhis, I saw immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the ten directions preaching this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddhas praised me, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!
When I originally sought the Prajñāpāramitā, I attained various samādhis, just as you do today.
Having attained these various samādhis, I universally attained all the Buddha-dharmas."
"The Buddhas extensively expounded the essential teachings for me and, having comforted me, suddenly vanished.
When I arose from samādhi, I thought:
'From where did these Buddhas come?'"
"Where has he gone?
Because I did not see the Buddhas, I was filled with great sorrow and anxiety. Then I thought to myself:

"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has made offerings to previous Buddhas, planted all manner of roots of goodness, long practiced the Prajñāpāramitā, and is well-versed in the power of skillful means. Having attained mastery within the path of the bodhisattvas, he is my spiritual friend who protects me."
I shall ask the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata about this matter:
"From where do all Buddhas come?
To where do they go?"
"I now ask the Great Teacher:
'From where do these Buddhas come, and to where do they go?
O Great Teacher!"
Please explain to me from where all Buddhas come and to where they go, so that I may know;
having known this, may I also never be separated from the sight of the Buddhas!
[Treatise] Commentary:

Because Sadāprarudita thirsted for and yearned to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, he saw the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma to the great assemblies; his heart was filled with joy and his aspirations were fulfilled.
Because their power of faith is firm and their diligence is unshakable, the Buddhas comfort their minds and praise them, saying:
"Excellent!
When I first practiced the bodhisattva path and sought Prajñā, I was just as you are now."
"Do not be sorrowful and consider yourself to be of meager merit!
At that time, Sadāprarudita attained great power through various samādhis, and his mind became deeply attached to them.

Therefore, the Buddhas taught him to seek the nature of these samādhis, seeing neither a substantial entity nor anyone who enters or emerges from samādhi, because of the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of phenomena.
The Buddhas briefly explain the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā:
"Do not conceive of these dharmas as existing; that is to say, because all dharmas are signless (animitta), they cannot be conceived of or clung to."
Abiding in this state of non-conceptualization, we are able to fulfill the six pāramitās;
by fulfilling the six pāramitās, we attain the golden body of a Buddha.
As it is said in the sūtras:
"The Buddhas teach, transform, benefit, and gladden [beings], comforting their minds.
Question:

The Transformation Buddha has already declared for you that "Dharmodgata is your virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) throughout successive lifetimes"; why do you now ask again, "Who is my virtuous friend"?
The answer is:
Because the Buddha has commanded that one should redouble one’s reverence and affection for spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);
furthermore, because he wished to hear of the virtues of Dharmodgata from the Buddhas of the ten directions, and desired to make his own faith firm and free from doubt, he asked.
The Buddhas of the ten directions replied as described in the sutra.
Because Sadāprarudita was a person whose karmic conditions were to be transformed by Dharmodgata, the Buddhas assisted him and provided guidance.
There were some bodhisattvas who assisted those whom the Buddha was to deliver, leading them to the Buddha’s presence.
A question is asked:
Previously, upon hearing the voice from space, he did not inquire about it and wept for seven days; [why is this different now?]

Now that you do not see the Buddhas of the ten directions, why are you not deeply distressed and seek further to see those Buddhas, instead desiring only to inquire of Dharmodgata about the matters of the coming and going of the Buddhas?
The answer is:
Previously, Sadāprarudita possessed only the fleshly eye and had not yet attained samādhi; because he believed deeply in and was attached to wholesome dharmas, he wept bitterly.

Now, having attained the power of various samādhis and seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions, his afflictions have become thin and subtle, and his mind of attachment has already departed; therefore, he simply maintains single-minded mindfulness:
"When shall I see Dharmodgata? He asked:

"If Sadāprarudita has attained the power of this samādhi, why does he not enter samādhi again to ask the Buddhas of the ten directions from where they come and where they go, instead of wishing to see and question Dharmodgata?"

Answer: The Buddhas of the ten directions have praised Dharmodgata with various causes and conditions, saying, "Dharmodgata has been your teacher throughout successive lifetimes. For this reason, he wishes to inquire.
At that time, Sadāprarudita thinks of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, considering him his karmic connection from previous lives; therefore, he gives rise to a mind of reverence and respect.
Because he possesses great merit, he is held in high esteem; because of his past-life karmic conditions, he is revered and cherished.
Question: Previously it was said that "Sadāprarudita did not cling to worldly affairs, but because he deeply loved the Prajñāpāramitā, he grieved and wept."
Why now do you disparage yourself for being poor and lacking the means to make offerings?
If one simply follows the teacher’s intention with a sincere heart, that itself is the offering of Dharma; what need is there for flowers and incense?
The answer is:
Although the Dharma-offering is supreme, worldly beings, seeing that those who have come from afar seeking the Dharma find it empty and non-existent, do not give rise to a joyful mind;
because of their worldly nature, they seek material requisites for offerings.
Furthermore, the five pāramitās serve as auxiliary dharmas to the prajñāpāramitā, and among these auxiliary dharmas, the dānapāramitā is foremost.
Sadāprarudita reflected:
"I have obtained the venerable field of merit, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; I shall offer him the fundamental auxiliary dharmas for the path."
Furthermore, he wished to inspire the multitude, saying:
"Sadāprarudita is a wise man and a virtuous person; if even one so impoverished can make such offerings, how much more should we!"
Furthermore, when practicing various wholesome dharmas or contemplating them, their flavors differ from one another;
Sadāprarudita desired the flavor of practicing generosity, and for this reason he sought the requisites for making offerings.
Question:
Sadāprarudita is a great bodhisattva who is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions and has attained various profound samādhis; why, then, is he poor?
Answer: Some say that this person has left his home to seek the Buddha-way; although born into a wealthy family, the distance is vast and remote, so he has gone alone, carrying no wealth or goods.
Some say: although one may be a great person, due to the causes and conditions of minor offenses in past lives, they are born into a poor family;
while others, though they may be lowly persons, due to the causes and conditions of having practiced even a little generosity in previous lives, are born into a wealthy family.
For example, Sudāyin, Nanda, and others were persons honored by the devas, yet they were born into lowly families.
There are two kinds of poverty:
first, poverty of wealth; second, poverty of merit and the Dharma.
To be poor in the Dharma of merit is the greatest shame!
While there may be good people who are poor in wealth,
there are no good people who are poor in the Dharma.
"Regarding 'having no flowers or incense,' it means there are no superior and exquisite jewel-flowers; furthermore, they are said to be non-existent because they are so few.
If I were to go empty-handed, although the Teacher may not require them, my own heart would not attain great joy; for this reason, I wish to sell my body."
Question:
If he sells his body to another, who will purchase this object and go to make offerings to the teacher? Answer:
Sacrificing one's body is itself a great offering; it is a matter of neither departing nor remaining. Some say:
"This person sells his own body to obtain wealth so that others may make offerings; for the sake of making offerings, I sell myself as a slave."
Furthermore, some say:

At that time, the world was in a state of prosperity and everyone knew the Dharma; thus, even if one were to sell oneself, the owner would surely permit it so that one might make offerings and return.

Moreover, this person has given rise to a profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*) and wishes to practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). To make offerings to the Dharma and the Dharma-teacher, he possesses no external objects and has only his own body; therefore, he sells this internal thing.
Among external and internal things, the internal gift is more significant because one cherishes it deeply.
Therefore, wishing not to break his vow of giving, he sold his body to make an offering.
In this regard, he himself explains the causes and conditions for his lack of regret:

"Throughout countless lifetimes, I have lost my body many times, yet never for the sake of the pure Dharma. Now, by sacrificing this body to make offerings to one who expounds the Dharma, I shall obtain great benefit from the Dharma."

Sadāprarudita fixed his mind in concentration, severed all thoughts of attachment and greed for his own body, and entered a great city along the way—entering this great city because he desired to buy and sell as he pleased.
Desiring with single-minded resolve to sell his own body in order to eliminate shame and humiliation and to break his pride, he cried out:
"Who needs a person?
He asked thus.
Why does Māra wish to destroy their resolve?
The answer is:
Māra is the constant enemy of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, he comes wishing to destroy it.
Furthermore, those minor bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) can be defeated by Māras and evil persons;

however, once they have attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and abide in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of bodhisattvas, none are able to destroy them.
Just as a young sapling can be broken by a small child, but once grown large, it cannot be broken;

furthermore, this very passage explains the causes and conditions for Māra’s failure to destroy him, namely: "Because Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma, he sells his own body to offer it to the Prajñāpāramitā and to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, so that he may correctly hear the Prajñāpāramitā," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Question:
If Māra intended to destroy Sadāprarudita, why did he not do so when [the Bodhisattva] first heard the voice from the sky and saw the Buddhas of the ten directions?
"Why do you now conceal yourself from the brahmins and householders, so that they do not hear your voice?
He replied:
"In the past, Sadāprarudita’s mind was not yet settled and his attachment to his body was not yet exhausted."
Having seen the Buddhas of the ten directions, he attained various samādhis, and his mind became settled.
Now that the signs of this settled mind appear, Māra is terrified.
If a bodhisattva’s mind were not yet settled, he would be unable to move Māra.
If a great bodhisattva’s mind is already settled, Māra will not come.
Sadāprarudita now wishes to settle his mind and exit the realm of Māra; for this reason, Māra has come.
For example, if a debtor does not intend to travel far away, the creditor does not obstruct him;
however, when he wishes to cross into another territory, the creditor will not permit his departure. Question:
Māra possesses great power; why does he not kill this bodhisattva, but instead merely destroy him?
The answer is:
Māra does not originally envy his life-span, but hates his resolve to become a Buddha; for this reason, he wishes to ruin him.
Furthermore, according to the laws of the various deities, if a person has not committed a grave offense, they must not be killed recklessly;
one may only cause them distress and terror. If the deities did not possess such laws, no human being would survive; therefore, they do not kill.
One born into the nature of a brāhmaṇa is called a brāhmaṇa because of having received the precepts;
apart from this, they are generally termed *gṛhapati* (householder).
A *gṛhapati* is truly a gentleman who dwells in a house, not merely a householder among the four castes.
As for the exclusion of the one daughter of the elder, it was because she had accumulated merit for the sake of the Buddha-way life after life, and thus Māra could not obscure her.
Furthermore, some say that because this Sadāprarudita ought not to die, [Māra] caused one woman to hear [the teaching].
Some say: It was by the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata that the merchant's daughter was able to hear him.
Thus she called out three times, but as no one bought [the flowers], she became deeply distressed.
Question:
Since Sadāprarudita does not cherish his body, he should not grieve even though no one buys it! Answer:
Having already resolved upon the Great Mind, he is deeply distressed because his vow remains unfulfilled.
Śakra-devānām-indra thought to himself:
"Sadāprarudita wishes to sell his body, yet there is no one to buy it."
As explained at length in the sutra. Question:
Since Śakra Devānām Indra has attained the knowledge of others' minds, he should have already known that Sadāprarudita’s resolve was firm; why, then, does he come now to test him?
The answer is:
The various devas only know the minds of worldly people—whether they will become Buddhas or not—but this is not within their knowledge.
Aside from a Buddha, there is no one capable of knowing that [a being] possesses the mind for the Buddha-way and thus bestowing a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Furthermore, Śakra-devānām-indra came to test him because he wished to guide many beings; he desired that all who heard or saw this would resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood.
Moreover, just as gold, silver, and other precious gems are not subjected to smelting, forging, grinding, or hammering merely because they are of little value, so too it is with the Bodhisattva:
if his mind remains unshaken even when he cuts his flesh, sheds his blood, and breaks his bones to extract the marrow, he is a Bodhisattva established in right concentration.
For this reason, Śakra, Lord of Devas, came to test him.
He asked:
"Śakra is the Great Heavenly King; why do you speak falsely, saying, 'I wish to sacrifice to the gods and require human heart, blood, and marrow'?"
Answer:
If one speaks falsely out of the afflictions of stinginess, greed, or anger, desiring to achieve one's own benefit, it constitutes a transgression.
However, if Śakra were to manifest his true body and speak truthful words, the Bodhisattva would not believe him.
"Therefore, according to the laws of that country, these items required for the celestial shrines are provided so that they may have faith and acceptance.
At that time, Sadāprarudita believed his words and was greatly rejoiced, thinking:
"I have attained a great benefit!"
The great benefit is the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika-bhūmi);
the supreme benefit is the Buddha-way.
The great benefit consists of the five perfections (pañca-pāramitā).
The foremost benefit is the perfection of wisdom;
the great benefit is the perfection of wisdom;
the foremost benefit is the power of skillful means within the perfection of wisdom.
"Great benefit" refers to the first stage of the bodhisattva;
"supreme benefit" refers to the tenth stage.
Furthermore, "great benefit" extends from the first stage through to the tenth stage.
The foremost benefit is the tenth stage;
the great benefit is the bodhisattva stages;
the supreme benefit is the buddha stage.
Although such distinctions as these are not yet fully perfected, they already abide in the causes and conditions for perfection; therefore, it is said that "they are already perfected. Question:
If Śakra Devānām-indra had come in an emanated form, why would he have said, "What price do you require"?
The answer is:
because [Dharmodgata] knew that [Sadāprarudita] wished to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and thus he fulfilled his wish.
Furthermore, Śakra-devānām-indra distressed Sadāprarudita, fearing that what he sought was too great; for this reason, he asked, "What price do you require?"
"Give it to me according to your own will" means:
"Give it to me if you do not feel great greed or attachment toward it, nor if it causes you regret.
Because Sadāprarudita lacked the power and influence to command the caṇḍāla, he took up the knife himself.
The brahmin was likewise unable to break [the door] because he feared the sin; for this reason, he took up a knife and tore open his own body.
Question: If the daughter of the elder heard the sound, why did she not come to inquire?
"Why have you come to sell yourself?
She replied, "To speak empty words of selling one's body is a light matter; to break open one's body to extract the marrow is a grave matter. Thus, the daughter of the elder conceived the resolve.
The daughter of the elder was staying on the upper terrace when she saw this man cutting and piercing himself, and she thought to herself:
"All sentient beings seek happiness and fear suffering, and they cherish their own bodies;
yet Sadāprarudita cuts and pierces himself—this is truly extraordinary!"
Furthermore, drawn by the causal conditions of the merit from previous lives, he went immediately to that place and inquired.
Sadāprarudita replied,
"I wish to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
He asked again,
"What benefit do you obtain?
He replied:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is what Bodhisattvas study; one should hear it from them.
By studying this path, I shall attain Buddhahood and serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.”
It is, for example, like a thick-leaved tree providing abundant shade;
or like a cool, great pool in a vast wilderness on a hot day.
To inspire the aspiration for awakening, he speaks of the Buddha’s meritorious qualities and manifest attributes: namely, his golden body, the thirty-two marks, and his great, immeasurable radiance.
Mahāprabha, for the sake of sentient beings in the evil world of Jambudvīpa, the true radiance of all Buddhas is limitless.
The meaning of great compassion up to the six supernormal powers is as previously explained.
Inconceivable pure precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom are as explained among the five aggregates, such as the Buddha’s own precepts.

Regarding the attainment of all unimpeded knowledge and vision among all phenomena: the Buddhas possess unimpeded liberation; this liberation is associated with knowledge and vision that is unobstructed regarding all phenomena.
The discernment of knowledge and vision is as previously explained.
Sadāprarudita said:
"Having attained such immeasurable merits of the Buddhas, I shall distribute this unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma to all sentient beings."
Regarding the "unsurpassed treasure," some say it is the Dharma-treasure among the Three Jewels; others say:

The entire assembly of eighty-four thousand dharmas constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma; by attaining this, one eliminates all afflictions, extinguishes all conceptual proliferation, and achieves liberation from all suffering.
Some say: "The unsurpassed Dharma-treasure is precisely Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for there is nothing superior to it. Others say:
Nirvana is the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) have that which is superior to them.
As stated in the *Abhidharma*:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), are called 'conditioned' (*sottara*) dharmas;
cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the 'unconditioned' (*anuttara*) dharma."
The exhaustion of the conditions for continued existence (*pratyaya-kṣaya*) is another name for *nirvāṇa*. Some say:
although the path to *nirvāṇa* is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it leads to *nirvāṇa*, it is supreme among all conditioned phenomena.
Such treasures of the Dharma as these are distributed among sentient beings according to the three vehicles.

These immeasurable teachings of the Buddha must be obtained from a teacher; therefore, I shall relinquish this impure, foul-smelling body that dwells in old age, sickness, and death, so that by making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, I may attain the body of a Buddha.
Her golden complexion and other features were as previously described.

Having made offerings to various Buddhas and planted roots of goodness throughout successive lifetimes, the daughter of the elder possessed sharp and keen wisdom; upon hearing this Dharma, her mind entered deeply into it, and she attained great joy in the Dharma, even to the point that her heart was struck with awe and her hair stood on end.
She spoke to Sadāprarudita, saying:
"How truly rare! The Dharma you have praised is most subtle and wondrous!
For the sake of each and every dharma, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, let alone a single body!"
The daughter of the elder did not know for what reason she was subjecting her body to such hardship; she felt pity for it and thought in her heart that it was unacceptable.
Now, having heard this immeasurable, boundless, and incomparable pure Buddha-dharma, she feels great joy because it can be attained through these causes and conditions. Therefore, it is said:
"For the sake of this Dharma, one should sacrifice bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The woman said, "Because of poverty, you have brought yourself to such hardship and exhaustion; you may now cease this.
Whatever you require, I shall provide it to you, for I too shall follow you in seeking this Way."
Question: Since this bodhisattva has already cut his own body to pieces, how is he able to preach much of the Buddha-dharma to the daughter of the elder? Answer:
This bodhisattva’s power of mind is so great that although he suffers physical pain, it cannot overwhelm his mind.

While the bodhisattva has just begun to cut his flesh with a knife until it bleeds, and is on the verge of breaking his bone to extract the marrow, the elder’s daughter arrives; because he is not yet in extreme agony, he is able to preach the Dharma to her.
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing that his mind was firm and that he had merely been testing him, said nothing; he immediately restored himself to his original form and praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
Regarding the phrase "Your mind is firm and accepts this matter," Śakra’s intention is as follows:

Since you, with your current physical body subject to birth and death and not yet having attained the Buddha-way, can thus disregard your own body, it will not be long before you attain non-attachment toward all dharmas, abide in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Taking the Buddhas of the past as witnesses, he comforted his mind with various causes and conditions such as these:
"I am a celestial king who loves and delights in the Buddha-way; therefore, I have come to test you, wishing to know whether your mind is firm or soft."
"In order to cause you to believe me, I said that human hearts and marrow were required for the sacrifice to the heavens, but in truth they are not required.
What do you wish for? I shall grant it to you."
"You are a good person and a member of the Buddha's lineage; I shall protect you.

Because Sadāprarudita’s mind was upright, faithful, virtuous, and gentle, and because he was deeply attached to the Buddha-way, he made no distinction between sentient beings. Upon hearing Śakra’s words, he said:
"Grant me *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!"
Śakra said: "This is not something that can be accomplished by my power;
it is the domain of the Buddha. Furthermore, some say:
“Śakra has greatly distressed Sadāprarudita; now he offers these words to apologize to him.
Śakra’s intention was that he sought gold, silver, and precious objects, not realizing that he was instead seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
since he cannot grant it, he is merely filled with shame and regret!”
He spoke again, saying:
"I shall certainly provide for you; ask for another wish.
This was the intention behind Śakra’s words:
"I am already so greatly distressed and exhausted that I cannot simply depart; I must make offerings to you.
Although Sadāprarudita did not begrudge his own body, he wished to use this very body to make offerings to Dharmodgata and hear the Prajñāpāramitā;
for this reason, he spoke these words:
"If you do not possess this power, restore my body to its former state.
Śakra replied, "It shall be as you say."
The wound was immediately healed and filled, no different from how it had been before.
He asked:
"Since the flesh had already been cut away previously, how did you cause it to become full again?"
Answer: The Buddha has taught that there are five inconceivable things.
Even the deeds performed by dragons are inconceivable, let alone those of the devas!
Furthermore, although the void of space is filled with subtle particles, when Śakra’s merit gives rise to a thought, they are able to harmonize and become level and full.

Just as the bodies of the various devas and those in the hells are not bodies born of the three [ordinary] births, but rather exist through the harmonization of the causes and conditions of sin and merit.
At that time, Śakra, knowing that his resolve was firm, granted him his wish and immediately vanished.

Then, as Sadāprarudita’s minor karmic offenses from past lives had been exhausted and his merit and virtue were radiant and flourishing, the merchant’s daughter took him back home, saying, "Whatever you require, ask it of my parents," as is explained at length in the sutra.
Question: This woman previously said, "Whatever goods you require, ask for them all from me"; why does she now say, "Ask for them from my parents"?
The answer is:

Now that he is about to return home, Sadāprarudita has witnessed with his own eyes that he will obtain [the teaching] from his parents upon entering the house; feeling ashamed that his previous words were not in accord with reality, he first said to himself:
"I shall seek it from my parents."
Furthermore, although the daughter was capable of obtaining the treasure by her own strength, because of the custom regarding daughters, she requested it from her parents.
Once the daughter had entered the house, she requested and received what had been previously promised from her parents.
Since there was no Buddha-dharma in that land, he asked the girl,
"Who is this Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita?
The girl then related everything she had seen and heard regarding the matters of Sadāprarudita to her parents.

"Now, parents, you should grant me permission to go together with the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, along with these five hundred female attendants and these offerings, to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
When the parents heard these words, they immediately granted his wish.
He asked:
"The Elder is noble and powerful; why did he not recognize Sadāprarudita before now?"
Because they heard of his meritorious virtues, were they able to cause the woman, her retinue, and their treasures to depart together with him?
He replied:
"The elder had also planted roots of virtue; however, due to minor causes and conditions, he was born in a land where no Buddha dwells."

Having briefly heard of the Buddha’s virtues, their latent predispositions from past lives were awakened; their minds immediately attained enlightenment, and thus they were able to dispatch [the messenger].
It is like a lotus flower that, once fully grown, blossoms upon seeing the sun.

The parents knew that their daughter’s mind was pure and mature, free from any impure conduct, and that she maintained her integrity without deviation; they knew she took no pleasure in worldly delights but sought only the benefits of the Dharma.
Recognizing the sincerity of her resolve and that it could not be restrained, they feared that if they were to oppose her wishes, she might bring harm upon herself.
Having reflected and deliberated thus, and having fulfilled his intention so that he himself might attain merit, he sent him away with joy.

Worldly conditions are deeply entangled and difficult to unravel; because of the extreme nature of such attachment, one cannot even go against them [in worldly matters], let alone refuse someone for the sake of the Buddha-way when their mind is pure and free from all defilement!
The daughter, having taken her parents as her authority, was granted permission; she did not begrudge the precious objects and, with a heart of sympathetic joy, rejoiced in their deed.
At that time, once the assembly’s minds were settled, they adorned a chariot of the seven treasures and, surrounded by the great multitude, proceeded slowly toward the east.
At that time, the five hundred women’s relatives and the multitude of people in the city, seeing this rare and unprecedented event, all followed along as well.
Once the crowd had gathered, they proceeded together in great joy, yearning for the City of Universal Fragrance as a thirsty person longs for a drink.

Gradually proceeding on their way, they saw from afar the city of Saṃghāṭa; then, accompanied by the daughter of the elder and five hundred women, who respectfully surrounded them, they set out for the place where Dharmodgata was.
Question:
Dharmodgata is a great bodhisattva who has attained various dhāraṇīs such as "retention" (dhāraṇī);

since he has already mastered and memorized the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā himself, why does he use a terrace of the seven precious gems to write out the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scrolls and place them within it for worship?
Answer: Although there are various causes and conditions, they can be summarized into two general meanings:
first, the mental activities of sentient beings differ; some delight in seeing the physical volumes of the scriptures, while others delight in hearing their exposition.
Second, Dharmodgata’s body appears as that of a layperson with a family.
Sentient beings of dull faculties might think:
"Since he has a household, he must certainly have attachments; how then can he benefit sentient beings with the ultimately pure and unattached Prajñāpāramitā?"
"Since I myself have not yet attained non-attachment, how can I use the Dharma of non-attachment to transform and teach others?
For this reason, he transcribed the text of the sutra and placed it upon tablets made of the seven treasures, making offerings of various jewels;
the devas, nāgas, and spirits all likewise came together to pay respect, offering flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, while raining down the seven treasures.

When sentient beings behold this, their faculty of faith increases; thus, one should demonstrate and transmit the Buddha’s words through this Dharma, expounding the teachings according to the text and exhorting others to resolve upon awakening.
All the ornaments of the jeweled terraces and Sadāprarudita’s inquiry to Śakra Devendra are as described in the sutra.
Regarding the "seal of the seven jewels": this is the true seal of Dharmodgata, which he constantly holds in his own hand to stamp upon the sutra.

Some say that the "seal of the seven jewels" refers to seven great deities who seek the Buddha-way; they hold vajra-clubs and constantly serve as attendants to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata to protect the script of the sutra, ensuring that Māras or the followers of Māra do not alter, change, or confuse it out of reverence for the Prajñāpāramitā.
There are those who resolve their minds upon awakening merely by hearing the discourse, and there are those who rejoice and resolve their minds upon seeing its magnificent textual adornments;
for this reason, the precious platform is adorned with writings inscribed on golden tablets and sealed with seals of the seven treasures.
Question:

Although the Prajñāpāramitā written on the terrace and the Prajñāpāramitā expounded by the mouth of Bodhisattva Dharmodgata both exist in those two places, the written copy cannot benefit people; why, then, did he go first to the terrace?
Answer: The written Prajñā enters among the Dharma-jewels.
Since the Dharma-jewel follows the Buddha-jewel in sequence, it should be honored first.
Because Dharmodgata alone is not included within the Sangha Jewel, one first makes offerings to the Dharma Jewel.
Furthermore, although that which is spoken by the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata is indeed the Dharma, sentient beings grasp at the mark of a person and thus give rise to much attachment;

if they see the written Prajñāpāramitā, they do not give rise to the mark of a person, and even if they grasp at other marks, their attachment is less than the affliction caused by attachment to a person. For this reason, one first makes offerings to the scripture.
The Buddhas themselves still make offerings to the sutras and the Dharma; how much more so for Dharmodgata and Sadāprarudita!
Since it is because of the *prajñāpāramitā* that Dharmodgata has received these offerings, how could one not first make offerings to the very source from which they arise?
Therefore, he divided the articles of offering into two portions.
A question was asked:
"Dharmodgata possesses sixty thousand court ladies, the five sensory pleasures, and palaces; how can he transform the flowers and objects scattered by others into flower pedestals?"
Answer: Some say that it was through the supernatural power of the Buddhas, acting upon the objects offered by Sadāprarudita, that this transformation was produced.
Some say: Dharmodgata is a great bodhisattva with a body born of the *dharmatā*; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he undergoes the five desires.
This is as explained in the section on the meaning of the name "Bodhisattva Dharmodgata."
Question:
According to the dharma of a bodhisattva, one first gives rise to compassion toward sentient beings; because one desires to deliver them from suffering, one seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Now you see only the supernatural power and majestic virtue of Dharmodgata; how then did he first resolve his mind [for enlightenment]?
He replied:
"There are various ways of resolving the mind."

There are those who resolve their minds upon awakening upon hearing the Dharma being taught; there are those who resolve their minds upon awakening by giving rise to compassion for sentient beings; and there are those who resolve their minds upon awakening by seeing supernatural powers and great majestic virtue. Thereafter, they gradually give rise to a heart of pity, as described in the *Jñānamudrā-sūtra*.
One abandons craving by relying on craving, and abandons pride by relying on pride.
For example, when a person hears the Dharma, because they develop a craving for that Dharma, they renounce the five desires and leave the household life.
Furthermore, there are those who, upon hearing that a certain person has attained the path of Arhatship, give rise to a haughty mind, thinking:
"This person possesses no qualities superior to mine; if he was able to achieve such a state, why should I not be able to do so?"
Thus they gave rise to great diligence and attained the path of Arhatship.
It is the same within the Buddha-way.

The daughter of the elder and the five hundred women had always deeply craved power, sovereignty, and pleasure; yet upon hearing that in ancient times there were those with supernatural powers and transformations who possessed all manner of treasures and enjoyed celestial bliss among humans, [they were moved].
Later, he saw Dharmodgata seated upon a great Dharma throne within towers, pavilions, and palaces, receiving offerings from devas and humans;

he further saw that the objects of offering transformed in mid-air into a vast platform. His heart was filled with great joy, and he conceived the thought that such a thing is difficult to encounter. He realized that all these matters could be accomplished through the causes and conditions of merit and virtue; therefore, they all resolved to attain Buddhahood.
Regarding those who have resolved their minds upon awakening as they have heard it taught, their practices are all sequential practices. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*:
"Afflictions such as craving and pride are all the very foundation of the Buddha-way."

Therefore, when women see these things, they give rise to a heart of love and joy; knowing that such things can be obtained through the causes and conditions of merit, they all resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
Because of this love and pride, one later attains a pure and wholesome mind; therefore, it is said that they are the root of the Buddha-way, just as a lotus flower grows from the mud.
Having resolved their minds, they made this vow:
"Just as Dharmodgata acts, we too shall attain this!"
At that time, Sadāprarudita and the others prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
Because flowers, incense, and other such offerings were not precious [to him], they offered them first;
because his own body was precious, they paid homage to it later.
Having paid homage, he recounted the causes and conditions for his original quest for Prajñā.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When I was originally seeking Prajñā, I heard a voice from the air... [and so on]... until now I ask the Great Master:"
"From where do all Buddhas come?
To where do they go? He asked:

Sadāprarudita has attained all the great samādhis, such as "Breaking Through Ignorance" and "Contemplating the Equality of All Dharmas. How could he not know emptiness and yet grasp at the marks of a Buddha, giving rise to deep attachment?
The answer is:

Although a bodhisattva who has newly resolved may possess a general understanding that all dharmas are empty and signless, because they harbor deep attachment toward the Buddhas, they cannot comprehend that the marks of the Buddha are ultimately empty; thus, although they know emptiness, they are unable to merge with it.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless real merits, and because these bodhisattvas have sharp faculties, they penetrate them deeply and become deeply attached to them.

If the Buddhas did not explain emptiness for the sake of these bodhisattvas, these bodhisattvas, out of their love for the Buddha, would be capable of sacrificing even their own kinsmen, let alone other people!
However, because of the realization of emptiness, such a thing does not exist.
Sadāprarudita, being deeply attached to the Buddhas, was unable to understand this and asked the Great Master:
"Now, for my sake, explain the characteristics of the coming and going of the Buddhas; because I never tire of beholding the Buddha-body, I shall never be separated from seeing the Buddhas."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Fascicle 98;
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra, Explanation of the Chapter on Dharmodgata,
Fascicle 89 (Fascicle 99).
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty. Chapter 89: Dharmodgata. [Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"Good son!..."
The Buddhas come from nowhere, and they go nowhere either.
Why is this? Because the suchness of all phenomena is an unmoving characteristic, and the suchness of all phenomena is itself the Buddha.
Good son! The dharma of non-arising neither comes nor goes; the dharma of non-arising is itself the Buddha.
The dharma of non-extinction neither comes nor goes; the dharma of non-extinction is itself the Buddha.
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is without coming or going; the reality-limit itself is the Buddha.
Emptiness is without coming or going; emptiness itself is the Buddha. Good son!
Stainless, there is neither coming nor going; that which is stainless is the Buddha.
Quiescent extinction, there is neither coming nor going; quiescent extinction is the Buddha.
The nature of space has neither coming nor going; the nature of space is the Buddha.
"Good son! Apart from these dharmas, there is no Buddha;
the suchness of all Buddhas and the suchness of all dharmas are a single suchness, without differentiation."
"Good son!
This Suchness is eternally one; it is without duality and without plurality, for it transcends all numerical dharmas because it is non-existent.
It is like the end of spring, at midday when the heat is intense: someone sees shimmering vapors moving and pursues them, hoping to obtain water."
What do you think?
From what lake, from what mountain, or from what spring does this water come?
Where is it going now?
"Or have you entered the Eastern Sea, the Western Sea, the Southern Sea,
or the Northern Sea? Sadāprarudita said,
"Great Master!"
“In the midst of a mirage there is not even water; how, then, could there be a place from which it comes or a place to which it goes?
Dharmodgata Bodhisattva said to Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva: “Good son!
Fools lack wisdom; oppressed by heat and thirst, they see flickering mirages and perceive them as water where no water exists.
Son of good family!
If there are those who discriminate that the Buddhas come or go, you should know that such people are all fools.
Why is this? Son of good family!
The Buddhas cannot be seen by means of their physical bodies; the Dharma-body of the Buddhas neither comes nor goes, and the places from which the Buddhas come and to which they go are likewise thus.
Good son!
It is like a magician who conjures various illusions—whether elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, men, or women—and all such diverse things.
What do you think?
From where does this illusory phenomenon come,
and to where does it go?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva said:
"Great Master!
Illusions have no reality; how could they have a place from which they come or to which they go?"
