“Good son! A person’s conceptualization that a Buddha comes and goes is also like this. Good son!”
Suppose, for example, one sees in a dream an elephant, a horse, an ox, a sheep, a man, or a woman.
What do you think?
Does that which is seen in a dream have a place from which it comes or a place to which it goes?
Sadāprarudita said: "Great Master!
What is seen in a dream is illusory; how could there be any coming or going?"
“Good son! This person’s conceptualization that the Buddha comes and goes is also like this.
Good son!”
The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like dreams.

If there are sentient beings who do not understand the meaning of these phenomena, and instead become attached to the Buddha through names and the form-body (*rūpakāya*), such persons discriminate that Buddhas come and go; because they do not know the true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, they are all counted among the ignorant and the witless.
Such a person repeatedly wanders through the five realms of existence, remaining far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and far removed from the teachings of all Buddhas.
Son of good family!
The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like illusions and like dreams.
If there are sentient beings who know things as they truly are, such persons do not discriminate among dharmas as coming or going, or as arising or ceasing;
if they do not discriminate among dharmas as coming or going, or as arising or ceasing, they are then able to know the true reality of all dharmas as taught by the Buddha.

This person practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and is close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they are called a true disciple of the Buddha, one who does not vainly consume the offerings of the faithful. Such a person deserves to receive offerings and serves as a field of merit for the world.

“Good son! For example, the various jewels within the great ocean do not come from the east, nor do they come from the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below. Rather, due to the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness of sentient beings, these jewels are produced within the sea.”

This jewel also does not arise without causes and conditions; this jewel arises entirely from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and even when this jewel perishes, it does not go away to the ten directions.
They exist because various conditions converge; they cease because various conditions disperse. Good son!

The bodies of all Buddhas are likewise: they arise from the karmic causes, conditions, and retributive fruits of the fundamental [karma]; when they arise, they do not come from the ten directions, and when they cease, they do not go to the ten directions.
"It is simply that they exist because various conditions converge, and they cease because those conditions disperse.
'Good son! It is like the sound of a lute:
when it arises, there is no place from which it comes; when it ceases, there is no place to which it goes.'"

It arises through the combination of various conditions: there is the hollow body, the neck, the skin, the strings, the bridge, and the plectrum; when a person strikes it with their hand, sound exists through the combination of these various conditions.

This sound does not emerge from the hollow body, nor from the neck, nor from the skin, nor from the strings, nor from the bridge, nor from the plectrum, nor from the person’s hand; rather, sound exists only when these various conditions combine.
When these causes and conditions disperse, there is likewise no place to which they go. Good son!

The bodies of all Buddhas are also like this: they are born from the causes and conditions of immeasurable merit; they do not arise from a single cause, a single condition, or a single merit, nor do they exist without causes and conditions, but exist because of the harmony of manifold conditions.
"The bodies of the Buddhas are not produced from a single cause alone; they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
'Good son, you should understand the manner of the Buddhas' coming and going in this way.'"
"Good son! You should also know that all dharmas have no characteristics of coming or going.

If you know that the Buddhas and all dharmas have no coming or going, and possess the characteristics of neither arising nor ceasing, you will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and you will also be able to practice the prajñā-pāramitā and the power of skillful means."
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra gave celestial māndārava flowers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāprarudita and spoke these words:
"O son of good family!
With these flowers, offer worship to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; I shall likewise protect and honor you. Why is this?
By the power of your causes and conditions, you today bring benefit to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, enabling them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Good son! Such virtuous persons are extremely difficult to encounter!
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they undergo various hardships and sufferings throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita accepted the māndārava flowers from Śakra Devendra and scattered them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"O Great Teacher!..."
"From this day forward, I offer my body to the teacher to serve and provide for him.
Having spoken thus three times, she stood before the teacher with her palms joined.
At that time, the daughter of the elder and her five hundred attendants said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
"From this day forward, we also dedicate our bodies to the Teacher.
By means of these roots of goodness, may we attain such a Dharma as that which the Teacher has attained;
together with the Teacher, may we make offerings to all Buddhas in every lifetime, and in every lifetime, may we constantly make offerings to the Teacher."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said to the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women:
"If you all entrust yourselves to me with sincere hearts, I shall accept you."
The women said, "We have entrusted ourselves to you with sincere hearts; we shall follow your instructions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the five hundred women, presented to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata all their ornaments, precious objects, and exquisite offerings, as well as five hundred chariots made of the seven treasures, and addressed him, saying:
“‘Great Master!
I offer these five hundred women to serve you, and these five hundred chariots for your use as you see fit.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:”
"Excellent! Excellent!
O son of good family!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having relinquished all that they possess, should practice giving in such and such a manner, and will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By making such offerings to those who preach the Dharma, one will certainly hear the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means.

When the Buddhas of the past were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they likewise abided in generosity and thereby heard the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means, attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, desiring to bring the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to full completion, accepted five hundred carriages, the daughter of the elder, and five hundred female attendants;
having accepted them, he gave them back to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata had finished preaching the Dharma, the sun set; he rose and entered his palace.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma; I should neither sit nor lie down, but shall attend to two matters:..."
"Whether walking or standing, I shall wait for the Dharma Master to emerge from the palace to preach the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata entered, with one-pointed mind, immeasurable and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) bodhisattva samādhis, as well as the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

For seven years, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita practiced walking meditation and remained standing; he neither sat nor lay down, slept not at all, and was free from desire, anger, and vexation, his mind unattached to sensory flavors.
He thought only this:
"When will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arise from samādhi and come forth to preach the Dharma?"
After seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I shall prepare a Dharma seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata shall sit upon it and preach the Dharma."

I shall sprinkle the ground to purify it, scatter various kinds of flowers, and adorn this place for the sake of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, who is about to preach the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and her five hundred female attendants, prepared a bed of the seven precious gems for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata. Each of the five hundred women removed her upper garment to spread upon the seat, thinking:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata shall sit upon this seat and preach the Prajñāpāramitā and the power of skillful means."
After the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had spread the seats, he sought water to sprinkle upon the ground but was unable to find any.
Why was this? An evil Māra had concealed it, causing the water not to appear.
Māra thought to himself:

"If the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita fails to find water, he may, in his practice for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, give rise to even a single thought of inferiority or a divergent mind; then his roots of goodness will not increase, his wisdom will not shine forth, and he will be delayed in attaining all-knowledge."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I shall pierce my own body and sprinkle my blood upon the ground so that no dust or soil may come to defile the Great Master."
"What use have I for this body!
This body must inevitably perish.
Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly lost my body, yet never for the sake of the Dharma."
He then took a sharp knife and pierced himself, sprinkling his blood upon the ground.
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva, the daughter of the elder, and the five hundred female attendants remained entirely resolute; even the evil Māra could find no opportunity to hinder them.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself: "How marvelous!
The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita’s love for the Dharma is such that he pierces his own body with a knife and sprinkles his blood upon the ground!"
Sadāprarudita and the women remained unmoved in mind; the evil Māra Pāpīyān could not destroy their roots of goodness.

Their resolve was firm, and they donned the great armor of adornment, disregarding even their own bodies and lives. With a profound heart, they sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, intending to deliver all sentient beings from the immeasurable sufferings of birth and death.
Śakra Devānām-indra praised the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Noble son!
Your power of diligence is great, firm and unshakable, and inconceivable!
Your love for the Dharma and your quest for the Dharma are unsurpassed!"
"Good son!

The Buddhas of the past were also like this; with a profound mind that loved the Dharma, cherished the Dharma, and revered the Dharma, they accumulated all merits and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Then the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita thought to himself:

"I have already prepared the Dharma seat for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata and finished sweeping and sprinkling it until it is pure; but where can I obtain fine, famous flowers to adorn this ground?"
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sits upon the Dharma-seat to preach the Dharma, you too should scatter flowers as an offering.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita was thinking in his heart, immediately gave him three thousand *droṇas* of celestial *mandārava* flowers.
Sadāprarudita received the flowers; he scattered half upon the ground and kept the other half to offer when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata sat upon the Dharma-seat to preach the Dharma.

At that time, after seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata arose from his various samādhis. For the purpose of expounding the Prajñāpāramitā, he proceeded to the Dharma seat and sat upon it, surrounded with respectful veneration by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings.
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, his mind was pure, joyful, and delighted, like that of a bhikṣu who has entered the third dhyāna."
[Treatise] Commentary:

Although the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita knew that all dharmas are empty and devoid of the characteristics of coming and going, he had not yet deeply penetrated them, nor could he understand the various gateways to the Dharma;
because his reverence for the bodies of the Buddhas was so profound and heavy, he was unable to contemplate emptiness.
Just as the waves of the great ocean, though they possess great power, recede and become useless upon reaching the slopes of Mount Sumeru;
so it is with Sadāprarudita: although he possesses the power of the wisdom of great emptiness, it becomes useless upon reaching the presence of the Buddha.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata now declares:
"The Buddhas come from nowhere, and when they depart, they go nowhere.
Within this, Dharmodgata himself explains the causal conditions, namely:
"All dharmas have the characteristic of immovability; the suchness of all dharmas is itself the Buddha.
Question: What is the suchness of all dharmas?
Answer:
The true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) refers to such dharma-gates as the emptiness of intrinsic nature, non-apprehensibility, and [the various forms of] emptiness.
Question:
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the foremost dharma among the six pāramitās of the Buddha-dharma Mahāyāna; if there were no Buddha, there would be no one to expound the Prajñā.

The thirty-two marks, the eighty secondary characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth—the harmonious integration of these pure and wondrous five aggregates, both material and immaterial—is therefore called the Buddha.
Just as the combination of five fingers is called a "fist," one cannot say that there is no fist;
since the name differs, the form differs, and the function differs, one cannot say there is no fist. Therefore, we know that the Buddha exists.
The answer is:
Not so! Within the Buddha-dharma, there are two truths:
There are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

From the perspective of conventional truth, it is said that "the Buddha taught the Prajñāpāramitā"; from the perspective of the ultimate truth, it is said that "all Buddhas are empty, neither coming nor going."
As you have said:
"Because the five pure aggregates are combined, they are called the Buddha.
If something exists because of a combination, it is then non-existent.
As the Buddha himself stated in a sutra regarding the causes and conditions:

"The five aggregates are not the Buddha; apart from the five aggregates, there is no Buddha. The five aggregates do not exist within the Buddha, nor does the Buddha exist within the five aggregates; the Buddha does not possess the five aggregates."
Why is this? The five aggregates are five and the Buddha is one; the one does not become five, nor do the five become one.
Furthermore, because the five aggregates lack intrinsic nature, they are deceptive and unreal.
The Buddha himself said:
"Among all dharmas that are non-deceptive, I am the foremost.
Therefore, the five aggregates are not themselves the Buddha.
Furthermore, if the five aggregates were themselves the Buddha, then all who possess these five aggregates would have to be Buddhas.
Question: Because of this objection, I previously stated:
"The first pure five aggregates, characterized by the thirty-two marks and so forth, are called the Buddha.
The answer is:
"The thirty-two marks and so forth also exist during the stage of a bodhisattva; why, then, are they not called the Buddha?"
Question:
At that time, although the body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, it lacks the knowledge of all modes;
if the knowledge of all modes were present within this first, wondrously beautiful body, that would indeed be called a Buddha.
The answer is:
"All-knowledge" (sarvākārajñatā) is described in the Prajñā[pāramitā] as having the characteristic of quiescence and being free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca).
If one attains this dharma, it is called "non-attainment"; because there is non-attainment, one is called a Buddha, and a Buddha is itself emptiness (śūnyatā).
For these and other such reasons, the five aggregates cannot be the Buddha himself;
nor is there a Buddha apart from these five aggregates. Why is this so?
Apart from these five aggregates, there is no other dharma that can be spoken of;
it is like how, apart from the five fingers, there is no further "fist" that can be spoken of. Question:
Why is there no such thing as a "fist"?
Because its form is different and its functional power is also different;
if it were merely the fingers, it should not be different.
Because the five fingers join together, the phenomenon of a "fist" arises. Although this phenomenon of a fist is impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing, one cannot say it does not exist.
The answer is:
if this phenomenon of a fist were definitively existent, then apart from the five fingers, there should be a fist visible on its own, and it would not need to depend upon the five fingers.
For such reasons as these, apart from the five fingers there is no fist;
likewise, the Buddha does not exist apart from the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
The Buddha is not within the five aggregates, nor are the five aggregates within the Buddha.
Why is this? Because difference cannot be apprehended.
If the five aggregates were different from the Buddha, the Buddha would have to exist within the five aggregates; however, this is not the case.
The Buddha is also not within the five aggregates. Why is this?
Apart from the five aggregates there is no Buddha, and apart from the Buddha there are no five aggregates.
For example, because a bhikṣu possesses the three robes and the alms bowl, one may say that he "has" them;
however, since the Buddha and the fivefold assembly are not distinct from one another, one cannot say that the Buddha "has" the fivefold assembly.
Since the Buddha cannot be found through these five kinds of seeking, one should know that there is no Buddha;
because the Buddha does not exist, there is neither coming nor going.
Question:
If one says there is no Buddha, that is a false view; how then can a bodhisattva resolve to seek Buddhahood?
The answer is:
what is meant here by "no Buddha" is the destruction of attachment to the notion of a Buddha; it does not mean adopting the notion of "no Buddha."
If even when a Buddha exists one is not permitted to grasp [at him], how much more so should one refrain from grasping at the false view that there is no Buddha!
Furthermore, the Buddha is eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristics of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
if a person discriminates or conceptually proliferates regarding the state of eternal quiescence, such a person also falls into false views.
To be free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence and to abide in the Middle Way is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The true nature of all phenomena is itself the Buddha. Why is this so?
To attain this true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called "attaining Buddhahood.

Furthermore, the mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena such as form is itself the Buddha; the emptiness of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of phenomena such as form is the mark of suchness, and the suchness of all Buddhas is likewise empty of intrinsic nature.
For this reason, it neither comes nor goes.

Non-arising, non-ceasing, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), emptiness, non-defilement, quiescence, and the nature of space are likewise without coming or going.
The suchness of [all things], up to the suchness of the nature of space and the suchness of the Buddha—this suchness is one; it is without duality, without triad, and without distinction.
Regarding this, the cause and condition are stated therein:
"For what reason?"
"They transcend all numerical dharmas because they are non-existent.
Such dharmas as these are real; within them there is no recollection or conceptual discrimination.
Because of grasping at marks, there are names, and within names there are numbers.
Within this, he himself states the reason:
"It is empty and not real, because nothing exists. He asks:
If these phenomena are non-existent, how can there be such distinctions as seeing or hearing, suffering or pleasure, bondage or liberation, and so forth?
The answer is:

herein, Dharmodgata himself explains through various distinctions and parables, namely, from "like seeing a mirage in the last month of spring" up to "this person does not discriminate whether dharmas come or go."
Just as in a mirage and the like, although there is no substantial reality, it can still deceive people by producing experiences of suffering and pleasure;
so too are all phenomena: although they are empty and non-existent, they can still cause people to experience suffering, pleasure, sorrow, and joy.
The phenomena of dreams and so forth are also like this.
Furthermore, the Buddha has two kinds of bodies:
first, the Dharma-body; second, the form-body.
The Dharma-body is the true Buddha; the form-body exists because it conforms to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the characteristics of the Buddha’s Dharma-body:

through various causes and conditions, the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) has been explained; yet this true nature of all phenomena neither comes nor goes. Therefore, it is said: "All Buddhas come from nowhere, and when they depart, they go nowhere."

If a person attains the characteristics of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas, this is called being "near" to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is called "near" because they have not yet attained omniscience, but because they are similar [to it].
The Prajñāpāramitā is named the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena;
if one can practice in this way, one is practicing the Prajñāpāramitā and is a true disciple of the Buddha.
Regarding those who are true disciples of the Buddha: one who realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is called a Buddha;
because they realize the distinctions within the true marks of all phenomena, there are those from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha* and the great *bodhisattvas*.
These individuals, from the *srotāpanna* up to the great *bodhisattva*, are called true disciples of the Buddha.

Regarding "not consuming in vain the faithful offerings of others": although giving to animals yields a hundredfold karmic reward, this merit is exhaustible and finite; because it cannot deliver sentient beings from birth and death, it is called "consuming in vain."
From the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) up to the Buddhas, all noble ones (*ārya*) receive the offerings of faith from others;
the fruit of this merit is inexhaustible and immeasurable even until *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that they do not consume the offerings of faith in vain.
This person should receive the offerings of all sentient beings: if a *srotāpanna* should receive the offerings of all ordinary persons;

a *sakṛdāgāmin* should receive the offerings of ordinary persons up to those who are *srotāpannas*; an *anāgāmin* should receive the offerings of ordinary persons as well as *srotāpannas* and *sakṛdāgāmins*; an *arhat* should receive the offerings of ordinary persons, *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, and *anāgāmins*; a *pratyekabuddha* should receive the offerings of ordinary persons as well as *srotāpannas* up to *arhats*; and a Great Bodhisattva who is close to attaining Buddhahood should receive the offerings of ordinary persons as well as *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

Regarding those who serve as fields of merit for the world: just as planting seeds in fertile soil will surely yield an abundant harvest, so too when sentient beings plant blessings in the fields of merit consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they obtain immeasurable fruits.

The preceding discourse stated that "all Buddhas neither come nor go. Sadāprarudita and the listeners then thought, "If even the Buddhas do not exist, then all dharmas must likewise be extinguished," thereby falling into the view of nihilism.
Therefore, I shall now explain the dharma of causes and conditions through an analogy.
Dharmodgata showed it to Sadāprarudita, saying:
"That which you are attached to and which you believe to exist substantially is non-existent."
"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, when there is a combination of causes and conditions, an image appears.
To prove this point, he spoke a parable:

"Just as jewels are produced within the great ocean, they do not come from the ten directions, and when they perish, they go nowhere; yet they appear through the conjunction of causes and conditions."
Nor does it arise without causes and conditions; rather, because of the merit and karmic conditions of the sentient beings of the four continents, this jewel is produced from the sea.
When the kalpa reaches its end and is extinguished, it likewise has no place to go;
it is like a lamp being extinguished, where the flame has nowhere to reach.
The Buddha’s body is likewise: the roots of goodness and merits planted from the first resolution for enlightenment are all the causes and conditions for the Buddha’s physical marks and signs;
yet the Buddha’s body is not independent, for it arises solely through the retribution of karma belonging to its original causes and conditions.

Although these causes and conditions endure for a long time, because their nature is that of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they must ultimately return to impermanence; when they disperse and perish, there is no body.
"It is like a skilled archer who shoots an arrow into the sky; though the arrow travels far, it must inevitably fall to the ground.

The bodies of the Buddhas are likewise: although they possess the marks and signs of excellence, radiant light, perfected merit, immeasurable renown, and limitless salvation of beings, they too return to extinction."
Question:

If precious jewels arise in the ocean due to the causes and conditions of the merit of sentient beings, why do they not arise near the dwelling places of sentient beings, but instead in the great ocean where they are difficult to obtain?
Answer: There are also sentient beings within the ocean, such as nāgas and asuras, who utilize these jewels.
Furthermore, if these jewels were produced among humans in a degenerate age, those possessed by greed would conceal them and not allow others to obtain them.
In times of prosperity, precious jewels arise spontaneously among humanity, and no one cherishes them as such;
it will be as when the time of Maitreya Buddha arrives, and precious jewels are regarded like common rubble.
Because people who are indolent and lazy cherish their own bodies and forcibly make vows to seek pleasure, they are unable to obtain the jewels even though they exist within the great ocean.
If one possesses a great mind and seeks with diligence, not sparing even body or life, then one shall obtain them.
The waters of the great ocean are a metaphor for the lands of the ten directions and the six realms; the various precious jewels are the Buddhas themselves.
Just as rare jewels arise for the sake of all sentient beings, yet cannot be obtained by those who are indolent and lazy;

so too it is with the Buddhas: although they appear in the world for the sake of sentient beings, those who are indolent, small-minded, or who are attached to the body and the self cannot be delivered.
Why is this so? All phenomena arise from the conjunction of various conditions. Sentient beings attain liberation due to two causes and conditions:
first, possessing right view within; second, having a teacher who skillfully expounds the Dharma without.
Although the Buddhas skillfully expound the Dharma, because sentient beings lack internal right view, they cannot all be saved.
It is like precious objects that, though produced for the sake of sentient beings, still leave some sentient beings in poverty;
so it is with the Buddhas: although they appear for the sake of sentient beings, because sentient beings possess little internal right view, they likewise cannot attain deliverance.
Furthermore, there is the analogy of the *vīṇā* (lute):
it has a hollow body, a neck, a skin, strings, and a plectrum; when a person strikes it with their hand, sound arises through the conjunction of these various conditions.
Just as the sound does not exist within the individual conditions, nor does it exist apart from the conditions, yet sound is audible because of the harmony of causes and conditions.
The bodies of all Buddhas are likewise: they arise through the convergence of various causes and conditions, namely the six pāramitās and the power of skillful means.
The Buddha-body does not reside within the dharmas such as the six pāramitās, yet it is not separate from the dharmas such as the six pāramitās.
Just as sound does not arise from a single cause nor without causes, so too is the body of the Buddha:
it does not arise without causes, nor does it arise from few causes; rather, because the causes and conditions of all wholesome dharmas are fully complete, the bodies of all Buddhas are produced.
Just as a reflection in a mirror exists through the combination of various causes and conditions, yet ceases when those conditions disperse;
so too it is with the Buddhas: they appear because of the presence of various causes and conditions, and they pass away when those causes and conditions disperse.
“Good son! You should contemplate the coming and going of all Buddhas in this manner; you should likewise know the characteristics of all dharmas.
Dharmodgata said to Sadāprarudita:

“Good son! Since you are able to know that the characteristics of all dharmas neither come nor go, you will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without falling back, and you will also certainly be able to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* and the power of skillful means.”
Why is this? Because all phenomena are without obstruction. He asked:
Question: Why did Śakra Devānām Indra manifest the *pāṭala* flowers for Sadāprarudita? Answer:
Because Śakra Devānām Indra loves and delights in the Buddha-way, he constantly makes offerings to all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to gather in sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha-way, manifested the body of a heavenly king and gave flowers to Sadāprarudita.
Because Sadāprarudita sought the Buddha-way with single-minded devotion, the devas came to make offerings to him;
and all sentient beings who saw him likewise resolved their minds on enlightenment.
Śakra-devānām-indra made offerings to Sadāprarudita for the sake of guiding sentient beings.

Some say: "Śakra-devānām-indra deeply loves and respects Sadāprarudita; having come to test him with the highest degree of severity, he has now restored his body to its former state and further given him these flowers."
Śakra Devānām-Indra has the power to give flowers to all people; however, because sentient beings lack the power of merit, if he were to give them, the flowers would immediately wither and decay.
Because Sadāprarudita has accomplished the perfection of merit, the flowers he receives will certainly not change; for this reason, Śakra gives them to him.
Furthermore, when all Bodhisattvas make offerings to their teachers, he does not give [the flowers] to everyone.

Regarding the protection and veneration [of the Dharma], the causal conditions have already been explained: namely, that one should protect it out of a desire to test whether old friendships can be maintained, even to the point of cutting one's own flesh and shedding one's blood.
Furthermore, Śakra Devānām Indra himself explains the causal conditions therein, saying:
"By the power of your causal conditions, you bring benefit to hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."
Sadāprarudita took the flowers and, according to his intention, made offerings to Dharmodgata.
Because Sadāprarudita had first heard his teacher’s name and later seen him with his own eyes and heard the Dharma that severed his doubts, he made this offering of his body.
The daughter of the elder and the others also followed the example of Sadāprarudita, offering their own bodies to him.
A question is raised:

Sadāprarudita offered his body as an act of worship to Dharmodgata; since Dharmodgata is a field of merit of great magnitude, why did the women not offer their bodies to him instead of giving them to Sadāprarudita?
The answer is:
Because women possess limited wisdom and many attachments, they should not abandon their original teacher to make offerings to another.
Furthermore, because the female body is sinful and defiled, even if the mind is pure, one must avoid external slander.
Question:
The daughter of the elder had already been given by her parents to Sadāprarudita; why does she now offer her body again?
Answer:

Previously, when they first left their parents to go with Sadāprarudita to Dharmodgata, it was for the sake of the Dharma that they made offerings, yet neither did they offer their own bodies, nor did their parents offer them to Sadāprarudita;

now, seeing Sadāprarudita inquire about the profound meaning and Dharmodgata explain it for him, Śakra Devendra rejoiced and made offerings. Therefore, having given rise to a heart of joy, he makes this offering of his body out of a mind of sovereign mastery.
Furthermore, all women are without independent status and thus incur ill repute.
According to the etiquette for women: in youth they follow their parents; in middle age they follow their husbands; and in old age they follow their sons.
Although these daughters of the elder came together along the road, they could not remain long without a protector; therefore, they offered their own bodies as a gift and made this vow:
"Just as our teacher has attained, may we also attain it."
At that time, Sadāprarudita wished to offer these women to Dharmodgata; fearing they might feel resentment, he asked:
"If you truly offer them with a sincere heart, I shall accept them from you."
"Sincere of heart" means not employing one's own will, but following whatever instructions are given,
like an insentient object. The women said,
"We truly act with a sincere heart."
Immediately, Sadāprarudita offered the merchant’s daughter, along with her handmaidens and five hundred chariots, to Dharmodgata.

Sadāprarudita did this because he wished to dispel the common suspicions of the world that he might be deceiving the merchant by bringing these women away; therefore, he gave them all as an offering to demonstrate his own lack of attachment.

Furthermore, Sadāprarudita, upon hearing the voice from the sky, attained understanding and rejoiced; he offered all his cherished internal and external possessions as worship, desiring to enter deeply into the gateway of the dānapāramitā.

Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing that although Sadāprarudita’s afflictions such as craving and greed were not yet exhausted, he was nevertheless able to relinquish all internal and external things through giving without any remainder, praised him, saying:
"Excellent!..."
Using the Buddhas of the past as an analogy:
because they performed difficult deeds, they attained a difficult-to-attain fruit of retribution, namely "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Question:

If Dharmodgata accepts [the offerings] because he wishes to cause Sadāprarudita’s roots of goodness to be fulfilled—roots of goodness being what is called the fulfillment of the dānapāramitā—for what reason does he then give them back to Sadāprarudita?
The answer is:
Dharmodgata’s great wisdom and skillful means cause Sadāprarudita to gain vast merit without any loss; this is called "receiving the superior."
Sadāprarudita practiced giving with a heart of utmost sincerity, severing all greedy attachments and not hoping for anything in return; thus his merit was fully perfected.

Dharmodgata reflected that Sadāprarudita had come from afar and his mind was untainted by the five desires, whereas those who had been there long were already providing him offerings; therefore, he gave them back to him.
Furthermore, it was heard that the daughters had previously offered their own bodies to Sadāprarudita—not out of material wealth, but because they wished to fulfill his original intention.
Moreover, these daughters had been the disciples of Sadāprarudita throughout successive lifetimes.
For such reasons as these, [the Buddha] returned them to Sadāprarudita.
[Sadāprarudita] asked:
"The great Bodhisattvas should not become exhausted by preaching the Dharma; why did he enter the palace?"
Answer: It is because he conforms to the ways of worldly people.
Furthermore, the sentient beings in the City of Universal Fragrance do not constantly seek the Way; at times they grow weary and desist, indulging in the pleasures of the five desires.
Because the various devas constantly indulge in the five desires, they obstruct and neglect the pursuit of the Way.
There are lands where Bodhisattvas dwell, where they always exert themselves with diligence and do not accept the five desires.

The sentient beings of this City of Universal Fragrance have various aspirations as their original vows; Dharmodgata, wishing to guide them according to their respective inclinations, was therefore born in that land.
For this reason, when the sentient beings grew weary from listening to the Dharma, he rose and entered the palace.

Furthermore, for those who have not yet attained the Way, although the Dharma is subtle and profound, because they hear it constantly, they give rise to a mind of weariness and distaste; this is because such people exist within this assembly.
Moreover, since Dharmodgata enjoys wealth and pleasure therein as a human being, he ought to rest when the sun sets.
At that time, Sadāprarudita had this thought:
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma; I should not sit or lie down. He asked:
"For the sake of the Dharma, why should one not sit or lie down?
Answer: "There is no fixed rule for this."
Because this person possesses great aspiration and great diligence, and out of reverence for the Dharma, they form this thought:
"If I were to sit or lie down, that would be laziness."
"When I first sought the Dharma, I did not even spare my own body, much less feel weary!
For this reason, he neither sat nor lay down;
for great desire and great diligence are incompatible with sitting and lying.

Furthermore, while sitting or lying down, he did not exert himself; however, while walking or standing, he was diligent and persevering. Therefore, he remained constantly in these two postures to await the teacher's emergence.
Question:
Did Sadāprarudita already know beforehand that his teacher would not emerge for seven years?
Answer: No.
Because he did not know [the situation] when he first arrived;
furthermore, Dharmodgata also remained without coming out for seven years, having made a vow to enter meditative absorption for seven years due to specific causes and conditions.
Sadāprarudita made this vow:
"Until my teacher emerges, I shall never sit or lie down.
Furthermore, a person of great capacity does not even contravene worldly laws, let alone those of the Dharma!
Furthermore, when he first sought the Dharma, he did not even spare his own body; now that he has undertaken this for seven years, how could it be considered difficult?
[The interlocutor] asks:
"The human body is frail and weak; how can one remain for seven years without sitting or lying down?"
The answer is:
At that time, the lifespan of human beings was long; thus, although seven years may have passed, it would be like seven days in the present day.
Furthermore, because the physical merit and power of people in that fortunate age were great, standing for seven years was not considered difficult.
For example, there was an energetic bhikṣu who left the household life at the age of sixty and made this vow:
"I shall not let my side touch the mat until I have fully attained all that is to be attained by a śrāvaka, up to and including the state of an arhat endowed with the six supernormal powers."
He composed the *Upadeśa* on the four Āgamas, which are widely practiced in the world today.
If this person was already thus in such a degenerate age, how much more so must it have been for Sadāprarudita, who was born in a favorable age!
Furthermore, although his physical strength may be weak, because his mind is powerful, he is able to accomplish the task.
Moreover, one who single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-way is held in the thoughts of all the Buddhas of the ten directions;

the great Bodhisattvas and the devas seeking the Buddha-way augment his vigor and surround him with protection. For this reason, even though he remains standing for seven years, he does not become exhausted.
Question:
Why did Dharmodgata enter into samādhi for as long as seven years? Answer:
This has already been answered:
for those of good fortune who live long lives, even seven years are not considered long.
Furthermore, the palace, the court ladies, and the exquisite five sensory pleasures of Dharmodgata are similar to those of the devas.

Sadāprarudita and others who have newly resolved their minds have not yet attained mental pliancy; though Dharmodgata preaches the Dharma of emptiness and praises the transcendence of desire, they suspect that his mind has not yet been able to relinquish [attachments].
Therefore, the seven-year samādhi was intended to eliminate the doubts of the multitude and to inspire in them a heart of noble reverence.

Upon hearing that Dharmodgata had practiced the seven-year samādhi with such harmony between mind and speech—being able both to preach and to practice—they would believe and accept his words, making it easy for them to attain liberation.
For example, when an abscess has not yet ripened, a physician does not lance it, but merely applies medicine to cause it to ripen; once ripened, it is easy to break open.
Furthermore, because one desires to experience the true bliss born of the mind, one enters immeasurable samādhis.
Furthermore, there are two ways of teaching the Dharma:
first, teaching through speech; second, manifesting the Dharma through the body.

Now, wishing to manifest the Dharma through the body, he enters immeasurable samādhis so that sentient beings may know how to gather the mind and enter into wisdom, thereby attaining knowledge of reality as it is.
The samādhis of a bodhisattva are as explained in the "Meaning of a Bodhisattva" section.
The practice of prajñā and the power of skillful means are as explained in the "Chapter on Skillful Means."
During those seven years, Sadāprarudita did not give rise to the three types of evil thoughts or reflections, nor did he relish sensory flavors.
Although this person had not yet destroyed his afflictions (*kleśa*), because he had accumulated all manner of wholesome dharmas, he restrained the afflictions so that they could not arise;
he focused his mind on this alone:
"When will Dharmodgata emerge?
I shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā from him.
After seven years had passed, he thought thus:
"I shall prepare a seat for Dharmodgata and sweep and adorn the place. He asked:
"How did Sadāprarudita know that after seven years had passed, Dharmodgata would emerge?"
Answer: Some say that in the past,
for seven years, he had heard and learned this through successive transmission.
Some say that when Dharmodgata first entered samādhi, he himself stated that seven years would be the limit.
It is as Śākyamuni Buddha told Ānanda:
"I wish to enter meditative concentration for one month or two months," Ānanda informed the fourfold assembly.
Because Sadāprarudita deeply loved the Buddha-dharma and revered Dharmodgata, he made offerings and adorned the place where the Dharma was being taught.
A renunciant bodhisattva merely adorns his own mind and approaches a teacher to receive the Dharma;
a householder bodhisattva, however, adorns the place where the Dharma is taught, making offerings of flowers and incense.

Furthermore, Sadāprarudita performed these adornments because he wished for Dharmodgata to know his love for the Dharma and his desire for the characteristics of the Dharma, and that his profound mind was filled with faith and joy;

therefore, he gave rise to the thought to exert his strength together with the five hundred maidens to sweep and sprinkle the ground, and personally arranged seats of gold, silver, and precious jewels.

Although Sadāprarudita and his companions possessed their own exquisite rugs and cushions, because their devotion to the Dharma was so profound, they spread the upper garments they were wearing upon the ground to serve as seats.
They sought water to sprinkle upon the earth, but because Māra had concealed it, they were unable to find any.
In this regard, he himself explains the causal conditions:
"Māra thought to himself:
'If Sadāprarudita does not find water, his mind will become discouraged, for his aspiration will remain unfulfilled.'"

Furthermore, it causes one to despise oneself, thinking, "Because my merit is meager, I cannot find water for the sake of making offerings to the Dharma"; thus, because the mind is shrouded by the sorrow of self-contempt, [one fails to attain the water].

Regarding the statement that "merit does not increase and wisdom does not shine with clarity," it is because the mind is shrouded by various sorrows and afflictions that merit and wisdom are unable to illuminate;
it is like the sun whose light is obscured and thus fails to shine clearly.
Māra knew that his mind was so great that it could not be utterly destroyed, yet he intended to cause some slight obstruction and delay him.
At that time, Sadāprarudita pierced his own body and shed blood to sprinkle upon the ground, wishing thereby to settle the dust.

Although human flesh and blood are foul-smelling, because he sought water with such utmost sincerity and failed to find it, his mind made no distinction between fragrance and stench, or good and bad; desiring to settle the dust, he did not begrudge his own body or life.
Furthermore, because Sadāprarudita deeply cherished and was devoted to the *prajñāpāramitā*, he had nothing he could not give away.

Some say: "There were many devas, nāgas, and spirits who constantly followed Sadāprarudita to assist and protect him; for this reason, the blood that flowed forth was transformed into fragrant water."
"Just as when the Rishi Kṣānti was being cut and mangled, his blood was transformed into milk.
Furthermore, because he has accomplished immeasurable merit and virtue, everything is realized immediately according to his vows.
Question:
If merit is perfected, one obtains whatever one wishes; why then would Māra conceal the water? Answer:
This Bodhisattva, having newly resolved his mind, is able to fulfill minor vows but has not yet been able to repel Māra.
In this context, Sadāprarudita himself explains the causes and conditions for shedding his blood:
"Since beginningless saṃsāra, I have repeatedly lost my body many times, yet never for the sake of the Dharma."
Question: If Sadāprarudita loves the Dharma so much that he pierces his own body and draws blood, and were his body to die, who would then listen to the Dharma?
Answer:
This matter is as explained in the response regarding breaking the bone to extract the marrow.
Furthermore, because the various devas and great bodhisattvas protect him therein, they cause him not to die.
Moreover, when the evil Māra realizes that his mind cannot be thwarted or destroyed, the water flows back out.

That Sadāprarudita and the others were all without divergent thoughts means this: suppose a person first practices the mind of loving-kindness; for the sake of sentient beings and for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not begrudge their own body or life.
Yet, once they have obtained a sharp blade and cut their own flesh, because they are oppressed by the pain, a sense of regret arises in their heart—this is called "divergence."
Because this bodhisattva possesses great power of faith and desires to attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not consider these [practices] to be suffering.
Furthermore, because they cherish sentient beings with a heart of profound compassion, they do not regard them as difficult even when undergoing various forms of affliction;
it is just like a compassionate mother who loves her child—though she undergoes long-term toil, hardship, and impurity for the sake of her child, she does not consider it evil.
Furthermore, because he perceives that the true mark of all phenomena is ultimate emptiness, he knows that this body is merely a deceptive combination;
since he has shattered this deception, when his body is being cut and dismembered, it does not hinder his *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for Māra not finding an opportunity: it is like a person who, having a sore, receives poison;
if a bodhisattva has the sores of greed and sorrow, Māra finds his opportunity.
Because they sprinkled their own blood upon the ground and their hearts were free from sorrow, Māra could find no opportunity.
Just as with the mind of Sadāprarudita, so too was the mind of the five hundred women;
because they revered Sadāprarudita, although they saw him piercing his own body, they felt no sorrow, for their own vows were being fulfilled.

At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, having witnessed this event, marveled at its unprecedented nature: "This person has not yet attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), nor have their afflictions been severed; yet for the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, they do not spare their own body or life, no different from those who are free from desire;
they cut and sever their own body as if it were grass or wood."
If it was thus at the initial stage, it becomes even more so in subsequent stages.
Furthermore, regarding the "extraordinary" aspect, herein Śakra Devānām Indra himself explains the causal conditions:
"Sadāprarudita’s love for the Dharma is such that he even pierced himself with a knife," and so forth.
Having thus rejoiced in his heart, Śakra Devānām Indra praised him, saying:
"Excellent! He praised his love for the Dharma, his delight in the Dharma, and his diligent application of effort.
He used the Buddhas of the past as an analogy:
"It is not only you who are now undergoing such hardship; the Buddhas of the past sought Prajñā in the same way.
Having heard Śakra Devendra’s consolation of his mind, Sadāprarudita felt like fire that has obtained ghee, becoming even more intense, and he thought to himself:
"I have already spread the seats and sprinkled the ground; where shall I find fine flowers to adorn this place of Dharma?
He asked: "When you do not see water, why do you not entertain this thought?"
"Where shall I find water to sprinkle upon the ground?
He replied:
"Sadāprarudita, the places where there was previously water have now all vanished; know this to be the work of Māra."
Therefore, from among the constituent elements of the four great elements within his own body, he drew out water and sprinkled it upon the ground.
Although the water element within his body was abundant, blood is where life resides; thus, he drew it out to sprinkle upon the earth.
The flowers do not belong to him of their own accord; as the time for Dharmodgata’s departure is approaching, he cannot seek them from afar.
Furthermore, the quantity required is vast, sufficient to cover the entire ground; therefore, he conceived the thought of obtaining them.
Śakra, knowing his thought, immediately gave him three thousand *droṇas* of the most exquisite celestial flowers called *māndārava*, sufficient to complete the task.
The reason Śakra did not give him human flowers was that he wished to cause him to give rise to a rare and extraordinary mind.
Having received the flowers, Sadāprarudita divided them into two parts:
he set aside the finer ones to scatter during his preaching of the Dharma, while the remaining ones were used to cover the ground.
According to the customs of that country, they cover the ground with flowers and cause people to walk upon them as an act of worship.

At that time, after seven full years had passed according to his previous commitment, Dharmodgata rose from samādhi and proceeded directly to the Dharma-seat, surrounded with respectful reverence by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers, in order to preach the Prajñāpāramitā.
Question:
If all bodhisattvas enter into subtle samādhi, who is able to cause them to arise from it? Answer:
When the practitioner first begins, they establish a limit for themselves before entering meditative concentration;
when the time arrives, their mind being autonomous, they arise from samādhi, and through a heart of compassion, they give rise to vitarka and vicāra.
For example, there was a bhikṣu who, when entering the samādhi of the cessation of perception and feeling, made a vow to himself that he would arise when he heard the gong.
Having already entered it, the monastery caught fire; the other bhikṣus were terrified and departed without striking the gong.
At that time, after twelve years had passed, a donor once again assembled the community of monks with the intention of building a monastery;
just as he was about to strike the *gandī* gong, the sound of the *gandī* reached his ears, and he died instantly, his body dissolving.
Later, those who attained the Way spoke of it in this way.
Furthermore, some say:
the Dharma-nature-born body of a Great Bodhisattva, like that of all Buddhas, constantly enters samādhi and is devoid of distracted or coarse thoughts.
By virtue of his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he is able to preach the Dharma, fly through the air, and deliver sentient beings.
According to worldly conventions, there are the signs of entering and emerging from samādhi.
Therefore, although he enters subtle and wondrous samādhi, he is able to emerge from it again, as he is drawn forth by his heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
For example, when a spell brings forth a dragon surrounded by a great multitude, these are its inner retinue;
they follow it out as it is respectfully offered flowers and incense, for the purpose of preaching the Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who preach the Prajñāpāramitā do so by means of worldly conventions, names, and language, desiring to reveal to sentient beings the sign of immovability in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
When Sadāprarudita saw Dharmodgata, he immediately attained pure joy; it pervaded his entire body like a bhikṣu entering the third dhyāna.

Why is this? Because sentient beings with many desires still feel joy and pleasure upon obtaining that which is not pure or sublime; how much more so when they behold one whose body is adorned with true merit!

Having heard of Dharmodgata from the Buddha in the sky, Sadāprarudita immediately conceived a great aspiration and attained various samādhis. He beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions and further heard those Buddhas of the ten directions explain the causes and conditions of his past lives:
"Only Dharmodgata is able to deliver you."
Having heard this, his heart was further inspired and he yearned with thirsting longing to see him; therefore, midway along the road, he wished to sell himself to provide offerings.
Now, for seven years in the city of Gandhavatī, he has neither sat nor lain down, desiring only to see Dharmodgata.
Thus have they long yearned with thirsty longing;
like a person oppressed by heat and thirst who finds even turbid, warm water in a puddle and yet rejoices, how much more so when obtaining clear, cool, and delicious water!
Since their longing has persisted for a long time and the merit of Dharmodgata is great, they are thus filled with joy and delight.
A question is asked:
There are four kinds of bliss; why is only the bliss of the third dhyāna mentioned, while the bliss of the concentrations of the higher stages and the bliss of liberation are not?
Answer:
Because sentient beings in the desire realm mostly crave pleasant sensations among the three types of feeling,
when they hear that the bliss of nirvana is characterized by non-existence, their minds do not find joy or delight in it.
Because suffering and pleasure have been abandoned within these aforementioned four dhyānas, the mind finds no further delight;
yet within the third dhyāna, there is bliss—the pinnacle of bliss.
Furthermore, some say:

Because Sadāprarudita had newly resolved his mind and had not yet entered the subtle, profound, and wondrous samādhi, upon seeing Dharmodgata, he experienced great joy, which was like the bliss of the third dhyāna.

Because Sadāprarudita realized for himself that he was greatly rejoicing, he immediately relinquished that joy and attained the pure nature of phenomena (dharmatā), whereby his entire body experienced bliss; therefore, the bliss of the third dhyāna is used as a metaphor.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Volume Ninety-nine.
The Mahāprāñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on the Chapter of Dharmodgata,
Volume Ninety-nine (Volume One Hundred).
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty. [Sūtra] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita, together with the daughter of the elder and her five hundred attendants, arrived at the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata was. They scattered celestial *mandārava* flowers, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and having completed their salutations, withdrew to sit to one side.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata saw that he was seated, he addressed the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying:
"Good son! Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
I shall now explain for you the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Son of good family!
Because all dharmas are equal, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also equal.
Because all dharmas are detached, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also detached.
Because all dharmas are immovable, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also immovable.
Because all dharmas are without mentation, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also without mentation.
Because all phenomena are fearless, one should know that the perfection of wisdom is also fearless.
Because all phenomena have a single flavor, one should know that the perfection of wisdom also has a single flavor.
Because all dharmas are boundless, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because all dharmas are unarisen, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also unarisen.
Because all phenomena are without cessation, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without cessation.
Because space is boundless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also boundless.
Because the waters of the great ocean are boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
Because Mount Sumeru is magnificent, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also magnificent.
Because space is without discrimination, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without discrimination.
Because form is limitless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also limitless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also limitless.
Because the element of earth is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless;
because the elements of water, fire, and wind are boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless;
because the element of space is boundless, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also boundless.
Because it is equal to the vajra and so forth, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also equal.
Because all dharmas are without discrimination, one should know that the prajñāpāramitā is also without discrimination.
Because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) cannot be apprehended, one should know that the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be apprehended.
Because all phenomena are equal in their non-existence, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also equal in its non-existence.
Because all dharmas are without activity, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without activity.
Because all dharmas are inconceivable, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also inconceivable.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāprarudita immediately attained various samādhis while seated upon his throne, namely: the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas, the samādhi of the detachment of all dharmas, the samādhi of fearlessness in all dharmas, the samādhi of the single flavor of all dharmas, the samādhi of the boundlessness of all dharmas, the samādhi of the non-arising of all dharmas, the samādhi of the non-extinction of all dharmas, the samādhi of the boundlessness of space, the samādhi of the boundlessness of the waters of the great ocean, the samādhi of the adornment of Mount Sumeru, the samādhi of the non-discrimination of space, the samādhi of the boundlessness of form, and the samādhi of the boundlessness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
as well as the samādhi of the boundlessness of the earth element, and the samādhi of the boundlessness of the water element, fire element, wind element, and space element.
The Vajra-like Samādhi, the Samādhi of Non-discrimination of All Dharmas, the Samādhi of the Inconceivability of All Dharmas—through such as these, he attained six million gates of samādhi.
At that time, the Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Just as I now, within this trichiliocosm, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus, teach the Prajñāpāramitā with these characteristics, with this appearance, and with these names;

so too did Sadāprarudita attain these six million gates of samādhi and see, in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, Buddhas in trichiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each surrounded by bhikṣus with reverence, teaching this Mahāprajñāpāramitā with such characteristics, with such an appearance, and with such names.”
From that time forward, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita’s vast learning and wisdom became inconceivable, like the waters of the great ocean;
he was never separated from the Buddhas and was born within Buddha-fields.
Even in their dreams, they have never failed to see the Buddha;
all their manifold difficulties have been completely severed, and they will be reborn in whichever Buddha-field they wish, according to their vows. Subhūti!
One should know that by means of this prajñāpāramitā, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish all merits and attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

For this reason, Subhūti, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to study the six pāramitās, wish to enter deeply into the wisdom of all buddhas, and wish to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), they should receive, uphold, recite, read, correctly contemplate, and extensively explain to others this Prajñāpāramitā; furthermore, they should transcribe it into volumes and make offerings, revere, and praise it with incense, flowers, and even music.

Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and it is that which is revered by all Buddhas of the ten directions.
[Treatise] Commentary:
After Dharmodgata had emerged and reached the place of the Dharma-seat, he surveyed the assembly and saw no one superior to himself; thereupon, he sat down.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, knowing that [Dharmodgata] was already seated, went to where Dharmodgata was, prostrated with his head at his feet, and sat to one side.
There are three kinds of prostration:
first, verbal prostration;...
Second, one bends the knees but does not touch the head to the ground;
third, one touches the head to the ground—this is considered the supreme form of salutation.
Among the various parts of the human body, the head is the highest and the feet are the lowest; to prostrate with the head at the feet is the ultimate expression of reverence.

When Dharmodgata saw that he was seated, he knew that [the seeker] had come from afar, not sparing his own body or life, and had undergone various hardships and sufferings solely out of a desire to hear the Dharma.
When they first met, the sun was about to set, so he heard the Dharma for only a short time;
because the sun had set, Dharmodgata rose and entered the palace.
Now, for the sake of the Dharma, he has yearned with thirst for seven years without giving rise to a single divergent thought;

as he was about to depart, he sprinkled the ground with his own blood, demonstrating that for the sake of the Dharma he does not begrudge his body or life, that his mind is non-regressive, certain and beyond doubt, and thus capable of receiving transformation through teaching.
Therefore, he said:
"Good son! Listen attentively with a single mind!"
The former doubt regarding the coming and going of the Buddhas has already been severed;
now, desiring only to hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he therefore explains "the characteristics of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Regarding the "characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*," it is as previously explained in the context of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*). Some may say:
it is by the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* that one contemplates all phenomena as being equal.
It is not that the nature of all dharmas is inherently equal;
rather, it is because all dharmas are equal that the Prajñāpāramitā is equal. Therefore, Dharmodgata said: "Because all dharmas are equal, the Prajñāpāramitā is equal."
Why is this so? Because cause and effect are similar.
Initially observing the equality of all phenomena is the cause; attaining a mind of certainty in the prajñāpāramitā is the fruit.
Question:
Since the contemplation of the equality of all dharmas is itself prajñā, and prajñā is itself equality, why are they distinguished as cause and fruit?
Answer:

Although Prajñā and all phenomena possess a single characteristic, being neither dual nor distinct, for the practitioner, the initial stage of contemplation is the cause, while the completion of that contemplation is termed the fruit—
just as there is the attainment of the path of a Srotāpanna and the stage of one who is approaching it.
Furthermore, just as the five aggregates with outflows are called "accumulation" at the time of their cause and "suffering" at the time of their fruit,
so too the equality of all phenomena such as form is itself the equality of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Question: One should explain the "characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā. Why, then, do you now speak of equality?
It is because of inequality that there is equality, and because of equality that there is inequality.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is neither a single characteristic nor diverse characteristics; why then do you wish to grasp at a single characteristic?
He replied:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep and subtle; if it were not taught through skillful means, no one would understand it."
Therefore, if one discriminates unequally, all afflictions arise and the three poisons increase—namely, hatred toward enemies and attachment to kin;
love for the good and hatred for the unwholesome.
When a bodhisattva abides in these two kinds of equality, they contemplate all dharmas as equal:
by abiding in the equality of sentient beings, they regard enemies and kin, and those they hate or love, as entirely equal; thus they open the gate of merit and close off the evil destinies.

By abiding in the equality of dharmas, they eliminate all conceptualization, discrimination, attachment, and grasping at signs regarding all dharmas; they see only that all dharmas are empty, and emptiness itself is equality.
There are those who, having attained this emptiness of the equality of all dharmas, proceed directly toward the bodhisattva path without engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding emptiness;
yet there are others who, despite attaining this equality, give rise to conceptual proliferation, thinking:
"If one contemplates universal emptiness, such faults will arise!"
For such a person, equality itself is inequality.
Therefore, it is for the sake of "true equality" within this context that the "equality of the prajñāpāramitā" is taught; it is not a frivolous conceptualization (prapañca).
To be free from the two extremes of equality and inequality is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Question:

Since the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is already fully established by "equality," for what reason is it further stated that "being free from [the extremes] is the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*"?
Answer: The sūtra merely states that "because all dharmas are equal, prajñā is equal. However, the practitioner grasps this mark of equality and gives rise to attachment. Therefore, it is said:
"The mark of equality of the *prajñāpāramitā* is by nature detached, because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and all other dharmas are detached."
The meaning of "detachment" is as explained in the "Chapter on Characteristics and Non-characteristics.

Having attained this equality of all dharmas, and further being detached from that very equality, one dwells securely in emptiness. In emptiness, one is immovable—neither can conceptual proliferation (prapañca) move one, nor can the mountains of afflictions (kleśa), nor even the onset of impermanence, cause one to waver.
Why is this? Because they have attained the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
When a bodhisattva abides in these two kinds of emptiness, they attain immovable *prajñāpāramitā*; this is the ultimate.
If there is mindfulness, that is precisely a point of attachment to signs;
therefore it is said:
"Because all dharmas are without mindfulness, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also without mindfulness."
The mark of immovability is the *prajñāpāramitā*, because all marks have been extinguished in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one does not keep this *prajñā* in mind, one may become bewildered and lose one's direction; those who engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) will give rise to fear when in the midst of the great assembly.
Furthermore, because they do not understand *nirvāṇa*, they likewise give rise to fear.
Therefore, it is said that "the mark of fearlessness is the perfection of wisdom.

Although such a person does not definitively grasp at the marks of phenomena, because they have deeply entered the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), their mind is without fear when confronted by those who challenge various marks within a great assembly; this is because they have attained the signlessness (*animitta*) of all phenomena.
Furthermore, when entering the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one knows that all phenomena are unattainable;
therein, there is likewise no fear.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has skillfully and thoroughly penetrated all phenomena.
Furthermore, all dharmas have a single characteristic, namely, emptiness of intrinsic nature;
therefore, because the Prajñāpāramitā conforms to all dharmas, it is also of the single flavor of emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Question: It has already been stated above that all dharmas are equal; why is it now further stated that they have a single flavor? Answer:
Emptiness is sometimes flavorful and sometimes flavorless.

If a practitioner, for the sake of various views, takes up signs, discriminates between the beautiful and the ugly, and engages in deliberation, they then attain this mind of emptiness that is equal toward all phenomena; because of the great joy [therein], it is called "flavor."
Just as when a person is oppressed by heat and thirst, they obtain clear, cool water and consider its flavor to be peerless; it is called "flavor" because it is used according to the occasion.
Ultimate reality is emptiness, and thus it is neither flavor nor non-flavor.
Furthermore, regarding "one flavor": when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), both the objects of focus and the objects of observation are of one flavor;
because the power of the knowledge of emptiness is great, all other phenomena follow suit and become empty.
It is like when rock honey is being boiled and is about to reach maturity; although various substances have been combined, they all become rock honey.
It is also like the great ocean, into which the hundred rivers flow and all become of one taste—namely, the taste of ultimate emptiness.
The various phenomena, such as form and so forth, are likewise distinct and separate within the minds of ordinary beings;
yet upon entering the Prajñāpāramitā, they all become of one single flavor.
"Extremes" are defined as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), whether they be existence or non-existence.
Because one observes that all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are neither existent nor non-existent, they are signless (*animitta*);
being signless is precisely being boundless (*ananta*). Having observed this, it is itself the boundless *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, some say that there are two kinds of extremes:
the extreme of permanence and the extreme of annihilation; the extreme of saṃsāra and the extreme of nirvāṇa; the extreme of evil and the extreme of goodness, and so forth.
Because there are no such extremes as these within it, it is called the "boundless Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, some say that "extremes" refers to the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and the posterior limit (*aparānta*).
Because the world is beginningless, it has no prior limit; because one enters nirvana without remainder, it has a prior limit;
and because one does not emerge from it again, it has no subsequent limit.
By thus discriminating these various extremes, one becomes attached to the world and fears nirvana.
Therefore, within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no such thing as these "limits"; one merely hears that the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is without entering or exiting.
Question: Since the equality of all phenomena and the detachment of all phenomena are both "limitless," why are they explained separately?
Answer: For those who know that all phenomena are equal and know that all phenomena are detached, there is no need for explanation;
however, because some grasp at signs and cling to this single flavor, it is therefore said to be "boundless."

Dharmodgata did not speak merely for the sake of Sadāprarudita, nor did Sadāprarudita ask merely for his own sake; rather, it was because sentient beings possess various minds and various practices that he briefly explained the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā.
There is neither arising nor ceasing, as previously explained in various causes and conditions within the section "Refuting Arising and Ceasing.
Space is boundless, as explained in the Mahāyāna analogies for space.
The waters of the great ocean are boundless and adorned by Mount Sumeru; because this has not been explained previously, it shall now be briefly discussed.
Question: Since space is an unconditioned and eternal phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*), no one can reach its limit, and thus it may be said to be "boundless."
The waters of the great ocean within the four continents, encircling Mount Sumeru, have a measurable extent in yojanas; since there are people who can cross them, why do you say they are boundless?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of "boundlessness":
first, actual boundlessness; second, boundlessness because people cannot reach it.
The ocean also has two kinds:
first, that which can be crossed;

second, that which encircles Mount Sumeru within the nine precious mountains, measuring eighty-two thousand yojanas in breadth, such that the people of the world cannot reach its edge, and is therefore called "boundless."
Just as a small sea can be crossed by the power of a boat,
whereas the waters of the great ocean cannot be crossed by the power of a boat— only those with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) being able to cross it—

so too do ordinary followers of external paths (*tīrthika*) produce the boat of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to cross the seas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is like a great ocean; because it is so deep and vast, one cannot cross it, for one cannot shatter the mind of self.

The noble sages (*ārya*), by the power of the wings of wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), shatter the false appearances of all phenomena and attain the true reality (*bhūtanimitta*); therefore, they are able to cross it. For this reason, the analogy of the great ocean is employed.
Question: Since Mount Sumeru is of a single color, why do you say it is "adorned"? Answer:
The non-Buddhist texts state that Mount Sumeru is of a single color,
being composed entirely of gold. In the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*,
it is said that each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru is formed of a distinct jewel, adorned with gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Whatever direction the various birds went, each became the same color as that place.
The dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, brothers, encircled [the Buddha] with their bodies seven times.

At the summit of the mountain is the palace of the Thirty-three Heavens; its city has seven concentric walls and is named Sudarśana. It has nine hundred and ninety-nine gates, and at the side of each gate there are sixteen powerful, blue-clad yakṣas who act as guardians.
On the high ground within the city, a palace was built named Vaijayanta; on its four sides were four great gardens.
On the four sides were the Four Great Kings, and there were mountains called Yugandhara, each forty-two thousand yojanas in height, upon which the Four Great Kings rule.
The four great oceans, the palaces of the various asuras and the palaces of the nāga kings;
the nine precious mountains, such as Yugandhara and others; and the sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, and all other stars surrounding and adorning them.
Adorned with such various and diverse ornaments, one never tires of beholding them.
The Prajñāpāramitā is likewise.
