By virtue of the retributive fruits of the six pāramitās, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), a Brahmā, a Śakra-devendra, a Śuddhāvāsa-devendra, or Maheśvara—receiving such retributive fruits as these adornments while the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā is not yet fully perfected.

When the perfection of wisdom is fulfilled, there is the adornment of the fruit of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, the fruit of the arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the irreversible bodhisattva, and the fruits of the path of all Buddhas.
Just as Mount Sumeru is adorned both above and below, so too is the adornment of the *prajñāpāramitā*:
when it is not yet complete, it is adorned by the various heavenly kings and others;
once it is complete, it is adorned by the fruits of the various paths.

Regarding Mount Sumeru: at the beginning of the kalpa, when it was first established, great winds blew from the four directions, gathering the essence and flavor of the earth and accumulating them to form Mount Sumeru;
further winds then blew upon it, making it firm and transforming it into precious jewels.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is also like this: among all wholesome dharmas, it is the foremost, solid, firm, and harmonious synthesis that constitutes *prajñā*.
Just as Mount Sumeru cannot be moved by the great winds from its four sides or by the waves of the great ocean;
so too the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be moved by false views, non-Buddhists, frivolous disputations, or the hosts of Māra.
Just as the four gardens atop Mount Sumeru provide various pleasures for the devas who reach them, so too is it with Prajñā:
the practitioner who can ascend to the summit of Prajñā reaches the gardens of the various meditative concentrations, such as the four dhyānas, and experiences manifold bliss.
Furthermore, some say: Just as all birds that reach Mount Sumeru become of one and the same color, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā;
all dharmas that enter into it become of one and the same characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Just as space is without discrimination—space does not discriminate between what is internal and external, distant and near, long and short, pure and impure, and so forth;
so too is the *prajñāpāramitā*. When all phenomena enter into *prajñā*, there is likewise no discrimination between internal and external, or between wholesome and unwholesome.
As for the boundlessness of the five aggregates, the five aggregates are eternally pervasive throughout the world;
the prajñāpāramitā is likewise, not being separate from the five aggregates, for the true reality (dharmatā) of the five aggregates is itself the prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, just as with phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), when analyzed and broken down even to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), they possess no spatial direction; because they lack spatial direction, they are boundless.

As for formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*), because they have no shape, there is no distinction between "this" and "that"; because there is no distinction between "this" and "that," they are boundless.

The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: regarding all phenomena, whether one analyzes form down to its subtlest atoms, or analyzes formless phenomena down to a single thought-moment, one does not perceive anything that is definitively permanent, blissful, self, or pure.
Therefore it is said that because form (*rūpa*) is boundless, prajñā is boundless;
this applies likewise even to the six elements up to space (*ākāśa*).
As for "like a vajra," it is like the vajra held by a celestial king (*devendra*): it has neither hatred nor attachment, and wherever it is applied, there is nothing it cannot shatter.

The mind prior to the omniscience (*sarvajñā*) of all Buddhas—within this mind, the samādhi is able to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and perversions (*viparyāsa*), as well as their residual impressions (*vāsanā*), such that they are entirely extinguished; therefore, it is called "like a diamond" (*vajropama*).
Just as the wisdom associated with the Vajra-samādhi contemplates all phenomena as equal, so too does the Prajñāpāramitā contemplate the equality of all phenomena.
Why is this? It is because one first contemplates the equality of all phenomena through Prajñā, and only thereafter attains this samādhi.
As for the non-differentiation of all phenomena: it is due to the power of afflictions that ordinary worldlings engage in various differentiations of phenomena.
When one attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they are seen to be subject to destruction and transformation.

Therefore, when a noble one (*ārya*) attains the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not follow after conceptualization or discrimination regarding phenomena; they enter into the three samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

When they encounter the transformation of all phenomena, they feel no sorrow, because from the outset they have not engaged in discrimination or grasping at the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena.

Regarding the fact that the nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended: all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; there is nothing that arises without causes and conditions, nor anything that arises from insufficient causes and conditions.
If something arises from causes and conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Nature" (svabhāva) refers to an originally existing, determinate, and real entity.
If nature were produced from the side of the conjunction of causes and conditions, one should know that it did not exist prior to such conjunction;
if it was previously non-existent and now exists due to the conjunction of causes and conditions, then it is known to lack intrinsic nature.
If that which arises from causes and conditions were by nature (svabhāva), then nature would be a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma).
Nature is defined as that which does not depend on others and does not rely on others; it should always exist independently.
If this were so, then conditioned phenomena would not exist.
Therefore it is said: "The nature of all dharmas is unattainable, and the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise.
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are equal in being non-existent": because the nature of all dharmas is unattainable, their various causes and conditions are also unattainable;
and because these various causes and conditions are unattainable, they are all non-existent.
Because one enters into the state of non-existence, all things are equal. Why is this?
Because where there is existence, there is discrimination.
Because there is no [self], there is no discrimination.
Just as with the fragrance of grass or the fragrance of sandalwood, there is discrimination while they are burning, but no discrimination when they have ceased.
All phenomena have no agent; because sentient beings are empty and phenomena are empty, all are without action.
That which is performed by sentient beings refers to the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome actions, and so forth.
That which is performed by phenomena refers to fire burning, water flowing, wind moving, consciousness cognizing, and wisdom knowing—such phenomena each possess their own specific power.
There are no sentient beings, up to and including no knower or seer; there is no form, up to and including no all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), as has already been refuted previously.
Because sentient beings have been refuted, there is no agent; because phenomena (*dharma*) have been refuted, there is no action.
It is only because ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are shrouded by inversion that they say:

"I have something to do. Regarding the inconceivability of all phenomena: one cannot definitively determine any phenomenon, such as form and so forth—whether it be permanent or impermanent, suffering or pleasure, real or empty, self or non-self, arising and ceasing or not arising and ceasing, quiescent or not quiescent, detached or not detached, existent or non-existent, and so on through various modes of differentiation; likewise, these are also inconceivable and cannot be grasped.
Why is this so? Because these dharmas all arise from the mind’s recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination, and they cannot be definitively established.
The true nature of all dharmas transcends the mind and its mental factors, and lies beyond the path of names and language.
As stated in the preceding chapter:
"All dharmas are equal; no noble ones or sages can practice them or reach them.
Therefore, they are inconceivable.
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this; it arises from contemplating these dharmas.
At that moment, Sadāprarudita immediately attained various samādhis while remaining on his seat.
Question:
Sadāprarudita already previously knew the mark of emptiness of all dharmas; what benefit did he obtain by now undergoing such various hardships and standing for seven years until he saw Dharmodgata?
The answer is:
In the past, Sadāprarudita had seen various Buddhas and attained various samādhis; thus, he came to value the Prajñāpāramitā and gave rise to a mind of attachment toward it.

Now, after seven years, Dharmodgata has arisen from meditative concentration and, for his sake, expounds the Prajñāpāramitā to shatter that mind of attachment, teaching that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is itself empty, and it is not the Prajñāpāramitā that makes them empty.
Therefore it is said:
"Because all dharmas are equal, the prajñāpāramitā is equal;
because all dharmas are devoid of marks, and so forth, up to because all dharmas are inconceivable, prajñā is inconceivable."
This is so that they do not treat other dharmas with contempt while holding Prajñāpāramitā in high esteem. Why is this?
It is so that they do not give rise to further defilement or attachment on account of Prajñāpāramitā.
Although the Prajñāpāramitā is ultimately pure and brings great benefit, one must not grasp at its characteristics and give rise to a mind of attachment;
it is like hot gold, which, though excellent, cannot be grasped by hand.
Having received this instruction, Sadāprarudita severed his attachment to the Prajñāpāramitā and immediately attained the various samādhis, such as the "equality of all dharmas.
To explain this point by point: within a distracted mind, although there may be wisdom, it is not called samādhi;
now, having heard it from the teacher, he contemplates with one-pointed attention, which is called samādhi. By gathering the mind so that it does not scatter, wisdom is transformed into samādhi.
Just as a lamp in the wind cannot illuminate, whereas in a quiet room with the doors closed its light shines everywhere,
so too, because the mind was previously distracted by the desire realm, the power of wisdom had not yet been perfected; now,
having entered into the concentration of the mind, all dharmas heard are called samādhi, capable of destroying all afflictions and the hosts of Māra.
Just as water, before the cold wind arrives and it has not yet become ice, lacks the function of solidity;
yet once it has formed into frozen ice, it can support those who tread upon it.
He attained six million such gateways of samādhi.
Sadāprarudita, having heard the Dharma taught by Dharmodgata, attained the great light of wisdom regarding all dharmas—namely, the various gateways to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
The equality of all dharmas—this equality is wisdom—which enters into the mind of Sadāprarudita’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and transforms into samādhi.
Now, because he wishes to explain the retributions of this samādhi and wisdom in both the present and future lives, at that time the Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“Just as I am now preaching the Prajñāpāramitā amidst this great assembly, so too do I preach the Prajñāpāramitā by these characteristics, by these manifestations, and by these names.”
Sadāprarudita obtained this samādhi from Dharmodgata; within that samādhi, he saw the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Prajñāpāramitā amidst great assemblies, just as it was here.
Subhūti! From that time forward, because Sadāprarudita deeply loved and delighted in the Dharma, he collected many sūtras and recited them extensively until he was widely learned.
Just like Ānanda, he was able to retain everything the Buddha taught.
Sadāprarudita was likewise; his extensive learning and wisdom were inconceivable, like the waters of the great ocean.
In this very world, he was never separated from the Buddha.
Such as these are called the retributions of the present life.

After casting off this body, one will always be born in a land where a Buddha resides; because one delights in the practice of the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, one shall not for even a moment be separated from seeing the Buddha, even in dreams.
All hardships such as those of the hells have been forever severed, and they may be reborn at will in the lands of all Buddhas;
because they have deeply entered the Prajñāpāramitā and accumulated immeasurable merit, they are not born according to their karma.
Sadāprarudita traveled from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to all the Buddhas, liberating sentient beings, and accumulating immeasurable merit;

he was like a wealthy and noble elder who went from one assembly to another, until now he has reached the presence of the Buddha Great Thunder Sound (Mahāmeghasvara) to purely cultivate the holy life.
If there are those who wish to seek the Prajñāpāramitā, they should, like the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, maintain a firm and upright single-mindedness that cannot be shaken or moved!

Therefore, one should know that it is by reason of the *prajñāpāramitā* that all merits can be accomplished. When bodhisattvas attain *prajñā*, the defilements of householders—such as greed, hatred, and the like—and the defilements of renunciants—such as wrong views, doubt, and frivolous proliferation—are all completely extinguished, and they attain purity of mind.
Because the mind is pure, they attain the accomplishment of all merits.
To attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) means to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the six *pāramitās*: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh stage, one attains the dharma of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
in the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, one enters deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom, attains the knowledge of all modes, and accomplishes Buddhahood.
Those who have attained mastery over all dharmas should all receive and uphold [this teaching], even using flowers, incense, music, and dance.

Although Subhūti constantly delights in the practice of emptiness, he was spoken to by the Buddha regarding Prajñāpāramitā, and furthermore, he has attained the Samādhi of Non-contention; therefore, he should not be the one to whom the entrustment is made.
Ānanda had attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, and because he was constantly in close attendance upon the World-Honored One, he was extensively entrusted with the teachings.
Chapter 90: Entrustment The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, Commentary on Chapter Ninety, "Entrustment" [Sūtra] At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What do you think? What is your opinion?"
"Is the Buddha not your Great Teacher?
Are you not a disciple of the Buddha?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha is my great teacher; the Sugata is my great teacher; I am a disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is! I am your great teacher, and you are my disciple."
If there is anything that a disciple ought to do, you have already completed it. Ānanda!
You have served and provided for me with the compassionate actions of body, speech, and mind; furthermore, you have always acted according to my wishes, without any transgression or failure.
Ānanda! While my body is currently present, you have loved, revered, made offerings to, and provided for me with a mind that is always pure;
after my parinirvāṇa, all these matters of love, reverence, offering, and provision should instead be directed toward the Prajñāpāramitā!
Up to the second and third time, I entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you.
Ānanda! Do not forget it, do not lose it; do not become the one who brings the lineage to an end!
Ānanda! For as long as the Prajñāpāramitā remains in the world, you should know that for that long the Buddha remains in the world teaching the Dharma. Ānanda!

If there is anyone who writes down the *Prajñāpāramitā*, upholds, reads, recites, correctly contemplates, and extensively explains it to others; and if they honor, respect, and praise it, making various offerings of flowers, incense, banners, canopies, precious robes, lamps, and candles—know that such a person is never apart from seeing the Buddha, never apart from hearing the Dharma, and is always in close proximity to the Buddha.

When the Buddha had finished preaching the Prajñāpāramitā, Maitreya and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the venerable Subhūti, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Ānanda, and the rest of the entire great assembly, as well as all the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced.
[Treatise] Question:

Since the Buddha has already severed craving for dharmas—even regarding everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and nirvana—and does not cling to or grasp at their marks, why now does he entrust this Dharma through various causes and conditions as if he were attached to it?
The answer is:
The great compassionate heart of all Buddhas has never been abandoned from the first moment they resolved their minds until their entry into the gate of *nirvāṇa*.

Even between the twin *śāla* trees, they used the *vajra-samādhi* to crush their own bodies for the sake of sentient beings like sesame seeds or rice grains; how much more so would they entrust the *sūtras* and the Dharma, which bring such vast benefit, without leaving instructions!

Furthermore, Ānanda is one who has not yet abandoned desire and has not yet fully understood the power, influence, and manifold benefits of the fruit of the *prajñāpāramitā*; for this reason, he was earnestly entrusted with these words:
"You must receive and uphold this well, so that you do not let it be lost or forgotten!"
"For this reason, although the Buddha has neither aversion nor attachment toward any dharma and always abides in the mark of quiescence, he entrusts this Prajñāpāramitā to Ānanda.
Question:
Ānanda is a śrāvaka; why is it that he is entrusted with the Prajñāpāramitā, while Maitreya and other great bodhisattvas are not?
Answer: Some say that Ānanda constantly attended upon the Buddha,
providing for all his needs, and having attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, he never lost what he had heard once.

Being the Buddha’s younger cousin, he was widely learned and renowned, serving as a refuge for the fourfold assembly; he was the third master capable of turning the wheel of Dharma following the Buddha.
The Buddha did not entrust [the Dharma] to Śāriputra because he knew that Śāriputra’s lifespan was short and that he would enter parinirvāṇa early.

Furthermore, Ānanda was the teacher of five hundred arhats who possessed the six supernormal powers, the three types of clear knowledge, and shared liberation; because he was able to provide such great benefit, the Buddha entrusted him with the Dharma.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the great bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and others will each disperse to the lands where they are to deliver sentient beings accordingly: Maitreya will return to the Tuṣita Heaven, while Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī will also go to the places where they are to deliver sentient beings.
Furthermore, because these bodhisattvas deeply understand the power of the prajñāpāramitā, there is no need for the Buddha to entrust it to them with such earnestness.
Ānanda, however, is a śrāvaka who follows the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, the Buddha entrusts it to him with great urgency.
Question:
If that is so, why do the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other Vaipulya sūtras entrust [the teaching] to figures such as the Bodhisattva Nandivikrama?
Answer: Some say that at that time,
the Buddha was preaching a most profound and difficult-to-believe Dharma, and the śrāvakas were not present.

Furthermore, as the Buddha taught in the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*, although five hundred arhats were in the presence of the Buddha, they did not hear [the teaching]; or even if they occasionally heard it, they were unable to apply it.
For this reason, [the Buddha] entrusts [this teaching] to the bodhisattvas.
A question is asked:
"What other dharma is more profound and superior to the Prajñā[pāramitā], such that the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* is entrusted to Ānanda, while other sūtras are entrusted to the bodhisattvas?"
Answer: The Prajñāpāramitā is not a secret teaching.
However, various sūtras such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* state that arhats receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, and it is the great bodhisattvas who are able to uphold and apply it.
For example, it is like a great physician who is able to turn poison into medicine.
Furthermore, as previously stated, there are two kinds of *prajñāpāramitā*:
first, that which is taught in common with the *śrāvakas*; [and second, that which is not].

Second, it is taught solely for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who dwell throughout the ten directions; it is not what is heard by those dwelling in the nine stages, much less by those who have newly resolved their minds!
Furthermore, there are distinct differences in what is heard by those on the ninth stage, down to what is heard by those on the first stage.
The general characteristic of the Prajñāpāramitā is one and the same, yet there are differences in its depth and shallowness; for this reason, there is no fault in entrusting it to Ānanda.
Question:
Previously, in the "Chapter on Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," there was an entrustment, and now there is another entrustment; what is the difference between them?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of bodhisattva paths:
first, the path of prajñāpāramitā; second, the path of skillful means (upāya).
The previous entrustment was made because the exposition of the essence of the *prajñāpāramitā* was completed;
now, having finished explaining the skillful means by which sentient beings may attain this *prajñā*, he entrusts it.
For this reason, after the "Vision of Akṣobhya Buddha" chapter, the "Upāyakauśalya" (Skillful Means) chapter is taught.
Although skillful means exist within the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā exists within skillful means, each receives its name according to what predominates.
Prajñā and upāya are identical in their essential nature; they are spoken of separately only because of slight differences in their application.
It is like a goldsmith who, through skillful means, fashions gold into various different objects; although all are indeed gold, each receives a distinct name.

When a bodhisattva attains this true mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*—namely, that all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, non-existent, and characterized by quiescence—they desire to attain parinirvāṇa;
yet, by the power of skillful means, they do not take up the realization of nirvāṇa.
At that time, he reflects thus:
"The nature of all dharmas is empty, and nirvāṇa is also empty. Since I have not yet fulfilled the merits of a bodhisattva, I should not realize [nirvāṇa];
only when my merits are complete may I realize it."
At that time, by the power of skillful means, the bodhisattva transcends the two stages and enters the rank of a bodhisattva;
abiding within this rank, they know the profound, subtle, and wordless Dharma and guide sentient beings—this is called skillful means.

Furthermore, there is skillful means: the bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are ultimately empty and non-existent, yet is able to give rise once more to wholesome dharmas and practice the six pāramitās, without following after emptiness.
If one can give rise to four things—
namely, doubt, wrong views, entering nirvāṇa, or becoming a Buddha—
the prajñāpāramitā possesses such discrimination; yet, if it can eliminate wrong views and doubt while not entering nirvāṇa, this constitutes skillful means (*upāya*).
Some say: "The benefit provided by the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme among all great heaps of jewels.

The Buddha knows that after his parinirvāṇa, there will be many enemies and thieves who wish to destroy it; even if he were to entrust it to them chapter by chapter, there would still be no fault, let alone in these two places!"
Question:
If it is a matter of entrusting [the Dharma], why is it so earnest and solemn? Answer:

The Buddha guides sentient beings in accordance with worldly conventions, just like a merchant leader who, wishing to travel far to another country, entrusts his wealth and treasures to his son; yet he does so with particular earnestness regarding the most precious and exquisite jewels, because the son does not yet recognize the great value of those marvelous treasures.
Other people, knowing that the caravan leader was one who recognized the value of jewels and had earnestly entrusted them to him, would surely consider them precious;
yet if they heard his son praise their value, they would not believe it.
The Buddha is likewise.

Furthermore, if he were to praise the entrustment of the Prajñāpāramitā within a different assembly of other people, those people would mock the Buddha for praising his own dharma, and they would harbor doubts and lack faith;
however, if he entrusts it among his own disciples, there will be no cause for suspicion.
Furthermore, some say:

In the "Superior Chapter," the Buddha spoke of the mark of quiescence as being free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), wherein there is no determinate dharma to be grasped, and thus people might consider it to have nothing worthy of esteem.
Now, by his earnest entrustment [of the Dharma], we know that the Buddha does not cling to the dharma of emptiness.

Among all sentient beings, none love and cherish the Prajñāpāramitā more than the Buddha; because the Buddha knows that the debt of gratitude toward the Prajñāpāramitā is profound, he holds it in high esteem and entrusts it with earnest diligence.
Some say: Because the Buddha wishes to manifest the Middle Way,
he entrusts [the teaching] by first explaining that all phenomena are empty, thereby negating the extreme of existence.
Now, this earnest entrustment serves to break through both extremes; this is the Middle Way.
If someone were to say that the Buddha has a greedy mind and is attached to this Dharma, the Buddha explains the mark of emptiness of the *prajñāpāramitā* through various causes and conditions.
If someone were to say that the Buddha falls into the extreme of nihilism, for this reason he earnestly entrusts [the teaching].
In this way, one is free from the two extremes.
Question: The Buddha knew that Ānanda was his disciple; for what reason did he ask Ānanda?
"Are you my disciple? Am I your teacher? He replied:

The Buddha had wicked disciples such as Sunakṣatra and others who, for some minor reason, became his followers with the desire to learn the art of archery from him. When the Buddha would not teach them, they renounced the precepts and said:
"I am no longer the Buddha's disciple."
Furthermore, for example, Susīma became a disciple for the purpose of stealing the Dharma;
such individuals as these are "disciples by name.

Moreover, non-Buddhists and others claim that Ānanda was at the Buddha's side against his will—Ānanda had previously been a disciple of non-Buddhists, wearing grass garments and seeking the state of a rishi.
Now, because the Buddha was his kinsman and out of respect for him, he served him.
For such reasons as these, he asked Ānanda in the midst of the great assembly:
"Are you my disciple?"
"If one says they are a true disciple, they should follow my instructions.
For this reason, Ānanda gave a repeated answer out of a desire to inspire faith in others.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The practices that a disciple ought to perform, you have fulfilled them all.
As for the duties of a disciple, they consist of serving the teacher through wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
There are disciples whose minds are excellent, but whose physical and verbal actions do not correspond;
there are disciples whose physical and verbal actions are excellent, but whose minds do not correspond.

If a disciple, with a virtuous mind, feels deep affection and joy for the teacher, such that their physical and verbal actions correspond, they do not begrudge their own body or life nor find toil difficult, setting aside their own inclinations to follow the teacher’s instructions—Ānanda has fully perfected all these qualities.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Just as you now show reverence to me, so too shall you show reverence to the Prajñāpāramitā after my parinirvāṇa."
Question: Prajñāpāramitā is the teacher of all Buddhas; why then does Ānanda not revere its teacher, but instead reveres the Buddha? Answer:
Although Ānanda had attained the first stage of the path, because his outflows were not yet exhausted, he did not deeply understand the reality of the Dharma as the Buddha knew it.
For this reason, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Revere Prajñā as you revere me."
Furthermore, sentient beings mostly feel love and reverence upon seeing the Buddha’s thirty-two marks, eighty secondary characteristics, great radiance, and golden body;
yet the Prajñāpāramitā is subtle, profound, formless, and colorless, and can only be known by the wise.

Whether the foolish or the wise gaze upon the Buddha’s physical marks and signs of excellence, none ever tire of beholding them; for this reason, the Buddha uses his own body as a metaphor for Prajñāpāramitā.
While the Buddha was in the world, he was able to ward off Māra himself; therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you must skillfully protect the Prajñāpāramitā."
Question: One entrustment would suffice; why does it extend to three? Answer:
Because the Buddha deeply loves the Prajñāpāramitā, he entrusts it three times.
A question is asked:
If he loves it so deeply, why limit it to three?
The answer is:
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that their speech does not exceed three times.
If [the request] is not heeded after the third time, the Vajrapāṇi deity will brandish his vajra-staff at them.
Furthermore, the Vajrapāṇi deity thought:
"If he does not comply after three [requests], he is a person who acts in opposition and must be killed.
For this reason, the Buddha did not ask more than three times.
Furthermore, if one speaks only once, it is too lax;
if one exceeds three times, it is too urgent, appearing as if one were an ordinary person attached to worldly things.
Moreover, there are three types of mental capacities among those who receive the teaching: for those of dull faculties, it is only upon reaching the third repetition that a wholesome mind arises.
Although Ānanda possesses keen faculties, his mind is directed toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas; he seeks liberation for himself alone. For this reason, [the Buddha] addressed him three times.
The purpose of this entrustment is to ensure that the Dharma does not perish.
You should instruct and transform your disciples, and those disciples in turn shall instruct others, passing the teaching on from one to another;
it is like one lamp lighting another lamp, so that the light becomes ever more abundant.

"Do not become one who severs the lineage at its end. In the world, when a person has a son, if that son does not carry on the succession, he is called "one who severs the lineage," which is considered most shameful.
The Buddha used this analogy to tell Ānanda:
"Do not allow the Prajñāpāramitā to be cut off within your own person!"

Question: As explained in the preceding chapter, it was clarified that "the Prajñāpāramitā neither increases when spoken of nor decreases when not spoken of; its ultimate characteristic is quiescence. Why, then, is it said here now that one must "not allow it to be extinguished"?
For example, who could extinguish space?
The answer is:

although the *prajñāpāramitā* is quiescent, characterized by neither arising nor ceasing, and like space, it is beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet one writes out the scrolls of the *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra through words and language and explains them to others. This is the *prajñā* within this context; herein, the fruit is explained on the basis of its causes.

When ordinary people hear that the Prajñāpāramitā is subtle and wondrous, they immediately give rise to a mind of attachment and grasp at the characteristics of Prajñā. They discriminate among all phenomena, saying, for instance, "this is wholesome" and "that is unwholesome," or "this is worldly" and "that is nirvāṇa.

Because of such discrimination, they develop a mind of attachment toward these phenomena; because of this attachment, they engage in contention; and because of contention, they give rise to various sinful karmas. Such persons are said to destroy the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should, in accordance with the characteristics of the Prajñāpāramitā, not cling to written words or speech as you teach and transform sentient beings.
This is called non-extinction.
“Ānanda! For as long as the Prajñāpāramitā remains in the world, for that long one should know that the Buddha remains in the world,” as is explained at length in the sūtra.

Out of earnest concern, the Buddha entrusts [the teaching] to the sentient beings present in the assembly; therefore, the Buddha explains the causes and conditions of this entrustment, namely: “Wherever the Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, there the Buddha exists.”
Why is this so? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas, and all Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher.
The Dharma is none other than the Prajñāpāramitā.
If the teacher is present and the mother is present, it is not called a loss of benefit. Why is this?
Because the source of benefit remains.
Therefore it is said:
"If Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, the Buddha also exists in the world.
Furthermore, the Jewel of the Dharma is not separate from the Jewel of the Buddha.
A bodhisattva who possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics is not yet called a Buddha; it is because of attaining the Dharma-jewel that one is called a Buddha.
This Dharma-jewel is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as a person gains benefit from the Buddha, even attaining liberation and nirvana;
so too, if a person can practice with faith within the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall likewise enter nirvana by means of the three vehicles of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that when Prajñāpāramitā exists in the world, it is as if the Buddha exists in the world; there is no difference between his teaching the Dharma and this. "Ānanda!

If there are those who hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, or who copy, uphold, and so forth, you should know that such persons are not separated from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and drawing near to the Buddhas."

Question: Suppose there is a person who has committed grave offenses and has fully accomplished the three unwholesome karmas, yet they listen to, receive, write down, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā. How can such a person ensure that they shall not be separated from the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and remain in close proximity to the Buddhas?
The answer is:
This matter has already been addressed in the preceding section. Specifically, there are two types of people who listen to the Dharma:
first, those who merely listen but do not believe, accept, or practice it; second, those who listen and then believe, accept, and put it into practice.
If a disciple does not listen to, believe, accept, or practice the words of the teacher, this is called "not listening.

If one listens with a single-minded focus, believing, accepting, and practicing them—feeling weary of the world, loving *nirvāṇa*, departing from the Lesser Vehicle, and delighting in the Great Vehicle—listening and receiving the teaching in such a manner is called "true listening."
Reciting and reading are likewise.
With right mindfulness, one follows the Buddha’s intention, remaining free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, and practicing the Middle Way.
One upholds what has been heard, as well as its meaning and interpretation, and explains it to others, with reverence, respect, offerings, praise, flowers, incense, and so forth.

Initially slight and thin, it eventually reaches the stage of right mindfulness and explaining it to others; its mind then becomes increasingly profound, its merit increasingly vast, and it becomes firm and unshakable.

Whether hearing the teacher’s exposition, seeing a scripture, or making offerings such as flowers and incense—if a wise person understands the merit of the *prajñā* and makes these offerings, their merit is profound;
if one who does not understand them makes offerings, their merit is slight.
Those whose merit and virtue are pure and profound will, upon changing bodies, never be separated from seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and drawing near to the Buddhas.

Those whose merit and virtue are slight and thin do not necessarily attain the three types of meritorious retribution upon changing bodies; yet, after their various karmic debts have been repaid, they too shall surely attain Buddhahood after a long time.

In this regard, the Buddha has spoken in general terms of merit being either pure and abundant or slight and thin; yet all shall gradually come to see the Buddhas of the ten directions and hear what those Buddhas teach, gradually fulfill the six pāramitās, and all attain Buddhahood.
Because the Buddha perceives with his Buddha-eye that *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such great benefit for sentient beings, he earnestly entrusts it to them.
A question is asked:

These great arhats have already realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are no longer subject to sorrow or joy; since they possess not even slight joy, how much less could there be great rejoicing!
The answer is:

Although the great arhats have abandoned the desires of the three realms, because they have not yet attained all-encompassing wisdom, they still harbor doubts and lack full understanding regarding the most profound dharmas.
Within this Mahāprajñāpāramitā, these [dharmas] are explained with complete clarity, thereby severing their doubts; for this reason, they experience great joy.
Furthermore, these great disciples have already realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The limit of reality is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*); it is free from all conceptual discrimination.

The Buddha extensively expounded this Dharma of quiescence through various distinctions of names, words, and parables; yet he neither subverted the nature of phenomena nor contradicted worldly conventions.
Because the Arhats have realized this Dharma, they rejoice greatly.

The Buddha has skillfully taught this Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, measurelessness, and cessation; although the rest of the great assembly had not yet exhausted all outflows, because their power of faith was profound, they too were greatly rejoiced and said:
"This Dharma can bring an end to our suffering of birth and death and enable us to attain the Way of the Buddha."
For such immeasurable reasons as these, the great assembly was filled with joy.
A question is asked:
If the Buddha entrusted this Prajñāpāramitā to Ānanda, why is it not mentioned here that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, together with Mahākāśyapa, compiled the Tripiṭaka?
Answer: The Mahāyāna is extremely profound, difficult to believe, difficult to understand, and difficult to practice.

During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were bhikṣus who, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, departed from their seats because they did not believe it and did not understand it; how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa!
For this reason, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka consists precisely of three hundred thousand verses, totaling nine million six hundred thousand words.

The Mahāyāna, however, is exceedingly vast, immeasurable, and limitless; for instance, within it, the "Prajñāpāramitā Chapter" contains twenty-two thousand verses, the "Mahāprajñā Chapter" contains one hundred thousand verses, and there are billions of verses in the palaces of the various nāga kings, asura kings, and devas.
Why is this? It is because these devas, nāgas, and spirits have long lifespans and possess powerful faculties of memory and cognition.

As for the people of this world today, their lifespans are short and their faculties of memory and cognition are weak; they cannot even recite the "Chapter on the Lesser Prajñāpāramitā," let alone the more extensive versions!
The Prajñāpāramitā known by all other great Bodhisattvas is immeasurable and limitless. Why is this?

It is because the Buddha does not teach with only a single body; throughout immeasurable ages, he may manifest as countless bodies through transformation. Therefore, that which he teaches is immeasurable.

Furthermore, there is the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* in one hundred thousand verses; the *Sarvabuddhapūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra*, the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, and the *Dharmamegha-sūtra*, each also in one hundred thousand verses; and various other great sūtras such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Kusuma-avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the *Upāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, the *Nāgarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and the *Asurarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. These are immeasurable and boundless, like jewels within the great ocean—how could they possibly be included within the Tripiṭaka?
Small things should be contained within the great; large things cannot enter the small.
If you wish to ask, you should say:
"Why is the Hīnayāna not included within the Mahāyāna?"
Because the Mahāyāna can encompass the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it should not be questioned as you have asked.
Furthermore, some say:

just as Mahākāśyapa led the bhikṣus to assemble the Tripiṭaka on Vulture Peak after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and other great bodhisattvas likewise led Ānanda to assemble this Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, Ānanda knows how to weigh the magnitude of the aspirations and karmic activities of sentient beings; for this reason, he does not preach the Mahāyāna among those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, for to do so would lead to confusion and result in nothing being accomplished.
The Buddha-dharma is entirely of one single flavor, namely, the flavor of liberation through the exhaustion of suffering.
This flavor of liberation is of two kinds:
first, that which is for oneself alone; second, that which is shared for the sake of all sentient beings.
Although both seek the same gate of liberation, there is a distinction between self-benefit and benefiting others; therefore, there is the differentiation between the Great and Small Vehicles.
For the sake of these two types of people, that which was spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth is divided into two kinds by means of written characters and language:
the Tripiṭaka is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, and the Mahāyāna is the Dharma of the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, when the Buddha was in the world, there were no names for the "Three Piṭakas"; there were only bhikṣus who upheld the Sūtras, bhikṣus who upheld the Vinaya, and bhikṣus who upheld the Mātṛkā.
*Sūtra* refers to the names of the sūtras within the four *Āgamas* as well as the names of the sūtras within the Mahāyāna.
There are two divisions of *sūtra*:
first, the *sūtras* within the four *Āgamas*; second, those Mahāyāna sūtras which are designated as "Great."
The Sūtras consist of two divisions: those of the Mahāyāna and those of the Hīnayāna.
The two hundred and fifty precepts and works such as these are called Sūtras.
Vinaya refers to when a bhikṣu commits an offense, and the Buddha establishes the precepts:
"This should be practiced; this should not be practiced; by doing such a thing, one incurs such a fault.
Briefly stated, there are eighty sections.
There are also two divisions:
first, the Vinaya of the kingdom of Mathurā, which includes the Avadānas and Jātakas and consists of eighty sections;
second, the Vinaya of the kingdom of Kaśmīra, from which the Jātakas and Avadānas have been excluded and only the essential portions taken to form ten sections.
There are eighty sections of the *Vibhāṣā* commentaries.

Therefore, it is known that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others are spoken separately among the *Sūtra* scriptures because they are extensive and their subject matter is distinct; for this reason, they are not included within the compilation of the Tripiṭaka.

The Dharma Master Kumārajīva arrived in Chang’an on the twentieth day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, when the year was Xinchou. In the summer of the fourth year, he translated this *Śāstra* for King Yao at the Xishengmen Pavilion in the Xiaoyao Garden; it was completed on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the seventh year.

Included therein were also copies of various sutras, Chan scriptures, the Vinaya, the *Śata-śāstra*, and essential expositions on Chan methods, totaling nearly five hundred thousand words; together with this commentary, they amount to one million five hundred thousand words.
The first volume of the treatise contains thirty-four chapters; the explanation of the first chapter constitutes the complete original text of the treatise.
From the second chapter onward, the Dharma Master has abbreviated it, taking only what is sufficient to elucidate the meaning of the text, and no longer providing the full extensive commentary.
Having obtained these one hundred fascicles, if they were all to be published, they would be ten times this amount.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Fascicle One Hundred.
